10083-the-house-of-the-whispering-pines:
Anna Katharine Green's 1910 mystery opens in smoke, with a hesitating step, a woman seen indeed, a cry of open, an odd candlestick, and a scrap of paper. Clifton accepts a case, and a chance is taken, in the first book of the novel.

Book two brings Sweetwater to the front, a letter no one knows, help offered, a coach house, and the thing they want, found at last. Green, author of The Leavenworth Case, builds her puzzle from small, concrete clues. Mystery readers get a classic detective tale from the writer who shaped the American whodunit.
10089-elves-and-heroes:
Donald A. Mackenzie's 1909 book gathers poems and tales of elves and heroes from Scottish folk belief. His preface notes that the immemorial folk-beliefs of his native land are passing away, yet keep a poetic appeal from early associations and glamour.

Inside are the wee folk in the greenest knoll, the remnant bannock baked with a spell, the banshee who will never more leave Scotland's shore, and Conn, son of the Red. Mackenzie writes as a folklorist and poet together. Readers get the old Scottish supernatural world in verse and story, before it fades.
10095-the-twilight-of-the-gods-and-other:
Richard Garnett's 1903 collection takes its title from The Twilight of the Gods, a tale of old divinities fading before a new age. Garnett, a librarian and scholar, dedicates the book to Horace Howard Furness and Georg Brandes, his two witnesses.

Other tales include The Potion of Lao-Tsze, where a maiden kneels by a drinker of strange tongues, and further stories of gods, philosophers, and marvels. Garnett writes with learning and wit, in a late Victorian manner. Readers get literary fantasy for grown-ups: elegant, ironic, and steeped in myth and legend.
10096-the-trojan-women-of-euripides:
Gilbert Murray, Regius Professor of Greek at Oxford, translated Euripides' Trojan Women into English rhyming verse in 1915, with explanatory notes. Murray says in his preface that the play, valued by stage usage, is not a perfect play. It is only the crying of one of the great wrongs of the world wrought into music.

Its narrow shape still makes a victorious injustice feel deeply sad. It holds the soul of the tragic, hinting that beyond defeat may come a greater glory. Readers get Greek tragedy at its most moving, in verse that can be read aloud or staged.
10123-aunt-jane-s-nieces:
Edith Van Dyne's 1906 novel introduces Aunt Jane's nieces, beginning when Beth receives an invitation. Mother and daughter, Patsy, and Louise's discovery follow, as the girls meet Aunt Jane herself and a boy who changes matters.

A first warning and a diplomat deepen the plot, in Van Dyne's friendly manner for young readers. The nieces learn to judge character, manage money, and stand by each other. Girls get a warm family story, the first in a long series, with humor, kindness, and a formidable aunt at its center. The book began a series young readers followed for years.
10139-the-faith-of-the-millions-2nd-seri:
George Tyrrell, a Jesuit priest, gathered this second series of Catholic essays in 1901. The pieces had first appeared one by one, and here they stand together as a defense of faith for ordinary readers. Tyrrell writes for people caught between modern doubt and old belief, not only for scholars.

Essays treat Juliana of Norwich, poet-mystics, art as a road to faith, and the making of religion. Others weigh Catholic life, naturalism, and whether a faith that adapts can still be true. Readers get a thoughtful, late Victorian Catholic voice, earnest about mysticism, art, and the needs of the multitude.
10164-the-black-creek-stopping-house-and:
Nellie L. McClung published this prairie story collection in 1912, dedicating it to the pioneer women of the West. The title tale follows a stopping-house on the Black Creek trail, a place that fed the hungry, nursed the sick, and sheltered travelers. McClung praises women who made hard life bearable for others.

Chapters treat the old trail, the house of bread, a sailors' rest, farm pupils, and a blizzard that tests every guest. Two shorter tales, on a runaway grandmother and a return ticket, close the book. Readers get warm, moral sketches of prairie kindness, grit, and neighborly faith.
1018-the-water-babies:
Tom, a poor boy who sweeps chimneys, runs from a harsh master and falls into a stream. There he wakes as a small water-baby, clean at last, and begins a new life among fish, crabs, and other sea folk. Charles Kingsley wrote this fairy tale for young readers in Victorian England.

Each creature Tom meets teaches him a plain moral: to be kind, to own his faults, and to help those weaker than himself. He must scrub away old grime, in body and in conduct, before he can grow. The tale mixes jokes, natural lore, and sermons, and it has stayed a much-loved children's story.
10225-their-crimes:
Translated from French and published in 1917, this wartime book charges German troops with crimes in Belgium and northern France. Its preface says the record rests on testimony attested by mayors of twenty-six French towns, and profits were pledged to relief work in Lorraine. The tone is angry and urgent, written to stiffen resolve.

Chapters list robbery, arson, murder, outrages on women and children, killing of the wounded, and the martyrdom of civilian prisoners. German excuses and appeals close the case. Readers get a fierce, period document of Allied war charges, best read as propaganda as well as testimony.
10322-miss-prudence-a-story-of-two-girls:
Jennie M. Drinkwater published this girls' novel in 1883, following two girls from school days into womanhood. Its motto, from Epictetus, says we follow events rather than lead them, and the story tests that thought through choices, work, and love. The tone is earnest, moral, and warm.

After school, an evangelist, a ride and a tumble, two promises, and letters shape the heroines' paths. Weddings, grandmothers, and Maple Street scenes fill the later chapters. Readers get a gentle, Victorian-era tale of friendship, faith, and growing up, with plain lessons on patience and duty.
10329-snubby-nose-and-tippy-toes:
Laura Rountree Smith wrote this animal storybook in 1917, with a later edition in 1922, for young children. Its heroes are small woodland folk with funny names, including Snubby Nose, Tippy Toes, and Dr. Cottontail. Pictures show their mishaps, from fainting fits to sailing away with a grumbling grandpa.

Short chapters follow washing dishes, sweeping chimneys with long tails, and splashing into lakes, all in a gentle, comic style. A second set, called More Cotton Tail Stories, adds further tales of the same crew. Readers get a sweet, old-fashioned picture book of animal manners and small adventures.
1036-joe-wilson-and-his-mates:
Henry Lawson, the voice of the Australian bush, tells here of Joe Wilson, a selector who works hard, drinks, quarrels, and loves his wife Mary through drought, debt, and lonely miles. Mates drift in and out of the tales: shearers, swagmen, and battlers, each with a yarn and a grievance.

The stories are plain and unsparing, with humor that bites and pathos that never turns soft. Lawson writes the bush as it was for poor folk, not as a romance. The book helped shape Australia's own literature, and it still reads as the truest short fiction of outback life.
10360-kitty-s-class-day-and-other-storie:
Louisa M. Alcott, author of Little Women, first issued these stories as Proverb Stories, reprinted here in 1882. Each tale turns on a proverb, from a stitch in time to other homely sayings, and each shows girls and women learning sense through daily life. The tone is warm, moral, and gently comic.

Kitty's class day, Aunt Kipp, Psyche's art, a country Christmas, picket duty, and the baron's gloves fill the set. Work, love, and duty test the heroines in turn. Readers get charming, old-fashioned tales that teach thrift, courage, and kindness without heavy preaching.
10376-american-indian-stories:
Zitkala-Sa, also known as Gertrude Bonnin, a Dakota Sioux writer and lecturer, published this memoir and essay collection in 1921. She had already written Old Indian Legends. Here she turns to her own life: a childhood on the Missouri, school days far from home, and work as a teacher among Native peoples. The book is personal and political at once.

Impressions of an Indian childhood, school days, a warrior's daughter, and a dream of her grandfather sit beside essays on the Great Spirit and America's Indian problem. Zitkala-Sa writes with beauty and anger about loss, faith, and reform. Readers get a vital Native voice on boarding schools and assimilation.
10403-twixt-france-and-spain-or-a-spring:
E. Ernest Bilbrough wrote this spring travel book on the Pyrenees, the range between France and Spain. With a map of peaks, rivers, and roads, he leads readers from Bordeaux and Pau toward mountain towns, castles, and spas. The tone is that of a pleasant, well-read tourist in the late Victorian age.

Chapters treat Pau, its castle and tapestries, Bagnères de Bigorre, peasant ways, vines, carnivals, and rides to Bétharram and Gan. Hunting, racing, polo, and church visits fill the days. Readers get a detailed, charming guide to Pyrenean spring, rich in local lore and routes.
10422-caesar-dies:
Talbot Mundy set this historical novel in the reign of the Roman emperor Commodus, opening in golden Antioch. Wide, marble-colonnaded streets swarm with fashionable folk, slaves, and chariots, while Romans and Antiochenes eye each other with scorn and fear. The city, gay and pleasure-loving, is broken only by earthquakes.

Against this rich stage, plots, loyalty, and the fate of Caesar himself drive the tale toward death and change. Mundy mixes adventure with Roman politics and Eastern color. Readers get a vivid, old-style romance of late empire, full of streets, courts, and danger.
10427-scientific-essays-and-lectures:
Charles Kingsley gathered these scientific lectures and essays, treating natural history, geology, and the study of nature. Kingsley, a clergyman and sanitary reformer, opens on bio-geology with a hint at preventable disease, drainage, and the lives lost to fever since the Prince Consort's death. Science, for him, serves human health and faith.

Essays treat superstition, science, thoughts in a gravel pit, how to study natural history, and the natural theology of the future. Kingsley urges close, humble observation of plants, rocks, and beasts. Readers get a lively, Victorian-era case for science as moral and practical knowledge.
10466-little-saint-elizabeth-and-other-s:
Frances Hodgson Burnett published this storybook in 1888, with drawings by Reginald B. Birch. Its title tale follows Little Saint Elizabeth, born in France in a beautiful chateau, heiress to a great fortune, yet feeling poor in a splendid New York house at age eleven. Burnett writes of wealth, loneliness, and childish faith.

Other stories include Prince Fairyfoot, the proud little grain of wheat, and Behind the White Brick. Each tale mixes fairy wonder with moral feeling. Readers get a charming, old-fashioned collection from the author of Little Lord Fauntleroy, full of tenderness and fancy.
10520-the-compleat-cook-expertly-prescri:
Printed in London in 1658 for Nathaniel Brook, this cookery book forms part of The Queens Closet Opened. It prescribes the most ready ways, Italian, Spanish, or French, for dressing flesh and fish, ordering sauces, and making pastry. The language is that of the seventeenth-century kitchen, full of sack, ale, and spice.

Recipes include a posset in the Earl of Arundel's way, with cream, nutmeg, sack, and ale, and a capon larded with lemons, with mutton broth, wine, herbs, and marrow. Each recipe gives plain, if old, steps. Readers get a historic cookbook, rich in period taste and household craft.
10531-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-05:
John Lord published this fifth volume of Beacon Lights of History, on the Middle Ages, in a later numbering that puts subjects in historical order. An earlier set had called the same lectures volume three, part one, by the order in which Lord gave them. The volume treats the age between Rome's fall and the Renaissance.

Mohammed opens the set, with Saracenic conquests, his early life, meditations, flight to Medina, and the Koran's doctrines. War, polygamy, and martial fanaticism follow in Lord's frank, Victorian-era account. Readers get a readable, moral history of medieval faith, empire, and change.
10548-the-westcotes:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch published this short novel, dedicating it to Henry James with a playful apology. Quiller-Couch says his tale wants James's penetrating insight and delicacy, and that his own work multiplies meaning only by invoking James's name like a figure outside brackets. The dedication sets a modest, witty tone.

The story follows Dorothea, a heroine whose worth the author hopes James might champion, through love, family, and social life in a small English world. Quiller-Couch writes with grace and humor. Readers get a charming, literary tale of character and manners, in the style of early twentieth-century England.
10554-right-ho-jeeves:
P. G. Wodehouse published this Jeeves novel, opening with Bertie Wooster struggling to begin his story. Bertie admits he always trips over where to start, fearing a slow opening will lose readers, while a fast opening will confuse them. He then harks back to a visit to Cannes, where he met Madeline Bassett and bought a white mess jacket.

Gussie Fink-Nottle, cousin Angela, Aunt Dahlia, Uncle Thomas, Tuppy Glossop, and the cook Anatole form the complex case Bertie must untangle, with Jeeves to save the day. Wodehouse writes in Bertie's inimitable, comic voice. Readers get a classic, hilarious tale of love, aunts, and a perfect valet.
10624-three-john-silence-stories:
Algernon Blackwood, an English writer of strange and supernatural tales, created Dr. John Silence, a physician who treats cases no ordinary doctor can touch. This book holds three of his cases: "A Psychical Invasion," "Ancient Sorceries," and "The Nemesis of Fire." Silence works with a trained knowledge of the occult, a calm manner, and a keen eye for fear.

Each story brings him a client haunted by something unseen, from a home under attack to old magic that will not stay buried. Blackwood builds dread slowly, through mood, place, and talk, rather than sudden shocks. Readers who like ghost stories with a thoughtful hero will find these three tales among the finest of their kind.
10659-three-more-john-silence-stories:
Algernon Blackwood brings back Dr. John Silence in Three More John Silence Stories, with three further cases: "Secret Worship," "The Camp of the Dog," and "A Victim of Higher Space." The first opens with Harris, a silk merchant, revisiting his old school in South Germany after thirty years, only to meet Silence tramping the same mountains. A strange case grows from that chance meeting.

Silence again treats troubles that baffle ordinary doctors, using calm reason and a knowledge of hidden things. Blackwood's dread builds through place and memory rather than shock. Readers who enjoyed the first Silence book will find the same thoughtful, eerie atmosphere here, with new puzzles of mind and spirit.
10669-at-last-a-christmas-in-the-west-in:
Charles Kingsley, the English novelist and clergyman, called At Last the fulfillment of a dream of forty years: a Christmas in the West Indies. Dedicated to Sir Arthur Gordon, governor of Mauritius, to whom Kingsley owed the visit, the book follows his Atlantic crossing and his time in Trinidad and neighboring islands. Chapters run from "Outward Bound" through island scenes.

Kingsley writes with a naturalist's eye and a traveler's delight, noting plants, people, and colonial life. His tone is warm and Victorian, full of wonder at tropical beauty. Readers get a classic travel book, and a view of the Caribbean as an Englishman of 1870 saw it.
10673-the-principal-navigations-voyages-:
Richard Hakluyt collected the voyages of the English nation into his great Principal Navigations, and this ninth volume, edited by Edmund Goldsmid, covers Asia, part two. Its chapters report English trade, travel, and discovery in Asian lands, including a Latin account of Cathay and the Tartars under the Grand Khan. Twelve great provinces and their kings fill that old geography.

Hakluyt's collection preserves sailors' tales, merchants' reports, and diplomatic notes that would otherwise be lost. The volume shows England learning Asia through ships, markets, and missions. Readers interested in exploration get primary accounts from the age when Europe first mapped the East.
10694-sea-power-and-other-studies:
Admiral Sir Cyprian Bridge collected Sea-Power and Other Studies from essays first printed in the Encyclopaedia Britannica, the Times, and other journals. The twelve studies cover sea-power itself, command of the sea, the press-gang, projected invasions of Britain, oversea raids, and Queen Elizabeth's seamen. Nelson and the Trafalgar centenary get a full essay.

Bridge writes as a serving officer turned historian, weighing strategy, supply, and the fleet's share in defending empire. His pieces mix history with practical lessons for navies. Readers interested in naval power will find clear, expert essays on how Britain ruled the seas and what that rule cost.
10735-christmas-eve-on-lonesome-and-othe:
John Fox Jr. published Christmas Eve on Lonesome and Other Stories in 1911, tales of the Kentucky mountains. The title story opens on a snowy Christmas Eve in a hollow called Lonesome, where cabins stand far apart and few know the date, though a holy hush fills the twilight. Companion tales include "The Army of the Callahan," "The Pardon of Becky Day," and "Christmas Night with Satan."

Fox writes of mountain feuds, faith, and rough kindness with local color and feeling. Illustrations by four artists add to the volume. Readers get Appalachian stories at their most atmospheric, mixing Christmas sentiment with the hard life of the hills.
10756-between-whiles:
Helen Jackson, known as H. H. and author of Ramona, published Between Whiles in 1888, a book of six stories written between larger works. Its contents include "The Inn of the Golden Pear," "The Mystery of Wilhelm Rutter," "Little Bel's Supplement," "The Captain of the Heather Bell," "Dandy Steve," and "The Prince's Little Sweetheart." Markets, knaves, and children at play open the first tale.

Jackson writes with sympathy for ordinary people and a keen eye for character, in stories that mix humor and pathos. The collection shows her range beyond the Indian cause that made her famous. Readers get a pleasant, varied set of tales from a leading American woman writer of her age.
10766-enquire-within-upon-everything-the:
Enquire Within upon Everything was the great Victorian household book, and this eighty-ninth edition, revised in 1894, records a total issue of over one million copies. Its editor promises answers for every domestic need: modeling a wax flower, learning etiquette, serving a relish, planning a dinner, curing a headache, making a will, getting married, or burying a relative.

Entries are arranged for quick reference, with an index at the end and companion dictionaries advertised alongside. The book taught generations of households how to cook, clean, nurse, and behave. Modern readers get both a usable reference and a rich picture of Victorian daily life.
10770-the-former-philippines-thru-foreig:
Austin Craig edited The Former Philippines thru Foreign Eyes, gathering outsiders' accounts of the islands before American rule. Its contents include Jagor's travels, Tomas de Comyn on the state of the Philippines in 1810, Commodore Wilkes on Manila and Sulu in 1842, and Lieutenant White on Manila in 1819. Virchow on the peopling of the islands and merchants' reports complete the set.

Craig corrected Jagor's out-of-print English translation from the German and modernized older texts for readers. The book lets Filipinos and others see their past through foreign eyes. It remains a valuable source collection for Philippine history.
10771-philippine-folklore-stories:
John Maurice Miller, writing from Boston in 1904, collected Philippine Folklore Stories from tales told in the islands. Fourteen stories fill the book, from "The Tobacco of Harisaboqued" and "How the World Was Made" to "The Anting-Anting of Manuelito" and "When the Lilies Return." The first is a legend of the Canlaon volcano on Negros.

Miller retells the tales plainly, noting where each was told, as with the Harisaboqued legend of western Negros and eastern Cebu. Kings of mountains, little men, magic charms, and creation myths people the pages. Readers get an early English doorway into Filipino storytelling, gathered just after American rule began.
10795-yorkshire-coast-and-moorland-scene:
Gordon Home painted and described Yorkshire Coast and Moorland Scenes, in a second edition of 1907 after a first edition of 1904. Chapters walk from Pickering across the moors to Whitby, along the Esk valley, and down the coast to Redcar and Scarborough. Whitby, Scarborough, the Cleveland Hills, and Rievaulx Abbey each get their turn.

Home's pictures show moors, cliffs, fishing villages, and abbeys, while his text gives history and local color. The book suits walkers and lovers of Yorkshire alike. Readers get a handsome, old-fashioned guide to a coast and moorland that still draw visitors today.
108-the-return-of-sherlock-holmes:
London believed Sherlock Holmes dead at Reichenbach Falls, but Watson learns otherwise. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's Return of Sherlock Holmes opens with the Empty House case in 1894. Holmes explains his survival and unmasks Colonel Moran, Moriarty's lieutenant.

Twelve more adventures follow, from the Dancing Men cipher to the Six Napoleons and the Abbey Grange. Watson narrates with loyalty as Holmes reads clues others miss. The collection restored the detective after public outcry. It stands among the finest short Holmes books. Fans still rank the Empty House and Dancing Men among the very best Holmes stories.
1089-moon-face-and-other-stories:
Jack London gathers short tales of men pushed to their limits. One plots murder by sunstroke, lovers bet on fate, and wanderers find gold or death in the wild. The title story turns on a grudge nursed under a tropic sun until it ends in a grim joke.

London's people are stark and his settings are hard, from the South Seas to the frozen north. His prose hits fast and leaves a sting. The book shows his gift for the short, cruel tale, and it pairs well with his novels for readers who like London at his most unsparing.
10891-algonquin-indian-tales:
Egerton R. Young collected stories told by Ojibway and other Algonquin peoples, publishing them in 1903 with a warm letter from Chief Keche Chemon, or Charles Big Canoe. The chief writes that hearing the tales again recalled boyhood evenings in wigwams and around camp fires, and he welcomes a book that saves them from being forgotten.

Trickster Nanahboozhoo, talking animals, and the gifts of trees and plants fill the tales, which often explain sickness, seasons, or human conduct. Young frames them with notes on storytelling in many lands, from Egypt to India. The collection preserves oral literature in readable English and shows how stories taught, warned, and entertained their first hearers.
10915-the-girl-s-cabinet-of-instructive-:
Uncle Philip wrote this 1856 story book for girls, pairing short tales with pictures and plain moral lessons. A doll's party opens the collection, where good girls who have done their lessons enjoy play after duty. Other stories follow a vain girl named Kate, who minds dress more than books, and a new girl arriving at boarding school.

Short explanatory pieces sit beside the tales, including a simple account of what a dispensary is and how the poor are treated there free of charge. The lessons are direct: obedience, kindness, and duty before pleasure. As a period piece, the book shows how mid-nineteenth-century publishers taught girls to behave, in stories meant to be read and discussed at home.
1092-the-description-of-wales:
Gerald of Wales, the same sharp-eyed clerk who rode with Archbishop Baldwin, turns here to describe Wales itself: its land, its people, and their customs. He praises Welsh music, wit, and hardihood, and he scolds their quarrels, their diet, and their morals with equal gusto.

The book lists rivers and saints, notes how the Welsh dress, eat, and fight, and adds tales of marvels and omens. Gerald writes as both a Welshman by birth and a Norman churchman by trade, which gives his view its edge. The work remains a key source for twelfth-century Wales.
10922-young-lives:
Richard Le Gallienne's 1899 novel follows a group of young people growing up in a small north-country town. Henry, Esther, Mike Laflin, and their friends leave home, choose professions, fall in love, and test friendship against ambition. An old desk, Atlantic liners, and a move to London mark stages in their passage from youth to adult life.

Le Gallienne writes with warmth about first love, literary dreams, and the pull of home, and he lets his characters argue about wives for poets, money, and fame. Mike's million pounds and a published book change fortunes without settling hearts. The novel reads as a semi-autobiographical portrait of youth, idealistic, restless, and tender toward the friends who shape a life.
10926-saxe-holm-s-stories-first-series:
Helen Hunt Jackson published these stories in 1873 under the name Saxe Holm. Six tales make up the first series, beginning with Draxy Miller's Dowry, about a lonely, book-loving father who names his daughter Darachsa after a heroine in a novel. Other stories follow wives, widows, and women holding marriages together through patience or quiet resolve.

The Elder's Wife, Whose Wife Was She, The One-Legged Dancers, How One Woman Kept Her Husband, and Esther Wynn's Love-Letters complete the set. Jackson writes about New England village life with sympathy for women whose strength shows in endurance rather than speeches. The stories were popular in their day and remain readable portraits of domestic courage and village judgment.
10947-the-best-american-humorous-short-s:
Alexander Jessup edited this anthology of American humorous short stories, pairing an introductory survey with stories by leading writers. The introduction places O. Henry and Jack London beside Henry James, Edith Wharton, and other masters, arguing that humour cannot be separated from the wider American short story. Earlier writers, from Sarah Orne Jewett to Ambrose Bierce, get their due as well.

Stories range from dialect comedy and tall tales to sharp social satire, showing how Americans laughed at boarding houses, business deals, and small-town life. Jessup chose pieces that still read well aloud, with strong plots and clear voices. The anthology works as both entertainment and a compact history of American humour in fiction.
10961-lawn-tennis-for-ladies:
Dorothea Lambert Chambers, Wimbledon champion, wrote this 1910 guide to lawn tennis for women. Chapters cover athletics for girls, practice and improvement, match and tournament play, rackets, courts, dress, and training, plus tournament management and personal reminiscences. Twenty-three illustrations show forehand and backhand drives, service, and Wimbledon finals.

Chambers advises plain white shirts and skirts, white shoes and stockings, and practical dress for rain and muddy courts. She also recalls leading players, including May Sutton's 1905 Wimbledon win and her own 1906 victory over Sutton. The book speaks with authority and warmth, encouraging girls to play seriously, and it captures women's tennis just as it gained a wide following.
10980-lady-john-russell-a-memoir-with-se:
Desmond MacCarthy and Agatha Russell edited this 1910 memoir of Lady John Russell, wife of the Victorian prime minister Lord John Russell. Chapters run from her early years in Paris and Berlin, 1815 to 1834, through her engagement and marriage in 1841, to decades at Pembroke Lodge. Diaries and letters carry much of the story in her own words.

Readers follow the Corn Law repeal, Chartism, the Crimean War, the breach with Palmerston, and the fall of the Russell government, seen from inside a political household. Literary friends, family illness, and foreign travel fill the private side. The memoir gives both a life and a view of nineteenth-century British politics, told by a woman close to its centre.
11027-grimm-s-fairy-stories:
Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm's famous tales appear here in a 1922 edition with coloured illustrations by John B. Gruelle and pen sketches by R. Emmett Owen. Twenty-five stories include the Goose-Girl, Hansel and Grethel, Little Snow-White, Cinderella, Rapunzel, Rumpelstiltskin, and the Frog Prince. Each tale is told in the Grimms' plain, traditional style.

The Goose-Girl opens the book, with a princess, a talking horse named Falada, and a lock of her mother's hair as a charm. Other tales follow clever tailors, faithful servants, and children lost in woods. The collection suits family reading aloud, and it shows why these German folk tales became children's classics around the world.
11028-philippine-folk-tales:
Four articles from the Journal of American Folk-Lore, joined into one volume, preserve folk tales from the Philippines. Clara Kern Bayliss contributes Philippine folk tales, including the Monkey and the Turtle, while Berton Maxfield and W. H. Millington give Visayan tales such as Jackyo, Truth and Falsehood, and Why Dogs Wag Their Tails. Fletcher Gardner adds Tagalog tales, including Juan stories and a Filipino version of Aladdin.

Laura Watson Benedict closes the book with Bagobo myths. Tricksters, giants, enchanted rings and shells, and children outwitting the powerful fill the tales. The collection, produced by Jeroen Hellingman, remains a valuable record of Philippine oral literature, gathered by early folklorists and now available in English for general readers.
11069-squinty-the-comical-pig-his-many-a:
Richard Barnum wrote this 1915 animal story for children about Squinty, a little pink pig with a curly tail, a nose like a flattened rubber ball, and one eye that squints. Squinty meets a dog, runs away, gets lost, gets home, learns a trick, and takes a balloon ride, meeting a squirrel and Mappo the merry monkey along the way. Harriet H. Tooker illustrated the book.

A boy on summer holiday picks Squinty out by his funny squint and hopes to take him home, while Squinty waits in the pen. Barnum writes in a warm, chatty voice for very young readers. The book belongs to his Kneetime Animal Stories, each following one animal's adventures in simple chapters.
11092-the-history-of-tom-thumb-and-other:
Chicago's M. A. Donohue published this profusely illustrated storybook, opening with the history of Tom Thumb. In King Arthur's days, Merlin the enchanter stops at a ploughman's cottage and learns the couple's sorrow: they have no children. The ploughman's wife says she would be happiest with a son no bigger than her husband's thumb, and the Queen of the Fairies grants the wish.

Tom never grows bigger, but he grows cunning, creeping into other boys' bags to steal cherry-stones, until one boy catches him and draws the bag string tight. Later Tom dances inside a miller, is thrown into a river, swallowed by a salmon, and found by a cook when the fish is cut open for the King. The book gives children the old tale in lively, picture-filled form, with further stories following.
11099-more-seeds-of-knowledge-or-another:
Miss Julia Corner wrote this sequel for children about Charles, a boy a year older and wiser than in Seeds of Useful Knowledge. Charles now writes well, reads without spelling long words, knows his multiplication and pence tables, declines Latin nouns, and loves geography best.

Chapters teach about black slaves who make sugar, a subject Corner presents as cruelty and injustice, about history, and about missionaries. Seven coloured engravings, including an Inca surprised by a watch, illustrate the lessons. The book mixes instruction with story, typical of early Victorian children's education.
111-freckles:
A one-handed orphan guards timber in the Limberlost swamp and dreams of belonging. Gene Stratton-Porter's Freckles follows the waif hired by lumberman McLean to watch valuable leases. Mrs. Duncan mothers him, the Bird Woman photographs birds, and timber thieves circle.

Freckles falls for the Swamp Angel, a girl glimpsed among the trees. Lord and Lady O'More arrive from Ireland seeking a lost relative, and the boy's past unfolds. Courage, nature study, and kindness carry the story. The novel made the Limberlost famous and Freckles beloved. Stratton-Porter's love of birds and swamp life fills the novel with vivid natural detail.
11107-theobald-the-iron-hearted-or-love-:
Reverend Cesar Malan wrote this tale from the French, published in 1808, about love toward enemies during the Hussite wars. In 1423, after a battle in a beautiful Bohemian valley, old Gottfried and his grandson Erard, barely nine, climb a hill and rescue a wounded chevalier. The wounded man proves to be Theobald, the Iron-Hearted, enemy of Erard's father Arnold the Lion.

Chapters follow kindness to an enemy, Arnold's arrival alive but wounded, family worship, and a friendly meeting where warriors forgive each other. Theobald, amazed at the kindness he receives, seeks instruction and learns the Bible's lesson of love to enemies. The story teaches children Christian forgiveness through a historical adventure, earnest and clearly told.
11111-only-an-irish-boy-or-andy-burke-s-:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote this boys' novel about Andy Burke, an Irish boy whose fortunes rise through pluck and honesty. The book opens not with Andy but with Godfrey Preston, a boy of fifteen, handsomely dressed and full of consequence, ordering John the stableman to saddle his horse. John refuses: the horse is sick, and Colonel Anthony Preston left orders it was not to go out.

Chapters follow Andy and his mother, Mrs. Preston, a profitable job, the two old maids, Andy's debut at school, a game of ball, Godfrey's rebellion, a midnight alarm, riding with a highwayman, the drop game, Colonel Preston's will. Preston unpleasantly surprised. Fairfax the adventurer draws a pistol on Colonel Preston and demands his money, calling himself the genuine article. Alger's tale rewards industry and punishes snobbery in his familiar formula.
11114-debate-on-woman-suffrage-in-the-se:
Senators H. W. Blair, J. E. Brown, J. N. Dolph, G. G. Vest, and George F. Hoar debated woman suffrage in the United States Senate on December 8, 1886, and January 23, 1887, during the second session of the 49th Congress. Blair moved joint resolution S.R. 5, proposing a constitutional amendment that the right to vote shall not be denied or abridged on account of sex, with Congress empowered to enforce it.

Speakers argued whether the amendment should go to state legislatures for ratification, and what women's voting would mean for homes, shops, and politics. One passage urges distinct women's departments in shops, run by motherly women, to rescue shoppers from tumult. The debate gives a primary source for the suffrage movement's long congressional struggle, in the senators' own words, three decades before the Nineteenth Amendment.
11148-aunt-harding-s-keepsakes-or-the-tw:
Daniel P. Kidder revised this 1851 children's story about two sisters and their aunt's keepsakes. Louisa and Emma sit at work in the summer-house, guessing what Aunt Harding will give them before she goes away. Louisa overheard her aunt wish to give something really useful, valued as the girls grow older, and the sisters dream of work-boxes and a writing-desk.

Chapters follow the presents, their use, two characters, letters from India, trouble between sisters, Aunt Harding's letter, the use of money, and her return. When Louisa gives way to her faults, her mother refuses to treat her as though she sought to overcome them, withholding a desk until improvement appears. The tale teaches care, honesty, and wise use of gifts.
11156-buddy-and-brighteyes-pigg-bed-time:
Howard R. Garis wrote these bed-time stories about Buddy and Brighteyes Pigg, first printed in the Evening News of Newark, New Jersey, and collected in book form by permission of that paper. The Pigg family lives in a pen: Dr. Pigg, named for a broken paw treated in hospital, his wife, and their children Buddy and Brighteyes, two queer little brown, white, and black guinea pigs.

Thirty-one stories follow Buddy in a cabbage, Brighteyes and Mrs. Hoptoad, Buddy playing ball, Buddy wanting a tail, walking a tight rope, Brighteyes in a tin can, and Buddy and the burglar fox. In one tale, a June bug sings of flipping, flopping, and buzzing around the room, then throws a mosquito out of the window to protect the sleeping Buddy. Garis's stories give very young children gentle animal adventures for bedtime.
11241-wee-ones-bible-stories:
Published in 1903, this small illustrated book retells Bible episodes in short sketches for little children. Stories include the feeding of the multitudes, where Jesus takes five loaves and two fishes and feeds a crowd on the far side of the Sea of Galilee. The language stays simple, the scenes stay brief, and each sketch ends before a child's attention wanders.

The book belongs to a tradition of giving children scripture as story rather than doctrine. Its illustrations were part of the appeal, inviting children to picture each scene. For modern readers, it offers a clear example of early twentieth-century religious publishing for the nursery.
11313-a-school-history-of-the-united-sta:
John Bach McMaster's 1897 School History of the United States, written by a University of Pennsylvania professor, covers American history from Europe's discovery of America through politics since 1880 in thirty-five chapters. Contents move from Spaniards, English, Dutch, and Swedes on the seaboard through colonial life, independence, the Constitution, parties, neutrality. the War of 1812, expansion, the Civil War, Reconstruction, and mechanical progress, with appendices printing the Declaration and Constitution.

Maps trace discovery, colonial claims, and war results. McMaster's narrative is clear and national in scope, designed for classrooms. The book shows what American schoolchildren were taught about their past at the century's end, including its silences and emphases. It remains a useful period textbook.
11315-friendly-fairies:
Johnny Gruelle, creator of Raggedy Ann, wrote and illustrated Friendly Fairies in 1919, dedicating it to his mother. Fifteen stories include the Three Little Gnomes, the Happy Rattle, a Recipe for a Happy Day, Grandfather Skeeterhawk, Crow Talk, the Fairy Ring, Mr. and Mrs. Thumbkins, Sally Migrundy, and How Johnny Cricket Saw Santa Claus. The opening tale finds three gnomes living beneath a fallen forest tree, hiding their fire when a huntsman's horn sounds.

Gruelle's fairies are gentle and domestic, teaching kindness through small adventures. His illustrations, in the Raggedy style, match the text's warmth. The book belongs to a kinder tradition of fairy writing, meant for bedtime rather than fright, and it charms young readers still.
11319-the-fairy-godmothers-and-other-tal:
Mrs. Alfred Gatty's Fairy Godmothers and Other Tales, published in 1851 and dedicated to her children, was written in hours of sickness for healthy and joyous young readers. Contents include the title tale, Joachim the Mimic, Darkness and Light, and The Love of God, with a frontispiece designed by Lucette E. Barker. The opening tale gathers fairies on a lovely July evening in a bay on the coast of Fairy Land.

Gatty states her aim plainly: to illustrate favorite, long-cherished convictions through story. Her fairies teach morals without preaching at length. The book is a fine example of Victorian fairy writing by a clergyman's wife, blending domestic piety with imagination.
11325-the-happiest-time-of-their-lives:
Alice Duer Miller's 1918 novel opens in a New York brownstone drawing-room, where young Miss Severance sits with hands cold as ice before an adventure her mother has carefully staged. The room, filled with beautiful objects and pink and yellow roses in Chinese bowls, frames a story about friendship, marriage, and the choices facing a young woman of good family. Miller dedicates the book to Clarence Day Jr.

The novel's talk is its engine: characters debate whether friendship can be as binding as marriage, since friends make no announcements or vows. Miller, author of Come Out of the Kitchen, writes with light irony about serious decisions. The book captures upper-class New York life on the edge of the First World War's end.
11337-cowmen-and-rustlers-a-story-of-the:
Edward S. Ellis's 1904 novel, Cowmen and Rustlers, follows Wyoming cattle ranges through warnings from the woods, flights over ice, reports of guns, hot pursuits, and a burned ranch. The story opens far from Wyoming, in a merry Maine household where Colonel Hugh Whitney, a Civil War veteran, anchors a family whose sons head west. Chapters build toward truces, hostages, underground missives, and a final summons.

Ellis, a prolific author of boys' adventure series, writes for young readers who wanted frontier action with clear heroes and villains. The novel's rustler war supplies chases, forts, and narrow escapes in steady supply. It represents the dime-novel western graduating into book form, still brisk and moral.
11360-sacred-and-profane-love-a-novel-in:
Arnold Bennett's 1905 novel Sacred and Profane Love, in three episodes titled In the Night, Three Human Hearts, and. The Victory, follows a young woman preoccupied with love as a noble, sensuous passion absorbing the soul. On the eve of her twenty-first birthday, she sits at a piano in a decaying drawing-room, playing Chopin by candlelight, weeping and wondering why she is what she is. A Maupassant epigraph on the immortal kiss frames the book.

Bennett, dedicating the novel to Eden Phillpotts, writes introspectively about desire, music, and destiny. The heroine's inner life carries the plot more than external events. The novel shows Bennett before his Five Towns realism fully took hold, experimenting with passion as a subject.
11376-autobiographical-sketches:
Annie Besant's 1885 Autobiographical Sketches answer frequent requests for an outline of her life, written to satisfy friendly questioners and defend against unfair attack. Besant begins with her birth in London on October 1, 1847, within sound of Bow bells. nicknamed little Pheasantina by a giddy aunt, and traces her Irish Morris family, a handsome, extravagant, decayed household whose pride survived its shrinking means. Her grandfather, bent and white-haired, dominates early memories.

The sketches stop well before Besant's later fame as a reformer and Theosophist, but they show the formation of her voice: candid, combative, and warm. Readers interested in Victorian women's lives will find a vivid childhood, told by a woman already accustomed to public controversy.
11381-sermons-for-the-times:
Charles Kingsley's Sermons for the Times gathers sermons on fathers and children, salvation, a good conscience, names, sponsorship, justification by faith, duty and superstition. sonship, the Lord's Prayer, Ahab and Naboth, providence, England's strength, death in life, shame, forgiveness, the true gentleman, toleration, and public spirit. The first sermon takes Malachi's closing prophecy of Elijah turning fathers' hearts to children as the bridge from Old Testament to John the Baptist.

Kingsley, a muscular Christian and social reformer, preaches plainly and practically, applying scripture to family and civic duty. His sermons were meant for ordinary congregations, not scholars. The volume shows Victorian preaching at its most earnest, connecting private conscience with public life.
11392-not-pretty-but-precious-and-other-:
This 1872 collection, Not Pretty, But Precious, and Other Short Stories, gathers American magazine fiction by John Hay, Clara F. Guernsey, Margaret Hosmer, Harriet Prescott Spofford, Lucy Hamilton Hooper, and others. Contents include the title story by Margret Field, Hosmer's Victims of Dreams, Guernsey's Cold Hand and Red Fox. Hay's Blood Seedling, Hooper's Under False Colors, De Forest's Hungry Heart, Spofford's Louie, and Minor's Old Sadler's Resurrection. An illustration shows an uncle exclaiming over a great gift.

The stories range from domestic realism to mild supernaturalism, typical of post-Civil War magazines. The title story opens with a letter to an injured man, Mr. Norval, about business best settled on paper. Readers sampling the era's short fiction will find the volume varied and accessible.
1148-the-itinerary-of-archbishop-baldwin:
Giraldus Cambrensis, a Welsh churchman of the twelfth century, rode through Wales in 1188 with Archbishop Baldwin, preaching a crusade and noting all he saw. His account lists towns, rivers, saints' wells, and the habits of the Welsh, with tales of wonders and portents along the road.

The journey took them from the border to the far west, and Giraldus writes as both guide and gossip, praising Welsh wit and scolding Welsh faults. The book is a prime source for medieval Wales, and it reads as a travel tale full of odd, vivid detail.
11501-laughing-bill-hyde-and-other-stori:
Rex Beach's 1917 stories open with William Hyde, called Laughing Bill, leaving Deer Lodge Penitentiary after three years. Prison has left him pale, weak in the lungs, and hating the law, though he can talk through stone walls and plait horsehair bridles.

Hyde means to bury his Montana past and start again in a kinder climate, and the title story follows his fresh schemes. Other tales in the volume range across the West and beyond, with a bridge contest in one story pitting an Atlantic company against a Patterson bid. Humour and hard luck carry them all.
11513-on-land-and-sea-at-the-dardanelles:
T. C. Bridges's On Land and Sea at the Dardanelles follows Ken Carrington and Dave Burney, a tall young Australian, from the transport Cardigan Castle through the Gallipoli campaign. Chapters cover the open port, the Cardigan Castle's last voyage, the landing, a ruse of war, promotion, guns, Lizzie letting loose. hunters hunted, battle by rocks, prisoners, a firing party, sweepers, tackling a trooper, a boarding party, and running the gauntlet. Photographs show Indian troops at Alexandria and landings at Sari Bair.

Ken opens by mocking fun, warning Dave about cliffs, quick-firers, barbed wire every five yards, and snipers. Bridges writes boys' war adventure with firsthand flavor. The book belongs to the wartime juvenile literature that turned Gallipoli into heroic story.
11514-balcony-stories:
Grace King's 1892 stories are set in Louisiana, where much of life passes on balconies through six long summer months. Women sit and talk on summer nights, and the tales that follow grow from that talk: a drama of three, a grande demoiselle, Mimi's marriage, and a miracle chapel.

Later pieces include a crippled hope, a little convent girl, a grandmother's grandmother, and a delicate affair. War and loss run through several stories, as in the tale of a sick woman moving from patient to patient after Sheridan passed through. The book keeps a Creole world in view.
11563-morning-bells-or-waking-thoughts-f:
Frances Ridley Havergal's Morning Bells offers waking thoughts for little ones, each headed by a Bible text. Early entries take up the holy child Jesus, Christ who pleased not himself, being held up and kept safe, and bearing one another's burdens.

Later thoughts cover garments always white, the beauty of the Lord, a new heart, the Lord fighting for his people, and being under his wings. One piece retells Israel at the Red Sea, with Egyptians, horses, and chariots behind and no boats ahead, and God fighting in a way no one had thought of. The book is meant for morning reading.
11582-old-greek-stories:
James Baldwin retells old Greek stories simply as stories, for young readers. Jupiter and his company stand at the centre, with the old Greek heroes beside them. His preface says the tales have delighted young and old for ages.

They have entered our language and thought, he argues, and form part of our heritage. Perseus and Andromeda supply one clear example. The hero slips the Gorgon's head back into his pouch. He speaks with the girl he saved, daughter of a king. Her queen mother had boasted of her beauty. Other tales follow the same plain pattern.
11592-children-s-hour-with-red-riding-ho:
Watty Piper's 1922 children's hour retells Little Red Riding Hood first: a sweet girl in a red cloak carries eggs, butter, and cake through the wood to her sick grandmother. Flowers, sunshine, and a happy dance open the tale before the wolf enters it.

Other stories follow in the same plain style, among them a false bride judged by her own sentence and Babes in the Wood, where two children are left to an uncle's care. The volume is a bedtime set, short, clear, and meant to be read aloud, with each tale ending in a firm, simple moral.
11603-the-house-of-cobwebs-and-other-sto:
George Gissing's 1906 stories, with an introductory survey by Thomas Seccombe, open with a survey of Gissing's work and a chronological record. The title story, The House of Cobwebs, is followed by A Capitalist, Christopherson, Humplebee, and The Scrupulous Father.

Later tales include A Poor Gentleman, Miss Rodney's Leisure, A Charming Family, and A Lodger in Maze Pond. One story follows a young man lodging with a bookbinder, paying for lessons by unpaid work, dreading the last fortnight of each quarter with its supperless nights. Poverty and pride run through the set.
11639-figures-of-earth-a-comedy-of-appea:
James Branch Cabell's 1921 comedy of appearances follows Manuel, who leaves the mire and climbs toward credit, spending, and settlement. Books divide the tale: the book of credit, the book of spending, the book of cast accounts, the book of surcharge, and the book of settlement.

Manuel lights four candles in a hut, one under each umbrella, and hears a thin voice call him to open the door, though no one stands in the forest dusk. Later chapters bring Niafer, Alianora, Freydis, and three women, with magic, duels, and a crown of wisdom. The novel is a fable of desire and its price.
11642-what-to-see-in-england-a-guide-to-:
Gordon Home's 1908 guide puts, in the smallest space he can, the means by which a traveller may see England's historic places, natural beauty, and literary sites. A sketch plan of London railway stations opens the book, listing Broad Street, Cannon Street, Euston, and Waterloo among the termini.

Later pages move county by county, with Oulton Broad full of smart yachts and Heigham lonely by contrast. Wroxham Broad shines with white sails, and its quiet waters thicken with yellow iris and purple loosestrife. The guide is a practical companion for a walking or rail tour.
11656-the-great-shadow-and-other-napoleo:
A. Conan Doyle's Napoleonic tales open with The Great Shadow, told by Jock Calder of West Inch, a man of fifty-five in the middle of the nineteenth century. He recalls beacons, cousin Edie of Eyemouth, and a shadow on the waters and on the land.

Later tales in the volume include The Crime of the Brigadier and The Slapping Sal. One letter in the book tells how a man took Edie as his wife and fled to old comrades, duty and honour calling him back. The stories mix Scots farm life with the wars against Napoleon, and they keep a storyteller's voice throughout.
11671-the-rudder-grangers-abroad-and-oth:
Frank R. Stockton's 1891 and 1894 stories open with Euphemia among the pelicans, on a yacht in warm winter sun off a semi-tropical river. Seven pelicans labour through the air, ducks rise, and mullet leap from the water like a sudden shower.

Later tales follow the Rudder Grangers in England, Pomona's daughter, a derelict, the baker of Barnbury, and the water-devil. A captain at sea hails a steamer with a speaking trumpet, asking after Bertha, while Mary Phillips answers that Miss Nugent feels unwell. The book is light, inventive comedy of travel and household adventure.
11683-where-the-trail-divides:
Will Lillibridge's 1907 novel, Where the Trail Divides, opens with a short, fat, greasy man, bowlegged as a greyhound, limping footsore under a hot August sun. His blue flannel shirt, open at the throat, shows a broad, hairy chest rising and falling with effort.

Chapters move from presentiment and fulfilment to discovery, reconstruction, and the land of licence. The red man and the white, a skeleton within the closet, and the voice of the wild follow. A later scene brings Landor and an Indian in a tent, parting in courteous silence, never to meet alive again. The book is a western tale of fate and reckoning.
11689-are-women-people-a-book-of-rhymes-:
Alice Duer Miller's book of rhymes for suffrage times opens with treacherous texts and campaign material for both sides. A consistent anti tells her son Willie, twenty-one today, not to go to the polls, since they are dark and dreadful places where many lose their souls.

Father, she says, casts her vote and Louisa's and Sarah's and Aunt Clo's, and would gladly cast Willie's too. Later rhymes quote a Wisconsin court of 1875, which called thirteen subjects unfit for women, three of them crimes against women. The verse is satire, turning anti-suffrage arguments back on themselves with a light, sharp hand.
11730-with-the-allies:
Richard Harding Davis, writing With the Allies, opens on the Lusitania slipping out of New York on 4 August, lights doused and ports sealed, three days ignorant of war's march. Sailors paint out Cunard scarlet and black for Admiralty grey.

Chapters cover Germans in Brussels, the burning of Louvain, Paris in wartime, Soissons, and Rheims. A later scene brings a cathedral turned stable, with wounded Germans on dirty straw, two killed not by wounds but by a shell from their own guns. Davis writes as a correspondent at the front, close to ruin and to ordinary soldiers.
11738-hindoo-tales-or-the-adventures-of-:
P. W. Jacob freely translated the Hindoo Tales, or Adventures of Ten Princes, from the Sanskrit Dasakumaracharitam, published in London in 1873. The original, printed more than twenty-five years before, had not yet appeared in any European language when Jacob took it up.

Turgid passages are condensed, indecent or tedious parts are left out, and the rest follows the original closely, with nothing added. The work, thought to date from the end of the eleventh century, was left unfinished, though the last narrator's story is nearly complete. Princes, nurses, crowns restored, and letters from old friends carry the tales forward.
11749-new-comedies:
Lady Gregory's New Comedies, copyright 1913, gathers four Abbey Theatre plays: The Bogie Men, The Full Moon, Coats, and Damer's Gold, with McDonough's Wife. The Bogie Men opens in a shed near a coach stop, where Darby, a sweep, tries on a showy suit from his bag.

Taig, another sweep, enters asking about the coach, and the two men spar over trade and shelter. Later plays bring a coat disputed over a spot of grease, a goose carved at table, and a man threatening libel in the Champion newspaper. Gregory's comedies are Irish country humour, quick, verbal, and played for a Dublin audience.
11752-chivalry-dizain-des-reines:
James Branch Cabell's Chivalry, dated 1921, opens with an essay on the chivalric code as an age's convenient illusions, minimising thought in dilemmas by posting a clear cleavage between right and wrong. The code, Cabell says, is prettier than most, and it puts God, honour, and mistress above all else.

Dizain des Reines follows, with a queen ordering a sick lord, Hastings, to rise from his couch and lead troops against the Scot. Hastings pleads illness, the queen retorts that the same illness killed Iscariot, and the army waits without. The book pairs an essay on codes with tales of queens, honour, and the price of living by a creed.
11759-the-bicyclers-and-three-other-farc:
Four farces, transcribed by David Price, open with The Bicyclers, set in the drawing room of Mr. and Mrs. Thaddeus Perkins in Gramercy Square. It is late October, moonlight, half past eight, and Perkins, in bicycle garb, awaits his first lesson from Bob and Jack.

Mrs. Perkins hopes the wheel will do her overworked husband good, though Perkins doubts that learning to ride is restful. Other farces in the volume include A Dramatic Evening, The Fatal Message, and A Proposal Under Difficulties. One rehearsal scene turns on yonder window, changed to yonder casement, lest it become yonder basement. The book is light stage comedy.
1187-war-of-the-classes:
Jack London gathers essays and talks on the class struggle, arguing that labor and capital fight a war that will end only when workers take control. He speaks for the socialist cause with his usual force, praising the working man and scorning the masters who live off his toil.

The pieces mix theory with stories of strikes, tramps, and the brutal terms of wage labor in his day. London's rhetoric is blunt and fiery, and his faith in the coming triumph of labor runs through every page. The book gives a clear window on American socialism before the First World War.
11877-monkey-jack-and-other-stories:
Edited by Palmer Cox, Monkey Jack and Other Stories gathers verse tales for children, opening with a little maid weeping piteously and demanding aid. The stories mix animals, seasons, and seafaring folk, with illustrations in the original edition.

Later verses describe Winter as a funny old fellow wrapped to the heels in a snow-white sack, painting noses a beautiful hue and whistling trills. Sailors who love a swinging breeze before the woods of Devon and the silver cliffs of Wales. The collection's charm lies in its musical, old-fashioned rhymes, meant to be read aloud to children who liked their stories short, funny, and slightly strange.
11930-more-fables:
George Ade's More Fables, illustrated by Clyde J. Newman and published in 1900, follows his Fables in Slang with a new set of comic moral tales. Titles show Ade's method: the fable of how Uncle Brewster was too shifty for the tempter, the grass widow and the mesmeree and the six dollars. The honest money-maker and the partner of his joys, such as they were.

Ade writes in American slang and newspaper English, turning everyday types, the shifty uncle, the grass widow, the sweetheart who flies the track, into figures of sly, unsentimental moralizing. The fables do not preach in the old manner; they let a character's own cunning or folly deliver the point, with a laugh.
11934-primitive-love-and-love-stories:
Henry T. Finck's 1899 study Primitive Love and Love-Stories, dedicated to one who taught him that conjugal affection is not inferior to romantic love, opens with a history of an idea. Chapters treat skeptical critics, Robert Burton, Hegel on Greek love, Shelley, Macaulay, Bulwer-Lytton, Gautier, and Goldsmith and Rousseau, before turning to Herbert Spencer's analysis.

Finck argues that love is a compound feeling, built from active impulses added to older theories, and he tests that view against literature and anthropology. The book belongs to a late Victorian effort to study love scientifically without losing its poetry, moving between philosophy, poetry, and the customs of peoples far from Europe.
11948-the-principal-navigations-voyages-:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques, and Discoveries preserves the great English collection of travel writing from the sixteenth century. This edition retains the spelling and abbreviations of Hakluyt's original, silently expanding manuscript forms such as vowels with macrons, q for que in Latin, and y for the, that, and with.

The collection gathers sailors', merchants', and explorers' accounts of voyages to the Americas, Africa, Asia. The Levant, with the documents, letters, and journals that made England's overseas enterprise imaginable. For modern readers it is both a source for early modern exploration and a monument of Elizabethan prose, ambitious, patriotic, and endlessly curious about the wider world.
1195-glasses:
Henry James tells of a young artist who meets Flora Saunt, a beautiful girl whose charm, he fears, will not survive the spectacles she must wear. The narrator watches her refuse glasses, marry badly, and fade, while he paints her portrait and ponders beauty, vanity, and sight.

The tale turns on a small, cruel irony: the thing that would let Flora see the world would spoil the face the world loves. James writes it in his subtle, winding manner, with much left between the lines. The story stands as a fine, sad study of looks and self-deception.
11969-duty-and-other-irish-comedies:
Seumas O'Brien's 1916 collection Duty and Other Irish Comedies gathers five one-act plays: Duty, Jurisprudence, Magnanimity, Matchmakers, and Retribution. The title play's characters include Head Constable Mulligan, Sergeant Dooley, and Constable Huggins of the Royal Irish Constabulary, with Micus Goggin and Padna Sweeney.

O'Brien's comedies use police, courts, and village disputes to satirize authority and human nature, with the dry-point study by P. Grassby as frontispiece. Written during the years of Irish political upheaval, the plays keep their humor local and concrete, finding comedy in constables, matchmakers, and magnanimity rather than in grand political statement.
1197-taras-bulba-and-other-tales:
Nikolai Gogol's Taras Bulba tells of a fierce old Cossack chief and his two sons, who ride to war against the Poles for faith and freedom. When one son betrays the cause for love of a Polish girl, Taras himself must judge him, and the tale ends in fire and revenge on the steppe.

The other tales in the volume show Gogol's range, from Ukrainian nights to Petersburg streets. His prose mixes comedy, horror, and lyrical praise of the land. Taras Bulba stands as a classic of Cossack romance, and it still stirs readers with its violence and its heart.
11980-a-tramp-s-sketches:
Stephen Graham's 1913 Tramp's Sketches, dedicated to the Celestials, records walking, sleeping out, and meeting strangers, with a frontispiece of night over the Black Sea. Contents move from farewell to the town and nights out on a perfect vagabondage to the Lord's Prayer, days. A still-creation-day, then to hospitality and the rich man and the poor man.

Graham writes about mercy through Shakespeare, quoting Portia's answer in The Merchant of Venice. About being pointed out as an Englishman in a Turkish coffee-house, where customers talked about England's role in war. The sketches value direct contact over comfort, finding religious and human meaning in roads, sunsets from the gate of Baidari, and the meaning of the sea.
11989-the-crime-of-the-french-cafe-and-o:
Three complete stories of Nicholas Carter, America's greatest detective, fill this volume: The Crime of the French Café, Nick Carter's Ghost Story, and The Mystery of St. Agnes' Hospital. The title story opens in a well-known French restaurant in New York's Tenderloin district, whose small, elegant private dining-rooms set the scene for murder.

Carter's cases move from a private dining-room, marked B, through a dinner invitation that turns strange, to folding doors behind which voices hush and slow, somber organ music rises. The dime-novel detective works by close observation and bold action, and the three stories together show why Carter, a rival to Sherlock Holmes in American popular fiction, held readers for decades.
12007-cousin-hatty-s-hymns-and-twilight-:
Cousin Hatty's Hymns and Twilight Stories was published in Boston in 1851 with illustrations including Mother Birds. It gathers simple verses written for a very dear child, with no thought beyond her gratification. Friends requested publication, hoping other children might derive the same pleasure as the little one for whom the verses were first written.

The hymns and twilight stories suit bedtime and Sunday reading, with plain language, gentle morals, and short forms a child could remember. As a mid-nineteenth-century children's book, it shows how family verse moved from private gift to printed volume, carried by affection rather than by literary ambition.
1203-dolly-dialogues:
Anthony Hope, author of The Prisoner of Zenda, gathers witty dialogues in which Lady Dolly, a clever young woman of society, trades barbs with her admiring friend and a circle of suitors. The talk runs over love, marriage, dress, and manners, with Dolly usually winning the last word.

The pieces are light, polished, and very much of the 1890s, when drawing-room wit was a fine art. Hope writes Dolly with charm and a touch of malice. The book suits readers who like Oscar Wilde's world without its sting, all sparkle and good humor.
12067-the-bee-man-of-orn-and-other-fanci:
Frank R. Stockton published this story collection with Scribner in 1887. Best known for The Lady, or the Tiger, Stockton here writes nine fanciful tales for older children and adults, each built on a single odd idea played out to its end.

The title tale follows an old man who tends bees and slowly learns who he truly is. Other stories send a minor canon to live with a griffin, trap a dryad in old pipes, and let a banished king and quarreling cousins settle scores by magic. Stockton humor lies in calm, logical narration of impossible events. The collection shows why his fairy tales lasted: wonder delivered with a straight face.
12069-joe-tilden-s-recipes-for-epicures:
Printed in San Francisco in 1907, this cookbook preserves the recipes of Major Joseph Tilden, a noted Pacific Coast epicure and Bohemian host. Friends gathered his dishes after his death, since he had shared them with only a few intimates.

The book runs from soups and chowders through fish, game, roasts, and sauces, with exact measures for dishes like onion soup, pheasant a la Savarin, and salmi of duck with olives. French technique meets California ingredients throughout, and short headnotes recall Tilden table. For cooks it remains a usable record of high-end home cooking in early San Francisco, before the earthquake scattered its dining rooms.
1208-south-sea-tales:
Jack London gathers stories from the South Seas he sailed himself: traders, planters, and beachcombers on atolls and in ports where fever, greed, and the law of the strong rule. The tales move from copra schooners to leper stations, with men and women tested by heat, sea, and each other.

London writes the islands without romance, showing both the beauty and the cruelty of the trade. His prose is hard and fast, and his endings are seldom kind. The book gives a vivid, unsparing view of the Pacific of his day, and it pairs well with his novels of the north.
12102-darrel-of-the-blessed-isles:
Irving Bacheller, author of Eben Holden, published this novel in 1903, illustrated by Arthur I. Keller. Set in the northern New York hills, it follows a village philosopher known as Darrel and the young people who gather around him.

Darrel, a clock tinker and dreamer, runs a rustic museum and a theater of the woods, teaching neighbors through stories, jokes, and odd inventions. Chapters move from a little red sleigh and a crystal city to a Christmas adventure, a schoolhouse day, and the coming of the railroad. The tone is warm and nostalgic, praising rural wit against new hurry. Bacheller novel celebrates simple wisdom, though its sentiment can feel thick to modern taste.
12116-struwwelpeter-merry-stories-and-fu:
Heinrich Hoffmann's Struwwelpeter, Merry Stories and Funny Pictures, was published by Frederick Warne and Company in New York. It first appeared in German in 1844 and in English translation in 1848, though this edition is undated. Color illustrations appear on every page, often playing with the text, a feature the transcriber notes.

The stories begin when the children have been good, and proceed to cautionary tales of naughty children and their fates, told in rhyming verse with alarming pictures. Struwwelpeter, or Shock-headed Peter, with his uncut hair and nails, became the most famous of Hoffmann's warnings. The book's blend of humor and horror has kept it in print, and in debate, ever since.
12136-government-and-administration-of-t:
Government and Administration of the United States, by Westel W. Willoughby, fellow in history, and William F. Willoughby of the United States Department of Labor, appeared in the Johns Hopkins University Studies in Historical and Political Science, edited by Herbert B. Adams. The series motto, from Freeman, declares that history is past politics and politics present history.

The volume, series 9, parts 1 and 2, opens with a preface and chapters on government, monarchy, and absolutism, before turning to American institutions. Written as a university study, it treats the federal government systematically, for students and citizens who wanted to understand how the United States was actually administered, not merely how its Constitution read.
12137-la-le-gende-des-sie-cles:
Victor Hugo long poem cycle La Legende des Siecles appears here in an annotated school edition prepared by G. F. Bridge for the Oxford Modern French Series. Hugo, exiled for opposing Napoleon III, wrote the poems as a vast panorama of human history, from Genesis to his own century.

The selection includes episodes of kings, heroes, saints, and outcasts, with notes aimed at advanced school and university students rather than beginners. Bridge omits basic geographical and mythological notes, trusting readers to know them, and gives fuller literary comment instead. The edition shows how Hugo was taught to English students: not as a curiosity, but as a major poet whose history of mankind still demanded close reading.
12143-the-three-comrades:
Kristina Roy, of Stara Tura in Slovakia, wrote this children story about three orphans, translated into English by Charles Lukesh in a first edition of November 1941. The comrades are Petrik, Ondrejko, and the dog Fido, who share a hard life on mountain sheep pastures.

Petrik, left a public charge after his parents died of fever, finds shelter with Bacha Filina, a shepherd overseer. Ondrejko, sent to the mountains for his health, slowly learns that the singing lady who visits him is his mother. The boys face hunger, work, and separation, and the story ends with a chance to buy the estate and stay together. Roy tale blends Christian faith with plain mountain life.
12164-strawberry-acres:
Grace S. Richmond published Strawberry Acres in 1911, a cheerful novel of a family that leaves city apartments for country life. Dedicated to the owner of Grasslands, the book follows the move in two parts: Five Miles Out, then The Lanes and the Acres.

Chapters follow exploring, telephones and tents, pine groves, old gardens, afternoon tea, and train timetables, as the family learns to live outdoors. Max compromises, hearts tangle, and a southbound limited carries lovers and plans across the map. Richmond writes light domestic comedy with a warm eye for housekeeping, neighbors, and courtship. The novel belongs to the back-to-the-land stories of its era, when country air promised health and happiness.
12184-abroad-with-the-jimmies:
Lilian Bell wrote Abroad with the Jimmies as a light travel book about touring Europe with a lively American party. Bell, author of The Love Affairs of an Old Maid and The Expatriates, dedicates the book to her father, praising his patriotism and loyalty.

Chapters follow a houseboat at Henley, Paris, Strasburg, and on through France and Germany toward Russia, with the Jimmies, Bee, and Billy in tow. Bell sister Bee manages everyone with diplomatic, velvety crookedness, and a skirt dance at a hotel delights the party. The tone is chatty and comic, full of hotels, trains, and national types. The book reads as an Edwardian American abroad tale, fond of its travelers and their mishaps.
12194-liza-or-a-nest-of-nobles:
Ivan Turgenev novel A Nest of Nobles appears here as Liza, translated from Russian by W. R. S. Ralston in 1873 for the Leisure Hour Series. Turgenev, author of Fathers and Sons, wrote the novel about the Russian gentry after serfdom reform.

Liza, a young woman of devout feeling, loves Lavretsky, a landowner returned from a failed marriage abroad. Their love collides with duty, religion, and the return of Lavretsky wife, and the novel ends in renunciation rather than union. Ralston translation keeps Turgenev clear, musical prose and his sympathy for both lovers. The book is a classic of the Russian novel of manners, where personal happiness yields to conscience and fate.
12228-home-geography-for-primary-grades:
C. C. Long wrote this primary school geography in the early twentieth century, arguing that children must learn geography from the ground at their doors before they learn it from books. Long, author of language lessons, addresses teachers directly.

The method is simple. Walk pupils to a hill, a pond, a stream, or a park. Then let a local slope stand for the Andes, a meadow for a prairie, and a brook for the Mississippi. Lessons on rivers, rain, and the water cycle build outward from what children can see and touch. Poems and questions follow each lesson. The book shows Progressive-era teaching faith: observation first, imagination second, and the wide world learned through the near one.
12241-poems-by-emily-dickinson-third-ser:
Mabel Loomis Todd edited this third series of Emily Dickinson poems, published after the poet death in 1886. Todd preface notes that Dickinson intellectual activity was so great that a large and characteristic choice remained among her papers.

Poems in this series keep Dickinson short lines, dashes, and slant rhymes, on themes of nature, death, love, and time. March appears with purple shoes, making mud for dog and peddler, while other poems weigh praise against blame and trifles against eternity. Todd edition regularized some texts, a choice later editors revised. Even so, the third series widened Dickinson audience and confirmed her as a major American poet, not a curiosity.
12280-the-grandissimes:
George W. Cable published The Grandissimes in 1899, a novel of Creole New Orleans in the early nineteenth century, illustrated by Albert Herter. Cable, a leading local-color writer, set the book among the proud, divided Grandissime family.

Chapters open with masked batteries and the fate of an immigrant, then follow Honoré Grandissime, a maiden who will not marry, family trees, and the question of who is my neighbor. The plot turns on race, caste, and hidden kinship: white and Black Grandissimes share blood and name, but not rank. Cable treats the color line with unusual frankness for his day. The novel remains a landmark of Southern fiction about race and family.
12281-cattle-brands-a-collection-of-west:
Andy Adams published Cattle Brands in 1906, a book of western camp-fire stories drawn from his years on cattle drives. Adams, a former cowboy, wrote with authority about trail life, and the book is dedicated to Mr. and Mrs. Henry Russell Wray.

Stories include Drifting North, Seigerman Per Cent, Bad Medicine, A Winter Round-Up, A College Vagabond, and The Ransom of Don Ramon Mora. A mid-book passage describes cattle brand burnt or blotched beyond recognition, guarded by twenty heavily armed men, twice as many as a herd that size required. Adams tells of rustlers, rangers, and poker steers around the spade wagon. The book is a plain, vivid record of cowboy work.
12308-winning-his-spurs-a-tale-of-the-cr:
G. A. Henty published Winning His Spurs in 1895, a boys adventure tale of the Crusades. Henty wrote dozens of such novels, each following a young hero through history with courage and good humor.

The hero, Cuthbert, begins among outlaws, rescues a captive, and helps capture Wortham Hold before sailing for the Holy Land. Chapters follow the lists, revenge, the princess Berengaria, pirates, capture by Saracens, a hermit tale, and a fight of heroes, ending with the accolade of knighthood. A mid-book escape has the hero stealing away while captors sleep, fearing slavery beyond Jordan. The novel teaches history through adventure, with the certainties of its day.
12315-shanty-the-blacksmith-a-tale-of-ot:
Mrs. Sherwood published Shanty the Blacksmith in 1852, a tale of other times set in the wild border country between England and Scotland. Sherwood, a popular moral writer for children, sets the story before revolution changed forefathers manners.

An ancient castle, of which only one tower and a few chambers remain, anchors the tale. Shanty, a blacksmith of low birth, argues that grace can counteract the nature of a vagrant child. It can counteract even such a vagrant himself, since the Spirit is sharper than a two-edged sword. The story blends border adventure with evangelical moral. Sherwood tale teaches that birth does not fix character, and that faith can remake the lowest life.
12370-bagh-o-bahar-or-tales-of-the-four-:
Mir Amman's Bagh o Bahar, or Garden and Spring, appears here in Duncan Forbes's 1874 translation from Hindustani. Forbes, professor of oriental languages at King's College, London, presents a work long held as a classic across British India, prized for correct idiom as much as for story.

Four wandering darweshes, or holy men, each recount the strange turns of his own life, and their tales braid adventure, love, magic and moral lesson in Eastern fashion. The frame lets Forbes show many modes of speech and many customs in one book. Readers meet it both as a story collection and as an introduction to Hindustani phrase, custom and thought.
12419-frontier-stories:
Bret Harte's Frontier Stories collects California tales, opening with Flip, a California romance. A red track climbs the Los Gatos road toward the Coast Range, past dwarf firs and heat-laden air, to a sheltered terrace that promises coolness. Miners, travellers and settlers move through that landscape in the stories that follow.

Other tales are set at Blazing Star, in the Carquinez woods, at the Mission of San Carmel, and on Lone Star Mountain, with a ship of 1849 among them. Harte mixes humour, dialect and sudden pathos, turning gold-rush camps into theatre. The collection remains a classic sample of the California story at its most vivid.
12441-the-house-of-a-thousand-candles:
Meredith Nicholson published The House of a Thousand Candles in 1905, illustrated by Howard Chandler Christy, and dedicated to his sister Margaret. Nicholson, author of The Main Chance, writes a mystery romance around a will and a strange house.

Chapters open with the will of John Marshall Glenarm, a face at Sherry, the house itself, a voice from the lake, and a red tam-o-shanter. Later chapters bring the girl and the canoe, the man on the wall, and a string of clues. A mid-book exchange has a businessman bound for California and Colorado stockholders meetings, scolded fondly by the narrator. The novel mixes inheritance intrigue with romance. It was a popular success of its day.
12472-bataille-de-dames:
Scribe and Legouvé's comedy, Bataille de Dames, or A Duel in Love, first played at the Théâtre Français in 1851, appears here in an edition by Benjamin W. Wells, with introduction, notes and vocabulary. Characters include the Comtesse d'Autreval, her niece Léonie de la Villegontier, Henri de Flavignoul, Gustave de Grignon, the Baron de Montrichard and a dragoon sub-officer.
