Set at the château d'Autreval, the three-act comedy turns love into a battle of wits, with women outmanoeuvring men by talk, letters and stratagem. Wells's notes make the French text usable for American students. The edition doubles as theatre and language lesson, a classic French comedy of manners kept alive in the classroom.
12485-the-three-brides:
Charlotte M. Yonge's The Three Brides opens in family talk, as sons tease their mother about an influx of daughters-in-law. Each bridegroom, they say, married a strong likeness of his mother, giving her three mirrors, and each married solely for her benefit. The mother answers with humour, warning a younger son against cynicism.

Three brides, three marriages and one mother-in-law give the novel its comedy and its moral testing. Yonge, a High Church novelist, examines duty, character and household rule through courtship and early married life. The book offers a gentle, domestic Victorian tale, where likeness to a good mother becomes both joke and standard.
12491-twelve-types:
G. K. Chesterton's 1902 essays, reprinted with changes from the Daily News and the Speaker, offer portraits of writers and rulers. Charlotte Brontë, William Morris, Byron, Pope, Rostand, Charles II, Stevenson, Carlyle, Tolstoy, Savonarola and Sir Walter Scott appear in turn, each essay taking one figure as a type.

Chesterton opens on Brontë by attacking realistic biography, which reveals, he says, exactly the points a person never noticed about himself. That paradoxical, combative method runs through the book, defending imagination against mere fact. Twelve Types shows the young Chesterton already in full voice, witty, dogmatic and fond of turning a commonplace inside out.
12506-critiques-and-addresses:
Thomas Henry Huxley's 1873 volume gathers critiques and addresses on education, science and philosophy, following his earlier Lay Sermons. Huxley calls them the high-water mark of work since 1870, a period that carried him onto the London School Board, where he served through its critical first year.

Health then gave way, and he resigned from colleagues whose practical work he praised. The pieces that remain argue for science in schools, for clear reasoning and for public education as a civic duty. Huxley writes with combative clarity, impatient with cant. The volume shows a leading Victorian man of science turning, in mid-career, from the laboratory to the classroom and the public platform.
12515-selected-english-letters-xv-xix-ce:
Arranged by M. Duckitt and H. Wragg in 1913, this selection of English letters spans the fifteenth to nineteenth centuries. Sir Thomas More writes to Margaret Roper, with a coal from prison, and she replies. Roger Ascham writes to Lady Jane Grey, Bacon to Bodley, Browne to his sons, Milton to a Cambridge friend and to Philaras the blind poet.

Evelyn writes to Pepys in retirement at Wotton, Dorothy Browne to her daughter in London, Berkeley to Pepys. Later letters carry the story toward modern times. The anthology lets students hear English prose grow, from Tudor prison notes to Victorian ease, in short, personal pieces.
12564-california-sketches-new-series:
O. P. Fitzgerald's 1883 California Sketches, new series, with an introduction by Bishop George F. Pierce, returns to gold-rush California in verse and prose. A prefatory poem recalls bearded men in rude attire, nerves of steel, hearts of fire, and women few but fair and sweet. The author sees them again as he peers down the past and treads hills of youth.

Fitzgerald admits encores are usually anticlimaxes, yet friends' wishes and six editions of the former volume induced a second appearance. Sketches, often in a minor key, draw on real life, where all lives are tragedies in his phrase. The book offers a nostalgic, moral view of early California, told by a preacher who knew its camps.
12606-the-great-speeches-and-orations-of:
Edwin P. Whipple's 1923 selection, The Great Speeches and Orations of Daniel Webster, carries an essay on Webster as a master of English style. It does not seek to replace the standard six-volume Works edited by Edward Everett in 1851. Whipple aims instead to call attention anew to Webster's genius and character, as lawyer, statesman, diplomatist, patriot and citizen.

Prominent orations and speeches of universally acknowledged excellence are republished, to revive public interest in the great body of Webster's work. Selection could not do full justice to his powers, Whipple admits, since omitted speeches hold passages of equal force. The volume offers a readable door into Webster's oratory, and into American public speech at its most classical.
12693-the-principal-navigations-voyages-:
This edition of Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques and Discoveries retains sixteenth-century spelling, while silently expanding manuscript abbreviations. Vowels with macrons become vowel plus n or m, q with a mark becomes que in Latin, and y'e, y't and w't become the, that and with.

Footnotes follow modern spelling, mostly added by the editor, while Hakluyt's own notes are not always marked. Sidenotes, Hakluyt's own, are labelled and placed before their sentences, or at their symbols in poetry. The edition lets modern readers sail with Hakluyt's explorers, in old spelling made readable, through voyages that built England's sea story.
12732-a-collection-of-short-stories:
Edited by L. A. Pittenger of Indiana University in 1914, this classroom anthology gathers ten famous short stories with an introduction on the form. Bjørnson, Stockton, Maupassant, Kipling, Poe, Hawthorne, and Stevenson all appear, with notes on history, qualities, and composition of the short story. The editor disclaims any claim to the ten best ever written.

Inside, readers meet Poe's haunted Usher house, Hawthorne's birthmark and Ethan Brand, Maupassant's piece of string, and Kipling's man who was. The set teaches by example: plot, character, and twist in short compass. It still works as a compact introduction to classic story craft.
12758-library-of-the-world-s-best-myster:
Julian Hawthorne's Library of the World's Best Mystery and Detective Stories, in six volumes, New York 1907, offers one hundred and one tales by famous authors of East and West. Sections divide American, French, Italian, English, Scotch, German, Russian, Irish and Oriental tales, with modern magic among them.

Contents open with Maupassant. The Necklace, The Man with the Pale Eyes, An Uncomfortable Bed, Ghosts, Fear, The Confession and The Horla are illustrated through a mist in the depths of a looking-glass. Mille, Villiers de l'Isle Adam, Erckmann-Chatrian, Apuleius, Balzac and Pliny follow. The anthology remains a grand, old-fashioned treasury of mystery, from ancient tales to Maupassant's horror.
12771-famous-americans-of-recent-times:
James Parton's 1867 volume profiles eleven famous Americans, most first printed in the North American Review. Henry Clay, Daniel Webster, John C. Calhoun, and John Randolph lead, followed by Stephen Girard, James Gordon Bennett, Charles Goodyear, Henry Ward Beecher, Commodore Vanderbilt, Theodosia Burr, and John Jacob Astor. Each sketch mixes life story with judgment.

Calhoun's essay, for example, turns on taxation and majority rule, warning that one section may be crushed to enrich another. Parton writes as a near-contemporary, close enough to gossip and far enough to judge. The book gives a vivid gallery of the men and women who shaped antebellum America.
12798-by-rock-and-pool-on-an-austral-sho:
Louis Becke's 1901 story book gathers tales from the Pacific islands and the Australian shore. Traders, sailors, island kings, and fisher folk people the pages, with scenes of barter, storms, and small wars over goods and pride. The title story sets the tone: life lived close to reef, tide, and boat.

Later tales move to Samoa, Nukufetau, and trading posts where muskets, powder, and provisions change hands at sunset talks. Becke knew this world from his own years at sea, and his plain style keeps the focus on people and place. The book offers a lively, if dated, window into the colonial Pacific.
12814-philippine-folk-tales:
Mabel Cook Cole compiled Philippine Folk Tales in 1916 from Tinguian, Igorot, Mindanao, Moro, and Christianized tribal sources, with notes throughout. Tinguian tales of Aponibolinayen and the sun lead, followed by Igorot creation and flood stories, Mindanao tales of moon and stars, and Moro tales of Bantugan. Ilocano animal tales close the set.

A turtle and lizard tale shows the book's humour: the lizard cries praise for stolen ginger until the man chases him, while the turtle hides under a shell and calls Kook. Cole's notes give each tale its people and place. The book remains a valuable early collection of Philippine story lore.
1285-the-water-goats-and-other-troubles:
Ellis Parker Butler wrote "Pigs Is Pigs," and he gathers humorous stories of suburban troubles here. A landscape gardener proposes water goats for the lake, a man's pockets rebel, and a family meets its first burglar. The tales turn small disasters into comedy.

Butler writes with a light, American wit, and his humor is gentle and domestic. The book suits readers who like old-style magazine humor and the comedy of everyday plans gone wrong. Butler's gentle humor turns each small disaster into a laugh, and the stories still read lightly today.
12859-ensign-knightley-and-other-stories:
A. E. W. Mason's 1901 story book gathers tales of soldiers, sailors, and adventurers, led by Ensign Knightley. The title story opens at night in Tangier, where Surgeon Wyley of the Bonetta walks to the Main-Guard and finds officers gaming at bassette. Duty, honour, and desertion recur through the set.

Other stories include The Deserter, set with the Army of the Rhine near Colombey, plus tales of cowards, crossed gloves, shuttered houses, and a cruise of the Willing Mind. Mason writes with crisp, military detail and a taste for moral tests. The book suits readers who like short, sharp tales of service life.
1287-the-poems-of-goethe-translated-in-t:
Edgar Alfred Bowring translates Goethe's poems keeping the original metres, so English readers can hear something of Goethe's rhythms as well as his sense. Lyrics, ballads, and songs from across Goethe's long life appear. Bowring, a Victorian translator, kept Goethe's metres where other translators loosened them.

Bowring, a careful Victorian translator, aims for fidelity to form as well as meaning. The collection serves readers who want Goethe's verse in English without losing the shape that made it music in German. Goethe's lyrics, from youth to old age, show a poet who mastered every form he touched.
1289-three-ghost-stories:
Charles Dickens gathers three of his finest ghost tales in this volume. "The Haunted House" sets a party of friends for a night among spirits. "The Trial for Murder" puts a murdered man's ghost in the courtroom. "The Signal-Man" follows a railwayman's dread of a warning spectre.

Dickens writes the supernatural with a storyteller's warmth and a journalist's eye for detail, and his ghosts carry guilt, warning, and pity. The three tales show his range, from comedy to horror. The book suits readers who like ghost stories told by a master.
12903-symphonies-and-their-meaning-third:
Philip H. Goepp's 1913 third series on symphonies treats modern masters from Berlioz and Liszt to Franck, d'Indy, Debussy, and Dukas. Chapters cover Berlioz's Romeo and Juliet, Liszt's symphonic poems on Tasso and Mazeppa, Saint-Saëns's Danse Macabre, Franck's D minor symphony, and Debussy's Sea. Musical scores illustrate the text.

Goepp describes the music in vivid listener's language, from clarinets breaking in with sentimental tunes to strings and woodwind sharing a melody two notes at a time. His aim is to help concertgoers hear form and feeling. The book suits music lovers who want guidance without heavy theory.
12923-the-laird-s-luck-and-other-firesid:
A. T. Quiller-Couch gathered The Laird's Luck and Other Fireside Tales in 1901, opening with a Horse Guards order of 1836 for regimental histories. Major Reginald Sparkes, sifting records of the Moray Highlanders, finds sealed memoranda on Ensign D. M. J. Mackenzie, and the tales unfold from that archive. Fireside storytelling frames military history.

A Peninsular War tale shows Trant hoaxing the French at Almeida with scarlet-coated guides, sham bivouac fires, and a governor's sortie in the dark. Quiller-Couch writes with Cornish wit and soldierly detail. The book suits readers who like short historical tales told by the fire.
1293-sesame-and-lilies:
John Ruskin was the great Victorian critic, and he gives two lectures that became a classic of reading and womanhood. "Of Kings' Treasuries" urges young men to read good books well. "Of Queens' Gardens" praises women's moral power in the home. The lectures were first given to working men and girls in Manchester.

Ruskin writes with eloquence and moral fire, and his advice on reading, choosing books, and living nobly still quotes well. The book's views on women are dated now, but its plea for serious reading endures. It draws readers who like Victorian prose at its most earnest.
12932-four-max-carrados-detective-storie:
Ernest Bramah's Four Max Carrados Detective Stories, published in 1914, introduces a blind detective whose other senses solve crimes. The Coin of Dionysius, The Knight's Cross Signal Problem, The Tragedy at Brookbend Cottage, and The Last Exploit of Harry the Actor make up the set. A rainy night visit to coin dealer Baxter opens the first tale.

A signal-problem scene shows Carrados at work: neither Mead nor Hutchins tampered with the signal, but a young Bengali named Drishna did, though a green light was indeed shown. Carlyle stares in disbelief at the bold solution. The book offers clever, unusual detective fiction with a memorable hero.
12995-the-matador-of-the-five-towns-and-:
Arnold Bennett's Matador of the Five Towns and Other Stories, published in 1912, gathers tales from his Potteries world. Contents include The Matador, Mimi, The Supreme Illusion, The Letter and the Lie, The Glimpse, Jock-at-a-Venture, and Three Episodes in the Life of Mr. Cowlishaw, Dentist. Tragic and frolic moods alternate.

A tram-conductor passage shows Bennett's social eye: in steam-tram days a conductor kept individuality, but electric traction brought dozens of miles of line and men reduced to numbers. The hero, an active politician who accepts a snub from no man, embodies Five Towns pride. The book offers Bennett's short fiction at its most characteristic.
13022-my-book-of-indoor-games:
Clarence Squareman's My Book of Indoor Games, published in 1916 with photographs lent by the Chicago Park Commission, gathers parlour play for all ages. Acting proverbs, animal vegetable or mineral, blind man's buff, cat's cradle, charades, checkers, consequences, and a feather game fill the index, with full-page plates throughout. The publishers thank the Park Commission for the pictures.

A stool-of-repentance game shows the fun: a culprit guesses who charged him with vanity, and if right takes a seat while the accuser becomes culprit. The feather game has players blow a flossy feather to keep it off themselves. The book suits families and party planners seeking old-fashioned play.
13046-the-historic-thames:
Hilaire Belloc's Historic Thames, in the Wayfarer's Library, argues that England was built on the frame of her rivers, with the Thames as the chief line. The river was the main highway of southern England, looked east to the Continent, and was better served by tide than any rival channel. Belloc follows its valley from source to sea as the spine of government and wealth.

He traces Norman fortifications up the valley, Oxford's rise as stronghold above Wallingford, and the great abbeys that held Thames land. His list counts only the eight largest monastic houses on the banks, setting aside smaller parcels and off-river holdings. The book is history told through a river, clear, opinionated, and meant to be walked as well as read.
13085-a-diversity-of-creatures:
Rudyard Kipling's 1917 collection mixes stories and poems written across the years before and during the First World War. Its contents range from the future-state tale As Easy as ABC, where an air board rules the planet, to school stories, sea tales, and village satire. Songs and verses sit between the prose pieces, each tied to the story it follows.

Readers meet soldiers, schoolboys, sailors, and villagers, and hear Kipling's familiar themes of duty, craft, and loyalty tested by war. One school tale ends with a prefect's blunt lesson in fair play; another piece mocks a village that votes the earth flat. The collection's range is its point: Kipling tries many voices, from comic to grim, and lets each creature speak for itself.
13124-history-of-kershaw-s-brigade-with-:
D. Augustus Dickert's History of Kershaw's Brigade gives the full story of a South Carolina brigade in the Civil War, with rolls of companies, sketches, incidents, and anecdotes. The volume opens with portraits such as Lieutenant Colonel Axalla John Hoole of the Eighth South Carolina. Dickert writes as a veteran historian, proud of his men and careful with names.

Camp anecdotes sit beside hard record: a captain's biscuits baked at night and kept in his tent, a fine breakfast planned for guests, and company lists from Anderson to Lexington. Rolls name captains, surgeons, chaplains, and quartermasters, company by company. The book serves both as regimental history and as a roster for families tracing men who served.
1316-some-reminiscences:
Joseph Conrad looks back on his life in this memoir: his Polish boyhood, his years at sea, and his turn to writing in English, a tongue not his own. The book moves from his father's exile to the ships that taught him his craft, and to the friends who urged him to write.

Conrad writes the memoir in his rich, reflective prose, with the sea and Poland as twin poles of his life. The book is short and personal. It suits readers who know his novels and want the man behind them, in his own words.
13168-dick-in-the-everglades:
A. W. Dimock's 1909 Dick in the Everglades, with thirty-two half-tone photos by J. A. Dimock, follows a boy through Florida waters and wilds. Chapters run from the chums and life on a sponger to a waterspout, a hunt for a lost friend, the capture of a manatee, and ghosts and alligators. Later chapters bring Seminoles, a wildcat, a prairie fire, and a fight with a panther.

Dick greets the Everglades at sunrise, with cypress and palmetto dotted across the prairie, and paddles a slough toward open water. On a Seminole island he finds turtle shells, deer and alligator bones, and a papaw tree twelve feet high with fruit of five to ten pounds. The book is a boy's adventure with real Florida detail, photographed as well as told.
13177-chocolate-and-cocoa-recipes-and-ho:
Issued in 1909 as a compliment of Walter Baker and Company of Dorchester, this book joins two recipe sets: chocolate and cocoa by Miss Parloa, and home-made candy by Mrs. Janet McKenzie Hill. A bird's-eye view shows Baker's mills, with 350,000 square feet of floor space. The book is both a cookbook and an advertisement for Baker's chocolate.

Opening pages explain cocoa as a corruption of cacao, from the tree Theobroma cacao, and trace chocolate from Mexican use to Spanish tables. Recipes give chocolate blanc-mange with sea-moss farina, moulded sweets with vanilla and cream, and candies coated in Baker's Dot chocolate. The book is a tasty record of early twentieth-century home candy making.
13201-evelyn-innes:
George Moore's Evelyn Innes, first published in 1898 and reprinted in the Essex Library in 1929, follows a singer torn between art, love, and faith. Moore dedicates it to Arthur Symons and W. B. Yeats, writers with whom he felt sympathy. The novel opens on a thin winter day, when Evelyn's father repairs an Elizabethan virginal by candlelight in a long concert room.

Evelyn, in Paris with Owen, wears fine dresses, rides in a carriage, and wonders at races, while Owen fears her scruples may bore him. Later, alone in a brougham, she faces the truth that she deceived Owen and herself about marriage. Moore's novel is a study of a woman artist, her voice, her lovers, and her slow turn toward a harder choice.
13203-original-letters-and-biographic-ep:
J. Atwood Slater, a designer and Royal Academy medallist, gathered these original letters and biographic epitomes in London from Sprague and Company. The book reprints his letters to the Western Daily Press on painting, social science, and sport. Slater writes as an artist and citizen with strong views on public taste.

One letter judges Munkacsy's Ecce Homo as inspired, though not highly, and laborious but average in ability. Another protests the misuse of locomotive steam whistles in towns, injurious to all who must work or live nearby. A third reports Slater's swim round St. Michael's Mount and his attempt to swim to Newlyn. The volume is a scrapbook of an Edwardian artist's public life.
13206-a-short-history-of-monks-and-monas:
Alfred Wesley Wishart, once fellow in church history at Chicago, published this short history in 1900 at Trenton, New Jersey. Contents run from hermits of Egypt and pillar saints to Benedictines, western monks before Benedict, and the spread of monasticism in Europe. Wishart also treats disorders, opposition, and monasticism and women.

He notes that Saint Patrick likely founded Irish monasteries apart from Rome, and that Bangor dates to about 450. Later pages recall monks chanting in chapels and bending over parchment books bound in purple and gold, seeking love and devotion more than knowledge. Wishart writes with sympathy for cloister life, while noting its faults and its end under kings like Henry VIII.
13273-out-of-the-ashes:
Ethel Watts Mumford's 1913 Out of the Ashes opens with Marcus Gard at his library table. He contemplates bronze inkwells, half man and half beast, while his thoughts center on vast schemes of destruction and reconstruction. His room, quiet despite Fifth Avenue outside, has green Genoese velvet walls and a carved, coffered ceiling. Mumford writes a society mystery with a sharp edge.

Later, Dorothy teases Aunt Lydia about mauve or pink and flirting in conservatories, until the telephone rings and Dorothy takes the receiver. A detective weighs whether Mahr caused a disappearance, noting Gard was the last to see him, and a bitter feud no one guessed. The novel turns on robbery as a blind for anger, and papers with a deeper meaning.
13279-a-yankee-in-the-trenches:
R. Derby Holmes's 1918 Yankee in the Trenches, illustrated from photographs, tells how an American corporal served in the 22nd London Battalion of the Queen's Royal West Surrey Regiment. Holmes dedicates the book to Marion A. Puttee of Southall, Middlesex, who befriended him as a stranger in a strange land. The memoir is plain, funny, and grim by turns.

He describes splitting seven onions nine ways among hungry Tommies, each holding out for his onion, and bully beef in cans that gets tiresome after a while. Later, under bombardment, men smoke fag after fag, faces hard-set and pale, while Fritz saves his fire for the moment they go over the top. The book is a vivid record of trench life.
13307-scattergood-baines:
Clarence Budington Kelland's Scattergood Baines follows a shrewd Yankee storekeeper who invades Coldriver Valley and takes root there, as told in post-office legend. Chapters run from kicking up dust and dealing in matchmaking to borrowing a grandmother, investing in salvation, and cracking an obdurate nut. Kelland writes in broad, comic dialect.

Scattergood appears in the capital on voting day, and President Castle, pocketing pride for business reasons, sends up his card. Scattergood sees him for a minute, well able to lead the talk. Later, he calls politics a side issue to hardware, a tasty dessert after a meal of business. The novel is a tall tale of small-town cunning, kindly meant and full of laughs.
13312-the-light-that-lures:
Percy J. Brebner's 1911 Light That Lures was published in England as A Gentleman of Virginia. It opens with a boy on a green hummock above a bay, knees up, head in hands, dreaming of strenuous times. His visions mix past and future, and the prologue, Across the Waters of the Bay, sets a tale of Virginia, France, and revolution. Brebner writes historical romance with a steady hand.

Later, Pauline accuses Lucien of deceit over Mademoiselle St. Clair, saying lie and deceit are one, while Lucien laughs that he learned her jealousy in ten minutes. A deputy named Latour, armed with a pistol, admits Seth, a Virginian servant, and hears his tale. The novel turns on love, loyalty, and intrigue across the Atlantic in revolutionary days.
13321-in-the-footprints-of-the-padres:
Charles Warren Stoddard's In the Footprints of the Padres, new and enlarged edition of 1912, gathers sketches of old California and the Spanish missions. Contents move from crossing the Isthmus and a boy's outing to Mission Dolores, social San Francisco, the Vigilance Committee, and a bit of old China. Stoddard writes from memory, with a traveler's fond eye.

He recalls Mission Dolores as a detached settlement with a Spanish flavor, one street lined with low adobe houses under red curved tiles. At the most famous Franciscan mission, roof wanting and arches crumbling, he found the nave crowded with neglected graves, and fifteen governors of the territory mingling dust there unmarked. The book preserves a California already passing.
13354-the-boy-knight-a-tale-of-the-crusa:
G. A. Henty's Boy Knight, a tale of the Crusades, follows young Cuthbert from outlaws and a rescue at Wortham Hold to the lists, pirates, the Holy Land, and the accolade. Chapters run from the capture of Wortham Hold and preparations for crusade to the Princess Berengaria, a hermit's tale, and a fight of heroes. Henty writes boys' adventure with history woven in.

Cuthbert rides through a wood without incident, halts at the only inn between two towns, and eats a hearty meal while his horse is held outside. Later, low on money, he turns back from Milan, then the richest city in Europe after Rome, hoping to meet King Richard at the court of Saxony. The tale is a stirring crusade romance for young readers.
13392-a-woman-s-impression-of-the-philip:
Mary H. Fee writes about her years as an American schoolteacher in the Philippines, from the sea voyage through San Francisco and Honolulu to Manila and then to Capiz. She describes first days in the city, housekeeping, classrooms, feast days, weddings, funerals, and children's games, with chapters on typhoons, earthquakes, and war alarms.

Fee also weighs Filipino character, schooling, social ranks, politics, and currency reform, often in the assured voice of an outsider judging a new colony. Storms at sea, sickbeds, gold hunting, and the daily work of teaching give the book its texture. It remains a vivid, if one-sided, record of American colonial life in the islands.
13414-love-and-other-stories:
Constance Garnett's translation of Chekhov, volume thirteen of his tales, gathers Love and a score of other stories. The title piece opens at three in the morning, with a sleepless narrator bursting with a strange, happy feeling he cannot analyse and will not try to. Lights, A Story Without an End, Mari d'Elle, and A Living Chattel follow.

Later stories turn darker: a man weighs suicide and finds today's reason worthless tomorrow, a doctor raps the floor at nine years of lying, and a government clerk dies of embarrassment. Fat and Thin, A Joke, A Country Cottage, and A Blunder show Chekhov's range from farce to pity. The volume is a fine cross-section of his short fiction in English.
13437-best-russian-short-stories:
Thomas Seltzer gathers nineteen classic Russian short stories in one volume, from Pushkin's Queen of Spades and Gogol's Cloak to Turgenev, Dostoyevsky, Tolstoy, and Chekhov. Gorky, Andreyev, Kuprin, Garshin, Korolenko, and Sologub widen the range from peasant life to fantasy and revolt.

Chekhov appears three times, with The Darling, The Bet, and Vanka, the apprentice boy who writes home by stolen ink on Christmas Eve. Tolstoy's God Sees the Truth, But Waits and Saltykov's tale of a muzhik feeding two officials show the moral bite of the older masters. Seltzer's anthology remains a broad, readable door into Russian fiction at its strongest.
13494-fables-for-the-times:
H. W. Phillips retells old fables for modern readers in Fables for the Times, illustrated by T. R. Sullivant. The Baa-Sheep and the Lion, the Dog and the Meat, the Fox and the Grapes, the Fox and the Crow. The Ass in the Lion's Skin, and the Horse and the Oyster lead a table of contents full of beasts and fools.

A sheep under a lion's paw must think fast to survive, a merchant meets a venerable fool who will pay for horses whenever he finds use for one. A monkey works eighteen hours a day only to learn people are not always such asses as they seem. An ass who kicks a brass idol breaks his leg and proves nothing except that he is an ass. Each fable ends with a sharp, modern moral.
13553-the-tidal-wave-and-other-stories:
Ethel M. Dell's 1919 collection gathers The Tidal Wave with The Magic Circle, The Looker-On, The Second Fiddle, The Woman of His Dream, and The Return Game. Rufus the Red, sitting on his boat with nets spread to dry, opens the title story in still waters before passion and betrayal rise like a tide.

A woman who gave herself freely and absolutely finds her lover gone his careless way, leaving her in the dark to think of the Death Current as the summer sea murmurs. Durant, in pain yet friendly, talks with a woman in a big bib apron whose feet are no longer bare. Dell's stories run on love, surrender, and the sudden wave that changes a life.
13560-nancy-macintyre-a-tale-of-the-prai:
Lester Shepard Parker tells Nancy MacIntyre, a tale of the prairies, in verse and prose for 1910, dedicated to his wee daughter Rachel Ellen Parker. Contents run from Billy's revery and the quarrel through disappointment, decision, search, return, and Nancy's story, with a frontispiece of leave-taking in the night.

A trail leads westward where once the red man's wild domain lay, now a shallow wagon highway where coyotes pass at night and meadow larks sing at dawn. Zach's cave-like prairie home, smelling of fresh-dug loam, holds a cracked stove, willow rafters, and grease-smeared paper for a window. Parker writes prairie life as ballad, with lovers, quarrels, and a home dug from the earth.
13569-tractus-de-hermaphrodites-or-a-tre:
A London treatise of 1718, printed for E. Curll in Fleet Street, describes several sorts of hermaphrodites and how law regards them in marriage. It also treats intrigues of hermaphrodites and masculine females, outward marks to distinguish them, and the material cause and generation of hermaphrodites, unnatural births and monsters.

The preface notes that prefaces nowadays are excuses rather than lessons, promising a funny scene for light works. Tales follow of Theodora and Amaryllis, raised like the finest folk in Italy, and of Diana, turned out of doors by a parson after an intrigue with his wife. The book is an early modern work of law, medicine, and racy tales in one.
1359-a-guide-to-the-best-historical-nove:
Jonathan Nield guides readers to the best historical novels and tales, listing and judging fiction set in every period from ancient times to his own day. Each entry notes author, period, and merit. Nield, a librarian, compiled the guide to help readers choose historical fiction wisely.

Nield writes for librarians, teachers, and readers who want good stories grounded in history, not mere costume romance. The guide remains useful as a bibliography of Victorian and Edwardian historical fiction. His lists, arranged by period, let a reader find novels set in any age from Rome onward.
136-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems for children from a sickbed memory of play. A Child's Garden of Verses opens with a dedication to his nurse, Alison Cunningham, who read him stories and watched long nights. Short poems follow on swings, shadows, rain, and beds.

Verses like The Swing, My Shadow, and The Land of Counterpane turn small hours into adventure. The language stays simple, musical, and kind. This early Gutenberg edition carries a note pointing readers to an improved text. The poems still delight young listeners today. Parents and teachers still read these verses aloud to children at bedtime.
13605-the-principal-navigations-voyages-:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations gathers English voyages, traffics, and discoveries in sixteenth-century spelling, with manuscript abbreviations expanded and editor's footnotes added. Sidenotes, some summarising and some keyed by symbol, guide readers through narratives of exploration, trade, and colonisation.

Sailors debate whether the sun heats by nearness or by angle of reflection, noting snow on mountain tops nearer the sun than valleys below. At Mount Raleigh they find ravens, withies like low shrubs, and primrose-like flowers, on a coast of huge stone mountains without wood, grass, or earth. The volume remains the great English record of an age of sailing into unknown seas.
13666-a-study-of-fairy-tales:
Laura F. Kready studies fairy tales for teachers and parents in 1916, with an introduction by Henry Suzzallo, president of the University of Washington. Chapters cover the worth of fairy tales, principles of selection, telling, history, classes, and sources, with appendix, outline, and index. Kready dedicates the book to children who may receive any good because of it.

Chaucer's lines on Arthur's days, when the land was full of fairy and the elf queen danced in green meads, open the argument. Kready teaches storytellers to grasp plot whole, note detail, atmosphere, and character contrasts, and realise a tale from three points of view. Sources run from Asbjörnsen and Moe's Norwegian tales to Dasent, Winther's Danish tales, and Lagerlöf's classic for children.
13673-the-pacha-of-many-tales:
Captain Frederick Marryat built this novel on the pattern of the Arabian Nights. A pacha, eager to rival Haroun al-Rashid, demands a new story every night. Storytellers answer with tales of sailors, slaves, monks, merchants, and rogues. Huckaback the traveller contributes several voyages, each stranger than the last.

Marryat links the tales with scenes at court, where the pacha judges each offering. Humour, adventure, and moral turns alternate from tale to tale. The frame lets Marryat range across the Mediterranean and the East without a single plot. Readers get variety and pace, plus a satire of rulers who crave flattery. The book shows Marryat's gift for brisk sea yarns.
13685-the-children-s-hour-v-5-stories-fr:
Volume five of The Children's Hour, selected and arranged by Eva March Tappan, retells seven old favourites for young readers. Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress leads, with Christian's passage through the wicket gate, his fight with Apollyon, and his arrival at the Celestial City, followed by episodes from Robinson Crusoe and Don Quixote.

The retellings keep the famous scenes while trimming the harder language, so children meet Friday and the cannibal shore, Quixote's bruising adventures, and the Giant Despair. Tappan's aim was to put classic stories within a child's reach without losing their shape. The volume shows how early twentieth-century editors passed the old canon on to a new generation.
13726-apology-crito-and-phaedo-of-socrat:
Plato wrote these three dialogues about the trial and death of Socrates in Athens. Henry Cary translated them into plain English, with an introduction by Edward Brooks Jr. The Apology gives Socrates answering charges of impiety and corrupting the young. Crito shows him in prison, refusing an escape plan. Phaedo follows his last day and his talk about the soul.

Socrates argues that a good life matters more than a long one. He questions his judges, his friends, and his own fear of death. Friends urge him to flee, but he holds that breaking the law would betray his own teaching. The talks move from courtroom defence to quiet reasoning about justice and what survives death. They remain a clear entry point to Greek thought.
13753-dorothy-dainty-s-gay-times:
Amy Brooks wrote this 1908 story for young girls about Dorothy Dainty and her school friends. Dorothy starts at a new school, where Arabella and other girls test her temper and manners. Dialogues, entertainments, and small crises fill the term. Patricia returns, Flossie misbehaves, and promises get made and broken.

Brooks keeps the tone gentle and the lessons plain. Kindness, honesty, and good humour win out over vanity and teasing. Dorothy's charm lies in her care for others, not in fine clothes. Illustrations by the author match the text's light mood. The book belongs to a popular series of girls' school stories. It still reads as a mild, old-fashioned school tale.
13774-rosa-mundi-and-other-stories:
Ethel M. Dell gathered stories under the title Rosa Mundi and Other Stories. The lead tale follows Rosa through hope, a magician, a visitor, and a friend in need. Later stories include A Debt of Honour, The Deliverer, and tales of races, enemies, and penalties. Dell's heroines face danger, pride, and love with strong feeling.

One sequence builds toward a race, an enemy's terms, and a night of despair before hope returns. Another follows a promise of marriage, a ring of value, and a grievous honeymoon. Dell writes in her usual romantic, high-coloured style. The collection suits fans of early twentieth-century romance. It shows Dell's gift for suspense and sentiment.
13799-old-fires-and-profitable-ghosts-a-:
A. T. Quiller-Couch gathered fourteen stories in Old Fires and Profitable Ghosts. Cornwall provides most settings: sea towns, ships, old houses, and lonely roads. Ghosts appear, but Quiller-Couch cares more for memory, guilt, and human folly than for fright. Titles include Oceanus, The Seventh Man, and The Room of Mirrors.

Some tales follow sailors and smugglers, while others watch prisoners, lovers, and penitent sinners. A small free-trader, a lady of the ship, and John Emmet each carry a past that will not stay buried. Quiller-Couch writes with a storyteller's ease and a historian's eye. The collection suits readers who like ghost stories with character and place at their heart.
13814-the-development-of-the-feeling-for:
Alfred Biese, director of a gymnasium at Neuwied, wrote this history of feeling for nature, translated from German in 1905. It follows his earlier work on Greeks and Romans into the Middle Ages and modern times. Biese admits the task daunted many since Humboldt's sketches, yet the subject would not let him go. His study ranges across literature, art, and thought.

Biese shows how writers learned to call a rock bold, fire furious, and a summer evening idyllic. Autumn rain, sighing willows, and flocks at sunset mark stages of feeling. He traces nature from backdrop to living presence in poetry. The book suits students of literature and aesthetics. It remains a classic survey of its theme.
13833-blackfeet-indian-stories:
George Bird Grinnell collected these Blackfeet stories from Native storytellers on the northern plains. The tales cover buffalo hunts, piskuns where herds were driven over cliffs, and tricksters who outwit wives and rivals. One story tells of a man whose wives tried to kill him by digging a deep hole. Others follow war parties, visions, and camp life.

Grinnell kept Blackfeet names and words, marking long and short vowels in the text. His notes explain customs, places, and terms for outside readers. The stories preserve oral literature with respect and care. They show humour, danger, and moral judgment in equal measure. The book remains a valued source for Plains Indian tradition.
13836-wide-courses:
James Brendan Connolly gathered sea stories in Wide Courses, published in 1912. The tales follow wreckers, light-ships, pump-men, and captains off New England and beyond. One story seizes the Aurora Borealis, another follows a hose-pipe ghost. A diver's tale opens with a boy who wanted to dive while his father went down instead.

Connolly knew Gloucester fishing life from the inside and wrote its speech with force. Wrecks, rescues, and hard bargains drive the plots. Humour and danger alternate, with the sea always close. The collection belongs with his earlier books on fishermen and sailors. Readers of sea fiction will enjoy its pace, talk, and salt air.
13872-the-ten-pleasures-of-marriage-and-:
The Navarre Society privately reprinted this 1682 work in 1922, attributing it to Aphra Behn. The Ten Pleasures of Marriage, with its second part, The Confession of the New Married Couple, satirises married life in Restoration London. Twenty plates and two engraved titles were re-engraved for the edition. John Harvey wrote the introduction.

The text jokes about courtship, weddings, lawyers, wills, and deeds drawn contrary to intent. Its humour is frank and of its time, with bawdy detail throughout. A publisher's preface notes the romance of old books and the rarity of the original. The reprint lets modern readers see Restoration wit in facsimile form. It suits students of Behn, satire, and book history.
13880-triple-spies:
Roy J. Snell wrote Triple Spies in 1920 as a mystery story for boys. The plot moves from a den of disguises and a mysterious Russian to treachery out of the night. A narrow escape, a mob, and an Eskimo turned Japanese agent add thrills. Chicago, its river, and its underworld close the chase.

Johnny and his friends face a Jap girl in peril, a three-cornered battle, and a submarine at the river bottom. Disguises of grey squirrel skins, shaped like a middy blouse with a hood, show Snell's love of detail. The story mixes wartime spy fears with boy adventure. Its pace stays fast throughout. Young readers get mystery, action, and a touch of the exotic.
13896-jacques-bonneval-or-the-days-of-th:
The author of Mary Powell wrote Jacques Bonneval, a tale of Huguenot persecution in France. Chapters open at the Fair of Beaucaire and the Feast of St. Magdalen, then follow trial by fire and flight. Jacques tells of his uncle Chambrun, a passport, and persecution yet not forsaken. The closing chapter bids farewell to native land.

Dragonnades, when soldiers were quartered on Protestant families to force conversion, drive the plot. Jacques recalls saints' legends, including Marguerite and cherry trees blossoming monthly. Family loyalty and faith sustain him through danger. The novel belongs to Victorian historical fiction on religious liberty. It offers a sympathetic view of French Protestant suffering.
1390-the-jimmyjohn-boss-and-other-storie:
Owen Wister's Western collection opens with its title tale of a ranch boss known as the Jimmyjohn, and moves through stories of cowboys, Eastern visitors, and the hard code of the range. Wister, who knew Wyoming at first hand, writes of roundups, camp talk, and the loyalties that bind men in open country.

The preface warns against fashion in letters, and the stories practise what it preaches: plain scenes, dry humour, and feeling held in check. Together they form a portrait of a West already passing. The book is a fine companion to The Virginian for readers who love Wister's range.
1391-penelope-s-irish-experiences:
Published in 1901, this travel tale follows Penelope and her two friends, Salemina and Francesca, on a long tour of Ireland. They move province by province, from Leinster through Munster, Ulster, and Connaught to Royal Meath, stopping in Dublin, Kerry, Donegal, and many small towns on the way.

Each stop brings a new lodging, a new guide, and a fresh set of local characters, songs, and customs, all told in Penelope's bright, chatty voice. The book mixes road mishaps with history, humour, and affection for Irish life, and reads as a friendly record of three women travelling on their own.
13912-be-be-e-or-two-little-wooden-shoes:
Louisa de la Ramée, writing as Ouida, published Bébée, or Two Little Wooden Shoes, in 1896. Bébée, sixteen, springs from bed at daybreak in a Flemish village. A cock crows her age, a kid bleats, a thrush sings, and a calf lows beyond the fence. She delights in being a woman quite, no longer a child.

Bébée sits quiet on a truckle-bed, eyes on an apple bough and a singing chaffinch, while friends advise her. Ouida writes with romantic feeling for peasant life and nature. The novel follows Bébée through love, loss, and sacrifice. Its sentiment and scenery made it popular. Readers of Victorian romance will find it tender and vivid.
13929-ilka-on-the-hill-top-and-other-sto:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published Ilka on the Hill-Top and Other Stories in a second edition in 1891. Boyesen dedicates the volume to Dr. Egbert Guernsey, thanking him for services to his family. Contents include Ilka on the Hill-Top, Annunciata, Under the Glacier, and A Knight of Dannebrog. Mabel and I, a philosophical fairy tale, and How Mr. Storm Met His Destiny follow.

Boyesen, a Norwegian-American writer, sets tales in Norway and America with equal ease. A cold meal served on a flat rock, with the Dornauberg in view, shows his eye for place. His stories mix romance, philosophy, and folk feeling. The collection suits readers of late Victorian short fiction. It also shows immigrant literature finding an American audience.
13930-african-and-european-addresses:
Theodore Roosevelt put his talks from a 1910 trip in this book, with an opening note by Lawrence F. Abbott. Talks include peace and just rule in the Sudan at Khartum, law and order in Egypt at Cairo, and good citizenship at the Sorbonne in Paris. A talk on world peace in Norway and one on U.S. rule abroad follow.

Roosevelt speaks of home-rule men unafraid to talk in the open and take firm steps. Boutros Pasha, Egypt's Christian chief minister, appears in Abbott's tale of the trip. The talks show Roosevelt as a man of state, a traveller, and a moral voice. His Sorbonne talk on citizenship stays well known. The book suits those who read Roosevelt and the politics of his day.
1396-rienzi-the-last-of-the-roman-tribun:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's historical novel follows Cola di Rienzi, the fourteenth-century Roman who rose from the people to become tribune and dream of restoring Rome's ancient glory. Friend of Petrarch and hope of Italy, he rallies the commons against barons who have turned the city into a den of thieves.

Rienzi's triumph, his pride, and his fall drive a long tale of crowds, conspiracies, and doomed idealism. Lytton fills Rome with colour, from the Forum to the palace, and weighs liberty against power. It is a grand, old-fashioned romance of a hero who aimed too high and fell too far.
13973-whistler-stories:
Don C. Seitz collected Whistler Stories in 1913, anecdotes about James Abbott McNeill Whistler. Seitz, author of writings by and about Whistler, arranged the tales for Harper and Brothers. A sketch from life by Rajon, courtesy of Frederick Keppel, fronts the volume. The book went to Sheridan Ford, discoverer of the art world, in dedication.

Whistler appears as wit, painter, and combatant in salons and studios. One story finds him asking a sitter not to take a picture until he returns, so he can watch finishing touches. Seitz lets friends' memories build the portrait. The stories suit art lovers and readers of artistic gossip. They preserve Whistler's sharp tongue in short form.
13980-mappo-the-merry-monkey-his-many-ad:
Richard Barnum wrote Mappo, the Merry Monkey in 1915, part of the Kneetime Animal Stories. Mappo, a young monkey, faces tigers, hunters, and circus life in turn. His mother warns of a tiger hiding under bushes, and the jungle fills with chattering alarm. Illustrations by Harriet H. Tooker picture his scrapes.

Mappo throws an empty cocoa shell with all his might in one scene. He learns caution, friendship, and courage through many adventures. Barnum, author of Squinty the pig and Tum Tum the elephant, writes simply for young children. The book suits bedtime reading. It offers animal fun with a gentle moral.
13984-in-the-wrong-paradise-and-other-st:
Andrew Lang gathered stories in In the Wrong Paradise in 1886, dedicated to Rider Haggard. Lang praises Haggard's romances for making readers boys again. Contents include The End of Phaeacia, In the Wrong Paradise, A Cheap Nigger, and The Romance of the First Radical. A Duchess's Secret, The House of Strange Stories, and In Castle Perilous follow.

Lang writes with wit, learning, and a taste for the uncanny. A shipwrecked narrator drags himself to a wood, dries clothes in warm sun, and keeps the dress of his calling. My Friend the Beach-Comber and The Great Gladstone Myth close the variety. The collection suits readers of Victorian fantasy and satire. Lang's range, from folk tale to parody, shines throughout.
13985-v-v-s-eyes:
Henry Sydnor Harrison published V. V.'s Eyes in 1913, a novel of class, faith, and love in Virginia. V. Vivian, M.D., and John the Baptist open a tale of two houses with a great gulf between. Miss Carlisle Heth meets an unwelcome swain at the beach in October. A Blue Book speaks of houses set upon poles of the world, joined by no thread of destiny.

Harrison follows doctors, society women, and reformers through romance and argument. Vivian's eyes, keen and judging, give the book its title. The novel weighs duty against desire and tradition against change. Its long, rich prose suits readers of Edwardian social fiction. Harrison, author of Queed, writes with wit and depth.
14015-the-discovery-of-witches:
Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled witch-finder, published this pamphlet in 1647 to answer his critics in Norfolk. Framed as queries put to the assize judges, it defends his methods point by point. Hopkins argues that watching, searching for marks, and keeping a suspect from sleep can expose a witch's familiar spirits. He also sets limits, rejecting confessions forced by torture, flattery, or leading questions.

Short and combative, the tract opens a window onto the English witch panic. Hopkins claims scriptural warrant, quoting the command not to suffer a witch to live, and insists that magistrates examine suspects with care after rest. Modern readers will find the reasoning chilling and the detail grim. Historians still use the pamphlet as a firsthand record of how accusations were built, tested, and justified in court.
1405-the-collection-of-antiquities:
Balzac's provincial novel centres on the d'Esgrignon family, an old Norman house clinging to its name in a town that has moved on. The aged marquis lives among relics of a past age, while his son Victurnien, sent to Paris, runs up debts and falls in with fast company that threatens the family honour.

When a forged bill brings the son before the law, friends and kin must act fast to save him and the name. The book contrasts old loyalty with new money, and country pride with city waste. It is a sombre tale of a house fighting ruin in a changing France.
14062-miscellanies:
Oscar Wilde's Miscellanies, transcribed from the 1908 edition, gathers essays, reviews, and short pieces outside his plays and novels. Editor's dedication to Walter Ledger praises his marvellous Wilde library and invites correction of errors of taste or type. Ledger's future bibliography, the editor hopes, will judge the edition kindly. Proofreaders and printers share thanks.

Pieces range over art, literature, and society with Wilde's paradox and polish. A Medusa-like grey phantom turns all it looks upon to stone, while Love's wings are rent, in one vivid passage. Comparisons with Sistine Chapel painting show Wilde's high critical standard. The volume suits Wilde readers beyond the famous works. It reveals his range as critic and essayist.
14098-hieroglyphic-tales:
Printed at Strawberry Hill in 1785, this slim volume offers six short tales in mock-Egyptian dress. A preface apologizes, with tongue in cheek, for grave matter in a trifling age of politics and satire. Princes, fairies, and courtiers then parade through absurd adventures: a dead prince fêted by fashion, a deaf-and-dumb governor who talks on his fingers, and courtiers copying hieroglyphs onto chairs and coats.

Satire is the true subject. Walpole mocks court flattery, fashionable folly, and learned nonsense by pushing each to comic excess. Three-legged furniture, cadaverous rouge, and endless addresses to a corpse all skewer the manners of his day. Short, witty, and deliberately silly, the tales work best read aloud. They show the Gothic imagination at play, turning ancient Egypt into a mirror for eighteenth-century London vanity.
14099-true-irish-ghost-stories:
St John D. Seymour and Harry L. Neligan compiled these Irish ghost stories in 1914, dedicating them to three lively poltergeists. Letters pour in from clergy, neighbors, and anonymous writers, each offering a haunting heard or seen. A phantom coach drives up unheard by some and plainly heard by others, while a hay-cutter watches an avenue for four hundred yards and sees what he cannot explain.

Banshees, revenge spirits, and death warnings recur. One woman, the notes admit, hardly counts as a banshee at all, while another tale echoes Scott's Drummer of Cortachy, where a murdered man's spirit dogs a family before a death. Westropp's Kilchrist story adds a fine, lightsome night walk between trees and high hedges. Told straight and sourced by name, the book preserves folk belief as local people told it, without apology or mockery.
14103-prose-fancies-second-series:
Richard Le Gallienne published this second series of prose fancies in 1896, dedicating verses to Maggie Le Gallienne. Contents wander from a seventh-story heaven and spring by parcel post to a merry-go-round, the burial of Romeo and Juliet, variations on whitebait, and the answer of the rose. Gifts of poets, the opening poem jokes, are nothing but words, while kings give gold, silk, and white horses.

Wit sparkles in dialogue. A Sphinx asks why the rose has thorns, then answers herself: to keep off nightingales. The narrator protests that without nightingales nobody would praise the rose, and the Sphinx dismisses lilies with equal scorn. Later essays tease poets who dress like publishers and men of letters who school themselves into mediocrity. Light, literary, and fond of paradox, the book suits readers who enjoy fancy as a form of thought.
14145-if-winter-comes:
A. S. M. Hutchinson's 1921 bestseller follows Mark Sabre of Penny Green from his 1904 marriage through war years. Four parts take their names from women: Mabel, Nona, Effie, and Mabel, Effie, Nona together. Sabre, aged thirty-four in 1912, talks publishing schemes with rapt listeners, dreaming of a Tidborough Press to rival Oxford and Cambridge. Enthusiasm pours out, then stops, as sympathy overwhelms him.

War narrows the world. Old Mr. Fargus, unfit for exposure, becomes a special constable on night duty in the Garden Home, since he rests by day while younger men work. His wife and daughters insist he is stronger than anyone imagines. Sabre watches friends age, hopes fail, and winter settle on a village. Shelley supplies the title's question: if winter comes, can spring be far behind? Hope and endurance carry the novel to its close.
14167-the-red-redmaynes:
Eden Phillpotts's 1922 mystery opens with rumor and a problem stated. Mark Brendon, detective, investigates the Redmayne family, where Robert Redmayne is seen, heard, and then lost. Chapters promise a compact, death in a cave, a piece of wedding cake, and a ghost. Mr. Peter Ganns takes the helm, and methods, confession, and a legacy close the case.

Shell shock and mercy complicate the crime. Robert, the dead man's wife treats with angel kindness, though he first fears she came to give him up. Bendigo shrugs off questions about his niece, insisting she goes her own way and hides her father's will under a woman's shape. Ganns presses Brendon on Doria, who may have entered the business at Crow's Nest or at Foggintor, and may have cut Michael Pendean's throat himself. Dartmoor mystery, told at leisure, keeps its secrets until the final confession.
142-the-30-000-bequest-and-other-stories:
A promised fortune of thirty thousand dollars ruins a couple's judgment in the title tale. Mark Twain's $30,000 Bequest and Other Stories gathers the bequest novella with A Dog's Tale and Was It Heaven? or Hell? Short pieces on blues, telephones, and writing machines follow.

The Five Boons of Life, a burlesque biography, and a humane word from Satan show Twain's range. Satire, sentiment, and jokes about language mix through the volume. The stories date from Twain's later years, when his humor darkened. They reward readers who know his earlier work.
14203-varied-types:
G. K. Chesterton collected these Daily News and Speaker papers in 1905 as Varied Types, reprinting them with changes. Contents range across Charlotte Brontë, William Morris, Byron, Pope, Francis, and Rostand. Charles II, Stevenson, Carlyle, Tolstoy, Savonarola, Scott, Bret Harte, Alfred the Great, Maeterlinck, Ruskin, Queen Victoria, the German Emperor, Tennyson, and Elizabeth Barrett Browning follow.

Paradox powers the portraits. Chesterton defends the Restoration as a human revolt against Puritan strain, yet calls it a fall and not an ascent, a recoil and not an advance. Puritanism bent the bow too far, he argues, but collapse stays collapse. Scott receives similar double judgment. His heroines speak stiffly, like Dr. Johnson, yet his books keep a breezy bachelorhood of clean adventure that later fiction lost. Readers meet Chesterton at his most quotable, turning each life into an argument about art, faith, and England.
14206-i-saw-three-ships-and-other-winter:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, signing as Q, gathered winter tales of the west country in I Saw Three Ships. Christmas Eve feasts of cake, cider, and crowding open the title story, where young Zeb fetches a stranger ashore, dances in his shoes, and faces a siege laid to Ruby. Zeb sells his soul and wins it back, while three ships mark the tale's turns.

Ghosts and mirrors widen the set. A haunted dragoon rides through one story, a blue pantomime unrolls at the Indian Queens inn, and two householders settle old scores. In the pantomime, a narrator dines at a place he swears he never visited, yet knows every furlong of the road to Huel Tor. Later, a woman's hands pass round a man's neck where a rope once passed round her own. Cornish speech, winter dark, and sly humor make the collection a fireside classic.
14220-the-tale-of-the-flopsy-bunnies:
Beatrix Potter's 1909 tale follows Benjamin Bunny, grown up and married to his cousin Flopsy. Their large family, cheerful and improvident, borrows cabbages from Peter Rabbit's nursery garden. One day the little rabbits eat too much lettuce in Mr. McGregor's garden and fall into a deep, soporific sleep among the lawn mowings.

Danger arrives with a sack. Mr. McGregor empties grass over the sleepers, spots brown ear tips, and counts six little rabbits for his bag. A friendly mouse wakes Benjamin, and the Flopsy Bunnies creep to the window to listen, then follow at a safe distance. Potter's pictures and dry wit carry the rescue, and the moral stays light: greed makes rabbits sleepy, and family must watch while they dream.
14241-more-english-fairy-tales:
Joseph Jacobs gathered these English folk tales, with pictures by John D. Batten, for young readers and for adults who love old stories. The tales come from oral lore and local lore, retold in plain, lively prose. Giants, clever lads, magic beasts, and sly folk crowd the pages. The book opens with a playful key-and-door game that invites the reader to step inside.

Among the tales are the Pied Piper of Franchville, Tom Hickathrift, the Black Bull of Norroway, and Tattercoats. One story tells of Jack, kept seven years as a giant's mill servant, who longs for a day at the fair. Another turns on a child sent back and forth to coax a cow to stand still for milk. The tales mix fear, jokes, and fair play. They keep alive the plots, voices, and tricks of English folk lore.
14253-flames:
Robert Hichens wrote Flames in 1897, a London novel of charm, sin, and power. Its hero is Valentine Cresswell, a young man ruled more by taste than by faith. He drifts past the sins of his age without joining any camp. Around him move Julian and Cuckoo, called Miss Bright, whose moods swing from shy fear to bold impudence. The novel watches how a fine soul can slide toward dark company.

Cuckoo's scenes turn on a broken hand glass, smashed on a cold night as frost bites. She laughs at the shards, then plants her bare feet in them, as if to bleed outside as she has bled within. A doctor climbs her step as she stands listening, blood on the carpet. The novel blends London rooms with low lodgings, and dread with occult hints. Its force lies in mood and in the pull of one will upon another.
14256-the-bell-in-the-fog-and-other-stor:
Gertrude Atherton wrote these ten stories in 1905, and gave the book to Henry James. The title tale follows an American author who buys an old English hall to live among ghosts of an ancient line. He loves the walls for their age, dignity, and aloof pride. Other tales turn on counts, snobs, and women caught between gold and rank. Atherton writes with a sharp eye for manners and for the price of social climb.

In one tale a doctor hears the cry of a lost soul in the night and fears his mind is going. He must choose whether to let a criminal die and save four people, or let her live and ruin their lives. Another tale follows Lady Carnath, a widow courted by Butler Hedworth, and Edith Ingoldsby, who bought her earl at a price. The stories mix dread with talk of money, marriage, and rank.
1429-the-garden-party-and-other-stories:
Katherine Mansfield's famous collection gathers fifteen stories of New Zealand and London life, opening with At the Bay and The Garden-Party. In the title tale, a girl preparing a garden party glimpses death in a workman's cottage nearby, and her bright day takes on a sudden, sober edge.

Other stories follow daughters after a father's death, a singing lesson, a first ball, and a woman alone in a hotel room. Mansfield's style is brief, sharp, and full of telling detail. The book is a landmark of the modern short story, praised for its light touch and deep feeling.
14302-principles-of-home-decoration-with:
Candace Wheeler wrote this 1903 guide to home decoration, with practical examples from real houses. A frontispiece shows a dining room at Pennyroyal, in Mrs. Boudinot Keith's cottage at Onteora. Wheeler treats decoration as an art, shaped by character, color, and use. She writes on builders' houses, kitchens, walls, floors, and light. The book speaks to women who make homes, and to builders who shape them.

Color rules fill the book: south rooms take cool blues, water greens, and silvery tones against strong sun. Wheeler tells of a painter whose red sunset canvas grew warm to the touch in the sun, while grey and blue pictures stayed cool. She seeks a missing textile, cheap, strong, soft, and true in color, such as old indigo denim once was. The book joins science, taste, and thrift. It still helps readers see why a room feels warm or cold.
14332-cleek-the-man-of-the-forty-faces:
Thomas W. Hanshew wrote this 1912 detective novel about Hamilton Cleek, a master of disguise. Cleek takes on forty faces, and the law knows him as a man who can seem to be anyone. The book opens on Blackfriars Bridge, where a constable named Collins meets a veiled woman in a maze of carts. From that meeting springs a chain of cases that test Cleek's wits. London streets and hotels form the stage.

Cleek poses as a servant to the Baron de Carjorac and watches a woman who seems to look for him. Later he chases a case that touches the Persian police and a blue belt said to come from a dead man. Cleek doubts the tale, since a dead man can send nothing. The novel mixes disguise, bluff, and watch on faces and rooms. Its fun lies in seeing how far a changed face can carry a man.
14347-plays-by-august-strindberg-second-:
Edwin Björkman translated this second series of August Strindberg's plays, in an authorized edition. It holds There Are Crimes and Crimes, Miss Julia, The Stronger, Creditors, and Pariah. Björkman adds introductions and defends his renderings of Swedish speech. In Miss Julia, he turns Jean's thou into a plain Miss Julia exchange for English ears. The book serves readers and players of modern drama.

Björkman argues that Strindberg's figures step from page to life as familiar human beings. His realism mixes with idealism, and each figure is doctored to drive home one truth. Strindberg sought pure cultures of single qualities, set in fitting mental groups. A miser drawn like Molière's Harpagon would be too crude for his art, Björkman notes. The plays join fierce feeling with sharp, modern craft.
14358-a-little-book-of-filipino-riddles:
Frederick Starr gathered this small 1909 collection from speakers of Ilocano, Tagalog, Pangasinan, and other Philippine languages. Each riddle appears in its original language, with an English rendering and a brief answer.

The riddles name the moon, a hammock, a coconut, a bamboo shoot, and other common things through vivid comparison and wordplay. Starr's short introduction notes set phrases, such as appeals to God, that open many items. The book preserves folk wit from Luzon and nearby islands, and it offers a window on daily life, farming, and household objects. Starr worked in the Philippines as an anthropologist.
14411-the-children-s-six-minutes:
Bruce S. Wright's 1922 book offers short devotions for children, each meant to take about six minutes. A contents list moves from New Year and snow through kindness, Easter, and harvest themes.

Each piece pairs a brief story or reflection with a Bible verse and a memory hymn, touching on honesty, work, worship, and care for others. One story recalls a peasant boy who learned to see God in a sunset. The book served Sunday schools and family prayers, and its simple language keeps it accessible to young listeners today. Parents could read one piece aloud each morning.
14416-stories-of-the-border-marches:
John Lang and Jean Lang wrote these stories of the Border marches in 1916, tales of the Scots-English frontier. The book ranges from the White Lady of Blenkinsopp to Kinmont Willie, the Laidley Worm, and vampires of Berwick and Melrose. Heroes, witches, packmen, and soldiers crowd its pages. The Langs draw on ballads, chronicles, and local lore. The tales are short, vivid, and made for fireside reading.

One tale recalls witch hunts at their height, when torture forced confessions and escape was rare. As late as 1722, a Sutherland woman was burned for turning her daughter into a pony and riding her all night. A second tale sets a vampire hunt by the Tweed, where a monk faces the Hundeprest with an axe at midnight. The monster flees, and the friar chases it to its grave. The book keeps the Border's grim, ghostly voice.
14420-the-exemplary-novels-of-cervantes:
Miguel de Cervantes wrote these short tales in Spanish in the early 1600s, and Walter K. Kelly rendered them into English for this 1881 London edition. Cervantes called them exemplary because each story was meant to instruct while it entertained.

Lovers, soldiers, rogues, servants, and gypsies cross Spain and Italy in plots built on disguise, mistaken identity, jealousy, and sudden reversals. Some tales end in marriage and pardon, others in sharp comic exposure. Together they show Cervantes working in miniature, with the same wit and humane irony found in his longer fiction. Kelly's plain English keeps the Spanish flavor close.
14449-dutch-courage-and-other-stories:
Jack London's collection gathers sea and adventure tales written in his early years, issued in New York in 1924 after his death. The table of contents runs from the title story to Yeddo Bay and the Sacramento.

Young sailors face typhoons off Japan, poachers, wreckers, and hard captains, while boys on the California coast learn courage the rough way. London's prose is vigorous and direct, with the sea as both workplace and test. The stories show the young writer finding the voice that later carried The Call of the Wild and The Sea-Wolf.
1445-aeroplanes:
J. S. Zerbe writes an early popular guide to aeroplanes, explaining how flying machines work and what they might do. Written when flight was still new, the book speaks to readers curious about wings, engines, and air. Zerbe wrote for boys and beginners, when aeroplanes were still a novelty at fairs.

Zerbe describes types of machines, their parts, and the problems of lift and control, in plain language for beginners. The volume captures the excitement of the first age of flight, before aeroplanes became common. His guide, published before the First World War, shows flight as sport, not yet as weapon.
14451-african-camp-fires:
Stewart Edward White's travel narrative follows a safari from the Red Sea through Mombasa and Nairobi into Masailand and the Serengeti, in the early days of British East Africa. White wrote as a popular American outdoorsman.

Chapters cover the voyage out, the Shamba Hills, lion hunts on the Kapiti plains, the Tsavo River, and the lost safari, with camp talk, porters, and big game throughout. The book celebrates hunting and open country in the style of its era, and it also records Nairobi as a raw new town. Modern readers will note its colonial attitudes alongside its vivid landscape writing.
14458-a-history-of-trade-unionism-in-the:
Selig Perlman, assistant professor of economics at Wisconsin, wrote this 1922 history in Richard T. Ely's social science series, drawing on the Wisconsin school's labor research under John R. Commons. The book carries the story from colonial beginnings to the 1920s.

Perlman traces the struggle for survival, the Knights of Labor's rise and fall after 1887, and the wage-conscious city unions that followed, with strikes, politics, and employer opposition throughout. His analysis stresses job consciousness over revolutionary aims. The history remains a foundational text for American labor studies, scholarly and readable at once.
14466-south-african-memories-social-warl:
Lady Sarah Wilson drew this 1909 memoir from diaries written at the time. It covers her South African years, from a first voyage to Cape Town through the Jameson Raid, Kimberley, and the Boer War. She dedicated it to her sister, Countess Howe.

Wilson describes Johannesburg and Pretoria in 1896, Mafeking under siege, risky drives past Boer patrols with false passports, and the social world of officers, nurses, and sportsmen. Her voice is frank, adventurous, and partisan. The book remains a lively woman's account of war and society at the edge of empire.
14480-twenty-six-and-one-and-other-stori:
Maxim Gorky, the Russian tramp turned writer, reached English readers in this 1902 collection from the Vagabond Series, translated from the Russian. An introduction presents him as a startling new voice after Tolstoy.

The title story follows twenty-six bakery workers and the girl they adore, while other tales pair a thief with a boy fisherman and trace outcasts, wanderers, and laborers on the Volga. Gorky writes with sympathy for the downtrodden and scorn for comfortable pity. The stories made his name abroad, and they still carry his rough, humane energy.
14494-scottish-sketches:
Amelia E. Barr's collection of Scottish stories, first copyrighted in 1883 and issued by Dodd, Mead in 1898, gathers six tales of Lowland and Highland life. The contents list runs from Crawford's money troubles to Lile Davie's fate.

Alexander Crawford counts his bank ledger with miserly pride, James Blackie nurses revenge, and other characters face confession, temptation, and a single wrong step. Barr writes in Scots dialect and moral earnestness, with village kirk and market town as backdrop. The stories are sentimental but vivid, and they show a popular novelist's affection for Scotland.
14542-the-lonesome-trail-and-other-stori:
B. M. Bower's 1904 collection gathers western stories headed by the title tale, in which a frightened man, like a frightened horse, shies at the same place until led firmly past it. Grosset and Dunlap published the volume.

Other stories bring first aid to Cupid, a cook falling ill, and a lamb. The spirit of the range and the unheavenly twins follow, with Happy Jack shy at dances and a schoolma'am leading him to talk. Bower's humor is warm and her range talk authentic. The book is a pleasant early sample of her Montana fiction.
14562-the-land-war-in-ireland-a-history-:
James Godkin, late Irish correspondent of The Times, published The Land War in Ireland in London in 1870, calling it a history for the times. Godkin had written on Ireland and her churches.

The preface compares Ireland to a sick patient under endless commissions, then traces the rule of the O'Neills, land tenure, and the long struggle over rents and eviction. Godkin weighs remedies proposed for a morbid condition. The book is a contemporary history of the land question, written before the Land League, and useful for the debate that led to it.
14593-norse-tales-and-sketches:
Alexander L. Kielland's Norse tales and sketches, translated by R. L. Cassie and published in London in 1896, gather stories from Norway and Paris. The contents run from A Siesta to Autumn.

A merry party at dessert in the Rue Castiglione meets Senhor José Francisco de Silvis, a rich Brazilian Portuguese notorious for incredible acquaintances. Other tales follow a student at variance with his father, a monkey, a sea tale, and a dinner. Kielland writes with irony about wealth, pride, and family. The collection is a fine introduction to a leading Norwegian realist.
14610-miss-elliot-s-girls-stories-of-bea:
Mrs. Mary Spring Corning's 1886 children's book gathers stories of beasts, birds, and butterflies told among Miss Elliot's girls. The Congregational Sunday-School Society first published it, and Burt reissued it.

Sammy Ray hunts a great green tobacco worm for Miss Ruth, a patchwork quilt society meets, and Furry-Purry the cat claims a master by laying a dead mole at his feet. The tales teach kindness to animals and neighbors. Corning writes gently for young readers, with country parsonage life as her backdrop. Her stories first served Sunday-school libraries and homes.
14634-sketches-and-studies-in-italy-and-:
John Addington Symonds, author of Renaissance in Italy, gathered this second series of sketches and studies in Italy and Greece, first published in 1898 and reprinted by John Murray in 1914. The contents run from Ravenna to the Orfeo of Poliziano.

Symonds wanders through Rimini, Umbria, Urbino, Parma, Canossa, and Florence, mixing travel description with literary history. He treats Vittoria Accoramboni, the Medici, Tuscan popular song, and Renaissance poetry with learned enthusiasm. The book is a classic of Victorian travel writing, rich in art, place, and allusion. Symonds's essays blend scholarship with personal travel notes.
1467-some-christmas-stories:
Charles Dickens's short Christmas stories, gathered from the 1911 Chapman and Hall edition, open with A Christmas Tree, a nostalgic look at childhood Christmases and the toys that peopled them. What Christmas Is as We Grow Older follows, with the Poor Relation's Story, the Child's Story, and the Schoolboy's Story close behind.

Each piece is brief and warm, mixing humour with a touch of melancholy about time passing. Nobody's Story closes the set with a parable of humble labour. The book is a gentle companion to A Christmas Carol for readers who love Dickens in miniature.
14678-the-war-of-the-wenuses:
C. L. Graves and E. V. Lucas wrote this 1898 parody of H. G. Wells's War of the Worlds, translated, in jest, from the Artesian of H. G. Pozzuoli. The book is dedicated to Wells as an outrage on a fascinating romance.

The Wenuses fall from the sky, London falls under them, and the narrator meets newspaper boys, Life Guards razed by a devastating glance, and his wife as commander-in-chief marshalling forces. The parody keeps Wells's shape while turning Martians into women. It is a witty period joke, best enjoyed beside the original it teases.
14699-shakespeare-study-programs-the-com:
Charlotte Porter and Helen A. Clarke wrote Shakespeare Study Programs: The Comedies, first printed in Poet Lore and reissued in book form by Badger in Boston. The authors edited the Pembroke and First Folio Shakespeares.

Each program gives act summaries and queries for discussion. In Love's Labour's Lost, readers ask whether Costard and Jaquenetta are the only happy lovers and whether the king shows youth and inexperience. The references follow Porter's First Folio edition. The book served clubs and classrooms, and it remains a useful guide to studying the comedies together.
14711-the-boy-allies-under-the-sea-or-th:
Ensign Robert L. Drake's 1916 boys' adventure sends Frank Chadwick and Jack Templeton to sea against German submarines around the British Isles. Frank wants to know how long England will put up with sinkings, including a big liner torpedoed off Ireland the day before.

Jack has stranger news: in thirty days, about a hundred German submarines have vanished, sunk or captured, and no one knows how. The Boy Allies must find the secret weapon or method behind those losses, and the hunt takes them under the sea into patrol, pursuit and danger. Fast dialogue and wartime daring carry a story written while the submarine war was still news.
14740-the-princess-passes:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson's 1905 romance follows a motor car across the Riviera, where a woman disposes, a Mercedes comes to the rescue and a lesson is learned. Pots, kettles, a search for a mule and wings of the wind keep the journey comic and brisk.

At last a mystery takes shape, a brat appears, acquaintance is scraped, and a shadow of night falls before the princess herself arrives. Afternoon calls, the path of the moon and a contessa from the dark deepen the plot. Motor travel, fashionable society and a love story run together, in a novel written when the car itself was still a novelty and a promise.
14776-the-arabian-art-of-taming-and-trai:
T. Gilbert's 1856 manual teaches the Arabian art of taming and training wild and vicious horses, printed in Cincinnati. Its introduction argues that horse domestication was man's greatest animal achievement, won not in a day but by gradual discovery and experiment.

Man first subdued ox, ass and camel, easier to catch and tame, and only later mastered the fleet, elegant horse, whose nature he long misunderstood. Gilbert builds on that claim: patience, knowledge of temper and steady handling beat force. The book suits readers of horse history and old training methods, and it shows a mid-century American faith in Arabian horsemanship as a model.
14783-the-twelve-tables:
P. R. Coleman-Norton prefaces, arranges, translates and annotates the Twelve Tables, the early Roman code that set out law for citizens of the Republic. Short, blunt rules govern summons to court, sureties, settlements and the conduct of trials.

Later tables extend the same plain logic to property, debt, family and wrongs. A defendant who will not come may be seized, a sick or aged man may claim a conveyance, and a freeholder must find a freeholder as surety. Notes explain terms such as asses and vindex.
