The volume gives students a direct route into Roman law at its root: terse, practical and meant to be known by all.
14797-the-tale-of-timmy-tiptoes:
Beatrix Potter's 1911 tale follows Timmy Tiptoes, a little fat comfortable grey squirrel with a nest thatched with leaves at the top of a tall tree, and a squirrel wife called Goody. Timmy sits out enjoying the breeze, whisking his tail and chuckling that the nuts are ripe.

He and Goody must lay up a store for winter and spring, for they will wake thinner when spring brings little to eat. Goody pushes moss under the thatch, making the nest snug for a long sleep. When they reach the nut thicket, other squirrels are already there. Potter's tale, for many unknown little friends including Monica, is a cosy lesson in prudence and sharing.
14812-a-midsummer-drive-through-the-pyre:
Edwin Asa Dix, former fellow in history at Princeton, drives through the Pyrenees in midsummer and writes a travel book illustrated from the route. He wonders why Americans visiting Europe in 1860 thought almost only of Switzerland and Italy, and sets out to show a grander, less crowded range.

Difficult bits on the Route Thermale, mountain passes, spas, villages and the border country between France and Spain fill seventeen chapters. Dix writes as a historian as well as a traveller, noting customs, legends and the look of the land. Published by Putnam in 1890, the book still tempts readers to take the slower road through the Pyrenees.
14817-the-white-wolf-and-other-fireside-:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, gathers fireside tales that range from Greenland to Cornwall and the sea. The miracle of the white wolf opens in early summer 1358, when a merchant ship from Norway reaches Brattahlid in Greenland with provisions for Christian settlements.

Sindbad on Burrator and Victor follow, with the capture of the Burgomeister van der Werf and King of Prussia. The man who could have told, cellars, a haunted yacht, Parson Jack's fortune and a burglary club come next. Talking ships, keepers of the lamp, two boys and a senior fellow close the set. Quiller-Couch tells each tale with a storyteller's pace, meant for reading aloud by the fire.
14823-a-student-in-arms-second-series:
Donald Hankey's second series of wartime essays, published in 1917 with an introduction by J. St. Loe Strachey, speaks from inside the army. A potentate, the bad side of military service and the good side of militarism open a set of reflections that refuse easy praise or blame.

A month's reflections, romance, imaginary conversations and the fear of death in war follow, with a letter to an army chaplain, advice not to worry, and a passing in June 1915. Hankey writes as a student turned soldier, thoughtful about comrades, officers and faith. The essays remain a humane record of how one educated volunteer tried to make sense of service, sacrifice and fear.
14855-a-few-short-sketches:
Douglass Sherley prints a few short sketches in Louisville in 1893, copyrighted in 1892, with unusual spellings kept as in the original. Those Russian Violets opens at a brilliant reception at Mrs. Adrian Colburn's house, honouring an attractive young woman from the East, from five to seven.

The narrator goes late and leaves early. He still makes an engagement with Miss Caddington, a debutante educated abroad, for a Bolton ball that night. She has not lost love of country or naturalness of manner. Through a short, fiercely gay season from October to Christmas she has made many friends and found two or three lovers hard to handle. Sherley's sketches are society vignettes, light and local.
14857-the-story-of-versailles:
Francis Loring Payne's 1919 history tells the story of Versailles from its beginning to its twilight as a shrine of royal memories. Louis the Fourteenth, builder of Versailles, stands on the frontispiece, and the making of his luxurious chateau and parkland opens the narrative.

Luxury, gardens, fountains and the Grand Trianon follow, with a day with the Sun King, golden days and red letter nights, and the women of Versailles. The Versailles of Louis the Fifteenth and the twilight of Bourbon kings close the arc. Payne writes for general readers who want palaces, courts and politics in one readable volume, not a dry architectural survey.
14877-the-tale-of-ginger-and-pickles:
Beatrix Potter's 1909 tale tells of a village shop called Ginger and Pickles, just the right size for dolls. Lucinda and Jane Doll-cook buy groceries there, the counter stands at a convenient height for rabbits, and the shop sells red spotty pocket handkerchiefs at a penny three farthings.

Sugar, snuff and galoshes join the stock, and all the animal customers come and go. Dedicated with kind regards to old Mr. John Taylor, who thinks he might pass as a dormouse after three years in bed without a grumble, the book is gentle comedy about trade, credit and village life. Potter's pictures make the small shop feel busy, familiar and very much alive.
14945-cato-maior-de-senectute-with-intro:
James S. Reid's edition of Cicero's Cato Maior de Senectute, on old age, revised for American students by Francis W. Kelsey of Michigan in 1882, presents Latin text with introduction and notes. Reid, of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, prepared the work for the Syndics of the University Press three years earlier.

His thorough scholarship, especially in explaining Latinity, won a cordial reception and a permanent place among English scholars. Kelsey's American edition, fully authorised by Reid, adapts that work for students in the United States. The volume pairs Cicero's dialogue on growing old with the notes a reader needs to follow its Latin and its philosophy.
14958-mother-west-wind-why-stories:
Thornton W. Burgess, author of Old Mother West Wind and the Bedtime Story-Books, explains animal traits in Mother West Wind Why Stories, illustrated in colour by Harrison Cady and published in Boston in 1920. Each chapter answers a child's why with a tale.

Why striped chipmunk is proud of his stripes, why Peter Rabbit cannot fold his hands, why Unc' Billy Possum plays dead and why Reddy Fox wears red open the set. Jimmy Skunk, Sammy Jay, Jerry Muskrat, Old Man Coyote, Miner the Mole, Mr. Snake, Bobby Coon, the buzzard family, Buster Bear, Flitter the Bat and Spotty the Turtle follow. The stories teach habits gently, with humour.
14960-the-silent-places:
Stewart Edward White's 1904 novel, illustrated by Philip R. Goodwin and dedicated to his mother, takes readers into silent northern places where woodsmen raise rifles together. A child utters a sharp cry of fright, Dick calls a girl pretty enough to kiss, and a brother tells his little sister he goes on a long journey.

Dick snatches aside a wigwam opening, a hound sniffs feather snow, and a voice croaks stop across the stillness. White writes wilderness adventure with a naturalist's eye and a storyteller's pace. The silent places are both landscape and state of mind: vast, beautiful and indifferent to the men who cross them.
14972-sketches-and-studies-in-italy-and-:
John Addington Symonds, author of Renaissance in Italy and Studies of the Greek Poets, gathers sketches and studies in Italy and Greece in a first series, new edition from Murray in 1914. A prefatory note explains that in preparing this edition of three volumes of travels, nothing changed except the order of essays.

For travellers' convenience a topographical arrangement was adopted, and a new title covers contents of all three volumes. Italian byways, Greek sites, art, history and landscape follow in place order. Symonds writes as a scholar traveller, learned and lyrical, and the volume still serves readers who want Italy and Greece seen through literature, art and a lifetime of walking.
14975-southern-horrors-lynch-law-in-all-:
Ida B. Wells-Barnett's 1892 pamphlet Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases, reprinted in 1893 and 1894, exposes lynching in the American South with evidence and anger. Dedicated to Afro-American women of New York and Brooklyn, whose effort at Lyric Hall on 5 October 1892 made publication possible, it opens with a letter from Frederick Douglass.

Wells-Barnett, writing from New York in October 1892, argues that lynching was not punishment for crime but terror used to control Black people and seize property and power. Acting on advice, leading citizens met in the Cotton Exchange and took steps that the pamphlet records. The work remains a founding text of American anti-lynching journalism.
14978-a-village-ophelia-and-other-storie:
Anne Reeve Aldrich's 1899 stories, published by Dillingham in New York, open with A Village Ophelia. The title tale is set at Long Island's eastern tip, where a pair of rural routes runs side by side for roughly thirty miles between Riverhead and Greenport. The northern route hugs the Sound, far from town life, passing isolated farmhouses spaced well apart.

A story of the Vere de Vere, a lamentable comedy, an African discovery and an evening with Callender follow the title tale. Aldrich writes Long Island country life with a sharp eye for class, courtship and eccentricity, and her Ophelia is a village girl whose romantic imagination meets hard local fact. The collection is period American short fiction, witty and melancholy by turns.
1498-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-3-p:
John Lord's popular history, in this volume's first part, surveys the Middle Ages through its great figures and turning points. From the fall of Rome through feudalism, the Church, and the rise of towns, Lord tells the age as a gallery of beacon lights, men and women whose deeds shaped Europe.

The style is that of the Victorian lecture hall: clear, moral, and full of anecdote, aimed at general readers rather than scholars. The volume pairs with a second part on Renaissance and Reformation. It offers an old-fashioned but readable road through a thousand years of history.
14980-outwitting-our-nerves:
Josephine A. Jackson and Helen M. Salisbury write Outwitting Our Nerves, a primer of psychotherapy published by the Century Company in 1922, dedicated to Mary Patterson Manly, a lover of truth. Part one, the strange ways of nerves, opens with most of us pleading guilty to the charge of nerves.

A drama of nerves follows, teaching what nerves are not and hinting what they are. Later chapters, sixteen in all, explain fear, habit, worry and the ways people can outwit their own nervous responses. Jackson and Salisbury write for lay readers, not only patients, in plain language. The primer is early popular psychology, humane and practical, though its advice now belongs to history.
15005-readings-in-the-history-of-educati:
Arthur O. Norton, assistant professor of history and art of teaching at Harvard, gathers readings in the history of education on mediaeval universities, published by Harvard in 1909. An introduction and the renaissance of the twelfth century open, with the rise of universities following.

Teachers and students of the twelfth century, Abelard and John of Salisbury, the new method and new studies follow, with Aristotle, Roman law, canon law, theology, medicine and other textbooks. University privileges, special protection by sovereigns and the right to teach, with exercises, degree requirements and academic letters, close the set. Norton lets medieval sources speak, in translation, about how universities began.
15025-prose-fancies:
Richard Le Gallienne's 1894 book gathers short essays first printed in London papers such as The Speaker and The Star. Spring mornings, silence, libraries, old playgoers, and the quirks of poets and publishers all get a turn. A portrait of the author fronts the collection, which he dedicates to his wife.

Le Gallienne writes in a light, musical prose, fond of fancy and gentle wit rather than hard argument. Pieces on genius, limited editions, and the measure of a man show a 1890s man of letters at ease. Readers who like reflective essays will enjoy its charm, even where its views now feel of their time.
15069-diet-and-health-with-key-to-the-ca:
Lulu Hunt Peters once chaired the public health group of the California Federation of Women's Clubs. She writes Diet and Health with Key to the Calories, published in Chicago in 1918 and dedicated by permission to Herbert Hoover. Illustrated by her small nephew Dawson Hunt Perkins, the book opens with a note on reading it.

Peters warns she cannot devise a key to read the book as well as a key to calories. Sometimes headings come before text and sometimes after, but order matters little if the reader follows. Calorie counts, menus and advice on weight follow. Peters, a pioneering nutrition columnist, writes plainly for home readers, and the book remains a landmark of American diet writing.
15078-idle-hour-stories:
Eugenia Dunlap Potts wrote The Song of Lancaster and A Kentucky Girl in Dixie. She gathers Idle Hour Stories, published by herself in Lexington in 1909. The book is dedicated to her beloved only son George Dunlap Potts, whose young eyes watched the weaving of these fancies.

A thrilling experience, a cluster of ripe fruit and the ghost at Crestdale follow. Her Christmas gift, a Pullman car, old Kentucky, his gratitude and the singer's Christmas come next, with turning the tables and how she helped a friend. Potts writes Kentucky tales for idle hours: ghosts, gifts, travel and gratitude, in a gentle, local voice. The collection is a memorial as much as a book, kept by a mother's dedication.
15143-famous-modern-ghost-stories:
Dorothy Scarborough selected this 1921 ghost anthology, with an introduction on the imperishable ghost. Tales include Blackwood's Willows, Freeman's Shadows on the Wall, Chambers's Messenger, Andreyev's Lazarus, and Harvey's Beast with Five Fingers. Poe's Ligeia, Machen's Bowmen, and Bierce's Middle Toe of the Right Foot also appear.

Scarborough, a Columbia lecturer on the supernatural in fiction, chose stories that haunt by mood as much as by shock. France, O'Brien, Dunbar, and Steele round out the set. Horror fans will find the book a classic sampler, still chilling, of how modern writers made ghosts feel real.
15145-my-book-of-favourite-fairy-tales:
Edited by Captain Edric Vredenburg and retold by the editor and others, this fairy tale book offers old favorites with pictures by Jennie Harbour. The Goose Girl fronts the color plates, and tales include Snow-White, Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood, Hansel and Grethel, and Beauty and the Beast. Bluebeard and Prince Chéri appear too.

Each tale is retold in clear prose for children, with the magic kept but the language kept simple. The White Fawn, Sleeping Beauty, and Thumbling round out a generous set. Families reading aloud will find the book a handsome, well-chosen gateway to the classic tales.
15174-memories-and-anecdotes:
Kate Sanborn's 1915 memoir gathers memories and anecdotes from a life among Dartmouth folk, Smith College pupils, and lecture halls. Early chapters recall village oddities, distinguished visitors, storytellers of Hanover, and a day with Bryant at his country home. A wedding trip to the White Mountains in 1826 rides in a one-horse shay.

Later chapters add friends at Andover, Hezekiah Butterworth, and her own family, with sixteen illustrations to match. Sanborn writes with a lecturer's ease and a New Englander's humor. Readers who like literary gossip and old New Hampshire life will enjoy her warm, chatty recollections.
15227-the-adventures-of-prince-lazybones:
Mrs. W. J. Hays's 1884 children's book opens with Prince Lazybones, of a family famed, in its way, like gems on the earth's surface. Other tales include Phil's Fairies, Florio and Florella at Christmas, and Boreas Bluster's Christmas present. Pictures show a swanlike boat, an eagle, and a useful sturgeon.

Hays writes in a fanciful, moral style, teaching industry and kindness through fairy adventure. Prince Lazybones must learn that ease alone brings no joy. Young readers who like old fairy tales will enjoy the book's whimsy, even where its lessons feel very Victorian.
15230-miss-mink-s-soldier-and-other-stor:
Alice Hegan Rice's 1918 story collection opens with Miss Mink's Soldier, in which a small, sharp-chinned woman sits in church, lips pressed, refusing a pulpit request. Other tales include A Darling of Misfortune, Pop Hoodooed, A Matter of Friendship, and Cupid Goes Slumming. The Soul of O Sana San closes the set.

Rice, known for Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, writes with humor and heart about Southern folk, soldiers, and spinsters. Her characters are drawn in a few vivid strokes, and her endings favor kindness. Readers who enjoy gentle, character-led short stories will find the book warm and easy.
15241-all-about-johnnie-jones:
Carolyn Verhoeff's All About Johnnie Jones, in a seventh edition, gathers stories of a little boy, dedicated to the memory of Meldrum Adams Hartwell, a child who lived from 1891 to 1896. Tales include Johnnie and the cookie, Johnnie lost, a squirrel, peach preserves, and Johnnie as Santa Claus. Diantha Horne drew the pictures.

Verhoeff says her sole aim was to give pleasure to little children while helping them grasp childhood's highest ideals. The stories are simple, kind, and domestic. Parents reading to small children will find Johnnie Jones gentle, funny, and full of everyday wonder.
15252-victorian-short-stories-stories-of:
This anthology gathers Victorian short stories of successful marriages, with Gaskell's Manchester Marriage leading the set. Thomas Hardy adds A Mere Interlude, George Moore A Faithful Heart, Walter Besant a solid gold reef company tale, and Henry James The Tree of Knowledge. Each story tests what a good marriage takes.

Gaskell opens with Mr. and Mrs. Openshaw moving from Manchester to London, where he must run a warehouse and she must learn city ways. The other tales probe loyalty, knowledge, and compromise. Readers who like classic short fiction will find the collection varied, thoughtful, and quietly surprising.
15281-uncle-wiggily-s-adventures:
Howard Garis's Uncle Wiggily's Adventures, number four in the bedtime series, offers thirty-one stories for reading aloud each night, with eight colored pictures by Louis Wisa. Cousin volumes cover rabbits, squirrels, ducks, dogs, pigs, cats, and chicks, each in handsome cloth. Uncle Wiggily's travels form number six.

The old rabbit gentleman, with his crutch, meets friends, foes, and funny scrapes, always kind and plucky. Garis writes in a simple, cozy style for little folks. The book pairs with his travels volume as a gentle classic of animal bedtime tales.
15283-disease-and-its-causes:
W. T. Councilman, professor of pathology at Harvard, wrote this 1913 book on disease and its causes, published by Holt in New York and London. Opening chapters define disease, describe living matter and cells, and use the amoeba as a type of single-celled life. Adaptation, environment, and body surfaces follow.

Councilman explains how germs, injury, and inner faults disturb the body's order, in clear prose for educated readers. The book captures medicine just as germ theory matured. Students of medical history will find it lucid, systematic, and full of early twentieth-century science.
15320-the-romance-of-the-milky-way-and-o:
Lafcadio Hearn's 1905 book gathers studies and stories from Japan, opening with The Romance of the Milky Way, where the River of Heaven is called the Ghost of Waters. Goblin Poetry, Ultimate Questions, The Mirror Maiden, and the story of Ito Norisuké follow, with a letter from Japan to close. Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston.

Hearn writes with a poet's eye for Japanese folk belief, ghosts, and star lore, blending scholarship with tale-telling. His prose is lyrical and respectful, if romantic in its gaze. Readers who love Japan and folk tales will find the book haunting, beautiful, and rich in wonder.
15328-the-lost-hunter-a-tale-of-early-ti:
This 1856 tale of early times, printed at New York and Cincinnati, opens with a Halleck verse. The verse praises a rough land of earth, stone, and tree, where no castled lord or cabined slave breathes. Friends find welcome there, while foes find a grave. An apology, in the voice of a clown at the door, fronts the story.

The lost hunter moves through frontier woods, settlements, and dangers, in a romantic American style that praises bold tongues and free hands. The tale belongs to the early American historical romance. Readers who enjoy frontier fiction will find it earnest, rugged, and full of period color.
15329-an-apology-for-the-study-of-northe:
Elizabeth Elstob's Apology for the Study of Northern Antiquities, first printed in 1715, appears here in an Augustan Reprint Society edition, edited by Charles Peake. A transcriber's note explains that Greek, Hebrew, Saxon, and Gothic scripts appear transliterated for readers whose devices lack those fonts. The reprint is number sixty-one.

Elstob defends the study of Old English and northern languages, then scorned as rude, as a path to history, law, and literature. Her apology is learned, spirited, and pioneering for a woman scholar. Students of medieval studies will find it a landmark plea for a neglected field.
15360-the-easiest-way-in-housekeeping-an:
Helen Campbell's Easiest Way in Housekeeping and Cooking, revised in 1903 from an 1880 original, teaches domestic work for home use or classes. A Macbeth motto on doing quickly fronts the book, dedicated to Agnes and the Southern girls who studied with her. The preface notes a firm Southern following.

Campbell keeps the plan small on purpose, refusing to bloat a plain, practical manual. Lessons cover cooking, cleaning, and order in clear steps. Home historians will find the book a useful, unpretentious guide to how American households were run. Its lessons still read as sensible advice for plain, good housekeeping.
15368-fugitive-pieces:
This volume reproduces Lord Byron's first book of verse, privately printed in the autumn of 1806 when he was eighteen. Marcel Kessel's bibliographical note, printed with the 1933 facsimile, traces how the poems grew. Byron doubled their number in late summer, adding lost pieces and new work. The last poem bears a November date.

The poems themselves are youthful and varied: verses on school days at Harrow, on childhood scenes, on friends, and on early love and loss. They show a schoolboy poet already fond of strong feeling and bold phrasing, before fame fixed his name. For readers of Byron, the book matters as a starting point, a record of the voice that would soon fill Childe Harold and Don Juan.
15387-jorrocks-jaunts-and-jollities:
Robert Surtees wrote this comic sporting book around his famous grocer-sportsman, Mr. Jorrocks. The narrator, styling himself the bard of Eastcheap, asks what city sportsman has not put off urgent business, even a wedding, to ride with the Surrey subscription foxhounds. That boast sets the tone for the whole volume.

Thirteen jaunts follow Jorrocks through the Surrey hunt, shooting trouble, staghounds, Newmarket races, Cheltenham, Margate, Paris, and a ride to Brighton on a coach called The Age. A dinner party and its hungover morning close the set. Surtees mocks city men who play at country sport, while loving the horses, hounds, and high spirits of the chase. The humor is broad, slangy, and very English.
15444-the-city-and-the-world-and-other-s:
Francis Clement Kelley published this second edition of short stories in Chicago in 1913. The title tale opens in Rome, in the cloister garden of San Ambrogio, where old blind Father Denfili tells his beads beside a goldfish pond. A younger priest, Father Tomasso, watches over him, and peace fills the small garden under a Roman sky.

Fourteen stories follow, mixing Catholic life, humor, and moral fable. Titles include The Flaming Cross, The Vicar-General, The Resurrection of Alta, The Man with a Dead Soul, and The Autobiography of a Dollar. Priests, saints in the making, tramps, and banknotes all take turns as narrators or heroes. The set reads as light, faithful fiction, meant to amuse while it points a moral about city life and the wider world.
15449-new-faces:
Myra Kelly published this book of short stories in New York in 1910, with pictures by Charles F. Neagle. An epigraph from Andrew Lang gives the theme: a hunger for new faces, since familiar ones grow dull after a fortnight. The eight stories that follow test that wish in comic and tender ways.

Titles include The Play's the Thing, There's Danger in Numbers, Misery Loves Company, The Christmas Guest, Who Is Sylvia, and The Spirit of Cecelia Anne. Lovers, guests, and strangers enter settled lives and stir them up, and marriage talk runs through several tales. Kelly, known for stories of New York schoolchildren, here writes for grown readers, with light dialogue and a fond eye for social comedy.
15466-victorian-short-stories-of-trouble:
This volume gathers five Victorian stories of troubled marriages, by five writers. Rudyard Kipling opens with The Bronckhorst Divorce-Case, first printed in the Civil and Military Gazette in 1884. Its husband, a middle-aged army man grey as a badger, grows to hate his pale, quiet wife, fifteen years his junior, and his coarse manner makes the home a battleground.

Ella D'Arcy follows with Irremediable, Arthur Morrison with A Poor Stick, Arthur Conan Doyle with The Adventure of the Abbey Grange, and George Gissing with The Prize Lodger. Divorce, cruelty, poverty, and murder test marriages that law and custom held fast. The set shows Victorian fiction at its least sentimental, asking what happens when love fails and duty, money, and reputation keep two people bound together.
15473-love-stories:
Mary Roberts Rinehart gathered seven love stories in this volume, published in New York in 1919. The first tale, Twenty-Two, opens in a hospital training school, where a probationer named Nella Jane Brown tends a man hurt when a warehouse wall fell. Outsiders assume young nurses have been crossed in love, but Rinehart's heroine has other plans, and the story plays against that easy theory.

Other tales include Jane, In the Pavilion, God's Fool, The Miracle, Are We Downhearted? No!, and The Game. Nurses, patients, soldiers, and ordinary lovers take turns at the center, and humor softens the sentiment. Rinehart, already a popular novelist, writes romance with a practical eye: love tested by work, illness, and war, rather than by fine speeches alone.
15486-edna-s-sacrifice-and-other-stories:
Frances Henshaw Baden published this small story collection, opening with Edna's Sacrifice. The title tale begins on a cold September night, after three days of almost ceaseless rain, with Nell, Floy, Aunt Edna, and the narrator huddled in shawls on sofa and chairs. Stoves are not yet ready, books are read, the piano begs for rest, and backgammon aches their arms.

Four more tales follow: Who Was the Thief, The Ghost, The Two Brothers, and What He Left. The narrator's imitations of celebrated actresses, until hoarse, give the opening its lively, domestic humor. Baden writes short, old-fashioned stories of home life, mystery, and sacrifice, in a voice that suits reading aloud on a rainy night. The collection is modest, but its period charm is real.
15566-notes-to-shakespeare-volume-iii-th:
Samuel Johnson's Notes to Shakespeare, volume three, cover the tragedies. Arthur Sherbo edited the volume, with an introduction. It appeared in Los Angeles in 1958, from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library. The Augustan Reprint Society series gathers Johnson's eighteenth-century notes in a clean modern text. A board of general and advisory editors from major schools guides the series.

Sherbo's introduction notes Johnson's curious reaction to the tragedies: deep emotional involvement in a few scenes, and a strange dispassionateness toward most of the rest. Notes then gloss single lines, as when Johnson explains that general means not speedy but compendious, a way to try many at a time. The volume lets modern readers see Shakespeare through Johnson's eyes, line by line, with a great critic's sense and prejudice both on show.
15592-old-fashioned-fairy-tales:
Juliana Horatia Ewing published this fairy tale book in London and New York, under the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, dedicated to her sister Undine Marcia Gatty. A preface warns readers not to mistake the tales for old ones told afresh. Except for common properties of fairy drama and care for tradition in color and detail, the stories are all new.

They appeared over several years in Aunt Judy's Magazine for Young People. Ewing wrote them to theories she sets out in the preface. Myths of all countries share ideas and types, such as the weak outwitting the strong. Any teller may use those shared types without plagiarism. Tales include Good Luck Is Better Than Gold, The Hillman and the Housewife, The Cobbler and the Ghosts, and The Ogre Courting. The book is gentle, moral fantasy, rooted in folk pattern rather than mere invention.
15600-matisse-picasso-and-gertrude-stein:
Gertrude Stein wrote this experimental volume, also known as G. M. P., with two shorter stories: A Long Gay Book, 1909 to 1912, Many Many Women, 1910, and G. M. P., 1911 to 1912. A transcriber's note warns that spelling oddities were checked against a modern edition and left as found, and that readers should consult an authoritative edition before quoting.

A Long Gay Book opens with a meditation on babies. When they are very little, one can never tell which is to be a lady. Some later feel inside them that they once were so little and knew nothing. Stein's sentences repeat, shift, and circle, building meaning by rhythm rather than plot. The book is difficult by design, a landmark of modernist prose that asks readers to hear language as much as to follow a story.
15616-hero-tales:
James Baldwin wrote The Story of Siegfried, The Story of Roland, and Baldwin's Readers. His book of hero tales appeared in New York in 1914, from Charles Scribner's Sons. It was copyrighted in 1904. It is dedicated to Carrie Edith and Nellie May. Seventeen tales run from Apollo's coming to Parnassus. They pass through the hunt in the wood of Calydon and the choice of Hercules. They reach the golden apple and Paris and Helen.

Later tales tell Iphigenia, the hoard of the elves, the forging of Balmung, and Idun and her apples. The doom of the mischief-maker, Ogier the Dane and the fairies, and Charlemagne crossing the Alps follow. What happened at Roncevaux closes the book. The first tale opens on Delos, where Earth smiles, nymphs sing, and swans fly seven times round the island at Apollo's birth. Baldwin retells Greek, Norse, and Frankish legend for young readers.
15649-a-philosophicall-essay-for-the-reu:
This philosophical essay for the reunion of the languages, or the art of knowing all by the mastery of one, was printed at Oxford in 1675 by Henry Hall for James Good. The printer's address to the reader explains the project: having met the offer in another dress, he thought it might speak another language too. Few nations, he notes, have not claimed supremacy for their tongue, with boasts of reason and authority.

The author's design wins praise for modesty and ingenuity. Without private regard for his own native tongue's flourishing air, he makes the noble language of the Romans the basis of his project. Free from prejudice and partiality throughout, he offers Latin as the key to all languages. The essay is a Restoration dream of a common tongue: learn one language well, and the rest follow, with scholars united across Europe.
15667-best-short-stories:
A 1922 anthology of short stories gathered by Thomas L. Masson for Doubleday, Page and Company. Masson chose tales that turn on a single sharp point, the kind of story that lands with a twist or a laugh. His foreword argues that a first-class joke, like a good tale, strikes home across trades and tempers. Doctors, lawyers, soldiers, and family men all appear as readers and as subjects.

The tales range across American life, from offices and farms to camps and city rooms. Each story is short enough to read in one sitting, yet built to be retold. Humour leads, but many pieces carry a sting about pride, money, or love. As a shelf of period humour, the book shows what American magazine readers prized in a tale: pace, surprise, and a clear human point.
15683-the-high-school-failures:
Francis P. O'Brien submitted this study of high school failures to Columbia University for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy, published by Teachers College in New York in 1919. The subtitle defines the field: school records of pupils failing in academic or commercial high school subjects. O'Brien asks how extensive failures are, what basis exists for predicting them, and what schools might do.

Early chapters define failure, set the scope and sources, and test their reliability. Later chapters distribute entrants by failure, by age and semester, and by subject, and track pupils dropping out by time and age. Possible factors follow: attendance, mental and physical defects, and class size, with school entering age as a predictor. The study is early educational science: numbers, not impressions, on why pupils fail and leave school.
15712-hugo-a-fantasia-on-modern-themes:
A fantasia on modern business by Arnold Bennett, author of Anna of the Five Towns. Bennett imagines a master shopkeeper who dreams of hats and wakes to build an empire. The book treats trade as high romance, with wit and large invention. It belongs to Bennett's group of fantasias, alongside The Grand Babylon Hotel.

Hugo rebuilds his premises after studying great stores in America and Paris, borrowing only the Bon Marche system of vouchers. His central office overlooks a court of fountains, an island calm in a sea of trade. Clerks, rivals, and a hat artist crowd his rise. Bennett uses Hugo to praise and mock modern commerce at once: its energy, its show, and its hunger for more.
15733-grey-roses:
Henry Harland wrote The Cardinal's Snuff-Box, Comedies and Errors, and The Lady Paramount. His story collection appeared in London and New York in 1911, from John Lane, fifth edition. The University Press at Cambridge did the presswork. An epigraph from Parashkine sets the tone: the conception was a rose, but the achievement is a rose grown grey. Nine stories follow, from the Bohemian girl to castles near Spain.

Contents list Mercedes, a broken looking-glass, the reward of virtue, a re-incarnation, and flower o' the quince. When I am king and a responsibility complete the set. The first story opens with a narrator waking slowly in Paris. He is a guest in the smart new house of his old friend Nina Childe. He has forgotten yesterday's journey from his Cromwell Road room. Harland writes urbane, melancholy tales of love, art, and expatriate life, where bright hopes fade to grey.
15737-the-torch-and-other-tales:
Fifteen short tales by Eden Phillpotts gather village life in rural Devon, where small choices carry sharp costs. Phillpotts sets most of them among farm folk, sailors, and neighbours who know each other too well. The title tale gives the set its name, but each story stands alone. First issued by Macmillan in New York, the set reads as plain, local fiction with a hard edge.

The opening tale follows Teddy Pegram, a handy newcomer who lodges in Little Silver and wins trust through odd jobs and kindness to children. Later tales turn on a returned native, a wise woman, and a pool with a grim past. Love, pride, debt, and revenge recur throughout. Together the tales show how one proud act can undo years of quiet standing in a small place.
15745-the-man-wolf-and-other-tales:
A set of tales by Emile Erckmann and Alexandre Chatrian, French writers of Alsace, in a translation issued in 1876. The pair, famous for stories of village life and war, mix the strange with the homely. Their tales move between forests, farms, and small towns. A translator's note praises their justice and their craft.

The title tale, The Man-Wolf, runs through thirteen chapters of mystery and fear. Myrtle, Uncle Christian's Inheritance, The Bear-Baiting, The Scapegoat, and A Night in the Woods complete the set. Superstition, greed, and kindness drive each plot. The book offers a fine taste of French popular fiction: eerie, humane, and told with a storyteller's pace.
1580-charmides:
Plato's Charmides, translated by Benjamin Jowett, asks what temperance, or self-control, truly is. Socrates, fresh from battle, meets the beautiful youth Charmides and his guardian Critias. The talk turns from a headache cure to the nature of knowing oneself and of a science of sciences.

No firm answer is reached, and the dialogue ends in puzzlement, as many early Platonic works do. Its charm lies in the portrait of Athenian youth and the gentle irony of Socrates. The Charmides is a brief, graceful introduction to Plato's method of question and answer.
15803-crime-and-its-causes:
A study of crime by William Douglas Morrison, of Her Majesty's Prison, Wandsworth, issued in London and New York in 1902. Morrison, a prison official, brings a scientific temper to a subject then ruled by moral talk. The press praised it as one of the first English books to study crime strictly. Swan Sonnenschein and Scribner issued it in the Social Science Series.

Morrison weighs heredity, drink, poverty, climate, and city life as causes, testing each against prison records. He compares Italian criminology with English facts, and asks what punishment can truly do. The argument stays modest: causes mix, and no single cure fits all. The book matters as an early, humane attempt to replace blame with evidence.
15807-among-the-forces:
A book of nature and faith by Henry White Warren, a bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church, issued in 1898. Warren, author of Recreations in Astronomy, takes the forces of nature as helpers of human life. Old Faithful Geyser fronts the book. Eaton and Mains in New York and Curts and Jennings in Cincinnati published it.

Chapters treat the sun's great horses, moon help, star help, and the fairy gravitation that pulls great loads. Seas, plants, gases, and metals each lend their aid, in Warren's lively telling. The Matterhorn, the Grand Canyon, and Yellowstone geysers close the tour, with spiritual dynamics at the end. The book charms as Victorian nature theology: science made friendly to faith.
15812-the-testimony-of-the-bible-concern:
A defence of the Bible by S. E. Wishard, issued by the Bible Institute Press in Los Angeles in 1909. Wishard sends his booklet to Sabbath-school teachers, young people, and all believers in the living Word. His target is destructive criticism, the scholarship that questions Bible authorship and truth. The foreword quotes Philippians on defence and confirmation of the truth.

Wishard argues that critics assume what they claim to prove, and that the Bible testifies for itself. Short chapters meet each assumption with scripture and reason. The tone is earnest and popular, not academic. The booklet shows fundamentalist argument at its early best: plain, confident, and aimed at ordinary church readers.
15829-memories:
A Civil War memoir by Mrs. Fannie A. Beers, issued by J. B. Lippincott in Philadelphia in 1888. Beers records personal experience and adventure during four years of war, on the Confederate side. She dedicates the book to the boys who wore the gray, living and dead. Friends among Confederate soldiers urged her to write it down.

Beers served in hospitals and camps, nursing the wounded and sharing the army's marches and losses. Her pages mix danger, humour, and grief, with portraits of officers and common soldiers alike. She writes as a witness, not a historian, and her voice stays warm and direct. The memoir gives the war's home and hospital side, seldom told in battle histories.
1584-laches:
Plato's Laches, or Courage, translated by Benjamin Jowett, opens with two aged Athenians, Lysimachus son of Aristides the Just and Melesias son of Thucydides, who wish to educate their sons well. Their own education, as often happens with sons of great men, was neglected, and they ask generals and Socrates what courage is.

The talk moves from fighting in armour to the nature of courage itself, and ends, as Socratic talks often do, without a settled definition. The dialogue's portraits of old Athens are warm. The Laches is a brief, humane introduction to Plato on virtue and education.
15853-one-of-life-s-slaves:
A Norwegian social novel by Jonas Lie, translated by Jessie Muir and issued in London in 1895. Lie, author of The Visionary, writes of working people caught in hard times. His hero moves from neglect and strict discipline toward a rise in life that never comes easy. Hodder Brothers published the translation for English readers.

Chapters treat a fight and its consequences, a stolen interview, and months among the unemployed. Factory girls, a postponed wedding, and a fair with a convict mark the road. Lie keeps sympathy with the lowly, showing how small chances shape great lives. The novel stands as a humane picture of labour, love, and the struggle to stand upright.
15859-the-piazza-tales:
A set of tales by Herman Melville, issued in New York by Dix and Edwards in 1856, with a London edition by Sampson Low. Melville, author of Typee and Omoo, gathers six pieces written for magazines. The title tale frames the book: a farmer builds a piazza to enjoy a country view. From there the tales darken and deepen.

Contents run from The Piazza to Bartleby, the scrivener who prefers not to, and Benito Cereno, a slave revolt told through fog and doubt. The Lightning-Rod Man, The Encantadas, and The Bell-Tower complete the set. Each tale probes pride, power, and human mystery. The book stands among Melville's finest short works, strange and lasting.
15862-afterwhiles:
A book of poems by James Whitcomb Riley, the Hoosier poet, in a text scanned and lightly corrected from print. A transcriber's note warns that Riley's spellings stand, with pretty as purty and dialect forms like sho'-nuff for sure-enough. The first poem appears as Proem on contents and headers, though later editions call it Afterwhiles. Old Aunt Mary's later grows by thirteen verses.

Poems treat the south wind and the sun, old aunts, and the small joys of home and field. Dialect gives the verse its music, and humour its warmth. Riley writes for reading aloud, by fire or porch. The book keeps Riley's voice close to print: plain folk, plain speech, and a poet's ear for laughter.
15865-noughts-and-crosses-stories-studie:
A set of stories, studies, and sketches by Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, known as Q. Two stories first appeared in Longman's Magazine, the rest in The Speaker, whose editors Q thanks. He dedicates the book to his wife. Q, a Cornish writer and critic, mixes humour, mystery, and seaside life.

Contents include The Omnibus, Fortunio, and The Outlandish Ladies, with the Statement of Gabriel Foot, Highwayman. The Return of Joanna, Psyche, and The Countess of Bellarmine follow, with A Cottage in Troy and stories of Bleakirk. Each piece is short, sharp, and well told. The book shows Q's range: a storyteller at ease in town, village, and open sea.
15868-the-man-without-a-country-and-othe:
A set of tales by Edward E. Hale, issued by Roberts Brothers in Boston in 1891, from an 1868 original. Hale, a minister and reformer, wrote fiction with a civic purpose. The title tale made his fame during the Civil War. Other tales in the volume mix satire, invention, and moral fable.

The Man Without a Country follows Philip Nolan, who curses his country and is sentenced never to hear of it again. The Last of the Florida, A Piece of Possible History, and The South American Editor follow. My Double, and How He Undid Me, and The Children of the Public close the set. Hale's tales still move readers: patriotism tested, and a country learned by losing it.
15881-the-flower-of-the-chapdelaines:
A New Orleans novel by George W. Cable, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1918, with a frontispiece by F. C. Yohn. Cable, a master of Louisiana fiction, sets his tale on Royal, Bienville, Conti, and Bourbon streets. A young lawyer, fresh in his new office, meets a fair stranger and her urchin escort at a corner. The scene repeats the next morning.

The stranger, with a nine-year-old boy in broad white collar and blue jacket at her side, draws the lawyer into a Creole mystery. Old families, old names, and old wrongs shadow the Chapdelaines. Cable writes with grace for a vanishing New Orleans. The novel stands as a late Cable romance: love, caste, and a flower that blooms in a walled garden.
15886-the-strength-of-gideon-and-other-s:
A set of stories by Paul Laurence Dunbar, issued in 1900 and dedicated to Captain Charles B. Stivers, his friend and teacher. Dunbar, the first Black American poet of national fame, writes here in prose of Black life after slavery. His tales mix humour, pathos, and sharp moral sense. Dialect and plain narration share the pages.

The title tale, The Strength of Gideon, leads a set with Mammy Peggy's Pride and Viney's Free Papers. The Fruitful Sleeping of the Reverend Elisha Edwards, The Ingrate, and The Case of Caroline follow, with The Finish of Patsy Barnes. Each story turns on pride, freedom, or faith. The book stands as Dunbar's lasting prose: tender, funny, and true to his people.
15905-collected-essays-volume-v-science-:
The fifth volume of Thomas H. Huxley's collected essays, on science and Christian tradition, issued by D. Appleton and Company in New York in 1902. Huxley, Darwin's bulldog, gathers his controversies of the 1880s and 1890s. A prologue on controverted questions opens the set. The essays defend science against dogma with wit and steel.

Scientific and pseudo-scientific realism, science and pseudo-science, and an episcopal trilogy follow. The value of witness to the miraculous, possibilities and impossibilities, and three great agnosticism essays complete the arc. Huxley coins and defends agnosticism as honest doubt. The volume stands as a classic of Victorian debate: reason against authority, argued brilliantly.
15922-a-loose-end-and-other-stories:
A set of stories by S. Elizabeth Hall, author of The Interloper, issued in London by Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company. Truslove and Bray printed the book at West Norwood. Hall writes of islands, villages, and roads by the sea, with a quiet, observant eye. Each story stands alone, yet all share a gentle moral light.

A Loose End opens one September morning, when the Channel Islands seemed further off than now, and some had hardly any contact with the outer world. In a Breton Village, Twice a Child, and The Road by the Sea follow, with The Halting Step and Tabitha's Aunt. The tales treat age, loss, and small kindnesses. Hall's book pleases readers who like short fiction with feeling and restraint.
15961-turns-of-fortune-and-other-tales:
A children's book by Mrs. S. C. Hall, in Francis and Company's Little Library for young persons of various ages. C. S. Francis and Company of New York issued the uniform series, neatly bound in cloth and illustrated with engravings. Choice volumes by distinguished writers for children fill the list. Hall's Turns of Fortune leads this volume.

Maria Child's Flowers for Children and Mary Howitt's Fireside Tales join the series, for ages three to twelve. Hall's tales treat fortune's turns with warmth and moral sense. Riches lost, friends found, and lessons learned fill the short pieces. The book shows Victorian children's publishing at its kindest: good stories, pretty bindings, and tales meant to form character.
15963-may-day-and-other-pieces:
A poetry collection by Ralph Waldo Emerson, in the 1867 George Routledge and Sons edition. May-Day leads, with The Adirondacs beside it. Occasional and miscellaneous pieces follow, with nature and life poems and a section of elements. Emerson, America's sage of Concord, writes here in his later, reflective manner.

Brahma, Nemesis, Fate, and Freedom join an ode sung in Concord town hall on July 4, 1857, a Boston hymn, and Voluntaries. Nature, The Romany Girl, Days, The Titmouse, Sea-Shore, and Song of Nature follow, with Two Rivers, Terminus, The Past, and In Memoriam. The book shows Emerson's range: philosopher, patriot, and lover of woods, in verse that thinks aloud.
1597-andersen-s-fairy-tales:
Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales, in this collection, gather his most loved stories. Among them are The Emperor's New Clothes, The Real Princess, The Fir Tree, The Snow Queen, The Little Match Girl, The Red Shoes, and The Shadow. Swineherds and emperors, fir trees and snow queens, move through a world where vanity is mocked and kindness is tested.

Andersen's voice is plain and intimate, as if told to a child at bedtime, yet his tales carry adult sorrow. The collection is a classic of world literature. It offers the essential Andersen in one volume, for first readers and for grown-ups returning to old friends.
1599-cinderella-or-the-little-glass-slip:
Anonymous authors offer Cinderella, or The Little Glass Slipper, as the head of this children's collection. Short tales follow, such as Fanny's Telephone Order, The Raindrops' New Dresses, Sir Gobble, and Something About Fires. Each story is brief, moral, and meant for reading aloud to young listeners.

Cinderella herself, kind amid cinders and stepsisters, leads the set, and the other tales mix fancy with lessons on kindness, care, and honesty. The book is a period children's miscellany. It will charm readers who love old-fashioned storybooks and their gentle morals.
15994-a-reckless-character-and-other-sto:
Ivan Turgenev's stories reach English readers here through Isabel F. Hapgood's 1907 Scribner translation from the Russian. Seven pieces fill the book: A Reckless Character, The Dream, Father Alexei's Story, Old Portraits, The Song of Love Triumphant, Clara Militch, and Poems in Prose. The title story dates from 1881 and opens with friends debating what reckless men are.

An old man answers with the tale of his grandnephew Misha Polteff, a young landowner whose wild energy has no aim. The other stories likewise watch love, faith, memory, and art press on ordinary Russians. Turgenev's prose is calm and exact, and the book offers a fine short path into one of Russia's great storytellers.
160-the-awakening-and-selected-short-sto:
Edna Pontellier, a wife and mother summering on the Gulf Coast, wakes to a self of her own. Kate Chopin's Awakening follows Edna from polite marriage to art, lovers, and a final swim toward freedom. Creole society watches her rebellion with shock.

Selected stories follow, including Beyond the Bayou, Désirée's Baby, and A Pair of Silk Stockings. Chopin writes Louisiana life with irony and sympathy for women trapped by custom. The Awakening was condemned in its day and later hailed as a feminist classic. The volume gathers her finest short work.
16018-the-black-prophet-a-tale-of-irish-:
A famine novel by William Carleton, The Black Prophet, a tale of Irish famine, in his collected works. The first chapter, Glendhu, or the Black Glen, scene of domestic affection, opens some twenty years before writing. A little cabin stands at the foot of a round hill, shaped like a cupola, commanding a prospect of singular beauty. The hill runs in a range from north to south-west.

A geologist's eye, Carleton notes, would prize the hill's distinct form. Domestic affection fills the cabin before famine strikes. Hunger, fever, and a prophet's grim warnings follow. The novel stands as Carleton's great famine book: a family, a glen, and a disaster that broke a nation.
16042-the-wonder-book-of-bible-stories:
Logan Marshall edited and arranged this children's Bible storybook, published by the John C. Winston Company in 1925 with roots in a 1904 edition. Its contents retell the great tales in short, simple chapters. Adam and Eve, Noah and the ark, Hagar and Ishmael, and Abraham and Isaac come first. Then follow Jacob and his ladder to heaven, Joseph and his coat of many colors, and Moses, the child found in the river.

Pictures, including the baby in the manger, help young readers picture each scene, and the plain retellings keep the stories moving. The book was made for family reading and Sunday schools, giving children the sweep of the Bible from creation onward. It remains a gentle, readable introduction to stories many readers meet first here.
16052-the-brownies-and-other-tales:
A set of fairy tales by Juliana Horatia Ewing, issued in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in 1871, with E. and J. B. Young in New York. Ewing dedicates the book to her very dear and honoured mother. The General Literature Committee directed the publication. Ewing, a beloved children's writer, mixes fancy with gentle morals.

The Brownies opens with a little girl sewing and crying on a garden seat, fair hair blown into her eyes. The Land of Lost Toys, Three Christmas Trees, and An Idyll of the Wood follow, with Christmas Crackers and Amelia and the Dwarfs. Each tale turns on kindness, tidiness, or unselfish help. The book still charms young readers: brownies who reward good children, in stories told with grace.
16090-the-exiles-and-other-stories:
Richard Harding Davis, the famed war reporter and storyteller, is gathered here in a 1919 Scribner volume with an introduction by Charles Dana Gibson. Gibson opens with a London memory of Davis at twenty-four, dressed as a Thames boatman after a night rowing for local color. Eight stories follow, drawn from Davis books of the 1890s: The Exiles, The Boy Orator of Zepata City, The Other Woman, and On the Fever Ship among them.

The tales range from exiles and fever ships to a reporter who makes himself king, all told with Davis's brisk, clean style. Adventure, romance, and a reporter's eye for strange places run through them. Readers who like turn-of-the-century action stories will find this a strong single-volume sample of his work.
16116-studies-of-trees:
J. J. Levison, lecturer on shade trees at the Yale Forest School and forester to Brooklyn's parks, wrote this 1914 guide for readers who want to know trees by sight. Early chapters teach identification step by step: pines, spruce, hemlock, cedar, larch, oaks, maples, hickories, and many more, told apart by leaf, form, bark, and trunk. Later chapters explain how trees grow and what they need.

The book then advises what to plant and how, with trees for streets, parks, and home grounds in mind. Its tone is practical and friendly, aimed at planters and nature lovers rather than scholars alone. Anyone learning to name the trees on their street will still find it a clear, useful companion.
16126-english-satires:
Oliphant Smeaton introduces this Gresham volume of English satires, dedicated to the memory of Alexander Balloch Grosart. Smeaton aimed for a representative book rather than an exhaustive one, since the limits of the series forced omissions of pieces readers might expect. The most typical satires of successive eras were chosen instead, to show each age's literary character and the trend of satiric writing.

The span runs from Langland in the Middle Ages to Lowell in the nineteenth century, centuries of mockery, moral anger, and wit. Permission to print the closing verses came from Mrs. C. S. Calverley, the preface notes with thanks. Students of English literature will find a useful, readable survey of satire's long career.
1615-old-english-libraries:
Ernest Savage's Old English Libraries, in the Antiquary's Books series, tells how books were made, collected, and used during the Middle Ages. Monks copying in scriptoria, abbots building libraries, and readers borrowing chained volumes all appear, with Abbot Whethamstede among the figures who shaped English book culture.

The book ranges from materials and scripts to catalogues, loans, and the fate of monastic collections at the Reformation. Its detail is scholarly but readable. It is a valuable guide to medieval reading, for lovers of books about books and of England's manuscript past.
16185-the-nest-in-the-honeysuckles-and-o:
Published in Philadelphia in 1855 by the American Sunday-School Union, this children's book gathers gentle stories written for Sunday-school readers. Its title tale watches a robin build her nest in the honeysuckles, rising before six to work, welcoming the rosy dawn with song, and resting only when the house is dry. The narrator urges young readers to rise with the birds and not lose the morning songs.

Other stories in the same spirit teach kindness, diligence, and love of nature through small, homely scenes. A frontispiece shows Mrs. Dudley and her little boy at a window, setting the domestic tone. The book survives as a sweet, old-fashioned sample of mid-Victorian moral tales for children.
16194-corporal-sam-and-other-stories:
Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch, known as Q, gathers ten stories in Corporal Sam and Other Stories. The title tale follows Sergeant David Wilkes of the First Royal Regiment, trudging down Mount Olia with a fatigue party after hauling a twenty-four-pounder into battery. Shells scream overhead as the men descend, distinguishing shell from round shot, while guns on the rocky platform keep firing.

The Copernican Convoy, Red Velvet, The Jew on the Moor, My Christmas Burglary, The Mayor's Dovecot, News from Troy, Colonel Baigent's Christmas, Doctor Unonius, and Mutual Exchange complete the set. Q writes with Cornish warmth and a soldier's eye for detail. Readers who like short, shapely tales of war, crime, and village life will enjoy this collection.
16206-analytical-studies:
Honore de Balzac's Analytical Studies gathers his anatomy of married life, opening with a warning to women readers. The author jokes that any woman tempted by the title has already read the work without knowing it. He adds that no man, however malicious, can say as much good or evil about women as they think themselves. He then inscribes, in effect, ladies must not enter on his title page.

Contents join Petty Troubles of Married Life with Unhappiness of Married Life, and an introduction declaring marriage no institution of nature, with the Eastern family entirely different from the Western. Balzac dissects love, money, and power in marriage with ruthless wit. Readers of The Human Comedy will find its sharpest, most provocative essays here.
16222-winter-evening-tales:
Amelia E. Barr's Winter Evening Tales, published in 1896 by the Christian Herald at Bible House, New York, gathers stories for leisure hours by the fire. The preface praises Barr's luminous genius and the spell of her fancy, calling each tale a perfect gem of romance in an artistic setting. Some stories sparkle with mirth, the preface says, while others show the sadder side of life.

Throughout, broad sympathy and intense humanity mark her men and women, creatures of real flesh and blood rather than painted figures. Barr, author of A Bow of Orange Ribbon and Jan Vedder's Wife, was a favorite storyteller of her day. Readers who like Victorian domestic romance will enjoy this varied, fireside collection.
1624-the-two-destinies:
Wilkie Collins's Two Destinies opens with a prelude in which a guest writes and tells the story of a dinner party. The party comes years after he and his wife left the United States for their first visit to England. Letters of introduction bring them to Greenwater Broad, where two lives, linked from childhood, move toward a fate neither can escape.

Through a divided narrative and a mystery of identity, Collins asks whether character or chance rules a life. The novel is less famous than his masterpieces, but its structure is clever. It is a thoughtful Collins tale of destiny, love, and the past's long shadow.
16248-the-opera-a-sketch-of-the-developm:
R. A. Streatfeild's The Opera, in a third revised edition from Routledge and Lippincott, sketches opera's growth with full descriptions of works in the modern repertory. An introduction by J. A. Fuller-Maitland opens the history, which runs from Peri, Monteverdi, Cavalli, and Lulli through Purcell and Handel. Later chapters treat Gluck's reforms, opera buffa and singspiel, Mozart, and the close of the classical age.

Weber and the romantics, Rossini, Donizetti, Bellini, and Meyerbeer follow, each with plot summaries and musical comment. Streatfeild writes for opera lovers who want a guide, not a textbook. The book remains a handy companion for anyone building a first acquaintance with the repertory.
163-flower-fables:
Louisa May Alcott wrote these flower tales for Ellen Emerson, daughter of Ralph Waldo Emerson. Flower Fables, dated Boston, December 9, 1854, gathers stories of the Frost King, Eva's visit to fairyland, and Lily-Bell and Thistledown. Little Bud, Clover-Blossom, and Ripple the water-spirit join them.

Each fable teaches kindness, patience, or the power of love through flowers, elves, and seasons. Alcott's early prose is gentle, musical, and moral without preaching hard. The book predates Little Women by fourteen years. It shows the young author finding her voice among fairy folk.
16310-cinderella-and-other-stories:
Richard Harding Davis's Cinderella and Other Stories, published by Scribner in 1896, gathers tales first printed in Scribner's, Harper's, and youth magazines. The title story opens at the Hotel Salisbury on Broadway, where servants plan their annual ball and volunteer concert, vowing to eclipse every earlier ball in the hotel's two-year history. Miss Delamar's Understudy, The Editor's Story, An Assisted Emigrant, and The Reporter Who Made Himself King follow.

Davis writes with a reporter's eye and a storyteller's pace, moving from hotel servants to editors and exiles. The collection shows his lighter, popular side beside his war reporting. Readers who like turn-of-the-century American stories will find a bright, varied volume.
16316-outdoor-sports-and-games:
Claude H. Miller wrote this 1911 boys' guide as part of the Library of Work and Play. It covers health and fresh air first, then Boy Scouts, camp choice, tents, fires, camp cooking, woodcraft, guns, and fishing. Later chapters take up games, sports, and the gear a boy needs to enjoy the woods safely.

The tone is brisk and practical, with lists of kit and plain steps for each skill. Miller stresses good food, clean air, and care with tools over mere daring. The book reads like a camp leader's handbook, and it still shows how American boys were taught to live outdoors in the years before the First World War.
1633-the-brick-moon-and-other-stories:
Edward Everett Hale's collection is headed by The Brick Moon, a story of a satellite built of brick and launched by accident into orbit around the earth. Its inhabitants signal home by Morse code. Hale, looking back thirty years after writing, adds a preface on how the tales have aged.

Other stories in the set share Hale's inventive, humane fancy, mixing science with moral reflection. The Brick Moon itself foresaw artificial satellites by a century. The book is a classic of early American science fiction, charming, earnest, and surprisingly prescient.
16380-the-odds-and-other-stories:
Ethel M. Dell's Odds and Other Stories, published in 1922, gathers seven tales from the author of The Way of an Eagle and The Rocks of Valpre. The title story opens with Dot Burton, blue-eyed and boyish in a tanned face, vowing to shoot Buckskin Bill if he comes her way. Her brother Jack, ten years older, warns her not to shoot at sight, or she might shoot a policeman, which would be awkward for them both.

Without Prejudice, Her Own Free Will, The Consolation Prize, Her Freedom, Death's Property, and The Sacrifice complete the volume. Dell writes passionate, popular romance with strong heroines and high stakes. Readers who like early twentieth-century romantic fiction will find a dramatic, readable collection.
16408-the-grey-wig-stories-and-novelette:
I. Zangwill gathers his newest and oldest short work in this volume, dedicated to his mother and sisters as mainly a study of woman. The Grey Wig opens with two old ladies in Paris, Madame Valiere and Madame Depine, lodgers at the Hotel des Tourterelles. Chasse-Croise, The Woman Beater, The Eternal Feminine, and The Big Bow Mystery follow.

Zangwill writes with wit and pathos about women caught between custom and desire. The tales range from Paris lodgings to London mysteries. Readers who know him from Children of the Ghetto will find here a lighter, sharper side, still keen on character and social edge.
16459-musical-memories:
Camille Saint-Saens looks back on a long musical life in these memoirs, translated by Edwin Gile Rich in 1919. Childhood and the old Conservatoire open the book, followed by Victor Hugo, opera, the organ, and portraits of Haydn, Berlioz, Rossini, Meyerbeer, Offenbach, and Liszt. A chapter on anarchy in music shows the old master's sharp tongue.

Saint-Saens writes with wit and strong opinions, praising friends and settling scores in turn. The book gives a first-hand view of French musical life across the nineteenth century. Music lovers will enjoy its gossip, its craft talk, and its firm sense of taste.
16462-with-the-boer-forces:
Howard C. Hillegas, correspondent of the New York World and author of Oom Paul's People, reports from the Boer side in this 1900 book, with twenty-three pictures and a plan. He travels by Delagoa Bay and Lorenzo Marques to the Transvaal, through fever country to the Boer capital, then follows burghers from farm to battlefield.

Chapters on the army's makeup note boys in commandos, great-grandfathers in battle, and homesickness in the laagers. Hillegas writes as a sympathetic eyewitness, keen on Boer character and camp life. The book gives the Boer War from the side least heard in Britain, vivid and direct.
16468-the-pot-of-gold-and-other-stories:
Mary E. Wilkins gathers short tales for young readers in this 1893 volume. The title story leads, with The Cow with Golden Horns, Princess Rosetta and the Pop-Corn Man, The Christmas Monks, and The Pumpkin Giant to follow. Later pieces turn to village life: a bound girl, a deacon's will, an adopted daughter, and a stranger in town.

Wilkins sets most tales in New England, with plain folk, thrifty homes, and a touch of magic where least expected. The stories are short and warm, meant for family reading. Together they show a beloved American storyteller writing for children without losing her keen eye for character.
16519-prime-ministers-and-some-others-a-:
George W. E. Russell recalls the great men he knew in this 1918 book of reminiscences, inscribed to Lord Curzon though he does not share Curzon's views. Prime ministers lead the contents: Palmerston, Russell, Derby, Disraeli, Gladstone, Salisbury, Balfour, and Campbell-Bannerman. Friendship, religion, and the church fill later sections.

Russell writes as an insider with long memories and a light touch, mixing anecdote with judgment. Many pieces first ran in the Cornhill, Spectator, and Guardian. Readers of Victorian politics will find a personal gallery, warm where he loved, frank where he differed.
16535-myth-and-romance-being-a-book-of-v:
Madison Cawein gathers verses of myth and romance in this 1899 Putnam volume, dedicated to his friend William Warwick Thum. Visions and Voices opens with the title poem, Genius Loci, The Rain-Crow, and The Harvest Moon. An Anthem of Dawn follows, with Morgan le Fay, The Dream of Roderick, and The Land of Illusion. Lines and Lyrics add wind-flowers, seasons, and songs for Yule.

Cawein writes in a lush, musical mode, full of woods, waters, and old tales. The book is long and rich, meant for slow reading aloud. Lovers of late Romantic verse will find a poet steeped in myth, singing of nature with a full, warm voice.
16540-melchior-s-dream-and-other-tales:
Juliana Horatia Ewing gathers eight tales in this volume from the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Melchior's Dream leads, followed by The Blackbird's Nest, Friedrich's Ballad, A Bit of Green, Monsieur the Viscount's Friend, The Yew-Lane Ghosts, A Bad Habit, and A Happy Family. The book is dedicated to four brothers and four sisters.

Ewing writes for children with warmth and moral clarity, mixing fancy with home life. Her tales are short, vivid, and kind, with ghosts and dreams kept gentle. The volume shows why Ewing remains a favorite among Victorian children's writers, tender without ever turning soft.
16553-burned-bridges:
Bertrand W. Sinclair's 1919 novel opens with a first problem, a man and his mission, and a deserted cabin. Mr. Thompson begins to wonder painfully, a slip of the axe bears fruit, and a man's job for a minister, a fortune and a flitting, and partners follow. The frontispiece catches a hammering heart against a breast on page ninety-five.

Sinclair writes of the Canadian west with knowledge of camps, cabins, and hard choices. The tale mixes romance with frontier work, and its reprints through 1920 show its popularity. Readers of northern fiction will find a warm, brisk story of love and new starts.
16554-foes:
Mary Johnston's 1918 novel opens in a Scottish glen in June sunshine, where English Strickland, tutor at Glenfernie House, fishes and talks with Mother Binning at her cottage door. A rose bush grows by the door, a hen crosses the yard with her chicks, and the old woman spins as she speaks of second sight: seeing behind the here and now.

The quiet opening gives way to a tale of old foes and divided loyalties, in Johnston's full romantic style. Scotland's glens, houses, and folk speech fill the pages. Readers of her earlier hits, To Have and to Hold and Audrey, will find the same strong storytelling and vivid scene-setting here.
16576-connor-magan-s-luck-and-other-stor:
M. T. W. gathers children's stories in this 1881 Lothrop volume, opening with Connor Magan's Luck. Connor, twelve, throws his brimless hat in the air with a jubilant shout and pushes off a skiff where his father waits. Why Mammy Delphy's Baby Was Named Grief, Sammy Sealskin's Enemy, Nannette's Live Baby, and Brothers for Sale follow.

The tales are short, warm, and funny, with a child's eye for luck and trouble. A story of a clock, a legend of the salt sea, and April fools round out the set. Young readers will enjoy the old-fashioned charm, and the book suits reading aloud in family circles.
1659-the-girl-with-the-golden-eyes:
Balzac's Girl with the Golden Eyes is the third part of the Thirteen trilogy, after Ferragus and The Duchesse de Langeais. It follows Henri de Marsay, a Parisian dandy who pursues a mysterious girl with golden eyes through salons and secret houses. Dedicated to the painter Eugene Delacroix, the tale is lush with Parisian detail.

Behind the seduction lies a hidden household, a jealous guardian, and a love that ends in violence and revelation. Balzac's Paris is sensual and sinister by turns. The novella is a feverish, beautiful study of desire, secrecy, and the dark side of romantic Paris.
16599-school-church-and-home-games:
George O. Draper compiled this 1923 book of school, church, and home games for the YMCA's community recreation work, rural edition, dedicated to his father. Part one gives schoolroom and schoolyard games for primary, intermediate, and advanced pupils. Part two adds home games, ice breakers, sociables for grown-ups and young people, trick games, and stunt meets.

Draper writes for leaders who need games that work with real groups. The book is practical throughout, with clear rules and age grades. Teachers, pastors, and camp leaders will find a useful old manual of play for country communities.
1661-the-adventures-of-sherlock-holmes:
Arthur Conan Doyle's collection brings together twelve of Sherlock Holmes's best-known cases, narrated by Dr. Watson from their rooms in Baker Street. A king in disguise, a league of red-headed men, a speckled band in a locked bedroom, and a blue carbuncle swallowed by a goose all pass through Holmes's hands.

Each story shows the method at work: small marks noticed, false trails cut away, and a chain of reason that ends in a single name. The book fixed the short detective story in its classic form. It is the easiest place to start with Holmes, since every case stands alone and needs no knowledge of the novels.
16624-no-and-yes:
Mary Baker Eddy wrote this short 1919 work of Christian Science, issued by the trustees under her will in Boston. In brief chapters it answers plain questions. Is disease real? Is this faith kin to spiritism? Is it pantheist or blasphemous? Is there a personal God or devil? Has man a soul? Is sin forgiven? Is there atonement or prayer? Each head states a doubt, then gives her reply.

Eddy holds that disease is error of belief, not true being, and that harmony is the truth of life. She sets her faith apart from spiritism and theosophy and defends it against church critics. The book is a compact creed in question form, useful for readers who want her views stated short and direct.
16636-makers-of-madness-a-play-in-one-ac:
Hermann Hagedorn wrote this short play in one act and three scenes, issued by Macmillan in New York in 1914. The title points to those who drive men mad: the makers of war fever, hate, and lies in the months before the Great War. Acting rights were kept tight, as the note on the title page shows.

Hagedorn packs a sharp charge into a small frame, with few players and a fast turn from talk to dread. The play asks who bears blame when a whole folk loses its mind to war talk. It reads today as a brief, fierce warning about crowds, press, and power, and it plays well as a short stage piece or a classroom read.
16645-sermons-preached-at-brighton-third:
Frederick W. Robertson's sermons at Trinity Chapel, Brighton, fill this third series, in a new 1884 edition dedicated to his congregation of 1847 to 1853. Sermon one, preached April 28, 1850, takes the tongue from James: a little member that boasts great things, a fire that kindles a great matter. The victory of faith follows on May 5.

Robertson was famed as a preacher of rare power, and these recollections preserve his pulpit voice. The sermons are earnest, literary, and humane. Readers of Victorian preaching will find a classic series, still warm with pastoral care and moral force.
16651-the-safety-curtain-and-other-stori:
Ethel M. Dell wrote this book of short stories, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York under arrangement with Putnam's Sons. The title tale leads, followed by The Experiment, Those Who Wait, The Eleventh Hour, and The Place of Honour. The first tale opens in a crowded hall with a dancer's Dragon-Fly Dance and a great shout of applause.

Dell writes of love, risk, and honor in high romantic style, with stage, sea, and desert backdrops. Her heroines face hard choices and wait, dare, or yield with full hearts. Readers who like old romantic tales will find strong feeling, brisk plots, and neat closes, all in the popular voice of her day.
16657-the-book-of-missionary-heroes:
Basil Mathews wrote this 1922 book of missionary heroes, issued by George H. Doran in New York. A prologue calls the work a relay race, then books take up pioneers, island adventurers, and later workers. Paul, Wilfrid of Sussex, Raymond Lull, and Francis of Assisi lead, followed by the ship Duff, John Williams, Kapiolani of Hawaii, and Elikana.

Mathews tells each life as a short adventure, with seas, beaches, and new lands as its stage. He frames mission work as brave, risky, and full of hardship, not as dry church history. Young readers get stirring tales of faith at the edge of the known world, and grown readers get a clear view of how 1922 told the mission story.
16693-stories-to-tell-children-fifty-fou:
Sara Cone Bryant gathers fifty-four stories to tell children in this 1918 volume, with suggestions for telling and a graded list for dramatizing. The Little Yellow Tulip, The Cock-a-Doodle-Doo, The Cloud, The Little Red Hen, and The Gingerbread Man lead the tales. The country mouse and city mouse, Little Jack Rollaround, and Brother Rabbit's tricks follow.

Bryant, author of How to Tell Stories to Children, also treats storytelling in teaching English. The book suits teachers, parents, and librarians. Each story is short and tellable, chosen for voice, rhythm, and child delight.
1671-when-a-man-marries:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's When a Man Marries follows a young wife who meant well, from the way it began through a closed door, a tree of love. A mighty poor joke, to an omelet, a correspondents' department, and a discovery on the stairs. Flannigan's find and a roof garden add farce to the domestic comedy.

Rinehart's heroine narrates with humour and a touch of exasperation, as a new marriage meets servants, guests, and misunderstandings. The novel is light and funny. When a Man Marries is a classic Rinehart comedy of married life, and a pleasant period piece of American humour.
16726-four-weird-tales:
Algernon Blackwood gathered four strange tales in this book: a study of rebirth, a man who learns too much, a snow-bound spell, and a desert tale called Sand. Each tale starts in plain life, then slips toward a hidden world that presses close behind it. Doors left ajar, faint stirrings, and a shift in mood mark the turn.

Blackwood writes of men whose inner senses wake to forces most pass by. Dread grows not from gore but from wonder, doubt, and a sense that causes lie just out of sight. These four pieces show why he is still read by fans of weird fiction: slow dread, rich nature scenes, and a firm belief that the strange is near at hand.
16739-the-greatest-thing-in-the-world-an:
Henry Drummond wrote this book of addresses, issued by Fleming H. Revell in New York and Chicago, with copyrights in 1891 and 1898. The title address on love grew from a Sunday evening in England in 1884. Friends asked Drummond to expound a portion of Scripture. He opened his small Testament at First Corinthians, chapter thirteen, and spoke on love. Other addresses take up doubt, the changed life, and boys.

Drummond speaks in warm, plain terms, with short texts and home examples. His theme is that love, not gifts or works, is the greatest thing in the world. The book has stayed in print as a devotional classic, best read a short address at a time for its gentle, practical faith.
16759-the-chronicle-of-the-canons-regula:
Thomas a Kempis wrote this chronicle of the Canons Regular of Mount St. Agnes, here in J. P. Arthur's translation from the 1906 Kegan Paul edition. It tells how Gerard Groote first pointed out the place, how the first house was built, who the first brothers were, and how John Kempen became first prior. Food, dress, chapel, burial ground, and moves of house all get their chapters.

The chronicle is plain monastic history: poor fare, hard work, prayer, and God's care for the house. It names brothers, priors, and gifts, and it keeps the tone of a community record, not a saint's legend. Readers who want late medieval religious life from the inside will find a short, clear, and humane house history.
16766-all-on-the-irish-shore-irish-sketc:
E. OE. Somerville and Martin Ross wrote this book of Irish sketches, second impression issued by Longmans in London in 1903, with pictures by Somerville. Sketches run from a tinker's dog and Fanny Fitz's gamble to a Connemara mare and a grand filly. High tea at McKeown's, a bagman's pony, and an Irish problem follow. A fair at Bandon closes the set. The pair were known for tales of an Irish resident magistrate.

Somerville and Ross write with humor and a sharp ear for Irish speech, horses, hunts, and country folk. Each sketch stands alone, full of talk, mishap, and local color.
