Chapters carry him through a tenement, a dangerous descent, and a lawyer's advice before the round-up ends the tale. Webster wrote brisk series fiction for boys. Roy's ranch honesty, set against city sharpers, drives every chapter.
21807-the-holy-cross-and-other-tales:
Tales by Eugene Field, the Chicago newspaper poet and humorist, fill this volume first gathered in 1893. Field was loved for his children's verses and his witty columns, and his prose tales show the same mixed moods: serious, gay, and tender. Five tales, beginning with The Platonic Bassoon, were added to the original issue from his later work. Roswell Martin Field, his brother, is honored in the dedication.

The title tale, The Holy Cross, moves its company to gentle pity, as the frontispiece shows. Field writes with a light hand even on sad subjects. This fifth volume of his collected works preserves stories that first lived in newspapers. They show why readers of his day wept and smiled over the same page.
21809-second-book-of-tales:
More tales by Eugene Field make up this second book, gathered in 1896 after the author's death. The editors chose pieces left unpublished in book form, down to The Werewolf. They added eight early sketches from Culture's Garland to show his first manner. The list mixes dialect stories, fairy tales, and tender sketches of mothers and children.

Humin Natur' on the Han'bul 'nd St. Jo tells of a railroad eaten away by war, told in broad dialect. Other tales bring angels, flowers, dream-fairies, and a moon-garden for Sweet-One-Darling. Field could shift from slang to sentiment in a page. The volume, tenth in his collected works, shows the full range of the newspaper storyteller his readers loved.
21824-the-old-stone-house-and-other-stor:
An unfinished stone house in the New York woods opens this set of tales by Anna Katharine Green, first published in 1891. The narrator rides up on a house whose scaffolding was never struck and whose windows mostly lack frames. Moss creeps over the blackened front, and the place feels steeped in tragic mystery. That mystery gives the title story its pull.

The other tales, A Memorable Night, The Black Cross, A Mysterious Case, and Shall He Wed Her?, work in Green's darker vein. Green was a pioneer of the detective novel, and her gift for dread shows here in short form. Gloom, secrets, and slow reveals fill the pages. It is a moody little volume from a mistress of mystery.
21832-the-wonder-island-boys-conquest-of:
War among the island tribes drives this volume of Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys series, published in 1914. Sutoto startles the camp, and the Tuolos, Kurabus, and Illyas draw together in confederation. A council of chiefs hears the case for unity against their common foes. Oma, Uraso, and Muro give their views before the allied tribes meet in the field.

The series follows two boys and an aged professor cast away with nothing, building every tool of civilized life step by step. Finlay folds science and craft into the fighting and scouting. Each book stands alone, and this one brings the tribal wars to their climax. Boys of the day got battle, invention, and two thousand facts in one cloth binding.
21863-derrick-sterling-a-story-of-the-mi:
Coal country dangers drive this boys' novel by Kirk Munroe, Derrick Sterling: A Story of the Mines, published by Harpers in 1888. The tale opens with cries of fire in the burning breaker, where boys work above the pits. White-faced miners of the night shift crowd the slope mouth as the chapters roll on. Derrick moves through a fearful ride, a lost wander in the mine, and a plunge down an air shaft.

A fatal explosion of fire-damp, a flooded mine, and a rescue fill the later chapters. Harry the bumping-mule and Socrates the wise mine rat give relief. Munroe knew hard trades and wrote them true. The book honors the boys who worked underground, and ends with Derrick promoted and restored to daylight.
21869-immortal-memories:
Toastmaster's speeches on great writers fill Clement Shorter's Immortal Memories, talks given to literary societies and gathered in 1907. Shorter admits in his preface that the addresses pleased him to write and seemed to interest their audiences. He aims them, he says, not at fellow journalists but at Hazlitt's sensible people: men of business and of the world.

One toast recalls a dear friend who proposed it the year before and has since died. Lord Acton's famous list of the hundred best books turns up in the talk. Shorter was a tireless champion of the Brontës and of popular literature. These speeches show him at the dinner table: warm, bookish, and quotable, keeping dead authors in living company.
21927-short-cruises:
Wapping sailors and their wives scheme and blunder through W. W. Jacobs's Short Cruises, a set of comic tales published in 1906. The first story, The Changeling, opens with George Henshaw wiping his boots in a too-still house, his wife's blazing stare waiting in the kitchen. Other tales bring mixed relations, a love-knot, a dreamer, and angels' visits. Jacobs's illustrations captions alone raise a smile: soft brown eyes, sarcasm, and a mate who smiled too.

Jacobs made the Thames waterfront his comic kingdom, and these short pieces show his hand at its surest. The humor is dry, the dialogue salted with dialect, and the plots turn on small vanities. Readers who know his longer novels will find the same world in miniature, perfectly timed.
21958-frank-merriwell-s-races:
Frank Merriwell goes to the races in this 1903 number of Burt L. Standish's famous dime-novel series. Diamond walks round Frank's bay gelding on the stable floor and calls him a swift one: rangey, clean-limbed, with a courageous eye. Horse talk leads to plots, eavesdroppers, and a strong accusation against the cleanest hero in American cheap fiction.

The chapters pile on a wrestling match, a boat race, a spurned bribe, and a fight on a special train. Yale spirit and pure grit carry Frank through every trap. Standish, whose real name was Gilbert Patten, built Merriwell into a national model of the all-round college man. This volume mixes the turf with the campus, and lets Frank win both ways, honestly.
21965-preventable-diseases:
Most sickness can be stopped before it starts, argues Dr. Woods Hutchinson in Preventable Diseases, published in 1909. Hutchinson, a clinical professor of medicine in New York, calls the body a republic with its own defenses. He grants that the human machine is imperfect, beaten at points by animals and machines alike. Yet heredity, air, and habits lie in our own hands, he insists.

Chapters take up colds and how we catch them, adenoids and mouth-breathing, pneumonia, and typhoid's natural history. Tuberculosis gets two chapters as a scotched snake, not a dead one. The writing is brisk, funny, and aimed at lay readers. The book helped carry the new gospel of prevention into ordinary homes.
21979-for-name-and-fame-or-through-afgha:
A lost child grows into a soldier of the Afghan war in G. A. Henty's For Name and Fame, or Through Afghan Passes. Sam Dickson finds little Willie Gale, and the foundling's road runs from a fishing smack through shipwreck and a fight with prahus to India. Henty's preface promises that following Will through the last Afghan war will teach a country of supreme importance to the British Empire. Lord Roberts's operations frame the hero's service.

The Peiwar Kotal, the Khyber advance, the massacre at Kabul, Maiwand, and Kandahar fill the war chapters. Will saves Colonel Ripon and is carried by a bayonet in the pictures. Henty mixes a boy's rise with a campaign history. It is his classic recipe: geography and glory, taught through one lad's luck.
22014-the-peter-patter-book-of-nursery-r:
Leroy F. Jackson wrote the rhymes in The Peter Patter Book of Nursery Rhymes, first issued in 1918. Blanche Fisher Wright drew the pictures. Peter Patter himself lives on a mountain near the sun, in a home among the alders. Squirrels, crickets, bats, and his Uncle Owl bring him every rhyme he knows.

The verses that follow are new nursery rhymes rather than the old Mother Goose stock. Goats, kings, platters of brisket and batter, and small boys fill the pages. Each rhyme is short, musical, and made to be read aloud. The book went on being reprinted for decades, with its copyright renewed in 1946.
22085-sir-jagadis-chunder-bose-his-life-:
Jagadis Chunder Bose was born in Bengal in 1858, in a village in the Dacca district. He grew up at Faridpur, where his father served as a local officer. The boy who watched plants and weather there became one of India's first modern scientists. Bose won world fame for work on wireless waves and on the responses of plants to touch, light, and wounds.

Sir Jagadis Chunder Bose: His Life and Speeches combines a biography with his own addresses. The life draws on his boyhood, schooling, and struggles for a laboratory in Calcutta. The speeches let Bose argue his case himself. The volume is a period tribute to a scientist who proved an Indian could lead world research.
22087-hazel-squirrel-and-other-stories:
Howard B. Famous wrote Hazel Squirrel and Other Stories for young children who like their heroes small and furry. Hazel is a young squirrel with a bad habit of hurrying. One morning he ties his tie sideways and brushes his tail the wrong way. He even forgets the breakfast his mother left out for him.

The other stories follow woodland animals through small scrapes and small lessons. Each tale is short enough for a single reading at bedtime. Manners, kindness, and care for one's mother come wrapped in fur and whiskers. Such animal storybooks were a staple of American childhood in the early 1900s, and Hazel is a typical busy hero.
221-the-return-of-sherlock-holmes:
Strand Magazine readers in October 1903 met a detective they thought dead. This edition of Arthur Conan Doyle's Return of Sherlock Holmes presents the stories as first serialized, beginning with the Empty House. Watson, writing in spring 1894, reports the murder of Ronald Adair.

Holmes steps back from the grave to explain his Reichenbach escape and to hunt Moriarty's surviving gunman. Later Strand installments add the Norwood Builder, the Dancing Men, and the Priory School. The serial form shows how Doyle rebuilt his hero month by month. It is a treat for collectors of the original run.
22114-a-plain-cookery-book-for-the-worki:
Charles Elmé Francatelli, once cook to Queen Victoria, wrote A Plain Cookery Book for the Working Classes in 1852. Francatelli aimed his skill at the poorest kitchens in England. Every recipe counts pennies and wastes nothing. Broths, puddings, cheap cuts, and vegetables fill the little book.

He gives exact measures and plain steps a beginner can follow. Even a breakfast-cup custard is broken down spoonful by spoonful. The book was sold cheaply and pushed by reformers who hoped good cooking would fight hunger and drink. It remains a landmark of social cookery, and a sharp record of what the Victorian poor could afford to eat.
22145-a-book-of-burlesques:
H. L. Mencken, the Baltimore critic, gathered A Book of Burlesques in 1916. These short pieces mock the solemn forms of his day: plays, sermons, novels, and official prose. One sketch opens with stage directions for a suffocating room, flowers everywhere, as if it rained outside, which it isn't. The joke lands before a word of dialogue is spoken.

Mencken's targets include puritans, professors, uplifters, and literary poseurs. His sentences snap; his slang was new and shocking in 1916. The burlesques are juvenilia by his later standard, but the voice is already his. Readers meeting Mencken here meet the sage of Baltimore warming up his famous act.
22168-the-golden-spears-and-other-fairy-:
Edmund Leamy, an Irish writer of fairy tales, published The Golden Spears and Other Fairy Tales in 1911. Corinne Turner drew the pictures. The title tale takes its name from an Irish mountain. The peak is bare and grey at its top. Yet it catches the sinking sun until it gleams like a spear of gold. So the children call it the Golden Spear.

Leamy retells Irish legends and wonder tales in gentle, literary English. Kings, heroes, and fairy folk move through his pages. He wrote to keep Ireland's old stories alive for children losing them. The book belongs to the Celtic revival's nursery shelf, where myth was handed down as national treasure.
22194-spring-street-a-story-of-los-angel:
Spring Street calls itself a story of Los Angeles, and it belongs to the city's early fiction. Children shout at a wild game a few doors down the street. Suddenly they stop, warned to be quiet: a neighbour has died, and the street must hush. The narrator remembers his own childhood shock at a death nearby, struck dumb for days.

From such street scenes the novel builds its Los Angeles. Spring Street was then the city's busy financial and shopping spine. Booth and local colour fill the pages in period style. The book survives as a curiosity of regional writing, when Los Angeles was still inventing itself in fiction as fast as in fact.
22195-little-tora-the-swedish-schoolmist:
Little Tora, the Swedish Schoolmistress, and Other Stories gathers tales of Sweden for English readers. The title story concerns Tora, a young schoolmistress in a Swedish village. One scene shows a family dinner laid in state: polished silver, shining glass, porcelain, flowers, and fruit cover the table. The plenty on the table seems, at first, to be all the dinner there is.

Mrs. Woods Baker, who wrote several books of Swedish life, gathered these tales from her years in Sweden. Village customs, schools, and family pride shape the plots. Such translated collections introduced English children to Scandinavian childhood. This one keeps the quiet, moral tone of the Swedish originals.
22198-two-sides-of-the-face-midwinter-ta:
Arthur Quiller-Couch, who signed himself "Q," published Two Sides of the Face as a set of midwinter tales. Quiller-Couch was a Cornish writer, anthologist, and champion of clear English. The title story opens behind a house where fields have cut back a plantation of noble ash trees. The modern farm buildings, shabby as they are, look friendlier than the old mansion brooding above them.

That contrast of faces, cheerful front and lost dignity, runs through the tales. Ghosts, doubles, and old houses suit the midwinter season of the subtitle. Quiller-Couch writes with a storyteller's ease and a scholar's vocabulary. The collection shows his fiction at its most characteristic: Cornish air, quiet uncanniness.
22217-my-reminiscences:
Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet who won the Nobel Prize in 1913, wrote My Reminiscences about his own formation. The English version reached readers through a translator who warns of the task's difficulty. Tagore's manner and matter, the translator says, combine in a way no second language easily carries. The effort was ventured anyway, from admiration for the original.

Tagore recalls a sheltered childhood in a great Calcutta house, servants, lessons, and early verses. He writes of his father's travels, his first songs, and the slow birth of a poet. The book is gentle, musical, and self-knowing. It remains the pleasantest door into Tagore's world for English readers.
22226-the-whispering-spheres:
The Whispering Spheres appeared in Comet magazine in July 1941, in that short-lived pulps attempt at wonder. An alien life form advances on Earth in the tale's opening picture, something like an inner eye glowing for a moment. In a factory town the whistle stays silent when it should blow. Three short blasts meant fire; one long blast, a breakdown; five toots, a layoff — but now nothing sounds.

The spheres whisper, and men must learn what the sound means before worse follows. The story works the classic pulp vein of first contact and strange invasion. Comet lasted only five issues, and tales like this one are nearly all that remains of it.
22278-a-master-of-mysteries:
L. T. Meade and Robert Eustace wrote A Master of Mysteries together, joining girls' fiction's queen to a master of scientific crime. Meade opens with a visitor laughing at his friend's special hobby. Yesterday, he admits, it struck him that those strange experiences might help him in a difficulty. The master of mysteries is that friend: a man whose trade is solving what looks supernatural.

Case by case, the tales explain hauntings, curses, and impossible crimes by science and patience. Eustace, a doctor, supplied the technical tricks; Meade supplied the storytelling. Their partnership fed the magazines with a new kind of detective tale. This set is an early, enjoyable sample of the scientific mystery story.
22290-me-and-nobbles:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote 'Me and Nobbles' as a story for children about a small narrator and her dog. The book opens inside a grand, gloomy house. The drawing room is awe-inspiring, its blinds nearly always down, with a musty, unused scent that says its grandeur is not for daily use. The library is gloomier still, with stained glass and dingy books lining the walls.

Through that gloom the child and Nobbles make their own cheerful world. Le Feuvre, whose Teddy's Button sold by the million, wrote faith and feeling in a child's own voice. This slighter tale shows her domestic vein: a dog, a lonely child, and a house learning to be a home.
22315-slain-by-the-doones:
R. D. Blackmore, famed for Lorna Doone, also wrote Slain by the Doones. The tales return to the wild West Country world of the Doone outlaws. One passage recalls a hard fanatic known as the Brewer.

The narrator's father, disgusted with England and banished from her, lost all his property. He took service on the Continent in exile. There he wandered for many years, until the throne was restored. Such backstory gives these short tales their sweep of loss and loyalty. Blackmore mixes family ruin, old violence, and moorland scenery into compact stories for readers who wanted more of the Doones.
22320-oldtown-fireside-stories:
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Oldtown Fireside Stories from the tales of old New England. The setting is a hearth, with crickets filling each pause. Aged tellers pass their memories down to the young by firelight.

The stories cover early life, war, and adventure in the forest. They tell of Native captivities and escapes, and of bears and panthers. Rattlesnakes appear, along with witches, wizards, and strange dreams. Appearances and providences round out the stock of tales. Stowe, famous for a very different book, here preserves village storytelling. Readers hear how old communities kept their past alive through winter nights.
22338-the-impossibles:
The Impossibles is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its hero, Malone, is caught lying curled up and daydreaming. He drifts toward a wonderful dream and hates to interrupt it.

In that dream stands a girl more wonderful than anything he had imagined. She has big blue eyes and long blonde hair. Her figure, Malone thinks, shames the average pin-up girl. Such a start mixes fantasy with a wry, male daydream voice. The title hints that impossible things drive the plot. Readers get a light period tale where longing and the impossible meet, told with a wink.
22357-danger-and-other-stories:
Danger and Other Stories gathers short fiction preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its title story opens with a summons to a royal Presence. Horli has been called in, and the narrator goes with him.

Horli knew the narrator had clear ideas on England's weak points. He also had schemes for taking advantage of those points. Only four men sat at that meeting. They were the King, the Foreign Secretary, Admiral Horli, and the narrator. Such a start promises invasion plans and high stakes. The other stories share the volume's taste for risk. Readers get compact tales built around danger at sea and court.
224-a-pair-of-blue-eyes:
Elfride Swancourt, a rector's daughter on the Cornish coast, loves two men and loses her way. Thomas Hardy's Pair of Blue Eyes follows Elfride from first love with Stephen Smith to a later passion for Henry Knight. Church restoration, cliffs, and social rank frame the tale.

Hardy's preface notes the craze for restoring churches that reached even remote western parishes. Elfride's blue eyes and quick heart draw both suitors toward tragedy. The novel's forty chapters build slowly to a bleak end. It shows Hardy's early power with love and fate.
22475-tortoises:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Tortoises, a small book of poems on the tortoise. Lawrence watched these creatures closely during his years in Italy. The opening poem addresses a baby tortoise in tender terms.

Voiceless little bird, he calls the resting creature fondly. Its head rests half out of its wimple in slow dignity. Alone, with no sense of being alone, it pauses eternally. Hence, he writes, it is six times more solitary. It pitches its little round house through immemorial ages. Such lines turn a small animal into a figure of endurance. Readers get Lawrence's intense, wondering nature poetry at close range.
22519-christmas-every-day-and-other-stor:
Christmas Every Day and Other Stories, dated 1892, opens with a father's tale. A papa rouses himself from his writing with great effort. His little girl wants a story before anything else will do.

Well then, he says, he will tell about a certain girl. She was the little girl who wanted Christmas every day. How would you like that, he asks his daughter slyly. The wish granted becomes the tale's comic and moral engine. Too much of a good thing teaches its own sharp lesson. The other stories share that playful, instructive spirit. William Dean Howells wrote the title tale. It remains a holiday favorite about gifts, greed, and enough.
22522-artists-wives:
Alphonse Daudet wrote Artists' Wives, a set of stories about creative men's marriages. Daudet knew Parisian art and literary life from inside its circles. One husband's outburst shows the book's dramatic, teasing tone.

You dare say that, he cries, and the lamp stays lit! The walls, he marvels, do not fall on your head. For two hours, he protests, she has shown him enviable happiness. It is the very happiness she forbids him to enjoy himself. Such scenes probe what artists demand of their wives. Sacrifice, patience, and rivalry run through these marriages. Daudet treats them with wit and a touch of cruelty. Readers get Paris studio life in sharp little portraits.
22559-the-day-of-the-boomer-dukes:
The Day of the Boomer Dukes is a time-travel story with a bored hero. Its narrator peers back and back through the centuries seeking interest. He finds no time better than his own to live in.

Back he peered as far as the Numbered Years themselves. The twenty-eighth century was boredom unendurable to his searching eye. The twenty-sixth was a morass of dullness without relief. Twenty-fifth and twenty-fourth centuries offered the same tedium everywhere. Wherever he looked, the narrator complains, tedium was the finding. That comic despair drives his hunt through future history for excitement. Frederik Pohl wrote the tale. Readers get future ages reviewed by their toughest critic.
22608-a-book-for-all-readers-an-aid-to-t:
A Book for All Readers is a practical guide to forming, using, and preserving libraries, public and private. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Written when public libraries were spreading across America, it taught new librarians and home collectors how to choose, arrange, and care for books.

The author calms the fear that books multiply beyond all use. Truly important books, the text reflects, form only a small share of the mass; most books repeat what has already been written, many times over. Originality is the rarest of literary qualities. Around that sober thought, the manual builds advice on selection and upkeep. It is a handbook from the heroic age of library building.
22660-king-candaules:
King Candaules is a tale by Théophile Gautier, the French master of lush, pictorial prose, set in the ancient kingdom of Lydia. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its subject is the old story told by Herodotus: a king so proud of his wife's beauty that he shows her, unseen, to a favored courtier, with ruin to follow.

The sample paints the royal wedding day in Gautier's richest manner. The road for the procession lies strewn with fine yellow sand, while brazen tripods send up smoke of cinnamon and spikenard, the only clouds allowed in the pure azure sky. Such splendor is the trap's bait. Readers who love gorgeous surfaces with a cold fate beneath them will find Gautier in full flower.
22673-plantation-sketches:
Plantation Sketches is a set of reminiscences of the Old South, written as that world faded from living memory. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its opening sets the tone: as the New South rises with all its changes and improvements, hearts that still cling to the old order look sadly backward.

The Old South, the writer sighs, fades into dimness. Soon it will survive only in the memory of the few who knew it. Sketches of plantation life, its people, and its customs follow from that elegiac start. Such books were written in great numbers after the Civil War, and they must be read with care, since nostalgia softens what slavery made brutal. As a record of how the region chose to remember itself, the volume is revealing.
22682-secret-armies:
Secret Armies is John L. Spivak's exposé of fascist and propaganda networks inside the United States, published on the eve of the Second World War. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Spivak, a muckraking reporter, devoted his pen for years to uncovering evidence of fascist activity in America.

The book's framing credits his reporting with setting off several official investigations into un-American, foreign-run propaganda. Secret Armies is presented as the climax of those exposures. Its pages name agents, front groups, and money trails as Spivak traced them. The book belongs to the alarmed literature of the late 1930s, when Americans first reckoned with organized extremist movements at home. It remains a document of that awakening.
22683-practical-pointers-for-patentees:
Practical Pointers for Patentees is a 1901 guidebook for inventors who hoped to profit from their ideas. The catalog record names no author. America's patent system promised that a good invention could make its maker's fortune. A small industry of guides arose in answer. They explained the path from workshop to patent office to market.

The opening insists there can be no doubt that demand for inventions of merit, ready to sell at a fair profit, is real. Never, the writer claims, was the demand for worthwhile inventions so great as at the present time. Around that promise the book builds cautions and steps: searching prior patents, drafting claims, and avoiding sharp dealers. It is a period handbook from the golden age of the lone inventor.
2278-condensed-novels-new-burlesques:
Bret Harte sharpens his parodist's knife again in this second batch of condensed novels, mocking famous authors by squeezing their styles into tiny plots. New Burlesques takes aim at the mannerisms of popular novelists, with heroes, heroines, and villains reduced to their most recognizable tics. The humor depends on knowing the originals, but the jokes land even without them.

Harte's gift for mimicry shows in every page: dialects, melodrama, and moralizing all get the same brisk treatment. The collection is short, sharp, and very much of its literary moment. Fans of parody will enjoy seeing Victorian fiction sent up by one of its own.
22782-the-buddha-a-drama-in-five-acts-an:
The Buddha is a drama in five acts and four interludes, telling the life of Siddhartha Gautama in verse for the stage. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Western writers of the era, stirred by translations of Buddhist texts, repeatedly tried the Buddha's story in poetry and drama.

The opening scene is set with a painter's care: a tropical garden in Kapilavastu, mountains behind, and in the distance, the Himalayas lift their snow-capped peaks. A marble bench stands among bushes. Behind it rises the Raja's palace entrance. At the left stands a fortified gate with its guard house. All is built in antique Indian style. From that luxury the prince's great renunciation proceeds. The play offers the Buddha's life as pageant and meditation.
2281-the-heritage-of-dedlow-marsh-and-ot:
Bret Harte returns to California in this collection of tales anchored by the title story of a marshland inheritance. The Heritage of Dedlow Marsh and Other Tales mixes courtroom disputes, lost heirs, and frontier romance, with Harte's familiar blend of pathos and dry wit. Each story turns on a document, a debt, or a disputed claim.

The marsh itself, foggy and treacherous, gives the title tale its mood. Other pieces range across mining camps and coastal towns. The volume shows Harte in his later manner, polished and fond of his old territory.
22818-an-alphabet-of-celebrities:
Oliver Herford wrote and pictured An Alphabet of Celebrities, printed in Boston in November 1899. Bertram Grosvenor Goodhue designed the border and initial letters, and E. Bird handled the end papers and cover. The result is a small, handsome gift book built around the alphabet itself.

Letter by letter, famous names of the day get brief, witty treatment in verse and drawing. Herford was known for light satire, and the fun here lies in seeing which celebrity he pairs with each letter and what joke he makes of them. The book doubles as a snapshot of who counted as famous in 1899. Many of its stars have faded, and that fading is half the charm now.
22829-no-animal-food-and-nutrition-and-d:
Meat is the enemy in No Animal Food, a health manual pairing arguments on nutrition and diet with vegetable recipes. Its authorities speak bluntly. One quoted physician warns against cheating. Add butter, cream, cheese, eggs, or lard to vegetables, he says, and the meal stops being vegetarian. It becomes mixed fare, with effects much like meat.

Readers get both doctrine and dinner. The early pages press the case that humans thrive without animal food, drawing on doctors and reform journals. The later pages turn practical, with recipes meant to prove the diet workable at an ordinary table. The book captures the vegetarian movement of its day at full confidence. Modern readers can test its claims, and its menus, for themselves.
2284-animal-heroes:
Ernest Thompson Seton, the naturalist who helped found the Boy Scouts, tells true-to-life stories of animals who showed courage, loyalty, and cunning. Animal Heroes follows dogs, horses, wolves, and other creatures through rescues, wars, and wilderness trials, each tale grounded in Seton's observation of animal behavior. The stories avoid sentimentality in favor of fact.

Seton's woodcraft knowledge gives every episode its texture: tracks, scents, and habits all matter to the outcome. Young readers learn natural history while cheering for animal protagonists. The book remains a classic of animal literature for children.
22885-hindu-gods-and-heroes:
East meets West by design in Hindu Gods and Heroes, part of a series meant to build goodwill and understanding between the two. The editors state their aim plainly in the front matter. Their small books would serve as ambassadors, following, in their own sphere, the highest example in the land.

Inside, the gods and heroes of India take the stage in retelling and explanation. English readers of the period often knew Hindu religion only through mission reports and rumor. A sympathetic survey, written to be read by general readers, filled a real gap. The volume keeps a respectful, introductory tone throughout. It remains useful as both a primer on its subject and a record of early cross-cultural publishing.
22886-cinderella-in-the-south-twenty-fiv:
A barroom question opens Cinderella in the South, Arthur Shearly Cripps's set of twenty-five South African tales. What's the good of him, the bar-tender asks, of a man who might explain how the Ruins came to be. A man who could explain the great ruins, he reckons, might earn a handsome monthly cheque for the knowledge alone.

Cripps lived in Southern Africa as a missionary priest, and his tales grow from that ground. Settlers, Africans, ruins, and veld talk fill the pages, with the great stone ruins of the region haunting several stories. His sympathy often ran against settler opinion of his day. The tales preserve a voice both inside and uneasy within colonial Africa, which gives them interest beyond their plots.
22891-simple-simon-silhouette-series:
Simple Simon meets the pieman in this little silhouette picture book for children. The hosted text presents the old nursery rhyme in the Silhouette Series format, where black paper-cut style figures act out the verses against the page. Simon's simple questions and the pieman's plain answers carry the whole joke.

Silhouette books were a cheap, cheerful staple of the nursery shelf. Their stark black shapes let even very young readers follow the story in pictures alone. Simon, the famous fool of rhyme, asks to taste the wares first and pay later, which never ends well for him. The charm lies in economy. A few lines, a few shapes, and a rhyme children have repeated for centuries.
22893-pygmalion-s-spectacles:
A philosopher argues about sight itself in Pygmalion's Spectacles. Sensations are mental phenomena, he insists. They exist in our minds. How, then, do we know the objects themselves do not exist only there too? That wall is never truly seen, he tells his listener. What reaches us is a visual sensation, and the mind supplies the rest.

Out of that argument grows one of early science fiction's most retold inventions, spectacles that make imagined scenes feel real. The story, first printed in the 1930s, plays with virtual experience long before the term existed. Its talk stays lively because the stakes stay personal. Readers who enjoy ideas dressed as conversation will find a small classic of the form.
22939-the-gypsies:
Charles G. Leland reports a discovery in The Gypsies, published in 1882. The Romanies of the East, he claims, speak a language much like the Gypsy speech of England, in vocabulary and in the slang of the roads. He learned this, he says, from a Hindu man who had himself been a Gypsy in his native land.

Leland traveled, listened, and wrote down lore, tales, and spells as insiders shared them. His book ranges across countries, always chasing the thread of Romany language and custom. Modern scholars treat parts of it cautiously, since Leland loved a good story. Yet few Victorian writers took Gypsy life so seriously. The book remains a rich, flawed, firsthand record of its subject.
22998-janet-of-the-dunes:
Harriet T. Comstock pits Janet against Cap'n Billy in Janet of the Dunes, published in 1907. Facing Janet undoes Cap'n Billy completely. He cannot meet her eyes and still hope to win an argument with her. Honest and simple as he is, he means to hold his course all the same, if she will let him..

The dunes of the title frame a Long Island fishing community, where Janet's will meets older men's custom. Comstock wrote regional fiction steeped in salt air and plain speech. Romance and stubbornness share the helm here. The book rewards readers who like their love stories weather-beaten, with the sea doing half the talking.
23051-the-two-shipmates:
A clever little vessel anchors The Two Shipmates. The little vessel nearly knows her own way through the harbor mouth. Her master knows it better than most traders using the port, and young Ralph Michelmore, his mate, is learning it fast.

Master and mate give the story its pair, age and youth working one small trade together. Sea tales for boys ran on such partnerships, where the junior learns seamanship and character in equal doses. Storms, cargoes, and harbor rivalries supply the incidents. The writing keeps a affectionate eye on the ship herself, treated as a third shipmate. Readers who like their adventure salted but wholesome will find this a snug berth.
23068-my-first-cruise-and-other-stories:
A prank at sea starts My First Cruise and Other Stories. The young narrator laughed just to keep the others company, thinking the joke was over. The crew seized him before he understood the joke. A handkerchief blinded him, and they lashed him spread-eagled in the rigging, arms and legs stretched wide. Then all fell silent.

Initiation, storms, and shipboard society fill this set of sea tales told from a boy's berth. The cruise teaches the green hand what books cannot, at the cost of a few such jokes. Collections like this one fed the great demand for naval yarns. Their value now is double, entertainment then, evidence now, of how the sailing services raised their boys.
23070-clara-maynard-or-the-true-and-the-:
An old sailor loves his yacht in Clara Maynard, or The True and the False, a tale of the times. Two men and a boy crew her, and she measures barely twenty-five tons. Even so, her owner swears he would take her round the world without a moment's doubt, if need arose.

Yachts and character tests give the tale its twin engines. Clara's story sorts the true from the false, as the subtitle promises, among suitors, friends, and fortunes. The sea scenes carry the freest writing, salt air clearing the drawing room's plots. Fiction of this school aimed to improve while it entertained, and the yacht chapters show the method at its best, adventure first, moral riding quietly astern.
23071-the-rival-crusoes:
An editor revives a girlhood book in The Rival Crusoes. Agnes Strickland, already known to readers, wrote the tale in her teens, the editor explains, more than fifty years before this reprint. He remembers the intense delight with which he read it in his boyhood, and was lately surprised to find it so long out of print.

Two castaways compete where Defoe's hero stood alone, and rivalry turns survival into sport and spite. Strickland, later a famous historian of queens, wrote this juvenile Robinsonade in her teens. The reprint frames it as a rediscovery, an old favorite rescued for new boys. Shipwreck fiction rarely shows its roots so plainly. Here readers can watch the Crusoe formula being handed down, girl author to boy readers.
2308-bunyan-characters-3rd-series:
Alexander Whyte, the Scottish preacher, continues his studies of John Bunyan's characters in this third series of lectures. Bunyan Characters takes figures from The Pilgrim's Progress and other works, treating each as a portrait of a spiritual type: the fearful, the faithful, the backsliding, and the steadfast. Whyte's pulpit style is warm, learned, and direct.

The lectures work as both literary criticism and devotion, unpacking Bunyan's allegory for ordinary readers. They show why Bunyan's people still feel alive centuries on. Readers interested in Bunyan or in Victorian preaching will find much to ponder.
23112-the-kitchen-cat-and-other-tales:
A child watches the street from high windows in The Kitchen Cat and Other Tales. From her high window, street traffic below shrinks to toys. Iron bars stop her leaning out for a better view. Her whole world is the facing row of houses and a strip of sky between chimney pots.

Amy Walton wrote these tales for children of the London streets and the houses above them. A kitchen cat, caged views, and small kindnesses carry her stories in the manner of the period's city tales for the young. The barred window does quiet work, childhood observed and confined at once. The collection keeps a tender, observant eye throughout.
23114-our-frank-and-other-stories:
A tired walker climbs home in Our Frank and Other Stories. A friend's talk cheered the first stretch of the walk home. After good-nights at the village edge came the steep chalky hill road. Each step up it tired her more, and the basket dragged heavier with every yard.

Village effort and village kindness fill this collection of tales. Frank, the title's hero, belongs to the world of that chalky road, where small earnings and large duties meet. The stories were written for readers who knew such roads themselves, and they honor endurance without dressing it up. Plain settings, plain people, and carefully kept sympathy make the volume a fair sample of its shelf.
23130-black-white-and-gray-a-story-of-th:
A cat hides in Black, White, and Gray, a story of three homes. At play today, the children spotted a white coat in a dusky hiding place. Madam the cat would rather have stayed hidden. Still, she accepted discovery calmly, even when Dennis reached in gently and drew out her black kitten.

Kittens sort the three homes of the title by color and fortune in this tale for young readers, credited to Amy Walton. A white cat, a black kitten, and the gray shades between carry a gentle plot about kindness to animals. Walton wrote many such stories for the era's children's lists. The hiding scene shows her method, small creatures, soft hands, and morals that arrive as naturally as the kittens do.
23171-the-tipster-1901-from-wall-street-:
Edwin Lefèvre studies a honest face in The Tipster, dated 1901, from Wall Street Stories. A great tenderness for the customer rises in Gilmartin, the narrator says, since the man's own credulity stings the lie out of the lie. Relief smiles on the tipster's lips. Three-and-thirty, pleasant in face and voice, he breathes health and an easy conscience. Honesty, it seems, shines in his eyes. People liked to shake hands with him.

A tipster with an easy conscience is Wall Street's perfect animal, and Lefèvre, the Street's great storyteller, dissects him gently. Tips, credulity, and the commission on both fill the tale. Lefèvre later wrote Reminiscences of a Stock Operator, the traders' bible. This early story shows the same eye at work, watching a smile do the work of a prospectus.
23250-the-skeleton-on-round-island-from-:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Skeleton on Round Island comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories. A hard-bitten lake traveller tells what hunger on the ice means. Sometimes, he says, he waits two or three days for a chance to move, drawing his belt in tighter as he waits.

Ice floes can carry a man miles, since they all drift east down the lakes when they start. He has landed on the far side of Drummond that way. But travel with a woman along, he adds, is different. Readers get a stark winter tale of ice, hunger, and hard choices.
23257-clair-de-lune-a-play-in-two-acts-a:
Michael Strange's Clair de Lune, from 1921, is a play in two acts and six scenes. Its talk is polished and teasing. One character, asked a question, glances about the room and remarks that everyone looks very much in tune with the Almighty, as if He had been telling them secrets.

The same speaker confesses a lasting weakness: a prey to the desire to hear what is said just before entering a room, and just after leaving it. Strange builds scenes from such drawing-room wit. Readers get a slight, elegant drama where conversation, curiosity, and social poise carry the action.
2327-some-short-stories-by-henry-james:
Henry James gathers five of his finest short tales in this volume, from the devoted servant of Brooksmith to the artists and patrons of The Real Thing. Some Short Stories by Henry James shows the master in miniature: social observation, moral ambiguity, and sentences that coil around their subjects. Each story turns on a small social fact with large consequences.

The collection suits readers who want James without committing to a long novel. Its pieces reward slow reading and rereading. For an introduction to James's art, few books serve better.
23310-bird-stories-and-dog-stories:
This children's book, printed in Cincinnati with pictures, gathers short stories of birds and dogs for young readers. A bird soldier fires a tiny cannon in play, and the narrator warns him not to kill himself or anyone else in his game.

Other tales follow dogs and birds in kind, funny adventures, each with a gentle moral. The book was made for reading aloud, with pictures to hold a child's eye and stories short enough for bedtime. Short tales suit reading aloud, with pictures to hold a child's eye. Beside the bird soldier stand stories titled The Canary and The Lost Boy.
23350-cecily-parsley-s-nursery-rhymes:
Beatrix Potter wrote and drew this small picture book of nursery rhymes, printed in nineteen twenty two. Cecily Parsley, who brews good ale for gentlemen in a pen, leads a set of short rhymes made for very young children to hear and repeat.

Geese that wander upstairs, pigs that go to market or stay home, and other farm folk fill the pages in turn, each rhyme paired with a picture. The verse stays short and easy, with a lilt that suits reading aloud at bedtime. Potter keeps the fun gentle and the scenes plain, so a child can follow the words and the drawings side by side.
23380-fighting-the-flames:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote this tale of the London fire brigade in the days before motors and phones, when horse drawn engines raced to fires and men pumped by hand. The alarm came by a runner to the station, and nearby stations were called so a district could get fuller cover.

Inside the action, firemen climb ladders, hunt through smoke for trapped folk, and carry them down with plain gear, at great risk to their own lives. A floating engine that serves fires by the river adds colour to the scenes. Ballantyne wraps a good story around true detail of brigade life, so young readers learn how fires were fought and why firemen were held in such high regard.
23406-dog-of-st-bernard-and-other-storie:
McLoughlin Brothers printed this Natural History picture book in oil colours, opening with the dogs of St. Bernard in the high Alps. Deep snow hangs loose on the slopes, avalanches roar into the plains, and storms block the passes so that travellers perish and lie buried in snow.

High on the mountain stands the convent of St. Bernard, home to the famed dogs trained to search the snow for lost folk. Other short stories follow, each with a picture, giving young readers plain facts about beasts and kind deeds. The book suits small children learning animal lore, with its clear text, bright plates, and tales of rescue that praise courage and care for strangers.
23409-acadia-or-a-month-with-the-blue-no:
Frederic S. Cozzens wrote this eighteen fifty nine travel book about a month spent among the Blue Noses, the folk of Nova Scotia. His opening verse calls Acadia a land weary souls have sighed for and heroic hearts have died for, yet one no settler has applied for, a joke that sets the tone.

Cozzens tours towns, shores, and farms, sketching Acadian faces, dress, and manners with a humourist's eye, helped by plates that show figures in antique dress. The book mixes road talk, local lore, and gentle satire, giving readers a lively, personal view of a province then little known to Americans. It reads less as a guide than as a month of company with a witty traveller.
23431-naughty-puppies:
Uncle Toby's series gave young children this rhymed tale of two puppies, Tiny and Toodles, who get into scrape after scrape like foolish noodles. Tiny, a brownish dog with a cunning eye, leads, while white Toodles, bright eyed, does whatever Tiny bids him.

Their tricks bring scoldings from their parents, and a bold plan to fight the turkey cock ends in flight when the bird answers with a gobble and a lecture from his beak. The verse stays bouncy and easy, with pictures to match each mishap. Small readers will laugh at the pups' pluck and fright, and learn, without a sermon, that bold plans often end in a chase home.
23433-the-kitten-s-garden-of-verses:
Oliver Herford wrote and drew this nineteen eleven book of kitten verses, printed by Charles Scribner's Sons. A kitten moves through a garden year, from winter and summer to rain, shadows, and night, with poems on the lion, the milk jug, and a happy thought along the way.

Herford's verse stays light and playful, with a cat's eye view of small wonders: a shadow that follows, a jug that tempts, a garden that changes with the light. His own pictures add to the joke, giving the kitten a face and a pose for each mood. Children who love cats will enjoy the rhymes aloud, while grown readers will catch the gentle wit tucked inside the fun.
23438-a-ribband-of-blue-and-other-bible-:
J. Hudson Taylor, of the China Inland Mission, wrote these Bible studies as a companion to his earlier books on union, communion, separation, and service. The title study takes up the closing passage of Numbers, chapter fifteen, where God sets out offerings and commands a ribband of blue.

Taylor moves through burnt offerings, vows, and free will gifts, stressing that no gift counts unless it matches what God appointed, in the spirit of not my will but thine. Other studies follow in the same devout, practical vein, aimed at readers who want Scripture applied to daily conduct. The book suits those who like plain, earnest exposition, with each passage turned toward prayer, obedience, and trust.
23446-picturesque-germany-first-series:
This first series of Picturesque Germany gathers photographs and short notes on German places, people, and art. Goethe, born at Frankfurt on the Main and dead at Weimar, opens the set in a Stieler portrait, with his Weimar castle room and a bust of Schiller beside it.

Frankfurt streets follow, with the Holy Ghost fountain and a cathedral tower whose base was laid centuries past. Then the Porta Nigra at Trier, a Roman gate on the Moselle from the fourth century, follows. Each plate pairs a view with a plain caption, so a reader can tour without leaving home. The volume suits armchair travellers and lovers of old photographs, offering Germany as the camera saw it in an age before colour and crowds.
23456-more-dollies:
Ruth Cobb and Richard Hunter made this Dumpy Book for Children, number twenty five in the series, as a follow up to Dollies. Short rhymes introduce one dolly after another, each with a picture and a trait to remember.

Ping Pong sings a song of racquet and ball and dares the reader to catch him. Uncle Jujuba loves sugar cane from his youth in South Carolina. Blue Coat carries a candle for night risers. Punch bears a hunch and a rose red nose. A shepherdess watches her sheep. The verse stays bouncy and brief, made for pointing, naming, and reading aloud. Small children will love meeting the whole doll family in turn.
23462-more-russian-picture-tales:
Valery Carrick wrote these Russian picture tales, translated by Nevill Forbes and printed in nineteen fourteen and nineteen twenty by Frederick A. Stokes. Ten tales fill the book, each with pictures: the cock and the bean, the goat and the ram, the hungry wolf, the peasant and the bear, and the dog and the cock.

King Frost, the bear's paw, the bear and the old man's daughters, the straw ox, and the fox and the blackbird complete the set. The first tale shows the pattern: a cock finds a bean, chokes on it, and lies gasping until help comes in a chain of favours. Carrick's tales mix wit, greed, and kindness in beast form, and Forbes keeps the English plain. Children will love the pictures and the folk humour, rooted in Russian village lore.
23464-a-life-of-william-shakespeare-with:
Sidney Lee wrote this life of William Shakespeare, in a fourth edition of eighteen ninety nine from Smith, Elder, with portraits and facsimiles. Parentage and birth open the book, from the poet's ancestry and his father's Stratford trade to his mother, his birth and baptism in April fifteen sixty four, and his alleged birthplace.

Childhood, schooling, money troubles, a visit by Queen Elizabeth to Kenilworth, withdrawal from school, and marriage to Anne Hathaway of Shottery follow, with documents and pictures to back each step. Lee writes with scholarly care, weighing legend against record at every turn. Readers who want a solid, readable Shakespeare life, built on evidence rather than on myth, will find this a lasting standard.
23490-pickwickian-studies:
Percy Fitzgerald, author of a history of Pickwick and books on Pickwickian manners and Bozland, wrote these eighteen ninety nine studies of Dickens's Pickwick Papers and the places behind them. The Great White Horse at Ipswich opens the book, an inn still little changed from the days when Mr. Pickwick put up there.

Fitzgerald recalls the lady in the yellow curl papers, the double bedded room, and the farce like fun that made readers' jaws ache. He then ranges over Ipswich churches, old houses, and the Tacket Street theatre where Garrick first played. Dickens lovers will enjoy the blend of literary gossip, local lore, and close reading. That reading treats Pickwick not as a mere book but as a map of real towns, inns, and stage memories.
23533-a-war-time-journal-germany-1914-an:
Lady Jephson wrote this war time journal of Germany in nineteen fourteen, with German travel notes, printed in London in nineteen fifteen by Elkin Mathews. The journal opens the book, followed by notes on fellow travellers, Mainz cathedral, Schlangenbad, Liebenstein, and Treves.

German newspaper pictures, captioned in the book, show how the Englishman makes war and how England finds help troops in Canada and Polynesia. They also show how, but not in London, the German idea of a Canadian or an Australian took shape. Jephson writes as a traveller caught by war, sharp eyed and wry about both sides. Readers of Great War history will find a lively, personal record of Germany at war's start, seen through travel, talk, and wartime cartoons.
23542-side-show-studies:
Francis Metcalfe wrote these side show studies in nineteen hundred six, with many amusing drawings by Oliver Herford, for the Outing Publishing Company. The liberty of Franz and the rebellion of Fuzzy Wuzzy open the set, followed by the bite of a rattler, the amorous baboon, and feeding the serpents.

A lioness skirt dance, an inconsiderate python, an animal barometer, a star lion, an interrupted temperance meeting, a kalsomined elephant, a hypnotic bear, and the tragedy of the tigers fill the rest. Madame Morelli, pretty and poised, leads the first tale's show folk. Metcalfe writes the midway with humour and a showman's eye, praising the beasts and their keepers alike. Readers who love circus lore will enjoy the tales as a backstage tour of a vanished show world.
23573-the-battle-of-bayan-and-other-batt:
James Edgar Allen, a war correspondent, and John J. Reidy wrote this history of the Moro campaign from April to December nineteen hundred two, eight months of service in the lake region of Mindanao. Printed in Manila, the book records events as they happened, with letters of praise from the President, Major General Adna R. Chaffee, and others.

The Battle of Bayan leads a set of battles, marches, and skirmishes against Moro fighters, told with a correspondent's eye for ground, troops, and action. Readers of Philippine war history will find a first hand, if period bound, record of a hard colonial campaign, written close to events and proud of its men. The letters add an official seal to a book that is part history, part report from the field.
23602-won-from-the-waves:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this late life tale, one of his very best, opening on a gloomy evening at a rough wooden pier at the mouth of a small river. Fishermen stand at the pier end as thick mist drives in from the German Ocean, hiding all beyond a few hundred fathoms. Dark leaden waves break lazily with a sullen roar that warns of a heavy gale.

Swimming feats, wrecks, rescues, and a hero won from the waves fill the book, with page turning incident at every turn. Kingston, near the end of his long career, writes with undimmed warmth for young readers who love the sea. Fans of his work will find this a fitting late triumph, a tale of shore, storm, and courage that earns its title again and again.
23613-las-casas-the-apostle-of-the-indie:
Alice J. Knight, a deaconess in the Protestant Episcopal Church of America, wrote this nineteen seventeen life of Las Casas, the apostle of the Indies, for the Neale Publishing Company. A frontispiece portrait of Bartolome de Las Casas opens the book, dedicated to Bishop Robert Lewis Paddock.

Chapters trace Bartolome the youth, a bit of history, a new world, a new life, disappointments, and knights of the golden spur. The pearl coast, the cloister, the land of war, bishop of Chiapa, revolt in Chiapa, and days at court follow. Knight writes for general readers, with a churchwoman's admiration for a friar who defended Native peoples. Those who want a short, readable Las Casas life, from youth to bishop, will find this a warm, accessible portrait.
23626-the-chemistry-properties-and-tests:
John Mastin, a London science writer, published this handbook in 1911 for readers who wanted to know what makes a stone precious and how to tell a real gem from a fake. It opens by asking what counts as precious at all, since fashion and rarity change over time. Then it moves through how stones form in the earth and what gives them color and shine.

Later chapters set out practical tests: hardness, weight, light effects, and the tricks used to improve poor stones, from gentle heat to chemical baths and X-rays. Jewelers, collectors, and students of gems will find here a clear, working guide to sorting, naming, and judging stones by evidence rather than by eye alone.
23634-italian-popular-tales:
Thomas Frederick Crane, professor of Romance languages at Cornell, gathered these Italian popular tales in eighteen eighty five, for Houghton, Mifflin, in a Riverside Press edition dedicated to Giuseppe Pitre. Growing interest in Europe's folk tales, Crane writes in his preface, led him to offer Italy's tales to general readers and to students of story alike.

Footnotes moved to paragraph ends and endnotes gathered at chapter ends aid the scholar, while the tales themselves, of kings, peasants, beasts, and saints, charm the casual reader. Crane's selection shows Italy's tale wealth in full: wit, wonder, cruelty, and kindness in village form. Folklore lovers will value the book as a classic English gateway to Italian oral lore, still readable and still rich.
23664-flamsted-quarries:
Mary E. Waller published this novel in 1910, opening not in a quarry but on Manhattan, where the daily drama of immigrant arrival still played out before the eye. From there the story turns to a girl raised in the world of the stage. She is a child from the vaudeville, whose singing — verse after verse without pause — wins the hearts of those who hear her.

Her path leads to the quarry town of Flamsted, to home soil, to work, and to a love tested by pride and fault, with Champney Googe kneeling before Aileen crying unworthy. Waller, who also wrote The Wood-Carver of Lympus, gives readers a warm, earnest tale of talent, toil, and the people who labor in stone.
23667-woodland-tales:
Ernest Thompson Seton, chief of the Woodcraft League of America, published Woodland Tales in 1922, with one hundred drawings by the author himself. The tales are nature stories for young readers, each explaining in story form how some flower, bird, or beast came to look or live as it does.

Contents include Blue-eyes the Snow-child, or the Story of Hepatica, and the Dawnsinger, or How the Bloodroot Came. How the Bluebird Came, Robin the Bird that Loves to Make Clay Pots, and How the Violets Came follow. Seton, who also wrote Wild Animals I Have Known, mixes woodland lore with gentle morals, teaching readers to look closely at springtime things.
23794-mother-goose-or-the-old-nursery-rh:
Kate Greenaway illustrated this edition of Mother Goose, or The Old Nursery Rhymes, published by Frederick Warne in London and New York. Greenaway's pictures, gentle and detailed, made the book a nursery classic, and its rhymes are the ones English-speaking children have chanted for generations.

Contents run from Hark, hark, the dogs bark and Little Jack Horner through To market, to market and Jack Sprat to Jack and Jill, Little Bo-Peep, and Polly put the kettle on. Later pages bring Mary, Mary, quite contrary, Little Miss Muffet, and Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall. It is the old rhymes in their familiar order, made to be read aloud.
23886-old-valentines:
Munson Havens published Old Valentines, A Love Story, in Boston and New York in 1914, with pictures by Griswold Tyng. Its opening offers two doors into the story. The stage door shows the beautiful actress Valentine Germain, married to Robert Oglebay the painter. The main entrance, more dignified, leads through his brother Sir Peter.

Sir Peter Oglebay, the great engineer, loves construction: massive machinery hoisting massive materials to incredible heights with calculated accuracy. Wherever building goes on, he stands at a little distance, silk hat in hand, leaning on his stick, an English gentleman. His portrait by Sargent hangs in the Engineering Society's lobby. Around him, and the baby Phyllis, Havens builds a love story across generations.
23892-carried-off-a-story-of-pirate-time:
Esmé Stuart published Carried Off, A Story of Pirate Times, in London in 1888, dedicating it to Clarissa and John. Stuart tells her young readers that the chief events are true, taken from a book over two centuries old. West Indies travel, she assures them, is now safe from buccaneers.

The story opens on a warm spring evening at Canvey Island, in the Thames estuary opposite South Benfleet, as the sun sets golden over marshy waters. Chapters follow a sacrifice, a capture, a beautiful island, and the pirates' coming, with scouts, treachery, a brave defence, and a secret passage. Harry's blood is up on the frontispiece, and Captain Morgan waits within.
2395-the-golden-fleece-and-the-heroes-wh:
Padraic Colum retells the Greek myths of Jason and the Argonauts for young readers in The Golden Fleece and the Heroes Who Lived Before Achilles. The book follows Jason from his youth through the gathering of heroes, the building of the Argo, and the quest for the fleece in Colchis. Colum's prose is clear, musical, and faithful to the old tales.

The volume also introduces Heracles, Orpheus, and other heroes before Achilles' age. Its storytelling has charmed generations of children. Mythology lovers will find a classic retelling. Colum also retold the myths of Troy and of Odysseus for children.
23990-moor-fires:
E. H. Young, author of William and The Mallets, published Moor Fires in New York with Harcourt, Brace and Company. It opens in the dusk of a spring evening, as Helen Caniper walks the long road from town, her laden basket no burden to her.

Past the high fir-wood, standing like a barrier against encroachment on the moor, Helen looks back at lights darting out to mark the streets. They shine as though a fairy hand lit a giant Christmas tree. The moor is inhabited by many winds, and she knows them all, though only the night wind cries among the trees. An old horse drawing a dog-cart rounds the corner, once Dr. Mackenzie's, now driven by his son. Young's moorland novel begins in that meeting.
23993-those-who-smiled-and-eleven-other-:
Perceval Gibbon published Those Who Smiled and Eleven Other Stories in London in 1920, dedicating the volume to his sister Muriel Gibbon. Gibbon was already known for Vrouw Grobelaar's Leading Cases, The Adventures of Miss Gregory, and the novels Souls in Bondage, Salvator, and Margaret Harding.

The title story opens in a marble-white North Italian villa where invaders have set up headquarters. A stout German captain and a young Austrian lieutenant walk through mulberry orchards in the still heat, toward the last houses of a village. The other eleven stories range from The Dago and Wood-Ladies to Miss Pilgrim's Progress and The Day of Omens. Gibbon's tales are sharp, worldly, and often set at the edges of war.
24016-photographic-reproduction-processe:
P. C. Duchochois published Photographic Reproduction Processes in New York in 1891, subtitled A Practical Treatise of the Photo-Impressions Without Silver Salts. The Scovill and Adams volume gathers the nineteenth century's alternative photographic printing methods into one manual.

Contents run from the cyanotype, or blue process, and Pellet's cyanofer process to the black or ink process, the ferro-tannate process, and Burnett's cuprotype. The aniline process, the primuline or diazotype process, tracing on metal, graphotypy, and the uranotype follow, with the platinotype, Artigues' process, and the carbon process. Each process uses light and chemicals to copy a drawing onto paper or cloth. The book explains each method step by step. For historians of photography, it is a record of how pictures were made before silver ruled the darkroom.
24062-a-history-of-the-united-states:
Cecil Chesterton wrote this history of the United States, published in London by Chatto and Windus in 1919, with an introduction by his brother G. K. Chesterton. He dedicated it to Lance-Corporal Wood, an American citizen from Massachusetts who had joined the British Army in August 1914. The book came from an English writer looking across the Atlantic just after the First World War.

Chesterton follows the country from its colonial roots through revolution, civil war, and growth into a modern power. He writes as a sympathetic outsider, judging American ideals against American deeds. Readers get a brisk, opinionated survey, useful as a view of how the United States looked to a British observer in 1919.
24063-a-handbook-of-some-south-indian-gr:
Rai Bahadur K. Ranga Achariyar of the Indian Agricultural Service, Agricultural College, Coimbatore, wrote A Handbook of Some South Indian Grasses, assisted by C. Tadulinga Mudaliyar. The Madras Government Press printed it in 1921, priced at four rupees and eight annas.

Grasses, the introduction notes, occupy wide tracts in all parts of the world, in every soil and climate. They dislike shade and are not abundant within forests, but in open places whole tracts become grass-lands, and a very great portion of the vegetation consists of grasses. Chapters cover vegetative organs, inflorescence and flower, histology, and classification, then the Panicaceae, Oryzeae, Andropogoneae, Agrostideae, and Festucaceae. For farmers and botanists, it is a working flora of economic plants.
24065-a-history-of-nursery-rhymes:
Percy B. Green published A History of Nursery Rhymes in London in 1899, reissued by Singing Tree Press in 1968. Green's history begins far back, with prehistoric man whose language was one of signs and sounds, and the story of Psammetichus and the two babies.

Modern types of early man follow, with the sign language of peoples living today. Examples include the custom of the Uvinza grandees, the good-morning of the Walunga tribe, and signs of hospitality in the vocabulary of the North American Indian. The Romans' attingere extremis digitis, clap-hands as a first nursery lesson, and Plato's rebuke lead to Agesilaus and his children. The Roman child's lalla, lalla, lalla and the baby dance of crow and caper, caper and crow show nursery classics surviving from antiquity.
24082-a-broader-mission-for-liberal-educ:
John Henry Worst, president of the Agricultural College in North Dakota, gave this baccalaureate address in the college chapel on Sunday, June 9, 1901. Speaking to graduates, he argued that America honors no birthright rank, only genius and character, and that a degree by itself is no badge of merit. Education, he said, is power only when it shows itself in action.

Worst pressed his hearers to join knowing with doing, since knowing without doing is idle and doing without knowing wastes effort. The graduate must carve a way by energy and grit, pitted against practical minds in open rivalry. The address still reads as a plain charge to use learning for real work in the world.
24117-a-apple-pie-and-other-nursery-tale:
George Routledge and Sons published this illustrated nursery book in London and New York, with forty-eight pages of pictures printed in color by Kronheim and Company. It opens with the alphabet rhyme of A Apple Pie. Each letter takes a turn with the pie, from B who bit it to Z who wished for a piece in hand. Short tales and rhymes follow for very young readers.

Among them are the Cats' Tea Party, with Miss Tabitha Pussycat and her monkey page Jacko, This Little Pig Went to Market, The Three Bears, and Little Red Riding-Hood. The large pictures and short lines suit children learning letters and first stories. It is a bright, old-style picture book of rhymes and animal tales.
2412-the-categories:
Aristotle's Categories opens the Organon, his works on logic, by sorting the ways things can be said to exist. The short treatise defines substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, and other categories, laying the groundwork for Western logic and metaphysics. Aristotle writes with terse, systematic care.

The work is technical but foundational: centuries of philosophers began here. Modern readers will find it demanding yet short, and its influence enormous. Students of philosophy meet it as a first text of the tradition. Medieval schoolmen built their whole logic course on this short text.
24130-andiron-tales:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote this children's fantasy, published in Philadelphia in 1906 with pictures by Clare Victor Dwiggins. A boy named Tom meets the andirons by his fireplace, and the poker, the bellows, and the other fireside tools begin to tell their stories. Their tales carry Tom off into the clouds, to the crescent moon, and onto a trolley cloud.

Along the way come a narrow escape on an oscycle, a jump by the man from Saturn, and a great bird's flight, before Tom wakes and comes home again. Bangs gives each household tool a voice and a past. Readers get a cozy fireside wonder tale, built for reading aloud by the hearth.
24167-careless-jane-and-other-tales:
Katharine Pyle wrote this book of verse tales for children, published by E. P. Dutton and Company in New York in 1902. It proved lasting, reaching a twenty-first printing by March 1928. Its contents run from Careless Jane, Boisterous Ann, and The Brother and Sister to Georgie Lie-a-Bed and Untidy Amanda. Later tales include The Child Who Would Not Go to Bed, The Beet, The Robber Rat, Grandfather Stork, Old Mother Webtoes, The Rabbit Witch, and Peter and the Ogress.

The book opens with a grandmother telling Jane it is time she learned to sew, a task Jane at her age should already manage. Pyle turns small faults into funny, gentle lessons in rhyme. Readers get a set of old-style cautionary tales, bright with mischief and meant for reading aloud.
24187-a-transmutation-of-muddles:
H. B. Fyfe wrote this science fiction story, with pictures by Van Dongen, about an arbitrator with a horse-trader's gift for turning two headaches into a single aspirin pill. A rugged scout ship sets down on Kappa Orionis VII, a mile from a native village, and pilot Lieutenant Eric Haruhiku takes care to scorch neither woodland nor shoreline. The Kappans fish the shallow seas and pick forest fruit, but farm little.

Louis Mayne, a retired space captain with a ranch on Rigel IX, stays on call as arbitrator to keep his grant, and Terra wants a friendly agreement for a spaceship base. Word comes that the Terran envoy arrived and left two days behind Mayne. Readers get a wry tale of frontier bargaining, where law is thin and a swap may settle all.
24205-breakfast-dainties:
Thomas J. Murrey, formerly professional caterer of the Astor House in New York, wrote this breakfast cookbook, published in New York in 1885. It is dedicated to his friend Frank B. Thurber, whose work to raise the standard of American food products Murrey praises. The book opens with remarks on breakfast cookery, then moves through its dishes in order.

Contents run from fruits, baked apples, bananas, berries, melons, and grapes, through beverages such as coffee, tea, cocoa, and chocolate. Breads, rolls, corn bread, muffins, and biscuits follow, with many toasts and egg dishes after. Readers get a practical Victorian guide to starting the day well, from a working caterer.
24222-the-story-of-eclipses:
George F. Chambers wrote this popular astronomy book, published in London in 1899 as a sequel to his Story of the Solar System and Story of the Stars. It was written because public attention already turned to the total eclipse of the sun due on May 28, 1900. That eclipse was partial in England but total no farther off than Portugal and Spain, with the line of totality also crossing the United States.

Chambers adds a temporary appendix on reaching Portugal or Spain by sea or overland from England, for watchers planning a trip. He doubts any reader will still doubt that an eclipse expedition brings pleasant, profitable, even amusing travel, citing Sir Francis Galton's trip to Spain. Readers get a plain guide to eclipses, made for general readers.
2428-an-essay-on-man-moral-essays-and-sa:
Alexander Pope's Essay on Man, with his Moral Essays and Satires, gathers the great Augustan poet at his most philosophical and his most biting. The Essay argues that the universe is ordered and that human pride blinds us to our place in it, in couplets of unmatched polish. The satires skewer dunces, flatterers, and the follies of his age.

Pope's verse rewards readers who love wit, balance, and epigram. His lines have passed into proverb: hope springs eternal, fools rush in. The volume serves as an ideal introduction to his art.
243-the-forged-coupon-and-other-stories:
A forged coupon, passed from hand to hand, spreads crime and ruin through Russian society. Leo Tolstoy's Forged Coupon and Other Stories opens with that chain of small sins growing into murder. Later tales follow its moral logic in reverse, toward repentance.

After the Dance, Alyosha the Pot, and The Young Tsar join the set, with essays on guilt and power. Tolstoy's late prose is plain, stern, and searching. The introduction frames spiritual power against an age of materialism. The volume shows Tolstoy the prophet in story form. Tolstoy's chain of sin and grace still challenges readers about moral cause.
24353-wired-love-a-romance-of-dots-and-d:
Ella Cheever Thayer wrote this telegraph romance, subtitled the old, old story in a new, new way. Its dedication was printed in American Railroad Morse dialect, which the transcriber notes cannot easily be shown in plain text. Chapters run from Sounds from a Distant C and At the Hotel Norman to Visible and Invisible Friends and Neighborly Calls. Quimby Bursts Forth in Eloquence leads to Collapse of the Romance, Good-By, and The Feast.

It opens with Miss Nathalie Rogers, called Nattie, sole presiding genius of a little country telegraph office. A clatter like no clock tells her that office B m is wanted by office X n, fifty miles down the line, whose operator she already holds in slight contempt. Readers get a love story told in dots and dashes, across a wire.
2436-the-marriages:
Henry James's tale The Marriages follows a young woman caught between her father's remarriage and her own engagement, in a tangle of money, loyalty, and social appearance. The story watches a family negotiate two weddings at once, with James's irony exposing every polite evasion. The heroine must choose between duty to her father and honesty to herself.

The tale is compact and psychologically acute, with James's late attention to motive. Readers of his short fiction will enjoy its quiet tension. It pairs well with his other tales of marriage and money.
24363-the-song-of-the-sword-and-other-ve:
W. E. Henley wrote these verses, published by David Nutt in the Strand, London, in 1892, and dedicated to R. T. Hamilton-Bruce of Edinburgh on March 17, 1892. With three exceptions, the numbers first appeared in The National Observer, by whose proprietors they are here reprinted by permission. The title poem, addressed to Rudyard Kipling, gives the sword itself a voice.

The sword sings, clanging imperious, forth from time's battlements, its ancient and triumphing song. In the beginning, before God breathed himself into the clay figure shaped in his image, the empty, naked shell soon to be man lay prone and helpless, fragile and open to attack. God drew a shape on the sand with his finger, a sign of his way, and that was the birth of the sword. Readers get Henley's hard, bleak verse of steel.
24374-the-romance-of-names:
Ernest Weekley, professor of French and head of the modern language department at University College, Nottingham, wrote this book on the romance of names, published by John Murray in London in 1922. Its first edition dates to January 1914, its second to March 1914, and this third, revised edition to May 1922. Weekley's other works advertised with it include The Romance of Words, Surnames, and An Etymological Dictionary of Modern English.

Chapters run from surnames in general, personal names, nicknames, mythical etymologies, and alternative origins. A medieval roll of London jurymen, Middlesex jurymen, and Steeple Claydon cottagers leads to spelling and sound. Variant spellings, dialectic variants, aphesis, epithesis and assimilation, metathesis, and baby phonetics follow. Brown, Jones, and Robinson follow, with occupative names, the absorption of foreign names, Tom, Dick and Harry, Goderic and Godiva, paladins and heroes, and local surnames. Readers get why names are what they are.
24437-the-last-penny-and-other-stories:
T. S. Arthur published this story collection in Philadelphia in 1852, with illustrations from designs by Croome. Its title tale follows Thomas Claire, a poor but industrious shoemaker whose skill went only to simple shoe repairs: half-soles, heel-taps, and patches, and who must make his last penny stretch.

Other stories include a tale of the American Revolution, an April Fool jest, and short moral pieces on how to attain true greatness and how to be happy. Arthur wrote for family readers, and his tales reward industry, honesty, and kindness while warning against waste and pride. The collection gives a vivid taste of mid-nineteenth-century American popular fiction.
24439-pirates:
Published in New York in 1922, with a foreword and decorations by C. Lovat Fraser, this book retells the lives and adventures of notorious pirates from the golden age of piracy. Its chapters take up Captain Avery, John Rackham, Edward Lowe, George Lowther, John Phillips, Teach, better known as Blackbeard, Major Stede Bonnet, Captain Kidd, Edward England, and John Gow.

Each life follows its captain from first voyage to capture or death, with sea fights, mutinies, and treasure hunts along the way. The tales come from old chronicles, retold in plain, stirring prose. Readers looking for true stories of the sea, wilder than any invented adventure, will find this collection hard to put down.
24473-the-cat-and-the-mouse-a-book-of-pe:
Hartwell James edited this book of Persian fairy tales, published at Philadelphia in 1906 with forty illustrations by John R. Neill. It belonged to Altemus' illustrated fairy-tale series, which also offered tales from India, China, Africa, and the South Seas. The title tale tells of a cat and a mouse.

Other stories in the volume follow the pattern of old Persian wonder tales: clever animals, foolish kings, magic, and quick justice. James's introduction sets the tales in their Eastern setting for young readers. The book gives children a bright, old-fashioned doorway into Persian storytelling, with pictures on nearly every page.
24478-the-nursery-may-1873-vol-xiii-a-mo:
