Boston publisher John L. Shorey issued this May 1873 number of The Nursery, a monthly magazine for youngest readers. It was the fifth issue of volume thirteen. Its prose pieces include Mabel's cow, Harry and the big pop-corn, a brindled cow, and the naming of a kitten.

Other tales follow Snip, Prince and Tip, and a sparrow's life, with Little Mischief returning as a regular feature. Verses include Jenny and Timothy Wren, Baby in the High Chair, and Mistress Mouse, with The Kitten set to music. The issue offers small children short animal stories and rhymes, plainly told and brightly illustrated.
24488-rollo-in-naples:
Jacob Abbott wrote this boys' travel story, published at Boston in 1864 as one volume of Rollo's Tour in Europe. Rollo, a young American traveller, reaches Naples with his party after earlier volumes took him to Paris, Switzerland, London, the Rhine, and Scotland. The series taught geography and manners through story.

In Naples, Rollo visits the orange gardens, the streets, and the sights of the bay, learning how Neapolitans live and work. Abbott mixes dialogue, description, and gentle moral lessons, as in all the Rollo books. Young readers get a cheerful, old-fashioned tour of southern Italy, full of curiosity about foreign ways.
24503-the-boy-slaves:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote this adventure of three midshipmen and an older sailor from a British warship. Their ship goes aground off the coast of Africa and sinks with all hands, but the four escape on a spar. They paddle with their hands for days until they reach the African shore.

There Arabs capture them and march them north to be sold in a distant town. Reid describes the Barbary pirates who seized European crews and held them for ransom, often pretending no ransom had come. The boys' struggle for freedom gives young readers a stirring tale of courage, endurance, and escape.
24569-a-treasury-of-eskimo-tales:
Clara K. Bayliss wrote this treasury of Eskimo tales, published at New York in 1922 with colour pictures by George Carlson. Bayliss had already written A Treasury of Indian Tales and Old Man Coyote. Her Eskimo volume gathers tales of the central Eskimo peoples and beyond.

Contents include The Baby Eskimo, Kiviung, The Giant, Kalopaling, The Woman Magician, The Bird Wife, and The Spirit of the Singing House. Later tales tell of the Tornit, a flight to the moon, and a summoned mascot in the form of a huge white bear. Young readers get a vivid doorway into Arctic storytelling.
2458-sermons-on-the-card-and-other-disco:
Hugh Latimer, the Reformation preacher and martyr, delivers his Sermons on the Card, using a deck of cards as a teaching tool for a congregation that knew games better than doctrine. The discourses preach repentance, honesty, and the Christian life in plain, vigorous Tudor English, with Latimer's famous directness. The sermons show why he moved crowds.

The volume preserves a voice of the English Reformation at its most popular and bold. Latimer's plain speech still strikes home. Readers of religious history will find a vivid primary text. Latimer was burned at Oxford in 1555 under Queen Mary.
2459-trent-s-trust-and-other-stories:
Bret Harte's Trent's Trust and Other Stories returns to California for tales of inheritance, trust, and frontier honor. The title story follows a man entrusted with a fortune and the temptations that follow, while the other pieces mix mining camps, romance, and Harte's familiar ironies. The collection shows his late style at its most polished.

Harte's California remains vivid even as the gold rush recedes into memory. The stories are compact and well-turned. Fans of his work will find a satisfying late volume. Harte wrote these tales near the end of his long career in London.
24596-history-of-the-thirty-ninth-congre:
William H. Barnes wrote this history of the Thirty-Ninth Congress of the United States, published at New York in 1868 with portraits. The Congress met just after the Civil War, and it faced Reconstruction, the Freedmen's Bureau, civil rights, and the struggle with President Johnson.

Barnes, author of The Body Politic, follows debates, votes, and leaders, with a portrait of Speaker Schuyler Colfax among others. His history is detailed and partisan, as befits a book written so close to its events. Readers of Reconstruction history will find it a rich contemporary record of a Congress that remade the nation.
24650-the-gentle-art-of-making-enemies:
James Abbott McNeill Whistler published this famous book of letters and quarrels, in which the painter answers his critics with wit and scorn. Its illustrations are sketches of butterflies, Whistler's own emblem. The book collects his battles with art critics, patrons, and the press, fought in public letters.

Whistler turns each dispute into a performance, defending his art and mocking his enemies with epigrams. The Gentle Art remains a classic of artistic self-defence, and a portrait of London's art world in the 1880s and 1890s. Readers will enjoy its sting, even where they side with the other party.
24658-the-loyalists-of-america-and-their:
Egerton Ryerson, chief superintendent of education for Upper Canada from 1844 to 1876, wrote this history of the Loyalists of America and their times, from 1620 to 1816. The second volume, published at Toronto and Montreal in 1880, carries the story through the Revolution and its aftermath.

Later chapters treat the alliance between Congress and France, the efforts of the Loyalists, and their exile to Canada and elsewhere. Ryerson writes from the Canadian side, sympathetic to men who lost homes for loyalty to the Crown. Readers of Revolutionary history will find this a detailed and distinctive account.
24659-hortense-makers-of-history-series:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this life of Hortense, Queen of Holland and mother of Napoleon III, as part of his Makers of History series, published at New York and London in 1902. His preface sets the French Revolution as a drama in three acts: the Revolution itself, with its terror and blood, and the struggles that followed.

Abbott follows Hortense from girlhood through the Empire, exile, and motherhood, with engravings throughout. His histories, written for young readers, mix narrative with moral judgement. Readers of Napoleonic history will find this an accessible, old-fashioned life of a queen caught in great events.
24662-the-grateful-indian-and-other-stor:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this short book of stories and verse, containing eight sections. Three of its pieces are nautical stories by Kingston, two are stories by lady writers, and the last three are collections of verse, including poems Kingston wrote while still at school. The title story gives the book its name.

One commended tale is An Adventure on the Black Mountain, by Frances Wilbraham, set in Montenegro, a Balkan country then little known to English readers. Kingston's sea stories and the guest tales mix adventure with feeling. Young readers get a varied, old-fashioned miscellany, short enough to enjoy piece by piece.
24689-new-italian-sketches:
John Addington Symonds published these New Italian Sketches in a copyright edition at Leipzig in 1884. His prefatory note explains that the volume gathers two earlier books. They are Sketches and Studies in Italy and Italian Byways. The new book forms a companion to his Sketches in Italy, though it is independent and no continuation.

Symonds includes only place studies, not literary or historical essays, chosen to suit travellers in Italy. His sketches visit towns, coasts, and hills with a scholar's eye and a poet's feeling. Readers planning Italy, or dreaming of it, will find this a graceful, learned companion to the road.
247-webster-s-unabridged-dictionary-1st-:
Noah Webster's revised unabridged dictionary of 1913 opens with the letter A and a history of the alphabet. This file gives the first hundred pages, from A through early entries, with pronunciation guides. The A entry traces the letter from Phoenician aleph through Greek alpha to Latin.

Definitions, word histories, and usage notes follow the dictionary's full pattern. Readers meet the 1913 editors' care for spelling, sound, and sense. The partial file suits browsing and reference alike. Later pages continue the alphabet beyond this opening stretch. The dictionary's first pages show how American English defined itself in print.
24709-bamboo-tales:
Ira L. Reeves, first lieutenant of the Fourth Infantry, wrote these bamboo tales of the Philippine War, published at Kansas City in 1900 with pictures by J. Alexander Mackay. Reeves dedicated the book to the first man up San Juan Hill. His contents include how the Spaniards campaigned in Luzon, Cougar Daly, and a dying Spaniard's request.

Later tales tell of Benito, the army mule, comedy and carnage, how the author saw Aguinaldo, and what the wounded say and do. Reeves writes as a soldier who was there. Readers get vivid, firsthand sketches of the Philippine campaign, humane, humorous, and unflinching.
2472-white-lies:
Charles Reade's White Lies is a melodrama of love, deception, and redemption set in France, where a woman's small falsehoods snowball into danger. The novel follows its heroine through a maze of secrets, duels, and revelations, with Reade's energetic plotting and reforming zeal driving every chapter. The lies of the title are white only at first.

Reade's theatrical sense keeps the story moving, and his sympathy for his heroine carries the sentiment. Victorian fiction fans will find a fast, emotional read. The book shows Reade at his most popular. Reade adapted the novel for the stage, as he did with many of his books.
24724-beyond-the-marshes:
Ralph Connor set this short prairie tale in the Canadian west, where a visitor joins a missionary on his rounds past the Great Marshes. Copyrighted in 1898, the story opens on a railway platform and moves on by rough trail to far-flung preaching stations. Along the way the narrator meets settler families, most of them Scots, making homes from logs and sod.

The heart of the book is the missionary himself: a tough, patient man who builds his own manse, endures swarms of biting flies, and preaches to scattered folk on Sundays. Connor writes with warmth about plain work, kind neighbors, and faith kept up in hard country. It reads as a gentle picture of frontier church life in early Manitoba.
24734-tommy-tatters-uncle-toby-s-series:
Tommy Tatters is a short picture book in verse from the Uncle Toby's Series, printed by McLoughlin Brothers of New York. It opens with Tommy in rags, cold and hungry, telling Master Peter Pink of his plight. Peter takes him home, feeds him, washes him, cuts his hair and nails, and dresses him in a new suit.

The verses are simple rhyming pairs, each facing a picture, and the whole tale runs only a few pages. Its lesson is plain: kindness and a wash can change how a child looks and feels. The book keeps the look and voice of a 1800s toy book, made to be read aloud to very young children.
24738-pleasing-stories-for-good-children:
Pleasing Stories for Good Children, printed in Cincinnati by Truman and Smith, offers short moral tales for young readers, each with a picture. A friend to youth, as the author signs himself, tells of Little Jane helping a lame poor man, of children learning hymns, and of small acts of kindness at home. Each story ends with its lesson stated plainly.

The book speaks straight to children in the voice of the 1800s Sunday school: be kind, share your pennies, mind your parents, and think of those worse off. Its tales are brief and its morals are never left in doubt. The volume keeps the tone of early American children's books, where a story and a lesson walked hand in hand.
24751-the-kitchen-cat-and-other-stories:
Amy Walton wrote this trio of stories for children, led by The Kitchen Cat. Ruth Lorimer, a lonely girl in a gloomy London house, longs for company in a nursery full of toys but short on warmth. A cat from the cellar becomes her friend, and later tales follow Sarah's Sunday out and a toad in a hole.

Walton writes gently about sickbeds, busy aunts, and small kindnesses that cheer a dull day. The stories suit reading aloud, with short chapters and homely detail. Young readers will find a kind, old-fashioned set of tales about pets, patience, and the comfort of one true friend.
24753-who-are-happiest-and-other-stories:
T. S. Arthur published this story collection in Philadelphia in 1852, with pictures from designs by Croome. The title tale asks who are happiest, and the tales that follow press the same moral question: Dick Lawson and his mocking-bird, the means of enjoyment, and man's judgment. Each story turns on a choice between kindness and cruelty, or between greed and content.

Arthur writes in the earnest voice of mid-1800s moral fiction, and one narrator confesses how copying a cruel act led him to worse ones. The lessons are plain and the endings point a clear moral. Readers of early American children's books will find a typical and well-kept sample of the genre.
24755-captain-cook-his-life-voyages-and-:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this life of Captain James Cook for young readers, stressing that it is plain biography, not invented adventure. Cook, born at Marton in Yorkshire in 1728 to a farm laborer, rose from grocer's apprentice to master of ships and then to the Royal Navy. His voyages carried him across the Pacific and round the world.

Kingston follows Cook's care for his crews, noting his fight against scurvy with fresh food, dry clothes, and clean ships. The book closes as a tale of steady rise by work and skill. Young readers get a clear, stirring life of one of the great seamen of the 1700s, told without tall tales.
24760-aunt-kitty-s-stories:
Aunt Kitty's Stories gathers nursery rhymes, short verses, and brief moral tales for small children, with 175 pictures. Familiar rhymes like Little Bo-peep and Simple Simon sit beside short stories with titles such as Thoughtless Julia, The Little Coward, and Careless Maria. Each piece is short enough to read aloud in a few minutes.

The tone is kindly and old-fashioned: good conduct wins praise, careless or selfish acts bring a small, clear lesson. Parents reading aloud will find plain rhymes and simple tales that suit bedtime or a quiet hour. The book keeps the charm of an early picture book, with verse and story mixed through its pages.
248-webster-s-unabridged-dictionary-2nd-:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary of 1913 continues here past page one hundred. This second hundred pages runs through entries near attract, with full etymologies and usage notes. Attractivity, attractor, and attrahent show the dictionary's Latin roots and careful marking.

Medical, obsolete, and figurative senses appear alongside everyday ones, with quotations from Browne, Glanvill, and Taylor. Pronunciation marks and part-of-speech labels guide the reader throughout. The file suits anyone tracing a word's history in early twentieth-century English. It continues the first hundred pages in sequence. The 1913 dictionary remains a favorite of word lovers and crossword solvers.
2480-under-western-eyes:
Joseph Conrad's Under Western Eyes follows Razumov, a Russian student who betrays a revolutionary assassin and is drawn into the world of spies and exiles he betrayed. The novel moves from St. Petersburg to Geneva, with Conrad's narrator piecing together Razumov's guilt and his doomed love. The book's political vision is dark and unsparing.

Conrad writes from his knowledge of Russian exile politics, and the novel's irony cuts every side. Its atmosphere of surveillance and conscience feels modern. Readers of political fiction will find a masterpiece. Conrad based his Geneva exiles on Russians he had known in London.
24811-viking-tales:
Jennie Hall wrote Viking Tales for schoolchildren in 1902, with pictures by Victor R. Lambdin. Drawn from the sagas, the stories follow Norse life in Norway and on the sea: babies, thralls, farms, fights, and kings. Olaf's farm and his fight with Havard open the book, and later tales show Harald kneeling to serve his bride Gyda at table.

Hall tells each tale in short, plain chapters that suit young readers, and a pronouncing index helps with Norse names. The book gives children a first taste of saga life: honor, hard work, and sea voyages. Teachers long used it as a gentle door into the Viking age, before the longer sagas themselves.
24879-curious-if-true-strange-tales:
Mrs. Gaskell gathered five strange tales in Curious, If True: The Old Nurse's Story, The Poor Clare, Lois the Witch, The Grey Woman, and the title tale. The first opens with an old nurse telling her charges how their mother, an orphan, came to the parsonage as a baby. Both parents died within a fortnight when little Rosamond was four or five.

Ghosts, witches, and wronged women haunt the rest, from a witch hunt to a grey woman's flight. Gaskell writes with warmth and dread in equal parts, and her narrators speak in homely, earnest voices. The set suits readers who like Victorian ghost stories with strong feeling and a moral spine.
24883-new-and-original-theories-of-the-g:
Henry Raymond Rogers, a doctor, published his New and Original Theories of the Great Physical Forces in New York in 1878, by subscription through booksellers. Rogers gives his own views, with an assurance born of conviction, on gravity, light, heat, and the atmosphere, quoting Faraday, Tyndall, and Dawson on science as a moving tide.

His central claim is that one current lights the earth, warms it, and draws all things to it, so gravity is no mystery but the work of that current. The atmosphere, he writes, is a veritable ocean at whose bottom we live and move. The book now reads as a bold, curious sample of Victorian amateur physics, argued with full confidence.
24914-wappin-wharf-a-frightful-comedy-of:
Charles S. Brooks wrote Wappin' Wharf, a frightful comedy of pirates, copyrighted in 1922, with pictures by Julia McCune Flory and music by Gordon Hatfield. The play is meant for reading, and its notice warns that no stage performance may be given without a royalty contract.

Its pirates wait for a merchantman known to carry gold, then tip off old Petey at the lighthouse to douse his light. They set up Flint's lantern on the rocks where the true light should show, and the ship strikes the cliff with a smash. Brooks mixes sea roguery with broad comedy, in the spirit of a pirate pantomime.
2492-orpheus-in-mayfair-and-other-storie:
Maurice Baring's Orpheus in Mayfair and Other Stories and Sketches brings classical myth into modern London, with the title story letting Orpheus walk Mayfair's streets. The sketches range from fables to wartime vignettes, many first printed in the Morning Post, with Baring's light, cosmopolitan touch. The collection is urbane and quietly melancholy.

Baring, a diplomat and man of letters, writes for readers who enjoy allusion and understatement. The book's variety suits dipping in and out. Lovers of the literary sketch will find a refined volume. Baring served as a diplomat in Russia and Persia before turning to letters.
24937-mike-marble-his-crotchets-and-oddi:
Francis C. Woodworth, writing as 'Uncle Frank,' published this 1852 collection of Mike Marble's crotchets and oddities with Phillips, Sampson and Company. Mike is a boy of fixed notions and funny habits, and each sketch turns on one of his notions meeting the real world. The humor is gentle, aimed at young readers who will recognize their own stubborn ideas in his.

One episode follows Jake, whose cruel treatment of a playmate gives the book its serious turn, as Jake later reflects on what he did. Woodworth uses the moment to teach without preaching, letting remorse do the work of a sermon. The result is a modest, old-fashioned storybook: funny, moral, and warm toward its young audience.
25024-the-night-of-the-long-knives:
Fritz Leiber's novel, illustrated by Finlay, opens one hundred miles from Nowhere, with a scavenger spotting a girl out of the corner of his eye. He watches for the other undead leftover from the murder party at Nowhere, still stalking him. Both follow high voltage towers canted at the same tipsy angle by an old blast, through dust showing metallic gleams and humps, possibly dead men or cattle.

Slim, dark topped, and on guard, the girl wears a scarf over the lower half of her face, as does the narrator. Neither waves as their paths converge, though both stay intensely watchful under a low dust haze. Later the pair reach a plane with its door above their heads, and Pop solves boarding with a light leap. The novel is postwar survival at its starkest.
25031-davy-and-the-goblin-what-followed-:
Charles E. Carryl's Davy and the Goblin, or What Followed Reading 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' published by Houghton Mifflin with illustrations by E. B. Bensell, sends Davy on a believing voyage after Alice. The dedication, addressed to his little boy Guy, recalls hours when the child sat throned on his knee hearing marvels of fay and goblin in days of old. Chapters carry Davy to the sugar-plum garden, among the butterscotchmen, to Jack and the Bean-Stalk's farm, and before the giant Badorful.

On the way Davy meets Robin Hood keeping a little shop, offering steaks and chops for to-day, to-morrow, or even yesterday, with the crossest manner imaginable. As Davy turns away, the path unfolds through the wood and the shop is swallowed up behind him. Carryl's nonsense runs gentle and inventive, a worthy companion to Wonderland.
25050-a-study-of-american-beers-and-ales:
United States Department of Agriculture Bulletin No. 493, by L. M. Tolman and J. Garfield Riley, studies American beers and ales to find whether a brew made entirely from malt can be distinguished from one made with malt plus rice, corn, or cerealin. Existing data covered mostly foreign beers, made with a very different malt, and few samples carried exact information about the raw materials in the wort. The investigators therefore collected samples across the raw materials ordinarily used.

Small scale laboratory brewings were rejected as unsatisfactory, since no laboratory can exactly duplicate commercial mashing or fermenting. Results track protein, ash, and phosphoric acid losses in beer, ale, and porter worts, finding no appreciable loss of protein or phosphoric acid during storage or aging. The bulletin is technical and precise throughout.
25062-a-study-of-recent-earthquakes:
Charles Davison's 1905 Study of Recent Earthquakes, published by Walter Scott with eighty illustrations, differs from a textbook of seismology. It gives brief, detailed accounts of individual earthquakes instead of a general discussion of phenomena and distribution. Fouqué's few chapters on the principal earthquakes of 1854 to 1887, and Lyell's chapters on still earlier shocks are, Davison notes, the only comparable ground covered. Otherwise the student must hunt through long reports in several languages.

Davison's object is to save that trouble, presenting the facts most worthy of attention, including a reprinted chapter on the Japanese earthquake. One passage works out a mean velocity from observations, weighting groups inversely as the squares of their probable errors, to reach 3.221 miles per second, probably nearer accuracy than any earlier estimate. Fissures and sand craters close the volume's miscellany of phenomena. Davison writes for readers who want facts.
25076-between-the-lines:
Boyd Cable's Between the Lines, published in Toronto in 1916, gathers short stories and sketches from the Western Front during the First World War. Cable writes from close knowledge of trench routine, and his pieces carry the slang, humor, and fatigue of men living within yards of the enemy.

Stories cover advanced trenches, shell fire, mining, artillery support, quiet nights when nothing is reported, and the spring advance. Civilians at home appear too, in scenes that measure what the war cost families far from the guns. The collection reads as wartime reporting in fictional dress, valued for its plain detail rather than for heroics.
2517-lincoln-s-yarns-and-stories:
Alexander K. McClure gathered this large set of funny and pointed tales about Abraham Lincoln, the president famous for settling hard questions with a story. The book opens with a sketch of Lincoln's life, from a Kentucky log cabin in 1809 to the White House and his murder in April 1865.

The anecdotes that follow show Lincoln teasing rivals, calming his cabinet, and answering critics with jokes drawn from farm life, courtrooms, and the army. Some tales are tall, some are sharp, and all show why his humor won friends and disarmed foes. Readers get Lincoln the man, not just Lincoln the monument, in his own best weapon: a well told story.
2518-the-hungry-stones-and-other-stories:
Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet and storyteller, wrote the tales gathered here, most of them turned into English by several hands, with one version by Tagore himself. Their settings run from old palaces and country villages to the streets of Calcutta, and their people include kings, priests, children, and travelers.

Ghosts haunt a ruined palace in the title story, a fruit seller from Kabul befriends a small girl, and a baby king rules a kingdom of cards. Across the set, Tagore blends folk wonder with sharp looks at pride, devotion, and family duty. The stories stay short, strange, and warm, and they show why his fiction traveled far beyond Bengal.
25235-a-dialogue-between-dean-swift-and-:
A Dialogue between Dean Swift and Tho. Prior, Esq., printed in Dublin in 1753, stages an imagined talk in the aisles of St. Patrick's Church. Its author, calling himself a friend to the peace and prosperity of Ireland, puts economic arguments into the mouths of two famous Irishmen.

Swift warns that Irish pride in drinking French wine enriches enemies, begs its own workmen, and drives genius abroad. Ireland, he says, would be richer, healthier, and happier drinking its own ale, beer, mead, and cider. The pamphlet is a sharp piece of Irish economic patriotism in dialogue form.
2525-john-ingerfield-and-other-stories:
Jerome K. Jerome opens this set with the title story of John Ingerfield, an oil and tallow refiner of Limehouse. Tales of a Norwegian mountain farm, stage patter, silhouettes, and the lease of a country inn called the Cross Keys follow. Jerome warns readers up front that the first three stories are serious, not comic.

That warning matters, because the book shifts between quiet tragedy and music hall jokes with ease. The Ingerfield story traces a hard family line, while the lighter pieces show Jerome's gift for talk and character. Together they show a writer wider than his comic fame, able to move from laughter to sorrow in a few pages.
25281-briefless-ballads-and-legal-lyrics:
James Williams's Briefless Ballads and Legal Lyrics, second series, published in London in 1895, turns law into light verse. Williams, a lawyer-poet, jokes that a lawyer has as little business with poetry as with justice, quoting Peacock's Melincourt for cover.

Poems include Justinian at Windermere, a vision of legal shadows, a garden party in the Temple, and lawn tennis in the Temple gardens. Cases become ballads, such as Mylward v. Weldon, where a plaintiff who filed a sixscore-sheet replication was paraded with his head through a hole in it. The book delights lawyers and lay readers alike.
25432-the-baby-s-bouquet-a-fresh-bunch-o:
This picture songbook gathers old nursery rhymes with tunes, as a companion to The Baby's Opera. The tunes were collected and arranged by L. C., while Walter Crane arranged and decorated the pages. Edmund Evans cut and printed the book in colours for Frederick Warne and Company. Its contents run from Polly Put the Kettle On and Hot Cross Buns to The Little Woman and the Pedlar.

Later pages give If All the World Were Paper, with its sea of ink and trees of bread and cheese. The Fairy Ship sails with white mice for sailors, satin sails, and a golden mast. Song titles appear as illustrations in the print edition, and a matching online version adds sheet music and audio for the songs.
2545-when-god-laughs-and-other-stories:
Jack London published this story set in 1911, opening with a tale of Carquinez, a man who claims Aztec, Inca, and Spanish blood and lives by a wise, instinctive temperance. The gods, London suggests, laugh hardest at men who think they have mastered fate.

An apostate factory boy, a wicked woman, a boxer past his prime in A Piece of Steak, and the crew of the Francis Spaight follow. The stories hit hard on labor, hunger, and pride, with London's blunt naturalism at full strength. Readers get a dozen sharp blows, each asking what a person is worth when luck turns.
25452-the-kangaroo-marines:
Capt. R. W. Campbell, author of Private Spud Tamson, writes a comic war tale of Australians. His hero Sam Killem advertises for one thousand cheerful toughs to join the Kangaroo Marines, barring boozers, shirkers, and loonies. Jackaroos, cattlemen, rouseabouts, and shearers answer, promised six shillings a day and the jewels of the Sultan's harem. The corps aims to be the crack unit of the Australian force.

Chapters follow the quartette from Melbourne versus Sydney through Egypt to the landing and Hell-Fire Post. A brave New Zealander, a chapter on what lady readers like, and a victory close the book. Cassell published it in 1915, dedicated to the conquerors of Anzac and to friends Campbell met in Australasia, Egypt, and the Dardanelles.
25500-a-london-life-and-other-tales:
Henry James gathers four tales in this 1889 Macmillan volume. A London Life follows Laura through a restless household, where strange voices frighten her and her sister Selina's flight shadows the children. Laura walks to Plash, the dower-house a mile and a half through the park, to see old Mrs. Berrington and Lady Davenant. She returns to the schoolroom tea, with bread and butter, candles, and her small nephews Scratch and Parson.

The other tales are The Patagonia, The Liar, and Mrs. Temperly, the last first published under a different name. Selina's children, Ferdy among them, do not miss their mother and ask no questions about her, adding to Laura's sense of dreariness. James writes London society with the close observation his readers expect.
25549-a-chosen-few-short-stories:
Frank R. Stockton gathers chosen short stories in this 1895 volume from Charles Scribner's Sons, with an etched portrait by W. H. W. Bicknell. Many tales come from earlier books, including The Christmas Wreck, The Watchmaker's Wife, and The Lady, or the Tiger?

A tale of negative gravity, Asaph, and His Wife's Deceased Sister appears beside the remarkable wreck of the Thomas Hyke. Old Pipes and the Dryad and the Transferred Ghost also appear. The volume includes his famous tale The Lady, or the Tiger? Stockton's humour turns on odd premises followed with straight-faced logic to a surprising end.
25582-daughters-of-the-puritans-a-group-:
Seth Curtis Beach writes brief lives of seven women shaped by Puritan New England in this volume, first published in 1905 and reprinted in 1967. A picture of Lydia Maria Child's home at Wayland, Massachusetts, opens the set.

Catharine Maria Sedgwick, Mary Lovell Ware, and Lydia Maria Child come first. Dorothea Lynde Dix, Sarah Margaret Fuller Ossoli, Harriet Beecher Stowe, and Louisa May Alcott follow. Sedgwick, once called queen of American letters, dates from 1789 to 1867. Alcott of Little Women fame dates from 1832 to 1888. Beach stresses character and public work beside writing. The Essay Index Reprint Series label marks the book as a reference work for libraries.
25584-the-purcell-papers-index-and-conte:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's Purcell Papers, in three volumes from Richard Bentley in 1880, gain a working index and contents list in this volume, with a memoir by Alfred Perceval Graves. The set was reprinted from the University of Chicago Library copy in a 1975 AMS edition.

Index entries cover an adventure of Hardress Fitzgerald, a royalist captain, Billy Malowney's taste of love and glory, the bridal of a Tyrone family tale, and the drunkard's dream. Readers use the index to find Le Fanu's Irish gothic tales across all three volumes without hunting through each book.
25600-bird-stories:
Edith M. Patch writes Bird Stories for the Little Gateways to Science series, published by Little, Brown in 1926 with a 1921 copyright and pictures by Robert J. Sim. She dedicates the book to Junior Audubon classes and to all boys and girls friendly to birds.

Chick, D.D., in his pulpit fronts the book, and contents follow with the five worlds of Larie, Peter Piper, Gavia of Immer Lake, Eve and Petro, Uncle Sam, Corbie, and Ardea's soldier. Each story teaches bird ways through a single bird's life, in prose clear enough for young naturalists.
25608-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson writes this child's garden of verses, issued by Dodge in New York in 1905 with pictures by Bessie Collins Pease. The volume ran through four editions by October 1908, a mark of its lasting appeal.

Contents list Bed in Summer and From a Railway Carriage. The Cow, At the Sea Side, and Autumn Fires follow. Block City, The Dumb Soldier, and Fairy Bread appear beside Foreign Lands, Garden Days, and Farewell to the Farm. Envoys close the contents. Stevenson speaks in a child's voice about play, travel, bedtime, and the small wonders of home and garden.
25609-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson writes this child's garden of verses in the 1905 Scribner edition, illustrated by Jessie Willcox Smith and reset in March 1955. Stevenson dedicates the book to Alison Cunningham, his nurse, in verse thanking her for story books, comforted pains, and long nights awake.

He calls her his second mother and his first wife. He calls her the angel of his infant life. He asks her, now that the sick child is well and old, to take the little book. The verses themselves speak of gardens, journeys, ships, and bedtime, in the child's voice Stevenson made classic.
25610-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson writes this child's garden of verses in the 1895 edition illustrated by Charles Robinson, published by Scribner in New York and John Lane in London. Edinburgh and Vailima, with the years 1850 and 1894, mark the title page, spanning Stevenson's life.

Stevenson dedicates the book to Alison Cunningham, his nurse, thanking her for long nights awake, story books read, and pains comforted. He calls her his second mother, his first wife, and the angel of his infant life. The verses that follow speak in a child's voice about play, garden, travel, and bedtime.
25611-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
This Philadelphia edition of A Child's Garden of Verses, illustrated by Millicent Sowerby and published by David McKay, keeps Stevenson's dedication to Alison Cunningham in full. For long nights awake, a comfortable hand through uneven land, story books read, and pains comforted, the poet thanks his nurse.

He calls her his second mother, his first wife, and the angel of his infant life. The little book goes to the nurse who tended him in childhood. A prayer closes the dedication, asking that every child who hears the rhymes find as dear a nurse at need in the bright, fireside nursery world.
25617-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Rand McNally issues this edition of A Child's Garden of Verses, illustrated by E. Mars and M. H. Squire, with a 1900 copyright and a 1928 edition. An introduction notes that Robert Louis Stevenson was still a boy at heart when he published the volume, though thirty-five by the calendar.

He had outgrown his knickerbockers, the introduction says, but never outgrew quick sympathy, a brave heart, a fresh outlook, and confident faith. Those qualities shape verses about gardens, ships, soldiers, and bedtime, spoken in a child's voice for children and for grown readers who sigh to be boys again.
25624-faces-and-places:
Henry W. Lucy writes this volume of faces and places for the Whitefriars Library of Wit and Humour. He had earlier written East by West, a record of a journey round the world. Henry and Company published the book in London. A portrait of the author fronts the book.

Lucy dedicates the volume to J. R. Robinson, editor and manager of the Daily News. He fills it with sketches of public men, scenes, and manners observed in London and abroad. The pieces mix humour, anecdote, and sharp comment, giving readers a journalist's gallery of late Victorian public life.
25627-the-hunted-heroes:
Robert Silverberg writes this Mars adventure, opening on a barren, desolate, forbidding planet tough enough to stop the most adventurous. A mad genius with a motto, death to all Terrans, stands against the heroes as well.

The narrator urges Val to keep moving, since giving up on Mars means death, and turns up the pressure on her oxymask to ease her breathing. Through the glassite, her face shows agony from fatigue, and she blames him for the failed sandcat. A grease monkey back at the Dome, who failed to fasten something down, may bear the real fault.
25634-christmas-roses:
Lizzie Lawson and Robert Ellice Mack write this small verse book, Christmas Roses, published in London by Griffith, Farran and Company. An opening poem offers a bunch of Christmas roses to a fairest child, plucked in a garden where drifting snow lies piled.

No violets, cowslips, or daisy chains can be brought in winter, when grassy meadows lie clad in snow and no sun smiles. The poets instead pluck verses from a garden wild, to cheer wet and wintry hours for a child. Short, tender rhymes make the book a Christmas gift in verse.
25645-the-principal-navigations-voyages-:
Richard Hakluyt collects the principal navigations, voyages, traffics, and discoveries of the English nation in this thirteenth volume, America part two, edited by Edmund Goldsmid. Letters and reports, not a single narrative, fill its pages.

Sir George Peckham's true report of late discoveries continues from part one. Letters from Sir Francis Walsingham to Hakluyt and to Thomas Aldworth of Bristol encourage cosmography and western discovery. Aldworth replies on a western voyage to the American coast southwest of Cape Breton, showing merchants, courtiers, and scholars planning new routes together. Goldsmid keeps Hakluyt's old spellings, such as discoueries, preserving Elizabethan flavour.
25647-holiday-tales:
Florence Wilford, author of Nigel Bartram's Ideal and An Author's Children, writes Holiday Tales, published in London by Griffith, Farran, Okeden and Welsh and in New York by Dutton. Planning out the ground fronts the book.

Seven Campbells opens the tales, with mother and sons, Johnnie's protege, and what seven Campbells can do. A poem about seven lovely Campbells whose father was Archibald prompts a child to ask if it means them. Cecil's memorable week follows, with a bachelor's lunch, good news, and an ending that declares it all right.
25655-the-skating-party-and-other-storie:
This children's story book, published in New York by George A. Leavitt, opens with The Skating Party, illustrated with skaters on a river. One cold winter morning, Willie's mother promises to take him to see skaters, and Willie, in great glee, wants to go on the ice himself.

His mother fears to venture, though the river lies frozen very hard and merry skaters seem almost to fly over the glib ice. Falls bring bursts of laughter, and each skater jumps up to go again. The tale warns that skating pleases and strengthens, yet breaks in ice can drown, so little boys should take care.
25665-popular-adventure-tales:
Captain Mayne Reid gathers three boy adventure tales in this illustrated volume from Simpkin, Marshall in London and Morison in Glasgow. The Young Voyageurs, or Boy Hunters in the North, The Forest Exiles amid the Amazon wilds, and The Bush Boys in southern Africa form the set.

A biographical sketch notes Reid was born at Ballyroney, County Down, in April 1818, son of a minister, educated for the church, then emigrated to New Orleans in January 1840. Plantation work, travel, and soldiering followed, feeding tales of fur countries, young voyageurs on the Red River, trumpeter swans, and castaways.
25698-think-before-you-speak-or-the-thre:
The author of The Peacock at Home writes this tale, Think Before You Speak, or The Three Wishes, in a third edition from M. J. Godwin's Juvenile Library in London in 1810. Its preface credits Madame de Beaumont's Magazin des Enfans, the delight of children of the last generation.

Beaumont's story, told with French simplicity and sprightliness, loses charm in literal translation, so this version retells it in English for nursery and schoolroom readers. Three wishes, granted without thought, teach children to weigh words before speaking, in a short moral tale of the kind early children's books loved.
25710-last-words-a-final-collection-of-s:
Juliana Horatia Ewing gathers her final stories in Last Words, published in Boston by Roberts Brothers in 1891 with pictures by H. D. Murphy. Ewing, author of Jan of the Windmill, Six to Sixteen, and Jackanapes, signs the book in a front illustration.

The preface notes that Mary's Meadow first ran in Aunt Judy's Magazine from November 1883 to March 1884, the last serial story Ewing wrote. After years of moving from place to place, its subject arose from her own unsettled life. The collection preserves a beloved Victorian children's writer at her close.
25786-american-sketches:
Charles Whibley writes American Sketches, published by William Blackwood and Sons in 1908, opening in New York. To land at Hoboken in quiet drizzle, Whibley says, is to sound depths of desolation, with a raw, half finished, unkempt street confronting the traveller.

A sad tram crawls along ruts, shops bear odd foreign names, and dark men lounging at doors suggest neither hustling spirit nor democratic grandeur. Memory of a great steamship's pomp and New York harbour shining in the mind heightens the letdown, as Whibley, fresh from apostrophising Liberty, sketches America with an English traveller's sharp eye.
25882-famous-islands-and-memorable-voyag:
Printed by D. Lothrop and Company, this book gathers eight island tales and sea voyages for young readers. A Venetian cruiser opens the set in 1431, when the port of Venice brimmed with ships bearing wine, spices, and fine cotton. Captain James's journal follows, with a winter in northern seas, and the finders of Madeira, St. Helena, and the Pitcairn islanders come next.

Norfolk Island, a solitary islander, and Captain Cook's last voyage close the book. One prison break scene shows men maddened by thirst for liberty rushing the deck, seizing a sentry's pistols, and throwing him overboard, though he was later saved. The tales mix true voyages with stirring scenes, and the frontispiece of castaways sets the tone for all.
25891-answers-to-prayer-from-george-mu-l:
Compiled by A. E. C. Brooks from the narratives of George Müller, this book gathers tales of prayer answered in the Bristol orphan work. Müller opens with his rule for finding God's will. First bring the heart to a state of having no will of its own in the matter. Then wait with patience for guidance through Scripture. He says that in some sixty nine years of seeking, he was always led right, while haste and trust in men's counsel led him astray.

Chapters follow the orphan houses from early days through waiting for help, gifts of one thousand pounds, and buildings raised by faith. Müller tells readers that answers may come in their own walks of life, in family, trade, or church work, not only in orphan care. The book is a plain record of trust, patience, and gifts that arrived just when they were needed.
25913-tales-of-folk-and-fairies:
Katharine Pyle writes and illustrates fourteen folk tales from many lands in this 1919 book from Little, Brown. A Scots worm tale, a Louisiana bull man, a Scandinavian widow's son, and a wise Serbian girl open the set. Ali Cogia from the Arabian Nights, a Cossack tale, talking eggs, a Russian frog princess, and Persian tales of magic turbans, swords, carpets, and silver citrons follow.

A Norse magic pipe, a Hindu triumph of truth, a Bengal life secret, and Dame Pridgett and the fairies close the book. One scene shows boys acting out the case of Ali Cogia and Abul Hassan before a hidden caliph and vizier, with a boy judge settling the suit. Pyle's pictures and plain retellings make old tales fresh for young readers.
25917-gold-out-of-celebes:
Captain A. E. Dingle sets a sea yarn of gold hunting off Celebes, printed by Little, Brown in 1920. Jack Barry, late mate of the Gregg, loafs three weeks at Batavia without a job, scorning shore work got through a consulate he rates as cocktails and reports. Fat jobs exist for men who grin at rebuffs, but Barry sticks to his own trade and waits for a berth at sea.

A frontispiece shows Natalie stepping back with a choking sob of horror at what stooping men have found. Night watches on a river grow dull, with little brown sailors dozing in corners and officers fighting sleep in the deckhouse. Hawsers twang, rats stir, and alarms fail, till danger slips close. Dingle writes of sailors, gold, and the East with brisk, salt humor.
25918-heads-and-tales:
Adam White, late assistant in the zoological department of the British Museum, compiles anecdotes of beasts and the distinguished men linked to them. Printed in 1870 in a second edition, the book treats mammals by story rather than by system. Dogs and horses stand as special friends who seem to grasp us, while cats and cows hold a different, cooler bond with man.

One tale honors Bussapa, a Mahratta hunter called the tiger slayer, who wore silver medals from the Indian government for his courage. Colonel Campbell records from his brother's diary how Bussapa faced a tiger with presence of mind after it knocked down its prey. The frontispiece shows the Tasmanian wolf, and tales of beasts and their masters run through a book fond of both.
2597-mrs-skagg-s-husbands-and-other-stor:
Bret Harte opens this set with Mrs. Skagg's Husbands, as the sun rises over the Sierra foothills east of Angel's camp. The tales that follow bring Santa Claus to Simpson's Bar, Princess Bob and her friends, the Iliad of Sandy Bar, and a prodigal Mr. Thompson.

A romance of Madrono Hollow, the poet of Sierra Flat, and a Christmas gift for Rupert round out the volume. Harte mixes camp humor with holiday feeling, and his miners, wives, and wanderers feel like old friends. The book shows his gift for turning rough California life into warm, surprising stories.
25973-birds-of-the-rockies:
Leander S. Keyser writes of Rocky Mountain birds in this 1902 book from A. C. McClurg, with plates by Louis Agassiz Fuertes and Bruce Horsfall. Dedicated to Katherine and the boys in memory of happy days indoors and out, the book climbs high and low. It moves from up and down the heights and bald peaks and green vales to birds of the arid plain, over the divide and back, and a Rocky Mountain lake.

A full checklist of Colorado birds closes the volume. One city scene finds Keyser spying a small finch-like bird through his glass, striped gray and brown, with face, crown, breast, and rump washed crimson. He wonders at the chipper chap's dressy coat and well bred manners. The book mixes field notes, local views, and plain love of birds.
2598-urban-sketches:
Bret Harte turns from mining camps to city streets in these sketches, opening with a venerable impostor glimpsed across his table. From a balcony, among melons, and along sidewalks, Harte watches neighbors, boys, dogs, and steamers with a journalist's eye.

A boy's dog, charitable reminiscences, and the act of seeing a steamer off each get a short, sharp scene. The sketches show Harte as a city observer, fond of small frauds and small kindnesses alike. Readers get a lighter Harte, sketching modern life in quick strokes rather than full tales.
2599-legends-and-tales:
Bret Harte gathers California legends in this volume, and warns the cautious reader himself that documentary evidence for them is thin. The Legend of Monte del Diablo, the adventure of Padre Vincentio, and the Legend of Devil's Point lead a parade of haunted hills and holy tricksters.

The Devil meets a broker, an ogress haunts Silver Land, and the ruins of San Francisco rise in a prophetic vision. A night at Wingdam closes the set with campfire color. Harte blends Spanish folklore, mining camp talk, and sly humor, and the tales work best read as fireside inventions, not history.
26023-the-league-of-nations-and-its-prob:
Three lectures on the League of Nations and its problems appear in Longmans' contributions to international law and diplomacy, edited by L. Oppenheim, Whewell professor at Cambridge. The lectures weigh what a new league could do for peace, law, and order among states after the Great War. Oppenheim's series also lists guides to diplomatic practice and monographs on conventions and third states.

One lecture argues that international law as it stands is largely book law, customary, controversial, full of gaps, and uncertain in many points. International legislation, the lecturer says, could slowly turn that book law into firm, clear, authoritative statute law. The task is full of difficulties, four of which the lectures take up in turn. The book is a sober, scholarly brief for law among nations.
2603-questionable-amusements-and-worthy-:
J. M. Judy wrote this book for readers worried about the amusements of a new century, with an introduction by George H. Trever. The manuscript was never sent to a publisher; friends put it into print in Chicago in 1904 through Jennings and Pye.

Judy weighs dances, theaters, cards, and other pastimes, judging which harm character and which wholesome substitutes might take their place. His tone is earnest and pastoral, aimed at parents, teachers, and church workers. The book now reads as a window on Edwardian moral worry, and on the search for clean fun.
26049-stand-by-naval-sketches-and-storie:
Taffrail, pen name of Henry Taprell Dorling, tells naval sketches and stories in Stand By, printed by Pearson in 1916 and dedicated to the ship's company, second to none. Contents run from the acting sub and the mother ship to out happy home, bloodless surgery, bunting, the lost sheep, a naval menagerie, and the Muckle Flugga hussars. Pirates, fog, traders, and Potvin of the Puffin follow.

The acting sub opens as a very junior officer, a mere sub lieutenant with acting after his name and a single gold stripe still new and untarnished. Not long before he was a snotty, a dog's body obeying nearly every officer aboard. The book turns passenger liners into men of war and enemy submarines into growing danger, with humor and salt pride.
26058-the-starvation-treatment-of-diabet:
Lewis Webb Hill and Rena S. Eckman set out the starvation treatment of diabetes with graduated diets used at Massachusetts General Hospital, second edition printed in 1916. An introduction by Richard C. Cabot praises Dr. Allen's changes to the classic treatment of saccharine diabetes, already proven in two years to advance the fight against the disease, though it demands detailed knowledge of food composition and calorie value.

Hill and Eckman's little book aims to aid physicians who lack that detail, with diets, urine tests, bran cakes, and muffins. A sample salad mixes cabbage and celery with walnut meats and cream dressing, and a cucumber cup is pared, quartered, hollowed, and filled. The book is a clinical record of a harsh but hopeful treatment from the years before insulin.
26064-problems-of-expansion-as-considere:
Whitelaw Reid gathers papers and addresses on American expansion in this Century volume of 1900, copyrighted 1898 and 1900. Reid says scattered pieces drew such praise that he set them in date order, from authorized texts or newspaper reports. The opening piece, on the territory with which we are threatened, was written before his appointment to the peace commission with Spain and printed days after. It drew sharp notice to his views on keeping taken territory.

Later pieces weigh the treaty of Paris, its purport and consequences, and later aspects of new duties. One note records American commissioners urging order over the whole Philippine archipelago pending ratification, with each nation's authorities keeping order where established. The book is a statesman's record of the annexation debate at its height.
26070-chinese-folk-lore-tales:
Rev. J. Macgowan retells Chinese folk lore tales in this Macmillan volume of 1910. Contents run from the widow Ho and Kwang Jui and the river god. The beautiful daughter of Liu Kung, the fairy bonze, a mysterious Buddhist robe, and the vengeance of a goddess follow. A wonderful man, the god of the city, and the tragedy of the Yin family come after. Two pages, three to four and thirteen to fourteen, are missing from the source copy.

The widow Ho opens at dawn, when mandarin Shih Kung leaves the city god's temple after incense and prayer, a just official revered through the provinces for Tien Li, divine righteousness. Later tales show Chang Lung twice fetching an old man's shoe from a brook and putting it on his foot, winning a fairy's book for his kindness. The book gives Western readers old Chinese wonders in plain dress.
26164-child-land-picture-pages-for-the-l:
Child Land, issued in London by S. W. Partridge and Company, is a picture book for small children holding nearly two hundred designs by Oscar Pletsch, M. Richter, and others. Each page pairs a picture with a short piece of verse or prose. The pages move through the small world of home, garden, and school. Subjects include the broken cup, the sick doll, feeding the birds, the washing tub, and the grocer's shop.

Later pages add the harvest field, a walk in wind and rain, a strolling fiddler, and lessons learned at school. The tone is gentle and moral, praising kindness, care, and good temper, and the book works as a window onto how Victorian children were shown their own daily lives in print.
26187-the-gentle-art-of-cooking-wives:
Elizabeth Strong Worthington's 1900 volume, a companion to her How to Cook Husbands, turns marriage advice into comedy. It opens with a girls' club in disorder, electing Prue Shaftsbury president so they can debate a scandalous article titled How to Cook Wives. Hilda Bretherton, Puddy Kennett, and Nannie Branscome trade jokes about officers, committees, and secret societies.

Later scenes bring Steve Loveland, settled in a rented attic with screens, old furniture, and a stove holding winter at bay. The book satirizes both the advice books that claimed to manage wives and the clubs that aped them. Its humour is light, its targets are manners and marriage talk, and its heroines answer back with wit.
26190-a-choice-of-miracles:
James A. Cox's science-fiction story opens with Andy Larson, a hard-headed Swede, lying helpless after a crash in the jungle. He can move nothing but his head, and he hears only water and the far whine of a patrol ship on a search grid. His ship skipped across a river into forest trees without fire or explosion, so he doubts the patrol will spot him.

His one hope is another survivor who can move, shout, climb, or light a flare. As hours pass, a voice reaches him, pleading and loving, and he tells her of the crash in light terms. The tale's teasing question runs through it: when prayer is all that is left, is life truly what you want above all else?
26307-the-wizard-s-daughter-and-other-st:
Margaret Collier Graham's 1905 volume, issued by Houghton, Mifflin in Boston and New York, gathers six California stories. The title tale opens on a mesa cabin, where a norther wind strips vineyard leaves and a young invalid named Palmerston sits on the porch. Mrs. Dysart sweeps eucalyptus leaves while valley haze turns golden at sunset.

Other stories include Marg'et Ann, At the Foot of the Trail, Lib, For Value Received, and The Face of the Poor. Mid-book pages show Marg'et Ann and Lloyd walking at dusk past fresh-plowed furrows, keeping a dead woman's house with scrupulous care. Graham writes of foothill folk, work, and loss with quiet sympathy and a sharp eye for place.
26346-our-bird-comrades:
Leander S. Keyser's Our Bird Comrades, issued by Rand, McNally in 1907, invites readers to know birds as comrades, studied with the glass and without the gun. Keyser, author of Birddom and Birds of the Rockies, watched birds day after day in their haunts, at cost of time, effort, and money. A sparrow-hawk fronts the book.

Keyser aims at scientific accuracy without heavy jargon, and he hopes to stir the young to use eyes and ears outdoors. Mid-book pages contrast honest brood care with the screaming cowbird, which drops eggs into the nests of bay-winged cousins and makes them rear its young. The book offers field notes, wonder, and a plea to watch birds alive.
26354-woodward-s-country-homes:
George E. and F. W. Woodward, architects, issued Woodward's Country Homes at New York in 1866, in a fourth thousand printing. The pattern book opens with domestic architecture and embellishment, then offers numbered designs for builders and owners. Early plans cover a labourer's cottage, small frame cottages, a gardener's cottage, and a farm cottage.

Later designs add stables and coach houses, a rural church, a suburban cottage, an ornamental summer house, and an ice house. A school house at Irvington, a country chapel, and an old house remodelled widen the range. Chapters on fences and gates, plus pumps and Kedzie rain-water filters, give practical detail. The book shows how mid-century Americans planned plain, useful homes.
26356-a-brother-to-dragons-and-other-old:
Amelie Rives's 1888 volume, issued by Harper and Brothers, holds three old-time tales first printed in magazines. The title story, from the Atlantic Monthly of March 1886, is set in 1586 and told by a man named Butter. His wife Marian nursed Lady Margaret, twin sister of Lord Robert of Amhurste, and the pair had quarrelled over a family ghost in a blue chamber.

The Farrier Lass o' Piping Pebworth, from Lippincott's of July 1887, brings a country courtship in song, with Robin falling at his lass's feet. Nurse Crumpet Tells the Story, from Harper's of September 1887, closes the set. Rives writes in old speech and old manners, with ghosts, pride, and love driving each tale.
2636-the-historical-nights-entertainment:
Rafael Sabatini set himself a task in this first series: to rebuild famous and bizarre events in full detail, with all the color surviving records allow. He chose episodes strange in themselves and born of intrigue, passion, or crime, rather than familiar textbook scenes.

Each night's entertainment retells a historical moment as a vivid tale, with courts, conspirators, and doomed lovers. Sabatini's preface owns his method plainly: color where records allow it, invention never where fact speaks. The book suits readers who like history as story, told by a master of adventure.
2639-villa-rubein-and-other-stories:
John Galsworthy gathers stories in this volume, led by Villa Rubein, a long tale of love and art in twenty nine chapters. A Man of Devon, A Knight, Salvation of a Forsyte, and The Silence follow, each showing Galsworthy's early range beyond the Forsyte clan.

Galsworthy writes of country houses, artists, soldiers, and families under strain, with the irony and pity that mark his best work. The preface to Villa Rubein frames a young writer finding his voice. The set offers a fine way into Galsworthy before the saga, and several stories that stand on their own.
26393-the-medicinal-plants-of-the-philip:
T. H. Pardo de Tavera, a Paris-trained doctor and scientific commissioner in the Philippines, wrote this survey of the islands' healing plants. Jerome B. Thomas Jr., a United States Army surgeon, translated and revised it for the 1901 Philadelphia edition, adding sizes, leaf lengths, flower colors, and English names to aid recognition in the field.

Each entry gives the plant's scientific name, local names, habitat, and blooming season, then the uses recorded for it, such as a leaf decoction used as an astringent. The book was aimed at medical officers posted far from towns. Its advice is over a century old and is offered here for history only, not as guidance for use.
26399-fairy-prince-and-other-stories:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott's 1922 collection holds six whimsical stories told by a child narrator who was nine at the time. The title story opens at Thanksgiving in her father's house, where the family buds the Christmas tree each year. A guest arrives from Cuba, young Derry Willard, whose steady gaze at seventeen-year-old Rosalee makes their father so nervous that he cuts his hand carving.

The other tales are The Game of the Be-Witchments, The Blinded Lady, The Gift of the Probable Places, The Book of the Funny Smells, and The Little Dog Who Couldn't Sleep. Throughout, grown-ups play along with children's fancies, and small household wonders, sights missed on a walk, and a contest of pictures carry the charm.
26407-an-arrow-in-a-sunbeam-and-other-ta:
This London collection of the 1880s gathers short tales, most by Sarah Orne Jewett, with pieces by C. S. Sleight and Frances Lee. The title story follows a minister who notices a shabby old widow in his fashionable church. He visits her topmost room, where a monthly rose and a heliotrope bloom beside rare books and fine engravings. Her crippled son repairs watches, and her patient endurance teaches the pastor more than he teaches her.

Other tales include Miss Sydney's Flowers, A Bit of Shore Life, and Lady Ferry, about a very old woman whose wandering mind holds strange fancies yet stays gentle and harmless. A Brave Boy and How Lily Got the Cat complete a volume of quiet, kindly stories, where small kindnesses carry the weight of the plot.
26414-fil-and-filippa-story-of-child-lif:
John Stuart Thomson's 1917 book introduces young readers to the Philippines through two children, Fil and his sister Filippa. The narrator, a visitor who sailed by Panama and San Francisco across the Pacific, meets Fil, Filippa, their playmates Moro and Favra, their parents, and the good Padre. The children tell him of their islands as a string of pearls hung from the equator.

Chapters cover names, climate and typhoons, worship, houses, cocoa and coffee, hemp and sugar, and the coconut, then forests, minerals, water buffalo, boats and fish, home life, dress, and an Adios feast. A piña gown, woven slowly from fine pineapple fibre, is promised to Filippa for the feast day. The book teaches geography through friendship and daily work.
26449-rambles-of-an-arch-ologist-among-o:
Frederick William Fairholt's 1871 papers, first written for the Art-Journal, ramble through art and archaeology with anecdote and curious lore. Ancient art, medieval art, and the Renaissance open the walk, followed by heraldry, enamelling, mosaic, glass-painting, Gothic metalwork, Raffaelle ware, wood panelling, and decorative furniture. Book illumination, engraved ornaments, metalworkers, and ancient jewellery extend the tour.

Two hundred and fifty-nine wood engravings, cut from the author's own sketches, illustrate the text. Wills and brasses supply telling details, such as Edward Lee's 1535 bequest of a double-wreathed gold ring worn on his thumb, matched by a gowned citizen's effigy at Hastings. Fairholt writes in a popular style, aiming to please general readers as well as antiquaries.
26451-a-stable-for-nightmares-or-weird-t:
J. Sheridan Le Fanu's 1896 collection gathers eleven tales of the uncanny, published in New York by the New Amsterdam Book Company. Dickon the Devil opens near Pendle Forest in Lancashire, where a visitor sent to divide a small property meets a garrulous inn host and learns of Barwyke house. A debt of honor, a dream, a quest, and a haunting follow in turn.

Later stories include Pichon and Sons of the Croix Rousse, The Phantom Fourth, The Spirit's Whisper, and Dr. Feversham's Story, closing with the secret of two plaster casts and the puzzle titled What Was It? Le Fanu, known for Uncle Silas and The House by the Churchyard, works here in his familiar mode: ordinary travelers, lonely houses, and dread that gathers slowly rather than striking at once.
26457-new-observations-on-the-natural-hi:
Francis Huber's New Observations on the Natural History of Bees, translated into English at Edinburgh in 1806, reports his hive experiments in thirteen letters. Early letters trace the impregnation of the queen bee, the retarding of fecundation, and Schirach's discovery. Later letters prove that common bees sometimes lay fertile eggs, and describe combats of queens and the massacre of males.

Huber studies what follows when a stranger queen replaces the natural one. He notes that bees seize and hold her captive in a dense cluster if she arrives within twelve hours of the old queen's removal. Further letters ask whether the queen is oviparous, how cell size shapes the bees produced, and how swarms form. An appendix and economical notes on beekeeping close the volume.
26475-the-boy-scouts-book-of-campfire-st:
Edited by Franklin K. Mathiews, chief scout librarian of the Boy Scouts of America, this 1921 collection, reissued in 1933, gathers stories fit for telling around a campfire. Mathiews calls the campfire a place of council, friendship, and story, where the glow quickens the mind and wakes happy tales. The stories aim at boys in their early teens, when growth of brain and body runs fast.

Professor George Walter Fiske, quoted in the introduction, urges boys to emulate the woodsman: keen vision, steady nerve, endurance, honesty, and faithfulness in friendship. The tales themselves range from winter travel, where small camp chores strain partnerships, to bold outdoor adventure. Notes by the editor help scoutmasters tell each story well.
26485-the-making-of-bobby-burnit-being-a:
George Randolph Chester's comic novel, copyrighted in 1908 and 1909, follows Bobby Burnit, idle heir to about three million, after his father's will shocks him into work. Old John Burnit writes that he believes his son a fool, but blames his own absorption in business for it. Bobby must run the John Burnit Store himself, as his only resource, while the rest of the fortune waits in trust.

Bobby, whose thoughts run to healthy amusements and Agnes Elliston, consults Agnes first, valuing her keen judgment. Later he faces a fifty-million-dollar corporation scheme, in which a watered stock, the Consumers', is raised from two to five million before consolidation. Chester, author of Get Rich Quick Wallingford, turns business education into farce.
26486-the-dukeries:
R. Murray Gilchrist describes and E. W. Haslehust pictures the Dukeries, the ducal country of Nottinghamshire, in this 1913 volume of the Beautiful England series. Worksop and its manor open the tour, with the Priory Gateway as frontispiece, followed by Robin Hood's Larder, the Major Oak of Thoresby Park, and the beech avenue at Thoresby. Welbeck Abbey, Clumber, Ollerton, and Rufford Abbey follow.

Welbeck draws special praise, nestled low in a wooded park, noble yet melancholy, and admired most by a wise, witty, and learned lady of its past. The book wonders whether her ghost still wanders those precincts, angered at enlargements of her home. Edwinstowe and the Japanese garden at Rufford close a gentle guide to a storied landscape.
26509-journal-of-the-third-voyage-for-th:
Captain William Edward Parry kept this journal on his third Arctic voyage, begun in 1824. The ships Hecla and Fury sailed to find a sea passage between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans through the far north of America. An opening life sketch traces Parry from his birth at Bath in 1790 through his first two voyages. Those voyages had pushed British Arctic knowledge far westward, but left the passage unfound.

Day by day entries follow the ships into Baffin's Bay and through pack ice. Parry records stores, warming stoves, and the grind of sawing ships free and hauling them off ice. He also records the slow unrigging of the Fury as ice pressed her hard. Readers get a commander's plain account of hardship, routine, and near-disaster in the search for the passage.
26513-a-spelling-book-for-advanced-class:
William T. Adams, master of Boston's Bowditch School, wrote this spelling book for pupils who already knew the rules of pronunciation and syllabication, the way words divide into spoken parts. First entered for copyright in 1868 and printed in 1873, it was meant to follow an ordinary spelling book, not replace it. Its aim was to test older scholars on harder words in common use.

Its plan is strict. Lessons hold thirty numbered words each, given with no pronunciation marks and no grouping by first letter or ending. Pupils must rely on their own knowledge and turn to a dictionary when stuck. Words range from everyday terms to rare ones such as flageolet and phantasmagoria. Teachers were told to set written lessons in lines, giving extra practice in dividing words.
26529-the-dakotan-languages-and-their-re:
A. W. Williamson of Augustana College, Rock Island, Illinois, published this philological study in the American Antiquarian for January 1882. It groups the Dakotan languages and asks how closely they relate to one another and to neighboring tongues. Four principal Dakota dialects anchor the study: Santee, Yankton, Assinniboin, and Titon.

Williamson sets beside them three allied groups, including Winnebago, Osage, Omaha, Mandan, Hidatsa, and Crow, with Pawnee and Aricaree noted as somewhat related. Tables of verb stems, nominal stems, and sound correspondences support his comparisons, judged against vocabularies such as Hayden's Indian Tribes of the Missouri. Population notes and remarks on pottery, houses, and speech habits round out a compact early survey.
26606-uncanny-tales:
C. Arthur Pearson published this collection of nine uncanny stories at London in 1916. The opening tale sets the tone. Professor William James Maynard, sole heir to his late cousin, strolls home content a month after murdering the old man for a fortune to fund his mathematics. No inquest was held, and the professor plans a great history of higher mathematics with the money.

Other tales promise an armless man, a tomtom clue, and the case of Sir Alister Moeran. A kiss, a Goth, a last ascent, a terror by night, and a tragedy at the Loup Noir complete the set. Murder, the East, and the supernatural mix through the volume. It is a period collection for readers who like their chills served with dry wit and a twist.
26629-werwolves:
Elliott O'Donnell, author of ghost books on haunted houses and byways of ghostland, published this study with Methuen at London in 1912. He begins by admitting that no single definition satisfies, since views of werwolves differ by country, sex, and age. The word itself joins Anglo-Saxon wer, man, and wulf, wolf, with kin in German Währwolf and French loup-garou.

Seventeen chapters cover metamorphosis, spirits of werwolves, how to become one, and exorcism, then tour the British Isles, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Spain, Scandinavia, and Russia. Cases include a lycanthropous brook in the Harz Mountains and the Countess Hilda von Breber. Sceptics, O'Donnell notes, call the belief an insane delusion, but centuries of testimony fill his pages.
26638-pictorial-composition-and-the-crit:
Henry Rankin Poore published this handbook for students and lovers of art with G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1903, dedicating it to his first teacher, Peter Moran. Poore teaches composition as a science of balance, line, and light, with the circle as a unifying and simplifying agent that can rescue a confused picture. His view-metre, a small finder, helps readers test arrangements in real scenes.

Examples range from Raphael, Michelangelo, Dürer, and Botticelli to Millet, Corot, Fortuny, Gérôme, and Detaille, with photographs beside paintings. Chapters weigh steelyard balance, opposition of light and dark measures, transitional lines, and Hogarth's line of beauty. Poore wants viewers to judge pictures by construction, not by subject alone, and to see why art without composition is crippled.
26703-the-children-s-book-of-celebrated-:
Lorinda Munson Bryant published this children's art book with the Century Company at New York in 1922, dedicating it to her daughter Bertha Cookingham Bryant. Bryant, author of Famous Pictures of Real Boys and Girls, presents celebrated pictures one by one, each with its artist, dates, and gallery, told in a child's friendly voice.

Early plates include Pintoricchio's Holy Family at the Academy in Siena, Constable's Valley Farm at the National Gallery in London, and Correggio's Madonna and St. Jerome at Parma. Later plates run from Rembrandt's Night Watch at Amsterdam and Titian's Assumption at Venice to Leonardo's Last Supper at Milan and Whistler's Mother at Paris. Of the Assumption, Bryant tells children to look past the bright colour to the cherubs circling the blessed mother.
26725-two-little-confederates:
Thomas Nelson Page published this boys' book with Charles Scribner's Sons at New York, copyrighted in 1888 and 1916, illustrated, in the Books for Young Readers series. Frank and Willy live at Oakland, a plantation in Old Virginia that ranked in old times among the best in the region. It lies between the Court-house Road and the great Mountain Road, with big woods reaching toward Holetown.

The great-house has as many wings as the angels in Ezekiel's vision, added generation by generation until a separate building was needed. Illustrations show the boys capturing a member of the conscript-guard, selling cakes to the Yankees, and watching men run. Wheat fails and corn turns out fine, soldiers pass, and the house fills with young officers, while the fearless boys ride horses to and from the stables.
2675-burlesques:
William Makepeace Thackeray parodies the popular novels of his day in these burlesques, with notes by eminent hands. George de Barnwell, Codlingsby, Phil Fogarty of the fighting Onety Oneth, and Barbazure each take a famous style and push it over the edge.

Lords and Liveries, Crinoline, and other pieces mock romance, fashion, and heroic history with glee. Thackeray writes as a critic in costume, showing how easily grand styles turn absurd. The book delights as literary satire, and as a young master's exercise in voices. Thackeray's targets knew themselves at once, and laughed anyway.
2676-the-bell-ringer-of-angel-s-and-othe:
Bret Harte opens this set at Angel's, where the North Fork of the Stanislaus River broadens from mountain youth into the plain. The bell ringer, Johnnyboy, young Robin Gray, and the sheriff of Siskiyou each take a story, with a rose of Glenbogie and a hacienda mystery to follow.

Chu Chu and Harte's own My First Book close the volume, mixing camp legend with literary memory. Harte writes with his familiar blend of dialect, irony, and sudden pathos. The stories show California in many moods, from comedy to quiet tragedy, all under a western sky.
26795-get-out-of-our-skies:
E. K. Jarvis wrote this science-fiction story. Its tagline says the long-suffering public tolerated billboards, singing commercials, and half a dozen sales pitches per radio or television show. They howled when hucksters made the wild blue yonder a vast television screen. Its hero is Tom Blacker, star of Ostreich and Company, public relations counsellors.

Then, on November's first cloudy day, Tom orders a rooftop engineer on the Cannon Building to fire a gigantic fifty-thousand-watt projector. Eyes the size of Navy dirigibles appear against gray cumulus. Then Monica Mitchell's whole face appears, close to a thousand feet from chin to hairline, crooning Love Me Alone, theme song of her newest picture. Traffic stops eighteen stories below as drivers leave their autos and raise hands to the heavens, while chief Ostreich demands the projector be turned off at once.
26801-village-improvements-and-farm-vill:
George E. Waring Jr., consulting engineer for sanitary and agricultural works, published these essays with James R. Osgood and Company at Boston in 1877. The papers on village improvements and farm villages were reprinted with amendments from Scribner's Monthly. An added Atlantic Monthly paper treats eastern farming and village residence as a cure for isolated country families' hardships.

Waring calls America par excellence a land of beautiful villages. Thousands of them show good taste in regulation and management. Badly kept private places and neglected public buildings often spoil the effect. Well-organized public sentiment, he argues, can remove the objectionable features and let a village's beauty show. Contents cover village improvements, village sanitary work, farm villages, and the life and work of the eastern farmer, with diagrams of drains, grease-traps, flush-tanks, and sewage disposal at Lenox, Massachusetts.
2684-five-tales:
John Galsworthy gathers five tales in this 1919 volume, opening with his motto that life calls the tune and we dance. The First and Last, A Stoic, The Apple Tree, and The Juryman each study a life caught by fate, duty, or desire.

Indian Summer of a Forsyte closes the set, and later became the opening of the second Forsyte volume. Galsworthy's prose is restrained and ironic, letting small choices carry large weight. The book offers a compact introduction to his art, and a bridge into the saga itself. Each tale turns on a single hard choice.
26874-rock-of-ages:
An illustrated edition of Augustus Montague Toplady's hymn, published by Cupples and Leon Company of New York in 1909. Its epigraph comes from the Second Book of Samuel, where the Lord is called rock and fortress. Its pages pair each verse with pictures: flowers, ocean waves, birds, an angel, a woman, and holly. The whole book is the hymn itself, set out verse by verse for reading or singing.

The singer asks to hide in the cleft rock, and pleads that the water and blood from its riven side be a double cure for sin's guilt and power. No labor of his hands can meet the law's demands, no zeal or tears can atone, and he brings nothing in his hand but clings to the cross. Naked, helpless, and foul, he looks to dress, grace, and the fountain, and closes facing death and the judgment throne.
26916-song-waves:
Theodore H. Rand's 1900 Toronto volume gathers lyric poems under the title Song-Waves, with a frontispiece portrait of the author. Rand, who also compiled A Treasury of Canadian Verse, writes in short musical stanzas about hills, brooks, gardens, and the sea. A dedicatory poem to Emeline opens the volume.

Many poems turn on faith and quiet reflection, with pieces listed by their first lines rather than given titles. The collection reads as a late Victorian Canadian book of verse: formal, devout, and tuned to the seasons, meant to be read slowly and aloud.
2692-a-protegee-of-jack-hamlin-s-and-oth:
Bret Harte returns to Jack Hamlin in this set, opening as the steamer Silveropolis cleaves the broad shallows of the Sacramento River. Hamlin's protegee, an ingenue of the Sierras, and the reformation of James Reddy each test the gambler's code.

The heir of the McHulishes, an episode of West Woodlands, and the home coming of Jim Wilkes round out the volume. Harte mixes river travel, camp society, and sentimental turns with his usual skill. The stories show his late California still rich in rogues, orphans, and second chances. Hamlin's gallantry toward the protegee anchors the set.
26938-esoteric-christianity-or-the-lesse:
