The book gathers jokes meant for telling after dinner, with 155 illustrations by John Leech, Charles Keene, George du Maurier, Phil May, L. Raven-Hill, and J. Bernard Partridge. F. H. Townsend, Reginald Cleaver, Lewis Baumer, and others also contributed illustrations.

The opening essay notes that all good stories are really for telling, and that post-prandial wit has its own pleasures: short, pointed, and sociable. Cartoons and anecdotes on progress, physique, and armor set the tone. Readers who enjoy Victorian and Edwardian cartoon humor will find a well-chosen anthology, complete in itself, from the magazine that defined British comic art.
33843-the-natives:
Katherine MacLean wrote this short science tale, first printed in Science Fiction Stories in 1953. An old one and a youngster of a strange people follow a dark, fast-moving thing that sucks heat and takes in light. The elder warns the child not to get too close, lest he take in too much and grow overcharged.

MacLean tells the tale from the aliens' side, so human readers must guess what the moving thing really is. The story turns on youth, teaching, and the danger of a power not yet understood. It is a clever twist on first contact, told in a few pages with warmth and wit.
33873-dolly-s-college-experiences:
Mabel Cronise Jones wrote this college tale, published in Boston in 1909 with the Roman date MDCCCCIX on its title page. Dolly, a new freshman at Westover, sits on her bed and looks around forlornly, far from home and known by no one. Old girls chatter outside her door, but no one takes notice of her yet.

Chapters follow Dolly through classes, walks with Beth, music, and introductions to new friends. Jones writes warmly for girls about to leave home. The book remains a sweet, early portrait of women's college life in America.
33899-optical-projection-part-1-the-proj:
Lewis Wright wrote this manual on the magic lantern, and Russell S. Wright rewrote it for a fifth edition in 1920. Part one covers the projection of lantern slides for shows and for scientific display. It explains lamps, light sources, lenses, screens, and the handling of the lantern itself.

Chapters move from oil lamps and gas burners through acetylene, limelight, and electric light to the optical system and the lantern body. Diagrams show each part in place. The manual gives a clear, hands-on account of a tool that once lit lecture halls, classrooms, and public shows.
33904-a-briefe-discription-of-new-englan:
Samuel Maverick wrote this brief account of New England in 1660, from a manuscript later found in the British Museum by Henry F. Waters and printed at Boston in 1885. Maverick describes the several towns of New England and the government then in place, in the spelling of his own age. A note on Greenwich leaves a missing distance blank.

The account argues that most inhabitants were shut out of rights they ought to enjoy, and it weighs their regard for the Church of England and for the king's power over them. The tract gives a rare, early voice from inside the colony, frank about its quarrels.
33916-the-dead-lake-and-other-tales:
Paul Heyse's tales appeared at Leipzig in 1870, translated from the German by Mary Wilson. The title tale spends a fortnight at a dead lake in the Alps, where a storm, an inn, and a restless household set a somber mood. Two more tales follow: Doomed Beatrice, and a tale of a beginning and an end.

Heyse writes with the polish of a practiced storyteller, letting landscape press on his people. Love, fate, and guilt run through the set, and each tale closes with a sharp turn. The book offers a compact sample of the short fiction that made Heyse a leading German voice of his day.
33921-cacao-culture-in-the-philippines:
William S. Lyon, in charge of seed and plant introduction, wrote this 1902 bulletin for planters in the Philippines. Issued as Farmer's Bulletin Number 2 by the Bureau of Agriculture at Manila, it gives practical advice on growing cacao. Lyon notes that Philippine cacao already won buyers at a premium over common Java grades, despite poor curing.

Chapters cover climate, site, soil, drainage, planting, pruning, harvest, pests, and the cost of a plantation. Lyon points to Mindanao and Negros, where the plant grew with striking vigor even under neglect. The bulletin still reads as a clear, hands-on guide for a tropical crop.
33923-special-method-in-primary-reading-:
Charles A. McMurry, director of practice at the Northern Illinois State Normal School, wrote this 1903 teacher's manual, reprinted in 1905. He argues that telling and reading stories to young children, before they can read alone, is a key step in learning. The book gives reasons for oral work, then sets out stories for first, second, and third grades.

Later chapters cover reading through games and side exercises, a method for primary reading, and a list of books for the early grades. McMurry writes for teachers in plain, practical terms. The manual still shows how story-first teaching was meant to turn listening into reading skill.
33931-popular-tales:
Andrew Lang edited this set of Charles Perrault's tales, first issued by the Clarendon Press at Oxford in 1888 and reprinted by Arno Press in 1977. Perrault, who lived from 1628 to 1703, wrote the classic French fairy tales that later readers know in many forms. Lang worked from the original editions and added an introduction.

The tales in the set are the stories of old France retold for English readers, with their morals and marvels intact. Lang's care for the source texts makes the book more than a nursery retelling. It serves readers who want Perrault as he first appeared, in a scholarly yet readable form.
33935-food-habits-of-the-thrushes-of-the:
F. E. L. Beal, assistant biologist for the Bureau of Biological Survey, wrote this 1915 bulletin on what thrushes eat. Thrushes, robins, bluebirds, and Townsend's solitaire form a small group of retiring birds noted as singers. Beal treats each kind in turn: wood thrush, veery, gray-cheeked, hermit, and others.

The bulletin sets out food by season and kind, drawn from stomach records and field notes. Farmers and bird lovers learn which insects, fruits, and seeds each thrush takes. It remains a solid early study of bird diet, useful to anyone who watches thrushes in garden or wood.
33942-beatrice-boville-and-other-stories:
Ouida, author of Strathmore and Chandos, published this third series of stories in Philadelphia in 1905. The title tale follows Beatrice Boville through pride, a first shadow, and a fall, as a narrator who once played rival in all innocence watches her fate. Other tales include a line in the Daily, holly wreaths, silver chimes, and slander.

Ouida writes of rank, love, and reputation with high color and sharp feeling. Her heroines pay dearly for pride or for the talk of others. The set gives a late sample of a once-famous novelist of society life, still readable for its drama and its polish.
33947-the-nerve-of-foley-and-other-railr:
Frank H. Spearman wrote this set of railroad stories, published in New York and London in 1900 by Harper and Brothers, with pictures. The title tale opens amid winter rumors that engineers will strike, while men of the operating department sleep with an ear alert, like soldiers. Andrew Cameron, one of the best men on a locomotive, is also one of the hardest.

Other tales follow Second Seventy-Seven, the Kid Engineer, Soda-water Sal, the McWilliams Special, a million-dollar freight train, and Siclone Clark. Spearman writes from inside railroad life, with engines, orders, and danger. The book remains a classic of American railroad fiction.
33955-remodeled-farmhouses:
Mary H. Northend wrote this book on remodeled farmhouses, published in Boston in 1915 by Little, Brown, with many pictures. Northend, author of books on colonial homes and historic homes of New England, visits house after house: Iristhorpe, Limovady, the Kittredge house, the Curtis house, Green Meadows, Nawn Farm, and Boulder Farm.

Each chapter shows how an old farmhouse gained new rooms, porches, and gardens without losing its character. Pictures of fronts, porches, dining rooms, and living rooms aid the text. The book serves readers who love old houses made fit for new life.
33956-true-politeness-a-hand-book-of-eti:
An American lady wrote this handbook of etiquette, entered for copyright in 1847 and published in New York by Leavitt and Allen. It lays down rules for introductions, salutations, dress, conversation, visits, and receiving visits. Later chapters cover ball-room parties, music, the dinner table, courtship, servants, letters, and funerals.

The rules are firm and detailed: the lesser is presented to the greater, and a lady takes precedence over a gentleman. The book shows how a mid-century American woman was expected to move through society. It remains a clear window on the manners of its age.
33970-the-raid-of-the-guerilla-and-other:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this set of mountain stories, published at Philadelphia and London in 1912, with pictures by W. Herbert Dunton and Remington Schuyler. The title tale opens at Tanglefoot Cove, where judgment day seems at hand as a noted guerilla with a reckless troop means to raid the cove.

Other tales ask who crosses Storm Mountain, tell of Una of the hill country, a lost guidon, Wolf's Head, an unquiet ghost, a Chilhowee lily, and a Christmas miracle. Craddock writes of Tennessee mountains with local color and feeling. The book offers a strong sample of her mountain fiction.
33974-candy-making-revolutionized-confec:
Mary Elizabeth Hall wrote this book on candy made from vegetables, published in New York in December 1912 with pictures. Hall opens with help for the novice, the candy-maker's table, the thermometer, steam, crystallization, chocolate coating, and sugar. A second section turns to decorative candies from potato paste and potato fondant.

Green leaves, violets, daisies, calla lilies, red apples, roses, pea-pods, and grapes all take shape from potato work, with potato caramels to follow. Hall writes for home candy-makers who want pure candy. The book offers a curious, practical piece of kitchen invention.
33976-jane-stewardess-of-the-air-lines:
Ruthe S. Wheeler wrote this girls' aviation tale, published in Chicago in 1934. Jane Cameron is one of seventeen senior nurses graduating from Good Samaritan Hospital at University City, held back half an hour by a surgery emergency on the third floor. Graduation night opens a story of opportunity, westward flight, and crash landing.

Chapters follow Jane's first call, an unexpected delay, a black plane, a flight through fog, a crash in flames, and a promotion. Wheeler writes briskly for girls who dreamed of the air lines. The book offers a lively early tale of a stewardess at work.
3404-april-hopes:
William Dean Howells opens this 1887 novel at Harvard, where Elbridge Mavering watches Class Day crowds from the floor of the gymnasium. Pretty girls in varied dress promenade with young men, and Mavering, older than the students around him, looks for one face in particular. The scene sets up a story of courtship, money, and manners among well off Boston families.

As the novel moves on, Mavering must learn what his hopes are actually worth. Howells follows his suit through drawing rooms, country visits, and family talk, testing charm against character. The book rewards readers who like social novels where the drama sits in conversation, conscience, and the small choices that shape a marriage.
34046-whispering-wires:
Henry Leverage wrote this mystery novel, adapted from his Saturday Evening Post story and published in New York in 1918. A rich Fifth Avenue mansion, with turret and tower and gates from Hyderabad, stands at the center of a tale of guilt and guile. A whispering voice, a magpie, a man in olive-drab, and a murder set the plot moving.

Chapters follow first clews, Harry Nichols, a spot of black, tangled wires, a woman's call, and a closing net, until a silent prisoner speaks and a voice sounds on the wire. Leverage writes in the brisk manner of the popular mystery. The book remains a lively period thriller.
34089-the-celestial-omnibus-and-other-st:
E. M. Forster published this set of stories in London in 1912, dedicated to the memory of the Independent Review. The stories first appeared in the Albany Review, the English Review, the Independent Review, the Pall Mall Magazine, and Putnam's Magazine. Contents run from The Story of a Panic and The Other Side of the Hedge to The Celestial Omnibus, Other Kingdom, and The Road from Colonus.

The opening tale begins in chestnut woods above Ravello, where Eustace, a boy of fourteen, stays with his aunts, the Miss Robinsons, and Mr. Sandbach, a former curate turned tutor. Forster writes with wit and wonder. The book shows his early gift for the uncanny in ordinary life.
34102-a-divided-heart-and-other-stories:
Paul Heyse's tales reach English readers in this 1894 volume translated by Constance Stewart Copeland, who also wrote the opening life of Heyse. Born at Berlin in 1830, Heyse rose to fame with a calm, fortunate career quite unlike the hard youth of most authors.

The book holds three pieces: A Divided Heart, Minka, and Rothenburg on the Tauber, a portrait of an old German town. Copeland's preface praises Heyse's poise and high ideals, and the stories show his gift for quiet feeling, clear scenes, and lives caught between duty and desire. Copeland's introduction also sketches Heyse's father, a scholar of words who kept a warm and bookish house.
34177-the-idyl-of-twin-fires:
Walter Prichard Eaton wrote this idyl of country life, illustrated by Thomas Fogarty and published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with copyright in 1914 and 1915 by Doubleday, Page. Chapters run from buying a farm on sight and watching money go as a farmer comes. New joy in an old orchard, pumping up a ghost, and being humbled by a drag scraper follow.

Later chapters seat Thoreau in the chimney nook, climb a hill together, welcome the Pilligs, bake a first lemon pie, build a pool, and praise country winter and spring in the garden. Eaton writes with humor and warmth. The book offers a gentle tale of a farm and its fires.
34185-recipes-for-eatmor-fresh-cranberri:
Eatmor put out this small book of ways to cook its fresh cranberries. The Good Housekeeping seal stands at the front, with a pledge of refund if the goods belie their billing. Bright plates show the red fruit at its best.

A 10-Minute Cranberry Sauce leads the book: sugar, water, and a bag of berries, boiled till the skins pop. Five twists on the sauce follow fast. Pour it over sliced oranges for Cranberry Ambrosia, stir in mint, or add sweet apricots. Bananas make Cranberry-Chiquita, and pear halves take a ruby spoon of sauce. Short, plain steps suit a home cook in a hurry at feast time.
34220-two-royal-foes:
Eva Madden's 1907 novel Two Royal Foes sets a girl named Bettina at Jena in the days of Napoleon's wars against Prussia. The mighty foe of the title is Napoleon, and the second royal figure is the Queen of Prussia, praised in the book as the mother of her people.

Thirty chapters follow Bettina from Jena to Memel and Tilsit, through flight, trouble, and the entry into Berlin, as war breaks a kingdom and tests a family. Madden tells the great clash through small eyes, keeping court and camp close to a child's home and heart.
34238-rural-rides:
William Cobbett's Rural Rides gathers his horseback tours across southern England, from London into Hampshire, Surrey, Sussex, Berkshire, and beyond. Each ride names its road town by town, from Newbury and Marlborough to Lewes, Brighton, and St. Albans.

Cobbett writes as he goes, on farming, wages, labourers, and the state of the land, with praise for good tillage and sharp words for what he saw as waste and wrong. The book remains a sharp, first-hand portrait of English country life between town and field. Cobbett's contents run from London rides to a Norfolk and Suffolk journal, widening the tour.
34252-vanitas-polite-stories:
Vernon Lee wrote Vanitas, three polite stories put out by Heinemann at London in 1892. The book opens with a long letter to Elena, a baroness and friend, at Pistoia. Lee recalls a talk on a terrace, with wind in the olives and cypress tops below. Elena had likened such tales to carved cherry-stones, fine toys of cheap stuff. Lee denies that these three tales are of that kind.

Round her sketches of frivolous women, Lee says, grave thoughts have grown and taken body. She writes of the waste of keen sense, quick feeling, and quiet strength spent on a frivolous life. That waste brings her sadness and anger as she looks on from outside. Lee hopes the tales may hold up a mirror to some vain reader. The book gives sharp, fine prose on high life and its costs.
34255-comrades:
Comrades is a story by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps, illustrated by Howard E Smith and published by Harper and Brothers of New York and London in 1911. Its frontispiece shows the remnant of a Grand Army post, captioned: We're All That's Left of the Charles Darlington Post.

Reuben, one-and-eighty, thrashes ill in bed on a late May evening while flowers crowd his room. His outrage is simple: he cannot march with the other boys tomorrow to decorate the graves. Patience, his wife of fifty years, swallows her surprise and calls him poor boy, as she always does when he is unreasonable. Behind the carpenter's shop the tobacco-fields of the Connecticut valley spring green, and young Jabez is locking up. The story turns on an old soldier's last muster, and on what fifty years of marriage has taught the woman watching it.
343-fables:
Robert Louis Stevenson lets his Treasure Island puppets step out for a pipe after chapter thirty-two. Fables, from the 1901 Longmans edition, opens with Long John Silver and Captain Smollett debating duty and character. Silver protests he is only a character in a sea story.

Smollett replies that he does not really exist either, which seems to settle matters. Later fables turn the same trick on morals, art, and human nature. Stevenson writes with wit about fiction's double life. The short book delights readers who love Treasure Island. Stevenson's fables show his playful side beyond adventure tales.
34378-hans-brinker-or-the-silver-skates:
Mary Mapes Dodge wrote a tale of Holland life for boys and girls, framed by a letter from Amsterdam dated 1873. Hans and Gretel Brinker had skated on the frozen Y more than twenty years past, she notes. Canals serve as both streets and rivers, and gabled homes, windmills, and masts fill each view.

Dodge says the customs, towns, churches, and art rooms of Holland all live in the tale itself. She calls the land the pluckiest small state on earth, held from the sea by sheer pluck. The book is given to her father, with thanks and love writ plain on the page.
34444-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Volume Eight of The Story of the Great War, Victory with the Allies, was issued at New York in 1920 by P F Collier and Son as a Canadian edition. Francis J Reynolds, Allen L Churchill, and Francis Trevelyan Miller edited the set. A preface holds pieces by Major General Leonard Wood, Rear Admiral Austin M Knight, and Frederick Palmer. A front print shows the signing of the peace treaty at Versailles on June 28, 1919.

Georges Clemenceau stands in that print and invites the German delegates to sign. Armistice and the peace congress lead the volume. Canada's war organizations and vast war industries fill a part. Canadian battles overseas close the set, under Lieutenant Colonel John A Cooper. Drawings, maps, and photos aid the official record of events to date.
34490-sweet-mace-a-sussex-legend-of-the-:
A Sussex tale of olden time opens in Sweet Mace, a Sussex legend of the iron times. Volume one, chapter one, is named How Gil Carr Heard a Concert in Spring. Gil bends among the sedges to pick the bright blue scorpion grass, a bunch for sweet Mace. Too soon for sweet mace itself, he muses, so she must have forget me not. I wonder whether she will keep some when I am far away.

He stopped and listened, for the morning concert was beginning, two hundred and fifty years ago. It was four o'clock in the morning, down in a Sussex valley near the sea. A long while since? Nay, the teller says, a mere instant. Though we now have steam and electric current, men then thought and spoke the same, perhaps a little more roughly. A trout darts in the stream at Gil's feet.
34492-the-master-of-the-ceremonies:
Volume one of The Master of the Ceremonies opens at dawn in Saltinville, a small sea town. Tide is out, and boats land mackerel, soles, and turbot on the sands. Fine fish go to town houses and great tables, not to London. Sun lights the cliff houses and the downs past them.

In one trim house, Isaac Monkley cleans panes that shine as they are. He serves Stuart Denville, the master of ceremonies of the town. Eliza, the housemaid, cleans from within, and the pair court through the glass as they work. Their hands move as one, from cloth to leather, into each corner. Readers get a bright first view of a prim town, its chief man, and love below stairs.
34515-lady-daisy-and-other-stories:
Caroline Stewart wrote Lady Daisy and Other Stories, published by Blackie and Son in London. Stewart also wrote A Kitten's Adventures. The title story is a doll story. Little Flora receives a small china doll on her fourth birthday. Larger dolls follow as she grows, until a tall baby doll needs a name. After much thought Flora calls her Lady Emily Mary Julia Gwendoline.

The book also holds Papa's Christmas Story and the Story of a Glowworm. The doll story turns on small household matters: a nurse's opinions, a cross old neighbour named Miss Higginson, and a ball that bounced into a flower garden. Stewart writes for young children about their own world of toys and family, where naming a doll is a serious affair and each gift marks a year of growing up.
3452-tea-leaves:
This short book from the New York tea merchants Francis Leggett and Company treats tea as a trade good and a daily pleasure. It explains where tea grows, how leaves are picked and prepared, and how different kinds reach the cup. The firm writes as sellers who know their stock, and the book mixes practical advice with the romance of far off gardens.

Readers learn how to judge leaf, judge a brew, and store tea so it keeps its scent. The book also reflects an age when grocers taught customers about imports face to face. It suits tea lovers and social historians alike, offering a small, clear guide to a drink that once linked China, India, and the American table.
34574-in-love-with-the-czarina-and-other:
Maurice Jokai wrote tales of Russia and the East, here turned from Hungarian. Louis Felbermann made the English form, issued by Frederick Warne in London. Felbermann had written Hungary and Its People before this work. A portrait of Jokai fronts the special authorized form.

A secret club called The Nameless meets in Jelagin's house at St Petersburg. Prince and private, lady and street singer, all use first names and thee and thou. Five tales fill the set, from the title tale to The Moonlight Somnambulist. Readers gain rich, strange stories from Hungary's greatest writer of tales.
34587-mrs-halliburton-s-troubles:
Mrs Henry Wood wrote Mrs Halliburton's Troubles, here in its two hundred and tenth thousand. Macmillan issued this copy at London and New York in 1904. Wood was the author of East Lynne, The Channings, and Johnny Ludlow. The first chapter is named The Clergyman's Daughter. It opens at a low, ancient church in a populous district of London, north of Temple Bar. One dark December evening a faint light glimmers inside.

The rector is giving away the weekly bread. Long ago a benefactor left money for twenty weekly loaves, one for each of twenty poor widows. Hard provisos bind the gift. The bread must be at least two days old, laid in the church a day before. Each widow must attend in person or lose her loaf. Four times a year a shilling joins the bread.
34588-some-of-sop-s-fables-with-modern-i:
Randolph Caldecott drew designs for twenty of Aesop's fables in a picture book. Macmillan issued the set in London in 1883, with cuts by J D Cooper. Alfred Caldecott made new English forms of the tales. A note says the pair aimed at plain, terse speech like the old Greek.

The Fox and the Crow leads, with cheese swapped for meat to fit the art. The Ass in the Lion's Skin, the Frogs Desiring a King, and the Wolf and the Lamb follow. Sixteen tales rest on Greek texts, and four on Latin or French forms. Children and art fans gain crisp tales with bold, fun pictures.
346-the-troll-garden-and-selected-storie:
Willa Cather gathers early tales of the Nebraska plains and the art world in this volume. The first half holds prairie stories of Norwegians, Bohemians, and lone dreamers on hard land. The second half, The Troll Garden, turns to artists, singers, and small-town folk who chase art in Boston and New York.

Paul's Case, the best known tale here, follows a restless boy who steals to taste city luxury for a few bright days. Other stories weigh the price of art, the pull of home, and the ache of exile. Cather's prose is spare and sure, and these tales mark the start of her mature voice.
34617-the-jews-of-barnow-stories:
Karl Emil Franzos tells The Jews of Barnow in stories translated from the German by MacDowall for Appleton in New York in 1883. A sonnet on the Jew's hunted face fronts the title page. Eight tales are listed, from The Shylock of Barnow to Nameless Graves.

The title story, dated 1873, opens on the Jew's great white house facing the Dominican monastery in Barnow, a gloomy town on the Lemberg to Skala road. Ghetto born townsfolk revere the house and its owner, old Moses Freudenthal, as the pride of Barnow. The house holds a lottery agency, a cattle insurance office, drapery and grocery shops, and rooms for wine and brandy. Agent, draper, grocer, and innkeeper are all Freudenthal himself, a tall, stern old man.
34627-the-dealings-of-captain-sharkey-an:
A Conan Doyle wrote The Dealings of Captain Sharkey and Other Tales of Pirates. George H Doran issued the set in New York, with tale rights held from nineteen hundred five onward. Four tales trace Sharkey’s foul career at sea. Two more pirate tales round out the first part.

Doyle opens with the peace that ended the Spanish war of crowns. Paid sea raiders lost their work when the Treaty of Utrecht was signed. Some turned to trade or to the fishing fleets. A wild few raised the black flag on their own. Sharkey leads that breed in these tales. A blue water set follows, with a striped chest and a polar ship. Sea fear in all its forms fills the book.
34653-the-three-eyes:
Maurice Leblanc wrote The Three Eyes, Englished by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and copyrighted in New York in 1921. Leblanc had written The Secret of Sarek. Contents open with Bergeronnette and the Triangular Circles, then an execution and Noël Dorgeroux's son. The Kiss, anxieties, and a fierce-eyed man follow in the heads. A man who will emerge from the darkness is promised, then the crowd sees.

The tale opens at Haut-Meudon Lodge, where the narrator lodges with his uncle Dorgeroux. None of them had set eyes on the uncle for a week. The last test of one of his inventions had thrown him into his usual fever, shut among his furnaces and retorts. Then he appears in the doorway, staggering and unhinged, livid and wild-eyed. His clean white tie has come undone, and his stained frock-coat hangs open.
34666-original-penny-readings-a-series-o:
Original Penny Readings, a series of short sketches by George Manville Fenn, dates to 1867. Routledge published the London edition of the working class sketches that year. Chapter one, Paying the Footing, opens the book in a potter voice. A pot worth is not in its clay, that first sketch begins in proverb style.

It does not matter what sort of clay a pot is made of, the speaker holds. If it turns out sound in the fire and rings well when struck, it serves. Common red ware without glaze may still be a good pot if it holds water. What he hates is pots on the grumble and murmur system of life, he says. Penny readings were cheap public entertainments where such sketches were read aloud.
34672-fish-stories:
Henry Abbott published Fish Stories at New York in 1919. The opening tale puts the narrator in the stern of a boat on a lake, casting toward shore for bass under ledge or lily pad while Bige rows gently along the bank.

A rival fisherman appears overhead: an osprey circling some two hundred feet up, crying its hunting cry. The bird's telescopic eye can read the lake bottom and locate prey exactly, the narrator admits, while human anglers guess. An illustration of the osprey accompanies the scene. Readers get Adirondack-style fishing tales told with a sportsman's humour about being outclassed by the wildlife.
34701-steam-engines:
Steam Engines is Number Seventy in Machinery Reference Series, a set of units on electrical and steam engineering, drawing, machine design, and shop practice. The small book treats the action of steam engines first. Rating and general proportions of steam engines follow. Plates and formulas aid the text throughout. Working men and students were the first readers.

Such reference numbers gave one topic at a time in brief, exact form. Engineers could learn how steam acts in a cylinder, how power is rated, and what sizes suit a given task. Shop terms, measures, and cuts are kept plain and close. The book shows how technical knowledge was sold in cheap parts to men who worked with engines daily. Trade readers still value its direct, no frills teaching.
3472-merton-of-the-movies:
Harry Leon Wilson writes a comic novel about a small town young man who dreams of becoming a serious film actor. Merton Gill leaves home for California, sure that the screen needs his noble talent, and he walks into a studio world of directors, cameramen, and actors who see him very differently. Chapter titles such as Western Stuff, The Watcher at the Gate, and Alias Harold Parmalee trace his education.

The joke, and the warmth, lies in Merton's blind spot. He aims at tragedy and finds fame as a comedian, winning laughs precisely when he tries hardest to be grand. Wilson satirizes early Hollywood without cruelty, and the novel suits readers who enjoy show business comedy and a hero who succeeds by accident.
34740-wayside-and-woodland-trees:
Wayside and Woodland Trees, by Edward Step, is a pocket guide to the British sylva from Frederick Warne of London. It holds one hundred and seventy-five plates, from water colours by Mabel E Step and photos by Henry Irving and the author. The preface is plain about its aim: not one more deep book on woods, but a straight tool for naming our own trees and big shrubs. It was made for the country rambler and the lover of nature.

Step owns the British list is short, yet each kind gets its clear marks, leaf, bark, and fruit. A Beecher line fronts the book: a great tree tops a great church as man's work of art. Walkers get a trim, sure friend for lane and wood, built to slip in a coat pocket.
34757-mashi-and-other-stories:
Mashi and Other Stories, by Sir Rabindranath Tagore, was published by Macmillan and Company in London in 1918, translated from the original Bengali by various writers. Publisher's lists of Tagore's other books, Gitanjali among them, front the title page.

The contents hold fourteen stories, from Mashi, The Skeleton, and The Auspicious Vision to Subha and The Postmaster. Also here are The Supreme Night, Raja and Rani, The Trust Property, The Riddle Solved, The Elder Sister, The River Stairs, The Castaway, Saved, and My Fair Neighbour. Mashi opens at a sickbed, where Jotin is urged to sleep because it is getting late, and answers that he has not many nights left.
34794-englefield-grange-or-mary-armstron:
Mrs Paull wrote this tale of a young woman's troubles for Warne's Star Series. Englefield Grange takes its name from a great house, and its motto from Timothy: the love of money is the root of all evil. Mary Armstrong stands at its heart.

By the Sea opens the tale, then Who Saved Her and a social dilemma. At the Review, a horse named Bucephalus, and Freddy's new school fill the early list. Henry Halford's new study, our antipodes, and first impressions mark the middle. Commemoration week and Christchurch meadows bring Oxford in. Mother and daughter, husband and wife, and Park Lane in June close the list shown here, in a grave tale of money and duty.
34812-london-days-a-book-of-reminiscence:
Arthur Warren wrote London Days, a book of reminiscences, for Little, Brown at Boston in 1920. Warren reached London at dusk in the autumn of 1878, at age eighteen. He was fresh from New England, out of Boston by way of New York and the Anchor liner Alsatia. Seventeen days had passed since he left his home town. His first chapter gives first glimpses of the heart of the world, as he calls it.

Later chapters recall London in the late seventies and men he came to know. Browning, Patti, Tennyson, Gladstone, Whistler, and Irving all get chapters of their own. Kelvin, Stanley, Meredith, and Parnell fill out the cast. Warren writes as an American who made London his school for life.
34827-memoirs-of-service-afloat-during-t:
Memoirs of Service Afloat, During the War Between the States, by Admiral Raphael Semmes of the late Confederate States Navy, was printed at Baltimore by Kelly, Piet and Company. Steel engraved portraits and six engravings from original designs fill the book. Semmes had written Service Afloat and Ashore, during the Mexican War.

A portrait of Semmes stands at the front. Seller houses are named in New York, Louisville, St Louis, Richmond, New Orleans, San Francisco, and London. Semmes commanded the cruiser Alabama, whose career drew many books, as was to be expected. He calls the Alabama the first steamship in the history of the world, with a fault in the claim left hanging in the head. His tale runs through commerce raiding on the high seas. War fans get the South most famed sea captain in his own defense.
34831-guilt-of-the-brass-thieves:
Mildred Wirt wrote this Penny Parker mystery, Guilt of the Brass Thieves, copyrighted in 1945 in New York. A publisher's list names the other tales in the series, from Tale of the Witch Doll to The Cry at Midnight. Chapter one, Adrift, opens on a creaking old dock in hot afternoon sun.

Anthony Parker, Penny's father, kicks his leather suitcase and paces in vexation, crying that this is the very limit. Penny stands in the shade of a shed and grins with good humour at him. The contents point the mystery ahead: a brass lantern, a problem boy, a sweeper who informs, a night prowler, a stolen trophy, loot in a basement, a fire, and a race.
34844-collection-of-nebraska-pioneer-rem:
The Nebraska Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution issued this Collection of Nebraska Pioneer Reminiscences in 1916, printed by the Torch Press at Cedar Rapids, Iowa. Lula Correll Perry's forethought dedicates the book to the daring men and women who carried the torch of civilization onto the prairies. She argues that reminiscence and personal experience are the foundation of history, and that the pioneer storytellers are passing beyond recall.

The contents gather county pieces: first things in Adams and Clay counties, frontier towns, Weeping Water, Plattsmouth, Custer and Dawson counties, and Plum Creek. A broken axle, a pioneer teacher, a pioneer woman's experiences, pioneer justice, and the legend of Crow Butte fill out the list. The Nebraska State Historical Society assisted the book committee. The portrait frontispiece shows Laura Pound, twice state regent.
34860-east-of-suez-a-play-in-seven-scene:
W. Somerset Maugham wrote this play in seven scenes, printed in 1922. The scene of the work is Peking, as the first leaf states. The folk of the play are named in a list: Daisy, George Conway, and Henry Anderson lead it. Harold Knox, Lee Tai Cheng, Sylvia Knox, and a nurse named Amah Wu fill out the cast. The first scene is a street in Peking.

The next scene is set on a small porch on a high floor of the house of the British American Tobacco Company. The title of the play points east of the Suez road, to the far ports where men of the West live and trade among the folk of China. A list of the author's past works stands at the front of the book.
34863-conversation-its-faults-and-its-gr:
Peabody compiled Conversation, its Faults and its Graces, in 1855. Munroe at Boston and Cambridge put out the little volume. It is dedicated to American teachers on its front page. Principles governing conversation among refined persons fill the aim. Common vulgarisms of colloquial English are pointed out in it.

An address before a young ladies' school makes the first part. A lecture in Reading, England, makes the second part here. Hints on current improprieties of expression make the third part. That part reprints an English book on writing and speaking well. Selections from two more English books make the fourth part. A day at an annual examination opens one of the pieces. Nearly two years ago that day was spent, its speaker says. Peabody gives talk itself a schoolmaster's rule book.
34865-great-mysteries-and-little-plagues:
John Neal, the Portland novelist, made Great Mysteries and Little Plagues, a book of essays published in Boston by Roberts Brothers in 1870. The front picture shows a child offering a kiss, under the title of the book's best known piece: Children, What Are They Good For?

The preface is a performance by itself. Neal swears he hates prefaces, and hates them more the older he grows. He had just finished what one daughter calls his naughty-biography. This little book was already under way, and a promise was a promise. The children piece, he says, came out some 40 years earlier, when children were overlooked. The title tells the rest of the plan: great subjects and small pests, in the same wry voice. Readers get Neal the essayist, chatty and funny about his own career.
3488-great-catherine-whom-glory-still-ad:
George Bernard Shaw writes a comic play about Catherine the Great of Russia, with a title borrowed from Byron. Shaw's apology warns readers not to expect the Catherine of diplomacy, campaigns, and letters to Voltaire. His Catherine belongs instead to the lighter pages of history, where gallantry, court intrigue, and sham cities built by scenic artists for a royal visit take center stage.

The play follows an English captain caught in Catherine's court, where flattery and favor rule and a ruler's whim can change a life. Shaw turns the empress into a witty, willful figure and the court into a theater. Readers who like Shaw's historical farces will enjoy the comedy, while those seeking a serious life of Catherine should look elsewhere.
34906-the-jumblies-and-other-nonsense-ve:
Edward Lear wrote The Jumblies and Other Nonsense Verses, for Warne. Brooke drew the pictures for this London and New York edition. Lear was the author of the Book of Nonsense, the title says. A first selection of his nonsense songs had pleased press and public. The publishers asked Brooke to do the same service for this second set.

The Jumblies stands as the titular piece of the volume. The Owl and the Pussy Cat stands among its prime favourites. The Duck and the Kangaroo and the Dong with a Luminous Nose follow. Lear did not draw these songs as fully as his custom. Some had no drawings at all, others a mere headpiece. Re-issuing them well pictured matches his other works. Drunk delight is what readers drew from them. Lear gives nonsense in its purest singing form.
3492-homespun-tales:
Kate Douglas Wiggin gathers stories set in a small Maine village in this collection, called Homespun Tales. Wiggin explains that the tales belong together because they share one background: an imaginary village, any village a reader chooses, within or near York County, Maine. Two of the stories first appeared as gift books with wide margins and decorative borders.

The village holds a meeting house and a Dorcas Society whose members once scrubbed the pews during a season of generous bankruptcy. Wiggin writes about neighbors, church suppers, and small kindnesses with warmth and humor. The book suits readers who enjoy gentle New England fiction, where character matters more than plot.
34922-a-history-of-pendennis-volume-1-hi:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote the history of Pendennis, here in Volume One. Harper and Brothers issued the work in New York in 1858, in two volumes. Pictures on wood by the author stand through the tale. A letter to Dr John Elliotson thanks him for care in grave illness.

First love breaks in on breakfast in the opening chapter's own words. A pedigree, the Major's campaign, and Miss Fotheringay's new engagement follow. Pen waits at doors, fights storms in a puddle, and goes up to Alma Mater. Readers gain half of a great, kind tale of a young man's folly and growth.
34935-consequences:
Delafield published the novel Consequences in New York in 1919. She dedicated it to a friend and to the memory of a London winter spent under the air raids of 1917 and 1918. The book is split into two parts and thirty chapters. It opens in a nursery, where three children learn the paper game that gives the novel its name.

Alex, the eldest at twelve, bosses her sister Barbara and their brother Cedric through the game while the nurse's stand-in looks on. The contents then carry the children through school, holidays, a London season, an engagement of marriage, and a diamond jubilee. The second book moves to Belgium and Rome and takes up a priest, an embezzlement, crisis, and forgiveness before an epitaph closes the story. Readers get a family novel that starts in small nursery spats and widens into the choices that shape a life.
34946-the-witch-doctor-and-other-rhodesi:
Frank Worthington, lately Secretary for Native Affairs in Northern Rhodesia, wrote these sketches of life in Rhodesia. The contents fall in three parts: The Mind of the Native, Man and Beast, and White Men and Black. The first tale gives the book its name.

In The Witch Doctor, a tired Native Commissioner ends a long court day and turns a new case away. The man begs to be heard, for his case is one of killing. Other pieces treat lions, bridge building, fishing, and the men who ran the territory. Worthington writes from long service on the spot. Tales of sport, courts, and camp life sit side by side with graver matter.
34970-pierre-or-the-ambiguities:
Herman Melville's Pierre, or The Ambiguities, came from Harper and Brothers at New York in 1852. Melville dedicates the novel not to a prince but to Greylock's Most Excellent Majesty, the mountain over his Berkshire amphitheater of maples and beeches. He signs the dedication from Pittsfield.

The twenty-six books carry Pierre from just emerging from his teens through love, delight and alarm to Isabel and her story. He crosses the Rubicon, departs the meadows with her, and comes to the city, where one book treats Young America in Literature and another reconsiders Pierre as a juvenile author. The Church of the Apostles, Lucy at the Apostles', Pierre immaturely attempting a mature book, and Enceladus fill the later books before a walk, a foreign portrait, a sail, and the end.
35013-chopin-the-story-of-the-boy-who-ma:
Thomas Tapper wrote this life of Chopin for the Child's Own Book of Great Musicians series, issued by the Theodore Presser Company of Philadelphia. The little book even ships with cord and needle, plus directions for binding it at home. Its series list names Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Handel, and many more composers.

Tapper tells the story of the boy who made beautiful melodies, written for young readers meeting the composer for the first time. Numbered pictures accompany the text through the volume. Readers get a starter biography from a long-running music education series that put a composer's childhood story into children's hands cheaply and simply.
35036-verotchka-s-tales:
Mamin Sibiriak wrote Verotchka’s Tales, bedtime tales told in a father’s voice, here Englished by Ray Davidson. E P Dutton issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty two. Boris M Artzybasheff drew the pictures. A lullaby frames the whole set.

One eye sleeps while one ear still hears, the frame song says. A bold rabbit with cock eyes boasts he fears no beast. A mosquito and a fuzzy bear named Mishka share one tale. Sparrow, stickleback, and a jolly sweep meet in a third. Vanka has a birthday full of guests. Milk, porridge, and a gray kitten named Moorka close the set. Young kids get beasts who talk, boast, and learn in short, soft tales.
35043-hybridization-between-two-species-:
Hybridization Between Two Species of Garter Snakes is a short work of wild lore by Hobart Smith. It is a set paper of a great school of the mid west. Its place in that set is set out at its head: the first book, the fourth count, a short span of pages. It was put out in the eighth month of nineteen forty six. The school press of that state struck the work.

The work sets out the chief marks that part the two kinds of snake. Those kinds dwell in the south of that state. The marks are set in two rows, one for each kind, point by point. The side light line is the first mark: in one kind it takes in one row of scales at the front, in the next two rows.
35051-ruthless-rhymes-for-heartless-home:
Col D Streamer wrote these ruthless rhymes for heartless homes, copyrighted in 1901 and issued at New York in 1902. A dedication in verse, signed only H G, asks no comments of the press and no critic's caress.

The author's preface offers the rhymes, with conscience-stricken tears, to children of maturer years, from seventeen to ninety-nine. Fond parents of the tender-aged are warned to keep the volume on an upper shelf and study it themselves. The first rhyme mourns Uncle Joe, borne by an angel beyond the stars: the speaker misses him so, for he had such good cigars. Impetuous Samuel breaks his baby sister's neck at breakfast. The black humor of Edwardian cautionary verse is the whole point. Readers get gleefully awful family poetry.
35059-familiar-faces:
Harry Graham had already made his name with Ruthless Rhymes for Heartless Homes. He had also written the two books of Misrepresentative Men and Women, and here he turns his comic verse on the stock figures of Edwardian life. Tom Hall's drawings carry the joke further, with The Man Who Knows It All facing the title page.

The pieces include The Cry of the Publisher, The Cry of the Author, The Fumbler, The Baritone, The Actor Manager, The Gilded Youth, The Gourmand, and The Dentist. Others take up The Man Who Knows, The Colonel, The Waiter, The Policeman, The Music Hall Comedian, The Reviewer, and L'Envoi. The book appeared from Duffield and Company in New York in August 1907.
35060-santal-folk-tales:
Santal Folk Tales, translated from the Santali by A. Campbell of the Free Church of Scotland Santal Mission, was printed at the Santal Mission Press at Pokhuria in 1891. Campbell's preface says the folk lore of the Santals had drawn little study, though collections from other parts of India were well known. He praises the Santals for keeping their language, customs, tribal order, and religion nearly intact.

Campbell sorts the tales into two classes: those purely Santal in origin, the more numerous, and those taken in from other sources. The first class, he argues, throws light on the social customs of the people and on the awe they feel toward their own fancies. The second shows how Hindu ideas reached the Santals only after passing through neighboring tribes. The volume opens a guarded people's stories to trained readers.
35063-the-negro-in-literature-and-art-in:
Benjamin Brawley wrote a survey of Black writers and artists in the United States. A revised form came out in New York in 1921. Brawley had wrote a short history of the American Negro. He gave the book to his father with thanks for stern teaching. A front plate shows Gilpin as the Emperor Jones on stage.

Parts deal with Phillis Wheatley and Paul Laurence Dunbar. Chesnutt, Du Bois, and Braithwaite get parts of their own. Douglass and Washington stand for the great speakers. Painters led by Tanner and sculptors led by Fuller close the set. All readers get a proud, clear roll of gifts.
35076-ghetto-tragedies:
Israel Zangwill's Ghetto Tragedies, copyrighted in 1899 and issued at Philadelphia by the Jewish Publication Society of America, gathers eleven stories of Jewish life. Zangwill also wrote Children of the Ghetto and The King of Schnorrers.

The first story, They That Walk in Darkness, opens with Zillah, who fasted every Monday and Thursday for a twelvemonth in hopes of a child. Her husband Jossel, a boot manufacturer of Bethnal Green, never guessed that his dinner was her breakfast. Other titles include Noah's Ark, The Land of Promise, To Die in Jerusalem, Bethulah, and Diary of a Meshumad. The Norwood Press printed the volume at Norwood, Massachusetts.
35173-the-bacchae-of-euripides:
Gilbert Murray translated this Euripides play into English, with explanatory notes. Issued in The Athenian Drama, a series for English readers, the volume appears here in its third edition. Each volume in that series presents verse translations of the Greek dramatic poets, with commentaries alongside. Ancient sculptures and vase painting supply the illustrations, twelve in Murray's volume. Murray's volume also contains Hippolytus and Aristophanes' Frogs.

Within the play, Dionysus returns to Thebes in disguise, son of Zeus and the Theban princess Semele. Pentheus rules Thebes as king, a grandson of Cadmus, while a chorus of inspired damsels follows Dionysus from the East. Murray's introduction weighs the play's significance in Athenian history, and his appendix surveys the lost tragedies of Euripides. Murray renders the Greek in English rhyming verse.
35179-the-three-sapphires:
The Three Sapphires is an adventure novel of India by W A Fraser, published in New York by George H Doran in 1918, with illustrations by Arthur Heming. Fraser was also the author of Fool's Gold. The tale opens on a marble terrace above the Lake of the Golden Coin.

Lord Victor Gilfain and Captain Swinton look down from a palace on the lights of Darpore City, six miles away on the plain. The illustrations promise the action: a leopard turned by a shot, an elephant in a python's deadly clasp, a gray stallion at the gallop. Pundit Bagh is shot into the air in another plate. Fraser mixes court intrigue, jungle danger, and horseflesh in the imperial romance manner. The sapphires of the title hang over the whole as the prize of the plot.
35191-some-notes-on-the-bibliography-of-:
Thomas Cooke Middleton surveys books on the Philippines in a library bulletin issued at Philadelphia in December 1900. Middleton read the paper before the Philobiblon Club, and the Free Library printed it as its fourth bulletin. The manuscript was lost once and burned once before reaching print.

The preface notes that W E Retana's short catalogue of Philippine writing runs to three thousand separate works. The library had by then gathered fifty-four volumes and references to near six hundred magazine pieces on the islands. A prized holding was the Flora de Filipinas in four folio volumes. Middleton aims to correct the notion that the islands' people had made little literature. Librarians and students get an early guide to a rich and little-known field.
352-buttered-side-down-stories:
Twelve short tales by Edna Ferber make up this 1912 set, first framed by a foreword that teases old fairy-tale endings. The stories stop short of happy-ever-after and end, as Ferber puts it, with life simply going on. Their people are actors, shop girls, small-town folk, and hopeful strivers.

Scenes shift from New York streets to home towns, stage doors, and kitchens, where pride, love, and work collide in small ways. A heroine may win a part yet lose her ease, or a man may come home changed by years away. The charm lies in Ferber's sharp eye for how plain hopes bend, but do not break.
35214-the-guerilla-chief-and-other-tales:
The Guerilla Chief and Other Tales, by Mayne Reid, was issued in London in an edition dated 1884. The title tale opens on the field of Cerro Gordo the night after the battle of April 1847, in the war between the United States and Mexico. A wounded voice cries for water in Spanish as the narrator lies in his tent.

The narrator tells how Santa Anna's routed troops fled toward Jalapa while others slipped down a cliff over the Rio del Plan into wild brush. He claims he alone saw Santa Anna escape and could have cut him off with a small guard, but for a timid colonel. Reid's tale mixes war fact, chase, and bold talk in his famed frontier style.
35222-white-slavery-in-the-barbary-state:
White Slavery in the Barbary States, by Charles Sumner, was printed in Boston by John P Jewett and Company in 1853. Original designs by Billings stand as plates. A Horace motto heads the book, with a verse from the Epistle to the Romans.

The Romans verse asks if a man who judges those who do such things, and does the same, thinks he shall escape the judgment of God. Sumner turns North African slavery of white captives back on American slave holders. He opens by calling history a gallery where the scenes and characters of the past are preserved in living forms. It may also be called the world great charnel house, he says, where coffins and dead men bones are gathered. Reform fans get a famed senator abolition lecture in book form.
35284-riven-bonds-vol-ii-a-novel-in-two-:
Riven Bonds is a novel in two volumes, turned into English by Bertha Ness from the German work of E Werner. Volume 2 was printed in London in 1877. The tale picks up with Captain Almbach, called Hugo, face to face with Ella at a quiet villa.

Hugo has a hard truth to tell her. He came to the house by chance, told he would meet a strange young lady who lived apart. Marchese Tortoni had sent him there. Ella hears him with a sad, stern look and turns to the window. Shame, pride, and old bonds pull at both in this tense first scene.
35289-hospital-sketches:
Hospital Sketches, by Robert Swain Peabody, published by Houghton Mifflin in December 1916, is a book of quiet, fanciful sketches. A poem by Yeats about spreading dreams underfoot opens the volume. An introduction leads to a view from a hospital terrace, and then to four small towns that never were.

Upthorpe in England, Ranconezzo in Italy, Rocher in France, and Aeginassos in the Greek world each get a walk of short chapters: minster, piazza, church, and tomb. A final part turns to sketches at the Johns Hopkins Hospital. The book reads like a convalescent's daydreams, drawn with an architect's love of place.
35316-dragons-of-the-air-an-account-of-e:
Dragons of the Air: An Account of Extinct Flying Reptiles, by Seeley, professor of geology in King College, London, was published in New York and London in 1901, with eighty illustrations. A frontispiece shows a flying reptile fossil with its wing membranes preserved, from the slate of Bavaria. A motto is from Job: I am a brother of dragons.

Contents open with flying reptiles, then how a reptile is known. A reptile is known by its bones, one chapter insists. Animals which fly, and the discovery of the pterodactyle, follow. The skeleton plan, backbone, and limbs get chapters. Evidences of the animal habits close the head list. Readers get a Victorian geologist popular book on pterosaurs, built bone by bone.
35346-the-ravens-and-the-angels-with-oth:
Ravens and the Angels is a set of stories and parables by Mrs Rundle Charles. Nelson published it in London, Edinburgh, and New York in 1894. Charles also wrote The Schonberg Cotta Family of Reformation times. Contents open with the title story at page seven of the volume. Ecce Homo and The Cottage by the Cathedral follow in her list.

The unknown architect of the minster and Only the Crypt come next. The sepulchre and the shrine and the cathedral chimes fill more pages. The ruined temple, the clock bell, and the black ship ensue. The island and the main land and the acorn vary the tales. Fern life, thorns, and household things close the parable set.
35351-fishing-and-shooting-sketches:
Fishing and Shooting Sketches gathers Grover Cleveland's essays on field sport, printed in New York by the Outing Publishing Company in 1906. Henry S Watson drew the illustrations. Cleveland begins by owning his devotion to hunting and fishing, and the criticism it drew during his years of official duty.

The contents run from the mission of sport and outdoor life to a defence of fishermen. The serene duck hunter, fishing pretences and affectations, and a word to fishermen fill the middle. Summer shooting, rabbit shooting, a duck hunting trip, and quail shooting close the book. Cleveland treats the mockery of newspapers as gnat stings on a stream bank, soon drowned in good memories. The sketches argue that sport restores men worn down by public work.
35357-curious-creatures:
Comic beasts fill Curious Creatures, a picture book in the Comic Animal Series, printed in New York with copyright in 1898. McLoughlin Brothers made the book. Short verses with plates show animals at human trades and games.

A talented giraffe plays the piano in the first plate. He is master of the keys, the verse agrees, so it is no wonder he holds his head high. A horse stands all day at a steaming washing tub: a clothes horse, the joke runs. Minnie Mousecatcher plays croquet, and Captain Kingfisher goes out for a day's sport. The Doggies' Promenade walks three dogs in their very best down a crowded street. A coatless cat laughs at their pomp, and the chase begins.
35367-mad-a-story-of-dust-and-ashes:
George Manville Fenn published Mad, a story of dust and ashes, in London in an edition dated 1868. Volume one opens with a chapter called The Thin End of the Wedge. Its hero is Septimus Hardon, an only child whose name carries no numerical reason.

His father Octavius, of Somesham, chose the name for its bold, sonorous, classical sound, hoping it would add importance nature denied. His mother shortened it to Sep, to her husband's disgrace, and Septimus himself troubled his father by being impressive in the wrong way. The narrator jokes that nature assembled him from leftover rough stuff. Readers get a Victorian novel opening with a comic portrait of its ungainly hero.
35378-the-strength-of-the-pines:
Strength of the Pines is a novel of the woods by Edison Marshall. Little, Brown published it in Boston in February of the year 1921. Dunton drew the frontispiece, showing eyes watched across a rifle sight. Marshall dedicates it to Lille Bartoo Marshall, his comrade and guide. Three books divide the tale: Call of the Blood, Blood Atonement, Coming of Strength.

Bruce is wakened by the sharp ring of his telephone bell at dawn. He hears its first note as the story plunges into motion and peril. Blood feud, pine forest, and a man's buried past drive the plot north. Marshall, a famed outdoor writer, sets strength against wild place and kin. Readers of frontier fiction found his stamp in every chapter here.
35402-poems-ballads-first-series:
Poems and Ballads, First Series, gathers verse by Algernon Charles Swinburne. The hosted text is taken from the first volume of his collected poetical works. A list at the front sets out six volumes of the set. The volume is dedicated to Theodore Watts Dunton, the poet's friend. A letter of dedication opens the book.

In that letter Swinburne says no man can comment on his own work without seeming full of himself. He addresses his friend as his best and dearest. The first printing of the series was in nineteen oh four, the title page notes. Reprints followed in later years, and a new publisher took it up in nineteen seventeen. The letter weighs whether remarks on one's own aims are worth making or reading at all.
35408-the-religion-of-geology-and-its-co:
Edward Hitchcock wrote The Religion of Geology and Its Connected Sciences as talks on faith and earth study. Phillips, Sampson, and Company issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred fifty four. Hitchcock led Amherst College and taught both fields. A cut of the earth’s crust faces the title page.

He gave the book to his wife, whose drawings taught his classes. The motto on the title page bids the two fields join their base. One court, it says, can hold learning, and the next can hold prayer. Hitchcock argues that rock facts do not war with faith. Each side, in his view, shows the same maker at work. Students of both church and quarry in his day took the book to heart.
35440-a-little-book-of-profitable-tales:
Eugene Field wrote a set of tales copyrighted in 1889 and dedicated to his daughter Mary French Field. He calls her his severest critic and most loyal admirer. The first tale, The First Christmas Tree, opens with the forest in commotion. Wise old cedars shake their heads and predict strange things.

The trees hear singing all night and see angels walk to and fro. Shepherd folk talk with the angels under bright stars. Other tales include The Mouse and the Moonbeam, The Robin and the Violet, and Margaret: A Pearl. Ezra's Thanksgivin' Out West adds dialect humor. Fido's Little Friend and Dock Stebbins close the list of tales.
35471-through-mountains-and-canyons-the-:
Through Mountains and Canyons presents the Canadian Rockies in photographs by Wm Notman and Son of Montreal. The album was entered under Canadian copyright in 1906.

The plates move west along the railway line. Early views show the Three Sisters at Canmore, the Banff Springs Hotel, and the Bow Valley. Lake Louise, the Victoria Glacier, and Moraine Lake in the Valley of the Ten Peaks follow. Yoho views give Twin Falls and the Takakkaw Fall, twelve hundred feet high. Further plates cross the Selkirks by Rogers Pass, showing the great glacier, snow sheds, and Glacier House. Captions note heights and feats of building, such as the Stony Creek Bridge at two hundred ninety-six feet. The text copy names each picture in turn.
35480-the-dusantes:
The Dusantes is a novel by Frank Stockton, the sequel to The Casting Away of Mrs. Lecks and Mrs. Aleshine, printed by the Century Company in New York in 1888. The narrator opens at the moment of farewell. His little party rows away from the Pacific island where he met his Ruth and made her his wife.

Aboard the long boat are Lecks and Aleshine, Enderton the narrator's father in law, the narrator and his wife, a red bearded coxswain, and two sailor men. A sail in the bow and steady rowing bring them by nightfall to a larger island of white traders and natives. Their arrival causes great surprise: the steamer's people, reaching the island earlier, had reported the three missing and mourned them as lost. Stockton keeps the party stranded there for more than a month, resolved to return to America.
35495-the-radicalism-of-shelley-and-its-:
Daniel J MacDonald traces the poet Shelley's bold thought to its roots in a doctoral dissertation. He submitted it to the Catholic University of America at Washington in June 1912.

Chapter one follows the young Shelley. A cold home, Eton, and a lost love mark him early. At Oxford he meets the cynic Hogg. The two print The Necessity of Atheism and are expelled. Marriage and love fill the second chapter. Godwin's thought runs through it, with Lawrence's Empire of the Naires. Politics fills the third. Godwin's Political Justice teaches that every kind of obedience is wrong. Later chapters weigh Shelley's views on belief. MacDonald judges him no atheist but an agnostic. He names Locke, Spinoza, and Drummond as sources.
3550-la-mere-bauche-from-tales-of-all-co:
Anthony Trollope writes a short story set in the Eastern Pyrenees, drawn from his Tales from All Countries. The valley holding the baths of Vernet is little known to English travelers, who rarely push beyond Luchon, though Trollope calls Luchon the loveliest spot in those mountains. Under the stern peak of Canigou lie the hot baths, in a close, secluded valley.

The tale follows visitors to Vernet and the household of La Mere Bauche, with Trollope's usual care for manners, money, and marriage. He writes as a traveler who knows the place, noting hotels, passes, and local life. The story suits readers who enjoy Trollope in short form and a glimpse of French spa life in the nineteenth century.
35550-archimedes:
Thomas Heath, a high scholar of Greek math, wrote a short life and study of Archimedes for the Pioneers of Progress set, issued in London in 1920. Heath notes that most folk know just two tales of the man. One is his cry of joy in the bath. One is his boast that with a place to stand he could move the earth. A third tale tells of his death at the fall of Syracuse.

Seven short parts first set out Greek shape lore up to his day, then list his works one by one. Later parts treat his proofs, his book The Sand Reckoner, his work on levers and weights, and his laws of bodies in water. A time line and book list close the volume.
35557-outa-karel-s-stories-south-african:
Outa Karels Stories holds South African folk tales by Sanni Metelerkamp. Constance Penstone drew the prints that dress the text. The gift page sends the tales to all who love folk lore, young and old. The book came out in London in the year nineteen fourteen.

The front note owns that the tales are not new, but drawn from a vast store. They rest in part on a famed set of Bushman lore by Bleek and Lloyd. Sun, stars, and the road of stars take their place in the sky tales. Tricksters, beasts, and first men fill the lore of the veldt fires. The tales were a shared stock of farm youth in that land.
35575-peculiarities-of-american-cities:
Willard Glazier wrote Peculiarities of American Cities, printed at Philadelphia in 1886, with illustrations throughout. Glazier had lived in more than a hundred cities and made their odd traits a study for many years. He gave the book to his wife, who helped picture and enrich all his literary work.

Glazier skips dry tables of figures and talks of cities as he saw them on daily walks. Favourite resorts, street scenes, and local customs mark each city chapter with fresh detail. Readers who could never travel could still picture the leading towns of America. The book is a lively early guide to how American cities differed in look, manners, and pride.
35641-uncanny-tales:
Mrs Molesworth, a famed teller of tales for the young, turned to ghostly ground in this set. Hutchinson printed Uncanny Tales in London, and she dated her gift note October 1896. A friend who helped her, unnamed in full, gets her thanks as a fellow worker.

The Shadow in the Moonlight opens the set with a bold claim. We never thought of Finster St Mabyn's being haunted, the teller says. The place was so old and curious that it needed no ghost to draw the eye. The Man with the Cough, Half-Way between the Stiles, and At the Dip of the Road follow. The Clock that Struck Thirteen closes the six tales.
35645-the-cavaliers-of-virginia-vol-1-of:
William Caruthers writes a historical romance in The Cavaliers of Virginia, volume 1 of 2, printed in New York in 1834. The sub title names it The Recluse of Jamestown, a romance of the Old Dominion. Harper made the book, and Caruthers had writ The Kentuckian in New York.

Chapter one hails the romance of the first years of Virginia. The mind turns at once to Raleigh, Smith, and Pocahontas, he says. It sees the ivy clad ruin of old Jamestown. In the tale's year, Jamestown is the capital, torn by factions like London. Roundheads and Royalists sway it in turn. Cavaliers who fled the death of their king came here and stayed as settlers.
35681-psycho-phone-messages:
Psycho-Phone Messages is a book of messages said to be spoken by the dead, recorded by Francis Grierson. The title page lists the speakers and their themes. General U. S. Grant speaks on fit preparation in America. Thomas Jefferson speaks on the future of American democracy. Benjamin Disraeli speaks on English and Irish affairs, and Prince Bismarck on the indemnities.

John Marshall is listed on the psychology of the Supreme Court, and Alexander Hamilton on the forces that go before revolution. Abraham Lincoln speaks on the future of Mexico, and Robert Ingersoll on our great women. Henry Ward Beecher is listed on the new Puritanism, and Benjamin Wade of Ohio on President Harding. General B. H. Grierson speaks on Japan, Mexico, and California. The book is a record of claimed spirit speech on public themes.
35736-life-and-death-and-other-legends-a:
Life and Death and Other Legends and Stories gathers short works by Henryk Sienkiewicz, translated from the Polish by Jeremiah Curtin. Little, Brown printed it at Boston in 1904, from copyrights reaching back to 1897. A photograph at the front shows a house presented to Sienkiewicz by the Poles, with author and translator in the foreground.

Five pieces fill the contents. The title legend is Hindu. Two immense plains lie side by side: the Plain of Life ruled by Vishnu, the Plain of Death by Siva. A clear river with a lotus covered ford runs between them. Brahma, having created both, told each ruler to do what he understood to be best. The other pieces ask whether he is the dearest one, tell a legend of the sea and a tale of cranes, and end with the judgment of Peter and Paul on Olympus.
35790-a-fantasy-of-far-japan-or-summer-d:
A Fantasy of Far Japan, or Summer Dream Dialogues, by Baron Suyematsu, is a book of talks on Japan. Constable printed it in London in 1905. Suyematsu had written The Risen Sun before it, and a French poem heads this one.

The contents read like a syllabus for the country. The war, forecasts, and the politics of 1905 open the talks. Japan is set beside Greece and Rome, custom by custom. Love stories, adoption, and Jane Eyre in Japan vary the run. Marriage rites are described: the rooms, the decorations, the banquet, the presents. The place of women, and of mothers and wives, gets treatment. A second talk turns to religion and to chivalry, east and west. What the Bushi is, and the great change of 1867, close the list.
35820-granny-s-wonderful-chair-its-tales:
Frances Browne wrote a fairy book for children, reissued in Everyman's Library with an introduction by Dollie Radford. First published in 1856, it was at once a favourite and quickly out of print. Strangely, it was not reprinted until 1880, after which new editions came thick and fast.

Browne's imagination, the introduction says, travelled into many lands in children's employ, and this was her most popular work. In 1887 Frances Hodgson Burnett published it again, retold, as Stories from the Lost Fairy Book. The chair of the title belongs to a granny, and its tales are of fairy times. Generations of children have sat in it since.
35824-all-about-the-klondyke-gold-mines:
The Miners' News Publishing Company of New York rushed out All About the Klondyke Gold Mines in 1897, the year of the great rush. A map of the Yukon gold diggings leads the book. The text under it traces the road every miner had to travel.

Steamers carried the gold seeker from Juneau as far as they could. Then he packed his load through Chilkoot Pass, boated a chain of lakes, and floated down the Lewis River to the Yukon, some 700 miles in all to the Klondyke River. The old camps at Forty Mile Creek and Circle City stood near deserted, the book says, in the rush for the new field. The contents promise the geology of the Yukon, the story of the first news, and tales of men poor yesterday and rich today. Stay-at-homes got the whole rush in one cheap handbook.
35853-japanese-fairy-tales:
Grace James gathered Japanese tales and legends, with pictures by Warwick Goble. Some tales come from the Ko-ji-ki, the record of ancient matters that holds the myths of Japan. Others she heard as a child from a school friend or a nurse, and some are stage favorites.

Thirty-eight tales fill the book, from Green Willow and the flute to the sea king and his magic jewels. Star lovers, a robe of feathers, a tongue-cut sparrow, and Momotaro all appear. One tale by Huish and one version by James's mother join the set by leave. The Moon Maiden, shown at the front, closes the list of tales.
35862-celtic-folk-and-fairy-tales:
Celtic Folk and Fairy Tales gathers tales from Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, chosen by Joseph Jacobs. Jacobs edited the journal Folk Lore and made this set for Putnam's Sons. Batten drew the pictures, and the book is dedicated to Alfred Nutt. Twenty six tales fill the contents, with notes and sources at the end.

Connla and the Fairy Maiden opens the book with a call to the Plain of Pleasure. Guleesh, the Horned Women, and Conall Yellowclaw follow in quick order. The story of Deirdre, the Wooing of Olwen, and Gold Tree and Silver Tree appear. King O'Toole and his goose gives the set one of its best loved tales. The Sea Maiden, Beth Gellert, and the Battle of the Birds close the run. A spell at the front bids the reader say words three times with eyes shut.
35928-a-syrup-of-the-bees:
Syrup of the Bees is a tale rendered from an old manuscript by Bain. Methuen of London issued the translation with a frontispiece plate. Francis William Bain Englished the text and gave it to Mrs Theodore Beck. A verse motto calls love the wine and jealousy the bitter lees.

Three chapters bear odd heads: A Twilight Epiphany and An Incomplete Oblivion. A Disjunctive Conjunction closes the triad of the strange love tale. The first page sings of Love bow, its string a line of bees. Love fell to ashes by fire from Shiva third eye, a note explains. A Poona poem dated nineteen fourteen fronts the book as a gift verse.
35946-true-and-other-stories:
George Parsons Lathrop published True and Other Stories at New York in 1884. Lathrop had written An Echo of Passion and Newport. The title tale, True, runs to sixteen chapters; shorter pieces follow, among them Major Barrington's Marriage and Three Bridges.

True opens with a lover of long ago: Guy Wharton, in love in 1587 with Gertrude Wylde of Surrey. Guy's father was a country gentleman, Gertrude's a small tenant farmer. Lathrop says an event of three hundred years past bears on his present day tale. Hawthorn lanes about Dorking set the old love in bloom.
3601-the-captives:
Hugh Walpole writes a novel that opens with the sudden death of the Reverend Charles Cardinal, rector of St Dreots in South Glebeshire, as he bends toward a drawer of his washstand. Walpole dedicates the book to Arnold Bennett and prefaces it with a reflection on the invisible world, suggesting that God himself may draw strength from human fidelity.

The story follows the rector's family after this loss, as faith, grief, and unseen forces press on ordinary lives. Walpole, known for his Lake District and London novels, writes here about spiritual hunger and the search for meaning after death. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth century novels where religion is felt as mystery rather than argued as doctrine.
36012-prairie-smoke-a-collection-of-lore:
Melvin Randolph Gilmore gathered lore of the prairies in a book first put out at Bismarck in North Dakota in 1921, here in a revised second edition. A map at the front shows where the native tribes of that country held their lands. Gilmore sorts the tribes of North Dakota into three tongue stocks.

Chippewa folk stand for the first stock, while Dakota, Mandan, and Hidatsa folk stand for the second. Arikara folk stand for the third, kin to the Pawnee and Wichita farther south. Gilmore traces where each folk held sway, from Lake Superior to the Missouri River, and how foes pressed the river tribes to join forces.
36027-silent-struggles:
Ann Stephens published Silent Struggles with Peterson of Philadelphia in 1865, adding it to a shelf of sensation novels: The Wife's Secret, The Rejected Wife, Fashion and Famine, and The Old Homestead. The verses on her title page state the theme.

A woman's heart, though delicate, is strong, the poem says. Great men have sought the battle in their pride. But women, braver still, have grandly died in silent struggles that fame may never tell. Stephens was the queen of the American story papers. She built her plots on women enduring in secret what men performed in public. The novel gives that doctrine a story: heroism without witnesses, suffering without a trumpet, in the domestic wars of her century.
36034-white-nights-and-other-stories:
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote the tales in this volume, and Constance Garnett turned them into English; Macmillan printed the book at New York in 1918. It forms the tenth volume of his novels in her translation. White Nights comes first, a sentimental story from the diary of a dreamer, set in Petersburg on a bright summer night.

The dreamer has lived eight years in the city with hardly an acquaintance, yet he knows every face on his walks. After it comes Notes from Underground, in two parts, then A Faint Heart, A Christmas Tree and a Wedding, Polzunkov, A Little Hero, and the tale of Prohartchin. The mix shows Dostoevsky early and late: tender romance beside the bitter, famous voice from underground.
36037-medical-experts-investigation-of-i:
Medical Experts is a paper by Doctor Thorne on insanity trials by jury. Thorne read it to the Santa Clara Medical Society in September eighteen seventy seven. The Pioneer print of San Jose issued the paper that same year. Thorne calls the legal ties of the insane among the most complex of affairs.

No duty tries a medical man like testifying in such trials, he says. Two points draw his focus for the talk that night in San Jose. First is the unsure place of medical experts in California courts now. Second is a civil code rule that lets a declared insane person demand trial. Such a person may claim a court probe before a jury instead.
36048-martine-s-hand-book-of-etiquette-a:
Martine's Hand-Book of Etiquette was entered at New York in 1866. Dick and Fitzgerald published the manual, written by Arthur Martine. Its long title promises a complete guide for those who want good breeding. Clear directions cover manners, dress, and conversation. Dinner parties get their rules, with hints on carving and taking wine. Ball and assembly room, evening parties, street deportment, and travel fill more chapters. Visiting and receiving calls are treated in turn. Courtship and marriage stand at the back, with domestic duties. Fifty six rules for general society close the book.

Martine opens with definitions. Politeness has been called artificial good-nature. Better, he says, to call good-nature natural politeness. Etiquette guards society against offences the law cannot touch, such as insolent staring. The manual maps American manners at the end of the Civil War.
3613-miscellaneous-pieces:
John Bunyan's short works are gathered in this volume, transcribed from the 1845 edition of the Works of the Puritan Divines. Contents include Of the Trinity and a Christian, Of the Law and a Christian, Bunyan's Last Sermon, and Bunyan's Dying Sayings. The opening piece advises a young or shaken Christian how to carry the weighty doctrine of the Trinity, or plurality of persons in the Godhead.

Bunyan writes in plain, earnest prose for ordinary believers facing doubt, law, and death. His last sermon and dying sayings give the book a farewell tone, as the author of Pilgrim's Progress speaks one final time to his flock. The volume suits readers interested in Puritan devotion beyond Bunyan's famous allegory.
36134-bat-wing-bowles:
