Dane Coolidge wrote a western tale called Bat Wing Bowles, issued in New York in 1914 with art by Hutchison. Coolidge had won fame with Hidden Water and The Texican. The tale opens in New York, where Dixie Lee of Chula Vista, Arizona, takes the Western Limited train and meets a glad young man at the gate.

Bowles is that man, an Easterner bound for the Bat Wing Ranch in Arizona. Twenty three parts put him through a round up, a fall to the ranks, a rise again, and fights with men and wild horses. A girl known as the Queen at Home, a postmistress's letter, and an English lord add spice. The tale ends with the custom of the country learned the hard way.
36149-songs-and-satires:
Edgar Lee Masters wrote these songs and satires after Spoon River Anthology. Macmillan printed the book in New York in March 1916. Masters thanks Poetry, The Smart Set, and The Little Review for first runs. Reedy Mirror and Cosmopolitan also first held some poems here.

Contents open with Silence, Saint Francis and Lady Clare, and The Cocked Hat. The Vision, Rain in My Heart, and The Loop follow in the list. Poems treat Helen of Troy, France at war, and city life. Portrait of a Woman and Love Is a Madness close early parts.
3615-john-bull-on-the-guadalquivir-from-:
Anthony Trollope writes a short story about an Englishman whose marriage connects him with the south of Spain. The narrator insists he is an Englishman living in England. His wife would not be pleased to be called anything but an Englishwoman, yet his tale requires him to describe Spanish trade and family life. The Pomfret and Daguilar families have long traded together, and their alliance shapes the plot.

Set on the Guadalquivir river, the story follows an English visitor, a Spanish household, and a young woman courted across national lines. Trollope writes with his usual humor about money, marriage, and national character. The tale suits readers who enjoy Trollope in short form, with Spain as a bright change from his usual English counties.
36185-the-sandman-his-farm-stories:
William J Hopkins wrote The Sandman: His Farm Stories, issued in Boston in 1902 with fifty pictures by Ada Clendenin Williamson. The book is given to Little John, who stands at the heart of the tales. Stories bear plain farm names, such as The Oxen Story, The Apple Story, and The Whole Wheat Story. Each tale turns a chore or crop into a small lesson for a child.

Later tales treat stumps, logs, hay, cows, chickens, and maple sugar. Others cover the rail fence, the fireplace, baking, and swimming. Pictures show corn being planted, cider running into a keg, and logs rolled onto sleds. Young readers learn how a farm works, step by step, in warm and simple talk.
36213-ypres-and-the-battles-of-ypres:
Ypres and the Battles of Ypres belongs to the Michelin Illustrated Guides to the Battlefields, 1914 to 1918. Michelin published it in 1919, in memory of the Michelin workmen who died for their country. A motor itinerary frames the guide.

The route runs from Lille through Armentières, Messines, and Poelcappelle to Ypres and Poperinghe, then back by Bailleul and Béthune. The history opens with the Race to the Sea after the Marne. The German offensive of October and November 1914 gets full treatment: the forces engaged, corps by corps, along the semicircle from Zonnebeke to Messines. A British sentinel before the ruined Cloth Hall illustrates the town.
36221-spinning-wheel-stories:
Louisa M Alcott gathered twelve tales for young readers in a set first held under rights in 1884. Little, Brown, and Company issued the Boston form shown here in 1902. A snow storm traps a group of young folk at a great country house at Christmas. Their grandmother keeps them glad with tales told by the fire.

Each tale stands alone, from Tabby's Table-Cloth to The Hare and the Tortoise. Heads name a cooking class, a jewel box, and a small house in a garden. Warmth, work, and kindness run through the set. Fans of Little Women will know the voice and the care for home life.
36228-the-eulogy-of-richard-jefferies:
Walter Besant wrote The Eulogy of Richard Jefferies, a memoir printed at London in 1888, a year after the death of its subject. Besant gives the book to the widow and two children of Jefferies. He names it a eulogy on purpose, since he finds pure praise for the late work on which fame will rest.

Heads trace a life from Coate Farm through youth, lean years proved by letters, and first taste of success. Fiction, full career, and the Longman letters fill the core, built from notebooks Jefferies filled in the fields. Those notes showed Besant how the great nature writer worked, eye on field and sky at once. Love of wild life and plain prose made Jefferies a voice his age prized and ours still reads.
36241-canadian-fairy-tales:
Canadian Fairy Tales, by Cyrus MacMillan, was first printed in 1922, with plates by Marcia Lane Foster and a lead note by John Grier Hibben. MacMillan had also written Canadian Wonder Tales. He gives the book to the memory of his father, a child of Canadian pioneers.

The list opens with How Glooskap Made the Birds, a tale of the great spirit of the eastern tribes. Rabbit tales follow, on grain buyers and an Indian chief. Other tales name Saint Nicholas and the children, the fall of the Spider Man, and a boy called Thick Head. How Raven Brought Fire to the Indians stands mid list. Later tales treat a cruel stepmother and a song bird with healing waters. Young readers get First Nations lore and settler tales side by side.
36269-a-few-words-about-the-devil-and-ot:
Charles Bradlaugh, the famed free-thought lecturer, published a set of sketches and essays at New York in 1874. The book opens with a page of his life, written as a farewell address on leaving for America. He vouches for the facts as far as he states them, and no further.

Bradlaugh was born on September 26, 1833, in a small house in Bacchus Walk, Hoxton. His father was a solicitor's clerk on a poor salary, and a splendid penman, fond of angling. Schooling ended before Bradlaugh was eleven, and at twelve he was an errand lad in his father's office. Chartist meetings on Bonner's Fields fill his youth, as the sketch tells it.
36293-nearly-bedtime-five-short-stories-:
Mary Wilson wrote Nearly Bedtime, five short stories for the little ones, for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, under its committee of general literature and education. She had written Crip. Longfellow supplies the motto, from the Children's Hour: between the dark and the daylight comes a pause in the day's occupations.

Her preface begins to state her motive in putting the stories before the public, and the society's list explains it. These are tales sized for the last reading of the day, short enough for candlelight and plain enough for the youngest listener who can follow a plot. The society published for exactly this hour: the nursery at dusk, a parent reading, and doctrine carried in under the story's coat. Five stories stand between the child and sleep, each with its moral burning low like a nightlight.
36309-the-water-babies:
Charles Kingsley wrote The Water-Babies, his fairy tale for children, here in the Dodd, Mead edition of 1916 with illustrations by Jessie Willcox Smith. Kingsley dedicates the book to his youngest son Grenville Arthur, and to all other good little boys. A riddle motto invites them in: come read me my riddle, each good little man; if you cannot read it, no grown folk can.

Eight chapters tell the tale. The pictures name its wonders: Tom looking up at the broad yellow moon, Tom entangled in a net, and the two great fairy ladies, Bedonebyasyoudid and Doasyouwouldbedoneby. The story opens in the old formula. Once upon a time there was a little chimney-sweep, and his name was Tom. Tom's fall into the river and his life under water made the book a nursery classic. Children got a sermon on cleanliness and kindness, disguised as a water fairy tale.
36366-dangerous-ground-or-the-rival-dete:
Lawrence Lynch, of the Secret Service, wrote a detective tale issued at Chicago in 1886. Lynch had written other tales of crime and chase, and this one joins a great detective series. The tale opens with a prologue set in May of the year 1859, when the West was new.

Rival detectives work the same ground, and the risks grow as they cross. A mother holds a candle close to shut eyes, by one picture's note, to test if the gaze will flinch. Names, clues, and false trails fill a long plot in the old style, with its roots in the West of the prologue years.
36385-tales-from-the-fjeld-a-second-seri:
Dasent translated these tales from the Norse of Asbjörnsen, in a second series of popular tales printed in London in 1874. Dasent had already made the first series, Tales from the Norse, and a third edition of those was on its way. Part of this second set had appeared earlier in the magazine Once a Week.

The preface tells the chain of making. Asbjörnsen sent the tales to Christmas books in Christiania, then gathered them in 1871 into a new collection, from which Dasent worked. His aim, as before, was to turn his Norse originals into plain mother English that any reader could run through. Asbjörnsen and his fellow collector Moe, he adds, praised the care and truth of the earlier version.
36419-the-white-hecatomb-and-other-stori:
The White Hecatomb and Other Stories is a set of tales by William Charles Scully. Methuen published the book in London in 1897. The title story opens with a verse from Hosea. They have sown the wind and shall reap the whirlwind.

An old blind woman narrates the title tale. A visitor has brought her snuff of a kind she loves. She thanks him and offers her life story in return. Her father's clan dwelt beyond the Tugela river. They were of the Amangwane tribe. Her childhood held nothing but fighting and wandering. Tshaka had fallen upon her people. They in turn fell upon their neighbours. She watched battles from the hills as a girl.
36424-army-boys-in-france-or-from-traini:
Army Boys in France is a boys' war novel by Homer Randall, one of the Army Boys series. Its sub-title runs from training camp to trenches. The contents march in step: The Bugle Calls, War, Off to Camp, A New Life, For France. The tale opens at home, with the storm of war gathering. Frank and Tom Bradford talk over the sinkings at sea. Three ships went down in a day, one of them American. The Kaiser counts on his U-boats to win before America can stir, Tom says.

Frank answers that the eagle is waking, and will scream soon. Talk turns to camp, drill, and the ship for France. Nick Rabig, the series' rogue, turns up on the way. The book gave its boy readers the war as a school of nerve and duty. It is a plain piece of 1919, writ while the guns were still warm.
36438-the-friars-in-the-philippines:
Ambrose Coleman, a Dominican friar, wrote this defence of his brethren in the Philippine Islands. Marlier, Callanan printed The Friars in the Philippines at Boston in 1899. The pieces had first run as magazine papers in England and America.

Coleman says the public has not heard the last of the friars' case. A real, pressing need for the facts, he holds, excuses the book's faults. He asks a fair hearing from a people famed for their love of justice. Truth, he writes, should have nothing to dread. In 1899 the islands had just passed to America, and the friars' lands and rule were a hot point of debate.
36493-owen-s-fortune-or-durable-riches:
Owen's Fortune, or Durable Riches, is a tale for the young by West, author of Frying Pan Alley and The Battle Field. Dutton printed it in New York. A front plate shows Owen making a dart after a little squirrel in the woods.

Owen Hadleigh, a strong boy of fourteen and a village schoolmaster's son, gathers nuts with Sam Netherclift one autumn day. He vows to make his fortune and share it with his father. Sam laughs, but Owen points to Squire Rowland, who grew rich by inventing a new dye. Six chapters follow: the resolve, changes, making his fortune, an unexpected trial, and sunshine and shade, closing on the text poor, yet making many rich.
36507-mary-wollstonecraft-s-original-sto:
Mary Wollstonecraft wrote tales for children that teach by small lives. Lucas wrote the first words for this form of 1906. Five plates by William Blake aid the old tales. Her boss, Johnson of Saint Paul's Churchyard, may have set the task. He sought a mate to a famed book on robins then in vogue, Lucas thinks.

She wrote it fast in 1787 or 1788, by his best guess. Her mind was more on women's state than on child books, he grants. Yet she made the tales bite with far more force than most. Small acts of care or scorn teach their point in each tale. A fine morn with birds and beasts shows in a plate.
36539-st-dionysius-of-alexandria-letters:
St Dionysius of Alexandria: Letters and Treatises presents the third-century bishop's surviving works in Charles Lett Feltoe's translation. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London and the Macmillan Company in New York issued it in the Translations of Christian Literature, Greek Texts series. A long introduction reconstructs a life thinly documented.

Dionysius was probably a priest past thirty when he became head of the Catechetical School in 231, and he pled age when excused from the Council of Antioch in 264. The introduction places his birth about or before 200, making him near of an age with Cyprian and a younger pupil of Origen. His letters come first in the volume, then the letter to Basilides. On the Promises, On Nature, and Refutation and Defence follow, the works of a bishop who governed through persecution and dispute.
36543-the-motley-muse-rhymes-for-the-tim:
The Motley Muse, by Harry Graham, is a book of light topical verse. Longmans issued this second impression at New York in 1913, Arnold at London. Lewis Baumer drew the plates for these rhymes for the times inside. Graham had won fame with Ruthless Rhymes for Heartless Homes and Boer War ballads.

Many verses first ran in the Observer, the Pall Mall Gazette, and the Graphic. Titles tease the last horsed bus, the Lyons cubs, and stage support in fun. Club cantos tour the Athenaeum, White, the Garrick, and Brooks in verse. Songs in season run from New Year Eve to the cynic Christmas close. Suffrage militants, model motorists, and parish pumps all get their rhyme.
36554-chaucer-and-his-times:
Chaucer and His Times is a study of the poet by Grace E Hadow. Williams and Norgate published it in London in 1914. It appeared in the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge.

Hadow lectured in English at Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford. Chapters cover Chaucer's life, his works, and his use of sources. Others treat his character drawing, humor, and descriptive power. A note explains how the final letter e sounds in his verse. The book closes with his influence and a bibliography. Short guides like this one carried scholarship to general readers before the First World War.
36571-the-book-of-riddles:
The Book of Riddles is a children's chapbook printed at Concord by Brown in 1846. Its title page carries the alphabet and the numerals as well as the title, marking it as a book for young readers. The riddles are short poems, each with its answer printed beneath. Pictures go with them.

A mole in velvet clothing complains of the gardener. A watch calls itself a faithful partner and favorite slave, bound with a golden chain beside the ladies. A rose tells its own sad story of being taken to a lover's breast, then thrown into the street. A pair of scales speaks as twins, square or round, of brass or iron, often hung by the neck in chains.
36581-four-american-naval-heroes:
Four American Naval Heroes is a book for young Americans by Mabel Borton Beebe, with an introduction by James Baldwin. The Werner School Book Company published it in New York, Chicago, and Boston. Its heroes are named on the title page: Paul Jones, Oliver Perry, Admiral Farragut, and Admiral Dewey. Baldwin's introduction maps them onto the nation's wars.

Four times, he writes, the American navy has achieved renown and won the gratitude of the nation. What would the Revolution have been without its Paul Jones, or the War of 1812 without its Perry? How differently might the Civil War have ended but for Farragut, and the Spanish War but for Dewey? The story opens six months after Lexington, when Congress decided to raise a fleet. Before the end of 1775 seventeen vessels were ready, and Paul Jones began his public career.
36625-the-cup-of-trembling-and-other-sto:
Mary Hallock Foote wrote The Cup of Trembling and Other Stories, in 1895. Houghton Mifflin put it out at Boston and New York that year. The Riverside Press at Cambridge printed it. Contents hold four tales: the title story, Maverick, On a Side-Track, and The Trumpeter. The title tale opens in the Coeur d'Alene mining country in winter.

A miner walks home alone on foot one winter evening. His road leads from the town in the gulch to his solitary claim. The way passes a lofty, abandoned mine that struck its vein too poor to pay. He had cached his snow-shoes at a cabin on the road going down. Snow works down from the high peaks, driving the game before it. Pack-trains still serve the outlying claims and distant cabins. Foote sets Western lives against snow, ore, and want.
36634-lest-we-forget-world-war-stories:
Lest We Forget is a set of World War stories for young readers, edited by two teachers. Thompson led a state normal school at Fitchburg, and Bigwood taught children's books there. Silver, Burdett published the volume in nineteen eighteen, while the war still ran. Kipling's Recessional poem stands at the front as the book's keynote.

Thirty five and more short pieces tell the war from Belgium's side first. The shot heard round the world, the defence of Liege, and Louvain's ruin open it. Cardinal Mercier, Edith Cavell, and Rupert Brooke each get a chapter in turn. Poems by Service, Burr, and Morley break up the prose of the set. Marshal Joffre, Verdun, war dogs, and the Russian upheaval follow in the list. A Punch cartoon shows the Kaiser taunting the king of the Belgians.
36668-polish-fairy-tales:
Maude Ashurst Biggs translated Polish Fairy Tales from the collection of A J Glinski for John Lane at London in 1920. Cecile Walton drew the pictures and dedicated them to her sons. Glinski printed his tales at Wilna in 1862, taken down just as peasants of Poland's eastern provinces told them.

Biggs shortened the tales, since the repetitions that charm in the original tire in English. Some parts came in rhyme or rhyming prose, like old ballads. Seven tales fill the volume: The Frog Princess, Princess Miranda and Prince Hero, The Eagles, and The Whirlwind among them. A good ferryman meets water nymphs, and a bear waits in a forest hut. Kinship with German, Celtic, and Indian tales strikes the reader at once.
36700-a-new-medley-of-memories:
David Hunter-Blair's A New Medley of Memories was published by Edward Arnold at London in 1922, with a portrait frontispiece. Hunter-Blair was a Benedictine, titular abbot of Dunfermline, and the book is dedicated to the master and scholars of Saint Benet's Hall, Oxford, in memory of ten happy years. Chapters dated 1903 onward string anecdotes by year: the Oxford chancellorship, Oxford under water, the Gregorian centenary in Rome, and Pope Pius the Tenth.

The contents promise Bismarck and William the Second, Liddell and Scott, Lord Rosebery at the Union, four thousand guests at Arundel, and a Warwick pageant. Later chapters bring Hugh Benson, a Jamaica tragedy, and an abbatial blessing. The medley is a Catholic don's diary of Edwardian society: weddings, pageants, country houses, and Oxford portraits, told in short dated paragraphs.
36707-charles-journey-to-france-and-othe:
Barbauld's tales for young children were issued at Worcester by Edward Livermore in 1847, in the series Uncle Thomas' Stories for Good Children. The series aims, its opening note says, to join facts with fun for the young. Greenfield printers Merriam and Mirick produced the small book.

Charles' Journey to France leads, as Charles sets out on foot through fields, churchyard, and lanes toward a far off land. Simple questions along the way teach him sheep, lambs, and cows as he walks. Other pieces include The Ball Players, The Little Boy Who Was a Coward, Stories of Dogs, and Lucy and Her Lamb, each a short moral tale.
36712-the-best-psychic-stories:
The Best Psychic Stories is a set of tales of the unseen, edited by Joseph Lewis French. French was the editor of Great Ghost Stories and Masterpieces of Mystery. An opening essay by Dorothy Scarborough, a lecturer in English at Columbia and author of a work on the supernatural in English letters, stands at its front. The book came out in New York in 1920 from Boni and Liveright.

The contents open with a preface by French and the opening essay. When the World Was Young, by Jack London, stands first among the tales. The Return, by Algernon Blackwood, stands next. The Second Gener— breaks the list in the part shown. The book is a chosen set of tales of ghosts and strange powers, made by a known maker of such sets.
36743-the-child-s-book-about-moses:
The Child Book About Moses was printed at Concord, New Hampshire, in 1843, by Rufus Merrill. The alphabet is printed at the front, in capital and small letters, before the story begins. The life then opens in Egypt, before Moses birth.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, feared the increase of the Hebrews. He gave orders to have every male infant of the Hebrews murdered. The father and mother of Moses were Hebrews, and loved their child too much to have him injured. They thought they saw something promising in his looks, as if he would make a great and good man. So they hid him three months. When they could hide him no longer, his mother Jochebed made an ark of bulrushes. She pitched it waterproof, put Moses in it, and laid it by the Nile. Readers get a Bible life retold in simple words for children.
36751-engraving-for-illustration-histori:
Joseph Kirkbride wrote Engraving for Illustration, notes on the craft’s past and use. Scott, Greenwood and Company issued it in London in nineteen hundred three. Two plates by the ink photo process show its newest art. Six more figures stud the short, dense trade treatise.

Cave men cut drawings on their tools when words failed them, he starts. Wood engraving rises first: block books, Durer, and Holbein lead it. Metal work follows, with each land’s own cast of burin hand. England’s line of cutters takes a full part of the survey. Etching brings Rembrandt and Hollar; mezzotint brings its soft tones. The engraver’s task weighs line, shade, and what to leave out. Photo process work, the new trade giant, fills the next part. Line, half tone, and photogravure each get their plain account.
36753-the-cavaliers-of-virginia-vol-2-of:
Volume two of The Cavaliers of Virginia, or The Recluse of Jamestown, closes a historical romance of the Old Dominion issued by Harper and Brothers in 1835. The novel was entered for copyright in 1834. Its author is named only as the writer of The Kentuckian in New York. The work ran to two volumes, sold by booksellers across the United States.

Romances of colonial Virginia crowded the market in those years. This one builds its tale on cavaliers, settlers, and the recluse of its subtitle. The second volume carries the plot to its end, after the grounding of the first. Readers of the day liked history dressed as a love tale and adventure. The book shows that taste at work in early American fiction. Its New York printing and wide sale mark its reach.
36759-daisy-or-the-fairy-spectacles:
Daisy, or The Fairy Spectacles, is a fairy tale for children printed in Boston in 1857. Its writer is named only as the author of Violet, a fairy story from the year before. The publishers praise that first tale for its simple style and its love of the good and the true. They commend Daisy to parents in the same words.

The tale opens in a great forest where a man named Peter lives alone and grows lonely. An old fairy and a pair of fairy spectacles shape the plot. Through them the world is seen in a new light. The book aims to teach children to see good in plain things and to love nature, truth, and kindness.
36788-critical-studies:
Ouida's Critical Studies, from Fisher Unwin at London in 1900, collects essays first printed in The Fortnightly Review, The Nineteenth Century Review and the Nuova Antologia. The volume is a second impression. Two of them she wrote in Italian and turned into English herself, and all but one, the piece on Blunt's poems, had appeared before.

The subjects run from Gabriele D'Annunzio, on whom hers was the first article printed in English, to Georges Darien and the Italian novels of Marion Crawford. Wilfrid Scawen Blunt, Joseph Chamberlain and Auberon Herbert also appear. Other essays treat unwritten literary laws, the ugliness of modern life, the quality of mercy and the decadence of Latin races.
368-acres-of-diamonds-our-every-day-oppo:
Russell Conwell, founder of Temple University, gives his famed lecture on finding wealth close to home in this volume. The core talk tells of a man who sold his farm to seek diamonds abroad, while diamonds lay in his own fields. Around it sits a life sketch by Robert Shackleton, tracing Conwell from Lexington to pulpit and lecture hall.

Conwell argues that chance lies in one's own town, trade, and neighbors, not in far lands. He backs the point with tales of small sums, hard work, and gifts that built a school. The book reads as both a speech and a brief life, and it kept its pull for crowds across the United States.
36803-rebel-verses:
Bernard Gilbert wrote Rebel Verses, issued at Oxford by B H Blackwell in MCMXVIII, with Longmans, Green and Company as New York agents. Gilbert had written Lincolnshire Lays, Farming Lays, Gone to the War, and War Workers, among many books. A long praise from The New Witness heads the volume. It calls Gilbert one of the discoveries of the War.

The notice holds that what William Barnes was to Dorset, Gilbert is to his native Lincolnshire. He has interpreted folk lives, sorrows, and hopes with surprising fidelity, it says. He knows the men he writes of in their most intimate moods, and records their defects without shrinking. Dreamy idealism, the notice grants, is scarce in his verse. Farm labour, war work, and county speech fill the poems. Readers get a plain, rooted voice of rural England in wartime.
36818-visits-and-sketches-at-home-and-ab:
The first volume of travel sketches by Mrs Jameson, in a second edition. Saunders and Otley published it at London in 1835. Anna Jameson also wrote Characteristics of Women. Tales and miscellanies are collected here for the first time. A fresco group of Siegfried and Krimhilde fronts the volume. It comes from the King of Bavaria's palace at Munich.

Dialogues on art, literature, and character open the sketches. A steamboat scene and a gallery at Ghent begin the travel. Cologne's Medusa, Schlegel, and Madame de Stael appear. Heidelberg and Elizabeth Stuart follow in the Rhine chapters. Frankfurt's theatre and museums receive their visits. Dannecker's life and German sculpture fill long sections. Goethe and his daughter-in-law close the German women chapters. Jameson wrote the Rhine for English readers before guidebooks ruled it.
36819-visits-and-sketches-at-home-and-ab:
Visits and Sketches at Home and Abroad holds essays and tales by Mrs Jameson. The hosted text is the second of three volumes in the set. This print is a second run, set in London in eighteen thirty five. Tales and loose pieces are here first gathered in book form.

Sketches of art and character from Munich fill the front of the volume. Wall paints, chapel art, an opera night, and a tomb all earn long notes. A plan of the new national gallery guides guests through its halls. The eye is sharp and warm for both paint craft and town life. Later parts roam past Germany to home ground and fresh tales.
36820-visits-and-sketches-at-home-and-ab:
Visits and Sketches at Home and Abroad is a work in three volumes by Mrs. Jameson. The third volume, in a second edition, came out in London in 1835 from Saunders and Otley. The full title adds tales and miscellanies now first gathered. Mrs. Jameson was the author of works on the traits of women and on famed female sovereigns.

The contents of the third volume open with a sketch of Mrs. Siddons, then a sketch of Fanny Kemble. Tales follow: The False One, Halloran the Pedlar, and The Indian Mother. A piece called Much Coin, Much Care ends the list as shown. The volume is a mix of life sketches of stage women and short tales, from a writer known for her books on women and art.
36861-the-green-casket-and-other-stories:
The Green Casket and Other Stories, by Molesworth, is a book of three tales for the young. Chambers printed it in London and Edinburgh in 1890. Molesworth had written The Cuckoo Clock, Carrots, and The Rectory Children before it.

The other tales are Leo's Post-Office and Brave Little Denis. A frontispiece shows Flossie's confession, a scene from the title story. That tale opens with Ruth's start in life, a place in service. Perry, the blacksmith's wife at Wharton, is called to the Tower House at Hopley. Lady Melicent Bourne wants to see her girl's mother herself. The under-housemaid's place is vacant, and Ruth has been approved for it. Lady Melicent, old-fashioned, takes a care of even her youngest servants. The cottage by the forge buzzes at the honour.
36890-the-english-church-in-the-middle-a:
English Church in the Middle Ages, by William Hunt, is a church history. Longmans Green of London issued it in eighteen eighty eight. The book forms one volume in the Epochs of Church History set. Mandell Creighton edited that series of short church era studies.

Hunt preface says the book shows church ties with papacy and state. Those two bonds, with Rome and with the English crown, form its theme. Sister volumes in the set treat the Reformation, Oxford, and the Puritans. The Arian clash and the Counter Reformation stand in the same series. Readers get a compact survey of the medieval English church order.
36925-indian-and-other-tales:
Indian and Other Tales is a book of tales and verse by Hope, issued at Toronto in 1911. William Briggs published it under Canadian copyright. The book opens with a poem to the west wind. The wind is asked to tell what it has seen. In the southern seas it wooed a Maori maid for a tree. A fern-tree pines for the girl in that tale. A tui-bird builds its nest in the lonely tree.

The wind then crosses to a land of apple blossom. A winding road runs through orchards to the sea. Twilight brings it to further shores in the verse. Such opening poems set the book's roaming mood. Its tales join Indian subjects to other scenes. Hope writes in the romantic verse of the day. The volume is a piece of early Canadian letters.
36977-the-village-of-youth-and-other-fai:
The Village of Youth and Other Fairy Tales is a story collection by Bessie Hatton, published in London in eighteen ninety five. Numerous illustrations by W H Margetson appear in the book. Six tales are listed, opening with the title story of a village where youth endures. A Child of the Winds follows at some length in the contents.

The Flower that Reached the Sun Lands, The Garden of Innocence, and A Christmas Rose continue the list. The Windflower closes the set of six. A verse motto on spring vanishing with the rose heads the title tale. Hatton writes gentle wonder tales in the literary fairy line for family reading, with pictures to match.
37024-the-express-companies-of-the-unite:
The Express Companies of the United States is a study of a public utility by Bert Benedict. It was put out in New York in 1919 by the Intercollegiate Socialist Society, at ten cents a copy. A foreword by that body presents the work to the public. It calls the pamphlet a careful study of its theme by Mr. Bertram Benedict.

The foreword holds the theme to be a weighty one, and the time well chosen. The nation was then at work, it says, to frame its course on the future control of the express trade and of kindred services. The study thus bears on a live public question of its day: who should own and run the firms that carry goods and parcels for the country at large. The pamphlet is a short work of public affairs.
37041-preservation-of-bull-semen-at-sub-:
N L VanDemark and four co-workers wrote a report on how to keep bull seed sound at deep cold. The report is Bulletin 621 from the farm test station of the University of Illinois. Its list of parts starts with the first work done on cold storage of seed. A part then asks which seed will freeze well.

Tests deal with first and second draws, and with seed that has been washed. A long part deals with the fluids used to stretch and shield the seed. Egg yolk and a salt called citrate are weighed in set shares. Rates of chill and thaw, and the gear used, fill the last parts. Farm breeders used such work to ship seed far and breed herds by plan.
37055-an-alphabetical-list-of-books-cont:
An Alphabetical List of Books Contained in Bohn Libraries is a publisher catalogue, arranged by author and title. A note says a detailed catalogue, arranged by the various libraries, will be sent on application. Entries give editions, editors, volumes, illustrations, and prices.

Addison Works open the list: six volumes, with the notes of Bishop Hurd, a portrait, and eight plates of medals and coins. Aeschylus follows twice, the dramas in English verse by Anna Swanwick, and the tragedies in prose. A book on comparative physiology, enlarged, with hundreds of woodcuts, comes next. Alfieri tragedies in verse, Allen battles of the British navy with steel engravings, and a Roman history in translation follow. Andersen Danish legends and fairy tales, and the thoughts of Marcus Aurelius, close the head portion. Readers get a Victorian cheap classics catalogue, the backlist of Bohn standard libraries in one alphabetical sweep.
37074-neghborly-poems-and-dialect-sketch:
Neghborly Poems and Dialect Sketches gathers early verse by James Whitcomb Riley. The Bobbs-Merrill Company published it at Indianapolis. Copyrights date to 1883, 1891, and 1897. Riley dedicated the book to his brother Humboldt. A salutation poem addressed to an old friend opens the volume.

That opening poem teases its subject gently. The old man's silver hair and patient pause please the speaker. Yet a sly twinkle betrays him. His soul still trembles at tales of Aladdin and Sinbad. He read novels on the sly as a boy. The same warm tears fall faster now. Age, the poem argues, only masks the childish face. The dialect sketches promised in the title follow in the same neighborly spirit.
37085-outlook-odes:
Crosland, author of The Unspeakable Scot, wrote a set of comic odes issued in London in 1902 and dedicated to Lord Windsor. Each ode is addressed to a person or a type of the day. The first, to the private member of Parliament, begins as a letter of mock pity.

Crosland tells the member that duty took him into Parliament, and duty likewise constrains the poet to odes. Other targets include the Cambridge crew, Dan Leno, the Pope, the Tsar, and Joseph Chamberlain. A motorist, a tripper, a golfer, and the stock exchange all take their turn. The verse is light, topical, and cheerfully rude about public life.
37121-charles-dickens-children-stories:
Charles Dickens' Children Stories is a set of the great tale man's works re told for the young. His grand child and more hands did the re tell. The book was put out in nineteen hundred with twelve full page plates. The front plate shows a famed small maid and her grand sire. That pair are the heart of one of the tales.

The first tale in the host text is of Trotty Veck and his daughter Meg. Trotty is a strange name for an old man. It was given to Toby Veck for his trot at his work. He was a door man who bore notes for folk in too much haste for the post. He did not earn much at that trade. He was out in all airs and all day long.
37142-how-to-care-for-the-insane-a-manua:
How to Care for the Insane is a manual for nurses by Doctor William Granger, in a second edition. Granger ran a private house for the insane at Mount Vernon, New York. He had served as first assistant physician at the Buffalo State Hospital. The revised edition came out in eighteen ninety one from Putnam's Sons.

The book grew from lessons Granger began in October eighteen eighty three at Buffalo. There he taught women attendants their duties toward the patients in their care. Those lessons became fixed training, and men attendants joined from eighteen eighty five. A two year course led to a certificate as a trained nurse of the insane. Granger believed every attendant should be taught in simple, patient ways. A note reports training schools spreading to nearly every asylum in the land.
37235-the-black-poodle-and-other-tales:
Anstey, who wrote Vice Versa, gathered these tales for Appleton in 1896. The stories had appeared in Belgravia, the Cornhill, the Graphic, Longman's, Mirth, and Temple Bar, and the preface thanks the editors for leave to reprint. The title story opens the volume. Its narrator, Algernon Weatherhead, a government clerk, sets himself to relate, without suppressing a detail, the painful and humiliating episode of his life.

His name for the dog in the frontispiece cry is Bingo: it is my Bingo, for all that. The confession is addressed to one reader, a woman who can think no worse of him than she does, and who will never hear justification by word of mouth. The other tales run lighter: a sugar prince, the return of Agamemnon, the wraith of Barnjum, a toy tragedy, and the curse of the Catafalques. Anstey's comedy had this undertow, laughter confessing itself in the first person.
37239-stories-about-famous-precious-ston:
Stories About Famous Precious Stones is Mrs Goddard Orpen's history of the great jewels, published in Boston by the D Lothrop Company in 1890. Twelve stories make the book, each built around one stone or one treasure. The illustrations show the gems in the rough, cut, and mounted.

The Regent leads: bought, sold, stolen, and lost, yet always traceable, it first appears for certain in December 1701, offered by the merchant Jamchund to Thomas Pitt at Madras. The Orloff, La Pelegrina, and the Koh-i-Nur follow, the Koh-i-Nur shown also as recut. The French Blue, with the Hope and Brunswick blues pictured, precedes the Braganza and the Black Prince's Ruby. The Sanci, the Great Mogul, and the Austrian Yellow come next. A famous necklace and, last, the Tara Brooch with the shrine of Saint Patrick's Bell close the collection.
37242-stories-and-pictures:
Stories and Pictures, by Isaac Loeb Perez, was translated from the Yiddish by Helena Frank and printed by the Jewish Publication Society of America at Philadelphia in 1906. Twenty six numbered pieces, besides a set of travel pictures, fill the contents, and a glossary closes the book.

The first story, If Not Higher, opens with a puzzle. Every Friday morning early, the Rebbe of Nemirov disappeared, melted into thin air, not to be found in synagogue, study house, or home, his door standing open. His people are sure he ascends to heaven, for who else shall answer the accuser when the Solemn Days draw near? A Lithuanian visitor laughs and cites the Gemara against them. Later titles include Domestic Happiness, In the Post Chaise, Bontzye Shweig, The Dead Town, In Time of Pestilence, Kabbalists, The Outcast, The Chanukah Light, and Between Two Mountains.
3725-famous-men-of-the-middle-ages:
John Haaren and Poland wrote this school history to teach the Middle Ages through lives rather than dates. The preface argues that a child grasps history best when a single person stands at the center of each scene, like a mountain peak in a landscape. Short chapters therefore follow kings, warriors, saints, and scholars one by one, each with a clear tale and a plain moral.

Harun al-Rashid of Baghdad stands as one example, a caliph who prized poets and scholars and whose court helped pass algebra and the numerals we still use into western Europe. Other chapters range from Rome's fall to the dawn of modern states. Teachers and young readers still use the book as a first map of the medieval world, short on jargon and rich in human incident.
37252-born-to-wander-a-boy-s-book-of-nom:
Born to Wander is a boy's book of nomadic adventures by Gordon Stables. Partridge published it in London, and Cheshire illustrated it. Book one opens at Grayling House by the silvery Tweed. The scene is an old baronial hall grey over the woods. A tributary of the Tweed runs by its banks. It was November, not the month for Michaelmas daisies, it begins. The chrysanthemums opened their great eyes to meet the light. They felt put about to see the daisies still in bloom.

Flowers are ever meek, albeit lovely, the narrator muses. Meekness and beauty hand in hand are charming, he holds. The daisies had not gone to sleep as they should. The chapter wonders why they linger into the cold season. Stables opens his wandering tale with a garden meditation. The boy hero's travels grow out of this Scottish home.
37295-soft-candy-for-bees:
Soft Candy for Bees is a short bulletin on bee feeding by Doctor Burton Gates of Massachusetts. It is bulletin number seven A of the state board of agriculture. The text comes from the board's sixty first annual report, printed in nineteen fourteen. Its subject is the so called Fuller candy for queen cages and feeding.

Gates lays down the rule that wise beekeepers now feed no honey at all. Honey, even from one's own yard, has spread bee diseases far and wide. Sugar syrups and hard candy serve instead, but the soft fondant is newer. Fuller of Blackstone and others had tested this English style candy for years. It feeds colonies in transit without combs and rouses them in spring. It does not harden past use, which is its chief merit claimed.
37300-henry-james:
Henry James is a critical study by Rebecca West, first published in 1916. Kennikat Press reissued it at Port Washington in 1968. Its chapters move from the sources of James's genius to his last great novel.

The contents promise a compact arc across a long career. Sources, the international situation, and transition carry the first half. The crystal bowl and the golden bowl of the late work close it. West opens with the crossings that made James an American of her kind. Two Irishmen, a Scotsman, and an Englishman crossed the Atlantic in one century. Their stock fixed the character of his genius, she argues at once. The essential thing about James was that he was an American. Such an American, she says, could feel at home only in exile.
37301-the-whale-and-the-grasshopper-and-:
Seumas O'Brien wrote The Whale and the Grasshopper and Other Fables, published at Boston in nineteen sixteen. Robert McCaig drew the front picture. O'Brien gave the book to Edward J O'Brien.

Twenty fables fill the set, most set in Ireland. Padna Dan and Micus Pat walk toward Castlegregory and trade sharp sayings on wealth and want. One says that if the poor were not decent they would be rich. Other tales treat kings, goats, a white horse, and the Lady of the Moon. The talk is witty, the morals plain, and the flavour strongly Irish throughout.
37315-the-boy-s-book-of-heroes:
The Boy Book of Heroes, by Helena Peake, was printed in London by Frederick Warne and Company, with fresh plates made for the book. Peake gathers ten heroes of old for boy readers. A front plate shows a sword thrust through a beast head.

The list opens with Hereward, last of the Saxons, a brave but wild youth of Mercia in the days of Edward the Confessor. Next come the Cid, Louis the Ninth of France, and Gustavus Vasa of Sweden. Later lives treat Columbus, the Chevalier de Bayard, Frobisher, Raleigh, and Sidney. Each life is told in short, bold strokes to fire young hearts. Boys of the day got courage, faith, and loyalty in stirring true tales.
37344-four-years-in-france-or-narrative-:
Four Years in France tells of an English family's residence there, printed in London in 1826. Before the narrative stands an account of the author's conversion to the Catholic faith in 1798. The author came from a line of Lincoln prebendaries and was schooled, then sent to Oxford as a young man.

Contents trace his path through cathedral services, college chapel, Catholic neighbours, and long argument over infallibility and antiquity. He took orders, held a Lincoln curacy, won a fellowship, and preached at St Mary's, Oxford. The family years in France then unfold against that faith journey of the head of house. Readers get travel, memoir, and religious controversy in one.
37363-making-up-with-mr-dog-hollow-tree-:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote these beast tales for children, with plates by Condé. Harper and Brothers printed Making Up with Mr Dog in New York, in the Hollow Tree Stories line. A gift plate sends good wishes to all Hollow Tree friends from the Story Teller.

The Hollow Tree folk are old friends in Paine's world: Mr Dog, Mr Rabbit, and Mr Possum. Mate tales in the line tell how Mr Dog got even and how Mr Rabbit lost his tail. A first dinner at the Hollow Tree Inn shows in one plate. This book's own tale turns on a quarrel made up, as its title says. Deep Woods and Snowed-In books kept the line going for years.
37381-snowdrop-other-tales:
Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm's tales appear in a volume drawn by Arthur Rackham, first issued in 1909 and reissued in 1920. Snowdrop opens the book, with a queen sewing at an ebony framed window in midwinter. She pricks her finger, and three drops of blood fall on the snow. The seven dwarfs find Snowdrop lying on the ground in the front picture.

Other tales include The Pink, Briar Rose, and Ashenputtel. The Wolf and the Seven Kids, The Queen Bee, and The Elves and the Shoemaker follow. The Goosegirl, The Golden Goose, and The Water of Life appear later. Rackham's color plates give the set its lasting fame.
374-fantastic-fables:
Ambrose Bierce packs short, biting fables into this 1899 volume, each with a sting in its tail. Kings, priests, politicians, poets, and fools act out small moral plays, then meet a twist that mocks their pride. Titles name the game: the moral principle, the crimson candle, the ingenious patriot, and the poet's doom.

Bierce writes in terse, polished prose, with a satirist's cold eye for cant and power. No party or creed escapes his lash. The book reads as a sharp tonic for readers who like fables with teeth, where virtue seldom wins and folly pays its own price.
37413-the-duke-decides:
Headon Hill wrote The Duke Decides, a novel first printed in 1903 and issued at New York in 1904. The tale opens on Broadway in New York, where crowds pour from a large dry goods store at six in the evening. A man with a mandate starts the plot in motion.

Chapters take the cast aboard the St Paul, to a terrace, and to a keeper's lodge. A cut panel, men on stairs, and a search for the duke build the mystery. The honor of a great house is at stake at the end. Readers get a brisk tale of secrets and duty.
37430-the-sin-of-monsieur-pettipon-and-o:
Sin of Monsieur Pettipon and Other Humorous Tales is a story set by Richard Connell, copyrighted in 1922. Doran of New York issued the book, dedicated to the author wife who helped with the tales. Magazine copyrights from Century, McCall, and Collier show where the pieces first ran. The title tale of Monsieur Pettipon leads the contents at page eleven.

Mister Pottle stands second in the list of comic pieces in the volume. Connell writes light, twist driven magazine fiction with a deft hand for surprise. His fame later rested on darker game, but here the mode is pure humour. Readers of 1922 short fiction gain a polished set of period entertainments.
37477-taking-chances:
Taking Chances is a story collection by Clarence L Cullen, author of Tales of the Ex-Tanks. The G W Dillingham Company published it in New York, with copyrights running 1898 to 1900. The stories first appeared in the New York Sun. Cullen's introductory note addresses two kinds of bitten men. One suffers from the horse bug, the other from the poker microbe.

The contents mix the turf and the green cloth. A colour-blind wiretapper and a whooped race-horse open the list. Ringers, verdant bookmakers, and men who knew all about touts follow. A race horse pays a church debt in one tale. Poker tales fill the second half: card-playing on ocean steamers, a dog that knew the game, and queer Pacific Coast poker. Cullen claims the stories belong largely to strict truthfulness. He disowns any didactic purpose; the tales were set down as he heard them.
37487-boy-scouts-in-the-northwest-or-fig:
Boy Scouts in the Northwest, by G Harvey Ralphson, was held under a 1911 copyright and printed at Chicago. Its second title is Fighting Forest Fires. Ralphson, a scout master, had written Boy Scouts in Mexico and in the Canal Zone.

The tale opens on a hot August afternoon in 1911, with three boys in khaki on a high plateau near the British frontier. Chapters name a mountain mystery and a signal in the sky. A typewriter ribbon serves as a clue, and an aeroplane stands in danger. Later heads bring a flight above the clouds at night and the chaos of a burning world. A forest ranger tells his tale near the close. Boys got scouting, flying, and fire fighting in one fast tale.
3752-voyager-s-tales:
This volume draws its tales from the great collections of Richard Hakluyt, the Elizabethan clergyman who spent his life gathering accounts of voyages. The introduction follows Hakluyt from Westminster School to Christ Church, Oxford, where maps, globes, and sailors' stories fixed his passion for a wider knowledge of the globe. His first book of 1582 on voyages toward America set the pattern for the vast work that followed.

The tales themselves range across seas and ports, with ships from Tripoli meeting at Zante amid drums, trumpets, and cannon fire. Readers meet merchants, mariners, and adventurers in their own words, often rough and direct. The book suits anyone who wants the age of discovery told by those who sailed it, rather than by later historians alone.
37521-the-broken-bough-no-435-iv-series:
The Broken Bough, number 435 of its fourth series, was revised by the Committee of Publication of the American Sunday-School Union at Philadelphia. The small tract carries no author's name, only the Union's Chestnut Street address on both title pages. A picture of lambs in a meadow suits its Sunday school scene.

Two brothers, Charles and John, walk home from class on a fine May Sunday, admiring lambs feeding in a green meadow. Their teacher Fulton had that afternoon expounded the fifteenth chapter of John, where Christ compares himself to a vine and his followers to branches. Fulton used the blossoming orchards to press the lesson: life and growth come from God, and branches draw nourishment from the vine as believers do from Christ. John remarks that the trees seem to explain the teaching.
3753-peacock-pie-a-book-of-rhymes:
Walter de la Mare wrote these rhymes for children, grouping them under headings that map a child's world. Up and Down opens the book with horsemen and huntsmen, Boys and Girls follows with windows and lost shoes, and Three Queer Tales add berries, thieves, and a castle. Later groups visit places and people, beasts, witches and fairies, earth and air, and close with songs.

The poems mix nonsense, eeriness, and tenderness in short stanzas, with an old soldier begging a crust at a door and a sailor wasting away far from home. De la Mare keeps his language simple and musical, so the verses read aloud well. Parents and young readers will find a book to dip into at bedtime, one rhyme at a time, without any need to read straight through.
37540-the-hearth-stone-thoughts-upon-hom:
The Hearth-Stone, thoughts upon home life in our cities, by Samuel Osgood, came out at New York in 1854. Osgood had written studies in Christian life tales. His preface says the pieces aim at want in the heart, not fame in the world of ideas, and breathe a kind spirit above sect and party.

The pieces follow a year of home life, lit from a fire lit at Christmas and New Year. Chapters treat the ideal of womanhood, the hope of childhood, and care in parents. More treat marriage, friends, master and servant, and the orphan. Later pieces treat the young prodigal, the schooling of girls, trade and the heart, and a church in the house. City families get warm counsel on love at home.
3757-the-white-bees:
Henry van Dyke gathers lyric and patriotic verse in this collection, crowned by its title poem. The White Bees retells the legend of Aristaeus, the shepherd whom Apollo made keeper of golden bees, with honey, music, and orchard light woven through the stanzas. Around it stand songs for America, a New Year's Eve sequence, and praise poems for poets from Milton and Wordsworth to Keats, Shelley, Browning, and Longfellow.

Later lyrics turn personal and wistful, with a hermit thrush, a firefly city, a window at twilight, and a ride through the Alps. Van Dyke writes in clear, musical lines that favor warmth over puzzle. Readers who like verse that can be read aloud will find a book of gentle craft, American feeling, and old legends made new.
37574-great-inventions-and-discoveries:
Willis Duff Piercy wrote Great Inventions and Discoveries, a school reader on how key finds changed life. Charles E Merrill Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred eleven. The set forms part of a Graded Supplementary Reading Series. A first sheet off the press fronts the book.

Praise of books from Carlyle, Kingsley, and Milton opens the course. The printing press then leads the things themselves in turn. Steam power, the telegraph, and the telephone follow in line. Light, street travel, and more wire uses fill a full part. The finding of America stands among the great turns. Guns, star tools, the cotton gin, and pain killers come next. Steel, rubber, short hand, the typewriter, and matches crowd the back.
37586-women-s-bathing-and-swimming-costu:
Claudia B Kidwell traced women's bathing and swimming dress in the United States. The Smithsonian Institution Press issued the study at Washington in 1968. The work stands as Bulletin 250, Paper 64, of the National Museum. It sold for fifty cents in paper covers from the government office.

Kidwell follows the shift from heavy bathing dress to a trim swim suit. Fashion of each age shaped the cloth, while use and modesty set its bounds. A bathing costume from The Delineator of July 1884 fronts the study. Museum readers gain a clear tale of dress, sport, and women's growing freedom in water.
37595-ecological-studies-of-the-timber-w:
Ecological Studies of the Timber Wolf in Northeastern Minnesota is a research paper of the Forest Service. It is Research Paper NC-52, issued in 1971. The North Central Forest Experiment Station at Saint Paul issued it. Mech and Frenzel edited the studies in this volume. The contents list four papers on wolves and deer. Movements, behavior, and ecology of timber wolves comes first. Mech, Frenzel, Ream, and Winship wrote that lead paper. An analysis of deer killed by wolves follows it.

That paper treats the age, sex, and condition of the deer. Snow conditions and the vulnerability of deer form the third study. The possible occurrence of the Great Plains wolf is the fourth. Mech had worked at Macalester College before joining the bureau. The volume is a founding document of modern wolf research.
37596-american-pomology-apples:
American Pomology: Apples, by Warder, is a grower's handbook on the apple in the United States. Orange Judd and Company issued the book in New York, entered in 1867. Two hundred and ninety drawings go with the text.

Warder led the Ohio Pomological Society and served as a vice-president of the national body. His standing made the book a standard work for orchard men of his day. The text treats the kinds of apples grown in America, their traits, and their worth. A added contents list warns readers that there is no chapter thirteen in the book. In the sorting chapter Warder uses classes and orders of differing rank. The book preserves the names and merits of many old sorts that later orchards let slip away.
37652-the-nameless-island-a-story-of-som:
Percy Westerman wrote The Nameless Island, a sea adventure published in London by Pearson in 1920. The subtitle calls it a story of some modern Robinson Crusoes. Eight full-page pictures illustrate the tale. The frontispiece shows an ensign broken at a masthead to cheers.

The wrecked ship is the San Martin, a Peruvian cargo steamer of 3050 tons. She was bound from Realejo to Tahiti when the hurricane struck. Chapters follow the castaways ashore and into camp. Unwelcome visitors and strange allies soon appear. A frustrated sacrifice and a knife-thrust in the dark raise the stakes. The boys find a buccaneers' cave and a treasure chamber. A great invasion and a last stand lead to the rescue.
37655-bye-a-baby-bunting-and-other-rhyme:
Bye a Baby Bunting and Other Rhymes is a small book of nursery rhymes with no named author. Old rhymes fill its pages, among them Bye a Baby Bunting and Pussy Cat Pussy Cat. Each verse has been bent a bit to praise the thread sold by Clark. Pictures go with the rhymes from page to page.

Betty Pringle and her pig, a counting rhyme, and a cat at London all turn up here. The last lines of most rhymes point the child back to the spool of thread. Books of this kind were ads as much as gifts for the young. It shows how firms once sold goods through songs that homes knew by heart.
37670-bible-stories:
Bible Stories, with fine engravings, was published at Worcester by J Grout. A full alphabet in capitals and lower case, with figures, stands in front as in old primers. The first head is Early Life of the Savior, but the text starts at the Creation. Adam and Eve are the first figures in the tale.

Near six thousand years ago, the book says, the first man and first woman were formed from dust. They were placed in a pleasant garden called Eden, with all they could wish. They might eat of all trees but one. Verse tells how they dared to taste the forbidden fruit and break God command. An angel drove them out to thorns, thistles, and hard work. Yet God promised that the seed of the woman should bruise the serpent head. Children get Scripture in plain prose and rhyme.
37679-ali-baba-or-the-forty-thieves:
Ali Baba, or The Forty Thieves, is a colored toy book from J Wrigley of 394 Grand Street, New York. Wrigley published all kinds of colored toy books. The tale opens in a town of Persia, with two brothers, sons of a poor man. Cassim, the elder, married money and lives at ease. Ali Baba, the younger, dwells in a mean cottage and cuts wood for his family.

In the forest Ali Baba sees forty horsemen ride to a rock. Their captain says, Open Sesame, and a door opens in the stone. Ali Baba tries the words himself and loads his asses with bags of gold coin. He tells his brother the secret. Cassim goes with ten mules and great chests, but the treasure makes him forget the word. The robbers find him inside and cut him in quarters.
37690-the-babes-in-the-wood-may-bells-se:
The Babes in the Wood is a picture chapbook in the May Bells Series, printed at New York by McLoughlin Brothers. It tells the old ballad of the children in the wood, in verse. Pictures show the parents' death and the ruffians' fight. A gentleman of good account in Norfolk lies sore sick, and his wife beside him, and both go to one grave.

They leave two babes, a boy not passing three years old and a younger girl. The son is to have three hundred pounds a year at full age. Jane is to have five hundred pounds in gold on her marriage day. If the children die first, their uncle takes the wealth. The dying father begs his brother to look to the children dear.
37691-the-travelling-companions-a-story-:
The Travelling Companions, a story in scenes by Anstey, author of Vice Versa, was reprinted from Punch and published in London in 1892 by Longmans, Green. Twenty-six pictures by Bernard Partridge attend the text. A score of scenes follow two men, Podbury and Culchard, through an uneasy partnership on tour.

Heads trace the pair: extremes meet, Podbury picks up acquaintances, Culchard comes out of his shell. A dissolution of partnership follows, then courtship according to Ruskin, crumpled roseleaves, and the pilgrims of love. Anstey builds the tale as dialogue scenes, letting the two tempers clash in talk. Podbury is open and warm; Culchard is dry, selfish, and too clever by half. The comedy rides on their friction from station to station.
37693-monks-popes-and-their-political-in:
John Alberger wrote this attack on the Roman Catholic Church and its part in world affairs. Monks, Popes, and Their Political Intrigues came out at Baltimore in 1871. Two mottoes head it: one from Saint Francis Borgia, one from Washington on watchfulness and freedom.

Alberger states his aim in the preface without gloves. He holds the church to be a vast plot against the freedom of the world, rich, wide-spread, and strong. He names the American republic as one of its marks. For proof he cites papal bulls, briefs, and letters, the rules of church councils, and priest-run papers. The book is a sharp sample of its era's fears.
37697-creed-and-deed-a-series-of-discour:
Felix Adler gave a set of talks printed at New York in 1880, put out at the wish of the society that heard them. The preface is dated September 1877. Adler thanks the friends whose hard work gave a risky venture hope of lasting life. Some talks are cut down, while others keep their first form.

The first talk takes up life after death under the motto, not by the creed but by the deed. Adler says his hearers had left the old faiths, or held them yet found no force in them. More talks review the year's work and the form of the ideal, and pieces on Hebrew faith are reprinted at the back.
37708-the-magic-bed-a-book-of-east-india:
Hartwell James edited a book of East Indian fairy tales, printed at Philadelphia in 1906 with forty illustrations by John Neill. The book sold for fifty cents in Altemus' fairy tales series, beside Persian, Chinese, South Sea, and African volumes. The magic bed leads the contents, then the wise jackal, the four brothers, the fish prince, and the talking turtle.

The princess Lalun, a tiger standing roaring, and a boy sitting under a tree stand in the picture list. Cannot I have supper with you, one caption asks. Spread it gently over the princess, says another of the magic bed. Two wild ducks are carrying a turtle in one scene. Hanging from the stick by his mouth is another. The rajah sent for the prince, and his tigers came in. James retells India's wonder tales in plain words for American children.
37718-elias-an-epic-of-the-ages:
Orson Ferguson Whitney wrote a long poem in epic form, issued in a revised and noted edition at Salt Lake City in 1914. Whitney says the poem tries to set out, in verse, the theme the world calls Mormonism. He treats that theme in past, teaching, and foretelling modes across the ages.

Twelve parts make up the work, a prelude, ten cantos, and an epilogue. Notes at the back explain points for students, since Whitney hoped schools would use the poem as a class text. A group of Utah men of public life helped bring the first issue through the press, and Whitney later polished the verse.
37752-poems-of-london-and-other-verses:
Poems of London and Other Verses, by John Presland, came out in London in 1918. A first set treats the great city street by street. Dawn over London opens the book, with pearly light on street and park, and houses white and strange in the hush.

Presland sees London as a city of old rhymes sunk deep in a clear sea of light. Yet on the pavement lies a thing of rags, fast asleep, cast off from the deep of the town. A police officer passes with kind eyes turned away. More poems treat spring in Oxford Street, sparrows, and the Tube. One marks an August night of 1914, and one mourns Rupert Brooke. A second set runs from a ballad of Knossos to love songs. Verse fans get tender, grave songs of a city at war.
37766-strange-stories-from-the-lodge-of-:
Strange Stories from the Lodge of Leisures is a set of Chinese tales translated by George Soulie of the French consular service in China. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in 1913. The contents promise wonders: The Ghost in Love, The Fresco, The Dwarf Hunters, and The Corpse the Blood Drinker. Love Rewarded, The Woman in Green, and The Laughing Ghost stand among them.

The first tale opens on the fifteenth day of the First Moon, in a town by the Eastern Lake. Streets throng with strollers, shops blaze with light, and boys carry lanterns. A student meets a pretty walker named Double Peony, daughter of a judge, who lives in a garden by the lake road. These are tales of fox spirits, ghosts, and love beyond death, from the great Chinese store of strange stories. Soulie's versions carried them to English readers.
37772-pioneer-day-exercises:
The Ladies' Library Association of Schoolcraft, Michigan, held this Pioneer Day on April 26, 1898. Old settlers and their kin wrote the papers for the day. The small book prints the whole program, songs and all.

A Thanksgiving hymn by Lakin Brown opens the set, sung by the ladies' quartette. Brown also reads on the beginning of Schoolcraft. Thomas recalls the early public schools, and Bates tells of the transplanting of a boy. Smith gives a young pioneer's life, and Fellows the early days in Prairie Ronde. The quartette sings The Young Pioneer and Michigan, My Michigan. A town honours its first comers here, in their own words.
37788-judith-shakespeare-her-love-affair:
Judith Shakespeare, Her Love Affairs and Other Adventures, is a novel by William Black, issued in New York by a popular reprint house. Judith was the younger daughter of William Shakespeare, and Black builds a romance around her life in Stratford. Black's other novels, including A Daughter of Heth and A Princess of Thule, are listed on the title page.

Chapter one is called An Assignation and opens on a fair, clear day. Love affairs promised in the title drive the plot, set against the fame of Judith's father. Black was a best selling novelist of his day, known for bright scenes and Highland settings. Here he turns that gift to a famous family in its home town.
37794-old-wine-and-new-occasional-discou:
Old Wine and New is a volume of occasional discourses by Joseph Cross, published at New York in 1884. Whittaker issued it; Cross had written Evangel and Knight-Banneret before. A dedicatory epistle to his publisher opens the book. Cross mocks the old custom of inscribing books to bishops and magnates. Such oaks once shielded the tender undergrowth of authors. Dew from their branches fell as showers of diamonds.

In self reliant America, he writes, authors walk alone. Their only patron now is the publisher himself. A book without intrinsic quality must go down under criticism's blasts. Cross couples his name with Whittaker's from esteem, not need. Two years before, he had trusted him with Knight-Banneret's manuscript. Sermons for occasions make up the volume that follows.
37814-the-story-of-magellan-and-the-disc:
Hezekiah Butterworth wrote this story of Magellan and the discovery of the Philippines. Merrill and others illustrated the tale in a uniform edition of Butterworth's books. A list at the front prices the cloth volumes of the series at $1.50 each for buyers.

The Treasure Ship, a story of Phipps, and the Pilot of the Mayflower stand in that list. True to his Home, a tale of Franklin's boyhood, joins them among the series titles. Magellan's own story sails from Spain through the strait that bears his name to the islands where he died, told for the young readers Butterworth loved.
37855-climatic-changes-their-nature-and-:
Climatic Changes: Their Nature and Causes was published on a foundation established in memory of Theodore Glasgow. The front matter lists other books by the same authors, grouped by theme. Four books show the development of knowledge as to historical pulsations of climate.

The Pulse of Asia, from 1907, heads that group. Explorations in Turkestan, Palestine and Its Transformation, and the climatic factor in arid America follow. Two books illustrate the effect of climate on man: Civilization and Climate, and World Power and Evolution. Four more illustrate general principles of geography, including a geography reader on Asia, The Red Man Continent, and principles of human geography. The named author is Ellsworth Huntington. His case, across all these books, is that climate pulses through history and shapes civilizations. Readers get a Yale geographer synthesis on climate and history, from the movement founder.
37860-poems-first-series:
Squire wrote this first series of poems, printed in London in 1918. Martin Secker issued the book from Buckingham Street in the Adelphi. A long dedication likens his poems to a harvest festival offering. Poor folk there bring fruit, grain, fish, and sea creatures to church.

Squire says his gifts are all products of mind, heart, and senses. Contents group poems by year, from 1905 through the war years. Titles range from In a Chair and The Roof to Starlight. Verse on town, friendship, faith, and fresh mornings fills the set. Martin Secker issued the poems from London in 1918.
37861-poems-second-series:
Squire published his Poems, Second Series, with Heinemann in 1922, dedicating the book to Edward Shanks. Squire edited the London Mercury and stood at the center of England's literary establishment in those years, poet and power in one. The contents are arranged by year, from 1918 to 1921.

The Birds opens the volume, addressed to Edmund Gosse: within mankind's duration, so they say, Khephren and Ninus lived but yesterday. A dog's death, a poet to his muse, and processes of thought follow. An airship over suburb and the invocation of Lucretius carry the war years. Constantinople, an elegy, and wars and rumours, 1920, date the next group. The rugger match closes the list. Squire wrote the Georgian poem at its most accomplished: regular, humane, and quotable. The second series is his bid to be remembered for the verse and not the editorship.
37877-goody-two-shoes:
Goody Two Shoes, in Walter Crane's picture books in a large re-issue from John Lane, retells the old tale of Margery Meanwell. In the reign of good Queen Bess, a hard landlord turned farmer Meanwell off his small farm. Care soon killed him and his wife, and their children Tommy and Margery were left in want. Margery had but one shoe for a long time, while Tommy had a pair.

The parish clergyman took the orphans in, and a London gentleman vowed to be their friend. He ordered new shoes for Margery and took Tommy to London to make his way abroad. Margery ran to show her shoes to all, crying two shoes, and so won her name. She learned to read and write from the clergyman, then taught poor children in her turn.
37878-life-of-oliver-wendell-holmes:
Brown wrote a life of Oliver Wendell Holmes, first copyrighted in 1884 and reissued in 1895. The poet, professor, and beloved physician was born on the twenty-ninth of August, 1809, in a gambrel-roofed house on Cambridge Common. His father, the Reverend Abiel Holmes, pastored the First Church there, where Washington had worshipped in Revolutionary times.

The contents map a sociable century: ancestry, boyhood, the professor, the lecturer, the naming of a new magazine, and a chapter on Elsie Venner. Favorites of song, the man of science, the Holmes breakfast, and the Harvard Medical School follow in turn. Tokens of esteem and last days close the record. Holmes quoted himself calls the old house a noble principality to be born into.
37881-the-golden-fleece-and-the-heroes-w:
The Golden Fleece and the Heroes Who Lived Before Achilles, by Padraic Colum, came out in 1921, with pictures by Willy Pogany. Colum gives the book to two children by name. A slave climbs Mount Pelion at noon with a small child in his arms, and blows three blasts on a horn.

Chiron the centaur comes, half man and half horse, great in limb and wise in face. So starts the tale of Jason and the ship Argo. Two parts tell the voyage to Colchis and the way back, with Medea and her spells. A third part retells peer tales, of Atalanta, Theseus, Heracles, and Orpheus. Young readers get the great Greek hero tales in clear, warm prose.
38007-memoir-of-john-howe-peyton-in-sket:
Memoir of John Howe Peyton gathers sketches by men who knew him, plus some of his public and private letters. The book was printed for private use in Staunton, Virginia, in 1894. Its maker also wrote a history of Augusta County. A preface laments how thin the record is, with few papers left after the civil war.

Old papers used include the Republican Farmer of 1811-12 and the Staunton Spectator of later years. The preface calls Peyton one of Virginia's purest men and greatest lawyers. It says he had no equal in crime law and torts, and no superior in any branch. A sketch of Ann M Peyton is also included. Like Patrick Henry, Peyton's fame rests largely on the praise of others.
38018-girl-scouts-in-the-rockies:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy wrote Girl Scouts in the Rockies, published in 1921. The Dandelion Troop spends its third summer together, this time camping in the Rocky Mountains. Verny, their captain, leads the talk as they outfit.

The girls recall tame first camps, with cooked food brought weekly, and a real one in the Adirondacks. This year they do without the tents and cots a friend furnished before. Chapters promise a prairie schooner, a mule's pleasantries, and a canoe trip. Later chapters bring a blizzard, a forest fire, and the bad lands, then back-trailing to Denver.
38024-dwarf-fruit-trees:
F A Waugh of the Massachusetts Agricultural College teaches small-tree fruit growing in a manual issued by the Orange Judd Company at New York in 1906. A two-year dwarf cherry fronts the book.

Waugh defines his subject plainly. A dwarf fruit tree is simply one that does not reach full size. Chapters weigh advantages and disadvantages first. Propagation and pruning follow. Special forms, like the cordon and the espalier, get their own treatment. Then come the fruits in turn: dwarf apples, pears, peaches, and plums. Bush fruits and fruit trees in pots close the course. Pictures show the same bush apple before and after pruning. Waugh wrote for American and Canadian growers who wanted fruit from small ground.
38041-old-celtic-romances:
Old Celtic Romances holds tales translated from the Gaelic by Joyce, printed at Dublin in 1920. Joyce wrote a social history of ancient Ireland and books on Irish place names. He served among the commissioners for publishing the ancient laws of Ireland. A line from Coriolanus stands on his title page: I shall tell you a pretty tale.

His preface recalls the old story-tellers of Ireland and northwest Scotland. Ollaves, shanachies, and bards held tales by heart for chiefs and guests. Good telling won costly presents. Men of learning shaped legends and events into stories, and the ones people loved passed down the generations. Joyce's versions carry that stock into print.
3805-the-vultures:
Henry Seton Merriman sets this novel among English travelers and a Polish family living on a volcano. Joseph Mangles, a dry and dyspeptic Englishman, opens the book smoking on an Atlantic deck, grumbling at fine weather because it brings women on deck. His path crosses Cartoner, a younger Englishman, and the Bukatys, who have lived with unsettled times since childhood, when they watched the streets from a nursery window in April 1861.

The Bukatys know what it means to live gayly on the edge of revolt, with fathers in the streets and empires overhead. Merriman writes with cool irony and a sharp eye for national pride. Readers who like political romance will find a tale of spies, families, and a Poland that refuses to lie still.
3806-a-modern-cinderella-or-the-little-o:
Louisa May Alcott gathers four stories for girls in this volume, led by the title tale of a modern Cinderella. Among green New England hills stands an old many gabled house, where sisters Nan and Di pass a summer morning with books, brooks, and birches. A little old shoe, lost and found, sets the romance moving, with a prince in modern dress and a heroine who earns her happy ending by kindness rather than by magic.

Debby's Debut, Brothers, and Nelly's Hospital follow, with Aunt Pen murmuring that propinquity works wonders as a young guest dresses for a hop. Alcott writes with warmth and humor throughout. Readers who know Little Women will find the same blend of home life, moral sense, and high spirits in shorter compass.
38063-the-sun-s-babies:
Edith Howes wrote these tales and verses for young children, first published in October 1910 and reprinted through January 1913. Frank Watkins supplied four colour illustrations. The contents run to dozens of short pieces about flowers, birds, insects, sea life, and the seasons. Titles include The Snowdrop Baby, Johnny Crocus, The Daisy Fairy, Billybuzz the Drone, and The Wheat People.

The opening poem has the Sun-Man claim a million babies on earth, all kissed good night by his beams. From there, gardens, hillsides, and rock pools supply small dramas of growth and change. Howes keeps each piece brief and gentle. Young readers get nature lore dressed as story, with spring, summer, autumn, and winter closing the set.
38067-a-select-collection-of-valuable-an:
A Select Collection of Valuable and Curious Arts is a book of practical arts and experiments. Rufus Porter published the third edition at Concord in 1826. The title page promises that each art is well explained. It also promises that the experiments are genuine. They can be done easily, safely, and at little expense.

An opening notice states the aim. The book does not try to deepen the skill of trained artists. It teaches first principles to people who practice an art now and then. Some readers will use it for profit. Others will use it for amusement. The chemical experiments mix recreation with useful knowledge. A district clerk's certificate from 1825 records Porter's claim of ownership.
3807-the-different-forms-of-flowers-on-p:
Charles Darwin devoted this botanical volume to a puzzle of flowers, why many plants bear two or three different forms of blossom. The cowslip and its kin lead the inquiry, with long styled and short styled forms that prove fertile only when crossed in the right way. Hybrid oxlips, flax with twisted pistils, and the purple loosestrife, with three forms of stamens matched to three pistils, supply the evidence.

Tables of pollen grain diameters, counts of seeds, and careful notes on legitimate and illegitimate unions fill the chapters. Darwin dedicates the book to Asa Gray and argues from experiment rather than from theory alone. Readers with patience for close science will find a classic of plant study, showing how small floral differences drive the whole business of crossing and seeding.
38081-the-inhabitants-of-the-philippines:
Sawyer wrote The Inhabitants of the Philippines, published in London in 1900, because he believed no English book did justice to the Filipino people. His preface sets his own favourable estimate against a row of harsher judges.

Sawyer lived fourteen years in Luzon, spoke Spanish and the Tagal dialect, and travelled widely, to Cebu, Iloilo, the Visayas, and Palawan.
