His work brought him into contact with officials, priests, landowners, mechanics, and peasants. He answers writers who called the islanders savages or ingrates, and praises Montano and Blumentritt for fairer treatment. The book appeared just as America took the islands from Spain, and it argues the case for the people at that turning point.
38095-heretics-and-heresies-from-the-god:
Heretics and Heresies is a lecture by Ingersoll. Its motto runs: liberty, a word without which all other words are vain. Ingersoll opens with a hard definition. Whoever honestly speaks his own opinion will be guilty of heresy. Heresy is what the minority believe, the name the powerful give the doctrine of the weak.

The word was born of hatred and cruelty, he says, and of thought's feudal ages. It served as an epithet in place of argument. When the Bible was printed and read, people began honestly to differ over its meaning. Catholics and Protestants vied to rid the earth of honest people. Ingersoll pleads for the right to think aloud.
38096-humboldt-from-the-gods-and-other-l:
Humboldt is the opening lecture in a volume of lectures by Robert Ingersoll. Ingersoll delivered it on the hundredth anniversary of Humboldt's birth.

He calls great men part of the infinite, brothers of mountains and seas. Humboldt rose above the superstition and prejudice of his time. Experience, observation, and reason were the only basis of knowledge. Ingersoll marvels that he grew great although born rich and noble. Wealth and position, he argues, are generally the enemies of genius. Poverty, by contrast, has nursed most of the intellectual giants of the world. They were reared in cottages, log-houses, and factories. Humboldt himself was born in the castle of Tegel, near Berlin, by a pine forest and a lake.
38098-individuality-from-the-gods-and-ot:
Individuality, a lecture by Robert G Ingersoll, opens a set of his lectures on free thought. Ingersoll was a famed American speaker for reason against creed. The lecture takes custom and suppression as the enemies of the free mind. Its motto is a line on a soul that dwelt apart, like a star.

Ingersoll argues that a child's wishes are treated as proof they should be denied. He holds that universal obedience would mean universal stagnation, and that disobedience is a condition of progress. Had the church held full sway over the mind, he asks, would the words liberty and progress have survived? The lecture sets his case for the free mind at full strength.
38099-mistakes-of-moses:
Robert G Ingersoll attacks the first five books of the Bible in Mistakes of Moses. The book grew from his lecture named Some Mistakes of Moses. It came out in 1880.

Ingersoll says he long saw the Pentateuch as the record of a barbarous people. He lists laws he calls absurd and unjust, and claims that clash with known facts. To teach that such a book was inspired struck him as a crime. He sets out the errors, clashes and impossibilities he finds in the text. The work is a famed blast from America's best known freethought orator. He dedicated the book to his sister and friend, Sue Farrell.
3810-the-man-eaters-of-tsavo-and-other-e:
Lieutenant Colonel J H Patterson wrote this plain account of two years building a railway through British East Africa. The famous chapters tell how two man eating lions stalked the Tsavo camps, killing workers night after night while Patterson hunted them. He insists he toned the facts down rather than up, and writes for readers who may doubt what they read.

Other chapters follow hippos, lions, and camp life, with one long watch ending as a great hippo hides behind a tree, tooting and splashing for hours. Patterson's prose is direct and unadorned, with the railway itself as a second hero. Readers who like true adventure will find a tense and vivid book, and a window on East Africa before the railway changed it.
38101-thomas-paine-from-the-gods-and-oth:
Robert G Ingersoll praised Thomas Paine in a famed lecture. The talk stands in From The Gods and Other Lectures. With his name left out, Ingersoll opens, liberty's history cannot be written. Praise of the brave dead is a labor of love, he says. Mind has been besieged by superstition for ages, he claims. Slow deliverance fights its way on, he adds.

Its soldiers die hated by those they would save, he says. Paine was one of the bravest of that host. Born poor, where children are burdens, Paine rose. Class privilege ruled his native land then. To plead for justice was treason there, Ingersoll charges. Poverty was Paine's mother, necessity his master. He had more brains than books, the lecture says. America's great freethought orator makes Paine a saint of reason in this rolling piece of platform prose.
38107-the-gods-from-the-gods-and-other-l:
The Gods is a lecture by Robert Ingersoll, the American orator known for his attacks on religion. The lecture is dated 1878 and stands at the head of a volume of his lectures. The book is dedicated to his wife, Eva Ingersoll, whom he calls a woman without superstition.

The lecture opens with a saying: an honest god is the noblest work of man. Ingersoll argues that each nation has created its own god, and the god always matches his makers. He hates and loves what they hate and love, and he is always found on the side of those in power. All these gods, he says, demand praise, flattery and worship. Most are pleased with sacrifice, and the smell of innocent blood is held a divine perfume. The lecture works through these charges in Ingersoll's flowing court room style.
38112-mighty-mikko-a-book-of-finnish-fai:
Parker Fillmore wrote this book of Finnish tales, printed by Harcourt, Brace and Company of New York with a 1922 copyright. Jay Van Everen drew the art. Fillmore gives the book to his niece Phyllis, calling the tales stories of her mother's native land. A plate shows Ilona floating up through the waves. Fillmore had written Czechoslovak Fairy Tales and The Laughing Prince.

His note tells how the Finns, swept by the same love of nation that moved small peoples across Europe, hunted their own lost tongue. Peasants had kept it alive in songs and tales. Elias Lönnrot spent a long life gathering those runos and built the national epic, the Kalevala, from them. Fillmore wandered the byways of Finnish lore with a native guide.
38115-book-of-50-pictures:
Book of 50 Pictures was printed at Concord, New Hampshire, by Rufus Merrill, as a small book for children. The pages are built round pictures, each with a short line or two of print. A peacock is called a very pretty bird, with tail feathers three feet long.

Other pictures show a cow and calf, a fine colt, a lion, and a zebra, called a small horse. A monkey drinks from a glass. Farm and home things follow: ox, mule, turkey, goose, duck, lamb, and beehive. Then come an engine, a bell, a steamship, a cart, a watch, and a stove. Readers get a first picture book that teaches young children to name beasts, birds, and things of daily life.
3815-rolling-stones:
O Henry's posthumous collection gathers stories, sketches, and fragments left at his death, with an introduction to frame them. The contents run from The Dream and A Ruler of Men to The Atavism of John Tom Little Bear, The Marionettes, The Marquis and Miss Sally, and A Fog in Santone. A German concert hall scene, with palms, marble tables, and soft shod waiters bringing beer, shows O Henry's eye for place even in an unfinished piece.

The book also holds an unfinished Christmas story, an apology, and a snapshot at the president, mixed with tales of sharp twists and tender endings. The quality varies, as in any posthumous gathering, but the voice stays unmistakable. Readers who want O Henry beyond the famous hits will find a miscellany worth browsing, story by story.
38168-from-veldt-camp-fires:
H A Bryden wrote tales from South African camp fires, in an edition dated 1900 from Hurst and Blackett of London. Chapter one is called A Secret of the Orange River. Bryden says many stories are told at the outspan fires of transport riders. Some are weird, some romantic, some of native wars or fierce beasts.

The transport rider, carrier of Africa, travels year after year with wagon and oxen over rough roads. He meets all sorts of men and picks up legend and adventure at evening fires. Bryden joins two riders at a farm outspan for a meal of steinbok and francolins. Good Cango brandy follows the meal, and the tales begin.
38172-atlantic-narratives-modern-short-s:
Charles Swain Thomas edits Atlantic Narratives, modern short stories, for the Atlantic Monthly Press at Boston with copyright in 1918. Thomas headed English at Newton High School and lectured at the Harvard Summer School. Biographical and interpretative notes close the volume after twenty-three stories.

His introduction, The Short Story, opens with a golf anecdote: a countryman's first swing lands inches from the hole, and the old man mutters that he missed it. Thomas likens that lucky feat to the untrained narrator who stumbles on a triumph of telling. Contributors include John Galsworthy with Buttercup-Night, Nesbit with The Marble Child, and Gerould with A Moth of Peace. Stories by Sedgwick, Canby, and Montague fill out the school anthology.
382-edinburgh-picturesque-notes:
Robert Louis Stevenson sketches his home city in this short travel book, first framed as picturesque notes. He opens with Edinburgh on its three hills above the Firth of Forth, a grand site cursed by wind, rain, and sea fog. Old Town closes, New Town streets, bridges, and views fill the chapters that follow.

Stevenson writes as a native who loves the city yet mocks its weather and its grim airs. He notes scholars, rogues, and ghosts of old Scotland in the same breath. The book gives a vivid walk through a city of stone, mist, and sharp contrasts, seen by one of its most fond and frank sons.
38245-atlantic-classics-second-series:
Atlantic Classics, Second Series, gathers essays from the Atlantic Monthly, printed at Boston. Copyrights run from 1899 to 1918, held by the magazine and its press. The book is dedicated to Atlantic readers everywhere, from Alaska to Zanzibar and from nine to ninety. Sixteen essays and biographical notes fill it.

Merwin opens with Dogs and Men, for people who live a dogless life without knowing what they miss. William Beebe gives Jungle Night, and Jane Addams writes of the devil baby at Hull-House. Other pieces treat intercollegiate athletics, car-window botany, and the Greek genius. The volume samples the magazine's best short prose of two decades, in one shelf-friendly form.
38262-wild-adventures-in-wild-places:
Gordon Stables wrote Wild Adventures in Wild Places for young readers, in a print dated 1881 from Cassell of London, Paris, and New York. Part one stays close to home, on the moors and fens of England. The tale opens in the depths of Epping Forest.

Young Frank Willoughby sits on a fallen tree with a book he cannot read. A great toad sits a yard away and stares up at him. Frank feeds it crumbs, and the two grow to know each other. A day with the hounds and a fox chase soon stir the calm. Boys who love the wild get hunts, woods, and bold deeds.
38268-aspects-of-modern-opera-estimates-:
Aspects of Modern Opera: Estimates and Inquiries is a book of music criticism by Lawrence Gilman, published by the John Lane Company of New York and London in 1909. Gilman had already written guides to Strauss's Salome and Debussy's Pelléas et Mélisande, and he inscribed these studies to Ernest Newman, a critic of breadth, wisdom, and independence.

Four essays make the book. An introduction on the Wagnerian aftermath argues that opera since Wagner's death, a quarter century before, had been a mostly barren page, and largely because of him. A View of Puccini follows, then a long study of Strauss's Salome, its art and its morals. A Perfect Music-Drama closes the volume. Gilman writes as a working critic weighing new opera while Wagner's shadow still covers the stage.
38269-a-history-of-the-philippines:
David P Barrows wrote A History of the Philippines, issued by the American Book Company at New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. Barrows was general superintendent of public instruction for the islands. Thirteen chapters and an appendix fill the book. Maps of the islands, of Malaysia, and of races and tribes aid the text.

Chapter One asks why the Philippines make a fit theme for history study. Peoples of the islands and Europe and the Far East about 1400 follow. Great voyages of discovery and Filipino life before the Spanish come next. The Spanish soldier and missionary get a chapter in turn. Conquest and settlement from 1565 to 1600 and life three hundred years ago fill the middle. Dutch and Moro wars, decline, and revolution lead to America and the Philippines at the close.
38274-ecclesiastical-curiosities:
Church doors, chests, mazes and churchyard lore fill this set of essays by several churchmen and antiquaries. Tyack opens with the church door, arguing that a shabby entry lowers what a visitor expects inside. A fine porch, by contrast, lifts the mind before worship begins and fits the building's high purpose.

Other pieces take up a leper window, big bones kept in churches, and Samuel Pepys at church. Theodore Johnson writes on churchyard beliefs, and Wilkins Rees collects odd notices read out in church. Old carving, custom and parish memory are the common thread running through the whole set of short studies.
38284-the-heart-of-denise-and-other-tale:
S Levett-Yeats published The Heart of Denise and Other Tales with Longmans, Green at New York in 1899, from a copyright of 1898. He also wrote The Chevalier d'Auriac and The Honour of Savelli. A plate shows de Clermont reporting on the defence of Ambazac.

The title tale opens in an anteroom before the Queen Mother's cabinet at the Hôtel de Soissons. A maid of honour watches a corridor hung with violet velvet and golden lilies while music drifts from the main salon. Other tales treat Captain Moratti, a treasure of Shagul, the foot of Gautama, and a devil's manuscript. Swordplay, courts, and far places give the set its colour.
38289-the-sa-zada-tales:
Fraser wrote The Sa'-Zada Tales, published by Scribner's Sons in New York in 1905 and illustrated by Arthur Heming. Fraser also wrote Mooswa and Others of the Boundaries and The Outcasts. Sa'-Zada is a zoo keeper who gathers his animal comrades for evening talks, and the animals tell their own stories.

The white, yellow, and black leopard opens the set. Hathi Ganesh, the white-eared elephant, follows, then Gidar the jackal debating with Coyote the prairie wolf. Raj Bagh, the king tiger, and the tribe of King Cobra come next. Tales of monkeys, birds, buffalo and bison, a camel, and a wild boar fill the book. The keeper himself closes it. Fraser mixes Indian jungle and Canadian north in one story-telling frame for young readers.
38302-the-lonely-ones:
The Lonely Ones is Edward Ludwig's story of a rocket crew eaten by loneliness. Paul Orban drew the pictures. The Wanderer carries six men through cold, silent space. They bear their loneliness like a shroud, yet a savage hope grows with each year. Nine years out, the forward screen shows a great gray globe.

Captain Sam Wiley holds his feeling corked inside him. Lieutenant Gunderson babbles his joy aloud. The new world is ten times the size of Earth, and it may hold life. Wiley dares not let the men hope too hard. The Moon was dead, and Mars was dead after centuries of dreams. The story asks whether this world will answer their prayers.
38310-the-wolves-of-god-and-other-fey-st:
Algernon Blackwood and Wilfred Wilson wrote The Wolves of God and Other Fey Stories, published in New York in 1921. The title page dedicates the book to the memory of their camp-fires in the wilderness. Blackwood was already known for John Silence and The Empty House.

The title tale opens as a small steamer enters the bay of Kettletoft in the Orkneys, where the shore at Sanday lies so low the houses seem to stand in water. Around it stand tales of Chinese magic, a running wolf, a tarn of sacrifice, and a valley of beasts. Egyptian sorcery, a decoy, an empty sleeve, and a wireless confusion fill out the fifteen pieces. The word fey runs through them all: strange, wild, and half in another world. Camp-fire dread is the flavor throughout.
38339-south-african-folk-tales:
South-African Folk-Tales collects animal tales and origin stories retold by James A Honey. The Baker and Taylor Company published the book in New York in 1910. Honey dedicates it to C F H and F I G. The table of contents is crowded with jackals, lions, and wolves. The tiger, the ram, and the jackal share one tale. Tink-Tinkje and the story of Hare stand among them.

The first tale explains the difference in life between Hottentots and Bushmen. In the beginning there were two men, one blind and one a hunter. The hunter found a hole in the earth where game came out. The blind man smelled the animals and knew them for cattle. Trickery over the anointing fat divided the two peoples forever. The Origin of Death appears in four versions, plus a Zulu one. A bibliography of South-African folk-lore closes the book.
38340-rules-and-practice-for-adjusting-w:
Rules and Practice for Adjusting Watches is a trade manual by Walter Kleinlein. Kleinlein had earlier written a book on the watch adjuster and his work. He held the rights to this manual in 1920. The contents divide the craft into two parts, on heat and cold first, then on timing and position.

The first part treats the balance that evens out heat and cold. Chapters tell where to place screws when a watch runs slow in heat or fast in cold. Gear for the work is described, from an electric oven to a cold box. Observatory and trade systems of rating are compared, with their cards and marks. The second part turns to even timing in all positions. Theory and practice of friction and the escapement fill its chapters.
38363-a-little-brother-to-the-bear-and-o:
William Long built these animal studies from his own notebooks and memory, reaching back some thirty years. The trail runs from the woods round his childhood home to a Canadian winter trip. The sketches carry Milicete Indian names drawn from each creature's sound. The bear of the title chapter keeps company with Whitooweek the Hermit and K'Dunk the Fat One. Moowen's Den and Kingfisher's Kin fill out the contents.

Ginn and Company published the book in Boston and London in 1903, with drawings by Charles Copeland. Long dedicated it to Lois, who likes bears, and warns that a few chapters, the toad's among them, are composites. The bear and eider-duck portraits, by contrast, come from single animals he knew.
3837-hospital-sketches:
Louisa May Alcott drew these sketches from her own months as a Civil War nurse, first printed in the Boston Commonwealth and then enlarged in book form. Chapters follow her from obtaining supplies and a forward movement to a day, a night, and off duty hours in a Union hospital. The publisher gave five cents of every copy to orphans made fatherless or homeless by the war, a fact the advertisement states with pride.

The sketches mix humor with horror, as a delirious patient flourishes a mug and an old boot for canteen and knapsack, declaiming in a toga while an attendant sleeps off whiskey. Alcott names no names, quoting Sairy Gamp for her warrant. Readers who know Little Women will find the same warm voice here, turned to wounds, laughter, and death in the wards.
38413-the-king-of-schnorrers-grotesques-:
Zangwill wrote The King of Schnorrers, subtitled Grotesques and Fantasies, copyrighted in 1893 and reprinted by Macmillan at New York in 1909. Zangwill had written Children of the Ghetto. Many artists, Phil May among them, drew the pictures.

The foreword states the plan frankly: the episodes make no claim to veracity. Zangwill embodies the floating tradition of the Jewish schnorrer, a beggar as unique among beggars as Israel among nations. He sets the tale at the end of the seventeen hundreds, the most picturesque period of Anglo-Jewish history. Shorter pieces follow: a semi-sentimental dragon, cheating the gallows, and a rose of the ghetto.
38464-tempting-curry-dishes:
Tempting Curry Dishes is a cookbook by Thomas Murrey of the chafing dish. James Smith of New York issued it in eighteen ninety one. Murrey also wrote Salads and Sauces, Fifty Soups, and Practical Carving books. Good Things from a Chafing Dish heads his long list of cookery titles.

An introduction sings three Hindoo kings famed for cookery in old ages. Nala of Nishadhades dressed dishes so well his kingdom grew famous thereby. Bhima served a full year as cook to King Virat in the third age. Pakasasana governed the making of celestial food as a distinguished chef too. A mysterious powder cured disease and appeased appetite in their dishes.
38469-the-life-of-benjamin-franklin-illu:
The Life of Benjamin Franklin, Illustrated by Tales, Sketches, and Anecdotes is a schoolroom life of Franklin. Its plates show the young Franklin carrying home his paper and making peace with his brother. The book was built for young readers and for use in teaching.

Chapters close with sets of study questions, a fact the transcriber's note is careful to flag. The preface argues that Franklin's life, rightly handled, is among the most instructive of all lives. It holds that the life stirs curiosity and wakes young minds as few can. Tales and short sketches are woven into the main line of the story to drive its lessons home. Industry, thrift, and self-help are the burden of the piece. The volume is a specimen of the moral biography that filled American school shelves in its century.
38489-gargoyles:
Gargoyles, by Ben Hecht, was published in New York in 1922. Hecht gives the book to his friend, the Chicago Daily News. Chapter one opens in 1900, by the calendars. It was growing warm, and George Cornelius Basine emerged from a house of ill fame at five on a Sabbath May morning.

He was twenty five, neatly dressed, unshaven, and whistling. The song he whistles is Won You Come Home, Bill Bailey. Considering the high estate that was to be his, as Senator Basine, the opening savors of malice. But that was twenty two years ago, the narrator says. It was before the forces of decency had triumphed, when saloons and hell holes still flourished in the city heart. Basine was of his time, neither ahead of it nor behind it. Readers get Hecht satirical novel of an American career, from brothel door to Senate.
385-the-redheaded-outfield-and-other-bas:
Zane Grey gathers eleven baseball tales in this volume, most set in the minor leagues of his day. The title story follows Delaney's red-haired outfield trio: Gilbat, Clammer, and Ray, each gifted, each a headache for his manager. Other tales track a country pitcher called the Rube through pennants, marriage, and defeat.

Grey writes the game in vivid, slangy detail, from circus catches to clubhouse rows. Managers, knockers, and old pros fill the dugouts. The stories capture early baseball as work, show, and gamble, and they still charm fans who love the game's rougher, smaller-town past.
38504-robin-s-rambles:
May Byron tells the life of a robin in a garden in the East Country of England. Milford printed the book in London for Oxford University Press. Muckley drew the plates, among them Robin feeding his young and a group of harvest mice. The tale is told close to the bird himself.

Robin thinks himself fine, clever, and brave, but his wife does not agree. She sits on five red speckled eggs in a nest by the stable, hard at work. Robin is a born rambler and flies off each day for news. He scorns the sparrows and starlings who fight for crumbs at the kitchen door. There he meets a kitten, till her mother steps in to stop the play.
38517-the-front-yard-and-other-italian-s:
Constance Fenimore Woolson published The Front Yard and Other Italian Stories with Harper and Brothers in 1895. The note records the first printings. In Venice ran in the Atlantic Monthly, The Street of the Hyacinth in the Century, and the other four stories in Harper's Magazine.

The contents add Neptune's Shore, A Pink Villa, and A Christmas Party to the title story. Woolson lived in Italy for years and wrote it as an insider-outsider. Her Americans meet Italian landlords, gardens, and streets, and the meetings unsettle both sides. She was among the first American writers to make Italy a subject rather than a backdrop. Six stories fill the volume, and Harper bound them as her Italian book.
38562-the-big-book-of-nursery-rhymes:
Walter Jerrold edited a big book of nursery rhymes printed at London and Glasgow by Blackie and Son, with pictures by Charles Robinson. The book is given to the youngest baby of all, with the love of the compiler and the artist. Curly Locks opens the pages: thou shalt sit on a cushion and sew a fine seam, and feed upon strawberries, sugar, and cream.

The very title, nursery rhymes, tells how the verse has passed from generation to generation, Jerrold begins. Who composed the little pieces is, save in a few cases, impossible to say. Some are very old and were repeated thousands of times before print. Ding Dong Bell was once called Plato's Song in an old song book, he notes. Mother Goose's whole crew marches here in a fine dress for the nursery shelf.
38565-cornish-catches-and-other-verses:
Bernard Moore's Cornish Catches and Other Verses, from Erskine Macdonald at London in 1914, is dedicated to his mother. Many poems are reprinted from papers ranging from the Academy and Country Life to the Sphere, the Westminster Gazette and the Western Morning News.

Dialect pieces carry the Cornish half: Well, There 'Tis, Eddication, In the Kittereen, Granfer's Proverbs, Seining Song, A Mevagissey Haul and The Old Fisherman's Lament. Well, There 'Tis runs a whole life in its refrain, from the crying child comforted at a warm breast to the lad at his games and the lover at a cottage door. A Ballade of Cornwall and The Fisherman's Prayer close the contents.
38596-notable-women-authors-of-the-day-b:
Helen Black wrote Notable Women Authors of the Day, published in Glasgow in 1893. David Bryce and Son issued the book with portraits. The sketches first ran as a series in the Lady's Pictorial. Black revised, enlarged, and updated them for this volume.

Each sketch pairs a life with a portrait photograph. Lynn Linton opens the list, and Riddell follows. Walford, Broughton, and Helen Mathers appear in turn. Florence Marryat gets a sketch of her own. Edna Lyall, Rosa Nouchette Carey, and Adeline Sergeant stand further along. Jessie Fothergill and May Crommelin close the portion shown. The book records the women who filled the fiction shelves of its day. It treats them as working authors worth a reader's notice.
38654-great-opera-stories:
Millicent Bender's retellings for children, in Macmillan's Everychild's Series, take six opera stories from original sources in old German. Copyrighted in 1912 and often reprinted, the book gives Children of Kings first, then Haensel and Gretel and The Master Singers. Lohengrin, the Knight of the Swan, The Flying Dutchman, and Tannhäuser, the Minstrel Knight, complete the set.

Children of Kings opens in a lonely mountain glade, where a hideous witch keeps a goosegirl in a tumbledown hut. The witch works to make the girl as ugly and wicked as herself, but the girl's heart stays too pure for evil to lodge in it. Each year leaves her face lovelier, her hair brighter than sunshine and her eyes bluer than the sky.
38680-the-thirteenth-greatest-of-centuri:
The Thirteenth, Greatest of Centuries, by James J Walsh, was first held under a 1907 copyright and printed in a popular edition at New York in 1920. Walsh was a doctor and a teacher at Fordham University. The book had reached its sixtieth thousand.

Walsh had also written Makers of Modern Medicine and The Popes and Science. His case here is that the 1200s, long called a dark age, were in truth a peak age. A front plate shows the Le Beau Dieu carving at Amiens. Walsh treats the age faith, learning, building, and law in that light. He argues that much called new in schools and medicine is in fact old. Church and past readers get a bold brief for the medieval world.
38683-mr-punch-s-golf-stories:
Mr Punch's Golf Stories was gathered from the magazine Punch. Hammerton edited the volume for a library of humour. That series ran to twenty five volumes of national wit. Each held the cream of Punch from 1841 onward. One hundred and thirty six illustrations fill this book. Phil May, du Maurier, and Raven-Hill drew the chief ones. Townsend, Furniss, Reed, and Partridge add more. Golf is the single theme of the collection. Told by his merry men, the title page promises. A short survey opens the volume's matter. Few pastimes, it says, give more innocent merriment than the royal and ancient game.

No outdoor game makes a beginner feel more worm-like, it adds. Golf looks absurdly easy to the onlooker. To the unpractised player it is preposterously hard.
38702-the-maker-of-opportunities:
George Gibbs wrote tales printed at New York and London in 1912, gathered from magazines of 1905 onward. But the Great Head rocks didn't hear, the frontispiece cries. I beg pardon, he repeated, but isn't this yours, a picture asks from page sixty six. What a lot of vermilion you use, says another. You are supposed to be playing the golf of the new era, a third teases.

It was two o'clock as the first tale opens. Mortimer Crabb pushed back the chair from his desk. Crabb raised a supercilious eyebrow at tennis, drawled his disparagement of polo and racquets, and recoiled at the mere mention of college football, the text shows. Yet those highest in Crabb's favor knew there were evenings when he met professionals in secret. Gibbs writes rich men's sports and schemes with a light, knowing hand.
38761-the-man-with-the-pan-pipes-and-oth:
A story collection for children by Mrs Molesworth. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published it at London. W J Morgan drew the illustrations, and Edmund Evans printed the book. Eight tales fill the contents. Pig-Betty, the Dormouse's Mistake, and the Christmas Guest follow the title story. A live dummy and a queer hiding-place add variety.

The title story opens with a childhood memory. A cousin from Germany came to stay, bright and hearty. Little Addie, the narrator, lived buried in storybooks. Cousin Meta scolded her fondly for reading in corners. The grown narrator now agrees with the scolding. Too much story world, she reflects, made her fanciful and delicate. Molesworth wrote dozens of such books. Her gentle moral tales defined Victorian childhood reading.
38785-secret-societies-of-the-middle-age:
Secret Societies of the Middle Ages is a volume in the Library of Entertaining Knowledge, a cheap set made to spread useful learning to plain readers. The set ran under the watch of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, whose board fills the front leaves. Lord Brougham chaired that board, with John Wood as his deputy and William Tooke as purse keeper.

Board names run from sea men and doctors to lords, bishops, and members of Parliament, a sign of how wide the scheme reached. The book itself treats the hidden leagues, courts, and sworn bands of the middle ages, in the plain style of the set. It was made for self taught readers who wanted real past events in short, cheap form.
38831-the-barb-and-the-bridle-a-handbook:
The Barb and the Bridle: A Handbook of Equitation for Ladies, by Vieille Moustache, was reprinted from the Queen newspaper and published at the Queen Office, 346 Strand, London, in 1874. The manual runs from the preparatory suppling exercises on foot to the form in which a lady should ride to hounds.

The introduction says ladies kept asking for the true principles and practice of equitation. The papers begin with the calisthenic practices a young lady needs before mounted lessons. No book alone can teach riding, the author grants, but a careful manual refreshes the memory on points a master explained.
38858-pictures-of-canadian-life-a-record:
Pictures of Canadian Life is a travel record by Ritchie, published by Fisher Unwin in 1886 with twelve illustrations. Ritchie, an English journalist, crossed Canada in the railway age and wrote what he saw. His itinerary runs from the emigrant ship and Quebec through Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto to the North-West, the prairies and the Rockies.

The first chapter begins with a Toronto alderman's indignation. Englishmen, the alderman complained over turtle soup, assumed Canadians were barbarians planted in a wilderness, of whom something might be made in the course of ages. Ritchie's book is the reply: interviews, cowboys, prairie farms, the Canadian Pacific Railway, and a pioneer store at Brandon all testify to a going country. A prefatory note corrects a story about Sir Charles Tupper on his own authority, after the chapter had gone to press.
38880-the-land-of-song-book-2-for-lower-:
The Land of Song, book two, is a poetry reader for the lower grammar grades, selected by Katharine H Shute. Larkin Dunton, head master of the Boston Normal School, edited the volume. Silver, Burdett and Company published it in 1899 in New York, Boston, and Chicago. Pictures go with the poems.

The compilers' preface sets out their rule of choice. Literature, they hold, should give healthful recreation, open the mind to larger views, and build ideals that shape the spirit. To win a lasting love of good reading, the poems must be true literature, of some scope, and matched to child interests. Those interests, they say, centre in the marvellous, in the natural world, and in human life, above all child life and the heroic.
38893-spiritual-adventures:
Spiritual Adventures holds short tales and self tales by Arthur Symons. The book first came out in the year nineteen hundred and five. A miscellany line reprinted it in the year nineteen twenty eight. A gift page sends the work to Thomas Hardy, the great tale hand.

A prelude to life leads, in which the author traces his own strange youth. He owns he recalls scant of those years, though they made the man he is. Homes lost in weeks, no fixed hearth, mark his root less boy days. Tales of a Kahn girl, a faith mad man, and a dead friend fill the set. Dream mood and keen art tune the whole to a poets prose key.
38894-vagaries:
Axel Munthe, a Swedish doctor who wrote Letters from a Mourning City, stands behind this odd, slight book. John Murray printed Vagaries in London in 1898. Instead of a preface, Munthe starts by saying he is no author at all.

His life, he writes, belongs to real work, with no peace for made tales. For near twenty years his best thoughts went to a craft whose only public is the drug shops. The book's stuff baffled even his friends: essays, tales, or what? Tales it is not, he swears, for he never tried to invent a thing. Such grave fun heads a set of sketches from a doctor's wide, strange life.
38895-the-cloister-and-the-hearth-a-tale:
Charles Reade wrote this tale of the Middle Ages, The Cloister and the Hearth. The copy at hand is one of The International Classics, a line that set Reade beside Eliot, Dickens, Scott, and Dumas. Sixteen plates in colour, the work of Evelyn Paul, grace this edition.

Reade's title sets two worlds against each other: the cloister and the home. His tale is the line's chosen work of his, among Adam Bede, David Copperfield, Ivanhoe, and Jane Eyre. The bright plates in colour suit a story of old times and strong feeling. Readers who like Scott and Dumas in this same dress will find Reade's Middle Ages told with the same sweep.
38898-poems-parodies:
Kettle published Poems and Parodies with the Talbot Press in Dublin in 1916. The poet, born in 1880, was an Irish writer, teacher, and politician who died in 1916. The volume opens with a memorial essay on Tom Kettle that stresses his talk, his wit, and his sad, joking nature.

The memoir calls him a genial cynic and a pleasant pessimist, full of paradox. It notes his essay book The Day's Burden and his gift for telling a story. His humour and sharp wit, the writer says, held listeners fast. Placed before the poems, the essay turns the book into both a collection and a tribute. Readers meet the man first, then the verse and parodies that made his name in Ireland.
38902-buzz-a-buzz-or-the-bees:
Buzz a Buzz, or The Bees, was done freely into English from the German of Wilhelm Busch by the author of My Bee Book. At Cologne station, waiting for a train to Aix-la-Chapelle, the translator browsed a stall covered with books about the late war of 1870. Sick of battlefields, he wanted something of a more peaceful nature for the journey.

A book titled Schnurrdiburr, oder die Bienen caught his eye, profusely illustrated with very comical cuts, and he paid his thaler gladly. The cuts are reproduced here, with verses written up to the pictures rather than translated line for line. Bee-friends had waited thirty years for his original Bee-Book's second edition. Comic verse readers get Busch's bees in English dress.
38922-pine-needles:
The author of The Wide, Wide World framed a set of mission tales in a light story of her own. Pine Needles, in a new London edition from Warne, carries a note dated the first of February, 1877. The tales come from the Missionsblatt of Pastor Louis Harms of Hermannsburg. The note says they might well be called Christian Heroes.

The frame story brings the Franklin children to Mosswood for a stay. Maggie and Esther plan treats for Meredith and Flora while the parents are away in California. Between the home scenes, the book tells the Harms tales in their plain, whole form. Hardly a dozen words, the note says, have been cut. The result joins a warm family story to tales of faith and courage from far mission fields.
38953-british-manufacturing-industries-p:
Bevan edited a set on the chief trades of Britain, and this part, in a second edition issued in London in 1877, treats pottery, glass, and silicates. Arnoux, art head at Minton's factory, wrote on pottery. Barff, a teacher, wrote on glass and silicates, and Pollen of the South Kensington Museum on wood work.

The set aims to draw each trade's main traits and present state into one clear view for plain readers. Growth of the past twenty or thirty years stands at its heart. Arnoux starts with clay pots as man's first step up from his first rude state, made to hold food and drink.
38976-the-necklace-of-princess-fiorimond:
Mary De Morgan writes fairy tales in The Necklace of Princess Fiorimonde and Other Stories, for Macmillan in London in 1880, with illustrations by Walter Crane. De Morgan, author of On a Pincushion, dedicates the tales to her six little nephews and nieces. Seven stories fill the contents.

The title tale opens with a widowed king whose daughter Fiorimonde is so beautiful that everyone assumes her good. In truth she is wicked, slipping out nightly to a mountain witch who taught her sorcery and made her beauty unmatched. The princess repays the witch by hiding her from all the world. Other tales follow Arasmon's wanderings, the heart of Princess Joan, a pedlar's pack, the bread of discontent, three clever kings, and a wise princess.
39026-our-journey-to-the-hebrides:
Joseph Pennell and Elizabeth Robins Pennell made this illustrated journey to the Hebrides, published in London in 1890. Most of the book first ran in Harper's Magazine. In their preface the Pennells say critics scolded them for not finding in Scotland what fashion expected, and for not giving second-hand accounts of the Scotch.

They chose instead to report what they saw themselves. A plate of crofters' cottages near Uig, on Skye, sets the scene early. The trip offers drawings and plain notes on islands, people and travel, written by two workers who trusted their own eyes over guide-book habit.
39062-the-last-lion-and-other-tales:
The Last Lion and Other Tales presents stories by Vicente Blasco Ibanez in English dress. The International Pocket Library issued it at Boston in 1919. Lorente wrote the introduction. Three printings in growing numbers attest its welcome. The tales came by arrangement with the author's American publisher.

The introduction sketches the author's life at length. He was born at Valencia in January 1867. His family came from Aragon. The Aragonese are painted as stubborn and freedom-loving. Their chief justice once told a king that the people were greater. Poverty and hunger marked the author's youth. He followed many trades before studying law. At eighteen he was a full-fledged lawyer. His later fame as a novelist grew from that hard schooling.
39072-the-a-e-f-with-general-pershing-an:
Heywood Broun wrote this report on the American Expeditionary Forces in France, printed in New York in 1918. Some of the pieces first ran in the New York Tribune. The opening chapter, The Big Pond, tells of the crossing itself: a sailor spots a submarine, the deck gun fires, and hundreds of passengers crowd the rail to cheer.

Later chapters take readers within sound of the guns, to General Pershing, to men with medals, and to letters home. Broun visits the French and British armies, sees Verdun, and meets men back from prison. Hospital and engineer units, marines, flyers, and big guns each get a chapter. The book ends as the American army marches to the trenches, written in a warm, chatty voice for readers at home.
39078-religious-folk-songs-of-the-southe:
A doctoral dissertation by Howard W Odum, reprinted in 1909. Clark University accepted it for the degree of doctor of philosophy. G Stanley Hall recommended its acceptance. The journal of religious psychology had printed it that July. Odum was then a fellow in psychology at Clark. His subject is the religious folk-songs of Black southerners.

To know a people's soul, Odum begins, find its folk-thought's source. Songs give the truest expression of the folk mind, he argues. Posterity often judges peoples without knowing their inner life. Treasures of song lie hidden beside us, wasting in obscurity. Odum collects spirituals as evidence of race character and feeling. His work helped open the academic study of Black folk culture. Later he became a leading Southern sociologist.
39103-the-circus-and-other-essays-and-fu:
Joyce Kilmer wrote these essays, edited with an introduction by Holliday and published by Doran in 1921. Kilmer's poems, essays and letters appeared in two companion volumes from the same editor. The circus opens the contents at page forty-five, and the abolition of poets follows at sixty.

Noon-hour adventuring, signs and symbols and kindred fugitive pieces fill the list. Kilmer, the poet of 'Trees,' died in France in 1918 before this gathering appeared. Holliday collected his light prose of circuses, streets and books for Aline Kilmer, the widow to whom this volume is dedicated.
39128-kensington-rhymes:
Kensington Rhymes holds verse for the young by Compton Mackenzie. Monsell drew the gay prints that fill the small book. A Punch and Judy show heads the front of the set as its plate. The book first came out in the year nineteen twelve.

Our house leads, with its high red walls, white steps, and bright knocker. Square games, dance class, kiss games, and a round pond song fill the list. Poor scent girls, a rare thief, and a band from abroad earn rhymes too. Street art men, sweeps, and green grocers walk the town in the set. Plain tune and fond sight tune the verse to a childs London.
39142-astronomy-the-science-of-the-heave:
David Todd's Astronomy: The Science of the Heavenly Bodies was published by Harper & Brothers in 1922, under a Collier copyright. Todd was director emeritus of the Amherst College observatory. A photograph from Mount Wilson fronts the book: an active prominence of the sun, 140,000 miles high, taken on July 9, 1917.

Todd opens with Hamilton's praise of the science as man's golden chain linking the heavens to the earth. Astronomy is the oldest of the sciences, he says, and the broadest in its ties. Geometry and the higher mathematics tell of motions and distances; physics and chemistry, of what planets and stars are made of. Even the riddle of life in other worlds falls, in part, to the astronomer.
39169-pictures-and-stories:
Pictures and Stories is a small book for young children, printed at Providence in 1847. Each page pairs a picture with a short tale in plain words. The tales show home life, school, work, and play, and each one points to a clear lesson about kind acts and good conduct.

Early tales tell of Susan, who sets her caged bird free though she weeps to lose it, and of a poor girl who sells radishes and still earns respect at school. Later tales take up tears over drowned kittens, good manners when a boy enters a room, and a girl who loves to obey her mother. Young readers get brief, gentle scenes that praise care for others over self.
39170-dorothy-and-other-italian-stories:
Constance Fenimore Woolson's Dorothy and Other Italian Stories was published in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1896. A note says A Florentine Experiment first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly and the other stories in Harper's Magazine. The five tales are Dorothy, A Transplanted Boy, A Florentine Experiment, A Waitress and At the Chateau of Corinne.

Dorothy opens at the Villa Dorio on Bellosguardo, above the Roman Gate of Florence. The American ladies of the villa receive Saturday visitors, and Giuseppe the gardener turns footman for the afternoon. Guests divide between the garden, where Dorothy is with Mrs North, and the salon and tea upstairs with Mrs Tracy.
39198-random-rhymes-and-rambles:
Random Rhymes and Rambles is a book of verse and prose in Yorkshire dialect by William Wright, who wrote as Bill o'th Hoylus End, printed at Keighley in 1876. Wright dedicates it to a local musician of North Beck Mills and introduces himself without pretence: the rhymes are the leisure musings of the uneducated.

His introduction asks only for credit for what the work is worth, from an author rough and ready, with no notion of Parnassus or the Muses. The first poem, Never Die in Thy Shell, is a creed of endurance in broad dialect. Never give up, old lad, though you be poor, though creditors seize your dish and spoon: night is always followed by morning, and fortune changes like the moon. Dialect pieces follow, like Old Betty's advice to a lass about to wed. The book is working-class Yorkshire verse, printed for neighbours.
39202-ever-heard-this-over-three-hundred:
Ever Heard This, over three hundred good stories, is a joke book by F W Chambers, printed at London in 1916. It reached its third edition by December of that year. The contents list hundreds of short tales by their titles. They run from What He Wanted and His Choice to A Good Pun and Something Like an Insult.

The titles map the humour of the day: the stutterer, the proud father, the unwelcome guest, and the thoughtful patient. Clerical wit, a canny Scot, the Quaker and his horse, and the relationship of hog to bacon all have their place. Later titles treat an inspector of taxes, the she bear, and fish as a brain food. Books of this kind served speakers, hosts, and after-dinner talkers who needed a story for every occasion. Chambers's collection is a storehouse of Edwardian jest, gathered for ready use.
39205-sheep-swine-and-poultry-embracing-:
Robert Jennings, veterinary surgeon, wrote Sheep, Swine, and Poultry. Its title page promises the history and varieties of each kind of stock. It adds the best modes of breeding, their feeding and management. It also covers the diseases to which they are subject, with the appropriate remedies for each.

The book served American farmers who kept all three kinds of stock on one place. Breeds are described and compared, rations and housing set out, and the common ailments matched to their cures in the manner of the period. Readers get a nineteenth-century livestock manual complete in itself, the small farm's whole animal economy between two covers.
39206-insect-stories:
Vernon Kellogg wrote these Insect Stories, printed in New York in 1908 in the American Nature Series. Mary Wellman, Maud Lanktree, and Sekko Shimada drew the pictures. Kellogg wrote the book at Stanford University in California, with a young companion named Mary. The dedication names Dorothy, Anna, and Mary as the Mary of the tales.

In his note Kellogg says the stories are true, seen by Mary and himself. He grants that Mary is a child of dreams, and some of her talk is fancy. The beasties and their doings, he insists, are quite true. The story list opens with a narrow-waisted mother and a fight of red and black against white. Argiope of the silver shield stands among the tales.
39217-the-king-s-stratagem-and-other-sto:
The King Stratagem and Other Stories is a tale set by Stanley Weyman, out in eighteen ninety one. A Cluett house of New York brought the set out that year. Six tales fill the scheme, from the name tale to The Fatal Letter. The name tale opens in the days when Henry of Navarre was king in name. His small hill realm held the faith war cause in the south west.

Each fort town from Garonne to the Pyrenees was a bone of strife then. Queen Catherine met him at La Reole town on its high cliff. She brought fair maids whose charm she trusted as much as state craft. Gay song rang in each house while both camps stood primed for arms. Two men at play in a deep set room frame the first night scene.
39221-flags-some-account-of-their-histor:
Macgeorge wrote Flags, some account of their history and uses, printed in 1881 in a large-paper edition of one hundred copies, this being number eighty. A plate shows the standard Napoleon presented to his guards at Elba shortly before invading France in 1815. Macgeorge also wrote Old Glasgow and its armorial insignia.

In a nation with dominion so extended and sea and land communication everywhere, flags cannot be without interest, the preface argues. Yet few subjects have less accessible information, so this volume gives a popular account of British and foreign flags, ancient and modern. Heraldic inaccuracies in the national flag and on bronze coinage are pointed out for correction. Flag history readers get a Glasgow antiquary.
39263-astronomical-curiosities-facts-and:
Astronomical Curiosities is a book of facts and fallacies by Ellard Gore. Chatto and Windus issued it in London in 1909. Gore was a fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society. He also wrote The Visible Universe and other popular works. The contents run to twenty-one chapters. They move outward from the sun to the whole heavens. Each body of the system gets its own chapter.

The first chapter treats the sun and its light. Pickering's measures from Jamaica are quoted there. Sunlight is put at 540,000 times moonlight. The moon's reflecting power is given a low figure. Comets, meteors, and the zodiacal light follow in turn. Double stars, variable stars, and nebulae fill later chapters. Old errors are set beside sound results. The book served amateur sky watchers of its day.
39281-a-dictionary-of-english-proverbs-a:
A shilling handbook gathers the proverbs of English speech into one ordered list. It formed number fifteen in a series of familiar quotation books. The front matter lists its shelf mates, from Latin proverbs to Lamb's Tales from Shakspeare.

The preface makes the case for the form. Long before books were common, proverbs were the chief means of teaching. Now they live on in papers and in literature, the editor argues. A reader meets them daily and needs a key. The entries run in letter order for quick finding. The series also sold a handy book of synonyms with about 33,000 words. Such cheap, cloth-bound helpers filled Victorian coat pockets and school desks across Britain.
39282-the-adopted-son-the-story-of-moses:
Willard retells the story of Moses for children in this 1905 volume of the Altemus Children of the Bible series. Each life in the series, from Isaac to the boy Jesus, sold at fifty cents. The tale begins far back with Abraham, chosen as founder of the Hebrew nation and promised the land of Canaan. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph follow in turn.

Joseph's brothers sold him into Egypt, where he rose to governor under Pharaoh, and Jacob's family settled in Goshen and grew great. But a new Pharaoh who never knew Joseph set the Israelites to unpaid labor, making bricks and building treasure cities. At last he ordered their baby boys destroyed, and into that danger Moses is born, the adopted son of the title. Pictures show him striking the rock and bringing the Ten Commandments down from Mount Sinai.
39298-modern-leaders-being-a-series-of-b:
Justin McCarthy sketches the modern leaders of his day in this book, published at New York in 1872. Queen Victoria and her subjects open the contents at page seven of the sketches. The real Louis Napoleon and the Empress Eugenie follow in the list of portraits at the front.

The Prince of Wales, the king of Prussia and Victor Emanuel of Italy come in turn. Thiers, Prince Napoleon, the Duke of Cambridge and Brigham Young fill the middle pages. The liberal triumvirate of England, English positivists and George Eliot with Lewes close a journalist's gallery of the famous in 1872.
39364-rich-relatives:
Rich Relatives, by Compton Mackenzie, was published in London in 1921. Mackenzie had also written Sinister Street, Sylvia Scarlett, and Poor Relations, to which this book is a kind of match. The tale is given to Alice and Christopher Stone, and dated November 1920.

Chapter one opens at York railway station. A porter, perhaps cross at Sunday duty, speaks rudely to Jasmine Grant. Her black clothes are not fashionable, and a journey from the south of Italy to the north of England has draggled what style they had. News of a near five hour wait for the train to Spaborough brings tears to her eyes. Yet her dark, southern beauty is there all the same. Readers get a Mackenzie novel of money, family, and a young woman adrift.
39414-the-masculine-cross-a-history-of-a:
The Masculine Cross, privately printed in 1904, traces the cross symbol through ancient and modern times and links it to old sex worship and kindred faiths. The title page names no author.

Pictures at the front show crosses from India, Buddhism, Assyria, and Mexico. Chapters first treat the cross itself, then the doctrine of a sacred triad. Later chapters turn to the golden calf of Aaron, circumcision, and gods of both sexes. The opening pages argue that things thought modern often reach back to the earliest ages. Meanings fixed on a symbol later, the writer warns, may not be the meanings it first carried. Greek words and two special symbols appear in the original text.
39425-the-mysterious-wanderer-vol-iii-a-:
Sophia Reeve wrote The Mysterious Wanderer, a novel in three volumes printed in London in 1807 for the author. The book is dedicated, by permission, to Lady Elizabeth Spencer. This third volume opens in mid-conversation, with Sir Henry beginning a narrative for Captain Howard.

The sudden death of Sir James Elvyn, Sir Henry says, and the loss of the fortunes he designed his daughters, were told to Howard long since by Jarvis. With her fortune, Eliza Elvyn lost every attraction in the eyes of a grandfather who had meant her for his son. He forbade the union accordingly, and the narrative starts from those circumstances. Fortunes lost and marriages forbidden are the machinery of the tale. Reeve wrote for the circulating libraries, where a wanderer mystery in three volumes was fare. Eliza's wrongs drive the volume home.
39431-young-folks-bible-in-words-of-easy:
Young Folks’ Bible in Words of Easy Reading retells the stories of Scripture for the youngest readers, in the language of childhood. Josephine Pollard wrote the book, as she had written histories of the Old and New Testaments. A front picture shows Christ the good shepherd, carrying the lambs in his bosom. An introduction by Milburn opens the volume.

The full title calls the tales the sweet stories of God’s word. Christian art fills the book with fine pictures of the scenes. The stated aim is to impress the mind and heart of young readers. It hopes to kindle a true love for the book of books. Pollard chose plain words so that small children could follow the sense. Such Bibles were staples of the Sunday school and the family shelf.
39447-shelburne-essays-third-series:
Shelburne Essays, Third Series, is a book of literary essays by Paul Elmer More, published in nineteen o five. Most of the essays first appeared in journals such as the Atlantic Monthly and the Independent. One essay, the last in the volume, had never been printed before. The book opens with a study of the correspondence of William Cowper.

Other essays treat Whittier as a poet and mark the centenary of Sainte Beuve. The Scotch novels and Scotch history get a joint essay in the volume. Swinburne, Christina Rossetti, and Browning each receive a full critical study. Shorter pieces take up Byron's Don Juan and the novelist Laurence Sterne. A life of the writer Shorthouse and an essay called The Quest of a Century close the set. More writes as a critic who weighs poets by their hold on letters.
39484-daddy-s-bedtime-bird-stories:
Daddy Bedtime Bird Stories, by Mary Graham Bonner, was held under a 1917 copyright and printed in New York. Four color plates by Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis fill the book. Bonner wrote the tales to be read aloud at bedtime.

The list opens with Old Mr Owl Writes a Book, in which the wise bird wants to know how to start a book. Other tales tell of woodpeckers who start a bird band, and of the cardinal bird and the robin. Winter wrens take dew drop baths, and seagulls move to Bluey Cove. One tale tells how the little redbird became red, and one gives poor Mr Owl a toothache. Small children get gentle bird fun with a fact or two tucked in.
39508-popular-scientific-lectures:
Ernst Mach's Popular Scientific Lectures reached English readers in Thomas McCormack's translation, here in a third edition, revised and enlarged, from the Open Court Publishing Company at Chicago in 1898. Mach had taught physics at Prague and now held the chair of the history and theory of inductive science at Vienna. Fifty-nine cuts and diagrams serve the 411 pages.

In his Prague preface of December 1894 Mach sets the terms of such lectures. They can give only a modest share of teaching, so they must pick easy subjects and keep to the simplest points. Yet a well-chosen problem can still carry the charm and the poetry of research, and show how close science stands to everyday thought. The new matter in this edition includes a lecture on some phenomena attending the flight of projectiles.
39543-a-holiday-in-bed-and-other-sketche:
J M Barrie wrote a set of short sketches, copyrighted in 1892, with a short life of the author at the front. That life notes his birth at Kirriemuir in Forfarshire on May 9, 1860. The town's trade was linen weaving. Barrie made the place famous as Thrums in his early Scots sketches.

The title sketch, A Holiday in Bed, leads the pieces. Life in a Country Manse appears twice, once with a wedding in a smithy. Other sketches treat a powerful drug, Gretna Green revisited, and running after a hat. Rules on carving and a piece addressed to influenza add humor. The tone is light and wry.
39548-the-forged-note-a-romance-of-the-d:
The Forged Note, A Romance of the Darker Races, is introduced by notes from the book's jacket. At twenty one the author was a homesteader on the Rosebud Indian Reservation in South Dakota. He was about the only Black settler there, the notes say. At twenty six he had prospered on the land.

When a new strip of the reservation was opened, he helped kin secure land. He furnished funds for claims and costs. He also secured a homestead for a young lady, the daughter of a minister. Six months later they were wed and lived on her claim. Strife grew between the husband and her father, who held unlike views. The wife, sick in bed, was led to forge her husband's name, the notes say. Race, land, and marriage drive the romance.
39576-the-radio-detectives:
A Hyatt Verrill writes a boys' tale of wireless sleuths in an Appleton volume held under rights from 1922 in New York and London. Verrill had written The Deep Sea Hunters and The Book of the Motor Boat before. Thirteen chapters run from Tom Takes Up Radio to Rawlins' Proposal at the close.

Tom Pauling bursts in at dinner with word of a new set he has built with his own hands. His father teases that the boys junk sets as fast as they make them, yet backs the craze in full. Strange messages, an under-sea wireless, a cry from the depths, and a battle beneath the river fill the heads. Tom's father urges him to learn the whole art from the ground up, not just buy gear and play.
39593-aunt-liza-s-hero-and-other-stories:
Aunt 'Liza's Hero and Other Stories, by Annie Fellows Johnston, author of the Little Colonel series, was printed by Page at Boston in 1904, gathering copyrights from 1889 to 1903. Taylor and others supplied the illustrations, including a frontispiece of a boy who at first always brought some boy with him.

Six stories fill the contents: the title piece, The Captain's Celebration, Jode's Circus Money, Jimmy's Errand, Washington's Birthday at Hardyville, and An Old Daguerreotype. The title story opens at a garden gate. Aunt 'Liza Barnes leans over the front gate at the end of her path and pulls her black sunbonnet farther over her wrinkled face against the glare. She had been weeding her vegetable garden when the shouting of voices reached her. Thinking it a runaway, she hurried to the gate as fast as her rheumatic joints allowed, while noise and dust came down the street.
39604-burlesques:
Burlesques, by Bateman, first published in 1916 by Duckworth of London, is a book of comic drawings with an opening note by Johnson. A plate shows the actor George Graves in Princess Caprice. Johnson praises Bateman as that rare thing, an artist whose very line is funny.

The note argues that Bateman does not force humor onto dull subjects; he finds the humor already in life and draws types everyone knows but no one has quite seen. A plumber in his pages is every plumber. Bateman went on to fame for silent, perfect single panel jokes, and this early book shows the gift forming.
39608-the-magic-of-the-middle-ages:
The Magic of the Middle Ages is a study by Rydberg, turned from its first tongue by Edgren. It came out at New York in the late eighteen seventies, and its rights were held that year by its house. Its parts run in four great heads.

First comes the world view of the mid ages and its growth in time. Then the magic of the church, the magic of the learned, and the magic of the folk. The fight of the church with that last kind closes the set. Its first words set the frame: the faith of that age held our globe the heart of all things. The earth stood fixed and still, ringed by ten heavens in their turns.
39610-riding-for-ladies:
W A Kerr wrote Riding for Ladies, issued at New York in 1891 by Frederick A Stokes Company. Kerr had served as second in command of the Second Regiment, Southern Mahratta Horse. A past book named Riding holds base chapters on action, aids, and bits. Those chapters are not repeated here, Kerr warns.

Chapters treat the lady's horse and give plain hints on how to mount. The seat, walk, trot, canter, gallop, and leap get steps in turn. The side saddle and dress for riding get chapters of their own. A part on riding astride follows. Notes at the back treat the training of ponies for children. Pictures show right and wrong ways to mount and turn.
39616-in-the-hands-of-the-malays-and-oth:
In the Hands of the Malays and Other Stories, by G A Henty, came from Blackie and Son of London and Glasgow. The title tale opens on May 1, 1669, on a rock isle off the south-west shore of Sumatra. A man of mixed blood stands by a rough grave with a wood cross and glares at a Dutch ship as it sails off. He has been marooned for some crime aboard the Dordrecht, a sixteen-gun merchantman bound for Java.

Dutch men of wealth had chartered her to plant rich crops on that isle. They took the man on at the Cape as cook, his hot, vengeful bent no bar with troops aboard. A second tale, On the Track, hunts a crime, and A Frontier Girl closes the book. Boys got sea peril in Henty's firm hand.
39628-the-expositor-s-bible-the-pastoral:
Alfred Plummer wrote on the Pastoral Epistles for The Expositor's Bible, a series edited by W Robertson Nicoll. The volume was issued at Toronto in eighteen eighty-eight. Plummer led University College, Durham, and had been a fellow of Trinity College, Oxford.

The first chapter weighs the character of the letters and whether Paul truly wrote them. Plummer then turns to Timothy, the beloved disciple of Saint Paul, and his life. A long part treats the false teaching the letters condemn, a Jewish form of early heresy. Letter by letter, the book explains the counsel given to young church leaders. Plain learning guides the whole.
39644-whilomville-stories:
Whilomville Stories is a collection of thirteen stories by Stephen Crane, illustrated by Peter Newell and published by Harper and Brothers in 1900. The stories concern the children of the village of Whilomville.

Titles include The Angel Child, Lynx-Hunting, Making an Orator, Shame, The Knife, and The Stove. One story stages the trial, execution, and burial of Homer Phelps, a boy's solemn game. Another sets a city urchin against the chaste villagers, and the last is A Little Pilgrimage. Illustrations show the Trescott children, a boy bandit chief, and a plea to borrow a father's gun. The first story begins one summer when the Trescotts receive a visitation: a cousin who is a painter of high degree.
39674-buffalo-land-authentic-account-of-:
W E Webb of Topeka, Kansas, wrote Buffalo Land, a true account of a hunting and science trip into the wild West, issued in 1872. Pictures from real photographs and drawings by Henry Worrall fill the book. Its long title promises finds, bold deeds, and mishaps of a sporting party, with close views of the country and of the red man, wild and settled. Hunts for buffalo, antelope, elk, and wild turkey fill its pages.

An added part gives a guide for sportsmen and men moving West. Webb gave the book, with deep regard, to the primeval man, the first Westerner and first buffalo hunter. A comic poem at the front paints the West as a wild spot where graves mark the prairies. The work mixes sport, humor, and hard fact for readers bound for the plains.
39701-heroines-of-the-crusades:
Heroines of the Crusades, by Bloss, is a set of lives of six women of the crusading age. It was published at Auburn, New York, in 1853, and dedicated to the author's pupils. Bloss taught history and wrote a school history of the ancient world. The six heroines are named on the title page in order.

They are Adela, countess of Blois; Eleanor of Aquitaine; and Berengaria of Navarre. Then come Isabella of Angouleme, Violante of Jerusalem, and Eleanor of Castile. In her preface Bloss tells her pupils that actions, not faint desires for excellence, form the character. Jerusalem, she writes, swayed men's minds more deeply in the dark after Rome's fall than at any earlier time. Her book brings queens who marched, ruled, and ransomed into schoolroom history. It stands as an early American attempt to write the crusades through their women.
39769-ghosts-i-have-seen-and-other-psych:
Violet Tweedale wrote Ghosts I Have Seen and Other Psychic Experiences, copyrighted in New York in 1919. Contents run to twenty-four chapters. Silk dress and rumpus opens the book, then the ghost of Broughton Hall. Curious psychic experiences and East End days and nights follow. The man in the Marylebone Road and the ghost of Prince Charlie come next. Pompey and the duchess and the unseen hands fill the middle heads.

The skeleton hand at Monte Carlo and the angel of Lourdes stand later. Haunted rooms, haunted houses, and the haunted lodge lead to auras and a farewell. The first chapter opens in the hard present. From its terrible terms, Tweedale writes, she has turned back to the past for a little joy and a great deliverance. A piece of music once loved, and the scent of mimosa flower, carried her back to a hillside in France.
39771-studies-in-modern-music-second-ser:
Studies in Modern Music, second series, by Hadow, treats three composers. Seeley of London issued the fifth edition in nineteen o four. Hadow was a fellow of Worcester College, Oxford, when he wrote. The composers are Frederick Chopin, Antonin Dvorak, and Johannes Brahms.

Outlines of musical form open the book, on taste, style, and function. Chopin study moves from Warsaw days to Paris and a lyric poet verdict. Dvorak study treats his days of training and his national traits in music. Brahms study traces growth, maturity, and the direction of new paths. Portraits of all three composers illustrate the volume for its readers.
39815-my-fire-opal-and-other-tales:
Sarah Warner Brooks's My Fire Opal and Other Tales was published by Estes and Lauriat at Boston in 1896. Brooks had written English Poetry and Poets. The tales are dedicated to the beloved memory of her grandmother, Isabel Cornwell. A preface dated January 31, 1896, states the book's aim: to interest readers in how convicted fellow sinners should be treated. The stories grew from personal observation behind the bars and are woven, she says, almost equally of fact and fiction.

Seven tales stand in the contents. The title story opens with Isabel, the narrator, staying home alone while her husband Alcibiades travels. She gives the servant Cicely a holiday and laughs at the idea of company and burglars. The Story of John Gravesend, A Bunch of Violets, and A Disastrous Sleigh-Ride follow. Tuckered Out, A Prison Child, and Escaped close the volume.
39831-a-study-of-splashes:
Worthington, headmaster and professor of physics at the Royal Naval Engineering College at Devonport, wrote A Study of Splashes. Longmans printed it in 1908 with 197 illustrations from instantaneous photographs. The study grew from boyhood watching at Rugby School.

Rain on a pool, Worthington says, raises a thousand little crystal fountains, each with its coronet of jets. Chapters follow a drop's splash at low and high falls, then bubbles below the surface. Solid spheres make two kinds of splash, smooth or sheath, and rough or basket. He explains why they differ, and ends with splashes left where shot pierces armor plate.
39850-cattle-ranch-to-college-the-true-t:
Cattle Ranch to College is Russell Doubleday's true tale of a boy's adventures in the Far West, printed at New York by Doubleday and McClure in 1899. Doubleday had written A Gunner Aboard the Yankee. He dedicated this book to his mother, his kindly critic, counsellor and friend. The illustrations include a bunch of cattle marked with the ranch's brand.

The preface is plain about the book's truth. The incidents described actually happened, and are described substantially as the boy related them. A ranch childhood gives the first half its matter: cattle, horses, and the work and mischief of a western boyhood. College gives the second half its destination, as the title promises. It belongs to the shelf of true boy's-life books that the nineties loved.
39860-the-evolution-of-states: Evolution of States bills itself as an introduction to English politics on its title page. Front pages list many past works by the same prolific author. Those works range over freethought, sociology, economics, and literary study. Titles like Pagan Christs and Pioneer Humanists show the author wide range of thought and study in print.
39911-the-army-mule-and-other-war-sketch:
Henry Castle served the Union as private, sergeant-major, and captain of Illinois Volunteers, and three decades later he turned his Civil War memories into humor. The Army Mule and Other War Sketches appeared in 1897 with illustrations by Vawter, and the mule on the title page climbs a tree without compunction.

Five sketches make the book: the army mule, the sutler, the shelter tent, dress parade, and the boys in blue grown gray. Castle wrote as a veteran for veterans, in the years when the Grand Army of the Republic filled halls. The comedy is camp comedy, fond and exact about the small miseries of soldiering, and the last sketch turns the laughter toward reunion and age.
39913-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-eccl:
The Book of Ecclesiastes, a commentary by Samuel Cox for the Expositor's Bible series, was published at Toronto in 1890. W Robertson Nicoll edited the series. Cox adds a new translation of his own. His motto is a line of Saint Augustine: all is vanity, save to love God and serve him alone.

The book grows out of lectures first given twenty five years before and printed in 1867. That edition sold out fast, then stayed out of print for over twenty years. Cox rewrote the work for this series rather than reprint it raw. He names the helps he used most: Delitzsch, Wright, Plumptre, and Perowne. Above all he praises the commentary of Ginsburg, from 1861, as still by far the best and most thorough.
39916-the-ranger-boys-outwit-the-timber-:
A boys' series novel by Claude A Labelle, published at New York in 1922. The A L Burt Company issued the Ranger Boys books. This is the fourth of five listed adventures. Garry Boone, Dick Wallace, and their friend form the trio. The series aimed at boys of twelve to sixteen. Packs, rifles, and northern woods supply its furniture.

A train conductor's cry opens the adventure. Bangor, all change for Portland and Boston, he shouts. Garry wakes sleepy Dick and grabs their knapsacks. Their father waits at the Bangor House with trouble hinted in a letter. Dick grumbles about walking when a car might come. Real action, though, is what the boys crave after quiet weeks. Timber thieves give the Maine woods their danger.
39974-handbook-of-alabama-archaeology-pa:
Handbook of Alabama Archaeology, Part One, is a guide to projectile point types. Cambron and Hulse wrote it, and DeJarnette edited the volume. The Archaeological Research Association of Alabama published it. A first printing came in November 1964. Revisions and reprints ran through November 1975. The contents open with a section on point shapes and features. An alphabetical index follows that guide section. The point types themselves fill the main body from page one.

Provisional types get their own section after the main types. A distribution chart maps where types are found. A glossary and a bibliography close the handbook. An illustration shows a Turkey Tail point form. Griffin of Michigan and Coe of North Carolina are thanked. The book is a field and museum reference for collectors and diggers.
39997-library-notes:
Library Notes, in a revised and enlarged edition of 1882, gathers Addison Russell's essays on books and character. The thirteen pieces bear single-word titles. Insufficiency opens the set, followed by Extremes, Disguises, Standards, Rewards and Limits. Incongruity, Mutations, Paradoxes, Contrasts, Types, Conduct and Religion complete the round.

Russell builds each essay from quoted voices. He begins with the thought that every object holds an inexhaustible meaning. The eye, he says, sees in a thing what the eye brings means of seeing. Goethe, Joubert, Johnson and Hazlitt all speak in the first pages. The method lets old writers argue the point while Russell steers, a commonplace book raised into criticism.
40020-the-thames:
Mitton described and Haslehust pictured this river book, The Thames, one of the Beautiful England series from Blackie and Son of London and Glasgow. A list of pictures follows the river upstream in paint: Hampton Court at the front, then Windsor, Richmond, Marlow Lock, Maidenhead Bridge, Cookham Church, Henley, Sonning, Pangbourne, and Folly Bridge at Oxford.

The text opens with a joke between nations. An American wondered what the fuss was about, since any of his home rivers could swallow the Thames. The Englishman answered that it would depend which end the swallowing began at, since London might give the bigger river indigestion. Size is not greatness in rivers, Mitton argues, and this book treats the Thames not as London's river but as a river of pleasure.
40027-the-scarecrow-and-other-stories:
The Scarecrow and Other Stories is a story collection by G Ranger Wormser, published in New York in nineteen eighteen. Twelve tales are listed, from The Scarecrow to The Stillness. Haunted, The Shadow, The Effigy, and The Wood of Living Trees promise a weird bent. The title tale opens at a ramshackle, tumble down shanty in hard wind.

A woman stands in that doorway with her hands cupped at her mouth, calling a name into the wind. Loose blond wisps whip around her face and her faded dress slashes in the gale. Farm Gothic in the American grain follows from that first scene. Wormser's tales mix rural poverty with haunting and dread.
40038-the-lone-ranger-rides:
The Lone Ranger Rides, by Fran Striker, was printed in New York in 1941 with drawings by Smith. The Lone Ranger company held the copyright, and Striker gives the book to George Trendle. The contents promise thirty chapters of western action.

The tale opens in a remote basin in western Texas, where the Cavendish clan raised cattle. Longhorns grew fat on lush grass across the level acres. The hills round the basin looked green and kind, but the text calls that pure deceit. Those hills were treacherous, and Bryant Cavendish loved them for that very quality. Chapter heads name a gap, a cave, and gray dawn before Tonto and Silver appear. Murder, a legal paper, and a gambler's talk build toward the unmasking of Andrew Munson. The badge of a Ranger closes the tale.
40124-poetical-ingenuities-and-eccentric:
Poetical Ingenuities and Eccentricities gathers curious and playful forms of verse. Dobson selected and edited the pieces. Chatto and Windus published the book in London in 1882. Dobson had written Literary Frivolities before it. That book's warm reception prompted this sequel. The publisher's list places it among light literary volumes.

A short preface states the bargain plainly. Reviewers had charged the earlier book with one sin only. That sin was omission. Dobson promises that readers will find it fully atoned here. Historical accounts of the verse forms appeared in the first book. This volume gives the examples themselves. Acrostics, echoes, and shaped verses are the kind of sport it collects. The tone stays antiquarian and amused throughout.
4016-prince-eugene-and-his-times:
L. Muhlbach's historical romance follows Prince Eugene of Savoy, the soldier prince whose honor and affections suffer a mortal wound. For a day he stays alone in his room, longing for the privilege of grieving without witnesses, while his servant Conrad keeps vigil outside.

Through the long night Conrad hears his master's slow, measured step, pacing out grief that no medicine can cure. Muhlbach builds the tale from court intrigue, war, and love, in the full manner of nineteenth-century romance. Readers who enjoy long historical novels will find a warm, old-fashioned life of a famous general.
40163-a-rminius-vambe-ry-his-life-and-ad:
Arminius Vambery wrote this account of his own life and adventures, first issued in London with portrait and pictures. The copy here is the fifth and popular edition. An opening chapter is given to the boys of England. Long quotes from reviews fill the front pages, from journals in London and from the Novoe Vremya in Moscow.
