Reviewers call the book a sketch of character and a tale of bold travel in a land then little known. They praise its vigour and its light on the peoples and tongues of the East. The contents start with his early years, spent in study and in work as tutor and waiter. Vacation rambles and literary studies come next in the list.
4018-japanese-fairy-tales:
Yei Theodora Ozaki's collection retells old Japanese tales for English readers, with princesses, stepmothers, and moral lessons at their heart. A dying mother tells her daughter Hase-Hime to honor her father and his second wife, to obey her superiors, and to be kind to those below her.

Hase-Hime listens in respect and promises to do all she is told, in the manner of a model heroine. Other tales in the book follow the same pattern of duty, kindness, and reward. The collection suits young readers and anyone curious about Japan's story tradition, told in clear, gentle prose.
40197-the-country-life-movement-in-the-u:
The Country Life Movement in the United States is a farm life book by Bailey. A Macmillan house brought it out in March of nineteen eleven. It stands in a set of four books on the rural view of life. Bailey gives it to Garfield, called seer of the best farm life to come. First heads swear it is not a back to the land move at all.

A state board on farm life and its three chief pleas fill next heads. Town and farm ties, two minds, and farm man odds stand mid scheme. Farm folk loss and lone farms get heads on what they mean. Drain work, held lands, and town craft fate fill more head ranks. Farm school in town class and state aid plans close the heads shown.
40203-arse-ne-lupin-versus-herlock-sholm:
Maurice Leblanc wrote Arsène Lupin versus Herlock Sholmes, and George Morehead translated it from the French for Donohue of Chicago in 1910. It belongs to the Extraordinary Adventures of Arsène Lupin, the gentleman thief. The table of contents lists eight chapters of duel and counter-duel.

The cases include Lottery Ticket number 514, the Blue Diamond, an abduction, and the Jewish Lamp. One chapter is bluntly titled the Second Arrest of Arsène Lupin, and another shows Herlock Sholmes opening hostilities. The first chapter opens in a Paris curiosity shop, where Professor Gerbois buys a small mahogany writing desk for his daughter Suzanne. An elegant young man in the shop wants the desk himself and follows Gerbois into the street with perfect courtesy. Readers get the thief and the detective, thinly renamed, matched wit for wit.
40235-the-expositor-s-bible-the-books-of:
William Henry Bennett wrote on the Books of Chronicles, in the Expositor's Bible. Hodder and Stoughton and Doran stand as its publishers in this form. Bennett was professor of Old Testament languages and literature. He had been a fellow of a Cambridge college in earlier years. His preface owns the odd place of Chronicles in the series.

To expound Chronicles after Samuel, Kings, Ezra, and Nehemiah, he writes, is gleaning. It gathers scattered ears from a field already harvested, he says. Sections shared with the older histories are treated briefly here. An exposition of Chronicles is not a history of Judah, he insists. To recombine what the chronicler left out would obscure his teaching. His selection of material has a religious significance, Bennett holds. That meaning is found by careful comparison with Samuel and Kings. Chronicles with Ezra and Nehemiah once formed a single whole.
40237-by-the-sea-and-other-verses:
H Lavinia Baily wrote By the Sea and Other Verses, published in Boston by Richard G Badger at the Gorham Press in nineteen seven. Copyright rests with Baily from the same year. A contents list of more than sixty poems fills the front pages. Myself and You opens the book. By the Sea, At the Close of the Year, and Risen follow near the start.

The poems turn often to faith and the sea. Psalm CXXI, Be Ye Also Ready, and A New Earth stand among them. Neal Dow and The White Ribbon Army show a temperance strain. The Ballad of the Boundary Line is one of the longer pieces. The opening poem argues that if two people were kind and true, the courts might all adjourn. Poetry readers get a Boston volume of devout, domestic verse.
40243-the-hittites:
The Hittites, The Story of a Forgotten Empire is a work of ancient history by A H Sayce, deputy professor of philology at Oxford. A second edition appeared in 1890 in the By-Paths of Bible Knowledge series. Sayce tells how scholars recovered a great people whom the modern world had forgotten.

His preface calls the discovery the romance of ancient history. The evidence came from Egyptian and Assyrian inscriptions, strange monuments in Asia Minor, and hieroglyphics still undeciphered when he wrote. Sayce's own paper on the monuments of the Hittites in 1880 laid the foundation, and Dr Wright's Empire of the Hittites built on it. The book mattered because the Hittites stand throughout the Old Testament, yet their empire had vanished from memory.
40249-in-a-cheshire-garden-natural-histo:
In a Cheshire Garden is a book of wild lore notes by Geoffrey Egerton-Warburton, the church head of Warburton. It was put out at London in nineteen twelve with all rights held. The notes first ran in a town sheet in the spring of that year. They then ran in a de town form in a next sheet. Plates from light prints stand in the book.

The first words thank two men for their light prints. One gave views of the old church, the great yew, and the flower gar den. One gave a shot of two nests told of in the text. The parts start with a lead in and with weeds and strange plants. Then come the birds in their kinds: the song birds, the chats and red breasts, the small tits and wrens.
4030-travellers-stories:
A mother's travel stories for her sons Frank and Harry open on a stormy evening, as the boys beg for tales of her five years in Europe. Seated on the old sofa, she recalls cities, coaches, and the small mishaps of travel.

One tale leaves mother and sons in the middle of a street, their noddy driver poring over a directory in a bright shop to find Dr. Nichol's house. The stories mix sights, manners, and mild comedy, told in a warm, fireside voice. Young readers will enjoy a book that turns a mother's journeys into lessons in curiosity and good humor.
40312-the-intoxicated-ghost-and-other-st:
The Intoxicated Ghost and Other Stories is a set of short tales by Arlo Bates. It came out in Boston and New York in 1908 from Houghton, Mifflin and Company. The contents list nine tales. The title tale stands first, then A Problem in Portraiture, The Knitters in the Sun, and A Comedy in Crape. A Meeting of the Psychical Club and Tim Calligan's Grave-Money stand in the list as well.

The title tale opens with a portrait of Irene Gaspic. It was not her beauty that made her out of the common run, the tale says, though she was of great charm. Nor was it her wit, her skill, or her wealth, though she had a full share of all those gifts. Other girls were fair and rich as well, the first page notes, as it sets up its lead figure.
40367-the-decoration-of-houses:
The Decoration of Houses is a guide to the dress of rooms in a home. Edith Wharton and Ogden Codman wrote it as a pair in 1897. The copy here is a New York print of 1914 by Scribner. A French line at the front sets its creed in one stroke.

The creed is that a form must be fair in its own right. Stuck-on trim must not be used to hide its flaws, they hold. The book starts with the old ways of the craft in past times. It then takes the house room by room and part by part. Walls, doors, hearths, and stairs each get a part of their own. Great rooms, the book room, the meal room, and bed rooms follow. Small goods and the close of the house end the guide.
40376-cork-its-origin-and-industrial-use:
Cork, Its Origin and Industrial Uses, a monograph by Gilbert Stecher, was published at New York in 1914. It treats the cork oak, whose Latin name heads the book. A front picture shows men gathering corkwood. Stecher offers the work as a summary of a most interesting subject, for others who seek knowledge of corkwood.

He says the material's character and makeup hold a mystery never yet fully pierced. Its uses and its native land, by contrast, are well known. The book follows cork from the bark of the oak to the many trades that use it. Stoppers, floats, insulation, and linoleum all depend on this light, springy bark. Stecher gives credit to the writers and workers he drew upon. His monograph is a compact guide to an industry that touched shipping, building, and the bottling of wine across the world.
40379-trench-ballads-and-other-verses:
Erwin Clarkson Garrett published Trench Ballads and Other Verses at Philadelphia in 1919, following his Army Ballads. He dedicates the book to his father, a Union Army captain in the Civil War, and to his mother. A portrait of the poet fronts the volume.

Part one holds the trench ballads: Trenches, Barb-Wire Posts, Your Gas-Mask, Slum and Beef Stew, and Shell-Fire. Other titles cover the Salvation Army with the American force, cooties, a gas-proof mule, and little gold chevrons on a cuff. Readers get soldier verse from the First World War that mixes danger with mess-tin humour, written for the men who lived it.
40424-surgical-instruments-in-greek-and-:
Surgical Instruments in Greek and Roman Times is a study by John Stewart Milne, printed at Oxford in 1907. Milne begins with the writers who mention such tools, from Hippocrates and Celsus down to Paulus Aegineta. A second chapter treats the metals and other stuff the tools were made of.

Later chapters sort the tools kind by kind, starting with knives. Scalpels, bistouries, fleams, and lithotomy knives each get their forms and uses traced. Milne also notes famous finds, among them the gear dug out at Pompeii and Herculaneum. The book maps what classical surgeons actually held in their hands, and how the tools changed across the centuries.
40425-chinese-mother-goose-rhymes:
Isaac Taylor Headland of Peking University translated and illustrated these Chinese Mother Goose rhymes, published by the Fleming Revell Company at New York, Chicago, and Toronto under an October 1900 copyright. Short rhymes in English couplets render the nursery songs of Chinese children, with pictures of little orientals.

The first rhyme, Sweeter than Sugar, calls a baby boy blue as sweet as sugar and cinnamon, sweeter than dates and cinnamon flowers. Little Small-Feet shows a small-footed girl crying over her spent money and her love of sweets. The Cricket climbs a hemp stock on a mountain top and answers that he is going out dining. The Butterfly is not worth catching, the Fire-Fly is coaxed home with sugar, candy, and meat, and The Cow counts four feet, eight toes, a tail behind, and a head in front. Grandpa Feeds Baby gives mutton dumplings with vinegar and tea.
40429-robinson-crusoe-s-money-or-the-rem:
Robinson Crusoes Money is a money tract by David Wells, a past chief of the tax desk of the land. It came out at New York in eighteen seventy-six. Its full name calls it the tale of the coin luck and ill luck of a far isle folk. Wells says hard coin friends urged him to set the first rules of coin and trade in plain dress for all.

He chose the old fable way and made a tale the cart of his lore. A far isle folk is feigned, one step past wild life, that climbs to a high state. Its path is traced past swap, coin, and notes, with the use and the wrong use of each. Side notes show that each folly of trade in the tale has its match in true past days, Wells holds.
40457-comparative-studies-in-nursery-rhy:
Lina Eckenstein's Comparative Studies in Nursery Rhymes, from Duckworth of London in 1906, treats the rhymes of the nursery as serious folklore. Her preface begins far from any nursery, with a carved scene in the temple of King Sety at Abydos in Egypt, fourteen centuries before Christ.

The carving, showing a dead figure mourned by hawks, reminded her of the toy-book tale of the Death and Burial of Cock Robin. She asks whether the two can be linked across the ages. Chapters then trace rhymes in print, toy-books, ballads, and country dances, and study the Sally Waters game, riddle-rhymes, counting chants, and creed chants. Later chapters turn darker, to sacrificial hunting, bird sacrifice, and the robin and the wren. The book argues that children's rhymes carry very old beliefs.
40501-the-blower-of-bubbles:
Arthur Beverley Baxter wrote a set of five long tales, published at New York in 1920 and dedicated to his mother. The title piece opens in Sloane Square on Christmas Eve, with snow quarrelling with rain as it falls. The narrator watches from his window and prays for Aladdin's lamp or a magic carpet.

A knock brings not the slave of the lamp but his landlady, Mrs Mulvaney, asking if he will dine in. He is twenty-five, and she counts all men equally immature. He calls himself one of intellectuality's hermits and thanks Heaven he has no friends. Petite Simunde, the man who scoffed, and an airy prince follow among the later tales.
40508-true-stories-of-girl-heroines:
True Stories of Girl Heroines is a story collection by Everett-Green, published with sixteen illustrations by Sherie. Twenty tales retell brave deeds of girls across history, from Inez Arroya to Agostina of Zaragoza.

The first story opens in alarm: a servant bursts in crying that the Moriscos are upon the house. Inez, a young Christian mistress in the Sierra Nevada country, pales at the words, then holds her breath to listen to the robbers below. Juana gasps out that when the wine and oil are taken, the men will come up and murder them both. The illustration captions promise the genre's pleasures throughout: stones hurled at Moors, girls defying judges, and a brave young wife riding out at the head of her whole garrison. The book is heroic history re-dressed as girls' adventure.
40510-the-watcher-and-other-weird-storie:
J Sheridan Le Fanu haunts the page in The Watcher and Other Weird Stories, from Downey and Company of London, with twenty-one illustrations by Brinsley Sheridan Le Fanu. A front plate shows a shape passing a man and whispering, furiously, Still alive. The preface, by the author's son, says most tales were written before Uncle Silas.

All but The Watcher first stood in The Purcell Papers, edited after Le Fanu's death by Alfred Perceval Graves. The preface notes that the seed of Uncle Silas lies in the Passage in the Secret History of an Irish Countess. Irish gothic chills follow.
40532-portrait-miniatures:
Portrait Miniatures, with text by Williamson and editing by Charles Holme, was issued by The Studio of London in 1910. Great collectors lent their treasures for the plates, among them Pierpont Morgan, Sir Charles Dilke, and Lord Hothfield. A color list opens the book, plate by plate.

Hilliard's Queen Elizabeth leads, followed by Isaac Oliver, Hoskins, and Samuel Cooper, whose sitters include Cromwell's daughter. Cosway, Smart, Engleheart, and Plimer carry the art into the age of elegance. The small portrait was once the photograph of its day, and this volume shows the finest hands that made it.
40553-the-queen-bee-and-other-nature-sto:
Carl Ewald wrote nature stories for children in Danish, and G C Moore Smith turned them into English for Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1908. The Queen Bee and Other Nature Stories is the first series. The tales first came out in 1882 and took final form in 1895.

Ewald's father, a noted writer of historical novels, praised the plan in a preface kept here. In place of trolls and bewitched princes, the tales take their matter from natural history. Bees, plants, and farm life give young readers true things to wonder at. The translator notes the tales were loved across Denmark and Scandinavia long before English readers met them.
40562-snowflakes:
Esther Nelson Karn wrote Snowflakes, a little book of verse printed at Philadelphia by the press of Geo F Lasher in nineteen hundred. Karn holds the copyright. She inscribed the book to her husband, S A Karn, whose kind encouragement enabled her to write it, she says. A first poem is Dance of the Snowflakes. Nature and home themes shape the set.

Let us dance to the brown old earth tonight, cried one little flake of snow, the poem opens. The autumn days have all passed by, and I am tired of my home in the sky, it says. They dressed themselves in a misty film of purest pearly white, it goes on. Their feet were clad in velvet down, as soft as the filmy gown. They flew over housetop, hilltop, and dell till morning light, it sings. Verse lovers get a gentle gift book of winter and hearth poems.
40573-the-other-side-of-the-sun-fairy-st:
Evelyn Sharp's The Other Side of the Sun, with pictures by Nellie Syrett, came out from John Lane in London and New York in 1900. Sharp gave the book to all the children she knew on this side of the sun. Eight fairy tales fill it, and the first tells of the Weird Witch of the Willow-Herb.

That witch lives in a pink cottage on a hill, dressed in pink and green, merry and kind, with eyes now full of laughs and now of tears. Other tales bring a magician's tea-party, the hundredth princess, somebody else's prince, and Princess Prunella's tears. A palace on the floor and a kite that went to the moon round out the set.
40584-lancashire-brief-historical-and-de:
Leo Grindon, a Manchester writer on plants and banks, set down brief historical and descriptive notes on Lancashire in a rich picture book issued at London in 1892. Twelve chapters treat the county's chief marks, Liverpool, the cotton district and its mills, and Manchester. Other parts cover trades of many kinds, the marks of the folk in speech and pastimes, the inland sights south of Lancaster, and the seashore and lake country.

The last chapters visit the old castles, stone houses of prayer, and old halls of the county, and the book closes with its wild life and fossils. The plates show emigrants at Liverpool, shipping on the Mersey, pay-day in a cotton mill, and glass-blowing. Grindon's book gives a full portrait of the great mill county at the height of its wealth and work.
40594-into-the-highways-and-hedges:
Into the Highways and Hedges, a novel by F F Montrésor, was published in London in 1896 and reached a seventh edition. The preface says the book is not meant as a debate in story form. The author states that she does not agree with all the views of Barnabas Thorpe, one of its figures.

The story turns on Margaret Deane, third daughter of Charles Deane. Her name stands in the family Bible with a thick line struck through it. No note of her marriage or her death stands beside it. The narrator calls her a woman who made one great mistake, and tells how she came through it. Men who fight for their ideals form the moral core of the tale.
40630-british-castles:
Charles Ashdown wrote British Castles, published in London by Adam and Charles Black in 1911. The book carries 32 full-page pictures in color, plus plans and diagrams through the text. A trebuchet, the great stone-throwing engine, stands on the title page, and Bodiam Castle in Sussex serves as frontispiece.

Ten chapters trace how the castle grew. They begin with natural strong places and fortified hill-tops, then take up the motte and bailey, the shell keep, and the keeps built square and round. The concentric castle and the castellated mansion follow, and a chapter treats the castles of Scotland. The book closes with the siege and defence of a medieval castle. Readers get the whole art of fortress building told step by step.
40650-christmas-roses-and-other-stories:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick wrote a set of tales named for flowers, issued in Boston and New York in 1920. The lead tale, Christmas Roses, opens on a walled garden border where white blooms push up between laurustinus and yew. An old, sad woman watches them force their way out of cold, dark earth each winter.

To her the flowers seem to will their own birth, as gifts to give more than lives to seek. They call up Christmas bells over snow fields and the star and manger of Bethlehem. Nine more tales bear flower names, from hepaticas and daffodils to pink foxgloves, carnations, and autumn crocuses. Each tale keys its mood to its bloom, in Sedgwick's fine, slow style.
40656-little-johannes:
Little Johannes is a tale of the fair kind from the tongue of the low lands, by Frederik van Eeden. Clara Bell made its English form. Andrew Lang wrote a lead in piece for the book. It was put out at London in the year eighteen ninety five. That lead in piece bears the name of the writ kind of the book: the tale of the fair folk.

The child's tale, Lang says at the start of that piece, is a form of writ of vast age. Yet it has a mint of strength to make its youth new at all times. Old wives' tales, tales of a lad and a lass and a cruel step dame, are its stock.
4066-wild-apples:
Henry David Thoreau's essay on wild apples celebrates the orchard tree and the old custom of wassailing it. Villagers throw cider about the roots, lay toast on the branches, and circle a good bearer to drink a toast three times.

Here's to thee, old apple tree, they sing, wishing hats full, caps full, bushels and sacks full of fruit. Thoreau uses the rite to praise wild flavor over tame orchard crops, and to link farming with poetry. Readers who love Thoreau's Concord walks will enjoy this short, fragrant essay on apples and autumn.
40692-foxholme-hall-and-other-tales:
Foxholme Hall and Other Tales, by W H G Kingston, was printed in London by Virtue and Company in an edition dated 1867. Kingston wrote sea tales for boys. The first story treats Christmas at an old country house in the New Forest.

Two boys get the choice of their Christmas holidays. They may stay in Russell Square with a kind old cousin, Miss Gillespie, and go to the theatre and panoramas. Or they may go to Foxholme, home of their great uncle, Sir Hugh Worsley. Foxholme for ever, cries brother Jack, making a face at the prim London plan. The Foxholme party holds Cousin Peter, Julia, Tom and Ned Oxenberry, Sam Barnby, and dogs Ponto, Hector, Beauty, and Polly. Boys of the day got a warm holiday tale with country sport.
40693-arctic-adventures:
Arctic Adventures is a boy tale by W H G Kingston. The narrator tells it in his own voice, as a young Scot who sailed for the far north. He had dreamed of icebergs and polar bears since he was a lad.

He lists the wonders he longed to see, from walruses and seals to the aurora and the midnight sun. Now he sails on the stout ship Hardy Norseman of Dundee, under Captain Hudson. Born in the Highlands and raised by his uncle, a keen sportsman laird, he roamed the hills with a rifle and scorned shoes. His brother Andrew serves as surgeon on the ship. A second brother, David, sailed on the Barentz and has not been heard of. The boy serves as doctor mate and captain clerk. Sea fans get whaling peril in the ice.
40697-sport-royal-and-other-stories:
Sport Royal and Other Stories, by Anthony Hope, was printed in New York by Henry Holt and Company in 1895. Hope had written The Prisoner of Zenda, The Indiscretion of the Duchess, and The Dolly Dialogues. A plate shows a princess rushing to a locked door and screaming.

Sport Royal is told as an extract from the journals of Julius Jason. It opens at Heidelberg, a tourist ridden place, where Jason tale begins with the sequel to a ball. The Mission of the Ruby closes the title tale. Shorter pieces follow, named A Tragedy in Outline, A Malaprop Parent, How They Stopped the Run, and A Little Joke. A Guardian of Morality, Middleton Model, My Astral Body, and The Nebraska Loadstone fill the rest. Tale fans get Hope light hand at court and town fun.
40718-atlantic-narratives-modern-short-s:
Atlantic Narratives holds modern short stories picked for school use. Charles Thomas chose the tales and wrote the lead in for the set. This copy is the second series of the Atlantic house school books. Rights date the work to the year nineteen eighteen.

A lie tale leads, then blue coats, a debt, and a shrine fire tale in turn. Hid gold, a sham princess, two apples, and a star fill the mid list. A coal mine year and a womans sphere earn parts of grave tone. A legion man and a road of rogues close the wide keen set. The book served class rooms that taught new prose in short form.
40745-short-stories:
Short Stories, by Fiodor Dostoievski, gathers nine tales in the World Popular Classics edition. Books Incorporated published it at New York and Boston for general readers. An Honest Thief opens the contents at page one of the volume. A Novel in Nine Letters and An Unpleasant Predicament follow in the list.

Another Man Wife, The Heavenly Christmas Tree, and The Peasant Marey fill the middle heads. The Crocodile, Bobok, and The Dream of a Ridiculous Man close the contents. An Honest Thief opens with the narrator cook Agrafena breaking six years of silence. She asks him to let the little room next to the kitchen, to his surprise. Small tales of clerks, dreamers, and holy fools show the great novelist in short form.
40756-the-nursery-may-1881-vol-xxix-a-mo:
The Nursery for May 1881 is one number of a Boston monthly magazine for youngest readers. It forms number 5 of volume XXIX. The Nursery Publishing Company issued it from 36 Bromfield Street. The pages mix short prose tales with verse, all cut to a child's measure. Pictures carry much of the weight.

The prose opens with The Bold Soldier-Boys. Colonel Bob charges four chairs, a table, and a sofa with his toy army. His papa finds the day's newspaper folded into the boy's soldier-cap. Other tales follow Papa Robin, Carlo and the ducks, and children picking oranges. The verse includes The May-Queen, The Naughty Cat, and The Mouse-Trap. One song, Daddy Frog, is printed with music. A drawing-lesson and simple natural history round out the number.
40765-the-story-of-our-submarines:
Klaxon told the tale of Britain's own dive boats in the Great War. The book came out in Edinburgh and London in 1919. He wrote a past work whose ship name is hid by dashes. Much ink had gone to the foe's U-boats, his first page says. Britain's own boats worked in dark and hush all that war.

Now and then a few state lines told of their deeds, he notes. With the navy's leave he tells some of that hid work here. Their own tales of meets with the foe fill these pages. On August 4, 1914, the fleet held boats of four kinds. Nine E, eight D, and more of C and B kinds stood there.
4077-the-mariner-of-st-malo-a-chronicle-:
Stephen Leacock's chronicle of Jacques Cartier follows the Mariner of St. Malo into the Gulf of St. Lawrence. On June 25, Cartier turned west from Newfoundland into what looked like open sea, then sighted land again near the Magdalen Islands.

Two abrupt rocks rose side by side, one pierced by surf into a passage that caught Cartier's eye. Leacock tells the voyages with the clarity of the Chronicles of Canada series, mixing navigation, first meetings, and French claims. Readers who like exploration history will enjoy a brisk, vivid life of Cartier.
40770-christianity-unveiled-being-an-exa:
Christianity Unveiled is an examination of the Christian religion by Nicolas-Antoine Boulanger. Johnson translated it from the French for this edition. Carlile printed and published it in Fleet Street, London, in 1819. Its subtitle promises an examination of principles and effects. A Pope motto about looking through nature to nature's God fronts it. A translator's preface opens in praise of the philosophic age. Nature, reason, and the rights of man have resumed their empire, it says.

The work ranks among those that changed the public mind, it claims. Rousseau, Mably, Raynal, and Voltaire are named as its company. Their writings concurred in bringing forward the French Revolution, it holds. That revolution may herald the complete triumph of reason, it hopes. Carlile was a famed radical publisher of such works. The book is an Enlightenment attack on revealed religion.
40786-the-black-riders-and-other-lines:
Stephen Crane's poems appear in The Black Riders and Other Lines, reprinted privately by courtesy of Small, Maynard with the 1905 copyright of Copeland and Day. Short numbered pieces fill the book, each a small parable or image rather than a rhymed song. The first gives the volume its title image.

Black riders came from the sea, the opening poem says, with clang of spear and shield and the rush of hair on the wind: thus the ride of Sin. A desert creature squats eating his own heart, calling it bitter and liked for that bitterness. Another piece shows God fashioning the ship of the world, then turning at a wrong's call while the ship slips rudderless down the ways. Three little birds mock a man who thinks he can sing.
40803-the-principal-navigations-voyages-:
Richard Hakluyt gathered the great voyages of the English nation in this famed storehouse, and Edmund Goldsmid edited this copy. Goldsmid printed volume fourteen at Edinburgh in 1890. America, part three, is this volume's main ground.

The end of part two fills the first pages: Virginia richly valued, from De Soto's four years of travel. Coronado's letter to a secretary of the viceroy Mendoza comes next in the list shown. Hakluyt's aim was to keep every English voyage from loss: Florida, Mexico, and the north coasts stand here in the words of the men who sailed them. Sea dogs and settlers speak in old spelling across these pages.
40832-the-veiled-man-being-an-account-of:
The Veiled Man is an adventure narrative by William Le Queux. Its full title promises the risks and adventures of Sidi Ahamadou. He was sheikh of the Azjar marauders of the Great Sahara. Alfred Pearce drew the pictures for the book.

In his opening note Le Queux tells how the tale reached him. He gathered the robber-sheikh's memories on a journey across that desert. A price sat on Ahamadou's head for twelve years of his life. The first chapter opens in his own voice, in a city of seven shadows. He recalls fifty years of wandering the silent sands. Feuds, revolts, raids, and battles against French troops fill that life. The book presents itself as his own account, shaped by an English editor.
40845-the-connexion-between-taste-and-mo:
The Connexion between Taste and Morals is a pair of lectures by Mark Hopkins, president of Williams College, printed at Boston in 1841. The first lecture asks whether the spread of cultivated taste is favourable to morals. Hopkins tells how he put the question to three educated men he met.

The first had not thought of it and doubted any such connexion. The second wished to see it proved before he would believe it. The third thought there was such a link. This split of opinion led Hopkins to take up the subject. He defines taste, after Alison, as the faculty by which we perceive and enjoy what is beautiful or sublime in nature or art. Feelings of taste, he says, can be known only by being felt, like colours to the blind. The lectures argue that what a people learns to love shapes how it learns to live.
40848-the-gully-of-bluemansdyke-and-othe:
The Gully of Bluemansdyke and Other Stories, by A Conan Doyle, was printed in London by Walter Scott Limited. A small edition of the book had come out in 1889 under the title Mysteries and Adventures. Doyle had written Micah Clarke, The White Company, and The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes.

Seven tales fill the book, named The Gully of Bluemansdyke, The Parson of Jackman Gulch, and My Friend the Murderer. The Silver Hatchet, The Man from Archangel, That Little Square Box, and A Night Among the Nihilists close the set. The title tale, opens at a store in Australia. The back room glows with firelight on polished flasks and shot guns, yet gloom rests on the two men at the hearth. Old Tom notes the missing party from the mine. Tale fans get early Doyle.
40866-the-rival-submarines:
A boys' naval adventure novel by Percy F Westerman. S W Partridge published it at London, and this copy is the third impression. C Fleming Williams drew the illustrations. The scene is Portsmouth during a practice mobilisation in 1917. Battleships at Spithead and aircraft from Dover join the final test. The fortress town believes itself impregnable once more.

Strange events then break the drill. Sub-Lieutenant Hythe discovers an unknown submarine. A man walks out of the sea, and signals rise from the depths. Captain Restronguet commands the Aphrodite, a remarkable private submarine. His rival sails the Vorwartz, and another rival flies the French La Flamme. The chase runs through Suez to the Red Sea. Westerman wrote scores of such sea tales for boys.
40869-true-bear-stories:
Joaquin Miller wrote true bear stories, copyrighted in 1900, with introductory notes by David Starr Jordan, president of Stanford University. Miller dedicates the book to his daughter Juanita, for whom he dug most of the tales out of his boyhood days. A thrilling account of the capture of the grizzly Monarch is included. The preface addresses his bright young reader directly.

Miller insists he disliked stories that seemed the least bit untrue as a boy. The modern bear, he says, is not a bloody, bad fellow. Keepers are killed by lions, tigers, and elephants, he notes, but never by tame bears. In half a century, he never knew a bear to eat human flesh.
40884-the-personality-of-american-cities:
Edward Hungerford tours the nation in The Personality of American Cities, from McBride, Nast in New York in 1913. Horter's etching of Madison Square fronts the book, which Hungerford dedicates to his little daughter Adrienne. Twenty-two chapters give each city a character sketch under a nickname.

Boston, Our Ancient Hub, opens the tour with a jab: more things are forbidden there than in Berlin. Park entrances post rule codes taking a quarter hour to read, and trolley cars, churches, and hotels all lay down sharp canons of conduct. Later chapters visit William Penn's Town, the Monumental City, the American Mecca, and Steel's Great Capital. The tour ends with Belfast in America and a city that never grows young.
40891-the-art-of-invigorating-and-prolon:
A health book of its age tells how to add strength and years to life. Food, clothes, air, and work acts are its named tools. Its print keeps old spell forms just as first set down. Word lists in the notes show toothache in three old forms. A third form of the book cleared dim spots in this text.

Long life by plain rules is the book's whole proud aim. What to eat, what to wear, and when to rest fill its parts. Sick rooms and sound homes share its sharp, close watch. Dose counts and meal plans stand in its neat lists. Health fans of that age kept it close at hand. Each rule claims proof in use.
40897-the-burglars-club-a-romance-in-twe:
The Burglars' Club: A Romance in Twelve Chronicles is a comic novel by Henry Hering, published in New York in 1906 with sixteen illustrations by Townsend. Its premise comes straight from the club's founders. They are rich young bachelors, ex-Army and Navy men and sportsmen, who have pretty well used up the pleasures of life. To help things on a bit, they start a club whose members commit burglaries for sport.

Each chronicle records one theft. The targets include Sir John Carder's cigars, a bishop's crozier, and the Fellmongers' goblet. Later chapters chase an ounce of radium, a Bunyan manuscript, and the Great Seal. A Holbein miniature and a Victoria Cross also figure in the list. The final chronicle closes the game. The book is a light-hearted Edwardian romp about gentlemen thieves, written long before such clubs became a stock device of popular fiction.
40915-johnny-ludlow-first-series:
Johnny Ludlow, first series, is a set of village tales by Mrs Henry Wood, printed in 1895. The title page boasts a fiftieth thousand, a mark of the series long public life. A verse from Longfellow on vanished scenes and the dead heads the volume. Contents open with Losing Lena and Finding Both of Them as paired tales.

Wolfe Barrington taming, Major Parrifer, and Lease the pointsman fill the early list. A hunt by moonlight, a tunnel trip, and Jerry Gazette add variety of scene. School, railway, and village folk supply Wood with her cast of plain lives. Johnny himself narrates as the boy who watches, learns, and grows through them.
40919-everyday-adventures:
Samuel Scoville wrote this book of outdoor pieces, Everyday Adventures, copyrighted in 1920 and printed at Boston with pictures from photographs. A note at the front says its chapters first appeared in magazines, among them The Atlantic Monthly and The Youth's Companion. Scoville dedicates the book to his wife, a brave and loyal fellow adventurer.

Contents name the fare: Zero Birds, Snow Stories, A Runaway Day, The Raven's Nest, Hidden Treasure, Bird's-Nesting, Orchid Hunting, The Marsh Dwellers, and The Seven Sleepers. A list of pictures fills in the cast. A gray fox and a screech owl stand on the frontispiece. Young red squirrels, deer mice, a banded rattlesnake, a great blue heron at breakfast, and a coon follow. Some of the animal portraits, a note admits, used tame or mounted models.
40928-johnny-ludlow-second-series:
Ellen Wood, who wrote as Mrs Henry Wood, wrote the Johnny Ludlow stories, of which this file holds the second series. Bentley published the volume in London, in an edition that had reached its thirty-third thousand by 1896. Wood was famous for East Lynne and The Channings. Johnny Ludlow, her narrator, tells tales of his Worcestershire town in the first person, as a boy growing up among its people.

Nineteen stories make up the series. The first, Lost in the Post, turns on money that vanished in the mail, a mystery that puzzled the family to the end. Others treat a life of trouble, a wedding day, earrings lost and found, and a syllabub feast. The final story follows Lee, the letter man. Wood's tales mix village incident with quiet moral weight, and Johnny's observant voice holds them together.
40936-johnny-ludlow-third-series:
Johnny Ludlow, Third Series, by Mrs Henry Wood, came out in London in 1899. Wood was known for East Lynne and The Channings. Nineteen tales fill the book, each told in the voice of Johnny Ludlow. The set mixes village mystery, family trouble, and quiet moral turns.

The first tale, The Mystery of Jessy Page, opens at Church Dykely and Copse Farm. A widower, Mr Page, falls ill, and his girls must run the house. A young farmer comes by day to watch the outdoor work, and love and doubt soon follow. Later tales treat Helen Whitney, the Caromel family, and Dorothy Grape. Readers who like slow village tales with a sting will find much here.
40940-johnny-ludlow-fourth-series:
Mrs Henry Wood gathers tales in Johnny Ludlow, fourth series, printed in London and New York in 1901. Macmillan made the book, in its twentieth thousand. Wood had writ East Lynne and The Channings, as the title page notes. A Longfellow verse on God's singers fronts the set.

Nine tales fill the book. A Mystery leads, then Sandstone Tor and Chandler and Chandler. Verena Fontaine's Rebellion and A Curious Experience stand in the run. Tales of a gipsy, a curate, and a tenant close the set. A Mystery opens at Timberdale, where Darbyshire the doctor takes his rest. He urges Johnny to tell of a strange disappearance that took place there.
40947-the-romance-of-his-life-and-other-:
Mary Cholmondeley, the author of Red Pottage, gathered eight short tales in a volume from John Murray in 1921. She gave the book to Percy Lubbock. The title tale opens with a friend's cool claim about his mate Barrett. The devil, he says, entered into Barrett at a set hour on a June afternoon, as the two stood at a door in a college court.

Barrett calls the story a romance. His friend will not name it, and says it covers him with shame to think of. The other tales bear teasing names. They include The Dark Cottage, The Ghost of a Chance, and The Goldfish. Her Murderer and Votes for Men stand among them, and The End of the Dream closes the set. Cholmondeley writes with a light, dry touch, and her tales turn on small hours that change a life for good.
40951-johnny-ludlow-fifth-series:
Johnny Ludlow, fifth series, by Mrs Henry Wood, was published in London and New York in 1899. Wood was the author of East Lynne and The Channings. Contents list six tales. Featherston Story opens the volume at length, then watching on St Mark Eve.

Sanker Visit, Roger Monk, and the ebony box follow. Our first term at Oxford closes the set. A Longfellow motto heads the text: God sent his singers upon earth, with songs of sadness and of mirth. Featherston Story opens in Buttermead, a wide straggling district in Worcestershire. Featherston is its doctor, and his house stands at the end of the village. Whitney Hall lies close by, as does the school. A few substantial residences, farmers homesteads, and labourers cottages are scattered round. Featherston himself is slim, long legged, grey, and careworn. Readers get Wood village tales, narrated by Johnny Ludlow.
40963-johnny-ludlow-sixth-series:
Mrs Henry Wood's Johnny Ludlow, sixth series, was published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1899. Wood had written East Lynne and The Channings before it. Five long tales fill the volume, and a verse from Longfellow about God's singers stands at the head of the first.

The Mystery at Number Seven opens the book, and its first part is Montpellier-by-Sea. The Squire, at home with the Todhetleys, springs a plan at breakfast: the whole household, children and all, will travel down tomorrow and take Mary Blair by surprise. Johnny Ludlow tells it, as he tells the rest. Caramel Cottage and A Tragedy follow, then In Later Years, and The Silent Chimes, whose bells are put up, play again, and fall silent for ever.
40964-tony-and-the-beetles:
Tony and the Beetles is a science fiction story by Philip Dick, printed in Orbit magazine in 1953. Its picture caption warns that a ten-year-old boy grows up fast when history catches up with the human race. Reddish-yellow sunlight falls through thick quartz windows into a sleep-room. Tony Rossi wakes, tosses off the covers, and dresses for the day outside.

He zips his mesh trousers, seals his boots and gloves, sets the pressure on his pump unit, and takes his helmet. In the dining room his parents have finished breakfast, and their voices drift to him, a disturbed murmur. Behind their voices rides another voice, cracked with static, bringing news that will end his childhood world.
4097-alice-of-old-vincennes:
Maurice Thompson's novel Alice of Old Vincennes sets a frontier romance in the Illinois country during the American Revolution. Father Gibault, a simple missionary of great worldly knowledge and force, brings the wave of revolution to Vincennes.

Colonel George Rogers Clark makes Gibault's acquaintance at Kaskaskia, and great movements reach even the quietest nooks like tides of the sea. Alice, the heroine, stands amid French settlers, soldiers, and shifting flags. Readers who enjoy historical romance of the old Northwest will find a spirited tale of love and loyalty on the frontier.
410-hell-fer-sartain-and-other-stories:
John Fox Jr. sets nine tales in the Kentucky mountains in this volume, told in rich mountain speech. The title story opens at a wild Christmas dance on Hell-fer-Sartain Creek, where two rivals fight over Nance Osborn. Later tales follow courtship on Cutshin, a trick of trade, a preacher on Kingdom Come, and a baby left in strange hands.

Fox writes feuds, loves, and church meetings with humor and a keen ear for dialect. His folk are proud, quick to fight, and slow to forgive. The book keeps a lost mountain world alive in story, where kin ties rule and a word carelessly said can start a war.
41016-the-land-of-song-book-3-for-upper-:
The Land of Song, Book Three, for upper grammar grades, is a school literature anthology selected by Katharine Shute and edited by Larkin Dunton, head master of the Boston Normal School. Silver, Burdett published the volume in 1899.

The compilers' preface concedes that literature's value for healthful recreation, larger views of life, and ideals that mould the spiritual nature is now granted by everyone who has considered education. The real question is the basis of selection. Their answer: the reading must be literature, literature of some scope rather than one small phase, and fitted to children's natural interests. Those interests centre in the marvellous, the natural world, and human life, especially the romantic and heroic.
41070-the-native-races-of-the-pacific-st:
The Native Races of the Pacific States is volume one of the works of Hubert Howe Bancroft, published at San Francisco in 1883. This first volume is subtitled Wild Tribes. Old and uneven spelling in place and people names is kept as printed in this text.

Bancroft vast project set out to gather the history and peoples of the Pacific side of North America. The native races volumes came first in the plan, before the histories of conquest and settlement. Wild Tribes treats peoples still living by hunt, fish, and gather ways when Europeans met them. Readers get a huge nineteenth century survey, built from many sources, of Indigenous peoples from Alaska toward Mexico, sorted by region and tribe.
41119-a-russian-proprietor-and-other-sto:
Nathan Haskell Dole translated A Russian Proprietor and Other Stories from the Russian of Count Lyof N Tolstoi. Thomas Y Crowell and Company issued the volume at New York. The tales, with one exception, come from the second volume of Tolstoi's collected works. They stand for his writing between 1852 and 1859. The title story is a fragment of a projected novel. Its hero quits his university and retires to his estate, as Tolstoi himself had done.

Recollections of a Scorer and Two Hussars come out of the author's gambling days. The Three Deaths, written in 1859, sets the death of a peasant against the death of a lady. A Prisoner in the Caucasus, a tale for children, closes the set. The shadowy Prince Nekhliudof runs through these early tales.
41142-book-plates:
W J Hardy wrote Book-Plates, here in a second edition issued in London in 1897. The first edition came out in 1893 as Volume II of Books about Books. Chapters start with the early use of book-plates in England and their styles. Later parts treat allegory and picture plates in English work.

Hardy then turns to German plates, and to those of France and other countries. American plates get a chapter, as do ladies' plates. One part collects inscriptions against book-stealing and book-spoiling, and in praise of study. Another names the main engravers of English plates. A long list of pictured plates includes work by Hogarth, Bewick, and Durer, with a plate from 1516.
41170-great-ghost-stories:
Great Ghost Stories is an anthology chosen by Joseph Lewis French. Dodd, Mead issued the book in New York in 1918. A foreword by James Hyslop opens the volume. Hyslop served the Society for Psychical Research. The contents list names twelve tales by known hands. Bulwer-Lytton, Hardy, and Gautier are among them.

The first tale, The House and the Brain, opens in London. A man of letters tells of a haunted house found by chance. Other pieces include The Open Door by Mrs Oliphant. Hoffmann's Deserted House and Hardy's Withered Arm follow. A tale of the Barchester stalls comes from James. What Was It, by O'Brien, closes the list. The set joins stage-fright tales to study of the unseen. It shows the ghost tale at its height.
41175-woodland-gleanings-being-an-accoun:
Woodland Gleanings is an account of British forest trees in one book. Verse at its front sings that each tree in the grove has its charm. Sixty four prints dress the text of this fresh, wide print. The book came out in London in the year eighteen fifty three.

The front note sends the book to town folk who flee to green lanes for rest. Home grown and brought in trees share the long list of kinds. Past, marks, plant lore, and farm ways are told tree by tree in turn. Words from the best hands on each kinds grace fill the notes. The aim is to wake fresh love for the woods in each reader.
41189-a-book-o-nine-tales:
Arlo Bates published this book of nine tales with Roberts Brothers at Boston in 1891, setting an interlude between each pair of tales. The tales are A Strange Idyl, The Tuberose, Saucy Betty Mork, John Vantine, Mere Marchette, Barum West's Extravaganza, A Sketch in Umber, April's Lady, and Delia Grimwet.

The interludes carry titles of their own, from An Episode in Mask and An Evening at Whist to The Radiator, Thirteen, and A Cuban Morning. The first tale opens in a sick-room by the sea, where an invalid lies staring at sunlight dancing on the ceiling, reflected from water outside. His young nurse, buried in her book, looks up at chapter's end to find his eyes open and the light of reason back in them, replacing the stare of delirium. He does not know who she is, where he is, or who he is himself.
41201-the-diary-of-a-superfluous-man-and:
The Diary of a Superfluous Man and Other Stories is a volume of Ivan Turgenev's tales, translated from the Russian by Isabel Hapgood and published in New York by Scribner in 1904. It is volume eleven of his novels and stories in English. A drawing shows the diarist crying out with rapture and turning to Liza.

Five stories fill the book. The Diary of a Superfluous Man comes first, then Three Portraits, Three Meetings, Mumu, and The Inn. The diary is dated 1850. Its writer records on March 20 that the doctor has just left him. Dodge as the doctor might, he could not help saying what he thought: the diarist will die soon, very soon. The streams are opening, he writes, and he will float away, probably with the last snows. The superfluous man, the gifted idler who fits nowhere, is Turgenev's great creation, and this is his testament.
41202-the-two-great-republics-rome-and-t:
James Hamilton Lewis wrote The Two Great Republics, Rome and the United States, issued by Rand McNally and Company in Chicago and New York in nineteen thirteen. A plate of ruins of the Roman Forum faces the title page. Lewis wrote from the United States Senate Chamber at Washington in September nineteen thirteen. Thirteen chapters and a preface fill the book.

Chapter one sets the two republics side by side under a line from Holmes, How like, how unlike, as we view them together. Lewis notes that near two thousand years have passed since the curtain fell on the Roman republic. Later chapters treat Roman assemblies, the first great melting pot, and foreign conquest. The Gracchi crisis, Marius and Sulla, Pompey, Cicero and Catiline, and Julius Caesar follow. A post mortem and a comparison close the tale. Readers get a senator parallel of Rome and America.
41236-the-little-washington-s-relatives:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy wrote a tale for young readers, issued in New York in 1918. George Parke and his sister Martha wait at home for city cousins from Philadelphia, Anne and Jack. The two trade fond tales of past visits as they wait.

Roy mixes play with the past. Chapter heads promise a Custis wedding party, Martha Custis's own story, Washington as general, the Boston Tea Party, and fights near Boston and New York. Games on the veranda, a bath tub used as a slide, and a zoo trip sit beside the grave tales. Prizes and new uniforms for the home army close the plan.
41317-the-bunsby-papers-second-series-ir:
John Brougham's Irish Echoes, the second series of The Bunsby Papers, came out in New York in 1856 from Derby and Jackson. Brougham dedicates the tales to Samuel Lover, and his preface praises Ireland's store of traditions and legendary tales as richer and more whimsical than any other country's.

The contents mix wonder tales and New York Irish life. Dan Duff's wish, the Blarney stone, a gospel charm, a test of blood, a fortune-teller, and a fairy circle appear alongside O'Bryan's luck, subtitled a tale of New York. The preface also traces an Irish flood story back through the historian Leland to Noah and the ark.
41349-historic-towns-of-the-western-stat:
Lyman P Powell edits a set of town histories for the western states, issued at New York in 1901. The volume belongs to an American Historic Towns series and is rich with pictures. Reuben G Thwaites adds an introduction and the chapter on Madison.

Each town gets its own writer, from Marietta and Cleveland in Ohio to Detroit, Mackinac, and Vincennes. Chicago is treated by Lyman J Gage, St Louis by William Marion Reedy, and San Francisco by Edwin Markham. Denver, Santa Fe, Salt Lake City, Spokane, Portland, Monterey, and Los Angeles close the sweep. Readers get the founding tales, growth, and landmarks of the West's chief towns as local writers told them at the century's turn.
41396-the-boys-of-1812-and-other-naval-h:
The Boys of 1812 and Other Naval Heroes, by James Russell Soley, author of The Blockade and the Cruisers, was copyrighted in 1887 and published in Boston by Estes and Lauriat. A front plate shows a cutlass breaking at the hilt. Nineteen chapters run from the beginnings of the navy through Biddle and the Randolph. Paul Jones's cruises, Barry and Barney, and the war with France follow, to Tripoli and impressment.

The War of 1812 fills the second half: the Constitution and the Guerriere, the first sloop action, Decatur and Bainbridge, and Captain James Lawrence. Perry on Lake Erie and Macdonough on Lake Champlain follow, then Stewart and Old Ironsides. Wars with Algiers and Mexico close the survey. Soley, a naval officer and historian, wrote the young republic's sea heroes for boys.
41408-affinities-and-other-stories:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote Affinities and Other Stories, printed in New York, copyright 1920. Contents name five pieces. Affinities stands first, then the family friend. Clara's little escapade, the borrowed house, and sauce for the gander fill the rest. The title tale opens the book.

Somebody ought to know the truth about the Devil's Island affair, the teller begins, and she is going to tell it. The truth is much of the time better or worse than the tales that get about. In this case, she owns, it is somewhat better, though she is not proud of it. It started with talk about wedded women having men friends. She had held it a clear duty, giving a snap to things. Six of them sat on the country club terrace, all of one mind, on a dull Sunday.
41415-studies-in-wives:
Studies in Wives, by Belloc Lowndes, bears a copyright of 1910 and was issued in New York. The book holds six long tales, each built around a wife and her marriage. The first is Althea's Opportunity, and it opens in an old house in Westminster.

Althea Scrope stands at a window in her outdoor dress, her mind back in Newcastle among girlhood friends. She has been buying Christmas gifts, and a footman's cough brings her back to the room. Her husband Perceval's old servant Dockett still treats her as an interloper in the house. The other tales bear names like Jarvice's Wife, A Very Modern Instance, and According to Meredith. The last is called The Decree Made Absolute, a hint of where its marriage ends.
41437-warriors-of-old-japan-and-other-st:
Yei Theodora Ozaki retold stories of old Japan in a volume published at Boston and New York in 1909, drawn by Shusui Okakura and other Japanese artists. Ozaki had written the Japanese Fairy Book. An introductory note says readers of that book will find old friends with new faces here. Storytelling, the note observes, long ago rose to a profession in Japan.

Tales open with Hachiro Tametomo the archer and Gen Sanmi Yorimasa the knight. The stories of Yoshitsune and of Benkei follow. The goblin of Oyeyama and Kidomaru the robber add wonders. A frontispiece shows a hero rushing upon a monster. The volume mixes legendary history, fairy tale, and myth.
41451-the-spell-of-the-hawaiian-islands-:
Isabel Anderson wrote the Spell of the Hawaiian Islands and the Philippines. The Page company at Boston issued it in its Spell series. Each spell volume sold boxed, with gilt top, at a set price. The book treats our Pacific possessions, its subtitle states. Their history and politics stand beside their natural charm there.

Strange and interesting customs of their peoples fill its promise too. Manila as we found it opens the Philippine half of the contents. The Philippines of the past and the insurrection follow in the list. Following the flag and healing a wounded land come later. A plate shows Mount Mayon in its fine volcanic cone. Anderson had written the Spell of Japan and of Belgium before. The series gave each land a volume in the same dress. Anderson gives two island worlds under one flag their spell.
41475-old-times-in-dixie-land-a-southern:
Caroline Merrick published her memories of the old South with the Grafton Press in New York in 1901. She calls herself a Southern matron, and the contents begin at Cottage Hall with home life in the old times. Rumors of civil war enter by chapter four, and her daughter Laura's diary follows.

War memories fill the middle chapters, with washing, gardens and women coming to the rescue. Laura's death in the epidemic of 1878 brings deep sorrow to the record. Later chapters treat noted women, Frances Willard and Julia Ward Howe among them, in the voice of a white Southern woman of her class and era.
41530-in-search-of-el-dorado-a-wanderer-:
In Search of El Dorado is a travel book by Alexander Macdonald, printed in London by Fisher Unwin. The first edition is of 1905 and this second impression of 1906. Admiral Moresby supplies an introduction. Macdonald dedicates the book to his mother. A portrait shows the author, signed yours very sincerely.

The contents run by camp-fire and goldfield. Camp-fire reminiscences and the sacred nugget stand in the middle parts. Into the Never Never Land and a chapter headed simply El Dorado follow. Where the pelican builds its nest closes the golden section. Promiscuous wanderings in the Australian back country fill the third part. Macdonald was a wandering Scot who chased gold and copy across the empire's edges. His book is the professional tramp's memoir, half prospecting diary and half fireside yarn.
41546-curiosities-of-olden-times:
Curiosities of Olden Times, by S. Baring-Gould, collects essays on odd customs and lore. John Grant of Edinburgh issued this revised and enlarged edition in 1896. First essay asks what mourning dress truly means in its roots. A black sleeve band is the shrunken last form of an old rite.

Baring-Gould argues mourning began with soot and tallow on bare skin. Grief garb kept its shape long after its first sense was lost. Later essays treat ciphers, strange wills, and queer culprits in courts. Ghosts in court, strange pains and penalties, and crazy saints follow in turn. The philosopher stone and Chiapa chocolate close the curious set.
41557-burial-mounds-of-the-northern-sect:
Cyrus Thomas wrote this study of the burial mounds of the northern sections of the United States for the Bureau of Ethnology. It formed part of the bureau's fifth annual report, for 1883 and 1884, printed at Washington in 1887. Plates and figures show groups of earthworks, sections cut through mounds, and pots taken from them.

Thomas works through the mounds district by district. He treats Wisconsin first, then the Illinois or Upper Mississippi country, then Ohio, then the Appalachian district. A long section asks whether the Cherokees were probably mound-builders. Closing remarks and a short extra note end the paper, which runs to more than a hundred pages.
41579-kimiko-and-other-japanese-sketches:
Lafcadio Hearn wrote this book of sketches, Kimiko and Other Japanese Sketches, copyrighted in 1896 and reprinted at Boston and New York in 1923. The first sketch gives the book its name. A short poem by Kimiko heads it, with a note rendering its sense. To wish to be forgotten by the beloved is a harder task of the soul than trying not to forget.

The name, the sketch begins, is on a paper-lantern at the entrance of a house in the Street of the Geisha. Seen at night the street is one of the queerest in the world, narrow as a gangway. Dark shining woodwork and tiny sliding doors with paper panes, lit from within, make it look like a row of passenger cabins. Lanterns of many shapes hang at every door, their Japanese signs written fair, and the street is silent, for its people live by night.
41583-burne-jones:
Burne Jones, by Lys Baldry, is a life and work study of the painter Edward Burne Jones. It belongs to a Masterpieces in Colour series, edited by Leman Hare. Eight colour plates reproduce the artist's paintings for the reader. The frontispiece is The Depths of the Sea, his one Academy picture.

That painting shows a mermaid dragging a drowning man to her cave below. Burne Jones made it for the Royal Academy show of eighteen eighty six. It was his sole gift to that body's exhibitions in his whole career. Other plates show Sidonia von Bork and Sponsa di Libano in colour. Baldry wrote the Leighton and Millais volumes of the same series as well. The text traces the painter's dreamy, medieval world of knights and ladies.
41589-lyre-and-lancet-a-story-in-scenes:
Anstey wrote Lyre and Lancet: A Story in Scenes, printed at London in eighteen ninety-five and first run in Punch. The cast pairs Galfrid Undershell, a minor poet, with James Spurrell, a horse doctor. A countess, her daughter, a bishop, and a house full of lords and ladies fill out the list. The scene is Wyvern Court, seat of Sir Rupert Culverin.

The tale opens on a wet February morning as guests fill the house. Lady Culverin asks who should take in Rohesia at dinner, and small talk turns to plans. Scene heads promise cross aims, borrowed plumes, and a trap. The poet's lyre and the vet's lancet stand for art and plain work, set side by side in a proud house.
41590-negro-tales:
Negro Tales is a book of stories by Joseph Cotter, published in New York in 1912. The Cosmopolitan Press issued the volume. A frontispiece portrait shows the author. An opening sketch tells his life in brief. Cotter was born in Nelson County, Kentucky, in 1861. He spent most of his life in Louisville. He was wholly self-taught in English letters.

The sketch tells how he rose from hard labour to teaching. He worked in a brick yard, a distillery, and as a teamster. Night school gave him his start at twenty-two. Within months he was teaching others himself. He became principal of a Louisville ward school. The tales mix sketches, fables, and dialect pieces. Caleb, Rodney, and Tesney head the contents list. Animal tales of rabbit and lion follow. The book is an early work of Black authorship in Kentucky.
41591-a-virginia-cousin-bar-harbor-tales:
A Virginia Cousin and Bar Harbor Tales, by Mrs Burton Harrison, was published in 1895. Lamson and Wolffe issued the book at Boston and New York. The author's note is dated at New York in November 1895. She calls the title story a tribute from an exiled child of the South. It was printed here for the first time. Two other tales join it. One had stood in an earlier volume of two tales. Another had run in The Cosmopolitan Magazine.

The title tale opens on Theodore Vance Townsend in New York. Young, rich, and well born, he wakes at odds with the world. His book of verse won him the nickname Laureate of the 400. The press mocks all he does as not in earnest. Harrison writes society tales with a Southern heart.
41592-the-laughing-mill-and-other-storie:
Julian Hawthorne gathered tales in a book printed at London in 1879. His preface defends the strange in fiction. Human interest grips most, he grants, but the marvellous has its own just pull. It feeds a hunger of the mind that fact cannot fill.

He names The Tempest, Faust and Consuelo as proof of the claim. Their makers soar past the level of plain chance and catch a higher light. A tale teller who holds all of man must hold the impossible too, Hawthorne holds. The risk of seeming crude stirs the writer to his best craft. The title tale and its fellows chase that unfathomed sky round us all.
41605-abigail-adams-and-her-times:
Laura Richards wrote Abigail Adams and Her Times, a biography printed at New York in 1917, illustrated from a Stuart portrait. Richards also wrote lives of Elizabeth Fry, Florence Nightingale, and Julia Ward Howe. She gave the book to the memory of Franklin Sanborn, friend to three generations of her family.

Chapters move from girlhood and marriage through the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, Lexington, and the blockade of Boston. Happy Braintree, independence at last, and Adams abroad fill the war years of Abigail's letters and labours. Abigail Adams, wife and mother of presidents, stands out as a sharp mind of the Revolution. Young and general readers get a warm, clear life.
41620-french-book-plates:
Walter Hamilton wrote French Book-Plates, issued in London in 1896 in the Ex-Libris Series under editor Gleeson White. Hamilton chaired the council of the Ex-Libris Society and held office in the French society of plate collectors as well. The first edition of the handbook came out in 1892 and was used up almost at once. This issue is limited to 750 copies of the ordinary edition, with 38 more on tall Japanese vellum.

A preface tells how fast the taste for collecting book-plates has spread. What was the hobby of a few has become the serious pursuit of the many, Hamilton writes. Societies for the study of plates have been founded in Britain, Germany, France, and the United States. Each society puts out a drawn journal of plates of all ages and countries. The taste has spread as far as Sweden, Italy, and South America.
41682-the-youth-of-parnassus-and-other-s:
The Youth of Parnassus and Other Stories gathers nine tales by Logan Pearsall Smith. Macmillan published the book at London and New York in 1895. The title story fills the first third of the volume. Smith dedicates the work to Philip Morrell.

The hero comes straight to Oxford from Parnassus City, a town in Indiana. A young don named Foley first sees him crossing a wet quad under a vast umbrella. He takes the pale stranger for a mission agent come to collect money. The thin young man in a long black coat proves shy, with an odd, striking voice. Later tales treat a broken trip, a sub-warden, and an optimist. Smith's prose stays cool and exact, with a feel for odd minds set down in strange rooms.
41693-lays-and-legends-second-series:
Lays and Legends, second series, is a book of poems by Nesbit. Longmans Green of London and New York issued it in eighteen ninety two. Edith Nesbit wrote as Mrs Hubert Bland on the title page here. She gives the book to Alice Hoatson, Helen Macklin, and Charlotte Wilson.

A portrait of the poet fronts the volume of lays and legends. The Bridal Ballad opens the poems with flagons of red and white wine. A bride decks her bower with roses and jewels for her wedding night. Tapers at the bed foot and head make it seem a death bed. Thanks go to editors who first printed verses gathered in this set.
41695-the-appendages-anatomy-and-relatio:
The Appendages, Anatomy, and Relationships of Trilobites is Percy Raymond's memoir in volume seven of the Memoirs of the Connecticut Academy, printed in December 1920. Raymond taught palaeontology at Harvard and kept its invertebrate collections. Charles Schuchert wrote the foreword. The work is dedicated to Charles Emerson Beecher, the great trilobite student.

Schuchert notes that trilobites have been described since 1698 and now run to several thousand species. Most fossils keep only the hard upper shell. The soft under side stayed hidden until a thin layer in the Utica black shales near Rome, New York, was found in 1892. That layer, under ten millimetres thick, kept the limbs, and this memoir builds on it.
41741-bound-to-succeed-or-mail-order-fra:
Allen Chapman wrote Bound to Succeed, or Mail Order Frank's Chances, copyrighted in 1907. Frank Newton tells his mother he must do something, and quickly. The lawyer's hopes of recovering their lost fortune, Frank says, are a bubble.

Chapters follow his rise: a five-dollar job, a business call, and a break for liberty. He rescues a balloonist and earns his nickname, Mail Order Frank. His own mail order house follows, with a nest egg, a mean enemy, and a suspicious visitor. A post-office inspector, a rival concern, and a mysterious Stet fill the later chapters. Good news and a heart of gold close the story.
41808-the-san-francisco-fairy-a-tale-of-:
The San Francisco Fairy, a tale of early times, is a comic poem issued in San Francisco by C P Kimball, with D E Appleton and Company as general agents. No author or date stands on its title pages.

Long years before Spaniards lived on California soil, the poem begins, an Indian of the Digger tribe rests from his toil by a vast inland lake. His youngest daughter, Li-Lamboni, loves a chieftain's only son but lacks the wampum to make him hers. Paddling out sad in her log canoe, she meets a fish of monstrous size, balanced on his tail, who asks what she is about. She tells him all her sorrows. The fish wags his fin, shakes his pointed nose, and invites his darling maiden to step into his mouth, where a splendid seat with wampum waits.
41816-ann-arbor-tales:
Ann Arbor Tales, a book of short stories by Karl Edwin Harriman, was published at Philadelphia in 1902. Jacobs and Company issued the volume, dedicated to the parents of the author. Nine tales fill the contents, led by The Making of a Man. The Kidnapping, The Champions, and The Case of Catherwood follow in that list.

The Door, a nocturne, and A Modern Mercury show the range of the set. The Day of the Game and The Old Professor close the volume with campus colour. The first tale opens in a little round room lit by low candles with tinted shades. Florence, its golden haired hostess, knows how that soft light sets her hair dancing. College town life in Michigan gives the tales their shared ground and cast.
41835-puvis-de-chavannes:
Puvis de Chavannes stands in the Masterpieces in Colour series. Stokes issued this New York printing under a 1912 copyright. Eight reproductions in colour carry the book. The artist's dates, 1824 to 1898, stand under his name. Plate one shows Saint Genevieve keeping watch over sleeping Paris. The mural hangs in the Pantheon at Paris. A note calls it his last work; his own wife posed for the saint. Contents give an introduction, then the first years, the glorious years, and the last years. A closing chapter treats him as a landscape painter.

Other plates show the Poor Fisherman, the Sacred Wood, and War, from museums at Paris and Amiens. The text opens with high praise: his glory shines uncontested. He stands, it says, as heir and equal to the fresco painters of the Renaissance.
41900-how-to-master-the-english-bible-an:
How to Master the English Bible, an experience, a method, a result, and an illustration, by James Gray, minister in the Reformed Episcopal Church, was published at Edinburgh and London in 1907. Gray wrote Synthetic Bible Studies and Primers of the Faith. Five chapters tell the story of his case, explain his method, show the plan at work, and trace its results in the pulpit, with outlines of talks.

Publishers on both sides of the Atlantic praise Gray as the man who knows what is in the Book. His synthetic plan reads whole books of Scripture at a sitting, then returns again and again until the text is mastered. Big interdenominational classes grew from the method, and Gray claims it put life into dead prayer meetings and remade Sunday school teaching.
41906-princess-sarah-and-other-stories:
John Strange Winter's Princess Sarah and Other Stories was published by Ward, Lock of London in 1897. Winter was the author of Bootles' Baby and Mignon's Secret. The title story runs seventeen chapters: Sarah orphaned, a new-found aunt, her future arranged, a taste of the future, the amiable Flossie, a brilliant marriage, a family catastrophe, and Sarah's opportunity.

Six shorter pieces follow it: Miss Mignon, Boy's Love, Yum-Yum: A Pug, Our Ada Elizabeth, Halt!, The Little Lady with the Voice, and Jewels to Wear. The title story opens in a poor little street of a crowded city, on a small house in a row of houses exactly like it. The bow window's frames are warped, the paint blistered and cracked, and the doorstep looks cleaned a week ago with whiting instead of pipe-clay. The cloth has daubed the door's lower part as well.
41921-the-maker-of-rainbows-and-other-fa:
The Maker of Rainbows and Other Fairy-Tales and Fables is a story collection by Richard Le Gallienne, illustrated by Elizabeth Shippen Green. Harper and Brothers published it in New York and London in October 1912. Le Gallienne dedicates the book, in fairy-tale fashion, to his publishers themselves.

Fifteen tales include The Old Coat of Dreams, The Maker of Rainbows, and The Man with Something in His Eye. Others are Mother-of-Pearl, The Mer-Mother, The Sleepless Lord, and The Man with No Money. The Rags of Queen Cophetua and The Wife from Fairy-Land follow, with The Buyer of Sorrows. Illustrations show a woman lifting the lid of a golden coffer to view a tattered robe. The prologue opens in London society, wondering whence a certain publisher's wealth had come.
41983-the-book-of-curiosities:
The Rev I Platts filled a book with ten thousand wonders of nature and art. Leary and Getz issued The Book of Curiosities at Philadelphia in 1854, the first American form. Entries run from the Abderites to customs, trials, and strange places of all ages. A plate shows the Grotto del Cani, engraved for the book.

Bees, ants, alligators, and the aurora each draw their curious notes. Joan of Arc, Noah's Ark, and the Alhambra stand among the great sights. Barometer rules help readers guess the weather from the glass. Browsers gain a fat, old store of facts meant to amaze and teach.
42018-natural-stability-and-the-parachut:
LeMaitre, honorary secretary of the Aeroplane Building and Flying Society, wrote Natural Stability and the Parachute Principle in Aeroplanes for Spon of London in 1911. The book carries 34 illustrations. Six chapters attack one problem: how to make a flying machine keep its balance on its own.

The first chapter states the case plainly. A practical machine must be one we can trust like a yacht or a motor car, keeping its balance by natural forces without effort from the pilot. A bicycle's fall is a small matter, he notes; an aeroplane's tilt mostly means sudden death. Present machines are the most unstable things alive: the least gust starts a sway that only instant correction can stop. Later chapters weigh speed, a low centre of gravity, and short span. Students of early flight get the safety argument of 1911 in full.
42035-dooryard-stories:
Dooryard Stories, by Clara Dillingham Pierson, was printed by E P Dutton at New York, with a copyright of 1903 and art by F C Gordon. Pierson gives the book to her father, who first taught her to love her dooryard friends. The first tale, Silvertip, opens on a cold, wet night. A tiny kitten, soaked to the skin, pads a board walk and cries for a home. A lady fights the wind past him; he will not be put off.

He rubs at her feet block by block till she must stop or tread on him. More tales fill the yard: a fight for the bird-house, brisk flickers, and the rude young robins. A wasp, a cuckoo, and a catbird each have their day. Young readers get the small folk of the lawn drawn true and kind.
42042-the-spell-of-the-rockies:
Enos Mills wrote The Spell of the Rockies, for Houghton Mifflin in 1911. The Boston and New York book came out in November of that year. Photographs by Mills himself fill its pages as pictures. The front plate is called The Home of the Whirlwind. Contents open with racing an avalanche on the high slopes.

Mills went into the San Juan Mountains in the first week of March. His errand was to learn the laws that govern snow slides, he says. Little conservationists, beavers at harvest time, and mountain-top weather follow. A beaver canal in his plates runs three hundred and thirty-four feet long. Forest fire, insects, a tree-surgeon woodpecker, and a boy grizzly take chapters. Alone with a landslide, a mountain blizzard, and the Estes Park region close the book. Mills writes as guide, watcher, and friend of the high country.
42099-frank-before-vicksburg-the-gun-boa:
Frank before Vicksburg is a boys' war novel by Castlemon. Carroll issued it at Cincinnati in 1866. It belongs to the Gun-Boat Series. Four mate volumes are listed on the series page. Frank the Young Naturalist heads that list. Frank on the Lower Mississippi closes it. The set sold at a dollar and a quarter a volume.

The hero, Frank Nelson, comes home in chapter one. He has passed through tragic adventures in the service. Harry goes on a scout in the next chapter. A fight in the woods and capture by the Johnnies follow. The trenches and the running of the batteries come later. A smuggler's cave ends the tale. Castlemon wrote as the Gun-Boat Boy himself. His books gave Northern boys the river war at first hand. They were among the first Civil War tales for youth.
42105-faces-in-the-fire-and-other-fancie:
F W Boreham wrote these essays, printed by the Abingdon Press of New York and Cincinnati. Boreham had written The Other Side of the Hill, Mushrooms on the Moor, and The Luggage of Life. Three parts hold the set. The first opens with a baby among the bombshells, then strawberries and cream, linoleum, and the editor. Nothing gets a chapter of its own.

The second part holds the title piece, Faces in the Fire, with the postman, an old maid's diary, and the menace of the sunlit hill. The third turns to a box of tin soldiers, the felling of the tree, and Christmas bells. His introduction recalls his first chill sight of New Zealand and landing, twelve thousand miles from home, where no soul knew him.
42124-american-forest-trees:
Henry Gibson's American Forest Trees was issued by the Hardwood Record at Chicago in 1913, edited by Hu Maxwell. The book treats the commercial trees species by species, starting with white pine. A footnote lists the twelve soft pines, from white and sugar pine to bristlecone. Gibson notes that white pine, the best known wood of the United States, carries few names. It is Weymouth pine in books and soft pine in Pennsylvania. Cork pine and pumpkin pine are trade names for old first-class trunks.

Northern spruce pine, in the South, is a name he thinks misplaced, since a dozen species get called spruce pine somewhere. Each account weighs the tree's names, range, wood, and uses for the lumber trade. Gibson's portrait fronts the volume. The Hardwood Record published for the trade, and the text keeps a lumberman's vocabulary of grades and grain.
42139-the-english-lakes:
The English Lakes, described by Bradley and pictured by Haslehust, was published by Blackie at London in 1910 in the Beautiful England series. Companion volumes treat Oxford, Canterbury, Shakespeare-land, the Thames, and Windsor Castle.

Its plates run from Windermere seen from Orrest Head, the frontispiece, through Coniston, Rydalmere, Grasmere, Thirlmere under Helvellyn, Ullswater, and Derwentwater. The text opens on Windermere, whose luxuriance is its dominant note, set against the noble array of mountains trailing from Kirkstone to Scafell. Orrest Head, a few hundred feet above the village, is the pilgrim's first viewpoint, since the railway made Bowness the first glimpse of the district for generations of visitors.
42156-the-nursery-july-1881-vol-xxx-a-mo:
The July 1881 number opens the thirtieth volume of The Nursery, a Boston monthly for youngest readers. The Nursery Publishing Company issued it from Bromfield Street.
