Everything in it is short, large, and kind. The first story, Hide and Seek, has a mother calling for Charley in the woods. She asks a bird, a squirrel, and a butterfly where he is, before he pops laughing from the bushes behind a tree.

The contents mix prose and verse for the very small. Outwitted, Zip Coon, and The Fuss in the Poultry-Yard stand beside pieces on swan-upping and winter on Lake Constance. The verses include a Hammock Song, Rosie and the Pigs, and Baby's Ride. One song, Under Green Leaves, is printed with its music. The magazine was built for reading aloud at the nursery table.
42171-gypsy-verses:
Gypsy Verses is a book of poems by Helen Hay Whitney, printed in New York by Duffield and Company in 1907. Whitney had also written Some Verses and The Bed Time Book. She gives this book to a friend marked only by initials.

The list runs to more than eighty short poems, from Atarah, Age, and Love and Dawn to Satan, Prince of Darkness. Later poems name ghosts, slave women, lotus eaters, and lost Aphrodite. Titles such as Down in Maldonado Town, Ballad of the Slave, and The Gypsy Blood keep the free, roving air of the title. Whitney writes in brief, song like forms on love, loss, and wild hearts. Verse readers get a full sheaf of turn of the age lyrics.
4221-shearing-in-the-riverina-new-south-:
Rolf Boldrewood's account of shearing in the Riverina follows a shed day from first bell to last count. At six o'clock the bell ends work, and each man's sheep are counted in his presence and noted with scrupulous care.

The record is written out in full and hung for public inspection in the shed next day, a ceremony of fairness in a hard trade. Master, men, manager, and laborers then part to separate lodgings, avoiding each other's company after the day. Readers who like Australian bush life will find a vivid, exact picture of shearing.
42226-mooswa-others-of-the-boundaries:
Fraser tells beast tales in Mooswa and Others of the Boundaries, printed in New York in 1900. Scribner made the book, with copyright the same year. Heming draws the plates. A frontispiece shows Black Fox calling the roll of the assembled animals: here ye have all assembled; for form's sake I will call your names.

A list of the dwellers of the boundaries gives their names in the Cree Indian language. Mooswa, the moose, is protector of the Boy. Muskwa is the bear. Black Fox is king of the boundaries, and the Red Widow is his mother. Cross Stripes is his baby brother. The contents open with Mooswa bringing help to the Boy. Northwoods animals speak and scheme in these tales, in a Canadian forest world shared with trappers and one human boy.
42265-the-comet-and-other-verses:
The Comet and Other Verses, by Irving Sidney Dix, was copyrighted in 1910 at fifteen cents. Munn Review press at Carbondale, Pennsylvania, printed the small book of poems. A dedication keeps the memory of a school mate, William Morgan, drowned in the Delaware. A note to the reader opens the verses with a word on their past.

Some of these verses had run before in periodicals in a slightly different form, he states. Binghamton, Scranton, Philadelphia, and New York City papers had carried them in their day. Most of the poems see print here for the first time in book form, he adds. A comet year showpiece heads a sheaf of small town American verse. Local poets of 1910 often printed their work in such slim home town volumes.
42274-with-the-indians-in-the-rockies:
With the Indians in the Rockies is a tale of the old West by James Willard Schultz, printed in 1912. George Varian drew its illustrations. Schultz dedicated the book to his wife, Celia Hawkins Schultz, whose good comradeship, he says, was his greatest help in writing the tale.

A plate shows shale sliding under the narrator's feet. The story opens in a quiet family of three, whose still life is broken every two or three years by a visit from a figure out of the wild days. Schultz had lived among the Blackfeet of Montana and married into the tribe. He wrote their world from inside, with a hunter's eye for game, weather, and danger. The book is one of his many tales that kept the northern Rockies alive for young readers.
42285-the-story-of-scraggles:
George Wharton James wrote The Story of Scraggles, printed at Boston in 1906, illustrated from drawings by Sears Gallagher and from photographs. James wrote on the Grand Canyon, California missions, and the Colorado desert. An introduction retells a Native tradition that animals and man once shared a common speech in old days.

Pride and contempt widened the breach between man and beast, while love looked on with tearful eyes, the preface says. Prophets such as Thoreau, Burroughs, Muir, and Seton now teach kinship with birds and beasts again for modern readers. James tells Scraggles's story from the bird's own viewpoint as a truthful record. Nature lovers young and old were his audience.
42306-the-calendar-and-other-verses:
The Calendar and Other Verses, by Irving Sidney Dix, was copyright in 1913. A first poem gives the book to Robert Meaker, a boy friend lost ten summers back. Dix wrote that piece in 1912, in grief and love. It asks if his words can reach the boy in paradise.

The Calendar, an idyll of the hills, walks month by month through the year. January brings deep snow, icy winds, and a warm fire at home. February brings the groundhog, the blue jay, and first hints of spring. Short verses follow on Niagara, frost fairies, and river men. More treat a miner, love of country, and the sinking of the Titanic. Two treat war and peace, and one speaks to Andrew Carnegie. Verse fans get plain, heartfelt songs of place and loss.
42308-overland-tales:
Josephine Clifford bound her tales and road sketches of the far west in one book. The book came out in San Francisco in 1877. She gave it to her mother, her kind, most constant reader. Her front words gather tales of three lands in the great west. California, Arizona, and New Mexico fill that wide road scope.

Small share of the tales is made up, she grants in front. The sketches ring true to life as she saw it then, she holds. Some tales first ran in the Overland Monthly of her day. Some are new in this book and had not run ere then. She begs a close, kind read from each guest of her pages. West fans get a woman's road eye.
4233-jeanne-of-the-marshes:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this romance around a princess who has withdrawn to a quiet life, only to be disturbed by the arrival of Major Forrest on urgent business. From that opening interview the story widens into a tale of rank, secrecy, and danger, set partly in the flat marsh country that gives the book its title.

Oppenheim, known for thrillers of diplomacy and high society, keeps the focus on the heroine's choices as old ties and new threats close in on her. Readers looking for an early twentieth-century popular romance, with a proud heroine and a plot driven by visits, letters, and revelations, will find it here.
42330-some-verses:
Helen Hay offers a slim book of verse issued by Duckworth and Company at London in 1898. She dedicates it to her father. Sonnets fill the first half, longer poems the second.

The sonnet titles run from The Days and The Everlasting Snows to Throne and Altar. East and West, The Battle, and Water and Wine follow. A Woman's Pride, Age, and In the Mist keep the inward tone. The poems section opens with Does the Pearl Know? Dear Dead Women, The Grave of Hope, and Trees of the Wilderness come next. The Flowers of Proserpine closes the book. One sonnet asks if the undaunted snows on the mountain crest shall still smile on a field where no blossom grows. Hay writes in the high, earnest mode of the 1890s.
42359-tales-and-legends-of-the-english-l:
Wilson Armistead, author of The Flora of Liverpool, gathered Tales and Legends of the English Lakes, issued at London by Simpkin, Marshall and Company and at Glasgow by Thomas Morison in 1891. Armistead had died before the book came out. His preface holds that no part of the world has so many charms for the thoughtful mind as the English Lake District. Its glens, silver lakes, white cottages, and wild mountains give, he says, the widest field for a playful fancy.

The ground from Lancaster and Morecambe Bay to the borders of Scotland holds, in his words, the richest valleys, the wildest mountains, the greenest meadows, and the smoothest rivers the salmon loves. The tales that follow draw on that ground: its falls, streams, mines, families, and stories. The book is a lover's guide to the lore of the lakes.
42374-to-kiel-in-the-hercules:
To Kiel in the Hercules is a war book by Lewis Freeman, a lieutenant in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve. It was printed at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1919. The book is illustrated with photographs by the author. A front picture shows the three admirals of the commission.

Eleven chapters tell the voyage into defeated Germany after the armistice. The Hercules goes into German waters and gets down to work. Merchant shipping and the bombing of Tondern follow. Then the ship passes through the canal to the Baltic, to Warnemünde and Rügen. One chapter gives the battle of Jutland as a German saw it. The last chapter is Back to Base. The book records the strange errand of a battleship sent not to fight but to take over a beaten fleet's ports.
4238-on-the-economy-of-machinery-and-man:
Charles Babbage's On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures, a founding text of industrial economics, asks how work, machines, and skill combine to make goods cheaply. A chapter on forces too great for human power notes the skill and apparatus needed for many men to exert full force at one point.

With hundreds or thousands at work, difficulties multiply, and no overseer can easily tell whether each man exerts his whole strength. Babbage turns that puzzle into principles of division of labor and machine design. Readers who like economics with a mechanical mind will find a classic still sharp today.
42388-the-solomon-islands-and-their-nati:
The Solomon Islands and Their Natives is a survey by Guppy, a former surgeon in the Royal Navy. Swan Sonnenschein published it in London in 1887. Guppy had been chosen for his naval posting with an eye to his tastes. The hydrographer of the day wanted a man with a bent for natural history in the post.

The book records what that service in the Pacific put before his eyes. Its title joins the islands themselves with the peoples who lived on them. Guppy's double training, in medicine and in field science, shapes the whole account. He writes as an observer stationed among the islanders, not a passing traveller. The result is a Victorian record of island life, custom, and nature. Such surveys became source books for later students of the Pacific world.
42409-sea-stories:
Sea Stories is an anthology for young readers, edited by Cyrus Townsend Brady for the Young Folks' Library. Hall and Locke copyrighted it at Boston in 1902. Thomas Bailey Aldrich edited the twenty volume series as a whole. Brady opens the book himself with Yarns of the Forecastle, arguing that the boy who never loved ships and salt water is fit only for the shore.

The selections range widely. The mutiny of the Bounty comes from a popular miscellany, and Bullen tells of a first whale. Cooper contributes the escape of the frigate Alliance and a piece among ice floes. Dana, Defoe, Dickens, Hugo, Kingsley, Marryat, and Melville all appear, with Hugo's struggle with a devil fish and Melville's chase among them. Stevenson closes the list with the cruise of the coracle, and eighty six black and white illustrations fill the text.
42501-new-york-sketches:
Jesse Lynch Williams wrote New York Sketches, a book put out in New York in 1902. Williams gave the book to Meade Creighton Williams. Plates from life and art fill the work. A first plate shows the Harlem River, with the heights of the town from Fort George.

Four prose parts make up the book, each a walk through the great town. The shore of the port leads, with ships that pass the Battery wall. A walk up town and the cross streets give the heart of the town. A last part finds a rural side to the vast town of stone. Plates show Grant Tomb, the old Dutch town, and the white towers of the new age. One plate shows the end of the day, with a look back at the isle from a boat. Williams writes with a fond eye for a town in fast change.
4253-dramatic-romances:
Robert Browning's Dramatic Romances collects some of his finest short poems, edited with introduction and notes by Charlotte Porter and Helen A. Clarke from the 1898 Crowell edition. The contents include The Patriot, My Last Duchess, Count Gismond, The Boy and the Angel, The Glove, The Last Ride Together, and The Pied Piper of Hamelin.

Other poems range from Porphyria's Lover and Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came to A Grammarian's Funeral and The Heretic's Tragedy. Each poem gives its speaker a voice and a moment of crisis, and the collection is a good entry point for readers new to Browning's dramatic monologues.
42542-lost-diaries:
Maurice Baring wrote Lost Diaries, printed in London in 1913. The pieces had first come out in three papers, the Eye Witness, the New Witness, and the Morning Post. Contents give twenty made-up journals. From the diary of Smith Minor opens the set. The diaries of Iseult of Brittany and King Cophetua follow.

Froissart as war writer, George Washington, and Marcus Aurelius keep diaries here. So do the husband of Mrs James Lee, Sherlock Holmes, and the Emperor Titus. Harriet Shelley, Tiberius, and Oedipus Rex stand in the list. William the Conqueror, Mary Milton, and Mark Antony follow. Ivan the Terrible, the private log of Columbus, and the Man in the Iron Mask fill the later heads. Hamlet at Oxford closes the set. The first piece is a schoolboy's diary of 1884, full of games, an eclipse of the moon, and chestnuts eaten in the garden.
42555-by-the-barrow-river-and-other-stor:
Edmund Leamy published By the Barrow River and Other Stories at Dublin in 1907, with a foreword by Katharine Tynan. Leamy had written Irish Fairy Tales. A note adds that the last story, The Ruse of Madame Martin, was the final tale he ever wrote, composed in France during his last illness.

The volume mixes legend, ghost lore, and love tales. The title tale opens in the guard-room of the fortress of Dun Righ, where Cathal, a guard of the usurper king, is famed for sight and hearing beyond other men's. His gift came, they say, from a wise woman of the Sidhe who touched his eyes and ears at birth. Other titles promise rapparees, spectres of Barcelona, a black dog, a message from the dead, and a pretty Quakeress. Readers get an Irish storyteller's shelf, touched by the knowledge that it was his last.
42568-the-cornish-fishermen-s-watch-nigh:
Cornish Fishermen Watch Night and Other Stories came from the Religious Tract Society in London, in a set of nine short tales. The lead tale opens on the last day of the year in Penwhinnock, a lone Cornish town on a rock point over the Channel. Rain pours and wind drives the waves wild.

Town talk says the hardy fishermen love wrecking, and that drowned men were thrust back so they could tell no tales. Rich loot from wrecks fills many homes, and guests shun the place as if plague lived there. A young minister comes in zeal and will not shun them. Heads for the rest promise gold from a book, scolding, a fool and a baron, and a harvest home, all told as plain moral tales.
42573-ingres:
Ingres is a small art book by Finberg, in the Masterpieces in Colour series. It was printed at London by Jack and at New York by Stokes. The series pairs each artist with a writer; this volume treats the French painter Ingres. It is illustrated with eight reproductions in colour. The plates are named at the front of the book.

The frontispiece is La Vierge à l'Hostie, in the Louvre. The note on it says the picture repeats, with changes, a version painted in 1840 for the Czar Nicholas. In no other picture from his hand, the note says, is the artist's deep admiration for Raphael so clearly shown. Other plates show Madame Rivière and Mademoiselle Rivière, both in the Louvre.
42576-the-common-spiders-of-the-united-s:
The Common Spiders of the United States is a field handbook by James H Emerton, published by Ginn and Company of Boston and London in 1902. Emerton was America's leading spider student of his day. His introduction covers the number and names of spiders before turning to their anatomy.

Silk and spinning organs, colours and markings, and habitats follow in order. A chapter on cobwebs and one on catching and preserving spiders serve the collector. Then the families march past: ground spiders, crab spiders, jumping spiders, and wolf spiders. Funnel weavers, cobweb weavers, and the round web orb weavers close the survey. Each family receives its genera and common species in plain accounts. Emerton wrote for amateurs with a hand lens and a pill bottle, and his book taught two generations to name what ran across the porch.
42606-mimicry-in-butterflies:
Reginald Crundall Punnett, Arthur Balfour professor of genetics at Cambridge, wrote Mimicry in Butterflies for the Cambridge University Press in 1915. Eleven chapters sort the subject: an introduction, Batesian and Mullerian mimicry, old-world and new-world mimics, criticisms answered, mimicry rings, and two chapters on the case of Papilio polytes. Later chapters take up the enemies of butterflies and mimicry and variation, with sixteen plates of oriental, African, and American species.

The introduction reviews fifty years since Darwin: natural selection has been magnified at the expense of use and disuse, discredited by Weismann's challenge, and of sexual selection. Punnett quotes Bates of 1861, that the process behind mimicry involves the origin of all species, and Fabre's warning to check whether the black thing is white. The book is a geneticist's brief for selection, written before the modern synthesis settled the argument.
42657-gleanings-among-the-sheaves:
Rev C H Spurgeon wrote Gleanings among the Sheaves, here in a second edition issued in New York by Sheldon and Company in eighteen sixty nine. The publishers gave the little volume to the numerous hearers and innumerable readers of Spurgeon sermons. The stems grow up every week, the shocks appear once a month, and the sheaves are bound together once a year, they say. Short extracts from the sermons fill the book.

A first piece treats the preciousness of the promises. The promises of God are to the believer an inexhaustible mine of wealth, Spurgeon says. Happy is he who knows how to search out their secret veins, he adds. They are an armory of offensive and defensive weapons, he holds. Blessed is he who has learned to enter the sacred arsenal, he says. Devotional readers get Spurgeon gold in small, daily pieces.
42677-fires-book-1-the-stone-and-other-t:
Wilfrid Wilson Gibson wrote these tales, printed at London in 1912 as the first book of Fires. A verse at the front is a gift to George Clausen. The man who speaks sits snug in his chair and stirs the fire to flame. Wild shapes of dream come with the flare: streams of gold wood, isles of dreams, towns of dusk in flame, and caves of bright stone.

The dreams turn at the close of the verse. The man shuts his eyes to heat and light, and sees in the dark a shape that crouches in the drip. It is the man who hews the coal that feeds his fire, with stark, damp arms. That turn sets the tone of the tales. The Stone, The Wife, and The Machine stand at the head of the list of parts.
42678-fires-book-2-the-ovens-and-other-t:
Fires, Book Two: The Ovens, and Other Tales is a book of verse tales by Wilfrid Wilson Gibson, published by Elkin Mathews at London in 1912. Gibson's earlier books, named at the front, include The Stonefolds and Daily Bread. Some tales here first appeared in the English Review, Rhythm, and The Nation. Six pieces stand in the contents.

The first, The Crane, speaks for a crippled boy lying in bed, watching the great crane swing over the wharf. His mother stitches trousers all day at three-and-three the dozen pair, yet cleans the window pane so he can see it plain. In dreams he stands above the wharf and works the crane himself. The Lighthouse, The Money, The Snow, Red Fox, and The Ovens follow.
42679-fires-book-3-the-hare-and-other-ta:
Wilfrid Wilson Gibson wrote these tales in verse, Fires, book three, The Hare and Other Tales, printed at London in 1912. Gibson also wrote Womenkind, Daily Bread, and The Stonefolds. Contents list six pieces: The Dancing Seal, The Slag, Devil's Edge, The Lilac Tree, The Old Man, and The Hare. Some first appeared in two named journals.

The Dancing Seal opens the book. Its teller was among the first men to live a night on a deep-sea isle, building a lighthouse. When chisels touched stone, friendly seals came ashore and sat watching, as if they had never seen men. They loved the boy's singing and whistling, and most of all his fiddle. Half-daft one moonlit night, the teller called a young seal to dance, and she rose, shed her black skin, and danced with him as a white maiden till morning.
42699-the-gilded-man-a-romance-of-the-an:
A romance of the Andes by Clifford Smyth, published at New York in 1918. Boni and Liveright issued the novel. Richard Le Gallienne wrote the introduction. The title points to El Dorado, the gilded man of legend. A chapter on the search for El Dorado stands early in the contents. Ghosts and an old mystery deepen the colour.

The story opens in an English garden, though. David Meudon arrives late at Stoneleigh Garden. His horse Comet has gone lame on the road. Una Leighton waits there and reads his gloom at once. From that quiet start the tale moves to Indian trails and rivers. A queen of the Indians, a black magnet, and subterranean photography await. Legend and reality meet in the closing chapters.
42728-forbidden-cargoes:
Roy Snell's Forbidden Cargoes, one of the Mystery Stories for Boys, was published by Reilly and Lee in 1927. The chapters promise A Strange Message, An Underground Sea, Johnny Thompson in Jail, An Earthquake Within a Cave, and Treasure at Last.

The book opens in a palm-thatched shack with the Caribbean Sea in front and the Central American jungle behind. Panther Eye, a boy who sees in the dark like a cat, paces the room where the safe stands rifled. The thieves left nearly a thousand dollars untouched, for it was the map they wanted. Johnny Thompson, unknown to Pant, sits in a stone jail three hundred miles away.
42733-the-brighton-boys-in-the-trenches:
The Brighton Boys in the Trenches, by Lieutenant James Driscoll, was copyrighted in Philadelphia in 1918. The Brighton Boys set also sent its heroes with the flying corps, the battle fleet, and the submarine and radio services. A front plate shows red streaks of flame stabbing the semi-darkness of no man's land.

Nineteen chapters move from enlistment and training to facing the foe and going over the top. A delicate mission, a traitor in camp, hunting big game in no man's land, and wing shooting with a rifle add pace. Herbert's little scheme and Lieutenant Whitcomb close the tale. Driscoll writes brisk, patriotic war adventure for boys while the Great War still raged.
42735-exotics-and-retrospectives:
Lafcadio Hearn's essays, copyrighted in 1898 and printed by Little, Brown in Boston, divide into two parts, Exotics and Retrospectives. Hearn was then lecturer on English literature in the Imperial University at Tōkyō, and his preface is dated there in February 1898. The Exotics treat Japan: Fuji-no-Yama, insect-musicians, a question in the Zen texts, the literature of the dead, frogs, and moon-desire.

The Retrospectives are shorter fantasies drawn from two hemispheres: first impressions, beauty as memory, sadness in beauty, azure psychology, and the eternal haunter. In his preface Hearn notes a curious likeness between the teachings of evolutional psychology and Eastern faith. He points to the Buddhist doctrine that all sense-life is Karma, and offers his pieces as hints of that truth.
42737-the-cape-peninsula-pen-and-colour-:
Rene Juta described the Cape Peninsula in pen sketches with paintings by Westhofen, printed at London and Cape Town in 1910. Cape Town from Table Bay fronts the book. Only those who see take off their shoes, the dedication quotes, the rest sit round and pluck blackberries. Stevenson on maps follows: names, shapes of woodlands, courses of roads and rivers, and the footsteps of early man make an inexhaustible fund of interest.

The castle opens the chapters, then eighteenth century society and slavery. In the blue shadow of Table Mountain, Paradise and the Barnards, and the Liesbeek river follow. Dutch commanders, a French explorer with a temperament, and Kolbe, a great liar with a sense of humor, crowd the person list. History and scenery share the pages of a fine travel book.
42754-good-references:
E J Rath wrote the novel Good References. W J Watt and Company issued it at New York in 1921. Paul Stahr drew its frontispiece. Rath had written Sam and Mister 44 before. Twenty-six chapters carry the tale. Mary Decides opens the action.

Aunt Caroline enters in chapter two. Engaged and The Web We Weave follow. Social Secretarying shows Mary at work. A night court scene fills one chapter. Miss Norcross Gets the Goods heads another. Mary Resigns comes at chapter thirteen. References and a sea trip build the late plot. Castaways and The Spoilers raise the stakes. Aunt Caroline plays referee near the end. A light romance of jobs and mix-ups, the book turns on the one thing every worker needs, a good word from the last boss.
42804-buff-a-collie-and-other-dog-storie:
Albert Payson Terhune wrote these dog stories, copyrighted in 1921, by the author of Lad, a Dog. The title story, Buff, runs four chapters, from the fighting strain to the end of the trail.

It opens on Nina, a mixture of the unmixable: chow-like coat, bulldog chest, collie eyes, a Great Dane's muzzle, and a mastiff's size. Her dam was a prize tricolour collie; her sire the fiercest pit-terrier ever loosed. Five of her six pups were ordered drowned, and the survivor thrived by chance. Around Buff stand shorter tales: Chums, The Grudge, One Minute Longer, and The Sunnybank Collies. Terhune writes from his own kennels. Dog lovers get his warm, unsentimental kennel craft.
4281-helen-s-babies:
John Habberton wrote this comic novel around Harry Burton. He is a twenty-eight-year-old bachelor salesman of white goods. His married sister Helen asks him to look after her two small children, Budge and Toddie, for a fortnight. Helen and her husband want to visit friends who have not invited the children.

The babies are therefore left with their uncle. Harry's account of those ten days made the book a popular success. It records the children's innocent, crafty, angelic, and impish ways. The comedy comes from a bachelor learning how little he knows about feeding, scolding, and amusing two lively boys.
4283-brazilian-sketches:
Rev. T. B. Ray, educational secretary of the Foreign Mission Board of the Southern Baptist Convention, wrote these sketches after traveling in Brazil with his wife. His chapters cover the country itself and Rio de Janeiro. They cover a visit to a country church, two presidents, and saint worship. They cover penance and priest, and the gospel withheld and then triumphant.

Later sketches tell of Jose Barretto, Captain Egydio, and Felicidade. They tell of persecution, of the Bible as a missionary factor, and of the mettle of native Christians. Ray writes as a missionary observer, interested in both the land and the people. The book gives a mission-board view of Brazil in the early twentieth century.
42837-aunt-kitty-s-tales:
Aunt Kitty's Tales is a set of moral tales by Maria McIntosh. Appleton published this new revised edition in New York in 1847. McIntosh also wrote Two Lives and Conquest and Self Conquest before it. Aunt Kitty greets her young friends again after years away in her preface. She hopes they have not forgotten her in that long gap of time.

No new acquaintance joins the group in this gathered volume. Blind Alice and her young benefactress return for young readers to meet. Jessie Graham and her ardent friend Florence Arnott stand in the cast. Grace, Clara, and Ellen Leslie fill out the company of girls. Aunt Kitty revised each tale by her own hand for this printing.
42839-popular-tales:
Popular Tales by Madame Guizot was turned from the French by Mrs L Burke and printed at London by Routledge in 1854. The preface hopes young readers will greet a fresh set from a loved hand. It claims the same sound morals and high tone as her Moral Tales, with one tale of still deeper pull. First comes Scaramouche, set at a village fair. Punch and Judy hold one side of the green, while a learned ass and a parrot draw crowds on the other.

More tales fill the book: Cecilia and Nanette, the life of Nadir, The Mother and Daughter, and Poor José. The Curé of Chavignat and New Year's Night close the front half. Young readers get tales of duty, grief, and grace, told with warmth and care for the home school room.
42864-the-story-of-john-paul-jones:
Chelsea Fraser tells the life of John Paul Jones for young readers in this 1922 volume of the Famous Americans series, from Barse and Hopkins. The story opens in the summer of 1759 at Arbigland, a fishing village across the Solway Firth from Whitehaven. The shipowner James Younger crosses to hire sailors there, as he has done before, among sturdy fishing families who know the sea better than books.

The contents carry the boy from young sailor to young planter, then to the young navy. Raising the first American flag, an inglorious cruise, and the young captain follow. Aboard the Ranger, in the enemy's own waters, and outwitting the Drake lead to the fight with the Serapis. Captain Landais, diplomacy, and society close the tale. Plates show the boarding of the Serapis and Jones's last burial at Annapolis in 1906.
429-the-magic-egg-and-other-stories:
Frank Stockton gathers twelve witty tales in this volume, opening with the title story of a magic egg shown at a private theatre. A traveler back from the East displays wonders to friends at the Unicorn Club, and each tale that follows turns on a trick, a bargain, or a surprise. A widow's cruise, a piece of red calico, and a Christmas wreck add their own twists.

Stockton writes in smooth, urbane prose, with a fondness for neat reversals. His folk are polite, clever, and often outwitted by their own schemes. The book charms as light, well-made entertainment, where humor and a gentle moral walk hand in hand.
42943-frank-forester-a-story-of-the-dard:
Herbert Strang wrote a boys' tale of the Great War, first printed in 1915 by Hodder and Stoughton of London. Cyrus Cuneo drew the pictures, and a map of the south part of the Gallipoli shore goes with the text. The first chapter is set in July 1914. Five men ride in close file through a pass in the hills of Armenia.

The leader is a fierce local horseman in a black turban and red boots, girt with knives and pistols. Two young men ride behind him, one English and one not. The chapters ahead bring arrest, a British shell, and a landing at Anzac. A submarine is captured, and the last chapter bears the name of the Victoria Cross. The tale mixes eastern travel with the Dardanelles fight, in the brisk style Strang's boy readers knew well.
42944-a-rainy-june-and-other-stories:
Ouida wrote A Rainy June and Other Stories, in a new London form put out in 1905. Ouida was the pen name of a famed teller of tales in her age. The book holds four long tales in all. The first tale gives the book its name and runs the longest.

A Rainy June opens with a sharp letter from a prince in London to a duchess. The prince scolds and pleads at once over a love he calls fate. Don Gesualdo, The Silver Christ, and A Lemon Tree make up the rest of the book. Each tale turns on love, pride, faith, or loss in a rich, warm land. Readers who like high drama in fine prose will find her mark on each page.
42963-the-weird-orient-nine-mystic-tales:
Henry Iliowizi, a rabbi and scholar, wrote these nine mystic tales, published at Philadelphia in 1900. The publishers' preface introduces him at length: born to a Chassidic family, raised in the Russian provinces of Minsk and Moghileff and in Roumania, then trained in Germany, London, and Paris.

He had served years in Morocco on school work for Jewish societies before settling in America as a minister. His earlier book, In the Pale, told stories of Russian life. Here he turns to Eastern tales, and the preface argues that his birth, faith, and long residence in the Orient fit him to interpret the East to the West. Some tales carry Hebrew text.
43016-chaucer-s-works-volume-5-notes-to-:
Notes to the Canterbury Tales is volume five of the complete works of Geoffrey Chaucer, edited from numerous manuscripts by Walter Skeat of Cambridge. Skeat was professor of Anglo-Saxon and a fellow of Christ's College. The transcriber's note explains the conventions of this copy. A special sign stands for the schwa, and another for the Middle English letter yogh, which is much like the numeral three.

Macrons, breves, and other marks on vowels are also shown by signs. The preface, summarized in a passage preserved in the copy, treats the text of the Tales. It discusses lines clipped at the beginning, the old black-letter editions, and Stowe's edition of 1561. Dryden's remarks on Chaucer's verse, brief rules for scansion, and the modernising of spelling follow. Skeat acknowledges the sources of his notes.
43084-a-widow-s-tale-and-other-stories:
Oliphant's A Widow's Tale and Other Stories appeared from Blackwood in 1898, a year after her death, with an introductory note by Barrie. He remembers being ordered to Windsor, where she lived. He went nervous as a subject summoned by the other lady resident in the same place, and bought his first umbrella to impress her.

She seemed tremendous to him, grand in manner, belonging to a politer age beside which the manners of today felt boorish. Oliphant wrote more than a hundred books to support her family, novels, tales, and history, at a pace that astonished even her publishers. Barrie's tribute opens her last collection like a door held by a friend; the widow's tale itself is her late manner, worldly, tender, and tired in the honorable way.
43087-total-per-cent-lambing-rules:
Total Per Cent Lambing Rules is a practical sheep manual by Thomas Boylan, copyrighted in 1915. Boylan addresses the inexperienced hand who must bring ewes through lambing on the range. His promise is plain: follow the rules and waste neither lambs nor ewes.

The philosophy comes first, before any rule of handling. Common sense, patience, and endurance carry the work. Sheep thrive when they stay content in their natural habits. Handled against their nature, they seem contrary and begin to fail. Boylan insists that trouble at lambing usually starts with the herder, not the flock. The rules that follow rest on that ground. Range lambing was skilled, lonely work done far from help. A short, blunt manual like this one served as the new man's teacher.
43097-chaucer-s-works-volume-6-introduct:
Volume six of Walter Skeat's edition of the complete works of Geoffrey Chaucer came from the Clarendon Press at Oxford in 1894. Skeat, a Cambridge professor of Anglo-Saxon, edited the poems from numerous manuscripts. This closing volume holds no poems at all, but the tools for reading them.

Inside are a general introduction, a glossary of Middle English words, and indexes to the whole edition. A transcriber's note explains marks for the schwa, the letter yogh, and accents used across the text. Readers get the scholarly apparatus of a landmark Chaucer edition, the volume students reach for when the language of the poems needs unlocking.
43127-an-enchanted-garden-fairy-stories:
An Enchanted Garden holds fairy tales by Mrs Molesworth, with pictures by W J Hennessy, issued by T Fisher Unwin. Chapter one, Madam Wren, opens under a great ilex tree in spring. Alix, aged nine, and Rafe, aged ten, sit and quarrel over a poor plan.

The pair are close in all they do, at lessons and at play. Their sore point is tales. They have read all their books too often, and told tales shared by two please them more. Their father, an old soldier, and their mother both fed that taste for years. Young readers get gentle tales framed by two real children who long for one more tale.
43143-a-ring-of-rubies:
A Ring of Rubies, by Meade, stands in a London edition of 1906. Ward, Lock published the novel. The narrator tells the ring's story for her children. She is nearly thirty now; she was nineteen when it happened. Chapter one is called Storming the Citadel. Home stood in the country, thirty miles from London. Her father and brothers took quick trains to town each day. She and her mother lived dull lives between their returns. Her father was a good man but an autocrat, she says. Girls, in his view, should be heard of as little as possible outside home.

The family was poor in the courage-sapping way: every penny looked at twice. Dresses were turned, fires kept small. The narrator wakes one sunny morning, thinks hard, and dresses with a purpose.
43190-blade-o-grass-golden-grain-and-bre:
Three tales share this volume: Blade-o'-Grass, Golden Grain, and Bread and Cheese and Kisses. Contents added for this edition lay out each tale's scenes in full. The first tale is set in Stoney-Alley, where a strange event gives a girl her name, and a legend of the tiger is told.

Its heads promise a battle of life, a talk on charity without judgment, a queer little old man, happy nights, a prison wall, and a plea to help the poor. Golden Grain moves through country roads and chapter questions about parting mother and child, to a golden mist at sunrise. The third tale turns on a lad, his Bessie, and his mother, and on parting at the dawning of a new year.
43192-afterwards-and-other-stories:
Afterwards and Other Stories, by Ian Maclaren, is a story set from 1898. The title tale opens on the Riviera in December, all sun and sea. Trevor, a hard worked man, takes a telegram in a garden there. His hostess teases him for tasting the luxury of contrast with London.

His wife stays in fog bound Bloomsbury with their boy Bertie, as always. Villa holidays for him, cheap resorts for her: the pattern stings him now. Clever talk at table mocks quiet wives who love only nursery and church. The telegram promises a turn in that settled, selfish routine of years. Tender moral tales of home and loss fill the rest.
4324-fifty-famous-fables:
Lida Brown McMurry collected fifty famous fables for young readers, retelling them in plain language for school and home. The tales come from Aesop and the wider fable tradition, where animals speak and act out human faults: foxes flatter, wolves threaten, and ants plan ahead while grasshoppers sing.

Each fable is short enough to read aloud, and each carries a moral stated or implied. McMurry's book was made for teachers as well as children, with stories chosen for clarity and for talk afterward. It remains a handy first fable book, where the lessons are simple and the animals do the teaching.
43245-luke-barnicott-and-other-stories:
Luke Barnicott and Other Stories by William Howitt gathers three tales: the title story, The Castle East of the Sun, and The Holidays at Barenburg Castle. The title story opens in Monnycrofts, a Derbyshire village set on a hill, its red brick houses and gray stone church steeple visible for miles. Howitt lingers on the view from the windmill hill: the valley of the Erwash, hedgerow trees, old coal mines, and the blue hills of the Peak beyond.

The young Luke of the opening illustration grows up in a country where colliers have worked coal and ironstone for ages. Howitt writes the village world with a rambler's eye, letting landscape carry much of the storytelling.
43248-little-playfellows-sugar-plum-seri:
Little Playfellows is a small book of moral tales for children, issued at Cincinnati by Peter Thomson in the Sugar Plum Series. Its stories are short and plain, each one built to teach a lesson a child can grasp. The first, The Little Cavalier, tells of little Johnnie and his hobby horse.

Johnnie makes a great noise at play until a sick old man next door asks for quiet. Forgetting himself, the boy keeps still, and his mother praises his kindness. A week later a box of lead soldiers arrives as thanks, proving the moral: kindness always receives its reward. A second tale follows little Pierre, a Savoyard boy lost in Paris.
43268-secrets-of-the-andes:
Secrets of the Andes, by James Foster, belongs to the Exploration Series issued by the Saalfield Publishing Company at Akron and New York in 1933. Companion volumes include Captured by the Arabs and Lost in the Wilds of Brazil.

The opening strands Bob Holton and Joe Lewis on a mountain road: the bridge is out, and Joe drives the brake pedal to the floor as the little car skids on. Chapters ahead promise train robbers, the pangs of soroche, an attack by Indians, a deadly snake, and at last the big secret and another hidden wonder.
43320-the-wonder-book-of-volcanoes-and-e:
Edwin Houston wrote The Wonder Book of Volcanoes and Earthquakes, for Stokes at New York in 1907. A plate of Mount Vesuvius in eruption fronts the volume. Chapter one opens with the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883. Krakatoa is a little island in the Straits of Sunda, the text says. It stands about thirty miles west of Java, and near the same distance east of Sumatra.

Chapters follow on Hawaii, Iceland, Vesuvius, and the volcanoes of Mexico. Coseguina and the peaks of Central and South America take their turns. The catastrophe of Martinique and the Lesser Antilles gets a full chapter. Jorullo, a young volcanic mountain, and the volcanoes of the moon pass in review. Earth's heated interior, lava forms, mud volcanoes, and hot springs close the fire half. Earthquakes end the book, with their shocks and sea waves.
43363-earthworms-and-their-allies:
Earthworms and Their Allies is a small science manual by Frank Beddard. The book stands in the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature set. Cambridge University Press and Putnam's of New York shared it in 1912. Beddard was a fellow of the Royal Society among his honours. Nine chapters run from structure and system to the worms' world spread.

Mode of life and external features in relation to habit follow first. Sense organs and senses of earthworms get a chapter of their own. Relative frequency in different regions of the world comes next in line. Peregrine forms and the earthworms of oceanic islands fill the middle. Movement and migration among earthworms lead to their geography at last. Leeches stand as the worms' next allies, the study notes plainly. Marine bristle-bearing worms stand a little more remote in kinship.
43383-galen-on-the-natural-faculties:
Galen on the Natural Faculties appears here in an English translation by Arthur John Brock. Heinemann published it in London and Putnam's Sons in New York in 1916. Three books of Galen's text follow a long introduction and bibliography. An index and glossary close the volume. The introduction sets Galen at the summit of Greek medicine. Hippocrates, six hundred years earlier, had laid its foundation.

Galen crystallised the best work of the Greek medical schools before him. Greek medicine reached later ages largely in Galen's form. The introduction retraces the temples of Aesculapius and their natural methods of cure. Fresh air, water cures, massage, and gymnastics were chiefly relied on there. Hippocrates of Cos separated the physician from the philosophical speculator. His watchword, Brock writes, was back to nature.
43406-herbs-and-apples:
Herbs and Apples is a book of poems by Helen Hay Whitney, printed at New York by the John Lane Company in 1910. Whitney had already published Songs and Sonnets and Gypsy Verses. Her opening verse gives the book its meaning: I give you this, the bitter and the sweet; it holds my heart. Apples and herbs, she says, are a poor gift, but the reader will understand.

Some sixty-five short poems fill the contents. The Search, Dust, The Peacock and The Architects follow. Later come The Lost Romany, The Song of Mokai, To the Gypsy Man, The Old Maid and The Wife Speaks. Illustrations face several poems, including the frontispiece: to be alone, to watch the dusk and weep. The volume is genteel American lyric verse of its decade.
43418-our-knowledge-box-or-old-secrets-a:
Our Knowledge Box, or Old Secrets and New Discoveries, presents cheap books sold by post in its opening pages. One star item is a fortune teller and dream book in Madame Lanormand’s name. It sold by mail for twenty cents. Palm lines, moles, tea leaves, and egg white all tell fate there.

A showman’s guide bares stage tricks for twenty five cents. Tricks there drive a cup through a table and turn water to wine. A conjuring guide in Houdin’s name makes hard tricks look easy. Dream lists run A to Z with a plain sense for each. Love charms, spells, and lucky days fill the gaps. The pages show what plain folk bought to peek at fate and fun.
43453-a-pickle-for-the-knowing-ones:
A Pickle for the Knowing Ones is the famous literary curiosity of Timothy Dexter, the eccentric Newburyport merchant who styled himself a lord. The fourth edition, printed at Newburyport in 1848, reprints his text verbatim, spelling and all, with a preface by a distinguished citizen of old Newbury. Dexter was born at Malden in 1747, apprenticed to a leather dresser, and grew rich on bold speculations.

The preface recounts his fortune, including the depreciated currency and the whalebone and warming pans he boasts of in the work itself. It also describes his house, crowned with minarets and ringed by forty wooden statues. The Pickle itself rambles on politics, religion, and his own greatness in glorious disorder. It remains America's best-loved monument of cheerful literary madness.
43482-a-book-of-bryn-mawr-stories:
A Book of Bryn Mawr Stories, edited by Margaretta Morris and Louise Buffum Congdon, was published by George Jacobs and Company at Philadelphia in 1901. Ten stories by Bryn Mawr women fill the contents, each signed with its author's class year.

Her Masterpiece, by Marian MacIntosh of the class of 1890, stands first. In Maytime, Within Four Years, and Free Among the Dead, by Georgiana Goddard King, follow. Studies in College Colour, Epoch Making, and A Reminiscence come next. Catherine's Career, The Apostasy of Anita Fiske, and A Diplomatic Crusade close the list. Her Masterpiece opens on Ellen Blake, a leader among progressive women. For the first time in many years she feels unable. She has promised a speech at the Women's Convention in Indianapolis, on the educational value of college life. On that very subject she can find no words.
4355-david-crockett-his-life-and-adventu:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this life of David Crockett for the American Pioneers and Patriots series. His preface admits Crockett was not a model man, but a representative one, of a large class whose modes of life most citizens know as little as the customs of the Comanche. Crockett's wild life, Abbott argues, deserves a patriot's study.

The book follows Crockett from frontier youth through hunting, soldiering, and Congress to the Alamo, in Abbott's popular style. It stresses character over legend, while keeping the tall tales that made Crockett famous. Readers get a nineteenth-century biography, admiring but frank, of a man whose name every American then knew.
43551-the-white-horses:
The White Horses is a novel by Halliwell Sutcliffe, the author of Ricroft of Withers and The Open Road. It came out in London, Melbourne, and Toronto in 1916 from Ward, Lock and Company. The book is given to the memory of the author's sister. A front picture shows Old Squire Metcalf, who broke into a roar of laughter as he went out to meet a guest.

The chapter heads mark the tale as a story of the English civil war age. Who Rides for the King? stands first, then Skipton-in-Craven and Some Men of Fairfax's. The Lady of Ripley, How Michael Came to York, and A Halt at Knaresborough stand in the list. How They Sought Rupert, The Loyal City, and The Riding In carry it on. A Stanley for the King and The Scots at Micklegate stand later in the list.
43555-selections-from-early-middle-engli:
Selections from Early Middle English, part two, is the notes volume of the set. The main volume holds texts from eleven thirty to twelve fifty. Notes to each selection stand alone here, with no index or glossary. Old letters like yogh, wynn, and thorn need Unicode display for reading.

Cross references point by page and line to the main text volume. Pages up to two hundred twenty two belong to the primary text book. Higher page numbers belong to this notes volume itself, the guide says. Greek transliterations close the sections where rare Greek words occur. Bracket marks show split prefixes and Orm special letter forms here.
4357-american-fairy-tales:
L. Frank Baum, author of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, wrote these American fairy tales for children. The contents include The Box of Robbers, The Glass Dog, The Queen of Quok, The Girl Who Owned a Bear, The Enchanted Types, and The Laughing Hippopotamus. Later tales bring the Magic Bon Bons, the Capture of Father Time, and the King of the Polar Bears.

The first tale leaves Martha alone one afternoon, while her family scatters to a card party, a drive, and the office. Baum sets his wonders in American homes and streets, rather than in a far kingdom. The stories are gentle, funny, and inventive, and they show Baum's gift for making magic feel close to home.
43571-the-mother-of-washington-and-her-t:
Sara Pryor published The Mother of Washington and Her Times with Macmillan in 1903. A supposed portrait of Mary Washington illustrates the front. The motto promises the book's method: that one who breaks the way with tears, many shall follow with a song.

Mary Ball Washington was famous for being difficult: the widow of Fredericksburg who held her son's career in her hands and was accused, even by his admirers, of holding it back. Pryor, a Virginia memoirist whose husband had been a Confederate general, writes the mother back into honor. Her times (the colonial Virginia of plantations, parishes, and early widowhood) explain the woman. Such books flourished in the decades when Mount Vernon was being saved and the republic was inventing its domestic saints. Pryor's Mary is the first of them: the mother as the unacknowledged founder of the founder.
4358-the-sea-fairies:
L. Frank Baum wrote this undersea fantasy for children, with pictures by John R. Neill. He begins by noting that two-thirds of the earth's surface is water, and that land folk have always wondered who inhabits it. Odd beings sometimes rise from the seas, and stranger ones may live unseen in the depths.

In Baum's story the sea folk speak and behave much like land folk, and the mermaids resemble fairies children already know. Trot and Cap'n Bill visit their kingdom, meeting its rulers and wonders. The book is fanciful throughout, but Baum insists its sea people are real within the tale, and young readers will take them as such.
43583-the-mystery-of-the-fires:
Mystery of the Fires is a girls detective novel by Edith Lavell, with a 1935 date in the record. Its heroine is Mary Louise Gay, named in the cast list as a girl detective. Her chum Jane Patterson and her brother Freckles join the Shady Nook summer cast. A young insurance agent, David McCall, visits the village in the tale.

Chapter heads run from the burnt bungalow through another fire, more suspects, and an arrest. A crazy woman, a threat, a search, and a captive stretch the middle acts. Release, return, and conclusion close the nineteen chapter summer mystery for young readers. Village families, an inn, and a hotel fill out the suspect rich setting.
43587-princeton-stories:
Jesse Lynch Williams wrote Princeton Stories, published by Scribner in New York in 1895 and dedicated to the class of 1892. The fourth edition is the text here. Eleven stories make up the book, all set at Princeton in the eighteen nineties. The Winning of the Cane opens the volume, and The Man That Led the Class closes it.

The cane story explains an old college custom. The Cane Spree, once a midnight rush watched kneeling on wet grass, had become a daylight event at the fall handicap games by Williams's time. Sophomores and freshmen fought over canes while girls watched from the bleachers. Other stories treat hazing, hero worship, a scrub quarter-back, and the rare visit of girls to Princeton. Williams wrote the first notable fiction of American college life, drawn from his own recent years on the campus, and students read it as a picture of themselves.
43599-a-picture-book-of-merry-tales:
A Picture Book of Merry Tales is an old English chapbook of comic folk tales, printed in London by Bosworth and Harrison at 215 Regent Street. Most of the book tells the pranks of Owlglass, a famed German trickster. From his odd birth and triple baptism on, he fools priests, tailors, smiths, and horse dealers.

Later tales shift to other folk leads, such as Tim Jarvis, Jock and his mother, Teeny Tiny, and the wise fools of Gotham. Dwarfs, a wee bannock, a false confession, and a donkey taught to read all play a part. The short, bold tales suit young readers and fans of old jest books.
43609-castles-and-chateaux-of-old-navarr:
Castles and Chateaux of Old Navarre and the Basque Provinces, including also Foix, Roussillon, and Béarn, is a travel book by Francis Miltoun. Page of Boston published it with illustrations reproduced from paintings made on the spot by Blanche McManus, in the author's series of rambles and cathedral books on France.

The introduction argues that no account of the life and historical monuments of an old French province can confine itself within geographical or topographical limits. The most a writer can do is centre the interest around an imaginary hub, from which lines of historic and romantic interest radiate. The castles and chateaux of the title give that hub its form, anchoring journeys through the Basque country and the Pyrenean provinces.
43630-pagan-origin-of-partialist-doctrin:
Pagan Origin of Partialist Doctrines is a theological work by John Claudius Pitrat, published at Cincinnati in 1857. Pitrat published the book himself, with Longley Brothers as printers on Vine Street. He is named as a member of the University of France and author of Jesuits Unveiled. 

The book argues, as its title states, that the partialist doctrines came from pagan sources. Partialism, in the disputes of that age, held that salvation reaches only a part of mankind by decree. Pitrat attacks that teaching by tracing its roots outside the Christian faith in his account. He dedicates the work to John Gurley, who had fed him when he was starving, a glimpse of the converts hard road. The book belongs to the fierce print wars of American universalism, in which ex priests and frontier preachers fought over the fate of the soul with pamphlets.
43665-java-facts-and-fancies:
Java: Facts and Fancies, by Augusta de Wit, was published in London in 1905, with a large number of illustrations. The text opens with a stage joke. Lady Dolly van der Decken, asked about her legendary husband whereabouts, murmured something vague: Java, Japan, or Jupiter.

She had Java in her mind, de Wit says, as the most impossible of those impossible places. But Java: what far, forlorn shore owns the strange sounding name? In what sailless seas may this other farthest island be fancied to float? There was a time, she confesses, when she never saw a globe without the same vagueness. The book that follows mixes fact and fancy from her own years in the Dutch East Indies. Readers get a Dutch writer Java, literary and observant, for English readers.
43666-the-german-emperor-as-shown-in-his:
Christian Gauss, a professor of modern languages at Princeton, gathered the public words of William II, German Emperor, in this 1915 book. A photo of the emperor, taken since the war of 1914 began, faces the title page. Gauss lets speeches and orders show the ruler in his own voice.

The contents start with the Hohenzollern tradition, then turn to the first acts of the reign. An address at Schloss Friedrichskron on June 15, 1888, opens the record of the reign. Messages to his people, the opening of the Reichstag and words to striking miners follow, giving American readers a wartime portrait from primary texts.
43684-eothen-with-an-introduction-and-no:
Eothen is a travel book by Alexander Kinglake, issued here by Methuen of London in 1900 with an introduction and notes and a frontispiece from a painting by the author. The Greek motto, from Herodotus, speaks of journeying toward the dawn. Its twenty-nine chapters run from Over the Border and Turkish Travelling to Constantinople, the Troad, and Smyrna, then Cyprus and Lady Hester Stanhope.

The Holy Land fills the middle: the monks of Palestine, Galilee, the Dead Sea, the passage of the Jordan, and the desert. Cairo and the plague, the pyramids, and the sphinx follow, then Suez, Gaza, and Damascus. The introduction calls Eothen Kinglake's earliest work; he is best known as the historian of the Crimean War. A passage preserved in the copy follows him after the tour.
43685-the-literature-and-history-of-new-:
The Literature and History of New Testament Times is a course of fifty-two lessons on early Christianity. Machen wrote the lessons. The Presbyterian Board published them at Philadelphia. The copyright dates to 1915. Part one treats the historical background of Christianity. A companion part was to follow.

Early lessons set the scene in three worlds. The Roman background comes first. Greek and Jewish backgrounds follow in turn. Palestinian Judaism and the Judaism of the dispersion divide one topic. The Messiah and the Book of Acts succeed. Paul's conversion and journeys fill the middle lessons. The council at Jerusalem marks a turning point. Later lessons present Jesus through each Gospel. The Christian hope closes the course.
43692-edward-buttoneye-and-his-adventure:
Cyril Austin wrote Edward Buttoneye and His Adventures, pictured by Hilda Austin, in the Little Mother Stories. Verses tell that Edward lay in a box made by those who stitched his eyes on, joined his toes, and gave him such a head and nose. Homeless on the broad countryside, another might have sat and cried.

But Edward takes what fortune brings and lives in hopes of better things, the rhymes insist for children. A farmhouse engages him to herd sheep by day and night, since the flock strays and hides whenever it can. He buys a paper, reads advertisements for a place to suit his bent, and forgets the sheep entirely in deep thought. Rag-doll adventure follows in verse and pictures.
43706-wounds-in-the-rain-war-stories:
Stephen Crane gathered war tales in a volume dated 1899 and 1900, dedicated to Moreton Frewen. Crane was already known for The Red Badge of Courage. The contents range from The Price of the Harness to War Memories and The Second Generation. One tale follows marines signalling under fire at Guantanamo.

The first story opens with twenty five men making a road up a hillside for guns behind them. Crane stays close to heat, dust, waiting, and hard work rather than glory. His soldiers dig, march, and endure while guns stay out of reach. The set shows his plain, sharp style applied to recent wars.
43713-the-butterflies-of-the-british-isl:
The Butterflies of the British Isles, by Richard South, fellow of the Entomological Society and editor of The Entomologist, came from Frederick Warne and Company at London and New York in 1906. It carries coloured figures of every species and many varieties, with drawings of egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, and food-plant.

The preface argues that wild flowers gain a second set of blossoms in the butterflies that rise from them, and that knowing the insects adds much to a country ramble. The volume belongs to Warne's Wayside and Woodland series for nature lovers.
43729-the-lost-pibroch-and-other-sheilin:
Neil Munro wrote Highland tales that open with a piece on a lost pibroch, a great pipe tune. Seven years of his own learning and seven ages before him go to the make of a piper, the tale begins. If the gift is in a man it will out, as an old Gaelic saying has it.

Only three pipers in the wide world today, the teller claims, can give a tune its full charm. They draw notes from the deeps of time and the tale from the heart of the man who made it. His own tale is not of those three, but of three fine pipers in a woodland place he calls Half Town.
43730-a-thousand-francs-reward-and-milit:
Thousand Francs Reward is a tale by Emile Gaboriau, rendered into English by Laura E Kendall. Military sketches go with it in the hosted volume. The tale opens on a Sunday afternoon in the Marais quarter of Paris. The whole quarter is in an uproar, the narrator says. A respectable merchant has disappeared, and no search has found him.

The event is discussed in every shop in the neighbourhood, the tale goes on. Groups stand at fruit sellers' doors, and housewives bring fresh details. A corner grocer has the latest news from the cook of the house. The merchant went down to his cellar for a bottle of wine after dinner, he reports. He was never seen again. The narrator adds that prudent people buy sword canes at such times.
43741-old-friends-and-new-fancies:
Old Friends and New Fancies is an imaginary sequel to the novels of Jane Austen, written by Sybil Brinton and published in London in 1913. Brinton says she built the after-adventures of Austen's characters from references Austen herself made, as recorded in Austen-Leigh's Memoir of her. She owns the difficulty, and the presumption, of the attempt. The fascination of the subject, she says, is the apology.

The cast list mixes figures from all the novels. From Pride and Prejudice come Elizabeth and Darcy, Jane and Bingley, Georgiana Darcy, and Lady Catherine. Mansfield Park lends the Crawfords and Tom Bertram, Northanger Abbey the Tilneys and Isabella Thorpe. A preserved passage shows the plot's matchmaking. Elizabeth and Darcy, from sincere affection and anxiety for the younger of the two, promoted an engagement between Georgiana Darcy and Colonel Fitzwilliam.
43816-incredible-adventures:
Algernon Blackwood wrote five long tales of strange and unseen things, printed in London in 1914. The tales are The Regeneration of Lord Ernie, The Sacrifice, The Damned, A Descent into Egypt, and Wayfarers. Blackwood was known for books such as Jimbo and John Silence.

The first tale follows John Hendricks, a tutor hired to take Lord Ernie round the world for a year. Hendricks hopes the trip will make a man of the boy. By the time they reach the lakes of Italy and Switzerland, he fears the trip has done little good. The other tales turn on faith, old rites, Egypt, and men who walk between worlds.
43840-poison-romance-and-poison-mysterie:
Poison Romance and Poison Mysteries, by Thompson, gathers tales of famous poisonings and the lore around them. The hosted copy opens on a long advertisement for a fruit salt remedy, as popular books of the day often did. Past the ads, the title page carries a warm word from a London gazette, calling the reading fascinating and pleasant.

Thompson treats poison as a subject with a literature of its own: secret doses at courts, Borgia legends, slow poisons and quick ones, and the trials that made them famous. Mystery cases sit beside tales of romance, where love and inheritance turned on a powder or a cup. The book belongs to the popular true-crime shelf of its decade, written for readers who liked their history dark and their chemistry explained in plain words.
43846-the-seer-of-slabsides:
Dallas Lore Sharp's The Seer of Slabsides, from Houghton Mifflin in 1921, is his portrait of John Burroughs, the naturalist of Slabsides and Woodchuck Lodge. Sharp dedicates the book to Henry Ford, named on the page as a lover of birds and a friend of Burroughs.

Sharp owns that the title fits loosely. Burroughs was a see-er rather than a seer, a poet and teacher of the near and simple things, not a prophet. Sharp recalls sitting with him one October on the boulder where Pietro set him resting. He notes that Burroughs was laid beside that rock the next April, on his eighty-fourth birthday. Even then the old man watched a woodchuck slip from its burrow and marvelled at it.
43862-in-the-morning-glow-short-stories:
Roy Rolfe Gilson, who wrote Miss Primrose, gathered these short tales of childhood at home. Harper held the rights of 1902, and Grosset and Dunlap reprinted the book at New York. Gilson gave it to his wife, and its cast is one family.

Grandfather and Grandmother head the list of tales. While Aunt Jane Played, Little Sister, and Our Yard fill the set. The Toy Grenadier, Father, and Mother close the roll. The plates sing the same tune: grandfather in his white vest, sail-boats whittled on rainy days, and a kiss at bed time. What a Beautiful Dream cries the front plate. Soft, fond scenes of a safe young world fill the morning glow of the title.
4387-present-at-a-hanging-and-other-ghos:
Ambrose Bierce gathered these ghost stories from his 1918 collection Can Such Things Be, in a selection titled Present at a Hanging. The contents divide into the ways of ghosts, soldier-folk, and haunted houses, with tales such as A Cold Greeting, A Wireless Message, An Arrest, and A Man with Two Lives. Later stories bring the Isle of Pines and the Spook House.

Bierce's ghosts are terse, ironic, and often military, reflecting his Civil War service. A hanging watched, a message from nowhere, and a field that cannot be crossed give the book its chills. The stories suit readers who like short, sharp supernatural tales, where the horror lies in a plain fact quietly stated.
43883-a-brief-history-of-the-u-s-s-imper:
A Brief History of the USS Imperator calls her one of the two largest ships in the United States Navy. The Imperator was commissioned in 1913 at Hamburg for the Hamburg-American Line. She ran from Hamburg to New York until late July 1914.

Her numbers fill the account: 919 feet over all, 98 feet 3 inches wide, and a top speed of 22 knots. She burned about 850 tons of coal a day. As a liner she carried 700 first class, 600 second, 1000 third, and 1800 fourth class passengers. As a transport she could carry some 9900 troops. Captain Casey Morgan's own service record follows the ship's figures.
43958-minnewaska-mountain-houses:
A resort booklet shows two mountain houses at a Shawangunk lake in a printing dated 1898, with plates of both houses. Lake Minnewaska sits on the summit of the Shawangunk Mountains, ten miles southwest of New Paltz in Ulster County. New Paltz stands eighty-eight miles from New York, about three and one-half hours by the Wallkill Valley Railroad.

Spring-fed, deep, and clear as crystal, the lake rests in a rocky, wooded bowl high above two valleys. Bracing air, select guests who return year by year, and grand scenery form the three claims of the house. Awosting Falls drop more than sixty feet within a mile, with cascades of one hundred feet below. Great crevices in the rock run over one hundred feet deep at three-quarters of a mile off.
43973-visions-and-beliefs-in-the-west-of:
Lady Gregory collected and arranged Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland, first series, printed in 1920, with two essays and notes by Yeats. Gregory had begun hunting news of the invisible world after reading Yeats's Celtic Twilight tales of Sligo. She felt jealous for Galway and its own store of wonders.

Sections gather sea stories, seers and healers such as Biddy Early, tales of the evil eye, and accounts of people taken away by the fairies. A closing essay treats witches, wizards, and Irish folklore in wider terms for the general reader. A Galway voice in the book says Irish folk simply talk more freely of such things. Folklore readers get gold.
43974-visions-and-beliefs-in-the-west-of:
Lady Gregory gathered the folk beliefs of the west of Ireland in a second set, printed at New York and London in 1920. Yeats adds two essays and notes. A view of Ballylee Castle stands at the front. The folk, a voice in the book says, talk of such things more freely here than elsewhere.

Heads open with herbs, charms and wise women. Straying and treasure, banshees and warnings follow. The unquiet dead and strange sights take long parts. Butter, smiths, friars and priest cures fill the middle. A fool of the forth and beasts of the little places close the tales. Swedenborg, mediums and waste places end the book, with notes at the back.
43983-wanted-a-cook-domestic-dialogues:
Wanted, A Cook is a set of home talks by Alan Dale, out in the rights year of nineteen four. Dale gives the book with thanks to a house wife who sent her four fair girls to his aid in his hour of no cook. Its first part tells how the voice came to wed his wife. Both were young, keen, and pure of the world, he says.

His wife was deep read, with a shine on her school that was no thin skin. She loved the old tongues and the great stage bard, and toyed with the wise men of France and the song lands. The pair held that grace was the till of the grand vain, and scorned the vile use of hands. Their home was to run on suave lines past no loss of that creed. The want of a cook tests that creed in the talks.
4399-a-few-figs-from-thistles:
Edna St. Vincent Millay wrote these poems and sonnets under the title A Few Figs from Thistles, thanking the editors of Ainslie's, The Dial, Pearson's, Reedy's Mirror, and Vanity Fair for reprinting several pieces. This edition adds poems not in earlier ones, and it opens with the famous First Fig, whose candle burns at both ends.

The Second Fig builds a shining palace upon sand, while Recuerdo recalls a night spent going back and forth on a ferry, tired and merry. Millay's voice is bright, defiant, and lyrical, with sonnets of love and independence. The collection made her a voice of her generation, witty about freedom and frank about desire.
43999-kitty-s-picnic-and-other-stories:
Kitty’s Picnic and Other Stories is a children’s book issued at Edinburgh and London by Oliphant, Anderson, and Ferrier. A plate shows Kitty sitting at the window in the first tale. The contents name seven short stories for young readers. Ellen’s Letter and That Dear Duck follow the title piece.

Little Miss Muffle and A New Red Riding Hood stand in the list. Lilla’s Doll Show and Selina and her Doll close the contents. The first story opens on a fine spring morning at that window. Green fields, young leaves, and far towers fill Kitty’s view. Small girls, dolls, ducks, and picnics make the world of the book. Such gift books filled Victorian nursery shelves at Christmas.
44000-the-origin-of-vertebrates:
Walter Holbrook Gaskell argues for a new view of how backboned life arose in a Longmans volume from London in 1908. Gaskell held posts at Cambridge in the study of the body and was a Fellow of Trinity Hall. Chapter heads show he rests his case first on the central nervous system, then on the organs of sight.

He picks the young lamprey, Ammocoetes, over Amphioxus as the best guide to early form. Young forms, he holds, keep old traits that grown forms lose, and the lamprey is no mere worn-down relic. Brain, pineal eyes, and side eyes in the lamprey are matched trait by trait with those of joint-legged beasts. Old rock finds and tissue growth serve as back-up proof in the plan.
44063-the-making-of-species:
The Making of Species, by Douglas Dewar and Frank Finn, was printed in London and New York by John Lane in 1909. Dewar served in the Indian Civil Service, and Finn worked on birds. Fifteen plates fill the book, one showing a hex curassow feeding a young bird.

The first chapter treats the rise of the theory of natural selection and its growth since Darwin. Dewar and Finn sort living writers on the theme into three classes, not two. They grant faults in plain neo Lamarck views and in Wallace views alike. The second chapter states the chief charges against natural selection, in two classes, those that strike at the root and those that do not. Mimicry, chance, and the struggle among the young get close tests. Science readers get a sharp Edwardian brief on how kinds arise.
44104-the-native-races-of-the-pacific-st:
Native Races of the Pacific States, volume four, Antiquities, is part of the works of Hubert Howe Bancroft. Bancroft and Company published the volume at San Francisco in 1883. It entered copyright in 1882 in the name of Hubert Bancroft at Washington. 

Antiquities is the volume of the set given to the remains of the native peoples in the region. Bancroft great survey of the Pacific states divided its matter among wild tribes, civilized nations, histories, and this study of what they built and left. Stone work, mounds, ruins, and objects of old craft are its field as the title states. The work came out of Bancroft library of sources at San Francisco, where clerks gathered reports from across the West. It remains a storehouse of early accounts of ruins and relics, many drawn from observers whose own writings are now hard to find.
44115-lady-sybil-s-choice-a-tale-of-the-:
Emily Sarah Holt tells a tale of the Crusades in Lady Sybil's Choice, in a new edition from John F Shaw of London in 1879. Her preface takes up the mystery of suffering: why those who know God do not see his days, and why waiting in trust is the one thing we can do. A hymn on walking in the dark with God stands with it.

The contents open with Guy Takes the Cross, pass two surprises for Elaine, and build through a calm before the storm to Sybil's Choice. A plate shows Sybil coming down the nave, sure where the crowned man stands.
44152-red-head-and-whistle-breeches:
Ellis Parker Butler wrote this short tale, issued by the Bancroft Company of New York in 1915 with art by Arthur D Puller. The publishers say a master story teller's tale, full of human interest and homely counsel, earns a lasting form. Tim Murphy, in the heat of a strike fight, cracked a deputy sheriff's head and joined the front rank of the strikers.

The court gave him two years in the penitentiary. The law's peace must be kept, the tale grants, yet the cost falls on his mother and his wife Maggie. His father Mike, a village hod carrier, has a small roll in the bank and a shanty of his own. When Maggie's baby comes, the strain peaks. Butler keeps the tone warm and plain.
44164-criminal-types:
Colonel Masten wrote a book on crime and the minds of men who commit it, printed in Boston in 1922. His first claim is plain. There are criminal types, but there is no one criminal type. Like crimes can spring from unlike causes in unlike men.

Chapters deal with marks of type, the moral criminal, and the work of mind doctors and crime experts. Masten warns that long fingers, close eyes, or a bull neck prove little, since honest men share the same marks. Later chapters take up prison rules, the chain of crime, lay critics, and what the study of the mind can and cannot tell about a criminal.
44191-gorillas-chimpanzees:
Gorillas and Chimpanzees, by Garner, reports ape study in the African jungle. Osgood, McIlvaine issued it at London in 1896 with many plates inside. Garner lived caged in the jungle to watch apes at close range. Man and ape compared opens the book in sober scientific tone at first.

Chapters treat chimpanzee speech, habits, and mind in long close detail throughout. Moses, a captured chimpanzee, gets two chapters for his life and death. Aaron and Elisheba follow, with their deaths told in full as well. Gorilla habits and Othello and other gorillas fill the later part. Care of apes in captivity closes this early primate study.
44233-plays-by-august-strindberg-third-s:
August Strindberg's Plays, third series, in Edwin Björkman's authorized translation, was published at New York in 1921. Five plays make the volume: Swanwhite, Simoom, Debit and Credit, Advent, The Thunderstorm, and After the Fire are listed on the title page. The set opens with After the Fire in contents order, then Swanwhite.

Swanwhite, a fairy play of 1902, has a duke, a stepmother, the prince, maids, gardeners, and the mothers of both lovers. Its stage shows a medieval stone castle, brocade draperies, a rose garden laden with white and pink roses, and the blue sea beyond a sandy beach. Readers get Strindberg's late, lyrical manner beside his chamber-play storms.
44257-cape-breton-tales:
Harry James Smith wrote Cape Breton Tales, published by the Atlantic Monthly Press at Boston in 1920, with illustrations by Oliver M Wiard. The catalog names Wiard, but the title page gives the tales to Smith and the pictures to Wiard, whose sketches were made on visits to Arichat.

The pieces gather around the French shore of the island. Contents run from On the French Shore of Cape Breton and La Rose Witnesseth to tales of the bucherons, La Belle Mélanie, and Siméon's son. A poem, At a Breton Calvaire, stands among the prose pieces. The opening sketch follows the Corpus Christi procession at Arichat, convent girls in white veils carrying banners up to the old Calvary.
44263-500-of-the-best-cockney-war-storie:
Five hundred short war tales told by London Cockney soldiers were reprinted from the London Evening News. Bert Thomas drew many of the pictures. General Sir Ian Hamilton opens the book with a tale of an older war. Hamilton led the British Legion work for old soldiers in London, and profits from the book aid that cause.

The editor says laughter at times saved men's reason in the war days. From countless tales sent in, these five hundred were chosen as the best. Each is short, told in the voice of Tommy Atkins himself. Mud, fear, luck, and mateship come through jokes that keep their grin. The book preserves how common soldiers bore a hard war.
44302-plays-by-august-strindberg-fourth-:
August Strindberg's Plays, Fourth Series, holds four dramas. Edwin Bjorkman translated them with an intro. Charles Scribner's Sons issued the book in 1916. The Bridal Crown leads the set. The Spook Sonata follows it in line. The First Warning and Gustavus Vasa close the volume.

The Bridal Crown is a folk play in six scenes. It dates to 1902 in Swedish. Mats and Kersti stand as its young pair. Kersti's kin are called the Mewlings in it. A child in white and a mewler ghost walk the cast. The headsman stands at the cast's dark end. Scenes run from hill pasture to mill. A church penance for Kersti fills scene five. The last scene plays on lake ice. Strindberg's folk tragedy of shame and custom reached English readers in the war years through Bjorkman's steady hand.
44322-a-bird-of-passage-and-other-storie:
Beatrice Harraden gathers tales in A Bird of Passage and Other Stories, printed at Chicago in 1890. Harraden had writ Ships That Pass in the Night. The title tale runs in eleven chapters, and two more tales fill the book: At the Green Dragon and An Idyll of London.

The title tale opens in a small hotel in Switzerland. A young girl comes in at four, soaked through, and draws her chair to the fire. An older lady urges her to change her clothes at once. The girl laughs: she has naught to change into. She had no luggage to lose, she says, but a knapsack. Chapters then bring Hieronymus, who comes, stays, and at last goes.
44385-bliss-and-other-stories:
