Katherine Mansfield gathers short stories in a volume issued in London in 1920 and reprinted many times by 1925. Mansfield gives the book to John Middleton Murry. Prelude opens the gathering, a long story of the Burnell family's move to a new house.

Lottie and Kezia, in coats with brass anchor buttons, cannot fit in the buggy for the move. Their mother Linda, tired and laughing strangely, agrees to leave them with a neighbor until the dray comes in the evening. Other stories include the title tale Bliss, The Wind Blows, A Dill Pickle, and The Little Governess. Mr Reginald Peacock's Day and Sun and Moon show Mansfield's eye for small humiliations. Readers get the stories that made her name, exact, musical, and unsparing.
44429-a-tour-through-the-pyrenees:
Hippolyte Adolphe Taine toured the Pyrenees in a narrative translated by J. Safford Fiske, with illustrations by Gustave Dore. Henry Holt issued the English edition at New York in 1875. Four books trace the route in full. The coast comes first, from Bordeaux and Royan through Les Landes to Bayonne, Biarritz, and Saint-Jean-de-Luz.

Inland books climb through the valleys of Ossau and Luz. Pau, Eaux-Bonnes, Eaux-Chaudes, Barèges, Cauterets, and Gavarnie each get chapters, with notes on people, plants, and high peaks. Bagneres and Luchon close the tour before Toulouse. Taine blends travel fact, landscape, and sharp portraits of local life. Readers get a classic French journey in careful English dress.
44463-red-and-white-a-tale-of-the-wars-o:
Emily Sarah Holt wrote Red and White, a tale of the Wars of the Roses in a new London form of 1882. Holt had told a past tale of the White Rose of Langley. A plate shows a girl called Nan who longs to be her father child once more. That scene sits at page 140 of the book.

Holt says that storm clears the air, and that those wars did the same for the land. She holds that the wars paved the way for the great change in the church to come. To the men of that day, she says, it was a fight for fame or for right. To the women, it could seem a pain with no end in sight. Parts bear names like Lilies Among Thorns and The Last Battle of the Rival Roses. Faith in God hand through dark days is her theme.
44536-georgian-folk-tales:
Georgian Folk Tales is a translated set of Caucasus tales by Marjory Wardrop, issued in 1894. David Nutt of the Strand published the translations for English readers in London. A dedication offers the tales to Tylor as a slight token of admiration. A Malcolm quote argues that a people is known through its popular stories.

Contents open with Master and Pupil, then The Three Sisters and Their Stepmother. The good for nothing, the frog skin, and fate fill the early tale list. Wardrop later became the great English translator of Georgian literature and epic. Folklorists gain early, faithful versions of tales from the Georgian mountains.
44550-the-hammer-a-story-of-the-maccabea:
Alfred Church and Richmond Seeley wrote The Hammer, a story of the Maccabean times issued by Seeley and Company in London in 1890, with pictures by John Jellicoe. Church was a professor of Latin who retold old history for young readers.

The story opens in Jerusalem in 174 BC, where a Greek circus stands under the Temple walls and the city has become a small province of the Greek kingdom of Syria. Chapters follow the persecution under Antiochus, the rising in the mountains, the death of Mattathias, and the battles of Emmaus and Beth-Zur. The tale ends with the cleansing and dedication of the Temple and the wars that followed. It turns the Maccabean revolt into a stirring adventure of faith and arms.
44563-thackerayana-notes-and-anecdotes:
Thackerayana is a set of notes and sketches by William Makepeace Thackeray. Chatto and Windus issued this new edition in London. Hundreds of his sketches illustrate the pages. They show jokes from his school life. They also show scenes and persons from his daily reading. The introduction opens with the shock of his death. That news broke at Christmas in 1863.

The editor recalls a public that would not easily forget the blow. Colonel Newcome's solemn end is named among his works. His two young daughters were left in sudden trial. The book gathers marginal drawings and idle notes. Such scraps show the novelist at play. His pen drew as readily as it wrote. Thackeray's sketches have a wit of their own. The volume serves as a portrait of his lighter hours.
44592-light-for-little-ones:
Mary Waterbury wrote Light for Little Ones, a tale for young children printed at Portland in 1872. Frankie lives in a white house on the bank of a large creek whose water turns the wheels of mills and factories. Trumpet honeysuckle climbs the piazza, poplars stand like guards, and maples flare red and gold in fall.

Chapter heads map a short, grave arc. Frankie has an adventure in the creek, makes a new friend in Aleck, and learns to keep the Sabbath day. He trusts in Christ, starts school, and races in a coasting match. Aleck goes home in a sadder sense, and a visit to his grave comes near the end, with a father return. Warm scenes and plain faith mark a Sunday school tale of home and loss.
44622-in-the-days-of-giants-a-book-of-no:
Abbie Farwell Brown wrote this book of Norse tales for children, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1902. Boyd Smith illustrated the tales for young readers throughout. A plate shows the giant Skrymir announcing himself, at a famous moment in Thor's travels among the giants.

A publisher's list of Brown's books fills the front page with titles. 'Songs of Sixpence,' 'The Christmas Angel' and 'John of the Woods' stand among them there. Brown retells old Norse myths of gods, giants and heroes in clear prose for children, keeping the wonder and strangeness of the northern sagas in a schoolroom form.
44623-the-golf-courses-of-the-british-is:
Bernard Darwin's tour of the golf courses of the British Isles, illustrated by Harry Rountree and published by Duckworth and Company in London in 1910, proceeds course by course. Two chapters take the London courses, and others follow for Kent and Sussex, the West and South-West, and East Anglia. Cheshire and Lancashire, Yorkshire and the Midlands, and Oxford and Cambridge come next.

Scotland takes three chapters: Saint Andrews with Fife and Forfarshire, the East Lothian and Edinburgh courses, and the west with Prestwick and Troon. Ireland and Wales close the book. Darwin opens by noting that a dozen or fifteen years earlier the London courses could be counted easily, most of them laid out on public commons such as Blackheath and Wimbledon.
44625-true-ghost-stories:
Hereward Carrington gathered tales of ghosts said to be true. The J S Ogilvie Publishing Company issued True Ghost Stories in New York in 1915. Carrington had written on spiritualism and death in earlier books. A first chapter asks what a ghost is and weighs the answers.

Death signs, doubles, and photos of ghosts fill the opening theory. Tales run from a Russian ghost to the Great Amherst Mystery. Hampton Court, Willington Mill, and a house in Georgia stand among the haunts. Curious readers gain a full, earnest tour of the ghost lore of its day.
44626-plantation-reminiscences:
A memoir of plantation life by Page Thacker, published in 1878. A transcriber's note identifies the name as a pseudonym. The Library of Congress catalogues the author as Letitia M Burwell. She dedicates the record to her nieces. Public prints, she warns them, call their ancestors cruel slave-owners. She writes so descendants may know the truth instead.

Martin Farquhar Tupper encouraged the project by letter. Her earliest childhood, she recalls, knew one vast plantation as the world. White cabins with gardens lined the quarters. The great house stood at the centre of her small universe. Nine generations of her family owned Virginia plantations. The book defends that world from inside, thirteen years after emancipation ended it.
44629-the-seashore-book-bob-and-betty-s-:
Boyd Smith wrote and drew this seashore book for children, copyrighted in 1912 at Boston and New York. Story and pictures are both his, in a series that also holds his farm book and railroad book. The tale tells how Bob and Betty spent the summer at the seashore with Captain Hawes.

Captain Ben Hawes was an old sailor. After forty years on the high seas he settled ashore at Quohaug, bluff and hearty, full of yarns of strange adventures and foreign ports. His home was a small museum of things brought from far lands, kept in shipshape order, with a green parrot that could call out ship ahoy. On the children's first fine day he took them out for a row in his boat.
44632-hell-s-hatches:
Hell's Hatches, by Lewis R Freeman, was printed by Heinemann at London, with art dated 1921. Its teller is a painter famed in Queensland for his South Sea sea views, and his mate in the tale is Slant Allen. The press hails Allen as a hero: he steered a plague ship of sick men through reef seas to save the few who might live. The teller alone knows the truth, with Bell and the girl both dead.

Allen did not choose the helm. A slight Kanaka girl forced him up the gangway at knife point to sail the doomed Cora Andrews. Heads ahead name a ship of death, Rona come aboard, and a fall down the flume. Sea fans get a bold tale of false fame, fear, and the price of a hid truth.
44644-philosophy-of-the-plan-of-salvatio:
Philosophy of the Plan of Salvation argues the truth of Christianity from the plan itself. The author signs only as an American citizen. The Religious Tract Society issued this revised edition at London. A preface tells how the book grew from a young sceptic's search.

The writer and a friend, a lawyer, both doubted in their early years. The usual evidences of the faith failed to convince either man. A fresh reading of the Bible led the writer to full conviction. He began letters to share his proof with the friend. Business broke the exchange, but the inquiry went on for years. The chapters set out a single method: judge the religion by whether its scheme fits man's nature and need. The book sold widely on both sides of the Atlantic.
44651-with-the-swamp-fox-a-story-of-gene:
James Otis wrote With the Swamp Fox, a story of General Marion young spies, issued by A L Burt in New York with a copyright of eighteen ninety nine. J Watson Davis drew six full page plates. Eleven chapters fill the tale. General Francis Marion last words, spoken February twenty seventh, seventeen ninety five, head the book. He thanks God he can say he never in intent did wrong to any man.

A boy teller starts with his uncle the major, then meets General Marion himself. Tory camps, a man named Samuel Lee, and an ambush fill the early chapters. Prisoners, a retreat, and Black Mingo Swamp bring hard marching. A battle and a push to Georgetown close the campaign, with a figure named Gabriel at the end. Boys got a brisk Revolutionary tale of swamps, spies, and the famed Swamp Fox.
44653-a-latin-grammar-for-schools-and-co:
George Lane, professor emeritus of Latin at Harvard, left a grammar for schools and colleges that reached a revised edition with an American textbook house, copyrighted in 1898 and 1903. Its preface is a memorial: Lane died on the thirtieth of June, 1897, with the book he had worked on for nearly thirty years approaching completion.

The first two hundred ninety-one pages were already stereotyped, and the chapters on the relative sentence and the infinitive stood ready. Other stretches survived in first draft, and the chapter on versification had arrived from a collaborator weeks before his death, unexamined. Editors finished what the classroom had shaped. A scholar's life work, completed by other hands, is the volume.
44703-the-eighteen-christian-centuries:
James White wrote a past of the church's first eighteen spans of years. His book came out in New York in 1878. White wrote a History of France as well in his day. This form comes from the second Edinburgh form with no cuts. Names of note have been swelled in its lists for this press.

Bad emperors mark the first span, and good ones the next. Strife and church growth share the third in his scheme. The move to Constantinople and Julian's fall mark the fourth. Rome's end and new states rise in the fifth span's tale. Each span gets one part in clear, brief prose. Church past fans get a long road in one book.
44745-the-world-on-wheels-and-other-sket:
Benj F Taylor published The World on Wheels and Other Sketches with S C Griggs and Co at Chicago in 1874. The pieces first ran in a New York paper in the summer of 1873. The main sequence follows travel itself, from the wheel instinct and the Concord coach to canals, railroads, engines, and train men.

A second part, headed Baggage, turns to shorter home pieces. Its sketches take up starry days, an old grandmother, outdoor preaching, the story of a bell, and the old road, closing with a bird heaven. The tone throughout is that of a newspaper man watching American life roll past his window.
44779-strange-teas-dinners-weddings-and-:
Strange Teas, Dinners, Weddings and Fetes, by sundry authors, came out at Boston in 1887 from D Lothrop Company. Twelve pieces fill the book. Each piece tells of a meal or rite in a far land, seen at first hand. A tea to Mehemet Ali leads the set.

A Japanese dinner and a Roman Christmas come next. A Coptic wedding, an Arab dinner party, and a West Indies birthday follow. A Siamese hair cutting and old English harvest ways get pieces too. Easter at Jerusalem and the Moqui Snake Dance close the book. The first tale starts in Syria when Midhat Pasha came as governor with great pomp. The set suits readers who like travel tales of food and custom.
44794-the-thames:
The Thames is a picture book of the river, with colour illustrations by Mortimer Menpes and text by Mitton. Black printed it in London in July 1906, in a series where each volume cost twenty shillings net. Menpes also made the series volumes on the Durbar, Japan, Venice, and India.

Nineteen chapters run downstream. They begin with the beauty of the river and the Oxford meadows, pass the old town of Abingdon and Dorchester, and rest at Sonning and its roses. Henley, Windsor and Eton, and a chapter on Magna Charta follow. The Londoner's zone and the river at London bring the course to its end, under the closing claim that the Thames is a national possession.
44813-sally-scott-of-the-waves:
Sally Scott of the WAVES is a girls' war novel by Roy Snell, printed at Racine, Wisconsin, with copyright in 1943. Whitman issued it, and Meixner drew the pictures. A notice says every name, character, place, and event is fictitious. Twenty-one chapters run from Up the Ladder to Dreams.

The contents promise a radio from the sky, a message in code, and a flight at dawn. Sally saves a life, steps out on a roof, and clings to a gable in the pictures. Danny Duke makes a catch and shares a secret. One picture caption has Sally murmur praise to her parachute. Snell sets his heroine among bombers and secret radios, in the women's naval service of the Second World War.
44852-yorkshire-battles:
Edward Lamplough wrote Yorkshire Battles, issued at Hull and London in 1891. Lamplough had writ The Siege of Hull and Medieval Yorkshire. The book is given to the Rev E G Charlesworth, vicar of Acklam, as a lover of Yorkshire letters. Twenty two chapters run from Winwidfield to a fight off Flamborough Head.

Stamford Bridge, the Standard, and Myton Meadows fill the early wars. Boroughbridge, Byland Abbey, and Bramham Moor follow. Sandal, Towton, Tadcaster, and Leeds mark the wars of roses and civil war. Adwalton Moor, Hull, Selby, and Marston Moor close the civil war set. Brunanburgh is set late though early in time. Lamplough holds that Yorkshire holds a chief place in the nation's growth. Valor and honor mark its wars, he says.
44894-social-life-in-england-through-the:
Wilton Hall wrote a survey of social life in England dated 1920, from cave homes to the planned suburb of his own day. Early chapters treat pit dwellers, earthworks, and barrows, then Roman and Saxon towns in turn. Churches, cloisters, and castles mark the long span of Norman and Saxon rule.

Later chapters take up fairs, markets, schools, and the great schools of Oxford and Cambridge. The Black Death, the wool trade, and care for the poor show as turns in the tale. Changes in homes, roads, and rail lines bring the long run of years down to modern streets and health.
44904-mrs-caudle-s-curtain-lectures:
Mrs Caudle Curtain Lectures is a comic book from Punch, issued at Philadelphia in 1845. John Leech supplied the illustrations for the lectures of the famous wife. Lecture one opens on Mister Caudle lending five pounds to a friend in folly. His wife wonders who would lend him five pounds in return for such trust.

A wife may work and slave, she cries, while five pounds go out the door. A black satin gown, wanted three years, would have been bought with that money. Everybody says she does not dress as becomes his wife, and he cares nothing. Nightly scoldings on money, drink, and friends make this a Victorian comic classic.
44916-modernities:
Modernities, by Horace B Samuel, author of The Land and Yourself, was published by E P Dutton and Co at New York in 1914, and dedicated to Mrs George Joseph. The contents list ten essays on modern writers and movements.

The subjects are Stendhal, Heinrich Heine, the psychology of Disraeli, Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals, and August Strindberg. Marie Corelli, Frank Wedekind, Arthur Schnitzler, and Émile Verhaeren follow, ending with the future of futurism. The Stendhal essay opens with his saying that he wrote only for a hundred readers, the happy few without hypocrisy or morality. Samuel calls him perhaps the most perfect type of the intellectual Europe has produced. He is no recluse scholar or rabid doctrinaire, but a man of the world and of action on the hunt of happiness.
44924-uncle-joe-s-stories:
Knatchbull-Hugessen, a member of Parliament, wrote these children's stories, published by Routledge at London and New York in 1879 with illustrations by Ernest Griset. The book is affectionately dedicated to all naughty children, if there be any such left in England, and a letter to them opens it.

The author tells his dear children he was once naughty himself, very long ago, when there were fewer pretty children's books. He advises them to be good as fast as possible, since in fairy stories the good people come out right at last and the naughty get into disagreeable scrapes. Six long stories follow: Uncle Joe, Zac's Bride, Evelyn with the Fairies, Cat and Dog, Ophelia, and The Crones of Mersham. The plates show Zac winning the pig-race, Evelyn meeting the fairies, the cat's last music-lesson, and Mary and Billy meeting the crones.
44951-the-motor-boys-in-strange-waters-o:
Clarence Young wrote another Motor Boys tale, printed in New York in 1909. A front picture shows a creature lashing about in a death struggle. The boys take their boat into strange waters this time, not their cars onto roads. The floating forest of the subtitle waits to trap them.

Saw grass catches the boat, a strange lake opens, and water begins to recede. A wanderer appears more than once, and Jerry seeks aid at a key point. The professor returns late in the tale. Alligators, swamp, and lost channels test the chums. Young keeps the pace fast, with a fresh peril in near every chapter for his boy readers.
44952-sixpenny-pieces:
Sixpenny Pieces is a set of sketches by A. Neil Lyons of London. John Lane at the Bodley Head issued it in the year 1909. Lyons also wrote Arthur's, then in its second edition in print. More than thirty short pieces fill the table of contents. Heads run from Concerning James and First Impressions to Sixpences themselves.

Hypocrites, the way of the East, and an apothecary sketch follow in order. A mother's trade union, a diagnosis, tuskers, and art lovers vary the fare. Dialogues with a bride, talks with James, and a case of low finance recur. Lyons drew his folk from the poor streets and pubs of London. Small coins and small lives carry the humour and pathos throughout.
44992-travelling-sketches:
Travelling Sketches is a set of essays on tourists by Anthony Trollope, reprinted at London in 1866 from a gazette. Its contents sort the travelling tribe into kinds, each with an essay of its own. The family that goes abroad because it is the thing to do comes first. The man who travels alone and the unprotected female tourist follow.

United Englishmen who travel for fun, the art tourist, and the tourist in search of knowledge fill the middle heads. The alpine club man and tourists who do not like their travels close the list. The first essay opens on a fixed habit of the age: men and women leave home at summer's end and go somewhere, though it be only to Margate. Incomes the most limited stretch themselves to fit the rule, Trollope notes with dry amusement.
44998-the-gentleman-from-san-francisco-a:
Bunin wrote these Russian tales, Englished at the Hogarth Press in 1922. Leonard and Virginia Woolf published the book at Richmond in England. Lawrence and Koteliansky Englished the title tale together, a note says. Three more tales come from Koteliansky and Leonard Woolf hands.

The title tale shows a rich man set out for two years pleasure. He sails with wife and daughter to the Old World in style. No one in Capri or Naples recalled his name, the tale says. Gentle Breathing, Kasimir Stanislavovitch, and Son fill the rest. Lawrence worked on the English text of the title tale.
45-anne-of-green-gables:
An orphan girl arrives by mistake at a Prince Edward Island farm. Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables wanted a boy to help Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert. Instead they get Anne Shirley, talkative, dreamy, and quick to blush.

Anne charms the island with mishaps at school, tea parties, and puffed sleeves. Diana Barry becomes her bosom friend; Gilbert Blythe becomes her rival. Matthew's quiet love steadies her temper. The book launched a beloved series about growing up with imagination. Sequels, stage shows, and screen versions spread Anne's island world far beyond Canada.
45044-the-great-small-cat-and-others-sev:
May Southworth wrote seven tales of cats dated 1914, with photos and art by Pedro Lemos. The lead tale tells of a black stray whose love for her young makes her brave a dark, swift river more than once. Her grit at last melts the cold heart of a ranch widow who had kept her at bay.

Thursday tells of an orphan kit fed by spoon who rules a grand Irish setter till a sad end. A miner tale makes the cat the shrewder prospector of the pair, first to find the rich mine. Maida, a Maltese mother, raises a brood of white rats as her own young.
45070-bobbie-bubbles:
Sherwood wrote and drew this children's tale, Bobbie Bubbles, with Budlong as fellow author. It opens by settling its hero's name. Bobbie's father was not named Bubbles, and bubble blowing was not the family trade: the boy earned the name himself, by being a famous person, and the tale tells how.

One day Bobbie, Betty, and Billy were blowing bubbles in the garden till teatime. Billy blew one as big as an apple; Betty one as big as a toy balloon. Bobbie blew, and his bubble grew past pumpkin size, past the Christmas snowball, and would not stop. Then the great shining bubble, glowing with all the colours of the rainbow, reached out and took in Bobbie, pipe, arm, and all. It rose with him, light as thistledown, above the garden.
45081-the-apostles:
The Apostles is a work of religious history by Ernest Renan. It forms volume two of his Origins of Christianity series. The Life of Jesus stands first in that series. Saint Paul was to follow as the third volume. Carleton published this English translation in New York in 1866. The book was translated from the original French. A publisher's notice praises Renan's works for power and learning.

Renan was a member of the French Institute. The volume takes up the story after the life of Jesus. Its subject is the first generation of the Christian movement. American readers met it as a companion to his famous Life. The series aimed to trace Christianity from its very origins. This instalment covers the apostles who carried the new faith outward.
45103-in-the-heart-of-the-christmas-pine:
Leona Dalrymple wrote a Christmas tale with pictures by Charles L Wrenn. McBride, Nast and Company issued it in New York in October 1914. Rights were held in 1913 and 1914 by the house. Eight chapters run from a cottage in the pines to the lady of the fire-glow.

Jean Varian rides three days through rain from Denver to a strange village. Fog, dripping trees, and one dim hotel light greet her odd whim. Aunt Cheerful Loring, a son's letter, and a small hermit wait ahead. Dalrymple builds a warm tale of loss, kindness, and a tree decked with crimson chains.
45114-the-children-s-book-of-thanksgivin:
Asa Don Dickinson edits a store of Thanksgiving tales for children in a book issued by Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City in 1915. Marks guide the choice: a star for younger children, a dagger for older ones.

The Kingdom of the Greedy opens the book. Mary E Wilkins Freeman gives a tale called Thankful. The First Thanksgiving is retold by Albert F Blaisdell and Francis K Ball. Harriet Beecher Stowe tells how Thanksgiving was kept at Oldtown. Nathaniel Hawthorne contributes John Inglefield's Thanksgiving. A frontispiece shows a gobbler insisting the wishbone was his. Wishbone Valley, a molasses cake tale, and a white turkey's wing season the list. Dickinson edited a matching Christmas volume. His holiday sets filled school and home shelves.
45153-historic-sites-of-lancashire-and-c:
James Croston wrote Historic Sites of Lancashire and Cheshire. John Heywood issued it at Manchester in 1883. Croston was a fellow of the antiquarian society. The Record Society's council held his name too. His notes mix history, legend, and family lore. A wayfarer's road book is his own frame.

The book goes to John Leigh of Hale manor house. Leigh helped found a Spenser reprint society. His work saved old halls' legends from loss, Croston says. A former book, Nooks and Corners, won warm praise. Press and public both took to it, the preface notes. That warmth bred this second volume, he adds. Samlesbury and Prestbury church stand in his past works. County pride in print, the book walks hall by hall through two shires where every gate had a ghost or a pedigree.
45172-fresh-leaves:
Fanny Fern wrote Fresh Leaves, printed in New York in 1857 and given to Grace Eldredge with her mother's love. A preface addresses her parish of readers directly. She offers, first, a new story that has never before appeared in print. Secondly, she offers the hundred-dollar-a-column story, about whose pay the paragraph writers have amused her so much. That story came out when the New York Ledger was in the dawn of its great circulation, and has appeared nowhere else.

Thirdly, she offers her late fugitive pieces, often requested by readers. Contents name a business man's home, a story for husbands, visiting and visitors, and our first nurse. To literary aspirants, summer travel, girls' boarding-schools, and a feminine view of Napoleon as a husband follow. The Boston woman, the New York male, my old inkstand and I, and lady doctors fill out the list of short pieces.
4518-madame-de-treymes:
Edith Wharton sets this short novel in Paris, where an American, John Durham, waits in a hotel doorway looking out toward the Tuileries gardens. He has come back to France with a personal stake in the city, and he soon meets Madame de Malrive, a woman caught between an American past and a French marriage. Around them stand old families, strict customs, and the glitter of a capital planned for pleasure.

Durham learns how hard it is for an outsider to move inside French family life, where divorce, honour, and duty carry a weight he did not expect. Wharton contrasts brisk American frankness with Parisian reserve and tact. Readers get a compact drama about love, social rules, and the cost of crossing from one world into another.
4519-the-descent-of-man-and-other-storie:
Edith Wharton gathers ten stories in this volume. It opens with The Descent of Man, in which Professor Linyard returns from a Maine holiday changed by an idea he picked up on his travels. The book then moves through The Other Two, Expiation, and The Lady's Maid's Bell. It goes on to The Mission of Jane, The Reckoning, The Letter, The Dilettante, The Quicksand, and A Venetian Night's Entertainment. Each story turns on a social choice made in polite company.

Wharton is sharp on marriage, money, reputation, and the small lies people tell to keep their place. Her characters often learn, too late, what a single decision has cost them. Readers get a polished set of early Wharton tales, witty and unsparing, showing the New York and European worlds she knew best, and the moral traps hidden inside good manners.
45201-fallen-fortunes:
E Everett-Green wrote a tale set in the days of Queen Anne and Marlborough. Thomas Nelson and Sons issued Fallen Fortunes in London in 1906. Twenty chapters run from the field of Ramillies to a merry marriage close. A scheming kinsman fronts the book as its first plate.

Grey Dumaresq and his man Dicon ride over a foggy rise into sight of war. French and allied troops stand drawn up as guns begin to roar. The youth hopes to meet the Duke of Marlborough, hero of Blenheim. Love, rank, and shifting fortune drive the tale through town and court.
45214-the-russian-grandmother-s-wonder-t:
Louise Seymour Houghton retold Russian wonder tales as if told by a grandmother to a little boy. Benda drew the pictures. Houghton gave the book to her five grandchildren, whose names stand at the front. Each chapter pairs a scene from the boy's life with a tale his grandmother tells.

The wolf, the sick lion, and the bear, the boar, and the fox fill early chapters. Reinecke the fox tricks Isegrim the wolf more than once. Later tales tell why dog and cat cannot agree, of seven stars, and of a golden apple tree with nine peahens. Frame scenes of suppers, snowy days, and bedtime keep the tales warm and close.
45232-the-blind-brother-a-story-of-the-p:
The Blind Brother, a story of the Pennsylvania coal mines, is a boys' book by Homer Greene. Crowell printed it in New York in 1887, in the Sunshine Library. The story won the first prize of 1500 dollars offered by the Youth's Companion in 1886 for the best serial story, and this copy is the fourteenth thousand.

Chapter one, Lost in the Mine, begins in the abandoned Dryden Mine in the Susquehanna coal fields. Its headings echo only to falling slate and dripping water, its robbed pillars crumbling. The contents promise a burned breaker, an unquiet conscience, a trial and a verdict, a fall, and a shadow of death, before the final chapter brings its hero out of darkness.
45279-american-indian-fairy-tales:
Larned retold American Indian fairy tales for children, with illustrations by John Rae, in a book reaching its twenty-ninth edition in 1921. A note says that all but one of the tales are adapted from the legends Schoolcraft collected and published in 1839. The storyteller of the frame is old Iagoo.

There never was anyone so wise and knowing as Iagoo, who understood the language of birds and beasts and kept the wonder stories of his grandfathers. Children asked him where the robin got his red breast, and how fire found its way into the wood. Winter was the telling time, when snow lay deep and the North Wind howled from the Land of Ice.
45292-the-placid-pug-and-other-rhymes:
The Placid Pug and Other Rhymes, by Lord Alfred Douglas, was published in 1906. Douglas signs himself the Belgian Hare on the title page in jest. He also wrote Tails with a Twist and The Duke of Berwick, the page notes. The title rhyme opens on a pug pacing in the park in silk.

Harnessed in silk and led by a leathern lead, that pug lives his dull life. He recks not of the shark in distant waters, the verse goes on to say. Lapped in sloth and greed, he makes no mark in strenuous life at all. Round the slow circle of his nights and days his life revolves in calm sameness. Light verse on pets and idleness fills this small book of rhymes.
45300-once-upon-a-time-and-other-child-v:
Once Upon a Time and Other Child Verses is a book of poems for children by Mary Wilkins. The title poem builds its whole story on its opening phrase, repeated like a spell.

Once upon a time, the poem chants, there was a nest of fairies under a wild rose tree, ringed thick with violets. Children found it dancing by, the fairies fluttered off on purple winglets, and the children searched for days and found only the empty nest. Other verses nurse a sick fairy on cowslip tea and poppy gruel served in a buttercup, and turn the Banbury Cross rhyme into directions past hollyhocks and gilly-flowers. Wilkins, famous for her stern New England stories, writes nursery verse of deliberate simplicity.
45303-the-life-of-john-taylor-third-pres:
The Life of John Taylor is a biography by Brigham Roberts. It was published at Salt Lake City in 1892. Taylor was the third president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Roberts dedicated the book to Taylor's family. He hoped it would stir his descendants to copy his virtues.

The preface makes no apology for the book. Justice to Taylor's character demanded a life, Roberts writes. The church annals alone could not hold his career. Roberts argues that Taylor would have led men in any cause. His gifts went instead to a church the world despised. The world called his devotion fanaticism. Roberts answers that praise and censure never swayed him where truth was concerned.
4533-the-hermit-and-the-wild-woman-and-o:
Edith Wharton gathers seven stories in this 1908 volume, opening with the title tale of a hermit living in a cave in a hill hollow. Below him runs a stream through oaks and alders. Across the valley stands a walled town that once flew a Guelf standard, and later fell to steel-clad men-at-arms. The hermit, once a town lad, now watches war, faith, and wildness from his lonely height.

The other stories, The Last Asset, In Trust, The Pretext, The Verdict, The Pot-Boiler, and The Best Man, return to Wharton's usual ground of money, marriage, art, and reputation. Together they show how private choices harden into public fates. Readers get a varied Wharton collection. A medieval opening gives way to modern social drama, and every tale turns on what a character will pay to keep, or lose, their good name.
45348-french-dishes-for-american-tables:
Pierre Caron wrote this book of French fare for the tables of America, printed in 1886. He had been chef of the sweet course at Delmonico's. Mrs. Frederic Sherman put his work in English dress. A few words at the front state the aim of the book. It is to put in front of the crowd a count of fine bills of fare, in a form so clear and brief that their make is in the reach of all.

That is a need long felt, the words go on. The books of worth on the art of the cook that have come out are in the main in French. Those in English, for all their bits of worth, in the main swarm with the terms of the trade. Such terms fret and maze the new hand.
45349-remarkable-rogues:
Charles Kingston wrote Remarkable Rogues, the careers of some notable criminals of Europe and America, printed in London and New York in 1921 with eight illustrations. A front picture shows Marie Tarnowska on trial. Contents open with a Russian Delilah, then an infamous female poisoner and Belle Star, the girl bushranger. The woman with the fatal eyes and Madame Rachel, the beauty specialist, follow.

A Monte Carlo trunk murderess, a female swindler, and a matrimonial agent fill the middle heads. The bogus Sir Richard Douglas, the enterprising Mrs Chadwick, and a million dollar ranch girl stand there too. James Greenacre, Catherine Wilson, Adam Worth, and a secret princess of Posen close the list. The first tale opens in a Russian country-house, where a girl of sixteen is presented to a prince, a baron, and a count. Each of the three, unknown to her, had asked her father for her hand.
45367-our-english-towns-and-villages:
Wilton Hall wrote Our English Towns and Villages, printed at London in 1906. Hall was library curator of the Hertfordshire County Museum and sub-librarian of St Alban's Cathedral. Verses on ancient ruins head the title page. Forty-nine chapters carry the long story.

Men who lived in caves and pits come first, then earthworks and barrows. Roman times, Saxon tuns and vills, and the hundreds and shires follow. Norman castles and monasteries, medieval town life, fairs, markets, and schools fill the middle. The Black Death, wool, and the poor mark the later chapters. Elizabethan houses and post-Restoration churches bring the account toward modern times.
45384-the-book-of-fables-and-folk-storie:
Horace Scudder's Book of Fables and Folk Stories is shown here in the new illustrated edition of 1919. Houghton Mifflin publish it from Boston and New York. A publishers' note dated October 1919 explains the edition: the book had been a prime favorite with young readers for more than a generation. All the old pictures were replaced by drawings from a modern artist. The old charm, the publishers hope, stands heightened by the new feature.

Little Red-Riding-Hood opens the collection, told in the classic form. The wolf meets the child in the wood, learns the grandmother's house beyond the mill, and races her there by the shortest way. She lingers chasing butterflies and plucking flowers while he knocks at the door. Pull the string, and the latch will go up, the sick grandmother calls. The book served American children from 1882 onward.
4539-back-to-god-s-country-and-other-sto:
James Oliver Curwood gathers nine northern stories in this volume. The title tale, Back to God's Country, opens the set. Other stories include The Yellow-Back, The Fiddling Man, and L'ange. They go on to The Case of Beauvais, The Other Man's Wife, The Strength of Men, The Match, and The Honor of Her People. Bucky Severn, His First Penitent, Peter God, and The Mouse close the set. The first tale begins on the Fraser River in British Columbia, when Shan Tung, a Chinese gold collector from Vancouver, sets out with Tao, a Great Dane.

Curwood's north is a place of gold trails and old grudges, where a fuse lit in one winter can explode forty years later. Heroes and villains meet in snow, river, and camp, and loyalty is tested by greed and love. Readers get a set of Canadian wilderness tales, full of animals, outlaws, and rough justice.
4542-checkmates-for-three-pieces:
Checkmates for Three Pieces is a working file for chess players, not a book of prose. It lists board positions in FEN notation, the short code that records where each piece stands, whose move it is, and the state of play. The positions cover endings with only three pieces on the board, such as a king with a queen or a rook against a lone king, in many different squares and corners.

Players can set each position on a board and work out the winning moves, or feed the lines into a chess program for study. Because the file gives positions rather than explanations, it suits readers who already know basic checkmate patterns and want practice material. It is a reference set for drill and testing, best used beside a board or an engine, not read as a story.
45425-guilds-in-the-middle-ages:
Guilds in the Middle Ages is a study by Georges Renard, with an introduction by Cole. Bell of London issued the work in its social and economic books line. Renard traces the guild as the working order of medieval town life. Craft and merchant guilds set rules for training, quality, and price in their trades.

Cole framing places the old guilds beside modern questions of labour and welfare. Publisher pages around the text praise works on women in industry and factory welfare. That setting shows the book spoke to reform debates of its own day too. Students of economic history gain a short, clear account of guild rise and rule.
45450-fern-leaves-from-fanny-s-port-foli:
Fanny Fern offers a second series of Fern Leaves from Fanny's Port-Folio, from Miller, Orton and Mulligan at Auburn and Buffalo in 1854, here at its eighteenth thousand. Fred Coffin supplied original designs, and the book is dedicated to Oliver Dyer, her truest friend in adversity. A preface confesses she knows no more of preface style than six months before.

Contents list dozens of short pieces: Shadows and Sunbeams, Aunt Hepsy, and Thoughts at Church. Soliloquies by a broadbrimmed man, a housemaid, and Sam Smith appear, plus sketches on critics, forgetful husbands, and summer friends. Titles such as A Model Husband, A Model Married Man, and A False Proverb show her comic targets. Boarding house experiences, a Broadway shop reverie, and newspaper life round out the portfolio.
4549-artemis-to-actaeon-and-other-verses:
Edith Wharton published this poetry volume in New York in 1909, opening with the title poem, Artemis to Actaeon. In that poem the goddess speaks to the hunter who could not look on her and live. He had seen her in cloud, wave, and bough, and in shapes that lurk between lid and eyeball in the dark. Part one goes on to Life, Vesalius in Zante, Margaret of Cortona, and A Torchbearer, mixing myth, history, and travel.

Part two, called The Mortal Lease, gathers Experience, Grief, Chartres, Two Backgrounds, The Tomb of Ilaria Giunigi, The One Grief, and The Eumenides. Part three adds Orpheus, an autumn sunset, moonrise, All Souls, All Saints, and other lyrics. Readers get Wharton as a poet: formal, learned, and moving, with classical myth used to speak about love, loss, and the limits of mortal sight.
45511-red-caps-and-lilies:
Katharine Adams sets a young tale in the French Revolution in Red Caps and Lilies, first published by Macmillan in 1924 and often reprinted. The contents move from a schoolroom and a bal masqué to the tenth of August 1792, a snowstorm, a hidden cellar, and a rescue. Marie Josephine, Jean, Lisle, Vivi, and Dian carry the action.

The book opens not with a child but with Flambeau, a strong dog listening hard for a call in the house of Madame la Comtesse. Jay Van Everen's pictures show the cast and the Old Green Mill-Inn. Young readers get history with peril.
45524-the-open-boat-and-other-stories:
Stephen Crane, author of The Red Badge of Courage, published this book of stories with William Heinemann at London in 1898, after opening pages listing the publisher's new novels for that year. Crane dedicated the title story to the memory of William Higgins and to Captain Edward Murphy and Steward Montgomery of the sunk steamer Commodore.

The Open Boat leads the first part, called Minor Conflicts, and Crane heads it as a tale intended to be after the fact, the experience of four men from the Commodore. None of them knew the color of the sky, the story begins; their eyes stayed on the slate waves. Other stories tell of a bride coming to Yellow Sky and of five white mice. A second part, Midnight Sketches, gathers short city pieces, among them An Experiment in Misery and The Pace of Youth.
45557-green-eyes:
Roy Snell writes a mystery story for girls in Green Eyes, printed at Chicago and New York with copyright in 1930. The Reilly and Lee Company made the book. Thirty four chapters mix island life, Gypsy lore, and a lost hoard.

Heads promise a mysterious islander, the lady of the island, and a Gypsy secret. A haunting melody, three rubies, and a dance of death build the case. A stolen trunk, strange signs, and a kidnapping raise the stakes. Petite Jeanne has a dark hour and a triumph. The tale opens on Morton's Bay at night. A half moon paints a silver path on still water, and a black rowboat rides at anchor in the bay's heart.
456-the-door-in-the-wall-and-other-stori:
H. G. Wells gathers eight tales of wonder and dread in this volume, opening with the title story. Lionel Wallace tells a friend of a green door in a London wall that led, in childhood, to a garden of delight. Each time he passes it in adult life, duty pulls him on, until one last chance decides his fate.

Other tales send a star toward Earth, dream an Armageddon, and blind a whole country to sight. Wells writes with clear, probing prose, mixing science with moral fable. The book shows his short fiction at its most haunting, where a single marvel tests a whole life.
4560-verses:
Susan Coolidge, best known for her children's stories, gathers her poems in this volume, opening with a dedication to two friends whose youth grew under peaceful suns and gracious dew. The opening poem praises friends who held beauty and ease as a trust. They scattered brightness on harder roads, so that roses, in the old saint's tale, turned to bread for hungry and weary souls. That note of kind, useful goodness runs through the book.

Coolidge writes in clear, musical verse about friendship, home, nature, faith, and the duties of a good life, without showy difficulty. Her poems suit reading aloud and quiet reflection, and they carry the same warmth readers know from her prose. This volume offers a gentle nineteenth-century poetry collection, modest in manner but sure in feeling, for readers who like verse that comforts and steadies rather than puzzles.
45606-the-little-glass-man-and-other-sto:
Wilhelm Hauff wrote his fairy tales in the 1820s, and Macmillan issued The Little Glass Man and Other Stories in the Children's Library in 1894. James Pryde's wash drawings illustrate the volume. An introduction by Eckenstein tells, in a fiction of its own, how the stories were found.

A Fairy Queen has turned publisher. She sends her fairies all over Europe in search of children's books. The tales they bring back here are Hauff's: the little glass man of the Black Forest, the caliph stork, little Muck, and Nose the dwarf. Hauff died at twenty-four, leaving tales that German children still grow up on. The English dress is handsome. The stories keep their strangeness, which is the point of them.
45622-the-curved-blades:
The Curved Blades is a detective novel by Carolyn Wells, printed in 1916. Lippincott brought the book out in February of that year in Philadelphia. Gayle Hoskins drew the colour frontispiece of Fleming Stone at work. Wells had writ A Chain of Evidence, the Gold Bag, and the Clue. Twenty-four chapters run from Miss Lucy Carrington to a closing confession.

A clash of tongues, the tragedy, and a paper snake fill the start. A man's glove, a neighbour's call, and the inquest come next in line. Anita's story, further testimony, and bizarre clues crowd the middle chapters. Fleming Stone himself enters the tale at the eleventh chapter mark. Who gave the poison and Pauline's purchase raise the stakes onward. Two wills and Pauline in Cairo lead to the confession close. Garden Steps, a show-place of Merivale Park, opens the tale.
45663-nan-of-the-gypsies:
Nan of the Gypsies is a novel for girls by Grace May North, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1926. Its heroine, Nan, travels with a gypsy caravan of covered wagons drawn by mule teams into the garden village of San Seritos, asleep by the Pacific. Chapters follow her escape, her return to a beloved garden, and the hard project of civilizing Gypsy Nan.

Across thirty-seven chapters Nan faces punishment, the lad next door, Thanksgiving rides, and surprises, until a trousseau and a wedding close the story. North wrote many such wholesome adventure tales for the girls' series market of the nineteen twenties. The book shows the period's fascination with gypsy life, romantic and stereotyped at once, and its faith that a spirited girl will find her place.
45720-jack-the-young-ranchman-a-boy-s-ad:
George Grinnell wrote this boy adventure tale of Jack, young ranchman. Stokes printed it in New York, copyright 1899, many printings on. Its ranch lies in a Rocky Mountain basin walled by peaks. The basin stands high above the sea, the preface notes.

The story is about real things and real people, Grinnell says. Antelope, elk, bears, and buffalo gave good hunting in those days. Wild Indians were far away yet near enough to be real. Contents open with Jack Danvers, prairie wolves and antelope next. Pawnee hero stories and Blackfoot lodge tales stand among his past books listed.
45747-climbing-on-the-himalaya-and-other:
J Norman Collie, a fellow of the Royal Society and a member of the Alpine Club, wrote this book of climbs, printed by David Douglas of Edinburgh in 1902. A stormy sunset fronts the book. Four chapters first ran in the Scottish Mountaineering Club Journal. Collie thanks friends for the use of pictures and for sketches of Himalayan peaks drawn for the text.

The title range runs from the Himalaya to other ranges, and the note names A Chuilionn and Wastdale Head among the pieces reprinted. Collie writes as a climber of the first rank of his day, at home on Scottish rock and Asian ice alike. The book joins route craft, weather, and the feel of high places in one record.
45751-nellie-s-housekeeping-little-sunbe:
Nellie’s Housekeeping is the sixth and last volume of the Little Sunbeams series of children’s stories by Joanna Mathews. Each volume of the set sold at one dollar, or six dollars in a box. Belle Powers’ Locket opens the list of the six tales. Dora’s Motto and Lily Norris’ Enemy stand among the middle titles.

Jessie’s Parrot and Mamie’s Watchword fill the fourth and fifth places. Mathews also wrote the Bessie Books and the Flowerets, tales on the commandments. Our Monthly praised the Flowerets as a charming set that families carried off. Nellie’s Housekeeping gives a small heroine a household to run and lessons to learn. Sunday school libraries of the age were stocked with such series.
45768-mr-sweet-potatoes-and-other-storie:
Mr Sweet Potatoes and Other Stories is a collection of tales for children published by the Werner Company in 1899. The title story is told by a child in China, where the family's milkman bears a name that translates as Sweet Potatoes. His Chinese neighbours call him Old Father Sweet Potatoes.

Some think the milkman a good man and others a bad one, for he is accused of watering the milk. He answers that he only does it when he has not enough to go round his customers. The sketch explains how new the milk trade is there, where few will taste beef and cheese is held in horror. His cows graze green patches by the brooks under child herds, since there are no fences and no grass fields, and the best milk comes when they are fed on peanut tops.
45784-gallery-of-comicalities-embracing-:
The Gallery of Comicalities gathers humorous sketches by the Cruikshank brothers and friends. Charles Hindley issued the book in London from Booksellers’ Row. Robert and George Cruikshank lead its cast of comic hands. Robert Seymour, a wood draughtsman star, joins the gay crew.

Most plates first ran in Bell’s Life in London in the late eighteen twenties. That paper’s sales leapt on the strength of these same cuts. George Cruikshank is praised here as a Hogarth of his age. His Time and Phrenology cuts fill a great share of the book. Bow Street morning scenes by Wright gain new life in it. Robert, the elder, drew Tom and Jerry’s London sprees. He died in March eighteen hundred fifty six at sixty five. George lived from seventeen hundred ninety two to eighteen hundred seventy nine.
45802-knock-three-times:
Marion Webb wrote a tale for young readers about Jack and Molly. Drawings by Margaret Tarrant fill the book. The tale starts when Aunt Phoebe sends a gift for a birth day. From that gift a strange trip soon grows.

Jack and Molly cross to the far side of a tree and meet odd folk. They pass a grey pumpkin, a black leaf, and a goblin heath. They must plan a search and face traps on the way. The book mixes fun, fear, and charm in a brisk fairy tale.
45804-elsie-and-her-namesakes:
Martha Finley wrote Elsie and Her Namesakes, published in New York in 1905, the last of the long Elsie list printed at the front. Twenty-eight Elsie books stand in a row there, from Elsie Dinsmore to this volume. Few series for girls ever ran so long.

The story opens at Woodburn, where things are going on blithely and everyone is deep in preparations for an approaching wedding. Relatives on the neighboring estates and connections on southern plantations share the excitement. Elsie, met first as a child in the early books, is here a grandmother at the center of a clan. Namesakes carry her name into a new generation. Finley wrote for girls who grew up with Elsie and then read her to their daughters. This closing volume gathers the family for one more wedding.
45812-insect-adventures:
J Henri Fabre wrote these insect studies, chosen from Alexander Teixeira de Mattos's English version of his Souvenirs Entomologiques. Louise Seymour Hasbrouck retold them for young people, and Elias Goldberg drew the plates. Dodd, Mead of New York issued the book in 1917. A motto from Maurice Maeterlinck heads it: there are no petty truths, only one truth seen in fragments.

The front matter tells Fabre's own hard road. At Avignon his fellow teachers, jealous of his packed lectures, nicknamed him the Fly and drove him from his house. Darwin called him the incomparable observer. France made him a knight of the Legion of Honour and offered him a prince's tutorship, which he refused for his country research.
45814-an-advanced-english-grammar-with-e:
An Advanced English Grammar with Exercises is a school textbook by George Lyman Kittredge and Frank Edgar Farley. Kittredge taught English writing at Harvard, and Farley at Wesleyan. Ginn published the book in 1913, with rights held by both authors. A contents table pairs each text page with its page of drills.

Opening essays treat language and grammar, then grammar and usage. The first main part covers the parts of speech within the sentence. It defines the eight parts and shows how one word can serve as several. The second part takes up word forms and sentence rules. Nouns, pronouns, and their cases fill long chapters with parsing drills. The plan suits advanced classes that need both rule and practice.
4584-mont-saint-michel-and-chartres:
Henry Adams wrote Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres as a private, jealously guarded book before it reached a wider public, and this edition carries an introduction by Ralph Adams Cram. Adams takes two great French monuments, the island abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel and the cathedral of Chartres, and uses them to open up the whole medieval world. Theology, philosophy, politics, art, and daily life all meet in his reading of stone, glass, and song.

At Chartres, Adams lingers on the great windows, where colour breaks from darkness into pools of sapphire and rose, and where the rose window hangs like a constellation. The book treats the cathedral as a living statement of faith, not a museum piece. Readers get a rich, personal work of cultural history, best read slowly, by an American writer trying to feel what the Middle Ages believed and built.
45854-chelsea-in-the-olden-present-times:
George Bryan writes a parish history of an old London suburb in a volume he printed and sold himself in 1869. Bryan lived at 4 Alfred Cottages, Camera Square, King's Road, Chelsea, and sold the book through all booksellers. A Bulwer Lytton line on honesty of purpose heads the title page in full.

A preface grants that men of greater gifts might have fit the task better than Bryan himself. More than forty years had passed since Faulkner last wrote a history of Chelsea, he notes with care. Bryan set type for much of Faulkner's first edition as a young man in the trade. He later read proofs for the two-volume edition, which gave him close sight of that work and its author.
45857-two-banks-of-the-seine-les-deux-ri:
Two Banks of the Seine is a French novel in English dress. Fernand Vanderem wrote Les Deux Rives, and George Raffalovich translated it. Dutton issued it in New York in 1919 in a French fiction library. Barnet Beyer edited that Library of French Fiction for English readers. A note sets the book in the class that Daudet made immortal.

That note hears a tone ironic yet good natured, as in Sapho. Paris life on both banks of the Seine forms the scene and subject. Family, love, and money move through drawing rooms on each shore. The two banks of the title hint at two worlds in one city. English readers of 1919 got a urbane Paris tale in translation.
4591-after-a-shadow-and-other-stories:
T. S. Arthur published After a Shadow, and Other Stories in 1868, gathering seventeen short tales. The contents run from After a Shadow, In the Way of Temptation, and Andy Lovell, through A Mystery Explained, What Can I Do?, On Guard, and A Visit with the Doctor, to Hadn't Time for Trouble, A Good Name, Little Lizzie, and Alice and the Pigeon. Later pieces include Dressed for a Party, Coffee vs. Brandy, Amy's Question, An Angel in Disguise, Which Was Most the Lady?, and Other People's Eyes.

The title story opens on a bright June morning, with Mrs. Mayflower calling to her little boy Arty from a window, in excitement at his new performance. Arthur's tales mix domestic comedy, temptation, and moral warning. Readers get a varied Victorian storybook for family reading, where small choices, a party dress, a cup of coffee, or a guarded tongue, carry a clear moral weight.
4595-heart-histories-and-life-pictures:
T. S. Arthur published Heart-Histories and Life-Pictures in 1853, opening with an introduction on how seldom we think of other people's inner lives. We are so given up to our own ends, hopes, joys, fears, and disappointments, he says, that we rarely consider the bright and sombre life-pictures other eyes look upon. Yet every heart has its history, and dreamy eyes, sober faces, and subdued, mournful tones on daily paths testify how sad many of those histories are.

Remembering this, Arthur argues, awakens a kinder feeling toward others, and draws our minds away from too exclusive thoughts of self. Whatever awakens sympathy and interest in humanity is both a personal benefit and a common good. The sketches that follow aim to create that sympathy, story by story. Readers get a gentle Victorian collection about compassion, written to make ordinary encounters feel less lonely and less judged.
45964-day-and-night-stories:
Day and Night Stories is a collection of tales by Algernon Blackwood, printed at New York in 1917. Blackwood also wrote Ten Minute Stories and Julius Le Vallon. Fifteen stories fill the volume. The first, The Tryst, opens at a little wayside station.

A man steps down from the train and recalls a talk of fifteen years before as if it were yesterday. His heart thumps so hard he almost hears it. Around that tale stand The Touch of Pan, The Wings of Horus, and an initiation. Other pieces treat a desert episode, the occupant of a room, and Cain's atonement. An Egyptian hornet, a bit of wood, and a victim of higher space close the set. Blackwood's eerie, tender manner is in full flower here.
46015-the-gypsy-s-parson-his-experiences:
The Gypsy's Parson is a memoir by George Hall, rector of Ruckland in Lincolnshire. Lippincott published it at Philadelphia, with Sampson Low at London. Its subtitle promises his experiences and adventures. Hall dedicates the book to his wife. She was his companion on many a gypsy jaunt, the dedication says. A photograph of Hall fronts the volume. An epigraph speaks of glamour cast over a man.

The quoted opening pages show a priest among desert Arabs. Sunshine, not shock, is his teacher there: he doctors, feeds, and befriends. That spirit matches Hall's own calling among English Gypsies. A parish priest who travelled with the Romany tells his roadside life here. Ministry, friendship, and adventure mix in his recollections. The book preserves a vanished world of horse drawn encampments. Hall writes as an insider by adoption rather than a tourist.
46019-capitals-of-the-northlands-tales-o:
Capitals of the Northlands is a travel book by Ian Hannah, with pictures by Edith Brand Hannah. Its subtitle calls it tales of ten cities. The frontispiece shows Trondhjem cathedral, three degrees from the Arctic Circle. The book is dedicated to the author's mother, with whom he once made a pilgrimage to the shrine of St Olaf.

The ten cities run in a ring round the northern seas. Thorshavn in the Faroe Islands comes first, and Reykjavik in Iceland second. Trondhjem, the old capital of Norway, and Christiania, its modern one, follow. Roskilde and Copenhagen stand for Denmark. Visby on Gothland and Upsala and Stockholm stand for Sweden. St Petersburg, capital of Russia, closes the ring. Churches, harbours, and market places fill the plates.
46024-origin-myths-among-the-mountain-pe:
H Otley Beyer wrote a study of origin myths among the mountain peoples of the Philippines. Beyer worked in the Division of Ethnology of the Bureau of Science at Manila. Four plates go with the paper. Beyer holds that tales of how earth, men, beasts, and plants began last longer than most parts of old culture.

Among plain folk the myths live on as folk tales told at home. In the mountains they stay part of daily rites and are sung or told at set rites. Beyer ranges from Mangyan and Tagbanwa tales to the rich faiths of Ifugao and Igorot groups. Scholars gain a map of beliefs kept by voice alone.
46039-dynamite-stories-and-some-interest:
Dynamite Stories, and some interesting facts about explosives, by Hudson Maxim, came out in New York in 1916. Maxim had written Defenseless America and a book on verse and speech. He gives the book to the men in its true tales, whose risks made the tales worth the telling.

He grants that past has been bent to tale, not tale to past. A long list names scores of short bits, most of a page or two. One treats a scrap of fulminate left and forgot. More treat a dog that ate dynamite, a hat that killed, and a race with death. Some treat nitro moved by motor car, and work on a fuel called Motorite. A mule gun and live bombs close the run. Fact fans get lore of blasts in tale form.
46049-twos-and-threes:
G B Stern wrote Twos and Threes, first published in nineteen sixteen by Nisbet and Company in London. Stern had earlier written Pantomime and See Saw. Three parts fill the novel. Chapter one of part one is headed To Bondage of Great Deeds. Stuart Heron is caught reading Nietzsche as the tale opens. His uncle by marriage, Baldwin Carr, entered the library unperceived.

That is a dangerous fellow, Stuart, Baldwin remarked, reading the title Thus Spake Zarathustra over his nephew shoulder. Stuart laid down the ponderous volume and smiled up lazily, the tale says. Oh, we are a depraved family, he answers. Not half an hour ago he caught Babs behind the drawing room screen reading Ella Wheeler Wilcox, he adds. Baldwin looked startled, since he himself gave the child the complete edition. Novel readers get Stern bright tale of a gifted, tangled family.
46051-south-american-jungle-tales:
Horacio Quiroga wrote the eight tales in South American Jungle Tales, shown here in English in 1922. Arthur Livingston made the English text from the Spanish. A L Ripley drew the pictures. The tales first came out in Spanish as Cuentos de la Selva.

Each tale turns on wild beasts and men in the jungle. Rays guard a ford in the Yabebiri River in the first tale. Other tales tell of raccoon cubs, a parrot, a blind doe, and a war with alligators. One tale tells how flamingos got their stockings. A lazy bee and a giant tortoise close the set. The style is warm and clear for young readers.
46055-among-the-birds-in-northern-shires:
Charles Dixon's Among the Birds in Northern Shires came from Blackie and Son in 1900. The publishers worked in London, Glasgow, and Dublin. Charles Whymper supplied a coloured frontispiece and forty other illustrations. Dixon calls the book a popular introduction, not an exhaustive faunal treatise. Still, he believes nearly every indigenous species is included. He had lived twenty years among these northern birds.

Dixon knew South Yorkshire and North Derbyshire best. He also visited the coasts of Lincolnshire, Yorkshire, and Northumbria, and parts of Scotland. Latitude and climate, he argues, mark the northern birds off from southern ones sharply. The northern avifauna is richer, above all in the breeding season. Migration unfolds there as it does nowhere else. Chapters run from upland streams and moorlands to crag and sea-cliff.
46079-evolution-in-art-as-illustrated-by:
Evolution in Art is a study of design by Alfred Haddon. Scott published it in London and Scribner in New York in 1895. Haddon was professor of zoology at the Royal College of Science in Dublin. It belongs to the Contemporary Science Series edited by Havelock Ellis. Eight plates and 130 figures in the text illustrate it. Its subtitle says art is shown by the life histories of designs. A preface thanks friends who helped prepare the little book.

Haddon collected his materials in museums in Britain and abroad. Curators opened cases and handed him specimens freely, he writes. Porters and guards rendered help at the time too, he notes. The method treats ornaments like living forms with descents. Patterns change, simplify, and travel between peoples, he argues. A zoologist's eye is turned on carved and woven design here.
46103-germany-s-vanishing-colonies:
Gordon Le Sueur, author of a life of Cecil Rhodes, published Germany's Vanishing Colonies with McBride, Nast of New York in 1915. A serving officer supplies a foreword under the single word Ichabod, the glory departed, and the motto that who sows the wind will reap the tempest.

The foreword praises the book as a concise and reliable description, performing a useful public service. In 1915 Germany's overseas empire was being taken from her piece by piece: Togoland, Samoa, New Guinea, and South-West Africa had already fallen or were falling. Le Sueur tours the vanishing possessions for British and American readers who needed the map explained. Imperial knowledge, the foreword argues, is essential to sound judgment. The book is a wartime inventory of an empire at the moment of its confiscation.
46107-the-german-lieutenant-and-other-st:
A story collection by August Strindberg, translated by Claud Field. T Werner Laurie published it at London in 1915. A biographical note from the Century Cyclopaedia precedes the tales. Strindberg, born at Stockholm in 1849, died there in 1912. The note calls him the Shakespeare of Sweden. Seven stories fill the contents.

The title story opens fourteen days after Sedan. September 1870 finds a Prussian lieutenant in Marlotte, France. Von Bleichroden was a geological survey clerk before the war. His dusty coat hangs on a chair like a corpse. He can read the local strata from orderlies' boot prints. Eocene or Pleiocene dirt tells him where they walked. Other tales treat over-refinement, funerals, and unwelcome guests. Field's translation brought late Strindberg prose to English readers.
46119-the-valkyries:
The Valkyries is a myth tale re told by Benson, out in nineteen three. An Unwin house brought it out in London, Leipzig, and Paris that year. Benson wrote Limitations and Dodo in past books of his own hand. A front plate shows the flight of the war maids in its cut list. Part one, The House of Hunding, heads the ten part scheme at front.

Spring had not come so late in man mind ere that year, it opens. Mid May still held the storms and squalls of the cold months fast. Men by their fires heard wind bugle and rain hiss night and day. Some said Erda, the earth ghost, grew old and frost crowned then. Some said Walhalla walls held shades where no shades should stand there.
46144-six-cups-of-coffee-prepared-for-th: Six Cups of Coffee is a small book on making coffee, whose title promises the drink prepared for the public palate. The opening pages of the hosted copy are not the work itself but the advertising matter bound with it. Those pages carry period notices for the Estey organ, Emerson pianos, Horsford's Acid Phosphate and Ridge's Food for infants and invalids. A nurse's letter from Boston, dated June 1886, praises the infant food. The coffee text itself lies past the pages shown here.
46145-the-book-of-princes-and-princesses:
The Book of Princes and Princesses belongs to the Fairy Book series edited by Andrew Lang. Those crown octavo volumes, with gilt edges, sold at two dollars a copy. The Blue Fairy Book heads the list with one hundred and thirty eight illustrations. The Red, Green, and Grey fairy books follow in their colours.

The Yellow and Pink books stand next in that famous roll. The Violet Fairy Book adds eight coloured plates to its fifty four pictures. The Crimson Fairy Book swells the rainbow of the series further. Lang’s princes and princesses are the real children of kings, told as tales. Their lives hold courts, wars, and weddings enough for any fairy story. The series taught history to children in the dress of romance.
46169-fishing-with-floating-flies:
Samuel Camp published Fishing with Floating Flies in New York in 1913 as one of the Outing handbooks. Camp also wrote Fishing Kits and Equipment and Fine Art of Fishing. His first chapter admits no one will ever know fly fishing in its entirety, and he claims no mastery himself.

The book is written for beginners at floating flies, not for seasoned experts. Chapters cover equipment, the fly rod, the reel, line, and flies, then how, where, and when to cast and fish the floating fly. A final chapter treats the insects of the trout stream. Readers get a plain starter manual for dry fly fishing.
46173-tourmalin-s-time-cheques:
Anstey's 'Tourmalin's Time Cheques' was first published in 1885 and reprinted by Greenhill Books in 1986, complete and unabridged. A prologue on shipboard, over curry and culture, brings Peter Tourmalin to an oath, a talisman, and a time bargain. Tourmalin opens an account, drawing cheques against time itself, and the chapter summaries promise startling results from the first experiment.

Later chapters draw the second, third, and fourth cheques, then a series of periodic drawings with advantages and drawbacks. Sophia presses questions, confidence breaks and is restored, and Peter's continued perversity brings unforeseen results. The tale climbs to a culminating cheque, a settling in his own coin, and compound interest. Anstey keeps the banking frame strict: every hour drawn must somehow be paid.
46262-pilgrim-sorrow-a-cycle-of-tales:
Carmen Sylva, the pen name of Queen Elisabeth of Roumania, wrote the tales in Pilgrim Sorrow. Helen Zimmern translated them from the German, and Henry Holt and Company published the book in New York in 1884. A long introduction presents the queen, her country, and her writing life.

The contents list twelve pieces: The Child of the Sun, Sorrow, The Realm of Peace, Earthly Powers, The Inexorable, Willi, The Hermit, Lotty, Medusa, Heavenly Gifts, The Treasure Seekers, and A Life. The introduction tells how the queen wrote in German, her native tongue, and took her pen name from the forests she loved as a girl on the Rhine. Roumania, it notes, had won respect in the Turkish war, and its queen had gained a name among German authors in a few short years. Readers get fairy-tinged tales from a throne, in an early English dress.
46292-selina-her-hopeful-efforts-and-her:
George Madden Martin wrote a novel in 1914 about an American girl of the eighteen eighties, with pictures by H D Williams. In a letter at the front, Martin explains the choice of subject. Selina was born late Victorian, when fine tenets had hardened into mere letter. The age around her, Martin says, grew sentimental, trite, and prudish.

Martin reads Selina as piteous rather than heroic, groping rather than grasping. Yet she and her companions repudiated their condition. In maturity they became pioneers for the women who followed. The subtitle promises her hopeful efforts and her livelier failures. The book studies a girl caught between two eras.
46304-the-silent-rifleman-a-tale-of-the-:
The Silent Rifleman, a tale of the Texan prairies from Jackson's Novels, opens an hour or two before sunset in late September. A lone horseman rides west across the high dry prairie between the upper Nueces and the Bravo del Norte. He is small and spare, with arms of extraordinary length, and he is armed like a walking arsenal.

A short heavy English rifle hangs across his shoulder, a two-edged sword and a hunting knife at his waist, duelling pistols in his saddle holsters, and a spiked hatchet at the pommel. A fat buck's loin rides behind him. Frontier danger plainly lies ahead.
46318-jungle-folk-indian-natural-history:
Douglas Dewar wrote jungle sketches of India's beasts and birds in their haunts. His book came out in London and New York in 1912. Of Indian Birds in General leads his list of parts. Sound cuckoos and the brown rock chat fill the first parts. The scavenge bird in wait and wagtails take their due turns.

The teesa, hawk craft in India, and small hawks build the mid. Bee eaters at rest and owls stand in his keen watch list. A pack of ill deeds and how beasts' acts read fill two parts. The coot, the fair porphyrio, and the cobra mark the late row. The mungoose and the swan close this part of the book. Field fans feast.
46366-down-the-ice-and-other-winter-spor:
Harold Sherman wrote these winter sports stories for boy readers at play. Goldsmith printed the book at Chicago in 1932. Contents hold Down the Ice, The Ice Cyclone, and Crabby tales. The Ski Battle, Ski Police, and Penalty Box fill the set.

Down the Ice opens with Carl Hemmer on a famed solo dash. Taber High great hockey star splits Howard Prep defence wide open. Twice he charged in to smack the puck past the goalie. No team yet had kept Carl bottled up in a game. Criss Crossed Skis closes the contents of the winter sports story set for boys.
46367-talbot-s-angles:
Talbot Angles is a story by Amy Blanchard, published by Dana Estes at Boston in 1911. Blanchard is named as author of A Journey of Joy and Wits End. A frontispiece at page 147 shows a proud greeting between two of her people. Contents list chapters of the Talbot household for the tale.

At End of Day, A Clinging Vine, and Leaving the Nest open the book in order. Departed Days, The Alarm, and An Inquisitive Neighbor follow in the list of chapters. Was It Curiosity, A Disclosure, and The Letters on the Trunk raise the family mystery in turn. Pursuing Clues, A Newspaper, A Brace of Ducks, and An Ancestral Pilgrimage fill the middle chapters. Blanchard wrote girls books of home and neighbourhood, and her angles here are the corners of a house of secrets: trunk letters, neighbours, and an ancestral journey worked into a quiet plot.
46397-legends-autobiographical-sketches:
August Strindberg bares a tormented season in Legends, autobiographical sketches issued by Andrew Melrose of London in 1912. The contents run from The Possessed Exorcist and Miracles through Studies in Swedenborg and extracts from his diary of 1897. Chapters on Paris and on Wrestling Jacob close the set.

It opens in December 1896 with Strindberg hunted by the furies and fixed fast at Lund, a small university town he calls his prison. Broke for three years, with twenty-four dramas unperformed and his books out of print, he reads his poverty as a penance laid on by Providence. Raw confession follows.
46403-the-cruise-of-the-make-believes:
Tom Gallon's novel of 1907 opens on Arcadia Street in Islington, where a thin young man in a glossy hat argues with a cabman over the fare. The contents give the story's shape in chapter titles: The Princess Next Door, The King of a Lean Kingdom, and The Great Game of Make-Believe.

Later chapters promise schemers and dreamers, farewell to Arcadia Street, pursuit, castaways, and the simple life. The frontispiece caption quotes the hero: to all intents and purposes I am a rich man. Gallon, author of Tatterley and Meg the Lady, builds a romance of pretending on a poor street, where make-believe money buys real feeling.
46414-a-history-of-bibliographies-of-bib:
Archer Taylor wrote this curious history for the Scarecrow Press in New Brunswick in 1955. His subject is bibliographies of bibliographies: lists of lists of books. The chapters trace the form from its beginnings, through its coming of age, to lists of books that carried the title 'Bibliotheca' on their pages.

Taylor then shows the field starting anew in a later age. He treats such lists as periodical and shared ventures before a short conclusion. His first case reaches back to Jerome, whose introduction of A.D. 392 may hold the first such list, naming nine men who had written bibliographies of various kinds.
46418-petals-plucked-from-sunny-climes:
Petals Plucked from Sunny Climes is a Florida book by Silvia Sunshine, printed at Nashville in 1880 for the author. A front picture shows the founding of Saint Augustine by Pedro Menendez on September 8, 1565. Its opening note describes the contents plainly. The book gives a brief account of Florida's early settlement and its Indian conflicts, with many amusing incidents of its present history.

It is also a collection of travels and sights in various parts of Florida, Key West, and Cuba. A gazetteer and Florida guide book are attached for tourists and settlers. In her history chapters the author says she sifted clashing accounts. She kept the most tangible events and rejected many tales taken as truth by shallow observers. Such sunny clime books sold the new state to northern readers after the war. This one mixes old Spanish days, Seminole wars, and steamboat era touring.
46438-archery-rules:
Archery Rules is a small guide to the sport of archery, sold by Hinrichs of Park Place, New York, for fifteen cents. It opens by praising the bow: archery trains the eye, gives a graceful carriage, expands the chest, and brings walking exercise without fatigue. The sport, it says, suits both sexes and holds its place as the first of English sports.

The guide then treats the archer's outfit: how to choose it and how to care for it. Price lists show bows for ladies in lemon wood and lance wood, and arrows from cheap practice shafts to the best footed kind. The writer warns against cheap gear from poor makers, since sound tools cost less in the end.
46486-rhymes-and-jingles:
Mary Mapes Dodge, the author of Hans Brinker, made this book of verses for children. Scribner, Armstrong published it at New York in 1875. The contents run to dozens of short pieces, sorted loosely as they come. Elfin Jack and The Mayor of Scuttleton open the book. Fire in the Window, Cousin Jeremy, and Thinking Aloud follow, with a song of St Nicholas and a stocking song for Christmas Eve among them.

A set of garden songs gives the book its freshest pages: the little green hummer, the tiger lily, and the evening primrose. The hollyhock must bend to make a cheese for a dolly's tea. Later come The Little Mother, Billy Boy, Shepherd John, and the star family. Dodge edited St Nicholas magazine for children, and these rhymes have its manner: quick, musical, and never talking down.
46528-whispering-tongues:
Whispering Tongues is a college novel for young people by Homer Greene, published in 1902. Crowell of New York issued it in the Golden Hour Series. Greene dedicates it to Professor William Wells of Union College. Generations of students knew and loved him as Billy Wells. Lines from Coleridge on whispering tongues stand as the motto. The moonlight rush opens the chapters in earnest.
