Twelve sophomores of Concord College march singing toward the grounds. The Gamma Questers, a college society, come next in the contents. The boys face the faculty before the quarrel of friends begins. A cowardly revenge and an almost tragedy darken the middle. The welcome home closes the tale. Greene, a Union man himself, writes of honour among college friends. Slander between friends is the book's true villain.
46552-the-story-of-bruges:
Ernest Gilliat-Smith wrote this history, The Story of Bruges, with pictures by Edith Calvert and Herbert Railton, printed in London. A verse about treading on reverend history heads the book. Editions ran from 1901 to a fourth in 1909, and tables of the counts of Flanders help the reader keep the rulers straight.

Twenty-five chapters tell the city's whole life. The first Flemings and earliest Bruges lead to Arnulph the Great, the murder of Charles the Good, and vengeance for it. Charters, counts, and the Battle of the Golden Spurs follow, then Bruges under Burgundy, its great humiliation, and its final catastrophe. Two chapters study the builders and painters of the fifteenth century, and one closes on modern Bruges.
46648-an-old-english-home-and-its-depend:
Old English Home and Its Dependencies is a survey by Baring-Gould of manor life. Methuen published it in London in the year 1898 with plates. Bond drew the illustrations of halls, cottages, and churches inside it. Contents open with paternal acres and the manor house in turn. The domestic hearth and old furniture fill the next two chapters.

Ceilings, the parish church, and the village inn follow in his survey. The manor mill, the farmhouse, and cottages complete the estate's buildings. The village doctor and scapegraces add the human furniture of the parish. Hedges and underground rights close the author's ground level tour. Baring-Gould preserves a vanishing rural England house by house.
46662-the-story-of-chartres:
The Story of Chartres is a guide and history by Cecil Headlam, printed by Dent at London in 1902. Herbert Railton drew its illustrations, one showing the Rue du Bourg. The title page gathers praise: Walter Pater called the cathedral a world to explore, as if one explored the entire Middle Ages. Lowell called it the most wonderful thing in France.

A verse of Robert Wace tells how the church of the Virgin's chemise was held in great cherishing. The chapters open with Druids and Romans at the crypt, then saints and barbarians. The book walks the reader from Paris, an hour and a half by train, into the town and up to the great church. Headlam writes the town's whole past as a road to its cathedral, in the manner of the medieval towns series.
46733-a-string-of-pearls-second-book-of-:
A String of Pearls is the second book of the Faith-Promoting Series, issued by the Juvenile Instructor Office in Salt Lake City. This second edition dates to 1882, and its preface says the first edition of 5,000 copies is exhausted. The series was designed for the instruction and encouragement of young Latter-day Saints.

The preface to the first edition, dated October 1880, explains the plan. The first book, My First Mission, was well received, so the publishers gathered more personal experiences from elders who had laboured in the ministry in various lands. The aim is to give young readers evidence that God hears and answers prayer, against an age of doubt and unbelief.
46734-scraps-of-biography-tenth-book-of-:
Scraps of Biography is the tenth book of a set made to build faith, put out at Salt Lake City in eighteen eighty three. Its bill says it is made for the teach and heart cheer of young folk of the Saints. The rights were sought that year at the great book house of the land's chief town. A first word at the front speaks to the sires and dames of that folk.

There is, it says, a growth of love for read and study past the young of this folk. It is now the hope of near each son and daughter of the Saints to be well taught. Sires and dames take a more deep share in the growth of the young mind as well.
46759-philosophic-nights-in-paris-being-:
Remy de Gourmont's Philosophic Nights in Paris, selections from his Promenades Philosophiques in Isaac Goldberg's translation, was published by Luce and Company at Boston in 1920. The introduction, called Footprints on the Sand, tells how Gourmont came to the Mercure de France. In the autumn of 1889 the founders wanted collaborators, and a cataloguer at the national library spoke of an extraordinary man at the library who knew everything.

That prodigy was Gourmont, who had published ten volumes and a hundred articles on every subject, yet lived in seclusion and was known to none of the literary set. Dumur's obituary note, quoted here, calls him the most complete representative of their literary generation. The selections that follow show the promenade manner: short walks of thought through Paris nights, on literature and everything else.
46769-flower-o-the-heather-a-story-of-th:
Robert William MacKenna wrote this story of the Killing Times, first printed at London in October 1922 and reprinted again and again through the decade. The Killing Times were the years when Scotland's Covenanters were hunted for their faith. The tale opens on a bridge and by a river, with a trooper of Lag's horse riding into the story.

Chapters follow a field meeting, a Covenanter's charity, pursuit, and hiding in the lap of the hills. There are tavern brawls, a flute player, a packman, and the tolbooth of Dumfries, where prisoners waited their fate. MacKenna builds a tale of love and loyalty under persecution, told in Scots speech and grounded in the cruel history every Scottish child once learned.
46802-the-biotic-associations-of-cockroa:
Louis Roth and Edwin Willis, of the Army Quartermaster Research and Engineering Center at Natick, Massachusetts, wrote this scientific study of the living things that associate with cockroaches. The Smithsonian Institution published it in Washington on December 2, 1960, as the whole of volume 141 of the Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections. Thirty-seven plates of photographs support the text.

The front matter explains the series, which since 1916 had carried the Institution's direct papers in every branch of science. The authors worked in the Pioneering Research Division, where cockroaches mattered as pests of food and stores. Their subject, the biotic associations of the roach, covers the creatures that live on, in, and around it. A fine photograph of a large tropical species opens the plates. Entomologists get a full-dress monograph on the company a cockroach keeps.
46849-animal-life-of-the-british-isles:
Edward Step wrote this pocket guide to the mammals, reptiles, and batrachians of the British Isles. It came out in London in 1921 in the Wayside and Woodland series. The book carries 111 plates from photographs by Stokoe, with 48 of them in colour, and opens with a frontispiece of a hedgehog facing a grass snake.

Chapters sort the animals by kind, from moles, shrews, and hedgehogs to bats, foxes, badgers, rabbits, and deer. Lizards, snakes, frogs, toads, and newts close the main text, followed by a classified index. Step notes that some past animals, such as the beaver and the wolf, are gone from wild Britain, which makes the guide a record of what still remains.
46851-the-preservation-of-antiquities:
Friedrich Rathgen's handbook for curators, in George Auden and Harold Auden's translation from the German, came out at the Cambridge University Press in 1905. Rathgen directed the laboratory of the Royal Museums at Berlin, and the translation was made by permission of the museum authorities. An epigraph from Sir Thomas Browne's Hydriotaphia heads the title page.

Rathgen's preface says that only one earlier work, the Merkbuch prepared by Voss for the government, had covered the whole field, and that only as a selection of methods. His own ten years in the Berlin laboratory, and journeys to learn methods in use elsewhere, stand behind the fuller treatment. The book addresses the keeping of antiquities against the decay that time works on them.
46894-volcanoes:
Volcanoes is a booklet by Tilling for the United States Geological Survey. Its cover pictures the eruption of Cerro Negro in Nicaragua in November 1968. A second picture shows lava fountains on Mauna Loa in July 1975. The text opens with the eruption of Mount St. Helens on May 18, 1980.

Tilling sets destruction against creation. Volcanoes form more than eighty percent of the Earth's surface, above and below sea level. Their gases built the first oceans and air. Their soils draw people to live on their flanks. The booklet gives the nature, workings, products, and hazards of the common kinds of volcano, and a word on how they are watched.
46923-epics-and-romances-of-the-middle-a:
M W Macdowall adapted Epics and Romances of the Middle Ages from the German work of Doctor W Wägner, and W S W Anson edited the version. W Swan Sonnenschein issued the second edition at London in 1884, with many illustrations. Anson also edited Wägner's Asgard and the Gods.

The opening essay argues that legend is not history, yet holds historical truth, manners, and beliefs that history drops. Alboin raising a goblet made from a royal skull stalks the first page. Siegfried with Chriemhild and the jealous Brunhild follow, with brave King Dietrich and the patient Gudrun and her mother Hilde. Evil men win for a time, the essay says, yet ever meet a stronger power in virtue.
46984-the-ga-takama-la-or-garland-of-bir:
The Gatakamala, or Garland of Birth-Stories, by Arya Sura, was translated from the Sanskrit by Speyer and published in London in 1895. The volume is the first of a series called Sacred Books of the Buddhists. That series was edited by Max Muller, and published under the patronage of the King of Siam.

In his editor preface Muller explains the series origin. After the Sacred Books of the East were complete, in forty nine volumes, he still had offers of good translations. They were chiefly of Buddhist texts, and he did not wish to leave them unpublished. Buddhist friends told him the King of Siam wished the true teaching of the Buddha to become more widely known in Europe. Readers get elegant Sanskrit tales of the Buddha past lives, told as a garland of stories.
46988-mother-west-wind-when-stories:
Mother West Wind When Stories, by Thornton Burgess, is a nature tale set for children. Little, Brown issued it at Boston in 1917 with colour plates by Harrison Cady. Burgess dedicates it to children and to elders who keep a child heart. Peter Rabbit loves Winsome Bluebird song as herald of Mistress Spring each year.

Grandfather Frog tells why Bluebird wears so fine a sky blue coat. His ancestor won it as reward for brave service to spring long ago. No one else would carry the glad message; he dared, and was honored. When stories explain how the meadow folk got their marks and ways. Bedtime nature lore in Burgess gentle style fills the book.
47018-a-dictionary-of-slang-cant-and-vul:
A London antiquary made a dictionary of slang, cant, and vulgar words, printed in London in 1860. Hotten issued this second edition, revised with two thousand more words. The full title claims speech from London streets, both universities, Parliament, and the dens of Saint Giles. A history of cant comes before the word list.

A cadger's map of a begging district stands at the front. Its signs warn where a house is no good, where a cold potato is safe, and where a dog waits. One sign marks a house as dangerous, with a month in prison sure. The preface says the first edition sold out in weeks. This one holds near five thousand words, with glossaries of the secret speech of costermongers and patterers.
47022-essays-on-the-greek-romances:
Essays on the Greek Romances is a work of classical scholarship by Elizabeth Hazelton Haight, professor emeritus of Latin at Vassar College. Longmans, Green and Company published it in New York in 1943. Two Vassar research funds helped make the book possible.

Haight's preface begins with a proverb: if all the world loves a lover, her book should win wide fame. The Greek romances of the first to the fourth century still sing, she writes, the refrain of the Vigil of Venus: let those love now who never loved before. At a time when fiction is the most popular form of literature, these wonderful old stories of love, adventure and worship are half forgotten. Their appeal, she argues, should be as great for the general reader as for the scholar. They mirror life round the Mediterranean under Rome: travel, piracy, kidnapping and reunion.
47108-deserts-geology-and-resources:
Walker wrote a guide to deserts for the United States Geological Survey. The guide opens with a Navajo chant on beauty in the desert. It asks a plain first question, what is a desert. About one third of the land on Earth is desert, dry land with scant rain and sparse plants.

Deserts may be hot or cold, sand or rock and gravel. The guide tells how deserts form, how wind and water shape dunes and stone, and what plants and beasts live there. It also covers the wealth found in dry lands, such as minerals and water held deep below ground, and the care such lands need.
47120-quarter-back-bates:
Quarter-Back Bates is a school football novel by Ralph Henry Barbour, printed at New York in 1920. Frank J Rigney drew the illustrations. The hero is Dick Bates, whose father is one of the very few persons left in Leonardville who can afford an automobile and still drives horses. The first chapter is called The Departure of a Hero.

The contents follow Dick through room-mates, enemies, and letters and rhymes. Blashington runs through the tale. Chapters treat the Phillipsburg game, the last quarter, and Captain Peters entertaining. Mr Bates protests, publicity follows, and two scraps of paper come into play. Blash confesses, Kenwood scores, and the last chapter gives the book its title. The frontispiece shows a forward pass, fairly high, with a defender reaching to spoil it. Barbour wrote many school sports tales; this is his quarterback's story.
4714-mr-achilles:
Jennette Lee published Mr. Achilles in 1912, opening with Achilles Alexandrakis arranging fruit on his stall in front of his little shop on Clark Street, Chicago. On a clear, breezy October morning, cool but not cold enough to endanger his fruit, he builds oranges into a yellow pyramid, grouping figs, dates, melons, pears, grapes, and pineapples around them. That happy moment, arranging fruit with dark, slender fingers, is the best of his day.

Already Alcibiades and Yaxis have left with pushcarts, north and south, calling antiphonally in clear, high voices that fade as they go. They will not return until night. From that shop grows a story of Greek immigrants, work, friendship, and American city life. Readers get a warm, humane novel about a fruit seller and his neighbours, told with care for small daily joys.
47232-the-book-of-roses:
The Book of Roses, by Francis Parkman, is a grower guide from 1871. Parkman opens with open air culture and the rose need for rich fare. Queen of flowers, the rose starves on a meagre diet, he warns. Sandy gravel soil is worst; wet dense clay is scarcely better in kind.

Deep rich loam, well manured, suits strong roses best, he advises. Poor sand beds can be dug out and rebuilt with heavy loam. Rotted sods, decayed leaves, and stable manure enrich the new bed in turn. One part manure to three parts soil is not excess, he says. Wet beds need drains, tile laid, or a sunken barrel trick.
47234-on-the-origin-of-inflammation-of-t:
Henry Lee, assistant surgeon to King's College Hospital, wrote this treatise on the origin of inflammation of the veins, printed in London in 1850. The full title adds the causes, outcome, and treatment of purulent deposits. A plate shows the first morbid look brought on by the stagnation of spoiled blood in the small vessels of the lungs. Lines from Hamlet on blood curdling like milk head the work.

A preface notes that since humoral pathology fell into earned disrepute, few have tried to define when morbid secretions pass into the circulation. The diseases raised by spoiled fluids far from their source, Lee argues, hold too low a place in systems of medicine and surgery. Tracing such secretions once mixed with the blood is hard and often fruitless work, he owns. The pathology of the solid parts has drawn a share of attention far beyond its due.
47274-history-of-company-k-1st-inft-penn:
Minnigh's History of Company K, 1st Infantry, Pennsylvania Reserves, subtitled The Boys Who Fought at Home, was published at Duncansville, Pennsylvania, under an 1891 copyright. Minnigh was the company's captain and a brevet major. He gives the little volume to the wives, daughters, fathers, and mothers who gave their loved ones to the Union cause.

His preface is frank about limits. He has gathered a few prominent incidents of the company's history, as they present themselves after the facts have passed almost beyond recall, and omitted much for brevity's sake. Children and children's children, scanning these pages, may boast of ancestors who were among the boys who fought at Gettysburg, their own home. He knows inaccuracies will be found; the collecting went on amid other duties. A larger revised edition, he adds, is already begun, and comrades are asked for corrections and additions toward it.
47283-lazy-matilda-and-other-tales:
Lazy Matilda and Other Tales is a book of verse tales for children by Katharine Pyle, put out in New York by Dutton in 1921. Thirteen tales fill the book, each told in rhyme. The first gives the book its name. Matilda is a shirk who would run a mile to get away from work. Her mother scolds her, but Mattie only shrugs and sulks. She leaves her room undusted and slips out to the fields.

In the wood she finds a grey house where a dwarf stands in the door. He takes her in as a servant maid, like it or not. He makes her cook and work all day, with no chance to run. A starved cat begs her for scraps, and the tale turns on that small bond. The rest of the book holds kindred lessons.
47284-favorite-nursery-rhymes:
Favorite Nursery Rhymes is a picture book of the old rhymes, printed in New York under a 1906 copyright with pictures by Ethel Franklin Betts. A color frontispiece shows Mother Goose and the children. The contents list the rhymes in order, from Rain, Rain, Go Away and Little Boy Blue onward. Curly Locks, Humpty Dumpty, and the dogs-do-bark rhyme stand early in the list.

Hey, Diddle, Diddle, Little Bo-Peep, and Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary follow. Jack and Jill, Jack Be Nimble, Hickory, Dickory, Dock, and Little Miss Muffet are all here. So are Little Jack Horner, Sing a Song of Sixpence, Peter, Peter, Pumpkin Eater, and Three Wise Men of Gotham. Color plates show Little Boy Blue, Mary at her garden, Miss Muffet, Jack and Jill, and Jack Horner at his pie. More pictures in black and white scatter through the pages.
47340-earthquakes:
Earthquakes is a general-interest booklet by Kaye Shedlock and Louis Pakiser, issued by the United States Geological Survey. It sold through the Government Printing Office in Washington. A picture shows Charleston, South Carolina, after the great earthquake of August 31, 1886. The authors call a severe earthquake one of the most frightening and destructive works of nature.

An earthquake, they explain, is a sudden movement of the earth when stored strain breaks free. The plates that form the earth's surface move slowly over, under, and past each other. When locked plates snap loose in a peopled place, deaths and great damage follow. The booklet closes with safety guidance for quake country.
4739-fly-leaves:
C. S. Calverley, author of Verses and Translations, published Fly Leaves at Cambridge in 1884, in a tenth thousand printing from Deighton, Bell and Company, with George Bell and Sons in London. Its contents run from Morning and Evening, through Shelter and In the Gloaming, to The Palace, Peace, and The Arab. Lines on hearing the organ, Changed, First Love, and Wanderers follow, with Sad Memories, Companions, and a Ballad.

Later poems include Precious Stones, Disaster, Contentment, and The Schoolmaster, with Arcades Ambo, Waiting, Play, and Love. Thoughts at a railway station, On the Brink, Forever, Under the Trees, and Motherhood lead to Mystery, Flight, On the Beach, and Lovers, and a Reflection. The Cock and the Bull and an Examination Paper close the set. Morning opens with white-horsed Day chasing Night's mares away, as Phoebus opens dawn's gates. Readers get witty, musical Victorian light verse, polished and playful.
47456-notes-on-bookbinding-for-libraries:
John Cotton Dana wrote Notes on Bookbinding for Libraries. The Library Bureau of Chicago issued this enlarged round in 1910. Dana ran the Free Public Library of Newark. A plate from Diderot's great work fronts the book. That plate of 1771 shows a binder's shop. A man beats a book at one bench.

A woman sews at a second bench in the plate. A third man trims book edges there. A fourth works a press beside them. Tools below run from marble slabs to thread balls. A quote from Naude warns on binding costs. Cut the vain spend on covers, he urges. Buy the books a library lacks with those funds. A working librarian's brief for sound, cheap binding that spends money on books, not show.
47471-the-girls-of-chequertrees:
Marion Webb wrote this girls' tale, first published by Harrap in London in September 1918. Percy Tarrant illustrated Chequertrees for the publisher, with a reprint in 1923. A plate shows Pamela reading the signature of Beryl's mother through a blur of tears.

The window opposite opens the contents, and Pamela receives a strange invitation next. Beryl, a room with a locked door and making plans follow in the chapter list. Millicent Jackson gives information, Beryl goes through an ordeal and Isobel makes trouble, in a school-and-home mystery by the author of 'Knock Three Times.'
47485-moral-tales:
Moral Tales, by Madame Guizot, was turned from the French by Mrs Burke and issued by Routledge at London. A plate motto asks whether the teller shall relate the history of a louis. All the adventures that coin has met with are promised there. The preface tells how celebrated the author’s writings are in France.

Some part of that fame may come from her place as a statesman’s wife, it grants. Her husband was an illustrious statesman and historian of France. Such a position draws a severer criticism than usual, the preface notes. But the works have merits of far too decided an order, it argues. Her tales teach children through small lives, gifts, and losses. A gold coin passing from hand to hand carries one famous tale.
47494-talks-on-writing-english-first-ser:
Talks on Writing English, First Series, is a style manual by Arlo Bates, a novelist and teacher of writing. Bates's novels, including The Puritans, The Philistines, and The Pagans, are listed in the front matter at set prices. The talks grew from his classroom work on prose craft. Seven footnotes are placed at chapter ends in the hosted text, its note explains.

Bates treats sentences, words, and clarity as matters a writer can study and fix. His talks speak to students who must write essays, letters, and stories that hold a reader. Against mere grammar drill, he sets taste and practice. The book pairs with his fiction as the workshop side of one writing life.
47506-the-coming-of-the-fairies:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Coming of the Fairies, illustrated from photographs, issued in New York by George H Doran Company with copyright in nineteen twenty one and twenty two. A front plate shows E L Gardner of the Theosophical Society. Plates show Elsie and the gnome, Frances and the fairies, and Cottingley Beck and glen. Eight chapters fill the book. Chapter one is How the Matter Arose.

Two girls at Cottingley in Yorkshire claimed to photograph fairies in nineteen seventeen and nineteen twenty. Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes and a convinced spiritualist, took up their case. The First Published Account, from the Strand Christmas number of nineteen twenty, fills chapter two. Reception of the first photographs and a second series follow. Observations of a clairvoyant in the glen and independent evidence for fairies close the case. Curious readers get a famed credulous classic.
47512-chats-on-old-miniatures:
Chats on Old Miniatures, by Foster, was published in London in 1908. Fisher Unwin issued the volume, with 117 illustrations. A portrait of a lady from the Wallace Collection fronts the book. Foster had written on British miniature painters and their works. Fourteen chapters make up the chats. The first treats collecting miniatures and the care of them. Chapter two gives the origin of the art and a method of painting. Enamels and enamel painters take the third.

Holbein, Hilliard, the Olivers, and Samuel Cooper each get a chapter. Petitot, the Georgian artists, and Cosway follow. Royal, private, and public collections are surveyed near the end. A last chapter treats the French school. Foster writes for collectors who want sound knowledge in a friendly form.
47520-our-pilgrim-forefathers-thanksgivi:
Loveday Nelson wrote a school book of Thanksgiving studies, printed at Chicago in 1904. It teaches young children how their country is ruled. A president serves four years, it says, and may be chosen again. No one knows the next president till the votes are cast.

Kings rule for life in some lands, and sons follow fathers. A good king blesses his land, and a cruel one makes poor folk suffer. The book then turns to church going in America. Each family picks the church that helps it most. Churches cost much to build, and the people give the money. Pilgrim tales stand behind the lessons, for young readers at school and home.
47524-elsket-and-other-stories:
Elsket and Other Stories, by Thomas Nelson Page, was printed in New York by Charles Scribner Sons in 1893, under an 1891 copyright. Page had written In Ole Virginia and Two Little Confederates. He gives the book to her memory. Five tales fill the volume.

The list holds Elsket, George Washington Last Duel, P Laski Tunament, Run to Seed, and A Soldier of the Empire. Elsket opens with an old Norsk proverb, the knife hangs loose in the sheath. The narrator spent a month of the summer of 188 in Norway, old Norway. His friend Dr John Robson, as great a fisherman as he is a physician, knew the narrator love of a stream where the trout and he could meet alone. Robson bound him by a solemn oath not to divulge the place. Tale fans get Page.
47527-lillian-morris-and-other-stories:
Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote the stories in Lillian Morris and Other Stories, translated by Jeremiah Curtin and published in 1894. Sienkiewicz was known to English readers for With Fire and Sword and for Without Dogma, a novel of modern Poland. A list of his writings stands at the front.

The title story gives the book its name, and shorter tales fill out the volume beside it. Curtin was the steady English voice of Sienkiewicz in these years, carrying his Polish tales to American readers. The same front matter sets the historical romances in a row: With Fire and Sword, The Deluge, and Pan Michael. Readers new to Sienkiewicz get a gentler door into his work than the great war novels. The stories trade swords for hearts, but the telling is the same.
4758-late-lyrics-and-earlier-with-many-o:
Thomas Hardy published Late Lyrics and Earlier, with Many Other Verses, at London in 1922, with Macmillan. In his apology, roughly half the poems date from recent months, and the remainder are older pieces set aside in manuscript while earlier books went to press. Those earlier books already offered readers enough pages at once, especially amid wartime distraction.

The oldest pieces here, he explains, were simply missed when earlier collections were assembled. Their freshness, now beyond recovery, seemed to offset their rawness and to warrant printing them. A few poems are dated, while other dates cannot be found. Launching such a volume in neo-Georgian days, by a writer who began in mid-Victorian times, called for a few words. Readers get late Hardy lyrics, with older pieces rescued beside them.
4765-loyalties:
John Galsworthy wrote Loyalties as a play in the fifth series of his plays. Charles Winsor, owner of Meldon Court near Newmarket, and his wife Lady Adela head the cast, with Ferdinand de Levis, young, rich, and new. Treisure, Winsor's butler, General Canynge, a racing oracle, and Margaret Orme follow, with Captain Ronald Dandy, retired, and his wife Mabel.

Inspector Dede, Robert, Winsor's footman, and a constable attend, with Augustus Bobbing and Lord St Erth. A footman of the club and Major Colford, a brother officer of Dancy's, appear. Edward Graviter, a solicitor, a young clerk of Twisden and Graviter's, Gilman, a large grocer, and Jacob Twisden, senior partner, complete the cast. Set among racing people, country houses, and clubs, the play tests what loyalty means when friendship, honour, and prejudice collide. Readers get a sharp Galsworthy drama of society judging one of its own.
47682-american-book-plates-a-guide-to-th:
American Book Plates is a guide to the study of book plates, by Charles Dexter Allen, printed in New York and London in 1894. Eben Newell Hewins made the list of books at the back. Allen sat in the Ex Libris Society of London and the Grolier Club of New York.

Book plates, or ex libris marks, are the printed labels owners paste in books to show the book is theirs. Allen says book plate writing would soon have its own place in library catalogues. He thanks collectors, among them a Miss Libbie of Boston, for loans of fine sets and for ready counsel. Many plates are shown in the book, some printed from the first coppers. Book fans get the art and past of the book plate in one rich guide.
47735-the-bull-calf-and-other-tales:
Frost, the famed American humorous artist, made a book of picture tales, copyrighted in 1892 by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York. The first tale, The Humane Man and the Bull Calf, is told almost wholly in captioned drawings. A humane man sees a pretty calf bound for veal and buys him to save him.

The former owner warns him not to tie the rope around his waist, but the calf proves no gentle thing. A small dog joins in, and the man is dragged down a stony hill in a circus performance. At the end he gives the calf to the boys, on condition he be made at once into minced veal. Nine more tales follow the same plan.
47761-the-dates-of-variously-shaped-shie:
George Grazebrook wrote this study of shields and their dates, printed at Liverpool in 1890 for private circulation. The work grew out of a paper read before the Historic Society of Lancashire and Cheshire. Grazebrook calls his line of enquiry one never before attempted.

His plan is to date shields by their shapes, matching each form to examples with known dates. He leans on seals as the chief source of evidence for old shields. In the preface he asks fellow antiquaries for firm criticism with exact references, hoping a later issue could serve as a handbook. He mourns that the seal knowledge of Albert Way and Charles Spencer Perceval died with them, unrecorded. The book is a small, earnest tool for students of heraldry.
47764-stories-of-heroic-deeds-for-boys-a:
Stories of Heroic Deeds for Boys and Girls is a school history reader by James Johonnot, book two of a historical series, published by the American Book Company. A view of Fort Ticonderoga from the eastern shore heads the text. The copyright of 1887 belongs to Appleton.

The preface sets out the plan. Three things were kept in mind: the plan of the series, the thought and sentiment of each lesson, and the language used. The stories are meant to give pupils a taste for history, to teach them to tell fact from fiction, and to stir them to high endeavour by noble example. The thought, Johonnot says, should be readily understood, and the moral lesson should be absorbed rather than learned. He warns the teacher against destroying a lesson by dealing out moral pap. The language is that of common life. American schoolrooms learned their heroes from such books.
47780-the-story-of-the-crusades:
Wilmot Buxton tells a long war tale in The Story of the Crusades, first published in London in December 1910. Harrap made the book, and reprints run on to 1930. Wilmot Buxton had writ Britain Long Ago and The Book of Rustem. A frontispiece shows the first crusaders in sight of Jerusalem.

Twenty two chapters run from Mohammed the prophet to the effect of the Crusades. Mohammed as conqueror, the spread of Islam, and the rise of chivalry set the stage. Peter the Hermit and the Emperor Alexios open the First Crusade. The siege of Antioch and the winning of the Holy City form its peak. Bernard of Clairvaux, Richard Lion Heart, and the Children's Crusade fill the mid run. The Crusade of St Louis and the fall of Acre close the long arc.
47803-coal-and-candlelight-and-other-ver:
Helen Parry Eden published a book of verses at London in 1918. A note from Begbroke that year explains that most had already been printed in England or America. Five numbers appear by special permission of the proprietors of Punch. All the war pieces, she adds, stand in their original order.

A long dedication poem leads the volume, over hills where cromlech and cairn wear lichen and moss, with a Roman road below. The title poem follows pieces called The Distraction and Sir Bat-Ears, and verses on trees and a figure named Simkin join them. Eden had earlier published Bread and Circuses with the same house. Verse written through wartime fills the book.
4783-riley-farm-rhymes:
James Whitcomb Riley wrote Riley Farm-Rhymes, inscribed to the good old-fashioned people. Its opening poem finds deadening and thicket boiling full of June, from cricket rattle to yellow-hammer tune. The catbird in the bottom and the sap-sucker on the snag seem able only to brag. Music fills the twitter of bluebird and jay, a sassy critter's pecking all day, the flicker, the thrush, and a chipmunk's snicker in the brush.

Music sends the speaker back in a sweeter-than-sleep dream, to a stream splitting the meadow where dandelions grew, where he stands knee-deep, redder than sunset down the road. Contents include Brook Song, The Canary at the Farm, A Clover, and The Country Pathway, with How John Quit the Farm, June, and Mylo Jones's Wife. Old-fashioned farm life, in Riley's dialect, runs through the book. Readers get musical farm rhymes.
47856-what-the-boys-did-over-there-by-th:
What the Boys Did Over There gathers first-hand accounts by Allied soldiers of the Great War. Fox edited the collection. A veterans' stories company published it in New York. The copyrights date to 1918 and 1919. The book is dedicated to the boys who rest in Belgian and French soil. Their more fortunate comrades offer it.

The contents list some twenty-five experiences. A dispatcher and a machine gunner tell their stories. Flanders, Verdun, and the Ypres salient supply the ground. The fall of Cantigny and the first tanks appear. A Dardanelles campaign closes the list. The editor explains his method plainly. The soldiers' own words are used wherever possible. Literary style was a secondary consideration. Truth unabridged, he judged, would please the public more.
47868-german-society-at-the-close-of-the:
Belfort Bax opened his series on the social side of the Reformation in Germany with this volume, published by Swan Sonnenschein at London in 1894. The theology and the politics, he warns, enter where they strike across social and internal affairs. The period runs from the closing years of the fifteenth century to 1525, the year of the peasant rising. Later volumes would treat the Peasants' War and the Anabaptist movement at Münster.

The chapters survey the ground of revolt: first signs of social and religious unrest, the German town, the revolt of the knighthood, and the new jurisprudence. Literature and folklore of the Reformation get chapters of their own. Bax drew on Ranke, Janssen, and Egelhaaf while reading them against the grain. His subject is the disintegration of a world: the economic and social causes under the religious storm, told for English readers by a socialist historian.
47898-grasses:
H Marshall Ward wrote Grasses, A Handbook for Use in the Field and Laboratory, issued at Cambridge in 1908 as part of the Cambridge Biological Series. Ward was late professor of botany at Cambridge. The book first came out in 1901. Arthur E Shipley edited the series. Ward hopes the book will be used with fresh grass in hand.

Most tasks in the book call for close study with a good hand lens. That mode is too much neglected in modern teaching, Ward holds. The book is not a full manual, he warns. It treats common native grasses in a way that teaches sharp sight. Meadow and pasture study, hay, weeds, and seed grasses are the chief uses. Wide claims on grass life and body fill out the lessons.
47928-time-telling-through-the-ages:
Harry Brearley wrote Time Telling Through the Ages, made by Doubleday, Page for the Ingersoll firm in 1919. The book marks twenty-five years since that firm joined the watch trade. It was planned in the midst of the world war, when plain celebration seemed out of place. Its issue waited till the peace covenant was signed, after the war. Research was done by Katherine Morrissey Dodge, in libraries, trade sheets, and watch schools.

Photos in the book are the work of Lejaren Hiller of New York City. His staged scenes show time tools of each age in use. Brearley traces clocks and watches from the first marks of hours to the modern wrist form. The Ingersoll name, famed for cheap watches, stands behind the work. Readers get a rich, pictured history of how man learned to keep and tell time.
47936-jersey-city-and-its-historic-sites:
Harriet Phillips Eaton wrote this local history at the request of the Woman's Club of Jersey City, which published it in 1899. The proceeds were to set memorial tablets on the city's historic sites. Eaton begins with the Lenni Lenape and their customs, the coming of the Dutch, Pavonia, and Communipaw, and the first ferry, the first roads, and the first church at Bergen.

The Revolutionary chapters cover the Battle of Paulus Hook, Lafayette in Bergen, and the Bergen patriots. Later sections treat early Dutch recipes, spinning and weaving, slavery, lotteries, the forming of the city, ferries, railroads, schools, and churches, down to the old houses and the city of the future. It is a clubwoman's labor of love, packed with small facts no larger history would keep.
47962-the-hidden-servants-and-other-very:
Francesca Alexander spent her life in Italy and gathered the legends of its peasants, and this book retells such very old stories in verse. David Nutt published it at London in 1907, though the copyright is 1900. The introduction recalls hearing the poems from Alexander's own lips, half chanted, half recited, in a quiet room, and speaks of the sunny charity and childlike faith of the people she loved.

Alexander drew as well as wrote: the frontispiece, Marianna and her Vision by the Fire, is from her own drawing. Ruskin had heralded her earlier work with enthusiasm. The tales themselves are saints' legends and folk stories of Tuscany, told over again with the simplicity of the tellers, for readers who want Italy as its poor lived and believed it.
47979-the-true-life-story-of-swiftwater-:
The True Life Story of Swiftwater Bill Gates was written by his mother-in-law, Iola Beebe, and copyrighted in 1908. Chapter heads trace Gates from his first word of the gold find on Bonanza Creek in the Klondike to fame as a big operator and promoter. A famed egg episode in Dawson is told as fact.

Beebe follows his loves, marriages, and flights with a frank, often bitter pen. She tells of gold given to win a bride, rich claims lost to debt, and hard lines for a deserted wife in Dawson, where mounted police showed kindness. Later chapters track more elopements and pursuits. The book is both a gold-rush record and a family reckoning.
47996-eighteenth-century-vignettes:
Eighteenth Century Vignettes gathers twenty papers by Austin Dobson, first printed in 1892. Sixteen of them appeared in America, and only one had been reprinted in England. The rest came from the Saturday Review and other magazines. Dobson arranged them in time order, saving two general papers for the end.

His preface promises more if the public takes to these first tries. A second series followed in 1894, and a third in 1896. The opening paper begins on May 19, 1708, with Queen Anne on the throne. A coach draws up at Lord Sunderland's office in Whitehall, carrying a lady in cinnamon satin. Dobson tells the century's small stories as scenes.
47999-natural-gemstones:
Natural Gemstones is a short guide from the United States Geological Survey, part of the Department of the Interior. It opens with color plates of quartz from Rhode Island and amethyst crystals from Mexico. The text starts by saying that hunting gemstones in the United States is a well liked pastime for collectors and hobbyists.

Plain definitions come first: a natural gemstone, a precious stone, a gem, a mineral, and the work of a gemologist and a lapidary. Diamond, ruby, sapphire, emerald, topaz, and opal are named as precious stones. Later pages tell where gems form, in igneous rock, stream gravels, and pegmatite veins, and why fine stones stay so rare.
48010-animal-parasites-and-messmates:
Animal Parasites and Messmates forms volume nineteen of the International Scientific Series. Monsieur Van Beneden, a professor, wrote the study. The series sold cloth volumes at a dollar fifty cents to two dollars each. Its list shows the wide range of the set.

Tyndall on forms of water leads the whole series. Herbert Spencer on the study of society stands in the roll. Books on descent and on light and photo art join it. Van Beneden’s part treats beasts that live on or in other beasts. Some guests harm their hosts, and some merely share their food. That split gives the book its twin theme. Plain readers in that age bought hard science in this cheap, neat form.
48044-facts-in-jingles:
Winifred Sackville Stoner wrote 'Facts in Jingles' between the ages of five and twelve, and the Bobbs-Merrill Company published the verses at Indianapolis in 1915. A photograph shows Winifred at twelve with her trained bird, Okikusan, and the book is dedicated to Katharine O'Shea of Madison, Wisconsin. The contents list runs to hundreds of short rhymes.

Some jingles carry school facts: England's kings in rhyme, a bony song, grammar in a nutshell, and an Esperanto grammar with an Esperanto poem. Others honour composers in verse, among them Bach, Beethoven, Berlioz, Brahms, and Chopin. Nursery figures get new treatments too, from Bo-Peep and Goosey Gander to Doctor Foster, while pieces on dentists, babies, and split pea soup keep the tone comic.
48051-the-story-of-the-thirteen-colonies:
Story of the Thirteen Colonies is a history for young readers of America. It appeared in The Youth's Library series with illustrations throughout it. A front plate shows Washington with his handwritten signature reproduced there. This edition dates to the year 1898 for school and home. A key to pronunciation in the index serves young readers aloud.

Planting, growth, and revolt of the colonies fill the plain narrative. Founders, wars with France and Indians, and rising taxes lead toward 1776. Portraits and maps guide the eye through the century and a half. Teachers and parents of 1898 bought such lives of the republic in sets. The road from Jamestown to independence is the book's whole arc.
48095-back-o-the-moon-and-other-stories:
Oliver Onions wrote Back o' the Moon and Other Stories, by the author of The Drakestone. The front pages carry press praise for that earlier novel of Yorkshire life. The Spectator called it unlike the usual flimsy modern story.

Reviewers praised Onions for strong drawing of character and a natural run of events. The Academy noted a canvas crowded with well-drawn figures. The Scotsman found the chief interest in Yorkshire country folk of the early eighteen hundreds. The Leeds Mercury said he writes of the dales with rare insight. The present tales share that ground: quiet tone, no cheap sensation, and close knowledge of rustic speech and ways.
48153-fables:
Fables by Ronald Ross was privately printed at the University Press of Liverpool in 1907, in an edition of two hundred and fifty copies. The poems are dedicated to his children, and a note says they were written in India between 1880 and 1890. Ross sets down twenty fables in verse, each with its own cast of beasts, spirits, and men.

The list runs from An Expostulation with Truth to The Poet's Retirement. On the way stand Ariel and the Hippopotamus, The Frog, the Fairy, and the Moon, The Virtuous Goat, and The Contest of Birds. In the first, a well meaning poet begs Truth to leave the world alone, since men must live by belief. The volume shows a man of science writing light verse for his family, and it keeps the moral fable in rhymed, playful form.
48181-six-bad-husbands-and-six-unhappy-w:
Six Bad Husbands and Six Unhappy Wives, by Ella Wheeler Wilcox and published at London in 1912, tells paired tales of marriage gone wrong. Wilcox was famed for volumes such as Poems of Passion and Poems of Power. Her name fronts a long list of verse books in the front matter. The prose tales here take up the same theme of love and its failures.

The first bad husband had been a very good man until he married, the tale begins. He built a sound business and a fair name with no help from others. He climbed without pulling others down on his way up the ladder. Small acts of kindness marked his path, and he gave a dollar where need called for it. What marriage changed in such a man sets the pattern for the six tales that follow.
48190-poganuc-people-their-loves-and-liv:
Poganuc People, their loves and lives, a novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe, was issued by Fords, Howard and Hulbert of New York at a dollar and a half. An engraving at the front shows the parson's daughter. Poganuc is Stowe's village of her Connecticut childhood, drawn from Litchfield, where her father was minister. The novel tells the loves and lives of a New England parish town.

The publisher's pages praise Stowe as a writer whose style is always fresh and whose depiction of human nature is apt and true. Doctor, parson, farmers, and church folk make the cast. The frontispiece catches a girl begging Nabby, the parson's daughter, for news of what they are doing up at the church, with armfuls of spruce and pine carried there all day. Church doings, courtships, and old quarrels of creed fill the village year.
48208-convict-life-at-the-minnesota-stat:
Convict Life at the Minnesota State Prison is an account by W Heilbron. The book was printed at Saint Paul in a run of one thousand copies. Many prints dress the text of jail life at Stillwater. This copy is a second run, set in the year nineteen nine.

New men are called fresh fish by the old hands in the first scene. Cuffs bear a slang name in the talk of the yard and the cell row. Papers are read in a room set between the two great gates of the jail. Notes go at once to each shop chief with the mans name and crime. Rules, work, and talk of the yard fill the plain told book.
48215-a-sheaf-of-roses:
Elizabeth Gordon wrote a book of rose poems in 1915, with pictures by Frederick W Martin. She dedicated it to kindred spirits who love the beautiful in nature, and to her loyal friends of the Pacific coast. The title poem says each rose is a sign of love divine and true. Gordon offers her sheaf of them to the reader.

Named roses get verses of their own. White Cherokee is born, in her telling, where an angel's tear fell to earth. Cecil Bruner carries a tale of two men who loved the same fair maid. The poems are short, tender, and floral in theme throughout.
48254-moni-the-goat-boy-and-other-storie:
Moni the Goat Boy and Other Stories is a set of tales by Johanna Spyri, translated from the German by Edith Kunz. Ginn and Company published it in Boston in 1906. Spyri is named on the title page as the author of Heidi. The title story runs five chapters, from Moni Is Happy through Moni Sings Once More.

Moni herds goats on a Swiss mountain and sings as he goes. A trouble silences his song until the tale's turn restores it. Other stories follow, among them Without a Friend. Spyri's Alpine tales taught generations of children in many languages. Kunz's translation was made for American school and home reading.
48297-a-soldier-s-daughter-and-other-sto:
G A Henty tells tales of war and risk in a volume issued in London in 1906, with pictures by Frances Ewan. The title story opens at the fort of Darlinger on the North-West frontier of India. Major Ackworth leads troops out to punish raiders, while his daughter Nita has grown up as a tomboy in the barracks yard.

Inside, Nita faces attack, capture, and escape across eight chapters of frontier fighting. Two more tales follow, one on Count Conrad von Waldensturm and one framed as a raid by Black troops. Readers who like Henty's mix of history, danger, and young heroes at the center of the action will find his usual pace here.
48354-cleg-kelly-arab-of-the-city-his-pr:
S R Crockett wrote Cleg Kelly, Arab of the City, issued in New York by D Appleton and Company in eighteen ninety six. Copyright rests from eighteen ninety five. Crockett had earlier written The Lilac Sunbonnet. A frontispiece shows a voice rising from a lake, mocking and bitter. The adventures are numbered in the contents. The Outcasting of Cleg Kelly is adventure one.

The Burning of the Whinny Knowes follows as adventure two. The tale follows a street arab boy in a Scottish city, cast out and making his way. Crockett uniform edition sold each book at one dollar fifty, the publisher list notes. The Lilac Sunbonnet is praised there as a love story pure and simple, wholesome and sunshiny. Boys and general readers get a Scots waif adventure of a city street boy.
48357-elsie-and-her-loved-ones:
Elsie and Her Loved Ones is a novel in the Elsie Dinsmore series by Martha Finley. Dodd, Mead of New York published it in November 1903. A list at the front counts the long shelf of Elsie books before it. Elsie Dinsmore itself stands first, and Elsie's Namesakes last in that line.

The story opens on a lovely spring day at Viamede, in the South. Grandma Elsie, as her young friends love to call her, sits under the orange trees. Her father and his wife, cousins, children, and friends gather on the lawn. Talk turns to the party's return to their more northern homes. Chester sighs that he has been neglecting his business shamefully there. Harold, the cousin who is a doctor, shakes his head with a smile.
48375-maybee-s-stepping-stones:
Maybee's Stepping-Stones is a book of moral stories for children by Archie Fell, published in Boston by Lothrop. Fell wrote other tales for the young, among them Earthen Vessels and Apron-Strings. The book is dedicated to the children of the Sabbath school whose faces the author had watched, week by week, for many years.

The dedication carries his prayer: that the volume may be to them stepping-stones towards heaven. The contents are arranged as a year of weekly readings, each story dated by its Sunday. Titles run from Mother Knows Best and Led Into Sin, and Out, through Naughty Dick and The Little Red House, to Walking With God. Bible verses head the book, and the stories teach their lessons through children, bargains, stratagems, and helping hands. It is Sunday school fare in its classic form.
48379-molly-and-kitty-or-peasant-life-in:
Molly and Kitty, or Peasant Life in Ireland, is a tale translated from the German by Trauermantel. Crosby, Nichols printed it at Boston in 1856. Two other tales stand with it.

The other tales are The Young Artist, by Maria Burg, and Benevolence and Gratitude, by Olga Eschenbach. Eschenbach wrote the title tale. A frontispiece is named Molly's Peasants. The translator gives the book to a young cousin, Ernest, in a letter. Sheltered childhoods, it says, may yet profit from scenes of struggle. The tales teach sympathy with all who suffer, and joy in triumph. Uprightness, perseverance, patient study, and forgiveness are the virtues praised. The tale opens in one of the desolate parts of Ireland. Hovels of rough stone stand there, looking more like graves than houses for the living.
48385-sylvia-arden-decides:
Margaret Rebecca Piper brings back a hilltop heroine in a novel issued in New York in 1917. Sylvia Arden stands by a white pillar at Arden Hall, bright and carefree in the sun, while her friends debate her one fault. Suzanne declares from her hammock that Sylvia is addicted to contentment.

Barbara answers that Sylvia has everything anyone could want and a perfect right to be content. Suzanne, loyal to the Cause, warns that another day among the flesh pots will ruin Barbara for good work. Chapter titles promise missions, city visits, frost, and revelations ahead. Readers get a cheerful tale of a rich, happy girl pressed to choose a serious path for her life.
48393-anecdotes-of-the-great-war-gathere:
Carleton Case gathered these jokes and short tales of the Great War from European sources for the Shrewesbury Publishing Company of Chicago in 1916. The pieces are brief, headed, and built on a single laugh. In one, a café keeper at Havre prints his menus in English for British customers, and the printer offers soup, fish, entrée, joint, sweet, wife and coffee included, for three francs.

In another, a captain orders a corporal to put a hole through a light on the opposite mountain, and the corporal reports that the light is the moon. The captain answers that he does not care for that, and to put a hole through it anyhow. A mother worries over her boy on the tented field, who turns out to work for a traveling circus. Tommy at the barber's fills out the humor.
48402-motor-matt-s-peril-or-cast-away-in:
Stanley R Matthews wrote a Motor Matt story for the Motor Stories weekly, number twelve, dated May 15, 1909 and sold for five cents. The series bills itself as thrilling adventure motor fiction. A picture caption announces that the Hawk was doomed. Motor Matt moves as quickly as he could in the scene shown. Cast away in the Bahamas gives the peril its place.

Motor Matt was Street and Smith's boy inventor hero of the motor age. His stories put engines in boats, cars, and airships. Weekly five cent numbers reached boys across the country. Matthews kept Matt in peril from wreckers, rivals, and the sea itself.
48411-studies-in-the-epistle-of-james:
Robertson, late professor of New Testament study at Louisville, Kentucky, wrote studies in the Epistle of James, first published as Practical and Social Aspects of Christianity. Heber Peacock revised and edited this edition for Broadman Press of Nashville. The first study gathers what is known of James himself.

Robertson takes the author to be James the brother of the Lord, not the brother of John, who died too early. Chapters then follow the letter's themes: joy in trial, the way of temptation, and the practice of the word. Class prejudice, the tongues of teachers, and God and business all get a study. Prayer and perseverance close the book.
48429-soliloquies-in-england-and-later-s:
George Santayana wrote these quiet musings in two sets, and Scribner's printed them at New York in 1922. The first set, Soliloquies in England, runs from 1914 to 1918. The later set runs from 1918 to 1921.

Air and light, praises of water, and cloud castles fill the English pieces. Hamlet's question, the British character, seafaring, and privacy take their turns. Dons, snobs, Dickens, English building, and the English church all pass in review. War shrines and skylarks close the war years. The later pieces turn to masks, plays, and the stage of the world: the tragic mask, the comic mask, carnival, and Queen Mab among them.
48458-within-the-capes:
Within the Capes is Howard Pyle's sea story, first copyrighted in 1885 and reissued at New York in 1901. The tale is told by Captain Tom Granger himself. His family begged him for years to write down his adventures. Granger always refused: a pen never fitted nicely between his stiff fingers, as his wife could tell them.

Now retired, with his sons running the business, he takes up the ink-horn at last. In two crowded years, he says, more happened to him than falls to most men in a lifetime. He rose no higher than second mate of a privateersman. He writes plainly, fearing that gossip would twist him into a pirate and murderer within three generations.
48485-psychologies:
Ronald Ross wrote Psychologies, issued in London by John Murray in nineteen nineteen. Five studies fill the book. The first two originally appeared in The Nation in nineteen thirteen, Ross notes. The last piece contains passages from a drama called Edgar, published in Madras in eighteen eighty three. The Marsh was intended to be a melodrama, but the music for it has not yet been developed, he says.

After Otho had been partially defeated by Vitellius, his soldiers clamoured to be led again to battle, the stage note says. Otho refused in the manner shown here in brief, it adds. Once more to battle, Otho, the soldiers cry. No, not for Rome sake, Otho answers. The Triumph, Evil, The Marsh, and The Boy Dream follow Otho. Readers get five short verse dramas of Roman and inner life.
48510-thirteen-stories:
Thirteen Stories, by Cunninghame Graham, was issued at London by Heinemann in 1900. Graham had written Mogreb el Acksa before this set of tales. He dedicates the sketches, stories, or studies to George Morton Mansel. The two men had galloped together over many leagues of pampa.

Day and night rides in South America stand behind the dedication. Graham hopes the tales are square by the lifts and braces, in a sailor’s joke. Some of the pieces had run in the Saturday Review and other papers. Graham wrote of Spain, Morocco, Scotland, and the pampas with one restless pen. His tales mix travel, character, and sudden death. The thirteen pieces show his range in a single volume.
48547-bees:
Bees is a guide by Phillips, who held charge of bee culture in the Bureau of Entomology. It was issued on May 23, 1911, as Farmers' Bulletin 447 by the United States Department of Agriculture. The bulletin took the place of two earlier ones, with a few new pictures and small changes in the text.

Phillips aimed to give, in brief form, what bee keepers most need and what the department is most often asked. The contents cover the placing of the apiary, hives and tools, the ways of bees, and the main tasks of the yard. Later pages treat queen work, disease checks, dealers in supplies, and laws that touch the trade.
48566-barracks-bivouacs-and-battles:
Archibald Forbes gathered his soldier tales and sketches into a volume issued at London and New York in 1891. All the pieces are reprints, he notes, with thanks to the periodicals that first carried them. The contents run from how a stray creature got on the strength to a forgotten rebellion and a campaign in Pall Mall.

The first tale follows Mick Sullivan, a private in the 30th Light Dragoons who could neither read nor write. His defaulter sheet was full, yet the Queen had a bargain in him. His grizzled captain remembered him limping out of the valley of death with a sword red from hilt to point and a wounded comrade on his back. Forbes writes as an old hand.
48593-as-the-goose-flies:
As the Goose Flies is a fairy tale by Katharine Pyle, written and illustrated by her. Little, Brown and Company published the book at Boston, copyrighted in 1901. Contents list twelve chapters for the tale of the child Ellen. A frontispiece shows a flight toward the dark line of a forest at the start.

Chapter titles promise a tour of the fairy tale world for the heroine in order. Behind the Bookcase and Beyond the Wall open her escape from the nursery world. The Five Little Pigs and the Goat, Up in the Cloud Land, and the House of the Seven Little Dwarfs follow in the list. The Great Gray Wolf, the Magic Lamp, and Bluebeard House fill the middle chapters of the tale. Pyle retold the old tales in her own pictures and prose, and this original tour binds them into one child journey.
48602-the-early-norman-castles-of-the-br:
Armitage wrote this study of the early Norman castles for John Murray, who published it at London in 1912. The plans are by Montgomerie. The frontispiece shows motte-castles as the Bayeux Tapestry draws them, at Dol, Rennes, Dinan, Bayeux, and Hastings. Armitage begins before the Normans, with Anglo-Saxon and Danish fortifications, then asks where the private castle came from. Her answer is the motte: a mound with a timber tower, thrown up fast by a lord who meant to hold new ground.

The middle chapters give the distribution and character of motte-castles, then survey them region by region: England, North and South Wales, Scotland, and Ireland. Stone castles of the Norman period close the argument. A schedule of English castles from the eleventh century and appendices on words like castrum, donjon, and bretasche serve the specialist. The book made the humble earthwork mound into history.
48613-across-the-andes:
Charles Johnson Post wrote Across the Andes, printed in New York in 1912, with pictures by the author. The subtitle calls it a tale of wandering days among the mountains of Bolivia and the jungles of the upper Amazon. Some chapters had first come out as pieces in magazines. A front plate shows a boat running the rapids of the Ratama. A long poem, the tropics, heads the book.

The legion that never was listed, the poem begins: the soft song, the starlight, and the shadowy tropics. Rubber or gold, it runs, the game is old: the lust, the lure, and the venture. The trails gleam white in the tropic night where the restless spirits mould. From dusk to dawn, when the heat is gone, home thoughts nestle and throb. The poem sets the mood for the travel that follows.
48636-stories-and-letters-from-the-trenc:
Stories and Letters from the Trenches was compiled by Ogilvie and published in New York in 1915 by the Ogilvie Publishing Company of 57 Rose Street. A frontispiece photograph shows Belgian soldiers behind an entrenchment on the road to Malines. The preface surveys the letters' writers.

Ogilvie notes that German letters from the field show wide liberty of expression. Allied letters, by contrast, pass under rigid censorship, with names of places, divisions, commanders and dates deleted. The writers range from nobles and royal family members to tradesmen, farmhands and street cleaners. Illiteracy, he adds, is rare even among the privates. The first piece is Bert Hall's account of three months in the trenches, written by an American who served with the French Foreign Legion and became an airman.
487-songs-of-travel-and-other-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers late verse in this volume, sent home for print months before his death in Samoa. Written mostly after he left England in 1887, the poems range from the vagabond's road song to youth and love, highland places, and winter lanes. An editor's note explains their tangled titles and order.

Stevenson meant them to join Underwoods as a third book. Their tone mixes wanderlust, longing, and a traveler's farewell. Lines on the open road and the fading light rank among his most quoted. The volume gives readers his last songs, brief, musical, and full of restless hope.
48703-john-porter-fort-a-memorial-and-pe:
Martha Fort copyrighted this memorial of her father, John Porter Fort, in 1918, printed by the Knickerbocker Press of New York. The foreword explains the book's making. The reminiscences were dictated to her by her father during the summer of 1916.

He touched only upon the main events. They sat together on the porch, or in the library by the open wood fire, while he told the story of a wonderfully full life. Countless unmentioned things would add to it, she writes, but she leaves it just as he told it. To his dictation she adds a few pieces of her own. Fort was a Georgia educator and college president. His daughter's book preserves the voice first and the record second, which is why she lets the porch and the wood fire stand in the foreword.
48722-making-fermented-pickles:
Edwin LeFevre of the Bureau of Chemistry wrote this Farmers' Bulletin, number 1438, issued at Washington in August 1924. The Department of Agriculture aimed it at housewives, pickle makers and extension workers. It revises and replaces an earlier bulletin, number 1159, on the same subject.

Cucumber pickles get the most space, in salt, sour, sweet, dill and mixed forms. Sauerkraut stands beside them as a main topic. String beans, green tomatoes, chayotes, mango melons, burr gherkins, cauliflower and corn on the cob are also covered. Peaches and pears appear too, and the methods suit both home batches and larger trade work.
48737-turkish-harems-circassian-homes:
Mrs Harvey of Ickwell Bury wrote this travel record of a summer in the East, published in London in 1871. Her preface hopes the little volume will recall pleasant memories to those who have visited the sunny lands, and interest armchair travelers for half an hour.

The contents move from Constantinople, the city of the sun, through the hour of prayer and a chapter on the harem. Then they run east: an eastern banquet, Eupatoria, Sevastopol with its traces of war, and Circassia. The book is built from the journals and letters of a yacht's mixed company, English owners with servants of five nations. The first chapter brings the Claymore into the Golden Horn. Ladies' travel in the Ottoman world gets a candid telling.
48747-who-ate-the-pink-sweetmeat-and-oth:
Who Ate the Pink Sweetmeat, and Other Christmas Stories is a holiday story book printed at Boston in 1884. The title tale is by Susan Coolidge. Other stories come from Mary Hartwell Catherwood, Kate Upson Clark, Lady Dunboyne, and E E Hale. Drawings by Smedley, Lungren, and other artists illustrate the book.

Coolidge's tale opens in a very little shop, scarcely larger than a stall, where only three pairs of stockings are left. Job Tuke, the keeper, is too poor to buy superfluous wares. Each spring he lays in thin stockings, cheap handkerchiefs, buttons, and a little stationery. In autumn he adds thick stockings, mittens, and knitted comforters. If his stock runs scant toward midwinter, Job rejoices and lays the money by for spring. The weather had been uncommonly cold since October. The book gathers Christmas tales of shops, rides, and gifts for young readers.
48778-the-sea-fairies:
Sea Fairies is a fairy tale novel by Frank Baum, author of the Oz books for children. Publisher pages in front praise Baum as the most inventive fairy tale writer of his day. John Neill pictures, in colour and in black and white, fill the Oz line adverts. The tale itself stands apart from Oz, turning from dry land to the sea.

Baum sends his young heroes under the waves to meet the sea fairies in their realm. Mermaids, sea folk, and perils of the deep replace the roads of Oz here. The book keeps the same warm address to child readers as the Oz tales. Wonder, peril, and kind magic drive the undersea adventure for its audience.
48794-pioneer-imprints-from-fifty-states:
Pioneer Imprints from Fifty States, by Roger Trienens, was issued in 1973. The Library of Congress published it at Washington. Trienens worked in its descriptive cataloging division. Contents give one entry to each state, in a set order. Each treats the first printing in that state. A picture shows the Lapwai press, brought to Idaho in 1839. Massachusetts opens the book. Stephen Daye set up the first press of English-speaking North America at Cambridge. He printed the famed Bay Psalm Book there in 1640.

That volume of 295 pages is the first substantial book from what is now the United States. Eleven copies survive; the last in private hands came to the Library in 1968. The catalog traces pioneer presses state by state, from colonial Cambridge to Alaska.
48809-plans-and-illustrations-of-prisons:
Hastings H Hart gathered Plans and Illustrations of Prisons and Reformatories for the American Prison Association. The Russell Sage Foundation issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty two. Hart led the group and showed the set at its Detroit congress. A chapel at the new Sing Sing faces the title page.

One paper floats a jail built like a tower for Cook County. Plans for Sing Sing show its clinic and mind wards. Wingdale and Kilby prisons get floor by floor study. Farms for women at Niantic earn a full section. Schools for bad boys show small house style dorms. Judges and builders who plan lockups will find costs and layouts side by side.
48862-little-pitchers-flaxie-frizzle-sto:
Little Pitchers is a children's story book by Sophie May, part of her Flaxie Frizzle Stories. Lee and Shepard of Boston held the copyright from 1878, and the edition shown is theirs of 1895. Sophie May wrote whole shelves of series for young readers. Her Little Prudy stories, Dotty Dimple stories, and Flyaway stories each ran to six volumes, sold separately.

The Flaxie Frizzle series likewise ran to six volumes. It begins with Flaxie Frizzle herself, continues through Doctor Papa, and reaches Little Pitchers as its third volume. Twin Cousins, Flaxie's Kittyleen, and Flaxie's Growing Up complete the set. Each volume was illustrated and sold for seventy-five cents. The publisher's catalogue bound into this copy lists her Quinnebasset books for older girls as well. Little Pitchers belongs to the gentle domestic world of her child characters, written for the youngest readers of the family.
48868-georgia-its-history-condition-and-:
Georgia, Its History, Condition, and Resources, by Samuel A Drake, was printed in New York by Charles Scribner Sons in 1879, with a map. Drake writes a short handbook on one of the thirteen first states of the Union. The book opens with the lay of the land.

Georgia has Tennessee and North Carolina to the north, the Atlantic to the east, Florida south, and Alabama west. The Savannah River parts it from South Carolina, and the Chattahoochee parts it from Alabama. Drake gives its length as 320 miles and its breadth as 256 miles, with 58,000 square miles in all. He sorts the state into three zones by soil, weather, and crops. Readers of 1879 got a plain guide to a Southern state in one slim book.
48890-studies-in-judaism-first-series:
Studies in Judaism, first series, is a set of essays by Solomon Schechter, printed at Philadelphia in 1911 by the Jewish Publication Society of America. Schechter gave the book to the memory of a rabbi of Berlin whom he held dear. The essays were written at Cambridge, and the first treats the Chassidim.

Schechter notes that English students knew little of this movement, though it was full and rich in its growth. The name means the Pious, and the sect rose in Eastern Europe as a revolt against dry, over fine debate by rabbis. Its heart was a hunger for direct touch with God, felt by plain people shut out by hard learning.
48891-front-lines:
Boyd Cable, author of Between the Lines and Action Front, wrote Front Lines for Dutton in New York with copyright in 1918. He dedicates the pieces, written at the front, to the front itself, wishing those there a quick end to the war. Twenty-one chapters run from trench art to stretcher bearers and conquerors.

Chapter one watches Corporal Richard of a London field ambulance return to his trade as a sculptor during a slack spell. Men of the ambulance found stream clay that served for modelling, and Richard made portraits and caricatures of his comrades. Sitters queued up free of cost, and soon half the squad tried the craft themselves. Later chapters cover a suicide club, a diving tank, a raid, and a roaring trade.
48916-outings-at-odd-times:
Charles C Abbott, a doctor of medicine, wrote these nature essays, printed by D Appleton and Company of New York in 1890. Abbott had written A Naturalist's Rambles About Home and Days Out of Doors. His prefatory piece, Nature and Books About It, opens with a long dusty midsummer walk and a wayside spring. Water drunk from the bosom of Mother Earth, he says, makes all other drink tame.

He draws the moral for graver things: he would gather his stores at the fountain-head, with his own hands. Age has softened the rule, and he now takes nature at second hand, yet asks how far another's eyes and ears can be trusted. A horse that seemed to ask him to let down the bars closes the argument.
48928-the-green-god-s-pavilion-a-novel-o:
Mabel Wood Martin wrote this novel of the Philippines, printed at New York under copyright in 1920. Her heroine, Julie, comes by ship to a golden far Eastern city of towers and domes, once the home of galleons and conquistadors. She crowds at the rail with the other passengers, trembling with joy at her first sight of the place.

Julie has lived a detached life under her uncle's roof, always outside the family circle, and she has come east seeking a place of her own. The new world presses on her like a hot weight, and seems to demand some special passport she does not hold. Martin builds a romance of an American girl finding her footing in a land of sun, strangeness, and old Spanish glory.
48985-the-english-flower-garden-with-ill:
The English Flower Garden, published by Macmillan in 1881, is Henry Bright's essay on what a garden should be. Bright had written A Year in a Lancashire Garden before it. The essay first appeared in the Quarterly Review a year earlier. Friends urged him to reprint it before the number was lost and buried.

Bright argues that a garden kept only for masses of gay colour loses half its delight. The true charm comes from making friends of each plant, with its history and associations. Bedding-out, he grants, has its place and can take care of itself. But he hopes flowering shrubs and hardy herbaceous plants will be grown far more widely. Garden owners wrote to tell him the reform was overdue.
48991-leyte-the-return-to-the-philippine:
Hamlin Cannon wrote this official history for the Office of the Chief of Military History in the Department of the Army. It was printed at Washington in 1954 and sold in cloth for six dollars and seventy-five cents. The volume belongs to the series United States Army in World War II. It is the fifth published in the subseries The War in the Pacific, under general editor Kent Roberts Greenfield.

Cannon took his doctorate in history at the American University. He served with the Navy in Australia and New Guinea during the war, and now covers the Leyte campaign of the return to the Philippines. The book stands in sequence with its sister volumes, running from The Fall of the Philippines and Guadalcanal through The Approach to the Philippines. Later volumes in the plan take up the triumph in the Philippines and Okinawa, the last battle.
49000-last-verses:
Last Verses is a book of poems by Susan Coolidge, printed at Boston in 1906. Coolidge, born Sarah Chauncey Woolsey, wrote the Katy Did books. A sketch of her life stands before the poems. She was born at Cleveland, Ohio, on January 29, 1835.

The sketch tells of a Euclid Avenue home with garden, orchard, and woodland. Sarah, eldest of five children, led the little tribe in play. Part of the woods, left uncut, served as their playground, which they called Paradise. To her the hiding places there were bowers. The verses that follow close the work of a writer whose books children had loved for decades.
49001-mother-s-nursery-tales:
Katharine Pyle both told and illustrated the tales in this book for young children, published by Dutton of New York under a copyright of 1918. Her introduction says plainly that these are not new fairy tales but old ones gathered together, some from one country and some from another. Pyle retold them freshly for the child who holds the book.

The contents run to more than thirty stories, among them The Sleeping Beauty, Jack and the Bean Stalk, Beauty and the Beast, Cinderella, Puss in Boots, and Little Red Riding-Hood. Lesser known pieces include Brittle-Legs, The White Cat, Star Jewels, Mother Hulda, and The Straw, the Coal, and the Bean. Color plates and black and white drawings by Pyle appear throughout, with headbands and tailpieces marking the start and end of each tale.
4901-the-only-true-mother-goose-melodies:
This essay traces Mother Goose in nineteenth-century Boston, asking which rhymes the city's old families actually grew up with. It discusses Whitmore's paper on the subject, Isaiah Thomas's 1785 edition reproduced in facsimile, and the French tales of Perrault's Mother Goose tradition behind them.

The author writes for readers who loved the rhymes as children and now want their history straight: which books carried them, and how a Boston line kept them alive. The record names no author for this work. The piece works as literary history for nursery-rhyme lovers, separating the true old Boston Mother Goose from later imitations.
4902-chess-history-and-reminiscences:
H. E. Bird's history of chess traces the game from its disputed origins to its growing popularity in his own day. Indian traditions, Persian and Arab courts, and early European mentions all get their turn, with figures from Chosroes and Harun to Charlemagne, Offa, and Alcuin appearing in the story.

Bird also gathers praise and censure of the game, including Pope's lines, and follows chess through India, China, Egypt, Greece, Rome, Scandinavia, and Spain. Reminiscences of players and play sit alongside the history. Readers who play chess, or who simply like games with long pasts, get both a chronicle and a memoir of the board.
49039-golden-dreams-and-leaden-realities:
Ralph Raven wrote Golden Dreams and Leaden Realities. G P Putnam and Company issued it at New York in 1853. Francis Fogie the elder wrote an opening chapter. The book went in under the copyright act that year. Fogie starts by calling himself an old man. Sixty-nine years pull at his rope of life, he says.

The seventieth year runs to join them, he adds. A strange dream of his fills the opening talk. The world stood on fire in that dream. Ten thousand bells rang the alarm through it. Engines raced while the ocean burned too. Etna and Vesuvius burst in the flames. A whimsical old man's voice frames tales where bright hopes meet dull fact, as the title's gold and lead promise from the start.
49074-the-garden-of-memories:
Henry Cooper wrote a novel of love, wealth, and a manor house. The book came out in Toronto in 1921. Cooper also wrote Sunny Ducrow and a tale of a baronet. Its parts run from a dream garden to a home-coming. Allan is the man who comes to the garden in the tale.

A match is planned, a fine house is sought, and Allan buys the manor. Sir Josiah opens his purse and proves a true gent in time. Hate, trust talks, and a dawn scene mark the heart's path. Ten years pass in one late part of the book. Readers get a warm tale of love that lasts.
49124-at-the-sign-of-the-sphinx-second-s:
At the Sign of the Sphinx, second series, by Carolyn Wells, was published in New York in 1906 by Duffield. Wells dedicates the book to William Bellamy. A motto from King Richard the Third heads the page: heyday a riddle, neither good nor bad. The body of the book runs to page 126, where the answers stand.

The pieces are charades in verse: riddles that build a word from its parts, my first, my second, and my whole.
