The first riddle climbs a scaffold with a condemned man, calm of gaze, garbed all in white with a rope about his waist. He calls for drink, drinks, and murmurs that men may say he did his work well. Wells made a specialty of such word play, turning the parlor guessing game into light literature.
49186-flaxie-growing-up-flaxie-frizzle-s:
Flaxie Growing Up is the sixth and last volume of Sophie May's Flaxie Frizzle Stories, published by Lee and Shepard of Boston. The copyright is 1884 and the edition shown is of 1895. The publisher's list bound in front shows the whole range of her little folks' books. The Dotty Dimple series and the Little Prudy stories each ran to six volumes at seventy-five cents.

The Flaxie Frizzle set runs from Flaxie Frizzle herself through Doctor Papa, Little Pitchers, and The Twin Cousins. Flaxie's Kittyleen comes fifth, and this volume closes the series. A scene preserved in the copy shows the book's world of lessons. A teacher tells Ethel she is obliged to be severe with her, for it will never do to let her play her piano practice carelessly. Ethel is worse than usual this morning because Kittyleen is waiting in the dining-room.
49194-the-history-of-coaches:
The History of Coaches is a lecture book by Thrupp, a coachbuilder, published in London in 1877 with numerous illustrations. Thrupp had been asked by the Society of Arts in 1876 to lecture on coachbuilding, and chose the art's history rather than its technique. His plates run from ancient vehicles to a child's carriage of 1700 and the Emperor of Germany's sociable.

In his preface Thrupp confesses the difficulty of his subject. No connected history of carriages existed, and the descriptions in books were vague and untechnical. He pieced together the shapes of early coaches from paintings and engravings. He appeals for news of surviving ancient carriages before they perish. The book is a tradesman's act of rescue for his own craft's past, taken down just as the motor age was about to end it.
49201-the-birch-and-the-star-and-other-s:
A story collection edited by Gudrun Thorne-Thomsen. Row, Peterson and Company published it in 1915, with pictures by Frederick V Poole. Thorne-Thomsen also edited East of the Sun and West of the Moon. The tales here come from Finland and the North. The title story opens in a war-wasted land. Cities lie burned and harvests destroyed. Families have scattered in every direction.

Two children, carried far from Finland, anchor the title story. Kind strangers raise them in comfort abroad. Peace at home rekindles their longing. They beg leave to walk home, hundreds of miles away. Other tales follow Viggo and Beate and a boy called Bikku Matti. The collection brought Nordic folk tales to American children.
49203-my-visit-to-tolstoy-five-discourse:
My Visit to Tolstoy: Five Discourses, by Rabbi Joseph Krauskopf, was printed at Philadelphia in 1911. The first discourse was given at Temple Keneseth Israel on December 11, 1910. Its theme is a trip to Russia made in the summer of 1894.

Krauskopf went to lay a plan before the Czar for easing the persecution of the Jews. The persecuted would move to empty lands in the interior and farm there, kept by fellow Jews abroad until they could stand alone. Russia barred him at the door because he was a Jew. President Cleveland and Secretary Gresham backed the plan and pressed his case. The answer cabled from Saint Petersburg was a flat regret: the government could not admit a Jewish divine. Krauskopf resolved to test his rights as an American citizen.
4921-young-canada-s-nursery-rhymes:
Young Canada's nursery rhymes gather the old favorites Canadian children learned by heart. The crooked man and his crooked cat and mouse lead the set. Curly locks will not wash dishes. The little old man quarrels over money. Bow-wow-wow's dog barks through another rhyme.

Multiplication is vexation, and the Rule of Three puzzles the schoolroom singer, just as in the English originals. The collection frames them for young Canadian readers. No author or editor is named in the record. Parents and teachers get a simple, singable treasury, useful for reading aloud and for sharing rhymes that crossed the Atlantic intact.
49216-the-threshold-covenant-or-the-begi:
H Clay Trumbull wrote this study of the threshold covenant, or the beginning of religious rites, published by Scribner in 1896. In his preface he is careful about what the book is not: it does not treat the origin of man's religious faculty.

Instead it traces how rites began, as evidence of belief that covenant relations between God and man were possible. The volume follows his earlier Blood Covenant, which sought the origin of sacrifice. Trumbull lists scholars of divergent schools, from Princeton to Oxford, who agreed on that work's freshness. The audience, he says plainly, is students of primitive life and culture. Readers get comparative religion built on the doorstep.
49227-kittyleen-flaxie-frizzle-stories:
Kittyleen is the fifth book of Sophie May's Flaxie Frizzle stories. Lee and Shepard of Boston published it in 1883.

A preface to mothers warns that Kittyleen is an interloper here. The book deals less with Kittyleen than with Flaxie Frizzle herself. Its aim is Flaxie's improvement under child-life's disciplines. Chapters promise crackers and cheese, sponge-cake, a friend, and Flaxie in church. Others bring runaway rings, a hunt, and Ethel's kettledrum. The story opens at Gray's house, where a brown and white dove walks the roof. Kittyleen arrives: three years old, in brown cloak, white fur cap, and tippet. Her name is Katharine Garland, and she demands to ring the bell herself.
49270-african-nature-notes-and-reminisce:
Frederick Courteney Selous, gold medallist of the Royal Geographical Society, gathers his African notes in a Macmillan volume of 1908. Theodore Roosevelt supplied a foreword, and the book is dedicated to him, since his urging led Selous to write it. Caldwell drew the pictures, and earlier Selous books are listed at the front.

The first chapter weighs protective colouring, recognition marks, and the force of surroundings on living things. Selous tests the theory against zebras, sable antelope, wild dogs, and lions, and notes how most hunters go by scent. Later chapters draw on years of hunting and travel in the far interior of South Africa.
49273-abc-of-the-steel-square-and-its-us:
Fred Hodgson compiled the ABC of the Steel Square and Its Uses, a condensed book drawn from his own larger works on the steel square and practical carpentry. The steel square, he notes, is a purely American product, made best by firms in New Haven, Ottumwa, and Southington. He calls it a simple calculating machine in an intelligent mechanic's hand.

Three divisions organize the book. Division A explains the kinds of squares, their markings, and their use on simple problems. Division B shows how the square gives the cuts, bevels, and lengths of rafters for roofs of every kind, plus brace cuts and raking cornices. Division C breaks new ground: easy solutions of handrailing problems by the square, drawn mostly from questions and answers by working mechanics. Hodgson keeps the pages severely practical, with no history padding. Readers get a pocket master class in the carpenter's key tool.
4932-a-knight-of-the-white-cross-a-tale-:
G. A. Henty's Knight of the White Cross opens in June 1470 at the royal chateau of Amboise. A stately lady watches from a window. A knight talks with a lady at a tambour frame. A lad of seventeen strokes a hawk at another window. A boy of nine studies pages at a table. The lady turns impatiently to ask what will come of it all.

The tale follows the Knights of St. John to the siege of Rhodes, where the White Cross stands against the Ottoman advance. Henty builds the siege from character and incident, with young heroes learning war. Readers get a historical adventure of chivalry and defense, told in Henty's brisk, instructive style.
49323-a-satyr-against-hypocrites:
A Satyr Against Hypocrites is a verse attack by John Phillips from the year sixteen fifty five. A Clark library set reprinted the rare piece in nineteen fifty three. Leon Howard wrote the lead in for the short sharp work. Its head cites a famed Roman wit as its mold for blame.

False faith and cant in church and state draw the poets hot fire. Verse lashes aim at men who mask base aims in pious talk. The set aims to keep rare short works in reach of study rooms. Editors of great schools lend their names to the list at its front. The piece shows the tart edge of prose and verse in that stern age.
49328-the-belgian-front-and-its-notable-:
Captain Willy Breton of the Belgian Army wrote this short account of the Belgian front, translated from the French and published by Chatto and Windus at London in 1918. He tells what the Belgian Army did from the first shock of invasion. He covers the stand at Liege from August 8, the fight at Haelen, and the fall back on Antwerp. The sorties that held German divisions away from the Marne in September 1914 get their due. The later war on the flooded Yser front is his main theme.

The photographs come from the Photographic Service of the Belgian Army Command, including a view of the front line through the floods. Breton writes to show British readers the notable features of a small front that held a corner of Allied ground for four years. It is part record, part tribute to his own army.
49336-seventy-years-among-savages:
Henry S Salt turns the traveler's tale inside out in Seventy Years Among Savages, first published in London in 1921. He is no explorer among far tribes but a native of the land he describes, and the savages of his title are his own civilized countrymen. His seventy years among them brought a slow awakening: the dark ages, he came to think, are not past but present.

The chapters map the charge in titles like Cannibal's Conscience, Twentieth-Century Tortures, Hunnish Sports and Fashions, and Hoof-Marks of the Vandal. A League of Humaneness and The Forlorn Hope point to his remedy. Readers fond of dry satire on modern manners will find the barb aimed home.
49342-the-stickit-minister-s-wooing-and-:
The Stickit Minister's Wooing and Other Galloway Stories is a story collection by Crockett. Hodder and Stoughton of London published it in 1900. It forms a second series of the Stickit Minister stories, eight years after the first.

Crockett dedicates the book to the memory of Stevenson. In a preface he tells how the first series found its welcome. The Stickit Minister had stood friendless outside the door. Two hands reached out: one from Stevenson in far-away Samoa, one from a London journalist. The London man, now his friend, prompted this second series. Crockett's debt, he says, is encouragement from men he had never seen. Stevenson first wrote in 1886, struck by a fragment of Crockett's verse.
49358-the-cyr-readers-book-8-arranged-by:
The Cyr Readers, Book Eight, published by Ginn in 1901, is Ellen Cyr's school reader arranged for the upper grades. A photograph of Stratford on Avon fronts the book. Cyr's preface argues that good literature shapes a life far beyond the schoolroom. Most grammar-school pupils, she warns, would never meet the classics unless a teacher woke their interest first.

The pieces run from Carlyle and Webster to Kipling's Recessional. Edward Everett Hale's tale of the man without a country stands here whole. Milton, Gray's Elegy and Spenser's Lady Una follow. Parkman tells the battle of Quebec, and Dana describes an iceberg. Portraits and short lives make the great writers familiar faces to a child.
49370-english-jests-and-anecdotes-collec:
English Jests and Anecdotes, collected from various sources, is a shilling book from Paterson of Edinburgh. It stands in a line called Nuggets for Travellers, with Scottish and Irish mates. The first tale turns on a boarding-school lady who wrote a novel near London. Her lordship in the tale could not weep, since sorrow had frozen his lachrymal canals. A reader, a keen skater, asked in pencil if those canals would bear.

The Duchess of Newcastle asks Bishop Wilkins how to reach his world in the moon. Your grace, he says, who built so many castles in the air, can be at no loss. Pennant, who hated wigs, snatched an officer's wig at dinner in Chester and threw it in the fire. The officer ran for his sword as the wig blazed.
4938-u-s-presidential-inaugural-addresse:
This collection gathers the inaugural addresses of American presidents from the early republic onward, in chronological order. Washington's successors speak in turn. Madison speaks in 1813. Monroe speaks in 1817 and 1821. John Quincy Adams speaks in 1825. Jackson, Van Buren, Harrison, Polk, Taylor, and Pierce follow.

Each address states a new administration's principles, fears, and promises at the moment of taking office. Read together, they trace how the presidency described itself as the country grew. Students of American politics get a primary-source survey, useful for comparing how different eras framed the same office.
49419-english-interference-with-irish-in:
English Interference with Irish Industries, by J G Swift MacNeill, came out in 1886. MacNeill taught law at Kings Inns in Dublin and had written on the Irish Parliament. His preface argues that farming is now near the sole trade left in Ireland, and asks why.

He quotes Gladstone, Bright, and Chaplin in the House of Commons on land hunger in Ireland. All three grant that the people have been driven to the land alone for a living. MacNeill then blames old English laws, made from fear and trade envy, that crushed Irish trades which once did well. Readers get a sharp brief for Ireland, built on the words of English statesmen themselves.
49426-a-country-idyl-and-other-stories:
Sarah Knowles Bolton published a volume of short stories copyrighted in 1898, headed by a country idyl. Bolton was known for books about poor boys and girls who became famous. Thirty stories fill the table of contents. Titles include Fifteen Thousand Dollars, The Ring of Gold, and The Unopened Letter.

The idyl opens in Nineveh, a quiet town amid New England mountains of pine and cedar, looking toward the sea. Its mills once sawed lumber and ground grain. Now the wheels stand idle, the dams are broken, and the water falls over scattered rocks. Decayed houses leave great chimneys standing like towers. Other tales treat college students, a dog tax, and a house warming.
49442-crusoe-in-new-york-and-other-tales:
Crusoe in New York and Other Tales is a set of short stories by Hale, the author of The Man Without a Country. It was published in Boston by Roberts Brothers in 1880. The preface takes up the case against tales like these, from both sides at once.

One set of critics says the moral sticks out too plainly, and that a preacher should preach outright. The other set says the stories have no purpose that anyone can find. Hale answers that teaching by parable has high authority for it. A parable may also wear a strong air of truth to life. People read short stories, he adds, more than they read anything else. That fact, learned in his years as an editor, is his defence for the form.
49484-my-friend-pasquale-and-other-stori:
James Selwin Tait wrote My Friend Pasquale and Other Stories, issued in New York with copyright in 1892. Tait also wrote Who Is the Man and The Neapolitan Banker. He gives the book to the dear memory of the woman who first inspired his pen. The title story, he warns, has never before been made public.

The narrator tells the tale with pain, from a sense of duty he can no longer shirk. The events changed his life from grave to gay, then to deep gloom. He was walking home from Hampstead Heath on a Saturday in early summer when the tale begins. His bank work done, his mind soared free as he strayed onto the Old North Road.
49503-a-hrenlese-a-german-reader-with-pr:
Ahrenlese is a book for the read of the tongue of Germany, with drills of use past each piece. The host text is made from the print of nineteen eighteen. A note at its head, in both tongues, sets out the marks of the host form. The tongue parts of the book are print in the black script of that land. The English parts are print in the round script of this land.

The note tells how slips of the pen in its marks were set right in the dark. The spell of the first form is kept where it is not a mere print slip. Twin slant marks show parts of words of that tongue that shift in use. In plain words of English, one straight mark is used in their stead.
49518-a-few-more-verses:
Susan Coolidge published A Few More Verses in Boston in 1889. Little, Brown and Company issued this later printing in 1907. The volume follows her earlier book called Verses. A short dedication poem opens the collection. In it the poet compares her gift to a tiny shell by the sea.

The first full poem is A Benediction. It prays that a loved one may gain the heart's desire. The speaker dares not bless or ban on her own judgment. Love, she says, often mars its song with sighs. She asks instead for love that counts no cost. She asks for a wider vision of the mind. A temper like a fragrant wind is the closing wish. The poems keep a gentle, household faith throughout.
49590-the-man-in-ratcatcher-and-other-st:
Sapper wrote short tales led by The Man in Ratcatcher, issued in London in 1921. Hodder and Stoughton brought out the set that year. Sapper was known for Bull-dog Drummond and The Black Gang. Eleven tales fill the contents, from a horse tale to a final poser.

A groom at Boddington's Livery Stable sizes up a tall, spare major at the start. The major knows tack, scorns a harsh bit, and rides the plain horse with ease. The groom mourns the fine riders lost in war and the poor crowd in their place. Ex-officers, hunts, and sharp tests drive Sapper's brisk, manly tales.
49595-when-the-king-loses-his-head-and-o:
When the King Loses His Head and Other Stories gathers tales by Leonid Andreyev in English. Archibald J Wolfe made the translation, and the book was issued at New York in nineteen twenty. A life of the author stands as preface. Andreyev was born at Orel in Russia in eighteen seventy one and died in Finland in nineteen nineteen, an exile.

The life sketch describes his surveyor father, a man of great vigour who died young. His mother, of Polish descent, was a woman of refinement and culture. The boy was a poor scholar who loved to play truant, yet he read literature without pause. Tolstoy and Schopenhauer shaped his later school years. His father's death and that reading gave his inner life a dark and brooding cast, the preface says.
49596-the-sorrows-of-belgium-a-play-in-s:
Leonid Andreyev, the Russian writer, wrote The Sorrows of Belgium, a play in six scenes, in the first year of the Great War. Herman Bernstein made the authorized translation, and Macmillan published it in New York in 1915. Andreyev's Anathema and The Seven Who Were Hanged are named beside his name.

The cast lists the two camps. On one side stand Count Clairmont, the famous Belgian author Emil Grelieu, his wife Jeanne, and their sons Pierre and Maurice. On the other stand the commander of the German armies in Belgium and his officers. An insane girl and a gardener fill out the persons. Scene One opens in the garden of Grelieu's villa at the start of the war of 1914, where peace still holds among the flowers. Theatre readers get the invasion of Belgium turned into a stage tragedy by a Russian hand.
49598-the-little-angel-and-other-stories:
L N Andreyev wrote the tales in The Little Angel and Other Stories in Russian, and W H Lowe turned them into English for Alfred A Knopf at New York in 1916. The title tale centres on Sashka, a boy of thirteen who hates his life. Contents also list a tale called The Spy.

Sashka dreads cold morning washes, the grammar school, and kneeling in a corner all evening as his mother orders. Bold and stubborn, he fights schoolmates, mocks masters, and lies to all but his father. When hurt, he howls without tears to scare hearers, then draws cartoons of himself. Andreyev mixes pity and dark humour in these short pieces on Russian life.
4960-on-picket-duty-and-other-tales:
Louisa May Alcott's On Picket Duty and Other Tales opens on a Civil War night. A great tree draped in gray moss stands scarred by lightning. It looks like a venerable warrior whose campaign is nearly done. Beneath it stands a guard of four. Campfires twinkle on a distant plain. A road strewn with the relics of a rout winds behind them.

A sluggish river glides toward jungle on one side. A Southern swamp breathes malaria on the other. The men on duty are friends as well as comrades. Alcott's tales mix camp humor, homesickness, and courage. Readers get war stories told from the picket line, where waiting and watching mattered as much as fighting.
49606-anathema-a-tragedy-in-seven-scenes:
Anathema is a tragedy in seven scenes by Leonid Andreyev, printed in New York in 1910 in Herman Bernstein's authorized translation. The translation is dedicated to Nathan Straus, in honour of his work saving children's lives. The cast joins biblical and everyday figures in one symbolic drama.

At the iron gates of the world stands the Guardian of the Entrances, guarding the Supreme Wisdom beyond. Anathema comes to question him, while on earth the poor scholar David Leizer, his wife Sarah, and their children draw crowds of the hungry and suffering. Bernstein quotes David promising bread and milk to children as the play's keynote. Andreyev's drama tests faith against poverty and doubt, in the stark manner that made him famous in Russia.
49653-stories-from-the-trenches:
Carleton Case's Stories from the Trenches, humorous and lively doings of our boys over there, gathered from authentic sources, was published by the Shrewsbury Publishing Company of Chicago in 1918. Some twenty-five pieces fill the contents: trench superstitions, life at the front, letters from the front, and the watch-dogs of the trenches among them.

Named exploits carry the book. Lufbery, the ace, bags his thirteenth; Harry Lauder does his bit; King George comes under fire; a fiddler's truce is kept at Arras. The man who taught the tank to prowl and slay, and the taking of moving pictures under shell-fire, show the war's new machinery. The first tale is of Elkington, cashiered in 1914 after thirty years of honored service, who vanished, then turned up a private in the French Foreign Legion, to win back his name.
49690-cities-of-belgium-grant-allen-s-hi:
Grant Allen wrote this pocket guide to the cities of Belgium for Grant Richards of London. It is the third of his Historical Guides, after Paris and Florence, at three shillings and sixpence net. The small green cloth book was made to slip in a coat.

A note tells how to use these guides, then the origins of the Belgian towns. An order for the tour sets the route. Bruges fills the first great part: its origins, its heart, and the Hospital of St John. Allen writes as a man of letters, not a mere list maker. His guides taught a whole set of travellers to look at old towns with an eye for their past.
4970-there-are-crimes-and-crimes:
August Strindberg's There Are Crimes and Crimes is a drama of guilt and judgment, published together with a companion piece called A Mystery under the common title In a Higher Court. The introduction places it after Strindberg's confessional works Inferno and Legends and the dream-play Toward Damascus, all finished between 1897 and 1898.

Behind those works lay a mental crisis in Paris, where Strindberg sought gold by transmutation while his spirit traveled through seven hells seeking heaven. The play itself weighs crime against conscience in a higher court than any earthly one. Readers get Strindberg at his most searching, turning personal crisis into drama.
49704-protection-from-fire-and-thieves:
Protection from Fire and Thieves is a trade book by George Hayter Chubb, out at London in eighteen seventy-five. Its themes are the make of locks, safes, strong rooms, and proof halls, theft and the means to bar it, and fire and how to find, bar, and quench it. A full list of grants for locks and safes is bound in. The front note says the aim is use, not show.

Parts treat locks and keys of old and new times, with the signs of a good lock and how pads are forced. The art of theft takes the next part, with famed bank and shop rob cases of the age. Safes past thieves, by their great makes, and fire walls take parts. The front plate shows a fire cart and a steam fire tool at work.
49716-sonnets-from-hafez-other-verses:
Sonnets from Hafez and Other Verses is a poetry book by Elizabeth Bridges. Oxford University Press published it in 1921. A note at the front explains the method of the Hafez pieces. The last fifteen poems rest on odes of the Persian poet Hafez. Bridges states plainly that they are not translations. Their aim is the spirit of the original, not a faithful rendering.

She admits to omitting, inserting, and even altering ideas as feeling dictated. A few of the pieces follow the Persian fairly closely. Others grow from a couplet or two. One poem springs from a quatrain by Baba Tahir. The rest of the volume is original verse. The opening numbered poems treat fading day, a drooped rose, and parting joy. The book mixes Persian homage with an English poet's own lyrics.
49736-the-khaki-boys-fighting-to-win-or-:
Gordon Bates wrote The Khaki Boys Fighting to Win, a war tale for boys, with rights held from nineteen nineteen. It is one of a set of books on the same young troops in France. Sergeant Jimmy Blaise leads men such as Bob Dalton, Roger Barlow, and Franz Schnitzel. The tale opens in a deep dugout while guns roar far off.

The boys clean their guns and talk of the next big fight. Part heads promise hard action: buried alive, a rush past cliffs, a cave fight, and an escape. Schnitzel, in spite of his German name, is praised as one of the best of Uncle Sam's boys. The book sells grit, team spirit, and hope that more fights will end the war soon.
49750-the-golden-breasted-kootoo-and-oth:
The Golden-Breasted Kootoo is a book of comic fairy tales for children by Laura E. Richards, first published in 1885. Richards was already known for Captain January and the Toto books. The contents list five pieces, ending with The Traveller, the Cook, and the Little Old Man.

The title story opens in full nonsense-fairy-tale voice. A king who loves music keeps four bands playing all day round his courtyard. They are a brass band, a string band, a rubber band, and one man on the jews-harp. At night, musical boxes in his pillow play him to sleep. One day the king decides to learn to sing, though he cannot take the bands hunting with him, and summons the Chief Musician to teach him. The humour is gentle, verbal and absurd, aimed squarely at young readers.
49751-three-minute-stories:
Three Minute Stories, by Laura Richards, is a book of short tales and rhymes for young people. The Page Company printed it in Boston, with a first impression in November 1914. Josephine Bruce drew the pictures, and Richards gives the book to her grandchildren.

Richards had written Five Minute Stories and the Captain January tales before this set. In her note she says many pieces first ran in the Ladies' Home Journal. Some were signed with her initials, and others with the names of figures from her books. A front list prices her other volumes, from a dollar and a half to two dollars and three quarters. The Hildegarde and Margaret sets are offered boxed at nineteen dollars and a quarter. Brevity is the book's whole promise: a tale in three minutes.
49765-some-eminent-women-of-our-times-sh:
Mrs Henry Fawcett wrote Some Eminent Women of Our Times, short lives printed at London in 1889. Twenty-three sketches fill the book. A line from Middlemarch on its title page sets the tone: desiring what is good makes us part of the divine power against evil.

Elizabeth Fry opens the set, followed by Mary Carpenter, Caroline Herschel, and Mary Somerville. Queen Victoria, Florence Nightingale, and Jane Austen each get a sketch. Charlotte and Emily Brontë stand together, and American abolitionists Prudence Crandall and Lucretia Mott close the list. Fawcett argues that learning makes women value their duties more, not less.
49798-the-boy-scouts-as-county-fair-guid:
The Boy Scouts as County Fair Guides is a boys' tale by Scout Master Robert Shaler. Hurst and Company held the New York rights in the year 1915. The book stands fourteenth in the Sterling Boy Scout Books line. Shaler's scouts had served as signal corps, life saving crew, and more. Fifteen titles at twenty-five cents each fill the list at its front.

Back from the fishing hole opens the tale, then the great undertaking forms. On duty at the fair puts the boys to work as guides for crowds. A fakir and his dupe, then a credit to the uniform, follow on. Strike while the iron is hot, a scout in trouble, and a rift come next. One boy's influence and the troop's backing carry the mid chapters home. The tale closes at the station as the fair days wind down.
49822-he-knew-lincoln-and-other-billy-br:
He Knew Lincoln, and other Billy Brown stories, is a set of tales by Ida Tarbell, author of a life of Abraham Lincoln. The contents list four pieces: the title story, one set back in 1858, one called Father Abraham, and one called In Lincoln's Chair. Copyrights in the front reach from 1907 to 1922, showing the stories gathered over years.

A picture caption sets the tone: an old man by a stove, telling stories and arguing by the hour. Billy Brown, the teller of the frame, is a small town man who had known Lincoln in the flesh. Through his talk the great man comes down to store and kitchen scale. Tarbell, who had written Lincoln's life in earnest, here lets neighbourly memory do the work of reverence.
49832-english-monasteries:
English Monasteries is a short history by Hamilton Thompson, one of the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature. The Cambridge University Press published it in 1913. A picture of Saint Mary's Abbey at York, its crossing and north transept, fronts the book. The first chapter treats the religious orders.

Thompson traces the growth of monastic life in the east and its beginnings in Italy, Gaul, and Ireland. He explains the rule of Saint Benedict and the order's coming to England. Saxon monasteries, the Danish invasions, and the monastic revival follow. The book gives a compact, clear account of the monks who shaped medieval England.
49838-jack-of-no-trades:
Evelyn E Smith wrote this short story, printed in Galaxy in October 1955 with art by Cavat. Kevin, the teller, is sick of psi powers for one plain reason: he has none, or thinks he has none. His whole family has them. His brother Danny sets tables by mind power and loses his grip when excited, so tablecloths fly and drape over Kevin.

Father teleports down to meals rather than walk, to show off. The family pities poor Kev, and their pity makes him sharper and worse. Only when they lose their tempers does he trust their feelings toward him. The tale plays a plain boy's grudge against a house full of gifted kin, for laughs and a sting.
49841-famous-persons-and-places:
Famous Persons and Places is a book of sketches by Willis, published by Scribner in New York in 1854. A preface refers readers to an earlier volume of the series. Pencillings by the Way is that previous number named there. A portion of the original pencillings is given here again. The size of the work compelled an unequal division, it says. Personal portrayings of distinguished contemporaries make up the volume mainly. Their readability has been proved in earlier shapes of publication, it claims.

Their value will increase with time, the preface holds. It is independent, to a degree, of literary merits, it adds. Sketches of the men of mark of any period are eagerly devoured. Willis was a famed magazine writer and editor of his day. His portraits catch celebrities in talk and travel settings.
49849-the-beginnings-of-libraries:
Ernest Cushing Richardson, keeper of Princeton's library, wrote this study of how libraries began. Princeton University Press printed it in February 1914. A set of quipus, the knotted cords of Peru, heads the plates.

Richardson starts with what a library is, and how to study its birth. Then he roams far and free: libraries before the flood, libraries of the gods, and beast and plant libraries with a question mark. Adamite and patriarchal stores come before the flood in his scheme. The growth of record keeping ties the tale. Few books range so wide on so plain a theme, or with such a scholar's zest.
49873-the-boys-book-of-submarines:
Frederick Collins and Virgil Collins wrote The Boys' Book of Submarines, published in New York by the Stokes Company in 1917. Frederick Collins had written Inventing for Boys and a manual of wireless telegraphy. A foreword addressed to the boy reader opens with the word submarine itself.

The foreword says everyone knows a submarine can travel on or under water and torpedo an enemy ship, but few know exactly how the boat works and fights. With the greatest war in history under way, the authors argue, boys who may be called to the colors should understand these craft. They trace the type from the first successful American submarines of 1900, five of which were sent to England.
49907-paris-grant-allen-s-historical-gui:
Paris, in Grant Allen's Historical Guides, was published in London by Grant Richards in 1900, the second edition of a book first printed in January 1897. The guides were small cloth volumes with rounded corners to slip in the pocket, marked 3/6 net each; Florence, the cities of Belgium, Venice, Rome, Dresden, and London made up the set.

A short chapter tells the traveller how to use the guide. Parts in brackets are for reading at home before a visit. The on-the-spot parts are printed large for the dim light of churches and galleries, with key-note words in bold. The Paris walk then runs from the origins of the city and the Ile de la Cite, with Notre-Dame and the Sainte Chapelle. It goes on to the Louvre and its paintings, the two banks, and St Denis.
49913-nine-unlikely-tales:
Nine Unlikely Tales is a book of fairy stories by E Nesbit, illustrated by H R Millar and Claude A Shepperson. Ernest Benn of London and Coward-McCann of New York issued this edition. The nine tales mix magic with schoolroom things, so that wonders keep turning up in ordinary places.

The contents include The Cockatoucan, Whereyouwanttogoto, The Blue Mountain, and Melisande, or Long and Short Division. Fortunatus Rex and Co, The Sums That Came Right, The Town in the Library, and The Plush Usurper close the list. The first tale opens on Matilda, whose ears burn from one of Pridmore's thorough good washes, the kind that makes a child smart and miserable. Nesbit's nonsense logic and sly asides made these tales favorites far beyond their first child readers.
49915-by-far-euphrates:
Alcock wrote By Far Euphrates, a tale, for Hodder and Stoughton at London in 1897. Her Spanish Brothers and Dr Adrian head the title page as earlier works. A verse about four men loose in the fire fronts the tale. Twenty-six chapters and an appendix trace an Armenian story in full order.

The dark river opens on a dreary plain at sunset in the east. An Englishman, Grayson, camps with his son under plane trees for night travel. Guides, Arabs, and Turkish guards wait for his signal to stir at dusk. Chapters promise a wedding, a ride, a revolver's use, and gathering storms in turn. Pastor Stepanian, a modern Thermopylae, and a great crime darken the road. Faith under empire fills a missionary tale.
49936-new-ideas-for-american-boys-the-ja:
The Jack of All Trades offers new ideas for American boys. Beard wrote and illustrated the book. Scribner published it in New York in 1900. It follows his earlier handy books for boys. Those volumes had proved unexpectedly popular. Letters from boys across two countries demanded more.

A preface tells the series' accidental history. Beard meant to stop after one handy book. Instead the first book only whetted appetites. Quaintly worded letters in boyish handwriting flooded his studio. A revised edition and an outdoor book followed. Now the mail demanded fresh ideas again. Beard laid aside brush and pencil to comply. The result is a third storehouse of projects. Making and doing, not reading, is its whole purpose.
49942-poems-poe-mes-autres-alliances:
Poems and Poemes, autres alliances, is a verse book by Natalie Clifford Barney, printed at Paris and New York in 1920. The title joins English and French, and the book does the same, with poems in both tongues. A Parisian roof garden in 1918 stands among the English pieces, a sign of the poet's home city.

The opening apology says that while soldiers share the mud, some must wear the colours of their hearts and sing. Poems named in the list treat night, Judas, Venus weeping, and a phantom guest. Barney writes of love in its many forms, with a light touch and a frank heart.
49949-the-logic-of-vegetarianism-essays-:
Essays and dialogues make up The Logic of Vegetarianism, a book that argues the case against eating flesh. The volume was sold with kindred works on humane and simple living. Its form is stated in the subtitle, essays and dialogues. That form lets the author meet objections in the mouth of a doubter.

Dialogue suits a cause that must win converts one by one. The vegetarian case rests on health, on mercy to animals, and on plain economy. Each of those grounds can be pressed and answered in turn. The book belongs to the vegetarian movement press of its day. Such books were cheap, earnest, and meant to be lent from hand to hand. Readers get the reasoning of the cause, set out as talk and essay in turn.
49987-forest-days-a-romance-of-old-times:
James set this romance of old times under Henry the Third, and Baudry's European Library published it at Paris in 1843. The dedication letter warns the reader of the surprise. Ballad and story have taught us to place Robin Hood in the days of Richard the First. James moves him forward: an English yeoman of superior mind, outlawed, in all probability, for his adherence to the popular party of the day. His struggle is with the weak and tyrannical Henry, against the great Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester.

The novel opens with a rhapsody on merry England and its yeoman-like hilarity. James promises striking scenes of the times and a struggle of feelings in the third volume. His Robin is a barons' wars partisan rather than a greenwood jester. The Paris edition carried the tale to the Continent's English readers.
50032-a-dog-of-flanders-the-nu-rnberg-st:
Louisa de la Rame, who wrote as Ouida, wrote A Dog of Flanders, The Nurnberg Stove, and Other Stories, issued in Philadelphia in 1909. Colour pictures are by Maria L Kirk. Contents hold four tales, with A Dog of Flanders first and The Little Earl last. In the Apple-Country sits between them.

A Dog of Flanders opens with Nello and Patrasche left all alone in the world. Nello is a little Ardennois boy and Patrasche a big Flemish dog. Both were orphaned and poor, and owed their lives to the same hand. They live in a little hut by a Flemish village a league from Antwerp. A picture shows little Nello taking his place beside the cart.
50033-morgan-s-men-a-narrative-of-person:
Henry Lane Stone told this story of his own war service in an address given at Louisville, Kentucky, on April 8, 1919. He spoke before a camp of United Confederate Veterans. Stone had served as a soldier in the famous cavalry command of General John Morgan, the men the South still called Morgan's Men.

A newspaper notice printed with the address praises its shape. In about thirty typed pages, the Evening Post said, Stone gives a vivid picture of those dashing cavalrymen in a form more condensed than any it had seen. The paper also notes what Morgan's men did after the war: where one of them settled, it says, the community gained a good citizen.
50040-st-benedict-s-rule-for-monasteries:
Benedict Rule for Monasteries is the rule of the Benedictine order, in a translation by Leonard Doyle. The Liturgical Press at Saint John Abbey, Collegeville in Minnesota, issued the translation. Its copyright is of 1948 by the Order of Saint Benedict there. The text follows the third edition edited by Cuthbert Butler of Downside Abbey.

 A table of contents lists the prologue and the chapters of the rule in order. On the Kinds of Monks and What Kind of Man the Abbot Ought to Be stand first. On Calling the Brethren for Counsel and the instruments of good works follow in the list. Doyle plain English made the sixth century rule the daily book of American Benedictine houses, in the form in which it is still read aloud in their refectories.
50064-proverbial-philosophy-the-first-an:
Proverbial Philosophy is a book of verse wisdom by Martin Tupper of Christ Church, Oxford. The edition shown is a new one, printed in London by Edward Moxon in 1867, with illustrations. Tupper's lines were among the most quoted of the Victorian age, and the book gathers his first and second series in one volume.

The contents of the first series read like a table of life itself. After a preface and opening words of wisdom come pieces on truth in things false, on anticipation, on hidden uses, and on compensation. Indirect influences, memory, and the dream of ambition follow. Each poem takes one theme and turns it over in aphorism and image, in the manner of proverbs set to verse. The form made the book a household companion and a preacher's storehouse for two generations.
50079-a-book-on-vegetable-dyes:
A Book on Vegetable Dyes, by Ethel Mairet, was published in 1916 by Douglas Pepler at Hammersmith. The book was printed at Ditchling in Sussex and sold at five shillings net. A Latin text from Genesis heads the work: God saw all that he had made, and it was very good.

Mairet opens with a claim about first makings: when man first learns to make a thing, that thing is good. Her own book was printed on one of the first iron presses made in this country, she notes. Yet trades now chase quantity over quality, she warns, and lose the use of good things. Her carpenter buys planks from a yard and forgets the tree. The dye book aims to restore a lost craft tradition.
5008-katherine-s-sheaves:
Katherine's Sheaves begins at four in the afternoon on the first day of Hilton Seminary's midwinter term, at a well-regarded school in a handsome old town in western New York. In a roomy recreation room, cheerful girls assemble noisily, like magpies, swapping holiday greetings, talking over their studies, classes, and roommates, and chatting about incoming teachers and pupils.

A tall, kindly woman of around thirty-five steps into the doorway, her pleasant face bright with amused delight at the lively scene. Katherine, the heroine, gathers her sheaves of friendship, study, and duty through the term. The catalog entry is anonymous. Readers get a girls' school story of the older kind, warm and orderly.
5010-state-of-the-union-addresses:
George Washington's State of the Union addresses gather the first president's annual messages, from the new government's earliest sessions onward. One message congratulates Congress on North Carolina's accession to the Constitution, on rising national credit and respectability, and on goodwill toward the Union, with concord, peace, and plenty blessing the country.

Later messages address finance, defense, Indian relations, and the whiskey troubles, always in Washington's measured style. The set shows a president inventing the office as he filled it. Students get the founding presidency in its own words, formal, cautious, and deeply concerned with union itself.
5011-state-of-the-union-addresses:
John Adams's State of the Union addresses gather the second president's annual messages to Congress, from his first message in November 1797 through the end of his term. The opening message deals with sickness in Philadelphia, where the legislature's meeting place itself became a question, and with the public expense and inconvenience of moving Congress.

Later messages carry Adams through quasi-war with France, naval buildup, and the partisan storms of the 1790s. Read together, they show a president defending a young republic's neutrality and institutions. Students get a primary source for the Federalist era, in Adams's own formal and anxious voice.
5012-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Thomas Jefferson's annual messages gather the third president's reports to Congress, written after years of war in Europe. Jefferson says with joy that the wars afflicting sister nations have at last ended. The links of peace and trade are opening again among them.

America's own peace, kept through a perilous season, draws his special thanks. Later messages cover the Louisiana Purchase, the Lewis and Clark expedition, and the road toward embargo. Jefferson's prose is spare and republican throughout. Readers get the early republic's growth and its foreign-policy caution, from the president who embodied both.
5013-state-of-the-union-addresses:
James Madison's State of the Union addresses collect the fourth president's annual messages, written through the long crisis with Britain and France. One message reports a deal with a leading belligerent nation. Then deep concern follows. Britain refuses to honor its minister's act. It pursues a harder policy toward the United States.

War, embargo, and the defense of a republic against the world's great powers run through the set. Madison's messages move from diplomacy to war and back to peace, always in the language of constitutional duty. Readers get the War of 1812 era from the desk of the president who asked Congress to declare it.
5014-state-of-the-union-addresses:
James Monroe's State of the Union addresses gather the fifth president's annual messages from the Era of Good Feelings. Monroe celebrates abundant harvests, extensive and profitable commerce, public credit at an extraordinary elevation, and defense preparations advancing under a well-digested system.

A free government founded on the people's interest and affections, he argues, has gained strength through experience. Later messages proclaim the Monroe Doctrine, address Florida, and manage a growing nation. Readers get the 1820s in the voice of a president who presided over prosperity and laid down the doctrine that would bear his name.
50147-beaver-an-alphabet-of-typical-spec:
John Kettelwell wrote Beaver, printed in London as an alphabet of typical specimens, with notes and a closing essay. The essay treats the manners and customs of beavering men. Each letter gives a type of beard, with a picture set by its account. A stands for an Admiral-Beaver, whose coat is good, harsh, and not silky. B gives a Bald-King-Beaver in full winter coat.

The accounts read like rules for a sport played by spotting beards. Fine specimens earn game and extra points, and players in the Service run real risk if the beard outranks them. No rule book settles the game's legality, so a court-martial might trip an unlucky player. The humour turns on treating beards as game animals to be scored.
5016-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Andrew Jackson's State of the Union addresses gather the seventh president's annual messages, beginning with his first address to a federal legislature of twenty-four sovereign states and twelve million happy people. Jackson presents a view of national affairs and proposes measures he judges necessary to promote the Union's objects, with unfeigned satisfaction at the trust placed in him.

Later messages defend the Bank veto, Indian removal, and the spoils system, and report on nullification and foreign affairs. The set shows Jacksonian democracy in full voice: popular, combative, and jealous of concentrated power. Students get the 1830s from the general who remade the presidency.
5017-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Martin Van Buren's State of the Union addresses collect the eighth president's annual messages, delivered as the young republic weathered financial panic and frontier conflict. Van Buren, Jackson's successor, defends the independent treasury, reports on the nation's finances, and addresses relations with Britain, Mexico, and Native nations.

The messages show a careful party manager turned president, arguing for hard money and limited government while the economy shuddered. Read in sequence, they trace a single-term presidency shaped by the Panic of 1837. Students get a primary source for Jacksonian democracy's second act, in Van Buren's precise and lawyerly prose.
5018-state-of-the-union-addresses:
John Tyler's State of the Union addresses gather the tenth president's annual messages, delivered after he succeeded William Henry Harrison in 1841. Tyler rejoices in general prosperity, civil and religious liberty, and unexampled means of education, knowledge, and improvement, with peace in American borders and plenty in American homes.

Disease visited a few portions of the land, he notes, yet the people's health was generally preserved. Later messages address Texas annexation, the tariff, and the veto fights that left him a president without a party. Readers get a primary record of the 1840s, from a president who governed alone and changed the map anyway.
5019-state-of-the-union-addresses:
James Polk's State of the Union addresses collect the eleventh president's annual messages, written during a presidency of territorial expansion. Polk reports on Texas annexation, the Oregon question, and the war with Mexico, along with tariffs, the independent treasury, and the growth of a continental republic.

The messages are businesslike and confident, setting out administration policy as accomplished fact. Read together, they show how a one-term president pursued a clear program and left the map changed. Students get a primary record of Manifest Destiny from the president who most deliberately carried it out.
5020-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Zachary Taylor's State of the Union addresses gather the twelfth president's annual messages, brief because his presidency lasted barely sixteen months. Taylor presents the United States as the most stable and permanent government on earth, its institutions vindicated against evil prophets who once foretold their downfall.

The country stands at peace with all nations, seeking amity abroad, while the future maintenance of free government depends on Congress. Taylor's messages also touch California statehood and the slavery question that would outlive him. Readers get a short, soldierly presidency in its own words, cut off just as the sectional crisis sharpened.
5021-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Millard Fillmore's State of the Union addresses gather the thirteenth president's annual messages, delivered after he succeeded Zachary Taylor in 1850. Fillmore reports on the Compromise of 1850, the Fugitive Slave Act's enforcement, California's admission, and relations with Britain and other powers during a decade sliding toward civil war.

The messages plead for union and compromise, in the voice of a president trying to hold a divided country together by law. Their limits are as instructive as their aims. Readers get a primary source for the 1850s crisis, showing how the center argued for itself just before it collapsed.
5022-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Franklin Pierce's State of the Union addresses gather the fourteenth president's annual messages, delivered as Congress fulfilled the duty imposed on a new president. Pierce reflects on a political system at once complex and symmetrical, in which the branches remain independent yet answerable to the same source of power, and no official escapes scrutiny or responsibility.

Later messages address Kansas-Nebraska, foreign affairs, and the Ostend Manifesto, as the republic slid toward disunion. Pierce's prose is formal and legalistic, trusting system over passion. Readers get a primary record of the 1850s, from a president whose faith in process could not hold the Union together.
5023-state-of-the-union-addresses:
James Buchanan's State of the Union addresses collect the fifteenth president's annual messages, from 1857 through the secession winter. Buchanan addresses the Kansas question, the Dred Scott decision, the Utah expedition, and the growing sectional crisis, arguing for constitutional limits on presidential action.

His final message confronts secession itself, denying both its legality and the federal power to prevent it by force. The set is essential, if painful, reading for the coming of the Civil War. Students get Buchanan's case in his own words, and a measure of how legal argument failed against a political crisis.
5024-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Abraham Lincoln's State of the Union addresses gather the sixteenth president's annual messages, written in the Civil War's darkest years. One message notes abundant harvests, then turns to profound solicitude over foreign affairs, because a disloyal portion of the people spent the whole year trying to divide and destroy the Union.

A nation enduring domestic division, Lincoln warns, invites foreign intervention, as tempted nations seldom resist counsels of seeming expediency. Later messages cover emancipation, finance, and the war's conduct. Readers get the war presidency in Lincoln's own annual reports, grave, legal, and increasingly determined.
5025-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Andrew Johnson's State of the Union addresses collect the seventeenth president's annual messages, delivered during Reconstruction after Lincoln's assassination. Johnson reports on the restoration of the Southern states, the Freedmen's Bureau, civil rights legislation, and his vetoes, defending a rapid and lenient reunion policy.

The messages show a president at war with Congress over the terms of peace, in language that grows sharper each year. His grief for Lincoln gives way to defiance of Radical Republicans. Readers get Reconstruction's central quarrel from the presidential side, in messages that explain both Johnson's principles and his political isolation.
5026-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Ulysses S. Grant's State of the Union addresses gather the eighteenth president's annual messages, opening with gratitude for peace at home and no entangling alliances abroad. Grant boasts of territory unsurpassed in fertility, equal to supporting five hundred million people, abounding in minerals sufficient to supply the world for generations, with exuberant crops and every climate.

Later messages address Reconstruction, the Ku Klux Klan, civil service reform, and foreign affairs, in the general's blunt prose. The set shows a soldier-president governing a continent and a divided country. Readers get a primary record of the 1870s, confident about America's resources and troubled by its politics.
50268-troubadour-tales:
Evaleen Stein wrote Troubadour Tales, published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company in Indianapolis in 1903. Virginia Keep, Maxfield Parrish, and others illustrated the book, which Stein dedicated to her mother. The tales return to the days of the troubadours, the poet-singers of old Provence in southern France.

The first story follows Pierrot, page to Count Reynaurd of Poitiers, a noble who is also a famous troubadour. The count rides from castle to castle with his lute, his horse decked in myrtle and periwinkle. He earns the favor of King René and wins a silver cup for cleverness in Latin. Three more tales follow: The Lost Rune, Count Hugo's Sword, and Felix. Stein writes medieval romance for young readers, full of song, courtesy, and bright adventure.
5027-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Rutherford B. Hayes's State of the Union addresses collect the nineteenth president's annual messages, delivered after the disputed election of 1876. Hayes reports on the end of Reconstruction, civil service reform, the resumption of specie payments, and relations with China and Latin America, in a tone of conciliation.

The messages balance a contested presidency's need for legitimacy against reformers' demands for a cleaner government. Read in order, they show Hayes withdrawing federal troops from the South while pressing for honest administration. Students get a primary record of the Gilded Age's opening, when reform and reunion competed for priority.
50271-tioba-and-other-tales:
Tioba and Other Tales is a collection of stories by Arthur Colton, published in New York by Henry Holt and Company in 1903. A frontispiece by Frost opens the book. The collection is dedicated to A G Brinsmade.

The title tale begins at a camp among birches and pines above flat meadow land. A slow river, called Still River in the tale, wanders the valley with no need to arrive anywhere. The campers settle for days to study the philosophy of the stream. Opposite rises a strangely ruined mountain side, its poised head three thousand feet nearer the stars. Colton's prose lingers over such scenes, making landscape itself the argument. The tales belong to the quiet, reflective school of American short fiction at the turn of the century.
5028-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Chester A. Arthur's annual messages gather the twenty-first president's reports to Congress, delivered after he succeeded the assassinated James Garfield. One message recalls a year of rare prosperity, with plenteous harvests, thriving industries, and preserved health. Yet grief shadows the year, for a mysterious act of will took the loved and illustrious citizen lately at the nation's head.

Arthur's messages then address civil service reform, the tariff, and the navy, as a spoilsman president surprised reformers by signing reform. The set shows an accidental presidency finding dignity in office. Readers get a primary record of the early 1880s, when reform began to tame the patronage system.
50286-the-wicker-work-woman-a-chronicle-:
Anatole France wrote The Wicker-Work Woman, a chronicle of our own times, translated by M P Willcocks for the limited English edition of his works edited by Frederic Chapman, published in 1910. Chapter one finds M Bergeret in his study.

Bergeret, professor of literature at the university, is preparing his lesson on the eighth book of the Aeneid. His daughters practise a hard piano exercise close by. His room has one large window filling a whole side, yet it admits more draught than light, the panes darkened by a high wall. His table stands close against it, catching the niggard daylight. Readers get the second Bergeret novel, France's irony at its most domestic.
5029-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Grover Cleveland's State of the Union addresses collect the twenty-second president's annual messages, spanning his first administration and the issues that defined it. Cleveland reports on civil service reform, the tariff, the surplus, pensions, and the regulation of railroads, arguing for honest and economical government.

His messages are famous for their bluntness: vetoes explained, abuses named, and party spoils condemned. Read together, they show a Democrat president governing against both parties' appetites. Students get a primary record of Gilded Age reform, in the voice of a president who trusted the veto more than the speech.
5030-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Benjamin Harrison's annual messages gather the twenty-third president's reports to Congress, written when the Union's state was known from day to day rather than once a year. Harrison notes that ideas for laws find an earlier voice than the president's yearly reports. Good will marks relations with other governments.

Few global questions of weight remain unsettled, he reports, and no block seems likely to postpone their settlement. Later messages address the tariff, pensions, and the Sherman Antitrust Act. Readers get a primary record of 1889 to 1893, from a president who governed a booming, confident, and increasingly corporate America.
5031-state-of-the-union-addresses:
William McKinley's State of the Union addresses collect the twenty-fifth president's annual messages, from his first message in 1897 through the Spanish-American War and its aftermath. McKinley reports on the tariff, the currency, Hawaii, Cuba, and the war that made America a colonial power, then on governing the Philippines and Puerto Rico.

The messages move from domestic prosperity to empire, in McKinley's calm and managerial voice. Their restraint is itself revealing: expansion presented as duty rather than conquest. Readers get a primary record of 1898 and its consequences, from the president who presided over America's turn outward.
5032-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Theodore Roosevelt's annual messages gather the twenty-sixth president's reports to Congress, opening under the shadow of a great blow. Congress meets in 1901 after President McKinley was shot by an anarchist at Buffalo's Pan-American Exposition on September 6. He died there on September 14.

McKinley is the third of the last seven elected presidents to be murdered, Roosevelt notes. That fact alone justifies grave alarm. Its sinister weight lies in an anarchist's deed. Later messages address trusts, the Panama Canal, and conservation. Readers get a primary record of the Progressive Era's most vigorous presidency, beginning in grief and turning to reform.
5033-state-of-the-union-addresses:
William H. Taft's State of the Union addresses gather the twenty-seventh president's annual messages, delivered between 1909 and 1912. Taft reports on tariff reform, the Payne-Aldrich Act, trust prosecution, the postal savings system, and conservation, while his break with Theodore Roosevelt splits the Republican Party.

The messages show a lawyer-president governing by statute and precedent, less rhetorical than his predecessor and more comfortable with detail. Read in sequence, they trace a presidency that achieved much and pleased few. Students get a primary record of Progressive Era lawmaking, in Taft's deliberate and candid voice.
5034-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Woodrow Wilson's annual messages gather the twenty-eighth president's reports to Congress, opening with a deliberate break from custom. Wilson tells Congress he will not offer the usual formal review of departmental business. That list is long, he says, and would suffer in shortening. Instead he will address several matters that ought to engage national attention.

The messages that follow cover the New Freedom, the Federal Reserve, tariff reform, and then war, neutrality, and the League of Nations. Wilson's professorial prose carries a moral argument throughout. Readers get a primary record of 1913 to 1921, from a president who treated the annual message as a lecture to the nation.
50349-a-basket-of-barley-loaves:
An unnamed writer gives these devotions, published by the Presbyterian Board at Philadelphia in 1870. There is a lad here who has five barley loaves, the title's text from John says. The author had written 'The High Mountain Apart' and 'Sacramental Sabbaths' before this basket.

The book is dedicated to the author's former pastor, Dickson, who taught the way of God. His thoughts and very words enter largely into these pages, the dedication confesses warmly. An editor's preface promises refreshment to readers who crave more of Christ in daily life, and the loaves are short meditations, small in size and meant to feed many.
5035-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Warren Harding's State of the Union addresses collect the twenty-ninth president's annual messages, written as America emerged from a decade of war and its aftermath. Harding reports with satisfaction that the country stands free from any impending menace of war, with growing assurances that the peace so deeply cherished may prove permanent.

Ten years of menace, war, and disordered aftermath had added difficulties to government that only those in immediate contact could appraise, Harding argues. The messages turn from war debts and disarmament to domestic normalcy. Readers get a primary record of the early 1920s, when a war-weary country tried to return to ordinary life.
5036-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Calvin Coolidge's annual messages gather the thirtieth president's reports to Congress, opening in tribute to his predecessor. Coolidge speaks of Warren Harding's humanity, greatness, and character. Justice grew more certain under him, and peace more secure. A surpassing tribute marked his journey across the continent to rest at home.

Those who knew and loved Harding, Coolidge says, need no long account of the man. But his associates cannot resume office without pausing to rededicate themselves to service in his memory. Later messages address tax cuts, economy, and business prosperity. Readers get Coolidge's laconic presidency, beginning with a eulogy and proceeding by restraint.
5037-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Herbert Hoover's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-first president's annual messages, opening with a nation grown in strength, comfort, and knowledge. Education spreads more widely, moral and spiritual forces hold, and peace grows more assured, Hoover emphasizes, while the problems ahead are problems of growth and progress.

The later messages, delivered as the Depression deepens, turn to unemployment, farm relief, and public works, with Hoover insisting on facts and relative importance before action. Read in order, the set traces optimism meeting crisis. Readers get a primary record of 1929 to 1933, from a president who trusted engineering and voluntary effort over federal expansion.
5038-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Franklin D. Roosevelt's annual messages gather the thirty-second president's reports to Congress, opening in January 1934 with a call to counsel rather than to request. Roosevelt tells Congress he comes not for special or detailed laws. He seeks joint work without party strife to continue national recovery. He aims to build, on the ruins of the past, a new structure for modern civilization.

Later messages cover the New Deal, the Four Freedoms, and war mobilization, in Roosevelt's confident and expansive voice. The set spans 1934 to 1945, the longest run in the collection. Readers get a primary record of depression and war, from the president who redefined what Americans expected of their government.
5039-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Harry S. Truman's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-third president's annual messages, from the postwar years through Korea and into the 1950s. One message explains the new executive budget: no longer piecemeal department programs, but a single comprehensive budget the president presents for Congress to act on, with tighter controls as federal programs grow.

Truman argues that budget and general policy are inseparable, since the president bears responsibility for recommending both. Later messages cover containment, civil rights, and the Fair Deal. Readers get a primary record of the early Cold War presidency, practical and plainspoken about government's new size.
5040-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Dwight D. Eisenhower's State of the Union addresses gather the thirty-fourth president's annual messages, opening with his first message to the Eighty-third Congress. Eisenhower welcomes the honor and states the joint purpose of congressional leadership and administration: to justify the summons to responsibility issued by voters the previous November.

That purpose involves applying American influence abroad with fortitude and foresight to deter aggression and secure peace, and establishing an administration of integrity and efficiency at home. Later messages cover the Cold War, interstate highways, and civil rights. Readers get a primary record of the 1950s, from a general turned president who prized steadiness.
5041-state-of-the-union-addresses:
John F. Kennedy's annual messages collect the thirty-fifth president's reports to Congress, opening with a return to the House he calls his oldest home. Kennedy recalls taking the federal oath there more than fourteen years earlier. He learned from leaders of both parties. He heard Churchill's eloquence, Nehru's idealism, and de Gaulle's steadfast words.

The messages that follow set out the New Frontier: Cold War rivalry, space, civil rights, and economic growth, in Kennedy's polished rhetoric. Readers get a primary record of 1961 to 1963, brief but consequential, from a president whose addresses shaped how America described its purposes.
5042-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Lyndon B. Johnson's annual messages gather the thirty-sixth president's reports to Congress, opening with a challenge to make the session historic. Johnson asks that it be known for civil rights above all. He wants it to do more for civil rights than the last hundred sessions combined. He also seeks the most far-reaching tax cut of the time. He declares all-out war on poverty and unemployment.

Health needs of older citizens, education, and conservation follow in the same ambitious program. The messages trace the Great Society from promise to legislation, and then to the strains of Vietnam. Readers get a primary record of the mid-1960s, when a president tried to remake American society by statute in a single session.
50427-the-nine-days-queen-lady-jane-grey:
Richard Davey wrote this life of Lady Jane Grey for the Romantic History series, first published in 1909 and edited by Martin Hume. In his author's note Davey says he tells the story from the personal rather than the political side, leaning on the human document.

He warns that Jane plays a shadowy part in the early chapters, since four conspiracies made her nine days possible. He traces them in order: the Howards against Katherine Parr, the Seymours against the Howards, Thomas Seymour against his brother, and John Dudley clearing his own path. Davey consulted archives at home and abroad for the men and women who used Jane as a tool.
5043-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Richard Nixon's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-seventh president's annual messages, and the 1970 message breaks deliberately with tradition. Nixon tells Congress that the address usually offers a lengthy account of past deeds and future requests, with election-year politics in between, but profound events command a different course.

The year 1970, opening a new decade, finds America rethinking Vietnam, the economy, and government's role, and Nixon uses the occasion to set a broader agenda. Later messages cover detente, wage and price controls, and Watergate's shadow. Readers get a primary record of a presidency that began with ambition and ended in crisis.
50438-jaunty-jock-and-other-stories:
Neil Munro wrote Jaunty Jock and Other Stories, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1919 in a third impression. A list of Munro's works fronts the book, naming The New Road, Doom Castle, John Splendid, and The Lost Pibroch. Eleven tales fill the contents. After the title story come Young Pennymore, A Return to Nature, The Brooch, and The First-Foot. The Isle of Illusion, The Tudor Cup, The Silver Drum, and The Scottish Pompadour close the list.

The title tale opens with the last of the West Bow balls, held before Lady Charlotte ran away with her dancing-master. Rain falls on an Edinburgh wrapped all day in haar, and the gutters run like mountain burns. Wives pick through the mud on pattens toward the fishwife for supper haddocks. Lady Charlotte, director of the dance, balloons about the room in her great hooped petticoat.
50439-english-eccentrics-and-eccentricit:
John Timbs, author of Clubs and Club Life in London, wrote English Eccentrics and Eccentricities, here in a new edition from Chatto and Windus at London in 1898. Forty-eight illustrations include the Earl of Bridgewater and his dogs. Timbs opens with a gentle word to the reader.

Odd company, he warns, may still hold good sense and good hearts. He quotes Swift: a little grain of romance preserves the dignity of human nature. Eccentricity can run to excess, like fermenting liquor turning acid, yet his subjects rarely stray so far. Most cases come from his own time, for novelty's sake. Sayings, doings, and fortunes of strange fellows fill the sketches, drawn to show oddity beside kindness.
5044-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Gerald R. Ford's annual messages gather the thirty-eighth president's reports to Congress, opening with a memory of his own beginnings. Ford recalls a young idealist who swore the House oath before Sam Rayburn. Two days later that freshman stood at the back of the chamber. President Truman then reported to the Eighty-first Congress that the state of the Union was good.

Ford's own messages, delivered after Watergate and the pardon, address inflation, energy, and restoring trust in government. The reminiscence frames a presidency that began without election and sought legitimacy through candor. Readers get a primary record of the mid-1970s, from a president governing in a predecessor's shadow.
50446-dictionary-of-explosives:
Dictionary of Explosives, by Arthur Marshall, is a reference list of explosive compounds and trade names. Blakiston printed the book at Philadelphia in 1920, from sheets printed in Great Britain. Marshall was chemical inspector in the Indian Ordnance Department.

The book sorts its entries first by class and country, starting with coal-mine explosives. American permissible powders fill a long list, from Aetna Coal Mine Powder to Xpdite. Austrian, Hungarian, Belgian, and British lists follow in the same order. Starred British names, a note says, are no longer on the permitted list for mines. Each entry then gives the make-up and traits of the compound in the main list. The book served chemists, mine men, and ordnance staff who needed to tell one powder from another at a glance.
5045-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Jimmy Carter's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-ninth president's annual messages, opening with a personal note about saving energy and a constitutional duty to report on the Union. Carter declares the Union sound militarily, politically, economically, and in spirit, and describes Americans as confident, hardworking, decent, and compassionate.

The messages that follow address energy, inflation, human rights, and the hostage crisis, in Carter's earnest and moralizing style. Read together, they show a president appealing to national character as a policy resource. Readers get a primary record of the late 1970s, when energy and confidence both ran short.
50458-the-toxins-and-venoms-and-their-an:
Em Pozzi-Escot wrote The Toxins and Venoms and Their Antibodies, in a form put into English by Alfred I Cohn. The book came out in New York and London in 1906. Cohn was a man trained in the craft of drugs. The first run was a set of a thousand copies in all.

The first words note that lore of these poisons is new in the world. Less than a score of years had passed since the first true facts were won. New cures by serum owe their rise to that lore, the book says. True poisons of germs are stuff of cells, of a sort not yet known in full. A second class, from the work of Selmi and Gautier, has a set and known frame. Snake poisons hold both kinds at once, the text warns.
5046-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Ronald Reagan's annual messages gather the fortieth president's reports to Congress, opening with a first address that recalls the tradition itself. Reagan notes that Washington began the custom in 1790. Washington reminded the nation that self-government was staked on the experiment entrusted to the American people. The sacred fire of liberty, he said, depended on that experiment.

From the same podium, Reagan adds, Churchill once asked the free world to stand together. His messages then address tax cuts, defense buildup, and the Cold War's final phase, in his warm and confident rhetoric. Readers get a primary record of the 1980s, from a president who told America's story as a tale of freedom renewed.
5047-state-of-the-union-addresses:
George H. W. Bush's annual messages collect the forty-first president's reports to Congress, opening with a claim about dates that divide history. Bush notes that for most lives in the chamber, the world was defined in 1945. That year's events set the shape of nations, the pace of progress, and freedom or oppression for millions.

His messages then address the Cold War's end, the Gulf War, and a new world order, in measured and managerial prose. Readers get a primary record of 1990 to 1992, when an old frame of reference dissolved and a president tried to describe what would replace it.
50479-far-away-stories:
Far-Away Stories is a set of short tales by William J. Locke, put out in nineteen nineteen. Locke was known for past tales with warm fame. In a note to the reader he says he dug these tales out of dead press files. Some he saved from pride in his work, and some in hope they still please.

The name points to the long span of years the tales cross, near all writ in calm days past the worlds great war. Tales bear names of love, of a song of life, of blind folk, and of a realm of a royal girl. Locke gives the two tales he loves best to his kind readers, with thanks for their grace past his due.
5048-state-of-the-union-addresses:
William J. Clinton's annual messages gather the forty-second president's reports to Congress, opening with a tribute to Tip O'Neill. Clinton jokes that he is not sure what speech sits in the TelePrompTer. He asks the chamber to recall the giant who presided over it with force and grace. O'Neill was a bricklayer's son who helped build the great American middle class.

O'Neill never forgot who he was, where he came from, or who sent him, Clinton says, and smiles down from the Lord's gallery for the first time. Later messages address health care, welfare reform, and the economy. Readers get a primary record of the 1990s, from a president who framed policy as a story about ordinary Americans.
5049-state-of-the-union-addresses:
George W. Bush's annual messages collect the forty-third president's reports to Congress, from 2001 through 2008. An early message opens with a new budget and a new approach to governing. It thanks Congress for its invitation. It jokes that the vice president may have had to break a tie to secure it.

Later messages address the September 11 attacks, the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, tax cuts, and the financial crisis, in Bush's direct and plainspoken style. Read in sequence, the set traces a presidency transformed by terror and war. Readers get a primary record of the 2000s, from the president who governed through them.
50504-the-battle-of-gettysburg-the-count:
The Battle of Gettysburg: The Country, the Contestants, the Results is a guide-history by W C Storrick. The J Horace McFarland Company copyrighted it in 1935. Storrick was retired superintendent of guides at the battlefield. He had served twenty years with the Gettysburg National Park Commission. The edition list runs from a first edition in 1931 to a seventeenth in 1957.

A foreword and Lincoln's Gettysburg Address open the book. The main account first sets the armies in motion. Lee's plan, Hooker's plan, and Meade's appointment frame the approach. The first day brings Reynolds's arrival and death. Highlights add the first soldier killed and the flag of the 16th Maine. The second day covers Little Round Top, the Peach Orchard, and the Wheatfield. The third day builds to the artillery duel and Pickett's Charge. Incidents, the military park, and the Soldiers' National Cemetery follow. Army organisations close it.
50531-on-sulphonfluorescei-n-and-some-of:
On Sulphonfluorescein and Some of Its Derivatives is a doctoral dissertation by C Willard Hayes, presented at the Johns Hopkins University in 1887.
