The transcriber's notes say the original was a handwritten thesis, and its spelling and punctuation are left unchanged. The contents divide the work into two parts.

The first part treats ortho-sulpho-benzoic acid: its preparation from toluene, its oxidation, and its conversion into sulphinide and back again. The second part turns to sulphonfluorescein itself, with earlier attempts, preparation, and purification. Analyses, properties, and salts of the substance are set down. Acetyl and bromine derivatives follow, with the action of strong acids and of reduction. The introduction notes the close likeness between phthalic acid and that benzoic acid. That likeness suggests that the second acid, acting on phenols, might yield new coloured substances. The thesis records bench chemistry of the dye-works age.
5055-plays-first-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, First Series, gathers the dramatist's earliest stage works, opening in a well-furnished London dining room at Rockingham Gate. John Barthwick's household anchors the first scenes. The Jones family's lodgings in Merthyr Street follow. A London police court closes the action across Easter Tuesday and the Wednesday of the following week.

Little girls left homeless, a relieving officer, a magistrate's clerk, and an usher fill out a drama of class and justice. A small act in a dining room ends before the law. Galsworthy's early plays already show his method: social questions argued through private lives. Readers get the playwright at his debut, sharp and compassionate.
5056-plays-second-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Second Series, gathers the dramatist's middle-period plays. One is a country-house drama set on December 7 and 8 at the Cheshires' house in one of the shires. Its cast lists Joan and Old Studdenham the head-keeper. Freda the lady's-maid and Young Dunning the under-keeper appear. Jackson the butler completes the household. Action moves from hall to morning room to smoking room.

Galsworthy's drama of class, property, and conscience unfolds through such households, where servants and masters watch each other closely. Readers get the playwright who would write The Forsyte Saga, working in the sharper, shorter form of the stage, with social criticism inside drawing-room manners.
50567-the-truth-about-the-congo-the-chic:
The Truth About the Congo, by Frederick Starr, gathers his Chicago Tribune articles into a book from Forbes and Company, 1907. Starr, a student of human races, first met Congolese people as an exhibited group at the Saint Louis exposition. Congo reform literature then reached him, and he sailed expecting horrors everywhere.

He stayed more than a year, traveling with his photographer Manuel Gonzales and two boys, Manoeli and Tumba, to whom the book is dedicated. His errand, he insists, was study, not exposure. The volume joined a fierce public fight over King Leopold's Congo, and readers on both sides quoted it.
5057-plays-third-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Third Series, gathers middle-period dramas set in flats, lodgings, and restaurants. One play opens in George Dedmond's flat in the evening. It moves to the rooms of Malise across mornings and afternoons three months apart. It closes in a small supper room at The Gascony. Waiters, managers, ladies in large hats, and a languid lord fill the company.

Galsworthy's characters argue loyalty, love, and reputation across those rooms, with time itself doing much of the dramatic work. The series shows the playwright's mature craft, compressing social judgment into dialogue. Readers get three acts of Edwardian life, polished and quietly devastating.
5058-plays-fourth-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Fourth Series, gathers later plays including A Bit o' Love, set on Ascension Day in a West Country village. In the Burlacombes' low panelled farmhouse hall sits Michael Strangway. He is a clergyman of about thirty-five in collar and Norfolk jacket. He plays the flute before a large framed photo of a woman, the room's only picture.

Strangway's rooms, the village inn, the church, and a barn carry the action through three acts of love, faith, and village judgment. Galsworthy's later drama grows quieter and more spiritual than his early social plays. Readers get a playwright turning from property and class to conscience and forgiveness.
5059-plays-fifth-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Fifth Series, gathers later dramas set in the Midlands town of Breconridge. Its cast includes Builder and his French maid Camille. Topping serves as Builder's manservant. The mayor and his secretary appear, with a justice of the peace, a constable, and a police sergeant. A journalist from The Comet joins them, with the figure of a poacher and the voices and faces of small boys.

Action moves between Builder's study after breakfast and at lunchtime and a studio, where respectability meets the wild figure from outside. Galsworthy's later plays probe conscience in provincial life. Readers get a playwright in his final manner, still finding drama in the collision of order and freedom.
50597-flute-and-violin-and-other-kentuck:
James Lane Allen's Flute and Violin and Other Kentucky Tales and Romances was printed by Harper in 1896, under an 1891 copyright. Allen gives the book to his mother, from whose frail body he drew life at the start and from whose strong spirit, he says, he will draw it to the close. The title tale first appeared in Harper's Monthly; the rest came from the Century Magazine.

Six pieces fill the contents: Flute and Violin, King Solomon of Kentucky, Two Gentlemen of Kentucky, The White Cowl, Sister Dolorosa, and Posthumous Fame. The opening tale begins in Christ Church, Lexington, at a marble tablet on a dim wall. It remembers the Reverend James Moore, first minister of the church and president of Transylvania University. He died in 1814, aged forty-nine, and the tablet calls him learned, liberal, amiable, and pious.
5061-the-children-s-book-of-christmas-st:
Asa Don Dickinson's Children's Book of Christmas Stories gathers tales acceptable to parents, teachers, and librarians, marked for younger and older children. Dickens's Christmas at Fezziwig's Warehouse and Andersen's Fir-Tree open the collection, followed by Freeman's Christmas Masquerade, The Shepherds and the Angels, and Olive Thorne Miller's Telltale Tile.

Younger children get starred stories, older children double-starred ones, with Susan Coolidge's Toinette and the Elves and a voyage of the wee red cap among the later entries. Dickinson edited the book for family and classroom reading. Readers get a Christmas treasury that mixes classics with lesser-known seasonal tales, ready for December evenings.
50626-manual-of-oriental-antiquities:
Manual of Oriental Antiquities, by Ernest Babelon, was printed in New York and London in 1906 in a new edition. Babelon kept the department of medals and antiques at the national library in Paris. Two hundred and fifty five plates fill the book.

The manual covers the building, carving, and craft arts of Chaldaea, Assyria, Persia, Syria, Judaea, Phoenicia, and Carthage. A new chapter treats the fresh finds at Susa. In his preface Babelon says the field holds all the old East save Egypt. He grants that so vast a field can only be summed in a small book, where Perrot and Chipiez took four large volumes. Two springs of art, Egypt and Assyria, run through the tale. Students get a compact guide to the ancient East.
50730-the-fleet-its-rivers-prison-and-ma:
John Ashton wrote The Fleet, its River, Prison, and Marriages, in 1888. Scribner and Welford at New York put out the illustrated book. Ashton had written social life under Queen Anne before it. A view of the mouth of the Fleet about 1765 fronts it. Pictures from original drawings and engravings fill its pages.

The book requires no preface beyond a statement of its scheme, he says. Time has wrought changes in this land, and especially in London. The old landmarks are gradually being effaced, he owns. This little river, with its prison and its marriages, is past. All are swept away and impossible to resuscitate now, he writes. He searched all available sources for a trustworthy history of it. A pleasant book for the general reader was his aim as well. Ashton gives buried London one of its best witnesses.
5074-aunt-judy-s-tales:
Aunt Judy's Tales gathers stories for children, told by an elder girl amusing the little ones of a large family. The contents list Vegetables out of Place and Cook Stories. Rabbits' Tails, Out of the Way, and Nothing to Do follow. The Little Victims opens the collection in verse about thankless eyes and saved blessings.

Mamma can nap by the fire because Aunt Judy, as the children call her, keeps the little ones entertained, and the tales mix nonsense, morals, and domestic comedy. The record names no author for this work. Parents and young readers get a Victorian storybook, gentle and imaginative, written for reading aloud to a nursery full of listeners.
50785-the-land-of-the-boxers-or-china-un:
The Land of the Boxers, or China Under the Allies, is a war account by Captain Gordon Casserly. Casserly served in the Indian Army and wrote from his own march. Longmans, Green brought the book out in London in the year 1903. Fifteen pictures and a plan back the text of the campaign tale. He gives the book to American and British officers of the force.

Chapter one rides from Wei-hai-wei to Tientsin past the Taku forts. The allied fleet, the Peiho river, and a mixed train crowd fill the road. Tientsin gets a chapter on its foreign town and Chinese city. Gordon Hall, brawls in Taku Road, and the siege fill that part. The allied armies of each nation then get weighed one by one. German, French, and other troops face his plain soldier's judgment.
508-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne gathers early tales of New England in this volume, twice told from magazine print. The Gray Champion defies a tyrant governor; the Minister's Black Veil hides a secret sin; Dr. Heidegger's experiment gives old folk a taste of youth. Legends of Province House, Wakefield, and the Great Carbuncle fill the rest.

Hawthorne writes in rich, shadowed prose, mixing history with moral allegory. Guilt, pride, and hidden sin recur in tale after tale. The book marks his rise as America's master of the short tale, where a single image can carry a whole moral world.
50817-juvenile-sports-or-youth-s-pastime:
A sixpenny chapbook for children fills this item: Juvenile Sports, or Youth's Pastimes, with coloured pictures, printed at London by Miller. Page by page it gives a sport, a picture, and a short rhymed caption that praises the game and warns of its risks in the same breath.

Skating comes first: beware of falls, for pain stands by pleasure's side, and broken heads are skaters' fare. Hoops, a toy vessel on the stream, leapfrog, and trap-ball follow. A boy whips his top and rests from the pleasing toil. A kite soars on a schoolboy's holiday, decked with stars and gay colours. Pins stand in even ranks like soldiers in a band, waiting for the bowler. Health and vigour, the verses keep saying, are what fit boys for the active games.
50819-a-bad-day-for-sales:
Fritz Leiber's short story from Galaxy Science Fiction in July nineteen fifty three follows Robie, a salesman who happens to be a robot. Robie is the demonstration model for a line of vending machines built by Shuler Vending Machines. His job on Times Square is less to sell goods than to draw a crowd. He charms onlookers into buying company stock.

Leiber sketches Robie from the crowd's side: a metal hemisphere on a sponge rubber skirt and a swiveling box of a torso. A built in sense of timing lets a pause ripen before the pitch begins. A child says he looks like a turtle. A legless veteran sees a war machine instead and rolls away. The story is a neat piece of nineteen fifties satire on salesmanship and automation. Its perfect salesman needs no feelings, only programming and patter.
50842-green-grew-the-lasses:
Ruth Laura Wainwright's story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in July 1953, begins with a smell. On a hot, humid September evening, Robert Raymond paces the living room from window to window, sniffing. His wife Helen watches him grow tenser by the minute. Her cousin Dora, arrived after losing a short-lived job, sniffs too: it is an odd smog, sweet and bitter, not sulphuric, not oil-well. It makes Helen think of rank tropical weeds.

Then she remembers her hands after weeding the garden. Strange weeds have sprung up, a foot high, with stiff stems of metallic green and rosettes of chartreuse leaves down one side. She fetches one from the vacant house next door, and the smell is beyond doubt. Something not of this earth is growing all over town. The motto over the story hints at the cure's logic: since evils cancel out, avoid odd numbers of them.
50875-the-business-library-what-it-is-an:
The Business Library: What It Is and What It Does is a handbook by Louise Krause, librarian of the Byllesby engineering firm of Chicago. The second, revised edition came out at San Francisco in 1921. The book is dedicated to her firm, whose support let library science be put to business use. The contents map the new field in full. The organization of the business library comes first. The service it renders to the house follows.

Periodicals, and how to use and file them, get a chapter. Government documents, trade catalogues, photographs, and lantern slides each have their place. Classification and cataloguing, and the mechanical equipment of the room, close the list. Krause holds that a business library is not a shelf of books. It is facts in any form, even word of mouth ahead of print. The book is a root text of special librarianship.
50896-northern-georgia-sketches:
Northern Georgia Sketches is a set of tales of the Georgia hills by Will Harben, published in Chicago by McClurg in 1900. The book is dedicated to Joel Chandler Harris, in thanks for the kind encouragement that made it possible. The sketches had first appeared in magazines of the day.

The first sketch is called A Humble Abolitionist. Andrew Duncan and his wife trudge a shadeless road in the beating sun. She wears a checked homespun gown and a cardboard-stiffened sun-bonnet. He is barefoot, in a soiled shirt and trousers worn to shreds. At a roadside spring the drinking gourd is gone. Duncan turns his broad hat inside out, folds it into a dipper, and holds the water up to his wife as he kneels. The talk on the road is given in the speech of the hills.
50943-rose-d-albret-or-troublous-times:
James wrote this historical novel for the Tauchnitz British Authors set. Tauchnitz printed the volume at Leipzig in 1844. Front pages list James past tales, from Morley Ernstein to Darnley. Chapter one takes up chivalry and its effect on Europe manners.

James says chivalry softened rude ages but left one hardship untouched. Women, whose honor knights swore to guard, stayed near slaves in law. Their own happiness in marriage was the point left unguarded most of all. The tale of Rose unfolds in those troublous, courtly times of old France. The Tauchnitz house issued it in its British authors line.
50963-future-development-of-japanese-dwe:
Future Development of Japanese Dwelling Houses is a thesis by Shigetsura Shiga, presented in June 1905. It earned him a master's degree in architecture in the graduate school of the University of Illinois. The work was transcribed from his hand written document, with its Japanese and Latin words kept as he wrote them. Plates stand at the starts of the paragraphs they illustrate.

Shiga looks at how the Japanese house might change as his country modernizes. He holds that Japan's progress rests not only on surface material gains. It has deep roots, he argues, in the mental training of its citizens. Talk and comparison run through every school in the empire, pushing the country a step further on its road. The thesis joins plans and plates to that faith in education. It is a rare record of a Japanese architect thinking aloud, in America, about his homeland's homes.
50981-garrity-s-annuities:
David Mason spins a space tale of a young engineer and his theory of women in a story from Galaxy Science Fiction for April 1956. The narrator warns that Garrity built his own disasters, though not in the way anyone foresaw. Jail or a lost ticket would have been the plain guess.

Aboard the Aloha, bound for Seranis, Garrity holds forth in the messroom on how women always cost a man more than they are worth. Gloster, who knows the port, praises its obliging people and plans to spend his pay there. Garrity, twenty-four and fresh from Lunar training, shakes his head and promises they will see. Readers get a wry tale whose title hints that one spaceman's port habits follow him to every planet.
51002-korean-folk-tales:
James Gale turned fifty three Korean tales into English from the work of Im Bang and Yi Ryuk. Dent of London and Dutton of New York published the book in 1913. Its full title adds the words imps, ghosts, and fairies, and the tales live up to that billing. Gale adds short lives of the two Korean authors at the front.

Im Bang was born in 1640 and rose to be governor of Seoul. The tales tell of foxes, seers, wizards, and a wild cat woman. Others treat a grateful ghost, a plucky maiden, and a man who became a fish. Some take the reader down to the king of hell itself. The set gives English readers a rich taste of old Korean folk belief, told in short, brisk tales.
51057-lady-jane-grey-and-her-times:
Lady Jane Grey and Her Times is a life of Lady Jane Grey by I A Taylor, published by Hutchinson in London in 1908 with seventeen illustrations. Taylor had written on Queen Hortense and Queen Henrietta Maria before. The book gives Jane's short life a wide stage, starting with the state of Europe and England under Henry the Eighth.

Chapters follow Katherine Parr and Thomas Seymour, Anne Askew's trial and burning, and the death of Henry. Under Edward the Sixth come the Seymour brothers' quarrels, Jane's time in the Admiral's house, and his fall. Roger Ascham's visit and Jane's letters to Bullinger show her standing among the reformers. The closing movement, as Edward sickens, brings Northumberland's plot and the rivalry with Mary. Court intrigue and religious persecution run through every chapter.
51085-helen-s-babies:
Helen's Babies, by John Habberton, stands in a 1908 printing. Grosset and Dunlap issued the comic tale at New York. Dwiggins drew the illustrations. A dedication mocks its own kind at the front. The book is given to the parents of the best children in the world. Each dedicatee, the joke runs, should buy and read a copy. Harry Burton narrates, a bachelor of twenty eight. He sells white goods for a living. A letter from his only married sister starts the tale. It reached him as he chose where to spend a fortnight's holiday. Helen asks him to take her boys for that fortnight.

Budge and Toddie, the imps of the plates, are the babies. Their sayings fill the picture list in child speech. Uncle Harry's holiday becomes their reign.
51143-the-waterloo-roll-call-with-biogra:
Charles Dalton's Waterloo Roll Call, with biographical notes and anecdotes, reached a second edition in London in 1904. Eyre and Spottiswoode published the revised and enlarged volume; the first edition had appeared in 1890. Dalton explains that relatives of Waterloo officers sent him much new information.

The bulk of the book is annotated tables of names, dates and ranks of the British Army at Waterloo, with brief biographical sketches. Dalton used an annotated copy of his own first edition made by O'Brien of the British Museum Library, once a ranker in the 4th Dragoon Guards. A special feature lists non-commissioned officers and men who served at Waterloo and afterwards received commissions.
51265-the-last-of-the-mortimers-a-story-:
Last of the Mortimers is a story in two voices by Mrs Oliphant, in a new edition. Oliphant is billed as author of Madonna Mary and Squire Arden. Contents split into five parts and a postscript. The parts alternate between two heads: the ladies at the hall and the lieutenant's wife. Each voice returns twice more after its first turn, the contents show.

Part one opens in a solicitor's office of quiet drama. The narrator discusses a matter with Mr Cresswell, their solicitor. Her sister Sarah, who never speaks except to her in a whisper, suddenly speaks aloud. Sarah names a man, Richard Arkwright, called after the cotton spinner. That naming was the chief thing against him in their father's days, she declares. The solicitor nearly upsets the ink in his start.
51314-in-bad-company-and-other-stories:
In Bad Company and Other Stories is a set of Australian tales by Rolf Boldrewood, author of Robbery Under Arms. Macmillan first issued it in 1901 and re-issued it in 1903 in the uniform edition of his works. The title story runs to 135 pages, the longest in the book. Bill Hardwick, its figure, is praised as a fine specimen of an Australian, active as a cat and strong withal.

A dozen shorter pieces follow the title story. Morgan the Bushranger and How I Became a Butcher come first. Then come Moonlighting on the Macquarie, an Australian rough-riding contest, and the mailman's yarn. A kangaroo shoot, the story of an old log-book, and Reedy Lake Station fill out the list. One title starkly promises five men's lives for one horse. The tales draw on bush life, the gold-era past, and station work, in Boldrewood's seasoned colonial manner.
51346-poem-outlines:
Sidney Lanier's Poem Outlines, printed at New York in nineteen eight, gathers the poet's rough sketches and fragments. A long list of Lanier's books heads the volume, from his poems and letters to his study of the English novel. A note at the start argues that an artist's finest work may never reach full finish. A painter's swift sketch can catch a colour that the finished picture loses.

So too, the note says, a poet may set down one note of his heart, or a heaven scaling thought, that will not fuse into a sonnet. Such fragments, caught by a subtle magic of genius, are what this volume keeps. Lanier's line at the front names the artist as one who walks lonesome amid a thousand friends. The outlines serve readers who want the poet's workshop, not just his finished songs.
51387-the-history-of-the-prince-of-wales:
The History of the Prince of Wales' Own Civil Service Rifles was printed in London in 1921 at Somerset House for past and present members. An editor's note says the pages were put together in haste so the record could reach members, kin, and friends without more delay. The book honors riflemen who laid down their lives in the Great War.

The record joins an older account of the regiment's first thirty years with new work that brings the story to the war years. Colonel Merrick gave much time to the task and let his early part be reprinted. The tone is plain and proud, a roll of service by clerk-soldiers who held their unit's honor as high as any in the army.
51413-the-ignoble-savages:
Evelyn Smith printed The Ignoble Savages in Galaxy Science Fiction in March 1957, with illustrations by Dillon. The blurb twists the anthropologist's cliché: Snaddra had but one choice in its fight to afford to live belowground (underhandedly pretend theirs was an aboveboard society).

Larhgan, high priestess of Snaddra, dismisses her suitor at the door. A beggar does not associate with the high priestess, she tells Skkiru. But the Earthmen aren't due for another fifteen minutes, he protests. Of what importance are fifteen minutes compared to eternity, she answers. We are going to keep this up as a permanent thing, she explains, and his disbelief is the story's engine. Smith wrote witty science fiction under several names. Her Snaddra stages a whole civilization as a performance for visitors, and the performance has eaten the performers.
51454-john-bunyan-and-the-gipsies:
John Bunyan and the Gipsies is a polemical pamphlet-book by James Simson, published in New York and Edinburgh in 1882. Simson edited a history of the Gipsies and wrote several other works on the subject. His motto, from Shakespeare, asks for a fair hearing: according to the fair play of the world, let me have audience. The preface returns to his Scottish Churches and the Gipsies.

There he had argued that almost everyone has joined in a settled belief about the destiny of the Gipsies. Gipsies, he says, cease to be Gipsies by conforming in dress and habits to others and keeping silent about their race. In bringing the subject forward he finds the way barred in every direction. Much of the book reviews Leland's work on the English Gipsies, also of 1882.
51455-the-fate-a-tale-of-stirring-times:
The Fate, a tale of stirring times by James, was reprinted at New York in 1864. Harper and Brothers issued it from Franklin Square in that year. It was first entered for copyright in 1851 in the Southern District of New York. James wrote The Commissioner, Henry Smeaton, and The Old Oak Chest, the title page lists.

A preface opens with a thought on change of scene for the mind. Change of scene braces the mind as change of air braces the body, he holds. It refreshes weary powers and prompts fresh activity of thought in his view. For a writer of fiction such change may be needful above all, he adds. Historical romance of love and fortune in troubled days fills the tale behind that preface.
51483-the-reluctant-heroes:
Frank Robinson wrote a science fiction story that ran in Galaxy in January 1951. Its headnote sets the twist: pioneers have always resented their wanderlust and hardships, but the future brings a new grudge, when pioneers stay put and scholars do the exploring. A very young man sits nervous on a sofa's edge.

He has a chance to go with the first research expedition to Venus, and blurts that he does not think he wants to spend two years there. An older man draws out the real reasons: home, familiar things, and a girl. Still the reluctant heroes, he murmurs. The scene cuts to Chapman, three years on the Moon, learning they do not want him back.
51521-the-prolongation-of-life-optimisti:
Élie Metchnikoff, a senior figure at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, wrote The Prolongation of Life as a set of hopeful studies. Chalmers Mitchell edited the English version, issued in nineteen hundred and eight. An earlier book by Metchnikoff, The Nature of Man, had set out the same broad line of thought.

Metchnikoff argues that much human gloom grows from a clash in our make-up. Parts of the body and old habits can outlast their use and cause harm. He looks at ageing, decay, and the gut, and asks how science might help people live longer in good health. The tone stays hopeful, as the subtitle promises.
51522-leather-for-libraries:
Five experts wrote a short handbook on book leather for the Library Association, issued in London in 1905. Hulme, Parker, Seymour-Jones, Davenport, and Williamson each took one part of the task. Their aim was to help libraries keep books bound in skins that last.

Hulme traces sumach tanning in England from a grant in the year 1565 and tells how trade work fell off. Parker then explains why new leathers rot, while later parts judge modern skins, show how to mend and bind books, and list the tools a small bindery needs.
51540-fun-for-the-household-a-book-of-ga:
Fun for the Household is a book of games by Emma Gray, copyrighted in 1897. The Christian Herald at the Bible House, New York, published the parlour manual. Contents divide the fun for little folks, boys and girls, and grown ups in turn. Special fetes, methods of choosing partners, and tangles and forfeits fill the middle pages.

Stories and side pieces mix with the games: Orrin the Bootblack and a Hebrew Christian among them. Hours with the poets, parlour fortune telling, and the flower test vary the evenings. An introduction starts when children have passed beyond the rattle age of play. Victorian and Edwardian homes gained a whole winter of evenings in one book.
51568-some-haunted-houses-of-england-wal:
Some Haunted Houses of England and Wales is a set of ghost inquiries by Elliott O Donnell, published in London in 1908. Eveleigh Nash issued the book from Fawside House in that year. O Donnell is named on the title page as an associate of the Society for Psychical Research. 

Contents name some twenty houses and places said to be haunted in the two countries. They open with the Green Bank Hotel at Bardsley and a house in Southgate Street, Bristol. Mulready Villa near Basingstoke, a house in Park Street at Bath, and the Minery in Devon follow in the list. Thurlow Hall near Exeter, the Guilsborough ghost, and Wolsey Abbey near Gloucester fill the middle chapters. The book belongs to the wave of Edwardian ghost hunting in which named houses, streets, and witnesses were set down as evidence for the unseen.
51733-bird-life-glimpses:
Edmund Selous's Bird Life Glimpses was published by George Allen at London in 1905. Lodge drew the six full-page plates and twelve chapter headings. Most observations were made at Icklingham, a little village of West Suffolk on the northern bank of the Lark. The country between Mildenhall and Bury Saint Edmunds is open, sandy, and barren. The geological survey, Selous notes, calls it more like an Arabian desert than an English landscape.

Wide warrens shelter rabbits, and stone-curlews roam them from April to October, wailing over the waste. The plates show wood-pigeons coming in to roost, hooded crows and rooks feeding, and herons descending on a nest. Headpieces run from a roosting pheasant and young nightjars to dabchicks on a nest. Selous watches single birds closely and reports what they do, hour by hour. The book is field observation written as narrative.
51762-manx-fairy-tales:
Manx Fairy Tales is a collection by Sophia Morrison, printed at London in 1911. The tales come from the Isle of Man. The first, called Themselves, tells of a man who met one of the Little Fellows. The fairy told him that if he went to London Bridge and dug, he would find a fortune.

The contents run to some fifty tales. There are bugganes of waterfalls and churches, the making of Mann, and the coming of Saint Patrick. One tale tells how the Manx cat lost her tail, and another how the herring became king of the sea. The Moddey Doo, the black dog of Peel Castle, has his tale, as do the Fynoderee and the witch of Slieu Whallian. The last pieces include an ancient charm against the fairies. Morrison's book preserves the spoken tales of the island in the days when they were still told by firesides.
51765-a-book-of-north-wales:
Baring-Gould toured North Wales for this book, published by Methuen in 1903 with forty-nine illustrations, many from photographs. He opens with the Welsh people and the English conquest, then takes the coast and the hills in order. Anglesey and Holyhead come first, then Bangor and Carnarvon, Snowdon, the Lleyn peninsula, and Conway with its castle. St Asaph, Denbigh, and Llangollen follow, with Vale Crucis Abbey and the ladies of Llangollen.

The last chapters cross to Dolgelley under Cader Idris, Harlech, Welshpool, Newtown, and Machynlleth. Baring-Gould wrote in the same series on Dartmoor, the West, and Brittany, and he brings the same mixture of history, folk-lore, and scenery. It is a carriage-and-railway Wales, described just before the motor car changed the tour.
51839-nacogdoches:
R B Blake writes the story of an old East Texas town in a booklet printed for the Nacogdoches Historical Society and the Chamber of Commerce. Karle Wilson Baker's poem Nacogdoches Speaks opens it.

Blake's note traces the booklet's own history. He and the Reverend George L Crocket prepared an earlier form in 1936 for the Texas Centennial. The Historical Society reissued it in 1939, in memory of Crocket. Crocket had preserved much material that would otherwise have been lost. Demand emptied the supply again, so the Chamber financed this third edition, free on request. Roy Henderson, Charlotte Baker Montgomery, and Crocket drew the pictures. The opening poem feels the dint of hoof and the print of booted heel in the town's streets. The shadows of its wild founders still fall there.
51881-the-lost-atlantis-and-other-ethnog:
Sir Daniel Wilson studies early man in The Lost Atlantis, and Other Ethnographic Studies, printed at Edinburgh and New York in 1892. Douglas and Macmillan made the book. Wilson was president of the University of Toronto, and had writ The Prehistoric Annals of Scotland and Prehistoric Man. His daughter writes the preface, and tells how the book came to be his last.

The preface is the most troublesome part of a book, she opens; her father often said so. In his notebook the work stands described as a few carefully studied monographs, linked by a slender thread of kinship. Coming home ill from Montreal, he found a bundle of proofs waiting. He set to work at once to correct them. It is my last book, he said. Through days of growing weakness he lay correcting proofs, till the pen dropped from his hand.
5195-cape-cod-stories:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Cape Cod Stories, also published as The Old Home House, gathers tales told in the voice of Cape Cod folk. Its contents include Two Pairs of Shoes, The Count and the Manager, The South Shore Weather Bureau, The Dog Star, The Mare and the Motor. The Love of Lobelia 'Ankins appears among them, each story turning on a local character or a small deception.

Lincoln writes with affectionate humour about fishermen, captains, and summer visitors, in dialect that gives the stories their flavour. The collection offers a gentle, nostalgic portrait of Cape Cod life before the motor age fully arrived. It remains a favourite among readers of American regional humour.
51972-priscilla-and-charybdis-a-story-of:
Priscilla and Charybdis is a novel by Frank Frankfort Moore, the author of The Jessamy Bride. Its subtitle calls it a story of alternatives. It was published in London by Constable in 1909.

The tale opens at a concert rehearsal in a schoolroom. Morley Quorn cannot see why people make such a fuss over the tenor Kelton. The bass singers grumble at the door about the airs the fellow gives himself. The curate of the parish stands by with his flute, and checks their free speech. He then makes the same joke himself: that it is natural for a tenor to give himself airs. The small scene sets the book's tone of comedy, music, and village talk.
51995-tanglewood-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote Tanglewood Tales, retelling Greek myths for children. This edition, published by the Penn Publishing Company in 1921, carries illustrations by Virginia Frances Sterrett. Hawthorne had earlier told the same kind of stories in A Wonder-Book, and these six tales complete the set.

The Minotaur opens the book, with young Theseus growing up at Troezene under his grandfather, King Pittheus. The Pygmies tells of the tiny people who warred with the cranes. The Dragon's Teeth gives Cadmus and the sown men. Circe's Palace and The Pomegranate Seeds retell Odysseus's sorceress and the rape of Proserpina. The Golden Fleece closes with Jason and Medea. Hawthorne softens the old myths into fireside tales, keeping their wonder while fitting them for young ears.
52001-the-little-child-s-book-of-divinit:
A grandmother explains the main points of Bible teaching to her small grandchild in this book for children, printed in London in 1855. Little Emma sits by the fire on a Sabbath evening and asks what the minister meant by doctrines. Her grandmother, Mrs Allan, agrees to teach her in plain words if she comes back each Sabbath night.

The talks run through eight nights, starting with the being of God. Each night takes up one point of faith and puts it in words a child can grasp. The frame is warm and homely: a Bible on the table, a fire in the grate, and a girl who has promised to listen well. Parents of the time used such books to teach faith at home.
52010-some-animal-stories:
Charles G D Roberts writes tales of wild beasts in a Dutton and Dent volume first published in 1921 and reprinted through 1932. Eleven tales fill the set, most named for their beast in the contents list. Quills the Indifferent, Stripes the Unconcerned, and Kroof the She-Bear lead that list of heads.

A psalm line gives the first tale its name: Do Seek their Meat from God in bold type. A great panther slips from a shadowy hollow in a ravine under a rising full moon at the start. His coat shows warm in daylight, yet moon rays turn it to a spectral grey on the steep. His shrill cry, keen and menacing, calls his mate to the night's hunt in that ravine.
52029-unvarnished-tales:
William Mackay wrote Unvarnished Tales, a story collection printed in London in 1886, given to Reginald Shirley Brooks. Contents list a queer quest, a sawdust man's curse, and Lord Lundy's snuff-box. A philanthropic masher, a dishonoured bill, a man of genius, a dignified dipsomaniac, old boots, and a missing heiress follow.

A Times notice of a novel opens the first tale: White's novels lack one element, a quarter-column review declares with cruelty. White must learn to study human nature from the life, since characters evolved from inner consciousness want backbone and turn flabby, the critic says. Teddy Martin's brief, Bluebeard's cupboard, and love and a diary close the list. Short story readers get Victorian variety.
52061-a-book-of-the-pyrenees:
A Book of the Pyrenees is a travel and history book by S. Baring-Gould, first published in 1907 by Methuen of London. Twenty-five illustrations and a map go with the text. The book opens with the mountain chain itself, its shape and passes. Then it moves west to east along the French side. Gascony and Bayonne come first. Chapters take up Saint Jean Pied de Port, Orthez, and Pau.

The east half runs through Luz and Cauterets, Tarbes, and Bagnères. The Val d'Aure, Luchon, and Couserans come next. Foix, the Cerdagne, and the Canigou close the high ground. Perpignan ends the tour at the Mediterranean end of the chain. Town tales, church lore, and old wars fill the pages beside the road notes. Baring-Gould writes for the traveller and the armchair reader alike.
52089-neighborhood-stories:
Neighborhood Stories, by Zona Gale, was published at New York in 1914. Macmillan issued the tales with copyrights from 1912 onward in the front. Gale wrote Friendship Village and The Loves of Pelleas and Etarre before it. A front plate shows an auction cry, now this one, who will bid on this one.

A dedication offers the book to the little towns of the time and place. Small town neighbours, gossips, saints, and sinners fill the tales of the volume. Gale made a Wisconsin village stand for all such places in her fiction. Magazine readers of 1912 first met many of these sketches in print. Gentle humour and sharp eyes for small lives mark the Gale manner here.
5223-the-satyricon-volume-06-editor-s-no:
This sixth volume of the Satyricon is not narrative but apparatus: the editor's notes to W. C. Firebaugh's translation of Petronius. It gathers chapter-by-chapter commentary, explaining Roman customs, words, and allusions, from gladiators and silver skeletons at Trimalchio's dinner to the gods, prostitution, and social habits of the Roman world.

The notes also discuss the forgeries and additions that entered the text over centuries, helping readers tell Petronius apart from later hands. The volume serves students and curious readers of the Satyricon who want the background that makes its jokes, obscenities, and satire intelligible.
5224-the-satyricon-volume-07-marchena-no:
This seventh volume of the Satyricon gathers six notes by Marchena, addressed to the Army of the Rhine, on the text of Petronius. Marchena writes of how the French conquests brought Egyptian monuments and convent manuscripts to light, enriching knowledge and letters, and he applies that learning to the puzzles of the Roman novel.

The volume holds only Marchena's notes, not the narrative itself, and it belongs with Firebaugh's translation as scholarly apparatus. Readers interested in how the Satyricon reached the modern world, through discovery, forgery, and emendation, will find here a compact record of that history.
52304-wonderful-escapes:
Richard Whiteing reworked a French book by Bernard on famed escapes and added fresh parts of his own, issued in New York in 1871. Twenty six plates light the text. The book stood in a set called the Illustrated Library of Wonders, beside volumes on heat, optics, glass, and the moon.

The tales run from old Greek and Roman flights to kings and queens of the middle ages. Mary Queen of Scots, Charles the Second, and the young Pretender all break free in their turns. Cellini tells his own bold flight, and Baron Trenck, Casanova, and Latude fill long, famed parts. Jacobite risings, wars, and jail breaks give the set its pace: each tale is a lock picked against the odds.
52329-under-blue-skies-verses-pictures:
Under Blue Skies is a picture book of verses for children by S J Brigham, published in New York in 1886. Song and picture share each page, as the title promises. The frontispiece poem sets the tone: daffodils dance and the oriole flies. Daisies and buttercups nod to the roses on the wall. Each day under blue skies brings a fresh surprise, the verse says. The contents list short pieces on small themes.

Little Neighbors watches bees and children at their summer play. Study-Hour sets a schoolgirl's lessons against a robin's free song in the lilac tree. Other pieces take up a letter, a family drive, and a camping song. Silent Voices gives the daisies and their kin a turn to speak. The lithographs are by Julius Bien and Company. The book is a bright keepsake of its age, made to be looked at as much as read.
52356-essays-and-dialogues:
Charles Edwardes translated the Essays and Dialogues of Giacomo Leopardi for a London edition of 1882, adding a biographical sketch. A motto from Rahel heads the sketch: manure with despair, but let it be genuine, and you will have a noble harvest. The contents are mostly dialogues.

Pieces include a history of the human race, dialogues between Hercules and Atlas, Fashion and Death, and a goblin and a gnome. Nature talks with a soul and with an Icelander; the Earth talks with the Moon. Tasso converses with his familiar spirit, and Columbus with Gutierrez. A panegyric of birds and the song of the wild cock lighten the set. Readers get Italy's great pessimist in English prose.
52388-whiteladies:
Mrs Oliphant published Whiteladies, a novel, at New York in 1875 in the Leisure Hour series. Oliphant also wrote Margaret Maitland and The Last of the Mortimers. The first chapter explains the name: an old manor house, not a deserted convent as a reader might suppose.

The convent buildings that named the place have dropped away, leaving one ivy-covered chapel wall behind the orchard. The Austin family has held the manor since Henry the Eighth's time, when the priory was destroyed and its lands transferred, though no one can say clearly how. A family tradition tells of a wild union between an emancipated nun and a secularised friar. Readers get a family mystery rooted in the Reformation.
52400-famous-men-of-ancient-times:
Goodrich wrote of famous men of ancient times in a book printed at Boston. Mohammed heads the contents at page seven, then Belisarius, Attila, Nero, and Seneca. Virgil, Cicero, Julius Caesar, and Hannibal follow. Alexander, Aristotle, Demosthenes, Apelles, and Diogenes stand in the middle of the roll.

Plato, Socrates, Alcibiades, Democritus, Pericles, and Aristides come next. Aesop, Solon, Lycurgus, and Homer lead to Confucius at the close. Mohammed has exercised a greater sway over the opinions of mankind than any other human being, save perhaps Confucius. He was born at Mecca in Arabia in the year 570, the first life begins. He was the only son of Abdallah, of the noble line of Hashem. Short, clear lives made the pagan and eastern past plain for young American readers.
52436-fifteen-discourses:
Sir Joshua Reynolds delivered these Fifteen Discourses in the Royal Academy, here issued as number 118 of Everyman's Library with an introduction by L March Phillipps. A biographical note heads the volume. Reynolds was born in 1723 in Devonshire, son of the Reverend Samuel Reynolds.

He lived at Plymouth, went to Italy, and settled in London in 1752, becoming the fashionable portrait painter of his day. He founded the Literary Club and in 1768 became the Academy's first president. He died in 1792 and lies in St Paul's. Readers get the classic lectures on art by the man who defined British academic taste.
52457-in-various-moods-poems-and-verses:
In Various Moods holds poems and verses by Irving Bacheller. The Harper house in New York put the small verse book out. Its first poem was penned for a school mark of fifty years past. Verse tales of hills, grain fields, and old school gates fill the set.

The Sowers leads, with its roll of names writ on water and on stone. Calls of loved lost voices echo through halls in the keen first piece. Joy, grief, and fond recall trade turns through the mixed set. Plain speech and warm tune mark the verse of the famed tale hand. The book forms his side shelf of rhyme next to the prose tales.
52485-commodore-paul-jones:
Commodore Paul Jones is a life of the sea captain John Paul Jones by Cyrus Townsend Brady, published by Appleton of New York in 1912. Brady had written lives of other naval heroes, among them Stephen Decatur. A portrait and maps go with the text. In his preface Brady owns that he began with warm admiration for his man. He says he tried to set that feeling aside and weigh the record with care. Faults and wrongs in the career are not hidden, he warns.

The verdict, after fresh study, is stronger praise than he began with. Jones was born a captain, in the phrase Brady borrows. His place among the great sea kings, as planner, tactician, and fighter, is now past dispute. The book is dedicated to George Clifford Thomas as a model citizen.
52521-grimm-s-fairy-tales:
Frances Jenkins Olcott edited this Grimm's Fairy Tales for the Penn firm at Philadelphia. Rie Cramer drew the plates, and the book holds rights from 1922 in this 1927 form. The tales come from the Brothers Grimm, whose names stand in the title. The first tale is The Frog-King, which starts in old times when wishing was having. A king had daughters all fair, and the youngest so fair that the sun marveled at her.

More than forty tales fill the book, from Rapunzel and Haensel and Grethel to Snow-White and Rumpelstiltskin. The Elves and the Shoemaker, the Bremen Town-Musicians, and the Golden Goose are here too. Olcott chose tales of kings, beasts, poor boys, and sly folk for young readers. The book gives the best-known Grimm tales in one neat, pictured set.
52534-true-manliness-from-the-writings-o:
True Manliness gathers selections from the writings of Thomas Hughes, the author of Tom Brown's School Days. Brown made the selection, and James Russell Lowell supplied an introduction. Lothrop and Company of Boston published the volume in 1880 in the Spare Minute Series.

Lowell's preliminary note tells an unusual story. Asked for facts, Hughes sent him an autobiographical letter that was never meant for publication. Lowell found it so interesting that he resolved to print it, cutting only a few intimate allusions. He confesses he purposely waited until Hughes was at sea on his way to America, so that he could not consult him first. The indiscretion, he says, is wholly his own. The selections that follow present Hughes's ideal of Christian manliness for American readers.
52539-beautiful-wales:
Robert Fowler painted the Welsh scenes of this book, and Edward Thomas wrote the words that go with them. Black printed Beautiful Wales in London in 1905. A note on Fowler's landscapes by Finberg ends the volume.

The Stack at Holyhead fronts the book, and Anglesey views crowd the early plates. Beaumaris by moonlight, a trout stream, and the Menai Straits show in colour. Thomas opens with broad remarks on men, authors, and things in Wales. Entering Wales, a farmhouse under a mountain, and fireside folk follow. Two ministers, a bard, a schoolmaster, and an innkeeper fill a long chapter. Wales month by month closes the main text.
52563-the-hand-of-the-mighty-and-other-s:
Vaughan Kester wrote The Hand of the Mighty and Other Stories, printed at Indianapolis in 1913. Kester had written The Prodigal Judge and The Fortunes of the Landrays. A likeness of the author goes with the book, and a sketch of his life by his brother Paul. Contents open with the brother's sketch, headed Vaughan Kester.

The title tale follows, then the bad man of Las Vegas and Mollie Darling. The blood of his ancestors, when we have waited, and the deserter come next. What Rearton saw, how Mr Rathburn was brought in, and the half-breed fill the middle. Willie, a social experiment, and all that a man hath close the set. The sketch tells that Kester was born in New Brunswick, New Jersey, and spent most of his boyhood in Mount Vernon, Ohio. A severe cold there left him a hoarseness of speech he never shook off.
52580-pearls-parasites:
Pearls and Parasites, by Arthur Shipley of Christ's College, Cambridge, was published in London in 1908 by John Murray. Shipley dedicates the book to his sister. Nine essays make the set. The title piece on pearls comes first, then the depths of the sea and British sea-fisheries. Zebras and horses and hybrids, Pasteur, malaria, the torment and danger of flies, and Cambridge itself follow.

Plates show zebra hybrids: a mare, her foal, and a hybrid foal by a zebra stallion, at a month old. Figures of the malaria parasite, after Ross, show the germ as it passes through the body of the Anopheles mosquito. Shipley wrote popular science with a researcher's hand, moving from oyster beds to horse breeding to tropical disease in one easy volume.
52596-czech-folk-tales:
Czech Folk Tales holds tales picked and turned by Josef Baudis. The teller taught word lore at the great school in Prague. Eight prints dress the text of the small book of old tales. The book came out in London, and no year is shown in its front pages.

Tales come from named Czech hands who wrote folk lore down in print. A tale of the twelve months leads the set, then a brave lad tale. Boots, cloak, and ring, a sleep lad, and three doves fill the mid list. Water sprites, twin lads, and wise girls share the back of the book. Plain English aims the lore at home and school shelves abroad.
52622-jane-austen-and-her-times:
Jane Austen and Her Times is a study by G E Mitton, with twenty one illustrations. Other books by the author are listed at the front. The London edition was first published in nineteen oh five. A painting called Morning Employments serves as frontispiece. Contents run to nineteen chapters. A preliminary and discursive chapter opens, then childhood. The position of the clergy and home life at Steventon follow.

The novels take a chapter of their own, then letters and post. Society and love making and visits and travelling take their turns. Contemporary writers and a trio of novels fill the middle. The navy, Bath, and dress and fashions follow. Last days closes the tale of her life in the list. Portraits of her father and brother stand among the pictures.
52697-five-years-in-the-alleghanies:
Five Years in the Alleghanies came out under the American Tract Society. The society issued it at New York in 1863. A plate shows the Hawk's Nest in Fayette County. That cliff is also called Marshall's Pillar. Chapter One treats the writer's preparation. Chapter heads sketch a rough mission field.

The grog-shop and the rolling mills mark chapter three. A new religion and a hard father mark the fourth. Book preachers get installed in chapter five. A governor of West Virginia enters chapter six. Surprising desolations greet the traveler there. A hunter seeks books for a Sunday school later. An Ironside preacher who distills stands in chapter eight. Colporteur tales from a hard mountain field show faith work among mills, mines, and cabins before paved roads came.
52703-mademoiselle-miss-and-other-storie:
Mademoiselle Miss, by Henry Harland, was published in 1893. Heinemann issued the stories in London that year. Five tales make the volume. The Funeral March of a Marionnette follows the title story. The Prodigal Father and A Sleeveless Errand come next. A Light Sovereign closes the list. The title story opens on a gloomy Paris. The day is a lovely one in April, yet the town is the dullest in Christendom. Mademoiselle Miss left last night for England. Her worshippers saw her off at St Lazare station. They found her a corner seat among ladies travelling alone. One brought violets; one, a book.

Jean brought claret, and Jacques sandwiches in a napkin. When the train rolled away, the city itself had changed. The narrator walks out into a new and dismal Paris.
52741-how-to-tell-fortunes:
How to Tell Fortunes was copyrighted in 1902 and published in New York by Frank Tousey. The title page promises Napoleon Oraculum and the key to work it. It also tells fortunes by cards, and gives lucky and unlucky days, signs, and omens.

The cards section opens with rank. In telling fortunes by cards, the ace ranks highest, then king, queen, knave, ten, nine, eight, and seven. Those are generally the only cards used. Suits have an order too. Clubs stand first, as they mostly portend happiness, and are rarely of bad augury. Hearts signify joy, liberality, or good temper. Diamonds denote delay, quarrels, and annoyance. Spades are the worst suit of all: grief, sickness, and loss of money. Position, the book warns, can change a card meaning entirely. Readers get a cheap fortune telling manual of the dime novel era.
52766-a-history-of-the-united-states:
Charles Kendall Adams, late president of the University of Wisconsin, and William Trent of Columbia wrote this school history of the United States. It appeared at Boston and Chicago in a revised edition, with copyrights of 1903 and 1909. It belongs to Allyn and Bacon's series of school histories, in half leather with maps and illustrations.

A portrait of George Washington fronts the book. Trent's preface explains that Adams's death left him to write it for their joint work. The duty would naturally have fallen to the senior author. Sister volumes cover ancient history, modern history, and England. Readers get an American school textbook history from the progressive era.
52810-the-border-boys-in-the-canadian-ro:
Fremont Deering wrote The Border Boys in the Canadian Rockies, a boys adventure printed at New York in 1913. Deering wrote Border Boys tales of the trail, the frontier, Mexican and Texas Rangers, and the St Lawrence. Contents open with the boy from nowhere, a torrent, peril of life, and Jimmie's pluck on the start for the Rockies.

A lynx trees a boy, a mountain mystery deepens, ponies vanish, a volcano erupts for Ralph, and boys face a grizzly in the high country. Caverns, a hut in the woods, underground passages, prisoners, Blood Indians, and mountain lions crowd the long tale. Carthew of the Mounted and an outlaw ranch close the plot. Boys got Rockies adventure.
52817-lightships-and-lighthouses:
Frederick Talbot wrote Lightships and Lighthouses in the Conquests of Science series, published in 1913. The frontispiece shows the Heligoland lighthouse throwing beams of forty-three million candle-power from a height of two hundred and seventy-two feet. Its range is twenty-three miles, and its rays are seen from Büsun on a clear night.

The contents march from the origin of the lighthouse to its building, its lights and illuminants, and its fog-signals. The Eddystone gets a chapter, as do the Bell Rock and Skerryvore lights together. The lonely lights of Scotland and the Fastnet, the outpost of Europe, follow. Talbot wrote popular engineering with a gift for the keepers' side: rocks, storms, and supply boats. Lightships share the title and the tale. Coast readers of 1913 got the lit edge of Britain explained.
52855-the-star-sent-knaves:
The Star Sent Knaves is a star tale by Keith Laumer from the June nineteen sixty three Worlds of Tomorrow. Dan Slane calls on a rich art man named Snithian at his strong house. Snithian guards his paint works with a host of men day and night. Slane claims the one weak spot stands bare in that scheme. No man sits in the vault with the works, he points out in plain words.

A past theft from a locked vault backs his claim with force. Seals on that vault door stood whole while the works went off. The guard chief warms to the plan, but Snithian scorns it as waste. He throws Slane out and blames the press for his risk. The tag asks what first meet of Earth and the star union brings.
52869-on-the-connexion-of-the-physical-s:
Mary Somerville's On the Connexion of the Physical Sciences reached its ninth edition, completely revised, from John Murray in London in 1858. She dedicates the book to her dear children, and its Bacon motto holds that no natural phenomenon can be studied alone, but only as it stands connected with all nature. Somerville had earlier written Mechanism of the Heavens and Physical Geography.

The opening sections treat gravitation: the attraction of a sphere, the form of celestial bodies, and the moon held in her orbit. Later sections take up elliptical motion, the elements of an orbit, and the perturbations, periodic and secular, that universal gravitation causes among the heavenly bodies.
52875-red-paint-at-oxford-sketches:
Two Oxford men, signing themselves Pish and Tush, published sketches of undergraduate life with Greening of London in 1904. Their preface warns that the pieces must not be taken too hard. They show, they say, only the lightest side of their friends' university years. Yet five Blues were won among the men in the book.

The Pilot, one of the set, beat odds of thirty three to one and took a creditable First. Freddy hopes for the Cabinet, and Squiff is on his way to rule a province in India. The sketches treat motoring to town, a quiet evening, the theatre, and rugger night. One tells how the set ragged a suburban train. Eights' Week closes the list. The first piece opens on a borrowed seven and sixpence and a motor car that will not start, its driver head down in the petrol tank.
52914-the-will-to-power-an-attempted-tra:
Friedrich Nietzsche left the notes gathered as The Will to Power, an attempted transvaluation of all values, and Anthony Ludovici translated this first volume into English. Foulis of Edinburgh and London published it in 1914 as volume 14 of the complete works, edited by Oscar Levy. Books One and Two stand in this volume.

The contents show the plan. Book One is called European Nihilism. It treats nihilism as the outcome of the values that had ruled so far. It reads the movement as a sign of decay, and as a crisis joined to the idea of recurrence. Book Two criticizes the highest values that have prevailed: religion first, then morality, with the herd, the good man, and the saint all weighed. A criticism of philosophy closes the book. Readers get Nietzsche's workshop notes arranged as an assault on the moral order of Europe.
52915-the-will-to-power-an-attempted-tra:
Friedrich Nietzsche's The Will to Power fills two volumes in Anthony Ludovici's English translation. Foulis of Edinburgh and London issued this second volume in 1913. The subtitle calls the work an attempted transvaluation of all values. Books three and four of the whole work stand here.

The third book sets out principles of a new valuation. It applies the will to power to science, nature, society, and art. Sections attack causality and the thing in itself. Others treat knowledge as a tool of life. The fourth book turns to discipline and breeding. Its order of rank sorts the strong from the weak. The noble man and the great man appear as types. Dionysus and the eternal recurrence close the volume.
52942-the-year-after-the-armada-and-othe:
The Year After the Armada is a set of studies in history by Hume. He was a fellow of the royal guild for the past. He served as editor of a great set of Spanish state papers. Those papers date from the age of Elizabeth, and rest in the public record rooms of London. Past books on the wooings of that queen bear his name as well.

The book is in its second form. It was put out at London in the late eighteen hundreds. Its front plate shows a famed earl of the age from a print of his own time. In a short word first, the author tells how his work led him down side paths. On those paths he oft struck rich finds. The studies in the book are the fruit of that work.
52944-prisons-prisoners-some-personal-ex:
Constance Lytton wrote Prisons and Prisoners, some personal experiences, printed at London with rights from 1914. Part of the tale runs under the plain name Jane Warton, spinster. Portraits front the work, and a publisher note owns that he does not share all her views yet is glad to print them.

Contents map a suffrage campaign through cells. Lytton tells her conversion, a deputation to the prime minister, a police court trial, and four spells in prison at Holloway, Newcastle, and Walton Gaol in Liverpool. Hospital days, types of prisoners, talks from the cells, and the Home Office fill the core. Calm, exact, and brave, the book bears witness to force feeding era protest and the price women paid for the vote.
52951-rhymes-of-the-rockies:
Rhymes of the Rockies, by James Whilt, is a book of verse in a second edition of 1922. Whilt and Masek held the copyright, and the Conkey company printed it at Chicago. His preface is dated at Eureka, Montana, on May 25 of that year.

Whilt spent most of his life in the Rocky Mountains as timber cruiser, packer, trapper, and guide. He says the peaks are part of him, and he gives the book to them and to Glacier National Park, their wonder child. The contents run to some thirty poems: a Chinook wind, an Indian trail, a pack train, and a trapper's story. The passing of the range, a pale horse, and a cabin of mystery show the range of his themes. Camp-fires and waterfalls run through the set.
52959-women-s-wages:
Women Wages, by William Smart, is a paper on pay for women workers. Smart taught political economy at Queen Margaret College and at Glasgow. James MacLehose of Glasgow issued the paper in eighteen ninety two. It was read to the Philosophical Society of Glasgow in December eighteen ninety one.

Smart opens that women wages are, as a rule, far under men wages. In British textile trades women earn about ten shillings a week on average. That work is skilled, as any who have seen a mill know well. A low average for a skilled man is twenty shillings a week. Smart sorts women workers into four classes from a Webb paper.
52984-the-right-to-be-lazy-and-other-stu:
Paul Lafargue's The Right to Be Lazy and Other Studies, translated by Charles Kerr and published by his Chicago company in 1907, takes its motto from Lessing. Let us be lazy in everything, he quotes, except in loving and drinking, except in being lazy.

The title essay attacks a disastrous dogma. A strange delusion, Lafargue writes, possesses the working classes of the capitalist nations: the love of work, a furious passion pushed to the exhaustion of the worker and his children. Priests, economists and moralists have haloed the curse instead of fighting it, and in capitalist society work stands as the cause of all intellectual degeneracy and organic deformity. Companion studies treat socialism and the intellectuals, the bankruptcy of capitalism, the woman question, the socialist ideal, and the rights of the horse against the rights of man.
53019-history-of-the-united-states:
A school history of the United States, published by the American Book Company in 1891. The preface holds that to American youth the history of their country is more important than any other branch of education.

The author says he put himself in the student's place, gathering the most important and romantic parts of the national story in a pleasing style. He promises research without the rubbish and scaffolding of showy scholarship. He also admits a western slant, refusing to despise the history of civilization in the Mississippi Valley or to find all heroism in the older states. The narrative runs from aboriginal times to the present greatness. Schoolrooms get a patriotic, readable text.
53023-the-history-of-the-assassins-deriv:
Joseph von Hammer wrote The History of the Assassins, derived from Oriental sources, translated from the German by Oswald Charles Wood and published at London in 1835. The translator dedicates the work to the Royal Asiatic Society. His preface gives two reasons for the translation.

The subject's own interest is the first. The second is introducing British readers to some portion of an author of such established reputation as von Hammer, historian of the Ottoman Empire. No earlier English account, he argues, makes the book superfluous. Readers get the first Western history of the Nizari Ismailis of Alamut, the Old Man of the Mountain's order, built from Persian and Arabic chronicles.
53053-by-the-aurelian-wall-and-other-ele:
By the Aurelian Wall and Other Elegies is a book of poems by Bliss Carman, issued in 1898. Carman was already known for Low Tide on Grand Pré and Ballads of Lost Haven. The title poem stands in memory of John Keats. It opens by the Aurelian Wall in Rome, near the tomb of Caius Cestius. There a weary traveller found burial far from home.

The elegy tells of that stranger who left a book of lyrics behind. A child finds his reed flute and one day wakes its wild music. Other poems mourn Phillips Brooks, Henry George, and John Eliot Bowen. A Norse Child's Requiem and Seven Wind Songs widen the range. The White Gull and The Country of Har add sea and travel themes. Elegy, in Carman's hands, turns grief into song.
53088-landseer-s-dogs-and-their-stories:
Sarah Tytler's Landseer's Dogs and their Stories was published in London in 1877 by Marcus Ward and Company. It gathers six of Sir Edwin Landseer's famous dog pictures as chromographs, each with its story told in prose. The plates are Low Life, High Life, Suspense, The Humble Friend, The Cavalier's Pets, and Dignity and Impudence.

Her introduction explains Landseer's hold on the public. His strength, and part of his weakness, lay in the human feeling he put into animals. Each picture tells a story not only of the dog but of the absent master and mistress behind it. The dog, she writes, is the humble friend of man, and Landseer interprets the ties between God's higher and humbler creatures. The book was made for the many readers who kept his prints on their walls.
53103-sop-s-fables:
Aesop's Fables, in the Banbury Cross Series, retells the old tales for children. Grace Rhys prepared this edition, and Charles Robinson drew the pictures. The book was printed in London in 1895.

A verse to a child named Enid opens the door of Aesop's house. The Lion and the Mouse and the Frogs that asked a king wait inside, the verse promises. The first fable tells of a jackdaw that dressed in peacock feathers to pass for a finer bird. His false strut betrays him, and the peacocks strip him bare and drive him home. His own flock then scorns him for his former airs. The Sun and the Wind follows, a trial of who can make a traveller drop his cloak.
53111-half-hours-with-the-highwaymen-vol:
Charles Harper wrote Half-Hours with the Highwaymen, a set of picturesque biographies of the road robbers of old England. Harper was the great chronicler of the English roads, author of books on the Portsmouth, Dover, Bath, and Great North roads. His name on a title page promised turnpikes, coaches, and inns.

The half-hour plan is the charm: each highwayman gets a short sitting, a life told at reading length. The robber was already a romantic figure when Harper wrote, half villain and half cavalier. His road books dug the records of the routes, and this volume stocks those roads with their inhabitants. Stand-and-deliver men step out of the hedges of his beloved highways. Readers who liked his coaching histories get the darker traffic of the same roads. Volume one implies a rogue gallery to come.
53112-half-hours-with-the-highwaymen-vol:
Half-Hours with the Highwaymen, in its second volume, offers short lives of famous road robbers. Charles Harper wrote the set, which calls itself picturesque biographies. Harper was a tireless chronicler of England's old roads. His books on the Portsmouth, Dover, and Bath roads stand listed at the front.

The argument of the volume can be felt in its treatment of legend. Harrison Ainsworth's romance Rookwood, the text complains, wronged a real highwayman. John Nevison, a distinguished robber of the sixteen-hundreds, lost his fame there. The glory of his wonderful ride to York was handed over to Dick Turpin. Turpin, the book insists, never owned the mare called Black Bess at all. Harper's half-hours aim to give the record back to its true owners. Romance is corrected, robber by robber, from the evidence of the roads.
53117-motion-picture-directing-the-facts:
Motion Picture Directing is a craft book on the facts and lore of the new art of film, by Milne. He was a film judge for years on the trade sheets and worked in the tale and make wing of a great film house. Its rights were set at New York in the early nineteen twenties.

It was used as a side text in a school of light craft in three great towns. Its parts take the great and the less great first, then the film sense. The prep for a make, and the ways of two famed chiefs of one house, fill the next run. When act skill helps, air and mood, and a giant of the art get their own parts.
53142-the-men-of-the-nineties:
Bernard Muddiman's The Men of the Nineties was published by G P Putnam's Sons in New York in 1921. Its prologue opens with the day Beardsley left his stool and ledger in a London insurance office. Then he took seriously to illustrating the strange comic world of Congreve.

About the same time, a coterie of young men, fresh from the Varsity in many cases, appeared in London proclaiming art for art's sake under the aegis of Oscar Wilde. Behind the English upheaval Muddiman sets France: the impressionists Manet and Monet in painting, and the symbolists who killed the Parnassian school of poetry about 1885.
53143-henley-s-twentieth-century-formula:
Henley's Twentieth Century Formulas, Recipes and Processes is a big reference book. Gardner Hiscox edited it for the Norman Henley firm of New York. The 1914 edition, revised and enlarged, holds ten thousand selected formulas. Household and workshop recipes serve makers, mechanics, and home workers alike. Hiscox also wrote Mechanical Movements and books on compressed air.

His preface aims to meet the practical needs of home and workshop. The mechanic, the manufacturer, the artisan, and the housewife all count. Care in selection marks the formulas gathered from many trades here. Soaps, inks, cements, polishes, and cures fill its ordered heads in bulk. Money saving methods for plain households stand beside factory processes in print.
53149-the-dyak-chief-and-other-verses:
The Dyak Chief and Other Verses is a book of poems by Erwin Clarkson Garrett. Barse and Hopkins published it in New York in 1914. Garrett also wrote My Bunkie and Other Ballads. He dedicated the book to his mother. A short verse on callings and yearning stands before the contents. The contents divide the poems into three parts. The title poem, The Dyak Chief, stands alone as part one.

Part two gathers American army ballads. Those poems treat camp life and service in the Philippines. Titles include Philippine Rankers and The Sultan Comes to Town. Part three holds a wide range of other verses. Shah Jehan, King Bamboo, and The Song of the Aeroplane appear there. Poems on Mark Twain, Keats, and Bryant honour fellow writers. War, sea, faith, and travel run through the collection.
53152-motor-tours-in-wales-the-border-co:
Rodolph Stawell's wife wrote Motor Tours in Wales and the Border Counties, published at Boston in 1909 with photographs by her husband. A frontispiece shows Valle Crucis Abbey, and a map opens the book. Five long chapters divide the ground by region.

The tours run through Shropshire, north Wales, the heart of Wales, south Wales, and the Wye Valley. Photographs show Ludlow Castle, Stokesay Castle, old streets in Shrewsbury, and abbeys such as Buildwas and Haughmond. One plate marks the hall where Comus was first performed. Readers get an early motoring guide, written when driving to castles and abbeys was still a fresh way to see Wales.
53190-absurd-ditties:
G E Farrow wrote Absurd Ditties, issued in London in 1903 with comic pictures by John Hassall. Farrow was known for The Wallypug of Why. The book holds more than sixty short verse tales, each named for its lead figure. Early pieces treat Mr Justice Dear, the late Mr Brown, and Captain Archibald McKan.

Justice Dear opens the set by lamenting his empty court and his many pairs of white kid gloves. Later ditties treat a tuck-shop woman, rival hairdressers, a plain cook, and a retired pork-butcher who meets a spook. Others cover a poet with buccaneers, converted cannibals, and a duel in France. An epilogue closes the book. The tone is light, rhymed, and proudly absurd throughout.
53219-the-history-of-bread-from-pre-hist:
John Ashton wrote The History of Bread, from Pre-historic to Modern Times, published in London in 1904. Ashton traces the staff of life from the earliest grain eaters to the bakeries of his own day. Pictures of Egyptians threshing corn by hand and storing it in sacks head the book, and many more drawings line its pages.

Fifteen chapters move across the world: bread in Egypt and Assyria, in Palestine, in the classic lands, in eastern lands, and across Europe and America. Ashton leans on the lake dwellings of Switzerland, whose people crushed corn, wove cloth, and baked bread. Later chapters show how grain becomes flour, the miller and his tolls, ovens old and new, and the religious use of bread. Gingerbread, charity bread, bread riots, and legends close the survey. Readers get a full popular history of the most common food on earth.
53225-a-society-clown-reminiscences:
A Society Clown is the book of reminiscences of George Grossmith, the comic singer and actor of the Gilbert and Sullivan stage. The title page dedicates it to his wife, his truest friend and best adviser. The contents run from early recollections to the provinces. A chapter at Bow Street police court stands odd in the list. Gilbert and Sullivan get a chapter of their own. The tale of how an amateur became a professional fills an other.

Grossmith opens with a quote from Ruddigore on his low view of himself. He tells of a talk in a dining room in February 1888. A friend held that any man who writes his life makes an ass of himself. He must praise himself or feign humility, and name-drop or starve the tale. Grossmith tells the story against himself, and writes on with a wink.
5324-the-book-of-were-wolves:
Sabine Baring-Gould's Book of Were-Wolves, published in London in 1865, gives an account of a terrible superstition. Chapters trace lycanthropy among the ancients, from Marcellus Sidetes, Virgil, Herodotus, Ovid. Pliny leads to a story from Petronius and Arcadian legends, then the book turns to the were-wolf in the North, with Norse traditions, the Volsung Saga, and Hrolf's Saga.

Baring-Gould, a clergyman and antiquary, collects folklore, history, and explanation in a single survey. The book offers readers a thorough, if Victorian, study of how men came to believe they turned into wolves. And it remains a classic of folklore scholarship.
53245-little-dramas-for-primary-grades:
Little Dramas for Primary Grades is a school reader by Ada Maria Skinner and Lillian Nixon Lawrence. The American Book Company published it in 1913. Skinner taught at a school in New York City. Emma Sebring, in a prefatory note, explains the book's purpose and place.

Dramatic readers, she writes, have passed beyond the stage of experiment. Their worth in stirring imagination and quickening appreciation is now proven. The true difficulty is the short supply of fit material for small children. This book was compiled to help meet that need in the classroom. It serves the end of the first year and the start of the second. Bunny Rabbit and the Timid Hare open the list of little plays. Fables like Belling the Cat and the Fox and the Crow follow.
53261-we-moderns-enigmas-and-guesses:
Edwin Muir sets out short numbered reflections in We Moderns: Enigmas and Guesses, published by Knopf in New York in 1920. Mencken edited the book and wrote its introduction. The first section, The Old Age, opens with a piece called The Advanced.

Muir notes a split in advanced minds: sure and eager on single questions, yet timid about life itself. A second piece, The Intellectual Coquettes, blames fear of decision for a habit of flirting with dangerous ideas. Such minds, he says, bear every burden except responsibility, and end by losing even the will to choose. A third piece attacks modern realism as art made by the average man for the average man.
53361-patsy-carroll-under-southern-skies:
Grace Gordon wrote a girls adventure tale printed in New York in 1918, with pictures by Emmet Owen. Patsy Carroll frowns at the start over the Easter vacation. She had hoped for three weeks, as it had always been at Yardley. Time to go wayfaring again, the first chapter cries, and glorious news soon lands.

The land of flowers, Florida, draws Patsy south. A cottage in a palm grove, the old ocean, and a timid caller open the new adventure. Patsy scents a mystery, meets Dolores and Carlos, and finds a secret drawer. A ghost, a memento, and the true sign of the dragon close a sunny tale of travel, friendship, and detection for girls.
53409-ocean-gardens-the-history-of-the-m:
Ocean Gardens is a book on the sea tank for the home by Humphreys, author of past works on the wing beasts and moths of Britain. Its full title tells its span: the past of the sea tank, and the best ways now in use to set it up and keep it. It came out at London in the late eighteen fifties.

A plate at its front names ten sea weeds in a row, each with its Latin name. Fans of red and green, a sponge like ball, and the pink coral weed stand in that list. The book then tells how the craze for glass seas rose, and how to stock one with weeds, shells, and small life of the shore, and keep it sweet.
53419-twenty-five-ghost-stories:
Holland compiled and edited this set of twenty-five ghost stories, copyrighted in 1904 by Ogilvie of New York. A line from Hamlet stands at the front, about more things in heaven and earth than philosophy dreams of. The contents mix famous names with popular magazine tales of haunts and horrors.

Edgar Allan Poe opens the book with 'The Black Cat' as its first story. A flayed hand, a tree that takes vengeance and a parlor-car ghost follow in the list. Phantom women, a burglar's ghost, a dead woman's photograph and the ghost of Washington round out a set built for late-night reading.
53433-west-virginia-trees:
Brooks wrote West Virginia Trees, Bulletin 175 of the Agricultural Experiment Station at Morgantown, dated September 1920. A stand of young white pines illustrates the front matter. Director John Lee Coulter heads the station staff list, with chemists, the state entomologist Rumsey, and plant pathologist Giddings among the specialists.

Bulletins and reports of the station are mailed free to any citizen of West Virginia on written application, the notice says.
