The state board of control directs financial affairs of state educational institutions from Charleston. Keys and descriptions of the state's native and planted trees serve farmers, foresters, teachers, and timber men identifying species. Forestry readers get a state flora bulletin.
53456-young-readers-science-fiction-stor:
Richard Elam wrote these space tales for young readers, and Victor Prezio drew their plates. Grosset and Dunlap issued the set at New York in 1957, from Lantern Press. Elam gives the book to the young travelers of tomorrow.

Beth and the Twilight Star opens the thirteen tales. Gib Takes a Space Test and the Space Mail Run follow. All Aboard for Space, Wheel in the Sky, and Danger on the Ice Canal fill the middle. Cargo for Callisto and the Big Show on Titan take the outer planets. Adventure on the Sun's Doorstep and the Flying Mountain run hot and strange. Castaways in Space, the Big Space Ball Game, and Paper Treasure for Mars close a set made for the first space age's children.
53467-prejudices-second-series:
Prejudices: Second Series, by H L Mencken, was published by Jonathan Cape at London in 1921. The long opening essay, The National Letters, runs from Prophets and Their Visions through The Ashes of New England to an epilogue.

Roosevelt: An Autopsy follows, then The Sahara of the Bozart and The Divine Afflatus. The contents also list a study of a stock virtue and a piece called Exeunt Omnes. Shorter groups treat the allied arts, the cult of hope, and the dry millennium of prohibition. An appendix on a tender theme, covering the nature of love and women as spectacles, ends the volume in Mencken's driest manner.
53474-prejudices-third-series:
Mencken published Prejudices: Third Series at the Borzoi in New York, with Alfred Knopf, in 1922. The third of his essay volumes gathers the Baltimore critic's shots at American life. A portrait front and a contents list of 19 pieces open the book.

On Being an American leads. Huneker gets a memorial, and criticism a footnote. Five Men at Random profiles Lincoln, Paul Elmer More, Frank Harris, and Havelock Ellis. Types of Men sorts the romantic, the skeptic, the believer, the scientist, the business man, and the average man. Advice to Young Men closes the set. The first essay watches the tender-minded boarding ships for Paris and Rome to escape American atrocities, and finds little to cavil at in their complaints. Readers get Mencken at full snort, between the war and Prohibition.
53486-the-three-fates:
Marion Crawford, author of Mr Isaacs and Saracinesca, wrote this novel, copyrighted by Macmillan in 1891 and published at London and New York in 1893. A dedication to Frederick Macmillan is dated from Rome in February 1892.

Jonah Wood was bitterly disappointed in George, his son. For twenty-five years he had looked in vain for business instincts in the boy. George could talk well enough about the great movements of business in New York, but he wasted his time trying to earn money with his pen. The old man, himself ruined by the exercise of his own business faculties, still pinned his faith to his theories of finance. He would have been content to see George a clerk on a nominal salary in a great banking house. He fought his wish to see the boy avenge the family's losses on Thomas Craik.
535-travels-with-a-donkey-in-the-cevenne:
Robert Louis Stevenson walks the Cévennes hills with a donkey named Modestine in this beloved travel book. Starting at Le Monastier, fifteen miles from Le Puy, he packs, prods, and argues with his stubborn beast through highland valleys. A dedication to Sidney Colvin frames the trip as a search for honest friends.

Stevenson writes with wit and warmth, noting monks, shepherds, and Protestant memories of the hills. Modestine steals every scene she enters. The book endures as a classic of walking prose, where a man, a donkey, and a pack prove that travel's best reward is friendship.
53506-a-collection-of-kacha-ri-folk-tale:
Anderson of the Indian Civil Service collected Kachari folk tales and rhymes, printed at Shillong in 1895. The little book serves as a supplement to Endle's Kachari Grammar and as a reading book for new learners. Anderson owns his vowel marks stray a bit from Endle's system, though the differences are small.

A rough translation is added for readers who may never learn Kachari. The tales show the folk lore of a simple and primitive people, Anderson says. He took them down as dictated on a tour of six weeks in the Kachari mauzas of Mangaldai. An accused person's statement is given in both Assamese and Kachari to show how close their syntax runs.
53538-prejudices-first-series:
Prejudices, First Series is a book of essays by Mencken, published in New York by Alfred Knopf in 1919. The front matter lists his earlier books, from A Book of Prefaces to The American Language. Four printings had appeared by March 1921.

The contents begin with an essay on criticism itself, then turn to named targets. Wells and Arnold Bennett receive chapters. The Dean, Professor Veblen, and the new poetry follow in the list. Mencken wrote as a critic who enjoyed the fight, and the series title warns the reader what to expect. The volume opens a run of Prejudices books that made his name in American letters. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
53601-the-academic-gregories:
Agnes Grainger Stewart traces one Scots kin group that held chairs at St Andrews, Edinburgh, and Oxford for two hundred years. Her Famous Scots volume came out in Edinburgh in April 1901. A family tree at the front links the line from John Gregorie of Drumoak and Janet Anderson down through sons and grandsons.

Chapter heads name David Gregorie of Kinairdy, who lived from 1625 to 1720, and James Gregorie, who lived from 1638 to 1675. Later men of the same name fill posts in maths and in the study of stars, then in healing and in thought. John Gregory and James Gregory close the main line, and a short last chapter looks back on the whole kin group and its mark on Scots learning.
53670-a-sketch-of-assam-with-some-accoun:
An officer in the East India Company Bengal Native Infantry, in civil employ, wrote A Sketch of Assam, with Some Account of the Hill Tribes. Smith, Elder and Company in London issued the book in eighteen forty seven. Plates from sketches by the author aid the text. The author had lived some years in the province. His narrative rests on official papers, with leave of Government, plus his own views.

The preface warns that vast forests, silence, and loneliness in Assam may not charm all travellers. Yet the land, he says, offers a wide field for discovery. Many wild tribes live there, and much about them is still to be asked and learned. His aims are to make Assam better known, to clear away bias against it, and to save the memory of fine scenes. Readers get an early British view of a frontier land and its hill peoples.
53723-early-english-hero-tales:
Jeannette Marks retells the oldest tales of England for young readers in a book issued by Harper and Brothers in 1915. Marks lectured at Mount Holyoke College. The volume opens her series Through Golden Doors to English Literature.

The tales run from the year 600 to 1340. The first golden door shows a hero, as it should be, she writes, for the English have always been brave. Yet the first poem may be the Far Traveller, not the hero's own. Welsh magic and the battle at the ford follow. Cædmon the cowherd sings in chapter four. The shepherd of Lauderdale and the boy who won come next. Marks chose master-stories not readily accessible elsewhere. A second volume was to bring Chaucer and the Middle English hero tales.
53766-merry-tales:
Eleanor Skinner and Ada Skinner made a book of tales for young readers. The book came out in 1915 with the American Book Company. Eleanor taught English in Columbus, Ohio. Ada taught in New York City. The tales come from many lands and many old sources.

Inside are folk tales, fairy tales, poems, and short plays in prose. Readers meet a monkey and a crocodile, a stone lion, and Finn with a fairy shoe maker. Some tales come from Chaucer, Andersen, and old Greek tales. Each piece is short and fits class or home reading. The mix shows how wide the old tale stock is.
53770-hymnological-studies:
Hymnological Studies is a study of church song by Matthew Lundquist of Wartburg College. The Wartburg Publishing House issued the work at Chicago, dated January 1926. Lundquist held degrees in letters and in music. The contents move from the hymnody of the Lutheran Church to a list of hymn writers.

The first section treats the hymns as both church songs and sacred poems. Their faith character, Lundquist argues, should mirror the church that bore them. Later sections survey Christian hymn singing from the earliest Greek and Latin hymns. Medieval song in Latin, German, and Scandinavian tongues follows. The long central part treats Luther himself and the hymnody of his church in three lands. An added part on Reformed church song closes the survey.
53794-within-the-gates:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps published the drama 'Within the Gates' with Houghton, Mifflin in 1901. A publisher's list of her earlier books fronts the volume, its titles running from 'The Gates Ajar' to 'Chapters from a Life' among them. A note explains the play's origin: it has so departed from the plan of her story 'The Gates Between' that it is in fact a new work with a new title.

The persons include Doctor Esmerald Thorne, a city physician, his wife Helen, and their child Laddie, between four and five years old. Fayth is an invalid patient and friend of the household. Doctor Gazell and a young surgeon named Carver complete the chief figures, and Maggie serves as maid. Beyond the cast stand a priest, nurses, patients, spirits, and the Angel Azrael. Act One opens in a city house library, the dinner table set beyond a portière.
53847-merry-s-book-of-puzzles:
Merry's Book of Puzzles, edited by Robert Merry and issued by Thomas O'Kane of New York, gathers brain-teasers from the pages of Merry's Museum. The preface greets the magazine's many readers with familiar faces and the same old jovial laughter. The stated aim is to instruct by smiles, not frowns, and to make the sad happy.

A verse greeting lists the stock: questions, conundrums, charades, puzzles, riddles of all shades, and rebuses. The puzzles open with picture problems, then ask who prolongs his work yet finishes in time, and why young ladies are like arrows. Parlor wits get a full workout.
53858-lowestoft-in-olden-times:
Lowestoft in Olden Times preserves lectures read before the members of Saint Margaret's Institute at Lowestoft, printed in an edition dated 1899 with additions to round out the story. The preface says modern Lowestoft, with its harbour, fishing fleet, and marine terraces, is a product of the nineteenth century.

The old town on the cliff survives as the nucleus of the enlarged modern one. Lowestoft's rise was bound up with Yarmouth, and records of contests between the two towns over the herring trade supply most of the surviving material. Readers get a small fishing port's history told through its long rivalry with its larger neighbour.
53861-the-apple-tree-table-and-other-ske:
The Apple Tree Table and Other Sketches, by Herman Melville, was printed by Princeton University Press in 1922, with a lead note by Henry Chapin. The sketches first ran in Harper and Putnam magazines from 1850 to 1856. None had been put in a book before.

Chapin singles out Hawthorne and His Mosses, the lone piece of criticism in the set. It gains from Melville friendship with Hawthorne when they lived near each other at Pittsfield. The other sketches treat home themes with fresh humor and rich, odd phrasing. The title piece opens in a dusty garret, with old vials and a worn quarto book. Readers meet the lighter, warm Melville of the magazine years, in short prose gems.
53873-old-coaching-days-some-incidents-i:
Old Coaching Days gives some incidents in the life of Moses James Nobbs. Nobbs was the last of the mail coach guards, and the tale is told by himself. The book was transcribed from the 1891 edition and sold for sixpence. A preface by the controller of the London postal service explains the occasion. A new rule retires civil servants at sixty-five, and the service loses its veterans at the end of 1891.

Nobbs, the preface says, has served the Post Office fifty-five years. He began as a mail guard on the coaches, and kept the work for years. When railways replaced the coach system, he rode as guard on the London and Exeter line. Later he superintended mail bags at Paddington Station. Now he retires to Uxbridge, and his short memoir keeps the guard's horn, the road, and the last years of the mails by coach.
53882-how-beauty-was-saved-and-other-mem:
How Beauty Was Saved and Other Memories of the Sixties, by Mrs James Madison Washington, gathers tales of the South during the Civil War. The Neale Publishing Company issued the book in 1907, and the author dedicates it to Southern girls.

The title story is set in the summer of 1862 in the Bayou Manchac country near Baton Rouge. Two girls ride three miles on one horse to a little schoolhouse called the Dove's Nest. Bands of Confederates, jayhawkers, and Federals roam the country, yet the girls carry a loaded pistol and a Spanish dirk and fear nothing. Beauty is the young bay horse one of them owns. Other pieces give the telltale gloves, a magic sign, memories of slave days, and a narrow escape.
53910-the-school-and-society-being-three:
The School and Society is a book of three lectures by John Dewey, supplemented by a statement of the University Elementary School. The University of Chicago Press published it, with copyright of 1900, and impressions ran on to 1913. A note preserved in the copy dates the lectures: they were delivered in April 1899. The audience was parents and others interested in the University Elementary School.

Dewey revised the lectures in part from a stenographic report, with unimportant changes and slight adaptations. The school described was his own laboratory school at Chicago, where his ideas of education were being tested in practice. The lectures argue that the school must grow out of the life of the home and community, not stand apart from it. Learning by doing, the occupation of the hands, and the social nature of the child run through them.
53915-folk-lore-of-west-and-mid-wales:
Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales is a gathering of Welsh tales, customs, and beliefs by Jonathan Ceredig Davies, a member of the Folk-Lore Society. It was printed at Aberystwyth in 1911. A preface by Alice, Countess Amherst, tells the author's own roving life.

Davies had lived for years in the Welsh colony in Patagonia, where he was a pioneer of the church. He then worked in a wild part of Western Australia, where he built a church. In 1901 he came home to Wales. There he found a great mass of Celtic lore still unrecorded in Cardiganshire and the mid counties. His command of Welsh fitted him for the task. The book is the fruit of that work.
53945-a-book-of-the-cevennes:
A Book of the Cevennes is a travel and history volume by Sabine Baring-Gould. John Long published it in London in 1907. Forty-four illustrations support the text. Eight of them are in colour. A map accompanies the volume. The book belongs to a series of regional guides by the same hand.

The contents move across the high country of southern France. Early chapters treat Le Velay and Le Puy. The volcanoes of the Vivarais earn a chapter. The canyon of the Ardèche follows. A long chapter treats the Camisards, the Protestant rebels of the region. Later chapters visit Alais, Ganges, and Le Vigan. The land of the novelist Ferdinand Fabre closes the tour.
53951-a-book-of-simples:
A Book of Simples prints a still-room manuscript found in the library of an Essex antiquary. Sampson Low, Marston issued the second impression at London, in a binding copied from the green vellum original. Experts judged the handwriting, by several hands, to cover some fifty years, ending about the middle of the eighteenth century.

Such a book held a manor house's cures, recipes, and household lore. Spelling and punctuation stand as written, quaint and uneven. A motto promises that delirious persons here may find a cure to stem the phrensy and calm the mind. In rural England of that age, roads were near impassable and doctors far off, so a still-room book was a working tool.
54019-farthest-north-the-life-and-explor:
Charles Lanman wrote Farthest North, the life and explorations of Lieutenant James Booth Lockwood of the Greely Arctic expedition, published in New York in 1885. A portrait of Lockwood in uniform stands at the front. A Thanksgiving sermon line from Phillips Brooks praises Arctic daring as the romance of the age.

In his preface Lanman says the book will interest the general public and gratify Lockwood's many friends. It will also correct false impressions raised by garbled extracts from the official journals of the Greely party. Those journals had been laid open to the public by order of the War Department. Lockwood sledged farther north than any man before him and did not come home. Lanman's life, built on the true journals, is the monument his friends wanted. Ice, hunger, and record distance fill its pages.
5403-short-stories-for-english-courses:
Rosa M. R. Mikels's Short Stories for English Courses, edited with introduction and notes for Shortridge High School in Indianapolis, gathers classic short stories for classroom use. Its contents include Henry van Dyke's First Christmas-Tree, Joel Chandler Harris's French Tar-Baby, Ruth McEnery Stuart's Sonny's Christenin', John Fox Jr.'s Christmas Night with Satan, and James Whitcomb Riley's Nest-Egg.

Later stories include Kipling's Wee Willie Winkie, Poe's Gold Bug, O. Henry's Ransom of Red Chief, and Ralph D. Paine's Freshman Full-Back, with notes on the requirements of the short story. The book offers students a varied anthology, with guidance on how each story may be used in class.
54060-beyond-the-gates:
Beyond the Gates is a tale by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps, first held by copyright in 1883 and printed at Boston in 1884. Phelps, also known for The Gates Ajar, wrote the book in grief. She gave it to the memory of her brother Stuart, who died in August 1883, while the work was in press.

The tale is told by a woman of forty who lives with her mother in a mill town in Massachusetts. She falls ill with brain fever, and on the fifteenth day of her illness strange events begin. Her account asks what lies past death, a theme her earlier work had made her known for.
54078-ruth-erskine-s-crosses:
Ruth Erskine's Crosses is a novel by Pansy, author of Ester Ried and the Chautauqua books. The Boston edition was copyrighted in eighteen seventy nine. A verse about God making all things beautiful in his time heads the pictures. Contents run to more than twenty six chapters, each named for a cross to bear or a stage in bearing it.

Early heads call her cross heavy, then a cross of lead. Bitter herbs, seeking help, and a drop of oil follow. Finding one's calling and other people's crosses take their own chapters. Later heads speak of duty's burden and shadowed joys. A verse frontispiece and the chapter plan mark the book as a tale of faith under trial. The heroine muses, in the text, on girls who rush into their mothers' arms.
54093-a-valiant-ignorance-vol-1-of-3-a-n:
Mary Angela Dickens opens a three-volume novel at a hotel table d'hôte in Nice in volume one. Macmillan and Company issued it at London and New York in 1894. She had written Cross Currents before it.

A child's letter leads the chapter. Young Julian reports that he is quite well, and Smut is quite well, and her tail is very fat. Uncle Richard gave him a box of soldiers. The captain has a horse, but there is a hole in the horse. Then the scene widens to the dining room. Long tables shine with white cloths, silver, and glass. Waiters glide, anticipating every wish. American chatter, French volubility, and a German and English undercurrent hum together. The motto comes from Browning's prince: thy gold is brass. Dickens was the novelist's granddaughter.
54094-a-valiant-ignorance-vol-2-of-3-a-n:
Mary Angela Dickens wrote A Valiant Ignorance, a novel in three volumes, and this second volume was printed in London in 1894. Dickens had written Cross Currents and A Mere Cypher. A motto, Thy gold is brass, stands on the title page. The volume opens in oppressive autumn weather, in the house at Chelsea, where the air has slowly cleared. Storms there had peaked in Julian's departure for the club.

As the days pass, Julian wins back his spirits and his careless ease. Yet his life this autumn is not the life of the past spring. Winter society is hardly formed, and hours of regular work have entered his routine for the first time. The house in Queen Anne Street now owns that work has something to do with life. A subtle change marks Julian too: a touch of self-standing, new to him.
54098-the-light-that-lies:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote a comic novel copyrighted in 1916 and published at New York. Its hero is Sampson, a rich man uncommonly successful in evading jury service. By some hook or crook he always managed to get off, and his trips to court three times a year became interruptions instead of annoyances.

Wise men advised him to serve once and be done, but he trusted his smartness over their wisdom. He escaped murder trials by professing reconsidered views on capital punishment, by doubting circumstantial evidence, and by denying insanity as a defence. Then the lower courts drew him, and his resourcefulness came under ever increasing strain. A jury-dodger's ingenuity, played for farce, opens the tale.
54109-round-the-fire-stories:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathered these seventeen tales, published by Smith, Elder and Company at London in 1908. A frontispiece by Castaigne shows a man bursting with a shriek into his own life. The titles promise strange doings: The Leather Funnel, The Beetle Hunter, The Man with the Watches, The Japanned Box, and The Lost Special among them.

The Leather Funnel opens the book in Paris, where the narrator's friend Lionel Dacre lives in the Avenue de Wagram in a small old house with iron railings. Dacre, a wealthy man of refined and eccentric tastes, has spent a fortune on a private library of Talmudic, cabalistic, and magical works, said to be unique. His tastes lean toward the marvellous and the monstrous, and rumor says his experiments in the unknown have passed all bounds of decorum, though to English friends he never alludes to them.
54130-wall-street-stories:
Edwin Lefevre wrote these tales of Wall Street stock trade and its folk. McClure, Phillips printed the book in New York in 1901. Contents open with The Woman and Her Bonds, a market tale. The Break in Turpentine and The Tipster follow in the list.

Fullerton Colwell of Wilson and Graves works hardest in his office. Partners leave much to him, and clerks own his industry freely. He raises pay, so men call him charming as well as busy. A Philanthropic Whisper, The Man Who Won, and Pike Peak follow. The book went through three printings in two months.
54149-a-history-of-advertising-from-the-:
Henry Sampson wrote a history of advertising from the earliest times. Chatto and Windus issued the work in London in 1874, with plates and facsimiles. The book is given to Thomas Milner Gibson for his services to advertising. A front plate shows a railway station of 1874 crowded with modern ads.

Early chapters split newspaper ads from street and general advertising. Anecdotes, curious specimens, and lives of advertisers fill the tale. Sampson traces how cries for wares grew into a press-shaping trade. Business readers gain a lively, first full chronicle of the ad trade's rise.
54159-busy-brownies:
Busy Brownies is a Brownie tale book with cuts by Palmer Cox, out in eighteen ninety six. Veale, a tale wife of fairy fame, wrote the tales of the set. A storm wind tore the Fairy Queen house to bits in the woods. That wind swept trees down and spread wreck as it ran its path. The sad queen lost the home of her line for long years past.

Brownies vowed to build her a house more fair than the lost one. Each small man bore a tool as the band set out by moon light. Ax, ham, nails, hod, and plane crowd their load in the fun list. Night is their work time, while the world sleeps in the dark. Ring of hams, grind wheel hum, and fast brush work fill the build night.
54247-beyond-these-voices:
Beyond These Voices, a novel by Braddon, was published in London by Hutchinson. A front caption shows a woman's stifled sobs as she lay on the floor. Chapter one presents Lady Felicia Disbrowe, who was held to stoop when she married Captain Cunningham of the first Life Guards. He was a handsome, fashionable man of old landed stock but no great wealth.

The captain's death in an Egyptian campaign left his widow with a small daughter, a pension, and about six hundred a year, half from the Disbrowes and half from small Somersetshire farms. For a grande dame to whom economy was degrading, the post was hard. As the orphan grew lovely at seventeen, Lady Felicia began to count her daughter her chief asset. Braddon sets up a tale of pride, money, and the marriage market.
5426-princess-polly-s-playmates:
Amy Brooks wrote Princess Polly's Playmates as another book about Polly, following earlier volumes such as Princess Polly at School and Princess Polly by the Sea. The story begins in a garden, where Polly imagines enchanted castles around her home at Sherwood Hall. Friends, visitors, and small adventures fill the chapters that follow.

Polly visits Rose, meets an unexpected guest, spends time at the shore, and deals with a runaway dog named Gyp. Chapters like The Village Nuisance and The Little Green Door show the gentle humor of the series. Young readers get a sweet, old-fashioned story of friendship, play, and everyday kindness.
54261-the-harvest-of-a-quiet-eye-leisure:
Leisure thoughts for busy lives fill a book called The Harvest of a Quiet Eye. The Religious Tract Society issued it in London, with art by Noel Humphreys and Harrison Weir. The author, who wrote My Study Chair, kept the name off the title page. Papers first ran in the Leisure Hour and in Sunday at Home.

Chapters follow the year from spring days to winter days and bare boughs. Woods, hay fields, sea shores, and hills prompt calm thought on faith and work. A Wordsworth verse at the front gives the book its name and aim. Busy readers gain short, restful pieces for spare moments.
54274-shakespeare-s-christmas-and-other-:
Shakespeare's Christmas, and Other Stories is a story collection by Q, the pen name of A T Quiller-Couch. Smith, Elder printed it at London in 1905. The title tale takes its motto from Bunyan, on the town through which the way to the Celestial City lies. It opens at the theatre in Shoreditch on Christmas Eve, 1598.

There the Lord Chamberlain's servants presented a new comedy. Never had the house known such a welcome, the tale says. A cutpurse in the twopenny gallery, paid to lead the applause, gave up toiling in its wake and leaned back with a puzzled grin. The other stories are Ye Sexes, Give Ear, Captain Wyvern's Adventures, and Frenchman's Creek. The Man Behind the Curtain, Rain of Dollars, and The Lamp and the Guitar complete the book. The frontispiece shows a woman commanding that a door be unbarred.
54309-ancient-apostles:
David McKay, general superintendent of the Deseret Sunday School Union, wrote these lessons for Sunday school teaching. The Deseret Book Company at Salt Lake City issued the second edition in 1921. The book presents the apostles of the New Testament as great men whose noble deeds still awaken good ambitions in boys and girls.

Part one follows Peter through his call, his testimony, his arrests, his visit to Samaria, and the closing scenes of his ministry, in a long run of short lessons. Shorter parts treat James the son of Zebedee, the first apostle to suffer martyrdom, and John the beloved disciple. Part four turns to Paul, from Saul of Tarsus and his conversion through his missionary journeys, his two years in prison, and the voyage to Rome.
54334-europe-in-the-middle-ages:
Ierne L Plunket, an Oxford graduate, wrote a history of Europe in the middle ages published at the Clarendon Press in 1922. Plunket had written The Fall of the Old Order and Isabel of Castile. Contents open with the greatness of Rome, then its decline. The dawn of Christianity and Constantine the Great follow. The invasions of the barbarians and the rise of the Franks come next.

Mahomet and Charlemagne get chapters of their own. The Northmen's invasions, feudalism and monasticism, and the investiture question continue. Humphrey Milford published for the university across the empire. Plunket wrote clear narrative history for schools and general readers.
54404-mehalah-a-story-of-the-salt-marshe:
Baring-Gould's novel of the salt marshes opens on the Essex coast between the mouths of the Blackwater and the Colne. The marshy tract is veined with water, contested by sea and land. At high tide only Mersea island and the Ray stand out of the flood.

The Ray is a gravel hill crowned with old thorn trees and an unfailing spring, reachable at ebb only by the old Roman causeway called the Strood. Chapter titles promise a decoy, a Dutch auction, and a forging of the ring. Smith, Elder and Company issued this new edition at London in 1884. Creeks run many miles inland, flushed with water twice in the twenty-four hours.
54415-nuggets-in-the-devil-s-punch-bowl-:
Andrew Robertson wrote these Australian tales, printed in London and Melbourne in 1894. Robertson also wrote The Kidnapped Squatter. Four stories make up the book: the title tale, Lanky Tim, Lost in the Bush, and Thunder-and-Lightning. The first and longest runs to nearly sixty pages.

The title story opens in a shearing shed. Bill Marlock, the ringer of the shed, is racing Norman Campbell sheep for sheep through a Saturday morning. Bill leads by one sheep on the tally, and Norman makes every effort to finish the week one better. A grab for the same small sheep leaves Bill with the old, shunned ram the shearers call the cobbler, to loud laughter.
54424-lotta-schmidt-and-other-stories:
Anthony Trollope collected short tales led by Lotta Schmidt in a volume from Chapman and Hall in London. The fourth form shown here is dated 1876. Lotta Schmidt opens in Vienna as workmen clear the old walls of the city. Two girls walk in the Burgplatz near a new bronze statue of Prince Eugene.

Talk of crowds and a grand gala day sets the social scene for the lead tale. Trollope mixes sharp notes on rank and fame with close views of young lives. The other tales in the set share his calm pace and close eye for manners. Readers who like his novels will find the same voice in brief form.
54470-tar-heel-tales:
Bryant, known across North Carolina as Red Buck, wrote Tar Heel Tales, printed at Charlotte in 1910. A front note says a letter sent to Red Buck, North Carolina, would find him, so wide was his fame. The red hair, rosy face, and gay ways that won the name came from his years on The Charlotte Observer.

Bryant roved the whole state and wrote human tales from each sand hill and mountain cove. Contents name fox races, forty acres and a mule, hounds of the old stock, and an owl called Minerva. Uncle Ben, Uncle Derrick in Washington, and Uncle George with an Englishman add folk leads. He gives the book to Joseph Pearson Caldwell, his chief and friend of fifteen years, in warm memory.
54491-more-short-sixes:
Bunner wrote More Short Sixes, a second gathering of his short tales, issued at New York in 1894 with pictures by Taylor. The first Short Sixes had made the form his mark: brief, neat stories with a turn at the end. Ten tales fill this volume, among them The Cumbersome Horse, The Ghoollah, Cutwater of Seneca, and The Man with the Pink Pants.

The opening tale sends a buyer named Brimmington to a farm house bought sight unseen in the Pennsylvania hills. His driver Skinner, postmaster, carpenter, teamster, and land agent in one, proves a trial on the road up. The house stands lonely in ragged fields on a steep slope, far below hope. Bunner plays the gap between hope and fact for dry comedy.
54502-vacation-rambles:
Vacation Rambles is a book of travel letters by Thomas Hughes, the author of Tom Brown's Schooldays. Macmillan published it in London in 1895. A line of Juvenal heads the book: the empty-handed traveller will sing in the robber's face. The rambles cover Europe in the years 1862 to 1866.

The first letter opens abroad in August 1862, addressed to an editor. Few moments in the year are sweeter, Hughes writes, than choosing the vacation hat. No other garment implies so much. A vista of coming idleness floats through the brain before the hatter's window. The bliss of escape from the chimney-pot hat of Cockney England rises before the mind. Two-thirds of all pleasure, he holds, lie in looking forward and looking back. Hughes writes as the holidaying lawyer and school storyteller he was, at ease in print.
54507-russian-memories:
Olga Novikoff, known in print as O.K., wrote her Russian memories, issued in London in 1917 with fifteen illustrations. Stephen Graham supplies the introduction. The frontispiece shows the Empress of Russia with Queen Alexandra, which sets the book's world of courts and diplomacy.

Graham calls her one of the most interesting women in the diplomatic circles of Europe. For many in English society, he says, she stood for Russia, was Russia. Gladstone learned from her what Russia was, and came to use her phrase, Holy Russia. Her life's work, as Graham frames it, was the great new friendship between England and Russia in her time.
54564-some-stories-of-old-ironsides:
Commander Holloway Frost of the United States Navy wrote Some Stories of Old Ironsides, published by the Naval Institute at Annapolis in 1931. Frost also wrote We Build a Navy. His subject is the frigate Constitution, the most famous ship in American naval history. Pictures show her in her great fights: against the Guerriere, the Java, and the Cyane and Levant together.

The book opens like a play, with acts and scenes. In September 1803 the Constitution sails along the Spanish coast toward Gibraltar. Frost describes her black hull, her broad white stripe, and the dark squares of her gun ports. A commodore's blue pennant flies at her mizzen. The stories that follow tell how the frigate earned her nickname in the Barbary wars and the War of 1812. British shot were said to bounce from her oak sides like iron.
546-under-the-andes:
Rex Stout, later famed for Nero Wolfe, writes this early adventure of a lost Inca world under the Andes. A New York gambler, bored at a Fifth Avenue club, is drawn into a quest for a hidden kingdom, a king's sweetheart, and a dance of the sun. Caves, courts, whirlpools, and an Inca spear mark the descent.

Stout writes with brisk, romantic flair, mixing modern talk with ancient rite. The hero must win a verdict before a strange court or die. The book charms as a lost-world romance, where gold, love, and danger wait beneath the mountains of Peru.
54601-a-treasury-of-canadian-verse-with-:
Theodore Rand chose and edited this treasury of Canadian verse, with short notes on each poet's life. Dutton of New York and Dent of London printed it in 1900. Rand had written At Minas Basin and Other Poems himself.

He gave the book to Louis Fréchette, whom he calls the Lamartine of Canada. A motto heads the title: love thou thy land. The Whitethroat, a piece by Rand himself, opens the verse. Margaret Alden's Mother's World and Joseph Allen's work stand at the start of the roll. Dozens of English-Canadian hands fill the pages, each with a brief life note, as the title promises.
54676-friendship-village-love-stories:
Zona Gale wrote Friendship Village Love Stories, copyrighted in 1909 and reprinted at New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Gale gives the book to her friends in Portage, Wisconsin. Many chapters first ran in magazines such as Everybody's and the Outlook.

Nineteen loosely linked tales fill the volume, from Open Arms and Inside June to Miggy, Splendour Town, and the Java Entertainment. The narrator opens in June, when a little child brings her white violets and one blue one. Months never die, the child says; they wait and show the next months how. Gale builds her village sketches on such small talk and small courtships.
54710-the-shame-of-the-cities:
Lincoln Steffens wrote The Shame of the Cities, issued in New York by McClure, Phillips and Company in nineteen four. The pieces first ran in McClure Magazine. Eight essays fill the book. An introduction and some conclusions opens it. This is not a book, Steffens warns. It is a collection of articles reprinted from the magazine, he says.

Done as journalism, they are journalism still, he insists. Tweed Days in St Louis follows. The Shame of Minneapolis and The Shamelessness of St Louis come next. Pittsburg, a City Ashamed, stands at the centre. Philadelphia is corrupt and contented, he finds. Chicago is half free and fighting on, he writes. New York, good government to the test, closes the survey. They were written to sound for the civic pride of an apparently shameless citizenry, he says. Reform readers get the founding text of muckraking.
54764-in-the-sixties:
In the Sixties is a collection by Harold Frederic, published by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York in eighteen ninety-three. The lead piece, The Copperhead, is narrated by a boy taken into a farmer's household. Abner Beech, his guardian, fills the first chapter in full length.

Beech is a stalwart, thick-shouldered man with a shaven upper lip and an iron-gray beard. He had been town supervisor and the first farmer nearby to use a mowing machine. Lightning rods on his buildings cost him his church, when an itinerant preacher damned them as defiance of heaven. The congregation grinned, and Beech never forgave them. The narrator dates his clearest memories from the news that Virginia had hanged John Brown. Frederic draws the rural North dividing against itself before the war.
54775-circus-life-and-circus-celebrities:
Circus Life and Circus Celebrities, by Thomas Frost, is a new edition published in London in 1881. Frost had also written The Old Showmen and the Old London Fairs, and Lives of the Conjurers. In his preface he says few persons do not count their first circus visit among the pleasant recollections of youth.

That first sniff of sawdust might come in a building made classical by Ducrow, or under the canvas of Samwell or Clarke. In his boyish days, Frost recalls, the cry of This way for the riders never failed to draw boys, and many grown folk too. It was bawled by the proprietor or ringmaster of a travelling circus at a fair. Fairs, he notes, have become things of the past near London, but tenting circuses still pitch. Readers get lives of riders and clowns from a man who loved the ring.
54783-mary-gresley-and-an-editor-s-tales:
Anthony Trollope wrote Mary Gresley and An Editor's Tales, in a new edition printed in London in 1873. Contents give Mary Gresley first, then The Turkish Bath, Josephine de Montmorenci, The Panjandrum in hope and despair parts, The Spotted Dog in attempt and result parts, and Mrs Brumby last.

Mary Gresley's face in supplication was more suasive, in grief more sad, in mirth more merry than any the narrator knew, Trollope opens. Her face compelled sympathy while she stayed unconscious of her own power over others. In her intercourse came much more sorrow than mirth, and in her sufferings the editor suffered too. Her extreme humanity, not society polish, made her charm. Short fiction readers get Trollope's editorial tales.
54799-balloons-airships-and-flying-machi:
Gertrude Bacon, who flew with her father in balloons, wrote this early history of flight. Dodd, Mead printed Balloons, Airships, and Flying Machines at New York in 1905, in the Practical Science Series. The authoress, her father, and Spencer making an ascent heads the plates.

The origin of ballooning opens the tale: two brothers by a fire at Annonay in 1782, watching smoke curl up the chimney. The coming of the gas balloon follows, then famous voyages of the past. The balloon as a tool of science and the balloon in warfare take their turns. The airship and the flying machine close the book, in 1905 still near-magic words. Bacon writes as one of the few who had truly been up.
54803-playing-santa-claus-and-other-chri:
Mrs Doughty offers holiday tales for children in a small volume issued at Boston in 1865. The preface tells young readers that true and lasting joy comes only from doing good to others. It urges them not to wait for great chances, but to use small acts of help all year long.

The title tale opens on Christmas Eve, with Caroline waking her sister Emma to talk of stockings, gifts, and cousins coming to dinner. Other pieces include Nothing to Give, Willie's Gold Dollar, The Little Match Boy, and The Christmas Tree, plus a Thanksgiving party tale. Readers get short, warm stories that tie feast-day fun to kindness, giving, and thought for the poor.
54822-a-roadside-harp-a-book-of-verses:
A Roadside Harp is a book of verses by Louise Imogen Guiney, published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1893. It followed her earlier volumes Songs at the Start and The White Sail. The title poem's motto takes the highway as the poet's chief Parnassus, her muse tuned to trampling horses' feet. The book is dedicated to Dora and Hester Sigerson in a prefatory poem.

The contents list short lyrics on set themes and persons. Titles include Vergniaud in the Tumbril, Winter Boughs, and The Vigil-at-Arms. Others treat a Madonna by Ghirlandajo, a spring nightfall, and a friend's song for Simoisius. Irish and historical notes sound in Athassel Abbey and Florentin. Later poems take up broken friendship, a lilac song, a ruin after a thunderstorm, and a cherry bough. The volume gathers brief, musical lyrics in the roadside spirit of its title, made for the open air rather than the chamber.
54870-philosophies:
Ronald Ross gathered his verse in Philosophies, first issued by John Murray in London in September 1910 and reprinted in August 1923. Ross held many honours in medicine and science, and the book shows his other side. Short pieces, not long poems, fill the volume.

Groups called Preludes, Apologues, Labours, and In Exile set the order. Titles such as Thought, Science, Power, Dogma, and Liberty show the range of his brief verse. India runs through the set, from a prelude called India to pieces on the Indian mother and Indian fevers. Parable-like tales, sonnets, and songs sit side by side. The style is terse, and each piece stands alone.
54880-letters-from-a-son-to-his-self-mad:
Letters from a Son to His Self-Made Father is a book of comic letters by Charles Eustace Merriman. It was printed at London by Putnam's Sons in 1904, with copyright in 1903. The pictures are by Fred Kulz. The volume is inscribed to Mark Twain, who is named a ready-made wit.

The son is Pierrepont Graham, a new freshman at Harvard. His father John is a pork packer in Chicago. The first letter, dated the 10th of October, answers his father's charge of slow reply. He reports that he talked his mother out of most of her travelling money on her visit. He calls a course in art, fitting up the flat, one of the most costly courses at Harvard. The letters give the son's side of a famous exchange, with the laugh on the father's side of the fence.
54881-the-laughing-bear-and-other-storie:
Robert Bell wrote a book of tales for children, printed in New York in 1917. Bell first told the tales to children at Saint Mark Church in Seattle. His note to them says their joy in the tales gave him the wish to print them for other children too.

Seven tales fill the book. The first tells of Princess Chonwa of Korea, her mother the queen, and a bold attack in the palace garden. Other tales tell of a gray witch, a rooster, small folk who live mid earth, a great sea beast, and a brown friar. Each tale is short, clear, and made to be read aloud.
54986-march-hares:
Harold Frederic starts a London tale in March Hares, printed in New York with copyright in 1896. Appleton made the book. Frederic gives it to a friend named Julia. The hero meets the reader on a bridge at a low hour.

On the morning of his thirtieth birthday, David Mosscrop leans on the low stone parapet of Westminster Bridge. He watches the crowd plod north into the polite half of London town. He had paused first to look down at the water, in a sad frame of mind. His head ached, as it so often did of a morning. He had done none of the great things his youth had promised, he owns. The wastrels and fools of last night's birthday eve made him sick to recall.
54991-poems-with-introduction-and-notes:
Ivan Panin translated poems of Alexander Pushkin from the Russian, with an introduction and notes, at Boston in 1888. He dedicates the book to a Mrs Gardner, the first to recognize helpfully whatever merit it holds. His text is the ten-volume Suvorin edition of Pushkin, printed at St Petersburg in 1887.

Panin says he has translated literally, word for word and line for line, with scarce five deviations. His aim was to make Pushkin himself speak to English readers, without a prompter. The contents sort the poems as autobiographical, narrative, nature, love, and miscellaneous. The Prophet, The Burnt Letter, and The Gypsies stand among the pieces chosen.
55024-the-queen-of-spades-and-other-stor:
Alexander Pushkin's stories were translated by Mrs Sutherland Edwards and published at London in 1892, beautifully illustrated, with a biography of the poet in front. The contents gather his famous tales: The Queen of Spades first, then The Pistol Shot, The Snowstorm, and The Undertaker. The Postmaster and The Lady Rustic follow, with Kirdjali and Peter the Great's Negro after.

The biography traces the poet from an ancient noble family to a Moscow birth on the 26th of May, 1799. An awkward, silent child, educated by French tutors, he read everything in his father's library and knew French literature nearly by heart at eleven. In October 1811 he entered the Lyceum of Tsarskoe Selo and led its literary society. Russia's national poet, introduced to English readers, is the volume.
55046-first-principles:
Herbert Spencer opens his System of Philosophy with this volume, issued by Williams and Norgate in London in 1863. The preface reprints the prospectus of March 1860 that announced the whole connected series. Part one treats the Unknowable, carrying further the doctrine of Hamilton and Mansel.

Science, Spencer argues, leads on every side to one belief: an Absolute beyond human knowledge and conception. In that shared belief lies the only possible reconciliation of science and religion. Part two states the laws of the Knowable, the highest generalizations true of all classes of phenomena. The series then skips inorganic nature and passes to the Principles of Biology.
55104-colony-treatment-of-the-insane-and:
Murphy gave a talk on farm colony care for the mind-sick and weak. His talk went to the North Carolina Medical Association in June 1906. It was held at Charlotte and reprinted from a state cure journal. Murphy wrote from Morganton in that same state. A plate shows the first house at the colony in his plan.

Work is the true cure at the core of his scheme. Sick men who can work are set in houses far from the main plant. There they farm under the care of the plant's own chiefs. Good air, plain food, and use for the hands do the work. Murphy holds such care kind and cheap at once. Cure men get a plan drawn from real use.
55107-little-songs-of-long-ago-more-old-:
Alfred Moffat harmonized these little songs of long ago for children. Augener printed the book in London in 1912 with Le Mair plates. Old nursery rhymes stand here with their original tunes in print. Dame Get Up and Bake Your Pies opens the song list.

Dance a Baby Diddy, Young Lambs to Sell, and Polly Flinders follow. Old King Cole, London Bridge, and Simple Simon fill the middle. A frog he would a wooing go and the spider and fly appear. Sleep Baby Sleep closes the contents of the rhyme book.
55114-teresa-of-watling-street-a-fantasi:
Arnold Bennett published 'Teresa of Watling Street' with Chatto and Windus in 1904, calling it a fantasia on modern themes, with eight illustrations by Frank Gillett. Chapter I, 'The Bank,' opens with a claim: since money is the fount of all modern romantic adventure, the City of London is the most romantic of cities. Bank clerks, Bennett says, ladle out romance from nine to four without knowing it.

A fair, thick-set young man in gold-rimmed spectacles stands opposite the headquarters of the British and Scottish Banking Company in King William Street. He had once been a clerk but is one no longer, and his boots and gloves are too well finished for a clerk's. At three minutes to twelve he crosses the traffic, for he has an appointment not just with chairman Simon Lock but with the Board itself.
55126-cloud-studies:
Arthur Clayden, principal of the Royal Albert Memorial College at Exeter, published 'Cloud Studies' with John Murray of London in 1905, fronted by a sunset sky. An introductory chapter leads into the cloud kinds one by one: cirrus first, then cirro-stratus and cirro-cumulus, the alto clouds, and the lower clouds. Cumulus and cumulo-nimbus get chapters of their own, as do wave clouds.

Later chapters measure cloud altitudes, settle cloud names, and teach cloud photography, closing with references and an index. The plates carry the burden of the teaching: more than fifty photographs and drawings are listed. They show high cirrus, thread cirrus, tailed cirrus, and hazy cirrus, each with a Latin name, then mackerel skies, turreted alto-cumulus, rain-clouds, and thunder-clouds forming. Clayden's aim is that a watcher of skies can name what he sees and know what it portends.
55147-tales-of-all-countries:
Anthony Trollope's stories, first printed in periodicals and gathered by Chapman and Hall in London in 1867, range widely in place. The titles alone map the range: John Bull on the Guadalquivir, Miss Sarah Jack of Spanish Town, Jamaica, George Walker at Suez, and A Ride Across Palestine. Others stay nearer home, among them The Courtship of Susan Bell and The Parson's Daughter of Oxney Colne.

The book opens with La Mère Bauche, set at the baths of Vernet in the Eastern Pyrenees. Trollope notes that travellers rarely get beyond Luchon, and that the fashion goes to the Eaux Bonnes while the truly ill go to Baréges and Cauterets. Vernet's valley, little known and quiet, is for him perhaps the loveliest among those mountains.
55160-the-war-and-the-gospel-sermons-and:
The War and the Gospel gathers sermons and addresses by Henry Wace, Dean of Canterbury. Thynne published the volume at London in 1917. Wace preached most of the pieces in Canterbury Cathedral. Cathedral deans preach on the chief festivals of the Christian year. His audiences often included soldiers, he notes in the preface. The Christmas message of 1914 opens the contents. Christmas and the war, preached a year later, follows it.

The things seen and the things not seen take a later place. Wace sought to bring the Gospel's light onto wartime suffering. The Gospel, he writes, has brought life and immortality to light. Its good news can support men under every trial and strain. He offers the sermons to a wider audience than his cathedral congregations. The preface is dated from Canterbury in January 1917.
55212-why-frau-frohmann-raised-her-price:
Why Frau Frohmann Raised Her Prices and Other Stories is a tale set by Anthony Trollope. Isbister of Ludgate Hill, London, published the volume in 1882. Contents give the title tale eight chapters, opening at the Brunnenthal peacock inn. The beginning of troubles, the question of the mitgift, and a zwansiger follow.

The frau returns to the simplicity of the old days as gold becomes cheap in the tale. Hoff the butcher and a closing indifference round out the innkeeper story. The Lady of Launay follows, telling how Bessy Pryor became a young lady of importance. Trollope late short fiction shows his ease in German and French settings.
55268-how-it-flies:
Richard Ferris's How It Flies, or The Conquest of the Air, was published in New York by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1910. A frontispiece shows Orville Wright in the 80-mile-an-hour Baby Wright racer. Over one hundred and fifty half-tones and line drawings trace the stages from the earliest balloon to the latest monoplane and biplane.

Ferris opens with the sudden awakening of 1908, when the world saw that mechanical flight had arrived. He recalls Santos-Dumont's flight of 720 feet in 1906 and the Wrights' public flights two years later. Chapters then treat the air, the laws of flight, biplanes, monoplanes, motors and gliders, and close with balloons, military aeronautics and biographies of prominent aeronauts.
55270-the-ways-of-life-two-stories:
Mrs Oliphant wrote The Ways of Life, two stories issued by G P Putnam’s Sons in eighteen hundred ninety seven. A short front essay is called On the Ebb Tide. The tales are titled Mr Sandford and The Wonderful History of Mr Robert Dalyell.

Oliphant says both tales grew from one hard find in life. A man may learn, all at once, that his rise has stopped. His wins are past and the tide now runs out. That find need not mean old age or weak health, she notes. It can strike while sails still look full. Most tales sing the flood tide and its rush to fame. Hers gives the ebb its own sad hue and truth.
55281-the-christmas-dream-of-little-char:
The Christmas Dream of Little Charles is a short children's tale published in New York by Redfield at Clinton Hall. Charles Estabrook, a good boy who loves horses, hangs his stocking by the chimney on Christmas Eve, says his prayers, and falls asleep. The day before, he had earned a shilling by watering a traveler's thirsty horse.

In his dream Saint Nicholas comes down the chimney on a small pony like Lightfoot, the pony his Uncle Ben had promised him. The rider's hair is made of crackers that pop as he nears the lamp, which makes Charles laugh in his sleep. Kind acts to horses and to his sister Lizzy frame the tale, a sweet moral dream for young readers.
55283-the-bet-and-other-stories:
The Bet and Other Stories is a set of short tales by Anton Chekhov, issued in Boston in 1915. Koteliansky and Murry translated the tales from the Russian for John Luce and Company. A translators note at the front explains Russian names and dishes for English readers. It glosses dumplings, sour cabbage soup, and porridge for the tale A Tedious Story.

The contents list thirteen tales in all for the volume. They run from The Bet and A Tedious Story through The Fit, Misfortune, and After the Theatre. Later titles are That Wretched Boy, Enemies, Expensive Lessons, A Living Calendar, and Old Age. The Bet opens on a dark autumn night in the study of an old banker. He paces his room and recalls a party at which guests debated capital punishment, a debate that sets the wager of the title in train.
55307-the-black-monk-and-other-stories:
Anton Tchekhoff broods and sparkles in The Black Monk and Other Stories, from Frederick A Stokes of New York in 1915. R E C Long translated the tales from the Russian. The contents list On the Way, A Family Council, At Home, In Exile, Rothschild's Fiddle, Sleepyhead, and Ward No 6 among the twelve pieces.

The title tale opens with Andrei Vasilyevitch Kovrin, a master of arts who has worn himself out and unsettled his nerves. A doctor friend advises a spring and summer in the country. A letter from Tanya Pesotsky calls him to Borisovka, her father's famous gardens.
55354-what-does-history-teach-two-edinbu:
John Stuart Blackie's What Does History Teach gathers two Edinburgh lectures, published by Macmillan and Co in London in 1886. Blackie delivered them to the Philosophical Institution of Edinburgh on the evenings of the 8th and 11th of December 1885. The first lecture treats the State, and the second treats the Church.

The first lecture opens with a refusal: history knows nothing of the earliest beginnings, and talk of primeval man descending from a monkey can never start a profitable philosophy of history. Man as revealed in history is generically different from the brute, and characteristically set against it, an inventive animal whose faculty is free.
55392-mackinac-and-lake-stories:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood wrote a set of tales of Mackinac and the Great Lakes, issued in 1899 and dedicated to her daughter Hazel, companion of all her journeys. The first, Marianson, opens as the British land on Mackinac Island at three in the morning of July 17, 1812.

Canadians must drag two six-pounders across the island to heights above the fort, a dreadful portage over sand, rock, and fallen logs. One young voyageur among the hundred and sixty hates the secret attack and the British who command him. Other tales treat Beaver Island's king, a skeleton on Round Island, and a penitent of Cross Village. French, British, and Indian pasts mix here.
55408-rounding-cape-horn-and-other-sea-s:
Walter McRoberts spins yarns in Rounding Cape Horn and Other Sea Stories, from the H S Hill Printing Company of Peoria in 1895, with pictures by Grant Wright. Byron's lines on the deep blue ocean front the book. The index lists ten tales, beginning with The Life-Savers and Thanksgiving on the Dicky Bird.

My Brazilian Adventure, Bringing in a Derelict, The Monomaniac, Crossing the Line, Missing, A Dangerous Cargo, and The Parson's Text fill the middle. The first tale opens on a wild March night at a New England life-saving station, surf thundering and patrolmen walking their beats. Storm work follows.
55443-psycho-analysis-and-the-war-neuros:
The International Psycho-Analytical Press issued Psycho-Analysis and the War Neuroses in London, Vienna, and New York in 1921. Ernest Jones edited the series, and the volume stands second in the library. Freud wrote the introduction.

The body of the book is a symposium. Ferenczi, Abraham, and Simmel spoke at the Fifth International Psycho-Analytical Congress at Budapest in September 1918. Their subject was war shock, the breakdown of soldiers under shell fire. The analysts argued that the neuroses of war proved the theory in the field hospital. Armies needed the men back, and the talking cure was put to national use. The papers were read while the war still ran.
55505-nequa-or-the-problem-of-the-ages:
Jack Adams wrote a utopian novel in two volumes, of which this is the first, issued at Topeka, Kansas, in 1900. He dedicates it to lovers of humanity who hold that the golden rule, applied in human affairs, would lift the burdens laid on the masses by ignorance and greed.

The tale opens beneath the midnight sun, with a strange visitor from above and a tale by an old physician. A woman in male dress enlists as scientist on the ship Ice King, bound for the North Pole. Ice, earthquake, and a lost ship lead to a strange tower and an open polar sea. Airships then bring the party to a highly cultivated people at Altruria.
55523-under-greek-skies:
Under Greek Skies is a story book for children by Julia Dragoumis, published at New York in 1913. Dutton and Company issued the book, printed by the Knickerbocker Press. Dragoumis dedicates it to her three grandchildren, Nico and Alexandra Yannicosta and Nadine Ralli. The book belongs to the Stories for Little Schoolmates set of tales.

A letter at the front speaks straight to the child who reads the book as a schoolmate. It recalls a sister volume on Pilarica and Rafael in sunny Spain in the same series. Those books, it says, tell of the child the reader might have been in another land. The new book tells how children work and play in Greece in its tales. It asks American children to imagine a life like their own led under Greek skies, with Greek schools, games, and family ways in place of their own.
55550-a-valiant-ignorance-vol-3-of-3-a-n:
A Valiant Ignorance, volume 3 of 3, closes Mary Angela Dickens's novel in three volumes. Macmillan published it in London and New York in 1894. Dickens had written Cross Currents and A Mere Cypher. The motto, from Browning's Prince Hohenstiel Schwangau, runs: thy gold is brass. The final volume opens in Marston Loring's chambers in the Temple.

Loring has come back from Africa with a new friend, Alfred Ramsay. Ramsay is small and insignificant, with sandy hair greying in streaks. They discuss young Julian Romayne. His name, Ramsay notes, belonged to a first-class swindler twenty years ago: William Romayne. Julian is the swindler's son, Loring confirms. The son has respectable capital and is exceedingly keen on increasing it. Ramsay muses: a chip of the old block. How far, he wonders, does it go? The volume's danger gathers in that question.
55577-tales-of-two-countries:
Maxim Gorky wrote Tales of Two Countries, issued at London in nineteen fourteen. A note gives his real name and his birth at Nijni-Novgorod in eighteen sixty-eight. Gorky had lived as a tramp among the poorest folk of Russia.

The book pairs Italian tales with Russian tales, as the title promises. The Italian set opens with Man and the Simplon, by a blue lake under snow-capped hills. White houses peer down like lumps of sugar, and all is quiet as a child's sleep. Other Italian tales treat a traitor's mother and the honour of a village. The Russian set treats a professor, a poet, and a liberal, among others.
55591-old-fashioned-flowers-and-other-ou:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote Old-Fashioned Flowers and Other Out-of-Door Studies, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and published at New York in 1905. Contents hold four essays: Old-Fashioned Flowers, News of Spring, Field Flowers, and Chrysanthemums. Illustrations quote their subjects, from the hollyhock flaunting her cockades to the sad columbine.

The first essay opens one morning at the author's garden fence. He looks at his flowers, safe from the cattle grazing beyond, and sees in mind all that blossoms in woods, fields, gardens, orangeries, and greenhouses. He muses on what we owe the world of marvels the bees visit. Readers get the poet of The Blue Bird writing prose poems on gardens.
55598-shifting-for-himself-or-gilbert-gr:
Shifting for Himself, or Gilbert Greyson's Fortunes, is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger, author of Ragged Dick and the Tattered Tom books. The Winston Company published it at Philadelphia, from a copyright of 1876. It belongs to the Brave and Bold series, and a dedication commends the art preservative of all arts, printing, without which authors write in vain.

The preface states the story plainly. Gilbert, in the course of a preparation for college, finds himself reduced to poverty. He is obliged to leave his books and give up his plans. How cheerfully he accepted the situation and settled down to work is the tale. What obstacles he encountered and overcame, and what success he met with in the end, the reader will learn. The preface concedes that Gilbert was more fortunate than most boys in his position, but claims he showed qualities that may wisely be imitated.
556-rewards-and-fairies:
Rudyard Kipling continues Puck's tales in this sequel, where Dan and Una meet folk from English history in field and wood. Cold Iron, Gloriana, King Henry VII and his shipwrights, a doctor of medicine, and Simple Simon each bring a song and a story. Puck's charm opens each visit with earth and flowers.

Kipling writes in rich, musical prose and verse, teaching history through talk and craft. The book, like its predecessor, treats the past as a living neighbor. It endures as a beloved companion to Puck of Pook's Hill, where England's makers speak again to children.
55601-lovers-saint-ruth-s-and-three-othe:
Lovers' Saint Ruth's and Three Other Tales is a book of stories by Louise Imogen Guiney, published by Copeland and Day of Boston in 1895. Guiney dedicates it to Clarence and Frances Blake, calling it a book finished on their own wild acres of the Maine coast, in October 1894. Her author's preface notes that the contents had never before been printed. One chapter among them needs explanation.

The Provider is based very literally on a tragic thing that happened some years ago in Dublin. It reached her as a cable despatch of some ten lines in a Boston daily newspaper. In the September 1895 Harper's, she notes, little Father Time in Hardy's Hearts Insurgent ends his life from a strange motive. Her own story, she is careful to state, was finished and laid by before Hardy's novel appeared in serial form.
55704-wilderness-babies:
Wilderness Babies is a nature book for children by Julia Augusta Schwartz. Little, Brown and Company issued this school edition in Boston. The copyright runs 1905 and 1906. John Huybers drew many of the pictures, and photographs supply the rest. Each chapter hides its animal behind a riddle title. The first chapter, The One with a Pocket, opens the series.

Inside that chapter, baby opossums crowd their mother's furry pocket. The biggest baby climbs over eleven brothers and sisters to peek out. Later chapters present the manatee, the one that eats grass in the sea. The whale is the biggest one, and the beaver the best builder. The fox has the prettiest tail, and the wolf is the fiercest one. The mole digs best of all. A squirrel fronts the book, tails curving over backs on the branches.
55707-john-brown-the-hero-personal-remin:
Winkley wrote these personal reminiscences of John Brown, printed at Boston under copyright in 1905, with an introduction by Frank Sanborn. The frontispiece shows a bust of Brown modelled from life while he waited in prison at Charlestown for trial. Winkley knew the Kansas struggle at first hand, and his book is a witness's account.

Chapters tell of a call for aid, a night march, a siege and its heroine, and the battle of Osawatomie. Brown's half sister kept a log cabin where he always found welcome, and the cabin still stood when Winkley went back to Kansas to see the old places. The tone is plain reverence: Brown as hero, told by a man who marched in his world and kept the faith.
55721-under-rocking-skies:
Under Rocking Skies is a sea novel by Frank Tooker, the author of The Call of the Sea. The Century Company published it in New York in 1905. Its plates show Captain March with a twinkle in his eyes, a brig sliding down the seas like a boy let loose from school, and a boat shooting in on a smooth.

The story opens ashore. For a quarter of an hour Thomas Medbury has stood at the east window of his mother's parlour, gazing across his neighbour's yard with eager intentness. The low room is shut and darkened, with a musty smell. Sea-fans stand before the fireplace, flanked by polished conch-shells, and a painting of a ship hangs on the wall. Medbury himself is tall and broad-shouldered, bronzed like overripe wheat, with the steady, far-seeing eyes of a seaman.
55781-willem-adriaan-van-der-stel-and-ot:
Willem Adriaan van der Stel and Other Historical Sketches is South African history. George McCall Theal wrote the sketches for Maskew Miller at Capetown in nineteen thirteen. Sketch one treats Portuguese exploration of the west African coast. The discovery of the Cape of Good Hope closes that first sketch here.

Sketch two follows French and English voyages to India and Dutch wars. The Netherlands war runs to the Union of Utrecht and on to sixteen o six. Sketch three gives Governor van der Stel rule and his faithless conduct. Proceedings in the Netherlands on his case close that long sketch. Sketch four chronicles leaders of the Great Emigration, Triegard and Uys.
55801-teen-age-super-science-stories:
Richard M Elam Jr wrote Teen-Age Super Science Stories for the Teen-Age Library, issued by Grosset and Dunlap under a 1957 copyright held by Lantern Press. The front pages list the whole series, dozens of volumes of sports, mystery, western, and adventure tales aimed at young readers. Frank E Vaughn drew the illustrations.

Nine stories of space flight fill the book. Cadet Marshall Farnsworth makes man's first trip into space in the opening tale, and the rest race around the sun, fly to Pluto and Luna, and meet peril from outer space. A ghost ship of space and a space steward close the run.
55807-verses:
Verses is a small book of poems struck at a shore town in eighteen seventy-eight. Its front line is a plea past a famed maid of song, to be kind to these fancies of mine. Its first set is of sonnets, each with its day of the fall of eighteen seventy-five past it. The first sings a soft sound of an organ stop, more sweet than the scent of blooms in wood dells.

That sound is as fond as the moan of a ring dove past the leaf tent of the wood. A next sonnet sets a lady at her dusk prayers in a church aisle past the choir has gone. Saints look down past the stained panes with a holy smile as the day fades. A third speaks to a great bard of the old world in the voice of that maid of song.
55839-the-law-s-lumber-room-second-serie:
Francis Watt wrote The Law Lumber Room, a second set of tales of old law, put out in 1898. Watt notes that this set is a book apart from the first set. Its themes are of wider pull and are told at more length. Most are as much tales of books as of courts, he says.

The tales first ran in The New Review, The Yellow Book, and The Ludgate. Watt warns that the book holds a great deal of death by the rope. Those were days of the rope, when law sought to end the bad man, not mend him. A line from Falstaff heads the book, on the rusty curb of law. Watt holds that such scraps bring the old world close, in all its strangeness. He asks what has been lost as life grew more just and more tame.
55859-the-west-indies:
The West Indies is a picture and travel book by Forrest and Henderson. Adam and Charles Black issued it in London in 1905. Forrest painted the scenes, and Henderson wrote the text. A companion volume on Morocco is advertised in front. Coming from Mass in Saint Lucia serves as frontispiece. The contents give Jamaica the bulk of the book. Twenty-eight chapters range across the islands.

Kingston, its people, and its politics fill many chapters. Turtle fishing and alligator shooting add sport. The West Indian army and a court house are described. Bog Walk and the hill stations show the island's ground. Commercial Jamaica and its flora close the survey. Haiti and the wider Caribbean end the book. The preface scolds Britain's jaundiced view of its colonies. Respect and sympathy are the author's plea. The colour plates were the book's chief selling point.
55861-the-outcasts-and-other-stories:
Maxim Gorky writes of the poor and cast off in tales turned into English in a Fisher Unwin volume from London dated MCMV. Dora B Montefiore and Emily Jakowleff turned the title tale and Waiting for the Ferry into English. Vera Volkhovsky turned The Affair of the Clasps, the third piece in the set.

The title tale opens on a high street of one-storey hovels squeezed wall to wall in a poor suburb. Leaning walls, crooked windows, and roofs patched with shingles and moss mark the row. A winding channel crawls down the street past holes washed out by storm rain from the town above. Grand stone houses and church steeples shine on the hill while the suburb takes the town's dust and flood water alike.
56020-the-power-of-truth-individual-prob:
William George Jordan wrote The Power of Truth, a set of essays on character issued in New York in 1902. The book sold so well that it ran through seven printings by 1916. Its sub title calls the parts individual problems and possibilities, and each part is a short talk on one trait or trial.

The lead essay calls truth the rock base of every great character, the compass of the soul and the guard of conscience. Jordan calls lying one of the oldest vices, born in the garden of Eden talk. Other parts treat the courage to face ingratitude, folk who live in air castles, the conquest of what can be stopped, and the way of the reformer.
5603-seven-icelandic-short-stories:
Seven Icelandic Short Stories, published in Reykjavik by the Ministry of Education, gathers Icelandic fiction across centuries, with an introduction by Steingrimur J. Porsteinsson. The anonymous thirteenth-century Story of Audunn and the Bear opens the set, followed by Einar H. Kvaran's A Dry Spell from 1905, Gudmundur Fridjonsson's The Old Hay from 1909, and Jon Trausti's When I Was on the Frigate from 1910.

Gunnar Gunnarsson's Father and Son from 1916, Gudmundur G. Hagalin's The Fox Skin from 1923, and Halldor Kiljan Laxness's New Iceland complete the book, each in translation. Readers get a compact survey of Icelandic storytelling, from saga to modern tale.
56036-inside-the-lines:
Earl Derr Biggers and Robert Welles Ritchie's 1915 novel, founded on Biggers's play, opens with Jane Gerson, a buyer, storming at a customs guard over a missing trunk on the wharf. She refuses to budge until it is found.

Jane brandishes her ticket, flourishes her French, and nearly breaks down before help arrives. Chapter titles promise a spy in the signal tower, a room lettered D, and a trap sprung at the quay. The war setting shows in chapters like Chaff of War and Her Country's Example, with the Wilhelmstrasse figuring early in the intrigue. The Bobbs-Merrill Company published the novel at Indianapolis.
56059-old-crosses-and-lychgates:
Aymer Vallance wrote Old Crosses and Lychgates, published in London by Batsford with a frontispiece of the Northampton Eleanor Cross. Eight chapters sort England's old crosses by kind, beginning with an introduction and monolith crosses, then the shaft-on-steps type.

Later chapters treat spire-shaped or Eleanor crosses, preaching crosses, market crosses, and unclassified varieties, before a full chapter on lychgates. A bibliography, an index, and a topographical list of illustrated subjects close the book, naming places from Aldborough to Bishop's Lydeard. Readers get an illustrated field guide to the stone crosses and churchyard gates that still mark English parishes and market towns.
5609-the-corporation-of-london-its-right:
William Ferneley Allen, sheriff of London and Middlesex and alderman of the ward of Cheap, wrote The Corporation of London: Its Rights and Privileges as a defense of the City's civic system. His preface apologizes for a newcomer to civic affairs standing forth as champion. Yet he insists no man of spirit could tamely submit to insulting charges and coarse insinuations long aimed at the Corporation.

Allen admits the system is not free from spot or blemish, but argues its rights and privileges deserve fair hearing. Readers get a Victorian civic tract, part history and part polemic, about London's ancient self-government.
56153-evening-tales:
Frédéric Ortoli wrote Evening Tales, done into English by Joel Chandler Harris in an authorized edition from Charles Scribner Sons. Copyright rests in eighteen ninety three, and the edition here is nineteen nineteen. Harris was the author of Uncle Remus. Fifteen tales fill the book. A French Tar Baby stands first. Corsican folk tales are the stock.

In the first tale, Brother Goat and Brother Rabbit live in the same neighbourhood, in days of hobgoblins and fairies. Proud of his long beard and sharp horns, Goat looks on Rabbit with disdain. His great pleasure is to make his small neighbour the victim of tricks and jokes. He cries that Mr Fox or Mr Wolf is coming, and poor Rabbit runs and trembles. Teenchy Duck, Mr Snail and Brother Wolf, and The Lion Secret follow. Children get French beast tales in Harris warm voice.
56206-my-book-of-ten-fishes:
My Book of Ten Fishes is a children's nature book by Rosalie G Mendel, illustrated by Hazel Frazee and published in Racine, Wisconsin, in 1916. Each of the ten fishes tells its own story in the first person, so young readers learn habits and anatomy as if from the animal itself.

The star fish explains its five arms, red eye spots, and the hundreds of suckers that catch oysters and clams. The salmon calls itself king of the fresh water fish, tells of swimming home to spawn, and describes curling its body to leap waterfalls. The plain, friendly voice suits the Whitman Publishing list of inexpensive picture books meant to teach while they entertain.
56208-philip-hale-s-boston-symphony-prog:
Philip Hale's Boston Symphony Programme Notes, edited by John Burk with an introduction by Lawrence Gilman, was published at Garden City, New York, by Doubleday, Doran in 1935. Burk draws the book from the programme books Hale wrote for thirty two years of Boston Symphony concerts. Hale's newspaper reviews of the same concerts, kept in scrapbooks at the Boston Public Library, supply the rest.

In the programme notes Hale held back his own opinion, writing for hearers with open minds; in the reviews he spoke freely. Burk sets review paragraphs before the notes on each work, so critic and historian stand together. Burk marvels that Hale, on a first hearing, so often judged new works by Strauss or Debussy more soundly than his fellow critics. The volume records one listener's forty years at the center of American concert life.
56210-the-lincoln-country-in-pictures:
The Lincoln Country in Pictures is a picture book by Carl and Rosalie Frazier, issued at New York in 1963. Its pages pair photographs of houses, fences, and wagons with the story of Abraham Lincoln. A caption at the front calls that story ever fresh. It grips the sight of many people, the caption says, and millions visit the humble homes where he lived.

A saying of Lincoln's own stands among the pictures. Every man is said to have his own ambition, the young Lincoln told his county in 1832. His own was to be truly esteemed by his fellow men, by making himself worthy of their esteem. How far he would succeed was yet to be shown, he said. Houses tied to his kin and his early years carry the book from page to page.
56238-deerfoot-on-the-prairies:
Edward Ellis wrote a boys' frontier tale printed at Philadelphia in 1905, with eight plates by Steeple Davis. Its hero is Deerfoot, a young Shawnee of the old tales. The book stands second in a set of three. Deerfoot in the Forest goes before, Deerfoot in the Mountains after.

The band's path runs from the Ohio to the Pacific through wild ground and plains. The time is that of Lewis and Clark's great trek. George and Victor, of the Log Cabin set, walk in these pages once more. Heads open westward bound, then the first camp and thieves of the night. An acquaintance and a close call follow. The set sold bound alike, one dollar a book, for boys who loved the trail.
56264-italian-fantasies:
Israel Zangwill wrote bright prose pieces on Italy and its dreams. His book came out in London in 1910. A color front plate shows an old Italian art work. Zangwill wrote Children of the Ghetto and The Grey Wig. His note tells the book's seed in three Harper's pieces.

Those pieces ran in 1903 and 1904 with art by Loeb. Loeb died, and the joint work stands half done in his name. All roads lead from Rome heads the main set of pieces. Beauty, faith, and death sing the book's first song. Naples, wives of carpenters, and earth's core fill the dreams. Wit and warmth mark each page.
56286-tudor-school-boy-life-the-dialogue:
