Foster Watson, professor of education at Aberystwyth, translated the dialogues of Juan Luis Vives for the first time into English and published them at London in 1908 as Tudor School-Boy Life. A long introduction treats Vives as a scholar of the Renaissance and weighs the dialogues' meaning.

Sections cover home and school life, subject matter and style, the Greek words in the dialogues, games, nature study, wine-drinking and water-drinking, and the vernacular. The dialogues themselves open with getting up in the morning and morning greetings. Vives wrote them as Latin exercises that pictured a schoolboy's whole day. Readers get Renaissance school life in the boys' own scripted voices.
56290-men-and-measures:
Men and Measures, a history of weights and measures ancient and modern, by Edward Nicholson, came out in London in 1912. Nicholson was a surgeon lieutenant colonel in the Army Medical Department. He had written a past book on weights and measures, and a manual on snakes in India.

Early chapters trace the cubits of Egypt, Greece, Rome, and Persia. Next come the talents, or old weight units, and the coin weights of Greece. Later chapters show how length units grew from weights, and how the English foot arose. Full parts then treat the yard, the acre, and old land terms. Readers get a deep, clear past of the units men still use each day.
56336-the-automatic-toy-works-manufactur:
The Automatic Toy Works of New York issued this trade catalogue in the spring of eighteen hundred eighty two. The firm made clockwork toys under letters patent. Its shop stood at Twenty College Place, near Park Place. The book lists each toy with a picture and a price.

All the toys move by wound patent works, the firm boasts. Each toy ships in a stout wood box, post paid, on receipt of price. A mechanical bear leads the stock at four dollars and twenty five cents. The bear stands, turns its head, growls, and snaps its jaws. Fur of black or white clothes its frame. A sewing machine girl charms girls next in the list. New kinds and finer dress mark this enlarged issue.
56357-the-laughing-willow-verses-and-pic:
Oliver Herford wrote and drew a book of comic verses and pictures, printed in New York in 1918. Herford had won readers with Artful Antics and other light works. The book takes its title from a jingle saying that the Kaiser's epitaph would make a weeping willow laugh.

Opening epitaphs mock Kaiser Wilhelm in brisk rhymes, praying the earth to swallow him and warning friends to tread softly lest he wake. War pieces follow on air raids, tanks, camouflage, and the Crown Prince. Later sections give verses on people met and not met, from Barrie and Mark Twain to cats, oysters, and a highbrow hen. Readers get sharp, playful satire from the war years, drawn and rhymed by one hand. The tone stays light even when the target is an emperor at war.
56401-fairy-tales-from-gold-lands-second:
Fairy Tales from Gold Lands, second series, is a book of tales by May Wentworth. Roman and Company published it in San Francisco and New York. This new edition, with illustrations, is dated 1870. The copyright was entered in 1868. Wentworth dedicated the little book to the children of California. She offered it with golden wishes for the Christmas time. An opening poem paints the land of gold for young readers.

That poem sings of bold mountains and deep canyons. Vineyards, orange groves, and deserts of priceless sand fill its verses. The tales belong to the Golden Gate series for children. A picture of the little lace maker stands at the front. The book brings fairy tales home to California's gold country.
56484-the-future-in-america-a-search-aft:
H G Wells wrote a search after the facts of America in 1906, after a trip across the Atlantic. A front picture shows Fifth Avenue in New York. His contents start with the prophet's turn of mind. Then come stuff progress, New York, and growth that cannot be stopped.

Later chapters treat the money process, some sides of American wealth, and certain workers. Corruption, the new comer, and what he calls state blindness follow. Two studies in let down hopes and the tragedy of colour lead to the mind of a modern state. The book opens with the sharp questions put to each new comer at the gate of the United States.
56501-a-comic-history-of-the-united-stat:
Livingston Hopkins jokes through the past in A Comic History of the United States, printed in New York in 1876. Carleton made the book, and Hopkins draws the plates himself, from sketches taken at a safe distance, the title page boasts. A mock gift chromo fronts the volume.

His dedication is a jest in itself. The printer left a blank for one, so he tells of a wealthy aunt once in his thoughts. On mature reflection he will send her a china shaving mug with Forget me Not in gold letters instead, he says; it will look less pointed. Chapter one treats a few stubborn facts not wholly unconnected with the discovery of America. The whole national tale gets the same sly handling.
56505-historic-bubbles:
Frederic Leake wrote these short lives and tales of the past, and Riggs printed them at Albany in 1896. Historic Bubbles takes its name from Banquo's line: the earth has bubbles, as the water has. A French tag adds that the shortest works are always the best.

The Duke of Berwick opens the set with the tale of a border town. Berwick was held first for Scotland, then for England, the tale says. Then the lawyers made it belong to neither, so no writ ran there. The Captivity of Babylon, the second house of Burgundy, and two Jaquelines follow. Hoche, an ancestor of Queen Victoria, and John Wiclif close the roll.
5651-dreams-and-dream-stories:
Anna Kingsford wrote Dreams and Dream Stories, a collection of vivid, symbolic dreams with a preface. Part one runs from The Doomed Train and The Wonderful Spectacles through The Counsel of Perfection and The City of Blood. The Bird and the Cat and The Treasure in the Lighted House follow, then The Forest Cathedral, The Enchanted Woman, and The Banquet of the Gods.

Later dreams include The Difficult Path, A Lion in the Way, A Dream of Disembodiment, The Perfect Way with Animals, and The Laboratory Underground. Kingsford, a mystic and vegetarian reformer, reads dreams as spiritual teaching. Readers get strange, earnest dream visions, part diary and part allegory.
56510-slicko-the-jumping-squirrel-her-ma:
Slicko, the Jumping Squirrel tells her many adventures for young children. Richard Barnum wrote the tale for the Kneetime Animal Stories set. Barse and Hopkins of New York brought the book out in 1915. Harriet Tooker drew the pictures that stand through the small book. Barnum had writ Squinty the Comical Pig and Mappo the Monkey before.

Slicko learns to jump in the first chapter of her adventures. She meets Squinty, goes on a visit, and sees a circus next. Tum Tum the jolly elephant joins her in the fifth chapter told. Halfway up a tall tree stood a round hole in the trunk. Soft dried leaves and milkweed fluff lined that snug little home. A little head like a small kitten's peered from that hole. Bright eyes watched the world from Slicko's tree-hole door each day. Forty cents bought each volume of the Kneetime set, postpaid.
56514-wild-roses-a-tale-of-the-rockies:
Wild Roses is a tale of the Rockies by Driggs, published by the University Publishing Company in 1916. The book is dedicated to the author's mother, who loved the wild roses. A plate shows a splendid mountain stream.

The tale opens in a mountain valley that an old frontiersman first called a trapper's hole. It lies on the western slopes of the great divide, next to the Yellowstone country. A rim of craggy, snow-streaked peaks rings it. Streams leap from its canyons and join in a bright network over the floor. The chapters that follow tell of a cowboy celebration, a dance, and fire water. The boys ride among the tepees and fish at a shadow pool. A fatal throw, a roundup, and the end of the long trail close the tale.
56570-breaking-into-the-movies:
John Emerson and Anita Loos, a famed pair of the silent screen, wrote this guide to getting into films. Jacobs of Philadelphia printed Breaking into the Movies in 1921. The pair had earlier written How to Write Photoplays, and knew the trade from inside.

A front plate shows a casting chief's office at work. Emerson and Loos study the faces of hopefuls with their shorthand clerk. When a face fits the tale, its owner goes straight to the studio floor. What the Jobs Are follows the opening talk, then Acting for the Screen. Would You Film Well tests the reader's hopes. Plain talk from two pros marks the book, in a year when all America dreamed of the screen.
56579-the-countess-of-lowndes-square-and:
Cynthia, Countess of Hampshire, takes sour milk by a famed doctor's rule and feels younger each June day. Benson opens his title tale with her letters, her gay post, and her gift for turning dull dinners into feasts. The Countess of Lowndes Square heads a shelf of Benson tales, sorted by kind.

Blackmailing stories come first, then general ones, spook stories, cat stories, and crank stories. Titles run from The Ape and The False Step to Philip's Safety Razor. Benson, a son of an archbishop, wrote these crisp society tales with a light, sly hand. Cassell printed the set in London and abroad. Each group shows Benson in a fresh key, droll to eerie.
56615-musical-studies:
Musical Studies, by Ernest Newman, was published in London in 1914 by John Lane, in a third edition. Newman also wrote Gluck and the Opera, a study of Wagner, and volumes on Elgar, Strauss, and Hugo Wolf. Six studies make the book. They treat Berlioz, romantic and classic, and Faust in music. Programme music and Herbert Spencer on the origin of music follow. Maeterlinck and music, and Strauss and the music of the future, close the set.

An appendix on Wagner, Berlioz, Liszt, and their chronicler closes the volume. The Berlioz study opens with a safe claim: no musician, Liszt perhaps excepted, divides opinion like Berlioz. On other men, Newman says, cultivated musicians roughly agree on the ranks. On Berlioz the world cannot make up its mind, not even as to whether he stands in the first rank at all. Newman argues the case afresh.
56638-hand-grenades-a-handbook-on-rifle-:
Major Ainslie compiled this handbook, Hand Grenades, on rifle and hand grenades, printed at New York and London in 1917. Contents move from the tool to its use in the field: the grenade establishment, the grenade squad, clearing a trench from a flank, frontal attack, and trench storming parties. French and German grenades get chapters of their own.

The opening pages give the tool's history in brief. A grenade is a hollow shell of metal, filled with explosive and burst by a fuse or on impact. Trained grenadiers threw them until the late seventeenth century, then the weapon fell out of use. It came back at Mafeking and in the Russo-Japanese war, and in 1914 it proved its worth against riflemen.
56652-kitty-of-the-roses:
Ralph Barbour wrote Kitty of the Roses, for Lippincott in 1904. Philadelphia and London shared the edition of the novel. Von Rapp drew its illustrations for the book. Perhaps I can help you, a voice says almost overhead in one. A basket weighted with pink and white blossoms fronts another plate.

Calmly she snipped two bunches of pink roses in a third. And me, Kitty, he whispered in the last of the plates. Through a wide-open door the tale steps in chapter one. On the edge of a table a cigarette smouldered in its talk. A thin filament of gray smoke rose from that cigarette. It lost itself in the upper gloom of the room above. Barbour had written the Land of Joy before this novel. Barbour gives a rose garden its slight summer romance.
56689-the-victories-of-wellington-and-th:
The Victories of Wellington and the British Armies, in Bohn's Illustrated Library, was printed by George Bell in London in a new edition of 1891. Its anonymous author also wrote Stories of Waterloo and a life of Wellington. A frontispiece shows a colonel's last charge at Assaye, and portraits of generals appear through the book.

The contents march in order. Seringapatam introduces the Indian service, then Assaye, the Egyptian expedition, and the battle of Alexandria. The Peninsular War fills the bulk: Rolica, Vimiero, Talavera, Busaco, the retreat to Torres Vedras, Salamanca, and Vitoria. Orthez and Toulouse lead to Napoleon's return, Quatre Bras, and Waterloo. Indian campaigns of 1838 to 1846, against Afghans, Biluchis, and Sikhs, close the volume, with an appendix on the storming of San Sebastian.
56690-adventures-of-the-teenie-weenies:
Adventures of the Teenie Weenies is a children's book by William Donahey, copyright nineteen twenty. Donahey drew the pictures himself. The Chicago edition is dedicated to his wife Mary, whom he calls his literary rival and better three fourths. An opening section tells who the Teenie Weenies are and where they live. They are a very tiny little people, it begins.

The Teenie Weenie children are about half an inch tall, the text goes on. A potato will keep the whole folk supplied for several months. One grain of rice makes one of them a square meal. Two baked lima beans make a meal for a whole family. A thimbleful of butter lasts them a week. Such measures set the scale of the tiny world the tales play in.
56711-poems-of-giosue-carducci-translate:
Poems of Giosue Carducci is a translation volume by Frank Sewall, issued in 1893. Osgood McIlvaine of London published the poems with two introductory essays by Sewall. Essay one treats Carducci and the Hellenic reaction in Italy in his age. Essay two treats Carducci and the classic realism of his poetic manner.

Translations open with Roma, then the famed Hymn to Satan in English dress. Homer, Virgil, and an invocation to the lyre follow in the translation list. A Bourget line on Greek art heads the book as its guiding motto. English readers met Italy greatest modern poet in this early selection.
56722-home-scenes-and-heart-studies:
Grace Aguilar wrote Home Scenes and Heart Studies, a book of tales for the home. Groombridge and Sons issued this thirteenth edition in London in eighteen hundred seventy six. Hyde W Briscoe drew the plates that grace the worn loved book. Aguilar’s Woman’s Friendship and Vale of Cedars won her name first.

The Perez Family opens the set in a mean Liverpool lane. Their small cot stands clean and bright amid dirt and cracked panes. A neat garden runs from its back door to the Mersey’s banks. Gossips of the alley can learn naught of the folk within doors. The Stone-Cutter’s Boy of Possagno takes the tale to Italy next. The Edict, a tale of fourteen hundred ninety two, turns to Spain’s Jews. The Escape and The Authoress follow. Cast Thy Bread Upon the Waters names one tale.
56765-the-bashful-earthquake-other-fable:
The Bashful Earthquake, and Other Fables and Verses is a book of comic verse by Oliver Herford, with many pictures by the author himself. Scribner's Sons published it at New York in the autumn of 1898. A poem at the front imagines this little world falling through space into the sun, shrivelling as it falls. Ants, philosophers, cattle, kings, beggars, and mice would vanish in an instant.

From some far planet, the poem ends, a child might watch the flash and cry at the pretty shooting star. The joke sets Herford's tone: light verse with a sting of wonder at man's small place. His own drawings carry the same wit through the fables that follow.
56797-the-invaders-and-other-stories:
Count Lyof N Tolstoi wrote tales of war and peasant life, turned from Russian by Nathan Haskell Dole. Thomas Y Crowell and Company issued the set in New York in 1887. Six tales fill the book, from The Invaders to the horse tale Kholstomir. The first tale is told by a volunteer who rides with troops in the Caucasus.

Captain Khlopof tells the young man that the battalion marches at dawn. Two days of food are ordered, though past marches lasted near a month. The captain urges him to stay safe and hunt at camp instead. Tolstoi shows war's wait, talk, and dread through small, true scenes.
5685-the-conservation-of-races:
Du Bois delivered The Conservation of Races in 1897 as Occasional Paper number two of the American Negro Academy. The paper argues that educated Black Americans bear a duty to their people. They should use learning and culture for uplift. It names two blocks to that work: disunity within the race, and persistent opposition to Black progress. Du Bois writes at a moment when the future relations of Black and white Americans stood at the center of public debate.

The essay's force comes from its plain claim about races. It treats them as real human groups with distinct gifts to preserve. Progress, it says, needs unity of purpose and honest facing of prejudice. Readers get a foundational text of African American thought, short enough to read in one sitting and rich enough to repay study. It still speaks to questions of identity, leadership, and collective duty.
56881-forged-egyptian-antiquities:
Wakeling wrote this warning book on forged Egyptian antiquities, published by Adam and Charles Black at London in 1912, with plates in color drawn from the objects themselves. He thanks workers on the Nubian Archaeological Survey and the Harvard University expedition for their help. His frontispiece shows a blue canopic jar with an Anubis head, its uneven modern glaze giving it away.

Chapter by chapter, Wakeling works through the faker's whole range: gold ornaments, lapis lazuli figures and glass, figures in wood and stone, and porcelain figures. Scarabs get a long chapter, then alabaster, mummies and mummy cases, and a whole forged tomb. He closes with the makers and sellers of forged antiquities and a chapter on Egyptologists, teaching buyers how imitations betray themselves.
56883-balaam-and-his-master-and-other-sk:
Joel Chandler Harris published Balaam and His Master and Other Sketches and Stories with Houghton, Mifflin at Boston in 1891. Harris also wrote Nights with Uncle Remus and Mingo. Six pieces fill the volume, from the title tale to The Old Bascom Place.

Harris opens with a flourish on the tricks of fate: war that redeems a nation, a university of slavery, a stroke of a pen that changes peoples' destinies. Tragedy drags comedy across the stage, he says, before he names the town of Billville. A Consript's Christmas, Ananias, and Where's Duncan follow in his Southern manner. Mom Bi and the Bascom Place close the set. Dialect, memory, and the old plantation world shape the tales.
56904-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy, new series number 40, for January 1901, is the annual journal of the Pennsylvania Prison Society. The society was instituted on May 8, 1787, and its office stood on State House Row in Philadelphia. The number prints the society's constitution in full. Its preamble argues the cause of prisoners in Christian terms.

The obligations of benevolence, the constitution says, are founded on the precept and example of the Author of Christianity. They are not cancelled by the follies or crimes of our fellow-creatures. It lists the miseries that attend prisons: penury, hunger, cold, unnecessary severity, unwholesome apartments, and guilt. By the aid of humanity, undue and illegal sufferings may be prevented. Better modes of punishment may be found, which, instead of continuing habits of vice, restore our fellow-creatures to virtue.
56931-suffrage-songs-and-verses:
A pamphlet of suffrage poems by Charlotte Perkins Gilman. The Charlton Company published it at New York in 1911. Ten cents bought the collection. Some poems came from her 1898 book In This Our World. Others appeared in the Woman's Journal and the Forerunner. A winged torch ornaments the title page.

She Walketh Veiled and Sleeping opens the set. Woman, Gilman writes, does not yet know her power. Coming answers with the mother's heart and hands entering public life. Anti-suffragists get their own mocking verses. A song for equal suffrage and poems to indifferent women follow. Girls of today and women of today frame the future. Gilman wrote the era's sharpest feminist economics. These verses carried her argument into meetings and marches.
56954-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy opens with the constitution of the Philadelphia Society for Alleviating the Miseries of Public Prisons. The constitution begins with a reflection. The obligations of benevolence, founded on the precepts and examples of the Author of Christianity, are not cancelled by the follies or crimes of our fellow creatures.

Penury, hunger, cold, unnecessary severity, unwholesome rooms, and guilt are named as the usual attendants of prisons. It becomes us, the society says, to extend compassion to those who suffer those miseries. By the aid of humanity, undue and illegal sufferings may be prevented. Modes of punishment may be found that restore fellow creatures to virtue and happiness, instead of continuing habits of vice. Readers get the founding document of American prison reform, and the journal that carried its work.
56963-fun-o-the-forge-stories:
Fun o' the Forge is a book of Irish stories by Brian O'Higgins, printed at Dublin by Whelan and Son. Twelve stories fill the contents, from The Blacksmith's Charm to The First Plum Pudding. Titles along the way promise How Jimmy Settled the Sojer, The Confiscated Bacon, and Ned's Trip to Dublin.

The first story sets the scene: Ned M'Grane's smithy stands by the roadside near the head of a glen, under great beeches. On winter nights the boys gather round the forge fire to talk of every subject under the sun and watch Ned at his work. Ned is as famed for his wit as for his trade, and his stories could draw laughter from the loneliest heart.
56978-the-book-of-the-feet-a-history-of-:
The Book of the Feet is a history of boots and shoes by Sparkes Hall. Hall was elastic-boot maker to the Queen. The book was printed in New York in 1847, from the second London edition. The title promises the fashions of the Egyptians, Hebrews, Persians, Greeks, and Romans, and the styles of Europe through the middle ages to the present day. Hints to last-makers and remedies for corns are added.

The American edition adds a history of boots and shoes in the United States. Lives of eminent shoemakers and Crispin anecdotes come with it. Hall says in his preface that twenty years of close practice in the trade stand behind the book. He tried to correct much that was bad in form and material. The work mixes trade pride, antiquarian plates, and practical foot care.
57036-a-slav-soul-and-other-stories:
A Slav Soul and Other Stories, by Alexander Kuprin, was printed in New York by Putnam Sons in 1916. Stephen Graham wrote the opening. Fifteen tales fill the book, in English dress for American readers.

The list opens with A Slav Soul, The Song and the Dance, and Easter Day. The Idiot, The Picture, Hamlet, and Mechanical Justice follow. The Last Word, The White Poodle, The Elephant, and Dogs Happiness stand in the mid part. A Clump of Lilacs, Anathema, Tempting Providence, and Cain close the set. Graham quotes Kuprin own view that the simplest events in life are the most strange and least understood. He calls the tales a torrent of Russian thought and feeling, a mirror of Russia herself. Story fans get a famed Russian voice in short form.
57057-healthful-sports-for-young-ladies:
Healthful Sports for Young Ladies is a book of games and exercises translated from the French of Mademoiselle Saint Sernin, printed in London for Ackermann's Repository of Arts. Eleven elegant engravings, from drawings by a draughtsman to the King of France, illustrate the games. Original poetry and anecdotes are mixed through the text.

The preface makes a medical case. Eminent physicians, it says, insist that young ladies growing toward womanhood need active and regular exercise, and should avoid sedentary amusements. Variety is the difficulty, since children tire of one game. The book answers with a great number of sports that require exertion. Its frontispiece shows a girl on a swing. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
57061-moonlight-schools-for-the-emancipa:
Cora Wilson Stewart describes the Moonlight Schools in a book issued in New York in 1922. Stewart led work against adult illiteracy for the National Education Association and allied groups. She gives the book to the unpaid teachers whose work, she says, blazed the trail for the whole effort.

Inside, chapters trace the first night classes in Kentucky, the shock of the first session, and new methods for grown learners. Stewart covers the first textbooks made for adults, schools in wartime, and the spread of the plan across the state and then the nation. Photos and letters from pupils, some past fifty and some past eighty, show what the classes meant in practice.
57090-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy number forty six is a year book. The Pennsylvania Prison Society, born in seventeen eighty seven, brought it out. This print bears January of nineteen seven from its Philadelphia house. Its front leaves give the full rule frame of that long lived group. Kind duty is not cut by the faults or crimes of men, that frame opens.

Want, hunger, cold, harsh rule, foul rooms, and guilt crowd jail life. Kind hands can bar those undue pains and keep the kin link whole, it holds. Fit pains may turn men from vice to worth and joy in that creed. Posts of the group span a head, two aides, quill men, and a funds man. Year meet votes pick those posts on a set day each year.
57135-guide-to-historic-plymouth-localit:
Guide to Historic Plymouth is a local guide book by Burbank, copyrighted in 1920. Burbank published the illustrated guide at Plymouth, Massachusetts, in the tercentenary year. A Mayflower image fronts the book for the pilgrim anniversary crowds of 1920. Contents list Pilgrim Hall, pilgrim antiquities, and the landing of the Pilgrims.

Cole Hill, Leyden Street, Burial Hill, and the national monument fill the site list. Governor Bradford house of 1621 and Clark Island stand among the pictured spots. Court house, old houses, industries, and Plymouth as a summer resort close the survey. Visitors to the shrine town gained a pocket key to its stones and stories.
57147-scott-burton-and-the-timber-thieve:
E G Cheyney wrote this third Scott Burton adventure, published by Appleton in 1922. Scott sits on his cabin porch above the Gulf of Mexico, reading a letter from Washington dated September 3, 1913 for the dozenth time.

The letter, from the Chief of Personnel, praises his cleanup of the sheepmen trouble on the Cormorant Forest. It appoints him deputy supervisor on the Okalatchee with a delicate job. Timber thieves have worked that forest for some time, and local officers have failed to catch them or stop the thefts. He is to report directly to Washington. Cheyney's forester hero gets a detective's assignment among the pines of Florida.
57165-mark-tidd-his-adventures-and-strat:
Clarence Kelland published Mark Tidd, His Adventures and Strategies, with Harper and Brothers in 1913. Clarke illustrated the volume. The frontispiece shows Mark shouting for Batten to go, and promising to look after Bill.

The publisher's list shows where the book led. Mark Tidd in Egypt, in Italy, and in the Backwoods followed. Mark Tidd in Business, as editor, and as manufacturer came after. Mark Tidd later filled a shelf of his own. Kelland built a boys' series on a fat, stuttering strategist who out-thought every rival. The first volume sets the pattern: a small town, a gang of boys, and a scheme worked out like a general's campaign.
57180-the-literary-shop-and-other-tales:
The Literary Shop and Other Tales is a set of satirical sketches by James Ford. The Chelsea Company published this new and enlarged edition in New York. The title piece first appeared in book form in the fall of 1894. Some of its papers had already run in the magazines Truth and Puck.

The enlarged edition adds sketches of a model literary community. That village was established by the McClure syndicate on a rise over the Hackensack River. Several hundred poets and prose hands live there in its telling. All are regularly employed on the syndicate's magazine and newspaper work. The title sketch moves through an old garret into the ages of letters. Ford writes as an insider of the New York literary trade.
57186-bayonet-training-manual-used-by-th:
The Bayonet Training Manual sets out the British army's method of teaching the bayonet. Van Nostrand reprinted it in New York in 1917. The text came from the latest British manual of 1916. That manual rested on war experience. An Infantry Journal printing spread it in America.

The preface gives the training two aims. The first is alertness of mind and quickness of muscle. The second is fighting spirit. Physical drill runs beside the bayonet lessons. The first chapter states the weapon's nature plainly. The bayonet is an offensive weapon. Its killing range is about five feet at most. Most killing happens at two feet or less. Later chapters give a progressive programme of instruction.
57206-morocco-its-people-and-places:
Morocco, Its People and Places is a travel book by Edmondo de Amicis, the Italian writer, translated by Rollin-Tilton and published in New York in 1882. A general view of Tangiers faces the title page. De Amicis travelled with an official mission, and his book became one of the most read accounts of Morocco in his century.

The contents follow the road inland. Tangiers fills the first long chapter. Then come halts at Had-el-Garbia and Tleta de Reissana, the city of Alkazar-el-Kebir, and the camp at Ben-Auda. Town by town and camp by camp, the party moves toward the Sultan's court. De Amicis writes with a novelist's eye for faces, dress, and ceremony, and the book holds the strangeness and splendour of a closed kingdom opening, street by street, to a European guest.
57266-cambridge-and-its-colleges: Cambridge and Its Colleges is a guide to the university city and its foundations, with pictures of the courts and chapels. Such guides led the visitor college by college through Cambridge. Kings, Queens’, Trinity, and St John’s stand among the great names on the river. Each foundation has its own age, arms, and famous sons. Halls, libraries, and walks fill a work like this. The guide mixes history with plain direction for the stranger. It turns a walk through Cambridge into a lesson in English history.
57272-the-depths-of-the-soul-psycho-anal:
William Stekel, the Viennese doctor of the mind, wrote these studies of the soul's depths. Tannenbaum turned them into English, and Kegan Paul printed the book in London in 1921. Stekel gave it to Bess and Oscar Blumenthal, in memory of a glad stay in Chicago.

The Second World opens the set, then thanks and its lack. Unpacking one's heart, laziness, and those who stand outside follow. What children aspire to, freedom, jealousy, and childhood friendship take their turns. Eating, running away from home, and refuge in disease fill the list shown here. Stekel reads small acts for the hid thoughts under them, in his famed free manner.
57277-a-dreamer-s-tales:
A Dreamer's Tales, a set of fantasy stories by Lord Dunsany, came out at Boston from John W Luce and Company, with pictures by S H Sime. Some tales first ran in the Saturday Review. Dunsany thanks its editor for leave to reprint them. Sime's drawings, dreamlike and strange, stand through the book.

The first tale, Poltarnees, Beholder of Ocean, opens on the Inner Lands: Toldees, Mondath, and Arizim, whose border sentinels never see the sea. Other tales tell of Bethmoora, of idle days on the river Yann, and of the city of Carcassonne. The Hashish Man, Poor Old Bill, and The Unhappy Body close the set. Dunsany builds whole worlds out of a few pages of rich, calm prose.
57289-studies-in-irish-history-1603-1649:
Studies in Irish History, 1603 to 1649, second series, gathers lectures given before the Irish Literary Society of London. R Barry O'Brien edited the volume, published at Dublin in 1906.

Four lectures fill the book. The Reverend SA Cox treats the Plantation of Ulster, opening with Sir Donnell O'Cahan, who served the English and was rewarded with nineteen years in prison without trial. Philip Wilson gives two lectures on Strafford, covering the Graces and the eve of the rising of 1641. Arthur Houston then treats the rising itself, called simply 1641. Dr Donelan closes with the Confederation of Kilkenny. The lectures trace the half century in which English rule was planted in Ireland and then shaken by rebellion and civil war.
57307-fighting-germany-s-spies:
French Strother wrote Fighting Germany's Spies, in 1918. Doubleday at Garden City put out the illustrated account. Its facts were verified by a bureau of investigation, it states. The attorney-general directed the nation-wide work against plotters then. Arresting and prosecuting them was that work, the plate says.

Dangerous enemy aliens were interned under the same direction there. The inside story of the passport frauds opens the contents. A first glimpse of a bridge-blower stands in that first chapter. The same man and the first ship bombs fill chapter two. Another agent and the ship bombs take the third chapter. A genius of the passport frauds came suddenly to earth, it says. Agents of the justice department took him in that fall. Strother gives the home front its spy hunt in documents.
57321-proverb-stories:
Louisa M Alcott gathered stray tales into Proverb Stories for young readers. Sampson Low, Marston, Searle, and Rivington issued the book in London in 1882. Alcott, barred from fresh writing, swept up waifs and strays, she writes. The Baron's Gloves shows the sort of tale Jo March wrote early on.

Kitty's Class Day opens under the saw, a stitch in time saves nine. Aunt Kipp, Psyche's Art, and A Country Christmas fill the set. Each tale hangs on a proverb as its quiet hinge. Young readers gain warm, wise tales from the author of Little Women.
57329-knuckles-and-gloves:
Bohun Lynch's Knuckles and Gloves came from Collins in London, with a first impression in October 1922. Theodore Cook supplied the preface. The book looks back at the bare-knuckle ring and the gloved game that replaced it. Lynch also wrote The Complete Amateur Boxer. His frontispiece prints a round-by-round account of a championship fight between Cribb and Molineaux. The report scores first blood, closed eyes, and a broken jaw in the ninth round. The fight ends in the eleventh, when the beaten man cannot stand again.

The caption calls that plate the close of the battle, or the champion triumphant. Its blow-by-blow shorthand shows the language of the old prize ring in full working order. Around such records Lynch builds his history of the sport. The story runs from knuckles to gloves.
57331-sexual-neuroses:
J T Kent, a doctor in St Louis, lays out a plain medical study of sex-linked nerve ills in an 1879 printing. Maynard and Tedford printed the work, and Kent states in his preface that he offers no excuse for the topic. He hopes fellow doctors will weigh facts that shame kept out of print for too long.

A long contents list names the ground: habit, restraint, and acts Kent links to harm, then states such as spermatorrhoea in its true and false forms. Chapters deal with the spine, the brain, and change in the parts themselves, with case notes to show each ill at work. Last pages turn to care, with steps for each form and notes on loss of power and its cure.
57411-the-magic-of-the-horse-shoe-with-o:
Robert Means Lawrence wrote The Magic of the Horse Shoe, With Other Folk Lore Notes, issued at Boston and New York in 1898 by Houghton, Mifflin and Company. Lawrence was a doctor of medicine. Seven parts fill the book. The horse shoe leads at page one and runs to page one hundred and forty.

Fortune and luck, the folk lore of common salt, and the omens of sneezing follow. Days of good and evil omen get a part too. Odd dealings with beasts and the luck of odd numbers close the set. A topical index ends the book at page three hundred and forty one. Verse lines from Whittier and Longfellow head the lead part. Lawrence traces shoe lore from old foot gear for draft beasts. Xenophon and more old writers are cited on hoof care.
57422-cliff-dwellings-of-the-mesa-verde-:
Don Watson wrote Cliff Dwellings of the Mesa Verde, a study in pictures. The Mesa Verde Museum Association issued it at Mesa Verde National Park, Colorado. The opening section tells the discovery of the first cliff dwellings. Spaniards were in the region as early as 1765, the book notes, with no record of their seeing the dwellings. They probably gave the great mesa its name, green table in Spanish.

Professor J S Newberry first printed the name in 1859. In 1874 W H Jackson came on a government photographic survey. He hired the miner John Moss to guide him into the Mancos River canyon. On September 9, 1874, the party scanned the cliffs all day and found nothing. At evening camp, Moss waved at the cliff above their heads. The last sun lit a small dwelling seven hundred feet up.
57483-the-napoleon-gallery-or-illustrati:
The Napoleon Gallery is a picture book of the life and times of the Emperor of France, published by Estes and Lauriat of Boston in 1888. Its engravings, by Reveil and other artists, copy the most celebrated paintings in France. A long list of plates opens the volume.

The plates march through the career. Early scenes show the action at Saint Roche, the entry into Milan, Rivoli, and the crossing at Arcola. Egypt follows, with the Pyramids, the revolt of Cairo, and the plague of Jaffa. Marengo, Ulm, and the later campaigns fill the rest of the list. Captions and letterpress explain each scene. Picture galleries like this one brought French history painting to American parlours. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
57500-a-history-of-economic-doctrines:
A History of Economic Doctrines is a survey by Charles Gide and Charles Rist, translated from the second French edition of 1913. Heath of Boston published the English version. Richards made the translation under the direction of the late Professor William Smart. The subtitle fixes its span: from the time of the Physiocrats to the present day.

Gide held the chair of social economics in the law faculty at Paris. Rist taught political economy at Montpellier. A prefatory note points to Gide's Principles of Political Economy, already known in several translations. The authors argue that France chose the history of theory for reasons in her own research tradition, while England kept to another path. Their book became the standard history of economic thought in its generation: schools, systems, and heresies in one long, clear line.
57530-volcanoes-of-the-united-states:
Steven Brantley wrote Volcanoes of the United States, a booklet sold by the Government Printing Office for the Geological Survey. A photograph of Mount Shasta in California heads the book, with the note that Shasta has erupted at least ten times in the past thousands of years. Sections treat Alaska, Hawaii, and the rest of the country in turn.

Survey scientists, the book explains, study the processes before, during, and after an eruption to cut the loss of life and property. They assess hazards and carry public outreach, turning science into terms the public and officials can use. Monitoring volcanoes is steady, watchful work, most of it done in quiet years. The booklet is the survey speaking to citizens who live in the shadow of volcanoes. Maps and photographs show where the danger sleeps.
57575-motherhood-and-the-relationships-o:
Gasquoine Hartley wrote Motherhood and the Relationships of the Sexes, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1917. Her earlier books, The Truth About Women and The Age of Mother-Power, stand under her name. The dedication is to her son Leslie, and it states her whole thesis.

The mother, she writes, is the main stream of the racial life, and all hope rests on faith in motherhood. Her son taught her that the single life is only foam on the great tide of humankind. The contents divide in two. Part one looks back: the position of women before the great European war, and as the war changed it. Part two studies the maternal instinct in the making, starting with parenthood among insects. Feminist readers of 1917 got motherhood argued as women's power.
5758-many-cargoes:
Jacobs gathers sea stories and shore comedies in Many Cargoes, a second edition published in New York in 1894. Contents include A Change of Treatment and A Love Passage. The Captain's Exploit, Contraband of War, and A Black Affair follow. The Skipper of the Osprey, In Borrowed Plumes, and The Boatswain's Watch add further tales of low water, inquests, elopements, and cooks. Sailors, skippers, and Thames-side folk fill every page.

The stories thrive on trickery, mistaken identity, and the gap between a sailor's plan and its outcome. Jacobs tells them in brisk, plain prose with a dry comic eye, letting dialogue carry the humor. Readers who enjoy short sea fiction will find a lively, old-fashioned collection, and fans of Jacobs will recognize the small boats and smaller ambitions that made his name.
57664-the-english-lakes:
The English Lakes pairs paintings by Heaton Cooper with descriptions by William Palmer. Adam and Charles Black published the book in London, first in 1905 and again in 1908. A misty morning at Newby Bridge on Windermere serves as frontispiece. The tour goes lake by lake through the Lake District of north-west England.

The reader rides a steam yacht on Windermere and walks by Wordsworth's Rothay to Rydal and Grasmere. Esthwaite Water, old Hawkshead, and Coniston Water follow. Later chapters give the moods of Wastwater, the glory of Ennerdale, and the charms of Derwentwater. Bassenthwaite, Thirlmere, Haweswater, and Ullswater close the circuit, with a chapter on mountain tarns. Cooper's plates carry the scenery that Palmer's prose explains.
5767-the-fireside-chats-of-franklin-dela:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt speaks directly to the American people in his Fireside Chats, radio addresses broadcast between 1933 and 1944. The first chat, on March twelfth, 1933, opens with banking, as Roosevelt promises to talk for a few minutes about a subject few fully understand. Later chats take up recovery, war, and the duties of citizenship, always in a calm, neighborly voice.

Readers hear a president explain policy as if sitting by a fire, turning complex measures into plain talk. The chats show radio as a new instrument of leadership, building trust in crisis. Historians, students, and general readers will find here the words that shaped American morale through Depression and war, in the informal style that made them famous.
57739-papuan-pictures:
Papuan Pictures is a missionary's account of life in Papua by Dauncey of Delena, printed at London in 1913 by the London Missionary Society. Sixty-three pictures from the author's own photographs fill the book, with Tima of Delena at the front. Dauncey greets the boys and girls whose meetings he attended in the old home land and in Australia.

The chapters move from games and school to keeping house, a sorcerer, and a chapter of accidents. Feasts and dances, doctoring, and peace making all get their turns. Dauncey writes of the hillside village of Korona and the district of Kabadi, closing with a chapter on the aim of the mission. The tone is warm and close to daily life.
57749-altruism-its-nature-and-varieties:
George Herbert Palmer gave these lectures as the Ely Lectures for 1917-18, printed by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York in 1919. The Ely foundation at Union Theological Seminary dates to May 8, 1865, when Zebulon Stiles Ely gave ten thousand dollars for lectures on the evidences of Christianity. The deed lets later lecturers range to other themes for the good of man, with the faculty's consent.

Palmer takes altruism as his theme: what it is, and the forms it takes. The lectures ask how far care for others stands at the heart of the Christian faith the foundation serves. Palmer writes in a clear, grave style, for hearers trained in pulpits and in classrooms alike.
57769-white-tail-the-deer-s-adventures:
White Tail, the Deer's Adventures, is a children's animal story by George Ethelbert Walsh. Walsh wrote a run of Bumper the rabbit books, his title page notes. Coloured pictures by Edwin J Prettie go with the text. The book belongs to a twilight animal series for boys and girls from four to ten. It was issued at Chicago, Philadelphia, and Toronto in nineteen twenty two.

A list of the series stands at the front. Bumper the white rabbit fills its first four titles. Bobby Gray Squirrel and Buster the brown bear follow. White Tail himself takes titles nine and ten. A washer the raccoon volume stands eleventh. The animals of the series are called a jolly lot, brave and fearless in danger, in the note shown.
5779-the-crushed-flower-and-other-storie:
Leonid Andreyev gathers stories of childhood, fear, and inner life in The Crushed Flower and Other Stories. The opening tale follows Yura, six years old, for whom the world is enormous, alive, and bewitchingly mysterious. Yura knows the sky by day. He knows its deep azure and its white-breasted clouds drifting slowly. He watches them lying on his back on grass or roof, though much of the world stays unknown.

Readers meet Andreyev's psychological realism, where a child's wonder borders on dread and adult certainties fail. The stories favor mood and inner vision over tidy plots, with images that linger after reading. Lovers of Russian short fiction will find a powerful, unsettling collection, and readers new to Andreyev will meet a writer who treats the soul as his true subject.
57810-it-was-marlowe-a-story-of-the-secr:
It Was Marlowe is a story by Wilbur Gleason Zeigler, built on the secret of three centuries of its subtitle. A motto at the front warns that no workman in tragic poetry should lightly take on the measuring of the great. The tale belongs to the long quarrel over who wrote the plays of Shakespeare. Its title gives the answer the story argues for its readers.

Marlowe, in the theory of the book, did not die in the Deptford tavern brawl of the records.  A story can carry a theory into parlours that a pamphlet never reaches, and this one dresses the Marlowe claim as a tale of discovery. The book is a document of the authorship controversy at its most romantic, when every missing year in a life looked like a door left ajar.
57845-fishing-from-the-earliest-times:
Fishing From the Earliest Times, by William Radcliffe, sometime of Balliol College, Oxford, was published by John Murray at London in 1921 with pictures. The Greek and Roman part alone runs to fifteen chapters, opening with Homer and the standing of fishermen. Aristotle is hailed as the first scale reader, and one chapter marks the first mention of a fly.

Later chapters reach the Macedonian invention, or first mention of an artificial fly, and the pike's first notice in classical letters. Cleopatra's fishing, costly fish suppers, and pickled fish all get their pages. Radcliffe dedicates the book to his fishing hosts on five shores.
57858-west-irish-folk-tales-and-romances:
William Larminie collected and translated West Irish Folk-Tales and Romances, published by Elliot Stock in London in 1893. The book belongs to the Camden Library. An appendix prints specimens of the Gaelic originals spelled phonetically, so readers can hear the tales' first language. Larminie added an introduction and notes.

His introduction argues a subtle point. Scholars expected the gain from Gaelic folklore to come from treating it as one uniform body. Larminie suggests the opposite. Ireland's districts stand far enough apart to isolate their peasant storytellers. The island may hold not one body of folklore but several, placed side by side for comparison. That variety, he argues, helps solve problems in the study of tales generally. The collection gathers stories and romances from the west of Ireland in the tellers' own shape, making it a record of a living oral tradition as the nineteenth century closed.
57862-popular-misgovernment-in-the-unite:
Alfred Cruikshank wrote Popular Misgovernment in the United States, published by Moffat, Yard and Company in New York in 1920. The book argues that unlimited suffrage has failed and threatens worse. Its chapter titles state the case in full, like heads of a legal brief.

Cruikshank holds that the oldest American traditions favor a restricted suffrage. The suffrage, he says, is not a natural right but a function of government, fit only for those competent to use it. He makes the capacity to create and preserve property the test of citizenship. Later chapters trace manhood suffrage to the French Revolution and blame it for the spoils system, the boss, and the machine. The book is a period document of anti-democratic argument, printed the year American women won the vote.
57890-the-comanches:
Comanches is a history of White's Battalion, Virginia Cavalry, in the Civil War. Frank Myers, late captain of Company A, wrote the battalion's record. Kelly, Piet and Company published it at Baltimore in the year 1871. All the officers of the battalion approved the history as written. The unit rode in the Laurel Brigade, Hampton Division, of Lee's army.

Myers preserves marches, fights, and names that regimental pride held dear. The battalion bore the nickname Comanches for its wild, swift style. Virginia horsemen in the Army of Northern Virginia form its cast. Postwar Baltimore gave many such unit histories to Southern readers in print. Veterans could trace their service company by company in its pages.
57893-the-country-school-an-entertainmen:
Orne wrote The Country School, an entertainment in two scenes, copyrighted in Boston in 1890. Suggestions at the front direct how the sketch should be played. The parts should be taken by prominent citizens of the town, the more elderly, staid, and ill-matched in years and bearing the better. Dignified professors, judges, doctors, lawyers, and teachers should be persuaded to forget their present greatness, don the costumes, and revive the scenes of their youth.

Costumes are left largely to taste, with short pantaloons, jumpers, caps, and broad-brimmed straw hats proposed for the gentlemen. Short dresses, the historic pantalette, sun-bonnets, and aprons are proposed for the ladies, their hair braided or in long curls. One or two may play the ragged fraternity: the bright boy, and the dullard who stumbles through his lessons. An indefinite number can take part.
57923-crystal-river-saga-lore-of-the-col:
Crystal River Saga, by Theresa Francis, tells lore of the Colorado Rockies. The book centers on Marble, a quarry town in Gunnison County, Colorado. Cover photos show the old marble mill fire walls still standing there. Sheep Mountain and White House Mountain frame the ruined mill site view.

Francis lived in Marble thirty three years, through boom and ghost town days. When Marble emptied in 1945 she stayed on, cheerful and neighborly still. Crafts teaching and a roadside stand kept her living in the town. Tourists by the thousand asked her the town story over the years. Her saga gathers that lore of mines, marble, and mountain folk.
57931-the-russo-japanese-conflict-its-ca:
Asakawa, a teacher of East Asian life and past at Dartmouth, wrote a study dated 1904 on the clash of Russia and Japan. A first note by Frederick Wells Williams of Yale backs the book for its calm tone. Maps show where the aims of the two powers meet in the East.

First pages weigh trade needs, as Japan shifts from farm life to mill life and looks to Korea and Manchuria. Chapters then trace the hand back of Liao-tung in 1895, rail pacts, and the grab of Kiao-chau. Port Arthur, an open door note from Secretary Hay, and troops in Manchuria close the chain of causes.
5797-youth-challenges:
Clarence Budington Kelland opens Youth Challenges with Bonbright Foote the Sixth rising behind a long table that serves as his desk, extending a hand across it. The elder Foote welcomes his son to his place in the firm with historic gravity, smiling as only he can smile. From that formal welcome, the novel follows a young man challenging his father's world, its business, and its values.

Here is a business and coming-of-age story, where youth tests tradition, ambition tests loyalty, and a family firm becomes a stage for character. Kelland writes with energy and clear moral stakes, favoring action and dialogue over introspection. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century American novels of work, family, and the price of independence.
57980-the-magic-and-science-of-jewels-an:
The Magic and Science of Jewels and Stones is a book of gem lore by Isidore Kozminsky, published by Putnam in 1922 with thirty-nine specimens in colour. Kozminsky wrote from Melbourne, where his dedication gathers a circle of Australian helpers and patrons. The frontispiece shows the great opal called the Flame Queen.

The contents join the two halves of the title. The magic comes first: early stone lore, the high priest's ephod and breastplate, and the zodiac. The science follows in the catalogue of precious and semi-precious stones. Kozminsky treats gems as charms with histories, and his book is a jeweller's grimoire as much as a mineral guide, written when occult revival and gem trade met.
58131-through-hell-with-hiprah-hunt-a-se:
Arthur Young made this picture book, Through Hell with Hiprah Hunt, printed in New York in 1901. The subtitle calls it the adventures of a modern Dante in the infernal regions. Satan fronts the book, billed as king of the infernal empire. A long list of plates maps the tour, canto by canto.

Hunt must register on the way down and cross the River Styx with Captain Charon. Judge Minos hands out justice in one plate, and the tour passes pits for lawyers and stock jobbers. Bribe-taking aldermen, careless dentists, and slow folk made active all get their due. The fun lies in seeing each trade and vice punished in kind.
58136-conscience-fanaticism-an-essay-on-:
Conscience and Fanaticism, subtitled an essay on moral values, is a work by George Pitt-Rivers, printed in London in 1919. A Latin line on the title page bids the reader keep an even mind. Pitt-Rivers starts from the great weight that public opinion, the state, and the church all give to the word conscience.

Chapters test the validity of moral judgments, then the meaning of moral obligation, arguing with the utilitarian standard and with Mill's defense of it. Religion and morality, the laws of suggestion, and the power of ideas follow. Later parts weigh instinct and heredity in how people value things, and how demagogues and fanatics sway crowds.
58180-my-knitting-book-second-series:
Miss Lambert wrote a second series of knitting patterns for ladies. John Murray issued My Knitting Book in London in 1847, at its twenty-third thousand. Lambert had written The Hand-Book of Needlework and a crochet sampler before. Patterns for quilts lead the contents of the new series.

Each pattern was reworked and its early faults fixed for this form, she writes. Terms are kept the same as in the first series for ease of use. Carriage socks, bassinet covers, and raised-stripe quilts fill the early pages. Knitters gain tested patterns from a famed hand of the craft's revival.
582-a-collection-of-beatrix-potter-stori:
Beatrix Potter's original Peter Rabbit books gather in this volume, with starred tales included here. Peter Rabbit, Benjamin Bunny, Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, Mr. Jeremy Fisher, Jemima Puddle-Duck, the Flopsy Bunnies, Two Bad Mice, Timmy Tiptoes, Mr. Tod, Pigling Bland, and Ginger and Pickles lead the set.

Potter writes and draws small animal tales with plain words and keen country detail. Peter, warned against Mr. McGregor's garden, runs straight there and eats lettuces till sick. The book charms young readers as a treasury of Potter's best, where naughty rabbits learn, gently, that rules have reasons.
58246-dagonet-ditties:
George Sims wrote light verse and prose bits in his Dagonet name. A second form of Dagonet Ditties is this book. His list names Rogues and Vagabonds and How the Poor Live. Those books sold in boards at two shillings in the ads. The ditties first ran in The Referee sheet of that day.

Short songs on town life, love, loss, and jest fill the book. Sims knew the poor streets of London from his own walks. That lore gives his light verse a warm, true core in it. Each piece is brief and built to be read aloud with ease. Such books sat in rail stalls and home shelves alike then. Wit with a heart marks the whole set.
58281-the-burton-holmes-lectures-volume-:
Volume One of The Burton Holmes Lectures is the first of a set of ten volumes of travel lectures. The set was printed at Battle Creek, Michigan, by the Little-Preston Company in 1901. The lectures are illustrated with photographs by the author. The original edition was limited to one thousand sets. A short life of Holmes stands at the front, in place of a biography.

Elias Burton Holmes was born in Chicago in January 1870. In 1883 he took up photography, and in 1886 he travelled abroad and took pictures. He has been travelling and taking pictures ever since. In 1893 he made his first professional appearance, describing a journey to Japan. These volumes are the printed form of the illustrated travel lecture at its height.
58289-roaming-through-the-west-indies:
Harry A. Franck wrote this book of roams through the West Indies, printed in 1920. He had made past books of long walks round the world and down the Andes. Photos by his own hand fill this book. It is sent forth to his wife Rachel, with whom the trip was the start of a far long road. His son Harry, who joined them on the way, is named in the gift as well.

A first word warns how the trip was made. Years past, the author made a tramp round the world for his own joy, and friends coaxed him to set it on paper. Since then more has been asked of him, but with one term: that it be on foot. He will not be told how to roam, he says flat.
58312-london-cries-public-edifices:
Luke Limner wrote and drew a picture book of London street cries and great buildings, printed in London in 1851. The publishers kept the shop at the corner of Saint Paul's Church Yard once held by Newbery and Harris. Each page pairs a street seller's cry with a famed London site.

The tinker cries pots and kettles to mend beside the Tower of London. The Tower is called fortress, palace, and prison, where great events of English history passed. Its oldest part is said to rise from William the Conqueror's time. Other cries and buildings follow in the same mix. Children and tourists alike get London work and London stone in one bright book.
58328-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra is a finding list compiled by David Widger. It gathers the tables of contents of Cervantes volumes in that library. Don Quixote in two volumes heads the contents. The Exemplary Novels of Cervantes follow in the list. Wit and Wisdom of Don Quixote and the play Numantia are included. Ormsby's translation of Don Quixote supplies the chapter heads. Chapter one treats the character and pursuits of the famous gentleman. The first sally and the dubbing as a knight follow.

The scrutiny of the library by curate and barber is listed too. The adventure of the windmills stands as chapter eight's head. The index serves readers navigating the Gutenberg Cervantes shelf. It is a map, not a work of Cervantes himself. Widger compiled many such author indexes for the project.
58381-battling-the-bighorn-or-the-aeropl:
Battling the Bighorn, or The Aeroplane in the Rockies, is a boys' tale by Ashton Lamar. It was put out at Chicago with rights held in nineteen eleven. It stands in a set of tales of boys and the new fly craft. Four plates stand in each book of that set. The price of each is set at the head of the list. Plates for this book are by a named hand.

The set list names the kin tales of the book. In the clouds for the state, a stole fly craft, and a swift fly post stand first. A club of boy fly men, a cruise in the sky, and a spy tale of scout meets scout stand past them. The parts of this tale start with a flight by night.
58386-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy, new series numbers 47 and 48, is the annual journal of the Pennsylvania Prison Society, published at Philadelphia in January 1909. The society, founded in 1787 for alleviating the miseries of public prisons, prints in its journal the laws and reports that govern its work of visiting and instructing prisoners.

The opening pages reproduce the legal basis of prison visiting. An act of 1903 extends the same standing to other incorporated prisoners' societies in the Commonwealth. A portrait of Bishop William White, the society's first president from 1787, faces the text. The journal documents a century-old Philadelphia tradition: lay visitors with a statutory right to enter every jail and penitentiary in the state.
58406-the-river-of-life-and-other-storie:
Alexander Kuprin, a Russian officer turned writer, stands behind these tales, turned into English by Koteliansky and Murry. Luce of Boston printed The River of Life in 1916. Kuprin was born in 1870 and served as a lieutenant from 1890.

Seven years later he quit the army for letters. His novel The Duel made his name, a ruthless tale of garrison life on the western frontier. Radicals took it as a charge against the army and the Manchurian war, and claimed him for their own. He fought that reading hard, the note says. His tales, here in English, keep that same cold, clear eye on rich, vivid Russian life.
58409-cossack-tales:
Cossack Tales is a set of stories by Nicholas Gogol, turned from the Russian by George Tolstoy. It was published in London by James Blackwood. A long introduction stands before the tales, in place of the usual front matter.

The translator says the title forces his hand. English readers know the Cossacks only as the horsemen who stopped Napoleon, camped in Paris, and vanished again. A short account of that warlike race is thus much wanted. He goes back to the Tartar invasion of the thirteenth century. Russia then lay split between two hostile branches of the house of Rurick. The southern princes held Kiev and clutched their old sway. The north bore its conquest in silence. From that broken land, the sketch argues, the Cossacks rose.
58412-ariel-dances:
Ethel Cook Eliot wrote a novel printed at Boston in 1931 and reprinted three times in its first month. The book is given to her mother. Chapter one finds Ariel in a deck chair on a ship called Bermuda, bringing crowds of folk to New York through a cold March wind.

Ariel takes nothing as a matter of course and never has, the tale says, since her first years. Her fellow riders seem gay and sure of their place, while she feels a dull ache of suspense. She longs for her father, who is gone, and feels the longed for day has come pale and thin without him.
5843-the-young-step-mother-or-a-chronicl:
Charlotte Yonge tells a chronicle of mistakes in The Young Step-Mother, opening as Albinia Kendal drives down the steep hilly street of Bayford on a March evening. The equinoctial sun has long set. Blue haze has deepened into twilight and darkness. The town, not large nor modern enough for gas, is lit here and there by a shop of more pretension. A young stepmother's trials begin in that dim light.

Readers follow Albinia through marriage, stepchildren, and household errors, as good intentions meet real family friction. Yonge writes with moral care and domestic detail, letting small mistakes grow into serious tests of character. The book suits readers of Victorian domestic fiction, and those who enjoy long novels where patience and humility are the true heroics.
58444-the-modern-bicycle-and-its-accesso:
The Modern Bicycle and Its Accessories calls itself a complete reference book for rider, dealer, and maker. The Commercial Advertiser Association copyrighted it in 1898. Its chapters republish a series written for that paper by Alex Schwalbach and Julius Wilcox under the caption Bicycles for 1898, setting out the changes in manufacture since 1816.

Chapter one traces the evolution of the bicycle from 1816 toward 1899, noting better quality, lower prices, and the return of the chainless wheel. The chainless types get two chapters, weighed against the chain wheel gear by gear. Frame and fork construction follows, then chain protection by the gear case, an English device improved in America.
58472-saint-vincent-with-notes-and-publi:
Saint Vincent, with Notes and Publishers' Prices, by Francis H Napier and E D Bacon, is one of the Stanley Gibbons Philatelic Handbooks. Stanley Gibbons Limited published it at 391 Strand, London, in 1895. The volume is the fourth of the series.

The publishers note that collectors on both sides of the Atlantic now chase the postal issues of the West Indian colonies. Prices in the handbook run higher than the general catalogue, they warn, because the specimens priced are of more than average quality. A handbook on the stamps of Barbados, by the same authors, was in preparation.
58486-the-rajah-s-heir-a-novel-in-3-volu:
The Rajah's Heir is a novel in three volumes, issued at London in 1890 and credited in brackets to Charlotte Despard. The contents open with a prologue and a chapter called The Heir. A general and his family stand near the centre of the tale. A mysterious legacy and a loss that cannot be repaired come early in the heads.

The heir speaks for himself in a chapter of his own, and a masquerade brings consequences. Delhi, Meerut, and Lucknow place the story in India at a time of revolt and siege. A model state, a ranee, and a rajah's reception widen the stage. News from Meerut is received in a small state, a general marches, and walls close around a garrison. The chapter heads alone sketch a tale of empire, kinship, and war.
58526-the-human-interest-a-study-in-inco:
The Human Interest is a novel by Violet Hunt, published at Chicago and New York in 1899. Its subtitle calls it a study in incompatibilities. The story opens in Newcastle, where a London authoress who writes under the name Egidia walks a dull street of matching houses. She is paying a call she expects to bore her, on a woman who takes writers very seriously.

Hunt writes with a dry, sharp eye for the talk of literary people. The heroine dreads Ibsen, Meredith, and Plato served up with tea, yet she rings the bell all the same. The novel turns on the clash between the London writer and the northern household that receives her. It is an early, witty work by a novelist of manners.
58571-foreign-butterflies:
James Duncan wrote a volume on foreign butterflies for a naturalists library edited by Sir William Jardine. Volume thirty one of the set, on insects, came out in Edinburgh and London in 1858. A life of Lamarck, the French student of nature, fills the first part, with his portrait at the front.

Plates then show butterflies kind by kind, starting with great bird wing kinds and swallowtails. Whites, orange tips, and brush foot kinds follow in order, each named in Latin and shown in colour. Duncan gives page length notes on where each kind lives and how it may be known by its marks.
58576-fifty-years-a-detective-35-real-de:
Fifty Years a Detective is a memoir of thirty five real detective stories. Its title promises cases from a half century of police work. The text was prepared from page images held by Internet Archive. A transcriber's note flags italics and bold face for plain text readers. Contents sit at the end of this edition by that same note.

Veteran case lore of theft, fraud, and pursuit fills the story set. Old methods of shadowing and of informers stand beside newer police craft. The detective's own voice carries the tales in workmanlike, direct prose. Readers of true crime in 1912 got a working man's casebook here. Each story turns on a clue, a chase, or a confession gained.
58611-new-hampshire-a-poem-with-notes-an:
Robert Frost wrote New Hampshire, a book of verse put out in New York in 1923. J J Lankes cut the wood plates for the book. Frost gives the book to two states, Vermont and Michigan. The book went through six print runs in five years, a sign of its pull.

A long poem on the state heads the book and gives it its name. A set of notes in verse follows, with tales in poem form. A star in a stone boat, a count man, and a star-splitter stand out. Paul and his wife, wild grapes, and two witch tales add dark hues. A set of short grace notes closes the book. Fire and Ice, Dust of Snow, and Nothing Gold Can Stay sit in that last set. So does the famed snow road poem of a stop by dark woods.
58621-war-time-breads-and-cakes:
Amy Handy wrote a war cook book of breads and cakes for lean years. The book came out in Boston and New York in March 1918. Handy wrote War Food, a mate book on save ways with food. No white flour is the badge of its bread craft in full. War Food treats how to keep greens, fruit, and meats as well.

Yeasts lead the book, with a dry yeast from sour milk first. Sponges and yeast breads fill the front parts in plain steps. Straight dough breads and no-yeast breads stand in the mid list. Hot cakes, cakes, and spice breads close the sweet end. Home cooks get thrift.
58657-a-little-colored-boy-and-other-sto:
A Little Colored Boy and Other Stories came out from the Methodist Book Concern at New York and Cincinnati. The title story centers on Ned, a young Black singer on a farm. Mrs Warner says the Lord must want him in heaven for his voice. Grandma calls it an angel's voice in his throat. Farmer Warner grumbles that the boy shirks his chores to sing. Milk slops and apple sauce starts the supper scene.

Ned comes in barefoot with a hat full of blackberries picked for the family. The women melt, and the farmer growls on. Other tales follow in the same Sunday school vein. The book shows the pious story form of its day, with dialect speech and a clear moral bent. Modern readers will also see the period's racial framing.
5867-rataplan-a-rogue-elephant-and-other:
Ellen Velvin gathers animal stories in Rataplan, a Rogue Elephant and Other Stories, with illustrations by Gustave Verbeek. Velvin, author of Tales Told at the Zoo and Jack's Visit, dedicates the book affectionately to Grace Gallatin Thompson Seton, and to the author coming as a stranger to this country. The title story follows a rogue elephant, with further tales of zoo and wild creatures.

Young readers join animals as individuals, with tempers, tricks, and troubles of their own. Velvin writes with naturalist care and storyteller warmth, favoring observation over sentiment. The book suits children who love elephants and zoo tales, and families reading animal stories aloud, where a rogue's mischief teaches respect for wild strength.
58684-finding-themselves:
Julia Stimson, chief nurse of an American hospital unit, published her letters from France in 1918 under the title Finding Themselves. A note explains that they were written as the daily record of a unit of Red Cross nurses sent to France in May 1917. The British had asked for them.

Almost at once the unit crossed the Channel to take over a British base hospital set up on a race course. There the sixty-five American nurses cared for a stream of from eight hundred to two thousand wounded men at a time. English volunteer aids helped for months, then some thirty more American nurses reinforced them. The letters were printed, the note says, as first impressions of lasting worth.
58693-a-wreath-of-indian-stories:
The missionary writer known as ALOE, an honorary missionary at Amritsar and author of The Young Pilgrim, wrote these Indian stories. Nelson and Sons published them at London, Edinburgh, and New York. Her preface says she wrote them after arriving in India, for the use of native readers, in an Oriental style with scenes and customs familiar to them.

ALOE argues that minds should be trained in the first principles of morality and religion through amusing fictions, since the people are fond of stories. She means to amuse and instruct through amusement. The contents list The Radiant Robe, The Church Which Grew Out of One Brick, The Pugree with a Border of Gold, The Pink Chaddar, and The Story of Three Jewels. She hopes the tales may wake interest in England for the small church in India, struggling against surrounding evil influences yet gaining strength year by year.
58697-american-architecture-studies:
American Architecture: Studies gathers Montgomery Schuyler's essays on the building of his own time, issued by Harper and Brothers of New York in 1892 with many illustrations. Schuyler wrote as the dean of American architectural critics, and the dedication page gives only initials. The essays first took stock of a young national architecture finding its feet.

The Point of View and Concerning Queen Anne open the argument. The Vanderbilt Houses studies the great Fifth Avenue palaces plate by plate, from recessed balconies to oriels. The Brooklyn Bridge as a Monument weighs the bridge as a work of art, and An American Cathedral examines a proposed cathedral at Albany. Glimpses of Western Architecture close the book in Chicago, St Paul, and Minneapolis, where a new building world was rising.
58712-campfire-girls-lake-camp-or-search:
Campfire Girls' Lake Camp, or Searching for New Adventures, is a girls' series book by Irene Elliott Benson. Donohue of Chicago published it in 1918. It stands among companion tales of mountains, rivers, hikes, and outings. Twin Lakes and the Alleghanies hold other volumes of the set.

The contents open oddly, with a chapter about teeth and teddy bears. A special meeting is called, and the girls vote aye on some plan. A boy and a fortune enter the story soon after that vote. Honours and spies, a telegram on the road, and a double-room mystery follow. Ammunition and catapults stand among the final chapter titles. Camp life and a light mystery carry the girls through their summer.
58718-bobby-blake-in-the-frozen-north-or:
Frank A Warner wrote a boys' tale of Bobby Blake in the frozen North. Barse and Company held the rights in New York in 1923. Walter S Rogers drew the pictures for the book. Thirty chapters run from school ball fields to a blinding blizzard.

Bobby pitches with speed to burn on the Rockledge School campus at the start. Fred Martin, Sparrow Bangs, and Mouser Pryde cheer their star chum. Shanghaiing, gold lure, a secret token, and an Eskimo hut crowd the road north. Boys of the time got a fast tale of pluck, peril, and treasure.
58726-small-talk-at-wreyland-first-serie:
Small Talk at Wreyland, by Cecil Torr, was published at Cambridge in 1918, and reprinted the same year. Illustrations are listed: Lustleigh Cleave from the oval lawn as frontispiece, an inner parlour, the Wrey at Wreyland, and a pixey garden.

May Day, a portrait of the author grandfather John Torr, a lower parlour, and the hall house follow. All the pictures but the portrait are from photographs taken by the author. The text opens in Devon talk. Down here, Torr writes, when any of the older natives die, he hears people lamenting. So much local knowledge has died with them, they say. The book does that work itself: notes on a parish, its families, and customs. Readers get a Devon antiquary small talk, learned and gossipy at once.
58727-small-talk-at-wreyland-second-seri: Small Talk at Wreyland appears here in a second series, issued by the Cambridge University Press. Its opening pages praise the author's earlier Ancient Ships for independent research, learning without pedantry, and a sound knowledge of seamanship, quoted from reviews in several languages. The same antiquarian temper stands behind these shorter pieces, which take their title from Wreyland, the author's home ground. Readers get brief, learned essays in a conversational frame.
58728-small-talk-at-wreyland-third-serie:
Small Talk at Wreyland, third series, is a book of country essays by Cecil Torr, printed by the Cambridge University Press in 1923. Wreyland is Torr's home in Devon, in the Wrey valley. Earlier series had made the place known to readers who liked quiet talk about old houses, old customs, and the slow life of a rural parish.

A photograph of men laying new thatch forms the frontispiece. The hall house, the author's desk, and a view across the valley fill the picture list. The talk opens with a stir in the slumbering place. Five years before, a single aeroplane had passed over, the only one ever seen from there. Now a cowboy on a bucking horse has come galloping down the lane, firing his pistols. Torr's art is to set such wonders beside tithe barns and church ales, and to let a small place hold a long memory.
58732-windmills-and-wooden-shoes:
Windmills and Wooden Shoes is a children's reader by Maude M Grant, pictured by Bess Bruce Cleaveland. The Dallas edition was copyrighted in nineteen nineteen. A note at the front tells its purpose for teachers. The book gives a continuous story of Dutch children, Jan and Katrina and their little friends, it says.

Teachers are urged to make the children in the book live for the children in class. Pupils should picture the big windmill and the canals with drooping willows. A slow moving barge and a busy market place are named as scenes to imagine. Words and music of a little song stand early in the book. Its chorus sings of Holland's children in wooden shoes. They can run, jump, and walk as fast as they choose, it says.
58752-the-ivory-workers-of-the-middle-ag:
A M Cust wrote The Ivory Workers of the Middle Ages, issued at London in nineteen hundred and two. The book formed part of a series on the great craftsmen, edited by G C Williamson. Cust gave the book to her father.

Early chapters treat paired carved panels made for consuls and other lay uses. Latin and Byzantine ivories follow, with caskets and a later flowering of the art. A front picture shows a fifth-century Byzantine panel leaf held by the British Museum. Lists of pictures and books open the volume. Cust traces how carvers in ivory worked and what they made for church and court.
58773-les-machines:
Les Machines, a science fiction story by Joe Love, ran in Worlds of If in December 1954. It opens with a murder trial set in the near future. Isobel Smith d'Larte stands charged with the killing of her husband Arnaud in March 1998. Friends call her too quiet and meek for such a crime.

The head note gives the true puzzle of the tale. Some people act like machines, and some machines seem almost human. The court must find not just who struck the blow, but which figure was machine and which was human. The trial scenes build that doubt step by step.
58803-the-witch-maid-other-verses:
The Witch Maid and Other Verses is a book of poems by Dorothea Mackellar, issued at London and Toronto in 1914. Dent published the collection, with Dutton at New York. The title poem, The Witch Maid, opens the contents. The Colours of Light and From a Town Window follow in the list.

The Santa Maria, a medieval song title, and Night on the Plains come next. Settlers and then My Country stand among the early poems. My Country is the famed lyric of a sunburnt land that Australians know by heart. Swallows, Fire, High Places, and The Closed Door fill the middle run.
