Mackellar wrote Australia with love and a painter’s eye for light. This early book holds the seed of her fame.
58817-the-praying-skipper-and-other-stor:
Ralph Paine wrote The Praying Skipper and Other Stories, printed at New York in 1906. The seven tales had first run in Scribner's, the Century, and other magazines between 1903 and 1905. A front plate quotes the psalm: cast me not off in the time of old age.

The title tale opens with a complaint letter: the captain of the Suwannee holds prayer meetings aboard, drives passengers on deck, and turns the ship into a gospel ark. Young Valentine wants the old man pensioned ashore. Other tales give a Yale crew victory, a deserter corporal, the last pilot schooner, a jade teapot, Captain Arendt's choice, and a surfman's day off.
58846-kate-aylesford-a-story-of-the-refu:
Charles J Peterson wrote a novel of the refugees, entered for copyright in 1855 and published at Philadelphia, with a motto from Scott's Lay of the Last Minstrel about one's native land. Contents open with a night at sea. Kate Aylesford is introduced in chapter two, and a shipwreck follows in chapter three. Morning, a country tavern, and Major Gordon come next.

An abortive attempt and a rescue build the middle. Sweetwater and a horse named Arab appear in later chapter titles. The refugees of the title belong to the American Revolution's loyalist story world, a popular setting for Peterson. He wrote many historical romances for the Peterson publishing house in Philadelphia.
58855-the-little-room-and-other-stories:
The Little Room and Other Stories, by Madeline Yale Wynne, is a story set. Way and Williams issued it at Chicago in 1895 with author decorations. Harper Magazine first ran the title tale in August 1895, a note says. A newlywed pair ride by train, teasing over a family mystery between them.

The wife tells of a little room in her Vermont aunts old house. Something queer began long before her birth and kept happening there since. Roger, her husband, mixes up yellow calico and blue chintz in fun. A sequel story, a ghost tale, and tales of Granada follow in the set. The Voice and The Scarf close the slim, eerie volume.
58863-an-englishwoman-in-the-philippines:
Mrs Campbell Dauncey writes home in An Englishwoman in the Philippines, published by E P Dutton of New York in 1906 with pictures and a map. The book is built of letters, the first from Manila: the run from Hong Kong, Manila Bay, the Pasig River, and old Manila's Spanish air. The second sails to Iloilo past Cebu and Mactan, where Magellan fell.

Later letters settle into a Philippine house: servants, prices, furniture, insects, and the washerwoman. A fiesta, native dress in pina muslin, a Filipino theatre, and carabaos fill the social chapters. New-rule island life is caught firsthand.
58881-a-philosophical-essay-on-probabili:
Pierre Simon, Marquis de Laplace, wrote this philosophical essay on probabilities, and two West Virginia professors turned it into English. Truscott and Emory translated it from the sixth French edition, and John Wiley and Sons published it in New York in 1902, with Chapman and Hall in London. It was the first edition in English, in a run of a thousand.

The table of contents shows a two-part plan. Part one is the essay itself: an introduction, the nature of probability, the general principles of the calculus of probabilities, and a chapter on hope. Analytical methods close the part. Part two applies the calculus, starting with games of chance and the unknown inequalities that may favor some events over others. Laplace wrote for general readers as well as mathematicians. Students get the classic statement of what chance is and how reason can count it.
58884-the-osbornes:
The Osbornes is a social novel by E F Benson, published in New York in 1910 with copyright held by Doubleday, Page and Company. The Osbornes are new money in Park Lane, London. Their house at 92 Park Lane is the newest, whitest, and most pretentious on the street.

Chapter one opens after a ball that has lasted all night. Mrs Osborne has ordered every window in the house kept lit until morning. The blaze is meant to look joyful, and a little electric light costs nothing. Her major domo Thoresby, once the boot boy Willum, has risen with the family. Benson watches this rise with a cool, amused eye. The comedy turns on display: what money buys, and what it cannot. Benson wrote many such studies of fashionable life. Few begin with so bright a house.
58900-where-animals-talk-west-african-fo:
Robert Nassau's Where Animals Talk, West African folk lore tales, was published in Boston by Badger, at the Gorham Press. Nassau had written Fetichism in West Africa before it. A pronunciation key opens the book, teaching English mouths the Bantu sounds: g always hard, a as in father, and every syllable closed with a vowel.

The tales are sorted by tribe. Part first gives the Mpongwe stories: Do not Trust your Friend, Leopard's Hunting-Camp, two versions of Tests of Death, and Tasks Done for a Wife, with the Giant Goat. Proverb tales follow, why mosquitoes buzz, who is king of birds, and why chickens live with mankind. Part second gives the Benga tales: the origin of the elephant, Tortoise in a Race, why goats became domestic, the Magic Drum, and the Lies of Tortoise. Nassau collected the tales in his mission years on the Gaboon coast.
58963-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy, new series number 50, is the yearly journal of the Pennsylvania Prison Society. The society was founded on 8 May 1787, and the journal is dated November 1911. Its office stood on State House Row in Philadelphia. The front pages print the law on official visitors to prisons.

Under the act of 1829, visitors include the Governor, judges, sheriffs, and the society's own acting committee. An act of 1903 added the visiting committees of other groups formed to visit and teach prisoners. The journal records the society's long work of watching prisons and pushing for kinder, wiser discipline in Pennsylvania.
58982-vagabond-adventures:
Vagabond Adventures is Ralph Keeler's account of his own life up to the age of twenty two. Fields and Osgood printed it at Boston in 1870. Keeler warns that the story is nothing if not true, and that he uses the first person only because no other form would hold the adventures together.

Book one, Among Wharves and Cabins, starts at age eleven with family matters, a flight, a stormy time, and a term taken prisoner. Book two gives three years as a touring minstrel performer, from a first company to an adieu to the stage. Book three is a tour of Europe made for 181 dollars in currency, starting on a cattle train and fighting famine on the road.
59015-the-shadowy-third-and-other-storie:
Ellen Glasgow gathers seven short tales in The Shadowy Third and Other Stories, printed at Garden City, New York. The tales bear copyright dates from 1899 to 1923. A front drawing by Elenore Plaisted Abbott shows a mother who stoops to lift her child.

The title tale opens in December with a nurse in a flutter. She has been called to Roland Maradick, a great surgeon she has met just once. She longs to watch him at work for one hour. The other tales are Dare's Gift, The Past, Whispering Leaves, A Point in Morals, The Difference, and Jordan's End.
59040-a-child-s-guide-to-pictures:
A Child's Guide to Pictures, by Charles Caffin, author of How to Study Pictures, was published at New York in 1908 by the Baker and Taylor Company. The frontispiece is Homer Martin's View on the Seine, also called The Harp of the Winds. Eighteen chapters teach a young reader how to look at paintings.

Chapters open with the feeling for beauty, and art and her twin sister, nature. Nature is haphazard, Caffin holds, while art is arrangement. Contrast and geometric composition follow, then the action and movement of the figure, the classic landscape, and naturalistic composition. Form and color take the later chapters, ending with brush-work, drawing, and the subject's point of view. The pictures studied include works by Raphael, Turner, Millet, Vermeer, Leutze, Velasquez, and Whistler.
59050-poker-jim-gentleman-and-other-tale:
Frank Lydston gathers stories in Poker Jim, Gentleman, and Other Tales and Sketches, from the Monarch Book Company at Chicago with copyright in 1906. He dedicates the book to the most indulgent of his friends and the least charitable of his critics, promising it will give both joy. Twelve pieces run from the title tale to A Great City's Shame.

The title story opens in spring 1860, when the University of Pennsylvania granted the narrator, William Weymouth, his medical degree. Weymouth jokes that the faculty may have let him graduate as western bands beg audiences not to shoot, since they were doing their best. His parchment, he soon learned, was no open sesame to fame or prosperity. Contents add Tommy the Outcast, Johnny, a suicide's diary leaves, a Yosemite legend, and Chicquita.
59054-my-two-countries:
Lady Astor's My Two Countries was published by Doubleday, Page of Garden City, New York, in 1923. The first part is headed America, and she opens by saying the welcome she gets is not for herself. Since she entered the Mother of Parliaments, she says, she ceased to be a person and became a symbol.

Her road to the House of Commons, she insists, was no sudden break but a slow growth. Her husband started her, urging her from home to the House, though he is, she says, a most home-loving man and a born social reformer. For eleven years she did the personal side of his Plymouth work: she found the wrongs, and he tried to right them.
59057-original-plays-first-series:
W S Gilbert wrote Original Plays, first series, issued in New York by Scribner, Armstrong and Company in eighteen seventy six. The book holds the same plays as the first volume of the Chatto and Windus set in London. A note dated London, November eighteenth, eighteen seventy five, stands in front. Six plays fill the volume. Trial by Jury closes the set.

The Wicked World opens the book, then Pygmalion and Galatea, Charity, The Princess, and The Palace of Truth. The Story on which The Palace of Truth rests is probably as old as the Arabian Nights, Gilbert notes. The Princess is a respectful parody of Tennyson poem of that name. If a dramatist uses a mere outline of an old story, he may call his play original, Gilbert holds. Theatre lovers get Gilbert fairy comedy and satire before the Savoy operas fame.
59071-inter-ocean-hunting-tales:
Inter-Ocean Hunting Tales is a book of hunt tales by Edgar Randolph. It was put out at New York in nineteen hundred and eight by a house of the stream and wood craft. Plates stand thick in it. The front plate shows a herd of the great deer of the west. The list of parts is a roll of trips in the wild west and past it.

A thought tale of the great hills heads the run. The cost of a trip and a hunt in a north shire of the new land come next. The round up of wild cats in a south west state and duck sport in a bayou shire fill the first run. A trip at a pass of two seas, camp life near a famed range, and blood less sport stand past them.
59078-streets-and-other-verses:
Douglas Goldring wrote Streets and Other Verses, for Selwyn and Blount at London. Seltzer sold the book at New York in the same dress. Goldring gives it to lovers of London as a ragged offering. His note is dated November 1, 1920, in the front pages. Fifteen pieces are printed in book form for the first time, he says.

The rest come from four volumes issued in ten years. Those four are all out of print by the date of his note. The title poem opens on the great grey city that bred him. Supreme, mysterious, dirty and divine, he calls London there. It is made up all of contrast, light and gloom, he writes. Green hills and parks stand against deserts of humble brick. All his life he has spent up and down in this unending town. Goldring gives the town in taverns, terraces, and alleys.
59107-aristophanes:
Collins, a clergyman and school writer, made a study of the Greek comic poet Aristophanes for Blackwood in 1872. A note owns that many of the turned passages come from the version by Hookham Frere. The opening chapter argues that true national comedy comes late in a people's growth. It asks for a full mind, high culture, and a keen taste in its hearers.

Athens in her glory gave Aristophanes just such a crowd, Collins says. The chapters then walk through the plays in groups. The Knights stands alone, and the war plays, Acharnians, Peace, and Lysistrata, stand together. The Clouds, The Wasps, The Birds, and The Frogs each take a chapter. The women's plays and Plutus close the book. Collins warns that this comedy is not like the modern stage kind. It is closer to burlesque, with broad fun and sharp satire joined.
59130-turkish-memories:
Sidney Whitman wrote Turkish Memories, from Scribner at New York and Heinemann at London in 1914. A portrait of Ghazi Osman Pacha fronts the book. It is inscribed to the memory of Ahmed Midhat Effendi, late vice-president of the Imperial Ottoman Board of Public Health. Whitman had written German Memories before this work. These pages grew from several long visits to Constantinople, Macedonia, and Asiatic Turkey.

The visits span twelve years, from 1896 to 1908, and some were made in rare conditions. Whitman holds that some of his experiences were of lasting public weight. Few travelers, he says, have had such access to an autocrat and his court. The book gives talks, scenes, and judgments from inside the late Ottoman world. Readers get a witness account of Turkey in the last years before the great war.
59148-the-cyber-and-justice-holmes:
Frank Riley placed his tale The Cyber and Justice Holmes in Worlds of If Science Fiction for March 1955. Old Judge Walhfred Anderson dreads his fate in the opening lines. A district attorney has pledged to replace human judges with cyber units across the county. Twice the prosecutions at half the cost is the campaign promise.

Anderson, at eighty-six, has researched law books for two hours before court. He winks each morning at his framed etching of Justice Holmes in a grey fedora, a ritual of fifty years. A surprise case waits, sprung by the smiling prosecutor that day. Riley pits habit, mercy, and human flaw against machine decisions. Courtroom science fiction asks what justice loses when error leaves.
59158-beggars-on-horseback-a-riding-tour:
Beggars on Horseback is a comic travel book by Martin Ross and E Œ Somerville, published by Blackwood in 1895. Its sub-title calls it a riding tour in North Wales. The pair had writ The Real Charlotte and other Irish tales. Somerville drew the many illustrations herself. The title page shows the two as beggars of a sort: ladies on tour with more pride than funds. The first chapter opens at an ironmonger's shop in a Welsh town, with talk of a horse once ridden by a kettle-drum player.

The plates list the tour's small disasters and joys. Packing the hold-alls, the first flies, and a fat ostler boy all get their cuts. Rain drives the riders to shelter more than once. Startled pony faces peer round a pile of boulders. A visitors' book closes the tour.
59181-tetherstones:
Ethel Dell wrote a tale printed at Toronto in 1923, and gave it to her friend Violet, who always stands by. A verse at the front sings of a lonely stone ring on a hill. Mist wreaths drift round the rough stones where Druids once lit their altar fire. Blue hare bells bloom at the grim stone's foot.

Contents fall in two parts. The first names a machine, a breakdown, a trade offer, and a blamer. The capture, a man named Roger, and a lions' den follow. The second part brings strangers, a beast, rebels, and a path through the woods. Dell's tales of strong men and proud women had a wide public in her day.
59197-angels-shoes-and-other-stories:
Pickthall wrote the short tales gathered in Angels' Shoes and Other Stories, printed in London by Hodder and Stoughton. The contents list holds twenty four stories in all. Names on that list range from The Sleeping Faun and Luck to The Lost Spring, The Distant Drums, and The Men Who Climbed.

The title tale opens where a great jungle river meets the sea. The small trader ship Dorotea Dixon waits for high water on the bar at dawn. A dugout drifts in with the tide, bearing a sick man named Brennan and a native girl. The crew lift them aboard in a hush of still light and glass clear air. The writing is rich in scene and mood, and the tales move between far ports and home ground.
59210-comediettas-and-farces:
Comediettas and Farces is a volume of short plays by John Maddison Morton, published in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1886. Morton tells the reader frankly that only two of the pieces are wholly original. The rest he adapted from French material, with great changes of plot and wholly new dialogue.

The famous Box and Cox leads the collection. First Come, First Served, Pepperpot's Little Pets, and After a Storm Comes a Calm follow. Express and Taken from the French complete the bill, with Declined With Thanks. Morton wrote with private performance in mind and addresses amateurs directly. These one-act farces were the stock of Victorian drawing-room theatre. Their quick mistaken identities and lodgings-house tricks kept generations of amateur actors busy.
59254-the-inimitable-jeeves:
The Inimitable Jeeves is a comic story collection by P G Wodehouse. Herbert Jenkins published it in London in 1923. The publisher's blurb explains the premise. When Bertie Wooster or his friends land in the soup, all turn to Jeeves. Jeeves understands human nature, especially gilded youth. His only failure, to Bertie's eyes, is purism in spats, socks, and ties.

Eighteen chapters recount Jeeves's remarkable achievements. Jeeves exerts the old cerebellum in the first. No wedding bells for Bingo opens the Bingo Little thread. Aunt Agatha speaks her mind, and pearls mean tears. Claude and Eustace, Bertie's twin cousins, are introduced and delayed in exiting. Sir Roderick comes to lunch in the most famous chapter. The great sermon handicap and the purity of the turf bring in betting. Jeeves floats in with tea exactly two minutes after Bertie wakes, never a drop spilled.
59299-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Works of Herbert Allen Giles is a guide list by David Widger. Giles wrote and turned a shelf of books on China in his long life. He held a chair of Chinese at Cambridge and served as consul in China. The index was made for a free text library on the web.

Heads list each book by Giles that the library holds in full text. Tables of parts for each work are set out in plain order in the list. Tales from a Chinese den, lore of faiths, and a past of Chinese verse stand in line. China and its Manchu chiefs earn their own head in the set. The guide serves as a map to a great China scholars whole shelf.
59311-gas-and-petroleum-engines:
Henry de Graffigny wrote on gas and petroleum engines in French, here in English form. A G Elliott edited the work for Whittaker and Company in London in 1898. Fifty-two figures show motors, sections, and gas plants throughout. The book stands in the Electro-Mechanical Series of handbooks.

Chapters run from the history of the gas engine to care of engines in use. Otto, Benz, Crossley, and Hornsby-Akroyd motors each get clear study. Gas making plants and engines for poor gases fill the later parts. The first gas engine, from 1678, used blasting powder, the history notes.
59319-adventures-of-martin-hewitt-third-:
Adventures of Martin Hewitt, Third Series, was written by Arthur Morrison. Ward, Lock published the tales in London in 1896. Crowther drew the illustrations. Six cases make the volume. Contents name a dead skipper and an elopement. A late Mr Rewse and a Mrs Seton's child follow. The Ward Lane Tabernacle closes the list. Brett, the narrator, tells each case. The first, the Flitterbat Lancers, is the one where he had a stake himself. It cost him, he owns, no more than a smashed pane of glass. He sat late over a volume of essays on social economy. Three evenings of attack had failed against its polysyllables.

On the fourth, a crash and jingle woke him from his doze. Hewitt's rule guides the book: nothing, however romantic, has not happened at some time in London.
59394-the-margenes:
The Margenes is a science fiction tale by Miriam Allen de Ford, printed in Worlds of If in February 1956. It opens with a bit of shore lore: the grunion, a small striped fish that rides the high tide onto California beaches to lay its eggs in the sand. Crowds once came by night with baskets and torches to catch them by hand.

On an April night in 1960, two students from Los Angeles, Marge Hickin and Gene Towanda, find something else riding in with the fish. The finds are tiny, live, straw coloured rings, harmless to the touch. The tale's own note warns that these small rings will be blamed for riots, revolt, and an atomic war.
59428-the-florentine-dagger-a-novel-for-:
Ben Hecht wrote a mystery novel copyrighted in 1923, subtitled a novel for amateur detectives, and dedicated to Josephine Ditrichstein, who promised to read his next book if it was a mystery. Wallace Smith drew five illustrations and the jacket. Smith, the text boasts, chose to illustrate the spirit rather than the letter. The result is a set of striking black and white designs.

Hecht was then a Chicago journalist becoming a novelist. Boni and Liveright published the book at New York. The amateur detective framing invites readers to solve alongside the story. Hecht's later fame as a screenwriter began in this decade of fiction and newspaper work.
59441-nacha-regules:
Manuel Galvez wrote a novel in Spanish, turned into English by Leo Ongley in an approved rendering printed at New York in 1922. Twenty four chapters and a short tail piece make up the book, none of them named. Chapter one opens on an August night in Buenos Aires in a year of great national fetes.

Fetes for the nations hundredth year had run since May, drawing crowds from each corner of the land and from Europe. Streets and houses seemed to move with the slow mass on the main roads, the tale says. At night, theatres, picture houses, and dance halls with tango bands took in the throngs.
59462-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Henry James. Roderick Hudson heads the contents, then The American, Confidence, The Europeans, and Pandora. The Turn of the Screw, The Aspern Papers, The Ambassadors, and The Portrait of a Lady in two volumes follow. The Golden Bowl, Italian Hours, What Maisie Knew, and The Awkward Age stand in the long list.

The Bostonians in two volumes, The Tragic Muse, The Sacred Fount, and The Spoils of Poynton are indexed too. James's letters in two volumes, Notes of a Son and Brother, Partial Portraits, and English Hours close the shelf. Some files lack linked tables of contents, the index warns, and those are listed apart. Readers hunting one tale in a vast free library get a map here.
59538-portraits-of-the-nineties:
Portraits of the Nineties is a book of biographical sketches by Raymond, published in London by Fisher Unwin in 1921. It joins a series that portrayed each decade of the Victorian age in turn: the sixties by Justin McCarthy, the seventies by Russell, and the eighties by Horace Hutchinson. A portrait of Gladstone forms the frontispiece. Four impressions were called for within five months.

The contents open with the nineties themselves, then turn to the men who filled them. The Earl of Rosebery and Cecil Rhodes come first. Gladstone and George Meredith follow, with Lord Salisbury and Lord Kitchener. The Duke of Devonshire, Archbishop Temple, and Lord Randolph Churchill stand in the middle. Herbert Spencer and Joseph Chamberlain belong to the later chapters. Raymond writes the decade through its faces: statesmen above all, in the last age before the wars changed everything.
59548-tappan-s-burro-and-other-stories:
Zane Grey's Tappan's Burro and Other Stories appeared in 1923. Publisher pages in front list his shelf of westerns. Riders of the Purple Sage, The Lone Star Ranger, Desert Gold, and The Border Legion stand among them. Tales of Lonely Trails and Tales of Fishes sit beside the novels.

The title story centres on a burro, the pack animal of the desert country Grey made famous. His short fiction works the same ground as the novels: lonely trails, desert water, and men and animals matched against empty land. Readers get Grey in short form, where a burro can carry a whole tale, from the most popular western writer of his day.
59554-house-flies:
House Flies is a United States government bulletin by Howard, chief of the Bureau of Entomology. The Department of Agriculture issued the pamphlet at Washington in July 1911. It is Farmers' Bulletin 459, sent free on request. Plates show the true house fly and its kin in fine detail.

Howard calls the common house fly the typhoid fly for its habits. The bulletin traces the fly's life from egg to winged adult. A chapter shows how flies carry disease germs on feet and mouth. Remedies and preventives take the longest share. Stable flies, blue bottles, and green bottles are told apart from the true pest. Towns and cities get advice on joint action. The pamphlet was part of a national war on the fly.
5956-gallegher-and-other-stories:
Richard Harding Davis gathers newspaper and city tales, headed by the story of Gallegher, an office boy. The newsroom has seen many boys come and go, sleepy ones, lazy ones, and smart ones who grew too familiar too fast. Gallegher stands apart from that composite of small boys in blue coats and nickel badges.

Alongside the title tale come Van Bibber stories, a walk up the avenue, and sketches of a disreputable friend and a cynical Miss Catherwaight. Davis writes with a reporter's eye for offices, streets, and sharp talk. The collection favors quick scenes and vivid figures over long plots.
59576-shasta-of-the-wolves:
Olaf Baker wrote Shasta of the Wolves, copyrighted in 1919 by Dodd, Mead, shown here in a 1952 printing. Charles Livingston Bull drew the pictures for the tale. Eighteen chapters trace a wolf child's path from den to kindred. Chapter one, The Wolf-Child, follows the old she wolf Nitka at dusk.

Nitka pads soundlessly through trees, hunting food for hungry, mischievous pups at home. Her nose reads the warm scent of flesh on the heavy summer air. Chapters promise a bear fight, a wise one named Gomposh, and the wolf chorus sung. Shasta joins the pack, sees his redskin kindred, and leaves his wolf kin at last. A boy raised by wolves anchors a rich northern animal tale.
59634-coronation-rites:
Reginald Maxwell Woolley wrote this handbook on coronation rites, printed at Cambridge in 1915. Woolley was rector and vicar of Minting and examining chaplain to the Bishop of Lincoln. The book sits in the Cambridge Handbooks of Liturgical Study. A picture shows the coronation of Henry the First of England.

The editors say the series aims to help students who are starting the study of liturgies. Each volume gives the history and the reasons of a rite, with lists of larger books for deeper study. Chapter One treats early ideas of kingship and the rites tied to a king's accession. Chapter Two turns to the crowning of a Roman emperor in pagan times, and the origin of the Christian rite.
59656-motion-pictures-1950-1959-catalog-:
The Copyright Office of the Library of Congress issued a cumulative catalog of copyright entries for motion pictures, covering 1950 to 1959. It was printed in 1960. The volume sold for eleven dollars and twenty five cents. A table of contents places the main listing first, then an index, then a series list. Registrations run from January 1, 1950 to December 31, 1959.

Class L, motion picture photoplays, accounts for fifteen thousand five hundred twelve registrations. Class M, motion pictures other than photoplays, adds eleven thousand seven hundred ninety eight. The total tops twenty seven thousand entries. Film historians use such catalogs to date and identify studio output, shorts, and sponsored films.
59677-the-costume-of-china-picturesque-r:
William Alexander made the drawings for a plate book on Chinese dress and manners, printed at London in 1814. Fifty coloured engravings show the people of China at work and at rest. Short texts explain each plate.

The plates range from Kien Lung, the emperor, to fishermen, porters, barbers, and boat girls. Readers see a mandarin in court dress and in common dress, a lantern seller, and a bookseller. There are also scenes of mourning, stage players, and two forms of punishment, the cangue and the arrow. Alexander drew from his own time in China. Each plate faces its own short account, so the book reads as a walk through daily life.
59678-woman-s-work-in-municipalities:
Mary Ritter Beard wrote this survey of women's work in city government, published by Appleton in 1915. It belongs to the National Municipal League Series. Beard was joint author of American Citizenship, and she writes here for readers who want to see what women were already doing in public life.

Eleven chapters map the field. They cover schools, public health, vice, play, and the drawing in of new races to city life. Housing, social service, prisons, public safety, and civic improvement follow, and the book ends on government itself. The first chapter shows women teaching most of the nation's high school pupils. Reform readers of 1915 got a plain record of work done and work open.
59685-original-plays-second-series:
Gilbert's Original Plays, second series, was published in London in 1899 by Chatto & Windus, uniform with the first series at half a crown a volume. Nine plays fill the volume. The contents list nine pieces: Broken Hearts, Engaged, Sweethearts, Dan'l Druce, Gretchen, Tom Cobb, The Sorcerer, HMS Pinafore, and The Pirates of Penzance.

The first series, named on the facing page, held The Wicked World, Pygmalion and Galatea, Charity, The Princess, The Palace of Truth, and Trial by Jury. The second series opens with Broken Hearts, billed as an entirely original fairy play in three acts, first produced at the Royal Court Theatre under the management of Mr Hare. The two famous operas close the volume, Pinafore as the lass that loved a sailor, and the Pirates as the slave of duty.
59699-history-of-the-u-s-s-leviathan-cru:
History of the U S S Leviathan was compiled from the ship's log and data gathered by a history committee on board. The Cruiser and Transport Forces of the Atlantic Fleet are its scope. A poem by Adele M Marshall opens the book, hailing the ship as a noble monarch of the seas. It asks that the ship bring sons safe across the waves.

The foreword calls the Leviathan's war career a brilliant chapter in sea history. Customs men seized her on April 6, 1917, as the Stars and Stripes replaced the German flag. The Shipping Board held her for near three months without her leaving dock. On July 25, 1917 the Navy took her for transport duty. Vice-Admiral Albert Gleaves led the force she joined.
59732-hernando-cortes:
Hernando Cortes is a life story for young people by Campe, Englished by Upton. McClurg of Chicago issued it in nineteen eleven with six illustrations. George Upton rendered the German text of Joachim Heinrich Campe here. A plate shows Cortes and Montezuma face to face in Mexico days.

The translator calls the conquest a tale of courage, resolve, and hideous cruelty. A little people were overcome and enslaved by a superior nation, he says. Lust for gold drove Spain to stratagem, cunning, and barbarous cruelty there. Early Mexican emperors were tyrants, yet their cruelty pales beside Spain acts. Cortes, Montezuma, and Guatemozin are the three chief figures of the drama.
59738-windmills-and-wooden-shoes:
Windmills and Wooden Shoes is a travel book on Holland by Blair Jaekel, published in New York in nineteen twelve. Jaekel had earlier written a book on the lands of the Turk. Fifteen chapters carry the reader across the whole of the Dutch kingdom. The route starts with an opening survey, then visits the island of Walcheren.

From Middelburg the tour goes to Rotterdam, Delft, and The Hague. Leyden, Haarlem, and Amsterdam, the city of ninety islands, follow in turn. Trips out from Amsterdam take in Volendam and its old fishing fleet. Cheese day at Alkmaar and the dike at the Helder get their own scenes. Friesland, Gelderland, and Utrecht close the tour of the provinces. Many photographs show dikes, canals, churches, and Dutch dress.
59757-james-lusk-letters-memories:
James Lusk: Letters and Memories is a memorial volume for a young officer of the Great War. Blackwell printed it at Oxford in 1916. James Lusk was a Cambridge graduate and a captain in the Cameronians. He held the cross of the Legion of Honour from France.

The little book was written first for those who had known him. It was made also for his sister's and brother's children, the preface says. They might ask for it one day, never knowing their loss in his passing. His life is described as a swift and shining track to the goal. Most of the letters printed here were written to his mother. The contents follow him from Falkirk in August 1914 to France. The last weeks, in November and December 1915, close the record.
59763-the-tariff-in-our-times:
Ida Tarbell published The Tariff in Our Times with Macmillan in 1911, gathering articles written over the previous five years. Tarbell had written the life of Lincoln and the history of the Standard Oil Company, which made her the most feared investigator in America. Here she turns the same patience on the tariff.

The tariff was the permanent question of American politics, and 1911 was a year of revision. Payne-Aldrich had satisfied nobody, the Democrats had taken the House, and reciprocity with Canada was collapsing. Tarbell explains schedules the way she explained rebates: by following the money through the machinery. Her premise is that the tariff is not an abstraction but a set of prices, paid at counters by people who never see the schedule that set them. The muckraker's method applied to customs law is the book.
59774-30-strange-stories:
Wells wrote Thirty Strange Stories, from Harper at New York and London in 1898. Rights were held in 1897 by Edward Arnold. Wells had won fame with The Invisible Man and The War of the Worlds. The first tale, The Strange Orchid, opens on the buying of orchids at sale. Such buying, Wells says, has a speculative flavor to it. The buyer faces a brown, shrivelled lump and must trust judgment, the auctioneer, or luck.

More tales treat a stolen bacillus and a red room. Aepyornis Island, the Plattner story, and the argonauts of the air mix science and wonder. Davidson's eyes, a cone, a purple fungus, and the lord of the dynamos fill the late set. The sea raiders and a treasure in the forest close the book. Wells gives thirty short shocks and marvels in one rich store.
59792-hume-s-political-discourses:
Hume Political Discourses is a set of essays by David Hume, here with an opening essay by William Bell Robertson. Robertson had written on the foundations of political economy and on the slavery of labour. The essays themselves are the classic core of Hume thought on trade and money.

Of Commerce comes first, then Of Refinement in the Arts. Of Money, Of Interest, and Of the Balance of Trade follow. Later essays treat the jealousy of trade, the balance of power, taxes, and public credit. Two long pieces close the main set: one on the populousness of ancient nations, and one on the original contract. Of Passive Obedience follows. Readers get Hume clear, cool essays on how trade, luxury, and credit work, in a handy one volume form.
59815-french-and-german-socialism-in-mod:
Richard T Ely wrote French and German Socialism in Modern Times, issued by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in nineteen hundred, from a work entered in eighteen eighty three. Ely taught political economy at the University of Wisconsin. He thanked Andrew D White of Cornell in a prefatory note. The book grew from lectures at Johns Hopkins and Cornell universities, largely rewritten.

Ely says his aim is a perfectly fair, impartial picture of modern communism and socialism in their two strongholds, France and Germany. A certain freedom of style from the lecture hall remains, he notes. He hopes the book stays neither less interesting nor less instructive for it. Students of politics get an early American scholar calm survey of schools, parties, and claims. The tone is measured, not partisan heat.
59850-hunting-reminiscences:
Alfred Pease wrote Hunting Reminiscences, printed in London in 1898 in a de luxe edition of two hundred copies only. Pease, a member of Parliament, had written on the Cleveland hounds and on horse-breeding for farmers. A coloured sketch by Frank Lockwood, Frozen Out, fronts the volume. Contents open with the Cambridge drag and the House of Commons steeplechases.

Hare-hunting takes the fourth chapter, fox-hunting the fifth and sixth, and cub-hunting the seventh. The greatest run I ever saw and badger-hunting close the book, with an index. The picture list shows Pease on Nora Creina, winner of the House of Commons point-to-point race of 1891. A drawing of that race and a painting of Queen Mab stand among the plates. Sketches by Lockwood and Newton appear as well, and a photograph of the Cleveland fox-hounds at exercise.
59865-the-elephant-man-and-other-reminis:
The Elephant Man and Other Reminiscences is a memoir book by Sir Frederick Treves. Treves served as serjeant-surgeon to the King in his high career post. Cassell brought the book out in London in the year 1923. Two printings ran in February of that year alone for the work. Twelve pieces run from the title sketch to a question of hats.

The old receiving room, a twenty-krone piece, and a cure for nerves follow. Two women, a sea lover, and a case of heart failure fill the middle. A restless night and a deathbed piece stand among the later sketches. The title piece opens in the Mile End Road by the London Hospital. A vacant greengrocer's shop showed the Elephant Man for twopence a head. Canvas hid the shop front with the bill painted large upon it. Treves tells what he found behind that sheet of canvas there.
59880-bird-biographies:
Alice Ball wrote this bird guide, Bird Biographies, printed at New York in 1923. It is a guide-book for beginners, and an introduction to one hundred and fifty common land birds of the eastern United States. Ball also wrote A Year with the Birds. Horsfall, a painter of backgrounds for a great museum's bird groups, made the pictures, fifty-six of them in colour.

Pages of thanks at the front show the book's debts. Passages are quoted, by leave, from Burroughs, Thoreau, Longfellow, and a roll of bird writers, and from Chapman's handbook of eastern birds. Colour plates came from an Audubon society's teaching leaflets. A curator at the museum in New York helped, and the book is dedicated to a friend whose aid, faith, and criticism, Ball says, never tired.
59892-changeling-and-other-stories:
Changeling and Other Stories is a book of short tales by Donn Byrne. It was put out at New York and London in nineteen twenty three. His past books are named on the title leaf. The first part of the book is not a tale but a set of sworn leaves. Each tale of the book is sworn to a friend of the hand. That odd start has a tale of its own.

You are to bring out a book of your tales, said the Old Bard. I think I am, sir, said the hand. I am sorry for it, said the Old Bard. It will not have a friend in the world, he said. When it comes to the print of books, the hand goes on, men are all of a sad mind.
59933-the-struggle-for-imperial-unity-re:
The Struggle for Imperial Unity, by Colonel George T. Denison, came out in 1909. Denison led the British Empire League in Canada and wrote on cavalry. His memoir traces Canada from before Confederation to 1906 in chapters. The Red River Rebellion and its expedition get early full treatment here.

Canada First, Hudson Bay lands, and national sentiment fill the next stretch. Chapters follow the Imperial Federation League at work in Canada and England. Fights over commercial union and the great election of 1891 stand out. Empire Day, the South African War, and missions to England close the tale. Speeches and a lecture on national spirit sit in the appendix.
59946-shapes-of-greek-vases:
Shapes of Greek Vases is a hall book of the great art hall in New York. It came out in the year 1922 from that hall's own press. The Greeks had a gift for fine form, the book holds at the start. That gift shows in no ware more than in their clay pots.

The pots were made for home use and for the rites of the gods. Each was shaped with skill to serve its own end in the best way. The book shows the chief shapes of the potters of Athens town. Those shapes are of the two great ages of that town's craft. Height to width and part to whole are set with care in each. Neck, lip, foot, and grips are planned for the hand that lifts. Most of the pots shown stand in that hall's own stock.
59956-gods-and-heroes:
George Upton translated and adapted 'Gods and Heroes' from the German of Ferdinand Schmidt and Carl Friedrich Becker. McClurg published it at Chicago in 1912 in the Life Stories for Young People series. A frontispiece shows Diana. In his preface Upton quotes a quaint 1810 history of the heathen gods by William Sheldon. Sheldon argued that all nations have believed in one almighty maker, alongside lesser gods as agents between God and man.

Upton adds that Greek myths hold rare beauty and moral lessons in the fates of lesser gods who offended the higher ones. The contents begin with Prometheus, then Deucalion and Pyrrha, Hermes, Phaethon, Orpheus, and Atalanta. Several of the greatest gods are left out on purpose, since they star in companion volumes on Achilles, Ulysses, and Hercules.
59963-halfway-house-a-comedy-of-degrees:
Maurice Hewlett writes a novel of love and rank in a Scribner volume dated June 1908, priced at one dollar and fifty cents. Ads at the front list his past books, among them The Forest Lovers and The Queen's Quair at the same price. Two books of chapters carry the tale from Germain's first notice to a wider world.

Book one heads name Duplessis, Miss Middleham, and a wedding day and night that close the first half. Book two moves to Southover, then to London nights, polls, and talks on the moral law. Heads hint at gypsy lore, a bird-catcher, and a dead hand that still grips the living. Hewlett calls the whole a comedy of degrees, which points to rank as the spring of both fun and pain.
60040-notes-on-novelists-with-some-other:
Henry James wrote Notes on Novelists, with some other notes, printed in New York in 1914. Contents open with Robert Louis Stevenson. Zola and Flaubert follow. Balzac takes two pieces, of 1902 and 1913. George Sand takes three, of 1897, 1899, and 1914. D'Annunzio, Serao, and the new novel of 1914 come in turn.

Dumas the younger, the novel in The Ring and the Book, and an American art scholar, Charles Eliot Norton, fill the later heads. London notes of 1897 close the book. The Stevenson piece opens on the man's happy lot. He had won a body of readers moved by feelings we keep for those we love in person. To read him, James holds, came to mean much the same as to meet him. He wrote himself outright into his prose, and still more into his happiest verse.
6005-celibates:
George Moore's Celibates returns in a 1915 edition with an introduction by Temple Scott, twenty years after its first publication. Scott finds the Moore of 1895 and the Moore of 1915 one and the same. He sees a novelist more concerned with how the world appears to him than with how it appears to casual observers.

Moore, Scott insists, was never a reporter or a philosopher, but always an artist expressing himself through facts and figures that stirred his imagination. That self-expression is not mere private sensation, but a shaping vision. The novel studies lives held apart from union, with suffering and privilege intertwined.
60068-an-ethical-philosophy-of-life-pres:
An Ethical Philosophy of Life, by Felix Adler, sets out the author's system of conduct in main outline. Appleton published it in New York and London, with rights dated nineteen eighteen. Four books divide the work, from the author's own story to his last outlook. An appendix treats spiritual self discipline and the use of force for freedom.

Book one traces Adler's path through the Hebrew religion, Emerson, and Jesus. Book two weighs Kant and builds an ideal of the whole and of worth. Book three faces the three shadows of sickness, sorrow, and sin in turn. Its supreme rule bids men act so as to call out the best in others. Book four applies the scheme to family, callings, the state, and mankind. Religious fellowship crowns the whole as the last social form.
60070-texas-gemstones:
Elbert King wrote Texas Gemstones, Report of Investigations number 42 of the Bureau of Economic Geology at the University of Texas at Austin, dated February 1961. John Lonsdale directed the bureau. The report saw five printings, the last in August 1991. Contents open with an introduction, then the properties of gemstones and crystals. The cutting and polishing of gemstones follows, under cabochon, faceted, and tumbled gems.

A long list of Texas gemstones then runs in letter order. Amber, beryl, celestite, diamond, fluorite, and fossil wood stand among the first. Garnet, jet, labradorite, obsidian, opal, and pearl follow. Quartz takes the fullest treatment, in its clear and cloudy kinds: amethyst, citrine, rock crystal, rose quartz, agate, and jasper. Topaz, tourmaline, and turquoise close the list. A glossary, chosen readings, and an index end the report. Figures show crystal forms and the steps of cutting a stone.
60084-life-in-southern-prisons-from-the-:
Life in Southern Prisons prints the diary of Corporal Charles Smedley, of Company G, 90th Regiment, Pennsylvania Volunteers. The Fulton Aid Society published it in 1865, in an edition of 400 copies voted that April. Smedley did not live to see it printed.

His title page carries the arc. The diary begins a few days before the Battle of the Wilderness, where Smedley was taken prisoner on May 5, 1864. A short account of the march to Gettysburg goes with it, and a sketch of the author. His own words stand at the front, from a letter home in 1862: if it is never my lot to return, remember me only as one who went to do his duty. The diary itself is the Andersonville record. Historians get a private soldier's prison book, printed by his neighbours as a memorial.
60099-cecilia-of-the-pink-roses:
Cecilia of the Pink Roses is a novel by Katharine Haviland Taylor, issued by Grosset and Dunlap from the Doran edition of 1917, with illustrations by May Wilson Preston. Taylor dedicates it to her mother, the source of her inner pink roses. The chapter titles trace a poor child's rise: Where Is Gawd, The Vision of a Promised Land, and The First Step into Canaan come first.

The opening scene is the Madden flat, hot with the smell of frying potatoes. Flies buzz and land on a small boy of four, who screams. His sister, a girl of seven, steps from the stove and shoos them away: aw now, Johnny, and Johnny quiets.
60126-pens-and-types:
Benjamin Drew wrote a book of hints and helps for those who write, print, read, teach, or learn, printed at Boston in 1889. A portion to seven, and also to eight, the motto runs. Drew gives the book to the memory of George Washington Hosmer, his early friend and instructor. The first edition was made for persons connected with the press, the publishers say.

It had a wide circulation among persons of all professions, and became a reference book in some notable schools. A lady teacher in a neighboring city found it of the greatest benefit in her teaching and in her writing for the press, they quote. Punctuation, capitals, proof marks, and clear style fill the lessons. Drew kept his own person out of sight behind the editorial we, the publishers note. Working writers get a bench manual here.
60136-the-sisters-rondoli-and-other-stor:
Guy de Maupassant wrote short tales in French, gathered here in an English issue from New York in 1923. Fourteen tales fill the book, from The Sisters Rondoli and My Landlady to The Umbrella and The Legacy. Other titles name a small cask, a cursed loaf, and a wise man.

The first tale opens with Pierre Jouvent telling friends he does not know Italy, though he tried twice to go. Each try stopped at the border, yet each gave him warm views of Italian ways. In June 1874 he set his heart on Venice, Florence, Rome, and Naples, then tells how train and hotel woes put him off travel.
60138-edith-and-her-ayah-and-other-stori:
A L O E, the pen name of Charlotte Maria Tucker, collects fifteen moral tales for children in Edith and Her Ayah and Other Stories. T Nelson and Sons published the volume in 1872. The shorter pieces include The Butterfly, The Penitent, The Vase and the Dart, The Jewel, The Storm and A Story of the Crimea. Each tale carries a scriptural motto and a plain lesson.

The title story opens in a bungalow in India, where little Edith asks her mother why Motee Ayah never comes to prayers. Mrs Tuller promises to teach the nurse, and her repeated talks with Motee meet only polite, uncomprehending agreement.
60154-the-red-cross-girls-in-the-british:
Margaret Vandercook sends girls to war in The Red Cross Girls in the British Trenches, printed at Philadelphia with copyright in 1916. The Winston Company made the book, with plates. Vandercook had writ the Ranch Girls and the Camp Fire Girls runs. A plate warns that a heroine stands in equal peril.

Twenty two chapters run from a social failure to a recognition. A farewell and a trial of fire start the girls out. Behind the firing lines, first aid, and the ambulance corps mark the war work. A girl's deed stands near the peak of the run. Chapter one closes a dance. Mildred Thornton climbs the long stairs in white lace and tulle, with no look of a conquering princess, and less of a belle.
60155-pen-pictures-of-british-battles:
Richard Wilson edits short takes on great fights from famed pens in an Eyre and Spottiswoode volume from London dated 1917. Eleven pieces run from the Falkland Islands to warfare under water at the close. Each piece names its battle and its writer on the contents page for quick choice.

Sir Arthur Conan Doyle writes the Marne, John Buchan writes the second battle of Ypres, and John Masefield writes the landing at V Beach. Philip Gibbs covers the Somme and Arras, while Rudyard Kipling closes the set on undersea war. An editor's note calls war writers the scene painters of history in Sir Walter Besant's phrase. No pen can show more than a corner of the vast drama, the note grants with care.
60168-mrs-ames:
Benson, the author of Dodo, published Mrs Ames in the years when his society comedies were the sharpest in England, and the opening wastes no time. The breakfast tongue at the Althams' table is the wrong color. It is cold mutton rather than the pleasant reddish hue a glass receptacle with an eminent label had promised.

Mr Altham escapes at a quarter past twelve to stroll to the local club in Queensgate Street. The novel settles into its true subject: provincial and London society observed at the level of its luncheons, its economies, and its small treacheries. Benson wrote with an ear for the sentence that wounds politely. Mrs Ames stands in the line of his waspish comedies of manners, where the tongue, in every sense, gives the trouble away.
60186-polite-conversation-in-three-dialo:
Jonathan Swift mocks empty drawing-room talk in three staged talks, here in a Chiswick Press edition dated MDCCCXCII. George Saintsbury writes the opening essay and notes, and the run is capped at five hundred copies. Copy number 438 is on handmade paper, with fifty more on Japanese vellum.

Saintsbury notes that Swift gave the work to a protégée, Mrs Barber, about 1736 and took no pay for it. The first edition came out in 1738 from Motte and Bathurst, late in Swift's life. Yet the piece grew from an essay on talk first planned in 1708 to 1710, he argues. Swift hides behind the name Simon Wagstaff on the title page. Three talks then pile stock phrases one on one until polite talk stands bare as pure form with no thought.
60189-from-the-heart-of-israel-jewish-ta:
Bernard Drachman, a rabbi turned storyteller, gathers Jewish tales and types in a book issued by James Pott and Company at New York in 1905. A Warshawsky drew the pictures. A glossary of Hebrew terms closes the volume.

His apology opens with a pointed question: is Saul also among the prophets? Some strict readers, he knows, scorn tales beside the Torah. The first long piece builds a village, the Village Kehillah, at Nordheim. Schnorrers, gendarmes, and Reb Shemayah people it. Later tales give the little horseradish woman, a general, and a scissors-grinder. The Shlemihl gets his own story. A rabbi's game of cards closes the set. Drachman wrote for American readers who wanted the old-world Jewish town from inside.
60192-spices-their-histories:
A trade book fills this item: Spices, Their Histories, valuable information for grocers, priced at fifty cents and copyrighted at Seattle in 1910 by a trade paper's company. Contents treat the spice shelf one by one: allspice, capsicum, cinnamon and cassia, cloves, ginger, mustard, nutmeg and mace, pepper, and cumin seed.

An introduction tells the book's making. The histories were first written by Fielding, of the staff of a grocery trade journal, and ran in its issues with their pictures. Grocers everywhere, the editor says, will find the little book of value for study and reference. Success in trade now depends on knowing where goods were produced, and how to judge their quality. It depends too on how they are prepared for market, and what their uses are. A first article takes allspice, the dried unripe berries of a Jamaican tree.
60215-galileo-galilei-and-the-roman-curi:
Karl von Gebler wrote a life of Galileo and his clash with Rome. His book rests on true sources, its title claims. An English form came out with his leave in London. Ads at the front praise grand books on the Renaissance. Those ads set the tone of high past work for the book.

Galileo's finds in the sky start the long fight. Rome's court calls him to face its charge of false faith. Gebler prints the proof and lets the reader judge the case. Trial tales by word of mouth are set right by his files. Science and faith fans share this grave old case. The book stays a key text on that clash.
60241-sheaves:
Sheaves is a novel by Benson, printed at New York by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1907. This printing is the fourth edition. Benson also wrote The Angel of Pain and Dodo. The title names a gathering of grain, and the book gathers a country house world. Its first chapter opens in the middle of a game that has just ended in a burial.

The intrepid trader lies dead on the hayfield. If his body and legs were buried, he hinted, that would be ritual enough. The Indians thought otherwise and covered his head also. Dead traders always have their faces uncovered, Hugh protests from underground. This one didn't, Chopimalive remarks. Benson's comedy of English leisure starts at full absurdity.
60283-the-birds-and-the-bees:
The Birds and the Bees is a short tale of future times by Dave Fisher. It first ran in a science fiction magazine in August of nineteen fifty seven. A note in the text says the story tag line jokes that heroics can be easy. The tale is told by an old man in a far calm age of man.

He walks in tall grass near a great city that guards an oracle shrine. Men in that age have left the stars and come home to live in peace. No wars or crises mar their soft and clear days on Earth. A youth named Xeon bursts in to break that calm at the start. Talk of a drunk watcher and a heat fault at a birth machine sparks the plot.
60294-welsh-rarebit-tales:
Harle Oren Cummins wrote Welsh Rarebit Tales, published by the Mutual Book Company in Boston in 1902, with pictures by Emmett Owen. His preface explains the joke of the title. Cummins belonged to a literary club whose fifteen members read their sharpest new work aloud after dinner. Running short of first-class plots, the club tried a gastro-literary experiment. Each member ate a heavy supper before bed: Welsh rarebit, a broiled live lobster, mince pie, and more.

The tales in the book are the dreams that followed, or so the conceit runs. Cummins calls them more like the creations of a disordered brain than anything else. A frontispiece shows a hideous thing creeping out of the darkness toward the dreamer. Welsh rarebit was proverbially supposed to cause strange dreams, and Cummins built a book of weird tales on the superstition, with his club's supper as the framing story.
60299-team-mates:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote the school story Team-Mates for the Century Company at New York in 1911, from a copyright of 1910. C M Relyea drew the pictures. A front plate shows the Obnoxious Kid waving a red and white banner beside Sandy. Barbour also wrote The Crimson Sweater and Captain Chub.

A new boy, Cal, arrives at West House and sits for judgment by the house. Chapters christen him, settle him, and feed him gingerbread for homesickness. Ned lays down the law, a ghost haunts the orchard, and money goes missing. Molly, the girl next door, takes a hand, and a Pippin Club forms. A falling-out, a second game, and an explained mystery close the tale of school loyalty.
60418-new-bed-time-stories:
Louise Chandler Moulton wrote these bed-time stories, first copyrighted in 1880 and reissued by Little, Brown in 1907. A verse dedication addresses a brown-eyed English girl, promising her peace and love at Christmas-tide.

The contents list fourteen tales, among them Helen's Temptation, The Surgeon of the Dolls' Hospital, Pretty Miss Kate, and Tom's Thanksgiving. The first story follows Miss Endell on a weary hunt for London lodgings near the British Museum. She needs economy, quiet, and pretty things while she researches a book on noted Irishwomen. Young readers get gentle tales of children, mothers, and small kindnesses, written for reading aloud at night.
60452-off-sandy-hook-and-other-stories:
Richard Dehan wrote short tales issued in New York in 1915 by Stokes. A list of his past books stands at the front, from The Dop Doctor to The Man of Iron. Twenty-six tales fill the set, most with short, sharp names.

The first tale rides a liner eleven days and a half out from Liverpool as the pilot yacht comes up off Sandy Hook. A young press man named Cyrus Pillson, of the New York Yeller, boards to quiz the second officer over drinks and a strong cigar. Later tales bear names such as Gemini, Gas, Air, a spirit flight, and the devil and the deep sea.
60469-the-hundred-and-other-stories:
The Hundred and Other Stories is a book of tales by Gertrude Hall, published by Harper and Brothers in 1898. It is dedicated to the author's mother. Five stories fill the book: The Hundred, The Passing of Spring, Paula in Italy, Dorastus, and Chloe, Chloris, and Cytherea. Pictures show scenes from the tales.

The title story opens on Christmas Eve in a house where the mistress dines out. Every heart in the little household rejoices, since the servants gain an evening of their own. The lady's-maid has plans she means to keep. Hall writes polished society tales of love and manners for the magazine readers of her day.
60472-london-clubs-their-history-treasur:
Ralph Nevill wrote a history of London clubs and their treasures, issued in London in 1911 with nine plates. He thanks club secretaries who helped him, and the St James's Club for leave to use its water-colour as frontispiece. The first chapter traces clubs to coffee houses and taverns.

Later chapters roam St James's Street, with Boodle's, Arthur's, and White's, then Brooks's and the Cocoa-tree. Nevill treats elections, rules, late sittings, fines, and card play. He ends with the Garrick, the Jockey Club at Newmarket, and the Royal Yacht Squadron at Cowes. Clubland's habits, houses, and valuables are all his subject, told with a member's ease and pride.
60482-steve-brown-s-bunyip-and-other-sto:
Steve Browns Bunyip and Other Stories is a set of tales by John Arthur Barry, in a fresh form of nineteen five. First verse by a famed bard of the realm heads the book. Barry was known for a shelf of sea and town tales of the south land. Past twenty tales fill the list, from the name tale to a feast day at the far cape.

A note at the front tells how the book lay long out of print, like a hulk in a snug cove with but its name left in minds. Kind asks past years brought it out once more, in new garb and in a new land. Barry hopes its timbers, made tough by rest, will let the old ship hold its own past the new craft of its kind. Sea, bush, school, and claim tales crowd its rows.
60487-verses:
Verses is a book of poems by Hilaire Belloc, with an introduction by Joyce Kilmer. It was published in New York in 1916. Belloc dedicates the book to a friend, with verses recalling the foolish painted toys the two of them loved as little boys. These poems, he says, are his imperfect toys, offered in the same spirit.

The contents show Belloc's range in short forms. Stanzas written on Battersea Bridge in a gale stand beside The South Country, his hymn to Sussex. A fanatic, a rebel, and a prophet lost in the hills appear among the ballads and songs. Pieces on courtesy, the early morning, the birds, and Our Lord and Our Lady show his Catholic and lyrical side. Verses to the Balliol men still in Africa date the book to the war years, when Belloc's light verse carried a heavier charge.
6051-stella-fregelius-a-tale-of-three-de:
H. Rider Haggard tells a tale of three destinies, opening with Morris, Mary, and the aerophone, then the colonel and some reflections, poor Porson, and Mary preaching while the colonel prevails. A proposal and a promise lead to good days at Beaulieu, sunk rocks, and a singer.

Miss Fregelius herself enters, with dawn and the land, a morning service, Mr. Layard's wooing, and two questions with one answer. Stella's diary, the evil gate, dreams and sleep, and Stella's coming carry the tale toward its close. Haggard mixes romance with strange invention and the pull of fate.
60512-a-hand-book-of-precious-stones:
A Hand Book of Precious Stones, by Rothschild, was printed by Putnam in New York and London in 1890. Its preface states the object plainly: to give the merchant, the workman, and the amateur condensed and accurate information on the properties of precious stones. Rothschild adds tests from his own practical experience that an amateur can readily make.

Early pages teach the physical characters: crystallization, cleavage, fracture, refraction, colors, lustre, hardness, and specific gravity. Then the stones march past one by one, diamond and corundum first, then ruby, sapphire, spinel, emerald, opal, pearl, and garnet. Quartz in its many forms, agates, jasper, amber, and coral close the list, with a table of hardness and specific gravity.
60518-military-architecture-in-england-d:
Military Architecture in England during the Middle Ages is a scholarly survey by Hamilton Thompson. Henry Frowde issued it for Oxford University Press in 1912. Two hundred photographs, drawings, and plans illustrate the text. Rochester's great tower serves as the frontispiece of the volume.

The chapters follow the castle from earthwork to fortified house. Early earthworks and Roman stations open the long story in England. The Saxon and Danish period precedes the castle of the Conquest. Attack and defence then advance together, art answering art across centuries. The stone castle begins, and the Norman keep receives two chapters. Cylindrical tower-keeps mark the period of transition that follows. The dwelling-house inside the castle walls earns study of its own. Edwardian castles on the concentric plan crown the medieval achievement. Fortified towns and the late fortified dwelling close the survey.
60526-jean-of-greenacres:
Jean of Greenacres is a novel by Izola L Forrester, published in 1917. It follows Jean and her sisters at their country home. The opening chapter arrives just five days before Christmas.

An express card hints at a heavy package waiting at the office. The girls wonder whether it holds books for their father. Kit hopes for word from the west and a promised silver fox skin. The table of contents promises guests, letters, a studio visit, and a fire. Forrester wrote warm domestic fiction for young readers. This story centers on family duty, small hopes, and country life.
60529-the-fascinating-stranger-and-other:
The Fascinating Stranger and Other Stories is a set of short tales by Booth Tarkington, printed in nineteen twenty three. Doubleday published the first edition at Garden City after a de luxe printing. Thirteen stories fill the contents, from the title tale to Mary Smith. Several had run in magazines such as the Red Book before this book.

The title story opens on George Tuttle waking in his limousine at dawn. He lies among shavings that make the car a snug bedroom for him. His one weak eye opens a crack, sheds a tear at the light, and shuts. His greeting to the new day is a plaintive, husky Oh, Gosh. Other tales name a party, a hundred dollar bill, and a spring concert. Willamilla, The Only Child, and Ladies' Ways fill out the middle of the set.
6054-mrs-caudle-s-curtain-lectures:
Douglas Jerrold presents Mrs. Caudle's curtain lectures, and his preface answers gentlewomen who asked in wonder, pity, and reproof what could have put Mrs. Caudle into any man's mind. He says some subjects fall like raindrops on a head, and the book grew like a night flower from a small seed.

The scene that sparked it was a thick, black wintry afternoon before a suburban school playground, where boys full of Saturday holiday ran, jumped, hopped, and shouted under leaden skies. Jerrold turns that chance sight into comedy. Mrs. Caudle's night-time lectures scold, tease, and rule the house from behind the curtain.
60564-radio-active-substances:
Radio-Active Substances, by Madame Sklodowska Curie, is her thesis presented to the Faculté des Sciences of Paris, reprinted from the Chemical News in a second edition at London in 1904. The Van Nostrand Company handled the book at New York.

Instrument advertisements front this copy: spinthariscopes as devised by Sir William Crookes, showing the scintillations of radium, at 21s each, and pure radium bromide when available. Harrington Brothers offer radium salts, pitchblende, and uranium screens. The thesis itself reports Curie's research on the new radio-active elements. The reprint spread those findings quickly through the English-speaking world of laboratories and instrument makers.
60581-more-bed-time-stories:
More Bed-Time Stories is a set of tales for the young by Louise Chandler Moulton. Roberts Brothers of Boston brought the book out in the year 1875. Moulton held the rights from 1874 and gives it to her daughter Florence. Addie Ledyard drew the illustrations that stand through the story set. A verse opens the book in tender tones.

Against Wind and Tide opens the fifteen tales of the collection. Blue Sky and White Clouds, the Cousin from Boston, and Missy follow. The Head Boy of Eagleheight School and Agatha's Lonely Days come next. Thin Ice, My Lost Sister, and what came to Olive Haygarth crowd on. Uncle Jack, Nobody's Child, and My Little Gentleman fill the middle. Job Golding's Christmas closes the set. Jack Ramsdale was a bad boy, the first tale opens plainly. A bad name given a boy may hang him, it warns.
60606-the-glebe-1913-09-vol-1-no-1-songs:
Adolf Wolff published Songs, Sighs and Curses as the first number of The Glebe, a little magazine issued at Ridgefield, New Jersey, in September 1913. The issue cost sixty cents and holds Wolff's poems alone. He dedicated the book to Leonard Abbott, whose sympathy, he writes, was the sunshine and rain that brought the poems forth. All were written in 1912 and 1913.

A note explains their order. Asked how he would arrange them, Wolff threw the manuscripts in the air and let fate decide. They appear in the order in which they were picked up from the floor. The proem states his creed: he sings, sighs, and also curses, because all life does the same. A zoo poem watches a great Numidian lion pacing his cage. The Glebe went on to print other young modern writers. This first issue survives as a small monument of American little-magazine beginnings.
60632-the-fortunate-island-and-other-sto:
Max Adeler, whose name was Charles Heber Clark, gathered The Fortunate Island and Other Stories at Boston in 1882, from the press of Lee and Shepard. He had also written Out of the Hurly Burly, Elbow Room, and Random Shots. His preface owns that a writer with nothing proper to say before the text finds the custom of prefaces a burden. He hopes these tales will be found as diverting as his earlier ones, and in some points more instructive.

The title tale opens as the good ship Morning Star, bound from New York to Liverpool, founders at sea. All escaped in the boats save Professor Baffin and his daughter Matilda, who trusted to a patent india-rubber life-raft the professor hoped to sell in Europe. Other tales treat the city of burlesque, an old fogy, Major Dunwoody's leg, and Jinnie.
60660-two-american-boys-with-the-allied-:
Two American Boys with the Allied Armies, by Major Sherman Crockett with pictures by Wrenn, was published in New York in 1915. Twenty-five chapters carry two boys behind the trenches, through battles in the air, a Zeppelin raid, and headquarters at Ypres, hunting a lost brother as they go. A transcriber's note warns that the brother's name shifts from Tom to Frank after chapter three.

Chapter one, The Story of the Old Windmill, opens with Jack urging a climb into a battered windmill to take an observation. Amos agrees but warns against showing themselves, since German raiding parties may be skirmishing near. Crockett writes the Great War as a boys' adventure of clues, narrow escapes, and good deeds repaid on the road to the front.
60705-meditations-and-moral-sketches:
Guizot, the French statesman and historian, collected these essays on religion, philosophy, and education, and the Marquis of Ormonde translated them into English. Hodges and Smith published the translation at Dublin in 1855. The Quarterly Review had praised the French volume as scarcely known in England and deserving of attention, and the translator hoped to ease access to sentiments he thought beneficial.

Guizot's preface states his great question: the debate between those who own a supernatural and sovereign order of things and those who deny it. Christians alone, he says, possess the living God, and the world needs that faith again. The translator died before the book appeared, and a short note asks that this solemn fact add interest to his labors for others.
60716-a-song-of-the-open-road-and-other-:
Louis J McQuilland wrote the poems in A Song of the Open Road and Other Verses. Heath Cranton issued the book in London. Gilbert Chesterton gave a verse proem addressed to the poet. Cecil Chesterton wrote the preface. David Wilson drew the art that goes with the text.

Cecil Chesterton sketches McQuilland as an Irish Catholic from Ulster now in London. The poet had held back talk of home and faith, he says, and turned to art. Some poems first ran in papers such as the Spectator and the Daily News. One lyric, When I Sail to the Fortunate Islands, had sold its song rights. The verse mixes Ireland, war, and hope for better days.
6073-smith-and-the-pharaohs-and-other-ta:
H. Rider Haggard opens Smith and the Pharaohs by teasing scientists who claim to know all worth knowing about man, tracing his bones and shape and intelligence from humble origins. Haggard doubts the dissecting table explains aspirations toward another life, rooted, some say, in fear of death, earthquake, or thunder.

The volume adds Magepa the Buck, The Blue Curtains, Little Flower, and Only a Dream. It also gives Barbara Who Came Back, whose chapters run from a rectory blind and a new year feast through wedded, parted, sin, and atonement. Haggard mixes Egypt, ghosts, and moral reckoning, letting the past press hard upon the present.
60782-beside-the-fire-a-collection-of-ir:
Publisher lists for works by Dr Hyde and Alfred Nutt fill the first pages of the hosted text. Then the title page of Beside the Fire appears. Douglas Hyde edited, translated, and annotated the collection of Irish Gaelic folk stories. David Nutt published it in London in nineteen ten, with added notes by Alfred Nutt.

Hyde dedicated the book to the memory of the poet scribes and hedge schoolmasters of the last century. The contents open with a preface. It treats earlier collections of Irish folk lore and the lack of the language among collectors. It also treats the link between Irish and Scotch Gaelic tales, the old bardic tales, and the date of the Irish versions. Folklore readers get Irish tales in English dress, with a scholar's notes on where they came from.
60790-the-spanish-royal-tapestries:
The Spanish Royal Tapestries is an art history by Albert Calvert, published at London in 1921. John Lane issued it in the Spanish Series, which Calvert edited. Two hundred seventy seven illustrations support the text. Five chapters structure this volume. A history of the art of tapestry weaving opens it. The foundation of the Spanish royal collection follows.

Gothic tapestries, the sacred pieces, take the third chapter. A transition group between Gothic and Renaissance comes next. Renaissance tapestries close the text at chapter five. The plates begin with the Story of the Virgin, from cartoons by Van Eyck. David and Bathsheba and the story of John the Baptist follow. The Passion appears from a cartoon by Van de Weyden. Calvert defines tapestry strictly: a fabric woven with coloured wools on warp threads. Hangings of other workmanship, he warns, are not tapestry.
60811-in-great-waters-four-stories:
Thomas Janvier wrote four tales of men in the grip of great waters. The book came out in New York in 1901. Janvier wrote In Old New York and The Aztec Treasure-House. A front plate shows a crew home along the beach once more. The wrath of the Zuyder Zee leads the set in full.

A Duluth tragedy on the great lakes comes next in line. Death fires of Les Martigues burn in the third tale. A sea upcast closes the set on a wild shore. Dutch dikes, lake storms, and French coasts give each tale its stage. Janvier writes of sea folk with a warm, sure hand. Salt and dread rule all four.
60842-yesterdays-in-the-philippines:
Joseph Earle Stevens, an ex-resident of Manila, wrote Yesterdays in the Philippines for Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1898. He dedicated the tale to his mother's memory. Chapter one sails from God's country by Hong Kong to Luzon, with a first view of Manila, its river Pasig, and the old city.

Later chapters shop at the Botica Inglesa, mark the chit system, and sit through Manila cooking and tram-car oddities. Roosters are everywhere, an epidemic of grippe strikes at seventy-four degrees, and a bull fights a tiger to a sorry fiasco. A Philippine valet, Chinese New Year, marionettes, and pony races at Santa Mesa fill chapter three. Stevens writes as an amused resident, not a tourist.
60858-bookplates:
Edward Almack wrote Bookplates for the Little Books on Art, a pocket series edited by Cyril Davenport and published by Methuen of London in 1904. The little book sells for two shillings and sixpence and carries 42 illustrations. The series list shows its company: miniatures, Greek art, the arts of Japan, and jewellery among the subjects.

The contents arrange the plates by age. A first chapter treats the modes of engraving and the styles in bookplates. Then the chronology begins: very early plates, Albrecht Dürer, and the German artists. Lucas Cranach and Hans Holbein follow. Early French and English plates come next, with Sir Nicholas Bacon and Queen Elizabeth. Collectors get the ex-libris from its cradle in German woodcuts, in a book small enough for the pocket.
60870-underneath-the-bough-a-book-of-ver:
George Allan England wrote a book of verses copyrighted in 1903, offered to Agnes in the tenth year of her reign, as he puts it. The edition was printed for subscribers only, with numbered copies. England thanks journals from the Literary Digest to the Boston Transcript for leave to reprint poems. A first part is titled The Race of the Mighty.

Songs and sonnets follow, on love, Dante, gardens, and Spain. Some pieces are versions from Horace and Charles d'Orléans. Ballades and rondeaux form a third part. A fourth part follows the year from spring to winter. A fifth treats death in many forms, from Gunga Din in Hell onward.
60900-merry-tales:
Mark Twain's Merry Tales appeared at New York in 1892 in the Fiction, Fact, and Fancy series edited by Arthur Stedman. The series aimed at busy Americans: short volumes for readers whose time came in scraps. Companion volumes held Poultney Bigelow on the German emperor, Whitman's selected poems, and Calabrian sketches.

An editor's note explains that the desire for brief reading had lately been fed from foreign sources, with many reprints and translations of little classics. Good was done that way, but much rubbish came too. This series offered American work in the same handy shape. Readers get Twain's comic tales issued as a pocket classic by his own publishing house.
60995-february-strawberries:
Jim Harmon works a dark trick in February Strawberries, a story from Worlds of If Science Fiction in March 1961. Its tag line asks how much the impossible is worth. Linton sits in a restaurant with Howell and spots Rogers Snead at a table, or a man who looks just like him. Howell squirms: that is not Snead, perhaps a twin, since Snead is dead.

Linton buried his wife Greta and did time in an asylum, and he knows what dead means. Howell hints that Snead may have been brought back, by the Mafia or whoever runs it. A chill tale follows.
61009-our-old-nursery-rhymes:
Alfred Moffat set the old nursery rhymes to their own true tunes, with drawings by Le Mair. The book was copyrighted in 1911 and sold in London and New York. Each rhyme stands with its music, ready to sing. The contents run to some thirty songs in all.

Well loved pieces fill the pages. Pussy Cat opens the book, and Mary Had a Little Lamb comes next. Sing a Song of Sixpence, Little Jack Horner, and Three Blind Mice follow. Later pages give Jack and Jill, Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, and Little Bo-Peep. Moffat aimed to keep the tunes as they had long been sung, not in new dress. For families of that day it was a sing at home book, words and notes on one page.
61016-the-black-dog-and-other-stories:
The Black Dog and Other Stories, by A E Coppard, was printed by Alfred A Knopf at New York in 1923. Coppard's thanks name the journals that first took some of the tales, from The Saturday Review to The Double Dealer. The contents run to eighteen: Alas, Poor Bollington, The Ballet Girl, Simple Simon, The Tiger, and Mordecai and Cocking. The Man from Kilsheelan, The Devil in the Churchyard, and Big Game stand late in the book.

The title tale opens at a lone small station at July noon. Loughlin, back from a charmed break, checks his bags with a one-eyed porter and waits for a late train.
