The best of his stay, a fair woman met at its end, pulls his thoughts back down the line. Tale fans get Coppard's fine, wry craft in a full first store.
61034-douris-and-the-painters-of-greek-v:
Edmond Pottier wrote Douris and the Painters of Greek Vases, turned into English by Bettina Kahnweiler and issued in London in 1909. Jane Ellen Harrison wrote the preface. Pottier was a member of the Institut in France. The frontispiece shows a kantharos and kylix by Douris, held in Brussels and the Louvre.

Five chapters trace how vase designs mirror the history of Greek painting. Pottier then treats the social state of a vase painter at Athens. Later parts enter the workshop and tools of Douris, and show how he worked. A final part surveys the work of Douris itself, with a bibliography and index. Pictures show potters at work, youths in the palaestra, and Eos carrying Memnon.
6106-definitions-essays-in-contemporary-:
Henry Seidel Canby, editor of The Literary Review and Yale English teacher, gathers essays in contemporary criticism under the title Definitions. He thanks the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's, Century, The Bookman, The Nation, and other journals for permission to reprint pieces first seen in their columns.

Canby says the book's unity lies in his point of view, not in chapters building one theme toward categorical conclusions. Literature in a civilization trying to be sophisticated and democratic at once has many sources and manifestations, tangled with social background. The essays open many doors before judging art and life.
61068-tiger-lily-and-other-stories:
Tiger Lily and Other Stories is a book of tales by Julia Schayer, published by Scribner's in New York in 1883. The contents hold five stories: Tiger Lily, Thirza, Molly, A Summer's Diversion, and My Friend Mrs Angel. The title story opens at the Ridgemont grammar school. A girl's shrill voice, raised in anger, breaks in on the teacher's reading.

School has just been dismissed, and boys' cries and the sounds of a scuffle follow. The small, fagged teacher rises in haste and goes out to the playground. The story begins in that schoolyard quarrel. Schayer's tales treat small-town and school life with a close eye for character.
61082-neddie-and-beckie-stubtail-two-nic:
Howard Garis wrote bed time tales of two nice bears for small children. Neddie and Beckie Stubtail are the bear cubs at its core. Louis Wisa drew the plates for the book. Garis wrote of Sammie Littletail and the Bushytail boys as well. The tales first ran in the Evening News of Newark.

Neddie and Beckie fall in strife in the first short tale. Beckie and the buns, Neddie and the bees' nest, come next. A trained bear, a run off, and a pole climb fill the mid set. Thanks Day, an elephant, and a monkey close the list. Each tale is brief and ends in a safe, kind place. Small ears get soft fun.
61084-the-standard-manual-for-baptist-ch:
The Standard Manual for Baptist Churches, by Edward T Hiscox, was entered for copyright in 1890. Hiscox wrote books for ministers and a pastors manual as well. The small book was made to be kept at hand, sized to fit a coat pocket.

Fifteen chapters set out what a Baptist church is and how it should run. Early chapters treat officers, rites, members, and church discipline. Later chapters treat doctrine, baptism, and the Supper of the Lord. One chapter gives model standing rules for church business. A last chapter gives Baptist history. Church officers get firm, plain counsel, argued with force for the Baptist way against other paths.
61138-contact-and-other-stories:
Contact and Other Stories is a story set by Frances Noyes Hart, published in 1923. Doubleday Page of Garden City issued the first edition of the collection. Hart dedicates the book to her father, Frank Brett Noyes, in a front line. Contents open with Contact, then There Was a Lady and Long Distance.

Philip the Gay, Green Gardens, Delilah, Her Grace, and the Honourable Tony complete the list. Magazine copyrights from Pictorial Review, Scribner, and Curtis show first printings of the tales. War and its after years hang over these polished stories of love and loss. Readers gain a once popular American storyteller at her interwar best.
61158-death-and-taxes:
Death and Taxes is a science fiction story by H A Hartzell, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction for May 1962. Its billing promises the genuine, inside, light-hearted story of its subject, remorseless or not. The scene is a town meeting in a metropolis of less than fifteen hundred souls.

Jerry Masterson, a young artist with paint on his sport shirt, pleads with the mayor to save the Waukeena Lighthouse. The council wants the picturesque landmark torn down, and with it the home of the town's only local ghost, Captain MacGreggor. The State Highway Commission backs demolition, the building is over seventy years old, and repairs cost too much. Mr Higgins of the Historical Society rises to fight beside Masterson. Hartzell turns the old saw about death and taxes into a small-town ghost's last stand.
61170-the-pastor-his-qualifications-and-:
H Harvey, a teacher at Hamilton Theological Seminary, wrote a book on the pastor's gifts and duties. It was first entered in 1879 and printed again at Philadelphia in 1904. The book is given to the memory of William Colgate, a rich friend of training for the ministry.

The preface says the thoughts grew from the writer's own years in the pulpit. They were first given as talks to his classes, most of them young men new to the work. The first part treats the call to the ministry. It weighs the call felt within, the call of the church, and the call of events in a man's life.
61171-the-expendables:
Jim Harmon wrote a crime tale that ran in Worlds of If in May 1962. A little black box, useful for getting rid of things, worked too well, the blurb warns. You see my problem, Professor, Tony Carmen begins, holding his pinkly manicured, flashily ringed hands wide. Professor Venetti sees the problem, and it is warmly embarrassing.

I am not a doctor of medicine, or a lawyer, he protests. They cannot help me, Carmen says, I need an operator in your line. I work for the United States government and cannot touch anything illegal, Venetti answers. Ever hear of the Mafia, Carmen asks, and tells of bodies dumped at his club. A disposal box and mob corpses make a tight, grim joke of a story.
61194-maid-marian-and-other-stories:
Molly Elliot Seawell wrote this collection, issued in 1891 as number 77 in Appletons' Town and Country Library. Seawell was already known for Throckmorton, a novel of Virginia in the years just after the war, and Little Jarvis, the story of a heroic midshipman of the frigate Constellation.

The title story takes its name from the Maid Marian of legend. The volume opens with long extracts of praise for her earlier books, where critics dwell on her grace of style, humor, and pathos. Readers who liked those novels will find the same hand at work in shorter form here.
61222-the-crochet-book-fourth-series:
Riego de la Branchardiere wrote The Crochet Book, Fourth Series, a pattern book printed in London in 1848 and sold for one shilling. The author had planned doyleys and antimacassars for this series, but patrons asked for collars instead. She deferred the other items to a fifth series to follow soon.

Patterns give a collar called Le Bouquet, a collar called La Rose, a manchette, a chemisette, and crochet edging, each with section views. Collar designs were registered by law, and makers needed her leave to sell them. Terms are explained in the first three series of the set. Needleworkers get a rare early crochet pattern book from a famed teacher.
61226-the-ark-of-1803-a-story-of-louisia:
C A Stephens wrote The Ark of 1803, a tale of Louisiana Purchase times for young readers. A S Barnes and Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred four. H Burgess drew the pictures. Jimmy Claiborne of Fish Creek stars in the tale.

School boys sign a plea for a holiday in the first scene. Feathers from plucked turkeys fly in the warm school room. The crew then builds and launches a great river ark. Perils crowd the long float down to New Orleans. Cave robbers, a tornado, and a landslide test the young hands. A keel from Saint Louis and a masked guess game join the fun. Napoleon and the Stars and Stripes end the ride. The year of the Purchase turns a river trip into high adventure.
61229-holiday-frolics-or-endless-amuseme:
Holiday Frolics is a sixpenny book of parlour tricks, printed in London for the Christmas fireside. Its title promises the most astonishing feats of legerdemain and astounding conjurings. It also offers experiments in various branches of science. Tricks with cards and dice and the art of making fireworks follow.

Puzzles, conundrums, riddles, and charades fill out the collection. The preface takes care to part legerdemain from conjuring. One deceives the eye by sound principles, it says, while the other is mere sleight of hand. Pictures show how to make a bird appear dead and a curious trick with a cup of tea. The book beguiled holiday hours cheaply.
61262-poirot-investigates:
Agatha Christie gathers eleven short cases for Hercule Poirot in a Bodley Head volume first printed in London in 1924. Captain Hastings tells each case and stands at Poirot's side through the work. The contents run from The Adventure of the Western Star to The Case of the Missing Will.

Cases in between cover a death at Marsdon Manor, a cheap flat, and a shoot at Hunter's Lodge. A bond theft, an Egyptian tomb, and a jewel theft at a grand hotel add range and risk. One case turns on a kidnapped prime minister, and one on a man who seems to vanish from his own home. The first tale opens in Poirot's rooms, where Hastings misreads a crowd that trails film star Mary Marvell.
61290-the-old-maid-the-fifties:
The Old Maid, the Fifties, by Edith Wharton, is one of the Old New York novellas. It was copyright 1922 as a magazine story and 1924 in book form, published in New York and London. Wharton other works fill the front list, from the Glimpses of the Moon to the Age of Innocence.

Part one opens in scene setting. In the old New York of the fifties, a few families ruled, in simplicity and affluence. Of these were the Ralstons. The sturdy English and the rubicund, heavier Dutch had mingled, Wharton writes. They produced a prosperous, prudent, and yet lavish society. It was built on the fortunes of bankers, India merchants, and shipbuilders. Readers get Wharton at her most exact: old New York money, manners, and a sacrifice hidden inside both.
61294-the-cruise-of-the-little-dipper-an:
Susanne Langer wrote fairy tales printed in New York in 1923, with pictures by Sewell. The title tale tells of a very poor boy with no cap, no shoes, and no penny. He has not even a name. His father sailed years ago in a ship called The Big Dipper and never returned.

The boy lives by the sea with a great aunt, old and cross and strict. She gives no sugar or butter and spanks him daily for the mistakes of today and tomorrow alike. From that hard home the cruise of the Little Dipper lifts him into wonder. Other tales tell of Nikko, Peter Dwarf, a crystal bowl, and a merciless tsar.
61297-false-dawn-the-forties:
Edith Wharton wrote a tale of old New York in the eighteen-forties, first of a set of four, published at New York in 1924. It opens on a July day scented with hay, verbena, and mignonette. Strawberries from the kitchen garden float in a pale yellow cup in an old Georgian bowl on the verandah.

The house is High Point, above the Sound, home of Halston Raycie, whose town house stands in Canal Street. His guest, known as the Commodore, is Jameson Ledgely, who served as a midshipman under Admiral Porter in the war of 1812. Raycie will not admit there are mosquitoes at High Point, though his guests slap their brows as furtively as they can. Old money at ease fills the frame.
61298-the-spark-the-sixties:
The Spark is a tale of old New York in the years of the great war of the states, writ by Edith Wharton and put out in nineteen twenty four. It stands in a set of four tales of old New York, one for each of four spans of years. The rights were held that year by her print house and by a great sheet firm. The tale is told by a young man who looks up to a great man of the town.

It opens at a card game in a rich house. You fool, says the wife of Hayley Delane, and throws down her cards. The young teller turns his head fast, that he not see the face of Delane.
61300-christmas-stories:
A story collection by Jacob A Riis, published by the Macmillan Company in 1923. The pieces carry copyrights from 1897 onward. Riis was the famous reporter of the New York tenements. His How the Other Half Lives had exposed slum conditions. These Christmas tales turn that knowledge into fiction. Thirteen stories fill the contents.

The first story opens in a boys' lodging-house on Christmas Eve. Six fat turkeys sizzle in the basement kitchen. Two-score boys guess at the pies to come. Checkers, a doodling pencil, and a dozing superintendent fill the quiet hall. A stage whisper then summons Tom to hear about the Kid. Other tales visit snow-sheds, tenements, and a burgomaster's feast. Riis wrote sentiment with a reformer's purpose.
61321-new-year-s-day-the-seventies:
Edith Wharton wrote a tale of old New York in the eighteen-seventies, the last of a set of four, published in 1924. Its narrator remembers his mother, spectacles slanted on her knitting, dropping a hissed sentence over a snowy baby-blanket. She was bad, always, the mother said, of Lizzie Hazeldean: they used to meet at the Fifth Avenue Hotel.

The precision of the phrase, the narrator says, characterized his old New York; a generation later people would have said merely that they met in hotels. Old Sillerton Jackson grumbles through his perfect china teeth that nowadays they might meet in the middle of Fifth Avenue for all anybody cares. A boy of twelve keeps the memory the tale unpacks.
61336-irish-memories:
Irish Memories is a memoir by the writing partners Somerville and Ross, published in New York by Longmans, Green in 1918. Twenty-three illustrations, from drawings and photographs, appear through the book. The partners had won fame with Some Experiences of an Irish Resident Magistrate and The Real Charlotte.

Twenty-eight chapters trace family and place. The Martins of Ross open the story, and Maria Edgeworth appears early. Chapters move through childhoods, mothers, and the years the contents call the years of the locust. Letters from Ross, dogs, horses and hounds, and the making of their famous books fill the later pages. Appendices print letters from a chief justice. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
61344-the-happy-isles:
The Happy Isles, a novel by Basil King, was published at New York in 1923. Harper issued it with illustrations by John Alonzo Williams in that year. King also wrote The Dust Flower and The Thread of Flame, the front list shows. The City of Comrades and The Empty Sack stand in the same roll of his books.

A front plate cries, they will say I stole him, it will be twenty years for me. The Happy Isles takes its name from a place of rest in the tale. Love, law, and a child at the centre of a storm fill the King plot. Popular religious tinged fiction of the 1920s often wore this gentle manner. Readers of The Inner Shrine met the same hand in this later novel.
61399-chain-of-colonial-houses:
Pictures and sketches of old Philadelphia houses fill this book, published by the Associate Committee of Women of the Pennsylvania Museum of Art. Its cover names the setting: Fairmount Park, Philadelphia. An opening essay calls Philadelphia the most important city in the colonies and the home of many leaders in the days when the American nation was born.

Eight old colonial houses are described, several dating back to the middle of the eighteenth century. The names given include Cedar Grove, Belmont, The Cliffs, Woodford, and Mount Pleasant. The essay credits the Pennsylvania Museum of Art, partner bodies, and generous Philadelphians with saving and restoring these landmarks in the park.
61401-don-a-runaway-dog-his-many-adventu:
Don, a Runaway Dog is a story for children by Richard Barnum, printed at New York in 1915. It stands in the Kneetime Animal Stories, beside Squinty the pig, Slicko the squirrel, and Mappo the monkey. Harriet Tooker drew the pictures, one showing Don marching like a soldier dog with a broom for a gun.

Don begins life as one of five puppies, cuddled close to his mother in a straw filled kennel. Chapter heads follow him to a new home, into the city, and into the net of a dog catcher. He sees Tum Tum the elephant and meets a bear before the end. Young readers get a dog's-eye tour of farm and town.
61437-set-down-in-malice-a-book-of-remin:
Gerald Cumberland wrote this book of reminiscences, Set Down in Malice, printed in New York in 1919. A prefatory note tells where much of it was drafted: in the trenches and dug-outs of Greece and Serbia, with a chapter or two added in Port Said, Alexandria, and Marseilles. Cumberland wrote, he says, far from books and documents, to refresh a mind dulled by active service.

The contents name the people he recalls. George Bernard Shaw gets the first chapter, and Frank Harris and Hall Caine get chapters of their own. Writers fill many pages, among them Arnold Bennett, Chesterton, John Masefield, and Max Beerbohm, while other chapters treat Elgar, Fleet Street, musical critics, and people of the theatre.
6144-report-of-commemorative-services-wi:
The Church in Connecticut kept a record of rites and talks for the Seabury hundred-year mark of 1883 to 1885, with an added part at the end. The list marks the hundred years since Bishop Seabury was picked, with thanks on Easter Day, 25 March 1883, and a rite at Woodbury two days later.

Bishop Williams gives talks and sermons, Dr. Beardsley gives talks, and church meets of 1883, 1884, and 1885 fill the book. Rites at Hartford and Middletown, a show of Seabury keepsakes, and an Aberdeen event close the record. The book keeps a church's mind on its first bishop. The added part gives the Aberdeen event of 1884.
61450-dido-the-dancing-bear-his-many-adv:
Dido, the Dancing Bear: His Many Adventures, by Richard Barnum, came out in 1916 from Barse and Hopkins of New York. It stands in the Kneetime Animal Stories, with Squinty the pig and Mappo the monkey as its kin, and art by C P Bluemlein. First we meet a bear clan in a snug den on a far peak: a father, a mother, and three cubs. Gruffo has a deep voice, and Muffo and Dido round out the young set.

Then men come, and Dido is caught and trained. He learns to dance, jumps a hoop of flame for an apple, and crosses the wide sea. A bakery, a circus, and a fire mark his road, and he helps a girl in need. Young readers get a warm beast tale of tricks, perils, and kind deeds.
61456-the-black-troopers-and-other-stori:
The Black Troopers and Other Stories came from the Religious Tract Society of London, with fifteen plates. Its long first tale is set in Australia in March 1849, on the Lower Murray. The teller, a doctor on the road with drays, is called to Lake Boga to aid a man shot in the leg. A war band had failed in a night raid and struck the lake camp in spite. He sets the limb with bark splints and rides on.

The heads run on: Old Man Toby, a night attack, a confession, and a chase to its end. Two more tales fill the book: Captain Stauncy's Vow and The Forged Will. Readers of brave tales get bush war, guilt, and grace in the plain, earnest style of the tract press.
61476-obstetrics-for-nurses:
Charles Reed's Obstetrics for Nurses was published by the Mosby Company at Saint Louis in 1917. Reed was obstetrician to Wesley Memorial Hospital in Chicago. One hundred and thirty illustrations support the text, and the book is dedicated to his friend Eugene Gilmore. Twenty-five chapters run the whole course of the nurse's subject, from anatomy and physiology through normal pregnancy and its hygiene. Abnormal pregnancy takes two chapters.

Preparations for labor, the mechanism of normal labor, and the care of the patient follow. The normal puerperium, unusual presentations, operations major and minor, and complications in labor fill the middle. Infection and the abnormal puerperium have chapters of their own. Four chapters treat the care of the child and one treats infant feeding, while cleanliness and sterilization, diets and formulas, and a therapeutic index close the manual. The illustrations begin with the female pelvis and the fetal skull.
61477-seneca-myths-and-folk-tales:
Arthur Parker's Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, volume twenty-seven of the Buffalo Historical Society Publications, was published at Buffalo in 1923 and edited by Frank Severance, to whom Parker dedicates it. Parker writes as archaeologist of the New York State Museum. A frontispiece painting by Richard Tucker shows the inside of a bark long house, the air in which legends were told.

Opening chapters weigh the makings of Seneca folk lore: gods and major spirits, folk-beasts, nature beings and magic beasts and birds. Then come the tales themselves, grouped as When the World Was New, boys who defied magic, tales of love and marriage, and horror tales of cannibals and sorcerers. Titles include How the World Began, The Coming of Death, The Boy Who Lived with the Bears and The Island of the Cannibal.
61478-the-court-of-the-king-and-other-st:
The Court of the King and Other Studies, by Margaret Benson, was first published in London in 1913. Benson other books listed include The Soul of a Cat, The Venture of Rational Faith, and The Temple of Mut in Asher, written with Gourlay. Contents list a preface and nine studies.

The gates of gold opens, then the lake within the world. A desert city, the other side, and the silent romance follow. The court of the king itself comes sixth. The golden dahabeah, the unseen world, and from the bank of the river close the set. The first study opens in a nursery. A favourite game with a Noah Ark, Benson writes, was to make the nursery table an island of delight. Readers get Benson studies, where childhood memory and Egypt meet in essays of faith.
61512-the-one-eyed-fairies:
Georgia Eldredge Hanley wrote this sewing book for children, with pictures and diagrams by Julia Greene. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard printed The One-Eyed Fairies at Boston in 1924. The fairies of the title are needles, each with its one bright eye.

The King of the One-Eyed Fairies opens the tale, then Sir Bodkin steps in and out. The Stitchers, Baster and Runner, teach their stitches as they come. Dainty Hemmer shows hemming, and the Crewel One the blanket stitch. Old Doctor Darner darns stockings. A doll's blanket, a marble bag, and a new middy blouse give each stitch its job. Buttons, patching, and ruffles close a bright way to teach small hands to sew.
61517-bread-and-circuses:
Bread and Circuses is a book of verse by Helen Parry Eden, issued by John Lane in 1914. She dedicates the poems to the memory of her sister, Joan Abbott Parry. An errata slip corrects a handful of small misprints in the text. Of the verses in the book, the greater part are new, her note begins.

The title takes the old Roman cry for bread and shows. Eden writes lyrics of faith, home, and the passing scene. Her verse has the plain music of the Georgian poets. War stood at the door in the year her book appeared. A sister’s memory gives the collection its tender frame. The poems are a young woman’s notebook of a world about to change. Lane’s Bodley Head list carried much such verse in those years.
61522-the-1-000-000-bank-note-and-other-:
Mark Twain leads this Toronto collection with The £1,000,000 Bank-Note, printed by the Musson Book Company. The narrator was a mining-broker's clerk in San Francisco at twenty-seven, alone in the world with his wits and a clean reputation. Sailing his little boat on the bay, he ventured too far and was carried out to sea. A brig bound for London picked him up at nightfall and made him work his passage without pay.

He landed in London with ragged clothes and one dollar, which fed and sheltered him for a day; the next day he went without both. Starving on Portland Place, he is called in by two elderly brothers who have settled an argument with a strange wager. Other pieces include Mental Telegraphy, Playing Courier, The German Chicago, and a petition to the Queen of England.
6157-what-men-live-by-and-other-tales:
Leo Tolstoy opens What Men Live By and Other Tales with epistles of St. John: we have passed from death into life because we love the brethren, and he who loves not abides in death. Love in deed and truth, not word or tongue, marks the passage, for God is love.

The title tale begins with Simon the shoemaker, who has neither house nor land, lives with wife and children in a peasant's hut, and earns his living by his work. Tolstoy asks what truly keeps men alive: not goods or strength, but love shown to a brother in need. The tales teach by parable and plain life.
61611-the-western-cowboy-and-arabians-in:
The Western Cowboy and Arabians in the Rockies is a small color book on ranch life, held in 1948 by the Trinidad Bean and Elevator Company of Denver. Its price was one dollar. The first half praises the cowboy as those who know him best see him: a plain, upstanding man, brave and loyal to his outfit and his friends.

His code, an old timer says in the text, calls for courage, loyalty, cheer under hardship, laughter at danger, no prying into a man's past, and respect for women. The book grants that dime novels and films have warped the public view. Real cowboys work from sunup to sundown in blizzard and sun, with no set hours, to put meat on the nation's tables.
61619-six-giants-and-a-griffin-and-other:
Birdsall Otis Edey wrote Six Giants and a Griffin and Other Stories, printed at New York in 1903 with art by Beatrice Baxter Ruyl. A verse by James Whitcomb Riley heads the book, on the child who begs a tale made up on the spot, held folded eyed in a mother arms. Contents hold six tales in all.

Teddy stars in the lead tale. An only child, he makes up playmates, most often gnomes, and slips each morning into the hollow trunk of an old oak at the foot of the lawn to start his adventures. Other tales send Gertrude to the moon, Jane to play with bears, and Sapphira to ride a flying pig. Christmas trees and a Mother Goose party close a gentle set of fancy tales for small children.
61654-blackie-a-lost-cat-her-many-advent:
Richard Barnum wrote Blackie, a Lost Cat for the Kneetime Animal Stories, printed in 1916 with art by Walter Rogers. Barnum had told tales of Squinty the pig, Tum Tum the elephant, and Flop Ear the rabbit. Blackie is black as coal or tar, with not one white hair in her glossy coat.

Smart and full of luck, good and bad, she hears a thing that starts her tale, then runs away from her fine large house. Chapter heads promise trouble and escape, a friend found, a ride in a basket and then in a train, and a chase. She meets Don the dog, scares a dog in turn, and swings from sad to happy. Warm, plain chapters suit young readers who love pets and mild peril.
61658-forest-lake-and-prairie-twenty-yea:
John McDougall told of twenty years of wild life in west Canada. A second form came out in Toronto in 1910. The years run from 1842 to 1862 in the book. McDougall gave the book to his dear mother with love. A front plate shows a chief and a buffalo at page 155.

Boy days with Indians, canoes, and old Isaiah lead the tale. School, guards, and a trip to Nottawasaga come next in line. The kin move far north to Garden River for his father's work. Storm peril, a lone store, and first boats mark those years. A move to Rama and school years fill the mid tale. Wild life fans get a true, warm voice.
6168-fifty-famous-people-a-book-of-short:
James Baldwin offers Fifty Famous People as short stories that, although not biographical, concern real persons who actually lived and played parts in the great drama of world history. Some were more famous than others, yet all left enduring footprints on the sands of time.

Each story holds a basis of truth and an ethical lesson of wholesome influence, with interest enough to disprove the doctrine that children delight only in tales of the imaginative and unreal. A few more than fifty famous people appear in the volume. Baldwin writes history as story, meant to teach and to please.
61688-flop-ear-the-funny-rabbit-his-many:
Flop Ear, the Funny Rabbit is a children's animal story by Richard Barnum, published in 1916. Barse and Hopkins issued it in the Kneetime Animal Stories. Walter Rogers drew the pictures. Barnum had written of Squinty the pig and Tum Tum the elephant before. Flop Ear belongs to a family of six rabbits. They live in the woods near the top of a mountain.

His mother, his father, and Lady Munch complete the household as the story opens. Twelve chapters carry Flop Ear through his adventures. He hears a noise, finds something, and gets lost in the hay. A boy teaches him tricks before he gets away again. He meets Slicko the squirrel and Dido the dancing bear. Helping some mice and meeting a monkey fill the later chapters. At last Flop Ear gets home again, as the contents promise.
61720-how-to-cook-in-casserole-dishes:
Marion Harris Neil wrote a cook book of dishes baked slow in one pot. A plate shows rabbit in its pot at the book's front. Neil once ran cook work for The Ladies' Home Journal. She wrote books on sweets, cans, thrift, and salads in past years. Word swaps in front fit the book for British homes from Yankee terms.

Whole spice is read as spice seeds in its clear note list. Squabs are read as young tame birds for the home pot. Soup rules lead the list, then fish rules take their turn. Fowl and game, meats, and cold meats fill the long mid span. Each dish is built for one dish from start to last. Cooks get a full set.
61736-bermuda-houses:
Architects of New York and Boston asked for this book on Bermuda houses to be made. Advance subscribers are listed at the front as an endorsement of the work. Aldrich of New York, Cram of Boston and the Harvard architecture library stand among those names in the list.

White roofs, thick limestone walls and cedar beams make Bermuda's building manner its subject. Rain caught from the roof fills the cistern in such houses, a design for islands without rivers. Measured drawings and photographs in such a volume taught American architects a colonial style shaped by sun, storm and scarce fresh water.
61755-o-henryana-seven-odds-and-ends-poe:
O Henryana is a small gathering of odds and ends by the writer known as O Henry, published in 1920. The sub-title calls it seven odds and ends of poetry and short stories. Doubleday, Page and Company of New York put it out ten years after his death. The contents list opens with a poem, The Crucible. It bids a man be tender when the roaring of battle ends. A Lunar Episode and Three Paragraphs follow in prose.

Bulger's Friend, A Professional Secret, and The Elusive Tenderloin stand in the run. The Struggle of the Outliers closes the set. The lunar piece opens on a world of black lakes and honeycombed crags, under immense stars. Two men step from a stone dwelling into that cold light. The book is a coda to a famed shelf: scraps and short pieces saved from the magazines of his day.
61762-the-bush-fire-and-other-verses:
Ida Lee wrote this verse book, The Bush Fire and Other Verses, in a second edition printed in London in 1897. She dedicates it to her father and mother. Seventeen pieces are named in the contents, mixing Australian bush scenes with English ones: Bill the Groom, White Sea Horses, Suffolk, and The Fish-Girl's Song among them.

The title poem is a spoken scene. A stockman wakes his boy at night: the grass is burning, and the sheep are still in the Flat Paddock. Mount the Arab, he cries, and take wet sacking, not dry. They must save the master's cattle if they perish trying. The riders beat at the flames with green branches while the fire takes the tall gum trees and the parrots flee screaming.
61784-paul-jones:
Paul Jones is a biography of the naval hero by Molly Elliot Seawell, first published by Appleton in 1893 and reprinted in 1936. Seawell wrote sea tales for the young, among them Little Jarvis and Decatur and Somers. A saying from the funeral discourse over Jones heads her introduction: the fame of the brave outlives him; his portion is immortality.

Seawell confesses her diffidence at using so mighty a name. Jones, as Cooper said, was not only a great seaman but a great man. Yet it is right and profitable, she argues, to set this heroic figure before American youth, even if the telling falls short. An illustration captioned the guns broke loose sets the tone of action. Her life of the Revolutionary captain, raider of British coasts and founder of the American navy's legend, was written to give boys a hero with salt water in him.
61798-venus-has-green-eyes:
Venus Has Green Eyes is a science fiction story by Carl Selwyn, taken from Planet Stories for Fall 1940. Flip Miller, an ex-prospector, is drinking with the trapper Charlie Mead on Venus.

Flip has a reason for the forty-day drunk. Two months earlier the Space Patrol found him marooned on Pallas with a pint of air. On Mars he won a fortune at poker and lost it in the next game. All he kept was a doubtful map of a Venusian xanite mine. The mine lies a few hundred miles east of Charlie's island in the Black Swamp. Xanite ore is worth over a thousand dollars a ton on Earth. The magazine's blurb sends Flip onward to worse trouble. He becomes prisoner of the lovely, cruel Venusian queen. His escape turns on remembering that women are women, on Venus as on Earth.
61847-tinkle-the-trick-pony-his-many-adv:
Richard Barnum writes for young readers in Tinkle the Trick Pony, one of the Kneetime Animal Stories, copyrighted in 1917 with illustrations by Walter S Rogers. Twelve chapters follow the pony from a swamp escape through trouble, a new home and new friends to the circus, a meeting with Tum Tum the elephant, sadness and a happy end. Tinkle's frontispiece trick is fetching the right flag in his teeth for Mr Drake.

The first chapter opens in the big green meadow, where Tinkle has lived over a year with his mother and father. Bored with grazing, he resolves to run away where no other pony can hear him plan it.
61875-animal-stories-from-eskimo-land-ad:
Renee Coudert Riggs retold animal stories from Eskimo land for young readers. Frederick A Stokes Company issued the book in New York in 1923. The tales came from true Eskimo stories gathered by Dr Daniel S Neuman. George W Hood drew the pictures and page ornaments.

Riggs gives the book to the children of Alaska with warm greetings. A father frames the set, taking two children in thought to a village house called a kasga. There folk pass long dark winter hours with song, dance, and tales. Bears, foxes, fish, and crows star in the short pieces that follow.
61959-anglo-american-memories:
George W Smalley wrote Anglo American Memories, issued by G P Putnams Sons in New York and London in nineteen eleven. Smalley had earlier written Studies of Men and a life of Sir Sydney Waterlow. A portrait of Smalley faces the title page. More than twenty chapters fill the book. Smalley looks back from a long life in press and public affairs on both sides of the Atlantic.

Early chapters treat New England in eighteen fifty, Daniel Webster, and Massachusetts Puritanism. Smalley recalls his Yale class of eighteen fifty three and Harvard Law School. He then treats the surrender of fugitive slave Anthony Burns in eighteen fifty four. Visits to Emerson and talks with Wendell Phillips and Charles Sumner follow. Civil War press work and the New York Draft Riots of eighteen sixty three fill later chapters. A talk with Count Bismarck adds a European crown.
61977-the-domestic-slave-trade-of-the-so:
Winfield Collins wrote The Domestic Slave Trade of the Southern States, copyrighted in 1904. Broadway Publishing of New York put out the book. Collins taught history and English at Claremont College. His preface says he began the study with no sense of where it would lead. That holds most for the third and fourth chapters of the work. His facts were drawn from the Yale library and the Congressional Library at Washington.

 Chapters sketch the rise of the African trade and the foreign trade of the South. Causes, amount, and extent of the home trade follow in order. One chapter asks if some states bred and raised Negroes for sale. A last chapter treats the kidnapping and sale of free Negroes. The book is a plain, sourced study of a grim trade.
61981-british-butterflies:
Stewart wrote this guide to British butterflies for the Peeps at Nature series, first published in 1912 and reissued in London in 1918. Sixteen full-page pictures show all the species, eight of them in colour and eight from photographs. The first plate alone names nine kinds, from the swallow-tail and black-veined white to the orange tip and wood white.

Three chapters make up the text. The first gives the life history of a butterfly, and the second tells how to catch and keep specimens. The third and longest part describes the British butterflies one by one. An index closes the book, which was plainly meant for beginners who wanted to name what they saw outdoors.
62001-the-cross-a-tract-for-the-times:
The Cross is a tract for the times by the Reverend J C Ryle, printed at Ipswich in 1851. Ryle was rector of Helmingham in Suffolk and had written Living or Dead and Assurance. The tract sold at two shillings a dozen for wide giving.

Ryle opens by asking the reader what he thinks and feels about the cross of Christ. He notes that the reader lives in a Christian land and most likely sits in a Christian church. A quote from Robert Traill of 1690 heads the piece, on faith built on a dying Christ. Ryle rests his case on Paul words to the Galatians, on glorying only in the cross. Church readers get a short, grave call to true faith.
62020-lightfoot-the-leaping-goat-his-man:
Lightfoot the Leaping Goat is a children's animal story by Richard Barnum, issued at New York in 1917 with pictures by Walter Rogers. It belongs to a kneetime animal series, the front pages say. Barnum's other animal tales are listed there: a comical pig, a jolly elephant, a runaway dog, and a trick pony. A front picture shows a man driving Lightfoot up and down a block, giving a boy and his nurse a fine ride.

The contents march Lightfoot through mishap and rescue in turn. His big leap, his hurt, and his saving of a girl open the tale. A wagon, a park, a butted boy, and a boat follow. Lightfoot goes on a voyage, comes ashore, roams the woods, meets a squirrel friend, and finds a new home at the end.
62030-a-capillary-crime-and-other-storie:
A Capillary Crime and Other Stories is a book of short tales by F D Millet, published by Harper and Brothers of New York in 1892. The title story is joined by A Faded Scapular, Yatil, Tedesco's Rubina, Medusa's Head, The Fourth Waits, and The Bush. A front picture shows the look of Mandel's studio on the morning after his death.

The title tale opens in a little street near the top of the hill in Montmartre, Paris. Grass grows between its paving stones, garden walls line much of its length, and no wheels pass. The lane turns and shoots up a slope too steep for a horse. Two minutes from the busy boulevards, the corner sits as quiet as a village. Millet anchors his mystery in that stillness.
62032-the-hypnotic-experiment-of-dr-reev:
Charlotte Rosalys Jones wrote The Hypnotic Experiment of Dr Reeves and other stories. Bliss, Sands and Foster issued it at London in 1894. Doctor Edward Reeves treats rheumatism by secret means. His fellow doctors shun him for that silence. Rivals call him a charlatan in print. The rheumatic public makes him a demi-god instead.

In genial moods Reeves tells curious tales, Jones writes. One strange experiment came in romantic settings. He tells that one in his own words here. A young man of twenty-eight came to his hospital. Heart rheumatism in severe form plagued the man. A younger brother attended him with rare devotion. The invalid hid a single great desire, Reeves says. He longed to shake the subtle disease off. Late Victorian tales of mesmerism and medicine trade on the era's hunger for mind cures and marvels.
62073-george-borrow-s-second-tour-in-wal:
George Borrow's Second Tour in Wales is a topographical paper by Cantrill and Pringle, printed in Y Cymmrodor in 1910. David Price transcribed the edition. The paper traces a journey that Borrow's readers barely know. Three years after the 1854 expedition to North Wales, Borrow made a rapid traverse of the south-west of the principality.

The incidents of the first tour formed the basis of Wild Wales. Of the second, the only published record is the brief itinerary in Knapp's Life of Borrow. The authors' professional duties took them for years into Carmarthen and Pembroke, the very counties Borrow crossed in 1857. Not content with the bald outline, one of them wrote to Knapp in Paris for details of the villages passed and the inns used. Their paper rebuilds the lost tour mile by mile from the ground itself.
62105-the-girl-scouts-vacation-adventure:
Edith Lavell wrote The Girl Scouts' Vacation Adventures, published by the Burt Company in New York in 1924. Lavell wrote a whole series about the Pansy Troop: at school, at camp, on a canoe trip, and on the ranch. A picture at the front shows the girls hanging a sign for the Pansy Tea-Room outside a hedge.

The story opens in spring vacation, with ten lazy days of April ahead. Daisy Gravers faces a lonely house while her mother visits a married sister. Then comes an invitation from Florence Evans: a week in New York, with parties and old friends home from college. The seven girls of the senior patrol, together the summer before in Wyoming, form the heart of the series. Their friendship drives this vacation tale.
62116-a-working-plan-for-colored-antitub:
Wertenbaker, a surgeon of the Public Health and Marine-Hospital Service, wrote this working plan in 1909. The Government Printing Office issued it as a reprint from the Public Health Reports. Its aim was war on consumption, the great killer of the age.

A plan for such leagues had run in the Reports of May 28, 1909. It dreamt of a league in each state, with a branch in every colored church. Once formed, though, the leagues stuck: the work was new, and their folk had no practice in it. Wertenbaker writes to cure just that fault. How to form a state league, run its branches, and teach clean air and rest fills the guide. A plain tool from a grim fight.
62127-on-the-processes-for-the-productio:
John Vinycomb wrote On the Processes for the Production of Ex Libris (Book-Plates) for A and C Black at London in 1894. The pieces were reprinted from the Journal of the Ex Libris Society, with extra illustrations. Vinycomb was president of the Belfast Art Society and a council member of the Ex Libris Society.

He dedicated the little book to Arthur Vicars, Ulster King of Arms and an eminent collector. The preface writer praises Vinycomb for taking a fresh path: not the history or styles of book-plates, but the modes of execution. Etching, engraving, and the many methods of making and copying plates are set out in a concise, clear account. A plate shows the Franklin Press, then at Philadelphia.
62135-chunky-the-happy-hippo-his-many-ad:
Chunky, the Happy Hippo is a children's animal story by Richard Barnum, published in 1918. It belongs to the Kneetime Animal Stories, a series that also includes Squinty the Comical Pig and Tum Tum the Jolly Elephant. Rogers drew the pictures. Twelve chapters follow Chunky from his home waters to a circus.

The chapter list tells the plot in brief: Chunky laughs, is bitten by a crocodile, falls in the mud, is caught, and takes a trip. He sails on a ship, falls overboard, and learns a new trick in the circus. A little girl named Alice rides on his broad back in the frontispiece. The tales were written as bedtime reading for young children.
62138-cannibal-land-adventures-with-a-ca:
Martin Johnson told of trips with a film box in the New Hebrides. Men of Espiritu Santo front his book in a bold plate. The book came out in Boston and New York in 1922. Its rights date to 1921 and 1922 in two claims. Nagapate is the chief whose name leads the first parts in line.

Sydney and New Caledonia start the road to that wild land. The lip of Cannibal-Land and a call from Nagapate come next. In his realm, the big men see their own selves on screen. Good bye to him and the ape folk fill the mid road parts. Paint dances and Tomman's head cure craft stand in the list. A feast ends it.
62173-mordred-and-hildebrand-a-book-of-t:
William Wilfred Campbell wrote this book of tragedies, Mordred and Hildebrand, printed at Ottawa in 1895. Campbell also wrote The Dread Voyage and Lake Lyrics. He dedicates the book to two friends named on its dedication page. The first play fills the hosted opening: Mordred, a tragedy in five acts.

A title page states its source: founded on the Arthurian legend of Malory. Campbell wrote it, a note adds, in the summer of 1893. The cast lists Arthur, king of Britain, Mordred his son, Launcelot, Merlin, Gwaine, Guinevere, Vivien, and Elaine, who loves Launcelot. Act one opens at a hermitage in the woods, where Arthur and Launcelot alight to rest and think on their sins. Arthur speaks first of his black mood, and Launcelot begs him to shake it off for Britain's sake.
62182-good-councell-against-the-plague-s:
Good Councell against the Plague is a plague tract printed in London in 1592. John Charlwood printed it for Thomas Nelson. Its title promises sundry present preservatives against the sickness. Wholesome fumes, drinks, and vomits are among the inward receipts. A perfect cure by plaster is promised for those already infected. The tract was writ, its page says, by a learned physician for the health of his country. It was made needful by the plague then rising in the city.

The first counsel is cleanliness. Houses, streets, yards, and sinks must be kept sweet and clean. Standing puddles breed stinking savours that feed infection. Dogs are a grave warning: they run from house to house on the foulest food. They take infection of any sickness and carry it in. The book is a plain Tudor guide to a householder's war on plague.
62234-shrubs-for-kansas-landscapes:
Shrubs for Kansas Landscapes, a circular of the Cooperative Extension Service at Kansas State University in Manhattan, was written by Gary McDaniel, the service's specialist in landscaping and environmental horticulture. McDaniel thanks Larry Leuthold for comments and Joe Roller for the illustrations.

The bulletin teaches choosing shrubs by purpose. A checklist names the uses: accent, border, softening a building's look, screening poor views, privacy, holding a soil bank, and ground cover. Accent planting belongs at the front entryway, McDaniel warns, and never make both sides of a door completely symmetrical. A strong accent on one side and a lesser one on the other serves better. Accent plants do not belong on the corners of a house at all.
62273-devonshire-witches:
Paul Q Karkeek read Devonshire Witches at Teignmouth in July 1874. The paper was reprinted from the Transactions of the Devonshire Association for the Advancement of Science, Literature, and Art. Karkeek opens with Buckle's theory: the climate and scenery of a country shape its people's creed. Devon's broad moors, deep valleys, and stormy coasts inclined its people to belief in the miraculous, he argues. Traces of that belief survive in his own day.

Scores in the western shires still believe in charms and consult the wise man, he writes. Sufferers from the evil eye are constantly heard of. Before James the First, the statute book looked mildly on witchcraft, with laws of 1551 and 1562. James the Demonologist brought matters to a climax. Belief and prosecution then spread like an epidemic, and the accused were seldom acquitted.
623-the-battle-of-the-books-and-other-sh:
Jonathan Swift satirizes the war between ancient and modern learning in this volume, with other short pieces. The Battle of the Books stages a fight in a library, where ancients and moderns clash over wit and worth. An introduction traces Swift from Dublin birth, seven months after his father's death, to Trinity College and fame.

Swift writes with cold, brilliant irony, mocking pride on both sides of the quarrel. The short pieces add wit and bite. The book serves as a fine entry to Swift, where a library brawl becomes a lasting joke on how ages judge each other.
62301-canoemates-a-story-of-the-florida-:
Kirk Munroe's Canoemates, a story of the Florida reef and Everglades, was published by Harper in 1893. Munroe had written The Flamingo Feather and Dorymates before it. Forty chapters cruise with Sumner and his companions Worth and Quorum. The canoes Cupid and Psyche start the voyage among the keys. Teaching a thief a lesson and the great Florida reef come early. The canoes vanish mysteriously, and life on a lonely island follows.

Sumner drifts away on a raft and is picked up in the Gulf Stream. A night in Alligator Light, pineapples and sponges, and an entertainment on the key fill the middle. The party turns off for the Everglades: a prehistoric mound, a closely guarded camp, and a night hemmed in by forest fire. The boys reach a Seminole camp and meet one of the rarest animals in the world.
62323-the-sword-of-johnny-damokles:
Hugh Frazier Parker wrote The Sword of Johnny Damokles, a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in March 1943. The Tsom clan of Neptune, a dread people, have taken root from the mad dreams of a crazed dictator of the past. Their invasion threatens a dozen peaceful worlds.

Little Timmy Gordon and Johnny Damokles can do almost nothing, for they are prisoners of the Tsom. They work on the monster bomb that is to signal the invasion. The scene opens at Spaceport X on Callisto, where dust beats gritty against the window and Neptune shines pale blue and clear. Timmy wonders where the planet ever got its name. Parker hangs his sword over two captive boys, in plain sight of the title. Pulp readers of 1943 got their war in space dress, with Earth tyranny reborn among the moons of Jupiter.
62398-a-trip-to-the-rockies:
The Knickerbocker Press issued a trip tale in New York in 1890, signed only with short initials by its writer. A party of bankers and trade men from New York and Brooklyn rode west for the yearly meeting of the American Bankers' Association. The meeting sat at Kansas City on September 24th and 25th.

Ben Blanchard wired that each guest would have a Pullman section and might bring his wife. The car was too long for the short curves by Washington, so the party rode through Harrisburg, Johnstown, and Altoona. A Brooklyn paper's report of the start from Jersey City on September 23d opens the gay record of the fortnight.
62402-galileo-and-his-judges:
Galileo and His Judges, a study by F R Wegg-Prosser, was published by Chapman and Hall of London in 1889. Few names in science, the preface says, have raised so long and fierce a fight. Historians, astronomers, and theologians have all taken shares in it. Wegg-Prosser enters the dispute to set the facts straight, not to write a full life.

He limits himself to the great crises of Galileo's career that drew the argument. Unfairness on one side, he holds, has been met by injudicious zeal and error on the other. The first chapter sketches the growth of astronomy up to Galileo's time. Only against that ground, he argues, can the worth of the man's work be judged, neither swollen nor shrunk by bias.
62411-dick-merriwell-s-glory-or-friends-:
Dick Merriwell Glory stands in the long Merriwell set of tales for young men. Front pages praise the set for sports thrills and clean moral tone. Frank and Dick Merriwell play fair with self and with all men. Half a million fans were said to follow the brothers tales.

The set was pitched to fire a boy aim to be a strong athlete. Tales span school days, Yale, races, and trips west and south. This volume bears the theme of friends and foes in its title. Readers get sport, grit, and high ideals in the Merriwell mold.
62441-sharp-eyes-the-silver-fox-his-many:
Richard Barnum wrote a children's tale of a silver fox, issued in New York in 1918 in his Kneetime Animal Stories. Each book in the set cost fifty cents and told of one animal, from Squinty the pig to Chunky the hippo. Sharp Eyes lives far up in the North Woods.

His fox family wear coats of red-yellow and gray, and must live by quickness and slyness, since a fox is not strong. Chapter heads promise that Sharp Eyes sees, catches, and hears things, is hurt, captured, and sold. He visits a zoo, meets Chunky, and at last gets home. Young children get the wild world told at their own scale.
62453-achilles:
Achilles, in the series Life Stories for Young People, was translated and abridged from the German of Carl Friedrich Becker by George P Upton. A C McClurg published it at Chicago in 1912, with three illustrations.

Upton's preface explains that Becker follows the lines of Homer's Iliad through the ten years' siege of Troy. The Greeks under Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, fight to redress the wrong done to Menelaus, whose wife Helen was carried off by Paris. The turning points are the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, the death of Patroclus, the death of Hector, and old Priam's visit to recover his son's body. The fate of Achilles himself is not told.
62486-ruffled-doilies:
Ruffled Doilies is a crochet pattern booklet from the American Thread Company, sold as Star Doily Book number 143 for ten cents. The company gives its address on West Broadway in New York. The patterns use the firm's own Puritan mercerized crochet cotton.

The first pattern, Blossom Ruffle, calls for four balls of white, cream, or ecru cotton and a number seven steel hook. Worked as directed, it makes a doily about seventeen and a half inches across, before the ruffle. Round-by-round instructions follow, with chains, single crochet, double crochet, and treble clusters spelled out in abbreviations. Later patterns in the booklet use the firm's Star brand cotton. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
62495-portland-oregon-a-d-1999-and-other:
Jeff Hayes wrote a futuristic romance of his own city, published at Portland in 1913, and dedicated to its citizens and the dear friends of his earlier life. The changes his tale reports as established facts, his preface says, are merely the signs of the times, and not one-half of the story is told.

Part one proceeds by prophecy: a visitor arrives, prophecies startle, old names are revived, and the prophetess grows jocose. Part two changes key entirely, gathering Western sketches and tall tales: the bad man from Bodie, a governor for fifteen minutes, gold growing on sage brush, and the office at Spirit Lake. Oregon boosterism in two registers, vision and yarn, fills the little volume.
62505-tamba-the-tame-tiger-his-many-adve:
Richard Barnum's 1919 children's story, from the Kneetime Animal Stories, follows Tamba, a tame tiger who lives in a circus-wagon cage next door to Nero the lion. The first chapter finds Tamba cross.

Tamba growls at Nero for letting his tail slip between the cage bars, while Tum Tum the elephant and Chunky the hippo wonder what ails their tame tiger. Chapters carry Tamba through a wreck, a barn, the city, the subway, a ship, and the jungle. Walter Rogers drew the pictures. Barnum's series also includes Squinty the pig and Mappo the monkey. Barnum also wrote Squinty the Comical Pig, Tum Tum the Jolly Elephant, and Nero the Circus Lion.
62509-russian-folk-tales:
Leonard A Magnus translated a set of Russian folk tales, first published in 1915 with an introduction and notes. A guide to pronouncing Russian words comes before the tales. Stories include The Dun Cow, tales of the dead, and The Bear, the Dog and the Cat. Others tell of Egóri the Brave, Danílo the Unfortunate, and a sorry drunkard.

Bába Yagá appears, as do Mark the Rich and a miraculous hen. One long tale follows Iván Tsarévich, the Bird of Light, and the Grey Wolf. Magnus kept the accented spelling to help English readers say the names. The book is a broad sample of Russian story tradition.
62514-jataka-tales:
Ellen Babbitt retells Jataka Tales for children, in a Century Company book from New York in 1912. Ellsworth Young drew the pictures, and Babbitt dedicates the volume to Dot. Eighteen short tales, told in plain words, feature animals who talk, scheme, and learn hard lessons.

The Monkey and the Crocodile opens the set, as a young crocodile offers a monkey a ride to an island of ripe fruit. His mother wants a monkey's heart to eat, and the ride turns into a dive meant to drown the passenger. Other tales include a turtle who could not stop talking, quails who quarrel, a banyan deer, and a crab who outwits a crane. Each story rewards quick wits over brute force.
62549-the-second-boys-book-of-model-aero:
Francis A Collins wrote The Second Boys Book of Model Aeroplanes, issued by The Century Company in New York in nineteen eleven. Collins had written a first book on the same theme. Many photos and drawings by the author fill the pages. The list of plates shows gliders, monoplanes, and biplanes. One plate notes an English mark of twenty six hundred feet.

Inside, boys learn how to shape planes, propellers, and frames for small flying craft. Designs include sling shot gliders, paper gliders, and a French model built of aluminium. Names of young builders appear with their work, such as Cecil Peoli and Harry McAllister. The book shows how keen boys were on flight in the first years of the aeroplane age.
62552-terrain-exercises:
Terrain Exercises, by Waldron, an infantry officer of the Army, was published in Washington in 1923 by the United States Infantry Association. Nine exercises drill officers over real ground with imaginary troops. They cover attack of a strong point by a rifle company, and approach march and deployment. A defensive position and a machine gun company in attack follow. An advance guard, a flank guard, an outpost, and two kinds of patrol close the set.

The introduction defines the method. In a terrain exercise, students carry on the operations of imaginary bodies of troops over the actual terrain. The step is the logical one between classroom theory and field work with real troops. Waldron argues the ground itself teaches: how to use cover, choose formations, and fit tactics to hills and roads. Commanders of the day used such exercises constantly to train their officers.
62571-wellington-s-men-some-soldier-auto:
W H Fitchett edited this set of soldier memoirs, printed by George Bell and Sons in London and Bombay in 1900. The edition was made for sale in India and the colonies only. Fitchett had won readers with Deeds That Won the Empire and Fights for the Flag. Here he gathers four rank-and-file accounts of the wars against Napoleon.

The men are Kincaid of the Rifle Brigade, Rifleman Harris, Anton, and Mercer of Waterloo fame. Their pages run from Torres Vedras to the Pyrenees, Quatre Bras, and the field of Waterloo itself. Fitchett says the book saves fine memoirs from neglect and shows great battles as the men who fought them saw them, not as later writers framed them.
62602-shakspeare-and-his-times:
Monsieur Guizot wrote Shakspeare and His Times, and Harper and Brothers issued the work at New York from their Franklin Square house. His essay on Shakespeare's life and works first served as the opening essay to a French edition of the plays at Paris in 1821. That edition rested on Le Tourneur's version, begun in 1776.

Guizot revised six tragedies, ten historical dramas, and three comedies himself. De Barante translated Hamlet, and Amédée Pichot revised the rest. Guizot doubts any version can pour Shakespeare's genius into French with its true character. He calls Shakespeare excellent in substance but deficient in form. The volume joins the life to essays on the plays and the age that made them.
62608-rat-proofing-buildings-and-premise:
Rat Proofing Buildings and Premises is a farmers' bulletin of the United States Department of Agriculture. It is bulletin number sixteen thirty eight, issued at Washington in December nineteen thirty. Three men wrote it: two biologists of the rodent control service and a senior architect. Contents open with an introduction and general principles of rat proofing.

Food and shelter are as essential to rats as to other animals, the text begins. Removing them offers a practical means of lasting rat control, it argues. The number of rats on premises matches the food supply and shelter there, it says. Rat proofing in the broad sense means more than barring rats from buildings. It also means cutting off their food and clearing their hiding places. All new buildings should be made rat proof, it urges.
62664-three-little-lines:
Josie Moore Crum wrote Three Little Lines, on the Silverton Railroad, the Silverton, Gladstone and Northerly, and the Silverton Northern. The articles first appeared in a Railway and Locomotive Historical Society bulletin in October nineteen forty eight. This volume, with copyright in nineteen sixty, adds new matter and pictures. The Durango Herald News at Durango, Colorado, published it. A cover picture shows the covered turntable at Corkscrew Gulch.

The Silverton Railroad is the most intriguing piece of narrow gauge in the world, Crum opens. It holds the steepest grades, the sharpest curves, the crookedest loops, and the highest altitude, she says. One switchback held a wye with a depot inside, and another a housed over turntable, she adds. The famous Otto Mears built the lines. Rail fans get a classic Colorado narrow gauge history.
62667-a-tale-of-brittany-mon-fre-re-yves:
A Tale of Brittany, known in French as Mon Frere Yves, by Pierre Loti, appears here in English dress by Baines, published in New York by Stokes. Loti dedicates the little tale to Alphonse Daudet, with affection. The book runs to one hundred and two short chapters, a sign of Loti's diary-like method. Front matter notes a stock charge against his books, that they hold too much of himself.

The tale, whose French title means My Brother Yves, centers on Yves, a Breton sailor, and the naval officer who treats him as a brother. Brittany ports, ships, drink, and duty shape their bond. Loti writes of the sea and of simple hearts with a lush, wistful prose that made the book one of his most loved works.
62677-street-trees:
Street Trees, by a Bureau of Plant Industry horticulturist named Mulford, is Bulletin Number 816 of the United States Department of Agriculture. The Government Printing Office in Washington issued it in January 1920. Mulford wrote for cities and towns that plant and care for trees along their streets.

The bulletin moves from the value of shade trees to public control of street planting, then to planning, spacing, and the conditions trees need in city soil. Long sections name the kinds of trees fit for city streets, by region and by special purpose, with plain descriptions of each. Later chapters cover choosing single trees, digging and planting, pruning, stakes and guards, and the feeding and spraying of mature trees. The aim throughout is practical: the right tree, in the right place, kept alive.
62749-strange-peoples:
Frederick Starr wrote a school book on strange peoples, printed at Boston in 1901 for forty cents. It stands first in a set of land and peoples readers. Starr owns he took his stuff where he found it. His aim was to make the maps in the school geography live for children.

He hopes the sketches give young readers a broader kindness toward other peoples. French and German works on the races of man fed the book most. Starr refused to hold other folk up to scorn. Their odd or dread ways are not paraded, he says. Our own way of life has faults enough to bar such sport. Few peoples are taken, here and there, from the whole wide field.
62771-horse-tales:
Mary Boyle wrote Horse Tales, with pen and ink pictures by Isabel Watkin, issued at London and New York by Ernest Nister and E P Dutton. Sally leads the first tale and gives it her name. A front print shows Sally the mare. John Dobbin's farm holds the scene.

John's stock holds a short horned cow, a limping calf, sheep, fowls, and a pig with eight young. Sally is an everyday lazy kind of horse, the tale says. One morning John feeds all, then leaves Sally loose to keep an eye on things. He goes to Farmer Peckett, who lies ill with rheumatism. Sally feels glum and lost without him. She watches the calf in the lettuces and the hen in the carrots. The tales give farm beasts thoughts and speech for young readers.
62783-lob-lie-by-the-fire-the-brownies-a:
Juliana Horatia Ewing gathers folk and fairy tales for young readers in the hosted volume. The title tale treats Lob Lie-by-the-fire, a rough brownie or house elf of north-country farms. Lob threshes in one night what ten men could not finish, then stretches by the fire for his bowl of cream.

Other tales include Timothy's Shoes, Old Father Christmas, Benjy in Beastland, and The Brownies, plus The Land of Lost Toys and Amelia and the Dwarfs. A short piece called Spoons, by Frances Henshaw Baden, is added at the end. Readers get kind, witty stories rooted in farm lore, feast days, and the secret work of household sprites.
62786-spain-and-her-colonies-compiled-fr:
Archibald Wilberforce compiled this history of Spain and her colonies from the best authorities, for a series called The World's Best Histories. A portrait of Alfonso the Thirteenth, king of Spain, fronts the book. The first chapter asks what Hispania meant and who came first: Greeks, Phoenicians, Romans, and Goths all left their mark.

Thirteen chapters run from Spain in antiquity through the caliphate of Cordova, Moorish Spain, and the Inquisition. United Spain and modern Spain follow, then colonial Spain, the fall of an empire, and the Philippines. A chapter on the Hispano-American war brings the story to the author's own day, and a last one treats Spanish art, literature, and sport. It is a full popular survey in one volume.
62794-toto-the-bustling-beaver-his-many-:
Toto, the Bustling Beaver is an animal story for children by Richard Barnum. Barse and Hopkins published the book at New York in 1920, with pictures by Walter Rogers. The tale belongs to the Kneetime Animal Stories, a shelf of beast tales by the same hand. Twelve chapters follow the young beaver's doings.

The story opens on the ice of Winding River in winter. Mother Beaver climbs out and calls for her little boy in beaver speech. She sits on her broad flat tail, which makes a fair seat, and scans the stream. Toto is off helping a friend, as the first chapter's title promises. Later chapters bring tramps, burglars, a trap, and a boat ride. A storm and a falling tree close the adventures. Barnum writes talking animals for the youngest readers.
62819-successful-baking-for-flavor-and-t:
Martha Lee Anderson wrote a baking book of tested methods, in a sixth edition printed at New York in 1937 by a soda making house. Kitchen hints fill pages at the back of the book, Anderson notes. Good baking, she opens, is one more way of keeping a family happy through the day.

Aroma of spicy gingerbread or a slice of rich chocolate cake can fill a home with joy of living, she says. Hot breads, cinnamon buns, lemon rolls, soda biscuits, and corn bread add zest to a meal. Her secret is baking soda, the same lift grandmothers used, which frees gas when it meets the mild acids in foods.
62822-exits-and-entrances:
Exits and Entrances is a book of stage memoirs by Eva Moore. It came out in London in 1923 from Chapman and Hall, with twenty pictures. A verse from As You Like It stands on the title page: all the world's a stage, and the men and women merely players, with their exits and their entrances. The book is given to Harry, whose words head each chapter, the author says, of what is in truth his book and hers.

The contents open with Home, then The Start and Wedding Bells. Plays and Players stand later in the list as shown. The front picture is a photo of the author by Claude Harris of London. The work is the life story of an actress, told from her home and her first steps to the stage world she came to know.
62854-stoles:
Book 161 of the Bernat Handicrafter, priced at twenty-five cents, is devoted to stoles. Julia Traphagen edited the series, with Carleen Goldsmith as associate editor. Before any pattern, the book preaches its one doctrine: stitch gauge.

The term stitch gauge, the hints declare, is the most important part of all knitting directions. The sizing of any garment is planned on this gauge, and you must work to the gauge given or the finished work will not be the size indicated. Cast on about twenty stitches, work three inches in the pattern stitch, bind off, block the swatch, and count. Too many stitches to the inch means a larger needle; too few, a smaller. Bernat, a yarn house, sold its wool by selling competence first. The gauge sermon opens thousands of pattern books like an oath.
62855-treasury-of-american-indian-tales:
Theodore Whitson Ressler's Treasury of American Indian Tales was published in New York by Bonanza Books, by arrangement with the Association Press. The copyright of 1957 was held by the National Board of the Young Men's Christian Association. Ressler dedicates the book to his son William Frederick, in words that set its tone. The ways of the Indian were good, honesty and truth sacred to them, courage a part of their lives.

Forty-four stories from twenty-seven tribes fill the treasury, grouped under heads like Adventure and Hunting and Fishing. Each tale is credited to its tribe. Little Rabbit Discovers a Secret of Strength goes to the Pueblo, and the secret lake of Atagahi to the Cherokee. Quarter Moon and Little Elk are Iroquois, and a kitten bringing a boy his feather is Nez Perce.
62875-the-queen-versus-billy-and-other-s:
The Queen versus Billy and Other Stories, by Lloyd Osbourne, was printed in New York by Charles Scribner Sons in 1900. Nine tales fill the book. Osbourne was the stepson of Robert Louis Stevenson and wrote with him on South Sea themes.

The title tale opens as the Sandfly, Captain Toombs, brings news to Sydney and stops a third class cruiser, the Stingaree, in Man of War Cove. The news is the same old story, one more white man sent to his account in the Solomons. Thomas Hysslop Biggar, known as Captain Tom, aged forty six, a British trader in copra, is dead. Other tales treat the Beautiful Man of Pingalap, the Dust of Defeat, Father Zosimus, and Amatua Sailor. Sea tale fans get sharp Pacific stories of trade, greed, and sudden death.
62903-greycliff-heroines:
Greycliff Heroines is a girls' novel of 1923 by Harriet Pyne Grove, put out in New York by the Burt Company. The title page lists it among the Greycliff Girls books, a run of tales for girls. Its frontispiece shows Cathalina diving from a point to catch Isabel in the water. The first chapter is called Guests on the Way. It opens at Bath, Maine, where a young camp councillor lands from a launch with two boys.

On the dock he meets his aunt, come in on the train from Portland. The girls are on their way from Merrymeeting Camp, and the party must be met and sorted. The meeting sets the stage for a summer of camp and shore life. Grove wrote four more Greycliff books, all named on the same page.
62910-the-spider-and-other-tales:
Spider and Other Tales gathers stories by Carl Ewald, rendered from the Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The New York edition was published in April nineteen oh seven. Nine tales fill the book, most of them nature pieces. Their heads name the spider, the mist, anemones, a queen bee, and a caterpillar.

A beech and an oak share one tale, weeds another. A water lily and a dragon fly pair off in a third. The title tale opens in a hedge once full of trees and bushes. The trees were cut down, and only long thin twigs shoot from their stubs. Weeds of the wild chervil sort crowd between the stubs. They strut and swagger as if they were bushes themselves, the tale says.
62944-experiments-of-spiritual-life-heal:
Roger Williams of Providence wrote these experiments of spiritual life and health. The tract first printed at London in 1652, reprinted 1863 at Providence. An introduction says the work was long unknown to scholars. Knowles memoir notes no copy had come to knowledge then.

The book presents evidences of personal piety and guards them from abuse. Part one treats weak, imperfect piety marks in the believer soul. Part two treats vigorous, maturer piety evidences in fuller growth. Part three gives directions for keeping and growing piety daily. No sectarian bitterness stands in it, the introduction says, only a Baxter like spirit.
62949-good-night-buenas-noches:
Good-Night (Buenas Noches), by Eleanor Gates, is a story of old California mission days. Crowell issued it at New York, rights held in 1906 and 1907 in turn. Arthur Rackham drew the plates, including a padre frontispiece in full colour. Loretta, a grey parrot, opens the tale on a perch by an adobe wall.

She snaps scarlet fuchsias onto Padre Alonzo open book as he reads below. The padre scolds her in Spanish and warns of the kitchen cats fate. Tomasso the cat stalks through the plate list, a threat in fur. Padre Anzar plant and the last fuchsias of the year set the scene. Spanish phrases season this gentle mission garden tale.
63014-masterpieces-of-adventure-stories-:
Nella Braddy edited a book of adventure tales of desert places, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1922. The set of masterpieces runs to four volumes. Braddy gives this one gratefully to Blanche Colton Williams. Seven tales by famed hands fill the table, each set in dry and dangerous country.

The Baron's Quarry by Egerton Castle leads, with a hunting tale told in a gentle, endless voice. Stephen Crane gives A Man and Some Others, and Selma Lagerlof gives The Outlaws. Bret Harte, Thomas Hardy, O Henry, and Hudson follow with princesses, strangers, eagles, and a devil child. Desert heat, loneliness, and sudden violence bind tales from five lands into one strong book for adventure lovers.
63015-masterpieces-of-adventure-oriental:
Nella Braddy edited Oriental Stories, one volume of Masterpieces of Adventure, printed at Garden City in 1922. Six tales from the East fill the book. Authors include Nathan Parker Willis, Washington Irving, and Jack London.

The first tale tells of a Chinese emperor who foils a plot by palace staff and then rides out to war. Other tales visit a pasha's garden, a hunt for a golden fleece, and two samurai. London adds a night scene in Goboto. Readers get a varied set of short adventure tales tied to lands and legends of the East. Short notes on each author help place the tales for new readers today.
63029-shaggo-the-mighty-buffalo-his-many:
Shaggo, the Mighty Buffalo is a children's animal story by Richard Barnum, published by Barse and Hopkins in 1921. It belongs to the Kneetime Animal Stories, a series of talking animal books for young readers. Walter S Rogers drew the illustrations. Barnum's other heroes line the series list.

Squinty the comical pig, Tum Tum the jolly elephant, and Sharp Eyes the silver fox keep Shaggo company on that list. Nero the circus lion and Tamba the tame tiger point toward Shaggo's own fate. The frontispiece shows the buffalo beginning to like life in the circus. In these books the animals speak, feel, and reason through adventures written in simple chapters. Shaggo's many adventures carry a plains buffalo from wild herd to show ring, in the gentle didactic style of the series.
63074-scottish-reminiscences:
Archibald Geikie looks back on a long life in Scottish Reminiscences, first printed in 1904 and reprinted at Glasgow in 1908. The metadata names the Glasgow press, but the title page names Geikie as the writer. His preface sets out a life of travel in every part of Scotland.

For sixty years, he says, he mixed with folk of all ranks. He watched old ways decay and new ways rise in their place. All that time he kept an eye out for native humour and told his tales to friends. Readers get warm tales of Scots folk, work, and wit from a man who saw much change.
63102-two-years-in-the-french-west-indie:
Two Years in the French West Indies is Lafcadio Hearn's travel book on Martinique. Harper reissued it in 1923 with photographs and drawings. Hearn dedicates the book to his friend Léopold Arnoux of Saint Pierre, in memory of their walks and talks in the land of revenants.

The Martinique sketches form the heart of the book: the porters, the washerwomen, the volcano Pelée, ghosts and devils of Creole folklore, and Creole melodies in an appendix. The foreword opens in siesta silence at a Fort-de-France hotel, where only a landlady's piping voice, bare feet on tiles, pigeons and a fountain break the midday sleep. The illustration list is elegiac: street after street of Saint Pierre as ruins, photographed after the eruption that destroyed the town Hearn had loved.
63168-the-soul-of-a-cat-and-other-storie:
The Soul of a Cat and Other Stories, by Margaret Benson, was published by William Heinemann in London in 1901, with illustrations by Henrietta Ronner and from photographs. A dedication in verse addresses the animals described in the book, its gracious creatures and tiny souls.

Twelve pieces follow. The title story gives Persis, a dainty Persian cat, blue and white and silky haired. Joey and Matilda, or Intellect and Emotion, and The Torpid and the Ill-Bred Cat come next. Vanity of Vanities, Taffy, and The Adopted Family follow. The Mysterious Ra and Mentu keep the Egyptian names. The Conscience of the Barn-Door Fowl and Confucius widen the menagerie. A Paradise of Birds and an epilogue close the volume. Persis, in middle age, had kittens and grew to hate them, with a hatred founded on jealousy and love.
63184-thrifty-stock-and-other-stories:
Ben Ames Williams collected these stories in a 1923 Dutton volume, dedicated to Robert Davis. Williams was known for Evered, the story of the famous red bull, and for Black Pawl, which the New York Times praised in high terms. Seventeen stories and a note fill the contents. Titles include They Grind Exceeding Small, Old Tantrybogus, One Crowded Hour, and Mine Enemy's Dog.

The title story opens above the village of Fraternity, where Lucia Moore storms out of the old farmhouse. Her father is stubborn, her mother supine, and the world at an ill turn, she feels. She crosses the wet stubble to a boulder under an apple tree and sits with her chin in her hands. The George's River winds through the valley below, backed up by the mill dam, in country Williams renders in loving color.
63191-winkie-the-wily-woodchuck-her-many:
Richard Barnum wrote a children's animal story for his Kneetime series, published in 1922 with pictures by Walter Rogers. Winkie is a woodchuck called wily because she is smart and careful, always on the lookout for traps and danger. Her sister is Blinkie, and their home is an underground house.

The first chapter opens on a hot day, with Winkie asking what they shall do next and Blinkie voting to sit by the front door. Chapters take Winkie through a storm, a trap, a new home, and lessons in tricks. She meets Don, a runaway dog from another book in the series. At last Winkie finds her folks, to her mother's cry of joy in the frontispiece.
