63221-travels-in-virginia-in-revolutiona:
Morrison edited this book of travels, Travels in Virginia in Revolutionary Times, copyrighted at Lynchburg, Virginia, in 1922. An advertisement at the front sets the span: from 1769 to 1802, when the United States still lay east of France and Spain, and Virginia reached west to the river Ohio. Virginia then, the editor says, was a proud commonwealth, thought at home and abroad the most weighty of the new states.

The travellers are named by kind. One was in the country before the war and shot for King George; another came with the king's troops and saw Virginia on parole. A chaplain and a general of the allied army follow, and a surgeon from Hesse whose book the editor praises. After the war came men of science, young sightseers, a missionary, a sad emigrant from France, and a sailor turned novelist.
63230-two-stories:
Two Stories is the first publication of the Hogarth Press, printed at Richmond in 1917. The press was the Woolfs' own, and the booklet was written and printed by Virginia Woolf and Leonard Woolf, as the title page proudly says. It holds two tales: Three Jews by Leonard, and The Mark on the Wall by Virginia.

Leonard's story opens on the first day of spring. The narrator sits restless at his window, watching the black trees break into bud and the tulips and hyacinths that even London cannot rob of colour. He wants clean trees, unsmoked grass, and above all the horizon. Something, he feels, waits beyond the houses and chimney pots. Virginia's companion piece, a meditation set off by a mark on a wall, became one of her most famous short works. The small hand-printed booklet is the seed of a great publishing house.
63232-the-epidemics-of-the-middle-ages:
Hecker, a Berlin professor of medicine, wrote the classic study of the great plagues of the middle ages. Babington turned it into English, and the Sydenham Society issued it at London in 1844. Three treatises stand in one volume here.

The Black Death is the giant of the set. The Dancing Mania, when folk danced till they dropped, stands beside it. Hecker worked from chronicles and town records across Europe. His lists of learned bodies, from Albany to Zurich, crowd the title page as a badge of weight. Babington, who gives his own Black Death rights to the society, frames the gift in his preface. A grim, founding book of the history of disease.
63243-hope-farm-notes:
Hope Farm Notes gathers the farm writings of Herbert Collingwood, reprinted at New York in 1921 from a farm weekly. Most of the notes first appeared week by week across some twenty years, the author says at the front. Readers of the paper asked to have them kept in lasting form between covers. Collingwood thanks his daughter for great help in choosing and ordering the pieces.

The notes stand in the order of their first printing. Two early pieces, a farm sermon and a sketch called Grandmother, date from 1902. The children named in the notes belong to two distinct broods, the author warns. A second brood appears just after one early sketch, and readers should not mix the two. Hens, neighbours, crops, and hard years fill the plain talk of a working farm.
63282-how-to-make-draperies:
Singer issued a home sewing guide dated 1960 on how to make draperies, as one book in its sewing set. First pages sort cloth by room and mood, from damask and satin for grand rooms to linen and chintz for plain ones. New man made cloth gets praise for quick wash and dry and for its light need of the iron.

Steps then cover how to pick needles and thread, take window sizes, and count the cloth a job will need. Work notes spell out hems, heads, and pleats, with counts for pleat width worked in full. Home sewers get a clear path from shop shelf to hung drapes.
63292-familiar-dialogues:
James Bellot, a gentleman of Caen, set forth these Familiar Dialogues in London in 1586. Thomas Vautrollier, dwelling in Blackfriars, printed the book. Each line stands in three columns: English, French, and English spelled as it sounds.

Bellot wrote for those who wish to learn to speak English well and say it right, and for French learners in mirror form. The sound-spelling is the book's charm: words are writ as the ear hears them. A gift page greets Sir Mark de Bussy of Beruille with good health in all three tongues. Few books show so plainly how English speech struck a French ear in the days of the first Elizabeth.
633-the-golden-mean-or-ratio-1-sqrt-5-2-:
This volume prints the golden ratio, (1+sqrt(5))/2, to twenty thousand decimal places, with a trove of other constants beside it. Catalan's constant, Artin's constant, the Feigenbaum numbers, Khinchin's constant, and zeta values share the pages, each to thousands of digits. The golden ratio itself opens at 1.6180339887 and runs on for pages.

The book serves less as reading than as a reference store for mathematicians, artists, and the curious. Its digits, checked and printed in blocks, let workers test code, art, and theory against a true value. For most readers it stands as a monument to precision, where beauty meets long arithmetic.
6330-amanda-a-daughter-of-the-mennonites:
Anna Balmer Myers opens on a scorching midsummer day in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, where a little red haired girl wades barefoot in a tree bordered creek. Her gingham skirt is tucked unevenly, her laughter breaks the Sabbath calm, and she declares the wading the best fun, with pebbles to pick and cool water against the heat. Amanda Reist, daughter of the Mennonites, grows up in that world of farms, markets, and plain speech.

Chapters follow a snitzing party, apple butter boiling, a visit to Martin's mother, school days, and Amanda as teacher, with a spelling bee, a market day, pink moccasins, and a boarder. A frontispiece shows her rescued from fire, still feeling the wonder of it. Myers writes Pennsylvania Dutch life with affection and detail, as a girl becomes a teacher and a woman in a community that values work, faith, and family.
63373-rain-and-roses:
Rain and Roses, a book of poems by Jeannette Fraser Henshall, was published in Boston in 1923 and dedicated to her daughter Beulah. The contents list more than sixty short lyrics. Titles range from Old Masonry and Hymn of Adoration to A City Guest, Sea Hunger, and Lines to Death.

The first poem, Inadequate, says that when a dear friend is away the speaker plans a thousand fine things to say. When the friend comes, the planned words flee like birds in wind, and the glad heart can say only that the friend has come. Faith, home, seasons, and loss shape most of the verse, in a plain and tender voice.
63395-freezing-combination-main-dishes:
Freezing Combination Main Dishes is a home guide from the agriculture department. The booklet stands as Home and Garden Bulletin number forty of the set. Stews, meat loaves, and casseroles fill the recipes on its pages. General directions for freezing such dishes stand before the recipes given. Vacant freezer space should be put to use, the guide opens.

Ready dishes, heated or cooked and served later, reward the foresight. For top quality, plan to use frozen dishes within two or three months. Properly packed foods keep safe up to six months in the freezer. After six months quality often declines fast, though food stays safe. Prepare the food as if it were to be served at once. Do not overcook, since reheating will finish the dish later on. Flour-thickened sauces may separate or curdle on thawing, it warns.
63398-the-hairy-ones:
Basil Wells wrote The Hairy Ones, printed in Planet Stories for winter nineteen forty four. A head note sets the tale. Marooned on a world within a world, Patrolman Sisko Rolf fights to bring life to dying Mars, it says. The outlaw ships are attacking, old Garmon Nash snaps as the tale opens. Five or six of them, he counts. Cut the searchlights, he orders.

Rolf stocky body was a blur of motion as he cut the rocket jets and doused the twin searchlights, the tale says. But here in the cavern world under waterless Mars, sound beams were of little value, it adds. Distances were far too cramped, it notes. Trapped us neatly, Rolf said through clenched teeth. Tolled into their underground hideout by that water runner we tried to capture, he says. Fans get a Mars cave war tale.
6340-literary-lapses:
Stephen Leacock's Literary Lapses runs from a financial career and Lord Oxhead's secret to boarding house geometry and the awful fate of Melpomenus Jones. A Christmas letter, how to make a million dollars, and how to live to be two hundred follow. How to avoid getting married, how to be a doctor, new food, and a new pathology come next. The poet is answered, statistics exert force, and men who have shaved the author take their turn.

A barber, Leacock jokes, pins his customer in the chair and covers his face with soap. He plants a knee on his chest and asks about yesterday's Detroit game, not as a question at all. Getting the thread, telling faults, winter pastimes, and number fifty-six keep the comedy coming, with a conjurer's revenge and hints to travellers. Leacock writes short, sharp humour, Canadian in setting and universal in its targets.
63408-report-of-the-committee-appointed-:
A committee appointed to investigate the causes and extent of the late extraordinary sickness and mortality in the town of Mobile published its report at Philadelphia in 1820. The committee examined all the wharves, docks, and vessels, and the buildings and lots near the river and elsewhere in town.

They found numerous local causes which, under the late season's influence, might have produced the fever without any foreign importation. First came the wharves, built of hewn timber closely laid, trapping water and filled with rotten logs, bushes, and shavings. Readers get an early American epidemic inquest, miasma theory at work on a Gulf port's yellow fever, evidence by evidence.
63417-the-wishing-stone-stories:
Thornton W Burgess wrote The Wishing Stone Stories, with illustrations by Harrison Cady, issued in Boston by Little, Brown, and Company. Copyright rests from nineteen fifteen and nineteen twenty one. Burgess dedicated the tales to the cause of love, mercy, and protection for our little friends of the air and the wild wood. Three story groups fill the book. Tommy and the Wishing Stone is the first.

Tommy learns to admire Thunderer the Ruffed Grouse in that group. What Happened When Tommy Became a Mink follows. Tommy Wishes Come True is the second group. Why Peter Rabbit Has One Less Enemy opens it. Why Tommy Became a Friend of Red Squirrels and The Pleasures and Troubles of Bobby Coon follow. Tommy Change of Heart closes the book. There Tommy takes up all his traps, the contents promise. Children get nature tales where a boy learns animal lives from inside.
63437-the-seven-plaits-of-nettles-and-ot:
Edric Vredenburg wrote The Seven Plaits of Nettles and Other Stories, with pictures by T Noyes Lewis, Hilda Cowham, and others. Raphael Tuck and Sons in London, Paris, and New York issued the book. Five tales fill the volume. They are the title tale, When Our Ship Comes Home, The Golden Wish, The Princess and the Frog, and The Three Snowflakes.

The title tale starts with a very bad king who ruled a very good land. The land was rich and the folk worked hard and saved with care. The king spent vast sums on fun, gambled the mint dry, and gave the poor no thought. When his chests were bare he raised taxes each few weeks. Young readers learn how greed in a ruler harms a whole land.
63463-the-gingerbread-boy-and-joyful-jin:
A children's story book of 1923 from Albert Whitman of Chicago belongs to a library of Just Right Books. The series list names The Tiddly Winks, Open Air Stories, and Surprise Stories. The Party Twins, Doll Land Stories, and The Treasure Twins follow. A picture caption shows all the people Bobby had been kind to coming to his party.

The Gingerbread Boy retells the runaway pancake tale in American form. Joyful Jingle play stories share the volume. Whitman's Just Right line sold sturdy, cheerful books for young children. The list mixes fairy tales, animal tales, and play games. Series branding helped parents choose by age and taste.
63468-occupations-of-the-negroes:
Occupations of the Negroes is a statistical paper by Henry Gannett of the United States Geological Survey. The trustees of the John Slater Fund published it at Baltimore in 1895. It is number six of the fund Occasional Papers on its title page. A list of the board, appointed from 1882, stands at its front.

The Slater Fund was set up to aid the education of the freed people of the South. Gannett paper belongs to its inquiry into the condition and progress of that people after slavery. His trade was census work, and the paper treats the jobs held by Black Americans as counted fact. Such papers were the data of the great debate of the 1890s on race, labour, and schooling. They let reformers argue from tables rather than from guesswork about how a people was earning its living one generation after emancipation.
63491-the-snow-baby-a-true-story-with-tr:
Snow Baby is a true story with true pictures for children. Josephine Diebitsch Peary wrote it from life in the far north. Stokes of New York published it in October 1901, in its fourth edition. Peary dedicates the book to her grossmamma in fond German style. A plate shows little Marie, the snow baby, in a fur costume.

Hundreds of miles away in the white frozen north the tale begins. Beyond where big ships hunt huge black whales lies that land of ice. Mountains, glaciers, and icebergs fill its wonderful, stark scenery in words. Strange brown people called Eskimos live there in snow houses of winter. In summer the sun never sets, and flowers spring up in brief bloom.
63574-the-rise-of-universities:
Charles Haskins, a Harvard professor of history, gave these lectures at Brown University for the Colver Lectures, and they were printed at New York in 1923. Haskins was dean of the Harvard graduate school and the leading American student of medieval schools. His subject is how universities began in the Middle Ages and grew into lasting bodies.

The lectures trace masters and students who banded together at places such as Bologna, Paris, and Oxford to win rights, fix courses, and grant degrees. Haskins shows how those guilds of learning set the pattern that universities still follow. The book is short, clear, and based on a life of work in the records, and it stays the standard short account of its subject.
63616-hagerty-s-enzymes:
Hagerty's Enzymes is a science fiction story by Haley. It ran in Planet Stories in the spring of 1955. Harper Breen is a man of shattered nerves. A new Relaxo-Lounge chair is meant to cure him. The chair rocks, vibrates, and rubs his back. His sister Bella urges him to give in to it. Five minutes is all Harper can stand.

He flees the chair for a plain, still sofa. Doctor Franz prescribed the thing, to Bella's defence. Harper has paid Franz a fortune in fees. He has not slept for weeks, he rages. Soup is all he can eat. The motto places the tale on robot-harried Mars. There every man has a place, but not quite. Haley spins comedy from a nervous age.
63625-broken-butterflies:
Henry Kinney wrote a tale printed at Toronto in 1924. It opens at sea by moonlight. The black bow of the Tenyo Maru cuts the broad ribbon of light toward Japan. Hugh Kent leans on the rail and looks into the dim.

A bamboo flute sounds from the deck below, and dance music drifts from astern. East and West draw near in his thoughts, yet stay too strange to blend in full concord. Kent left Japan at fifteen, twenty years before. He hopes to win back the tongue he prattled as a small boy in Kyoto. A changed, more knowing Japan waits for him across the water.
63730-books-and-printing-a-treasury-for-:
Paul Bennett edited a treasury for typophiles, lovers of type and printing, published in Cleveland and New York as a Forum Book in 1951. Essays by many hands on books and printing fill the volume. Different articles are set in different type families, Times, Gill Sans, Garamond, Bodoni, Baskerville, Centaur, Perpetua, and Bell among them, so the book shows its subject as it tells it.

Old texts are quoted in ancient style with the long s and fine ligatures kept. Printers' errors have been corrected for the modern reader, the notes say. Readers who love the craft get lore on letters, presses, binding, and book design from experts. The treasury is both a history and a specimen of the printer's art.
63781-a-group-of-famous-women-stories-of:
Edith Horton tells lives for the young in A Group of Famous Women, published by D C Heath in 1914 and dedicated to the women teachers of America. The contents run from Joan of Arc through Dorothy Payne Madison, Elizabeth Fry, Lucretia Mott, and Mary Lyon. Dorothea Dix, Margaret Fuller, Harriet Beecher Stowe, and Maria Mitchell follow.

Later lives take up Lucy Stone, Julia Ward Howe, Queen Victoria, Florence Nightingale, and Susan B Anthony, closing with Clara Barton, Harriet Hosmer, and Louisa M Alcott. A last chapter honors women on the battlefield and in pioneer life. School readers get heroines aplenty.
63790-rosemary-and-pansies:
Rosemary and Pansies is a book of poems by Effie Smith, printed at Boston in 1909. The Gorham Press issued it. Smith dedicates the book to the memory of her brother Marvin. Thirty-eight poems fill the contents, from At the Grave of One Forgotten to Good Night.

The opening poem stands in an old, still churchyard, where giant oaks shade a sunken grave. No stone bears the name of the dead. Only blossoms clothe the place with trembling light. Was the sleeper young, or old and tired? No wise person on earth can tell. But the flowers bear witness that those who laid the sleeper there loved him well. Smith's verse is plain, gentle, and mournful.
63805-old-sports-and-sportsmen-or-the-wi:
Old Sports and Sportsmen is a Shropshire sporting memoir by John Randall, printed in 1873. Its other name is the Willey Country. Randall also wrote The Severn Valley. A portrait of Lord Forester fronts the book. Sketches of Squire Forester and his whipper-in Tom Moody fill its heart.

You all knew Tom Moody the whipper-in well, runs the motto from the old song. Randall's preface says his object is to gather facts of local history and set them plainly before the reader. If too many details of the country's earlier features crept in, he pleads the close tie of cause and effect. The old forests, he argues, shaped the sport and the men. Squire Forester stands as a fair sample of the squirearchy of his time. The book is fox-hunting nostalgia with a county's memory in its saddlebags.
6381-two-years-in-the-french-west-indies:
Lafcadio Hearn dedicates his West Indian book to Leopold Arnoux, notary at Saint Pierre, Martinique, in memory of walks, voyages, and talks. On an unshadowed day in Saint Pierre, a visitor with poetry and study in mind feels he has seen it all before, in a happy dream half recalled. Quaint architecture and bright narrow streets aglow with warm colour fill the view. Roofs and walls streaked with mould greens and greys, and no window sashes, glass, gas lamps, or chimneys, make the scene feel past rather than present.

Chapters follow porteuses, Grande Anse, a revenant, la guiablesse, washerwomen, Mount Pelee, little canoes, and a coloured girl, with bonnes haggling for first fish as boats return. Hearn writes Martinique as colour, sound, and custom, with a French epigraph on the passion to return. The book is travel as portrait, tender toward a city soon to vanish.
63812-grandma-perkins-and-the-space-pira:
Grandma Perkins and the Space Pirates, by James McConnell, ran in Planet Stories for March 1954. McConnell sets the tale on a luxury space ship named Kismet, among the moons of Jupiter. His cast pairs glamour with age in a sly way.

The front blurb says star actress Darling Toujours lit hearts across the whole system with her smoke and flame eyes. Yet it took sweet old Grandma Perkins, of the pirate ship Dirty Shame, to set the Jupiter moons on fire. The tale opens with Toujours trading barbs with Carlton E Carlton, a sharp tongued author of famed books. Captain Homer Fogarty of the Kismet joins their drinks and talk. Fans of pulp space tales get stars, pirates, and a grandma who steals the show.
63850-eyes-and-no-eyes-and-other-stories:
O'Shea, a professor of education at the University of Wisconsin, edited this school reader for Heath in 1900. He opens with praise from Oliver Wendell Holmes for the title story, 'Eyes and No Eyes' in name. Holmes said he had never seen anything of the kind half so good. He urged any child under forty-five to read it at once.

The story comes from 'Evenings at Home' by Aiken and Barbauld, and its subtitle calls it the art of seeing. Holmes thanked its writer for turning his mind to common things. Notes and an introduction frame the tales for young readers in the Heath Supplementary Readers series.
63863-the-four-masted-cat-boat-and-other:
The Four-Masted Cat-Boat and Other Truthful Tales, by Charles Battell Loomis, with illustrations by Florence Scovel Shinn, was published by the Century Company in New York in 1899. Forty sketches fill the book, grouped under four heads: A Few Idiotisms, At the Literary Counter, Unrelated Stories Related, and Essays at Essays.

Griggs and his mind, a Spanish parrot, a calculating bore, and a dialect store appear among the pieces. A note thanks the editors of the Century, the Saturday Evening Post, Harper's Bazaar, Puck, the Critic, and the Criterion for leave to reprint. The title sketch opens as an etching of the sea by a landlubber. White caps ride like pond lilies, and a full rigged four masted cat-boat lugs and luffs in the calm.
63879-siam-and-laos-as-seen-by-our-ameri:
Siam and Laos, as Seen by Our American Missionaries is a fully illustrated volume issued at Philadelphia by the Presbyterian Board of Publication. Copyright rests in eighteen eighty four. A front plate shows Chulalongkorn the First, King of Siam. A remark of the late ex regent of Siam heads the book, that Siam has been opened by missionaries, not by English and French guns. A score of missionaries contributed chapters.

Some chapters were written amid the crowded field life, others during brief visits home, the preface says. Several writers are children of missionaries, born in Indo China. Others are pioneer workers whose long service abroad is now ended. Two of the writers have entered into rest, it adds. The editor drew also on Pallegoix, Bowring, Crawford, and Mouhot. Church readers get Siam and Laos through missionary eyes, with kings, temples, and schools.
63882-war-s-embers-and-other-verses:
Ivor Gurney published War's Embers and Other Verses in London in 1919, following his earlier Severn and Somme of 1917. A dedication poem thanks a friend whose kindness his art is too poor to repay. Several poems had already appeared in The Spectator, The Westminster Gazette, and a Gloucester paper.

Titles in the contents mix war and home: The Volunteer, In a Ward, The Battalion Is Now on Rest, The Farm, Omens, and Fire in the Dusk. Gurney wrote as both soldier and composer from Gloucestershire. Readers get poems where the trenches and the Severn country sit side by side, neither one letting go of the other.
63911-hard-pan-a-story-of-bonanza-fortun:
Geraldine Bonner's Hard Pan: A Story of Bonanza Fortunes was published by the Century Company in 1900. The first chapter sits at a family dinner table as coffee arrives in tiny gold-rimmed cups. Letitia Mason asks her brother-in-law John Gault whether he knew that Colonel Ramsay Reed had a daughter. Maud Gault, splendid in white and yellow, answers that bonanza men who lost their bonanzas drop out of sight. Nobody really knows anything about them.

Mortimer Gault adds the facts: White Pine scooped the last dollar Reed had, and the old fellow has not a cent in the world. What does he keep a daughter on, but the memory of his glories? The dinner party is small: the Gaults, Letitia, and John. Bonner lets the talk sketch San Francisco society and its fallen mining kings. Reed's hidden daughter is the thread the talk throws out.
63940-the-ecclesiastical-architecture-of:
The first volume of a survey of Scottish church architecture. David MacGibbon and Thomas Ross wrote it. David Douglas published it at Edinburgh in 1896. The pair had already covered Scotland's castles and mansions. Years of travel gave them notes and sketches of churches as well. Those materials grew into this companion work.

The survey runs from the earliest Christian times to the seventeenth century. Its authors apply the known Gothic period system to Scottish buildings. That system, they note, was already settled for Europe. Their earlier castle study needed fresh terms and periods. Church work instead needs careful measurement and drawing. Plates throughout show plans, mouldings, and towers in detail. The volumes remain a standard record of Scotland's medieval churches.
63947-rue-and-roses:
Angela Langer published Rue and Roses with Doran of New York in 1913, with an introduction by Courtney. The first chapter opens in a little shop, where the narrator's parents sold candles, soap, brushes, and many other articles. The child narrator regards them all with respect.

Each Christmas her father received a wooden chest. Its opening and unpacking was her greatest joy. Sometimes her father showed no hurry about the sacred ceremony, and she reminded him of it. At last he declared he would open it. She got so excited she hardly knew what to do. She asked to help; he said she was a bother and in his way. Fearing dismissal, she sat still for two minutes. Rue and roses are remembrance and love in the language of flowers, and the book is a childhood recalled in that language.
63967-the-timeless-ones:
The Timeless Ones is a science fiction story by Frank Belknap Long, printed in Planet Stories for July 1951. A blurb sets the puzzle: a peaceful green world under two golden suns, and visitors from Earth sitting terrified in their rocket ship. Ned Jackson and his wife Cynthia, the co-pilot, approach that world in the contact rocket Star Mist.

They are returning to colonists they remember: Clifton and Helen Sweeney and their children, planted five thousand light years from Earth. A century has passed since the first prospect ship crossed by warp-drive, yet Ned pictures Tommy Sweeney still a tow-headed boy of ten. The story's tension turns on time itself, and on what the green world has done to the people who settled it.
63978-the-ecclesiastical-architecture-of:
The Ecclesiastical Architecture of Scotland, volume two, is a survey by David MacGibbon and Thomas Ross, printed at Edinburgh in 1896. The authors also wrote The Castellated and Domestic Architecture of Scotland. This volume holds drawings and descriptions of the First Pointed and Middle Pointed periods, the finest of the medieval buildings.

The preface weighs the place of these churches in the general system of Gothic architecture in other countries. There can scarcely be any question, the authors say, that the Gothic style was imported into Scotland, not native to it. The Norman style came gradually from England and was superseded by the transition style. The first pointed buildings also show their design brought from England. The middle pointed ones, though allied to English examples, show signs of other influences in their details.
63995-the-art-of-conversation-twelve-gol:
Good talk follows rules, and The Art of Conversation sets out twelve golden rules for it, by Josephine Turck Baker. The book was published at Evanston, Illinois, in 1907 by the Correct English Publishing Company. Baker was the author of a full grammar called Correct English. She also edited a magazine on correct English and its use.

A companion work by Baker taught the pronunciation of ten thousand words. Her art of conversation belongs to the same campaign for correct and pleasing speech. The twelve rules give plain counsel for talk in company. Readers of the day used such guides to gain ease in drawing rooms and at table. The book shows how much store its age set by smooth, correct, and tactful talk. It is a window on the manners teaching of its time.
64017-the-dare-boys-in-vincennes:
Stephen Angus Cox wrote The Dare Boys in Vincennes, a Revolutionary War adventure for boys published by Chatterton at New York in 1912, with pictures by Rudolf Mencl. The story opens in a Patriot hospital at Charleston, where Tom Dare reads a letter to the wounded Ben Foster, whose recovery the surgeons have just promised. Dick Dare returns from the commander's quarters, and the brothers Dick and Tom, lately serving under the Swamp Fox, take up new duty.

Sixteen chapters carry the Dare Boys aboard a sloop, on the march, into an ambush and a night attack, up to a cliff drop and a final reunion. The British hold the country round Charleston, so every errand beyond the lines runs a gauntlet. Cox keeps the period dialogue and camp detail plain, and the plot moves on rescues, trails, and narrow escapes in the series manner.
64047-boys-of-other-countries:
Boys of Other Countries, by Bayard Taylor, appears here in an enlarged edition. Putnam issued it at New York and London. First copyright dates to 1876, with later renewals into 1912. Taylor tells young readers he met many children in his travels. He chose tales where story and fact come together. Children in other lands, he notes, often start work young. Their courage and self-reliance struck him on the road. The Little Post-Boy opens the book, set in northern Sweden in winter.

The Pasha's Son and Jon of Iceland follow. Two herd-boys and a young serf widen the map. Studies of animal nature break the run of lives. A new last tale treats a robber region of Southern California. The volume mixes travel knowledge with adventure for boys.
64077-a-description-of-a-new-invented-st:
A Description of a New Invented Stove Grate is a short sales tract by the maker, J Durno, printed in London in 1753 and sold for six pence. Durno claims his grate beats all others in cost and in use for a chamber fire. He sold it from his house in Jermyn Street.

Durno notes that the British weather is so changeable that folk must keep fires near eight months of the year. Coal duty has made fire dear, most of all in London. His grate, he says, makes rooms warm and snug for less, with no smoke and a cheerful blaze. One grate had stood in a room at his house since last winter for guests to test. Readers see early home tech sold in bold print.
64127-the-cambrian-tourist-or-post-chais:
A post chaise companion through Wales reached a sixth edition, corrected and considerably enlarged, at London in 1828. A picture shows the suspension bridge over the Menai at Bangor Ferry. The whole promises cursory sketches of the Welsh territories. Manners, customs, and games of the natives are described. An account of the Welsh language opens the text.

The force of the letters, a list of primitive words, and the character of Welsh poetry are treated there. It supposes that the Welsh or British language once spread widely. Such companions guided carriage tourists before the railway age. Routes, inns, antiquities, and scenery fill their pages for travelers hiring post chaises.
64132-the-cambrian-tourist-or-post-chais:
The Cambrian Tourist, or Post Chaise Companion through Wales, is a guide book in its eighth edition, issued at London in 1834. The whole was corrected and much enlarged for that edition, its title page says. A picture of the Menai Bridge heads the text. Cursory sketches of the Welsh territories fill the plan of the work.

The book describes the manners, customs, and games of the Welsh people. An account of the Welsh language opens the body of the guide. That account treats the force of the letters and lists primitive words. The character of the tongue and of its poetry is weighed there. Travellers by post chaise used the book as a companion on the road. It mixes routes with lore, in the manner of its age.
64161-idylls-of-the-sea-and-other-marine:
Idylls of the Sea, by Frank Bullen, was first printed in 1899. Grant Richards issued this London printing in 1900. Strachey wrote the introduction. Bullen was a first mate, and author of The Cruise of the Cachalot. He gives the book to his wife. Thirty sketches fill the contents, most reprinted from magazines. The Spectator lent many of them. The Passing of Peter opens the set. A true shark story and a slaver follow. The birth of an island and a submarine earthquake stand midway. Studies in marine natural history form a second group. The kraken, sharks, and devil-fish are treated there.

Flying-fish catching at Barbados is described from the deck. Other sketches end the book: the loss of a ship, the truth about the merchant service. Bullen writes as a working sailor.
64195-the-tourist-s-guide-through-north-:
Bennett wrote this tourist guide through North Wales, with Clint etchings. Whittaker printed the book in London in 1853. A view of Llangollen faces the title page as frontispiece. Plates show Chirk Castle, Valle Crucis Abbey, and Bala Lake.

Bennett aims to show the finest Welsh scenery in a month tour. He claims the route variety can scarce be matched on earth. Higher hills stand in Asia and America, he grants at once. Yet Snowdonia views, castles, and falls reward the traveler close at hand. Snowdon from the pass and the Llanberis pass stand among its views.
64197-magna-carta-and-other-addresses:
William D Guthrie wrote these addresses, printed by Columbia University Press of New York in 1916. The lead address marks the seven-hundredth anniversary of Magna Carta, given at Albany on June 15, 1915, before the Constitutional Convention of New York. A Mayflower Compact toast at the Hotel St Regis follows, from November 23, 1915.

Constitutional morality went to the Pennsylvania bar at Cape May in 1912. The Eleventh Amendment speech dates to 1908, and a piece on criticism of the courts follows. Graduated taxation, the duty of citizenship, and nominating conventions fill the back of the book. Guthrie speaks as a lawyer of the old school, tying American practice to English roots.
64242-the-carcellini-emerald-with-other-:
Burton Harrison's story collection The Carcellini Emerald, with Other Tales was published by Herbert Stone and Company in Chicago and New York in eighteen ninety-nine. The title tale leads a contents list of seven stories. They include An Author's Reading and its Consequences, Leander of Betsy's Pride, The Three Misses Benedict at Yale, A Girl of the Period, The Stolen Stradivarius, and Wanted: A Chaperon.

The illustrations came by courtesy of the Saturday Evening Post, the Woman's Home Companion, and Harper and Brothers, where the tales had periodical lives. The title story opens on Ashton Carmichael, a dictator in New York smart society. Nobody knew how he won that place, and in his set nobody really cared.
64255-the-city-of-comrades:
Basil King's novel, copyrighted by Harper and Brothers in 1919, takes its epigraph from Walt Whitman's dream of a city of friends. The story opens at Columbus Circle in New York in June 1913, where the narrator, a seedy drifter, shuffles along with Lovey at his ear. Lovey is pressing him to join a good thing, dead easy, against two old ladies.

The narrator refuses, again and again, though Lovey warns he will be sorry and calls him not even a beginner. The frontispiece shows a woman hushing a visitor so as not to frighten her nervous friend. Other plates promise stolen pearls pocketed, a sudden proposal of marriage, and a welcome home spoiled.
64296-model-flying-machines:
Model Flying Machines: How to Build and Fly Them is a manual by Morgan, published at Newark in 1913. Cole and Morgan issued the little book. Its introduction calls model aeroplane building essentially simple. A well balanced machine soaring under its own power delights maker and spectators alike. Detailed plans for several machines fill the volume. Most are designed for distance rather than for looks.

General principles of flight open the teaching chapters. Construction remarks treat resistance and the fuselage, or framework. Bearings, thrust blocks, and gears get their own sections. The plans aim to aid the experimenter's judgment, not to replace it. Morgan writes for novices in the new science of aeronautics. Practical knowledge, he argues, comes best from building and flying small machines.
6434-a-brief-history-of-the-united-state:
Barnes's One-Term History offers a brief history of the United States for school pupils, with a preface on why children dislike history books. Teachers testify, the preface says, that pupils prefer real incidents to improbable tales, yet find their books dry. The remedy is method, not shorter facts: each pupil first draws an outline map of North America, at least eighteen by twenty four inches, showing only coast line, mountains, lakes, and rivers.

Six epochs carry the story: early discoveries and settlements, development of the colonies, the Revolutionary War, development of the states, the Civil War, and reconstruction with passing events. An appendix adds questions for class use, historical recreations, the Declaration of Independence, and the Constitution. A mid passage shows Washington's Princeton feat kindling patriotism afresh, with expiring enlistments renewed and Howe alarmed.
64350-among-the-scented-ones:
Basil Wells wrote this far-world tale for Planet Stories, where it ran in the Winter 1947 issue. Its head note names a man called Besan Wur. To him a backward planet of wild beasts and rank men was a haven, till men found he gave off no scent.

A vast dark flood of beasts opens the tale on the Saaaran plain. Green-crested saurians stampede west by the thousand, past the ruins of a score of old towns. Their mad rush rolls through a five-mile gap in low hills at noon. Walls grown over with jungle show that men once held this world. Fear drives the herd, and the land shakes with their feet.
64360-the-pirate-frog-and-other-tales:
The Pirate Frog and Other Tales is a book of nonsense verse for children by W A Frisbie, with pictures by Bart. Rand, McNally and Company of Chicago and New York copyrighted it in 1901. Frisbie and Bart had already made The Bandit Mouse together.

The fore word warns that the book is no arithmetic to vex the young, and that its lying tales teach children to know a lie when they see one. The title poem sets boys' toy boat adrift on Plunkett's Pond, where the Pirate Frog and his crew lie in wait behind a log. The frogs cut the line, raise their flag, and seize the helm. Ashore they turn three basking turtles onto their backs, and a lasso of cord goes round a duckling's neck. Mrs Muskrat rights the turtles; the pond war sails on.
64365-anne-of-green-gables:
Montgomery published Anne of Green Gables with Page of Boston in 1908, and the impressions tell the story: a third in August and a fourth in September of the same year. The Claus brothers illustrated it. She dedicates it to the memory of her father and mother.

The contents begin with three surprises in a row. Rachel Lynde is surprised, Matthew Cuthbert is surprised, and Marilla Cuthbert is surprised. Morning at Green Gables follows, then Anne's history, Anne saying her prayers, and Rachel Lynde properly horrified. The orphan sent by mistake to a Prince Edward Island farm became the most beloved heroine in Canadian fiction. Montgomery wrote from her own island girlhood, and Anne's imagination, which renames every lane and lake it meets, is the book's engine and its apology. The world has kept the appointment the Cuthberts never made.
64387-egyptian-art-studies:
Gaston Maspero studies pieces of Egyptian art in essays Englished by Elizabeth Lee and issued in London in 1913. One hundred and seven pictures back the text. Maspero ran the antiquities service at Cairo and taught at the College de France.

In a prefatory note Maspero says the essays span more than thirty years and first ran in art journals. He wrote them for general readers, not for experts, to show how fine works of Egyptian sculpture and goldsmith work should be approached. Some pieces he met in museums at Paris or Cairo, others on the day they came out of the ground. Readers get a great excavator's eye for single works, and his reasons for prizing them, in clear and lively prose.
64506-notes-on-noses:
Eden Warwick wrote Notes on Noses, a comic study. Richard Bentley issued this new edition at London in 1864. A Tristram Shandy line heads the book. Learned men write no dialogues on long noses for nothing, it says. Three great difficulties face a preface writer, Warwick opens. The first is talking the publisher out of one.

Writing one yourself is the second trouble, he says. Getting another to write it is the least. Of divers evils choose the least, the saw runs. Slawkenbergius prefaced his folio on noses in Sterne. That clause states Warwick's own call to the theme. Ever since he knew what was what, he quotes, the point of long noses lay loosely handled. A mock-learned treat on the nose riffs on Sterne's great joke with Victorian good humor.
64537-modern-cosmogonies:
Agnes Clerke, who wrote a popular history of astronomy in the nineteenth century, surveyed modern theories of how worlds began, in a book issued in London in 1905. Its motto is Young's line that the world is a prophecy of worlds to come. The first chapter runs from Thales to Kant.

She opens with the thought that few peoples, however rude, take the world as it is without asking how it came to be. Later chapters weigh the nebular hypothesis and its critics, tidal friction, and world-building out of meteorites. Protyle, the ether, and the forms of nebulae follow. Life as the outcome closes the survey.
64564-a-tale-of-two-monkeys-and-other-st:
A Tale of Two Monkeys and Other Stories was published by the Methodist Book Concern in New York and Cincinnati. The title piece tells of the late Dr John Torrey of Columbia College, fond of pets. A friend back from Brazil gave him a pair of pretty Brazilian monkeys with gentle, human faces and mouse coloured coats. They lived in a cage in his study, petted by all.

One Sunday the family went to church and left the monkeys alone. They forced their cage door and ran wild through the house. In the cellar they dumped a bag of hops and ten baskets of strawberries together. They skimmed pans of milk with their tails. Clothes from the line went into the cistern, and the cook things suffered too. Children get animal mischief and other short moral tales in lively prose.
64565-a-happy-new-year-and-other-verses:
A Happy New Year and Other Verses is a book of poems by Beresford. Spottiswoode printed it at Eton in 1913. The book is dedicated to the poet's dear wife. Some verses had run in magazines before. The title poem greets young, brave, strong, and old in turn. Its wish is spoken for frail and weak as well. A cradle song follows close behind.

Queen Tamar's castle and dark Donegal come next. Ulster's prayer and Hy-Brasail lend an Irish note. Samarkand, Florence, and the Thames widen the range. Two Londonderry elections, thirty years apart, are marked. A regiment at war in 1900 is honoured. Beresford writes in a plain, loyal, outdoor voice.
64573-the-children-and-the-pictures:
Children and the Pictures is a book on art for young readers by Pamela Tennant. The London and New York edition is dated nineteen oh seven. Pictures are reproduced in colour by a special process, the title page notes. A sketch by Arthur Rackham ornaments the title page. Contents run to twenty seven short chapters, listed by number alone. A painting by Hoppner, of two girls, serves as frontispiece.

Advertisements at the front praise Rackham editions of Rip Van Winkle and Alice in Wonderland from the same publisher. A list of pictures names portraits by Romney and other painters of children and sitters. Verses on dreams for sale appear in the text shown. If there were dreams to sell, what would you buy, the poem asks.
64578-magic-shadows-the-story-of-the-ori:
Martin Quigley wrote this history of how motion pictures began, first copyrighted in 1948 and reissued in 1960. The contents start with a chapter called 'It Started With A' in the book's playful scheme. Friar Bacon's magic and da Vinci's camera come next, reaching far back before film itself.

Porta is named the first screen showman, and Kepler and Kircher follow as men of light and lenses. Musschenbroek and motion, phantasmagoria shows and a toy by Doctor Paris trace the path onward. Plateau, who first made moving pictures in this account, and Marey carry the story toward the cinema age.
64607-seeking-his-fortune-and-other-dial:
Seeking His Fortune, and Other Dialogues is a collection of short plays for young performers, by Horatio Alger and his sister Augusta Cheney. Loring of Boston published the volume in 1875. Cheney dedicates it to her father and mother.

Alger's preface explains the division of labour. Only the first dialogue is his. The remainder are his sister's work, first printed in a New York juvenile magazine, and he served merely as editor. The pieces had been used at school exhibitions across the country. Titles include One Week an Editor, Keeping Genteel Boarders, Taming a Wife, and John Smith's Trials. Dialogue books like this one stocked parlour theatricals and school stages. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
64615-honor-bright-a-story-of-the-days-o:
Mary Rowsell wrote Honor Bright, a story of the days of King Charles, printed at Philadelphia under a 1900 copyright with twenty-three illustrations. A front picture note describes a boy with dark locks and swarthy cheeks smudged with dirt, taken by good folks for some gipsy boy. The first chapter, The Cedar Room, opens one fine autumn morning long ago. A little boy lies in the broad seat of a latticed window.

The room sits high in a tower at the corner of a big old house. Below stretch terrace walks, stone steps, and yew-hedges as thick as walls, with flower-beds ablaze at midday. Fruit gleams on the garden walls, and beyond lie wood, dale, and green meadows. A stream winds like a silver ribbon toward the house. The boy, whose name is Charles, gazes as tears brim up in his great dark eyes.
64646-goma-s-follicles:
Goma's Follicles is a science fiction story by John and Dorothy de Courcy, taken from Planet Stories in the summer of 1948. Its teaser asks who would have thought that getting a haircut on Procyon IV could be a matter of life and death. The tale opens aboard the Franklin, the newest ship of the Morgan Interstellar Transportation Corporation.

Captain Webster, proud of his ship, fumes at an unscheduled stop at Procyon IV. A dispatch orders him to pick up a passenger for Earth at Iridium City. The stop sets the plot in motion, mixing space-trade routine with an odd danger tied to hair. The copyright on the story was never renewed, the transcriber notes.
6465-short-cruises:
W. W. Jacobs gathers twelve cruises, with drawings by Will Owen. The tales are The Changeling, Mixed Relations, His Lordship, Alf's Dream, A Distant Relative, The Test, In the Family, A Love Knot, Her Uncle, The Dreamer, Angels' Visits, and A Circular Tour. The tales run on sailors, families, and talk, from a voice demanded in one illustration to a lordship exclaiming over eyes in another. Jacobs writes in cockney voice and humour, where a joke lands like a rope's end.

A mid passage shows Alf questioning his uncle: why sign them so, and never mind, it is his handwriting and good enough for her. The uncle tried writing backwards once, but would not do it again for fifty pounds, and Alf muses that if her first husband were alive she could not marry him. Jacobs writes short stories where folk scheme, blunder, and talk their way out of trouble.
64659-the-night-has-a-thousand-eyes:
John and Dorothy de Courcy wrote a tale of the space ways for Planet Stories in the winter of 1949. Its blurb tells of a tough old pirate captain named Brace, who balked at casting an unwanted girl into space. The tale opens in a crude bar on Titan.

Brace stands at the bar. The captain is ape like, with a flat nose and long arms. He calls for Borl and drinks it straight, as a show. The stuff is drawn from the roots of a poisonous tree, and burns like acid. No other man he knows can drink it. Aliens of five worlds watch in their own ways, in the sump where the leavings of five races gather.
64685-secrets-of-making-frozen-desserts-:
Secrets of Making Frozen Desserts at Home offers 150 tested recipes, promising results easier, more economical, and more delicious than bought desserts. The opening lesson tells how to freeze ice cream at home, step by step.

Scald the freezer can, prepare the mixture, and pack ice and salt around the can, in the proportion of three to six parts of ice to one of salt. Turn the crank slowly, then rapidly as the mixture stiffens; three to five minutes should freeze the cream. Directions for letting it set and for molding the cream in solid form follow.
64686-forgers-and-forgeries:
Forgers and Forgeries is a book by Constable, printed at New York and Toronto with copyright in 1954. Constable curated paintings at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Harry Abrams published it in the Art Treasures of the World line, at one dollar. Its covers show a forged Greek bronze statuette and a genuine one.

Constable starts by correcting the common idea of a forgery. Many things made for innocent ends are later used to deceive, by false claims or handling. The heart of forgery lies in how a thing is presented, not why it was made. Money is the main motive for pieces made to deceive. He tells of a Sleeping Cupid the young Michelangelo is said to have carved and buried.
64707-nicaraguan-antiquities:
Carl Bovallius wrote this archaeological study, published at Stockholm in 1886 for the Swedish Society of Anthropology and Geography and dedicated to the royal antiquary of Sweden. It reports two years in Central America.

Nicaragua, he found, is a very rich field for the student of American archaeology, and the literature on its antiquities is very poor. The book describes and figures the more important statues, rock-carvings, and ceramic objects he found, drawn or photographed on the spot. His pottery went home to the Swedish State Museum; the statues were too large to carry. He corrects some of Squier's figures against the originals. Sources named include Oviedo, Las Casas, and Thomas Gage. Archaeologists get an early Swedish survey of pre-Spanish Nicaragua.
64749-upper-canada-sketches:
Thomas Conant wrote Upper Canada Sketches, published by William Briggs at Toronto in 1898 with portraits, pictures, and a map. Conant dedicated the book to a friend in Chicago, hoping that Canadians living in the United States would enjoy these random sketches of home. His first chapters dig into family roots: the name Conant in Normandy and Devon, and Roger Conant, the Pilgrim who became the first governor of Massachusetts.

The story then crosses to Canada. Roger Conant's descendant removed there after the American Revolution. Sketches follow of a home in the wilderness, salmon fishing, logging, and the fur trade. Durham boats on the St Lawrence rapids, trade with the Indians, and maple sugar making fill the middle chapters. Conant writes as a settler's heir preserving the pioneer world of Upper Canada before it vanished, mixing genealogy with the daily work and dangers of the early settlements along the lakes.
64752-the-life-of-cervantes:
Albert F Calvert wrote The Life of Cervantes in a 1905 London and New York edition. The book holds many portraits and prints from early editions of Don Quixote. It came out three hundred years from the first part of Don Quixote in Madrid. Calvert had writ books on Spain and Australia too.

Calvert calls Cervantes a great peer of Shakespeare. He notes that few lives of Cervantes exist in English. Yet the life was as full and varied as that of his own knight. Don Quixote may be read as a kind of sequel to that life, he says. The book seeks to fill that gap for English readers. It treats the man as much as the famed book.
64762-some-historic-trees:
The boards of the Public Library of Fort Wayne and Allen County issued this pamphlet on famed trees, as one of a historical series. A plate shows Penn's Treaty Tree at the front. The tales are short and plain, each tied to a place and a date in the nation's past.

Near the line of North and South Carolina stood a tulip tree where Americans beat part of Cornwallis's army in October 1780, and ten Tories were hanged from its limbs. A pine by the Hudson bore the cut name Jane McCrea, 1777, until about 1852. Under a black walnut in 1779, Mad Anthony Wayne gave night orders before storming Stony Point. Each tree stands as a marker of memory.
64807-turkish-fairy-tales-and-folk-tales:
Turkish Fairy Tales and Folk Tales, gathered by Ignacz Kunos and turned from the Hungarian version by Bain, was published in London in 1901 with drawings by Celia Levetus. Nineteen Turkish tales make up the main part, from The Stag-Prince to Stone-Patience and Knife-Patience. Four Rumanian tales close the book.

The Stag-Prince opens with a Padishah who dies and leaves a son and daughter. The son soon spends the whole estate, then tells his sister they must leave home before their poverty is known and they are driven out in shame. Magic turbans, carpets, dragons with seven heads, and peris fill the set, told in a plain once-upon-a-time voice.
64808-modern-swedish-masterpieces-short-:
Modern Swedish Masterpieces is a book of short stories selected and translated by Charles Wharton Stork, editor of Contemporary Verse, published in New York by E P Dutton and Company in 1923. Stork had earlier translated an anthology of Swedish lyrics and poems by Gustaf Fröding, and he dedicates this volume to Thorsten Laurin, a patron of the arts.

Hjalmar Söderberg contributes the largest group, including The Chimney-Sweeper's Wife, The Fur Coat, and The Kiss. Sigfrid Siwertz, Verner von Heidenstam, and Per Hallström follow with tales of fishermen, fortified houses, and falcons. The first story opens grimly in a cobbled Stockholm courtyard under an old linden tree. Such translated collections carried Scandinavian fiction to American readers between the wars.
64814-little-mexican-other-stories:
Aldous Huxley wrote Little Mexican and Other Stories, published in London in 1924. The same-author page lists Antic Hay and Crome Yellow among his novels, and Limbo and Mortal Coils among his story books. Six pieces fill this volume, and the first, Uncle Spencer, runs to more than half the book.

Uncle Spencer opens with a meditation on childhood holidays. Some people, the narrator says, look back on always different landscapes: chalk downs, Swiss mountains, a blue sea or the grey fringe of ocean. He envies them the variety of their impressions. His own memory holds the untroubled waters of Como, the cypresses, and the Easter roses. The title story, Hubert and Minnie, Fard, The Portrait, and Young Archimedes follow. Huxley in these years was turning from poetry to the cool, ironic fiction that made his name.
64854-little-dinners-with-the-sphinx-and:
Richard Le Gallienne published a book of prose fancies at New York in 1907, dedicated to Eva. The title piece supposes a series of little dinners with the Sphinx, parted into meditations on starlight, the mysticism of gastronomy, the wearing of opals, and new loves for old. She and the author had not dined together for four years.

Across the glitter of crystal and moon-white roses they ask whether they are the same people, and she notes that he is growing grey. Sorrows, he quotes, would blanch an angel's hair; pleasures, she answers, grey the butterfly's wings. Other fancies follow: the death of the poet, a castle in Spain, the little joys of Margaret, and dream documents. Whimsy at table is the manner.
6487-the-new-boy-at-hilltop-and-other-st:
Ralph Henry Barbour gathers The New Boy at Hilltop and other stories. It opens with Hilltop School closing its fall term at ninety five students and reopening two weeks later, January third, with ninety six. Kenneth Garwood, booked for autumn but delayed by family plans, journeys to Moritzville on a cold January afternoon. Curled in a heated day coach, he wonders why the Connecticut Valley runs colder than Cleveland, Ohio.

Other tales follow. They are the proving of Jerry, McTurk le, the band, the triumph of Curly, and Patsy. Then come a first assignment, Pemberton's fluke, the seventh tutor, a race with the waters, a college Santa Claus, the triple play, and the dub. A mid passage shows Jerry on a bridge, grasping Welch's wrist as the boy hangs swinging over water, praying for strength and endurance while his shoulder hurts worse every moment. Barbour writes schoolboy sport and pluck.
64904-some-frightful-war-pictures:
Some Frightful War Pictures, by W Heath Robinson, was first published by Duckworth and Company in 1915 and reprinted in 1916. The full-page drawings first appeared in The Sketch and in The Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News.

The captions promise Robinson's absurd war machinery. The true reason of the war is a frontier incident in Alsace in July 1914, and the Hague Convention is defied by button magnets, directed draughts, and the Tatcho bomb. Krupp's great reconnoitring mortar and the war lord's morning tub aboard the imperial campaigning car follow in the same vein.
64928-the-tournament-its-periods-and-pha:
R Coltman Clephan wrote The Tournament, Its Periods and Phases. Methuen and Company issued it at London in 1919. Charles J Ffoulkes wrote its preface. He kept the Armouries at the Tower then. A colored frontispiece shows a German gestech course. Twenty-three other pictures aid the text.

An intro and book list front the study. Chapter One traces the tournament's origin. Rules made in the year 1066 stand cited there. The word's derivation gets its own study. The behourd and the joust stand defined apart. The Round Table game gets full treatment. Edward the Third revived Arthur's table glories, it says. Winchester keeps an actual table of old fame. The quintain and running at the ring follow. A Tower man's history of the lists gives sport's most dangerous game its rules, ages, and armor in order.
65014-the-ecclesiastical-architecture-of:
David MacGibbon and Thomas Ross wrote The Ecclesiastical Architecture of Scotland, and volume three closes the set. David Douglas issued the work in Edinburgh in eighteen hundred ninety seven. The survey runs from the first Christian age to the sixteen hundreds. The pair had mapped castles and homes of Scotland before.

The front notes air fights with fellow scholars in print. Galloway, Watson, and Chalmers each get a fair reply. Glasgow Cathedral and Melrose Abbey drew sharp words in past parts. Late church work, they find, sank in craft past the mid fourteen hundreds. A few late aisles shine bright in that dim age. Plans and views let readers judge each claim on the stones themselves.
65064-the-old-ones:
Betsy Curtis wrote this tale, first printed in a journal of tales of the mind in December 1950. A note at the head states its theme in brief. The old ones had lived past their use on Earth. The world of men waited with calm for them to die. So it was but plain that they should seek a new world of their own.

The tale opens in a house of the sick. Dr. Warner comes into the office of Dr. Farrar in a rush, not in his slow wonted way. He brings word of two deaths by their own hands in one block that same day. The names are Saul Forsythe and Madam LePays. Farrar, who had sat and sighed that no stir was left in life, is caught short by the news.
65079-autobiography-of-mother-jones:
Autobiography of Mother Jones is the life story of the labour organizer Mary Harris Jones, edited by Mary Field Parton and published in Chicago by Charles Kerr in 1925. A late photograph of Mother Jones fronts the book. Twenty-two chapters carry her from early years to old age.

The contents read as a strike history of America. The Haymarket tragedy, wars in the West Virginia coal fields, the march of the mill children, and child labour north and south stand out. One chapter tells how the women mopped up Coaldale, another how women sang themselves out of jail. She tells the reader at the start that she was born in Cork, Ireland, in 1830. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
65099-with-john-paul-jones:
With John Paul Jones is a boys' historical novel by John T McIntyre, printed at Philadelphia in 1906. Clyde O Deland drew the illustrations. It opens about noon on a day late in September 1777. A group of young men and boys lounge on benches in the shade of two big buttonwoods across from the old State House at Philadelphia.

The chapters tell how Ethan Carlyle brought the news of Burgoyne's surrender, and how a spy listened at the window. The shallop attacks the Island Queen, and the Ranger sails for France. Ethan faces the bully of the Ranger and strikes with Longsword by night in the harbour of Nantes. Benjamin Franklin opens the secret dispatch. Later chapters sail the cruise of the Ranger and the fight with the Drake in the darkness.
65107-knole-and-the-sackvilles:
Knole and the Sackvilles is a house history by Sackville-West, printed in London by Heinemann in 1922. A chronological table opens the book. A portrait of John Frederick Sackville, third Duke of Dorset, after Gainsborough, fronts it. The story is of a great Kent house and the family that has held it since Elizabeth's day.

The table runs from 1456, when Archbishop Bourchier bought Knole. Cardinals and archbishops hold it in turn: Morton, Dean, Warham, and Cranmer. Cranmer gave Knole to Henry the Eighth in 1539. Edward the Sixth granted it to John Dudley, and Mary to Cardinal Pole. In 1586 Elizabeth granted it to Thomas Sackville, Lord Buckhurst and first Earl of Dorset. Sackville-West, born in the house, writes its annals as family memory and national record together.
65132-wild-pastures:
Wild Pastures is a nature book by Winthrop Packard, printed at Boston in 1909 with pictures by Charles Copeland. The dedication goes to the author's wife and wee boy, who shared the pasture sunshine with him. Its first line calls a New England pasture on a June morning the most beautiful place on earth.

The contents read as a year of walks. Chapters waylay the dawn, stalk the wild grape, keep a frog rendezvous, and chase butterflies. Others go down stream, find magic in a brook, and enter the Ponkapoag bogs. Later pieces treat the resting time of the birds, a pond at low tide, and the coming of rain. The plates show a fox watching a hen coop and a mother bird on the dance. The book is a close, fond watch kept on small wild lives.
65140-not-in-the-rules:
Mack Reynolds sends Jak Demsi, a second-rate gladiator, to Mars with bad news waiting at the spaceport. A yellow spacegram tells him the spacer carrying Earth's gladiator to the Interplanetary Games was lost. Jak has been appointed emergency replacement to represent Earth. He narrates the fix himself, still trying to impress Suzi with antique phrases.

Imagination printed the story in April 1951. The blurb explains the stakes: a planet's strength is settled in the Arena, where brute force usually wins. The Earthman, it promises, will choose a forgotten weapon, strategy. Alger Wilde, a fellow student of ancient times, congratulates Jak while Suzi's eyes widen at the honor.
65194-jingles:
Frank J Medina wrote Jingles, a book of short poems issued in Denver with copyright in 1919. In My Jingles, Medina admits some pieces are fair and some are simply rot. He jokes that he had to fill the book. Contents list more than thirty poems, each with its first line noted.

Topics run from love at dawn and the Rocky Mountains to a small town hotel. A boarder's soliloquy plays on Hamlet, asking whether to board or not. Other poems treat Lawyer Taffy and Doctor Pill, the wild and woolly West, and the school house on the plain. Pieces such as That's My Pa and That's My Wife show a homely, comic bent. Medina writes in plain rhyme for general readers.
65204-around-the-boree-log-and-other-ver:
John O'Brien was the pen name of an Australian priest. Around the Boree Log, published by Angus and Robertson of Sydney in 1921, became the best-loved book of bush verse in Australia. This copy is the 1964 impression.

The title poem asks to be stuck in the old caboose this night of wind and rain. The contents proceed through the little Irish mother, ten little steps and stairs, and the trimmings on the rosary. The old bush school and the birds that will sing again complete the world: Irish Catholic settlers in the back country of New South Wales. O'Brien wrote of his own parishioners with humor and without a drop of condescension. The boree log, a campfire log, is where his people warm themselves, and where the verses still live.
65223-mixed-pickles:
Mixed Pickles, by Evelyn Raymond, was copyrighted in 1892 by Thomas Crowell of New York. A plate of Fritz and Don, at page 158, fronts the tale. The book opens in a pleasant room thrown into dismay by a telegram.

Grandmother Capers throws up her hands and calls the news a terrible infliction. Grandmother Kinsolving, on a lounge, still holds the telegram in trembling fingers. Aunt Ruth speaks with asperity, though her plain Friend's dress should soften her temper. The voice from the lounge is firmest: the visitors cannot come here, and if they do, she will leave. Ruth answers that she is at perfect liberty to do so. The clash of old folks and kin sets the household comedy in motion.
65252-captures:
Captures is a collection of short stories by John Galsworthy, first published in London by William Heinemann in 1923. Galsworthy dedicates the book to R H Sauter, who illustrated some of his other works. A motto from Don Quixote warns gentlemen not to look for this year's birds in last year's nests.

The contents open with A Feud and continue with The Man Who Kept His Form. The list of Galsworthy's earlier books runs long: The Man of Property, The Country House, and the Forsyte Saga among them. By 1923 he stood near the height of his fame as England's humane novelist. The stories in Captures take up men and women caught by habit, class, and old quarrels. His manner stays quiet and ironic, letting small defeats speak for the whole of a life.
65305-christmas-magic-for-all-your-gifts:
Christmas Magic for All Your Gifts, a 3M booklet with a copyright of 1950, shows how to wrap with Scotch brand tapes and Sasheen brand ribbon. Its pitch is plain: the tape sticks like crazy and makes plain things shine. The first trick is the stay-pretty wrap: lid and base wrapped apart, so the box opens neat. Thin strips laid in crosses on the table are picked up with tape and set as trim.

More ideas crowd in. Mag scenes serve as wrap; tape loops take glitter; new pennies line the money tree. Snowflake cut-outs backed with tape make the dazzler, and tapes draw a shirt or toy train on the box. Home craft fans get a gay pack of cheap tricks.
65326-baker-s-coconut-recipes:
Baker's Coconut Recipes, copyright in 1922 by the Franklin Baker Company, is a small brand cook book for canned coconut. First pages praise coconut as a sound, body building food. They say a pound of dried coconut feeds as much as more than twice that weight in beef, by state reports.

Two cans are set out with care. The blue can holds fresh coconut in its own milk, and cooks must press the milk out first. The yellow can holds sweet coconut with pure cane sugar. Tested dishes follow, all made in the Baker test kitchen. They run from Coconut Charlotte with whipped cream to a rice dish with raisins. Home cooks get clear, short dishes built on one store food.
65362-harry-fenimore-s-principles:
Harry Fenimore's Principles is a moral tale for the young, issued by the American Tract Society. The society published it in New York with rights dated eighteen seventy seven. Its author hides behind earlier books, A Summer in the Forest among them. Chapter one sets two city houses side by side on an October evening.

One house stands poor at the city's edge, under a great gnarled butternut tree. The other fronts a fashionable avenue, with ivy walls and a conservatory of flowers. Gaslight flashes up in both at the same moment of the short dusk. Hal Fenimore sits in the rich house's library, elbows planted, hair rumpled with thought. He waits on his friend Tom Haggarty to move in their game together. Something unseen before stands plain in the new light before his eyes.
65452-american-dangers-and-duties:
American Dangers and Duties, by Mayo, is number twelve of Tracts for the Times, volume two, whole number twenty-four. The Ladies' Religious Publication Society published the tracts at Albany in 1861. A circular to friends at the front tells the story of the line. The trial of issuing a run of tracts on liberal Christianity began in October 1858. It proved a marked success at moderate cost.

The circular then lists both volumes by title and author. The first volume holds Liberal Christianity by Mayo himself, The Gospel of the Day by Frothingham, and The Natural History of the Devil by Conway. Starr King, Clarke, and Osgood stand among its other writers. The second volume opens with Bartol, Dewey, and May, and gives Parker, Bellows, and Collyer places. Mayo's own American Dangers and Duties closes the second list, as its twelfth number.
65475-a-list-of-english-american-sequel-:
Thomas Aldred compiles a list of English and American sequel stories for librarians, issued in London in 1922. The Library Assistants' Association published the list for use at the desk. Entries run by author, with each series set out in its reading order.

Anonymous series open the list, from the Cheveley stories to the Saul Weir tales. Jacob Abbott's many boys' series fill long entries, with the Rollo books alone running to fourteen titles plus a European tour of ten more. The Franconia, Marco Paul, and Jonas stories are likewise set in order. Librarians and collectors get a compact guide to which book follows which, a real help where series were sold one volume at a time.
65497-buried-cities-and-bible-countries:
Buried Cities and Bible Countries is a work of biblical archaeology by George St Clair. He was a fellow of the Geological Society and a member of the Society of Biblical Archaeology. The frontispiece shows the ruins of a Galilean synagogue, by favour of the Palestine Exploration Fund. St Clair lectured for ten years in his field.

The book joins the spade's findings to the Bible's lands. It treats the old cities dug up in Egypt, Palestine, and the east, and what their ruins prove. Such works fed the Victorian wish to test scripture by stones and inscriptions. St Clair writes for general readers, with pictures of the sites throughout.
65501-my-hundred-favorite-recipes:
My Hundred Favorite Recipes is a cookbook by Mary Blake, of a milk products company's home economics department. The copyright is held by that company and dated nineteen twenty seven. A quotation at the front finds the road to people's hearts lying through their mouths. The little book is sent in the hope that readers find many new and tasty dishes in it, Blake writes.

Her own favorite recipes are contained herein, one hundred of them, she says. She promises they will all prove thoroughly practical. An opening essay treats the delight of the new in cookery. No matter how old a story cooking is, a new recipe revives our interest, it argues. Even milk has new secrets to reveal, it adds. Doctors insist upon a quart of milk a day for each member of the family, it notes.
65506-certo-a-short-cut-to-better-jams-a:
General Foods issued this recipe booklet in 1943 to teach the short-boil method of jam and jelly making with its Certo pectin. The booklet promises perfect jams and jellies by a quicker road than the old long boiling. Steps to follow come first, then a page of do's and don'ts, then the recipes.

The jelly index runs from apple, grape, and currant to beach plum, chokecherry, guava, and pomegranate. The jam pages add conserves, marmalades, and relishes: cherry conserve, ginger marmalade, grape butter, and orange marmalade among them. Every recipe is built around measured sugar and bottled pectin, made for the home kitchen in wartime. It is a neat piece of branded cookery, complete and practical.
65510-delicious-recipes-including-toll-h:
Delicious Recipes is a booklet for Nestle's Semi-Sweet Chocolate, copyrighted in 1939 by Lamont, Corliss and Company of New York. Its prize piece is the story of the famous Toll House cookies. On the outskirts of Whitman, Massachusetts, stands a Cape Cod house that served travellers in the early 1700s as a toll house.

There, in 1930, Ruth Wakefield, dietician and lecturer, opened her inn, the Toll House. Her chocolate cookie comes from her own cook book. It creams butter with brown and granulated sugar and eggs, and folds in flour, chopped nuts, and two economy bars of the chocolate cut to the size of a pea. Ten to twelve minutes in the oven makes a hundred cookies. The booklet adds Bishop's Cake and more, every recipe a reason to keep the yellow-label bar in the pantry.
65561-jungle-tales:
Croker, a much-read teller of Anglo-Indian tales, gathered these Jungle Tales from her years in India. Press praise heads the book: the Athenaeum sets her in the temple of such fiction, with Kipling as its high priest. Her Diana Barrington had made her name before this.

Woman praises her fine, fresh touch and her close grasp of India. The Glasgow Herald adds that she writes with deep warmth for the folk she lived among. Village griefs and grim turns, shared at close hand, fill her pages. The Scotsman calls the tales new, well made, and sure to please. Readers at home got the daily life of the East in sharp, lived scenes.
65582-causes-and-consequences:
John Jay Chapman fires five essays at the America of the 1890s in a book issued by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1899. He dedicates it to the members of Club C.

Politics opens the set with a hard claim. Misgovernment in the United States, he writes, is an incident in the history of commerce. The growth and massing of capital, made by railroad and telegraph, sits at the bottom of the trouble. New wealth strove to control the laws that touched it at every point. The machinery of government stood in a purchasable state after the war. Society, education with Froebel, democracy, and government fill the other essays. Chapman wrote with a prophet's anger. His essays still cut at the joint of money and public life.
6562-the-pretentious-young-ladies:
Molière turns his eye on Parisian ladies who aped high style in speech and manners, and made a fashion of fine words. His one-act comedy, first played in 1659, marks the point where he left Italian and Spanish plots behind and began to paint living people as they were. The note that opens the text sets that shift out with care.

Two young women, keen to seem grand, fall for false suitors and fine talk, and the fun comes from the gap between their airs and plain sense. Molière keeps the jokes sharp but the target clear: a craze for polish that had grown coarse in the civil wars. The play is short, brisk, and still easy to grasp today.
65706-money-saving-main-dishes:
Money-Saving Main Dishes is a cookery booklet built round cheap, hearty main courses. Its opening pages lay out the food science in plain terms. Protein builds and repairs the body, the book says, and each day needs its share. The booklet gives recipes and plans for about one hundred and fifty main dishes. Most of them give four full servings. Most also give about a fourth of the day's need for protein. Where a dish gives less, the menu note names a food to add.

The book ranks the protein foods in clear tiers. Meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, and cheese stand at the top. Soybeans, nuts, dry beans, and peas come next. Grain foods stand third, and gain when matched with a top food. Milk gets a note for its calcium.
65708-the-philosophy-and-theology-of-ave:
The Philosophy and Theology of Averroes presents tracts of the great Arab thinker Englished from the Arabic by Mohammad Jamil ur Rehman. It was printed and issued at Baroda in 1921, as one of a series of studies in religion and philosophy. The translator was a professor of Islamic history at Hyderabad. He dedicates the book to the teacher at whose feet he first learned to value research.

The following pages, he writes to that teacher, are the earliest fruits of the labour that teaching set going. Averroes, the famed reader of Aristotle in Muslim Spain, argued in such tracts for the harmony of faith and reason. His defence of philosophy against its critics shaped thought in three faiths. An Indian college press here carries that medieval debate to English readers.
6577-the-junior-classics-volume-6-old-fa:
Volume six of The Junior Classics, chosen for boys and girls, gathers old-fashioned tales from writers young readers still know. Mary Mapes Dodge opens with a race for silver skates, Louisa Alcott follows with a hospital tale, and Lucretia Hale, Sophie May, and Mary Freeman add their own stories. A reading guide and a Harvard introduction frame the set.

Each tale stands alone, yet all share a plain, moral warmth and a love of home, work, and play. The book was made as a library for the young, not as a school text, and its tales reward reading aloud. Old-Fashioned Tales gives families a solid shelf of classic short stories in one handy volume.
65774-facts-for-the-people-of-the-free-s:
Facts for the People of the Free States is Liberty Tract number two, an anti-slavery pamphlet. William Harned published it in New York for the American and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society. It sold at a dollar per hundred, and a plate shows a private slave-prison at Washington.

A section named Southern Scenes in 1846 gathers reports of that year. The Abbeville Banner tells of two of Governor McDuffie's slaves killed by drivers, a killing the law termed moderate correction. The Baltimore Sun reports a woman who leaped from her place of confinement. Rescued from the water, she begged to be let drown rather than go back to beatings. At Richmond, a man asked to be hanged instead of whipped. While his master fetched the cowhide, he ran and drowned himself. A Louisiana item follows, of a man hunted by dogs.
65784-the-annes:
Annes is a novel for girls by Marion Ames Taggart of America. A long list of Taggart books fronts the volume in this printing. Her Beth books, Six Girls books, and Nancy books fill that list. Titles run from At Aunt Anna's to Treasure of Nugget Mountain. The Annes stands in that catalogue among her tales for young readers.

Taggart wrote wholesome fiction of home, school, and friendship for girls. Two Annes, by the title's hint, likely share the stage of this tale. Her books sold in series that libraries and Sunday schools trusted widely. Clean peril, kind hearts, and small triumphs form her steady formula. Readers who loved Beth and Nancy could follow the Annes as kin.
65793-international-harvester-refrigerat:
International Harvester Refrigerator Recipes is a company recipe booklet tied to its home refrigerators. The record dates the booklet to 1950, in the first great age of home cold storage. Its pitch promises recipes that are tempting, different, and easy to make for families. All dishes in the set were tried, tested, and checked before printing.
