Sparkling drinks, rich desserts, and crisp salads made for cold keeping lead the list. The text sells the joy of meals that bring children racing to the table. Hostess fame for the unusual in food is the carrot held out to readers. It is a period piece of appliance marketing as much as a cookbook.
65836-drawings-in-pen-pencil-from-du-rer:
George Sheringham wrote notes and appreciations for a book of drawings in pen and pencil from Durer's day to ours, edited by Geoffrey Holme and printed at London in 1922. Malcolm Salaman was to have written the letterpress, the editor's note says. Owing to serious illness, Salaman has been unable to fulfil that intention, and the editor voices his sincere regret.

Owners who lent drawings for reproduction are thanked at length: galleries, collectors, and critics across London and Paris. The Leicester Galleries, William Burrell, Campbell Dodgson, and Oppé stand in the roll. Francesco Albano leads the list of illustrations. Plates run from old masters to living men, each with Sheringham's word on line and character. Collectors and art students get a gallery between covers here, in the Studio's fine printing.
65850-the-house-of-spies:
Warwick Deeping wrote a novel issued in New York in 1913, with a coloured frontispiece by Michael. It opens at night, when Jasper Benham tumbles out of bed at the crack of a pistol shot. Moonlight lies patterned on his floor through a long casement window.

Below the window, his groom John Bumpstead howls that horse thieves have broken into the stable. The thieves have pistols, and Jack dares not face them, even when offered the blunderbuss. Jasper dresses in haste, in a frilled shirt and the red coat of a lieutenant of volunteers, and takes a hanger from the bedpost. Forty chapters carry the tale from that alarm.
65909-a-smaller-dictionary-of-greek-and-:
A Smaller Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities is a reference book for students of the classics. It belongs to a series of historical class books for advanced scholars. Its entries are Latin names, with marks showing how vowels are pronounced. Greek words appear in full polytonic Greek type. Tables at the back run to sixteen, some very dense. The original was printed in two columns, with indexes citing page and column.

A transcriber's note explains the conventions of this edition. Fractions appear in several period forms, kept as printed. Footnotes sit at the end of each entry. The single column text makes the old column references useless, so pages alone are cited. The dictionary covers the things of daily life in Greece and Rome. Law, dress, money, houses, and rites all find their entries. It served school and university readers who met antiquity in Latin texts.
65913-tirant-lo-blanch-a-study-of-its-au:
Tirant lo Blanch is a scholarly study by Joseph Vaeth, printed by Columbia University Press in 1918. Vaeth taught Romance languages at New York University. The study belongs to Columbia's series in Romance philology and literature. Its three questions stand in the subtitle: the work's authorship, its principal sources, and its historical setting.

The Tirant is the great Catalan romance of chivalry, printed at Valencia in 1490. Who wrote it, from what books, and against what history, are hard problems, and Vaeth takes them in order. He thanks Professor Todd, who advised and guided the work from beginning to end. The monograph is a dissertation in full dress: exact, sourced, and made for the small company of scholars who read medieval Catalan. It helped fix the Tirant's place for English-speaking study.
65932-the-royal-regiment-and-other-novel:
The Royal Regiment and Other Novelettes is a set of war tales by Grant, author of a long shelf of novels of war and Scots arms. A list at its front names those books, each at a set cheap price in boards. It came out at London in the late eighteen seventies.

His past tales fill that list: a romance of war, an aide of a chief, a Scots horse man, and a famed queen tale. The black watch, a queen of France, fusileers, and a yellow ship crowd the run. This set weds its title tale of a royal band to short tales of the same cast: camps, marches, duels of honor, and love in time of war.
65974-carry-on-jeeves:
Carry On, Jeeves, a set of ten comic stories by P G Wodehouse, was first published in Great Britain by Herbert Jenkins in 1925. The stories pair Bertie Wooster, a rich young idler, with Jeeves, his unflappable valet. This text follows the Penguin edition.

The opening story, Jeeves Takes Charge, brings the pair together. Others follow the artistic career of Corky, an unbidden guest, and a hard boiled egg. The Aunt and the Sluggard and The Rummy Affair of Old Biffy fill the middle. Fixing it for Freddie and Clustering Round Young Bingo come near the end. Bertie Changes His Mind closes the set. In each tale Bertie blunders and Jeeves quietly sets things right.
66012-identifying-hardwoods-growing-on-p:
Clair Brown of Louisiana State University and Harold Grelen of the Southern Forest Experiment Station wrote Identifying Hardwoods Growing on Pine Sites. The report is General Technical Report SO-15 of the United States Forest Service, dated 1977. A summary states its scope. The book shows and describes twenty-six hardwood species or varieties, among them sixteen oaks and hickories. Photographs show leaves, bark, buds, flowers, and fruits.

Line drawings give the winter outline of each species, and a key is included to help in naming them. Contents open with an overview of southern hardwoods, then the key, then the species one by one. Hickories come first, then a long run of oaks, then elms, sugarberry, yellow-poplar, sweetbay, and sweetgum. Red maple, black tupelo, and the ashes close the list. The overview counts some forty-nine billion cubic feet of small, low-grade hardwoods on southern pine sites.
66045-creepin-tintypes:
Creepin Tintypes is a western story by Tuttle, told in cowboy slang. Tuttle also wrote Tippecanoe and Cougars Two and Between Pike Peak and a Pickle. The narrator and Dirty Shirt Jones open in flight from Piperock town. They had helped Sheriff Scenery Sims jail Tombstone Todd one dark night.

Scenery had no handcuffs, so the pair helped handle his prisoner there. By morning the town had to dynamite the jail to free its own sheriff. Tombstone had vanished, and the town rose and followed the pair to the border. The narrator swears they were only joking and meant no real harm. A sad eyed stranger at a strange bar starts the tale within.
66089-balancing-and-shoeing-trotting-and:
Balancing and Shoeing Trotting and Pacing Horses is a practical treatise by Wm J Moore. The Judson Printing Company printed it in Cleveland in 1916. Moore ran the horse shoeing department of the Allen Farm at Pittsfield, Massachusetts. The farm billed itself as New England's greatest nursery of speed. W R Allen's introduction, dated June 1916, vouches for the author.

Moore was born in Richmond, Virginia, in 1865. He began as a shop apprentice at sixteen. Thirty-five years of shoeing followed, over twenty of them at Allen Farm. The introduction calls the book plain and unvarnished, in everyday words. Its index runs from foals and preparing the foot to gait faults. Shin hitting, knee knocking, paddling, and forging each get remedies. Sideweights, speedy cutting, and converting a pacer close the list. A photograph shows Kremlin 2:07 3/4 at the farm's blacksmith shop, aged twenty-nine.
66136-home-canning-of-fruits-and-vegetab:
Home Canning of Fruits and Vegetables is Home and Garden Bulletin Number 8. The United States Department of Agriculture issued it at Washington, checked in 1965. Staff of the Human Nutrition Research Division made the guide. It sold for fifteen cents from the Superintendent of Documents.

Heat kills mold, yeast, and germs that spoil food, the guide first explains. Fruits, tomatoes, and pickled goods go in a boiling water bath canner. All other common vegetables need a steam pressure canner for safety. Steps, times, and answers fill the pages for home canners who want safe jars.
66139-the-fugitives:
Malcolm B Morehart Junior wrote The Fugitives, a short tale first printed in Imagination in September 1953. Jeff Engel works for the Missing Persons Bureau in his town. Off duty, he still scans each face in a crowd by habit. A card file in his mind holds the faces he seeks.

A small man slips through a gate and bumps a fat shopper in the subway. Engel spots a pen at his feet, marked with the same two marks as the case the man bears. He calls out, gets no turn of the head, and gives chase. The hunt leads through a park and down a still lane to a new world. White towers, swift round ships, and a sky like a vast web greet him there. The folk of that world hate all who come from afar, and now he is one.
66150-gleaner-tales:
Robert Sellar wrote tales set in the southwest corner of Quebec, entered in Canada in 1895 at Huntingdon. A glance at the map, he says, shows that corner as a wedge of territory. The St Lawrence bounds it on one side and the United States on the other. Most of the tales first appeared in a newspaper called the Gleaner, which gives the book its name.

Sellar states a purpose: to present this corner of Canada in readable form. The first tale, Hemlock, opens at Montreal barracks in 1813. Heat beats on the yard while a black cloud hangs over the river. An orderly gallops in from headquarters. War era Canada frames the stories that follow.
66157-joe-napyank-or-the-river-rifles:
Joe Napyank, or The River Rifles, is a dime novel by Billex Muller, printed by Beadle and Adams of New York. The hosted copy is number fifty six of its series, dated August 19, 1876. Its chapters open on the Ohio river, on a night of premonitions and a visitor. Teddy O'Donnell and his love adventure bring a startling catastrophe.

On an island the party stands ringed by peril, with sad forebodings. Young Smith has a desperate adventure, and a rifle is recovered after sad news. Teddy is captured, taken to a flat boat, and thought of rescue stirs his friends. A night voyage down the river leads into the dark and bloody ground of Kentucky. There come capture, an Indian camp, pursuit, and a desperate conflict. Such ten cent tales fed the frontier hunger of city readers. This one packs river, rifles, and Irish humour into weekly parts.
66180-sketches:
Willis wrote these sketches at different periods of a college life. Goodrich printed Sketches at Boston in the year 1827. A Barry Cornwall verse on stories bringing man to humanity fronts it. The volume stands dedicated to his father with warm respect.

The preface says the Scripture Sketches came at a very early age. The rest were written as college days ran out just now. Press of the Christian Examiner at Boston printed the sheets here. A district clerk record of the copyright stands in front matter. The book was entered in the Massachusetts district clerk office in November of 1827.
66229-the-warden-of-the-marches:
Sydney Grier's The Warden of the Marches, sixth in the Modern East series, came from Page of Boston in 1902 with pictures by Alfred Pearse. The frontispiece caption has Sinjāj Kīlin Sahib Bahadar riding out by night, and the chapter heads promise honour, duty and a fire on the hill.

The tale opens in India, where Major North, called Dick, takes his letters from his wife Georgie on the verandah. Both are anxious about Mabel, whose own letters have grown strange and hurried since her uncle's illness and death left her alone in a big house. Before they settle what to do, Mabel herself canters up the drive in a grey riding-habit.
66257-impressions-and-experiences:
Howells wrote Impressions and Experiences, for Harper in 1896. A Hazard of New Fortunes stands among his works on the title. My earliest memories open one of the pieces in this set. Some early hearsay we mistake for remembrance, he warns there. The concern of those memories is his childhood's world itself.

His list of books fills the front pages of the volume. A Boy's Town and My Literary Passions stand in that roll. A Traveler from Altruria and April Hopes stand there also. Criticism and Fiction and the Mouse-Trap farces join the list. The pieces here gather a novelist's looking back and looking round. American scenes and literary life furnish their matter by turns. Howells writes with the plain ease of his best essays. The book gives his impressions the permanence of a volume.
66303-the-art-of-story-telling-with-near:
The Art of Story-Telling, a handbook by Julia Darrow Cowles, was published by A C McClurg and Company of Chicago in 1914. Cowles also wrote Stories to Tell. The book holds nearly half a hundred stories, as its title promises. Its motto calls the word painter the greatest human artist.

Part one treats the craft. It asks why stories belong in the home and in school, and how to choose stories for telling. Chapters cover the telling itself, the use of the story in the primary grades, and set kinds: jingles, fables, folk lore, myth and hero tale, holiday stories, and Bible stories. Part two gives the chosen stories to tell, with two indexes and a list of books for the story teller.
66317-inside-illinois-mineral-resources:
Inside Illinois, Mineral Resources surveys the Prairie State's wealth. The Illinois State Geological Survey issued it in 1965. The book is Number Nine of an education line. John C Frye led the survey then. The state seal of 1818 fronts the text. Illinois runs 385 miles from north to south.

The state spans about 218 miles in width. Its area counts 55,947 square miles. Mean height stands near 600 feet above the sea. Charles Mound tops the state at 1,241 feet. That hill sits in Jo Daviess County, far northwest. Cheap water carriage serves its trade, the book notes. Lake Michigan and great rivers aid its works. A school-level survey joins land forms to the coal, oil, and stone that fed Illinois industry.
66366-dead-men-tell-tales:
Dead Men Tell Tales is a Bible archaeology book by Harry Rimmer, copyrighted in 1939. Eerdmans of Grand Rapids issued the eleventh edition of the apologetic work. Thirty seven plate illustrations run through the text of the volume. A frost memorial library note frames the book as dealing with Old Testament finds.

A companion volume, Crying Stones, was promised for the New Testament records to follow. Rimmer gathers tombs, inscriptions, and digs that bear on the Old Testament problem. Dead men tell tales through their stones to his believing audience of readers. Popular apologetics of the age gains a lively, pictured standard bearer here.
66391-a-book-of-marionettes:
A Book of Marionettes, by Helen Haiman Joseph, was published in New York in 1920. Joseph dedicates the book to her father, Elias Haiman, with pride in his brave, simple, gentle life. A note says the story of the marionette is endless, with neither beginning nor end, since puppets have been everywhere and are everywhere.

Joseph calls her purpose modest: to be a sign-post to better historians and friends of the puppets, and through them to more puppet play. A bibliography lists the chief modern works on marionettes and much curious comment. Thanks go to scholars and players who gave time and help. Photos of fine puppets, such as a dryad and fauns, adorn a warm survey of the puppet stage.
66408-our-nuclear-future-facts-dangers-a:
Our Nuclear Future is a plain language survey of atomic science by Edward Teller and Albert Latter. Criterion Books of New York issued it in 1958 for general readers. Its subtitle promises facts, dangers, and opportunities in equal measure for the public. Early chapters ground readers in atoms, nuclei, and the law of radioactive decay.

Fission and the chain reaction come next, then the action of radiation on matter. Tests, the radioactive cloud, and the path from soil to man fill the middle. Danger to the person and to the race, the cobalt bomb, and reactor safety follow. The book weighs civil and war uses in the first atomic age.
66428-the-frightful-ones:
Frightful Ones is a science fiction story by Richard Maples. It first reached print in a magazine of science and fantasy in November nineteen fifty four, the hosted note says. Its headnote asks what a boy does when he meets a danger from another world. Should he run for help, or fight bravely face to face with it, it asks.

Right then he was the scaredest he had ever been in his life, the tale opens. A spaceship turns within the glow of its flaring jets above him. His father's warning runs in his head as he watches. A boy's duty is to keep eyes and ears open and give the alarm, his father had drummed into him. The rockets of years before were a test by beings of another planet, he recalls.
66458-the-dog-s-medical-dictionary-an-en:
Sewell, canine surgeon to the King and to the Kennel Club, wrote this medical dictionary of the dog, in a second edition revised and printed in London in 1907. The full title calls it an encyclopedia of the diseases of dogs, their diagnosis and treatment, and the physical growth of the dog. Portraits of prize dogs appear through the book.

Entries run in alphabetical order, each split into symptoms and treatment. Abrasions, the first entry, directs the reader to clean the raw skin with hot boracic lotion, dry it, apply ointment, and bandage the part. Abscesses call for hot linseed meal poultices kept warm under oil silk, repeated as needed.
66502-yellow-butterflies:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews wrote a war tale for Scribner of New York in 1922. She gave the story to those Americans who gave even more than life in the Great War, the blinded. A note owns a debt to Kirk Simpson's press account of the coming home of the American Unknown Soldier, and takes lines from it word for word.

The tale opens in a garden. A small boy named Dicky, five years old, races from the house with his young mother after him. His hair is as yellow as the tulips, and a swarm of yellow butterflies rises from the clover and settles on his head. His mother calls a butterfly a sign of the life that does not die. Later the boy's father finds a book of butterflies and reads of the Cloudless Sulphur. The bright scene carries the grief of the war years within it.
6655-tom-slade-boy-scout-of-the-moving-p:
Percy Fitzhugh sends Tom Slade, boy scout, into a tale adapted from the photo play The Adventures of a Boy Scout. The story starts in Barrel Alley, where Tom, as usual, is the one who does it, picking up a barrel stave for a scrape. Sticks and stones, hats off, jail and out again, and Camp Solitaire follow in brisk order.

Tom turns detective, faces revenge, rescues Roy, and learns first aid by wireless, all with scout honor as his guide. Fitzhugh keeps the action clean and the jokes boyish. Tom Slade, Boy Scout of the Moving Pictures, is a lively early scout book, tied to the new thrill of the movies.
6658-owindia-a-true-tale-of-the-mackenzi:
Charlotte Selina Bompas tells the true tale of Owindia, a girl born on a pretty open spot by the great Mackenzie River. Pine woods stand behind the camp, low shrubs and willows ring it, and mossy grass carpets the ground. Her father Michel the Hunter pitched his lodge where the banks rise sixty feet above the river, near other camps drawn by abundant fish.

The story follows Owindia's life among the Mackenzie River Indians, with its hunts, camps, and hard northern ways. Bompas writes with missionary warmth and a keen eye for place. Owindia is a short, vivid true tale of the Canadian north, told for readers far from its cold rivers.
66596-the-punishment-of-the-stingy-and-o:
George Bird Grinnell gathered tales told by Native peoples, printed at New York and London in 1901 with pictures. An opening note tells how the tales came from story tellers, some from sea shore folk and some from folk of the high plains. With no writing of their own, elders passed tales down by word of mouth with great care.

Bluejay tales open the set, with Bluejay as a copy cat and as a guest of ghosts. The title tale punishes a stingy man, and other tales tell of first corn, a star boy, and a bears strong charm. Coyote, Thunder Maker, and Cold Maker also walk through these pages.
66654-all-time-favorite-cranberry-recipe:
All Time Favorite Cranberry Recipes is a cook booklet on cranberries, billed as the year round berries with the bounce. The book opens with the beginning of the berries. Cranberries are truly North American berries, it says.

Before Columbus came to the new world, tangy wild cranberries held an important place in everyday life here. Indian women used cranberries to brighten up food. The Wampanoag Indians of the Cape Cod area treated wounds from poisoned arrows with a cranberry dressing. Pilgrim women learned of the wild berry from the friendly Indians. They soon made their own ways of fixing cranberries, in sauces, bubbling tarts, and nogs. The naming of the berries follows, from names like Sassamanesh and Atoqua to crane berry, for blossoms shaped like a crane head. Cooks get berry history with the recipes.
66688-hans-andersen-s-fairy-tales:
Hans Andersen's Fairy Tales is a large illustrated edition of the Danish storyteller's tales, with pictures by Heath Robinson, published in New York by Henry Holt in 1913. Coloured plates stand among the many drawings. The contents hold the heart of Andersen's work in one thick volume.

The Marsh King's Daughter opens the book at length. Tommelise, the thumb-sized girl, follows. Then comes The Snow Queen in its seven parts, from the mirror and its fragments to the palace of ice. Elfin-Mount and The Little Mermaid stand in the middle. The Nightingale, The Wild Swans, The Real Princess, and The Red Shoes follow. The Emperor's New Clothes, The Flying Trunk, The Shepherdess and the Chimney-Sweeper, and The Ugly Duckling close the list. Robinson's fanciful line was a perfect match for Andersen, and the edition served as many families' Andersen for a generation.
66802-the-man-with-the-golden-eyes:
The Man with the Golden Eyes, by Alexander Blade, first appeared in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in August 1956. Lee Hayden had sent eleven men to their death in deep space, and now he wanted only to die himself.

The story finds Hayden in the gutter, mud and filth on his two-week shirt, while a tape recorder in his mind plays his fall from boy genius to washed-up wreck. A plump, cheerful stranger with an air of confidence stops, offers help, and lifts him to his feet. Something more in the man keeps Hayden from swinging at his chin.
66829-gentlemen-prefer-blondes:
Anita Loos wrote Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, the diary of a professional lady, printed at New York in 1925. Ralph Barton drew the pictures. Six long chapters carry the diary from March into travels abroad.

The diarist, a young woman from Little Rock, Arkansas, starts because a senator friend sent her a blank book and praised her brains. Her educator is Gus Eisman, the Button King of Chicago, who takes her to dinner at the Colony and to the Trocadero. Chapters headed London Is Really Nothing and Paris Is Devine record her trip. The spelling is the joke: brains, she insists, are really everything.
66861-history-for-ready-reference-volume:
The second volume of a five-volume historical encyclopedia edited by J N Larned. The C A Nichols Company published it at Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1895. Its span runs from El Dorado to Greaves alphabetically. Historical maps by Alan C Reiley illustrate the set. The title page states the method plainly. Best historians and specialists speak in their own words.

Larned built the work as a complete system of history for all uses. Long articles quote standard authorities at length. Cross-references tie subjects into a web. A transcriber's note explains this digital edition's rearrangements. Page numbers move to paragraph breaks for clean searching. The set aimed to put a library of history on one shelf. Students and readers were its promised audience.
66870-tibetan-tales-derived-from-indian-:
F Anton von Schiefner translated Tibetan Tales from the Tibetan of the Kah-Gyur. W R S Ralston then did them into English from Schiefner's German, with an introduction. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Company published the volume at London in 1906. Fifty tales fill the contents. King Mandhatar opens the set, and the Kusa Jataka follows. Adarsamukha, the Clever Thief, and the Sudhana Avadana come next.

Prince Jivaka, Visakha, and Mahakashyapa stand among the human tales. The Blue Jackal, the Hypocritical Cat, and the Grateful Animals stand among the beast fables. The Monkeys and the Moon, the Peacock as Bridegroom, and the Revengeful Crow close the run. Ralston's introduction leans on Schlagintweit's list of books on Buddhism in Tibet. The Kah-Gyur, Tibet's great canon, carried these Indian stories north. English readers got them at two removes, through German.
66871-the-doves-nest-and-other-stories:
Katherine Mansfield's stories were gathered after her death in a volume printed in New York in 1923. Mansfield died at Fontainebleau on January 9 of that year, the introductory note records. The book ran through four printings by November. She gives the book to Walter de la Mare, and a line calls reverence the angel of the world.

Finished tales open the book, The Doll's House, Honeymoon, A Cup of Tea, Taking the Veil, The Fly, and The Canary among them. Unfinished stories follow, with The Doves' Nest itself, Six Years After, and A Married Man's Story. Her earlier work between her first and second books was set for later volumes. Delicate, sharp tales of small moments fill the set.
66916-another-man-s-shoes:
Victor Bridges wrote a novel copyrighted in 1913, told in the first person by Jack Burton. It opens on a small problem: a hungry man with precisely one and sixpence to spend on dinner. Parelli's wins, for its four decent courses at a shilling, dirty tablecloths and all.

Inside sits Billy Logan, known by the long red scar from the corner of his eye, a keepsake of a failed rising in Chile. Billy grips his hand, amazed, for a man named Goldley had reported Burton knocked on the head in Bolivia. Burton lets the report stand, admitting it suited him not to contradict it. Burgundy replaces lager, and the old acquaintance reopens, with trouble plainly ahead.
66923-west-african-folk-tales:
West African Folk-Tales gathers tales collected and arranged by Barker, once head of the Government Institution at Accra, and Cecilia Sinclair. Harrap and Company published the book at London in 1917, with twenty-three drawings by Sinclair. Its first and longest part holds the Anansi, or spider, tales.

The spider tales explain how wisdom became the property of the human race, why the lizard moves his head, and why spiders live in ceiling corners. Other tales tell how the tortoise got its shell, and how beasts and serpents first came into the world. A second part of mixed tales and a set of riddles round out the Gold Coast store.
66926-hoppy-toad-tales:
William Hennessey wrote a set of animal tales for children, published at Boston in 1923 and dedicated to the memory of Annie Lucy Libbey. Hoppy Toad is a wee bit of a toad, newly come to the light of day. His home is a hole in the ground, at the roots of a tree, close to a pond.

In the first tale he strays from home against his mother's word, and is followed by a bull-frog who means him no harm. Lost among paths at nightfall, he shakes with fright when Billy Bull-Frog speaks. Later tales bring a narrow escape, a rescue, Sally Woodpecker, Bimby Squirrel, and Billy Crow. Gentle peril is the pattern throughout.
6694-in-midsummer-days-and-other-tales:
August Strindberg, in a translation by Ellie Schleussner, opens with midsummer in the north, when the earth is a bride and brooks still run. A dove flies from the wood to a cottage where a ninety-year-old granny, bedridden twenty years, watches through her window. Flowers, birds, and untouched meadows frame the scene.

Other tales follow: a big gravel-sifter, a sluggard, a pilot's troubles, a photographer and a philosopher, and a tree-swallow's song. Strindberg mixes folk fancy with sharp, modern observation. In Midsummer Days is a varied, lovely set, full of northern light and strange, short wonders.
66951-wireless-possibilities:
Wireless Possibilities is a short book of forecasts by Low, a physicist late of the Royal Artillery College, published in New York by Dutton in 1924. It belongs to a series on today and tomorrow. Companion volumes include Haldane's Daedalus and Bertrand Russell's Icarus.

Four diagrams support the text. Low opens with invention itself. Every comfort that parts us from the cave-man, he argues, comes from the science of invention, yet the faculty waited long for recognition. The inventor must be a strange person, since his doings must be new to be of value. From that ground the book turns to what wireless might still become. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
66968-the-cruise-of-the-scandal-and-othe:
Victor Bridges wrote The Cruise of the Scandal, and Other Stories, published by Putnam's Sons in New York and London in 1920. Bridges had earlier written A Rogue by Compulsion and The Lady from Long Acre. Several pieces first appeared in the Red Magazine and the Bystander. He dedicated the book to Cousin Rose.

Fourteen stories fill the volume, among them The Man with the Chin, Tony and His Conscience, and The Ordeal by Water. The title story opens at a dinner table. George, the narrator's elder brother and a Cabinet Minister, urges him to accept an invitation from Lady Bulstrode and settle down. Rank, George says, has duties as well as privileges. The younger man's dismay at settling sets the cruise in motion. Bridges writes light adventure with a clubman's ease.
66991-memories-and-adventures:
Arthur Conan Doyle's Memories and Adventures was published by Little, Brown of Boston in September 1924, with the author's photograph, taken in America in 1923, at the front. The contents run from early recollections through school, medicine, the sea, and the making of his books, each chapter with its string of sub-heads.

The early chapters are a life in outline. Under the Jesuits recalls Spartan schooling and corporal punishment; the student chapter at Edinburgh names the originals of Professor Challenger and of Sherlock Holmes. Whaling in the Arctic aboard the Hope, and the voyage to West Africa in the Mayumba, follow, with blackwater fever and a ship on fire. Then practice: a strange character's Bristol venture, a telegram from Plymouth, and the start at Southsea, with queer patients and an income-tax joke.
66997-plantation-echoes:
Elliott Blaine Henderson wrote Plantation Echoes, a collection of original dialect poems printed at Columbus, Ohio, in 1904. A modern note warns that the writing captures African American dialect of its time but contains slang and racial stereotypes likely to offend modern readers. Henderson gave the book to Columbus friends including a Dispatch literary editor.

Contents list dozens of short poems: When the Moon Hangs Low, Good Bye Honey, laments, sermons, possum and coon pieces, Memorial Day, and Christmas tree verses in dialect form. Titles such as Stick to Your Race and Learn to Help Yourself show uplift themes inside the plantation frame publishers demanded. Poetry historians get a period Black dialect collection, read with care.
67029-minos-of-sardanes:
Charles B Stilson wrote Minos of Sardanes, an adventure tale with a nineteen hundred sixteen copyright held by Popular Publications. Stilson had won readers with Polaris, a tale of the snows. The first chapter is named The Drive Against Death. Two men watch vast fires from the bridge of a fast ship.

Their gray cruiser flies the Stars and Stripes through Antarctic seas. Ice floes crash round her steel sides. On shore a whole range of peaks has split in a huge blast of lava. Falls of white hot rock pour to the sea in clouds of steam. One man wears the skins of a white bear. His mate Hinson hears him hail the fires. Peril and wonder strike at once.
67056-the-japanese-new-year-s-festival-g:
Helen Gunsaulus, assistant curator of Japanese ethnology at the Field Museum, wrote The Japanese New Year's Festival, Games and Pastimes as the museum's anthropology leaflet number eleven, printed at Chicago in 1923. The leaflet begins with Japanese prints. The familiar nishikiye, or brocade pictures, show actors, beauties, landscapes, and nature studies.

Other woodcuts called surimono picture historical and folk figures, household gods, daily life, and festivals, above all the New Year. From careful study of these prints, Gunsaulus says, we may learn many of Japan's most distinctive customs. Surimono are enriched with metal dusts and embossing beyond the colour blocks. Readers get a museum curator reading a holiday from its greeting cards.
67062-life-among-the-butterflies:
Life Among the Butterflies is a natural history by Vance Randolph. It appeared as Little Blue Book number 796, edited by E Haldeman-Julius. The Haldeman-Julius Company of Girard, Kansas, copyrighted it in 1925. Peter Quinn drew the illustrations. Seven chapters give the butterfly story. The first surveys the literature, from Linnaeus onward.

Randolph notes that the first American species were described around 1750. Clerck, Fabricius, Cramer, and Hübner followed Linnaeus. Smith and Abbot, Scudder, and Holland built the science. The butterfly's body takes chapter two, part by part. Metamorphosis follows: egg, larva, pupa, and imago. Chapter four traces one species, the red silverwing, through every stage. Classification occupies two chapters. Randolph explains the four families and subfamilies. The four-footed butterflies, gossamer-wings, swallowtails, and skippers are distinguished. Enemies and protection close the book. Protective coloration, warning colours, and mimicry explain how butterflies survive their hunters.
67085-icelandic-fairy-tales:
Icelandic Fairy Tales was translated and edited by Hall, with original illustrations by Mason. Warne printed it in London and New York in 1897. The contents list runs through more than a dozen tales, several told in numbered chapters.

Thorstein loses his kingdom and comes to a giant's castle, where a locked room holds a mystery. Sigurd wrestles with giant sisters and escapes on the wonderful horse Gullfaxi. Other tales tell of a giantess and her granite boat, and of Greybeard outwitting a king to win Princess Sigrid. Laughing Ingibjorg is cruelly treated by a stepmother and cast onto a witch's island. Kings' sons, five brothers, and three peasant maidens fill out the set.
67100-bumps-and-his-buddies:
Bumps and His Buddies is a set of child tales by Gulbransen, with prints by a named hand. It came out at Philadelphia in the mid nineteen twenties, made in America. Its rights were held that year by its house.

Its parts are named like small dreams. A charm purse comes first, then a trip to a land of no such place. Queer wee beast folk and their cod oil, a lad who is now seen and now not, and a wee dance girl fill the mid run. A lad with a wish ring and a girl in bird land close the set. Its front print shows a boy who had never heard of a bridge made of fish.
67124-father-thames:
Father Thames, by Walter Higgins, was printed in London by Wells Gardner, Darton and Company. Maps show the river Thames from its source to Windsor. The book falls into three parts, on the London river, the great city the river made, and the upper river.

Early chapters treat the estuary and its towns, the Medway, and Gravesend and Tilbury. Later heads cover the marshes, Woolwich, Greenwich, and the port and docks. The city part runs from Roman and Saxon days through Norman times and the first bridge. Heads name the Tower of London and the great fire that ate what the river had made. River fans get past, trade, and town life along England famed stream.
67180-korean-fairy-tales:
William Elliot Griffis told the fairy tales of Korea for young readers. Griffis wrote much on Korea and on the tales of Japan and Wales. Color plates aid this book, out with Crowell of New York. A note calls Korea the Land of Morning Splendor. Griffis hopes one day to write its full past as well.

A rude tiger leads the tales, and Tokgabi's pranks come next. East Light, Prince Sandalwood, and the Rabbit's Eyes fill the first parts. Topknots, odd hats, and a bird who aids a girl named Fancha add fun. Each tale is short and bright for home reads. Young fans of far tales get a fresh land.
67183-aspects-of-nature-in-different-lan:
Alexander von Humboldt wrote these aspects of nature, translated by Sabine and published in London in 1849. Volume one of two gathers papers born in the presence of grand natural scenes. The ocean, the forests of the Orinoco and the steppes of Venezuela stand in his preface's list.

Mountain wildernesses of Peru and Mexico join that catalogue of his travels there. Fragments were written down on the spot and afterwards moulded into a whole, he explains. Humboldt shows the concurrent action of nature's forces on an enlarged scale, joining science to feeling in the book that taught a century to see landscapes whole.
67191-serbian-fairy-tales:
Serbian Fairy Tales, translated from the Serbian by Elodie Mijatovich, was published at New York in 1918. Sidney Stanley supplied the illustrations, some in colour. The contents open with The Bear's Son, then The Golden Apple Tree and the Nine Peahens. Papalluga, or The Golden Slipper, and Satan's Jugglings and God's Might follow.

Good Deeds Are Never Lost, The Wicked Stepmother, and Bird Girl stand among the tales. Bash Chalek, or True Steel, takes the longest place in the book. The Biter Bit, The Three Suitors, and The Golden Haired Twins come after. One picture shows a great alligator with three heads, and another an old man on his great goat. Mijatovich brought her homeland's tales to English readers in clear, simple English. The book preserves the heroes, witches, and wonders of Serbian storytelling for children abroad.
67201-more-beetles:
More Beetles, by J Henri Fabre, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, was published by Dodd, Mead and Company at New York in 1922. The translator counts it the fourth and last beetle volume of the collected English edition, after The Sacred Beetle and Others and The Glow-worm and Other Beetles.

Fourteen chapters treat the Cetoniae, saprini and dermestes, and the beaded trox. Four chapters follow Minotaurus Typhoeus through its burrow and its morality. The pine cockchafer, the vegetarian insects, the dwarfs, and the gold beetles, their food and their nuptial habits, close the volume.
67207-the-box-of-smiles-and-other-storie:
The Box of Smiles and Other Stories is a children's story book by Laura Rountree Smith, with pictures by Pettee. The Whitman Publishing Company issued it at Racine, Wisconsin, in 1920. All its pictures are in colour. The front one shows a witch dropping two straws from her broom. Eight stories make the book.

The Fairy Shoemaker follows, then Tell Tale and Tattle Too. Little Stay at Home and the Wishing Pin, Little Girl Throw Away, and The Enchanted Staircase come next. Little Dwarf Courage and Dorothy Ann and the Wee Little Man close the set. In one tale a little fairy called Light Heart whispers to a mother that she can help her crying boy. Before you could wink, little Boo Hoo is nodding off to the land of dreams. Smith's tales join fairies, dwarfs, and wee folk to gentle lessons for the very young.
67239-reflections-on-the-music-life-in-t:
Roger Sessions, who taught the craft of music writing at Princeton, set down his thoughts on music life in the United States for the Merlin Music Books. Only fifteen hundred copies of this form were made, and the copy at hand is number 175. Sessions tries to account for the huge growth of serious music in the land since the end of World War One.

Seven parts treat the past and present state of concerts, the stage, school training, and public taste. A last part weighs the ideas of the men who write the music, under heads such as love of country, the hunt for fame, and cross currents. Counts of seats and sales, he warns, show size but not worth.
67256-belgian-fairy-tales:
Belgian Fairy Tales, by William Elliot Griffis, gathers wonder tales from Belgium for young readers. Crowell published the volume in New York, and Griffis had written Dutch tales before. Twenty six chapters run from a story for a preface to a closing society tale. That society aims to make fairy tales come true in real life.

The opening chapter sorts Belgium into Flemings in the north and Walloons in the south. Griffis notes Walloons settled New York and New Jersey in sixteen twenty four. Tales follow of swan maidens, ogres, poppy fairies, and a Bluebeard of Flanders. The long Wappers, pilgrim pigeons, and an enchanted windmill fill the middle chapters. Rinaldo and his horse Bayard, a golden dragon, and kitchen fairies close the set. Pictures and old lore of the Low Countries colour every page.
67265-researches-on-the-visual-organs-of:
Researches on the Visual Organs of the Trilobites, by Lindstrom, was communicated to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on September 12, 1900, and printed at Stockholm in 1901. Six plates go with the memoir. Contents open with an introduction, then blind trilobites.

The eyes of the trilobites follow, then marks on the hypostoma, conclusions, and an explanation of the plates. At the outset, Lindstrom says the memoir is in fact a joint work. The first discoverer of the remarkable structure to be described was Liljevall. He searched out a large amount of the material with great discernment. He prepared it for microscope sections, and drew the figures. Lindstrom arranged the observations. Readers get a classic paper on fossil eyes, built on microscope sections.
67301-southern-soldier-stories:
Southern Soldier Stories is a set of Civil War tales by George Cary Eggleston, printed in eighteen ninety eight. Macmillan published it in New York and London, with pictures by Zogbaum. Eggleston had written A Rebel's Recollections from his own service in the war. He dedicates the book to Joe, his loved comrade in arms throughout.

More than forty short pieces fill the volume, most only a few pages long. A first essay explains how battles are fought for readers who know nothing. Joe, camp fires, an unfinished fight, and a cradle captain follow in order. The women of Petersburg, a woman's hair, and a midnight crime add home front tales. Stuart the cavalier fronts the book as its hero's picture plate. Tar Heels, gunboats, and a dead man's message close the soldier's set.
67323-the-best-of-fences:
Randall Garrett wrote The Best of Fences, printed in Infinity Science Fiction for February nineteen fifty six. A head note sets the stakes. It was a race between man and alien to rule the stars, it says. The aliens were decades ahead, but their real advantage was their incredible elusiveness, it adds. The tale opens inside Interstellar Communications Central.

Romm Parmay stepped in and eased the door shut behind him. Nobody paid much attention to him, the tale says. The five hundred ICC men at the boards filled the room with a murmur of talk. At Number One board, Kerrman stared moodily at the dead screen, blowing cigarette smoke at the panel. Parmay stopped behind him and said, Boo. Kerrman jerked and turned glaring. Parmay then announces he is not the boss any more. Fans get a first contact puzzle of unseen aliens.
67359-comparison-of-woods-for-butter-box:
Comparison of Woods for Butter Boxes is an agricultural bulletin by Turnbow, issued at Berkeley in August 1923 by the California experiment station. It is bulletin number 369 of the university's agriculture series. A picture shows the proper method of packing cartoned butter in sixty pound boxes. The text opens with the trade's custom and its problem.

Butter boxes for shipping and storing butter in California are usually made of spruce, the bulletin says. That spruce is largely shipped in from other states, Washington and Oregon above all. With the late war came a sharp shortage of spruce on the Pacific coast, and a matching rise in price. Makers tried to find a stand in, but the trade did not readily accept a change. Both lumber and butter interests asked for a study of a fit substitute.
67383-little-foxes:
Little Foxes, by Christopher Crowfield, the pen name behind House and Home Papers, was published by James R Osgood and Company at Boston in 1875. It was entered for copyright in 1865 by Harriet Beecher Stowe. A list of Mrs Stowe's writings, from Uncle Tom's Cabin to Oldtown Folks, fronts the volume.

Seven household essays name the foxes: fault-finding, irritability, repression, persistence, intolerance, discourtesy, and exactingness. The frame is a father's winter evening readings for his children, from a text found in the pamphlet-barrel: take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines.
67405-woman-in-the-golden-ages:
Woman in the Golden Ages is a history by Amelia Gere Mason, printed by the Century Company at New York in 1901. The contents march through the ancient world. Woman in Greek poetry opens the book. Sappho and the first woman's club follow, then glimpses of the Spartan woman.

The Athenian woman, Aspasia, and the first salon take a long chapter. A revolt of the Roman women, the new woman of old Rome, and famous women of imperial Rome carry the story west. Marcella, Paula, and the first convent mark the Christian turn. The learned women of the Renaissance and the literary courts of platonic love close the set. In Greek poetry, Mason notes, early poets denounced women while Homer took a kindlier view. Her heroines are Penelope, Nausicaä, Andromache, and Helen.
67436-autumn-leaves:
Autumn Leaves, a book of poems by Ardelia Maria Barton, was published at San Francisco in 1908, printed by Bruce Brough. Barton dedicates the volume to her mother, who watched with loving care over her childhood's tender years, soothed her little woes, and kissed away her tears. The dedication verses thank the mother who guided her over life's rough road and pointed out the snares.

The contents run to some fifty poems. Titles include Dreamland, What Will the Harvest Be, Meridian, and The Indian Lover's Plea with Winona's Reply. A Prayer, Where Is Heaven, Destiny, Liberty, and My Soul and I follow. Verses on the race of life with time, a Mohammedan's prayer, and the progression of the rose fill the book. Barton's poems turn on faith, nature, and the conduct of life.
67438-a-united-states-midshipman-in-the-:
A United States Midshipman in the Philippines is a boys' naval adventure by Yates Stirling, a lieutenant commander in the Navy, published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1913. Ralph Boyer illustrated the book. Stirling wrote companion volumes set afloat, in China, in Japan, and in the South Seas.

Twenty-five chapters carry the midshipmen through capture and escape. A polite captor, a leak of military information, the Katipunan Society, and a traitor unmasked mark the middle chapters. A gunboat cooperates, takes a hand, and stands guard in turn. River expeditions and a struggle for a stronghold fill the close. The frontispiece shows someone turning on an electric current at a tense moment. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
67476-the-automaton-ear-and-other-sketch:
The Automaton Ear, and Other Sketches, was written by Florence McLandburgh. Jansen and McClurg published it at Chicago in 1876. She gives the book to John McLandburgh. A note dated April 1876 explains the contents. Some sketches had run in Scribner's Monthly, Appleton's Journal, and the Lakeside Magazine. They appear here revised, by the editors' kind leave. Others are printed for the first time. Eleven pieces fill the volume. The Paths of the Sea and Reinhart the German follow the title sketch. Silver Islet, a stroller, and a death-watch come next.

The title sketch opens on a summer day like many others. A paragraph stops the narrator in his book: sound is never lost. A strain of music vibrates in the air forever, weakening by a fixed ratio. Some ears, it says, catch sounds wholly lost to others.
67485-the-little-fig-tree-stories:
Mary Hallock Foote wrote The Little Fig Tree Stories, with illustrations by the author, issued in Boston and New York by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in eighteen ninety nine. The stories first appeared in St Nicholas Magazine. Foote gave the profits to the Children Hospital of San Francisco. A first story is Flower of the Almond and Fruit of the Fig. A garden on a hill slope opens it.

There is a garden between the snows of the Sierra Nevada and the warm rich valleys, the tale begins. The Lamb That Could Not Keep Up, Dream Horses, and An Idaho Picnic follow. A Visit to John Camp and November in the Cañon fill the middle. The Gates on Grandfather Farm and The Garret at Grandfather close the book. Foote western tales for children carry her own drawings. Young readers get Idaho ranch life in gentle stories.
675-american-notes:
Charles Dickens paired two travel works in this volume: his notes on a visit to America and his sketches of Italy. The American part records what he saw on his 1842 tour, from cities and prisons to hotels, courts, and daily manners. The Italian part follows his later stay in that country, with scenes of streets, churches, and country life.

Dickens writes as a keen-eyed visitor, quick to praise warmth and wit and just as quick to fault slavery, boast, and harsh jails. He dedicates the American notes to friends in the United States who could bear plain truth told in good humour. Read together, the two halves show a famous novelist testing his own first views against places he knew only by report.
67533-the-book-of-alfalfa-history-cultiv:
F D Coburn, secretary of the Kansas Department of Agriculture, wrote a book of alfalfa covering its history, cultivation, and merits, and its uses as forage and fertilizer. A publishers' note presents Coburn as the man who declined a United States Senate seat. He chose instead to direct the Kansas State Board of Agriculture and serve farmers. Verse by Joaquin Miller calls alfalfa Spanish clover.

Miller's lines praise it filling Sacramento's valley with sweet fragrance. The book argues alfalfa's value to American farms at length. Coburn's Kansas reports had already made him the crop's best known champion. The volume gathers his case in one place for growers weighing a new forage crop.
67575-riallaro-the-archipelago-of-exiles:
Godfrey Sweven wrote a utopian satire printed in New York and London in 1901. An introduction tells of a mysterious shot, and a wounded albatross flashing its broad wings in twilight wakes a camp. Resurrections follow, and the voyagers land on Riallaro, an archipelago of exiles. Its language and its Aleofanian society and religion are set out in order.

Aleofanians worship truth, run a bureau of fame, and organise repute itself. Chapters mock church and journalism, freedom and revolution, and imprisonment and escape. Island after island, from Tirralaria to Coxuria, skewers a fresh modern folly. Sweven uses a lost world voyage to hold a mirror to his own age with a sly, steady hand.
6758-the-adventures-of-sir-launcelot-gre:
Smollett's Sir Launcelot Greaves opens with a set of personages introduced to the reader, then brings its hero onto the stage of action. A chapter the reader may wish were the last, a knight hard to wake, and a recapitulation that draws to a close follow in Smollett's teasing chapter titles. Madness, it seems, may prove catching.

Launcelot, a modern knight-errant, rides to right wrongs in a world of lawyers, madhouses, and rogues. Smollett mixes Don Quixote with English satire, to comic effect. The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves is a lively, odd novel, for readers who like a knight out of time.
67591-famous-colonial-houses:
Paul Hollister wrote a book on famed old houses from the colony days. The book came out in Philadelphia in 1921. James Preston drew the pictures, and Julian Street wrote the front note. Each part takes one house and tells its tale. The set runs from south to north.

Monticello leads, with praise for how Jefferson used fine art at home. A haunted house in New Orleans and Doughoregan Manor come next. Mount Vernon, the Longfellow House, and Cliveden fill the mid part. Hollister mixes build lore with tales of the folk who dwelt there. Home lovers get a grand tour in print.
67607-in-the-nursery-happy-hours-for-the:
The Lothrop Publishing Company of Boston issued In the Nursery in 1897, happy hours for the little ones, with the syllables hyphenated for beginning readers: lit-tle ones, but-ter-cup, meas-ur-ing. The pictures carry equal weight with the words.

Jack and Jill open the contents. The three model mice, the mice and the egg, and in the swing follow. Buttercup the bossy, measuring Tommy, the twins, and a brave girl proceed in tiny chapters. An outline picture to color and a slate picture close the exercises. Books of this kind were the kindergarten's first readers, printed large and kind. The hyphenated words teach the eye to break language into pieces small enough to swallow. A century later the typography looks like a code; to its first readers it was the sound of a mother's voice at reading time.
67610-three-loving-ladies:
Three Loving Ladies is a novel by Mrs Dowdall, printed at Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in 1921. The book was printed in Great Britain. It is dedicated to Katie Burrill. The story opens in Millport, one of the largest and richest cities of the empire. Furniture vans from Burridge and Company bump along its streets early in the morning.

The opening chapter is a satire of the rising suburb. Nobody lives in Millport for choice, the narrator says, but for the chance of making money. Families mark their rise by removing to houses farther from the breadwinner's premises. Each move adds servants, greenhouses, garages and acres needing upkeep. The heights of Elysium are reached by train. Into this world of removals and rising the three ladies of the title are placed.
67643-prosper-me-rime-e-s-short-stories:
Prosper Merimees Short Stories holds four tales by the French master of the form. George Ives turned the tales from French into English for this set. Grace King wrote the front talk on the man and his cold keen art. The set stands in a line of small French master works in print.

Carmen, the famed tale of a wild gypsy girl, leads the book at length. A fort storm tale and a son who kills his sire in pride chase follow. A bronze maid of old myth who slays her groom closes the set list. The front talk calls the tales stars in the French tale sky. Crisp prose and dark turns mark all four of the short works.
6765-mogens-and-other-stories:
Jens Peter Jacobsen's Mogens and Other Stories, in Anna Grabow's 1921 translation from Danish, opens with a decade of ferment in Denmark, 1870 to 1880. Georg Brandes lectured on main currents of literature, Ibsen probed from Norway, and Darwin's ideas echoed from England. Old and new fought with bitterness, each side going to extremes.

The stories that follow, Mogens, The Plague at Bergamo, There Should Have Been Roses, and Mrs. Fonss, show that new spirit in human terms. Jacobsen writes with a poet's eye for mood and a scientist's care for detail. Mogens and Other Stories is a fine, short gateway to Danish realism at its most lyrical.
6768-the-man-upstairs-and-other-stories:
Wodehouse gathers short stories under the title The Man Upstairs, with Something to Worry About, Deep Waters, When Doctors Disagree, and Ruth in Exile among them. The title tale opens with Annette Brougham, composing a waltz, and the knocking from above in three stages: vague discomfort, physical pain like red-hot pincers, and at last insult.

Other tales follow: a man who disliked cats, a tuppenny millionaire, a goal-keeper and a plutocrat, and Sir Agravaine. Wodehouse's wit, light and precise, runs through them all. The Man Upstairs is a delightful, varied set of comic stories from a master of the form.
67758-mandalay-to-momien-a-narrative-of-:
Mandalay to Momien is a narrative of two expeditions to western China, by John Anderson. Anderson was medical and scientific officer to both expeditions. The London edition of eighteen seventy six carries maps and pictures. A view of Mandalay from its hill serves as frontispiece. The expeditions of eighteen sixty eight and eighteen seventy five were led by two colonels, Sladen and Browne, the title page says.

In his preface Anderson notes that seven years had passed since the first expedition. Its results were recorded in official reports printed in India, he says. Those reports were not open to the general reader. Public interest in the overland route from Burma to China had revived, he adds. A repulse and a tragedy attending the recent mission drew that interest, he writes.
67761-stories-from-the-crusades:
Stories from the Crusades, by Janet Harvey Kelman, retells crusade tales for youth. Jack of London and Dutton of New York issued the pictured book. John Lang edited the Stories from History series for young readers. Luard drew the pictures, with Richard in hot battle on the front plate.

Kelman opens that her heroes caught sight of a lovely dream long ago. They lived and died to make that dream come true in the East. Greedy men rode with them, as men still ride with dreamers today. Five tales treat Peter preaching, Tancred, the kings, Frederick, and Louis. Tancred and Louis are praised as knights who fought for poor and weak.
67778-history-of-the-transmission-of-anc:
Isaac Taylor's History of the Transmission of Ancient Books to Modern Times was published in London by Jackson and Walford in 1859. This new edition, revised and enlarged, joins the history to its sequel, The Process of Historical Proof. Together they explain how the genuineness of ancient literature is ascertained.

Taylor's preface says both books were long out of print, and that the reprint removes matter of secondary importance and adds whole new chapters. The work also weighs the evidence usually offered on behalf of the Holy Scriptures against the general case. Taylor cut some chapters on the Biblical argument, holding that the broad subject, fully understood, carries that argument home by itself.
67803-a-list-of-philippine-baptismal-nam:
The Bureau of Education in Manila issued this list of Philippine baptismal names in 1905 as its Bulletin number 9. A teacher named Schneider first made the list because American teachers found it hard to spell the names of Filipino pupils on school rolls. Filipino teachers, too, often spelled names with careless slips, and no fixed standard existed to check against.

The list holds more than a thousand names, drawn in large part from Roman Catholic calendars, with others from school registers. In Manila, Emerson Christie then checked the names against the city cedula lists, going through tens of thousands of entries. He fixed doubtful spellings by an authorized Roman Martyrology and set accent marks by the rules of the Royal Spanish Academy. A preface warns of common letter mixups that twist the names.
67844-hoisting-appliances:
Hoisting Appliances is a correspondence-school textbook from the International Textbook Company of Scranton, Pennsylvania. This file holds Parts Three and Four, copyrighted in 1906. The book is made of separate sections, each with its own page numbers and its own synopsis in the contents.

The text teaches the machines that lift loads in mines and works. One device, the hoist indicator, is fixed to the drum shaft of a hoisting engine. It shows the engineer the position of the cage or skip in the shaft at every moment of the lift. Such plain, exact teaching was the school's trade: working men studied at home, by mail, for better posts. The volume is a specimen of that system at full stretch, diagrams and rules alike reduced to lessons.
67891-the-two-great-canyons-excerpts-fro:
Cyrenus Cole published The Two Great Canyons at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, in 1908, as excerpts from letters written on a western journey. The letters first ran in the Cedar Rapids Republican and Evening Times. Cole dedicates them to the woman who, he says, made all the ways pleasant and all the places happy for three traveling men.

The first letter is dated August 14, 1908, at Mammoth Springs Hotel in Yellowstone National Park. Cole tells of the night train from Minneapolis and the morning spent crossing the wheat country of Minnesota and North Dakota. He finds the towns mere wheat stations, though Fargo, Bismarck, and Mandan hold some interest. At Bismarck he recalls a Bryce story of the state house cornerstone, laid in 1883 before Grant and Sitting Bull.
67898-the-bungalow-boys-on-the-great-lak:
The Bungalow Boys on the Great Lakes is a boys' adventure novel by Dexter J Forrester, published by Hurst and Company of New York in 1912. Tom Dacre and his younger brother Jack cruise the lakes in their sixty-foot motor craft, the Sea Ranger. Four illustrations by J Paul Burnham picture the action.

A Lake Huron storm opens the tale, with the boys refusing to run for shore. Tom is lost overboard and meets old foes. A craft of mystery crosses their path. A Mr Ironsides keeps a submarine on Lake Huron, the strangest vessel on the lakes. Captain Rangler reappears, a submerged wreck strikes, and the boys end within a tower. The frontispiece shows Tom's limp form hauled aboard just in time. The Great Lakes give this one cold water and real danger.
67960-tramping-with-a-poet-in-the-rockie:
Tramping with a Poet in the Rockies is a travel book by Stephen Graham, printed at New York and London in 1936. Appleton-Century issued it, under a copyright of 1922. Vernon Hill drew its thirty-eight emblems. Graham also wrote The Gentle Art of Tramping and A Tramp's Sketches. The poet of the title is Vachel Lindsay.

Graham thanks the Great Northern Railway at St. Paul for pictures, maps, and books on Glacier Park. The two tramps then eluded the railway's kind care, as they wished, and got out on their own. Lindsay had been an art student before he was a poet. On the trail the two discussed emblems and picture writing, and Hill's emblems try to express that side of the trip.
67970-chinese-pottery-and-porcelain-vol-:
R L Hobson wrote Chinese Pottery and Porcelain, Volume One, Pottery and Early Wares, issued in 1915 in a limited run of one thousand five hundred copies. Copy Number 669 is shown here. Hobson worked at the British Museum in old arts and peoples. Forty plates in colour and ninety six in black and white aid the text.

The full work runs from the earliest times to the present day. Volume One starts with the first periods and the Han line of rulers. Han wares run from 206 before Christ to the year 220. The Tang line, from 618 to 906, comes next. A front print shows a Tang statue of a Lohan at the British Museum. Hobson had writ past books on English pottery and Worcester ware.
67978-prejudices-fourth-series:
Prejudices: Fourth Series is a book of essays by Mencken, published by Knopf in 1924. The Borzoi imprint issued it at New York in a limited first edition. Thirty six hundred and ten copies made up that printing, some signed. The contents open with The American Tradition. The Husbandman follows as the second essay. High and Ghostly Matters gathers shorter pieces on faith and the church.

One opening passage mocks a hullabaloo among native scholars. A 1917 book called Standards, by Brownell, had started the row. Mencken watches the white Protestant learned men of the republic with amusement. His titles promise the same sport throughout: the devotee, the cosmic secretariat, the nature of faith. The fourth series kept the manner of the first three. Knopf listed Mencken's whole shelf on the front pages.
67985-little-guzzy-and-other-stories:
Praise for Helen's Babies fronts this 1878 volume before its own title page appears, since its author was known by that famous nursery tale. The book is Little Guzzy and Other Stories, by John Habberton. The Brooklyn Eagle notice in the front matter praises the mix of stories, various in length and grave, gay, and pathetic by turns. Carleton of Madison Square sold the book in cloth at $1.50 and in paper covers at $1.00.

Habberton dedicates the volume to Frank Leslie, who gave him a publishing medium while other publishers only advised him to write. The first story, The Schoolteacher at Bottle Flat, opens in a California mining camp. The forty miners who founded the place argue about freedom, feeling that the founders' voices were spent in vain. The rest follow in the same vein of humor and pathos.
67992-twentieth-century-french-writers-r:
Twentieth Century French Writers is a book of reviews and reminiscences by Mary Duclaux. Scribner's Sons published it in New York in 1920. It was printed in Great Britain for that American edition. A portrait of the author serves as the frontispiece.

In a preface written before the war, Duclaux states her aim plainly. The book should be an image of the century in France. Literature of its first fourteen years would supply that reflection. Her book is small and the subject vast, she confesses at once. A living movement will not keep still to be copied, she writes. That child tried to gather the ocean into a little shell. She has brought away only a sample of the waters, she says.
68032-diabetes:
Diabetes: Its Cause and Its Treatment with Insulin is Little Blue Book number 875, written by Russell M Wilder and edited by E Haldeman-Julius. The Haldeman-Julius Company of Girard, Kansas, copyrighted it in 1925 for its Health Series. Morris Fishbein edited the series and supplied an introduction.

The contents move from the nature of diabetes to the story of insulin, then to cause, diet, and treatment in mild cases. Fevers and operations in diabetic patients and miscellaneous complications close the plan. The book opens in rejoicing: the discovery of insulin in a usable form, it says, is cause for genuine rejoicing, and the sensational newspaper articles may be forgiven their exaggeration. Wilder writes that the diabetic death rate in New York City trebled between 1880 and 1920 for the younger ages, and quintupled above forty-five.
68049-book-of-detective-stories:
The Book of Detective Stories is an issue of the Multum in Parvo Library, a monthly magazine that boasted of being the smallest in the world. A B Courtney of Boston published it in November 1894 at five cents a copy. Its stories are framed as extracts from the diary of a New York detective, edited by Frank Pemmon.

The first tale is called Betrayed by a Dog. Dogs, the narrator begins, have played an important part in the affairs of men. A Chicago dog now assists a policeman in ferreting out thieves. In the case at hand, a dog led at last to the detection of his own master. The store of John Camden had been broken into and its safe blown open. Pocket format detective fiction like this fed the same appetite as the great dime novel houses, at half a dime a month.
6807-pickle-the-spy-or-the-incognito-of-:
Andrew Lang traces Pickle the Spy, the secret agent who shadowed Prince Charles, from papers he found in the British Museum. The Pelham Papers held letters of Pickle and of James Mohr MacGregor, transcripts of which Lang sent to Robert Louis Stevenson for a novel Stevenson did not live to finish. Pickle, like the Master of Ballantrae, tempts romance writers.

Lang resists that temptation, telling Pickle's woeful history as fact, not as fiction's villain. His preface sets out sources with scholarly care. Pickle the Spy is a vivid, true tale of Jacobite intrigue, spies, and a prince in hiding.
68071-the-fir-tree-fairy-book-favorite-f:
The Fir-Tree Fairy Book, edited by Clifton Johnson, holds favorite fairy tales retold for the fireside. Little, Brown printed it at Boston in 1912, with pictures by Alexander Popini. It came out that November, in a series of fairy books.

The cover sets the game: little men guard the road that leads to Fairy Land. If you believe, they let you pass; if not, they turn you back. A plate shows the Pied Piper ordering the rats into the water. Johnson's note explains his editing of the wonder tales. The charm and sweetness are kept, Johnson says, but savagery and distressing detail are dropped. Falsehood, gluttony, drunkenness, torture, and gore go out with them. Cruel fathers and wicked stepmothers can be spared too. The book, he promises, may be read aloud to children with confidence.
68092-cargoes-for-crusoes:
Grant Overton wrote Cargoes for Crusoes, held in 1924 and issued at New York by D Appleton, George H Doran, and Little, Brown in joint form. Overton had writ About Books and Authors and The Women Who Make Our Novels. A droll note gives the book to all who, though having one book, sometimes enjoy another. Two lines of talk head that note.

The book opens in the voice of Robinson Crusoe on his desert island. Crusoe says Defoe's ending is indifferent and that truth is often happier than fiction. He tells of long loneliness and distress of soul on the isle. Overton then turns to books as cargo for lone readers. Essays treat authors of the day and the books such readers should pack. The frame is witty and the aim is a guide to good reading.
68113-jingles:
Winifred Sackville Stoner wrote Jingles, a book of verses published in 1909 by Smith and Butterfield of Evansville, Indiana. The title page carries a remarkable note. Stoner wrote the poems when she was five and six years of age. Karl Knecht drew the pictures. The book is dedicated to dear friends, and its pages are dated by photographs of the author at one, two, and three years old.

The verses run through a small child's year. Christmas pieces open the book, with Santa's reindeer and Nissen, the Santa Claus of Norway. Other poems treat a kitten, the new baby, too many dolls, and whooping cough. Simple Simon, the giant Arithmos, and King Teddy all appear. The collection preserves the rhymes of a child poet whose work her family and town thought worth printing, spelling slips and all.
68129-carlyle-s-laugh-and-other-surprise:
Carlyle's Laugh and Other Surprises gathers essays by Thomas Wentworth Higginson, printed at Boston in 1909. Higginson wrote lives of Margaret Fuller Ossoli and Longfellow, and a memoir of a Black regiment. Some papers here first stood in his earlier book called Book and Heart.

A note at the front thanks publishers for leave to reprint pieces on Keats and Shelley manuscripts. Other essays treat Brown, Cooper, and Thoreau, and one looks at a woman of Thackeray's making. Higginson moved among the writers of his century and knew many of them. His surprises are the small true stories a long life among books and authors leaves behind.
68151-early-candlelight-stories:
Early Candlelight Stories holds short tales for the young by Stella Shetter. Dorothy Gregory drew the prints that dress the text of the book. A front print shows three children drawn close to hear a gran read. Rights date the work first to the year nineteen twenty two.

A gran tells the tales by lamp light to Bobby, Alice, and Pink. Wolf chases, a yellow gown, a war tale, and a sugar camp fill the list. Fair fun, a dare, dog tales, and a last red man mark the range. A word list at the end helps young readers with hard terms. Plain home faith tunes the set for school and hearth alike.
68162-the-bushwhackers-other-stories:
The Bushwhackers and Other Stories is a set of Tennessee mountain tales by Charles Egbert Craddock, the pen name of Mary Noailles Murfree. Herbert Stone of Chicago published it in 1899, and this copy is the third impression. Craddock had written In the Tennessee Mountains and The Story of Old Fort Loudon. The title story fills the first 119 pages.

Two shorter tales follow: The Panther of Jolton's Ridge and The Exploit of Choolah, the Chickasaw. The Bushwhackers opens on a young mountaineer, Hilary Knox. Some enchantment seemed to draw his steps daily to a rocky promontory above the wooded valley. He would climb the almost inaccessible steeps between sunrise and sunset and stand shading his eyes, gazing far and near. At first he searched with eager expectation; at last he dwelt on the scene dully and wistfully.
68204-ballads-from-the-danish-and-origin:
Smith-Dampier made this verse book, Ballads from the Danish and Original Verses, printed in London in 1910 and dedicated to the memory of her parents. A contents page divides it cleanly in two. The Danish ballads come first, eleven of them, and the original verses follow, six pieces in a sterner, Scottish key.

The Danish set runs to trolls, mermen, and wronged lovers. King Olaf and the Trolls stands first. Sir Karl's Lykewake, The Avenging Sword, and The Avenging Daughters follow. The Knavish Merman, The Wood-Raven, and The Rime of the Dead Lover close the set. A note promises that in the renderings the measure of the original has in all cases been strictly kept. The original verses turn to Prince Charlie, the Forty-Five, and a traitor's head.
68225-australian-fairy-tales:
Australian Fairy Tales is a story book by Atha Westbury, issued by Ward Lock in 1897. Johnson drew the pictures for the London, New York, and Melbourne printing. Contents open with Golden Cloud, a five chapter tale from The Lone Rock onward. Mother Dot, Dusk Stronghold, and the ring dove fill that first long tale.

Twilight brings Baron Thimble, Prince Picnic, and Lady Lollypop in short chapters. Tim, Three Sparrows, King Dunce, and The Bank Cat fill the middle of the list. Gumtree Hollow plants the fairy world in the Australian bush for child readers. Colonial children gained home grown magic in place of imported wonder alone.
68235-one-hundred-one-mexican-dishes:
May Southworth compiles One Hundred and One Mexican Dishes, printed at San Francisco with copyright in 1906. Paul Elder made the book, in a second printing of 1914. Small chile outlines grace many heads, the notes say.

The classes run soup, fish, meat, fowl, and vegetables. Meat dumplings, desserts, enchiladas, and tamales follow, with olla podrida at the end. Soup leads with Almendra, a rice and almond soup in milk and cream. A touch of ground chile warms it. Caldo de Pescado follows, a fish soup with tomatoes, wine, and a chile pepper. Cooks get clear, short receipts in the style of the day.
68248-my-twin-kitties:
My Twin Kitties is a picture story for small children by Edna Groff Deihl, printed in New York by Samuel Gabriel Sons and Company in 1924. Deihl also wrote tales of a little dog, a teddy bear, and twin puppies. Her twin kitties wear no mittens, only coats.

One kitten is yellow and one is black, and both have blue eyes, sharp teeth, soft feet, and scratchy claws. They are the same age to the day. At first they live on a farm with too many kittens, eat only mice, sleep on hay, and have no names at all. At last they set out to seek their fortune, which is a home and two pretty names. Young readers follow two small strays on a brave, sweet hunt.
68254-my-twin-puppies:
Edna Groff Deihl wrote My Twin Puppies, issued at New York in 1924 by Saml Gabriel Sons and Company. Deihl had writ tales of a little dog, a kitten, a teddy bear, and a chick. Pictures fill the small book. The tale is told in large, clear lines for young children.

Two puppies are born on the same day, so they are twins. Jimmy's father brings them home in a big basket. One pup has a big black eye and one has two brown eyes. Jimmy names the brown one Bubbles for a girl next door who blew bubbles. The black eyed pup chews Jimmy's shoe at once. Short scenes and prints carry the pet tale.
68255-a-history-of-the-zulu-rebellion-19:
J Stuart, once an officer in Natal and an aide on native affairs, tells how Natal rose in arms in 1906. His Macmillan history from London in 1913 pairs the rising with the arrest, trial, and exile of Dinuzulu. Five maps, six plans, and twenty-five pictures support a long, close account built in part from official reports.

Stuart says the Natal government first asked for an official history near the end of the fight. When the Union of South Africa formed, that backing ended, and he chose to finish the work at his own cost and risk. Help from officers, returns, and maps still gives the book weight, and he thanks those who stood surety for its printing.
68334-best-laid-schemes:
Best Laid Schemes is a story collection by Meredith Nicholson, published by Scribner's in 1922. The six stories had appeared in magazines over the previous decade. Their titles promise the book's world: the susiness of Susan, the girl with the red feather, Arabella's house party, the third man and wrong number.

The first story follows Susan Parker, twenty-six, to whom Man had never happened. Suitors had come and gone on slight grounds: a weak sonnet, a sermon, and a careless remark about Harvard. Orphaned and not rich, she has adjusted by taking a library course in Syracuse. Nicholson's comedy is gentle and exact about the marriage market of the educated middle class, where a careless sentence can sink an argosy of young affection.
68341-the-book-of-witches:
Oliver Madox Hueffer wrote The Book of Witches, printed in New York in 1909. A frontispiece in colours by Heath Robinson goes with the book. Contents run to sixteen chapters. On a possible revival of witchcraft opens the set. A sabbath-general, the origins of the witch, and the half-way worlds follow. The witch's marks and ways, and some leading English witches, come next.

The witch of the oldest times, and the witch in Greece and Rome, take their chapters. From pagan days to Christian days, the witch-bull and its effects, and the later trials in England follow. Trials in Scotland and elsewhere, love-drinks and potions, and the witch in tales end the set. The first chapter owns the oddity of its theme. The witch, to schooled minds, is as long gone as the dodo.
68351-in-the-three-zones:
In the Three Zones is a book of three tales by Stimson, who wrote past a pen name. It was put out at New York in eighteen ninety three. The three tales are named at the front with their sub heads. The same hand's past tales of tale craft are list past them with their prices. The first tale bears a strange name in a tongue of the north.

That first tale works out the creed of a man who held that mind is stuff. Its hand would tell how its chief came to his end, he says at the start. That chief was a prey of that creed, as his sire had been past him. Past death he left this tale past his rolls, writ to the hand.
68364-book-of-brief-narratives:
Book of Brief Narratives is number twelve of the Multum in Parvo Library, volume one, December 1894, published monthly by Courtney at 671 Tremont Street, Boston. It bills itself the smallest magazine in the world: fifty cents a year, single copies five cents. It opens with detective stories, from the diary of a New York detective, edited by Pemmon.

The first, A Chance Meeting, is told by the detective himself. A robbery at the house of Bond had baffled the police for a month; two detectives failed, and the case came to him. Among the jewelry gone was a gold watch, Bond's daughter's birthday present from her mother. The thief left one trace, a piece of paper reading Remember the poor, which he thought nothing of. He confesses a complication: Bond's daughter Clara is pretty, and he fell in love at first sight, which made him work all the harder.
68374-friends-and-enemies:
Friends and Enemies is a short star tale by Fritz Leiber from the April nineteen fifty seven Infinity. Two plain men are marched out of town at dawn by a fat chief and two armed lads.
