One is Ellenby, a math teacher at Ozona College in the tale world. His fault is a hid past as a man of the atom craft. That past marks him for ban in a world wrecked by super bombs.

His mate has spent his life in warn cries against men of science. Bombs, screen shows, and fax craft are the blights that mate names. Thugs rule the blast world and fear all book craft alike. Art and science clash as a death debate in that world, the tag warns. New Angeles spires gleam far off as the two walk the hot road.
68380-the-guest-rites:
The Guest Rites is a science tale by Silverberg, with art by Giunta, first set in a pulp sheet in the late nineteen fifties. A tag at its head sets its trap: the Earth mans god was not Carthule, but Carthule shields him while he is a guest in the shrine. That holds, it says, even if he tears the shrine down.

Its first scene is a priest at his noon rite. The first priest of Carthule ends his spare meal and goes out to sit in the noon breeze. He watches the sands drift over the bare flat plains. His thoughts turn on the word of his god: why did Carthule wait so long to tell his folk they are not alone in the vast void? A bright dot glows in the grey sky wall. That, he knows, is the sun.
684-worldwide-effects-of-nuclear-war-som:
A 1975 report from the United States Arms Control and Disarmament Agency sums up what was then known about the wide, long-term effects of nuclear war. It draws on a National Academy of Sciences study and related agency work, and it is frank that much stayed unsure. Its aim was to give the public a clear, plain account, not a technical one.

The chapters cover how nuclear blasts work, local and worldwide fallout, dust high in the air, and harm to the ozone layer. Short notes add facts on yields, bomb design, and radioactivity. The value lies in its scope. It looks past the blast zone to effects that could touch the whole globe, and it warns that statecraft should aim to never learn these lessons from real war.
68408-argonaut-stories:
Argonaut Stories, selected from the San Francisco Argonaut by its editor Jerome Hart, was published in 1906 by Payot, Upham of San Francisco. Twenty-two stories stand in the contents, a roll of the magazine's writers: Jack London leads with Moon-Face, and Frank Norris follows with A Caged Lion. Stewart Edward White, Morrow, and Sinclair are among the rest.

The tales are of the West the Argonaut served. London's Moon-Face opens the book, its narrator explaining his hatred of John Claverhouse. The man's round face, its nose flattened at the centre like a dough-ball on a ceiling, had become an offence to his eyes. Other heads promise a double shot, ten thousand years in ice, leaves on the river Pasig, the man-dog, and under flying hoofs. Kathleen Thompson's The Colonel and The Lady closes the contents.
68479-windmills-a-book-of-fables:
Windmills, a book of fables by Gilbert Cannan, was published by Huebsch at New York in 1920. Cannan dedicates it to Lawrence, the famed novelist. Its motto names a four armed monster who battles the gods. The fables divide into Samways Island and Ultimus.

Samways Island runs through short headed chapters: Tittiker, the bishop, Arabella, the skittish navy, and Captain Courageous. Hostilities, love, music, hunger, and national feeling follow in a few pages each. George Samways awakes one night with a vague distress that all is not well with his island. The moon casts the shadow of his palm tree over his cooking hollow in a way it never did before. Cannan's fables mock nations, churches, and emperors in the voice of a tale. They are brief, dry, and aimed at recent follies.
68542-free-and-other-stories:
Free and Other Stories, by Theodore Dreiser, was issued at New York by Boni and Liveright in 1918. Four printings of the book were called for in that first year. Free, the title tale, opens the contents at page nine. McEwen of the Shining Slave Makers follows in the list.

The Lost Phoebe and The Second Choice stand among the middle stories. A Story of Stories and Old Rogaum and His Theresa come next in order. The Cruise of the Idlewild, Married, and When the Old Century Was New close the book. Dreiser had written Sister Carrie and Jennie Gerhardt before this set. His tales show small lives ground by money, custom, and desire. The title story opens in the comfortable rooms of an architect on Central Park West.
68585-puppies-and-kittens-and-other-stor:
Carine Cadby wrote tales of young pets, told with real photos of them. Will Cadby took the photos, thirty-nine in this book. A front tale tells of dolls who take a day off. That tale, The Dolls' Day, drew praise from a London daily. It calls the book a trip through a lens to a child's dream land.

Belinda and Charles slip from their cots while Stella naps. They roam woods and fields, meet a cat, and find a kind rabbit. In the main tales, pup and kit lives fill the pages. Each photo pins the tale to a real small beast. Young pet lovers get charm with a true look.
68589-sandman-s-rainy-day-stories:
Abbie Phillips Walker wrote these fairy tales for Harper and Brothers in 1920, with pictures by Chase. The book is dedicated to the memory of her father, Thomas Phillips. Twenty-three stories fill it, most short. Princess Cantilla opens the volume. She lives in a decayed castle with her father, an old king who has lost his lands quarreling with other kings. She cooks their meals like a peasant girl.

An enchanted dwarf steps out of her soup kettle and offers to restore everything. The Tree of Swords, the Silver Horseshoes, and the Blue Castle follow. There are ogres, dwarfs, and an enchanted boat. Animal tales close the book: how the elephant got his trunk, why rabbits have short tails, and the hunter's friend Johnnie Bear. Walker wrote the Sandman books for the hour before sleep, and the tales keep that size and temper.
68624-the-red-cross-girls-with-the-stars:
The Red Cross Girls with the Stars and Stripes, by Margaret Vandercook, was published at Philadelphia in 1917. Vandercook also wrote the Ranch Girls series and the Camp Fire Girls stories. Earlier Red Cross Girls books put the girls in British trenches, on the French firing line, and in Belgium, Russia, and Italy.

Chapter one is the call, and chapter two another volunteer. Somewhere in France, and with the American army in France, follow. Introductions, carrier pigeons, and the days before the great day fill the middle. Loneliness, a dispute, and the two sides of a shield come later. The undertow is named near the end. Readers get a girls war service novel, written the year the United States entered the First World War.
6864-average-jones:
Samuel Hopkins Adams opens Average Jones in the Cosmic Club, where three men ask what is the matter with Jones. Waldemar, owner of an important newspaper, wears a look of good-humored power; Robert Bertram, the club idler, sits slender and languid; Jones himself is the third. His nickname, Adams notes, was foreordained by parents who gave him an average name.

Chapters on a B-flat trombone, a red dot, an open trail, mercy signs, blue fires, and a million-dollar dog follow, each a small mystery Jones solves by keen, average sense. Adams writes with wit and pace. Average Jones is a delightful set of detective tales, where plain logic beats showy brilliance.
68655-six-modern-women-psychological-ske:
Six Modern Women is a book of psychological sketches by Laura Marholm Hansson. It was translated from the German by Hermione Ramsden and printed at Boston by Roberts Brothers in 1896. The six women are each given a heading that names her type. The sketches are studies of the inner life of women who had lately come before the world.

The first is The Learned Woman: Sonia Kovalevsky, the mathematician. The second, Neurotic Keynotes, treats George Egerton, the novelist. The third takes Eleonora Duse as The Modern Woman on the Stage. The fourth calls Amalie Skram The Woman Naturalist. The fifth is A Young Girl's Tragedy: Marie Bashkirtseff, the diarist. The last is The Woman's Rights Woman: Edgren-Leffler. But she pays for this knowledge with her death, as the sketches of the dead Bashkirtseff shows.
68657-a-book-of-images:
William T. Horton drew the plates of this book of images, printed at London in 1898. W. B. Yeats wrote the word at its front. It is the second book of a set named the Unicorn Quartos. The list of plates gives the cast of the work. By the Canal, The Old Pier, and Notre Dame de Paris stand for its scenes of place. Trees Walking and The Wave stand for its turns of dream.

More plates name the themes of faith and dread: Mammon, St. George, and a call to be strong. The Angel of Death, Sancta Dei Genitrix, Rosa Mystica, and a rise into the sky fill the last half. The plates are all of one kind: black shapes of a world of dream and of souls, drawn by a man whose gift was the sight of such things.
68681-the-cross-word-puzzle-book-second-:
The Cross Word Puzzle Book, second series, printed in New York in 1924, is a second gathering of fifty new cross word puzzles. They were chosen as the best of the thousands sent in to the New York World, and appear here for the first time. Buranelli and co-editors made the choice. An opening piece by William Stern, cross word puzzle champion of the world, tells how he came to the game.

Two years before, Stern writes, he saw a friend poring over a checkered pattern in a Sunday paper and asked if he had taken up cross-stitching. Told it was a puzzle, he laughed, holding puzzles childish time-wasters. His friend, angered, dared him to try. He finished that first puzzle the next day, with little thought to food and rest. He then sets out the rules in simple terms.
68685-moon-madness-and-other-fantasies:
Aimée Crocker Gouraud wrote a set of eight fantasies, here in a fourth edition issued at New York in 1910. The book is dedicated to those who know. Its first tale, Our Lady of Red Lips, is set in Paris, where a big, handsome American man stops before an art dealer's window.

The portrait that holds him shows a small French woman with creamy skin, black hair, green eyes, and lips of a red he has never seen or dreamed. The dealer tells him the painter, Paul Gaspard, died six months before, in peculiar circumstances. Other tales treat a cobra dance, pearls, and the title piece, Moon-Madness. Decadent glamour is the book's vein.
68706-modern-house-plans-for-everybody-f:
Reed's Modern House-Plans for Everybody, published in New York by the Orange Judd Company in 1900, offers designs for village and country houses. The title page prices the range from two hundred and fifty dollars to eight thousand dollars. Each design carries full descriptions and detailed estimates of materials, labour and cost.

The preface calls this a modernized and revised edition, with nearly all the elevations redrawn to current taste. The first design is a cottage costing $250, meant as the wing of a future main house. A country cottage at $450 and two at $550 follow, with practical suggestions on roofs, linings and outside plastering throughout.
68732-the-moral-pirates:
The Moral Pirates, by W L Alden, was published by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1881. The illustrations promise the boys' cruise: the Whitewing at Harlem, lifting the boat over the piles, going through the lock, a soup explosion, and a fight with the tramps.

Mr Wilson troubles over his son Harry, idle from July to September and caught reading a wretched story about pirates. His brother answers that all boys like piratical stories, and that he himself once dreamed of being a moral and benevolent pirate. He offers to find Harry something better to do all summer.
6874-canada-and-the-states:
Sir Edward Watkin recalls his work in Canada and the United States between 1851 and 1886, years spent crossing the Atlantic on railway and trade business. He opens with an American report urging that the Maritime Provinces, with their hardy folk, harbors, fisheries, and seamen, would strengthen the United States at sea. That bold claim frames his own hope for Canada as a great part of the British Empire.

Dedicating the book to his wife, who bore long absences while he traveled the continent, Watkin mixes personal memory with public argument. He writes of routes, deals, and the men he met, and he keeps returning to one theme: Canada's place in the Empire and its ties, friendly and rivalrous, with its southern neighbor.
68792-the-cross-word-puzzle-book-third-s:
Prosper Buranelli, F. Gregory Hartswick, and Margaret Petherbridge edited the third series of a cross word puzzle book issued in New York in 1924. The volume holds fifty new puzzles chosen from thousands sent to the New York World. The editors print them here for the first time, under the rules of the Amateur Cross Word Puzzle League of America.

Inside, a ballade by Ruth Franc von Phul, named as cross word champion of the world, praises the puzzle book as a cure for dull hours. A comic dialogue shows two neighbors whose talk has swelled with rare words learned from clues. Readers get fifty fresh puzzles plus period humor about the craze that made cross words a national habit.
68796-the-blue-peter-sea-comedies:
Morley Roberts wrote The Blue Peter, a set of sea comedies published at London in nineteen hundred and six. Roberts had earlier written The Promotion of the Admiral and other tales of the sea. He gave the book to his father.

The first tale, The Extra Hands of the Nemesis, opens at Tilbury in November fog. The steamer Nemesis loads cargo for Capetown and ports beyond, while Captain Jordan gloomily boards. Jordan, once keen, now sails for a hard firm and feels his chances gone. Other tales bring a captain wrecked on the Manacles, a crowded iceberg, and a parson's strange change of heart. Salt humour rules.
688-the-goodness-of-st-rocque-and-other-:
Alice Dunbar wrote these stories of Creole life in and around New Orleans, where French, Spanish, and African roots mix. The title tale follows Manuela through the streets of the old city, and the other pieces move between bayous, fishing towns, feast days, and small shops. Love, faith, pride, and hard luck run through them all.

Dunbar gives close portraits of women and men who live by custom and by heart, from a praline seller to a violin player. The local speech, food, and rites are part of the scene, not mere colour. The book is prized as an early, insider view of Louisiana Creole society, told with warmth and a sharp eye for social rank.
68806-the-land-of-the-hittites:
The Land of the Hittites, by John Garstang, reports digs in Asia Minor. Constable issued it at London in 1910 with maps and plans. Ninety nine photographs and a bibliography back the text in full. Garstang held the Liverpool chair in methods and practice of archaeology there.

Professor Sayce intro note frames the Hittite realm as a forgotten empire. German digs at Boghaz-Keui found the Hittite capital north of the Halys. Garstang scouted other Asia Minor and north Syria sites for like remains. At Sakje-Geuzi he began digging and found art of real weight in time. Monuments described here link east and west in one old culture.
68831-il-novellino-the-hundred-old-tales:
Edward Storer turned these hundred old Italian tales into English for the Broadway Translations line. Routledge of London and Dutton of New York issued Il Novellino with a long opening essay. The tales are short, sharp, and very old.

A proem opens the set, then the rich embassy Prester John sent to the Emperor Frederick. A wise Greek in a king's prison judges a horse in the next tale. A jongleur pleads before Alexander, and a young prince carries a king's reply to Greek envoys. King David counts his people, and an angel warns Solomon's house. Such brief, bright tales fed the stream that later filled Boccaccio's great book.
68888-how-jack-mackenzie-won-his-epaulet:
Gordon Stables wrote this boys' tale of war, printed in London in 1906. In his preface Stables says war has a glamour that rightly stirs young men. Yet a real soldier, he warns, must be a good camp man as well as a brave fighter. That skill, he argues, is learned on the tented field in peace, not in barracks.

The first book sketches a sailor's life in peacetime, drawn from real service. The second book turns to the Crimea, where Stables says the tale is all true, sadly and terribly true. Britain had not fought for forty years before 1853. Its army sailed ill prepared, saved only by courage and luck. Stables quotes General Evelyn Wood on why such waste must be recalled. Jack Mackenzie's road to his officer's epaulettes runs through that hard school.
689-the-kreutzer-sonata-and-other-storie:
Leo Tolstoy wrote the title novella as the confession of a man who murdered his wife in a fit of jealousy, told to a fellow traveller on a train. Music, marriage, lust, and rage are argued through at length, and the narrator's guilt gives the tale its force. Benjamin Tucker's translation carries the work into English.

The volume adds further short tales, including the folk fable "Ivan the Fool", in which simple goodness defeats cunning and greed. Together they show Tolstoy's late moral fire: plain stories that preach against pride, wealth, and sexual vanity. The book remains a stark, unsettling read, and a key to Tolstoy's thought after his great novels.
68902-really-so-stories:
Elizabeth Gordon wrote Really-So Stories, with pictures by John Rae, issued in 1924. The frame is a boy named Billy, who spends a summer in the woods with a friend. Billy does not care much for made-up tales, even of wolves and bears. He wants tales that are really so, about how things began and what days mean.

Short pieces then answer his kind of ask, month by month through the year. Topics run from the telegraph and the military salute to Lincoln's birthday and Flag Day. Others treat silk, coal, cotton, coral, clocks, and carrier pigeons. Holiday pieces cover Easter, the Fourth of July, Thanksgiving, and Christmas. Each piece is brief and plain, made for young readers.
68919-the-promotion-of-the-admiral-and-o:
Morley Roberts, author of The Colossus and The Fugitives, gathered eight sea tales in The Promotion of the Admiral and Other Sea Comedies. Page and Company issued the book at Boston in 1903, in its third impression. The tales bear names like The Settlement with Shanghai Smith, The Policy of the Potluck, The Crew of the Kamma Funder, and The Scuttling of the Pandora. Each turns on the tricks, feuds, and luck of men who live by the sea.

The title tale opens at a sailors' boarding-house on the Barbary Coast of San Francisco, run by Shanghai Smith. Smith is drawn as hard, rough, and tough, with the bold head of a mad steer and the sly wit of a monkey. Roberts writes of the waterfront with a seaman's own knowledge, and the humor is broad, salt, and quick.
68920-captain-balaam-of-the-cormorant-an:
Captain Balaam of the Cormorant and Other Sea Comedies is a book of sea stories by Morley Roberts. It was published in London by Eveleigh Nash in 1905. Roberts was also the author of The Promotion of the Admiral. The contents list six tales in all. They run from The Owner of the Patriarch to The Comedy of the Oriana. The title tale stands third in that list.

The first tale opens with the ship record of the Patriarch in Lloyd's List. Its owner was Thomas Tyser, a man of great wealth. He owned a dozen other vessels, all beginning with a P. He held a large block of land in Melbourne. He held streets in London and a heavy banking account too. The tales promise comedy built on owners, captains, and ships. Sea trade and its odd characters fill the frame.
68928-unpopular-government-in-the-united:
Albert Kales's Unpopular Government in the United States was published by the University of Chicago Press in 1914, with a second impression in 1915. Kales was professor of law in Northwestern University. A frontispiece map shows the thicket his book attacks: the election districts, state apart, in which one elector of Winnetka, Illinois, must vote.

Part one is called The Rise of the Politocrats. Kales defines unpopular government and shows how it was formerly maintained, then how it grew in America despite the precautions meant to prevent it. The burden on the electorate is his engine: an inverted pyramid of governmental and electoral districts, and more offices to fill than any voter can judge. The result is political ignorance, and with it real disfranchisement. Power passes to those who direct the ignorant how to vote: an extra-legal government that uses its power selfishly to maintain itself.
68933-the-commune-of-london-and-other-st:
The Commune of London and Other Studies is a history book by J H Round, published at Westminster in eighteen ninety nine. Round was already known for books on Geoffrey de Mandeville and on feudal England. A prefatory letter by Sir Walter Besant opens the volume. Besant thanks Round for advance proofs and praises his facts.

Besant singles out Round's work on twelfth century London as a first working theory of its facts. The title study deals with the commune, the city's sworn self governing body of that age. Other studies in medieval records sit beside it. The book shows a strict record scholar at work, testing legend against charters and rolls.
68942-red-stripes:
Hugh Pendexter tells a frontier tale of capture on the Big Sandy in the hosted story. A Virginian, newly come from Richmond, scorns the garrison's caution and steps outside the station against advice. Wyandot raiders seize him within gunshot of the stockade and carry him toward the Ohio.

On the march he sleeps bound with rawhide, a warrior tied on each side, and is led by a cord at his neck by day. The Wyandot chief, marked by a red stripe down his back, treats him kindly in camp, feeding him meat and water. Hope of ransom grows, then darkens when young men return with scalps and a second prisoner. Readers get a hard, close tale of frontier war and a captive watching for one careless minute.
68953-aspects-of-nature-in-different-lan:
Alexander von Humboldt wrote wide studies of nature in many lands. Sabine turned this set into English. Volume two came out in London in 1849. Humboldt drew on his long trips in the New World and in Asia. Long notes add fact to each part.

One part deals with how plants shape the look of a land. One deals with fire hills and how they act round the globe. A tale part, The Rhodian Genius, deals with the life force. The last part climbs to Caxamarca and a first view of the Pacific. Science fans get grand scenes with hard fact.
6896-a-brief-history-of-the-united-state:
John Bach McMaster wrote this history for elementary schools, on the view that most Americans learn their country's past at school. The text proper gives the essentials in as few words as truth and fairness allow, so young readers meet the main line of progress first. Notes carry matters of less weight, with outline lives of men whose deeds need mention.

Teachers may set the notes as lessons or leave them to be read alone, as they judge best. The preface stresses fairness over flourish, and it aims to give every young American both the facts all should know and useful things beside. Portraits, including Washington by Rembrandt Peale, add a visual thread to the narrative.
68961-portraits-of-places:
Portraits of Places is a book of travel essays by Henry James. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published it at Boston and New York. A note explains that the papers first appeared in magazines such as the Century, the Atlantic Monthly and the Galaxy, and in the New York Tribune and The Nation.

The essays open in Venice and move through Italy, Paris, Rheims and Laon, Chartres, Rouen and Etretat, then from Normandy to the Pyrenees. English pieces follow, on Easter, London at midsummer, Warwickshire, abbeys and castles. The last chapters cross the Atlantic to Saratoga, Newport, Quebec and Niagara. James warns that those four were the earliest published, and that thirteen years will have changed the places. Venice, he begins, is a great pleasure merely to name, and the easiest city to visit without going there.
68983-cook-book-of-tested-receipes:
Ida Cary published her Cook Book of Tested Receipes at Poughkeepsie in 1920, printed by Haight. She was the originator of the Vassar Tea Room, and the book opens with the story of the tea room. She dedicates the recipes to her daughter Eula.

She started by serving college students lunches and waffle suppers in her parlor, and selling homemade candy. The business grew so popular that she had three rooms arched into one large room, seating a hundred and four students comfortably. The college yell for Cary Cottage is printed with pride. Rules for measuring follow: two cups of butter or lard make a pound, and four cups of flour another. A tea room that fed Vassar was a laboratory with customers. Cary's tested recipes carry the authority of a dining room that could not afford a failure.
68998-cape-coddities:
Dennis and Marion Chatham wrote these thumbnail sketches of Cape Cod, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1920 with illustrations by Harold Cue. Their foreword warns that the essays are no serious attempt to describe the Cape or delineate its people.

They merely express a perennial enthusiasm for the summer holiday land. The contents include the ubiquitous clam, a by-product of conservation, motor tyrannicus, summer bargaining, and scallops. The first essay sorts summer people into three classes: Maine loyalists, North Shore devotees, and those who place Cape Cod second only to heaven. It then quotes the earliest verdicts, from Captain John Smith's scant praise to Gosnold's rapture in 1602. Summer readers get the Cape loved lightly and well.
69011-australian-fairy-tales:
Hume Cook wrote fairy tales of Australia for three young kin. Christian Yandell drew the plates for the small book. It came out in Melbourne, its tales told by 1925. Keith, Madge, and Kevyn are the three names on the gift page. Are there fairies in Australia, Father, one child asked in haste.

Why yes, whole tribes of them, he said ere thought gave pause. Then tell us of them next tale night, came the swift charge. Hughes, once prime head of Australia, wrote the front words. War and science had swept old marks away, he holds in front. Yet man's faith in fairies stands firm through all change, he says.
69075-the-fairy-babies:
Laura Rountree Smith wrote tales of fairy babies for small children. A Flanagan Company issued The Fairy Babies at Chicago in 1924. Pictures by Dorothy Dulin stand through the ten chapters. Smith had written many Cotton-Tail and Bunny books for the same house.

Fairy Ink-Bottle Babies, born from a bottle of ink, start to school in chapter one. One tumbles off the desk and leaves black footprints on the floor. Magic pitchers, spoons, kites, and a rocking chair drive the later tales. Little readers gain gentle, funny tales of wee folk and home joys.
6911-the-majesty-of-calmness-individual-:
William George Jordan, author of The Kingship of Self Control, offers seven essays on calmness and the conduct of life. He calls calmness the rarest quality in human life, the poise of a great nature in harmony with itself and its ideals. It is not the stillness of stone, he warns, for petrifaction is death, nor is it the surrender of the fatalist, whom he calls a coward slave of fate.

Later essays attack hurry as the scourge of America, praise personal influence and the dignity of self reliance, and read failure as a form of success. Doing our best at all times and the royal road to happiness close the set. Jordan writes in short, plain maxims, urging readers to meet each crisis with singleness of purpose and quiet power.
69114-our-wonderful-selves:
Our Wonderful Selves is a novel by Roland Pertwee, issued at New York in 1919. Its contents divide the story into eight parts with striking heads. The first is called A Question Mark in Suburbia, and the second The Purple Patch. Later parts move to Paris and to the pen and the boards, meaning writing and the stage.

The story opens with its hero, Wynne Rendall, as a baby of seven months' birth. The narrator calls that fact a sign of a nature seeking early prominence on this planet. The child weighs under three pounds and is kept wrapped in cotton wool by the fire. A doctor who loves figures shakes his head over the sums. From that frail start the novel follows Rendall toward the leap of its final part.
69134-coal-and-the-coal-mines:
Homer Greene wrote Coal and the Coal Mines for the Riverside Library for Young People, under copyright in 1889. Greene drew most of his facts from his own time in the mines of Pennsylvania, and he thanks mine superintendents and the Wyoming Historical and Geological Society for help. He aimed at sound facts without heavy technical detail.

Sixteen chapters explain coal from the ground up. Early pages ask how coal was formed, what it is made of, and how the beds lie under the earth. Then come the discovery of coal, its spread into daily use, and the way down into a mine. Readers meet the miner at work, learn what happens when a roof falls, and study air, water, and the dangerous gases underground. Later chapters show the anthracite breaker, the bituminous mines, the boy workers, and miners' wages. Greene's own drawings illustrate the book.
6917-the-gerrard-street-mystery-and-othe:
John Charles Dent, born at Kendal in Westmorland in 1841, came to Canada as a youth when his parents emigrated. He learned in Canadian schools, studied law, and joined the Upper Canada Bar, but practice in an obscure village soon felt uncongenial. Dreams of literary labor drew him to London, the world's literary center, once he could afford the move.

The tales that follow show the Canadian author and historian in a stranger vein, with mystery and the weird as their matter. The title tale of Gerrard Street leads a set that trades on secrets, shadows, and sudden turns. Dent's own restless move from law to letters mirrors the unease his stories stir in their readers.
69170-the-essenes-their-history-and-doct:
Christian Ginsburg's essay on the Essenes was reprinted from the Transactions of the Literary and Philosophical Society of Liverpool and published by Longman at London in 1864. The Essenes, a strict Jewish sect of the ancient world, were much admired by Greek and Roman writers, yet little known to Christian readers. Ginsburg complains that the evidence comes from only seven ancient witnesses, Philo, Pliny, Josephus, Solinus, Porphyry, Eusebius, and Epiphanius, each colored by his own dogmas.

His aim is an impartial statement of the sect's history and doctrines, and of the likeness between some of its practices and those of early Christianity. He charges one party with hiding that likeness and the other with magnifying it. The essay weighs the old testimony with care, and remains a clear Victorian account of a puzzling order.
69180-the-cobbler-of-ni-mes:
Imlay Taylor wrote The Cobbler of Nîmes, a historical romance published at Chicago in 1900. Taylor had earlier written On the Red Staircase and The Cardinal's Musketeer. The contents open grimly with the body of a damned person.

The shop of two shoes and slippers for a young lady set the cobbler craft at the center. Rosaline enters, the cobbler takes a guest, and a military suitor presses his suit. A string of trout, a visit from Babet, and a candle burned by Charlot lighten the middle. A dangerous suit, a pledge by François, and a battle hymn raise the stakes toward the end. The temptation of Le Bossu and the cobbler faith close the list. Nîmes in the days of religious war gives the romance its ground: a humble craftsman among soldiers, priests, and plotters.
69202-the-cost-of-wings-and-other-storie:
Richard Dehan wrote The Cost of Wings and Other Stories, issued in New York by Frederick A Stokes Company with a copyright of nineteen fourteen. Dehan had earlier written One Braver Thing and Between Two Thieves. Some thirty short tales fill the book. Titles range from A Faded Romance and Yvonne to In the Fourth Dimension and The Lost Room.

The title tale opens with Sheldrick back from a fast car run with a friend. His wife sits still in a dull room at the Pavilion Hotel by Greymouth Links. Sheldrick has a pact with the Aero Club of France to fly for Cherbourg the next day if wind and sky allow. Flight, love, chance, and strange turns shape the tales that follow. Readers get brief, sharp tales of that age.
69225-365-bedtime-stories:
Mary Graham Bonner's 365 Bedtime Stories, from Stokes at New York in 1923, gives a tale for every day of the year. Twenty illustrations in colour by Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis brighten the pages, and the book is dedicated to Eugene Edward Early.

The contents march by date. January opens with A New Year's Party and The Rhyming Years, then Naughty Wind, The Selfish Oyster Crabs and Brownie's Toothache. February brings Mice Are Discovered, How the Inkfishes Protect Themselves, the life-saving St Bernards and Abraham Lincoln, and March brings Lucy's Tonsils, Elephant Ways and the reason the shamrock is worn.
69256-considerations-on-the-negroe-cause:
Samuel Estwick, a member of Parliament for Westbury, wrote a legal tract on the slave cause in a third London form dated 1788. The work is cast as a letter to Lord Mansfield, chief justice of the King's Bench. Its spark was the famed Somerset case, which had ruled in a way that shook the old view of a master's rights.

Estwick sets out to fix the ground on which an owner claimed a right to his slave, and to clear the theme of mist and doubt. He grants that the case has grown huge in the public mind and now faces a formal inquiry in Parliament. The tract answers the most heard claims of the other side, point by point, in the cool tone of the law.
69260-my-friend-the-murderer-and-other-m:
A Conan Doyle wrote My Friend the Murderer and Other Mysteries and Adventures, a set of short tales. The International Book Company issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred ninety three. Doyle had written The White Company by then. A prison doctor tells the first tale in his own voice.

Warder McPherson hints that convict number eighty two holds a great tale. The doctor scoffs at more work till the point lands. Eighty two killed a man on the Corinthian brig once. His night fits of screams gnaw at the prison staff. Twelve more tales fill the volume past the first. Bluemansdyke, Sasassa Valley, and a gold field parson star in turns. Doyle’s crime and yarn craft shows here in brief, sharp form.
69273-the-history-of-silhouettes:
The History of Silhouettes is a book on the art of the black profile portrait by Nevill Jackson. It was printed at London by The Connoisseur in 1911. A stance from Fitzgerald's Omar Khayyam fronts it, calling life a magic shadow show played in a box whose candle is the sun. The author was a collector of silhouettes, and the book holds his pictures of the art.

The chapters then lay out the subject. The first treats black profile portraiture and its place in art, literature and social life. The second tells the coming of the silhouette and its passing. Three chapters give the processes: brushwork; shadowgraphy and mechanical aids; and freehand scissor work. An alphabetical list of silhouettists and makers closes the volume. Jackson writes as a lover of a fallen craft, gathering its traditions before they were lost.
69283-the-necessity-of-disinterment-unde:
William Cooke, a surgeon, wrote a long letter dated 1827 to the mayor of Exeter in plea for the use of the dug up dead. Teachers of anatomy, he notes, must rely on a chance stock of bodies left to rot and then dug from graves. A quote from Abernethy calls that state of things a shame for the whole land.

Newspaper talk had blown the trade wide open, so Cooke saw no gain in hid facts. Much of the letter fights the charge of bias in his own case, moved to a court in the next county. Fair trial, free of prior ill will in the jury box, is the ground he takes.
69302-land-of-play-verses-rhymes-stories:
Sara Tawney Lefferts chose verse, rhymes, and tales for a child's play land. Kirk and Nosworthy drew the plates for the gay book. It came out in New York in 1911 from Cupples and Leon. Their First Kiss fronts the book in a sweet plate. A Stevenson verse heads it: shut eyes and sail the skies.

My Ship and I and The Little Land stand in Stevenson's share. James Whitcomb Riley and Eugene Field lend verse to the set as well. A Dutch lull and a Dutch cold scene come by leave in it. A tale of Washington stands by leave of its own house. Bath and Good Listening close the thanks list in the front. Young guests get a rich store.
69313-volume-of-anecdotes:
Volume of Anecdotes is number 24 of the Multum in Parvo Library, volume 2, for December 1895, published monthly at Boston by Courtney. The little magazine calls itself the smallest magazine, at fifty cents a year and five cents a copy. Its whole stock is short, true-seeming stories told for their point.

The opening set, Humor of the Battlefield, gathers Civil War tales. A Confederate colonel at Malvern Hill swears his men forward with the cry, do you want to live forever. A dying private, read Samson's slaughter by a chaplain, begs not to be deceived and asks if the name of John Pope is signed to that. A gun crew at Fair Oaks jokes that a shattered wheel is lucky, since their powder was spent. Such pocket libraries sold cheap reading by the handful in the 1890s.
69361-dr-vermont-s-fantasy-and-other-sto:
Dr Vermont's Fantasy and Other Stories is a book of tales by Hannah Lynch. It was published in London by Dent in 1896, with a Boston issue the same year. Three of the stories had already appeared in Macmillan's Magazine.

The title tale is the longest piece and is told in two parts. The first part gives the story of Mademoiselle Lenormant, told by a traveller. It opens on an island off a hot southern city. The second part brings Dr Vermont and his guests to the same island. Around it stand shorter tales: Brases, A Page of Philosophy, Armand's Mistake, and The Little Marquis. The mix joins tales of travel and dream with studies of character.
69370-leaves-from-our-tuscan-kitchen-or-:
Janet Ross wrote Leaves from Our Tuscan Kitchen, a book on how to cook green stuff the Italian way. J M Dent issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety nine. Ross lived at Poggio Gherardo near Florence. A drawing of her kitchen opens the book.

Ross took most dishes down from her cook, Giuseppe Volpi. He had served the house for more than thirty years. Some dishes came from an Italian book on greens printed in Milan. The lists run long for each plant. Artichokes get ten forms, and asparagus gets more. Beans, peas, and greens fill page after page. Cooks who want new ways with plain garden food will find plenty here.
69379-prince-ragnal-and-other-holiday-ve:
Prince Ragnal and Other Holiday Verses is a book of Christmas poems by Eleanor Donnelly, of 1898. Kilner and Company published the book at Philadelphia, copyrighted by its author that year. A dedication to Matthew Russell, editor of the Irish Monthly at Dublin, stands at its front. A finding list sets out the poems of the little book for the reader.

Prince Ragnal, a Christmas legend of early Christian Ireland, opens the volume at page nine. A Christmas Carol, At Dame Noel, and A Murillo follow in the finding list. The Stable of Bethlehem, The Three Masses on Christmas Day, and The God Man fill the middle of the list. Donnelly, a Philadelphia Catholic poet, writes holiday verse in the devotional manner of her church. Ragnal, her Irish prince, gives the book its tale in verse, around which the carols and stable pieces are hung like ornaments.
69386-origin-of-modern-calculating-machi:
Turck, a member of a western engineers' society, wrote this history, Origin of Modern Calculating Machines, printed at Chicago in 1921 under that society's wing. Its subtitle calls it a chronicle of the growth of the principles that make up the modern calculating machine as a kind.

Chapters march the art forward: kinds of ancient and modern machines, the early key-driven art, and the key-driven calculator. Early efforts at a recording machine come next, then the first practical recorders. The modern accounting machine, the high-speed calculator, the improved recorder, and bookkeeping and billing machines close the march. A long list of pictures mixes patent drawings with photographs. Pascal and one of his machines appear, and the inventors Felt and Burroughs. The first comptometer is shown, and the bill for its first making tools.
69397-tales-of-the-supernatural-six-roma:
Tales of the Supernatural: Six Romantic Stories, by James Platt Junior, was sold for one shilling by Simpkin, Marshall at London in 1894. The six are named on the contents page: The Seven Sigils, The Hand of Glory, The Rabbi Lion, The Evil Eye, The Witches' Sabbath, and The Devil's Debt. The first opens at the Bottomless Lake of legend, said to vent the Bottomless Pit. On sabbath nights the witch hosts of Italy crowd its cliffs.

Two men stare down at the black altar at the witching hour. Tosca of Venice, bravo and poisoner, drills young Janko in a grim catechism of his past. His stock was sorcerer kin, crushed by the Council of Ten, and his trade is blade and dose. Horror fans get lush, dark romance in the high Gothic key.
69401-mr-and-mrs-santa-claus-musical-chr: Mr and Mrs Santa Claus is a musical Christmas play in four scenes, sold for 25 cents by the Beckley-Cardy Company of Chicago. Beckley-Cardy made school books, and the play sits inside their catalog of supplementary readers and classroom classics. It was built for the school stage: a Christmas entertainment in four scenes, with music, small enough for a school hall and a class of children to perform at the holiday season.
69416-christmas-stories:
Christmas Stories, by Georgene Faulkner, who was billed as The Story Lady, is a book of holiday tales for children. Daughaday and Company of Chicago published it in 1916, with pictures by Frederic Richardson. Faulkner dedicated the book to her father, whom she calls a generous Santa Claus to his large family.

Five tales make up the volume, among them A Visit to Santa Claus Land and The Legend of Saint Nicholas. The others are Squeaky and the Scare Box, A Christmas Tree for Santa Claus, and The Gift of Love. The first opens with two children, Willie and Annie, who can hardly wait for Santa Claus to come. The pictures face the text at set points, showing Santa's laugh, a fall into a funny square box, and the boy holding a baby lamb. The book aims at the fireside read-aloud market its author's Story Lady name already served.
69427-stonepastures:
Stonepastures is a novel by Eleanor Stuart, published by D. Appleton and Company in 1895. The scene is Soot City, a raw iron town with three districts: By the Bridge, By the Tracks, and the Stonepastures. Its tale is told through Simeon Quarry, who lived By the Tracks and knew more of the story than the narrator.

The opening recalls the year 1830, when surveyors came with strings and water levels, and strange words like ile, iron, and smelt-oven were first heard. The chapters move through wedding gloom, a blast rite, a bad bargain, and breaking up a home. A strike chapter and one called The Eye of God lead to an epilogue.
69446-the-massarenes:
The Massarenes is a society novel by Ouida, the author of Under Two Flags. Fenno and Company published it in New York in 1897, with Sampson Low in London. Ouida dedicated the book to Lady Howard of Glossop, and added a notice about its African episode.

That episode, she insists, was written four years before the Jameson raid occurred, lest readers suppose recent events in the Transvaal suggested it. The novel opens at Homburg, where Lord Kenilworth points out a large, pale, superbly dressed woman sitting alone. She rolls, he tells his wife: she wallows in money, the biggest pile ever made out West. Yet nobody has discovered her, nobody has taken her up, and she has the desolate air of not being in it. Ouida builds her satire on new American wealth knocking at the doors of European society.
69500-the-queen-s-cadet-and-other-tales:
The Queen's Cadet and Other Tales is a book of stories by James Grant, published by Routledge in London in 1874. Grant also wrote The Romance of War and The White Cockade. The title tale is followed by The Spectre Hand and The Bombardier's Story. Kotah tells of the Indian Mutiny, and other tales treat a Greek outlaw and the Franco-Prussian War.

A second part gathers apparitions and wonders: leaves from old London life, the wild beast of Gévaudan, and a string of ghost stories. The Queen's Cadet opens with its narrator confessing a forced belief in an unseen world. Grant mixes military tales with the supernatural in the popular Victorian manner.
69532-what-luck-a-study-in-opposites:
Abbie Farwell Brown wrote a small tale put out by a Boston eye and ear hospital for its friends alone. It bears the dates 1827 to 1920 on its title page. Two women sit side by side on a crowded waiting bench. Each holds a child at her elbow, and each judges the other in silence.

One envies the rich mourning of her neighbour and scorns her own saffron coat. The other mocks a purple velvet hat and weeps into a black edged cloth. Little Stephanie, five years old, has red and swollen eyes that shun the light. The pale boy Paolo hangs his head and never looks up. The tale sets the two mothers and children face to face.
6956-in-divers-tones:
Charles G D Roberts sings in divers tones in this collection, dedicating its medley to his friend Edmund Collins. His opening verses invite a friend who can rightly hear to listen, promising serious things, light laughter, and here and there a tear. Roberts, professor of English at King's College in Windsor, Nova Scotia, and author of Orion and Other Poems, gathers themes far and near.

The contents range from a collect for Dominion Day and poems on Canada to Actaeon, the pipes of Pan, and scenes out of Pompeii. Fredericton in May time, September, the Tantramar revisited, and a ballade of Calypso sit beside a serenade off Pelorus and a poem on a slave woman. The book is a varied songbook from a young Canadian voice.
69563-everyday-birds-elementary-studies:
Bradford Torrey wrote a beginner's bird book issued in Boston in 1901, with twelve color plates after Audubon. The studies start small, with two kinglet species that wear bright crowns on their heads. Torrey notes that a chickadee looks like a giant next to these tiny birds.

Inside, short chapters treat the chickadee, brown creeper, brown thrasher, and butcher-bird, then move to tanagers and sparrows. Later chapters cover the blue jay, kingbird, hummingbird, chimney swift, flicker, and bittern. Closing pieces take up winter guests and the fall flight south. Readers who are new to bird watching get clear, close looks at common birds and habits they can check outdoors.
69580-colonial-facts-and-fictions-humoro:
Colonial Facts and Fictions is a set of laugh sketches by Mark Kershaw. A Chatto and Windus house of London brought it out in eighteen eighty six. North Australia opens the set with talk of who writes of far lands. Long dwellers write least, since day sights bore them by long use. Birds of flight write most, though they know least of the place.

Small lore leaves room for dreams, which makes the tale gay, he jokes. Fact books read like word books and need weak mix to go down. Parts roam Queensland, boomerang trials, and the Darling Downs in turn. A Newcastle tale of a dark room and a bath jest fill mid ranks. New Zealand, quake talk, and hot lakes close the scheme of the set.
69620-library-of-the-best-american-liter:
Library of the Best American Literature promises the best writing of the nation together with the lives of its authors. Notes explain the text's rules: punctuation made even, nested quotes re-marked, and small capitals set in full. Spellings from the days when American words were not yet fixed are left as printed.

Such sets were the parlour's school, binding poems, essays, and speeches between lives of their makers. The lives frame the writing as a national story told author by author. Readers get the canon of the young republic as its own editors built it, marble busts and all.
69700-the-case-book-of-sherlock-holmes:
The Case Book of Sherlock Holmes is the last set of Holmes stories by Arthur Conan Doyle, first published in London by John Murray in 1927. Twelve adventures fill the contents, from The Illustrious Client to The Retired Colourman. Among them stand the Mazarin Stone, the Sussex Vampire, the Three Garridebs, and the Lion's Mane.

The first tale opens in a Turkish bath on September 3, 1902, where Watson at last wins leave to tell what he calls the supreme moment of his friend's career. A note from the Carlton Club summons Holmes: Sir James Damery, a man known for arranging delicate matters kept out of the papers, will call at half past four.
69739-swiss-fairy-tales:
William Elliot Griffis's Swiss Fairy Tales was published by Crowell at New York. Griffis had written Dutch and Belgian fairy tales before it. The dedication honors his Swiss maternal ancestry near Valley Forge, from whose lips he first heard stories of Washington, Lafayette, and Steuben. Twenty-four chapters follow. The first explains how Swiss fairy tales came to America, through the Harby family of Barren Hill. Grandmother Hess, born a Harby, tells them.

The tales themselves begin with the wonderful Alpine horn and the whimsical avalanche. Mountain giants, a dwarf and his confectionery, two good-natured dragons, and the fairy in the cuckoo clock follow. The yodel carillon of the cows, the tailor and the giant, and the fairy of the edelweiss fill the middle. A white chamois, the siren of the Rhine, and the ass that saw the angel close the book.
6974-tomaso-s-fortune-and-other-stories:
Henry Seton Merriman gathers short stories here, from Sister and A Small World to Tomaso's Fortune, Stranded, and Putting Things Right. The contents run through a crooked way, a tale of a scorpion, life on the rocks, Golossa, a mule, and love and war. Later pieces follow Juanita's sake, the front, the end of the Mooroo, a caravan, and the track of the wandering Jew.

The opening story, Sister, begins with a guard: it does not matter where it was, and the narrator does not want those around them to know Sister or himself. That note of discretion runs through the set, as Merriman sketches soldiers, travelers, and lovers in far places. The stories favor incident, irony, and a quiet moral turn.
69741-the-house-of-five-gables:
Mary Holmes wrote the House of Five Gables, for Hurst in 1892. The Columbian series issued it quarterly at fifty cents. Ashes and Sins of the Fathers stand among her earlier books. Many years ago a house stood on a high bluff, it opens. The bluff overlooked an island now part of Wheeling in Virginia.

Far and near the place was known by the book's title. Sandstone and brick built it, wood on top. No thing of beauty, the opening owns. Its rare ugliness enchained the eye of a first beholder. It began life as a modest cottage of two gables only. Change of owners brought change of architecture over the years. A settler's ancestor is named Sir Roger in it. A hundred settlers came from England under Gates in 1607 there. Holmes gives an ugly house a family history to match.
69751-the-inequality-of-human-races:
An English translation of Gobineau's essay on the inequality of human races. Adrian Collins translated it, and William Heinemann published it at London in 1915. Oscar Levy wrote an introductory essay on Gobineau's life work. The French original dated from the 1850s. Its contents list the argument chapter by chapter.

Civilizations die from general causes, the book claims first. Fanaticism, luxury, and irreligion do not by themselves kill societies. Governments' merit does not set a nation's lifespan either. Gobineau defines degeneration as the mixture of racial elements. Later chapters call racial differences permanent and unequal. Languages, too, are ranked by the races using them. The essay became a notorious source for later racial theories. Historians read it as a document of nineteenth-century race thinking.
69755-women-for-votes:
Women for Votes, a farce in three acts by Elizabeth Hughes, was printed by Dutton in New York in 1912. The action takes place in New York City during a week in November, in the present day. The persons of the play centre on the Tilsbury household: George, his wife Josephine, and his daughter Mildred by a former marriage.

Their friends include Imogene Brown, who brings a pet pig named Cochon, blanketed and ear trimmed, everywhere she goes. Against the bridge parties stands Mary Henrietta Thom, a leader of the women suffragists, with a minor partisan named Sophie Slavinsky. Act one opens in the Tilsbury drawing room. The lady of the house returns from a suffrage meeting full of reported horrors. Her friend, in dinner dress, turns the talk to a purse won as a prize at bridge.
69779-something-about-eve-a-comedy-of-fi:
Something About Eve, a Comedy of Fig Leaves, by James Branch Cabell, was first printed in London in 1927. Cabell gives the book to Ellen Glasgow, in honor of the wit of women. A verse from Genesis heads it, on Adam fear at being naked.

The book falls into many named parts, from the Book of Outset to later books of twilight and far lands. Heads name Evelyn of Lichfield, two Geralds, and a devil in the library. Later parts treat wives, glass people, and the holy nose of Lytreia. Cabell mixes myth, satire, and fine talk in his lush manner. The tale plays Eve long line through time and tale. Readers who like rich, sly prose will find Cabell in full form.
6978-made-over-dishes:
Sarah Tyson Rorer, author of the Philadelphia Cook Book and Bread and Bread Making, offers a revised and enlarged book on made over dishes. Her contents run from stock and cooked fish through beef, mutton, chicken, and game, both cooked and uncooked, to bread, eggs, potatoes, cheese, sauces, salads, cereals, vegetables, and fruits. Sour milk and cream close the list, showing how far thrift can reach.

Rorer opens with a rule: wise forethought, which means economy, stands first among domestic duties, and poverty need not dull skill in cooking. The cook's aim is to draw out each ingredient's proper flavor and make it easy to digest, using little leftovers that too often reach the garbage bucket. Buy small amounts of the best, use them wisely, and waste nothing.
69780-mrs-hallam-s-companion-and-the-spr:
Dillingham's catalogue of the popular novels of Mary Holmes, printed here, runs to thirty titles at a dollar and a half each, sent free by mail. Tempest and Sunshine leads, then English Orphans, Homestead on the Hillside, Lena Rivers, and Meadow Brook. The volume itself is Mrs Hallam's Companion, with The Spring Farm and other tales.

A reviewer quoted in the list gives the formula due. Holmes is a peculiarly pleasant and fascinating writer, it says. Her books enlist the sympathy and affections of her readers and hold their attention with absorbing interest. Holmes was among the most popular American novelists of her century, and among the least reviewed by the critics who mattered. Her readers bought fidelity, feeling, and fortunes lost and found. The tales in this volume are her shorter work, bound for the mail-order trade.
69800-christmas-stories:
Mrs Mary J Holmes wrote Christmas Stories, a set of tales issued by G W Carleton in New York in eighteen hundred eighty five. A steel portrait of Holmes faces the title page. She gave the book to a Clarkson woman tied to Saint Luke’s parish. Some tales, she says, hold more fact than made-up tale.

Alice and Adelaide opens the set on Christmas Eve. Parlors at forty six Shelby Street blaze with light and scent. Young Alice Warren makes her first bow to town life that night. Red-Bird and Ruth and Rena follow in longer tales. Benny’s Christmas and a tale of a font add soft notes. A view of the Passion Play at Oberammergau closes the book.
69823-public-health-and-insurance-americ:
A set of American addresses by Sir Arthur Newsholme. The Johns Hopkins Press published them at Baltimore in 1920. Newsholme lectured on public health administration at the Johns Hopkins school of hygiene. He had run England's Local Government Board medical work. The dedication honours John Burns, without permission. Burns made the public centre the mother and her child, Newsholme writes.

The first lecture surveys fifty years of English progress. Urbanisation, industrialism, and laissez-faire teaching frame the story. Cholera, typhoid, and typhus mark the old regime. Vital statistics and epidemiology earn praise as tools. A second lecture traces the policy's historical growth. Poor law, insurance, and a national medical service all enter the argument.
69828-the-bride-s-fate-the-sequel-to-the:
Southworth wrote The Bride's Fate, the sequel to The Changed Brides. The Burt Company issued it at New York in its line of her popular books at sixty cents a volume. Her name stood on a shelf of tales: The Hidden Hand, Ishmael, A Beautiful Fiend, and many more, several with sequels of their own. A line from Shakespeare heads the book: the writer has set her life upon a cast and will abide the hazard of the die.

The front matter is a catalogue of that shelf, title by title. It maps the work of one of the widest read American novelists of her century. The Bride's Fate takes up the threads of The Changed Brides and carries its heroines through fresh trials in Southworth's high melodramatic manner.
69830-my-experiments-with-volcanoes:
My Experiments with Volcanoes is the life tale of Thomas A. Jaggar, put out in nineteen fifty-six by a Hawaii guild that bears his work. Jaggar lived from eighteen seventy-one to nineteen fifty-three. He gave his last years to writ of his sixty years of hard and risky work on fire hills. His wife shared that work at his side for long.

The guild was set up in nineteen eleven to back a new watch post on a fire hill in Hawaii. Jaggar came there in nineteen twelve and ran it past his death. The book runs from his young years as a man of lore, past craft tests at school, to ten year spans of trips and of life by the fire hills. Its close holds his hopes for what the craft may guard.
69838-captain-chap-or-the-rolling-stones:
Frank Stockton, author of Rudder Grange, wrote this boys' adventure, first copyrighted in 1882 and reissued by Lippincott in 1897 with pictures by Charles Stephens. The contents send Chap and his friends to Florida waters.

Chapters promise a sea voyage, Chap's alligator, a rolling stone, two orphans, and Chap leading the Indians. Later come the metropolis of the Indian River, a race through the woods, and a plot against Chap. The story opens in October, with school kept shut because Mr Wallace is ill and the boys studying loosely at home. The frontispiece shows a panther within feet of the boat. Readers get a sunny boating expedition with wild company.
69875-the-windfairies-and-other-tales:
Mary De Morgan wrote these fairy tales, published by Seeley in London in 1900 with drawings by Olive Cockerell. De Morgan had earlier written 'On a Pincushion' and 'The Necklace of Princess Fiorimonde' for young readers. She dedicates the tales to Angela, Dennis and Clare by name.

The title tale opens at a windmill on the downs by the sea, far from any town. A miller lives there alone with his little daughter, whose mother has died. Vain Kesta, Nanina's sheep, a gipsy's cup, a cat, Dumb Othmar and a rain maiden fill the rest of the set.
69881-preservation-of-forests-as-a-measu:
Preservation of Forests as a Measure of Public Safety is an address given by Baeta-Neves before the seventeenth National Irrigation Congress at Spokane, Washington, in August 1909. The speaker came as Brazil's delegate: a mining and civil engineer of the Ouro Prete school, chief of the technical department of railways and public works in Minas Geraes. He also spoke for the foreign representatives at the opening session.

The address opens in thanks. He is glad and honoured to come again before the congress, and warm in praise of North American welcome and of Spokane's hospitality. He brings greetings from the Brazilian government and from the nations represented. Then he turns to his theme, speaking, as he says, with his whole soul on behalf of the countries of Columbus: the keeping of forests as a guard of public safety.
69897-women-artists-in-all-ages-and-coun:
Women Artists in All Ages and Countries is a survey by Mrs Ellet. Harper and Brothers of New York brought the book out in 1859. Ellet had writ The Women of the American Revolution before this work. She inscribes the volume to Mrs Coventry Waddell, a friend of artists. Her preface owns no such grouping of women artists had appeared before.

Ernst Guhl's Berlin volume on women in art history stood alone then. Guhl closed his survey with the eighteenth century, poets included too. Ellet used his facts, adding details he left out of the work. Vasari, Descampes, and Fiorillo stand among her consulted authorities named. Lives of Bonheur, Fauveau, and Hosmer come from late papers of the day. Painters, sculptors, and engravers fill her pages across the centuries. Many living women artists had yet to prove their full powers.
69904-animal-intelligence-experimental-s:
Edward Thorndike of Teachers College, Columbia University, wrote Animal Intelligence, published by Macmillan in 1911. The book gathers his experimental studies, the work that founded a science. Thorndike put cats, dogs, and chicks in puzzle boxes and timed their escapes. He measured how animals learn by trial, error, and success, and drew the learning curves that made his name.

The contents show the program. After apparatus and experiments come chapters on reasoning, imitation, and the formation of concepts. Thorndike asks whether animals reason or merely associate, and how delicate, complex, and permanent their associations are. Shorter studies treat young chicks, fishes, and monkeys. A final section applies the findings to teaching and to human psychology. The book's dry reports changed how the world understood learning, in animals and in schoolrooms alike, and it remains a landmark of experimental psychology.
69934-early-british-trackways-moats-moun:
Alfred Watkins gave Early British Trackways as a lecture to the Woolhope Naturalists' Field Club at Hereford in September 1921, printed at Hereford in 1922 with his own illustrations. Watkins was a fellow of the Royal Photographic Society and past president of the club. Much added matter swells the lecture into a book.

Watkins argues that mounds, moats, camps, churches, castles, and mark stones line up on straight sighted tracks he calls leys. Peak, water, tree, and stone served as sighting points for ley men in early Britain. Place names, traders' roads, Roman roads, and wells add proof, he holds. Hints to ley hunters close the work. The book launched the ley line idea.
69972-the-changed-brides:
Emma Southworth wrote a novel printed at Philadelphia in 1869. Southworth had written How He Won Her, Fair Play, The Brides' Fate, The Discarded Daughter, and a long shelf more, each complete in one large volume. Tis an old tale, and often told, a maiden true, betrayed for gold, Scott is quoted at the front. The Brides' Fate follows as a sequel to this tale.

Southworth's works sold by the wagon load to story paper readers. Hidden marriages, swapped brides, lost heirs, and ruined girls fill her plots. The changed brides turn on gold, betrayal, and the long arm of a buried past. Peterson's cheap volumes carried her into farmhouses across America. Her fans read her as they read no one else, and this is one of her most reprinted tales of love wronged and righted.
69995-report-on-the-lands-of-the-arid-re:
Powell wrote the Report on the Lands of the Arid Region of the United States. The Government Printing Office at Washington made this second edition in 1879. Maps go with the book, and Utah gets a more detailed account. Powell was geologist in charge of the survey of the Rocky Mountain region. Congress ordered five thousand copies printed on March 3, 1879.

One thousand copies were for the Senate, and two thousand for the House. Two thousand more went to the Department of the Interior. The Secretary of the Interior sent the report in on April 3, 1878. It sets forth how the dry lands of the West should be held and used. Powell argues from the land itself: its rain, rivers, and soil. The report became a landmark in the shaping of the American West.
70000-wakeman-s-handbook-of-irish-antiqu:
Wakeman's Handbook of Irish Antiquities appears here in its third edition, revised by John Cooke. Cooke was a fellow of the Royal Society of Antiquaries of Ireland. The edition was issued at Dublin and London in nineteen oh three. A picture of the Knockmany chamber stands near the front.

In his preface Cooke owns he took up the revision with hesitation. The field of Irish archaeology is wide, he says, and the first author was an acknowledged master of it. W F Wakeman gave his whole long life to the subject, by pen and pencil. The handbook had grown out of date as new work piled up. Cooke says he enlarged its scope to cover the whole of Ireland and rewrote much of it.
70014-how-to-paint-permanent-pictures:
Maximilian Toch, professor of industrial chemistry at Cooper Union, wrote How to Paint Permanent Pictures, printed at New York in 1922. Toch had written The Chemistry and Technology of Paints. The manual serves makers, dealers, artists, and collectors.

Ten colours, Toch says, suffice for the average painter, and all but madder lake mix freely without fading. He lists lamp black, zinc white, red iron oxide, ochre, umber, two chromium oxides, ultramarine, cadmium yellow, and madder lake. Chapters warn against bitumen and fugitive lakes, and treat tempera, water colours, grounds of wood and metal, oils, and varnishes. Cleaning, restoration, and framing close the book.
70029-biography-and-bibliography-of-jess:
A career record opens the Biography and Bibliography of Jesse Walter Fewkes, with the bibliography compiled by Mrs Frances S Nichols. Fewkes, Chief of the Bureau of American Ethnology, was born at Newton, Massachusetts, on November 14, 1850. He took his Harvard degree with honor in natural history in 1875, studying under Louis Agassiz at Penikese Island.

Zoology came first: Leipzig, Naples, and charge of the lower invertebrata at Harvard's museum. He also ran Alexander Agassiz's Newport marine laboratory in the summers. A California trip in 1887 turned him to the Pueblos, and in 1889 and 1890 he recorded Zuni melodies and Hopi songs on the phonograph, a method then new.
70075-palm-trees-of-the-amazon-and-their:
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote Palm Trees of the Amazon and Their Uses, published in London by John van Voorst in 1853, with 48 plates. Wallace had spent the years from 1848 to 1852 traveling the Amazon and its tributaries, chiefly collecting animals. The palms, he says, soon claimed him.

In the preface he describes the forest: huge buttressed trees, tangled climbers, and everywhere the graceful palms rising over all. They are, he writes, the most striking feature of the tropics. He learned each species by its native name, though the Indians' kinds were hard to separate by eye. Closer study found the marks that divide even near allies. Naturalists get the young Wallace, fresh from the river, describing the Amazon's emblem tree by tree.
70135-the-lost-oases:
Hassanein Bey tells here of his explorations in the Libyan Desert, copyrighted by the Century Company in 1925. A photo shows the Egyptian explorer in Bedouin clothes starting a trek of twenty-two hundred miles. Rodd, a former ambassador, supplies an introduction to the narrative of the journey.

Two lost oases, known to legend but not to modern maps, were his goal. The book is dedicated in homage to King Fouad the First of Egypt, whose help made the journey possible, the dedication states. Ball, director of desert surveys, summarized the scientific results, and Hassanein's photographs of wells and dunes fill the pages.
70172-catherine-s-coquetries:
Camille Debans wrote a tale of French country life, translated by Leon Mead and copyrighted in 1890. It opens with a village game that ends badly. Sidonie, a lame young girl called the Little Crook, chases a young peasant of two and twenty round the trees, a cluster of red raspberries crushed in her hand.

Bruno slips and falls, and Sidonie daubs his face with the juice, to general applause. The peasants feel no pity for her lameness, and she would be piqued if they did. Catherine of the title, and her coquetries, enter a world of hardy, laughing country folk. Mead's version keeps the scene brisk and sunlit.
70188-advertising-by-motion-pictures:
Ernest Dench wrote this handbook, Advertising by Motion Pictures, copyrighted at Cincinnati in 1916. Dench also wrote Playwriting for the Cinema and edited a photoplay magazine. Thirty-one chapters lay out the whole young trade of selling by film, from telling an advertising story on screen to the future of the business.

The contents range over every kind of seller. One chapter weighs the dollars and cents of film advertising, and another sets slides against films. Methods follow for makers, dry goods stores, railroads, food firms, car dealers, and farm machinery men. Dench treats foreign trade, working-class audiences, and children in turn, and even shows publishers and newspapers how to fight the film men at their own game.
70198-seven-xmas-eves:
Seven writers each told one part of a linked Christmas tale, billed as the romance of a social evolution. Dudley Hardy drew twenty eight illustrations. The first eve gives the testimony of Mrs Mary Cheevers, written by Clo Graves. She admits she had little book learning in her time. Her speech is rendered in broad dialect.

The second eve gives the opinion of David Dix, night watchman, by B L Farjeon. Florence Marryat writes a constable's stray recollections next. G Manville Fenn, Mrs Campbell Praed, and Justin Huntly McCarthy follow. Clement Scott closes with old memories by a lonely clergyman. A front picture bears the words God bless us all.
70214-peeps-at-many-lands-wales:
Wales, in the Peeps at Many Lands series, is a travel book for young readers by Wilmot Buxton. The London edition of 1911 carries twelve full page pictures in colour. Contents pages map a tour of the whole country, from wild Wales and Snowdonia to the valley of the Wye. A transcriber's note records small fixes to names and page numbers.

Chapters visit a Welsh market town, Anglesey and Holyhead, and a great singing festival. Others recall the men of Harlech, a buried village, and a sacred river. Pembroke, the great hill Plinlimmon, and the Devil's Bridge each get a chapter. The tour closes with a glowing mountain, giving a full circuit of Welsh places and tales in short, pictured steps.
70223-two-colored-women-with-the-america:
Addie W Hunton and Kathryn M Johnson wrote an account of their YMCA welfare work with black troops in France, published in 1920. A plate shows the highest ranking colored officers in France and in the United States Army. Colonels Denison, Duncan, and Charles Young are pictured. The two authors served canteens and huts for the American Expeditionary Forces. Few black women were permitted such service.

Their book records the black soldier's war: segregation, labor battalions, and courage under fire. It is also a claim on memory, written so the record would not omit them. Hunton was a veteran clubwoman and organizer. The volume is a primary source on race and the Great War.
70228-old-and-new-favorites:
Old and New Favorites, book number 173, is a crochet design book priced at ten cents, copyright in 1941 by the Spool Cotton Company. Its cover vows designs for tablecloths, bedspreads, lunch sets, chair sets, and doilies. A front note says fans in each state wrote in to ask for these designs.

The picks made crochet history in past books and come back by request. Star Wheel, Queen Anne's Lace, and Wheel of Fortune lead the set. Motif, popcorn, and filet work all appear, plus cameo crochet. One fine motif, Snowdrift, joins piece to piece like first snow. Full lists name the thread, hook, and size for each job. Makers are told to use famed threads to give the work heirloom worth. Home crafters get a best loved set in one cheap book.
70231-everyday-experiences:
Everyday Experiences is a book of the new thought school of its day. Sears wrote it, with a long list of past works on the mind. The book came out in New York and London in the year 1916. Its set name says its books hold no if in their creed at all.

His past books took up how to draw luck and how minds are made. Cause and fruit, the life past death, and wealth by law fill the list. This book brings such lore down to the round of each day. What a man meets in his hours is read by the light of mind law. The school held that thought shapes the world a man walks in each day. Plain tales from his own days are the stuff of the book's proof. It is a guide for those who sought a creed of the mind then.
70235-the-expendables:
Science fiction from the pulp age fills The Expendables, a story by van Vogt printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in September 1963. Art by Finlay went with the tale in the magazine. The story opens 109 years after a starship left Earth. The ship, Hope of Man, has gone into orbit around the planet Alta Three.

Captain Browne tells his shipload of colonists that a manned lifeboat will drop to the surface. The colonists are fourth and fifth generation voyagers, born in space. Every member of the crew must count himself expendable, the captain says. A deadly and inhuman alien waits below as the feared foe. Yet the tale warns that the alien is not the most feared enemy on the ship. Suspense turns on the crew itself.
70266-lyrical-tales:
Lyrical Tales is a book of verse tales by Mrs Mary Robinson, out in eighteen hundred. A Longman house of London brought the book out that year. All Alone opens the set with a lone boy by a church yard. His dam lies pale and cold in a grave stone bed in the tale. A roam man stops to hear the boy tale and soothe his grief.

Mistletoe at Yuletide, a poor sing dame, and a cat tale fill next ranks. Lascar, widow home, and sheep dog tales stand in the scheme list. Ghost beach, monk tale, and Mont Blanc hermit give a grave cast mid set. A gypsy fate tell, a lost cot, and a Swiss Goth tale close the list. Verse runs in short four line bands through the shown first tale.
7027-a-hive-of-busy-bees:
Effie Williams writes A Hive of Busy Bees as a children's book of virtues, each chapter named for a bee: obedient, honest, truthful, kind, polite, gentle, helpful, grateful, loving, content, and prayerful. The tale opens after Christmas, with Grandpa calling cheerily that the sun has gone under a cloud, while Grandma laughs that it is the brightest day in two weeks. Don's face and Joyce's tell another story.

The children, Daddy explains at last, are thinking about next summer already, borrowing trouble months ahead. Grandpa throws back his white head and laughs at such little trouble borrowers, amid dolls, trains, and pictures from the holiday. The chapters that follow teach each virtue through home scenes, closing with home again.
70282-ella-a-little-schoolgirl-of-the-si:
Eva Tappan wrote this tale of Ella, a schoolgirl of the sixties. Houghton Mifflin printed it at Boston in 1923 with Ruth Best plates. The book serves children and grown ups who remember that age. A gift line sends it to Boy Cousin and Bearcamp days.

Contents open with a little girl and a big seminary school. Three tragedies of seminary life and graduation misfortunes follow fast. The real New Hampshire, rainy days, and books and play appear. Public school days, a principal, and 1869 exam questions close it. Ella first day in public school and the Tories Alphabet stand in the later contents.
70284-dream-tapestries:
Louise Morey Bowman, author of Moonlight and Common Day, gathers her poems in groups under pictured titles. The Macmillan Company of Canada published the book at Toronto in 1924, and a verse from Ralph Hodgson stands at its head.

The groups run from The Wingéd Cloak and the title group, with Hyacinth, Enchanted Wood, and Green Apples, to Oranges and The Mountain That Watched. Songs of Women holds Blue Moon, Mistress Mary, Daffy-Down-Dilly, The Dead Violin, and more. Cinquains follow, with a City Child's Easter, Deep Snow, and twelve hokku on a Canadian theme. Cold Tragedy stands alone, and Homespun closes the book with Twins, The Witch, The Post Box, and Bread and Fire.
70298-the-deformities-of-the-fingers-and:
William Anderson, surgeon to St Thomas's Hospital and professor of anatomy in the Royal Academy of Arts, wrote this surgical monograph, published at London in 1897. None of these affections threaten life, he admits, but they cause much pain and crippling.

The contents treat contractions of the fingers first: Dupuytren's contraction, trigger finger, and contractions from ruptured tendons, paralysis, and birth. Toes follow, with hammer toe and the hallux group, some blamed on misshapen shoes. A last section covers congenital deformities: extra fingers, webbed digits, and giant digits. Anderson argues for studying hand and foot together, since nearly every contraction of one appears in the other. Surgeons get a compact Victorian specialty text.
70314-english-monasteries:
English Monasteries, from Saxon days to their dissolution, was printed at Cambridge in 1904 and reprinted from The Church Times at the request of many readers, in somewhat extended form. A photograph of the chapter-house chapel at Newstead Priory, in continuous use since the Dissolution, fronts the sketch.

The writer lists authorities for students: monastic chartularies and customaries, episcopal registers, the great Monasticon of Dugdale in eight volumes, and the English Monastic Life of Abbot Gasquet. The sketch itself walks through the features of the monastic life that Protestant England had abolished and was learning to study again. Church-party archaeology of this kind rebuilt the medieval abbey in the imagination, stone by documented stone.
70341-moo-cow-tales:
Moo Cow Tales is a book of farmyard stories for children by Rosamund Nesbit Bland, illustrated by Stuart Hardy. Ernest Nister of London and Dutton of New York issued it, the copy shown dated 1860. The first tale is The Little Bull-Calf and the Poppy. Its hero is a little calf who was always unhappy, though he had a dear mother, two white cousins, and a beautiful field.

The field was full of buttercups, daisies, and cow-parsley, which little calves must not eat. His trouble was that the other cows and calves could not understand him. This little calf loved everything that was red, though cows and bulls generally hate red things. In the next field, among the corn, grew many scarlet poppies.
70382-the-music-of-the-spheres:
The Music of the Spheres: A Nature Lover's Astronomy, by Florence Armstrong Grondal, was published by Macmillan of New York in 1926. It is dedicated to Samuel Boothroyd, professor in charge of the Fuertes Observatory at Cornell University. The book is a night sky guide for nature lovers.

Fifteen chapters move from a sight of the stars through their stories. The Andromeda group brings Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Perseus, and Pegasus. A parade of zenith constellations follows, then the southern stars Spica, Antares, Formalhaut, and Sirius.
