Orion and Taurus follow, with Betelgeuse, Rigel, the Belt, and the great nebula, then the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds. Closing chapters come home to the sun, its surface and eclipses, its children the planets, planetoids, comets, and meteors, and portraits of Venus, Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, Mercury, Uranus, and Neptune.
70393-prejudices:
Charles Macomb Flandrau gathered notebook pieces printed at New York and London in 1911. Flandrau had written Viva Mexico, The Diary of a Freshman, and Harvard Episodes. The pieces first ran in the Bellman, and he thanks its editor for leave to reprint. The book is a birthday present for a friend. Some Dogs opens the set.

When the hour is right, he likes to ask a person he does not know well if he or she is fond of dogs. The answer is a fine barometer of sympathy, he says, above all when a dog stands in the room. Little pictures of people, wanderlust, travel, fellow passengers, parents and children, and what is education follow. An essay on Ann Veronica, holidays, servants, and writers fill a light, sharp, club man's notebook.
70419-history-of-christian-names:
Charlotte Yonge, author of The Heir of Redclyffe, wrote the History of Christian Names, here in a new revised edition from Macmillan of London, 1884. The book traces what Christian names mean, where they came from, and how they travelled. A long glossary, running to more than a hundred pages, serves as its index.

In her preface Yonge apologizes for the attempt itself. Her excuse, she says, is the attraction the subject has held for her for at least 20 years. Names, in her hands, become small histories: saints, kings, and languages folded into the words parents choose at the font. The volume follows each name's changes of form and fortune across Europe. Parents choosing a name get the standard Victorian book on the subject.
70424-old-nurse-s-book-of-rhymes-jingles:
Old Nurse's Book of Rhymes, Jingles and Ditties is a nursery collection edited and illustrated by Charles Bennett, author of Shadows. Griffith and Farran of London published it in 1858 with ninety engravings. Bennett's dedicatory letter, dated November 1857, addresses a playmate of his, Sydney Rogers. If you laugh heartily at the pictures, he writes, he shall not have laboured in vain.

He hopes the boy will find the rhymes as they both remember them, and recognise a few old ones now printed for the first time. He asks him not to forget the little children at the corners of the pages. They represent all the different sorts of boys and girls he could easily call to mind. The first rhyme brings a cat fiddling out of a barn with bagpipes under her arm.
70431-between-two-thieves:
Between Two Thieves, by Richard Dehan, is a novel of Swiss lake country. Stokes issued it at New York with rights in 1912 for the book. Dehan had won notice with One Braver Thing, called The Dop Doctor there. An old paralytic in a velvet skull cap opens the tale at sunset.

He watches light die on Riedi and Donatus peaks above the Blau See. A Sister of Charity turns his chair from the glare to the lake. A Bleriot type monoplane rises from the shore, droning over the water. Garden villas, ruined castles, and rich peasant farms ring the blue lake. Age, youth, and flight set the stage for the thieves.
70436-devil-tales:
Devil Tales is a set of folk tales by Virginia Frazer Boyle. Harper and Brothers published it in 1900. Frost made the illustrations. The contents list ten tales. They include Old Cinder Cat, The Devil's Little Fly, and Stolen Fire. One tale is called Asmodeus in the Quarters.

The first tale opens with a quarrel. Solon and Juno have been models of married happiness for eighteen years. Their standing in the Quarters makes their fight a public matter. The tales draw on Black folk belief in the devil and hoodoo. Charms, conjure, and animal shapes run through the list of scenes. Titles and pictures alike promise bargains, tricks, and terrors.
7057-david-poindexter-s-disappearance-an:
Julian Hawthorne tells of David Poindexter's disappearance and other tales, opening with a note on English state trials. Strange stories there would make a modern novelist's fortune, he says, yet other cases, known only locally and barely touched by law, stir as much wonder. Among them none is better worth recalling than Poindexter's, which he aims to tell simply and briefly, much as he heard it years ago near the scene.

The contents add Ken's Mystery, When Half Gods Go the Gods Arrive, Set Not Thy Foot on Graves, and My Friend Paton. Hawthorne writes as a collector of half forgotten mysteries, where law stops and talk begins. The tales favor quiet dread, odd circumstance, and a past that will not quite explain itself.
70573-bucolic-beatitudes:
A writer signing as Rusticus wrote these farm essays, printed by the Atlantic Monthly Press of Boston with a 1925 copyright. Decie Merwin drew the plates. The writer gives the book to his wife, who lets him do these things. Each chapter blesses a farm creature or the garden, on the pattern of the Beatitudes.

Blessed be the Dog opens the set, with a one-eyed dog who began it all. The writer confesses he bought the dog, a sin in his creed: a dog may be rescued, given, borrowed, found, or even stolen with dignity, but never bought. Blessed be the Pig, the Hen, the Cow, the Horse, and the Garden follow. The tone is warm, wry, and fond.
70596-the-byzantines:
Thomas Caldecot Chubb wrote The Byzantines, published by the World Publishing Company in 1959 as one of its books on the major cultures of the world. Richard Powers illustrated the volume. Chubb wrote history for young readers, and the book introduces the Byzantine Empire in short, clear chapters.

It opens with a crusade that went astray: the great armada that sailed from Corfu on May 24, 1203, the force that would sack Constantinople. Chapters then treat Byzantium as crossroads of the world, the Roman roots of Constantinople, and the holy Augustus. A Roman army on horseback, one church, and the golden bezants of Byzantine money follow. The Byzantine way of life and the last days of the empire close the story, with a chart, reading list, and glossary.
70642-historical-vignettes-1st-series:
Historical Vignettes is a set of short tales from the past, told as scenes. Bernard Capes wrote the set, and it came out in London in 1910. Each tale takes a name from the past and puts him in a tight hour. Kings, queens, and stark men of the sword fill the cast list.

One tale halts a king's coach on a flat road at dusk. A queen's nurse, a fair outlaw maid, and a slain rose all have tales. The death of a Borgia and the fall of a queen are in the set. A priest of the Tower and the chief of Nantes stand in the run. Capes writes each scene as if the reader stood in the room. The past is shown in short, sharp cuts, not in long briefs.
70666-the-ethics-of-hercules:
Robert Chenault Givler, professor of philosophy at Tufts College, argues The Ethics of Hercules for Knopf in New York in 1924. His subtitle calls the book a study of man's body as the sole determinant of ethical values. Givler dedicates it to the thousand men of his generation whose thought he claims to make articulate.

An Ostwald motto heads the contents: waste not free energy, treasure it and make the best use of it. Chapter two promises a bodily account of why value words come in opposed pairs, good against bad, right against wrong. Givler notes that beauty pairs with ugliness, truth with falsehood, and cheap with costly across every field of judgement. Later chapters treat right as a gestural sign, virtue and vice as functions of the organism, and conscience as perhaps a sickness.
70667-the-diagnostics-and-treatment-of-t:
Stitt wrote a cure book on the ills that strike men in hot lands. Stitt was chief surgeon of the United States Navy. He had run the Navy's school of hot-land cures. He taught the same art at two schools in Washington as well. Charts in the book need a fixed-width type to read well.

Signs of each ill are set out so a cure man can name it. Drugs, doses, and care steps come with each ill in turn. Germ ills, worm ills, and heat harms all find a place. Ship and camp doctors were the chief users of the book. Clear rules in brief form suit field work far from aid.
7067-the-magnificent-lovers-les-amants-m:
Moliere's Magnificent Lovers, given by Louis the Fourteenth, was acted before the king at Saint Germain en Laye on February 4, 1670. It was never played in Paris, and it was printed only after Moliere's death. Wall calls it one of Moliere's weakest plays, since the whole weight of court entertainment then rested on him. Its attack on astrology stands as the most interesting part, and Moliere himself played Clitidas.

The author's preface notes the king wanted nothing but what is magnificent, and wished his court an entertainment gathering all the stage could furnish. Linking so many different things into one vast idea taxed the playwright hard. The play remains a court spectacle of love, splendor, and star reading, curious for its royal occasion.
70671-harvard-episodes:
Charles Macomb Flandrau's Harvard Episodes, published by Copeland and Day at Boston in 1897, went through two editions within two months, 3,500 copies and then 5,000. His letter to his friend calls the book a very little corner of a very great place.

The first story, The Chance, sets sophomore Horace Hewitt against the older Robinson Curtiss in a Claverly Hall room. Their talk turns from chaffing to earnest perplexity about whether Hewitt's college life will always be a fizzle. Other pieces include The Serpent's Tooth, Wolcott the Magnificent, Wellington, Butterflies, and The Class Day Idyll. Flandrau signs his opening letter with initials only.
70681-slavery-letters-and-speeches:
Horace Mann's Slavery: Letters and Speeches came out in Boston in eighteen fifty-one from B. Mussey and Company. Mann, the first secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education, dedicates the volume to the young men of Massachusetts. His opening address sets the book's frame. It comes from a man whose present memories are taking the place of early hopes, and speaks to readers whose future memories will soon replace their hopes.

The desire of happiness, he argues, sits fixed in the core of life before conduct can touch it. Youthful hopes can become happy memories of age by following sound principles. Citizens hold their welfare bound up with their country's institutions and laws, which is why slavery demanded his letters.
70685-historical-vignettes-2nd-series:
Bernard Capes wrote Historical Vignettes, a set of short lives and scenes from the past. The second set was first put out in London in 1912. Ten pieces came from a first book of 1910. Twelve more appear in book form here for the first time, by leave of the Truth sheet.

Fair Rosamond, Maid Marian, and Raleigh lead the list of themes. Marlowe, Queen Elizabeth, and the priest of Drake follow. James the Second, George the First, and George the Third each get a piece. Beau Brummell, Paganini, and Napoleon stand for a later, gay world. The first piece tells of Elfrida, wife of Athelwold, a famed beauty of old England. Capes writes each scene as a small, sharp tale with a twist of fate.
70709-victorious-life-studies:
Robert C McQuilkin, secretary of the Victorious Life Testimony and editor of The Sunday School Times, published Bible studies in a revised and enlarged edition of 1918. The Christian Life Literature Fund of Philadelphia issued the book. Its headquarters for Victorious Life literature sat at Sixteenth and Chestnut Streets. The publishers ask readers to report any definite blessing received from the book.

Oliver Richard Heinze directs the fund's note. The Victorious Life movement taught that Christ living within gives victory over sin. Its conferences at Keswick and in America spread the teaching. McQuilkin later founded Columbia Bible College. These studies carry the movement's message in lesson form.
7073-specimens-of-greek-tragedy-aeschylu:
Goldwin Smith translates specimens of Greek tragedy by Aeschylus and Sophocles in this 1893 volume. His preface traces Greek drama to the festival of Dionysus, god of wine, celebrated with dance, song, and recitative. Recitative in character grew into drama, chiefly through Thespis, tradition says, while dance and song remained as the chorus, that peculiar feature of the Greek play.

Thirlwall, still perhaps the soundest and most judicious historian of Greece, traces drama to great choral compositions joining music and action to lofty poetry. Smith's specimens let English readers hear the lyric and dramatic elements combined, through the mist of an unrecorded age. The book serves students and lovers of the ancient stage.
70740-the-dalrymples:
The Dalrymples, a novel by Agnes Giberne, was published in London by Nisbet. Giberne wrote Beryl and Pearl and Saint Austin's Lodge. A line from Holmes heads the book: the great thing is not where we stand but in what direction we move. Thirty-five chapters follow the Dalrymple household and their kin and neighbors.

The tale opens at a rectory garden, where an old gardener calls Miss Herminy an angel and thumps his spade for stress. Contents name Marjory, Hermione, Julia, and a sum of twenty thousand pounds that stirs the plot. Sudden peril, a trying position, and a siege fill later chapters. Questions of right and wrong, duty, and giving in shape a firm, warm family tale in the Victorian mode.
70769-old-times:
Old Times, published at New York in 1885, is John Ashton's picture of social life at the end of the eighteenth century. Ashton had written on social life under Queen Anne. Eighty-eight illustrations, many from satirical prints, fill the book. His source is the daily newspaper, starting with the Times of January 1, 1788.

Political histories and diaries, Ashton argues, cover only the great. The middle classes, the vast bulk of the people, live in the papers instead. Without railways, steamships or the telegraph, news came slowly and dear. Editors filled their sheets with social paragraphs, anecdotes and satire. Gathered and sorted, those paragraphs show daily life as nothing else can. Ashton trusts them, since readers could correct them at the time.
70795-a-forgotten-prince-of-wales:
A Forgotten Prince of Wales is a life of Frederick by Captain Henry Curties. An Everett house of London brought the book out in its day. A front plate shows the prince with his sisters at Kew in paint. Part one seizes the prince as he comes in to the world in rank jest. Born at Hanover in February of seventeen seven, he crept in with small noise.

His sire in late years called him the great ass and worse names in scorn. Parts run through a vast will gain, age nine days, and a new crown pair. Court notes by Wentworth, cash woes, and a duchess big throw fill mid parts. Child bride, wed rites, a rope stair, and storm scenes crowd late parts. Cash votes, a cast out, and the queen death close the scheme.
70836-too-close-fisted-and-other-stories:
Ruth Lamb wrote these moral tales for the Religious Tract Society in London. A plate shows Burton, who could hardly bear to part with her, pointing to the title story's theme. The contents list four pieces, starting with 'Too Close Fisted' in four chapters of its own.

Looks and ways, mistaken kindness and new arrivals at a house called the Nest fill those chapters. A king's stamp closes the first tale, and three shorter pieces follow in the book. 'What Came of a Talk,' 'It Is Mother's Way' and 'Nothing Beats Trying But Doing' carry plain lessons on giving, help and effort.
70939-the-jimmyjohns-and-other-stories:
Mrs A M Diaz wrote The Jimmyjohns, and Other Stories, published at Boston in 1878. Diaz also wrote The William Henry Letters and Lucy Maria. A list of her writings prices her illustrated story books for young folks at a dollar and a half in cloth. An illustration captioned How Easy She Goes points into the title story.

Contents open with the Jimmyjohns themselves, starting with a morning with them, then the sad fate of a character named Polly. The stories were written for children and sold as wholesome home reading. Readers get a nineteenth-century American story collection for the young, from a writer who specialised in letters and tales about boys and their households.
70957-the-treasury-of-languages:
The Treasury of Languages is a rudimentary dictionary of universal philology, issued by Hall and Company of Paternoster Row, London. The advertisement is dated February seventh, eighteen seventy-three, and the compiler thanks Bagster and Sons for matter from The Bible in Every Land. He also thanks Longmans for Dr Latham's Elements of Comparative Philology, without which the book could not exist.

An opening essay surveys the geographical distribution of languages, chiefly from Latham, and Africa's philology begins at the frontier of the Semitic tongues. Entries then give the skeleton outline of each language, with the initials of each contributor at the end. A pointer symbol refers readers to an appendix that was never included, and a planned second volume never appeared. Small in scale, the treasury still aims wide, and it stays incomplete.
70992-escape-from-east-tennessee-to-the-:
Captain Ragan's Escape from East Tennessee to the Federal Lines was published at Washington in 1910. James Dony was the publisher, and Ragan held the copyright. Ragan claims to be the only East Tennessee pilot still living. He names his fellow pilots: Daniel Ellis, James Lane, Fondren, James Kinser, and David Fry. All are dead, and Lane was killed conveying men to Kentucky.

Ragan was born in Greene County, Tennessee, near the Nolachucky River. The family moved in 1845 to the French Broad River in Cocke County. In 1860 he was elected a militia lieutenant-colonel. The next fall he drove hogs to South Carolina markets with Frank Clark. Spartanburg was excited and in rebellion, and the rebel flag flew there. At that sight, he writes, he became a Union boy in the wrong latitude.
70999-the-human-species: The Human Species stands as volume twenty seven of the International Scientific Series. That set gave general readers sound science books at low prices. Its list at the front names works by Tyndall on water and Spencer on society. Jevons on money and Draper on religion and science stand there too. A book on mankind takes its place in that company. It treats man as a subject for calm study, like any part of nature. His races, his past, and his place among living things form its theme.
710-love-of-life-and-other-stories:
Jack London gathered stories of men and women tested by cold, hunger, and gold in the far north. The title tale follows a prospector left alone in the wild, who crawls toward life with a broken leg while a sick wolf stalks him. Other tales turn on claims, dogs, boats, and the hard code of the trail.

London writes with stark force about hunger, fear, and the will to live. His people are not heroes in fine clothes; they are workers and wanderers pushed to the edge. The book shows his gift for the short tale of survival, where nature is foe and judge, and where life itself becomes the prize.
71013-the-turk-and-his-lost-provinces:
William Eleroy Curtis wrote this study of Turkey and the lands it had lost: Greece, Bulgaria, Servia, and Bosnia. Revell brought out a second edition in 1903. Curtis had written on Thomas Jefferson and on the East before this tour of the Balkans.

The Great Turk and his capital fill the first part. Curtis treats Turkish rule, the Sultan and his house, the Selamlik rite, and scenes in Constantinople. Mosques, palaces, Robert College, and the men of the missions all get chapters. Then come Bulgaria, with the kidnaping of Miss Stone, Servia and its capital, and Bosnia. Greece closes the book, from Corfu on, in a land-by-land survey.
71032-fanciful-tales:
Frank R Stockton's fairy tales appear in a school edition prepared by Julia Elizabeth Langworthy, a Chicago teacher. Mary E Burt adds an introduction, and the text carries notes for classroom use. The tales were first gathered in 1894, and this edition renews that gathering for young readers.

Five tales make up the book, opening with Old Pipes and the Dryad, about a piper grown too weak to call the herds home. The Bee-Man of Orn and The Clocks of Rondaine follow, then The Griffin and the Minor Canon, a widely loved tale. The Christmas Truants closes the set. Readers get Stockton's dry humor and gentle morals in stories built on odd wishes and kind hearts.
71057-a-libell-of-spanish-lies:
A Libell of Spanish Lies is a small pamphlet tract of the Armada years, kept here in a faithful copy of the edition printed around 1600. The note at the front says only five copies are known, three of them in public libraries and two of those imperfect. The tract was found, its title says, at the sack of Cales. It tells of a fight in the West Indies between fourteen English ships and twenty sail of the king of Spain.

It also tells of the death of Sir Francis Drake in that enterprise. An answer follows, briefly confuting the Spanish lies, with a short relation of the fight according to truth by Henrie Savile, a captain in one of her Majesty's ships. Sir John Hawkins, who also died on the voyage, shares its interest.
71082-political-and-commercial-geology-a:
Spurr led a team of experts who wrote Political and Commercial Geology and the World Mineral Resources, printed at New York in 1920. Gains from sale of the book were pledged to fund more study of the same kind. Each chapter takes one key resource and treats its supply as a world question of trade and state.

Petroleum opens the set, then coal, iron, and a run of rare metals: manganese, chromium, nickel, and tungsten. Vanadium, radium, and uranium get chapters too, as do copper, lead, zinc, and tin. Bauxite, graphite, mica, asbestos, and phosphate round out the list. After a great war fought with steel, oil, and coal, the book maps who holds the earth wealth that new industry must have.
71092-gypsy-folk-tales:
Gypsy Folk Tales is a set of tales gathered by Francis Hindes Groome, published in London in 1899. Hurst and Blackett issued the book from Great Marlborough Street. Groome is named as author of In Gypsy Tents, Two Suffolk Friends, and Kriegspiel. His preface opens with a confession that frames the whole work.

Groome says he is no folklorist and has merely dabbled in folklore for twenty years. In those years he tried to interest folklorists in Gypsy folk tales, in vain so far. He names scholars and tellers who have died in that span, with whom much has perished. Against that loss he hails a Romani Grimm in John Sampson, librarian of University College, Liverpool. The book is thus both a collection of tales and a plea that the lore of the Gypsies be taken seriously before its carriers are gone.
71103-the-pillars-of-hercules:
David Urquhart's The Pillars of Hercules, a narrative of travels in Spain and Morocco in 1848, was published in London in 1850 by Richard Bentley, in two volumes. The copy at hand is the second. Urquhart sat in Parliament and had written Turkey and Its Resources and The Spirit of the East before it.

Book three, continued, opens on Arab domestic industry, the ruins of baths, and the bath itself, then moves to the helot and the Arabs of the desert. One chapter gives the history of muffins, the origin of butter, and the English breakfast. Book four crosses to Rabat and Tangier, with the gardens of the Hesperides, the Jews in Barbary, and druidical circles near Tangier. Book five lands at Seville: the cathedral, Spanish painting, the dance, and Gothic architecture traced from Spain.
71119-aunt-caroline-s-dixieland-recipes:
Emma and William McKinney serve up Southern cooking under the name of Aunt Caroline. Laird and Lee issued the book at Chicago in 1922. William McKinney holds the copyright.

The breads alone fill twenty pages. Virginia beaten biscuit and sweet-potato biscuits lead. Spoon bread, corn fritters, and Sally Lunn follow. There are Jeff Davis muffins and salt rising bread. Drinks include Maryland egg nog, Louisiana coffee, and an Uncle Remus mint julep. Cakes run from devil's food to Martha Washington cake, with its own filling. Betsy Ross pound cake and plantation cookies round out the sweets. Books of this kind preserved the dishes of plantation kitchens for Northern buyers. The names alone chart a whole food culture of the old South.
71135-an-englishwoman-s-adventures-in-th:
Gladys Lloyd wrote An Englishwoman's Adventures in the German Lines, printed in London in 1914. A sketch map shows the position of the places named in the tale. Contents open with war, then getting ready and how the Uhlans came. Anything for bread, the terrible French, and spies ahoy follow. Threatened with death, to leave or not to leave, and what the Uhlans think fill the next heads.

The sign of the Red Cross, on the road, and a Teuton feast come in turn. Prisoners of war and the march past follow. Arrest and homeward bound close the list. The first chapter opens at a village inn. Albert has gone, the narrator hears as she steps down from the little light-railway train. Madame Job's son the baker is in the forts at Liège. A dispatch rider warns her to return to England that day, while she can.
7114-une-vie-a-piece-of-string-and-other:
Guy de Maupassant's Une Vie, the history of a heart, leads this volume in translations by McMaster, Henderson, Quesada, and others. The contents follow Jeanne from the home by the sea through happy days, Monsieur de Lamare, marriage and disillusion, and Corsica and a new life. Disenchantment, Jeanne's discovery, maternity, the death of La Baronne, and retribution follow, with the development of Paul, a new home, Jeanne in Paris, and light at eventide.

Shorter stories join the novel: A Vagabond, The Fishing Hole, The Spasm, In the Wood, Martine, All Over, The Parrot, and the famous Piece of String. A study by Pol Neveux recalls Maupassant's boast that he entered literary life as a meteor and would leave it like a thunderbolt. The volume gathers his art at its sharpest.
71164-two-bad-blue-eyes:
Rita, author of Joan and Mrs Carr, Darby and Joan, and Vivienne, wrote Two Bad Blue Eyes, a novel issued by Ward, Lock and Company at London, Melbourne, and Toronto. The tale opens on Lauraine Douglas' wedding-day. Sunlight streams through the curtained windows over lace, linen, and needlework strewn about the room, and wakes the bride on her pillows. Her first thought is that in a few hours she will be Lauraine Douglas no longer.

Her mind runs back to Keith, the boy-and-girl love her mother calls a fancy, long unheard from while he sought his fortune. A front piece shows Lady Etwynde visiting Lauraine in her boudoir and praising her roses. The novel is a society tale of love, loss, and marriage of the kind Rita's many readers knew well.
71184-a-reference-hand-book-for-nurses:
Amanda Beck's handbook for nurses, first copyrighted in 1905, appears here in a fourth edition, revised, from Saunders in Philadelphia and London in 1919. Beck was a graduate of the Illinois Training School for Nurses in Chicago. The book is inscribed to Isabel McIsaac, long the school's superintendent, and to her successor, Idora Rose.

In her preface Beck tells how the book began as her own memorandum book of formulae and directions, gathered in class and hospital work and on private duty. She used it until its leaves fell apart, then rewrote it for others. The fourth edition adds new subjects and recent advances, while keeping the volume small and compact for daily service.
7120-knock-knock-knock-and-other-stories:
Ivan Turgenev's Knock, Knock, Knock and other stories appear here in Constance Garnett's translation. The contents list the title study, The Inn, Lieutenant Yergunov's Story, The Dog, and The Watch. The first story opens in a circle of friends. Alexandr Vassilyevitch Ridel, German by surname but Russian to the marrow, promises a brief tale from the eighteen thirties, forty years past, and begs not to be interrupted.

Ridel, fresh from university and living in Petersburg, often stayed with his brother, a lieutenant in the horse guard artillery whose battery stood at Krasnoe Selo. The brother lodged in a neighboring village, where Ridel met his circle. Turgenev's tales that follow mix the uncanny, the comic, and the military, in Garnett's clear English.
71221-a-history-of-tithes:
Henry William Clarke, a Trinity College Dublin graduate and clergyman, wrote a history of tithes in a second edition published at London in 1894. Clarke had written on the revenues of the Church of England in Wales. His preface takes Selden's History of Tithes of 1618 as chief authority. He adopts Selden's reading of King Ethelwulf's charter as the first legal grant of tithes.

After consulting Kemble, Haddan, and Bishop Stubbs, Clarke qualifies that view, the preface continues. The tithe question was live politics in Wales and Ireland then. Swan Sonnenschein published the book, with Scribner's in New York. Clarke writes church history with a lawyer's care for title deeds.
71240-poppy-ott-s-pedigreed-pickles:
Poppy Ott's Pedigreed Pickles is a boys' book by Leo Edwards, author of the Poppy Ott and Jerry Todd books. Grosset and Dunlap published it at New York in 1927, with pictures by Bert Salg. Edwards dedicated it to Aunt Dell. The frontispiece shows a girl crying out at how perfectly delicious the pickles are.

Chapter one opens Poppy's Pickle Parlor. The narrator owns that Poppy usually knows where he will land when he jumps into a thing, but his wits tangled the day the pickle plan struck. Twenty-two chapters bring a silent partner, a gold cucumber, a cat killer, and a banker's threats. A man in a cave, midnight excitement, and Poppy's surprise carry the pickle business to its close.
71260-essays-and-soliloquies:
Essays and Soliloquies is a book by Miguel de Unamuno, translated from the Spanish with an introductory essay by J E Crawford Flitch. Alfred A Knopf printed it at New York in 1925. Flitch, the author's friend and translator, made the selection as an anthology of the shorter articles and extracts from the longer writings.

The aim was to present a conspectus of Unamuno's whole literary work. In his own preface, dated 6 June 1924, Unamuno writes from the island of Fuerteventura. The island, he says, is propitious to calm thinking and to a laying bare of the soul. Its parched land is bare even to the bone, as the writer means to be. The title joins essays with soliloquies, the talk of a man with himself. Unamuno was Spain's great philosopher of the tragic sense of life.
71279-the-emperor-of-elam-and-other-stor:
H G Dwight gathered short tales in a book printed at Garden City in 1920, though many tales date from years well before that. Dwight had earlier written on Constantinople old and new and on Persia in small art form. A long giving note thanks an army colonel who helped invent one tale in the set.

Fourteen tales fill the book, from Like Michael and The Pagan to White Bombazine and Retarded Bombs. The Emerald of Tamerlane was written with John Taylor, the colonel praised in the giving note. The title tale, The Emperor of Elam, closes the set, after tales of bathers, a bald spot, and a door with a secret.
7128-indian-fairy-tales:
Joseph Jacobs selects and edits Indian Fairy Tales, illustrated by John Batten, with an illustration of Princess Labam among its plates. Jacobs, editor of Folk Lore, draws on Indian story tradition for English readers, with page images from the Internet Archive behind the text. A transcriber's note explains a letter after a carat marks a superscript, as in 2e, and notes a fuller HTML version with the original illustrations.

The tales themselves bring princes, princesses, beasts, and magic from the Indian story store, told in Jacobs's clear, scholarly style. Batten's pictures give the book its visual charm, from palace scenes to forest paths. The volume stands as a classic gathering of Indian wonder tales for children and for students of folk lore.
71347-wrecked-on-the-feejees:
Wrecked on the Feejees tells the true tale of William Cary, a Nantucket whaler. Cary sailed on the Oeno in 1824. The book was printed at Nantucket in 1949. The ship wrecked on Turtle Island, and Cary alone of the crew lived. He spent nine years among the islanders of Fiji. Chapter heads move from wreck to massacre to life with the islanders.

The log style start tracks whales taken and oil stowed down. Three whales gave 45 barrels early in the voyage. At the Bay of Islands two men deserted. Later chapters treat trade in beche de mer and a trip to Manila. The last chapter brings Cary home to Nantucket. His account is a stark record of whaling risk and survival.
71383-the-look-of-the-thing-and-other-st:
The Look of the Thing and Other Stories is a set of four moral tales by the writer who signed herself with the initials of A Lady of England. The Project Gutenberg text follows the New York edition of 1865. That edition was paid for by the offerings of a Sunday school in Bridgeport, Connecticut.

The contents list four stories: the title tale, Good-Bye, Good for Nothing, and How Like It Is. The first opens over tea in a poor neighbourhood. Rebecca Burton, who earns her living by washing and cleaning, gossips with the widow Lydia White. The widow's small daughter Agnes listens hard to every word. The tales are built to teach through scenes of daily life among working people.
71400-trapping-wild-animals-in-malay-jun:
Trapping Wild Animals in Malay Jungles is a book by Charles Mayer. It came out at Garden City, New York, with copyright dates of 1920 and 1921. The book is given to the author's sister Dora. A front picture shows a native in the grip of a great snake, with a caption that tells the end of the scene.

The contents set out the course of the work. Circus Days stands first, then Jungle Stratagems and Elephants. Shipping Wild Animals and The Sea Tragedy of the Jungle Folk stand next in the list. Killing a Man-Eater and Up a Tree in the Jungle close the row. A second picture shows the author who looked up just as a black leopard— as its caption breaks off. The book is a trapper's tale of the Malay wilds, told for the trade that fed the zoos and shows.
7141-suburban-sketches:
William Dean Howells sketches suburban life in pieces named for Missus Johnson, doorstep acquaintance, a pedestrian tour by horse car to Boston, and a day's pleasure. A romance of real life, scene, jubilee days, lessons from the school of morals, and flitting complete the contents. Illustrations, not available in this edition, once showed a potent pipe lit, a young lady in black alighting, and a sweet young blonde arriving by most trains.

Missus Johnson opens on a morning of lovely New England May, when the narrator leaves the horse car, spreads an umbrella, and walks down toward a suburban scene. Frank and Lucy stalk ahead with shawls dragging, while questioners skirmish about a gaunt figure of forlorn and curious smartness. Howells writes Boston's suburbs with gentle humor and a close eye.
71464-florentine-palaces-their-stories:
Janet Ross's Florentine Palaces and Their Stories was published by Dent in London and Dutton in New York in 1905, with many illustrations by Adelaide Marchi. Ross gives the book to Angelo Bruschi, librarian of the Biblioteca Marucelliana, in memory of much kindness and ever-ready help. The form is a palace-by-palace tour: some seventy houses, each with its story told under its name.

The list of palaces is the book's table of its city. Acciaiuoli, Alberti, Albizzi, and Alessandri open the alphabet; the Antinori takes its plate as frontispiece. Great names fill the middle: Bardi, Capponi, Corsini, Davanzati, Gondi, Guicciardini, Pazzi, Peruzzi. The Pitti palace gets the longest stay, from page 182 to page 208, and the Bargello, the Palazzo del Podesta, runs close behind. Riccardi, Rucellai, Salviati, Strozzi, and Torrigiani carry the tour toward its close.
71466-queer-questions-and-ready-replies:
Queer Questions and Ready Replies gathers four hundred questions with their answers. Grant Oliphant made the set, and this copy is the fourth edition. The New England Publishing Company of Boston brought it out in 1888. Oliphant gives the book to Carrie Norris in thanks at its front. Fields run from history and geography to myth, science, and word lore.

His preface says the aim is quaint facts in a handy form. False notions held by many get corrected across the question list. Phrases of daily talk get their roots laid bare for the reader. He swears each claim rests on good authority he checked with care. Much of the matter had never stood in reach of most readers. An index by letter lets the reader hunt a topic fast and sure. One answer retells the Saint Albans raid from Canada in 1864.
71478-railroad-building-and-other-storie:
Railroad Building and Other Stories gathers tales from The Pansy, the magazine of Isabella Alden, who wrote as Pansy. Lothrop published the book at Boston with an 1888 copyright. The title tale opens with Will proposing a new game to his friends. He is tired of humdrum play, and wants something new and big: a railroad.

The boys shout for it, but ask who knows how. I do, says Will: his father is an engineer, and he hears him talk of the work every day. The boys laugh, thinking of the men who run the engines, and Will laughs back. His father builds railroads rather than driving them, he explains. You cannot build roads in the air, he tells them: you must have ground, and that is the right of way. Other stories in the book include A Very Sly Fellow, Fretting Lettie, and How Rosie Helped.
71492-the-beautiful-garment-and-other-st:
The Beautiful Garment and Other Stories, by the writer known as ALOE, was printed at Rock Island in 1927. The contents list names three tales: The Beautiful Garment, The Captive, and The Voyage. The first opens with talk about Lydia, an only child praised by her father, Captain Neill.

Captain Neill says Lydia goes from cottage to cottage reading and talking, like a grown woman. Her uncle, back from India, is more grave and less warm in his praise. Her mother, ill on a sofa for months, calls her a very uncommon child. The talk raises a clear theme of the book: faith, good works, and the risk of spoiling a child. Readers get moral tales for the young, told in a warm home setting.
715-the-moon-endureth-tales-and-fancies:
John Buchan gathered tales and fancies in this volume, ranging from the Pentland hills of Scotland to Avignon in 1759. Some pieces are short stories of folk, soldiers, and wanderers; others are songs and sketches, such as the grove of Ashtaroth and the ride of Ninemileburn. A lucid interval, a gipsy's song, and a tale of Babylon sit side by side.

Buchan writes with a love of border country, old faiths, and plain folk, and with a storyteller's pace. The mix is uneven by design, moving from eerie fancy to homely tale. The book shows the lighter, more fanciful side of the man later known for thrillers, and it rewards readers who enjoy short, atmospheric fiction.
7153-elder-conklin-and-other-stories:
Frank Harris gathers Elder Conklin and other stories, published by Macmillan in New York and London in 1894. The contents list the title tale, The Sheriff and His Partner, A Modern Idyll, Eatin Crow, and The Best Man in Garotte, with Gulmore the Boss. Elder Conklin opens as the elder leaves the supper table and his daughter walks out with the new schoolmaster onto the stoop, or verandah, running round the frame house.

The day was warm, but evening chill betokened the near approach of Indian summer. The house stood on the crest of a prairie roll. The pair leaned on the railing looking over a small peach orchard to Cottonwood Creek, two hundred yards away at the bluff's foot, fringed by the trees that named it. Harris writes prairie life with sharp, unsentimental eyes.
71532-colonial-dames-and-good-wives:
Colonial Dames and Good Wives tells of the women of the first age. Alice Morse Earle wrote it, out in Boston in the year 1895. She gives the book to the dames whose blood runs in her own veins. Their names are set in a roll at the front of the book.

Wives and lone widows head the first part of the work here. Women of trade and sharp tongued wives fill the next two parts. Town mates in Boston and a dame who bore a hard trip come next. Two bold dames of chance and a dame called the Friend fill the midst. The dress, the joys, and the crafts of such dames are set out in turn. Girls of the free cause and a house wife of the war close the run. Lists sent home in the first days tell what a wife must bring.
71536-books-and-their-makers-during-the-:
George Haven Putnam wrote Books and Their Makers during the Middle Ages, published by Putnam in New York in 1896. The work studies the production and distribution of literature from the fall of the Roman Empire to the close of the seventeenth century. This file holds the first volume, covering 476 to 1600. Putnam dedicated the book to his wife's memory; her hand, he writes, transcribed much of it.

The second volume's contents show the design. Chapters treat the first printer-publishers of France, Caxton and printing's arrival in England, and the Kobergers of Nuremberg. Erasmus and Luther appear as authors in the book trade. Plantin of Antwerp and the Elzevirs of Leyden follow. National chapters close with privileges, censorship, and the slow growth of literary property. Putnam, himself a great publisher, wrote the history of his own trade's beginnings with a practitioner's knowledge.
71563-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy, new series number 57, for March 1918, is one issue of the journal of the Pennsylvania Prison Society. The head prints the law on official visitors to prisons. It comes from section seven of the act of April 23, 1829.

The old act names who may visit without special leave. The list holds the governor, the speaker and members of the senate and house, and the secretary of the commonwealth. Mayors, recorders, commissioners, and sheriffs stand in the list. The acting committee of the Philadelphia Society for Alleviating the Miseries of Public Persons stands there too. A supplement act of March 20, 1903, widens the rule to visiting committees of prison aid societies. Reform fans get the legal frame of prison visiting.
71574-six-months-in-the-gold-mines:
Six Months in the Gold Mines is a journal of California in 1847 to 1849 by Gould Buffum. Lea and Blanchard published the book at Philadelphia in 1850 from his journal. Buffum was lieutenant in the First Regiment of New York Volunteers in the war years. 

He inscribes the book, by permission, to John Charles Fremont, the first senator chosen to represent California. The dedication praises Fremont pioneer labours in the mountains, valleys, and plains of the West. Buffum six months in the mines form the heart of the volume as its title states. His account is one of the earliest books of the rush by a man who worked a claim. It records prices, camps, and the temper of the crowd in the first seasons of the Sierra gold country.
71598-danger-cliff-and-other-stories:
Danger Cliff and Other Stories is a book of moral tales for the young, taken from The Pansy, the magazine of Isabella Alden. It was printed at Boston by Lothrop and Company, with copyright in 1884. Sixteen stories are listed, among them Danger Cliff, My Mocking-Bird, A Queer Kind of Salt, Joseph and Richard, The Broken Promise and Grandmother's Darlings. The rest include Noble and Tricksy, Giessbach, A Bit of Logic, Interlaken, White and Clean, Boy Wanted, Sightseeing, and Slings and Stones.

The title story is a parable. He wanted to show how near he could come to danger and yet escape. The tale is a parable of temptation, of the boast that one can go close to harm and stop. Alden, who wrote as Pansy, was a famous teller of Sunday school tales.
71615-loaves-and-fishes:
Bernard Capes gathered twenty one short tales in a book first printed at London in 1906. A note thanks the magazine editors who first ran many of them. The Pall Mall Magazine and the Illustrated London News stand first in the list. Idyllic names hide sharp plots.

A gallows bird opens the set. The ravelled sleave, the soul of a teacher, and a ghost child follow. A breeches bishop, the strength of the rope, and a ghost leech fill the middle. The unluckiest man in the world and a jade button come near the end. The first tale opens at the siege of Saragossa in 1809, where a French army flavours its soup with salt from its own cartridges.
71661-holiday-stories:
Ruth Lamb wrote Holiday Stories, printed in London in 1892 with pictures. Lamb had written Arthur Glynn's Christmas Box and Her Own Choice. Contents name six tales. Dear Miss Meg stands first, in seven chapters. Its heads run from a bride's homecoming to brighter days for Margaretta and a painful find. A Tale of a Penny and Borrowed Feathers follow, in five and three chapters.

A Story of an Angle Window comes next, with heads on a stepbrother and golden silence. A Mere Flirtation and By a Girl's Hand close the book. The first tale opens in a great house. A lady orders Thorley to tell Miss Margaretta to make less noise. How can she get her afternoon nap, she cries, with that girl screaming loud enough to be heard beyond the park? Margaretta's voice, she says, is like a railway-whistle.
71665-brown-leaves-and-other-verses:
Ella Stevens Harris's Brown Leaves and Other Verses was copyrighted in 1912 and privately printed in one hundred copies, this being number 68. A note says the verses had appeared from time to time in newspapers and periodicals and are collected at the request of friends.

The contents run from the title poem through To the Daisies, Absence, A Valentine, A Spring Reverie, My Prayer, and Columbus, to To a Rosebud and Trees. The opening poem watches winter's blast cast a mantle of snow over the gray earth, sheltering the brown leaves of autumn at last. It reads the leaf on the ground as a link in time's endless chain.
71676-edwin-the-young-rabbit-fancier-and:
Edwin, the Young Rabbit Fancier, and Other Stories was printed at Boston in 1866. The first story opens on Edwin himself. He was a very tender-hearted boy, and very eager about a thing when he took it into his head. But his first heat very often left him just when it ought to have stayed. So he never followed any study or pastime long with profit.

One day he begs his mother for a pet. Charles Jones has a sweet little bird, and cousin James has a squirrel. Edwin wants a guinea pig, pigeons, or a rabbit; he saw a beautiful white rabbit yesterday. His mother fears he would soon tire of it, as he did of his gun, his bow and arrow, his ship, and his rocking-horse. A rabbit is quite different, Edwin pleads: you can love it, coax it, and feed it.
71683-miscellanies:
Emerson's Miscellanies, printed at Boston in 1856 by Phillips, Sampson and Company, gathers his essay Nature with his early addresses and lectures. The American Scholar, his Phi Beta Kappa oration of August 31, 1837, stands second.

The Divinity College address of 1838 and Literary Ethics follow, then The Method of Nature, Man the Reformer, and lectures on the times, the conservative, and the transcendentalist. Nature opens by asking why we should not enjoy an original relation to the universe, instead of groping among the dry bones of the past. The sun shines today also, Emerson insists. The Riverside press at Cambridge stereotyped the volume.
71699-ralph-trulock-s-christmas-roses:
Ralph Trulock's Christmas Roses is a story by Annette Lyster, printed in London by the Religious Tract Society. Lyster also wrote The Boy Who Never Lost a Chance. The tale is set at Fairford, a large village in one of the midland counties of England, split by a shallow stream into High and Low Fairford.

Near the forest stand twelve pretty houses in a row, built more than a hundred and fifty years ago by a lady who owned all the land there. The contents move from Lady Mabel's rest to Ralph Trulock's own story, with May Cloudesley speaking her mind. A small seamstress, a dinner party, a nurse, and a letter lead to the chapter where the Christmas roses bloom at last.
71718-lake-country-sketches:
Lake Country Sketches is a book on the lake lands of the north by Rawnsley, a church man of rank of that shire. His past book on the writ bonds of those lakes is named past his name. It was put out in nineteen hundred and three by a school press of a great town. The front plate shows the great bard of the lakes at the age of seven and seventy. The book is sworn to a true friend of the wild world and of those lakes: the wife of the hand.

A long quote from that bard stands past the sworn leaf. From the wild world and her full soul, that quote says, I had took so much. All my thoughts were steep in sense, it goes on.
71742-the-prince-of-the-pin-elves:
Charles Lee Sleight's The Prince of the Pin Elves was published at Boston in 1897 by Page and Company, with illustrations by Amy Sacker. His Majesty, the prince himself, fronts the book. Fifteen chapters carry the tale, from Where the Pins Go to On Top.

Chapter one asks the question every boy has asked. Harry, examining the lapel of his coat, is sure he stuck two or three pins there that very morning, and wonders where all the pins go. His mother's cushion is the only sure place to find one; his own vanish by the day, and he hardly ever finds one again. Just then he spots a pin lying in the path, bends to pick it up, and watches it disappear from sight. Taken prisoner, pursued, a trip to the gnomes, three jewels, and a mighty battle follow in the contents.
71792-cobwebs-to-catch-flies:
Cobwebs to Catch Flies is a book of talks in short lines for the young. Its sub name tells its span: it fits young folk from the age of three to the age of eight. The host print is a new form of the book, with fixes and plates. It was put out at New York and Boston in eighteen fifty one. A plate at the front shows a dame with the book in her hand.

Here is a sweet, new book, made to catch the eye of my dear one, that plate word says. A first note tells why no long word of the book's aim stands at its front. The hand of the book was bid by a friend to set such a word there.
71811-the-books-of-chronicles:
The Books of Chronicles, in the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges, carries maps, notes, and an introduction by Elmslie, fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge. Kirkpatrick, dean of Ely, edited the Old Testament side of the series. The Cambridge University Press issued the volume in 1916, a second edition of a book first published in 1899.

The series was made for school and college reading of the Bible, book by book, each with its own scholar's apparatus. Here the transcriber's notes explain the plain-text dress: punctuation made uniform, abbreviations opened out, small capitals shown in full capitals, and footnotes set under the paragraph they belong to. The general editor's preface follows the title pages, ahead of Elmslie's introduction and the text of Chronicles itself.
71812-miscellanies:
Miscellanies gathers thirty speeches, sermons, and addresses by Ralph Waldo Emerson. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued the volume at Boston and New York, printed at the Riverside Press in Cambridge. The copyrights run from 1878 to 1906, the later ones held by Edward W Emerson. The first piece is The Lord's Supper, the sermon Emerson preached before the Second Church in Boston on September 9, 1832.

The contents run to the Historical Discourse at Concord, the letter to President Van Buren, and the address on emancipation in the British West Indies. Two pieces take up the Fugitive Slave Law, and two speeches honor John Brown. The Emancipation Proclamation, Abraham Lincoln, and the Harvard Commemoration Speech stand in the Civil War years. Woman, Robert Burns, Shakspeare, Humboldt, and Walter Scott close the run, with The Fortune of the Republic last.
71818-roman-pictures:
Percy Lubbock wrote Roman Pictures, a novel printed at New York. Lubbock also wrote Earlham and The Craft of Fiction, a famed study of novel writing. Contents tease each chapter with a string of hints: fountains, streets, palaces, St Peter's, and the Villa Borghese in Rome.

A lonely young pilgrim named Deering, a citizen of the world with a Roman accent, threads through the scenes. English residents, priests, dancers, sculptors, and sweethearts crowd the tables and piazzas of the eternal city. Lubbock builds the book as a set of pictures rather than a single driving plot of action. Readers who love Rome and fine prose get an elegant, witty portrait of expatriate life.
7182-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's great collection gathers the voyages, traffics, and discoveries of English seamen, keeping the spelling of his sixteenth-century original while expanding old manuscript short forms for modern eyes. The editor's notes explain that footnotes follow later spelling, while Hakluyt's own sidenotes stay his, marking the line between the old text and new help.

Readers meet a vast store of sea tales, trading ventures, and coastal claims, told in the voices of captains, merchants, and chroniclers. Hakluyt built the book as a record of English enterprise abroad, and its bulk still shows how wide that enterprise ran. This text preserves both the journeys and the manner of their first telling.
71824-twilight-stories:
Catharine Shaw wrote Twilight Stories, published at London by a religious house. Shaw also wrote Sunday Sunshine and The Strange House. Twenty-seven short chapters fill the book. A Ticket for Each opens it, then What the Shepherd Knows and Following.

Kept at Home, Robbie's Christmas Eve, The Flower of Hope, and Milicent's Music follow. Serves Him Right, Nellie's Hindrance, The Earwig, and Lost on the Common keep the fireside pace. The first story opens on New Year's Day: children beg their visiting aunt for a twilight talk by the bright fire, something to help them on their way. Readers get Victorian Sunday-school tales built for the hour between tea and bed.
71859-accept-no-substitutes:
Robert Sheckley wrote Accept No Substitutes for Infinity magazine in March 1958. Ed Emsh drew the pictures. A tagline pits the fierce Sexual Morality Act against a fiercer Algolian import. Its hero is Ralph Garvey, owner of a private space yacht.

Garvey waits on yellow standby at Boston Spaceport. The radio orders him to await a customs inspection. Spot checks are rare, and he paid eight hundred dollars to know the team was far away. A twenty-year sentence hangs over his hidden cargo. In the after cabin sits a packing case ten feet high. It holds a sex surrogate banned by the Act. He locks the cabin door and sweats at the rap outside. Blasting off for Mars tempts him, but patrol ships would catch him first.
71862-the-box-of-whistles:
John Norbury wrote The Box of Whistles, an illustrated book on organ cases with notes on organs at home and abroad, published at London in 1877. A frontispiece shows the old organ of St Paul's Cathedral. His preface disclaims three ambitions at once.

It is not his wish, Norbury writes from Gordon Square, to teach the player how to use, the maker how to build, or the architect how to encase the instrument. He puts before the descendants of Jubal what may incite them to improve the noble instrument that taste, science, and skill have brought to its present excellence. Readers get the organ as furniture and architecture, cases praised and blamed across Britain and Europe.
7187-seven-english-cities:
William Dean Howells walks through seven English cities in this illustrated book of travel and comment, opening with a view of Monk Bar. Howells was already known for books on Rome, English towns, and London, and here he turns the same easy eye on streets, buildings, and local life in a set of linked sketches.

The charm lies in observation rather than in guidebook fact: a gate, a market, a quiet lane, and the talk that rises around them. Howells writes as a friendly visitor, noting what pleases him and what puzzles him without pretending to master each place. The result reads like good company on a slow tour, full of small scenes that stay in mind.
71873-in-old-narragansett-romances-and-r:
Alice Morse Earle gathered these sketches of old Rhode Island life from Wickford, where she signed the preface on Midsummer Eve 1897. Charles Scribner's Sons published the volume in New York in 1898, in the Ivory Series.

The sketches mix story and local lore: A Narragansett Elopement, Narragansett Weavers, Where Three Towns Meet, Tuggie Bannocks's Moonack, A Black Politician, The Witch Sheep, and The Crusoes of the Noon-House. Later pieces cover The Doctor's Pie-Plates, My Delft Apothecary Jars, The Dancing Turkey, and Cuddymonk's Ghost. The opening sketch lingers on the old South Ferry and the great house on Boston Neck built by Rowland Robinson in 1746, once one hundred and ten feet in length.
71883-the-high-ones:
Poul Anderson wrote this tale of the stars, first printed in a journal of such tales in June 1958. A note at the head sums the plight of the crew. A revolt has given the Whites charge of the starship. But that means they can never go back to an Earth ruled by the Reds. The tale opens with Eben Holbrook at a port of glass. He sees a world of green and blue and white cloud, across many cold stars.

The sight gives him a sense of home, and brings tears to his eyes. The ship is three units of the void and fifty-eight years from Earth. The wait drags, and the nerves of the crew are worn thin by strife. No man knows if the star Tau Ceti has a world where men can walk free.
71958-edinburgh-sketches-memories:
Edinburgh Sketches and Memories gathers essays by David Masson. Masson taught English literature at the University of Edinburgh in his day. Adam and Charles Black brought the book out in the year 1892. His prefatory note owns the papers came from different times and aims. One piece reprints a Westminster Review article from as far back as 1856.

Seven pieces ran first in Macmillan's Magazine, The Scotsman, or The Scots Observer. Five more stand printed here for the first time from his papers. Queen Mary's Edinburgh opens the set with her return in August 1561. Robert Rollock and the beginnings of Edinburgh University follow that piece. Allan Ramsay, Lady Wardlaw, and the Baroness Nairne fill the middle. The Dundas despotism and Scott's last years stand among later pieces. Carlyle's Edinburgh life takes two full parts near the end.
71968-chinese-pictures:
Chinese Pictures gathers notes on photographs made in China by Mrs Bishop, and it was issued by Cassell and Company in 1900. Bishop was a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society and a famed traveller. The small book grew out of talks with her over her own photographs. Those pictures came from her journeys into and across China.

Some of the photographs had already appeared in her larger books. Those books include The Yangtze Valley and Beyond and Korea and Her Neighbourhood. The notes here were, in substance, dictated by Bishop herself. They tie each view to the place and people it shows. For readers at home, the book turned travel photographs into a guided tour. It stands as a record of China at the turn of the century, seen by a sharp eyed visitor.
71978-old-comrades:
Old Comrades is a novel by Agnes Giberne, published in London by John F Shaw and Company. Giberne also wrote Life-Tangles, Ida's Secret, and Won at Last. The story centres on Colonel Tracy, a retired Indian officer, and his daughter Dorothea, who has been home one week.

The opening chapter, A Christmas Card, starts with a small quarrel. The Colonel calls for the first volume of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, which stands upstairs where he himself put it. Dorothea fetches it without reminding him, having learned that whatever goes wrong will be laid at any door but his. The Colonel gives orders as if to a sepoy and mutters approval of her quietness. The contents promise Dolly's journal, a Mrs Effingham, afternoon tea, and a tennis party. Chapters ask Was Something Wrong and later answer with The Something That Was Wrong.
71991-a-boy-s-text-book-on-gas-engines:
Fay Leone Faurote, a former instructor at the Detroit Motor School, wrote and published at Lansing, Michigan, in 1908 a text book on the automobile gas engine, in simple language for boys. Its first problem is the four-stroke cycle, which the author calls a bugbear to be tackled at once. He starts with the word cycle itself.

A relay race around a block, he tells his reader, runs down one side, across another, back on the third, and home: a four-street circle, no harder than that. Suction, compression, working, and exhaust strokes are figured in section again and again. A gas engine is even compared, in a drawing, to a cannon joined to a grindstone. Plain talk and pictures teach the motor.
71999-stars-of-the-southern-skies:
Orr guides southern star gazers in Stars of the Southern Skies, printed in London and New York in 1915. Longmans Green made the book, with illustrations. Orr, also named as Evershed, had writ An Easy Guide to Southern Stars and Dante and the Early Astronomers. She gives the book to Miss Mary Proctor. Lines of Tennyson stand as motto: all experience is an arch wherethrough we glimpse the untravelled world.

Chapters open with the Greek letters and the constellations of the south, in their modern groups and their ancient ones. The ten brightest stars of the southern hemisphere follow, then stars of different ages. Some near neighbours and double and multiple stars come next. The astonishing star Eta Argus and Mira, the wonderful star, get chapters of their own. Eclipsing stars, clusters, nebulae, and the clouds of Magellan close the survey.
72060-an-introduction-to-the-study-of-fi:
Albert Günther, keeper of the zoological department in the British Museum, wrote An Introduction to the Study of Fishes, printed at Edinburgh in 1880. A preface states the scope: a concise account of the chief facts of the structure, naming, and life-history of fishes. The book is meant for students of the elements of the science. It serves as a reference to zoologists, and as a source for travellers who often meet with fishes.

One earlier work, an encyclopedia article by Richardson, had partly met these wants, Günther writes. He undertook to rewrite that article, and prepared this handbook at the same time. He departs from his plan in the chapters on the spread of fishes over the earth. That subject, never before treated in a full manner, called for lists of the kinds found in each region. Twenty illustrations copy originals by Cuvier, Owen, and others.
72063-once-upon-a-time-animal-stories:
Once Upon a Time is a set of animal stories for children by Carolyn Sherwin Bailey, printed at Springfield, Massachusetts, with copyright in 1918. Milton Bradley issued it. Bailey also wrote For the Children's Hour and Stories Children Need. Her introduction explains where the tales come from, and why they suit story telling.

Old-world stories bear the stamp of one source, she says: early peoples gave animals human impulses and conduct. The Kid Who Would Not Go matches the tale of the Old Woman and Her Pig, in Hebrew dress. Southern Black storytellers gave the tales of Elephant and Frog and why the bear sleeps all winter. American Indians gave camp fire tales of the rabbit and the squirrel. A picture asks where the woodchuck is.
72077-the-fog-princes:
The Fog Princes is a tale by Florence Warden, out in eighteen eighty nine. A Lovell house of New York holds that right claim from its front leaves. Warden wrote Saint Cuthbert Tower and The House on the Marsh in past years. Llancader Castle stands first in the tale, seat of the Earl of Saint Austell. No seat is more fit for new life, lifts and bells mix with old cloth there.

The earl is the great land lord of that part of the realm by far. In town he has a free hand name at the dance stage doors there. His wife grieves not at his wild ways but at no son to heir him. Three girls get a boy school at her free hand in their home. Plain girls, that train just puffs their pride, the tale voice hints there.
72102-a-voyage-to-guinea-brasil-and-the-:
A Voyage to Guinea, Brasil, and the West-Indies is a sea journal by John Atkins, surgeon in the Royal Navy. It was printed at London in 1735. Atkins sailed in His Majesty's ships the Swallow and the Weymouth. The book describes the islands and settlements on the way: Madeira, the Canaries, Cape Verde and Sierra Leone, and others on the Guinea coast, then Barbados and Jamaica in the West Indies.

The title promises the colour, diet, languages, habits, manners, customs and religions of the natives and inhabitants of those places. It also promises remarks on the gold, ivory and slave trade, and on the winds, tides and currents of the several coasts. Bound with the voyage is a treatise on the venereal disease, its causes, symptoms and cure by mercury. An appendix holds physical observations on the heat, moisture and density of the air on the coast of Guinea.
72110-the-brother-s-return-and-other-sto:
A L O E wrote The Brother's Return and Other Stories for Nelson and Sons in 1886. Her Fairy Frisket and Giant-Killer head the title page as earlier tales. Six stories fill the contents, from the title tale to Beware of the Wolf. Sarah May's kindness remembered pictures the front of the volume in soft tones.

Ralph Daines comes home after more than twenty years in a distant land. He and his brother John parted in anger and never wrote in all that time. Ralph seeks the old house by the church and finds waste land and thistles. A little girl with fagots crosses the meadow toward his questions at last. Black yarn, a shepherd's dog, and hero tales fill the companion stories.
7212-memories-of-canada-and-scotland-spe:
The Marquis of Lorne gathers speeches and verses on Canada and Scotland in this volume, dedicated with respect and affection to the members of the Royal Society of Canada. Verses on Canadian subjects lead the way: a Canadian national hymn, river rhymes, a robin, legends of the St John river, Mohawk guides, prairie roses, Cree fairies, and the Qu'Appelle valley.

Speeches follow the poems, joining public voice to private verse, and the whole book moves between two northern lands the author knew well. Lorne writes as a statesman with a poet's ear, praising lakes, rivers, and peoples in measured lines. The collection preserves a late Victorian view of Canada from inside its public life.
72129-puzzles-and-oddities:
Puzzles and Oddities gathers pieces found floating on the surface of current literature, or tossed to dry land by the waves of memory. An editor signing with initials arranged them. Russell Brothers published the book at New York in 1876. An opening reflection quotes Saint Aloysius Gonzaga. Asked what he would do if he had an hour to live, he said he would go on with his game of chess.

An index sorts the pieces by kind. Charades and conundrums run into the hundreds, numbered through the book. French and Latin riddles follow, with further classes beyond. The volume is a storehouse of parlor amusements drawn from the magazines and papers of its day, meant for recreation taken in a pure spirit.
72154-the-golden-pennies-and-other-stori:
Madeline Leslie wrote The Golden Pennies and Other Stories, issued at Boston by Henry A Young and Company as part of the Little Favorites Library. Twelve short tales fill the book. Old Tom the Cat and How My Pigeon Helped Me follow the lead tale. The Mother's Secret, Little Willie, and Robert and His Dog sit in the middle.

The lead tale turns on coins dropped in a mission box. One boy gives a tin penny with a laugh and no thought of Christ. One gives a brass penny with pride in his own act. One gives an iron penny from cold duty. One gives a silver penny with tears of pity. One gives with a throbbing heart for Christ's sake. The tales teach faith, kindness, and help for others to young readers.
72199-westy-martin-in-the-rockies:
Westy Martin in the Rockies is a boys' adventure novel by Percy Keese Fitzhugh, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1925. Fitzhugh also wrote the Tom Slade, Roy Blakeley, and Pee-Wee Harris books. Richard Holberg illustrated this volume, which carries the approval of the Boy Scouts of America.

Forty chapters carry Westy from Temple Camp into the Rockies. Chapter titles promise a captive, a rescuer, a lost agreement, and a mysterious hollow. Characters include Uncle Jeb, Artie, and a silent figure named Ollie Baxter. Ghosts, evidence, and a man without a soul appear late in the list. The frontispiece shows a boy whose blood turns cold at some mountain sight. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
72223-lolly-willowes:
Sylvia Townsend Warner's Lolly Willowes, or The Loving Huntsman, was first published by Chatto and Windus in 1926. Laura Willowes, called Lolly, loses her father and goes to live in London with her brother Henry and his wife Caroline. The opening chapters sit inside Caroline's planning: the small spare room, an eiderdown to buy, and their mother's walnut bureau to fit in. Lolly is twenty-eight, gentle, and loved by the little girls of the house. Her family expects London to give her a better chance of marrying before thirty.

The dedication is to Bea Isabel Howe. The novel follows a spinster aunt fitted neatly into a brother's household, where every kindness also confines her. Warner tells the settling-in from both sides of the spare-room door. The book became known as the story of a woman who escapes that arranged life by a strange bargain.
72231-the-silica-gel-pseudomorph-and-oth:
Edward Hart, a chemist by trade, wrote the 20 short pieces in this book, published at Easton, Pennsylvania, by the Chemical Publishing Company in 1924. He dedicated it to Harvey Washington Wiley, the food crusader, calling him scholar, teacher, poet, and friend. His earlier book, Our Farm in Cedar Valley, is named on the title page.

Hart explains the mix in a short note. He had a boy who loved stories, and true tales told plain went dull, so he dressed them up. Some of these pieces are true, some part true, and some pure invention, written at night as rest from graver work. The titles run from The Silica Gel Pseudomorph and Death Valley to The Professor's Story, Jumping Steel, and The Red Devil. Readers get a scientist at play, with tales of labs, deserts, and odd men.
72241-the-willow-weaver-and-seven-other-:
The Willow Weaver and Seven Other Tales, by Michael Wood, came out at New York in 1916. Wood had written The House of Peace and tale sets of saints and kings. Eight tales make up this book. The first gives its name to the whole set.

An elder man gives young Campion one day to vanish in. He does it, he says, for the sake of the youth's dead father. In his mind he hints at a darker way out, self death, yet dares not say it. Campion is the sole child of a poor, proud widow, and a court dock waits if he stays. More tales treat a minor poet, a bent twig, and a glamour land. Readers get grave, strange tales with a sting of guilt.
72267-westward-hoboes:
Westward Hoboes, the ups and downs of frontier motoring by Winifred Hawkridge Dixon, was issued by Scribner in 1921. Photographs by Katherine Thaxter and Rollin Dixon illustrate the run. A front plate shows the silver bracelet of Walpi. The book was reprinted twice in December of its first year.

Westward Ho is the title of the first chapter of the contents. From New York to Antoine’s and a long ways from home follow. Chivalry versus gumbo mud makes the fourth chapter head. The party nibbles at the map of Texas, then rides down by the Rio Grande. Sandstorms, bandits, and dead soldiers fill the seventh chapter. The Apache Trail and the Tonto Valley wait ahead in the book.
72282-books-and-their-makers-during-the-:
Books and Their Makers during the Middle Ages is a study by Putnam of how books were made and spread. The front pages list his other works, from The Question of Copyright to The Censorship of the Church of Rome. The study runs from the fall of the Roman Empire to the close of the seventeenth century, in two volumes sold apart.

Volume one covers the years 476 to 1600, and volume two 1500 to 1709. Putnam's preface notes that the centuries after printing's invention belong chiefly to the printer-publishers. Their operations fill much of the account. Before them stand the scribes and stationers of the middle ages. The book traces who made books, who sold them, and what rules governed both.
72283-memoirs-of-the-life-of-david-ritte:
David Rittenhouse was the leading American astronomer of his century, a maker of fine instruments, and late president of the American Philosophical Society. William Barton, a counsellor at law in Philadelphia, published these memoirs of his life in 1813. Barton mixes the life with notices of many distinguished men of the time, so the book doubles as a portrait of early American science and its circle.

An appendix prints philosophical and other papers by Rittenhouse, most of them never published before, and Barton registered the book at Philadelphia in October 1813. The memoirs remain a chief source for Rittenhouse's life, valued for how close their author stood to the world of the Philadelphia societies and the men who ran them.
72289-canaries:
Alexander Wetmore's Canaries, Their Care and Management is Farmers' Bulletin number 1327 of the United States Department of Agriculture. It was issued at Washington in May 1923, revising and replacing bulletin 770. Wetmore, an assistant biologist in the Bureau of Biological Survey, compiled it from many sources and his own observation.

The contents run from the bird's history and varieties to cages and their care, indoor and outdoor aviaries, and food. Bathing, the molt, color feeding and breeding follow, then vermin, care of feet and bill, and diseases and injuries. The introduction notes that more than 3,250,000 canaries were imported into the United States in the ten years before 1915, mainly from Germany and England.
72365-at-home-in-the-smokies:
At Home in the Smokies is Handbook one hundred twenty five of the Park Service. The National Park Service issued this new form at Washington in nineteen eighty four. Fifty years had passed since the park’s founding in nineteen thirty four. Wilma Dykeman and Jim Stokely wrote its long heart part.

Part one walks the guest through the park’s chief old sites. Part two, Highland Homeland, first came out in nineteen seventy eight. Cherokee days open that tale of a high border folk. Rail fences, rifle making, and spinning fill its craft side notes. The pioneers come, the sawmills roar, and a park is born in its arc. A band of Cherokees holds on through the worst years there. Part three guides the road: Oconaluftee, Cades Cove, and more old sites.
72380-radio-mates:
Benjamin Witwer wrote this science fiction tale under the title 'Radio Mates' in its magazine form. A plate quotes a witness in wonder at a living piglet dissolved by a twist of a switch. The piglet vanished along wires to an aerial, passed as waves through the ether, and came back alive at a receiver.

Witwer argues in his own voice that each step in sending has grown from the last. Telegraph to telephone was one step, and telephone to radio another, he says. X-ray particles, real as bullets though smaller, point the way toward sending solids through space, a feat not yet achieved in his telling.
72401-how-deep-the-grooves:
How Deep the Grooves is a science tale by Philip Jose Farmer, with art by a staff hand of its pulp home. It first ran in a famed science sheet in the early nineteen sixties. A short head note sets its hook in a few lines of dread.

Till one mans trial, the note says, each of us held one voice in the mind that at all times told the truth. After a far world named in the tale, there were all at once two such voices. And just one of them was the voice of good sense and right. The tale opens in a lab, where a stern doctor bends his will on his own wife to put their unborn child to the test, to sway a state chief.
72440-the-smart-ones:
Jack Sharkey's story, printed in Amazing Stories in February 1963, begins with a forty-second news bulletin. Russia has uttered a flat or-else at the United Nations, and the United States has countered with a steely just-try-it. Then regular programming resumes. Pete Crolin and his wife Beth feel that this time it is the last straw. So do their friends Lucille and Corey, who are out checking their fallout shelter and stocking it with books.

The title asks who knows the secret of survival after the day of the big Blast. Beth urges Pete to join the shelter across the way: there is room, and they have food of their own. Pete wrenches away and refuses. Sharkey builds his chill on that refusal, and on the ordinariness of the evening: a western, a beer, a phone call. The smart ones of the title may not be the prepared.
72456-childhood-s-happy-home-and-other-v:
Lemuel Kayhart wrote Childhood's Happy Home and Other Verses, a small book of poems printed in 1921. The title poem looks back to a mother's arms, green fields, and safe sleep in a childhood home. Age and grey hair now press on the poet.

Other verses retell the fall of Adam and Eve in Eden in plain rhyme. Faith, home, and loss shape much of the verse. Kayhart writes in short, song-like lines that are easy to read aloud. Readers get a sincere set of home and Bible poems in the plain style of their time.
72482-modern-cookery-for-private-familie:
Eliza Acton published Modern Cookery for Private Families in 1845, and this new edition of 1882, from Longmans, shows how long the book ruled English kitchens. Her preface argues like a reformer's pamphlet. An improved system of practical domestic cookery, she says, is still much needed in this country.

Daily waste of excellent provisions, from ignorance or mismanagement, almost exceeds belief. Worse, the positive disease caused by improper food, or food rendered unwholesome by bad cooking, is a greater evil still. Acton writes as if the nation's health were on the stove, because she believed it was. Her great innovation was the recipe itself: ingredients listed, times given, methods exact. Modern Cookery made the modern cookbook, and every later writer, from Beeton onward, worked in its shadow.
72510-prejudices-fifth-series:
Mencken's fifth series of Prejudices came out at the Borzoi in New York, under Alfred Knopf's imprint, in 1926. The essays group themselves in runs: four moral causes, then four makers of tales, then single pieces that range from Beethoven to life in Baltimore. The moral causes are birth control, Comstockery, capital punishment, and war; the tale-makers are Conrad, Hergesheimer, Lardner, and Masters.

The volume also holds an In Memoriam piece, a prose piece called The Hills of Zion, and essays on Protestantism in the republic and the last New Englander. It closes with a catechism. Mencken's manner throughout is the one his readers knew: blunt, funny, and happy to give offense where he thought offense was earned.
72548-the-alligator-and-its-allies:
The Alligator and Its Allies is a zoology book by Reese, printed at New York in 1915. Reese taught zoology at West Virginia University and wrote on vertebrate embryology. Sixty-two figures and twenty-eight plates illustrate the volume. A coloured frontispiece shows Alligator mississippiensis after Ditmars.
