Nine chapters run from the biology of the crocodilia to the development of the alligator. Reese treats the skeleton and the muscles, then the nervous and digestive systems. Later chapters cover breathing, blood vessels, and the organs of generation. Pictures show hunters in the Okefinokee, a typical alligator hole, and nests made chiefly of grass or flags. The book is a full anatomy of a living fossil.
7255-cambridge-sketches:
Frank Preston Stearns sketches Cambridge men he knew without ever seeking them out. His preface owns a regret: he never introduced himself to distinguished persons or sought their notice, and only later wished he had seized chances his youth let pass. Knowing these men, he writes, gave him a more elevated idea of human nature than he might otherwise have held.

Charles Sumner faces the volume, and the sketches that follow mix memory with portraiture, letting talk and habit reveal character. Stearns writes as a neighbour rather than a biographer, fond and frank by turns. The book preserves a Cambridge of friends, teachers, and talk before fame fixed them in print.
72578-tom-swift-and-his-talking-pictures:
Tom Swift and His Talking Pictures is a boys' invention novel by Victor Appleton, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1928. Its sub-title calls the talking picture the greatest invention on record. The frontispiece shows Tom thrown overboard. The first chapter is called Blasting Fire, and Ned stands in its second title. The front pages list the whole Tom Swift shelf, from his motorcycle to his circling of the globe. The Don Sturdy series stands beside it as a stable mate.

Tom is the boy inventor of Shopton, rich in tools and nerve. Here his work turns to the new art of sound film. In 1928 the talkies were the wonder of the hour in real life as well. The tale gives Tom rivals, perils, and a machine to perfect. It is the series at its most up to date, science worn as adventure.
72598-the-meaning-of-pictures:
John Van Dyke, professor and critic, published The Meaning of Pictures as university lectures delivered at the Metropolitan Museum in New York, with thirty-one illustrations. The publisher's list prices his other studies beside it: Art for Art's Sake, Studies in Pictures, and the text-book of the history of painting.

Van Dyke taught Americans how to look at the old masters hanging in their new museums: what a picture means beyond its subject, in composition, color, and handling. His lectures belong to the moment when the great collections crossed the Atlantic and a public had to be trained to see them. He wrote as a technician of looking, plain-spoken and exact, and his little handbooks guided a generation of gallery visitors.
72629-the-curse-of-the-reckaviles:
Walter Masterman wrote The Curse of the Reckaviles, a novel of mystery in two books. The frontispiece shows a man with a fire poker staring at a white-bearded face at his door, a vacant, dead-looking face in a mass of white hair streaked with yellow. The tale promises a family horror.

Book One, The Curse, runs to 14 chapters. It opens at the Hospital Cup final between Guy's and Bart's. Then come the coming of the stranger, the end of the line, and the Reckavile horror itself. A mysterious bungalow and the meaning of the Red Cote fill the middle. Book Two steps back into the family's past: a convent school, a flight, two marriages, a divorce, and a nameless wife. Roy at Oxford and a ghost from the past lead to the secret out. Mystery readers get a curse, a castle, and a buried family story.
72670-a-year-among-the-trees:
Wilson Flagg wrote a year among the trees, subtitled the woods and by ways of New England, copyrighted in 1881 and reissued at Boston in 1890. Flagg had written Studies in the Field and Forest and A Year with the Birds. An index runs from ailantus and alder to the American elm. Animals of the primitive forest get an early section.

Apple tree, arbor vitae, and arrow wood appear in the index's first page. Flagg writes nature essays in the Thoreau tradition, tree by tree and season by season. His books taught New England readers to see their own woods closely. The Educational Publishing Company kept them in print for schools.
72696-last-winter-in-the-united-states:
F Barham Zincke wrote Last Winter in the United States, table talk from a tour of the land. John Murray issued the book in London in eighteen hundred sixty eight. Zincke was vicar of Wherstead and chaplain to the Queen. His road ran through the late Southern Confederation and the far West.

Winter sea travel has real charms, he urges at the start. A cabin to oneself comes free in that cold season. New York’s vast menu at the Fifth Avenue Hotel amazes him. Churches crowd the town, and Beecher packs his Brooklyn house. Baltimore first turns his sense of talk to the South. Debt denial there finds friends in all ranks of men. Washington shows Congress as no school for great statesmen. Zincke gives his wife the book, she who stayed home for their child.
72700-the-scots-brigade-and-other-tales:
James Grant wrote tales of war, issued in London in 1882 by Routledge. A camp song on the old Scots Brigade, Holland's bulwark in many fights, stands at the front. Grant had won fame with The Romance of War, named on the title page.

The lead tale opens as a young officer begs his uncle, a general, to call with him on some ladies. The old man scorns love as a wreck for a soldier and rates his heir, who loves a girl named Dolores. Sword play, a fair widow, and a kidnap fill the heads. Shorter tales tell of the Cid, Jean Cavalier, a bugle boy at Badajoz, and a retreat from Cabul.
72704-the-great-persian-war-and-its-prel:
Grundy, lecturer at Brasenose College and university lecturer in classical geography at Oxford, published 'The Great Persian War and Its Preliminaries' with Scribner and Murray in 1901. The subtitle calls it a study of the evidence, literary and topographical. In his preface Grundy admits that retelling so old a story needs an apology, and offers new evidence as his justification.

Much modern criticism of Herodotus and Thucydides, he argues, rests on maps without accuracy, drawn from travellers' sketches. Grundy made his own surveys of Thermopylae, Plataea, and Pylos between 1892 and 1899, and Marathon had lately joined the German survey of Attica. With real ground under the narratives, he sets out to test which doubts about the old historians stand and which demand reconsideration.
72735-jamaica-anansi-stories:
Martha Warren Beckwith gathered Jamaican Anansi stories for the American Folk Lore Society, published at New York in 1924, with music recorded in the field by Helen Roberts. Animal stories open the contents. Tying Tiger leads, with parts on a fish basket and a storm. Tiger as substitute and Tiger as riding horse follow.

Tiger's sheep skin suit and Tiger catching the sheep thief come next. Eggs and scorpions, Tiger's bone hole, and a christening fill the early list. Anansi the spider tricks his way through Jamaican folk tradition, carried from West Africa. Beckwith's fieldwork preserved the tales with their songs. The volume is a landmark of Caribbean folklore study.
72761-a-commentary-on-ecclesiastes:
A full note book on Ecclesiastes sets the old text next to fresh wording. The print book put the Authorized Version on the left page. The writer's own plain form sat on the right page. Notes on each verse came right after the pair. This typed form stacks the pair in two rows for ease.

Verse by verse, the notes weigh what the Preacher means. Hard lines get care, and short forms are spelled out in full. The aim is to help a home reader track a hard book. Bible students get text, gloss, and note all in one place. Slow, close study is the clear goal.
72852-the-age-of-the-crusades:
The Age of the Crusades, by James M Ludlow, belongs to the series Ten Epochs of Church History. The Christian Literature Company published it in New York in 1896. Ludlow begins with the state of society that made the Crusades possible. His chapters survey ignorance, superstition, and a low sense of justice. Chivalry and the feudal system each get a study.

Further chapters cover the poverty of Europe and the policy of the papacy. The Mohammedan menace, from the rise of Islam to the Turks, fills another. Pilgrimages prepare the narrative. The story itself opens with Peter the Hermit and Pope Urban. The crusade of the crowd goes first, under Walter the Penniless. Then the chieftains march: Godfrey, Raymond, Bohemond, and Tancred. The fall of Nicaea, the battle of Dorylaeum, and the siege of Antioch follow.
72880-jewish-fairy-stories:
Gerald Friedlander translated Jewish Fairy Stories, published in New York by the Bloch Publishing Company, with illustrations by Beatrice Hirschfeld. The tales are drawn from old Jewish books, and the contents name the sources: the Babylonian Talmud, the Midrash, and the Ma'aseh Book among them.

The first tale tells of King Solomon and the worm. Solomon, resolving to build the temple, remembers the law that no iron tool be lifted on the altar stones. That worm could cut stone without iron. Other stories give falsehood and wickedness, a wicked king and his bride, two jewels, and a beggar at a wedding. The clever wife, the coins of Elijah, and the fox and the raven close the list. Friedlander retells the tales plainly for children. Wonder and moral travel together.
72890-the-eternal-moment-and-other-stori:
Forster gathered these stories, written at various dates before 1914, in a volume published at New York by Harcourt, Brace and Company under a 1928 copyright. His preface says they join the tales in The Celestial Omnibus as all he is likely to do in a particular line, the line of fantasy. One story had already appeared in the Atlantic Monthly.

Six stories make the book: The Machine Stops, The Point of It, Mr Andrews, Co-ordination, The Story of the Siren, and the title story. The Machine Stops opens it, in a hexagonal room like the cell of a bee, where a woman sits swaddled in an armchair worked by machinery. She knows several thousand people, yet she grants her son Kuno only five minutes of talk before her lecture.
72922-authors-and-their-public-in-ancien:
Geo Haven Putnam wrote this sketch of how writers reached readers in the ancient world. Its full title covers literary conditions and the ties between authors and their public, from the earliest times to the fall of the Roman Empire. The copy here is the third edition, revised, issued in New York and London in 1896.

Putnam says his aim was plain and modest. He traced an outline record of steady literary work from scattered notes in the writing of the period. He covered how books were made and shared, and how authors stood with their readers. Readers get a short, clear survey built on the work of earlier scholars he names in his preface.
72928-ten-minute-stories:
Algernon Blackwood wrote short tales first printed in three London papers, gathered in a first edition in February 1914 and reprinted the same month. Blackwood thanks the editors who let him reprint them here. Twenty nine tales fill the book, each short enough, as the title promises, for a brief sitting.

First comes Accessory Before the Fact, in which a walker named Martin stands at moorland cross roads with a map gone out of date. Dusk falls, his pack grows heavy, and he sees he took a wrong turn two miles back for the lure of a short cut. Other tales name a prayer, a lease, a goblins hoard, and a house of the past.
72946-turrets-towers-and-temples:
Turrets, Towers, and Temples gathers great writers on the great buildings of earth. Esther Singleton edited and rendered the pieces for Dodd Mead of New York. The book was first copyrighted in eighteen ninety eight, this printing nineteen twelve. Ruskin opens on Saint Mark at Venice, and Dixon on the Tower of London.

Thackeray writes on Antwerp Cathedral and Hugo on Notre Dame of Paris. Chevrillon treats the Taj Mahal and Gautier the Kremlin at Moscow. Dickens describes Saint Peter at Rome and Ebers the Pyramids of Gizeh. Loti writes on the Mosque of Omar at Jerusalem in the set. Many plates picture the famed towers, temples, and shrines described.
73016-david-ives:
Arthur Stanwood Pier wrote David Ives, a story of St Timothy's school, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1922 with pictures by Franklin Wood. David's father is a doctor in a raw new suburb of unpaved streets, billboards, and two-family houses. The boy leaves that home, in a chapter called Farewell to Rosewood, for boarding school life.

The contents trace a school career. Hostilities and friendships come first, then probation, blindness, and an examination for a boy named Wallace. A torn page, hero worship, and an anti-climax mark the middle terms. The book ends with chapters called Relinquishment and Attainment. Pier wrote many school stories, and this one follows his pattern. A boy is tested by school customs, rivals, and masters. He learns what honour costs before he can claim the prizes of the place.
73029-half-loaves:
Margaret Culkin Banning's Half Loaves was published in New York by the George Doran Company under a copyright of 1921. Banning had written This Marrying before it. The copy at hand is inscribed to a set of initials, and Book One opens at dusk in a convent.

Cecily sits on a window ledge opposite a statue of the Blessed Virgin, watching the world darken before Benediction. The convent is holding a mission for its pupils, above all for the small class of girls about to graduate. The Jesuit missionary, tall and emphatic, has laid three paths before them in his last talk. A woman in the world may stay unmarried, may marry, or may become a nun. One must choose, he tells them.
73041-compromises:
Compromises, by Agnes Repplier, is a book of essays from the Riverside Press. Houghton, Mifflin issued it at Boston and New York in 1905, from a copyright of 1904. A line of Voltaire heads the book: error, too, has its merit.

Fourteen essays run from the luxury of conversation to an Allegra. The gayety of life, the point of view, and marriage in fiction come early. Our belief in books, a beggar's pouch, and a pilgrim's staff fill the middle. A Quaker diary and French love-songs add voices to the set. The spinster, the tourist, the headsman, and crime consecrated close the run. The first essay, on conversation, takes a motto from Mark Pattison. Repplier opens on the age of reminiscences, when nothing is left untold. Old men, she notes, claim the wit died with their youth.
73047-auld-lang-syne-second-series:
Auld Lang Syne, second series, subtitled My Indian Friends, is a book of life notes by Max Muller. Muller was a teacher of note and the hand of a famed work on the lore of tongue. It came out in eighteen ninety-nine. Its front note owns that its notes reach back past seventy years in spots and may not all be fresh.

The first book of the set held notes of song men, bards, crowned heads, and beg men. This book is in the main for his friends of the far east land and for the turns that first drew his mind there. He has never set foot in that land, he says. Yet he has long known its writ wealth, the bold flights of its old thought, and the hot zeal of its old faith.
7306-autobiographic-sketches:
Thomas De Quincey's Autobiographic Sketches gathers selections, grave and gay, from writings published and unpublished, chosen for an American edition he was revising in 1853. His letter from Lasswade that January explains his plan: to revise and considerably alter, for republication in England, such of his writings as it seemed proper deliberately to avow.

De Quincey stresses that he does not disown anything he published, only that some pieces served a transient occasion and need not stand unchanged. The sketches that follow mix memory, confession, and wit in his famous winding prose. Readers meet a master of the personal essay sorting his own past for a new public.
73079-the-soul-of-henry-jones:
Ray Cummings wrote a tale of a man's starving soul. At the age of thirty two Henry Jones awoke one brilliant summer morning with the sudden realization that the soul in him was starving. He lay quiet, staring idly at the white ceiling, his mind groping dully with this abrupt enlightenment. Then he raised himself upon one elbow and looked at his wife sleeping beside him.

He had always thought her pretty in a quiet way. He did not remember ever having noticed before the wrinkles beginning to show around her eyes. Her neck seemed very thin and stringy, and the line of her lean jaw very sharp. The thin locks of black hair on her pillow were shot through with gray. A vision of wavy golden tresses flashed into his mind, the crowning glory of no particular woman. What Henry does with his hunger drives the tale.
73093-swedish-fairy-tales:
Herman Hofberg's Swedish Fairy Tales, translated by Myers, was published at Chicago by Belford-Clarke in 1890. Hofberg's preface draws a line between tradition and saga: tradition clings to a spot and names its actors, while saga moves free of time and place. Many traditions, he notes, grow from real events retold by the peasantry until they turn to folklore. Others descend from old myths dressed in historical clothes. Hofberg chose the most typical tales rather than gathering everything.

Each tale carries a historical and ethnographical note, stating where else the tradition is found. The illustrations come from several of Sweden's best artists. Myers, the translator, dropped some notes as unimportant and set the rest after each story. The contents are arranged by province, beginning with Skane and its Ljungby Horn and Pipe. A faithful rendering, without embellishment, is the translator's stated aim.
73141-american-short-stories:
American Short Stories is an anthology edited by Charles Sears Baldwin of Columbia University. Longmans, Green and Company first issued the book in 1904, and this is a later impression of 1921. Baldwin was professor of rhetoric at Columbia, as the title page states. The volume carries his introductory essay on the short story as a form.

Baldwin reprints run through 1906, 1909, 1910, 1912, and 1916 before this impression of the book. That long classroom life marks the place of the volume in American teaching of its day. The short story was then claiming rank as the national form of American fiction among critics. Baldwin selection, with his essay on its laws, helped fix a canon for schools. Poe and Hawthorne stand behind it in that canon. The modern masters of the brief tale hold the place of honour before the student reader.
73155-ashes-to-ashes:
Isabel Ostrander wrote Ashes to Ashes, a novel of money and marriage. The contents promise a lie, a trap, a blow, and a verdict in the first seven chapters. The story opens in a lawyer's office. Wendle Foulkes, an attorney with keen old eyes, faces his client Norman Storm across a wide desk. The last batch of securities, he warns, is all that remains of Storm's inheritance.

Storm has squandered nearly four hundred thousand dollars in ten years on wildcat schemes. Three thousand a year is all the remnant would yield, and he protests that it would not cover the car and the country club. He insists his new investment is a sure thing, on straight inside information. Foulkes sighs: so had all the others. Ostrander builds her drama on that weakness, a rich man's son who cannot stop speculating while his fortune turns to ashes.
73169-betty-wales-decides:
Margaret Warde wrote this story for girls, published by Penn at Philadelphia in 1911. Eva Nagel illustrated Betty's deciding year for the publisher that season. A slump in Ploshkins opens the contents, naming the college candy shop of the series in its first chapter.

Montana Marie O'Toole dawns upon Harding College in chapter two of the list. Her initiation, her ride and her rescuing fill the middle chapters with comedy. Suffragists, a dignified dinner and popping mascots follow, as Betty, done with college, decides what work and love will fill the life after Harding in this late series volume.
73213-ida-s-new-shoes:
Madeline Leslie, writing as Aunt Hattie, wrote a tale for small children that Young of Boston published in 1870. Little Ida Kent dances in to show her aunt the new shoes her papa has brought her. The aunt hopes the shoes will never carry her into mischief. Ida vows she will be a real good girl now.

She does not keep the vow for ten minutes. Her mother lies ill with a bad headache in a dark room. Ida pushes a stool to the bed and jumps up, boots and all, to show the shoes. The sick woman groans, and the aunt takes the child firmly by the hand. Ida screams and clings to the bedpost. The shoes are taken off till she can behave better. Snarled hair, oranges, and dandelions teach the same lesson in turn. The book aims each small fault at a change of heart.
73221-anti-semitism-in-the-united-states:
Rabbi Lee Levinger wrote this history of anti-Semitism in the United States, published by Bloch in New York in 1925. Levinger had earlier written 'A Jewish Chaplain in France' from his war service. He dedicates the book to his parents, who first taught him the meaning of tolerance, he says.

Lines from William Blake stand under the dedication, urging love for the human form in heathen, Turk or Jew. Levinger writes from Wilmington, Delaware, in May 1925 in his preface. He traces the history and causes of hatred of Jews in America, from early slurs to the organized campaigns of his own day.
73259-horses:
Roger Pocock's book on horses, published by John Murray in London in 1917 with a preface by Cossar Ewart, ranges from the origin of the horse to the soldier horse. Its chapters treat the origin of varieties, the habits of outdoor horses, the conquest of the horse, and the horse in history. Horsemanship, the pleasure horse, and the soldier horse close the argument.

Ewart warns that Britain forgot the loss of over 300,000 horses in the Boer War, and so entered the war of 1914 as short of horses as of men and munitions. Pocock's own opening holds that in the horse's world man is its god, the source of oats, salt, and weather. Better horses, he argues, require better gods.
73293-japanese-folk-stories-and-fairy-ta:
Japanese Folk Stories and Fairy Tales retells old tales of Japan for young readers, by Nixon Roulet. The American Book Company published it in nineteen o eight in New York. Nixon Roulet had written the Little Cousin books on Spain and Alaska before. Thirty two tales fill the contents, from a princess's choice to two brothers.

The Choice of the Princess opens the book with the beauty of Inaba. Her skin is velvet, her hair night dark, her eyes soft as stars. She is sweet but willful, and puts off marriage with one small answer. But I don't want to, she says, and no counsellor can reply to it. Her father is dead and her mother can do no more with her. Gods, swords, phantom cats, and the angel's robe fill the tales ahead.
73352-the-heel-of-achilles:
The Heel of Achilles is a novel by Delafield, published by the Macmillan Company at New York in 1921. It opens with a girl of twelve, Lydia Raymond, reflecting with great satisfaction that she is an orphan. Her father died in China three years before, and she remembers how all pity then went to her mother, not to her.

The dedication is a long verse letter to the author's sister, recalling their childhood games and shared plans. That tone of family memory runs under the fiction. Delafield writes of a clever child watching the grown world with clear eyes. Readers meet Lydia first, and the grown world only as she sees it.
73355-the-deadly-ones:
The Deadly Ones is a science fiction story by Wallace. It appeared in Fantastic Universe in July 1954. An editor's note praises Wallace as an engineer who designs presses. It warns that his sound science may carry readers across the universe. A head note says the villain preyed on nightmare fears. The dread food he craved was his in abundance, it adds. The narrator names himself Rathsden and asks that it stay unknown. There are legends from old Germany, he concedes.

Colonial America has legends of him too, he says. But nothing damaging or concrete can be proved from legends. He has kept his name out of the stories with care. A clever person shuns publicity, he explains. It may involve tampering with history to stay hidden. The narrator is something old that feeds on human dread. Wallace tells the tale in the monster's own calm voice.
73403-the-dissolution-of-the-monasteries:
Francis Aidan Hibbert wrote a history of how the monks' houses in Staffordshire fell. The book came out in London in 1910. Hibbert led Denstone school and had won prizes at Cambridge. He had wrote on guilds and on monks in the same shire. A long list of rolls and old books backs his work.

King Henry's break-up of the great houses is the theme. Hibbert shows it house by house in one shire's bounds. Charters, state rolls, and church lists ground each claim. Small houses and great ones share the same fate here. Local past fans get a close, sourced case study. The tale stays grave and fair.
73496-an-eye-for-the-ladies:
Darius John Granger wrote a tale of a sleuth who hops from man to man. The tale ran in Fantastic in October 1956. His task is to find a client's lost wife, a gay girl. She has found a fresh body and plays wife to a new man. To find her, he must be a new wife's husband each night.

His first client is a plump man dressed stiff as a penguin. Last week the sleuth sold fraud hunts, this week he hunts folk. Sharp talk fails him as the odd case opes. He vows to find her though he wed all the town in turn. Pulp fans get a wild, wry hunt.
73499-reminiscences-of-my-life-in-camp-w:
Susie King Taylor wrote memories of her life in camp with a Black regiment in the Civil War, printed at Boston in 1902 at her own cost. She gives the pages to Colonel Higginson, who led the regiment. A letter from a field officer and a portrait of Taylor lead the book, with group photos of officers inside.

Contents run from her forebears and childhood to St Simons Island in 1862 and Camp Saxton in 1863. War trips, life on Morris Island, a shipwreck, and the taking of Charleston follow in her tale. Later chapters tell of mustering out, the years after the war, a womens relief corps, and a trip to Louisiana.
73507-stories-of-elizabethan-heroes:
Edward Gilliat wrote Stories of Elizabethan Heroes, published by Seeley, Service and Company in London in 1914. Gilliat had been a master at Harrow School and wrote other books of adventure for the young. The volume belongs to a series of true stories for boys and girls, sold at two shillings and sixpence.

An opening chapter sketches the Elizabethan world. Then come the sea captains: John Hawkins, Martin Frobisher, and Humphrey Gilbert, founder of Newfoundland. Lord Howard of Effingham, Richard Grenville, and John Davis follow. Francis Drake gets two chapters, as the scourge of Spain and the queen's greatest seaman. Full-page pictures support the text. The book presents the age of Elizabeth as a school of bravery and resource for young readers.
73520-five-nights-at-the-five-pines:
Avery Gaul's Five Nights at the Five Pines was published by the Century Company in New York in 1922 and dedicated to Mary Fenollosa. The contents build the book in nights: the first night at Five Pines, the second, third, fourth, and fifth nights, then dawn.

Around the nights stand chapters on Mattie, the winkle-man and the will, a boycott, a little coffin, and a séance of horns. The first chapter, The House of the Five Pines, opens on a sea of yellow sand, dunes like combers that never burst into spray. The head of the cape, with the town in its jaws, fights the encroaching sea that thundered against it.
73532-the-model-village-and-its-cottages:
Alexander Harvey, the architect of Bournville, wrote this book on the model village and its cottages. Batsford of London and Scribner's of New York printed it in 1906. Fifty-seven plates of plans, views, and details fill the book.

Harvey gave the work to Mr and Mrs George Cadbury, whose firm built the village. In February 1904 he read a paper on cottage homes in London, drawn from his Bournville designs. Much had to be cut for that talk, and more left out whole. The book gives the full tale: real cottages, their plans and looks, with measures. A block of four cottages fronts the plates.
73545-the-ranch-of-the-tombstones:
The Ranch of the Tombstones is a Western novelette by Tuttle, author of The Range Boomer and Flames of the Storm. Tuttle wrote for the pulp magazines, and his tales of the range ran to dozens. The story is billed on its first page as a complete novelette.

Two men ride through the broken gateway of the Half-Moon Ranch. The leader is tall, thin, and unshaven, with a sad face and bright, grin-wrinkled eyes. His partner is shorter and heavier, with half-shut eyes. They rein in and look the place over, then ride around to the back. From the kitchen comes a voice raised in anger, scorning the man who calls himself a cook. Can he even burn food decently? Tuttle opens in mid-quarrel, with the easy slang and dry humour that made his cowboys favourites of the magazine racks.
73569-comfortable-mrs-crook-and-other-sk:
Ruth Lamb wrote these sketches, printed by the Religious Tract Society of London. Lamb had written Look on the Sunny Side and Taught by Experience. A plate shows Fanny bringing in the tea-tray to the minute. The lead sketch follows Mrs Jemima Crook, a widow ten years, who allows in good temper that Crook left her comfortable.

She keeps her affairs to herself as a rule, and no one saw a tear for her husband. Six chapters trace her through a silent messenger, an invitation accepted, and waiting and trusting. Shorter pieces follow: Can't Afford to Play, Walking Too Big, and Winkles. Lamb writes warm, plain tales for home reading, in the tract society's line of improving fiction.
73580-procrustes:
Pink wrote Procrustes, or the Future of English Education, published in New York in 1927. Four chapters make the book. An introduction on the Procrustean bed leads, then the schools and their present-day problems and leanings. Future growth of the schools follows, and the universities close the work, with the academic mind of today and tomorrow.

The first chapter opens with a speech by Undershaft in a play by Bernard Shaw, against snapping up foundlings for scholarships. Pink then takes up a speech by Lord Hugh Cecil in the debate on the education estimates of 1925. Cecil had held that teaching should not be spread alike to all, apart from each child's real capacity. The clever should be picked out and given the fullest chances, Cecil argued. The great body of children should get a low standard, built on reading.
73602-little-frank-and-other-tales:
Darton and Harvey published this child's book at London in 1838. Its subtitle promises tales chiefly in words of one syllable, made for the youngest readers. A verse address to the little book opens it, hoping girls and boys will prize it above bat, ball, and doll. The pages, the poem says, tell of the bird by the sedgy stream, the hawk darting on prey for his young, and the glow-worm's light.

The first tale, The Owl, puts Tom and Grace in a dark nut-walk by moonlight. Grace fears the rising clouds will hide the moon, and a strange noise frightens her until Tom stays to see the bird. Other pieces tell of the north with its ice and snow and reindeer sledges, and of the rat who dives beneath the stream to hide. Short words carry real incident here, which was the reforming point of such books.
73607-a-thousand-miles-on-an-elephant-in:
Holt S Hallett wrote A Thousand Miles on an Elephant in the Shan States, issued by William Blackwood and Sons in MDCCCXC. Hallett was a civil engineer and fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. He gave the book to the American missionaries in Burmah, Siam, and the Shan States. Their noble work wins his high esteem, he says. A preface treats trade.

The importance of the Eastern markets to European commerce has long been recognised, Hallett opens. Since Vasco da Gama rounded the Cape of Good Hope, the trade of Western China and Indo China has been a prize for every maritime community in Europe, he says. The Portuguese were ousted from Burmah in sixteen thirteen, he notes. A railway survey journey on elephant back follows. Travel readers get Burma and Siam from the howdah.
73609-a-guide-to-the-shell-and-starfish-:
A Guide to the Shell and Starfish Galleries is a museum handbook printed in 1901. The Trustees of the British Museum ordered its printing. The museum's natural history branch stands on Cromwell Road in London. Its zoology department arranged the galleries the guide describes. Mollusca, polyzoa, brachiopoda, tunicata, echinoderms, and worms fill the subtitle. Numerous illustrations support the text throughout.

One large north gallery, entered from the Bird Gallery, holds the molluscs. Types of every principal division stand there, in spirit or as models. Shells, the preface admits, have always drawn collectors more than the animals. The shell series is therefore as complete as the space allowed. A separate series of British shells lines the west wall. The Starfish Gallery shows echinoderms and the creatures called worms. Small or soft bodied kinds resist display, so types are chosen with care.
73622-the-english-moths-and-butterflies:
Benjamin Wilkes sells a grand picture book of English moths and butterflies, drawn and coloured from the insects themselves. He printed it in Fleet Street, London, and sold it in parts. The coloured set cost nine pounds.

One hundred and twenty copper plates fill the work. Each fly is shown with the plants, flowers, and fruits it feeds on. The text gives the true times of each stage: caterpillar, chrysalis, and fly. It teaches how to find them, rear them, and keep them. Wilkes dedicates the book to Martin Folkes, president of the Royal Society. Buyers could take the natural history alone for ten shillings and sixpence. Such costly plate books taught British collectors their home fauna before cheap field guides existed.
73626-insect-manufactures:
Insect Manufactures is a small work of natural history issued in London in 1847. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge printed and sold the book at its depository. It was published under the direction of the society committee of general literature and education. Its contents turn the work of insects into a set of manufactures for the reader.

Chapter one treats the manufacture of silk by caterpillars of various kinds in the book scheme. Chapter three turns to the manufacture of silk by spiders in their turn. Wax by the hive bee, the humble bee, and the white wax insect of China follows in chapter four. Honey by the hive bee and cochineal by the cactus insect complete the survey. The book is a neat example of the cheap improving tract, where natural theology and useful knowledge were bound together for general readers.
73637-white-and-black-lies:
Madeline Leslie wrote White and Black Lies, or Truth Better than Falsehood, a Sabbath-school book entered for copyright in 1867 and published at Boston. Leslie had written Tim, the Scissors-Grinder and other tales for the same shelf. A verse stands on the title page: lying lips are an abomination to the Lord.

In her preface Leslie ranks truthfulness among the cardinal virtues, at the foundation of success and enviable fame. The passion for the marvellous, she warns, fills the age with temptations to deception, and the young are exposed on every side. A childhood reading of a treatise on lying by Opie had deepened her own conviction. The tales that follow sort lies into white and black and weigh them by their fruits. Sunday schools bought such books to give as prizes. Plain moral story was the method.
73645-home-labor-saving-devices:
Home Labor Saving Devices is a handbook for farm homes by Rhea Scott, given here in its second, revised edition. Scott taught home demonstration work at George Peabody College for Teachers at Nashville. She had served as a state demonstration agent in Louisiana. The book is dedicated to the women and girls of the farm. It aims to make the rural home a place of light, health, and beauty. Illustrations by Mrs Gamble go with the text.

The pages give plans and pictures of devices that ease house work. Kitchen arrangements lead the set. Experts of the Department of Agriculture helped with facts and photographs. Dairy men, poultry men, and home agents across the states lent their best tools. An iceless refrigerator and a dish drainer stand in the list. The book belongs to the home demonstration movement of its age.
7366-three-comedies:
Björnstjerne Björnson was Norway's leading writer and a public voice in its national life, and these three plays show him turning from peasant tales to the stage. The volume opens with The Newly-Married Couple, follows with Leonarda, first performed in 1879, and closes with A Gauntlet, written in 1883. An introduction traces Björnson's life from a remote parsonage in the north to literary fame.

The plays take up marriage, reputation, and the rules society sets for women and men. Leonarda and A Gauntlet stirred sharp controversy in Norway, since they pressed social and religious questions that audiences were not used to hearing on stage. Read together, the three comedies show a dramatist using domestic life to argue about freedom, duty, and the cost of defying convention.
73668-music-after-the-great-war-and-othe:
Carl Van Vechten wrote these music essays in the first years of the Great War, and Schirmer of New York published them in 1915. He dedicated the book to Fania. The title essay asks what the war will do to music, and six more studies follow it.

The contents range wide. One piece asks whether music belongs in museums, and another claims to give the secret of the Russian ballet. A long study presents Igor Strawinsky as a new composer, with the accent his name carried in 1915. Massenet and women, stage decoration as a fine art, and the stage reformers Appia and Gordon Craig round out the set. The first essay opens with Leo Stein in Florence, calling the day of the cubists over. Concert readers get a young critic thinking in public.
7368-lifted-masks-stories:
Susan Glaspell, a playwright and novelist of the American Midwest, writes here about people caught between who they seem and who they are. The stories often place Americans abroad, as in the Paris scene where a young woman's clothes, bought in France, still cannot hide that she is American. Manners, money, and marriage all act as masks her characters wear.

The title points to the moment each story builds toward: a mask lifted, a pretense dropped, a truth spoken at last. Glaspell's people are plain speakers in elegant rooms, and their small rebellions carry real weight. Readers who know her plays will find the same interest in women's inner lives, told here in compact, quietly dramatic fiction.
73746-the-proud-girl-humbled-or-the-two-:
The Proud Girl Humbled, or The Two School-Mates, is a moral tale for children by Mrs Hughs. Lindsay and Blakiston published the book at Philadelphia in 1849. Hughs had written Frank Worthy and May Morning among other tales. The title page addresses the story to little boys and little girls.

A preface tells young readers the point of the tale. We make our own unhappiness by selfish conduct, Hughs writes. To be happy, we must be good, and kind to all who deserve it. The story opens with two schoolgirls on the steps at Fairmount. Matilda Hamilton refuses a party invitation with contempt. She will not own the hostess, Rosalba Pearson, as an acquaintance, though they share a school. Her friend defends Rosalba as a favourite loved by all the girls.
73789-primitive-athens-as-described-by-t:
Jane Ellen Harrison, of Newnham College, Cambridge, wrote this study of early Athens. The University Press printed it at Cambridge in 1906. Her guide is Thucydides, the great Greek writer of the war with Sparta, who tells how Athens began.

Harrison says in her preface that her old book on Athens is out of print and will not be reissued. Frazer's vast notes on Pausanias have since changed the field for scholars. These pages set out what Thucydides shows of the first Athens: its shrines, tribes, and old ways. She gives the book to Wilhelm Doerpfeld, the digger of Greek sites, with thanks in Latin and Greek verse.
73790-automobiles:
Automobiles, by Zerbe, is a volume in Every Boy's Mechanical Library. The book was made for boys who want to know how cars work, part by part. Zerbe says few boys will build a car, but knowing each device helps them fix and set right the cars they meet.

Each part is shown in drawings made for the book, with the parts pulled apart so their jobs can be seen. The text weighs the good and bad points of the main types in use. As an early guide from the first age of the motor car, it shows what young readers were taught about engines, parts, and care.
73791-thirsty-blades:
Otis Adelbert Kline and Hoffmann Price wrote a tale first printed in Weird Tales in February 1930. Rankin finds the side gate of an inn shut and turns back down an alley, straight into a half ring of drawn blades. Six desert swordsmen close in while their red-bearded chief watches from his horse.

Rankin's gun clicks on empty shells, for a thief had drawn its load while he smoked and drank coffee in the market that day. He draws his curved blade and cuts his way through the first rush. His aim in the town of Tekrit is to free the lady Azizah from a threat out of the hills of Kurdistan.
73825-wild-flowers-of-the-north-eastern-:
Wild Flowers of the North Eastern States is a flower book of three hundred and eight kinds, drawn and told from life by Miller and Whiting. Its prints are the size of life, one for each kind. It came out at New York and London in the mid eighteen nineties, and its rights were held that year.

A front print shows the wild senna in bloom. Its gift word makes it out to two mums of the two hands. Its first words own its aim at the front. It was made, they say, with no wish to vie with the lore books of plants. Its hope is to make the flowers easy to know for plain folk, more so than the tight hand books of the flora can.
73844-the-history-of-the-seal-of-the-uni:
Gaillard Hunt, chief of the Division of Manuscripts, writes The History of the Seal of the United States for the Department of State, printed at Washington in 1909. His letter of transmittal to Secretary Philander C Knox explains that his meager 1892 sketch, prepared for Secretary James G Blaine, is here replaced with gathered additions. Nine chapters run from the first device to the uses of the seal, with a glossary of heraldic terms.

Chapter one opens late on July 4, 1776, when Congress appointed Franklin, Adams and Jefferson to prepare a seal device. Hunt acknowledges Charles A L Totten's two-volume work on the great seal for much valuable information.
73858-the-twelve-adventurers-and-other-s:
Charlotte Bronte's The Twelve Adventurers and Other Stories gathers her juvenilia, written between the ages of twelve and twenty-one. Clement Shorter's note says the twelve fragments were never meant for print. They came to him in a little house at Banagher in Ireland from Arthur Bell Nicholls, Charlotte's husband, who wrote that they would have been burnt had Shorter not arrived. Hatfield transcribed the minute handwriting and prepared the volume, published by Hodder and Stoughton.

The contents mix the Glass Town world with later tales: An Adventure in Ireland, The Search After Happiness, The Adventures of Ernest Alembert, Albion and Marina, The Rivals, and Mina Laury. Napoleon and the Spectre stands among them. Shorter offers the book as a document for child psychology as much as literature. The new cover art uses a pencil drawing by Bronte herself. Several pieces are printed here for the first time.
73860-among-the-gnomes:
Among the Gnomes is an occult tale of adventure in the Untersberg, by Franz Hartmann. Hartmann also wrote books on magic and on Paracelsus, his title page notes. The London edition of eighteen ninety five carries many pictures. A portrait of the Princess Adalga serves as frontispiece. Contents run to eight chapters, from an introduction and a dragon's den into the mountain itself.

Two long chapters pass among the gnomes, then one is named for Lucifer. Digging for light and war close the list. The introduction asks who has studied the night side of nature in earnest. Such a reader will know the Untersberg, it says, the mountain of the lower world. It stands like a giant outpost of the Austrian Alps on the frontier of Germany, the text goes on.
73941-empty-bottles:
Raymond S Spears wrote Empty Bottles, a short western tale of a saloon and a strange ask. A tall, clumsy man shambles into the One Way Thru Saloon. He sidles to the bar and speaks in a voice too low to hear. Cock Eye Baer, the bar man, leans close and asks him to say it once more.

The man blurts out that he wants a bottle, a quart in size. The bar man grins and asks what drink shall fill it. The guest then shocks the room by his plain wish. He wants no drink at all, just a clean, bare bottle. The bar man sends him to the yard in back, where bare stock lies in heaps. He comes back and sniffs at two flat quarts in turn, as the crowd looks on.
73954-sunday-stories:
Catharine Shaw wrote Sunday Stories, stories from the Old and New Testaments, published by John Shaw and Company in London. Shaw had earlier written Cherry's Choice and Mother's Bible Stories. The Flight into Egypt serves as frontispiece. The book retells the Bible for children, in short chapters for Sunday reading.

The New Testament stories come first in the contents: the message to the shepherds, the star, the flight into Egypt, and the boy Christ in the temple. The life of Jesus follows, through the temptation, Lazarus, Gethsemane, the cross, and the resurrection. Then the book turns back to the creation, Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, and the tower of Babel. Joseph, Moses, the Passover, and the tabernacle close the set. Such retellings were staples of the Victorian nursery and Sunday school.
73958-thoughts-on-the-mechanism-of-socie:
The Marquis de Casaux's Thoughts on the Mechanism of Societies, in Parkyns Mac Mahon's translation from the French, was printed in London in 1786 by Spilsbury of Snowhill. Casaux, a fellow of the Royal Society, let the translation pass under his own inspection. A line from the Spectator on grafting upon nature heads the title page.

The editor's preface warns that what follows is no treatise, only thoughts, and so bound to no regular plan. One object, it says, fixes every state in Europe: the national debt of England, all of them being debtors or creditors. Casaux begins there, with that formidable debt and its influence on the wealth of the state and the ease of the people, approaching it through general reflections on England's present situation.
73964-the-golden-heart-and-other-fairy-s:
Violet Jacob wrote The Golden Heart and Other Fairy Stories, published in London in 1904 with pictures by May Sandheim. Jacob dedicated the book to six children by name, three boys and three girls. She was already known for novels such as The Sheepstealers, and here she turns to fairy tales for young readers.

Eight stories fill the book. The title tale opens at night on the North Sea. A little boy lies awake in his father's fishing smack and talks with a great shining fish that stares up at him. Other tales bring a sorcerer's sons and two princesses of Japan, a dovecote, a peacock's tail, a pelican, and cherry trees with a witch in a hut. A short Jack Frost story closes the set, made for very little children. Readers get gentle wonder tales with princes, talking creatures, and pictures on nearly every turn of plot.
7399-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
This last volume reaches back to Holmes's oldest portfolio, to verses first printed in The Collegian in 1830 and in illustrated annuals of his youth. The Meeting of the Dryads, The Toadstool, The Spectre Pig, and The Ballad of the Oysterman show a student poet trying on masks: classical fancy, comic parody, and Yankee humor in turn. A poem called The Poet's Lot already wonders what a life in verse will cost.

The charm of the book is its earliness. These are the experiments of a young man who did not yet know he would become Boston's beloved doctor-poet. One of the poems, the preface hints, won kind words from Thackeray. Read after the later volumes, the collection shows where Holmes began: playful, curious, and already fond of the odd corners of New England life.
74057-a-book-of-bridges:
A Book of Bridges is a work on the great spans of the world by Frank Brangwyn and Walter Shaw Sparrow. It was put out at London and New York in nineteen fifteen. The front plate shows a famed part span past a great stream of France. That span was built in the years past seven teen seventy seven. A first note at the front sorts the kinds of book work.

Some book works, that note says, are like steam ships. They go in a set course straight to their port. More are like sail ships that tack here and there. Their course is a zig zag, rul by the winds. The theme of spans is of this last class, the note holds. For five and twenty years the hand has tried to sort it to a set sport.
74067-powers-of-the-president-during-cri:
Smith and Cotter wrote a study of emergency power for the Public Affairs Press of Washington, copyrighted in 1960. The opening chapter sets the stakes. A modern nation's welfare hangs on a web of making and moving, and a break at any of a myriad of points can starve its people and its army. Crowded cities and the arts of swaying opinion add the risk of panic.

Fear of attack, the authors say, drives the ceaseless rebalancing of shared power and private freedom. The book sorts the grants of emergency power made to presidents since 1933. Chapters treat the idea of emergency in free thought and in American law. Powers over persons, property, and news follow. Checks by the law makers and the courts close the study.
74084-history-of-the-waldenses:
History of the Waldenses, by Wylie, retells the tale of a persecuted church people. Cassell issued it, reprinted from his larger History of Protestantism work. The Waldenses held their faith in Alpine valleys through ages of conflict. Martyrdoms and wars in defence of faith and liberty fill the book.

Wylie preface ties their fight to the freedoms Italy won in 1848. Piedmont constitution makers heard their demand for freedom of conscience then. That principle entered the charter, then spread with it across Italy in time. Wylie credits five hundred years of Waldensian struggle for that root gain. Their new work of preaching across Italy closes his hopeful preface.
74118-the-seven-missionaries:
Major McNeile wrote a tale of Jim Maitland and modern pirates aboard the Andaman. Drawings by Gage stand in the text. It never got past the rumour stage at home, the teller says. Captain James Kelly of the ship saw to that. England was busy with rail strikes and war scares.

Two short news notes are all that reached print. One said the Andaman had put in at Colombo for wireless repairs. The other, months later, feared the yacht Firefly lost with all hands. In truth the sea lay flat calm when the Firefly sank in deep water near the Cocos Islands. The tale is set down for one reader's eyes alone, since Maitland's deeds may not stand strict law.
74177-tirzah-ann-s-summer-trip-and-other:
Josiah Allen's Wife wrote Tirzah Ann's Summer Trip and Other Sketches, copyrighted in 1892 and reprinted from Peterson's Magazine. The author had written Samantha at Saratoga and Sweet Cicely. Samantha Allen narrates in rich dialect.

Tirzah Ann, Josiah's daughter, and her husband Whitfield make a likely couple, Samantha allows: he is industrious, she economical. But Tirzah Ann is dreadful ambitious and wants a genteel summer rest, like other folks. Samantha would rather rest at home on her own feather bed with a fan and newspaper. Rest and change, she argues, must happen on the inside of a body, not the outside.
74201-instructions-in-gardening-for-ladi:
Instructions in Gardening for Ladies, by Loudon, was printed by John Murray in London in 1840. The author dedicates it to her husband, the noted gardener Loudon, from whom she says she owes all her knowledge of the subject. When she married, she confesses, she could imagine no person more completely ignorant of plants and gardening than herself.

Ten years of being taught gave her the lessons she now passes on, with the reasons for every task. Chapters stir and manure the soil, make hotbeds, and sow seeds and plant bulbs. Propagation by suckers, layers, cuttings, budding, and grafting follows, then pruning, training, frost protection, and the kitchen garden's vegetables.
74292-south-african-anecdotes:
South African Anecdotes, gathered from many sources, oral and written, by Ellman, was published at Johannesburg in 1914 by the Transvaal Leader. Short tales, each a few lines or a page, make up the book. The first tells of a Dutch schoolmaster brought to the Zoutpansberg district some forty years before.

Elders were shocked to learn the children were taught that the earth turns on its axis and rounds the sun. The minister asked the master to let the sun go round the earth in that district for a few years more, as sudden changes were not liked. Other tales treat a cursing soldier on the road to Kimberley and a digger at Barberton who paid his fine in advance. Dry Boer and mining humor marks the set.
74307-wales:
Wales is a short history of that land by W Davies. The author was a law man and a fellow of a past lore group. Past books by his hand teach how to read the tale of lands. Rights date the work to the year nineteen twenty five.

Parts run from first folk to the Roman hold and the long hunt for one rule. Faith, laws, and the fight for free rule fill the mid age heads. A great revolt chief, the Tudor age, and the faith split earn parts. Home rule dawn and a new birth close the brief keen survey. A note on books at the end points keen minds to more lore.
74350-london-street-games:
Norman Douglas made a breathless list of the games of London streets. The book first came out in London in 1916. Douglas also wrote Fountains in the Sand and Old Calabria. He gave the book to a friend in fond terms. Grown men, he notes, have few sports of their own.

Boys with bats go to the park, and girls take their shuttle cocks. Most young folk have no gear at all to play with. They lark in the street with what they have at hand. Paper chase and rounders are the plain games he names first. Egg-in-cap and more odd games fill the list. Past fans get a lost world of play.
7437-a-peep-behind-the-scenes:
Mrs. O. F. Walton, author of Christie's Old Organ, looks behind the fairground in this moral tale for young readers. The show people, who seem gay and carefree from the front of the booth, live hard lives in their caravans, grumbling at the weather and counting their takings. The story follows Rosalie, a girl of the little theatre, through the day after the fair and the actress's story.

Later chapters bring a circus procession, a doctor's visit, a family secret, and a lone lamb lost and found, as Rosalie learns what lies behind the painted scenes. Walton writes plainly and kindly, with a Victorian evangelical's eye for suffering and hope. The book's charm is its backstage view: the fair as work, home, and hardship, not only as a holiday show.
74379-old-celtic-tales:
E M Wilmot-Buxton retold Old Celtic Tales, a book for the young put out in London by Harrap. The tales were drawn from her large set called Britain Long Ago. That set sat in a line of books told through the ages. A plate at the front shows Kilhugh and Olwen, from page 22.

The Children of Lir leads the set of tales in the list. Lir lost his wife while his young ones were still small in years. He wed once more, a fair wife named Eva who hid a dark gift. She was a witch who could not bear his love for the young ones. In time she set her mind to do away with them for good. A quest of seven great men, and more old tales of the Celts, fill the book.
7438-friends-in-council-first-series:
Sir Arthur Helps was a Victorian civil servant who wrote his way into literature, and Friends in Council, first published in 1847, was the book that made him known. Born at Streatham in 1813, educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge, Helps served as private secretary to the Chancellor of the Exchequer before turning to letters. The book takes the form its title promises.

Friends meet in council and talk through the questions of life: conduct, work, friendship, and the duties of ordinary people. The dialogue form lets Helps argue with himself, giving each side a fair voice. Later series followed, but this first one sets the pattern: thoughtful, good-tempered conversation as a way of thinking, written for readers who enjoy ideas at leisure.
7439-english-fairy-tales:
Who says that English folk have no fairy tales of their own? Joseph Jacobs opens his collection with that challenge, and answers it with a selection from some 140 tales of which he found traces in England. He admits the oddity in his title: few of these stories actually speak of fairies, just as few in Grimm speak of them. The name covers a wider kind of folk tale.

Jacobs invites the child reader in with a playful key and door, then tells the tales plainly, in the voice of the storyteller. Giants, clever youngest sons, talking beasts, and tricksters all appear, in stories that had lived by word of mouth long before they were printed. The collection stands as the classic English counterpart to Grimm, and the source of many tales children still know.
74437-those-barren-leaves:
Those Barren Leaves is a novel by Aldous Huxley, published by Doran in New York in 1925. Huxley's earlier books, Antic Hay and Crome Yellow among them, stand listed. The novel is built in five parts of very unequal weight. The first and longest is an evening at a great house in Italy.

The little town of Vezza stands where two torrents join below the Apuan mountains. Above it a huge house rises among ilex trees and cypresses. Its solemn front, twenty windows wide, looks down over terraced olive groves. There the company of the novel gathers for its talk and intrigues. Fragments from the autobiography of Francis Chelifer form the second part. The loves of the parallels, a journey, and conclusions complete the design. Wit and talk, more than action, carry Huxley's satire of cultivated idleness.
74533-the-triumph-of-the-nut-and-other-p:
Christopher Ward wrote these parodies, printed by Henry Holt and Company of New York in 1923. Two printings ran in its first autumn. Ward gives the book, timidly, to the seventeen writers whose aid, he jokes, made it possible. The names run from Sherwood Anderson and Edith Wharton to Sinclair Lewis, Willa Cather, F Scott Fitzgerald, and T S Eliot. Several pieces first ran in The Literary Review of the New York Evening Post.

The Triumph of the Nut, or Too Many Marriages, opens the set in the manner of a small-town chronicle. The Flame That Failed reworks The Vehement Flame, and Blacker Oxen comes signed by Gertrude Otherton. Glimpsing the Moon bows to Wharton. Ward mimics the famous voices of his day with a light, exact hand.
74565-how-to-study-the-best-short-storie:
How to Study the Best Short Stories, by Blanche Colton Williams of Hunter College and Columbia, was published in Boston in 1919. The book studies Edward O'Brien's yearly volumes of the best short stories of the year, for writers and other students of the form. Williams also wrote a handbook on story writing and edited a book of short stories.

Contents work tale by tale through the yearbooks of 1915 to 1918. Names include Gertrude Atherton, Thomas Beer, Theodore Dreiser, and Irvin Cobb. Each entry takes up plot, character, and craft in turn. The book treats the short story as a form that can be learned by close reading of the best new work, year by year.
74583-wood-folk-comedies:
William J Long wrote Wood Folk Comedies, a book on wild beasts put out in New York in 1920. Its short title calls the work the play of wild life on a stage of the wilds. Long had written on how beasts talk and on trails of the north. The book opens at dawn on Moosehead Lake.

A first part sets the birds at their board, like guests at a meal. A fox plays the lead in one part, and beasts in sable in the next. Wolves, ears that hear far, and night life in the deep woods follow. Tales from the trail and a bear tale told two ways add fun. Beaver meets otter, and a night of spells closes the set. Long treats each beast as an actor with a part to play.
7466-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations is the great Elizabethan collection of English voyages, traffics, and discoveries, and this volume is one part of it. The edition retains the spelling of Hakluyt's sixteenth-century original, expanding only old manuscript abbreviations, so readers meet the accounts in something close to their first form. Editor's footnotes in modern spelling guide the way.

This volume opens amid grim eastern history: Tartar chieftains and their followers destroying whole provinces without respect for condition, fortune, sex, or age. From such accounts the collection builds its picture of a world opening to English ships and traders. For readers of travel history, Hakluyt remains the first source, vast, vivid, and unmistakably of its age.
74695-the-old-house-and-other-stories:
The Old House and Other Stories, by Blanche Sellers Ortmann, is a book of five tales. Ortmann published it herself at Chicago in 1910 and held its copyright. The dedication names the child: Rosanne, for whom the stories were written.

Tante Blanche, as she signs it, hopes they turn Rosanne to the soul in nature. They are to teach love of plain things, and to know and answer the good in all. The other tales are The Boxwood Flats, Bar-Gee, The Soul of a Violin, and The Story of the Goldfish. The title tale gives the house a voice of its own. For a hundred years it has weathered mountain storms and basked in Virginia sun. Its bricks were made on the place, from the clay of the hills. Blinds like green eyelids open and shut with the day.
7471-the-man-with-two-left-feet-and-othe:
P. G. Wodehouse's 1917 collection takes its title from a story about a man who cannot dance, but its pleasures run wider. The contents include Bill the Bloodhound, about Henry Pifield Rice, a detective whose trade is not quite what it seems; Extricating Young Gussie; Wilton's Holiday; and two parts of The Mixer. Crowned Heads at Geisenheimer's and The Romance of an Ugly Policeman add restaurant and street comedy.

Dogs, chorus girls, policemen, and young men in scrapes fill these stories, all told in Wodehouse's bright, effortless voice. The book shows him between his school stories and his mature Jeeves and Blandings work, already master of the comic short story. Readers who want Wodehouse in small, perfect doses will find this collection ideal.
74714-the-black-ship-with-other-allegori:
The Black Ship, with Other Allegories and Parables, is a book of tales by Elizabeth Rundle Charles. Nisbet of London published it in 1861. Charles had written Tales and Sketches of Christian Life, and The Voice of Christian Life in Song.

Contents include The Ruined Temple, The Jewel of the Order of the King's Own, and The Cathedral Chimes. Shorter parables treat household things, thorns, and two bells. Others are The Ark and the Fortress, The Three Dreams, and Thou and I. The Black Ship opens on an island, the King's Garden, beneath the Pine Mountains. A mother lives there with her son Hope and her daughter May. The children are never separated or quarrelling. Hope leads every expedition, and May believes all he plans is best.
74718-miss-ayr-of-virginia-other-stories:
Julia Magruder wrote tales of the South that Stone of Chicago published in 1896. The first and longest gives the book its name. When Miss Ayr of Virginia comes down to take her place on the coach for the races, the contrast with her cousins is plain. The New York cousins have style, height, and bearing. Their cousin has beauty, and little else to show.

Her dress, made in her village, hides her slight figure. She knows her cousins count her a burden; the call came from their father, not from them. She is the belle of her county, an only child who lost her mother young. The New York branch is rich. The Virginia branch was made poor by the war. Seven more tales fill the volume, of a bartered birthright, a masked singer, and an old soul.
74737-the-santa-claus-brownies:
The Santa Claus Brownies is a children's Christmas book by Ethel Calvert Phillips. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in 1928. The contents list five long tales in the volume. The Rocking-Horse Pony Who Wanted Blue Eyes comes first. The Gay Little Town of Bo-Peep and Buttons and Boots follow. The Book of Good Children stands fourth in the list. The Brownie Who Found Christmas closes the book.

The first tale opens at Santa's Snow Palace on the North Pole. A bright cold March wind sweeps round its corners. Some brownies have not finished their household tasks yet. Crusty, oldest of the brownies, brushes the eight tiny reindeer in the stable. Sweet-Tooth, chief of the candy cooks, is busy in the kitchen. An illustration shows a brownie finishing a great white furry rabbit. The tales stick close to Santa's workshop world.
74754-elizabeth-betsy-and-bess-schoolmat:
Amy Blanchard wrote girls' tales of the wars of the young United States. Her lists name books on the war for free rule and on 1812. This tale brings three school friends back for a new year. Elizabeth, Betsy, and Bess had starred in a past tale. A color front plate aids this one, sold at one dollar.

School days, home days, and friend tests fill the new book. Blanchard wrote of pioneer days and of the Texas edge as well. Her girls face small trials with pluck and grace. Each book stands on its own for new young readers. Fans of the first tale get more of the three. Warm, clean fun rules the whole book.
74756-aztec-place-names:
Aztec Place Names treats the meaning and the mode of composition of Mexico old town names. Frederick Starr of the University of Chicago chose the matter from the Spanish of Agustin de la Rosa, Antonio Penafiel, and Cecilio A Robelo. Starr printed the book himself at Chicago in 1920, in a second, revised edition.

The rules of making open the work, after Penafiel. Place names commonly end in a special particle that marks place, as co. When such a particle joins a noun, the noun stands in its singular form, even with a plural force. The noun also commonly drops its last letters or syllable, as Anahuac from atl and nahuac. With two or three nouns joined, each sheds its ending in turn. Examples give house of stone from tetl and calli. Language fans get a compact key to the names.
7476-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
This volume of Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations opens with its author's own preface, a defense of recording English deeds at sea. Hakluyt notes how nations love to blaze abroad their pedigrees, painting ancestors' arms on their walls, while poets trace obscure heroes back to the gods themselves. Against fable, he sets the undoubted truth of voyages, traffics, and discoveries, gathered from sailors and merchants.

Like its companion volume, this edition retains Hakluyt's sixteenth-century spelling, expanding only manuscript abbreviations, with editor's footnotes in modern spelling. The collection as a whole remains the foundation of English travel literature. This volume's preface is the place to start for readers who want to know why Hakluyt gathered his vast library of voyages at all.
74778-keynotes:
Keynotes is a collection of short stories by George Egerton, first copyrighted in 1893 and published in Boston by Roberts Brothers and in London by Elkin Mathews and John Lane in 1894. Egerton dedicates the book to Knut Hamsun. A fragment of a letter serves as motto.

Nine pieces make up the contents. A Cross Line opens the set, and stories follow under titles like A Little Gray Glove and An Empty Frame. A group called Under Northern Sky closes the book. The first story opens on a spring day spoiled by a music-hall tune floating into clear air. Egerton's stories of women's inner lives made the book a landmark of its decade. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
74857-empty-churches:
Empty Churches, subtitled The Rural-Urban Dilemma, is Charles Josiah Galpin's study of country religion. Galpin was in charge of farm population and rural life work for the United States Department of Agriculture. The Century Company copyrighted the book in 1925, and he had also written Rural Life and Rural Social Problems.

The opening scene is a cross-roads with four churches of four denominations within two stone's-throws, almost identical in doctrine. In three of them the congregation can be counted on a pastor's fingers; the fourth is shut that day, its flock too poor for more than an occasional shepherd. Together they cannot muster one fair congregation nor pay one living salary. Yet other farm country he travelled had no church at all, where children had never heard preaching. Competitive religion, wrote one young pastor, is the stiffest problem of the countryside.
74888-no-talent-and-phil-s-pansies:
No Talent and Phil's Pansies are two Golden Text stories by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, published by the American Sunday-School Union of Philadelphia. Guernsey also wrote Irish Amy, Opposite Neighbors, and Twin Roses. Each tale is built on a Bible text. No Talent takes its motto from the Gospel of Matthew: what is done for the least of these is done for Christ himself.

No Talent runs in five chapters, from the summer-house through a dog named Pug, patchwork, and knitting, to the knitting finished. Its heroine is Amity, a plain girl sitting in a mournful posture on a rustic sofa. Yet Amity owns the great place around her, with its stone house, gardens, and smooth lawns. Phil's Pansies follows in five chapters of its own: the seeds, seeds by the wayside, the weeds, the flowers, and the fruit. Both stories teach Sunday-school lessons through small domestic acts.
74897-chinese-fables-and-folk-stories:
Chinese Fables and Folk Stories, by Mary Hayes Davis and Chow Leung, was printed by the American Book Company in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. Yin Chwang Wang Tsen Zan wrote the opening. Davis gives the book to her friend Mary F Nixon Roulet. Each tale carries its Chinese title as well.

The contents open with How the Moon Became Beautiful and the Animals Peace Party. The Widow and Her Son, the Evergreen Tree and the Wilderness Marigold, and the Snail and the Bees follow. A Boy Who Would Not Tell a Lie and a Lesson from Confucius stand later. The first tale says the moon is very beautiful with his round, bright face. But once, six thousand years ago, his face was not so beautiful as now. Young readers get Chinese tales in English dress.
74926-the-golden-windmill-and-other-stor:
Stacy Aumonier wrote The Golden Windmill and Other Stories, in 1921. Macmillan put out the set that March. A Source of Irritation follows the title tale. The Brothers and Old Iron stand after it. A Good Action takes the middle pages.

The Bent Tree closes the contents list. At the top of a hill the party halts in the first tale. The trek up was long and the sun hot. A Frenchman fanned himself with his hat on that hilltop. His eye fell on a large pile of cut fern-leaves there. This will suit me admirably, he remarked as he settled down. He plumped down and stuffed his English pipe. Afternoon sleep gives an indisposition, talk runs. This position suits me admirably, he answers in the same scene. Aumonier gives small lives their exact comic weight.
74947-fairy-tales:
Wilhelm Hauff wrote these fairy tales, here in Weedon's English translation with pictures by Dixon. Hauff's tales are German classics, set largely in the East. The Story of Caliph Stork opens the book.

Chasid, Caliph of Bagdad, lounges on his couch after a nap, sipping coffee and smoking a rosewood pipe. His grand vizier Mansor comes with a troubled face, vexed that a pedlar below the wall has fine goods and he no money. Other tales tell of Little Mouk, the False Prince, Dwarf Long-Nose, and the Cold Heart. A Scottish legend, the Cavern of Steenfoll, closes the set.
74971-a-b-c-of-motion-pictures:
Robert E Welsh writes a primer on the film trade in Harper's A-B-C series, published in April 1916 in New York and London. A front plate shows the interior of a typical motion-picture studio, credited to Edison at the start. Series mates treat cooking, golf, gardening, correct speech, and automobile driving in the same small form.

Welsh opens with history and principles, granting that no one man invented the motion picture as it stands. A score of workers over half a century built it piece by piece, he writes in that first head. As far back as 1795, scientists strove to make pictures move in some early form of the art. Edison's kinetoscope of 1893 dawned the modern day of the screen, Welsh holds at the start.
74998-profiles:
Profiles is a set of moral tales by Pansy and Livingston for young readers. Lothrop of Boston issued the volume with rights in 1888 for it. Pansy, the pen name of Alden, leads with the tale Clean Hands. Elsie Burton hears a strange parting charge from her pastor in it.

Keep your hands clean while you are gone, Doctor Falconer tells her gravely. Elsie puzzles whether he means her dainty hands or something deeper meant. Circulating Decimals and Fishing for Phil follow, each in four short chapters. Our Church Choir runs seven chapters, the longest piece in the set. Livingston adds His Friend, Ten Bushels, and other tales of conduct.
75047-the-amouretta-landscape-and-other-:
Adeline Adams wrote The Amouretta Landscape and Other Stories, in 1922. Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York put out the book. Nine stories make the contents of the volume. Bits of Clay and The Young Lady in Blue follow the title tale. Their Appointed Rounds and Speaking of Angels stand in the middle.

The Marquis goes donkey-riding, and a face called forgiveness, come late. The artist's birthday closes the set of tales in the contents. The title story opens on a painter of New York, Maurice Price. Search the city through, it says, and find none less spoiled by fame. It was in his nature to know that luck makes kindness easy. Nothing wild marks his attire or his way of living, it adds. Yet his good looks set him apart and give him away. Adams gives artists and their loves in gentle tales.
7505-half-past-seven-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson wrote these stories for half-past seven, the bedtime hour, and the Toyman tells them. That is what the Toyman used to say, the book promises. If you ever go to the White House with the Green Blinds by the Side of the Road, the Toyman will say it still, whatever the weather. Dorothy Hope Smith's color illustrations picture the tales.

The contents run from The Little Lost Fox and The Big Bobsled to The Jolly Roger. Then come The Blue Croaker, the Bright Agate, and the Little Gray Mig, and the old woman who lived on the canal. Anderson dedicates the book to Sarah Davis Anderson, the youngsters' Aunt Sally. The stories are gentle, funny, and just strange enough for bedtime, told for children who are not quite ready to sleep.
7506-the-huge-hunter-or-the-steam-man-of:
Edward S. Ellis wrote one of America's first science-fiction adventures in this dime novel of the prairies. A colossal figure strides across the plains, looking like some Titan taking giant steps, with a black volume of smoke issuing from its mouth or the top of its head. At a distance no one can scrutinize the phenomenon closely, and terror spreads before it.

The terror is the Steam Man, a giant machine built by a genius. It travels with a trapper and an artisan up the Yellowstone, among miners and Indians, on buffalo hunts and against a grizzly bear. Chapters promise the steam man as hunter, in wolf ravine, and in an appalling danger. Ellis's huge hunter is the ancestor of the robot tale, a wonder of steam and iron loose on the frontier.
75081-notices-on-the-outlasting-war-site:
The Belgian Army issued Notices on the Outlasting War Sites in 1923 at Brussels from the Ministry of National Defence. A map at scale one to one hundred thousand goes with the book. Four sketches and thirteen photos by the Army Photographic Service aid the text. A portrait of King Albert of Belgium heads the work.

A state list ties each site to its number on the map. German battery Wilhelm the Second at Knocke leads the list. Guns at Zeebrugge and batteries at Breedene and Ostend follow. A great redan at Nieuport and a post at Pervyse station get notes. The Death Trench on the Yser and posts at Dixmude fill the middle. The book keeps war sites marked for guests and for the record.
75101-binney-the-beaver-and-other-storie:
Binney the Beaver and Other Stories is a children book by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, published at Boston in 1875. Henry Young and Company issued the book from School Street, entered for copyright that year. Contents give the title story a run of chapters at the head of the volume. Binney home, and the driving out of idlers, open the beaver tale.

Bad Companions, Disobedience Punished, and Caught in a Trap carry Binney downhill in the list. The beaver is the moral animal of the Sunday school tale: industrious by nature, ruined by bad company, and saved by kindness. Guernsey wrote many such nature tales for children, in which an animal life carries a lesson in each chapter. Her beaver dam is a little commonwealth, and its laws are the laws she wishes her young readers to keep in their own homes and schools.
75132-selected-papers-on-hysteria-and-ot:
Selected Papers on Hysteria and Other Psychoneuroses, by Sigmund Freud, appeared in English in 1909. Brill made the authorized translation for the New York publisher that year. The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease company issued the volume. The psychic mechanism of hysterical phenomena opens the contents at page one.

The case of Miss Lucy and the case of Miss Elisabeth follow as chapters. The psychotherapy of hysteria fills the fourth chapter of the collection. The defense neuro-psychoses brings a theory of hysteria, phobias, and obsessions after it. These papers from the 1890s carried the young psychoanalysis to American readers. Case talk on a couch in Vienna changed medicine through books like this one.
7515-the-glory-of-the-trenches:
Coningsby Dawson, author of Carry On: Letters in Wartime, wrote this interpretation of the trenches from his own service as a Canadian officer. His father, W. J. Dawson, introduces the volume. The epigraph gives its thesis: the glory is all in the souls of the men, nothing external. Dawson had been wounded, removed to a base hospital and then to a military hospital in London, where amputation of his right arm was gravely feared but happily avoided.

As soon as he could use his hand, he was asked to write for Canada about its forces. The book opens with letters from home carried by runners through battle smoke, up Death Valley spouting flame, and down roads no one uses by day. Dawson writes for those at home, to show what the trenches meant to the men who held them. It is a soldier's book, earnest and unsentimental.
7516-crucial-instances:
