Edith Wharton's Crucial Instances gathers seven stories in which a single moment decides a life. The contents run from The Duchess at Prayer and The Angel at the Grave through The Recovery, a dialogue called Copy, and on to The Rembrandt, The Moving Finger, and The Confessional. Italy, art, and old houses provide much of the scenery.

The opening story asks the reader to question the shuttered front of an old Italian house, a motionless mask behind which buzz the secrets of the confessional. Other houses declare the lives they shelter, Wharton writes, but the old palace in its narrow street is as impenetrable as death. Each tale turns on such a masked moment, when character shows itself and cannot be hidden again.
75165-chesterton-as-seen-by-his-contempo:
Chesterton As Seen by His Contemporaries is a life built from others' memories. Cyril Clemens wrote the book for the Mark Twain Society in 1939. Bentley, author of Trent's Last Case, wrote the introduction for it. Massaguer drew the front portrait of Chesterton just for this book. The volume stands eighth in the society's biographical series from Missouri.

Fifteen chapters run from boyhood days to Chesterton the man at last. Literary apprenticeship, meetings, and friends fill the early part of it. The English platform and the American platform get a chapter each. Visits to Notre Dame and New Haven stand among the memories told. Father Brown, the poet, and appraisals by many hands close the book. Clemens gathered a vast store of other folk's memories, Bentley says. Those voices show how his own age saw Chesterton, better than one critic.
75168-secret-remedies:
Secret Remedies, What They Cost and What They Contain was published in London in 1909 by the British Medical Association. The book rests on analyses made for the Association, and its twenty chapters sort the patent medicines by the ills they claim to cure. Catarrh and cold cures come first, then cough medicines, consumption cures, and headache powders.

Blood purifiers, kidney medicines, cures for diabetes, obesity, baldness, and cancer follow, with soothing powders for infants and cure-alls near the end. The preface gives the game away: secrecy itself sells the stuff. The quack, it argues, hides behind mystery to pass off cheap or old-fashioned drugs as costly wonders, said to be culled on remote prairies or confided by venerable chiefs.
7518-more-jataka-tales:
Ellen C. Babbitt retold the Jataka tales, the Buddhist birth stories, for children, and this second volume answers the cry for more. The first collection, published ten years earlier, had won readers young and old, and Felix Adler had confessed himself captivated by the charm of the tales. Babbitt dedicates this companion volume to Rudyard Kipling, in the name of all children who troop to his call.

The stories come from a Guild of Jataka Translators under Professor E. B. Cowell of Cambridge, and Babbitt turns their scholarship into simple, lively tales. Animals talk, kings learn, and kindness wins, in stories first invented to please and instruct cousins far away in the East. Here East meets West, as the foreword says, in a book meant to be read aloud.
7519-the-nomad-of-the-nine-lives:
A. Frances Friebe tells this story through a cat. Her nephew Tom finds his uncle in a brown study before a comfortable fire. He asks why the uncle does not write the story of his life. The uncle, who has spent hours relating his thrilling adventures, finally grants the request. The book that follows hopes to interest people as well as cats, and Clara R. Atwood's illustrations picture its hero.

The hero is the Nomad, a cat of nine lives, whose wanderings carry him through streets, seashores, and homes. Friebe dedicates the book to the Reverend Francis H. Howley, president of the S.P.C.A., and its spirit is humane throughout: June, the preface notes, is when people abandon dogs and cats as they move to the seashore. It is an animal story with a conscience, told by the animal himself.
75212-a-mirror-for-witches:
Esther Forbes wrote A Mirror for Witches, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1928 with woodcuts by Robert Gibbings. The title page tells the story in the old style. Here is reflected the life, machinations, and death of famous Doll Bilby, who preferred a demon to a mortal lover, and the awful judgement that destroyed her body and soul.

The first chapter marshals examples. Devils in human shape, or with horns, hoofs, and tails, may fancy mortal women and prevail by flattery and promises. Forbes cites the burning of Meslie Ry in 1616 and the confession of Christie Goose. Her novel, set in colonial New England, is written as a Puritan chronicle: a witch narrative in period voice, wrought with a historian's care for how such beliefs were actually recorded.
75226-light-interviews-with-shades:
Light Interviews with Shades is a book of comic imaginary interviews by Robert Webster Jones, published in Philadelphia by Dorrance in 1922. A reporter questions the ghosts of famous figures. Nineteen interviews make up the contents list.

Bluebeard explains why he killed his wives. Queen Elizabeth discloses why she never married. Hippocrates holds forth on modern doctors, Methuselah gives longevity secrets, and Jesse James talks on tipping. Shakespeare mentions the movies, Nero discusses jazz, and Old King Cole gives his views on Prohibition. The first interview opens with the girl reporter backing out of the Bluebeard assignment. The narrator draws the job instead, and meets a monster with a long blue beard. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
75293-the-war-drama-of-the-eagles:
Edward Fraser's history of Napoleon's regimental eagles, published by John Murray in London in nineteen twelve, follows the gold standards of the French army. It runs from Austerlitz to Waterloo. Fraser calls it a record of hard fighting, heroism, and adventure. He builds the book around the men sworn to defend each eagle with their lives.

The chapters move battle by battle. They cover the presentation on the Field of Mars and the first campaign under Marshal Ney. They tell of the twelve eagles lost at Eylau and the captured eagle with the golden wreath shown in London. The disasters after Moscow and the last stand at Waterloo close the story. Fraser quotes Napoleon's own addresses, in which losing an eagle is an affront no later glory can repair. Maps and portraits of the marshals support the narrative.
75310-the-secret-of-the-caves:
Franklin Dixon wrote a Hardy Boys mystery, copyrighted in 1929, with illustrations by Walter Rogers. Frank and Joe Hardy open the tale on a drowsy Saturday afternoon in June, circling in motorboats on Barmet Bay within sight of Bayport. The stealing of autos in the neighbourhood, Frank says, has come to an end.

Joe hopes something will turn up before they get rusty, and of course it does. The contents promise an overboard rescue, a Miss Todd, a missing motorcycle, and strange doings. A storm, a cave, footsteps in the night, and stolen supplies follow. A prisoner, a shotgun, and swirling waters lead back to Bayport and a hospital.
75345-the-process-of-gilding-and-bronzin:
The Process of Gilding and Bronzing Picture Frames is a trade manual. Isaac Walker entered its copyright in 1884. Nesbitt printed it in New York. Opening remarks survey the art of gilding through history. Scripture mentions the art, the writer notes. The Egyptians used it on burial cases.

The Romans took up gilding after the fall of Carthage. Medieval Italy and Moorish Spain used it with lavish hand. The Chinese have practised it from ancient times. Walker then turns to the gap his book fills. Gilders work as tradesmen, he says, and write little. Encyclopedias give only thin and unworkable accounts. His aim is a clear description of the processes. The frame itself, he notes, is made by others.
75356-do-you-believe-in-fairies:
Do You Believe in Fairies, by Leonora de Lima Andrews, was copyrighted in 1924. The subtitle calls the book a book of fantasy for grown-up children. Some forty short pieces mix tales, verse, and sketches. Titles run from The Little Girl and The Music Charm to a Ballade for Believers in Fairies.

The first piece sends a little girl running with the wind in her hair. The air is so clear and blue that she thinks a small jump would land her on the mountaintop. She will not jump; that would take a mean advantage of the mountain. Instead she flies up its side, meaning to reach up and squash a fleecy cloud between her hands. Later pieces turn to city rain, Christmas, adolescence, and day dreams, in a light, whimsical key.
75364-enemies:
Marian Isabel Hurrell wrote Enemies, a tale for little lads and lasses, published in London by Partridge and Company. Her earlier books, Cecily Mordaunt and A Three-Fold Promise, are named on the title page. A line from the Sermon on the Mount sets the theme: love your enemies.

The story opens in anger. Young Hugh storms at the news that his grandfather turned his mother away from the door like a stranger. He swears his grandfather shall never insult her again, and that the children will soon be big enough to work for her. The chapter list shows where the feud runs: a council of war, an uncle's generosity, school conflicts, a terrible fall, and a grandfather's penitence. The last chapter is called Peace at Last. Young readers get a family quarrel carried through to forgiveness.
75369-the-pyrenees:
The Pyrenees is a travel and topography book by Hilaire Belloc, describing the great chain between France and Spain. Belloc walks and rides the range and writes of its passes, valleys and peoples. The edition here carries a later preface, written some twenty years after the book, correcting the compass variation and the new frontier rules.

Belloc's counsel is practical and wry. Spain entered over the main range is entered by its most remote and difficult frontier. The wise traveller has nothing to explain. Only at the two ends of the chain, by the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, do common international highways cross. The book remains the classic English account of the Pyrenees: part guidebook, part meditation on a frontier.
75395-the-racer-boys-on-the-prairies:
The Racer Boys on the Prairies, or The Treasure of Golden Peak, by Clarence Young, was printed in New York by Cupples and Leon under a 1913 copyright. Young wrote the Racer Boys, Motor Boys, and Jack Ranger sets.

Chapters open with what is he afraid of, planning the hazing, and a needless alarm. A mysterious man, a strange attack, and Billy tells something follow. News from the West, a thrilling rescue, and an invitation set the trip. Off for the West, a railroad smash, and the man who limped pace the road part. On the prairies, we are being followed, at the ranch, and warned away raise the stakes. The missing paper, the chase, camping out, and a cloudburst drive to Golden Peak. Boys of the day got school fun turned to gold hunting.
7541-quotes-and-images-from-celebrated-c:
Alexandre Dumas père, famous for romantic novels, also wrote histories of famous crimes, and this volume gathers quotations and images from that series. Dumas, the notes remind us, was a novelist who knew his history. He was meticulous in research in his early works, and these books are histories that place most romantic novels in the shade. They cover many centuries and many lands.

The contents list reads like a rogue's gallery of Europe. There are the Borgias, the Cenci, and the Massacres of the South. There are Mary Stuart, Karl-Ludwig Sand, and Urbain Grandier. There are Nisida, Derues, La Constantin, and Joan of Naples. The Man in the Iron Mask appears as an essay, not the novel, beside Martin Guerre, Ali Pacha, and Murat. The Renaissance popes, the notes say, are especially intriguing.
75423-my-life-and-balloon-experiences:
My Life and Balloon Experiences, by Henry Coxwell, came out in London in 1887, with an added chapter on military ballooning. Coxwell was born on March 2, 1819, at Wouldham, near Rochester, on the banks of the Medway. His father was a naval officer who had seen much active service and bore wounds from it.

Coxwell tells of his first view of a balloon as a boy, and of school days near Chatham dockyard. His list of flights runs from Amsterdam and Belgium to Berlin, Cologne, and Leipsig. One flight in Hanover ends in a narrow escape. Later parts treat flights of 1852 and 1853, and ascents more than five miles high. A last part weighs balloons in war, with air torpedoes and bombs. Readers get the life of a famed air man in his own words.
75431-abracadabra-other-satires:
Abracadabra and Other Satires gathers short pieces by John Galsworthy, published in London by William Heinemann. The works list at the front places the volume among his stories and studies, beside A Commentary, A Motley, and Tatterdemalion, and below the novels. The title piece heads the contents, and its illustration is dated 1924.

The contents run from Abracadabra through The Voice of ---- and A Simple Tale to Ultima Thule. Studies of Extravagance, For Love of Beasts, Reverie of a Sportsman, and Grotesques complete the book. The opening tale remembers Minna, a child of eight who hid in the bathroom whenever the governess brought visitors round. She stayed a symbol of shyness for months, then proved a tomboy of hardihood, climbing every tree in a blue jersey and red cap. Galsworthy's satires keep that light, exact touch.
75446-a-history-of-slavic-studies-in-the:
A History of Slavic Studies in the United States is a scholarly survey by Clarence Manning, associate professor of Slavic languages at Columbia University. The Marquette University Press published it in 1957, as the third volume of the Marquette Slavic Studies. Roman Smal-Stocki edited the series.

The contents trace the field from settlement to Cold War. First come the Slavs in America and the age of mass immigration. Then Slavic studies in the nineteenth century and the beginning of formal study. Efforts before the First World War, the years from 1914 to 1939, and the great growth since 1939 follow. A closing chapter sets out the future tasks of Slavic studies. Manning writes as an insider of the small world he chronicles, when Russian and East European studies were moving from the margins of American universities to their centre.
75460-they-re-a-multitoode-and-other-sto:
They're a Multitoode and Other Stories was compiled by the secretary of the Young People's Forward Movement for Missions, printed at Toronto for the Methodist Church. The title story motto runs: we ain't expected to do only our part, in a missionary appeal to young people. Stories promote giving to foreign missions.

Christopher Morton was looking through morning mail when a knock came five minutes before office hours for visitors. Gaunt, hollow-chested Jim Perry entered without ceremony, an old friend sent home with fever by missionaries abroad. Jim might better have stuck it out there, he says, but had no breath to argue, and returns in September. Christy finds his faith in missions tried by losing Jim. Church youth readers got appeal stories.
75466-famous-stories-from-foreign-countr:
Edna Worthley Underwood turned tales from many lands into English in Famous Stories from Foreign Countries, issued in Boston in 1921. Underwood had Englished the songs of Hafiz from the Persian. She gave this book to Calvin Thomas, a scholar and tongue master, in thanks for his help.

Eleven tales fill the book, each with a short life of its maker. Rudolf Hans Bartsch of Austria leads with The Little Blanchefleure, a tale of a young French marquise who lost her head in 1792. Czech, Armenian, Hungarian, Dutch, Czech, and Finnish hands follow, with tales of an exchange, a prison, an elopement, and a king's clothes. Saidjah by Multatuli brings the Dutch East Indies into the set.
75484-anthropoid-apes:
Robert Hartmann, a professor in the University of Berlin, wrote Anthropoid Apes for the International Scientific Series, and Kegan Paul, Trench and Co published it in London in 1885. Sixty-three illustrations show skulls, skeletons, ears, hands, and whole animals, from the aged male gorilla to the white-handed gibbon.

The chapters first trace how knowledge of the apes grew, then set out their external form and their anatomy beside the human frame. Later chapters take up varieties of form, the apes' homes and habits in nature and their native names, and life in captivity. A closing summary weighs the place of the gorilla, chimpanzee, orang, and gibbon in the zoological system.
75485-the-secret-commonwealth-of-elves-f:
The Secret Commonwealth of Elves, Fauns and Fairies is dated 1691. This London edition by Nutt was printed in 1893. Lang added the commentary for that issue. The book reprints a printing of 1815, from Kirk's manuscript. Kirk was minister of Aberfoyle when he wrote. Five hundred and fifty copies of the edition were struck. A dedication in Scots verse goes to Stevenson. Louis, it teases, is far from kelpie, wraith, and ghost. No heather, peat, or trout burns grace his exile. Yet his island folk love tales of gods and giants too. Lang half believes the Highland stories himself, he owns.

Kirk's text is subtitled a study in folk-lore and psychical research. The minister set down his neighbours' beliefs in the second sight. Fairies, co-walkers, and the folk of peace fill his pages.
75490-d-eon-de-beaumont-his-life-and-tim:
Octave Homberg and Fernand Jousselin compiled a life of the Chevalier d'Eon from unpublished papers and letters, Englished by Alfred Rieu and printed at London in 1911. The chevalier in 1770, from a portrait by Huquier, fronts the book. From Tonnerre to Saint Petersburg opens the life: childhood, first successes and friends, and entry into the diplomatic service.

He was employed also by Louis the Fifteenth in his secret diplomacy, on a mission to Russia beside Chevalier Douglas. Diplomatic and military chapters follow: aide de camp to Marshal de Broglie, bright service in the Seven Years' War, then London and the peace of 1763. The English government trusted him to carry the treaty home. Spy, soldier, and the most puzzling figure of his age stand in one life.
75538-bog-land-studies:
Jane Barlow published Bog-Land Studies in a third edition with Dodd, Mead of New York in 1895. She wrote of the Irish bog country as its laureate, and the contents mix tale and verse: Th' Ould Master leads, at the head of seven pieces.

Walled Out, or eschatology in a bog, follows. Last Time at McGurk's gives Mick Flynn on old age. By the Bog-Hole, Past Praying For (the souper's widow), Miss Honor's Wedding, and A Curlew's Call complete the set. The title piece opens in dialect verse on Inish Fay: it mayn't be so much of a place when you reckon by land, a trifle of fields and a bog. But consider the sea, spreading out like a floor to Ratheen. Barlow's bog is a civilization, funny and theological, rendered in the speech of its turf-cutters.
75587-a-creel-of-irish-stories:
Jane Barlow's A Creel of Irish Stories was published in London in 1897 by Methuen, and Barlow had written Irish Idylls before it. A Greek line about a creel heads the book: what we caught we left, what we missed we carry. Ten tales fill the creel, and The Keys of the Chest comes first.

That tale opens in the little valley of Letterglas, a green and lonesome place the snow seldom lies on. A great grassy curtain cuts it off from the sea, and halfway along one side a sharp dip in the ridge makes a gap called the Nick of Time. Ask why, and a boy's answer is all the reason there is: sure, what else would they be calling it? The Snakes and Norah, Three Pint Measures, and A Proud Woman stand among the rest.
756-arizona-sketches:
Joseph A. Munk wrote these sketches of Arizona when it was still a rough frontier of desert, mines, and small towns. He describes the land, its climate, its people, and its ways, from prospectors and ranchers to Native peoples and new settlers. His eye is that of a visitor who stayed long enough to learn the country.

Munk mixes travel notes with local history and anecdote, praising the clear air and wide skies while noting the hardships of desert life. The sketches give a vivid picture of Arizona at the turn of the century, before dams and cities remade it. Readers who love the old Southwest will find here a plain, first-hand portrait.
75655-moufflou-and-other-stories:
Moufflou and Other Stories is a book of tales for the young by Louisa de la Rame, who wrote past the name of Ouida. Kirk made its plates in hue, and Garrett its pen draws. It was put out in nineteen ten. It stands in a set of the tales of youth, whose list stands at the front. That list is a roll of the great tales for the young of the age.

A maid at a wild town by the same hand who wrote this book heads that list. The tale of a drowsy hol low and the tale of a man who slept past years stand past it. Both are by the great hand of the new land's tales.
75758-dames:
Dames is a tale of fog, sea, and perplexity by Murray Leinster. Leinster also wrote Buck Comes Home and kindred magazine fiction. A headnote says the man swimming in the fog found a fog in love. Even before the echoes came, the swimmer felt sure he would drown. The nearest echo, on which his hopes were set, kept receding fast.

A current bore him away from whatever headland echoed the steamer's horn. Thick mist let him see a circle of twenty feet in each direction. In that circle lay nothing but oily water in long, sluggish swells. A power boat's motor beat somewhere, but fishermen mind no fog there. Inside Passage boats ran on while the swimmer's hope sank with each horn.
75765-wee-babies:
Ida Waugh drew the babies of this picture book, printed in colours from her own designs. Amy Blanchard wrote the verse that goes with them. Dutton of New York and Griffith and Farran of London issued Wee Babies in 1882.

Babies short and tall, big and small, open the rhymes. Blue-eyed babies, brown-eyed babes with lots of hair, and babes too tiny to sit up fill the first page. Some drink from a silver cup, some can only eat and sleep. Dimpled fingers and feet draw the praise. Twins get their own spread. Mothers of 1882 got a sweet, bright book to share with the very young.
75771-the-faa-s-revenge-and-other-tales:
John Mackay Wilson leads a set of Scottish tales issued by Gall and Inglis at London and Edinburgh. His own tale of the Faa's Revenge heads the book. The Faa folk are the gypsy people of the Borders.

The title tale is also called The Laird of Clennel. It opens at the Three-Half-Moons Inn in Rothbury, as brown October ends. A stranger sits by the parlour fire for half an hour. Visitors enter and call for brandy and warm water. Other hands fill out the volume. Alexander Campbell gives The Rival Nightcaps and The Merchant's Daughter. Walter Logan writes The Story of Clara Douglas. Theodore Martin adds Country Quarters. James Maidment tells a legend of Morton. George Howell closes with Major Weir's Coach.
75799-stories-and-folk-lore-of-west-corn:
William Bottrell printed his third series of Stories and Folk-Lore of West Cornwall at Penzance in 1880, for the author, with illustrations by Joseph Blight. The preface is a sad one. Before the whole was completed, Bottrell was stricken by a severe stroke of paralysis, which left him unable to hold a pen.

He asks the indulgence of critics and the public for this, his last literary testament. Folklore was then at the height of fashion, with journals like Melusine gathering tales from every nation. Bottrell's Cornwall is the far west of saints, giants, and mine spirits, told in the dialect of the people who remembered them. He collected where Hunt and others had collected before him, in the parishes around his Penzance home, and the third series closes the store.
75806-colonial-memories:
Colonial Memories is a memoir by Lady Broome, published by Smith, Elder and Company in London in 1904. Some chapters first appeared in the Cornhill Magazine. The contents roam the empire she lived in as a colonial governor's wife. Old New Zealand takes three chapters, with a modern New Zealand after. Natal memories follow, then Mauritius under its Latin motto. General Charles Gordon gets a chapter of his own.

Western Australia fills two chapters, with the Enrolled Guard between. Trinidad takes two more, and Rodrigues one. The personal story that opens it reaches back to childhood. A gipsy on Cannock Chase read the little girl's palm. Gold would flow through it, never quite dry, yet the hand could never close on money. Her foot, the gipsy said, would wander the earth. Lady Broome was born in Jamaica, where her father was the last Island Secretary.
75827-lukundoo-and-other-stories:
Edward Lucas White, author of El Supremo and Andivius Hedulio, gathered Lukundoo and Other Stories, published in New York by the Doran company. The copyrights run from 1906 to 1927, a score of years of tales. Ten stories stand in the contents, with an afterword.

Lukundoo leads, and its opening sets White's method. In a club room, Twombly lays down the law: a man must accept the evidence of his own eyes. Not always, Singleton puts in softly. Singleton, effaced in his corner, says he was thinking of something he both saw and heard in Africa. No one has ever drawn a story of his African years out of him before. The other titles promise the same mixture: Floki's Blade, The Snout, The Message on the Slate, and The House of the Nightmare. Tale readers get the club story raised to dread.
75835-legal-antiquities:
Legal Antiquities is a collection of essays upon ancient laws and customs by Edw J White. The F H Thomas Law Book Company published it in St Louis in 1913. White edited Tiedeman on Real Property and wrote The Law in Shakespeare. He dedicates the pages to the memory of his mother. Her faith in humanity, he says, made her charitable for the frailties of the past.

The essays open with marriage laws and customs. Witchcraft and sorcery follow, then the recall of judges. Trial by battle and trial by ordeal get chapters of their own. Peine forte et dure, the wager of law, and benefit of clergy come next. The privilege of sanctuary and ancient punishments continue the survey. Quaint and curious wills close the volume. White's introduction warns against reviving old remedies that failed.
75836-six-mrs-greenes:
Lorna Rea's novel follows one family through the women who married into it. Six wives of Greene men carry the chapters, from Lavinia Forster, who married William Greene in the middle of the last century, down to the wives of his great-grandsons. The family tree printed at the front maps the Greenes from 1808 onward: Geoffrey, Hugh, Rodney, Edwin, and their sons and daughters.

The book opens with the old matriarch, tired and talking to herself, her mind wandering among sons and grandchildren while her companion, Miss Dorset, listens. Heinemann published the novel at London in March 1929, and it was reprinted again and again that spring and summer. Rea builds the story generation by generation, letting each new wife see the family from a fresh angle.
75847-the-singing-leaves:
The Singing Leaves, a Book of Songs and Spells, by Josephine Preston Peabody, was published at Boston and New York in 1903. The book is in its tenth impression in this copy. Thanks are given to the editors of Harper Monthly and Scribner Magazine, for leave to reprint many of the poems.

A short dedication invites whoever cares to look in her little book to look again. Songs and spells open with the house and the road, a charm to be said in the sun, and grace before meat. Sad truth and glad truth sit side by side. Road songs, cedars, an inn, sins, and a watcher follow. Later groups treat young things: a sapling, a hero, nests, and a fir tree. Readers get lyrical poems of home, road, and nature.
75849-aggravating-ladies:
Aggravating Ladies lists books published under the pen name A Lady, with lessons on describing books. Olphar Hamst wrote the work while gathering matter for a handbook of false author names. Quaritch published the book at London in 1880. A long quote from Professor De Morgan heads the title page.

Hamst says the list began as a note in Notes and Queries. He hoped owners of such books would send him true names and full details. The front half teaches how to describe a book well. Chapters treat cataloguing, styles of printing, marks of punctuation, and common errors. A chapter tells how to unmask unknown and false named authors. The list itself runs to twelve pages of titles. The book is a small classic of the book trade's back room.
75869-a-doctor-enjoys-sherlock-holmes:
Doctor Enjoys Sherlock Holmes is a book of Holmes essays by Edward Van Liere, published in 1959. Vantage Press of New York issued the first edition, copyrighted to the physician author. Van Liere dedicates the book to his two grandsons in a front note. Pieces in it had run in medical journals and in the Baker Street Journal.

A West Virginia medical journal and a Harvard alumni journal carried his Holmes pieces. The Physiologist and a medical fraternity quarterly also printed the doctor essays. A physician reading Holmes brings clinical eyes to Watson medicine and Holmes method. Sherlockians gain a genial doctor fan readings of the canon cases.
75879-essay-and-speech-on-jewish-disabil:
Lord Macaulay's Essay and Speech on Jewish Disabilities appears here in a second edition, printed at Edinburgh in 1910 for the Jewish Historical Society of England. Israel Abrahams and Levy edited the volume, with an introduction and notes. Contents give the editors' introduction, then Macaulay's essay, then his speech, then the editors' notes. A portrait of Macaulay fronts the book.

The essay, on the civil disabilities of the Jews, first appeared in the Edinburgh Review in January 1831. It opens on a member of the Commons who has given notice he will renew his motion for the relief of the Jews. Reason and power are now on the same side, Macaulay writes. He will pass in review the phrases used to defend a system full of absurdity and wrong. The claim that the constitution is of its nature Christian stands first among them.
75882-a-history-of-the-colonization-of-a:
A History of the Colonization of Africa by Alien Races is a volume of the Cambridge Historical Series. Prothero, a fellow of King's College, Cambridge, edited the series. Cambridge University Press issued the book, with sellers from Edinburgh to Bombay. Its maps carry notes of the lands and peoples treated.

The author tells the story country by country as a rule. In one or two cases the tale starts at an earlier date, and for the colonies it generally begins later. Separate treatment, he holds, lets the thread of events be followed more clearly, save in great shared epochs like the French Revolution. The book surveys how outside powers planted colonies across Africa, from early trading posts to the partition of the continent. It served students as a single, sober account of a vast and tangled subject, written when the colonial map was still new.
75896-arse-ne-lupin-intervenes:
Arsene Lupin Intervenes, by Maurice Le Blanc, was published in New York. The contents open with a foreword, then Drops That Trickle Away. A narrator explains Jim Barnett, whose notice promises information free, with no fees of any kind.

That was, the text says, paradoxically true. Barnett income was not fees but levies. Sometimes he took toll of his clients, sometimes of their enemies. A kind of poetic justice marked his takings, and the poor and innocent had nothing to fear. Inspector Bechoux was likely his only close friend. Yet even Bechoux knew nothing of Barnett private life, his past, or even his identity. Later chapters name a royal love letter, a game of baccarat, a man with gold teeth, and arresting Arsene Lupin. Readers get Lupin tales of disguise and daring.
75914-on-the-distribution-of-intensity-i:
Cecilia Payne and Harlow Shapley wrote On the Distribution of Intensity in Stellar Absorption Lines, a research paper of 1926. It appeared in the Proceedings of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, volume sixty-one, number ten. A grant from the Rumford Fund met the cost of publication. Payne was then a National Research Fellow.

The authors note that theory on line contour abounds, while careful measurement is scarce. Their study measures the broad, strong lines in the spectra of stars of various types. They base the work on objective prism spectra, read by a photographically recording microphotometer. That method, they argue, gives a steady photometric scale across the whole spectrum. They test how far scattered light distorts the true contours, and check their results against slit spectrographs. The paper is early work by the astronomer who reshaped the study of stars.
75942-lectures-and-biographical-sketches:
Lectures and Biographical Sketches is volume ten of Emerson's Complete Works, in the Riverside Edition, published by Houghton, Mifflin of Boston in 1884 under Edward Emerson's copyright of 1883. An editor's note by Cabot sorts the pieces: some Emerson printed himself, from the Dial and elsewhere; others Cabot prepared from the manuscripts for readings, after Emerson had given up regular lecturing.

The contents mix lectures and lives. Demonology leads, then Aristocracy, Perpetual Forces, Character, Education, The Superlative, and The Sovereignty of Ethics. The Preacher, The Man of Letters, The Scholar, and Plutarch follow. The sketches remember Ezra Ripley, Mary Moody Emerson, Samuel Hoar, Thoreau, and Carlyle, with historic notes of life and letters in New England. Several pieces, Education and The Scholar among them, appear here for the first time, the note says.
75953-a-day-in-the-country-and-other-sto:
A Day in the Country and Other Stories, taken from the magazine The Pansy, was published by Lothrop of Boston under an 1885 copyright. Fourteen short pieces fill the contents: the title story, Why Madge Changed Her Mind, Nannie's Lesson, Some Curious Fishes, On Nantucket Wharf, The Greenlander, and Some Young Heroes among them.

The title story follows four Boston girls to Sabbath-school on a pleasant September morning: Maggie and Lottie Barnes, Delia and Sallie Shaw. The narrator warns against picturing them in silk and plumes. Their dresses are faded and worn, Maggie in her mother's trailing shawl, Delia in a rusty black velvet sack too large for her. Lottie has a soiled silk handkerchief for a wrap and a hat that sails off at every gust. Sallie's shoes are too large and keep slipping down at the heel.
760-enoch-soames-a-memory-of-the-eightee:
Max Beerbohm wrote this tale as a mock memoir of Enoch Soames, a would-be poet of the 1890s who fades into obscurity. Soames, a pale young man in a waterproof cape, haunts London cafés and dreams of fame, while the narrator watches with amused pity. A deal with the devil lets Soames glimpse his future fame, or lack of it.

Beerbohm mixes real figures of the decade with invention, and the joke turns tender as Soames learns his fate. The tale is a small masterpiece of irony, poking fun at artistic vanity while mourning lost youth. It remains one of the most quoted stories about the nineties, and about the cruelty of literary fame.
76004-the-problem-of-lay-analyses:
Sigmund Freud wrote The Problem of Lay-Analyses, put out by Brentano at New York in 1927. Maerker-Branden translated that treatise from the German for this volume. James Strachey translated the autobiographical study bound with it. Freud opens by explaining his title in plain terms. The problem, he says, is whether laymen should practise psychoanalysis. Laymen here means men and women not trained as physicians.

Up to now, he notes, nobody cared who was practising the new science. The one shared wish was that nobody at all should practise it, he adds. Now legislatures in some lands are pressed to reserve it to physicians. That demand itself proves a more tolerant view is gaining ground, Freud holds. His treatise argues the case for trained lay analysts. The study of his own life and work closes the volume.
76009-piccino-and-other-child-stories:
Piccino and Other Child Stories is a set of tales for the young by Frances Hodgson Burnett. It came out at New York in eighteen ninety-seven, with rights of two past years. Four tales fill it. The first tells two days in the life of its name boy. The next tells of a sea chiefs last child, and a third is told by a small girls cat in its own voice.

A last tale tells how the famed small lord of her great book came to be. The first tale opens past a boy who could not lose those two strange dread days past a full span of years. If he lived to be as old as the white head who plays with string in the sun, he would still hold them, it says. His mates thought him a fool past those days.
76041-lighthouses:
Hardy traces Lighthouses, Their History and Romance, in a London print of 1895 from the Religious Tract Society. Plates show the first lighthouse at Dungeness, from a dues receipt of 1690, and the Eddystone medal of 1757. The book is a coastwise tour as much as a history.

Early heads treat old and middle age lights, the Trinity House, and old methods of lighting. Grace Darling gets a head of her own. The tour then runs from Spurn Head to the Thames, past the Nore lightship and the Goodwin Sands. The Eddystone takes four heads, from the plans of Henry Winstanley to the fourth tower. The Lizard and the Scillies close the run.
76047-agricultural-prices:
Henry Wallace, of Wallaces Farmer, wrote this study of farm prices in 1920. Wallace Publishing Company issued it from Des Moines, Iowa. Part one takes up the present price registering system at length. Three price making forces and their faults get early chapters.

Supply and demand, cost of production, and ratio methods fill part one. Hog cost by ratio, cattle prices, and milk prices get worked cases. Part two gives a math study of supply and demand in hogs. It tries to predict hog prices and owns the method limits. Wallace wrote it while editing Wallaces' Farmer in Iowa.
76055-malay-sketches:
Malay Sketches, by Swettenham, was published in 1903. John Lane issued this third edition in London and New York. Swettenham's Unaddressed Letters are praised at the front. The Real Malay, his pen pictures, stand beside them. Twenty two sketches and an introduction make the book. The Real Malay opens the contents, as in his other volume. The tiger, a fishing picnic, and a murdered hawker follow. Amok and the joget get sketches of their own. The story of Mat Aris and the state called latah come midway. Malay superstitions and a casting-net fill later pages. The death of Birch, a British resident, is told at length. An opening address, headed Voltaire, sets the scene.

Eternal summer rules the golden peninsula, Swettenham writes. It lies between Hindustan and far Cathay.
76071-bed-time-stories:
Bed-Time Stories is a children's collection in verse and prose, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1914. Saalfield printed the book in Chicago, Akron, and New York. An illustration of Tom Tinker's dog opens the pages with a nursery rhyme. The stories mix animal tales with rhymes for the nursery hour.

The first tale stars a frog who would sing. Froggie thinks his voice very fine, and the fishes next door agree. Fishes, having no voices at all, may not be the best judges, the narrator allows. Proud of such praise, the frog sets off to charm the world. The book belongs to Saalfield's mass produced nursery line. Cheap, bright, and sturdy, such collections put a small library of tales beside American children's beds in the years before the First World War.
76153-the-stone-dragon-and-other-tragic-:
The Stone Dragon and Other Tragic Romances, by Murray Gilchrist, was printed in London by Methuen in 1894. Gilchrist gave the book to George Alfred Garfitt. Fourteen tales fill it, and some first ran in The National Observer.

The title tale opens with a son who finds his father journal years after his death. The journal tells of a last visit to Furnivaux Castle and a breach with great aunt Barbara. She was a gross, worldly woman who loved to meddle for sport. Other tales name a lost mistress, a basilisk, and a pageant of ghosts. One is cast as excerpts from a journal plus a letter. Readers who like dark, lush tales of love and doom will find Gilchrist rich fare.
76176-kitty-cat-tales:
Kitty-Cat Tales is a book of cat stories for children by Alice Van Leer Carrick, printed at Boston in 1907. Homer Eaton Keyes and Bertha Davidson drew the pictures, and Carrick gave the book to Margaret and John. The tales are framed as nine nights of story telling, with a cat named Impty curled by a child's pillow.

Each night brings a fresh tale: the white cat, the king of the field mice, and the cat who married a mouse. Old favorites join them, such as Dick Whittington and his cat, Puss in Boots, and Venus and the cat. The frame tale opens with Dolly, a lonely child who cannot sleep.
76184-further-memories:
Further Memories is a second volume of reminiscence by Lord Redesdale. Hutchinson published it in London in 1917. Edmund Gosse wrote the introduction to the volume. A portrait of the author and sixteen other plates illustrate it.

Redesdale's earlier Memories had reached an eleventh large edition by then. Reviewers quoted at the front praise that book without reserve. Its author was born some months before Queen Victoria came to the throne. He had been everywhere and seen everything, the Times declared of him. Courts and princes across East and West crowd his long experience. The new volume adds the gist of later conversations and thoughts. Many of them arose in idle moments in a Cotswold garden. That garden gathered features unusual in Western pleasure grounds, he notes. Social, historical, and personal matter mix in his treasury as before.
76295-notes-from-calais-base-and-picture:
Montague wrote Notes from Calais Base and Pictures of Its Many Activities, printed in London in 1918. The first piece treats training in France. All our troops are trained before they go to France, it opens, whether a man goes out with his battalion or in a draft. But when drafts are landed in France they are put through a further course, before they go up to join their regiments at the front.

That last spell of teaching is very short and tightly packed with work. It takes the men as knowing their work already, needing only greater finish. It is given by the army's best experts in trench warfare. The base schools live in close touch with the front, Montague writes. Their teachers come fresh from the trenches and show the young soldier how a new trick of bomb-throwing will help him at the pinch.
76332-collected-poems-of-clarence-edwin-:
Clarence Edwin Flynn's verse is gathered in a first series covering work of 1929 and earlier. The poems are ordered by year of printing, then by title within each year, as the notes explain. Where Flynn reused a title, the year marks which version is shown.

The opening poem, Si Gidders, from 1902, is a dialect piece about an old farmer who wonders at everything. Gidders asks why leaves are green, why things fall down, and why three times three is not ten. Short notes and three added lists round out the volume, one naming poems the editors could not obtain. Readers get a plain record of a working poet's early verse, humor, and rural speech.
76365-ant-ventures:
Blanche Elizabeth Wade wrote a storybook of ant adventures, with pictures by Harrison Cady, copyrighted in 1924. A table of contents lists some two dozen short tales, from Around the World for a Change to a venture of mottoes. The first tale opens on an ant sitting on a leaf to think.

He is tired of carrying out earth all day and of hunting food for the family, and says so aloud. A beetle with horn-rimmed spectacles appears, writing on a prescription pad, and offers a cure: a change is all he needs. Later tales visit the angleworm's doorway, a wild-rose tea house, and the hollow-log inn. Gentle morals ride on small legs throughout.
764-hans-brinker-or-the-silver-skates:
Mary Mapes Dodge wrote this tale of Holland, where canals freeze in winter and every child skates. Hans Brinker, a poor boy, hopes to win the silver skates offered in a great race on the ice. His father lies ill from a fall, and the family scrapes by with little money and much pride.

Dodge mixes the race with lessons on Dutch life: dikes, windmills, markets, and the customs of town and farm. Hans and his sister Gretel face hardship with pluck, and the race becomes a test of heart as much as speed. The book, aimed at young readers, has long served as a friendly guide to Holland and to honest effort.
76407-telephone-troubles:
Telephone Troubles, Their Location and Remedy, by Wev, was published at New York in 1907. McGraw Publishing Company issued the little manual for telephone workers that year. A note says the book aims to help the beginner and guide the experienced man. Its word comes from fifteen years of practical work in the trade.

Direct line troubles open the contents at page one of the guide. Two party line and four party set faults follow as the next chapters. Testing for and clearing troubles in private branch exchange boards gets a long chapter. Inspection closes the contents of the practical manual for linemen and repairmen. Early telephone plant needed such pocket guides in every tool bag of its crews.
76438-hints-on-writing-short-stories:
Charles Finger wrote these hints on writing short stories for beginners. Haldeman-Julius printed the ten cent pocket booklet at Girard, Kansas, 1922. Finger says this is his third attempt at the booklet. Two drafts went into the waste basket as too stiff, formal.

He aims at curtness and directness, as true instructors use them. Children teach each other games with a few simple directions, he notes. Parents and teachers flounder in mist of explanation too often. A sudden warning word taught him swimming where books had failed. Tons of theory failed where a caution word worked, his swimming lesson shows plain.
76439-historic-towns-of-the-southern-sta:
Historic Towns of the Southern States surveys eighteen old cities of the American South. Powell edited the volume. Putnam published it in New York and London in 1900. Trent wrote the introduction. Each town has its own local author. Illustrations fill the book.

Baltimore opens the set with a long chapter. Annapolis and Frederick Town follow from Maryland. Washington, Richmond, and Williamsburg come next. Charleston, Savannah, and Mobile carry the story south. New Orleans closes the river towns. Knoxville, Nashville, and Louisville end the inland group. Augustine, the oldest town, comes last. A frontispiece shows the Library of Congress. Old prints and portraits support each chapter.
76441-some-points-in-choosing-textiles:
Some Points in Choosing Textiles is a household science bulletin by Charlotte Gibbs, issued by the University of Illinois on November 25, 1912. It is Volume Ten, Number Thirteen of the university bulletin, from the Department of Household Science at Urbana. Gibbs writes for the woman who now buys what her grandmother made.

In the past century, she begins, a great change has come in the position of the woman in the home. In early America nearly every woman produced her family's clothing and the household linens, from raising the sheep or flax to the finished product. Now manufacture has left the home, and even sewing is going. Homespun was the best the materials allowed; bought cloth is a guess. Women, Gibbs finds, depend more and more on the word of clerks, who are often as ignorant as themselves. Her bulletin teaches buyers to judge fibre and weave for themselves.
76461-voyage-to-the-east-indies:
A friar reports the east in A Voyage to the East Indies, an English rendering of a work by Fra Paolino da San Bartolomeo. The author was a barefooted Carmelite who resided thirteen years in India. Notes kept from the original illustrate parts of the text, a note states.

He was born at Hof, in the Austrian dominions, in 1748. Before he embraced the monastic life, he was known by the name of John Philip Wesdin. He was seven years professor of the Oriental languages, the account adds. Such a man may be supposed well acquainted with the subject on which he treats, the English editor holds. His long stay in India is the book's warrant: the voyage and the country are told by one who lived there, not by a passer by.
76466-glimpses-of-the-dark-ages:
Glimpses of the Dark Ages sketches the social condition of Europe from the fifth to the twelfth century. The Religious Tract Society of London issued the book. Its preface confines the plan to one branch of medieval history. Political affairs and the rise and fall of dynasties are set aside.

Military deeds and the lives of heroes do not come within the plan either. The author takes the first six centuries of the middle ages apart. In the twelfth century a new epoch commences, he argues. So he glances instead at homes, laws, faith, and daily work. How men ate, prayed, learned, and obeyed fills his sketches. The book is popular history with a moral aim, in the tract society manner.
76522-pythagoras-and-the-delphic-mysteri:
Edouard Schure's Pythagoras and the Delphic Mysteries, in Rothwell's translation, was published by the Theosophical Publishing Company of New York in 1909. A saying from the temple of Delphi heads it: know thyself, and thou wilt know the universe and the gods. Three laws stand beneath: evolution is the law of life, number the law of the universe, unity the law of God.

Five chapters carry the life: Greece in the sixth century, the years of travel, and the temple of Delphi, with the pythoness Theoclea and the theory of divination. Then the order and its doctrine, in four degrees from preparation to epiphany. Marriage, the rising at Croton, the master's end, and the school's destiny close the book. Chapter one opens on Orpheus, whose soul crossed the new-born Greece like a divine meteor.
76537-plays-for-small-stages:
Mary Aldis wrote these one-act plays for small stages, printed by Duffield and Company of New York in 1915. The set holds Mrs Pat and the Law, The Drama Class, Extreme Unction, The Letter, and Temperament. Aldis gives the book to her boys. A front plate shows Hugh and Gladys mid-quarrel over music.

A note thanks friends who helped prepare and stage the plays. The prefatory matter scorns the amateur habit of reviving professional hits with a punch. Amateurs cannot match professionals at their own tricks, the book argues. So these pieces are built for small rooms and plain means, where a home cast can shine. The plays sit in a line with festival and holiday play books of the day.
76541-red-aces:
Red Aces, subtitled Three Cases of Reeder, is a detective book by Edgar Wallace. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London. Wallace dedicated the volume to his friend and secretary Curtis. The three cases are the title story, Kennedy the Con Man, and The Case of Joe Attymar.

The title case opens with a young man very much in love. Kenneth McKay, a bank clerk, spends his days counting other people's money and his lunch hours writing impassioned, ill-spelt letters to Margot Lynn. Everybody at the bank knows he is desperately in love. His father George, meanwhile, broods in a gaunt riverside house at Marlow over a vanished fortune. The old man gives his whole mind to the folly that dissipated his money, and to fantastical schemes for getting it back. Reeder, Wallace's mild ex-criminal detective, unravels the crimes that follow.
76547-jibby-jones:
Jibby Jones is a boys' story by Ellis Parker Butler, published by Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York in 1923. Its full title promises a story of Mississippi River adventure for boys. Arthur G Dove drew the pictures, starting with Jibby in his big suit.

The narrator is one of the Riverbank boys, proud of their stretch of the great river. Jibby himself is Oliver Parmenter Jones. Chapters promise pearl-diggers, a climbing rabbit, and a fishing prize. A red-headed bandit abducts the dog Rover. A treasure hunt, a worm mine, and a Viking ship follow. Skippy shares the fun, and one chapter asks where Greenland is. Butler was a humorist, and the tall-tale tone runs through every scrape. The book gives boy readers the river as a playground of schemes, prizes, and buried gold.
76573-chinese-recipes:
Chinese Recipes gathers the recipes of the Nellie Wong Tea Shop in Peking, copyrighted by Nellie Wong in 1927. Explanatory notes set out the pantry. Soy bean sauce and ginger season universally, the sauce often taking the place of salt. Mushrooms, water chestnuts, and bamboo shoots are the distinctive vegetables, and peanut oil or lard serves for frying. Each recipe makes six portions.

Tea opens the contents, then egg flowers soup, Chinese rice, and left over rice. Shrimp dishes run several pages: shrimp straws, shrimps and toast, fried shrimps, and shrimp cakes. Sweet and sour fish, fish balls, and pineapple fish follow. Pork appears broiled and with bean sprouts, and spring rolls and cabbage rolls come next. Corn and white meat of chicken, walnut chicken, stuffed mushrooms, string beans, and almond chow mein fill the middle, and sweet potato balls, precious pudding, and a sauce close the book.
76637-wee-johnnie-paterson-other-humorou:
Grant Stevenson's Scots sketches appear here in a new edition with added pieces, printed at the Ballantyne Press in Edinburgh and issued by Foulis in 1914. Henry Kerr and other hands supply the pictures, one of them facing the title page.

The title sketch follows Mrs Johnstone, who can never tell one story at a time and whose talk wanders off to sugar at a shillin' the pund and the loaf at eleven-pence. The other pieces include Boys, An Amateur Cook, The M'Crankys at a Party, Johnnie Gibb's Funeral, Spring Cleaning, A Marriage, and After-Dinner Speeches. Golf, football, and a singing lesson fill out the later pages.
76641-the-molly-maguires-and-the-detecti:
Allan Pinkerton wrote The Molly Maguires and the Detectives, Book Six of his tales of his own trade. The new and full form came out in New York from Carleton and his firm. Pinkerton had told tales of a rail man, a model town, and men of ghosts and fraud. Plates show a trial scene and a talk in his own rooms.

Pinkerton states his aim at the front of the book. He means to give the facts of the Molly Maguires in full, and to stick to the truth. His men spent three years in the midst of that gang, at great risk. The trial at Mauch Chunk drew all the great law men of Carbon County. The tale blends a true crime case with the craft of the spy sent in to break it.
76710-ellice-quentin-and-other-stories:
Julian Hawthorne wrote the short tales in Ellice Quentin and Other Stories, here in a new edition printed in London. Hawthorne had written Garth before this book. His preface makes a case for the short story as a form. Conciseness, he argues, is not mere brevity, and the writer who packs a tale tight does his readers a service.

He grants the points against his case at length. Padding is easier for the writer and pays better under the rules of the trade. A thousand-page novel can hardly miss a few strong pages, while a short tale may say nothing worth hearing. Still, he holds, most long novels would shrink to short tales if stripped of matter that does not belong.
76718-russian-essays-and-stories:
Maurice Baring's Russian Essays and Stories was first published by Methuen in London in 1908. Baring had written A Year in Russia and With the Russians in Manchuria. He dedicates this book to Evan Charteris, and the dedication letter serves as his preface.

Baring says the essays and stories deal entirely with Russian subjects but are in no sense political. His only object, he repeats, is to give a record of things seen. He jokes that Conservatives called his last book a revolutionary pamphlet while English Liberals called it an apology for reaction, which he takes as proof of its impartiality. A story about bluffing a German examiner enlivens the letter.
76733-celtic-art-in-pagan-and-christian-:
Celtic Art in Pagan and Christian Times, by Romilly Allen, first came out in 1904 from Methuen in London, in the Antiquary's Books series. Allen begins with the continental Celts and how they came to Britain, then follows their art through the Bronze Age and the early Iron Age. Three chapters close the book with the art of the Christian period.

The plates and figures show the Hallstatt sword, bronze sheaths from La Tene, gold lunulae, mirrors, torques, and the spiral carving at Newgrange in County Meath. Allen sorts chevrons, spirals, cup and ring marks, and interlaced work, and ties each pattern to the things that bear it. Christian chapters bring in the carved stones and metalwork of the church age. The book served for years as the standard short account of Celtic ornament.
76745-many-marriages:
Sherwood Anderson wrote Many Marriages, a novel from Huebsch at New York in 1923. The book came out on February 20 and ran to a third printing in March. Anderson gives it to Paul Rosenfeld. An explanation at the front speaks to readers of the Dial magazine. The story had run in that sheet in serial form, and Anderson thanks it for leave to print.

In book form, he says, the tale has been greatly expanded from the serial. A foreword holds that to seek love directly, in modern life, is perhaps insane. A small act, like opening a door and saying a few words, can turn huge in the mind. A man stands in a hallway, with a closed door and a figure by a window past it. Anderson builds his tale on that strain between wish and act.
76750-the-two-countesses:
The Two Countesses came out as number twenty-seven in the Unknown Library, a line of short tales. The tale is told in a warm letter voice, as if to a dear friend. Its teller jokes that she will plunge her reader at once into the midst of things. She teases her friend that the Latin phrase for that plunge is a bit of learned show. From that light start, the tale turns to news of two countesses.

The Unknown Library mixed tales from many lands and hands in small, cheap books. Names in the line run from John Oliver Hobbes to Juhani Aho and tales from France and Russia. This volume gives a brief, chatty tale in that cosmopolitan mix. Readers get gossip, wit, and high life in a pocket form made for the train and the fireside.
76755-ojibwa-myths-and-tales:
Colonel Geo E Laidlaw gathered Ojibwa Myths and Tales, reprinted from the Archaeological Report of nineteen fifteen. The series was obtained from Peter York in the summer of nineteen fifteen, Laidlaw says. Peter camped with his family of basket makers, and later told the tales at the Rama Reserve by Lake Couchiching in Ontario. The tales told by John York were told in Ojibwa to Peter and written down in English by Peter, he notes.

I have followed York phraseology as closely as possible, Laidlaw says, not changing his meaning in any sense. Some stories may appear crude, but he left them as they are, he adds. John York is an old man of ninety six, named Big Thunder, he notes. Peter York is forty eight, named Thunder. Nanabush, the trickster hero, stands at the centre of the tales. Folklore readers get Ojibwa myth in the tellers own English.
76764-landscape-with-figures:
Landscape with Figures is a tale of a trip east by Ronald Fraser. The text draws on the diary of a man named Ambrose Herbert. Seven men who call their band the Seven Sages make the tour. Rights date the work to the year nineteen twenty six.

A lily smell and a faint lake scent hang on the first page in dream tones. The seven find wise men in that far vale who best them in deep talk. Good sense rules their days, with rare gleams of soul at soft hours. They do not let dreams of the whole sway their plain road of life. East thought and west ease clash in the lush, wry tale.
76770-aspects-of-jewish-power-in-the-uni:
Aspects of Jewish Power in the United States is volume four of The International Jew, a reprint of articles from the Dearborn Independent, the newspaper published by Henry Ford. The twenty articles gathered here, numbered sixty-two to eighty in the series, appeared as a campaign against supposed Jewish influence in American life.

Their titles announce the argument: liquor control, a liquor trust, bootlegging, and Arnold's associates. The volume opens by claiming that most organized bootlegging under Prohibition was in Jewish hands, and by presenting Jewish solidarity as the key to American demoralization. Historians treat the series as a landmark of American antisemitic publishing; the text is preserved here as a record of that propaganda and of the Prohibition-era resentments it exploited.
76776-minor-tactics-of-the-chalk-stream-:
Minor Tactics of the Chalk Stream and Kindred Studies is an anglers book on the fine art of the fly for trout. Its fronts list the shops that sell it round the world, in New York, Melbourne, Toronto, and the towns of India. A plate of flies heads the copy at hand.

That plate names its flies like a roll of troops. A rough spring iron blue dun and an olive stand at its head. A green fly of a famed name, in its counts and twin forms, fills the rows. A pale dun of summer, a black gnat, and a lure named for its need in all kits close the plate. The text then weighs when each fly, and each cast, will take a shy trout.
76807-another-year-with-denise-and-ned-t:
Gabrielle Jackson wrote this children's book, Another Year with Denise and Ned Toodles, copyrighted at Philadelphia in 1904 with pictures. Jackson also wrote Caps and Capers and Doughnuts and Diplomas. A frontispiece shows Denise raising her head to listen for a second call. Twenty-two chapters cover another year with the pair and their pets.

Contents promise what the wood-thrush told, and an old friend and a new one. A circus, the earth opening to swallow a pet, troubles coming in troops, a timely rescue, and an aunt's arrival in town follow. A birthday frolic, a rescue by Denise, and a coasting episode lead to a Christmas for all the pets. Chapter one finds Denise alone in her carriage, chin propped on her hands, brown curls about her face, gazing dreamily toward a glassy river.
76814-ghosts-in-the-great-war-and-true-t:
Giraud edited Ghosts in the Great War and True Tales of Haunted Houses, published in London by Fleetgate Publications for the Daily News. The book is number four in a series of readers' ghost books. Earlier numbers gathered true ghost stories, warnings from beyond, and uncanny stories, all told by readers of the Daily News.

The first tale is called A Pal in Life and Death. Two friends joined the army together on September 21, 1914. The narrator's mother sent him off with the words: be a man, do your duty. The pal, a soldier from head to foot, answered that they would come back. Side by side they fought for two long years. Such collections fed the hunger, after the war, for word that death was not the end of comradeship.
76842-fools-and-mules:
Ray Humphreys wrote Fools and Mules, a Shorty McKay tale of snow, mines, and a pay roll at risk. Snow had capped the peaks of the Sangre de Cristos late in August. By slow weeks it had rolled down and smothered the town of Monte Vista in drifts. Roads to the silver mines were blocked to all but horse men and men on snow shoes.

The First State Bank of Monte Vista had to send a three-thousand-dollar pay roll to a mine in the heart of the snow land. It called on Sheriff Joe Cook for a plan and a guard with guns. Talk said Buck Bancroft, a road thief, had been seen on that side of the range. Cook scoffed at the talk and praised the rule of law in his bounds. That pride sets the trap the tale will spring.
76902-the-history-of-the-bastile-and-of-:
Davenport wrote a history of the Bastile in Paris and of its chief prisoners, issued in London in 1838. He had meant to tie the tale to the whole history of France and its parties and sects. One volume proved too small, he warns, even with more and larger pages.

He says he read every record he could reach and tried to be just while he taught and pleased. Contents list the towers, dungeons, rooms, food, library, and chapel of the fort. Sealed royal orders that jailed men without trial, the search of new prisoners, and the hush laid on guards all come under his eye.
76942-yachting-wrinkles:
Yachting Wrinkles, a practical handbook for the racing and cruising yachtsman, was written by Captain Kenealy, author of Boat Sailing, Fair Weather and Foul. The Outing Publishing Company printed it in 1899. A subtitle defines a wrinkle, from a nautical lexicon, simply as something worth knowing.

The preface disarms the critics. Kenealy confesses he went to sea at thirteen and spent years afloat where books were scarce; nautical experts must let the work speak for itself. Twelve chapters follow: yacht racing as a sport from its inception, the racing yacht's material and construction, and the choice between keel, centreboard, and bulb fin types. Fitting out and tuning up, duty and discipline afloat from skipper to sea cook, and a down to date yacht race come next. Later chapters treat racing rules, the evolution of the racer under measurement rules in America and Britain, etiquette, insurance, and cost.
76948-silence-and-other-stories:
Silence and Other Stories is a set of tales by Mary Wilkins, published by Harper in 1898. Wilkins is named as author of Jerome, a Poor Man, Madelon, and Jane Field. An illustration at page thirty eight shows a woman calling a name, David, three times.

The title story takes its name from a stillness at the heart of a New England village life in her manner. Wilkins tales are of farmers daughters, spinsters, and poor relations in the hill towns of Massachusetts. Her people speak little, and the silence between them carries the weight of the story in her art. She was, by 1898, the acknowledged master of the New England tale in America. This volume is a fair measure of the gift that made her name. It is the drama of those who cannot say what they feel.
76950-the-ghost-of-charlotte-cray-and-ot:
Florence Marryat gathers ten tales in The Ghost of Charlotte Cray and Other Stories, printed at Leipzig in 1883. Tauchnitz made the book as a copyright edition, with the right of translation held back. Marryat had writ Love's Conflict and Facing the Footlights.

The title tale opens on Sigismund Braggett in his small study. He is a publisher and bookseller, well to do, with a trade in the city and a fair villa at Streatham. He is just forty, sound in tooth and hair. He has wed three months back one of the fairest women in England. Yet a mournful mood wraps him. His trouble is that he has got more than he wanted, the tale says.
76970-the-orphan-nieces:
Noon recess at Granger's school finds the girls round the piano, deep in talk of the near examinations. Olive McHenry finds something pleasant in the tests; her cousin Charlotte sees no good in them but the holiday after. So Lucy Ellen Guernsey opens her tale of orphan nieces, out in 1856.

Its full title joins the girls' state to its theme: Duty and Inclination. Twenty chapters carry the school world and the home claims that pull against it. Guernsey wrote many such tales for young readers, warm in faith and firm on doing right. The talk rings true to schoolgirl life of its time. Home scenes soon test what the schoolroom taught.
76971-the-black-spaniel-and-other-storie:
Robert Hichens wrote The Black Spaniel and Other Stories, put out by Stokes at New York in 1905. Forestier made eight plates for the book. The title tale opens in the great hall of the Grand Hotel at Rome. The narrator brings Peter Deeming and Vernon Kersteven together, two friends of his own. He hopes the pair will like each other and form a happy trio. The front plate shows a cry of murder, and the dog of the title soon takes the stage.

Later tales turn to the desert. Desert Air, Halima and the Scorpions, and The Desert Drum draw on North African scenes. The Princess and the Jewel Doctor, The Figure in the Mirage, and Safti's Summer Day add more of the same mood. Hichens gives readers tales of love, fear, and fate in hot lands.
76997-wigwam-wonder-tales:
William Thompson wrote wonder tales for young readers, printed at New York in September 1919 with art by Carle Michel Boog. Thompson gives the book to a friend who shared ten years of travel with him, from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean. That friend, the giving note shows, is a dog who rode fourth class with a first class ticket.

Ten tales fill the book, starting with a giant butterfly and a mouse who offers to free the sun. Wactu, an animal painter, Alitoci and giant birds, and a tale of why dogs do not talk follow. Fire Boy and Water Boy, underwater folk, and talking birds close the set.
77017-some-forgotten-pennsylvania-heroin:
Henry W Shoemaker speaks for overlooked women of his state in an address given at Bellefonte on May 6, 1922. He spoke to the Bellefonte Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, and the Times Tribune Co of Altoona printed the talk that year. A newspaper query from Washington sparks his theme.

That query named Betsey Ross, Rebecca Biddle, Lydia Darrah, and Lucretia Mott as the state's greatest women. Shoemaker grants Mott her fame as preacher, teacher, and reformer who broke the bonds of caste. Ross, Biddle, and Darrah rest on shaky tales and social ties, he argues with care. Wealth and rank too often buy a name in his age, he warns, while a servant girl may spring from a noble line.
77020-ten-recreational-parties:
Helen Durham wrote a handbook of ten recreational parties, published at New York under a 1924 copyright by a press for women's work. It revises and enlarges her earlier six parties; the last three pieces, she owns, are not parties strictly speaking, but ways of adding variety to larger entertainments. The first party is built on peanuts.

Invitations for the peanut party are written on tissue folded inside a split peanut shell, tied with orange ribbon, or pinned to cards with decorated peanut faces. Guests receive orange bags for the peanuts they win at guessing and piercing games, and the fullest bag at the final counting takes the prize. Newspaper, balloon, doll, Japanese, Washington, and circus parties follow the pattern.
77065-the-barbarous-babes:
The Barbarous Babes, being the memoirs of Molly, by Edith Ayrton, Mrs Israel Zangwill, was printed in London and Edinburgh by R Brimley Johnson in 1904. Ayrton gives the book to the memory of her mother. Molly tells the tale at the age of ten.

Chapters hold the martyrdom of Humphrey, Samson and Delilah, and Violet visit. The whipping of Teddy, the rage of the heathen, a first night, and mother close the set. Molly opens by saying it all started because Humphrey and she generally play together, and they generally play at torturing games. Sometimes they let the little ones, Violet and Ted, come in too, but they spoil things rather. Teddy is so tiny, and Violet does not properly enjoy even the loveliest tortures. Young readers get nursery cruelty played for comedy.
77080-collected-writings-of-clarence-edw:
The Collected Writings of Clarence Edwin Flynn, First Series, gathers the author's shorter pieces from 1929 and earlier. Two appendices were made for this book, one of them a set of selected quotes and zingers. A line from Flynn's Obligation of Good Cheer stands at its head: it is the glad service which lifts the world a little farther in its long, hard climb.

The categories are named for their aim. Another says the issues of life have always proceeded from the heart, and that the heart of any age expresses itself in its music. Lifting Christianity follows, with pieces on the Sabbath and on light as the knowledge of the truth that makes men free. The collection shows a small town American man of letters at work across twenty years.
77138-through-green-glasses:
Through Green Glasses collects Irish tales by F M Allen, illustrated by M Fitzgerald. D Appleton and Company published it in New York in 1887. The subtitle names the lead story, Andy Merrigan's Great Discovery. Six tales follow it in the contents. From Portlaw to Paradise and King John and the Mayor come first. The Wonderful Escape of James the Second adds mock history.

The Last of the Dragons, The Siege of Don Isle, and Raleigh in Munster complete the volume. An introduction presents the source of the lore. Allen once met, in a southern Irish town, a little old man named Dan. Dan was thoroughly illiterate, yet his mind stored strange legendary matter. Kings and saints in his yarns wore his own shabby clothes. They thought as Dan thought and spoke with his brogue. The tales that follow retail Dan's Ireland.
77151-the-olive-branch-and-other-stories:
Olive Branch and Other Stories is a set of moral tales by A L O E, printed in 1885. Nelson of London issued the book for young readers in home and school. Seventeen short pieces fill the table, from The Olive Branch to The Two Standard Measures. The ass in the lion skin and the boy and the bird nest show the fable strain.

A peep into a back kitchen and the two patients bring the lessons close to home. Never mind scoffs, go and do likewise, and it is very hard preach by their titles. Thorns and flowers and heir to something better close the list of tales. Each brief story drives one clear duty or kindness home to its reader.
77172-codes:
Codes is a novel of the telegraph office by Romaine Lowdermilk and Arch Giddings, authors of The Boomer. Its first page says the world of the telegraph man is strange to the man in the street. It offers romance and excitement to those who know it, the authors promise. The tale opens at Los Angeles, in the operating room of the National Consolidated Telegraphs. DeMars blows in one autumn afternoon. He talks two minutes with the chief and goes to work that night on the fastest wire in the house.

DeMars is dark, slender, and fond of fine clothes, a dandy among drifting operators. June Harmon works the same room. She is pretty, capable, and wise past her twenty-four years. Her father was once chief of that very room. Since his death she has run her family's affairs. The spark code and the heart's code cross in the tale.
77173-the-crusades:
The Crusades is a short history volume in the series Epochs of Modern History, edited by Edward Morris. The head of the text is given to the series lists, which set this book among its companions. Metadata names Andrew White as creator, while the series pages credit the Crusades volume to Cox, the Oxford historian. The text itself follows the series list.

The Epochs series sold each volume at one dollar, with maps and plans throughout. The ancient series runs from Troy and the Greeks to the age of the Antonines. The modern series begins with the early Middle Ages and the Normans, and this volume on the Crusades stands third in its line, before the early Plantagenets. These were school and home histories, written by scholars for general readers, and the Crusades volume tells of the wars for the Holy Land in that compact form.
77213-pop-corn-recipes:
Mary Hamilton Talbott compiled Pop Corn Recipes, a small cookbook issued from Grinnell, Iowa, in 1916. The publisher bought the recipes from Talbott, a well-known recipe writer for leading magazines. The booklet promotes one brand of popping corn above all. It still treats popcorn as everyday food, not a fairground treat.

A publisher's letter opens the book. It praises the corn's popping test, its Iowa-grown Amber Rice stock, and its rat-proof storage cribs. Readers are urged to insist on the ten cent package. The recipes begin with breakfast dishes. Popped corn can be served hot or cold as a cereal. The hot kind is soaked overnight in water, then cooked. The book argues that popcorn matches sweet corn in protein and fuel value.
77240-the-romance-of-the-oxford-colleges:
Francis Gribble wrote The Romance of the Oxford Colleges, printed in London in 1910 with seventeen illustrations, including Merton College. Gribble was sometime scholar of Exeter College and author of George Sand and Her Lovers. Contents open with University College: founders, Alfred the Great claims, William of Durham, statutes, and Shelley.

Shelley's printing freaks, his friendship with Hogg, his Necessity of Atheism, and his expulsion fill the University College tale. Balliol follows with a birching, Snell exhibitioners, Adam Smith, Southey, Coleridge, and Jowett's reforms and sermons in the mastership years. Merton brings town and gown rows and Civil War queens. Oxford lovers get anecdotal college history.
77274-historic-towns-of-the-middle-state:
Lyman Powell edited a volume on the historic towns of the middle states, printed at New York and London in 1899. Albert Shaw wrote the introduction. The Half Moon on the Hudson in 1609, from a painting by Seavey, fronts the book. Albany opens the town tales in Battershall's hands, then Saratoga by Walworth and Schenectady by Landon.

Newburgh, Tarrytown on Hudson, New York City, and Brooklyn follow. Princeton by Sloane, Philadelphia by Talcott Williams, Wilmington, Buffalo, and Pittsburgh close the roll. Each town gets its own writer, its old streets, churches, and battles. Dutch charters, river trade, and revolution fill the pages. The book stands in a set with a New England volume at three dollars fifty. Antiquaries and travelers get a portrait shelf of old America.
77294-memories:
Memories is a memoir by Gordon Cumming, the traveller who wrote Wanderings in China and At Home in Fiji. Blackwood published it in Edinburgh and London in 1904. A portrait by Angelica Kauffmann, of the beautiful Duchess of Argyll with her daughters, faces the title page.

Her apologia opens the book with a confession. She has inherited many pleasant things, she writes, but also one trying heritage: a total inability to recognise acquaintances when meeting them face to face. Even real friends, known well in mind, go unidentified at a sudden meeting. Her father suffered the same failing all his life. She mentions it in hope that the confession may meet the eye of someone she has thus unwittingly offended. A memoir that begins by apologising for its author's blind spot promises candour, and hers roams from Fiji to the great houses of Scotland.
77297-annals-of-the-great-strikes-in-the:
Dacus, late of the editorial staff of the St. Louis Republican, wrote Annals of the Great Strikes in the United States, published at Chicago in 1877. The book calls itself a reliable history and graphic description of the labor strikes and riots of that year. A picture of troops fighting rioters at the Halstead Street viaduct sets the tone.

The preface says the events mark an epoch in the nation's history. Dacus argues that the strikes would feed political debate and social movements for years to come. He wrote close to the events, in the year of the great railroad strike that spread across the country. The book preserves how the crisis looked to a newspaper man while the smoke still hung over it.
77314-ladies-old-fashioned-shoes:
Ladies Old-Fashioned Shoes, by Watson Greig of Glencarse, was published at Edinburgh in 1885. Greig was a vice president of the Literary and Antiquarian Society of Perthshire. Eleven illustrations from originals in his own collection grace the book. A shoe said to have belonged to Mary Queen of Scots leads the list of plates.

Such a study treats footwear as a window on dress, craft, and rank in past ages. Collectors and students of costume are the clear audience for the volume.
