Each plate lets readers see the shape and trim of shoes that women wore in old times. Perthshire antiquarian circles stood behind the work in its local roots. David Douglas issued it at Edinburgh for a niche but keen readership.
77377-eva-s-apples:
William Gerhardi published a novel at New York in 1928, subtitled a story of jazz and jasper, in homage to the genius of Wells. Its title joins Eva to the jasper stone of the book of Revelation, clear as crystal. A second large printing followed quickly.

The first chapter argues in a taxi outside a tall Fleet Street building crowned by the sign of the Daily Runner. Eva will not run away, nor sit and wait, though the meter ticks shillings away. The narrator, a young man of nervous complex who fears waiters and hall porters, has an appointment with Lord Ottercove. Eva teases that his lordship might like to see him too, if he knew. Comic dread carries the scene.
774-essays-and-lectures:
Oscar Wilde gathered essays and lectures that show his wit at full stretch before his plays made him famous. He writes on art, dress, the English Renaissance, and the value of beauty, arguing that art needs no excuse beyond itself. The lectures, given on tour, carry his gospel of aestheticism to new audiences.

Wilde's prose sparkles with paradox and epigram, turning each topic into a performance. Beneath the glitter lies a serious claim: that beauty and form matter as much as morals or facts. The volume gives readers the young Wilde as critic and prophet, and it helps explain why his later plays still dazzle.
77405-romantic-castles-and-palaces:
Esther Singleton edited and translated Romantic Castles and Palaces, published by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1901. Singleton compiled several such volumes, gathering famous pictures, scenes, and buildings as great writers described them. Conway Castle in Wales fronts this one. Each castle or palace is presented through the words of a well-known author, and numerous illustrations accompany the texts.

Grant Allen opens with Conway and returns for Fontainebleau. Théophile Gautier describes the Ducal Palace at Venice, the Winter Palace ball, and the Generalife. Walter Scott gives Linlithgow, and Alexandre Dumas the Palazzo Vecchio and the Riccardi Palace. Alice Meynell writes on Arundel, Lady Wilde on Dublin Castle, and Edmondo de Amicis on the Alhambra. The book is an armchair tour of Europe's great houses, and a few beyond, in the age before cheap travel: the buildings seen through literary eyes.
77406-old-glory-and-verdun-and-other-sto:
Elizabeth Frazer wrote Old Glory and Verdun and Other Stories, published at New York in 1918. The pieces first ran in the Saturday Evening Post. A front plate, passed by the Committee on Public Information, shows a French field hospital wrecked by a shell.

Ward Eighty-Three opens the set: a new volunteer nurse, an auxiliaire, reports at an American war hospital in France, fearing her ignorance might cost a man his life. Other pieces take up nursing the French wounded, a greenhorn nurse, children of the war zone, and a canteener. The title story and pieces on Château-Thierry and a spite attack close the book.
77423-the-twenty-six-clues:
Isabel Ostrander wrote this detective novel, first printed by Watt in 1919 and reprinted by Grosset and Dunlap. The Twenty-Six Clues sits among her tales of suspense. The Clue in the Air and The Heritage of Cain stand on her list at the front.

One of her books was made with William Burns, the famed real-life detective chief. That link marks her trade: yarns built like case work, clue by clue. Twenty-six clues is a bold count to promise a reader. Each must land, mislead, or turn in the hand. Ostrander was one of the most-read American mystery hands of her day, and this tale shows her pace and polish at full stretch.
77426-the-three-glass-eyes:
William Le Queux unmasks a financier in The Three Glass Eyes, a story of to-day from Anthony Treherne of London. His letter to the reader names the target: Ventris Blake, the noted American financier in London, whose doings have made British industries tremble. Public men, Le Queux says, keep a fair self for show and a hidden self for private life.

Under the expose runs a simple love story, that of Winifred Pontifex and her mysterious vicissitudes, temptations, and dangers. The contents promise a marriage certificate, a hole in the wall, a strange scene in church, and all about those glass eyes.
77456-geological-and-solar-climates:
Marsden Manson, a civil engineer, set out his theory of Earth's past climates in this thesis. He read it for the University of California in May 1893, in geology and physics. George Spaulding printed it at San Francisco the same year.

Its title holds the claim: geological and solar climates, their causes and variations. Manson sought the springs of the ice ages and the warm ages between them. The errata sheet at the front, with its wavers and eras set right, shows the print's care and haste at once. A working engineer's reach for the great question of his day: why the Earth's heat has swung so wide across deep time. The thesis still stands in the debate's early record.
77476-commonplace-and-other-short-storie:
Commonplace, and Other Short Stories, by Christina Rossetti, author of Goblin Market, was published by Ellis in London in 1870. In a prefatory note dated April 1870, Rossetti explains that the earliest of the tales goes back to 1852 and the latest was finished that year.

Rossetti notes that two tales, Pros and Cons and The Waves of this Troublesome World, were each written with a special object. She insists that not one of the stories is founded on fact. One friend, she says, had taken The Lost Titian as an imposture, and she puts on record that she knows no tradition of any lost picture by that master. The title story opens at Brompton-on-Sea in April, with three maiden sisters at the breakfast table. The volume gathers the prose fiction of a poet better known for verse.
77478-a-history-of-english-lotteries:
A History of English Lotteries is John Ashton's account of the lottery in England, billed on its title page as now for the first time written. The Leadenhall Press of London published it in 1893, with Simpkin, Marshall and Charles Scribner's Sons of New York. Twenty-eight old lottery bills are inserted in facsimile, their tinted papers and dirty red ink imitated.

Ashton traces the subject from the year 1569 to his own day. He drew on the British Museum library and on the fine collection of Andrew Tuer, placed unreservedly at his disposal, and picked his handbills and engravings from a plenty that embarrassed him. Dates and Acts of Parliament are verified with a scruple meant to make the book an authority. The first chapter opens with the antiquity of the lot itself and the scheme of the first lottery in England.
77484-the-isle-of-lies:
Shiel's novel The Isle of Lies, published in London by Werner Laurie, begins in a professor's diary and reaches back to Abyssinia in 1868. Professor Reid records the birth of a son to Lepsius and sets down what he knows of the story behind it.

Reid recalls how Lepsius joined a British mission to Abyssinia after the capture of Magdala, hunting Jurassic limestones and old Bible manuscripts. The chapter list then points the tale forward: a stele, Molly O'Hara, the isle itself, a ship, towers, terraces, a garden, and stops at Egmond and Serapis. Shiel blends diary, history, and romance into one strange tale, in the rich and odd style that marked his fiction.
77496-pretty-creatures:
Pretty Creatures is a gathering of five long stories by William Gerhardi, published by Duffield in New York in 1927. Gerhardi had already won fame with Futility and The Polyglots, novels of Russia and diplomacy. The title story opens in Salzburg. Its hero falls in love mainly because other men swarm after the prize he thought his own.

The other pieces are The Big Drum, A Bad End, In the Wood, and Tristan und Isolde. Gerhardi writes of drawing rooms, dancers, and middle-aged suitors with a gentle comic touch. Awkward conversations carry his scenes, and vanity does the rest. The stories show the bright, melancholy manner that made him one of the admired English stylists of the nineteen twenties.
775-when-the-sleeper-wakes:
Herbert George Wells wrote this tale of Graham, a man who falls into a trance in 1897 and wakes more than two hundred years later. He finds a London of moving roads, vast halls, and a Council that has grown rich on his sleeping wealth. A leader named Ostrog seeks to use him as a figurehead for revolt.

Graham must choose between the Council and the people, and his choice leads to war in the streets of the future city. Wells uses the sleeper to judge his own age and the age to come, on wealth, power, and the crowd. The novel is a founding work of dystopian fiction, and it still grips as a tale of a man out of time.
77523-immunity-in-infective-diseases:
Immunity in Infective Diseases is a medical work by Elie Metchnikoff, professor at the Pasteur Institute in Paris. Francis G Binnie of the pathological department at Cambridge translated it from the French. The Cambridge University Press printed it in 1905, with forty-five figures in the text.

In his preface to the English edition the translator calls the book the sum of Metchnikoff's labours of twenty-five years. His aim was a faithful rendering of the ideas and argument of the original, even at the risk of a crude phrase here and there. An index was added to this edition as a key to the many authors cited and the maze of detail in the work. Marginal references point to the pages of the French original. Metchnikoff's book set out his account of how the body defends itself against infective disease. It is a foundation text of the science of immunity.
77548-the-philoctetes-of-sophocles:
An English translation of Sophocles' Philoctetes was printed at Dublin in 1725, with a dedication to Lady Carteret. The translator thanks her for the honor her husband, the lord lieutenant, did him. His scholars had acted a play of Sophocles in Greek before him. He chose the same author for this version. A motto from Horace heads the title page.

Philoctetes, marooned with his bow on Lemnos, is the tragedy's subject. The dedication's schoolroom scene shows how Greek drama was taught in Georgian Ireland. Hyde and Dobson printed the book for R Owen of Skinner Row. School and college editions like this one kept Greek tragedy in circulation in English.
77559-the-story-of-the-great-lakes:
Edward Channing, a professor of history at Harvard, and Marion Florence Lansing wrote The Story of the Great Lakes for Macmillan in 1909, with maps and pictures. A portrait of La Salle fronts the book. The tale runs in three parts, from first discovery to the shipping of their own day.

Part one follows Champlain in 1615 and 1616, the Jesuit mission to the Hurons, and La Salle's building of the Griffon. Part two takes the fight for the lakes: the founding of Detroit in 1701, Pontiac's plot, Wayne's campaign, and the conquest of Lake Erie in 1813. Part three turns to roads, the Erie Canal of 1825, railroads, and the great trades of the lakes.
77569-the-wondrous-sickle-and-other-stor:
A L O E wrote The Wondrous Sickle and Other Stories, issued at London and Edinburgh by Gall and Inglis. The author had writ Ned Franks and The White Bear's Dean. A front print shows a king go out day by day to reap his corn. Tales in the set treat India and faith in short form.

The lead tale turns on Fath Masih, a Christian patwari in a large village. A patwari measures land and keeps the district map, a note says. The post gives much chance to fleece the poor. Fath Masih took no bribes and heard the humblest, folk said. Hindus and Muslims who had scorned his post came to praise his just life. The Zamindar runs to eight chapters. Short tales named The Strait Gate and The Bad Bargain close the set.
77619-cordage-and-cordage-hemp-and-fibre:
T Woodhouse and P Kilgour, both heads of departments at Dundee Technical College, wrote this handbook on cordage in Pitman's Common Commodities and Industries series. The frontispiece shows a rope drive for a mill shaft.

The contents define cordage and classify fibres, then treat the cultivation of hemp and its retting, breaking, and scutching. Hard fibres follow, with the preparing and spinning machinery for each class. Closing chapters cover twines and lines, ropes and rope-making with yarn numbering, and marketing. Photomicrographs show fibre sections, and plates show sisal breakers and baling presses. Mill men get the whole trade from plant to rope walk.
7763-the-law-breakers-and-other-stories:
Robert Grant's The Law-Breakers and Other Stories opens with George Colfax, a passive reformer. He reads the Nation, hates the spoils system, votes for the best men, and gives a dollar a year to civil-service reform. He talks well about public decay, yet does little beyond talk.

Other tales in the volume include Against His Judgment, St George and the Dragon, and The Romance of a Soul. An Exchange of Courtesies, Across the Way, and A Surrender follow. Together they satirize genteel Boston morals, where right views cost little and real action costs much more.
77648-the-friends-and-other-stories:
Stacy Aumonier wrote stories published at New York in 1917, under copyrights of 1915 and 1917. A line of Dostoevsky stands for epigraph: people, even the wicked, are much more naïve and simple-hearted than we suppose. The title story fills two-thirds of the book; two shorter pieces, The Packet and In the Way of Business, follow it.

White and Mapleson, the friends, cannot recall when their friendship began; they drifted together across commercial London and founded it in the saloon bars off Oxford Street. White agents for a wire-mattress firm; Mapleson manages the brass bed department at a Bloomsbury emporium. Either man might drink ten to fifteen whiskies in a day, yet neither was ever really drunk, nor ever really sober. A drinking friendship, studied with tenderness, is the story.
77680-yiddish-short-stories:
Isaac Goldberg edited this set of Yiddish Short Stories as Little Blue Book number 489 for Haldeman-Julius at Girard, Kansas. Copyright rests in 1923 with the Haldeman-Julius Company, and Goldberg thanks Brentano's for a Pinski tale. The first story, Three Gifts by Isaac Leib Perez, opens after a man's death. His soul rises to judgment in the court above.

Advocate and accuser pour white and black sacks of deeds onto the scales of justice. Good deeds glow like stars while evil deeds reek of tar and pitch below. The balance sways by hairs as angels empty the sacks grain by grain. Perez turns a folk trial into a study of small virtues. Cheap print carried fine Yiddish tales to all.
77686-my-tussle-with-the-devil-and-other:
A volume of stories credited to O Henry's Ghost appeared at New York in 1918, opening with a piece called The Barrage Fire. Its frame claims the tales come from the dead author himself. A quote from Algernon Blackwood's fiction arms the ghost against critics: the beloved dead step nearer when their bodies drop aside. Scoffers, the text says, will call the stories impossible.

They are not a bit like O Henry's, the scoffers will say, lacking his virility. The ghost answers that of course they differ. O Henry's earthly tales were written in bold black and red, the colors of human passion. The premise sells spiritualist curiosity in wartime.
77689-the-sword-decides:
Marjorie Bowen founded her novel The Sword Decides on the story of Giovanna of Naples, and the McClure Company issued it at New York in 1908. The subtitle calls the tale a chronicle of a queen in the dark ages. Chapter one opens on the night of June 3, 1343.

Andreas of Hungary camps by the Adriatic on his way to wed Giovanna, a wife he has never seen. Silver olives and wild cherry foam fade in the dusk around his splendid train. Later chapters bring an entry into Naples, a masquerade, executions, and a battle in the streets. Queens move, kings move, and the sword decides at last, as the final chapter promises.
7769-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques, and Discoveries of the English Nation gathers the great age of English sea travel, edited here by Edmund Goldsmid. This edition keeps the spelling of Hakluyt's sixteenth-century original, while expanding old manuscript shortenings for modern readers.

Footnotes follow nineteenth-century spelling, sidenotes stay Hakluyt's own, and two kinds of notes guide the reader through dense old texts. Sailors, merchants, and explorers fill its pages, from first Atlantic ventures to far eastern trade, making it a first source for how England learned the wider world by ship.
77762-tom-gillies:
Mrs George Gladstone wrote a tale of a boy named Tom Gillies and the knots he tied and untied. James Nisbet and Company issued the new form in London in 1881. Gladstone gave the tale to her nieces Flo, Bessie, Bella, and May. Fifteen chapters run from Tom at home to two years later.

Norton Island, with cliffs, caves, and lime quarries, forms the wild scene. Tom and Dick Potter raid sea bird nests in the high rocks. Mr Pender owns the quarries and the one great house on the isle. Work, mishap, and first wages test the lad in a tale for the young.
77764-soap-bubbles:
Max Nordau gathers tales in Soap Bubbles, printed in New York in 1896. Neely made the book, in a rendering by Mary Safford. Nordau had writ Degeneration and The Right to Love. A story index stands in front, each tale summed in a line.

Cant and Humbug leads, a story of English selfishness and American thriftiness. Wife Versus Native Land shows how a man may quit smoking for spite, but not for love. Ali Hadji Effendi gives the adventures of a wandering fanatic of Islam. The Cross at the Corner treats the devotion of an aged Hungarian. A Christmas Eve in Paris recalls suffering in the siege of Paris. Within an Inch of Eternity tells how a prison physician's hair turned white in a night, from horror inflicted by two escaped prisoners.
7780-notes-to-shakespeare-volume-01-come:
Samuel Johnson's Notes to Shakespeare, volume one on the comedies, appears here in the Augustan Reprint Society edition, edited with an introduction by Arthur Sherbo. General editors from Michigan, California, and London universities frame a text that returns to Johnson's famous critical work.

Johnson's preface to Shakespeare, the general introduction notes, ranks among the great essays of the eighteenth century, yet students often forget it is, precisely, a preface. This volume collects his notes on the comedies, where his plain sense, learning, and sharp judgment meet the plays line by line.
77809-verses:
Verses is a book of devotional poems by Christina Rossetti. Its motto, out of the deep have I called unto thee, O Lord, stands on the title page and again at the head of the first poem. The opening sonnet asks to be lifted above the transitory scope of earth.

Pleasures that begin and cease, the waning moon, and the decreasing seasons all pass. We turn to Thee, the poem says, as wheat on an eastern slope feels the dawn. A second poem asks what can hold God's mercy save His own infinitude. Seven vials hold His wrath, but His lovingkindness overflows all bounds. Rossetti's verse is spare, scriptural, and turned wholly to patience and desire. The volume gathers her sacred poems in their plainest dress.
77843-collected-poems-of-clarence-edwin-:
This second series of the Collected Poems of Clarence Flynn gathers the verse of an American poet whose work appeared in the magazines across the first decades of the century. The edition orders the poems by publication year, and within each year alphabetically, so that the reader watches the manner form.

The editors have standardized the titles and investigated spellings, with the help of modern tools. Where Flynn reused a title, the version is marked by its year. Two appendices, created for this collection, index the poems. Alternative text describes the illustrations. Flynn wrote in the genteel tradition that the little magazines were then displacing: lyrics of nature, faith, and season, worked to a polish. A collected edition of this kind is an act of rescue, assembling a magazine life between covers before the paper yellows away.
77859-the-starry-skies:
Agnes Giberne wrote these first lessons on the sun, moon and stars, copyrighted by the American Tract Society in 1894. An eclipse of the sun forms the frontispiece picture at the front. Chapter one starts with this earth of ours, and chapter two asks why men do not fall off it.

By day and by night, how the world spins and how it journeys fill early chapters. The moon by night, its changes and its face through a telescope come next in the contents. Storms on the sun, other worlds, eclipses and the planets from Mercury to Saturn give children a plain tour of the sky.
77870-talkies:
Eddie Cantor, star of Whoopee and author of Caught Short, wrote Talkies, a comic look at the new age of sound, with drawings by Holton. Silence has left the city, Cantor begins. In the old days a man wearied by street noise could slip into a telephone booth, drop a nickel, rest his ear on the receiver, and nap for half an hour. Now, after three minutes, they say your time is up.

The subway once served for sleep, and the movies were the last retreat of silence, where a man could flee a debating wife and twelve vocal children. Now even the screen shoots and shouts. A phonograph record hitched to a roll of film has wrecked the last temple of quiet, Cantor jokes, and made a new market for ear-muffs. Talk has become goods like salmon, he says, caught, canned, and sold.
77879-the-barge-of-haunted-lives:
The Barge of Haunted Lives, a novel by Aubrey Tyson, author of The Scarlet Tanager, was copyrighted by Macmillan in New York in 1923. Twelve chapters run from a salt marsh adventure through destiny's crossroads, the mystery of a derelict, and the shadow of nemesis, to the drained glass.

Chapter one keeps a hunter waiting. For more than two hours a thick set, sullen man crouches in a reed covered sneak boat by a muddy bank north of Great South Bay. A score of decoy ducks bob near him, unvisited by wildfowl. He has one eye, a greenish yellow left eye with an uncanny effect. For five years he has come down to Sellersville on the first day of November, known to Peters as Colonel Canbeck. There he hires a sloop with a motor and shoots alone for a week, seldom ten or twelve miles from the boathouse.
77881-old-mexico-and-her-lost-provinces:
Old Mexico and Her Lost Provinces is a travel book by William Henry Bishop. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1883. Bishop reached Mexico by way of Cuba. Part one climbs from Vera Cruz up the long mountain slope to the capital. Railways, money, shopping, and social life get their own chapters.

The Mexican chapters range widely. Bishop visits lakes Xochimilco and Chalco and old Texcoco. He climbs Popocatepetl and tours Puebla, Cholula, and Tlaxcala. Mines at Pachuca and a week at a country-house fill later chapters. Part two turns to the lost provinces, lands once Mexican. San Francisco, Monterey, and Los Angeles pass in review. The journey ends across Arizona, at Tombstone, Tucson, and San Xavier del Bac. Felix Parra's picture of Las Casas protecting the Aztecs fronts the book.
77896-masquerades:
Shane Leslie, author of The Oppidan and Doomsland, calls his studies in the morbid Masquerades, published by John Long in London in 1924. A publisher's list at the front prices the latest library novels, and a note states that all persons in the book are fictitious. A motto from the Apocrypha of Solomon declares that all is masquerade.

Leslie dedicates the work to the soul of Frederick Rolfe, Baron Corvo, placed in purgatory in the dedication line. A long prayer from Baudelaire's family prayers, asking pity for mad men and women, stands before the contents. The first study, The Pope's Temptation, begins the set, with Connemara and Inspiration after it.
77900-vile-bodies:
Vile Bodies is Evelyn Waugh's novel of the bright young things. It was first published in 1930. This text follows the reset edition of 1965. Waugh dedicated the book to Bryan Moyne and Diana Mosley. The first chapter crosses the Channel in rough weather. The ship carries a load of queasy passengers. Among them are Father Rothschild, a Jesuit, and Mrs Melrose Ape, an evangelist.

Mrs Ape travels with a troupe of angels. They bear names like Faith, Charity, and Chastity. Her hearty gospel of hope sets the tone for the parties ahead. Waugh strings together debutantes, gossip writers, and crumbling country houses. The scenes swing between farce and chill. The novel became the defining portrait of a generation dancing through the ruins of the old order. Its glitter has kept a hard edge ever since.
77923-very-good-jeeves:
P G Wodehouse wrote Very Good, Jeeves, issued by Doubleday, Doran and Company at Garden City, New York, in nineteen thirty. Parts hold copyrights of nineteen twenty six, twenty seven, twenty nine, and thirty. Eleven tales of Bertie Wooster and his man Jeeves fill the book. Bertie tells each tale in his own loose, bright voice. Jeeves solves each scrape with calm wit.

The first tale, Jeeves and the Impending Doom, opens on a grim morning for Bertie. He must visit his aunt Agatha at Woollam Chersey in Herts for three full weeks. His heart is heavy at the breakfast table, and he tells Jeeves he is far from his old merry self. Later tales treat a song, a dog named McIntosh, a spot of art, and an uncle in late bloom. Fans of light farce will find Wodehouse at his best pace here.
77946-snow-flakes:
Snow-Flakes, a chapter from the book of nature, was published by the American Tract Society at Boston, entered for copyright in 1863. A text from Job heads the title page: hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? Lines from Cowper urge the reader to acquaint himself with God through his works.

Contents promise snow structure, unity in diversity, perfection, and purity as the first four topics. The little book reads a snowflake as natural theology, moving from crystal form to moral lesson. Readers get a tract society meditation where winter weather becomes evidence of design, written for general and Sunday reading.
77958-turkey-and-the-armenian-atrocities:
Edwin Munsell Bliss, late of Constantinople, wrote a book dated 1896 on the wrongs of Armenians in Turkey. Help came from Cyrus Hamlin, founder of Robert College, from Grosvenor of Amherst, and from men who saw the kills. Frances Willard wrote the first words, with the Red Cross held up as aid to come.

Bliss paints Armenians as a brave, chaste, book dear folk who harm no one and seek to farm in peace. Their land near a famed mount held three million souls in old time, by his count. Pledges broke, then raids and kills came, from Tartar huts to the great city, in his charge.
77977-handbook-of-fictitious-names:
Book hunters and librarians still reach for a Victorian guide to false names on title pages, built around the life of the French scholar Joseph-Marie Quérard. Its author signs himself Olphar Hamst, a name that is itself a puzzle of the kind the book explains.

The volume first gives a life of Quérard, the worker called a martyr to bibliography, drawn from his own account and from notices by Gustave Brunet and others. Then comes the handbook proper, with notes and an index that doubles as a supplement, dropping in facts and good stories that missed the main text. Press notices from 1867 praised its store of facts about hidden authorship. The guide serves anyone who has held an old book signed by nobody and wondered who wrote it.
77989-the-gostak-and-the-doshes:
Miles Breuer, a doctor who wrote science tales, built this story on a famous puzzle of words. The Gostak and the Doshes runs on one made-up line: the gostak distims the doshes. Morey drew its plates, and the magazine note warns readers to come to it with a clear, rested mind.

You know nothing of gostaks, the tale says, yet grammar tells you much. The doshes are distimmed; one distimmer is a gostak. From such bare bones of speech Breuer spins a whole strange world. His frame tale talks of Einstein, weight, and the pull no one can name. Meaning itself is the hero here, and the tale is a small landmark of its kind.
78-tarzan-of-the-apes:
A lord's infant son grows up among apes after his parents die on an African shore. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Tarzan of the Apes traces the boy from a jungle cabin to lord of his tribe. Books left in the cabin teach him to read before he can speak with men.

Tarzan battles apes, lions, and a village of black warriors, then meets Jane Porter and her party. He learns his true name and rank, yet hesitates between two worlds. The novel's final choice leaves him apart from Jane. Burroughs launched a century of Tarzan tales with this book.
7802-seven-o-clock-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson's Seven O'Clock Stories, told first to Jean and Malcolm, offers twenty nights of bedtime tales. Early nights bring three happy children, their playmates, noisy folks, the toyman, a willow whistle, and Mr Scarecrow. Then comes the prettiest fairy story in the world.

Later nights add Mother Hen and Robber Hawk, Duckie the stepchild, and a tall enemy. A sleigh and tiny reindeer, Jack Frost and the Man in the Moon, a circus, a jolly clown, and lions of the north wind follow. Pictures show a fat old man on a hill with pipe and sack, ready for story time.
78035-the-old-lady-flies:
Raoul F Whitfield writes of a worn war-surplus Jenny and the circus flyer who loves her in a tale told by a fellow pilot. Russ Healy bought the plane right after the war at a government sale, unused. He has flown her ever since, through joy rides, smoke writing, stunts, and crop dusting in the South.

The Jenny shows oil stains, patched wing cloth of mixed hues, and struts bare of varnish, yet her wires stay true. An old Hall-Scott engine makes her slow and heavy on the controls next to new ships. Brooks' Flying Circus fields eight ships and five true pilots for town-to-town jumps. Tough luck and a word from Bob Brooks's wife set the plot in motion.
78047-the-dogaressas-of-venice-the-wives:
Edgcumbe Staley wrote on the dogaressas of Venice, the wives of the doges. Charles Scribner's Sons issued the book in New York, with plates throughout. Staley had written The Tragedies of the Medici before this work. A front plate shows Dogaressa Teodora Selvo dressed as Cleopatra.

Early chapters run from the flight to the lagoons to the first doge of Eraclea. Marriage rites, the Festa delle Marie, and the rape of the brides fill the lore. Later parts treat lace guilds, quakes, and dogal rights cut back. Readers gain a rich, gossipy chronicle of women beside Venetian power.
78048-sandhills-sketches:
Sandhills Sketches, by Williams Haynes, was copyrighted in 1916 at New York. Haynes also wrote Casco Bay Yarns, as the title page notes for readers. Photographs by the author and others illustrate the little book. A front plate shows the Lumbee river twisting through the sandhills country.

The book is just what its title implies, Haynes says in a front note. Its pages come from a notebook kept during a winter in the Piedmont country of North Carolina. The story of the Sandhills had not been told before, he holds, so the sketches earn their print. Most first ran in magazines such as Travel, Forecast, and Outing in their day. Dodging Winter opens the contents, and a Sandhills Christmas carol follows in the set.
78110-verses:
Violet Jacob, Mrs Arthur Jacob, wrote Verses, published by William Heinemann at London in 1905. She was the author of The Sheep-Stealers and The Interloper. Some poems here are reprinted from the Westminster Gazette, the English Illustrated Magazine, and Country Life. The contents open with Half-way, White Magic, and Serenade. The Shadow, The Mill-house, and The Two Queens follow. The Ballad of Hakon stands among the early poems.

Three poems for children and a Valley of the Kings come midway. The Lowland Ploughman and Late February turn toward Scotland. A group of India poems closes the main run: a mango grove, night in the plains, and evening in the opium fields. A Mahommedan graveyard and cherry-blossom at Dagshai stand among them. Jacob, a Scotswoman who had lived in India, writes both countries from inside.
7813-madame-de-mauves:
Henry James's Madame de Mauves opens on the terrace at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, where Paris lies spread in dusky vastness, domed and fortified, girdled by the silver Seine. Behind the viewer stands a stately park, then a forest of turfy avenues where one may forget the boulevards half an hour away.

One mid-spring afternoon a young man, fond of rural things yet drawn to the city's hive, watches Paris with wistful curiosity, feeling that to miss it is to miss a thrilling chapter. His winter there proved fruitless, yet the view still pulls him. The tale that follows tests honor, love, and restraint.
78196-a-dictionary-of-geographical-names:
A Dictionary of Geographical Names was compiled by Leo Markun. It appeared as Little Blue Book number 1259, edited by Haldeman-Julius. Girard, Kansas printed it under a copyright of 1927. Entries run in alphabetical order, each in a few plain lines. Aachen opens the book: the ancient Aquisgranum, once capital of Charlemagne. The Aar is a Swiss river, and Aargau a Swiss canton. Aberdeen is an old Scottish city, now a manufacturing centre. Aboukir village stands fifteen miles from Alexandria.

Abydos, Abyssinia, and Acadia follow in the same terse style. Africa gets a fuller note, with its area given. Ancient names sit beside modern states and battlefields of the Great War. The pocket dictionary aimed at quick answers for common readers: what a place is, where it stands, and why it matters.
78202-the-changing-of-historic-place-nam:
George P Donehoo, secretary of the Pennsylvania Historical Commission, wrote The Changing of Historic Place Names, published at Altoona, Pennsylvania, by the Tribune Press in nineteen twenty one. Henry W Shoemaker suggested the monograph and paid for its publication, Donehoo notes. An introduction and glossary of historic names changed or misspelled in Pennsylvania come from Shoemaker. The pamphlet is brief by design.

Enough is written to call attention to the evil of changing place names, Donehoo says. A partial list of historic place names changed or misspelled in Pennsylvania follows the essay. The Spirit of the Name Vandal and Changing the Face of History get short sections. Exit Muckelrat and Enter Woodland Hills mocks a real swap. Pennsylvania readers get a preservation plea for old names, Indian, pioneer, and homely alike.
78224-the-dreams-of-chang-and-other-stor:
The Dreams of Chang and Other Stories holds short tales by Ivan Bunin. Bernard Guilbert Guerney turned the Russian text into English. The book came out in New York in 1923.

The title tale leads a set of sixteen stories in all. Names such as Brethren, Gautami and The Grammar of Love hint at the range. The Gentleman from San Francisco, Bunin's best known tale, closes the book. Settings run from Russia to the East and the sea. The prose is spare and keen, and each tale turns on a sharp moment in a life. Bunin writes of love, death and fate with a cool, clear eye.
78253-an-idyl-of-the-wabash-and-other-st:
Anna Nicholas's An Idyl of the Wabash and Other Stories, published by Hurst in New York under copyrights of 1898 and 1912. It opens with a motto from Riley: the tales are made of stuff smart folks think too common to use. Eleven stories fill the contents, from the title idyl to At a Way-Station, A Farmhouse Drama, An Occult Experience, and The Quickening of a Soul. The book is given to the author's mother.

The title story brings Miss Callista Rogers from her Vermont home to Honeyport, a small Indiana town on the Wabash. She feels something like the peril of the pioneer women, though she allows there are no Indians and no scalps to fear. Her letters home call the people queer but friendly. Her fixed New England faith, that only New England ways count, sets up the comedy of her settling in.
78256-a-brief-outline-of-the-history-of-:
A Brief Outline of the History of Libraries is an old tract by Justus Lipsius. John Cotton Dana turned it to English from the print of sixteen oh seven. That Antwerp print was the last from the hand of the man himself. A Chicago house brought out the English form in nineteen oh seven. Only two hundred fifty prints of the form were made at Boston that spring.

A front note says the life men of Lipsius pass this work by too fast. His church, past, and book works draw their gaze in its place. Bayle great word book gives the strange faith shifts of his life in brief. Those shifts shocked minds of his own age and the next as well. The tract gives book house lore a first short map in print.
78268-dancing-beauty-and-games:
Lady Constance Stewart Richardson wrote Dancing, Beauty, and Games, put out by Humphreys at London in 1913. Photos show the author, Isadora Duncan, Adeline Genee, and Karsavina at their art. The book opens with physical culture, which she will not split from mind and morals. A tree, she says, can no more live shorn of bark and leaves than a body can thrive alone. Most folk, she holds, miss that plain truth.

Parts follow on games, beauty, teachers, and dancing in turn. Swimming and big game shooting get parts of their own, and faith closes the book. Plates show barefoot dancing in the Greek style and fine diving forms. Richardson writes for women who sought health, grace, and sport in a new age. The book mixes how-to counsel with bold views on the trained body.
78278-the-authorized-life-of-marie-c-sto:
The Authorized Life of Marie Stopes is a life book by Aylmer Maude. A Williams and Norgate house of London brought it out in nineteen twenty four. Maude wrote the Life of Tolstoy in a past work of like kind. A front cut shows Stopes as crowds saw her on the talk boards. Part one, The Theme, heads the scheme of nine parts at front.

Child days peeks, the school girl, school life, and world roam fill ranks. Match, wed love and its growth, and foes fill mid part scheme. In life and three back lists close the scheme of the book. One list names all her books and tracts in that back scheme. One names her lore tracts and new finds in plant past lore there.
78333-the-geographical-lore-of-the-time-:
Geographical Lore of the Time of the Crusades is a study by John Kirtland Wright, issued in 1925. Wright was librarian of the American Geographical Society, which published the work. It stands as number fifteen in the society research series of monographs. Contents open with the time of the Crusades and the scope of the term lore.

Origins of that lore and the plan of the present work fill the introduction. Part one treats origins, sources, and place in the classification of knowledge. Maps, marvels, scripture, and old science braid in medieval ideas of the earth. Historians of geography gain a deep guide to what crusading Europe thought the world was.
7838-fifty-one-tales:
Lord Dunsany's Fifty-One Tales, published in 1915, gathers brief fantasies. They run from The Assignation and Charon through The Death of Pan, The Sphinx at Giza, and The Hen, to Wind and Fog and The Raft-Builders. Death meets Odysseus and an orange, a flower prays, and time trades with a tradesman.

Later tales bring a giant poppy, a man with golden earrings, and King Karna-Vootra's dream. A mistaken identity and the true history of the hare and tortoise follow. Short, polished, and strange, the book shows Dunsany's gift for turning myth, jest, and melancholy into tales a few pages long.
78403-brazilian-short-stories:
Monteiro Lobato wrote short tales of Brazil, here in a small cheap form. The Haldeman-Julius Company issued the book at Girard, Kansas, in 1925. It stands as Little Blue Book Number 733, with a front note by Isaac Goldberg. Three tales fill the set: Modern Torture, The Penitent Wag, The Plantation Buyer.

Modern Torture calls the postman's job the heir of rack and wheel. A set wage and pension lure the victim into years of slow pain, Lobato jokes. Old tortures killed fast; this one stretches the agony, he writes. Readers gain sharp, wry tales of Brazilian life from a famed pen.
78420-bush-studies:
Barbara Baynton writes of the Australian bush in Bush Studies, printed in London in 1902. She gives the book to Helen McMillen of Sydney, New South Wales. Six tales fill the book, and two short notes gloss hard bush words for town readers.

Scrammy marks a hand or foot ill formed, one note says. Skywonkie marks a weather prophet. The tales are A Dreamer, Squeaker's Mate, Scrammy 'And, and Billy Skywonkie. Bush Church and The Chosen Vessel close the set. A Dreamer opens at a small station in wet night. A lone woman lands, finds no buggy sent for her, and faces a dark street and a stray dog.
78464-picture-frames:
Picture Frames, by Thyra Samter Winslow, came out at New York in 1923 and ran through five printings that year. Eleven tales make up the book, each a frame round a life. The first, Little Emma, opens in Black Plains, Iowa, and moves to Chicago.

Emma Hooper comes to the great city to carve out her luck, and her family is glad to see her go. She lacks money and kin pull, and never fixed her spelling at the town trade school. Cash comes to her in a sudden way. More tales treat a grandma, Mamie Carpenter, and a cycle of Manhattan. Late tales treat city folk, an Indian summer, and the end of Anna. Readers get sharp, sad tales of small lives in a big town.
78530-i-buy-me-couple-horses:
Tuttle's I Buy Me Couple Horses is a tale of horse trading told in a drawl. It opens with the sentence that started all the trouble: all the narrator said was, I'm movin' out where I can have couple horses. Before the moving vans had his plunder through the gate, the horses began to come.

Trailers of horses arrive, peddled by cowboys on commission. One, worth twelve hundred, five gaited and kind, proves the wrong kind: he eats the narrator's shirt, a twelve-dollar shirt. A polo pony whirls till his hat sits backwards; another, taken because he does not bite, has no teeth left. At dusk Johnny brings the Horse, five hundred bucks, shadeable to four hundred. By morning the stable and corral are a wreck, and the beast, a cross of battering ram, tiger, and rattlesnake, is hog-tied to an old oak.
78538-the-trey-of-spades:
The Trey of Spades is a western tale by the writer Tuttle. Tuttle had written The Dead-Line and Just for a Laugh before it. The tale opens in the saddle with two riders in high country. Hashknife Hartley looks down on the Thunder range and dreams aloud. Here, he tells Sleepy Stevens, is the range of their dreams at last.

No fences and few ranches mark that wide, rolling cattle land. The Bitter River cuts its green thread near the heart of it. Cottonwoods and live oaks dot the hills of that fine spread. Hashknife is tall and lean, Sleepy short, stout, and weather lined. Both wear well-worn cowboy dress and ride tired horses that day. A match with no head starts their talk on that high ridge.
78617-dangerous-trades:
Thomas Oliver, a doctor and professor of physiology at Durham, edited this set of expert studies, printed by John Murray of London in 1902. Oliver served the Home Office on its white lead, dangerous trades, pottery, and lucifer match committees. He gives the book to Asquith and Ridley, home secretaries who gave him his chances to learn the field at first hand.

A M Anderson, the principal lady inspector of factories, traces the growth of law for harmful industries in England. Other chapters weigh the rules of the chief European lands. Infant mortality and factory labour, child labour by Margaret McMillan, home work, and the physiology of fatigue follow. The book maps how work ruins health, and what law can do.
78624-life-tangles:
Agnes Giberne wrote a tale in journal form for Shaw of London, the diary of a girl named Rhoda Frith. The first entry is dated December 12. Rhoda counts the days to a great event. Her mother is coming home from India with the little twins, after nearly seven years away.

Rhoda can paint her mother's face from memory, young and pretty with its soft color and gentle smile. Her father's face is less clear, for he was much away from the children. Grief stands inside the joy. A sister, Connie, died while the parents were gone, and her father must still stay in India. Rhoda also dreads that her sisters Clarissa and Juliet will stay on in the house. The chapters ahead bear names of banishment, choice, and tangle. The journal tells a young life of duty, loss, and slow growth.
7865-jackanapes-daddy-darwin-s-dovecot-a:
Juliana Horatio Ewing's Jackanapes, Daddy Darwin's Dovecot, and Other Stories, pictured by Randolph Caldecott, opens with Byron on battle's stern array, where rider and horse lie in one red burial. The title tale follows a gallant boy soldier, Jackanapes, from village green to battlefield, loved for pluck and heart.

Two donkeys and geese, a dovecot, and other short tales follow, in Ewing's warm, moral style for young readers. Through humor, pathos, and country life, the collection praises courage, kindness, and duty, and remains a classic of Victorian children's writing, tender without preaching, and still readable today.
78713-the-loom-of-lies:
The Loom of Lies is a western tale by W C Tuttle, who also wrote Blind Trails. Tuttle sets it in the valley of the Bunch Grass in a dry August year. No rain has come since the winter snows melted.

Poplars and cottonwoods by the Lost Horse River have turned yellow early, and willow leaves crackle under thirsty stock. The river is a shallow, foul stream, and the hills are as brown as burlap. At the north end stands the JHF ranch of John H Fann, called John the Baptist for his huge size and great white beard. John sits on the ranch steps with his hands hid in his beard. Range readers get drought, cattle, and lies spun tight in Tuttle plain style.
78715-sticky-ropes:
W C Tuttle wrote Sticky Ropes, a western by the author of The Ranch of the Tombstones and Tramps of the Range. The story opens on Dusty Corbett waking in pain in the middle of a corral, staring at the forefeet of a shaggy-legged bronco.

A lanky cowboy on the top pole tells him he has been drunker than seven hundred snakes. Dusty, still in his twenties but looking forty, with a nose deformed from many smashes, scratches his dust-coloured hair and asks what is going on. Readers get a hard-used cowhand sobering up into trouble, in Tuttle's rough and comic western voice.
78728-brasses:
A short handbook on monumental brasses by J S M Ward. Cambridge University Press published it in 1912. It belongs to the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature. Fifteen chapters divide the subject by period and type. Edward the First and Second open the story. The last brasses, dated to 1773, close the medieval tale.

England, Ward begins, holds more brasses than all Europe together. English examples also differ curiously from foreign ones. Chapters treat clergy, monasteries, and special types in turn. Architectural details and foreign brasses get their own sections. Twenty-five plates show knights, ladies, and families in engraved brass. Such memorials covered church floors across England. Ward teaches readers to date them by armour, dress, and lettering.
78740-sir-piegan-passes:
W C Tuttle wrote the western tale Sir Piegan Passes. Solomon Kane stands at its center, rich and sly. His heart would make fine arrowheads, Tuttle opens. His conscience would cut into corkscrews, he adds. Outside of that, Solomon Kane was normal. Kane had plenty of money in hand.

Earning by sweat never moistened Kane's brow, though. He came to Micaville with ten dollars in cash. An assaying outfit was his other capital there. A big strike had just been made then. Prospectors swarmed thicker than fleas, Tuttle says. An assayer was sorely needed in that camp. Kane read each sample's true gold in his crucible. He then cut the count to a bare trace. Fooled men sold out and moved on fast. Kane picked their claims up cheap behind them. A crooked assayer's comeuppance drives Tuttle's dry, hard western humor.
78742-four-gates:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote Four Gates for Pickering and Inglis, in the Golden Crown Library of stories by authors of high repute. The subtitle promises the different outlook on life of four young women. The motto counts the gates of the city in Revelation, three on every side.

An illustration shows Doctor Verner turning furiously to Audrey. I decline the honour, he says. That is my reply to that astonishing letter. Le Feuvre wrote Probable Sons and a shelf of evangelical tales for girls. Her heroines face the world in four directions, and the novel compares what each makes of it. Religious publishers like Pickering and Inglis ran a parallel literature to the secular shelves. It sold in Sunday schools and prize givings, and its best writers, Le Feuvre among them, could tell a story straight.
78750-famous-mystery-stories:
McSpadden edited this anthology for Crowell at New York in 1922, in the Mystery Library that also offered famous ghost, psychic, and detective stories. Ten tales make the volume. Barham's Spectre of Tappington, from the Ingoldsby Legends, opens it in comedy: Lieutenant Seaforth cannot find his pantaloons, and his man Barney swears he went to bed in them. Erckmann-Chatrian's Mysterious Sketch and Hoffmann's Deserted House follow.

Washington Irving's Adelantado of the Seven Cities represents America. Crawford's Upper Berth is the sea's contribution, a berth no passenger keeps for long. The Diamond Lens, by O'Brien, turns a microscope into an instrument of obsession. Maupassant's Horla and Gautier's Mummy's Foot bring the French fantastic, and Anna Katharine Green's Thief closes the book with detection. Each tale, the editor promises, comes from a powerful writer, and the set is a small canon of the weird as 1922 understood it.
78790-the-voices:
Edward Wellen wrote The Voices, a tale with art by Joseph Eberle. Nicholas Kane was sitting at his desk when he heard the voices, the tale opens. He heard them only once, but that once was once too often for Kane. A chain of small accidents in his body sets the trap, the early pages show.

At fifteen Kane drove a pencil point into his left palm over homework. He did not pry out the point and the flesh healed over it. A faint gray speck stayed visible under the scar. Body currents washed the speck along at one billionth of an inch per second, the tale reckons. At eighteen he lost a tooth on the football field and got a metal screw tooth. Twenty three fillings, steel rimmed glasses, and chemical work followed by age twenty four. Metal in the body becomes the path for the voices.
78809-more-secret-remedies:
More Secret Remedies: What They Cost and What They Contain was issued in London in 1912 by the British Medical Association, from 429, Strand. It is the second series of tests on secret cures, made for the association. The preface says the first book opened the eyes of the public and the law to the trade in such goods.

Chapters sort the cures by their claims: rheumatism and gout, skin ills, nerve tonics and elixirs of life, coughs and consumption, kidney medicines, and fat cures. Soothing syrups for infants, epilepsy medicines, and hair preparations each get a chapter. The book ends on the men behind the trade: the unqualified seller by post, and the advertising that moves the goods.
78849-a-calendar-of-dinners-with-615-rec:
A Calendar of Dinners is a cook book by Marion Harris Neil, out in nineteen twenty-two. It bears the name of a great food firm of the north land, and its price was a few coins. The front list counts six hundred and fifteen ways to cook in the book. A tale of the firms fat brand takes a long part at the front.

Parts give hints to young cooks, the pick of foods, ways of cook, time charts, and the art of the carve. Ways then run by kind, from soups and fish to breads, cakes, and sweets. A day book of meals for the year takes the last great part of the book. A full guide lists each dish by its first mark.
78874-miss-polly-wiggles:
Miss Polly Wiggles is a children's novel by Edna Clark Davis, printed at Boston in 1925. Julia Greene drew the illustrations. Davis dedicates the book to her niece Elizabeth, the original Polly Wiggles of the story. The first chapter is set at The Lilacs, the country home of Grandmother and Grandfather Carr.

Every summer the Eatons come there, and Aunt Elsie, Elizabeth's young-lady aunt, makes part of the household. The chapters run through a dolls' bathing-picnic, games, and Cubby's adventure. Limericks, tea at Miss Helen's, and a storm follow. Grandmother's story-quilt and Grandpa's story fill two chapters. The enchanted palace wakes, Gabriel has a surprise, and the children hail the king and queen of the May. The May frolic closes the book. The frontispiece shows Marion crying that hers is ahead. Davis writes a summer of adventures for a little girl.
78936-the-eighteen-nineties:
The Eighteen Nineties is Holbrook Jackson's survey of the literature and art of the eighteen nineties, the decade of Beardsley, Wilde and the Yellow Book. In 1895 Max Beerbohm declared, with whimsical irony, that he belonged to the Beardsley period.

The remark gives Jackson his frame: a short, intense period style, already passing at its height, by which a whole generation of writers and artists can be named. The book treats the nineties as a state of mind: aesthetic, decadent, and conscious of its own brevity. Its sympathy is with the period's makers, and its method is the portrait and the anecdote rather than the bibliography.
7894-the-fallen-leaves:
Wilkie Collins's The Fallen Leaves, dated Gloucester Place, July 1, 1879, opens with the author refusing prefatory pleading. Readers who followed its serial run at home and abroad, he says, already grasp its design and its delicate treatment. He leaves the book to speak on its own merits.

A prologue traces remote causes shaping a young man's life. A stranger household's misfortune, falling while he still wore his first jacket, steers his happiness years later. Through love, shame, and social judgment, Collins follows fallen leaves of society with sympathy and firm moral sight.
78942-the-espadrilles:
Espadrilles is a science fiction story by Margaret Clair, set in Marsport on Mars. A bar blurb at its head sets the tone of hard luck among the stars. Barkeepers, it says, have heard hard luck tales for centuries, and will for centuries more. When a man hard luck spans the starry galaxy, the trouble can be really bad in that bar.

The tale is told in the first person by a man carrying quite a lot of money in Marsport. A stranger in rope soled espadrilles sits down beside him on the bar bench in the first lines. He is gaunt, hollow eyed, and unshaven, burned almost black by the rays of space on his skin. Clair wrote wry, sharp tales for the science fiction magazines of the postwar years, and this bar room encounter in space is in her driest manner.
7900-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques, and Discoveries of the English Nation, in this second hosted copy, again keeps sixteenth-century spelling while expanding old shortenings. A transcriber's note explains macrons, Latin endings, and the old y-for-th spellings, so modern eyes can follow the text.

Footnotes use nineteenth-century spelling, Hakluyt's own sidenotes stay marked, and marginal notes sit at their points except in verse. Sailors, merchants, and explorers crowd its pages, making this a core source for England's first age of ocean travel and trade, in a faithful, readable reprint.
79068-katy-hunter-s-homes:
Livingston wrote Katy Hunter's Homes, a children's story published at Boston in 1876. The first chapter, Alone in the World, opens in a dismal old house in a narrow city alley, its windows broken and stuffed with old clothes against the cold. In one gloomy room a girl of about seven sits on a straw bed, crying for her mother.

Katy's mother died two days before and has just been carried to the grave, leaving the child unnoticed. The tale then looks back: Katy's father, a small ship owner, went down with his vessel in a storm when she was four. Her mother sewed, sold the village cottage, and came to the city chasing high wages that never appeared. Chapter titles promise friends, a new home, gleams of sunshine, and Christmas presents. Readers get a tender tale of an orphan passed from home to home.
79076-how-to-keep-bees:
How to Keep Bees is a handbook for beginners by Anna Botsford Comstock, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1905. Comstock writes for the use of people starting an apiary, and the book is illustrated with plates of hives, smokers, brushes, and bee tools.

Chapters explain why to keep bees, how to begin, and where to place the apiary. Others describe the inhabitants and industries of the hive, swarming, and how to keep from keeping too many bees. Feeding, wintering, rearing and introducing queens, robbing, and the enemies and diseases of bees all get chapters. A closing study of the anatomy of the honey-bee and the interrelation of bees and plants gives the practical advice a natural history frame.
79102-emil-and-the-detectives:
Erich Kästner wrote this story for children, translated by May Massee and published by Doubleday in 1930. Walter Trier drew the pictures for Emil's adventure in the English edition. A first chapter explains that the story does not begin yet, in the contents list.

Emil helps to shampoo, then the trip to Berlin can start in the early chapters. A dream with much running, a wrong station and street car line 177 follow in turn. Emil's money is stolen on the train, and a crew of boy detectives in Berlin helps him track the thief through the great city.
79107-a-treatise-of-civil-power-in-eccle:
John Milton wrote A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes, first printed in 1659 and reprinted at London in 1790. Its full title states the claim: it is not lawful for any power on Earth to compel in matters of religion. The new edition is inscribed to Richard Price as a defender of civil and religious rights.

Milton addresses the Parliament of the Commonwealth of England. He argues from scripture and Protestant maxims that rulers hold civil power just, while faith stays free. He bids men in power for a time to guard the consciences of others as they would their own under a turn of fortune. Brief, firm, and scriptural, the treatise is a root text of the case for liberty of conscience.
79110-wild-medicinal-plants-of-the-unite:
A government bulletin fills this item: Wild Medicinal Plants of the United States, issued at Washington on January 16, 1906. It is bulletin number eighty-nine of the Bureau of Plant Industry in the Department of Agriculture. Its author is Alice Henkel, an assistant in the bureau's drug-plant investigations. A roster of the bureau's offices fills the front pages.

A letter of transmittal, dated October 30, 1905, sends the manuscript to press. In it the bureau's chief reports the paper's title and author, and recommends it for publication in the bulletin series. The drug-plant office behind it, the roster shows, stood beside work on tea culture and poisonous plants, under its own chief, with a small staff of experts and assistants.
79118-on-england-and-other-addresses:
Stanley Baldwin, prime minister of Great Britain, gave the addresses gathered in On England, first printed at London in April 1926. Five impressions ran within the year. A short chronology traces Baldwin's rise from member for Bewdley in 1908.

The speeches sort into groups: on England and the West, on peace in industry, on political life, and on literature and the arts. Shakespeare, Byron, and Hudson get addresses of their own. Others treat Bonar Law, Lord Curzon, and Lord Oxford. Empire Day messages and talks on Scotland, Ireland, and Wales close the set. The England address was given at the Royal Society of St George dinner in May 1924.
79122-the-mouse-miller-and-other-stories:
The Mouse Miller and Other Stories is a set of fairy tales by Cooke Don-Carlos. Don-Carlos also wrote Virginia's Inheritance. The book came out at Boston in 1917.

Nine tales fill the table of contents, each with a touch of magic. The Baker of Coblentz opens the set on Christmas Eve. Baker Gottlieb looks out on his snowy street as the sun sets. Other tales tell of a daughter of the stars and a broom master. Rose-Marie meets a witch, and little Hans meets the kobolds. The title tale of the mouse miller sits near the end. Each tale is short enough for one sitting with a child.
79239-mixed-pickles:
Mixed Pickles is a tale for girls and boys by Mrs Field with a long scheme. Thirty one cuts by Pym line the book from a New York Burt house. Bryda, a lone girl in her grand dam old plot, opens the tale. She loves to roam off and talk to birds, blooms, and brooks at will. But no mate to play with is a sad sort of lone, the tale notes.

She wishes for a kit if naught more at the sun dial stone. Parts run through a prince in guise, a tale by Uncle Jack, and Beppo woes. Beppo, a lad of the tale, fills scrape on scrape through the mid parts. Moll, a poor soul of the place, finds a use in a late part. Thief breaks and a call to rise close the scheme of parts.
79240-stray-leaves:
Alexander MacDonald wrote Stray Leaves, or Traces of Travel. The Christian Press Association issued it at New York. MacDonald was Bishop of Victoria in British Columbia. The book sold for the Propagation of the Faith. One dollar was its stated price. The copyright dates to 1914.

A pilgrim's diary leads the contents. Misty Atlantic and London open that road. Paray le Monial and Swiss towns follow. Milan, Venice, Rome, and Florence fill the road. Lourdes closes the pilgrim's path in France. Jottings of a trip in Scotland join the set. Rome at Christmas gets its own piece. New York to Naples and Naples to Cairo extend it. A poem, The Sound of Another Sea, fronts the prose. A Canadian bishop's travel pages mix devotion with the plain joy of roads and shrines.
79248-a-scarlet-poppy-and-other-stories:
Harriet Prescott Spofford gathers seven short tales in a Harper volume dated 1894, issued in the Harper American Story-Tellers line. The contents list A Scarlet Poppy, Best-Laid Schemes, An Ideal, and a tale of a hidden skeleton in a family home. Later pieces cover Binns, a composite wife, and a daughter-in-law, each with its own cast and setting.

The title tale opens at a breakfast table, where Mark Dunmore scolds his wife Helena for buying a scarlet paper poppy. She paid twenty-five cents for the lamp shade ornament, and he calls the small cost a path to ruin. Their sharp back and forth sets a tense, witty tone for the stories that follow.
79263-our-insect-enemies:
Our Insect Enemies, by Vance Randolph, is Little Blue Book number 860 from Girard, Kansas. Haldeman-Julius edited the series and published this number in 1925. Drawings by Peter Quinn illustrate the cheap pocket volume for its readers. Houseflies and their kindred open the contents at page four of the book.

Mosquitoes and disease follow at page twenty eight in the contents list. Life among the bedbugs, then lice and their kin, fill the middle pages. Our friend the cockroach gets a wry chapter of his own in the set. Chiggers, ticks, and fleas close the parade of pests in the volume. The common housefly lives wherever man has settled, Randolph writes, and thrives nowhere else.
7927-the-celibates:
Honore de Balzac's The Celibates, the longest single-titled section of the Comedie Humaine after Lost Illusions, joins three tales whose only firm bond is bachelors and old maids as heroes. Its introduction admits the union is weak, and judges Pierrette, the opening tale, below its companions.

Written for the young Countess Anna de Hanska, Pierrette carries a studied, artificial air, the introduction says, unlike the freer later tales. Linked loosely to the Arcis series with The Tenebreuse Affaire, the volume shows Balzac turning single lives into a panorama of French society.
79297-the-telling-of-the-bees:
The Telling of the Bees, a story by Helen Hull, was printed in Liberty magazine on January 4, 1941. It is billed as a haunting tale of human hearts and the tragic trail of a woman's outlawed love. Marcia wakes in a rough cabin divided by an unpainted wooden partition. She thinks the week long spring rain still beats on the roof, but sunlight fills the room.

A gay north wind shakes the new green of larches and birches and strips petals from the apple trees. Marcia lights the stove, draws well water, and eats her breakfast standing in the doorway. She remembers last spring and calls it back on purpose, drinking it like wine. Hull sets a mood of spring beauty over a story of longing and loss. The title points to the old custom of telling bees of a death in the household.
79304-what-to-do-in-cases-of-accidents-a:
Joseph Lawrence, a medical and surgical nurse, issued his first aid guide at New York in 1888 with Vail and Company. The preface states the aim in plain terms for lay readers. People should learn what to do at once when help is far off, in language any person can grasp and use.

Contents run from apoplexy, broken bones, burns, and choking to drowning, fits, frost bite, and sunstroke in turn. Long sections cover poisons, their signs, and their antidotes, plus wounds, sprains, and snake bites. Closing pages urge calm and show how to avoid accidents at home and on the water. Families get a shelf ready manual for the minutes before a doctor can arrive.
79327-french-fairy-tales:
French Fairy Tales, translated by M Cary and pictured by E Boyd Smith, was published by Thomas Y Crowell Company of New York, under copyrights of 1887 and 1903. An introductory note speaks first to the elders of the house. Popular tales, it says, have left the nursery for the parlour and the study. Students in the line of the brothers Grimm have made a science of them.

The note states the sources of the tales and vouches for the truth of the rendering. The stories come from the French provinces, and in one or two cases from the colonies. The first part was chosen from a French folk lore journal of high standing. The tales promise the usual rewards: kindness repaid, pride humbled, and the youngest child coming into a magic prize.
79339-the-spectacles:
The Spectacles is a tiny tale by Frank Belknap Long. A house note jokes that Long wrote it with no help from prophetic glasses, though the editors doubt him. They say they once saw him hide a pair of glasses that glowed with magic.

A blurb sets the scene in a chill, sunless future where man is a relic under glass, and a museum must have its guards. A small boy named Willie slips into a hall on a crisp autumn day, though the place is barred to him. He climbs into a huge case and comes out with spectacles from a pale, dried brow. Gulls wheel over a bay past the window. Readers get a short, sly tale of sight, time, and a boy theft of wonder.
79384-recluses:
Raymond S. Spears wrote this tale of a dog, as its first leaf states. The dog is of a kind bound by long years of habit and drill in the ways of man. Yet she thrills to the call of the wild, which no drill can still. A cut at the front shows a man named Danvers as he smashes the big hand of a man who breaks in. The tale opens with the breed of the dog.

A vast count of breeds was used to breed the ugliness out of the wolves of the Black Forest, to make them tame guards of sheep. That work could not fail to rub out some of the wolf in them as well. Their shape, looks, and frame stayed the same, but their minds grew soft and kind. At the end of that line stands Queen.
79402-preludes:
Preludes is a book of verse by Thompson, put out at London in eighteen seventy five with all rights held. Its plates and trim are the work of Elizabeth Thompson. The book is sworn to the sire and the dame of the hand. A French line from a great bard stands at the head of the first piece. That line says that men know the sea, but the soul is yet to sound.

The list of parts is a full year's round of the heart. In the first spring, parted, to a poet, and songs of spring to the warm time lead in. To the loved one, a deep thought piece, and to the loved dead come next.
79460-plays-and-controversies:
Plays and Controversies is a volume of prose by Yeats, the Irish poet, published in New York by Macmillan in 1924 in a new and revised edition. A portrait of the young Yeats, from a charcoal drawing by John Singer Sargent, faces the title page. The book is dated from Dublin in February 1923.

The contents are led by a long essay on the Irish dramatic movement, running to more than two hundred pages. The Countess Cathleen follows, with a note on the play. The controversies of the title are the fights of the Abbey Theatre's birth. They were fought over plays accused of insulting Ireland, over the language of the stage, and over what a national theatre should be. Yeats wrote these pieces across the years of the fight. The volume is both memoir and manifesto of the movement that remade Irish drama.
7949-the-historical-nights-entertainment:
Rafael Sabatini collected this second volume of historical tales from The Premier Magazine, dedicating it in London in June 1919 to its editor, David Whitelaw. Each story takes one dramatic night or episode from history: the absolution of Afonso Henriques, first king of Portugal; the False Demetrius. Pretended son of Ivan the Terrible; and an episode of the Inquisition in Seville called The Hermosa Fembra. Further tales follow the same pattern.

Sabatini's gift is to find the human turning point inside a famous event and tell it as a short, tense story. The volume reads quickly, story by story, and needs no knowledge of the first series. For readers who like history with a plot, it is an entertaining way to meet figures and crises that textbooks usually flatten.
79502-old-new-england-houses:
Albert G Robinson wrote Old New England Houses, issued in New York in September 1920. Robinson also wrote Old New England Doorways. The book draws on his unique collection of photographs, with the Old Manse at Concord as frontispiece. Plates list houses town by town across New England, with dates where known.

Massachusetts houses include the Fairbanks House at Dedham from 1636 and the Abbott House at Andover from 1685. The Lexington house where Samuel Adams and John Hancock slept when Paul Revere roused them appears. Orchard House, home of the Alcotts at Concord, is also pictured. Later plates reach Maine, New Hampshire, and Connecticut, including the Judge Oliver Ellsworth House at Windsor.
79538-traditions-and-stories-of-scottish:
A H Millar gathered traditions and stories of Scottish castles in a book printed in 1927, with many photographs. Crookston and Cathcart castles open the set. Lochleven and Burleigh follow, then Dumbarton and Neidpath. Dunnottar, Castle Campbell, and Rothsay each get a chapter.

Later chapters treat Threave, Dunoon, Erchless, and Duart. Tantallon, Hermitage, Stirling, and St Andrews appear in turn. Dunbar, Inveraray, Fowlis, Mains, and Bothwell close the list. Millar opens by noting the Celtic fondness for local tales. Every ruined keep, he says, holds some marvellous tale handed down with faith. The book pairs place history with legend.
7955-historical-miniatures:
August Strindberg's Historical Miniatures, translated by Claud Field, offers short visions from the whole sweep of human history. Julian the Apostate and Peter the Hermit appear alongside Attila and Luther, Alcibiades and Eginhard. While the scenes range from the empires of the Pharaohs and the Czars to the Athens of Socrates and a Merry England. Critic Maximilian Harden praised it in 1907 as a book the public should read.

Strindberg writes as philosopher and poet rather than historian, letting each episode stand as a vivid scene. The miniatures are brief, so the book can be read in sittings, each one a different age. It suits readers who want history as imagination: famous lives and turning points, lit up by one of Scandinavia's most restless minds.
79569-ashes:
T T Flynn wrote Ashes, a story of how a man's soul was tested in a railroad yard pit. The shops of the D and R system sprawl in soot-coated buildings, steel rails, travelling cranes, and belching smokestacks. Over all lies dirt and grease and noise.

On the fringe of the plant is the ash pit, deep still waters capped with tongues of vapour under slatwork covers. The pit was covered after men blundered into it at night and vanished, hauled out days later by Juan Mendoza and his clamshell bucket. High over the pit Juan sits in a travelling cage from midnight to eight. Readers get pulp fiction set in the grime of a locomotive works.
79573-snow-berries:
Snow-Berries, a book for young folks by Alice Cary, gathers poems and stories for children. Ticknor and Fields published it in Boston in 1867, with pictures throughout.

A prelude in verse warns the small reader at once: there is not a single fairy tale in the book. Cary calls her muse plain and homespun, given to workaday ways, strongest on her native soil. She sings little of elves and queens and more of meadows, rivulets, and hedgerows. The prelude tells of a hunt for late flowers across stubble land and lowland moss to Callamus Pond. After three weary hours the children find the white snow-berries shining in a thicket. The book keeps that same love of the near and common things of country life.
79600-undream-d-of-shores:
Frank Harris wrote Undream'd of Shores, a set of tales. Brentano's issued it at New York in 1924. Two printings ran by July of that year. Harris had written Oscar Wilde's life in two volumes. The Man Shakespeare and The Bomb bear his name. Thirteen pieces fill the contents.

A Mad Love opens the set at page three. Akbar, called the Mightiest, follows it. A Fit of Madness and A Chinese Story come next. Saint Peter's Difficulty stands at page 141. Love Is My Sin and As Others See Us follow. In Central Africa takes the reader far afield. The Extra Eight Days and The Great Game build the end. A temple to forgotten dead stands near the close. My Last Word ends the book. Vienna in the early 1890s sets the first tale, where a student narrator falls into the city's gay contrasts.
79699-the-fortune-hunters-and-other-stor:
Violet Jacob gathered thirteen tales in a book printed at London in 1910. A note tells where each tale first appeared. Three come from the Pall Mall Magazine, two from The Woman at Home. Others come from The Acorn, a Newcastle paper, and the Cornhill Magazine. Four had never been printed before.

The first tale lends the book its name. Its heads range from Léonie and a black man's hand to the Wythan tree and the lights of Jerusalem. One tale treats a windmill, one a picture gallery, and one the claims of friendship. The first tale opens in Venice, where Mrs Wylde walks in May heat with a book under her arm.
79701-too-many-heroes:
Too Many Heroes is a western tale by Ray Humphreys. The scene at the start is the office of Sheriff Joe Cook of Monte Vista. The sheriff is in a foul mood and calls out his deputy, Shorty McKay, for being gone all morning. A bold robbery the day before has set the town on edge. A lone masked bandit had robbed the Second National Bank and got away with three thousand dollars in cash.

Shorty gives a soft answer: he has been in the public library. The sheriff sneers at the thought of a book as a help in the hunt for a bank robber. Shorty is a deputy who, as the sheriff puts it, is of little help in a hard hour. The tale opens as a clash of tempers in the law office, with a manhunt still to come.
79738-the-stratagem-and-other-stories:
Aleister Crowley gathers three tales in The Stratagem and Other Stories, printed by the Mandrake Press of London at 41 Museum Street. The title tale opens at a bare junction station where travellers wait on the fiery sand for a missed train. An Englishman rails at the railway while his small, keen-eyed fellow traveller listens in silence.

The book is dedicated to the memories of three dead friends: Joseph Conrad, who applauded the first story, and Allan Bennett, who suggested the second. Eugene John Weiland bowled the author out over the third. The Testament of Magdalen Blair and His Secret Sin fill out the volume.
79757-suggestions-for-seat-work-and-game:
Suggestions for Seat Work and Games, Primary Grades is a handbook for teachers by Eleanor Troxell, copyrighted in 1921 and printed by the Tribune Publishing Company of Dillon, Montana. It sorts its help under two heads, seat work and games. The aim is useful, quiet occupation for young children at their desks.

Seat work covers paper cutting, drawing, and modeling, then textiles, reading and writing, and number. Children model nature objects, dress paper dolls, design wallpaper for a doll house, and cut fruit and vegetables for a play store. Indian beads are made from salt, corn starch, and water, with the recipe given in full. The games half offers word games, spelling games, and number games. A recipe for paste closes the little book.
79759-medieval-cities:
Henri Pirenne of the University of Ghent wrote Medieval Cities, translated from the French by Frank Halsey and published by Princeton University Press in 1925. The book holds the substance of lectures Pirenne gave in American universities from October to December 1922. He dedicated it to Princeton, in gratitude for sympathy shown during the war.

His theme is the economic awakening of Western Europe and the birth of urban civilization. Chapters treat the Mediterranean world and the ninth century, then city origins and the revival of commerce. The merchant class and the middle class follow, with municipal institutions after them. A final chapter weighs cities in European civilization. Pirenne calls the book a synthesis from long years of study, with a bibliography for readers who want the details.
8007-the-bible-king-james-version-book-7:
Judges tells of Israel between Joshua and the kings, when the people fell into a repeated cycle: they turned from God, suffered under oppressors, cried out, and were rescued by a judge. Deborah leads an army, Gideon tests God with a fleece and routs Midian with a handful of men. Jephthah makes a tragic vow, and Samson, strong and reckless, brings down a Philistine temple on himself. The book ends in anarchy, with everyone doing what was right in his own eyes.

The stories are rough, vivid, and morally unsettling, which is why they endure. Judges refuses to tidy its heroes, showing deliverers who are flawed and a nation drifting. In the King James Version, its battles, songs, and betrayals read like a dark chronicle of freedom without leadership, and a warning about what follows when a people forgets.
8013-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
Adam, Seth, Enosh: First Chronicles begins with a genealogy that runs from the first man through Noah, Abraham, and Israel's tribes. After the long lists, the narrative turns to David, his wars, his preparations for the temple, and his organisation of priests, singers, and gatekeepers. The book ends with David's death and Solomon ready to build.

The chronicler writes history as a family record, tracing how worship was ordered and why it mattered. Readers who push past the names find a portrait of David as temple planner rather than warrior king.
