Rudyard Kipling wrote these notes on America, gathered from his travels in the United States in 1889. The introduction recalls a paragraph in the London World of April 1890. It named Kipling, the literary hero of the hour, the man who came from nowhere, in two small rooms joined by a tiny hall.

Kipling writes of American cities, trains, and people with a young reporter's eye, praising energy while mocking boast and bad manners. His notes are vivid, opinionated, and sometimes harsh, as a visitor's notes often are. The book gives readers Kipling's America at first sight, before fame softened his pen.
9777-riley-child-rhymes:
James Whitcomb Riley wrote Riley Child-Rhymes, a book of Hoosier childhood verse with pictures by Will Vawter. Dedicated to children everywhere, the book gathers poems from Little Orphant Annie to The Bumblebee, Circus-Day Parade, and Our Hired Girl. A frontispiece shows a child listening to witch tales Annie tells. Riley's verse favors dialect, laughter, and tender memory.

Poems range from aunty's house and farm boys to grandfathers, naughty Claudes, and down-around-the-river days. The Hoosier pictures match the rhymes' warmth. A reader gets a beloved children's classic, rich in Indiana speech and the magic of small days.
9790-traffics-and-discoveries:
Rudyard Kipling wrote Traffics and Discoveries, a book of tales and verse on empire, sea, and modern war. Contents include The Captive, The Bonds of Discipline, A Sahibs' War, and Their Lawful Occasions, with Steam Tactics, Wireless, and The Army of a Dream. Mrs. Bathurst and They add mystery to the mix. Kipling opens with a captive's march, chained yet nobly at ease.

Tales move from barracks and ships to wireless rooms and dream armies, with verse woven between. Kipling writes with terse craft and imperial confidence, shadowed by doubt. A reader gets a strong, varied Kipling collection, where soldiers, sailors, and signals tell the age's story.
9806-mr-justice-raffles:
E. W. Hornung wrote Mr. Justice Raffles in 1909, a tale of Raffles the gentleman thief turned judge of rogues. The book opens with Raffles vanished, then cabling his friend to meet the 7.31 at Charing Cross from Carlsbad. Chapters promise an inaugural banquet, a council of war, and our Mr. Shylock, with Camilla Belsize and a triple alliance. A dash in the dark and trial by Raffles follow.

Later chapters bring a secret service, the death of a sinner, and an apologia, as Raffles rights wrongs his own way. Hornung writes with light, daring wit. A reader gets a charming Raffles adventure, where a thief plays justice with style.
9815-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt, an English preacher and collector, gathered the accounts of his countrymen's sea voyages in the sixteenth century. This eighth volume, edited by Edmund Goldsmid, covers the English in Asia, from early trading ventures to longer stays in eastern ports and markets.

Sailors, merchants, and envoys describe storms, markets, rulers, and customs they met far from home. The spelling keeps the flavor of Hakluyt's age, with notes to help modern readers follow old names and terms. Together the reports show how England first learned Asia by ship, bargain, and hard travel.
9867-riders-of-the-silences:
Max Brand's 1919 western opens on the legends of the old West: gunmen whose bullets never missed, and stallions faster than the wind. Greatest of these legends, the prologue says, is the tale of Red Pierre and the phantom gunfighter McGurk.

The two men, unlike in every way, share one trait: neither can be beaten. Their rivalry drives the novel through mountain deserts, chases, and showdowns. Brand writes with speed and a storyteller's relish for myth. Fans of classic westerns get a tale that knows it is a legend and enjoys being one.
9888-the-spread-eagle-and-other-stories:
Gouverneur Morris published this story collection in 1910, with The Spread Eagle as its title tale. Morris, author of The Footprint and other stories, sets his characters in drawing rooms, Swiss winters, and Nice holidays, where pride, love, and money collide.

The title story opens with a youth spoiled by the praise of everyone around him, and the other tales follow men and women learning what praise and position are worth. Morris writes with wit and a light hand. Readers get polished, early twentieth-century short stories about society people discovering their limits.
9959-the-armourer-s-prentices:
Charlotte M. Yonge's 1889 novel follows prentice lads in an armourer's household in an earlier England of craftsmen, guilds, and faith. Published by Macmillan in London and New York, with illustrations by W. J. Hennessy, it belongs to Yonge's long shelf of historical tales for young readers.

The story moves through workshop life, old haunts, and the duties of apprentices learning a trade and a code. Yonge's interest lies in character formed by work, loyalty, and patience. Readers who enjoy historical fiction about ordinary craftspeople will find her earnest, detailed picture of a vanished working world.
9994-the-indian-lily-and-other-stories:
Hermann Sudermann's story collection, translated by Ludwig Lewisohn in 1911, takes its title from The Indian Lily. That story opens at seven in the morning with Herr von Niebeldingk and his dark, weary eyes. Sudermann, a leading German dramatist and novelist, writes of love, guilt, and fate.

The other stories are The Purpose, The Song of Death, The Victim, Autumn, and Merry Folk, each turning on a moral crisis. Lewisohn's translation keeps Sudermann's serious, polished manner. Readers get German short fiction of the naturalist age: somber, thoughtful, and attentive to the costs of desire.
a-book-of-prefaces: Henry Louis Mencken writes critical prefaces on Joseph Conrad, Theodore Dreiser, and James Huneker. A further essay treats Puritanism as a force in American letters, judging its effect on writers and readers. Mencken argues with vigor and wit, praising strong work and attacking pious cant. The book stands as an early statement of his critical voice and his case for honest art.
a-brief-history-of-the-united-states:
Joel Dorman Steele wrote his one-term history, Barnes's, on a teacher's complaint: pupils find history books dry, and the interesting ones are too long. His preface promises an attractive book that can be mastered in a single term. The copyright page dates the work 1872. Six epochs organize the whole.

Early discoveries and settlements, development of the colonies, the Revolutionary War, development of the states, the Civil War, and reconstruction and passing events carry the story to his own day. Questions for class use, historical recreations, the Declaration of Independence, and the Constitution fill the appendix. Steele's brief histories taught more American schoolchildren than almost any rival, and this is the pattern book.
a-changed-man-and-other-tales:
Thomas Hardy reprints a dozen shorter tales from the periodical press in this collection, transcribed from the 1920 Macmillan edition. His prefatory note, dated August 1913, says he gathered the pieces so readers could have them in the complete series of his works. The title tale, A Changed Man, opens the volume.

The Waiting Supper, Alicia's Diary, and The Grave by the Handpost follow. Enter a Dragoon and A Tryst at an Ancient Earthwork come next. A committee-man of the French Terror and a duke's reappearance stand among them. Soldiers, shepherds, and waiting women fill the Wessex scenes. Hardy mixes ghostly hints, class-crossed love, and his usual irony about fate in these late, polished stories.
a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems for children, many of them from the memory of his own sickly childhood. The volume is dedicated to Alison Cunningham, his nurse, with a verse letter thanking her for the nights she watched over him. The contents group the poems in three parts: the first under his own name as the child speaker, then The Child Alone, then Garden Days.

Short rhymes cover bedtime, rain, swings, shadows, foreign lands, and the land of counterpane, where a sick child turns bedcovers into hills for toy soldiers. Favorites such as My Shadow and The Lamplighter sit beside marching songs and farewells to the farm. The poems speak in a child's voice without talking down, which is why the collection has stayed a nursery classic.
a-collection-of-beatrix-potter-stories:
Beatrix Potter's animal tales are gathered here from her little Peter Rabbit books. A front list names the titles and marks those included: among them The Tale of Peter Rabbit, The Tale of Benjamin Bunny, The Tale of Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck, The Tale of the Flopsy Bunnies, The Tale of Two Bad Mice, and The Tale of Mr. Tod.

Peter opens the collection, squeezing under Mr. McGregor's garden gate and losing his jacket and shoes in the chase, as his mother warned. The other tales follow hedgehog washerwomen, fishing frogs, cats, mice, and foxes through small domestic adventures in the Lake District countryside. Potter's exact, unsentimental animal observation carries the charm: the creatures wear clothes and keep house, but they eat and are eaten like real animals.
a-collection-of-short-stories: Lemuel Arthur Pittenger gathers a collection of short stories with an introduction to the form. His opening essay treats the history, qualities, and composition of the short story. The stories that follow include Bjornson, Stockton, Maupassant, Kipling, Poe, and others. Pittenger's volume serves both as an anthology and as a classroom guide to reading stories well.
a-desperate-character-and-other-stories: Ivan Sergeevich Turgenev gathers stories headed by a desperate character. The volume also includes a strange story, Punin and Baburin, old portraits, the brigadier, and Pyetushkov. Its opening party of eight talks of contemporary affairs and men. Turgenev writes with quiet irony about Russian character and fate. Readers meet old Russia in tales that are brief, sharp, and true to life.
a-diversity-of-creatures: Rudyard Kipling gathers a diversity of creatures in stories and verse. The volume includes As Easy as ABC, Friendly Brook, In the Same Boat, The Village that Voted the Earth was Flat, and Mary Postgate. Poems such as MacDonough's Song and The Land stand beside the tales. Kipling ranges from future fancy to war, village life, and the sea.
a-few-figs-from-thistles:
Edna St. Vincent Millay's A Few Figs from Thistles collects short poems and sonnets of love and independence. The title promises small sharp fruit, and the opening poems deliver it. First Fig boasts of a candle burning at both ends. Second Fig builds a shining palace on sand.

Recuerdo remembers a night spent riding a ferry back and forth until dawn. Thursday coolly dismisses a lover who complains of Wednesday's change of heart. Macdougal Street walks a noisy New York immigrant street at night. Other pieces sing of travel, roses, and the not impossible him. Millay's voice is musical, witty, and unrepentant. These brief lyrics made her the emblem of a young generation that meant to live brightly and briefly.
a-few-short-sketches: Douglass Sherley offers a few short sketches of social life. The first sketch, Those Russian Violets, opens at a brilliant reception for a young woman from the East. Hours from five to seven frame a ball engagement and the talk of guests. Sherley writes light, observant pieces on manners and feeling.
a-great-emergency-and-other-tales: Juliana Horatia Ewing gathers a great emergency and other tales for young readers. The title tale follows Rupert's lectures, school cricket, a boys bridge, and an unexpected emergency. Other stories treat Henrietta, a family chronicle, and a school mimic. Ewing writes school and family life with warmth and moral sense.
a-group-of-noble-dames:
Thomas Hardy groups ten tales of Dorset ladies of past centuries, first collected in 1891, as the title page of this 1920 edition records. The dames are named like a roll of honor. They include the First Countess of Wessex and Barbara of the House of Grebe. They include the Marchioness of Stonehenge, Lady Mottisfont, and Squire Petrick's Lady. The Lady Icenway, Anna Lady Baxby, the Lady Penelope, the Duchess of Hamptonshire, and the Honourable Laura complete the roll.

A map of Wessex faces the tales, which are told as after-dinner stories among a club of antiquarians, in parts before and after dinner. Each turns on a marriage, a pride, or a strange fate in an old great house. Hardy treats his dames with irony and pity in equal measure.
a-guide-to-the-best-historical-novels-an:
Jonathan Nield sorts the best historical novels and tales ever written so that readers can find their way through a huge field. After an introduction on the rise of the form, his lists run by period: pre-Christian times, then century by century up to the nineteenth. A supplementary list covers semi-historical works.

Each section names authors and titles worth reading for that age, from ancient Rome to the age of Scott and Dumas. Suggested courses of reading for young readers and a bibliography close the volume. Nield's guide served for years as the standard map for readers who wanted the past told as story, arranged so a reader could march through history in fiction.
a-history-of-trade-unionism-in-the-unite: Selig Perlman writes a history of trade unionism in the United States. Part one treats the struggle for survival, from labor movements before the Civil War through equal citizenship and wild cat prosperity. Perlman builds on the Wisconsin school of labor history under John Commons. The book carries American union history forward with new research.
a-hive-of-busy-bees:
Effie Mae Hency Williams frames her children's book as a visit to Grandpa and Grandma, where Don and Joyce are caught worrying about next summer just after Christmas. The contents tell the plan: after How It Happened and The Sting of the Bee come chapters named Bee Obedient, Bee Honest, Bee Truthful, Bee Kind, Bee Polite, and more.

Each bee chapter tells a small story from the children's days. It turns a fault or a kindness into the lesson of its title. Bee Grateful, Bee Loving, Bee Content, and Bee Prayerful pass in review. The book ends with Home Again. Williams writes for young readers in plain, warm sentences. The book is Sunday-school moral teaching in story dress, gentle and old-fashioned.
a-knight-of-the-white-cross-a-tale-of-th:
G. A. Henty's A Knight of the White Cross tells the first siege of Rhodes through an English boy's eyes. His preface to his dear lads explains the Knights of St. John. Born as hospitallers to pilgrims, they became a great military order. At Rhodes they fortified the town against the Turks.

The tale opens at the chateau of Amboise in June 1470, with a lad of seventeen stroking a hawk. Gervaise Tresham's path leads from English faction fights to the white cross of the order. Page, squire, and knight, he rises through the Rhodes campaigns. The siege itself, against Sultan Mahomet's host, crowns the book. Henty chose the episode, he says, as the most full of incident in the order's history. Research and adventure march together in his most chivalrous tale.
a-little-book-of-filipino-riddles: Frederick Starr edits a little book of Filipino riddles. Dedicated to informants from Agoo in Union Province, it gives riddles in Ilocano and Pangasinan with English notes. Set phrases at riddle openings and closings mark the tradition. Starr's book introduces Filipino folk wit to English readers. Young readers can try the riddles and learn how folk wit works.
a-little-book-of-profitable-tales: Eugene Field gathers a little book of profitable tales for his daughter Mary French Field. Its tales include the first Christmas tree, the symbol and the saint, the coming of the prince, and the mouse and the moonbeam. The divell's Christmas, the mountain and the sea, and Margaret a pearl follow. Field writes tales that teach through fancy.
a-loose-end-and-other-stories: Elizabeth Hall gathers a loose end and other stories of the Channel Islands and Brittany. The title tale opens one September morning when the islands seemed further off than now. A Breton village, twice a child, the road by the sea, and Tabitha's aunt complete the volume. Hall writes quiet stories of place, memory, and character.
a-lover-in-homespun-and-other-stories: Frank Clifford Smith gathers Canadian stories headed by a lover in homespun. Other tales treat faith that removes mountains, a pair of boots, a prairie episode, and a daughter of the church. A perilous encounter, Le Loup Garou, and a Christmas adventure follow. Smith dedicates his book to his mother, who loved his literary work.
a-midsummer-drive-through-the-pyrenees: Edwin Asa Dix drives through the Pyrenees at midsummer in this travel book. Chapters visit a Biscayan beach, Bayonne the invincible, and Saint John of Light. Dix wonders why Americans visit Switzerland and Italy while passing the Pyrenees by. His drive, illustrated and learned, argues for the mountains of the south.
a-modern-cinderella-or-the-little-old-sh:
Louisa May Alcott gathers four stories, opening with the title tale in an ancient, many-gabled New England house, where a brook runs through the orchard and patriarchal elms stand on the lawn. One summer morning a humble history begins there: Nan, a poor relation with a kind heart, and Di, the restless invalid she tends. A little old shoe carries the Cinderella plot into this household.

Debby's Debut, Brothers, and Nelly's Hospital complete the volume, the last drawn from Alcott's own nursing in the Civil War. The stories mix romance, sacrifice, and domestic duty in her early manner. Readers who know her through Little Women will find the same warmth in shorter compass.
a-pair-of-blue-eyes:
Thomas Hardy's novel tells, in his own preface's words, an imaginary history of three human hearts. The preface sets the frame: a craze for restoring old churches had reached the wild coast of western England, and the story grows out of such a restoration. The scene lies near Castle Boterel, at the furthest west of Hardy's Wessex settings, a region he calls one of dream and mystery.

Across forty chapters, the architect Stephen Smith comes to restore a church tower and falls in love with Elfride Swancourt, the vicar's daughter. Her later attachment to the man of letters Henry Knight, and the misunderstandings between the three, drive the tragedy. Hardy mixes cliff scenery, coincidence, and his early interest in how chance governs feeling.
a-peep-behind-the-scenes:
Mrs. O. F. Walton wrote A Peep Behind the Scenes as a Christian story for young readers, by the author of Christie's Old Organ, as the title page notes. It begins in rain at a fair, where little Rosalie belongs to a travelling theatre company, brightly lit on Saturday night and dreary by Sunday afternoon, when the crowds have gone.

Rosalie's story runs through the little theatre, the actress's own tale, a family secret, circus processions, and lodging-house poverty. Kind and cruel adults cross her path while the book presses its lesson, that the showy world backstage is poor and sad beside a Christian home. Chapter titles like 'The Lost Lamb Found' and 'The Green Pasture' announce the ending Walton's Sunday-school readers expected.
a-philosophicall-essay-for-the-reunion-o: Pierre Besnier proposes a reunion of languages in this essay printed at Oxford in 1675, promising that mastery of one tongue might open all the rest. Rejecting pride in any native tongue, he takes Latin, the noble language of the Romans, as the basis of his project. The printer commends the author's modesty and freedom from prejudice, presenting a scheme by which one well-learned language might open the rest of Europe's tongues.
a-practical-directory-for-young-christia: Harvey Newcomb writes this practical directory as letters written by an elder brother for his younger sister, left partly dependent on him by the death of her parents. Written for the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society, the letters guide a young Christian woman through conduct, devotion, and daily duty. The preface stresses that the letters were truly written to his sister, giving familiar counsel the weight of family affection.
a-protegee-of-jack-hamlin-s-and-other-st:
Bret Harte opens aboard the steamer Silveropolis, cleaving the Sacramento River with foam at her paddle-boxes, where the gambler Jack Hamlin steps quietly from his stateroom. Hamlin, Harte's recurring gentleman of the camps, takes a young woman under his protection, and the title story follows what his chivalry costs him. Five more tales fill the volume.

An Ingenue of the Sierras and The Reformation of James Reddy come next. The Heir of the McHulishes, An Episode of West Woodlands, and The Home-Coming of Jim Wilkes follow. They range across mining towns, ranches, and river landings. Harte writes his California with sentiment and irony in equal measure, and Hamlin remains one of his most graceful creations.
a-reckless-character-and-other-stories: Ivan Turgenev gathers stories in this volume translated from the Russian by Isabel Hapgood, opening with the title tale told among eight people discussing contemporary matters. An old man answers talk of modern recklessness by recalling earlier reckless men, whose enthusiasm had no object. He narrates a story of his own youth. Other pieces in the volume include a dream tale, a priest's story, old portraits, a song of love triumphant, Clara Militch, and poems in prose.
a-ring-of-rubies:
A Ring of Rubies is an 1892 novel by L T Meade. Rosamund Lindley, an English girl, begs a wealthy but eccentric relative to aid her in a cherished project. He puts her off with a promise to answer definitely after a week. Within that week he dies, and his will leaves Rosamund an antique ruby ring.

The ring is the hinge of the story: an unexpected inheritance that changes what Rosamund can do and what others expect of her. Meade, a hugely productive writer of girls' and domestic fiction, builds the tale around the gift and its consequences. The novel shows her gift for turning a single striking object into the engine of a young heroine's fortunes.
a-school-history-of-the-united-states: John Bach McMaster, professor of American history at the University of Pennsylvania, writes this school history of the United States, published in 1897. The contents run from Europe finding America through Spanish, English, Dutch, and Swedish settlements, the planting of New England, and the struggle for New France. Independence, the Constitution, the rise of parties, and progress between 1840 and 1860 carry the story toward a continental nation.
a-short-history-of-monks-and-monasteries: Alfred Wesley Wishart writes this short history of monks and monasteries, moving from eastern monasticism to the orders of the west. The contents pass the hermits of Egypt, the pillar saint, and the cenobites of the east into ante-Benedictine monks, the rules of Benedict, and the struggle against barbarism. Reformed and military orders, then mendicant friars including Francis Bernardone, complete a survey of lives withdrawn from the world for prayer.
a-short-history-of-wales:
Owen Edwards tells the whole story of Wales in twenty-five short chapters, first published in 1906 and in its fifth impression by 1922, as this Fisher Unwin edition records. He begins with what Wales is made of and what it is like, then the wandering nations: Iberians and Celts. Rome, the coming of Christ, and the Welsh kings follow.

The laws of Howel, the Normans, Llywelyn the Great and the last Llywelyn, Owen Glendower, the Tudors, the Reformation, and the Civil War carry the tale forward. Closing chapters treat the religious awakening under Howel Harris, the Reform Acts, education, and self-government. Edwards writes with love and clarity, in a small book meant for every Welsh home.
a-student-in-arms-second-series: Donald Hankey continues his student in arms in this second series, published in 1917 with an introduction by J. St. Loe Strachey. The contents weigh the bad side of military service against the good side of militarism, add a month's reflections, romance, imaginary conversations, and the fear of death in war. A letter to an army chaplain, Don't Worry, a passing in June 1915, and memories of home and school complete a soldier's reflections.
a-study-of-fairy-tales: Laura Fry Kready studies fairy tales for teachers in this volume, with an introduction by Henry Suzzallo and a dedication to children who may receive any good from it. The chapters treat the worth of fairy tales and principles of selection. The telling of tales, their history, their classes, and their sources follow. A Chaucer epigraph and a Tuileries statue of Perrault, among his Red Riding Hood and Sleeping Beauty, open a practical guide to choosing and telling.
a-thief-in-the-night-a-book-of-raffles-a:
A Thief in the Night, subtitled A Book of Raffles' Adventures, is E W Hornung's 1905 collection of stories about A J Raffles. It is the third book of the series and the last of the short story collections. In it, Raffles, the gentleman thief, commits his crimes behind the perfect cover of an England cricketer admired by the society he robs.

Bunny Manders, his devoted friend, shares the dangers and tells the tales. This edition gathers those adventures under the book-of-adventures subtitle, with the full original content. For new readers it serves as a complete entry into the Raffles world: elegant theft, loyal friendship, and the police forever one step behind.
a-thoughtless-yes: Helen Hamilton Gardener gathers stories in this volume, dedicated to the many strangers whose letters, thoughtful, gay, or sad, came from far and near. Letters arrived from rich and poor, Christian and unbeliever, a bishop's palace and behind prison walls. She hopes the collection gives back as much pleasure and mental stimulus as they gave her. The contents include a splendid judge of a woman, the lady of the club, a rusty link, the Boler House mystery, and Florence Campbell's fate.
a-touch-of-sun-and-other-stories: Mary Hallock Foote gathers stories in this volume, opening with a touch of sun at a famous mining property in northern California. The five-o'clock whistle drones through the heat for the Asgard group, whose square league of foothill land keeps fire lines cleared, forest trees respected, and roads maintained. Everything is painted monopoly brown. The Maid's Progress, Pilgrims to Mecca, and The Harshaw Bride join the title story in a book of western light and heat.
a-tramp-s-sketches: Stephen Graham sketches a tramp's life in this 1913 volume, dedicated to the celestials and frontispieced with night over the Black Sea. The opening declares that a town is one large house whose little houses are rooms and whose streets are stairs. Farewell to the town, nights out in perfect vagabondage, hospitality, a Turkish coffee house, and a great monastery open the wandering. A boy who never grows old and a pilgrimage to Jerusalem carry the wanderer toward a message from the hermit.
a-village-ophelia-and-other-stories: Anne Reeve Aldrich gathers stories in this 1899 volume, opening with the title story, set on Long Island's east end. Two roads run side by side for the thirty miles from Riverhead to Greenport. The north road near the Sound passes lonely farmhouses and desolate settlements, while the south road runs through small hamlets. North roaders drive across to church or purchases, and the title story, a Vere de Vere story, a lamentable comedy, and an African discovery follow.
a-wodehouse-miscellany-articles-stories: P. G. Wodehouse brings together early pieces, poems, and tales in this mix put up for Project Gutenberg, with first print dates in the contents. The pieces take up team leadership, a half-done set, the new ads, the hidden joys of Reginald, a bout with drink, astigmatism, indoor golf, and the odd spread of verse. The tales include When Papa Swore in Hindustani, Tom Dick and Harry, Jeeves Takes Charge, and Disentangling Old Duggie.
a-woman-intervenes: Robert Barr tells how a woman intervenes in this 1896 novel, illustrated by Hal Hurst and dedicated to his friend Horace Hart. The first chapter finds the managing editor of a New York paper, the Argus, at his desk. He frowns under shaggy eyebrows at a young man who has thrown a huge fur overcoat over one chair. A telegram opens the business, and illustrations of Wentworth, Miss Jennie, Edith Longworth, and a walk alone up and down the promenade promise a story of newspapers and society.
a-woman-s-impression-of-the-philippines: Mary Helen Fee gives a woman's impression of the Philippines in this volume, dedicated to her schoolmate and lifelong friend Martha Parry Gish. The contents run from the voyage's beginning through San Francisco and Honolulu to Manila, then to Capiz and first experiences as a teacher of Filipinos. An analysis of Filipino character, housekeeping, youths and maidens, typhoons and earthquakes, war alarms, Christmas festivities, weddings, and children's games follow.
a-yankee-in-the-trenches: Robert Derby Holmes, corporal of the 22nd London Battalion of the Queen's Royal West Surrey Regiment, writes a Yankee in the trenches, published at Boston in 1918. Illustrated from photographs, the volume carries a glossary of army slang. Its pictures show a heavy howitzer under camouflage, a raid over the top, cooking under difficulties, and a British tank. Dedicated to Marion Puttee of Southall, it follows an American stranger in a strange land into war.
abroad-with-the-jimmies: Lilian Bell travels abroad with the Jimmies in this volume, published by Ward, Lock and Company in London, New York, and Melbourne. Dedicated to her father as the origin of her ideals of patriotism, loyalty, and devotion, the book opens on a house-boat at Henley. Paris, Strasburg, and the Black Forest follow, with the Passion Play and Munich after them. Salzburg, Ischl, Vienna, and a first interview with Tolstoy complete two years of travel with her sister and the Jimmies.
acres-of-diamonds-our-every-day-opportun:
Russell H. Conwell, founder of Temple University as the title page notes, built his fame on a single lecture, Acres of Diamonds, delivered thousands of times across America. This volume prints that lecture together with Robert Shackleton's account of Conwell's life and achievements and an autobiographical note. The contents trace the life first: the story of his sword, his start at Lexington, and the fifty-seven cents that began his work.

The lecture itself argues that wealth and opportunity lie close at hand, in one's own town and trade, rather than in distant strikes. Its title story tells of a man who sold his farm to hunt diamonds abroad, while diamonds lay under his own land. Shackleton's biography then shows the doctrine financing a university built for working students.
aeroplanes:
James Slough Zerbe explains the flying machine while it is still new, in chapters that move from theory to practice. His contents begin with theories and facts about flying: gravity, momentum, resistance, lift and drift, and the flight of birds. Later chapters take up the shape of machines, fore and aft control, and lifting surfaces.

Construction, power, propellers, and accessories follow, with chapters on experimental gliders and model aeroplanes for the beginner. A chapter on the aeroplane in the Great War brings the subject up to its military present. Zerbe writes in plain terms for curious readers and amateur builders, and his tables and arguments show an inventor thinking on paper.
aesop-s-fables-a-new-revised-version-fro: Aesop offers short animal fables in a revised version drawn from original sources, each tale closing with a plain moral for daily conduct. Foxes, wolves, lions, and asses act out folly, greed, cunning, and pride in brief scenes a child can grasp at once. Illustrations by Harrison Weir, John Tenniel, Ernest Griset, and others add humour and detail to this enduring store of proverbial wisdom.
african-and-european-addresses: Theodore Roosevelt gathers speeches delivered in Africa and Europe, on peace and justice in the Sudan, law and order in Egypt, and citizenship in a republic. Other addresses treat international peace and the colonial policy of the United States, stating his views on duty, order, and national character. Together they show a former president speaking as a statesman abroad, blunt, moralising, and confident.
african-camp-fires: Stewart Edward White recounts an African safari in camp-fire tales, opening with the voyage to the island of war and moving inland through hunting country. He describes camps, trackers, game, and the long evenings when stories were told under the stars. The book mixes sporting adventure with vivid sketches of landscape and people, in the style of early twentieth-century travel writing.
after-a-shadow-and-other-stories:
T. S. Arthur's After a Shadow, and Other Stories appeared in New York in 1868. The title tale begins on a bright June morning with baby Arty. The child escapes his nurse and runs laughing down the pavement. He is chasing his own long shadow on the ground.

Seventeen stories follow, among them In the Way of Temptation and Andy Lovell. Coffee versus Brandy brings Arthur's temperance cause into the parlour. A Good Name, Little Lizzie, and An Angel in Disguise treat children and disguise. Which Was Most the Lady tests manners against worth. Arthur writes short fiction for family reading, each piece turning on a small incident with a moral inside it. The shadow of the title is the kind adults chase too, an emptiness mistaken for a prize.
after-long-years-and-other-stories: Sophie Antoinette Miller offers stories translated from the German, led by the title tale of return after long years apart. The collection moves through domestic scenes, partings, and reconciliations, with feeling kept plain rather than sentimental. Agnes M. Dunne shares the translation work, and the Sunshine and Shadow series setting suits these gentle tales of home, memory, and second chances.
afterwhiles: James Whitcomb Riley gathers poems of home, memory, and Hoosier life, written in the warm, plain voice that made him a popular American poet. The verses move between humour and tenderness, recalling childhood, neighbours, and seasons past with a storyteller's ease. Readers find here the dialect charm and gentle sentiment at the heart of Riley's appeal.
algonquin-indian-tales: Egerton Ryerson Young collects Algonquin Indian tales, opening with a letter from Chief Big Canoe of Georgina Island on Lake Simcoe. The stories pass on the lore, humour, and teaching of Algonquin storytellers, as heard and retold by a missionary long among them. They preserve Native narrative traditions in a form meant for general readers, young and old.
ali-pacha-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas tells the true story of Ali Pacha of Janina in this volume from his Celebrated Crimes set, printed here in the 1910 edition. His first chapter sets the scene: while Napoleon remade the West, the old Ottoman East crumbled, and bold adventurers carved pieces from its ruins. Ali, a brigand's son, carved the largest piece in Greece.

Eleven chapters trace his rise from robber chief to pasha ruling Albania and much of Greece, his courts, cruelties, and wars, and his long defiance of the Sultan. Dumas writes history like a novel, with scenes, speeches, and a villain of real grandeur. The fall of Ali, besieged in Janina, closes the tale in fire.
alice-of-old-vincennes:
Maurice Thompson's novel Alice of Old Vincennes opens under the Roussillon cherry tree, a French seedling old Vincennes remembered into statehood days. The Wabash town of French habitants and British soldiers is the stage: Fort Sackville flies the British flag over the Illinois country. Alice Tarleton grows up among priests and traders while George Rogers Clark's Virginians move toward the river forts. The contents promise an attack, a flag of Alice's making, and Clark's counsel.

Inside, the novel follows the 1778-79 campaign that took Kaskaskia and Vincennes for Virginia and lost and retook the fort. Alice's flag, sewn for the American cause, gives the romance its emblem of women's part in the frontier war. Thompson fills his pages with French patois, river weather, and the diplomacy of the old Northwest. Readers get the standard American historical romance of its decade, the book that made Vincennes famous in fiction.
all-about-johnnie-jones: Carolyn Verhoeff tells all about Johnnie Jones, a boy hero of illustrated stories for young children. The book follows Johnnie through everyday doings and small adventures, with pictures to carry the youngest readers along. Its simple scenes and gentle humour made it a durable nursery favourite, reaching a seventh edition.
all-on-the-irish-shore-irish-sketches: Edith Oenone Somerville sketches Irish life on the Irish shore, from a tinker's dog and Fanny Fitz's gamble to a Connemara mare and high tea at McKeown's. The stories catch the talk, humour, and hardship of country Ireland with an insider's ear. Written with the author's usual warmth, they offer a vivid, affectionate portrait of a vanishing rural world.
alonzo-fitz-and-other-stories:
Mark Twain gathers stories and sketches, opening with The Loves of Alonzo Fitz Clarence and Rosannah Ethelton. Alonzo sits in snowbound Eastport, Maine, on a bitter winter morning, courting by the new telephone a Rosannah he has never seen in California. The contents continue with On the Decay of the Art of Lying, Punch Brothers Punch, and The Great Revolution in Pitcairn.

The Canvasser's Tale, An Encounter with an Interviewer, Paris Notes, a legend of Sagenfeld, and speeches on the babies and the weather fill out the volume. Twain mixes tall tale, satire, and platform humor, much of it from his earlier years. The telephone courtship, with its cross-country mix-ups, remains the best-known piece in the set.
amanda-a-daughter-of-the-mennonites:
Anna Balmer Myers sets her novel in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, opening on a scorching midsummer day with children splashing in a small stream. Amanda Reist grows up Mennonite, plain in dress and strict in church, in a farm world of snitzing parties and apple butter boiling. Helen Mason Gross illustrated the book, as the title page notes.

Twenty-six chapters follow Amanda through school days to work as a teacher, a spelling bee, the market, a boarder, a trouble maker, and Aunt Rebecca's will. Martin, the boy of the farm, and Lyman, a voice from the wider world, divide her heart. Myers writes the Pennsylvania Dutch country from inside, with affection for its faith and food alike.
american-fairy-tales:
L. Frank Baum, fresh from The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, wrote American Fairy Tales as a set of comic wonder stories. Baum sets his magic in modern American homes, attics, and streets rather than old European kingdoms. The first tale leaves little Martha alone in a big house. She opens a brass-studded chest from Italy and lets out trouble.

Twelve tales follow, among them The Glass Dog, The Queen of Quok, and The Enchanted Types. A dummy comes alive, a boy captures Father Time, and magic bonbons cause chaos. A laughing hippopotamus and the king of the polar bears join the company. Baum mixes slang, satire, and nonsense with his enchantments. The stories gently mock fashion, wealth, and pride while keeping a child's view of wonder at the centre.
american-indian-stories: Zitkala-Sa writes American Indian Stories from her own life, opening with impressions of an Indian childhood, her mother, and the legends she heard. The book moves between Native tradition and the boarding-school world that sought to remake her, in prose both lyrical and pointed. It stands as an early and powerful Native American voice in English letters.
american-notes:
Charles Dickens wrote this travel book after his first tour of the United States, published here in an edition that also carries Pictures from Italy. His dedication thanks the American friends who welcomed him and left his judgment free, and who can bear the truth told good-humouredly. A preface to the cheap edition insists, years on, that his opinions stand unaltered.

Dickens travels through Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Washington, and the West, touring prisons, asylums, factories, and schools, riding steamboats and trains, and watching Congress and frontier manners with the same sharp eye. He praises American energy and kindness and attacks slavery, the press, and the national habit of spitting. The book made him enemies in America and remains a vivid outsider's portrait of the young republic.
among-malay-pirates:
Among Malay Pirates, published in 1893 by G A Henty, is a collection of short adventure stories for boys. Henty was the era's best-known writer of such tales, and this volume ranges widely. Its title story takes readers among the Malay pirates of the East, and other stories turn to India and to a shipwreck around the Channel Islands.

The collection also includes a tale of a dam within California and an escape from Chinese captors. Each story delivers the brisk danger and resourceful heroes that made Henty famous. Together they show the full spread of his adventure map, from Eastern seas to American engineering, in the short form his young readers devoured.
among-my-books-first-series: James Russell Lowell gathers his first series of essays among his books, on Dryden, witchcraft, Shakespeare once more, and New England two centuries ago. The pieces show Lowell as scholar and humorist, at home in old books and American history alike. They remain a model of the familiar literary essay, learned without pedantry.
among-my-books-second-series: James Russell Lowell continues among his books with a second series on Dante, Spenser, Wordsworth, and Milton. The essays weigh four great poets with learning, humour, and a critic's judgment, linking their art to their times. Together with the first series, they form Lowell's chief contribution to American literary criticism.
among-the-forces: Henry White Warren writes among the forces, a study of the powers at work in nature and human life, with illustrations to aid the argument. The book treats physical forces as signs of a larger order, in the spirit of popular science wedded to faith. Warren speaks to readers who sought science and religion in harmony.
an-apology-for-the-study-of-northern-ant: Elizabeth Elstob defends the study of northern antiquities, in a work reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society with Hebrew and Gothic matter. Her apology argues for the value of Old English and northern learning at a time when it was little prized. Elstob, a pioneering woman scholar, speaks with learning and quiet confidence.
an-author-s-mind-the-book-of-title-pages: Martin Farquhar Tupper edits An Author's Mind, the book of title-pages, described as a bookful of books, or thirty books in one. The volume gathers title-pages as a playful survey of authorship, publishing, and literary vanity. Its Hartford edition offers a curious window onto Victorian book culture. The joke is gentle, and the love of books is real.
an-essay-on-man-moral-essays-and-satires:
Alexander Pope's poems fill this 1891 Cassell volume, whose introduction divides his career by reigns: original poet under Anne, translator of Homer under George I, and moral poet as his genius ripened. The Essay on Man stands first, a poem in heroic couplets that surveys man's place between angels and beasts and argues that whatever is, is right.

The Moral Essays take up the characters of men and women, riches, and taste, through portraits of real people thinly veiled. The Satires close the book with Pope's attacks on dunces, hirelings, and corrupt taste. Line after line has passed into common quotation, and the volume shows why Pope defined poetry for his century.
analytical-studies: Honoré de Balzac gathers analytical studies, including the petty troubles and unhappiness of married life, in a volume dedicated with his usual ambition. The studies dissect marriage, money, and manners with Balzac's keen, unsparing observation. They show the novelist as analyst, turning social life into a science of motives. The pieces still bite, two centuries on.
andersen-s-fairy-tales:
Hans Christian Andersen's tales fill this collection, opening with The Emperor's New Clothes. The contents list nineteen stories, among them The Swineherd, The Real Princess, The Fir Tree, The Snow Queen, The Shadow, and The Little Match Girl. Andersen wrote as a Dane telling stories aloud, and the voice stays close and warm.

Some tales are funny, like the emperor parading in invisible clothes. Others are sad: a match girl freezing on New Year's Eve, a fir tree longing for greatness, a mother searching for her dead child. Andersen mixed folk material with stories wholly his own, and his blend of wonder, humor, and sorrow changed children's books for good.
angling-sketches:
Andrew Lang writes as a fisherman in sketches first printed in periodicals such as Macmillan's Magazine and the Fishing Gazette, gathered here from the 1895 Longmans edition. The Confessions of a Duffer opens the book honestly: Lang owns his failures with rod and line. Loch Awe, Loch Leven, and Tweedside supply the waters.

The Lady or the Salmon, The Bloody Doctor, and The Complete Bungler mix fishing fact with story and joke. Lang salts his sport with classical learning and Border memories from his boyhood. The result is sporting literature for readers who may never cast a fly: a book about patience, hope, rivers, and the tales fishermen tell.
animal-figures-in-the-maya-codices: Alfred Marston Tozzer studies animal figures in the Maya codices, in papers of the Peabody Museum of American Archaeology and Ethnology at Harvard. The work identifies beasts and birds painted in Maya books, and what they meant in ritual and calendar. Tozzer's study links Maya art to the natural world its scribes knew.
animal-heroes:
Ernest Thompson Seton tells the life stories of animals he calls heroes, and his note to the reader insists each tale rests on a real animal's life. The contents list the Slum Cat and Arnaux the homing pigeon. They list Badlands Billy the wolf and the Boy and the Lynx. Little Warhorse the jack-rabbit, Snap the bull-terrier, the Winnipeg Wolf, and the White Reindeer complete the set.

Seton, a working naturalist, follows each animal's habits, enemies, and escapes with a tracker's knowledge. Some tales end in triumph, others in the hard deaths nature deals. He wrote the White Reindeer in Norway with herds in sight, and Arnaux's flight from people who knew the bird. The stories helped create the realistic animal story as a form.
anna-st-ives: Thomas Holcroft writes Anna St. Ives, a novel in three volumes whose contents span a heroine's trials in love and society. The story follows Anna through family pressure, suitors, and moral choice, in the radical, sentimental manner of the 1790s. Holcroft's novel remains a notable example of Jacobin fiction in English.
anne-of-green-gables:
Lucy Maud Montgomery wrote this novel about Anne Shirley, an orphan sent by mistake to Green Gables, the Prince Edward Island farm of Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert. The brother and sister had asked for a boy to help with work. Anne, talkative and full of imagination, wins Matthew over at once and slowly softens Marilla. The contents list thirty-eight chapters following her first years in Avonlea.

Anne renames places, befriends Diana Barry, feuds with Gilbert Blythe, and lands in scrapes at school and at tea. Later chapters take her through the Queen's class, examinations, and a scholarship path, ending with loss at home and a bend in her road. Warmth and comedy carry the story of a child remaking a strict household.
apology-crito-and-phaedo-of-socrates: Plato presents Socrates in the Apology, Crito, and Phaedo, translated by Henry Cary and Edward Brooks. The three dialogues follow Socrates at trial, in prison refusing escape, and on his last day discussing the soul. Together they form the classic portrait of the philosopher facing death with reason and calm.
applied-psychology-for-nurses: Mary F. Porter writes for student nurses from her work in schools, a nerve hospital, and a large city hospital. She argues that restoring bodily health matters little if a patient keeps a sick outlook through a long life. The book links habits of mind, fear, and mood to ward care, and it offers ways to speak and act that calm rather than alarm. Its plain cases aim to help nurses read patients with more patience and skill.
april-hopes:
William Dean Howells dates his novel 1887 on the title page and opens at Harvard's Class Day, in the Hemenway Gymnasium. Tall Mr. Elbridge G. Mavering watches the gaiety from the floor, struck by how young the students look. Among the promenading girls is Alice Pasmer, and young Dan Mavering's April hopes begin.

The courtship runs through a Newport summer and a winter of misunderstandings, family pride, and second thoughts on both sides. Alice's mother, a widow with a sharp tongue, and Dan's easy nature complicate every step. Howells studies the small change of feeling — a word, a visit, a silence — with his famous fineness. The novel is a comedy of manners with real pain under it.
are-women-people-a-book-of-rhymes-for-su: Alice Duer Miller answers anti-suffrage talk with short, sharp rhymes that turn its own claims back on the speaker. One poem has a mother warn her son Willie against the polls, then admit that his father already casts votes for her and other women. Others mock fears about danger, coarseness, and lost womanhood at the ballot box. The verse is witty rather than solemn, and it was made to be read aloud at rallies and in print.
arizona-sketches:
Joseph A. Munk wrote these sketches of Arizona from his own trips and ranching experience there. The contents list fourteen chapters. The first, A Romantic Land, warns the newcomer that Arizona judged by Eastern standards looks a disappointment: it seems all desert at first glance. Munk answers that the country must be taken on its own merits, for its scenery, climate, minerals, and strange plants and animals.

Following chapters describe his first trip, the open range, ranch life and the round-up, and a model ranch. Others treat desert plants, Hooker's Hot Springs, echoes in the canyons, and the fallen star at Meteorite Mountain. The ancient cliff dwellers and the Moqui Indians come next, and the climate closes the book. The book is part travel narrative, part settler's handbook for a territory still new to most American readers.
ars-ne-lupin-versus-herlock-sholmes:
Arsène Lupin versus Herlock Sholmes is a 1908 book by Maurice Leblanc, pitting his gentleman thief against a great detective. Arsène Lupin is everything expected of a French aristocrat: witty, charming, brilliant, and sly, and possibly the greatest thief in the world. Against him stands Herlock Sholmes, the British gentleman detective, the one man who may be able to stop him.

The book stages their duel of wits across a set of linked cases. Each man reads the other's moves and answers with a bolder stroke, so the contest stays open to the end. It remains a classic of the Lupin series, loved for the rare pleasure of watching thief and detective test each other at full strength.
artemis-to-actaeon-and-other-verses: Edith Wharton's 1909 book of verse opens with Artemis to Actaeon, in which the goddess speaks to the hunter who saw her and must die for it. Later poems take up Vesalius in Zante, Margaret of Cortona, Chartres, tombs and grief, then Orpheus, autumn sunsets and All Souls. Classical myth, Italian places and mourning run through a collection written in strict, musical verse.
arts-and-crafts-in-the-middle-ages: Julia de Wolf Addison surveys medieval workmanship in gold and silver, jewelry, enamel, metals, tapestry, embroidery, stone sculpture, wood and ivory carving, inlay, mosaic, and book illumination. She names fine pieces such as the Crown of Charlemagne and the Tara Brooch, and she notes artisans of the early Renaissance. The book is a clear, illustrated guide for readers who love craft history. Its charm lies in close looking at objects made by hand.
asser-life-king-alfred-giles:
Asser, a Welsh monk from St David's, wrote his Life of King Alfred in 893, during the king's lifetime. J. A. Giles's English translation is the text here, from his Six Old English Chronicles. Asser had joined Alfred's court in 885 and wrote as a friend and daily companion.

The life mixes a chronicle of the Viking wars with intimate detail: Alfred's childhood, his illnesses, his hunger for learning, and his program of translating Latin books into English. Asser shows the king dividing his income and his hours with a monk's exactness. It is the first biography of an English king by a man who knew him. Its authenticity has been debated; its charm has not.
at-home-with-the-jardines:
Lilian Bell's comic novel of young married life appeared in book form in 1906, after serial runs in several magazines. Bell follows the Jardines, newlyweds learning housekeeping in New York, through the small wars of a first home. Chapters promise the tone at once: theories, janitors, an angel and an agent, and how the couple tamed the cook.

Mary, the maid, anchors the household and eventually breaks up in a chapter of her own. Moving house, a first house-party, and Bee's campaign to make the couple smart supply the incidents. A letter from Jimmie widens the cast before the closing chapter grants the pair their happy ending. Bell writes domestic chaos with affection, turning rent, servants, and callers into light social comedy.
at-last-a-christmas-in-the-west-indies:
Charles Kingsley wrote this travel book after a Christmas voyage to the West Indies, a dream he says he had held for forty years. Kingsley, clergyman and naturalist, dedicates the volume to Sir Arthur Gordon, the governor whose invitation made the trip possible. Trinidad is his base, and the Spanish Main his horizon.

Chapters mix voyage narrative with close natural history: tropical plants, birds, and sea life observed by a trained collector. Ashore, he watches cane cutting in fierce heat, where gangs haul carts from mud while sucking sugar-cane at every pause. Humboldt-style wonder and a parson's moral reflections run side by side, making the book both a holiday record and a Victorian study of colonial island life.
aunt-harding-s-keepsakes-or-the-two-bibl:
An anonymous Sunday-school tale, revised by Daniel P. Kidder and dated 1851, this story follows sisters Louisa and Emma as their aunt Harding prepares to leave for India. The girls guess what keepsake she will give them. Emma thinks her doll, cradle, and baby-house furniture have exhausted generosity; Louisa is sure something more is coming.

Aunt Harding's presents turn out to be Bibles, and the chapters test how each sister uses hers. Letters from India, trouble between the sisters, and lessons on the use of money carry the moral. When Emma begs pity for Louisa, her mother explains that treating a faulting child as faultless would betray the aunt's wish. The tale ends with the aunt's return and the two characters fully contrasted.
aunt-jane-s-nieces:
L. Frank Baum wrote this girls' novel under his Edith Van Dyne pen name, publishing it in 1906. Three cousins — Beth, Patsy, and Louise — receive invitations from their rich, eccentric Aunt Jane, who means to choose an heiress among them. Professor De Graf sorting the breakfast mail opens the story of Beth's summons.

At Aunt Jane's estate the girls meet Uncle John, the mad gardener, and the boy Kenneth, whose story James later tells in strange detail. Chapters run through a first warning, a man with a bundle, duplicity, and the reading of the will. Patsy adopts an uncle, loses her job, and speaks frankly at the crisis. Baum writes brisk series fiction about money, character, and which niece deserves a fortune.
aunt-judy-s-tales: Mrs. Alfred Gatty's 1859 children's book gathers stories told by Aunt Judy to the little ones of a large family. The Little Victims, Vegetables Out of Place, Cook Stories, Rabbits' Tails and Out of the Way mix drollery with gentle moral teaching. Each tale is framed as fireside talk, with an elder girl amusing younger children while their mother rests nearby.
autobiographic-sketches:
Thomas De Quincey's Autobiographic Sketches gathers selections, grave and gay, from his published and unpublished writings. De Quincey writes to his American editor from Lasswade in January 1853, as he revises his works for republication in England.

He does not disown anything he has published, De Quincey insists, though some pieces served only a transient occasion and others might as well have been suppressed. Even pure levities, he adds, may lack any justifying principle of life within them. The sketches that follow mix memory, confession and wit. Readers of De Quincey will find here the opium-eater in reflective, autobiographical mood.
autobiographical-sketches:
Annie Besant published these sketches in 1885, answering friends who kept asking for an outline of her life. She also meant them as a defence against unfair attack. Born on the first of October 1847 within the sound of Bow bells, she was three quarters Irish by blood, her mother a Morris whose name had shifted from Maurice. A giddy aunt nicknamed the baby little Pheasantina.

Pages trace the road from devout childhood toward doubt. A Mr. Scott lets the young Besant write a tract on the nature and existence of God, warning that she faces the problem at last. Reading Bradlaugh's Plea for Atheism sharpened the turn. The sketches stop early in her public career, but they show the making of a famous freethinker in her own brisk words.
average-jones:
Samuel Hopkins Adams's Average Jones introduces a hero nicknamed by his own initials. Average Jones, whose parents gave him the initials A. V. R. E. before the surname Jones, seems a composite photograph of a thousand well-conditioned, clean-living young men.

Three men at the Cosmic Club open the book by asking what is the matter with Jones, and the stories that follow answer them case by case. Chapters include The B-Flat Trombone, Red Dot, Open Trail, The Mercy Sign, Blue Fires, Pin-Pricks, and The Million-Dollar Dog. Adams writes crisp, witty detective stories in which an apparently ordinary man notices what others miss. Readers who like clever, short mysteries will enjoy Jones immensely.
b-b-e-or-two-little-wooden-shoes:
Ouida — Louisa de la Ramée — wrote this Flemish tale, printed here in an 1896 edition. Bébée is sixteen as the story opens, springing out of bed at daybreak to a crowing cock under her lattice. She laughs at being a woman quite, with a kid bleating in the shed and a thrush in the sycamore. Her two little wooden shoes name her trade: an orphan flower-seller of Brussels.

Kindness from a great artist lifts her hopes, then teaches her the distance between worlds. Watching music and bright women through trees, she walks the stones with tears falling, sure he has not seen her and does not think of her. She has the dog's soul, the narrator says, without knowing it. Ouida builds a sentimental favourite on faithful, unrewarded love.
b09-luther-95theses:
Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses on October 31, 1517, under the formal title Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences. An indulgence was a church grant that cut the penalty for sin, and its sale had grown into a trade. Luther, a monk and teacher at Wittenberg, wrote in Latin for debate among scholars.

The theses attack the sale point by point and deny that the pope can free souls from purgatory at will. Luther asks what true sorrow for sin is worth next to a bought pardon. Few short texts have changed so much: this one lit the spark of the Reformation. It remains the most cited single document of that break.
b09-melanchthon-loci-communes:
Philipp Melanchthon was only twenty-four when his Loci Communes appeared in 1521. The Latin title means commonplaces, the main topics of theology set in order. No one had yet given the young Reformation a full, ordered system of teaching, and this book did it first.

Melanchthon builds the system straight from Paul's letter to the Romans, topic by topic. Sin, law, grace, and faith stand at the center of the scheme. The Latin text here follows the first form of the work, in the edition of G L Plitt as revised by Th Kolde. Students of the Reformation still treat it as the movement's first dogmatics.
baby-pitcher-s-trials-little-pitcher-sto:
Mrs. May — Carrie L. May — wrote these children's stories, published at Boston by Clark and Fiske in 1869 as part of the Little Pitcher Stories. Baby Pitcher is Flora, a small girl whose trials fill ten chapters. The frontispiece shows a funeral at page fifty-two, from the chapter where the children plan one in play.

Flora waits for the sun to drink up water, hears the story of the poor robin, and visits Grandma, where tarts are distributed and grievances get a hearing. Bertie meets Jack Midnight at the spring, a deadly snare waits for the muskrat, and Flora suffers exile before matters mend. May writes household morality at child scale: small faults, small sorrows, and forgiveness served with lunch, in the manner of postwar American Sunday reading.
back-to-god-s-country-and-other-stories:
James Oliver Curwood collected Back to God's Country and Other Stories from his tales of the Canadian north. The title story opens forty years before its climax, with Shan Tung travelling up the Fraser River. His Great Dane Tao, the biggest dog on the Height of Land, pulls his sledge alone. A drunken man's shot at Copper Creek Camp starts the long fuse.

Tao's blood survives in Wapi, a giant fighting dog of Coronation Gulf, born generations later. Other stories include The Fiddling Man, Peter God, and The Honor of Her People. Curwood sets gold camps, fur trails, and Eskimo igloos against each other. Dogs and men alike fight cold, hunger, and each other. His north is violent and romantic, a God's country judged by endurance and loyalty.
backlog-studies:
Charles Dudley Warner named these essays studies, and the first of them studies a disappearance: the open fire on the New England hearth. The hearth has gone out, he writes, and the family has lost its centre. No more toast-and-cider, no roasting apples before the coals, no grey-haired sires dozing in the chimney corner.

Warner builds the study into a small philosophy of the home. A house without a fire has no soul in it, nothing to rally round, and people move between rented rooms as they change clothes. The gas log with painted iron logs he calls a fraud and a blasphemy, because a fire you cannot poke is no fire. The later studies work the same vein of domestic observation, half lament and half comedy.
bagh-o-bahar-or-tales-of-the-four-darwes:
Duncan Forbes translated this Urdu classic from the Hindustani of Mir Amman of Dihli, publishing his version in 1874. Forbes, professor of Oriental languages at King's College London, notes that Bagh O Bahar — Garden and Spring — had stood for fifty years as a classical work across British India. Students used it to learn correct, idiomatic Hindustani and the manners behind the language.

Four dervishes tell their life stories to pass a night, each tale opening into marvels. One narrator wakes in a grave-like place, hears voices he takes for Nakir and Munkir, the angels who question the dead, and fumbles over bones in the dark while something chews nearby. Frame tale, romance, and language textbook in one, the book remains the standard doorway into Urdu prose.
balcony-stories:
Grace King published this set of New Orleans stories in 1892, framed as tales told on a balcony in the old Creole city. King knew that world from inside: French-speaking families, convent girls, and grandmothers whose memories reached back generations. Contents list La Grande Demoiselle, Mimi's Marriage, The Miracle Chapel, and The Little Convent Girl among fourteen pieces.

One story follows Little Mammy, who nursed sick white women across a war-stricken countryside, moving from patient to patient as emergencies of pain held her fast. She never travelled further than one refuge town of soldiers' wives and widows, and there she stayed, the only alleviation those poor women knew. King writes Creole Louisiana with a native's ear: charm, caste, and loss balanced on a balcony rail above the street.
ban-and-arriere-ban-a-rally-of-fugitive-:
Andrew Lang rallied his fugitive rhymes in Ban and Arriere Ban, printed at Edinburgh in 1894 and dedicated to Eleanor Charlotte Sellar. His verses, ghosts returning from dusty papers, are offered for the sake of other times. The contents open with A Scot to Jeanne d'Arc and a ballad of how Jacobites held the Bass Rock for King James in 1691 to 1693.

Three portraits of Prince Charles, versions from Omar Khayyam and Meleager, a haunted tower, and a ballade of Yule fill the middle. Poems address Stevenson and mourn places like the deserted spa hotel of the mid-book sonnet. Lang's occasional verse mixes Jacobite sentiment, Greek translation, and pure play with his usual polish.
baring-gould-curious-myths-1867-second-s:
Sabine Baring-Gould, a Devon priest with a vast store of lore, made this second set of his Curious Myths in 1867. The text here is the 1868 print. He dealt with the odd tales of the Middle Ages and sought their roots.

One long part traces the tale of Melusina, the fairy bride, from land to land. Swan maids and the Fortunate Isles, the isles of the blest in the west sea, fill other parts. The set was the main Victorian guide to such tales, read far past its own age.
bataille-de-dames:
Eugène Scribe and Ernest Legouvé wrote this three-act comedy, first played at the Théâtre Français in 1851; the hosted copy is a school edition with introduction, notes, and vocabulary by Benjamin W. Wells. Its subtitle is a duel in love. The Countess d'Autreval, her niece Léonie, and the young Gustave de Grignon and Henri de Flavigneul fill the château near Lyon where the scene is set.

Politics sharpens the flirtation: Grignon is a wanted man, and Baron de Montrichard can protect him only until the president of the provost court arrives. The countess, gazing at Grignon, assures the baron of her ascendancy over his spirit — he will not resist her. She must work fast, and the baron will not say why. Scribe's vaudeville machinery turns courtship into statecraft, with two clever women fighting the duel of the title.
be-be-e-or-two-little-wooden-shoes:
Louisa de la Ramée, called Ouida, published this tale in the edition of 1896, and the hosted text matches the printing found elsewhere in the library under a near-identical title. Bébée wakes on her sixteenth birthday in Brabant, wishing the crowing cock good day and laughing that no one may call her a child again. Bells from many steeples seem to agree how good it is to be so old.

Pretty, orphaned, and poor, she sells flowers in Brussels in her wooden shoes. A great man's kindness opens a brighter world she may watch but not enter. Coming home from the lacework she finds him among gay women and music; he does not see her, and the tears fall as she walks the stones. Ouida's sentimental story of faithful love unrewarded became a durable favourite.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-05-the-m:
John Lord's fifth Beacon Lights volume covers the Middle Ages, and the hosted text follows the later edition that numbers volumes by historical sequence. Mohammed and the Saracenic conquests open the lectures: public opinion about the prophet has changed, Lord notes, while the triumph of Mohammedanism still astonishes. Arabia's old religions and the systems it displaced set the scene.

Church and schoolmen fill the middle lectures. Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, gathers the Fathers' sayings into four books of Sentences, a manual shaped partly by Abelard's unsettling Sic et Non. That textbook, appearing near the middle of the twelfth century, ruled theological schools for generations. Lord moves from prophet to pope to friar with a lecturer's confidence, fitting the thousand years between Rome and the Renaissance into character sketches.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-3-part-1:
John Lord's Beacon Lights of History reaches the Middle Ages in this third volume's first part, an older lecture-order edition whose note points readers to a later renumbering. The lectures open with Mohammed and the Saracenic conquests, reviewing his early life, his wife Cadijeh, his meditations, and the flight to Medina. Lord tracks the astonishing triumph of Islam against older Arabian religions.

Later lectures treat the medieval church, Charlemagne's age, and the scholastic world, ending near Abelard, who died at Cluny in the arms of Peter the Venerable after condemnation. Lord, a popular American lecturer, wrote history as moral biography for lyceum audiences. His medieval volume shows both his narrative gift and his century's Protestant frame.
beneath-an-umbrella-from-twice-told-tale:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this sketch for Twice Told Tales, among the pieces he grouped as Night Sketches. Its whole action is a man staying indoors on a rainy winter's day, reading a book of travels beneath his umbrella of a roof. Pleasant is such a day within doors, he begins; the best amusement for it is a voyage on the page.

Fancy, he finds, works best against the rain. Strange landscapes glimmer through familiar walls, and outlandish figures press almost within the sacred precincts of the hearth. His small chamber proves wide enough for the ocean-like circumference of an Arabian desert, its sands tracked by a caravan's long line. The sketch is Hawthorne in miniature: no plot, only a mood studied until the room, the book, and the desert share one dusky light.
bert-wilson-in-the-rockies:
J. W. Duffield wrote this boys' adventure for the Bert Wilson series, copyrighted in 1914 and reprinted at Racine in 1924. Bert, an all-round athlete of Duffield's earlier track and wireless tales, goes west to a ranch in the Rockies. Contents promise the full frontier syllabus: busting a broncho, a grizzly at bay, a wolf pack, an Indian outbreak, and quick work on the draw.

One tale is told as a campfire memory: a winter ride, snow falling at four in the afternoon, the narrator cold and hungry and thinking only of a late supper. Danger arrives as a sound in the distance. Trailing outlaws and a race for life close the contents. Duffield writes the Stratemeyer-era series formula straight, with Bert's cool head settling every crisis the mountains arrange.
best-russian-short-stories:
Thomas Seltzer compiled and edited this anthology of Russian tales in translation, fronted by a portrait of Chekhov as Russia's greatest short-story writer. The contents run the whole nineteenth-century school: Pushkin's Queen of Spades, Gogol's Cloak, Turgenev's District Doctor, and Dostoyevsky's Christmas Tree and the Wedding. Tolstoy, Saltykov, Korolenko, and Garshin follow, then three Chekhovs — The Darling, The Bet, and Vanka.

Seltzer's motto claims everything in Russian fiction bows to humanitarian ideals and fidelity to life. Garshin's Signal supplies the sample: a railway line made perfect for an inspection, ballast laid, sleepers examined, yellow sand sprinkled at the crossings, while great personages approach from St. Petersburg. Sologub, Gorky, Andreyev, and Kuprin carry the book into the modern age, making it a one-volume survey of the Russian story's golden century.
best-short-stories:
Thomas L. Masson collected this volume of comic tales for Doubleday, Page in 1922, under the Review of Reviews imprint. Masson, editor of Life magazine, opens with a foreword to everybody on the point of a good joke. Doctors, lawyers, family men, and soldiers, he says, are each sensitised to their own fields. A first-class joke, though, strikes home to the majority because human nature works by universal laws.

The pieces are magazine humour at its most polished: anecdotes, dialogues, and twist endings. One suitor, nerve failing him nightly, takes his Maria to their favourite seat — a gravestone in the village churchyard. Inspiration strikes: when you die, he trembles, how should you like to be buried here with my name on the stone over you? A section headed Knew More About Hens Than History promises the level: bright, brief, and built for the train.
between-whiles:
Helen Hunt Jackson published this set of stories in 1888, signing herself H. H. beside the titles of Ramona and A Century of Dishonor. The Inn of the Golden Pear opens the contents in verse: children sell their diamond stones for glass while knaves pass worthless stones for diamonds. The Mystery of Wilhelm Rütter, The Captain of the Heather Bell, Dandy Steve, and The Prince's Little Sweetheart follow.

Wilhelm's mystery is a cure that looks like a curse. The silent man rattles with merry talk till the old kitchen echoes with laughter. Carlen grows cold with fear: surely this ringing laugh means but one thing, and Wilhelm himself says he has been ill till today and now is well. Jackson, dying as she wrote, fills these tales with her Colorado light and her pity for the misjudged.
beyond-these-voices:
M. E. Braddon published this late novel with Hutchinson of London in 1910, in the firm's sevenpenny copyright series. Lady Felicia Disbrowe was supposed to condescend when she married Captain Cunningham, and the marriage's strains drive the tale. Braddon, the queen of sensation fiction since Lady Audley's Secret, here writes of faith and doubt inside a household rather than bigamy and arson.

A wife's consolation gives the sampled scene its title's meaning. Hand on her husband's shoulder, she reminds him of his happy, innocent boyhood and its unquestioning faith, before the leaven of doubt made the Christian youth a trifler and cynic. He listens in silence, eyes downcast. Beyond these voices — the world's and doubt's — Braddon sets an older music, and her doubter must decide whether he can still hear it.
billy-whiskers-adventures:
Frances Trego Montgomery continued her goat's career in this later volume of the Billy Whiskers books. Billy now travels with two dogs, Button and Stubby. The front matter shows the trio at work. Button runs off with a big lamb chop between his teeth, Stubby with a huge steak. Billy contents himself with a head of lettuce. Appetites launch most of the adventures.

Stubby turns messenger in the sampled tale. A note arrives at a country store folded in a handkerchief tied round the little dog's neck. The storekeeper lifts him to the counter and reads it aloud to the men: no person brought it, the dog carried it himself. Montgomery writes animal slapstick with a farm wife's knowledge — goats butt, dogs steal, and every creature's character is its species turned up loud for child readers.
biographical-sketches-from-fanshawe-and-:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's biographical sketches appear here as printed in Fanshawe and Other Pieces, his posthumous miscellany. Five lives make the set: Mrs. Hutchinson, Sir William Phips, Sir William Pepperell, Thomas Green Fessenden, and Jonathan Cilley. Anne Hutchinson opens the series. Hawthorne turns her story toward his own century with uneasy wit. He notes portents of public women in the press, and the changing habits of the gentle sex.

Fessenden, the poet-lawyer of Tractoration fame, gets the warmest treatment. His grotesque rhymes fit each to each as accurately as echoes, Hawthorne says, and his thoughts are thrown off as distinctly as impressions from a type. A man who caricatured his own features, he laughed heartily at perceiving the resemblance. These magazine sketches show Hawthorne practising biography as moral portraiture, years before the custom-house introductions.
biographies-of-distinguished-scientific-:
François Arago's biographies of scientific men appear here in English, translated by Admiral W. H. Smyth, the Reverend Baden Powell, and Robert Grant for Ticknor and Fields of Boston in 1859. This first series joins Arago's own autobiography to his memoirs of eminent men of science, continental and British. The translators warn that the autobiography bears the stamp of his ardent and energetic disposition throughout.

Arago's life runs from observatory to revolution. One passage defends the Paris regime of 1848 against bitter blame. The red flag raised under martial law was too small, a pocket flag. Worse, it stood in the column where the crowd could not see it. The astronomer who measured the meridian also governed France for a season, and his éloges of Fourier, Fresnel, and their peers carry a statesman's authority into the history of science.
blackfeet-indian-stories:
George Bird Grinnell published these Blackfeet tales in 1915, a companion to his Blackfeet Lodge Tales. Grinnell, who had wintered with the tribe and been adopted into it, addresses the reader directly before the stories begin. Names throughout carry the breves and macrons of the printed book, marked in this text the first time each word appears. Cold Maker, spirit of winter, fronts the volume as frontispiece.

Fisher and Weasel Heart carry one tale of a water lodge. Fisher waits long by the stream, afraid something bad has happened to his friend. Weasel Heart comes out and reports another lodge in the water, painted with yellow buffalo, still there to be entered. Go you into the water as I did, he says. Grinnell's stories keep the tribe's own tellers' manner — medicine, animal helpers, and instruction carried inside adventure.
blister-jones:
John Taintor Foote made his first book, Blister Jones, from life around American race tracks, and Indianapolis publisher Bobbs-Merrill issued it in 1913. Foote frames the tales through a narrator who takes a magazine horse story to a real trainer. The trainer's verdict starts the book.

Blister Jones, horse trainer by trade and gent by instinct, tells what the printed story got wrong. Linked sketches follow horses, owners, grooms, and hangers-on in their own rough speech. Foote knows the stable yard at first hand, and the talk rings true. Poems on the thoroughbred break up the prose. The result honors the men who work with horses while it gently mocks fine writing about them from the outside.
bob-chester-s-grit-or-from-ranch-to-rich:
Frank V Webster wrote Bob Chester's Grit, a boys' novel issued by Cupples and Leon of New York in 1911. Webster sends young Bob Chester west under a cloud, with a kind waitress, a reporter, and railroad men as his helpers. Oklahoma and a ranch at Fairfax form the goal.

Bob misses the woman he seeks, rides alone in a strange city, and earns his passage at the throttle of a freight engine. A tale of the plains and a kind act done on the road shape his luck. At Fairfax he finds work, a partner, and a ranch of his own. The firm of Ford and Chester thrives by the close. Young readers get a plain tale of pluck, honesty, and reward in the West.
boethius-consolation-philosophy-james:
Boethius, a Roman senator and scholar, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison in 524, awaiting execution under King Theodoric. H. R. James's English translation is the text here. Boethius had been the king's chief minister; now, stripped of office and wealth, he wrote his way toward calm.

Lady Philosophy visits his cell and talks him out of self-pity, step by step. She shows that fortune's gifts were never truly his, and that the good cannot be taken by force.
