The famous wheel of fortune turns through the book. Verse and prose trade places as the argument climbs. It was among the most loved books of the Middle Ages.
bohemian-days-three-american-tales:
George Alfred Townsend, who signed himself Gath, published Bohemian Days with H Campbell of New York in 1880. Townsend gathers three American tales with short verse chords between them. A preface dates the first tale to 1864 and a reading among its own subjects.

The Rebel Colony in Paris shows Southern refugees and skedaddlers abroad in the Civil War. Married Abroad etches a young Northern truant overseas in the same years. The Deaf Man of Kensington recalls an old Philadelphia suburb then being swallowed by the city. Verse pieces on grisette and pigeon girl lighten the frame. Townsend claims the set as a rare record of refugee life. Readers get war-era bohemia on two sides of the Atlantic.
brazilian-sketches:
T. B. Ray's Brazilian Sketches reports his travels in Brazil for American church readers. Ray, Educational Secretary of the Southern Baptist Foreign Mission Board, dined with a businessman ignorant of missions and resolved to write what missions do. His contents run from the country and its capital, Rio de Janeiro, to a visit to a country church. Two presidents, saint worship, and penance frame his argument. Brazil is Catholic in form, hungry in fact, and open to the Bible carried by native Christians whose mettle he praises.

Inside, travel alternates with testimony: converts like Jose Barretto, persecution endured, and the Bible as a missionary factor. The urgent call and the last stand of the Latin race close the appeal. Readers get a primary document of Protestant missions in South America, part travelogue, part fundraising sermon, wholly certain of its cause.
britannica-1911-abbadides:
Abbadides names a dynasty in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, the Muslim house that ruled Seville from about 1023 to 1091. The entry calls the line short-lived yet singularly active, a type of its age. Abd-ul-Qasim Mahommed, cadi of Seville, founded the house from an Arab family grown rich in the city.

His son El Motaddid, poet, poisoner, and sceptic, kept his enemies' skulls as flower-pots and chests. Wars with Granada and tribute to Castile marked the reign. El Motamid, the last king, loved verse, his poet-vizir Ibn Ammar, and his wife Romaica past prudence. False coin paid to Alphonso brought ruin, and the Almoravides he called in ended his house. Poet-kings fill a vivid, grim page of Spanish history.
britannica-1911-abencerrages:
Abencerrages names a family in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, a faction of note in Moorish Granada in the fifteenth century. The name likely springs from Yussuf ben-Serragh, who served Mahommed the Seventh well in his fights to hold a crown lost three times. Certainty ends there, the entry warns.

Romance carries the name further than record can. Perez de Hita's Guerras civiles de Granada tells their feuds with the rival Zegris and the cruel end dealt them. Florian and Chateaubriand borrowed the tale for French readers. The Alhambra holds a hall of the Abencerrages, named for the massacre said to have stained it. Family, feud, and fiction blend so fully that the entry sorts them with care.
britannica-1911-abington-frances:
Frances Abington receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. Abington, a soldier's daughter born in 1737, began as flower girl and street singer. Service with a French milliner taught her dress and French, tools of her later trade.

The Haymarket saw her first in 1755. Drury Lane under Garrick held her eighteen years from her Irish success as Lady Townley, and she created Lady Teazle in 1777 among thirty new parts. Portia, Desdemona, and Ophelia stood beside her Hoydens and Prues. Reynolds painted her as Miss Prue. Fashion copied her frocks, and the Abington cap spread her name. Covent Garden, a late return, and death in 1815 close the life.
britannica-1911-abipones:
Abipones receives a tribal entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Abipones, a Guaycuran people, once held the Paraguay Chaco till Spanish hostility drove them between Santa Fé and St Iago. Jesuit Martin Dobrizhoffer lived seven years among them and counted some 5,000.

Foreheads plucked bare as a tribal mark, tattooed women, and pierced lips and ears mark their look in his account. Bow and spear, tapir-hide armour under jaguar skin, fine swimming and riding fill the war sketch. Flood months meant island or tree-shelter living. Marriage bargains could be refused by the girl outright, a custom Darwin quotes. Two children at most were reared, by hard subsistence rule. The tribe is now believed extinct, the entry closes.
britannica-1911-aborigines:
Aborigines receives an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The word first names a mythical people of central Italy, tied in legend to Aeneas, Latinus, and Evander. They were said to descend from the hills near Reate, drive out the Siceli, and settle as Latini.

Name study divides scholars: ab origine, the original folk, clashes with Cato's view of them as Greek immigrants. Tree-born and nomad readings fare no better, and the entry grants no result. Modern use widens the word to any land's first-found inhabitants. The Aborigines' Protection Society, founded in 1838 after Buxton's inquiry, closes the entry with its work against colonial cruelty.
britannica-1911-abrahamites:
Abrahamites receives a sect entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Abrahamites were deists of eighteenth-century Bohemia who claimed the pre-circumcised Abraham as their pattern. One God, the Decalogue, and the Paternoster bounded their whole profession of faith.

They refused classing as Christians or as Jews. Joseph the Second's edict of toleration of 1781 therefore left them outside its shelter. Deportation scattered the sect, the men drafted into frontier regiments. Some turned Roman Catholic. The rest could not hand their views to the next generation, and the movement died with its holders, the entry records in a handful of lines.
britannica-1911-abrantes:
Abrantes receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Portuguese town crowns a hill of olive woods, gardens, and vines above the Tagus's right bank, where two railways join. Fruit, olive oil, and grain drive its trade.

Command of the highway down the Tagus valley to Lisbon makes Abrantes a standing military prize. An Iberian settlement of about 300 B.C. took the Roman name Aurantes, perhaps from alluvial gold in the river. Mosaics, coins, and an aqueduct mark the old ground. Junot took the town for France in 1807 and gained a dukedom from it. The Convention of Cintra restored it in 1808. Some 7,255 folk lived there in 1900.
britannica-1911-achaemenes:
Achaemenes, in Persian Hakhamani, is the ancestor who gave his name to the royal house of Persia, the Achaemenidae, a clan of the Pasargadae tribe. Darius, in the Behistun inscription, makes him father of Teispes and great-grandfather of Cyrus the Great. Cyrus himself, in his proclamation to the Babylonians, never mentions the name, so the entry admits we cannot decide whether he was a real person or a mythical founder.

Kingship followed the line. Teispes and his successors ruled Anshan as vassals of Media until Cyrus founded the Persian empire in 550 B.C. Every later Persian king called himself an Achaemenid, and the house ended with Darius III in 330. A second Achaemenes, son of Darius I, governed Egypt and died fighting rebels there.
britannica-1911-achates: Achates is the companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid. That epic tells of Rome's founding hero. This entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica is a single sentence. Achates has almost no story of his own. His fame is a phrase. Fidus Achates, faithful Achates, became proverbial in Latin. Later languages use it too. It names a loyal and devoted companion. His constancy needs no adventures to prove it.
britannica-1911-achilles:
Achilles is one of the most famous heroes of Greek legend and the central figure of Homer's Iliad. Son of Peleus, king of the Myrmidones in Thessaly, and of the sea nymph Thetis, he was raised with his friend Patroclus and taught war, eloquence, music, and medicine. When called to the Trojan war he sailed at once with fifty ships.

Later writers added the tales everyone knows. Thetis dipped the child in the river Styx, making him invulnerable except at the heel she held him by, hence the heel of Achilles. Hidden in women's clothes on Scyros, he betrayed himself by seizing a spear. The epics beyond Homer tell of his killing Penthesileia and Memnon, then falling to Paris's arrow, guided by Apollo.
britannica-1911-achimenes:
Achimenes is a genus of plants in the family Gesneraceae, kin to the gloxinia and streptocarpus, native to tropical America. Gardeners know the plants well as stove or warm greenhouse favourites. They are herbaceous perennials, plants that live several years without woody stems, generally with hairy, serrated leaves and handsome flowers whose tubular corolla spreads into a wide limb.

Colour is their selling point. Flowers run through white, yellow, orange, crimson, scarlet, blue, and purple, and many hybrids exist in cultivation. Growers keep the plants in the warm stove until flowering, then move them to the greenhouse. Propagation is easy several ways: by cuttings, by leaves pricked into sandy soil, by scales from the underground tubers, or by the very small seeds.
britannica-1911-acid-amides:
Acid-amides are chemical compounds derived from ammonia by replacing its hydrogen atoms with acid residues. Replacing one, two, or three hydrogens gives primary, secondary, and tertiary amides, of which the primary kind matters most. Chemists prepare them by distilling ammonium salts of acids, by partly hydrolysing nitriles, or by treating acid chlorides, anhydrides, or esters with ammonia.

Behaviour fills the technical entry. Primary amides are mostly solid crystals, soluble in water when small, and they break back into acid and ammonia when boiled with acids or alkalies. Nitrous acid frees their nitrogen, and a famous reaction with bromine and potash converts an amide into an amine with one carbon fewer. Formamide, acetamide, and benzamide serve as worked examples.
britannica-1911-acinaces:
Acinaces was an ancient Persian sword. It was short and straight. Persians wore it on the right side of the body. Romans wore their swords on the left. Some Persians wore it in front instead. Reliefs at Persepolis show it carried that way. Persepolis was the old Persian capital. The entry treats the weapon as more than a sidearm. It was partly a badge. It was partly a sacred object.

Gold marked rank. Among Persian nobles the sword was often made of gold. It served as a badge of distinction. Herodotus is cited for a stranger fact. The Scythians treated the acinaces as an object of worship. Other peoples did the same. A sword set up could be honoured as a god's emblem.
britannica-1911-acotyledones:
Acotyledones was the name Jussieu gave in 1789 to the lowest class in his system of botany. The class embraced all flowerless plants. Ferns, lycopods, and horse-tails belonged to it. So did mosses, liverworts, sea-weeds, lichens, and fungi. The name points to a missing seed-leaf. A cotyledon is the seed-leaf inside a seed. Flowering plants bear seeds with embryos. Those embryos carry one or two cotyledons.

Flowerless plants have no seed at all. Hence they can have no true cotyledon. Later systems replaced the term with Cryptogams. That word means plants with hidden reproduction. Readers of older botany books meet both names. They mark an era when flowerlessness defined a whole kingdom rank.
britannica-1911-adamites:
Adamites, or Adamians, were a sect of heretics. They flourished in North Africa in the second and third centuries. Gnostic and ascetic doctrines probably formed their basis. Members claimed restoration to Adam's original innocency. That claim drove their rejection of marriage. Marriage, they said, existed only because of sin. They lived in absolute lawlessness instead. Whatever they did, they held, was neither good nor bad.

Survival of the sect was brief. The obscure group did not itself last long. Its doctrines revived in medieval Europe, though. The Brethren of the Free Spirit took them up. Sisters of the Free Spirit shared the revival. The entry treats a small sect with a long shadow.
britannica-1911-adhemar-de-chabannes:
Adhemar de Chabannes is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born about 988 at Chabannes in France, he was a monk and writer of chronicles. He was schooled at the abbey of Saint Martial at Limoges and lived as a monk there and at Angouleme.

The article centres on his main work, a history of the Franks in three books. It spans from the fabled King Pharamond down to the year 1028. The first two books mostly copy an older work on the Frankish kings. The third book, on the years 814 to 1028, holds real worth for later readers. He died about 1030, most likely at Jerusalem while on a pilgrimage.
britannica-1911-agapemonites:
Agapemonites, also called the Community of the Son of Man, were a sect founded in 1846. The 1911 Britannica article names its founder as Henry James Prince, a Church of England clergyman. Prince first trained in medicine and worked at a Bath hospital. Ill health drove him out, and in 1837 he entered a Welsh college for the church. There he drew a band of keen young men around him, known as the Lampeter Brethren.

Prince held that he had been taken into the person of God. His first charge was a Somerset parish, where his rector read a sermon of his and was won to his views. The two men drew many converts, but the church cast them out. They set up a free church of their own for a short time. The sect's aim, says the article, was to raise marriage to a holy state under odd rules.
britannica-1911-agatharchides: Agatharchides of Cnidus, a Greek writer on lands and past events, lived in the time of Ptolemy Philometor, who reigned from 181 to 146 BC. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his works on Asia, on Europe, and on the Red Sea. Long parts of the Red Sea work survive in Photius, who praised his style, which was shaped on that of Thucydides. Short as the notice is, it gives a clear fix on a lost Greek author whose words now reach us only in part.
britannica-1911-agathocles:
Agathocles, a tyrant of Syracuse who lived from 361 to 289 before Christ, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in Sicily, the son of a potter who had moved to Syracuse. He learned his father's trade, then joined the army. Twice he was exiled for bids to topple the ruling few.

In 317 he came back with hired troops and made himself master of the city. He built a strong army and fleet and took most of Sicily. At war with Carthage, he broke a siege and struck at the foe in Africa. He won at first, then lost and fled home. Peace made, he called himself king of Sicily.
britannica-1911-agonothetes:
Agonothetes was the president of the sacred games in ancient Greece. He superintended the contests at the festivals. At first the games' founder filled the role. That founder also defrayed the expenses personally. Great public games changed the arrangement later. Olympic and Pythian presidents represented different states. Host peoples also chose presidents from themselves. Athens elected ten athlothetae for its Panathenaic festival. Their term ran four years at a time.

Names for the office vary widely. Aisymnetai, brabeutai, and agonarchai all appear. Athlothetai was the Athenian title specifically. Rhabdouchoi took their name from the rod. That rod symbolized their authority over contests. Functions stayed generally the same throughout Greece. Superintendence of sacred contests was the core duty.
britannica-1911-agricola-johannes:
Johannes Agricola (1494-1566) was a German Protestant reformer. Schneider was his birth name, later Schnitter. Eisleben was his birthplace, hence Magister Islebius. Wittenberg study gained him Luther's friendship early. He recorded proceedings at the Leipzig assembly in 1519. Frankfort and Eisleben posts followed in reform work. In 1536 Wittenberg recalled him to teach. Controversy erupted almost at once with Luther.

Doctrine split the old friends bitterly. Agricola taught Christians are free from Mosaic law wholly. Only the gospel binds the regenerate, he held. Luther branded those views Antinomian, against law. Agricola left secretly for Berlin in 1540. Brandenburg's elector made him court preacher there. He helped prepare the Augsburg Interim of 1548. He died in a plague epidemic in 1566.
britannica-1911-agriculture-agricultural:
Agricultural Population and Wages charts Britain's rural shrinkage. The last half of the nineteenth century saw remarkable diminution. Before 1871 rural labour supply exceeded demand. Many labourers were only in partial employment then. Their withdrawal mattered little at that stage. Permanent workers' shrinkage later turned serious. Tables track persons engaged in agriculture across decades. Numbers fell from over three million four hundred thousand in 1851. By 1901 they stood near two million two hundred thousand.

Causes and a counter-trend close the section. Less cultivated area reduced demand for hands. Land laid down to pasture needed fewer workers. Machinery spread through farms in the same decades. Cash wages rose steadily all the while, though. Board of Trade figures show ordinary labourers' weekly pay climbing. Eastern counties lagged the national average consistently.
britannica-1911-agriculture-breed-societ:
Breed Societies are voluntary associations of British stockbreeders. Their object is promoting their respective breeds of livestock. Formation of such societies marked the late nineteenth century. The Shire Horse Society is the typical example given. It incorporated in 1878 to improve Shire cart-horses. Sound, healthy sires were distributed through the country. Annual shows and a stud book serve that aim. Medals at agricultural shows reward the best animals.

No public money supports any of them. The entry stresses that voluntary character pointedly. Hackney and Hunters' societies follow the same lines. Cattle societies keep herd books for each breed. Shorthorn, Hereford, and Aberdeen-Angus societies head the list. Sheep and pig breeders have their own associations. Addresses appear yearly in the Live Stock Journal Almanac.
britannica-1911-aguascalientes:
Aguascalientes, an inland state of Mexico, is covered by an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Zacatecas bounds it on the north, east, and west, and Jalisco on the south. Its people numbered about 102,416 in 1900, over an area of 2,970 square miles. The state sits on a high plateau between spurs of the Sierra Madre and fertile eastern plains.

Streams and the Aguascalientes river water the land, and the climate is mild with moderate rain. Northern and western valleys farm, while the plains raise stock, and corn, flour, cattle, horses, mules, and hides go out to neighbouring states. The capital, also Aguascalientes, takes its name from hot springs used as medicine nearby. Its cotton mills, smelting works, potteries, and tanneries made it a busy rail centre northwest of Mexico City.
britannica-1911-aigues-mortes:
Walls make Aigues-Mortes famous: few towns in France keep their medieval ring so whole. The town of the Gard department stands twenty-five miles south-south-west of Nimes on a branch rail line, alone in the marshy plain at the west end of the Rhone delta. Its people numbered 3,577. The ramparts form a long box of walls with notched tops, up to thirty-six feet high, studded with towers.

The Tour de Constance, raised by Louis IX, holds two round rooms with vaulted roofs. Protestants were jailed in them after the edict of Nantes was called back. The rest of the walls date to the reign of Philip III. Canals join the town to Beaucaire, to Cette, to the Lesser Rhone, and to the sea. Fishing and soda making keep it fed.
britannica-1911-aire-landes:
Aire, in the Landes department of south-west France, is a bishop's seat on the left bank of the Adour, twenty-two miles south-east of Mont-de-Marsan along the Southern railway. Its people numbered 2,283 in 1906. A cathedral from the twelfth century and a bishop's palace give the old centre its weight, though both have been rebuilt and mended again and again.

A church in the suburb of Mas d'Aire beats both for interest. St Quitterie, built of brick in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, hides Gallo-Roman tombs in its crypt, among them the fifth-century stone coffin of the saint herself. Aire went by the name Atura in Roman days and housed Visigoth kings. Alaric II set down his famed code there, and its line of bishops runs back to the fifth century.
britannica-1911-albery-james:
James Albery (1838–1889) wrote plays at a desk in an architect's office before the stage would have him. Born in London in May 1838, he quit school for that office and penned plays on the side. Loss after loss came first. Then Dr Davy, a piece he had adapted, reached the Lyceum in 1866 and his stage career began.

Two Roses, a comedy staged at the Vaudeville in 1870, proved his biggest hit. In it Sir Henry Irving won one of his first London triumphs, as Digby Grant. Albery turned out many more plays and adaptations. Jingle, his take on Pickwick, played the Lyceum in 1878. Pink Dominoes came from his run of French pieces recast for the Criterion, where his wife, the famed actress Mary Moore, took the lead roles. He died in August 1889.
britannica-1911-alcala-de-henares:
Alcala de Henares, a town of Spain, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Madrid, seventeen miles east-north-east of the capital, on the river Henares and the Madrid to Saragossa railway. Its 11,206 people in 1900 lived in a town of slight trade but great historical interest. The place has been identified with the Roman Complutum.

Complutum was destroyed about the year 1000 and rebuilt by the Moors in 1083. Cardinal Jimenes de Cisneros founded its richly endowed university in 1510, which at its height held 12,000 students and ranked second only to Salamanca. The famous Complutensian Polyglot Bible was prepared there from 1514 to 1517. Cervantes, Spain's greatest writer, was born in the town, as were the emperor Ferdinand I and the dramatist Solis. When the university moved to Madrid in 1836, Alcala declined fast.
britannica-1911-alcamenes:
Alcamenes, a Greek sculptor tied to Lemnos and Athens, worked in the shadow of Pheidias, the great Athenian master of the age just before his own. Fine detail and a polished finish marked his output. Two pieces won special note: his Hephaestus, and his Aphrodite, the one called of the Gardens.

Pausanias gives Alcamenes one of the gable groups on the temple of Zeus at Olympia. That claim fails on dates and on style alike. A copy of his Hermes Propylaeus head, dug up at Pergamum in 1903, helps little either, since it shows the god in a stiff, old-fashioned mode. Sound ground for judging him lies in the carved work of the Parthenon. He all but surely had a hand in it, under the lead of Pheidias.
britannica-1911-alcibiades:
Alcibiades, an Athenian general and politician who lived from about 450 to 404 B.C., receives a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Athens to the Alcmaeonid family, he was a near relative of Pericles, who became his guardian after his father Cleinias fell at Coroneia in 447. Beauty, great wealth, and no father's control shaped a self-willed, passionate youth.

His teachers taught him to laugh at common ideas of justice, temperance, holiness, and patriotism. Socrates' hard, simple life he could admire but not imitate, and his vanity, loves, and impious revels grew notorious. Yet his abilities outran his vices, the entry insists. War made him Athens' brilliant, unstable champion. Later, Sparta ordered his execution on Agis's urging, and Alcibiades crossed to the Persian Tissaphernes in 412, advising him to let Athens and Sparta wear each other out.
britannica-1911-aldehydes:
Aldehydes, a class of chemical compounds, are treated in a long technical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their general formula is given, with a variable group joined to the CHO group that defines them. The name comes from alcohol dehydrogenatum, alcohol stripped of hydrogen, since aldehydes can be prepared by oxidising alcohols. The article works as a chemist's survey of the whole family.

Lower aldehydes are neutral liquids with a characteristic smell, soluble in water and quick to evaporate, though formaldehyde is a gas. As carbon content grows, the members dissolve less, smell less, and end as odourless solids. Preparation methods include careful oxidation of primary alcohols, distilling calcium salts with calcium formate, and breaking down acetals. Long tables then list individual aldehydes, from acrolein and crotonic aldehyde to benzaldehyde, with their boiling points, the working data of the laboratory.
britannica-1911-algae-uses:
Uses, a short section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, takes stock of algae in human industry. Its verdict is modest at the start. Algae, it says, cannot be regarded as directly important in the industries. The uses that follow are local, coastal, and mostly old, drawn from what the sea throws up or what nearby communities gather.

On European coasts, marine algae torn loose by autumn gales are commonly carted onto the land as a convenient manure. Two kinds serve as food locally: Porphyra laciniata, and Rhodymenia palmata, the latter known as dulse. Agar-agar, a gelatinous substance used to set foods and cultures, comes from an eastern species of Gracilaria. Seaweed ash, called kelp in Scotland and varec in Brittany, was once a major source of iodine, though less so by the time of writing.
britannica-1911-almogavares:
Hard frontier foot-soldiers from Spain, the Almogávares won fame in the Christian reconquest and then sold their spears across Italy and the Levant in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Their name comes from an Arabic word for a scout. First raised in the Pyrenees, they were later drawn mostly from Navarre, Aragon, and Catalonia.

Skins served them for clothing, and armour they had none. Each man carried two heavy javelins, a short stabbing sword, and a shield, much like a Roman legionary, and their order, fierceness, and throws could break heavy cavalry. After serving Peter III of Aragon past the Sicilian Vespers, they marched east under Roger di Flor against the Turks. His killing in 1305 turned them on the Byzantine emperor: Gallipoli became their base while they laid waste the lands near Constantinople.
britannica-1911-almohades:
One God, with no separate traits standing apart from him: that hard teaching on God's unity drove the Almohades. Their founder, Mahommed ibn Tūmart, was a Berber of the Atlas, a mosque lamplighter's son famed for piety from youth. He made the pilgrimage to Mecca, studied at Bagdad in the school of al Ashāri, and shaped his own system with mystic touches drawn from Ghazāli.

Home in Morocco, Ibn Tūmart preached against loose living, struck at wine-shops, and clashed with the ruling Almoravides. The power he raised, properly Muwāḥḥadis or Unitarians, founded the fifth Moorish dynasty in the twelfth century and won all northern Africa up to Egypt, together with Muslim Spain. Strict law and teaching on fate mark the movement, and its later rulers are listed down to 1269.
britannica-1911-almoravides:
A pilgrimage set the Almoravides in motion. About 1040 the Lamtūna chief Yahya ibn Ibrāhīm travelled to Mecca and, through teachers at Kairawān, brought back a missionary, Abd-Allah ibn Yāzīn. Turned away at first, the man withdrew to an island monastery in the Niger, and from there his strict teaching spread. The Lamtūna, the veiled men of the upper Niger, were the strongest tribe behind the movement.

Properly Murābiṭis, the Almoravides were a Berber people from the Sahara whose name comes from an Arabic word for a religious ascetic. Converted early, the Lamtūna at first knew little of Islam past its creed's formula. In the eleventh century they founded Morocco's fourth dynasty, and through it the Moorish empire grew over Tlemcen and much of Spain and Portugal. Arabic and European sources for that rise close the account.
britannica-1911-anne-of-cleves:
Anne of Cleves is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a queen of England. She lived from 1515 to 1557. She was the fourth wife of King Henry the Eighth. Her father was John, duke of Cleves. Her mother was Mary, heir of the duke of Juliers. Anne was born on the twenty second of September 1515. Her father led the German Protestants of his day.

After Queen Jane Seymour died, Cromwell eyed Anne as a match. She had been raised in strict retirement at home. She spoke no tongue but her own, the entry says. Her gifts were needlework and a meek, gentle temper. She brought no dowry to the marriage plan. A portrait by Holbein pleased the king, all the same. A treaty for the marriage was signed in 1539. She landed at Deal late that year. Henry met her at Rochester and was taken aback.
britannica-1911-antibes:
Antibes is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a seaport town of France. It lies in the department of the Alpes-Maritimes. It once lay in the department of the Var. It moved when the new department formed in 1860. Counts from 1906 give the town 5730 people. The wider commune held 11,753 in that count. Nice lies to the north east by rail. The town sits on the east side of the Garoupe peninsula.

It was formerly fortified with strong ramparts. All those walls, save one fort, have been demolished. That fort, the Fort Carre, was built by Vauban. A new town is rising on the site of the walls. Its chief exports are dried fruits, salt fish, and oil. Much perfume distilling is done in the town. Antibes is the ancient Antipolis of Greek settlers.
britannica-1911-antilles:
Antilles, a name for the West India Islands, is traced in a brief place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name rests on Antilia, a land of old sea charts from before the New World was found. Such lands shifted in size and place on those charts from age to age. In time the name was tied to the lands found by Columbus. When those lands proved to be a great chain of isles, the name took its plural form.

The chain rings the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico on the map. A split is made in the text between two sets of isles. The Greater Antilles hold Cuba, Jamaica, Haiti, and Porto Rico. The Lesser Antilles hold all the rest of the chain.
britannica-1911-antiphanes:
Antiphanes was the most important writer of the Middle Attic comedy after Alexis, and this short 1911 Britannica entry sums up his work. He lived from about 408 to 334 before Christ. He seems to have been a foreigner who settled in Athens, where he began to write about 387. He was extremely prolific as a playwright.

Of the comedies credited to him, counted at 365 or at 260, more than two hundred are known by their titles. Large pieces of them survive in the writings of Athenaeus. They deal chiefly with matters of the table, the entry says, but hold many striking thoughts as well. The entry closes by pointing to the printed collection of his fragments and to studies of the Greek comic poets.
britannica-1911-antipodes:
Antipodes is a term from Greek for feet set against feet, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a strict sense. It means two places on far sides of the earth, so placed that a line from one to the other cuts through the centre of the globe. London and Antipodes Island, near New Zealand, serve as the near case.

Such places stand a half circle of longitude apart. One lies as far north of the equator as the other lies south. Noon at one is midnight at the other, and the longest day at one matches the shortest at the other. The entry then takes up the snarl of dates. A sailor who goes east gains hours, and one who goes west loses them, so the two can differ by a full day when they meet. A set line where dates are brought into line is the fix.
britannica-1911-antisthenes:
Antisthenes, who lived from about 444 to 365 before Christ, founded the Cynic school of thought. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his path from rhetoric lessons to the feet of Socrates. Born at Athens to a Thracian mother, he first studied speech under Gorgias and others. A fall into poverty may have turned his mind to plainer values.

So keen was he to hear Socrates that he walked each day from Peiraeus to Athens. He set up his own school in the Cynosarges hall for outcast youth. There he drew the poor by a life and teaching of stark simple form. His cloak, staff, and wallet became the badge of his followers.
britannica-1911-apelles:
Apelles is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a painter of the ancient world. The text calls him in all likelihood the greatest painter of that age. He lived from the time of Philip of Macedon past Alexander's death. Born Ionian, he trained at the famed school of Sicyon under Pamphilus.

At Philip's court he painted the king and the young Alexander with success. That work made him the named court painter of Macedon. His Alexander with a thunderbolt was his most famed piece of art. Portraits of Clitus, Archelaus, and Antigonus are also listed by name. A great piece on Calumny and an Aphrodite rising from the sea are named. None of his works live on in copy form, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-aphides:
Aphides are tiny insects known as plant lice, blight, or green fly. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places them among the true bugs. They have long feelers and legs and paired tubes on the body. Those tubes give off a waxy fluid. The sweet honey dew that ants seek comes from the gut instead. Both winged and wingless forms occur in each sex.

Their breeding is the marvel of the entry. The rose plant louse serves as the type case. Eggs laid in autumn sleep through winter on the plant. Spring hatching yields females only. Those females bear live young with no males at all. Brood follows brood all summer in the same way. One spring insect can thus leave thousands of kin. In autumn winged males at last appear. Mating then yields the eggs that carry the line through winter.
britannica-1911-apollonius-of-rhodes:
Apollonius of Rhodes was a Greek epic poet and grammarian of Alexandria under the Ptolemies. The 1911 Britannica entry places his flourishing between 222 and 181 before Christ. He learned under Callimachus, then quarrelled with his old master in later years. In youth he wrote the Argonautica, an epic in four books on the Argonauts.

Read at Alexandria, the poem was rejected through the sway of Callimachus party. Stung, he withdrew to Rhodes and won fame there as a teacher of rhetoric. A revised epic met warm praise, and Rhodes gave him the freedom of the city. Back in Alexandria he recited to applause and became head of the great library.
britannica-1911-apsines:
Apsines of Gadara, a Greek rhetorician of the third century, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. After study at Smyrna, he taught at Athens. He gained such fame that the emperor Maximinus raised him to the consulship, which he held from 235 to 238 in the emperor's reign span. He was a friend of Philostratus, author of lives of the sophists.

Philostratus praises his fine memory and his accuracy, the entry notes. Two works on rhetoric by Apsines survive. One is a handbook of the art, though much meddled with by later hands. A large part of it is taken from the rhetoric of Longinus, scholars hold. The smaller work treats claims that are put in a figured, indirect form. The article closes with editions and studies of the author.
britannica-1911-aramaic-languages:
Aramaic languages are a class of Semitic languages. Their name comes from Aram. Aram is an old Semitic geographical term. It designates nearly the districts of Greek Syria. Aram excludes Palestine, unlike Syria loosely used. It comprehends Mesopotamia, though. Hebrew calls Mesopotamia Aram of two rivers. Greeks often distinguish it from Syria proper.

Geography therefore defines the class. Aramaic dialects were current in Mesopotamia originally. They spread south-west from the Euphrates. Their range extended toward Palestine. The entry is brief and definitional. It points readers to related articles instead. Semitic Languages gives the family context. Syriac Language covers the chief literary form. Targum covers the Aramaic scripture versions. This short notice functions as a map of terminology.
britannica-1911-arbaces:
Arbaces appears in Ctesias's history of Assyria. Ctesias made him a general of Sardanapalus. He credited him with founding the Median empire. That founding is dated about 830 B.C. The entry flatly rejects the story. Ctesias's whole Assyrian history is absolutely fabulous. His Arbaces is not a historical personage. His supposed successors are not historical either.

Inscriptions give a different, smaller figure. Sargon's records name one Arbaku of Arnashia. He was a dynast of a Median district. He paid tribute to Sargon in 713 B.C. Forty-five Median chiefs paid alongside him. Eduard Meyer signs this sceptical notice. It points readers to the Media article. The contrast is the entry's whole point. Legend built an empire founder. Epigraphy shows only a tributary chief.
britannica-1911-archimedes:
Archimedes (about 287 to 212 before Christ) was a Greek mathematician and inventor, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens its long entry with his circle. He was born at Syracuse in Sicily. His father, Pheidias, was an astronomer. Archimedes stood on close terms with Hiero, king of Syracuse, and with Gelo his son.

He studied at Alexandria and met Conon of Samos there. He admired Conon as a mathematician and cherished him as a friend. He made a habit of sending his new findings to Conon before he published them. Back in his native city, he gave himself to mathematical research. The entry stresses a proud trait of the man. He set no value on the clever devices that made him famous. He held them beneath the dignity of pure science.
britannica-1911-ares:
Ares is a mythology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Greek god of war. Ares, son of Zeus and Hera, is the god of battle rather than of wise war. He delights in bloodshed and takes either side without care for justice.

The article then asks what Ares was before this. Scholars have read him as a storm god, a sun god, or a god of the world below. In Scythia an old iron sword stood for him, drawing yearly offerings. In the Homeric hymn he is even addressed as a helper of justice and an enemy of tyrants, a sign of how later ages softened him.
britannica-1911-ariobarzanes:
Ariobarzanes is a name borne by kings and satraps of Pontus and Cappadocia. Its kings entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Three rulers of Pontus and three kings of Cappadocia held that name. A Persian satrap of the same name is also treated here.

One Pontic ruler, son of Mithradates the First, rose against Artaxerxes in three sixty two. He may be seen as founder of the kingdom of Pontus itself. A Cappadocian king ruled in name from ninety three to sixty three before Christ. Mithradates the Great drove him out three times, and Rome restored him. The Persian satrap fought Alexander the Great on his way to Persepolis.
britannica-1911-aristomenes:
Aristomenes of Andania is the semi-legendary hero profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He led his people in the second Messenian war against Sparta. He came from the Aepytid family. His father is named as Nicomedes in one tale, or Pyrrhus in another.

The article tells how he stirred up revolt against Sparta. He won the help of Argos and Arcadia for the cause. At Derae, the first clash, he fought so well that a crown was offered to him. He refused the crown and took only the rank of commander-in-chief. One bold tale has him slip into Sparta by night. There he set up his shield in the temple of Athene of the Brazen House. Its words said it was a gift to the goddess, taken from the Spartans.
britannica-1911-armour-plates:
Armour plates, metal shields for warships and forts, are treated in a 1911 Britannica article. The first known plan to armor warships was made in England by Sir William Congreve in 1805. He drew an armored floating gun battery he held proof against shot. None of his plans came to use.

John Stevens of New Jersey put like plans to Congress in 1812, with the same cold result. His family kept at the work and by 1841 had proof of the iron thickness needed. Shell fire made the need plain to all by 1841. The loss of the Turkish fleet at Sinope in 1853 at last spurred real builds. French armored batteries then won a clear success at Kinburn in 1855.
britannica-1911-arses:
Arses, a Persian king, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the youngest son of Artaxerxes the Third. The courtier Bagoas raised him to the throne in the year 338 before Christ, after murdering his father and all his brothers. When the young king tried to stand on his own, Bagoas killed him too, with all his children. That came in the third year of his reign, in 336.

The article lists the forms his name takes in old sources. Plutarch calls him Oarses, another writer calls him Arsamos, and the canon of Ptolemy gives Aroges. A clay tablet from Babylon shortens the name to two letters. The entry rests on Diodorus, Strabo, and Arrian, and points readers to the history of ancient Persia for the wider tale of a throne ruled by murder.
britannica-1911-art-galleries:
Art Galleries, halls built to show paintings, are weighed as more than picture stores in a 1911 Britannica essay. A hall for pictures is set apart from a broad hall of art in the text. Such a hall shows how hue, form, and lay out are handled. It holds true faces of great men of the past as well. Dress, homes, and faith of past ages can be read in its frames.

Feel is called the most weighty part of a good painting in the text. Grief in a Pieta and calm pride in a Velasquez face serve as proofs. With no care and study, the high sense of a work is lost. The painter asks the guest to share his spirit as he views. Rest for mind and eye is the last gift the hall is said to give.
britannica-1911-art-sales:
Art sales by auction in England date from the later part of the seventeenth century. In most early cases the names of the auctioneers were held back. A diary note of sixteen ninety three speaks of a great auction of pictures at Whitehall. Other writers of the time refer to the practice in like terms. Before set auctions, art was sold as other goods were sold in trade.

Each object was priced, and buyers were invited to take it at that price. That way was slow, above all for pictures, and lacked the spur of a contest. The first great store of art to come under the hammer was an earl's in seventeen forty two. That sale ran for six days, with six more days for the coins alone. Prices ran from five shillings to one hundred sixty five guineas.
britannica-1911-art-societies:
Art societies are the subject of a survey entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry opens with the claim that artists have always been keen to band together. By forming societies they can hold shows of their work. Those shows give members a chance to earn reward for their labour.

As art practice and public interest grew, the entry explains, new aims appeared. Some societies were formed where selling work was absent or only one aim among others. Shared devotion to a style and focus on a narrow field also drove new groups. The text traces how such bodies spread and what work they did for artists and the public.
britannica-1911-artaxerxes:
Artaxerxes is a 1911 Britannica article on a name borne by kings of ancient Persia. The name stands for a Persian word, Artakhshatra. Its sense is, he whose empire is well-fitted or perfected. Forms of the name appear in Hebrew, Babylonian, and Greek. Herodotus gave a Greek rendering of it.

Herodotus, the text notes, plainly knew nothing of the Persian tongue. His reading of the name was a guess built on Xerxes. The later Persian form of the name is Ardashir. It also appears as Artaxias, a name of some kings of Armenia. Three kings of the Achaemenian dynasty bore the name Artaxerxes. While its meaning was still understood, kings can only have taken it on their accession. The article then turns to the first of those kings, surnamed Longimanus. Name lore here opens the door to royal history.
britannica-1911-arteries:
Arteries are the elastic tubes that carry blood from the heart. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains their build and branching. The name was first given to the windpipe in Greek. Ancients found arteries empty after death and thought they held air.

Two great trunks, the aorta and the pulmonary artery, leave the heart. They split again and again into ever finer tubes. The smallest of these bear the name arterioles. Large trunks keep a set place and get fixed names. Small twigs wander much more from body to body. Side links join small arteries freely near each other. If a main tube is blocked, those links swell and carry the flow. Some brain and spleen branches have no such links at all.
britannica-1911-augereau-pierre-francois:
Pierre Francois Charles Augereau, who lived from 1757 to 1816, was a marshal of France. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his bold and roving life. Born in Paris in humble station, he joined the carabineers at seventeen. He fled France after a duel and served in foreign armies.

Augereau came home when revolution broke out and rose fast. He became a general of division late in 1793. In Italy his moves helped win at Millesimo, Lodi, and Castiglione. Napoleon praised his courage, drive, and luck in action. In 1797 his troops backed a coup in Paris against the moderates. He later won a marshal baton under the Empire.
britannica-1911-autochthones:
Autochthones are the original inhabitants of a country. The Greek word means people sprung from earth itself. Latin calls such people terrigenae, earthborn. Settlers are the contrasting category. Descendants free of foreign admixture also count. Greek legend strengthened the doctrine of autochthony. Heroes were described as earthborn in it. Athenians wore golden grasshoppers in their hair. That token proclaimed their birth from Attica's soil.

Thucydides and Plato both record that custom. Thebes had its own earthborn race. The Sparti sprang from a field sown with dragons' teeth. Phrygian Corybantes were forced from the hillside like trees. Rhea, the great mother, produced them so. Aeschylus shows primitive men living like animals. Gods and heroes later raised them to civilisation. The entry surveys the myth's political uses.
britannica-1911-averroes:
Averroes (1126-1198), born at Cordova in Spain, was an Arabian philosopher trained in theology, law, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy. The vizier Ibn-Tufail brought him to Prince Yusef, and the physician Avenzoar was his friend. Skilled in Malekite law, he became cadi of Seville in 1169.

For twenty-five years he held posts at Seville, Cordova, and Morocco, discussing philosophy and faith with his rulers. About 1195 hostile feeling against free thought brought charges of heresy, loss of honors, and banishment near Cordova, while liberal learning was stamped out across Andalusia. The storm passed, he was recalled to Morocco, and he died restored to honor shortly before his patron al-Mansur. His sons followed him in law, one writing on his father's theory of the intellect.
britannica-1911-avesnes:
Avesnes is a town of northern France on the Helpe river, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Nord, with 5,076 people in 1906. It has a subprefect, a court of first instance, a chamber of commerce, and a communal college.

Its church of St Nicholas, from the 16th century, carries a 200-foot tower with a fine chime of bells. Wool-spinning is the chief industry, with trade in wood. Founded in the 11th century, Avesnes formed a countship that passed to Burgundy and then to the Habsburgs. Louis XI destroyed it in 1477; France gained it by treaty in 1659, Vauban fortified it, and Prussians captured it in 1815.
britannica-1911-aviles:
Avilés, or San Nicolás de Avilés, the Roman Flavionavia, is a seaport of northern Spain in the province of Oviedo, on a winding inlet of the Bay of Biscay west of Gijón. Its 1900 population was 12,763. Ancient palaces and Gothic churches give the town its old-fashioned air.

The bay, crossed by a fine bridge at its narrow landward end, shelters a fishing fleet and many coasting vessels. Coal from the Oviedo mines moves out coastwise, and in 1904 shipments from Avilés passed those of Gijón for the first time, topping 290,000 tons. Glass, coarse linen, and woollen cloth are made in the town, and valuable stone quarries lie nearby.
britannica-1911-avranches:
Avranches is a town of north-western France, capital of an arrondissement in Manche, standing on a wooded hill above the river Sée south of Cherbourg. Its 1906 population was 7,186. Botanical gardens on the hill command a fine view westward over the bay and rock of St Michel.

A bishop's see from 511 to 1790, Avranches lost its cathedral, once Normandy's finest, after the Revolution found it unsafe; one stone marks where Henry II received absolution for Becket's murder. Leather-dressing leads local industry, with brewing, dyeing, and gardening around it, and trade in cider, cattle, and butter. A Roman military station and medieval county chief place, the town endured sieges and led the Nu-pieds revolt against the salt tax in 1639.
britannica-1911-ax-les-thermes:
Ax-les-Thermes is a watering place of south-western France in the department of Ariège, set where the Ariège river meets three tributaries, south of Foix by rail. At 2,300 feet up, the town had 1,179 people in 1906. Its Roman name was Aquae, waters.

About sixty warm sulphur springs rise here, running from 77 to 172 degrees Fahrenheit. Romans used the waters, and in the entry's day they were still held effective for rheumatism, skin diseases, and other maladies. A small mountain town thus rests its fame on hot springs known since Roman times, their heat and number set out plainly for health seekers.
britannica-1911-azores:
Azores, or Western Islands, are a Portuguese archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, 922 square miles in area with 256,291 people in 1900. Nine chief islands fall into three widely spaced groups running north-west to south-east, farther from any continent than any other Atlantic group.

Volcanic birth shows everywhere: high, steep coasts, peaks rising to Pico's 7,612 feet, and a long record of earthquakes and eruptions, centred mostly on St Michael's. Basalt and scoria are the chief rocks thrown up. St Mary's and some western islands have escaped eruptions so far. One blast in 1522 buried Villa Franca, then capital of St Michael's. Though nearer Europe in climate and plant life, the islands sit over 800 miles from Portugal's Cape da Roca.
britannica-1911-azoximes:
Azoximes, also called furo-diazoles, are a class of organic compounds holding a five-part ring of carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. Their making goes step by step. Nitriles are turned into amidoximes with hydroxylamine. Those are treated with acid chlorides or anhydrides. Water is then driven out by heat, closing the ring.

They can also arise from a dioxime through the Beckmann change. Most azoximes are very volatile, sublime readily, and dissolve easily in water, alcohol, and benzene. Workers wanting detail are sent to papers by Tiemann, Schulz, and Müller from the 1880s and to the Chemical Society's annual reports. Formula diagrams in the text show the ring forming from a worked example.
britannica-1911-azymites:
Azymites, from Greek words meaning without leaven, is a name the Orthodox Eastern Church gave to the Western or Latin Church. The quarrel was over a point of ritual: the West's use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist. The practice arose in the 9th century, following the Jewish passover custom, and Armenians and Maronites share it.

The Orthodox side holds its ground firmly. Their case, as the entry reports it, rests on the very name bread and on the mystery's holiness. It rests also on the example of Jesus and the early church. All are said to testify against unleavened bread in this use. A single Greek label thus carries a whole East-West quarrel over the communion loaf.
britannica-1911-bailey-philip-james:
Bailey, Philip James (1816-1902), was an English poet born at Nottingham, where his father owned and edited the Nottingham Mercury. Locally schooled, he entered Glasgow University at sixteen without taking a degree, then read law at Lincoln's Inn without serious practice, settling at Basford to write.

For three years Bailey worked on Festus, published anonymously in 1839 to instant success in England and America, running through a dozen home editions and nearly three times as many abroad. The vast poem, a pageant of theology in some twelve parts, argues God's goodness, the soul's immortality, and a gospel joining faith and reason. Fine lines and dignified thought fill it, the entry grants, but its huge theme and loose working keep it hard reading. Bailey published other verse, yet stayed a man of one book.
britannica-1911-baily-edward-hodges:
Baily, Edward Hodges (1788-1867), was a British sculptor born at Bristol, son of a celebrated carver of ships' figureheads who meant him for trade. Even at school the boy modelled wax figures and busts of schoolmates, and the habit survived his placing in a merchant's house.

Two Homeric studies shown to Flaxman won such praise that in 1807 Baily came to London as Flaxman's pupil. The academy gold medal followed in 1811 for Hercules restoring Alcestis to Admetus, and in 1821 he became a Royal Academician, showing Eve at the Fountain among his best works. He carved bas-reliefs for the Marble Arch and made statues and busts of Nelson, Earl Grey, and Lord Mansfield, among many others, before dying at Holloway in 1867.
britannica-1911-bain-andrew-geddes:
Bain, Andrew Geddes (1797-1864), was a British geologist from Scotland. He emigrated to Cape Colony in 1820. For some years he worked as a saddler at Graaff Reinet. During the Kaffir War he led a frontier battalion.

Bain was next hired to build a military road. The road crossed the Ecca Pass. His skill won him steady work under the Royal Engineers. He surveyed military roads across the colony. That work woke his love of geology. A loan of Lyell's Elements in 1837 fed it. Bain found many fossil reptiles near Fort Beaufort. They included the Dicynodon, later described by Owen. In 1852 he finished the first full geological map of South Africa. The Geological Society published it in 1856.
britannica-1911-baird-james:
Baird, James (1802-1876), was a Scottish iron-master. He was born at Kirkwood in Lanarkshire. His father was a coal-master there. In 1826 the family leased coalfields at Gartsherrie. Iron mines followed in 1828. Blast furnaces rose in 1830.

James Baird took active control that year. The firm became William Baird and Company. His machine improvements raised furnace output sharply. By 1864 nearly fifty furnaces stood at work. They made 300,000 tons a year. They employed 10,000 hands. The brothers became great landowners too. Baird sat in parliament for the Falkirk burghs. He died leaving three million pounds. His gifts were large and public. He founded schools and the Baird Lectures. His Baird Trust gave half a million pounds in 1873.
britannica-1911-bala-series:
Bala Series, in geology, names a rock series in North Wales. Dark slates and sandstones form it. Beds of limestone run through it. The Bala neighbourhood of Merionethshire shows it well. Sedgwick first described the series. He placed it in his Cambrian System.

Modern placing puts it atop the Ordovician. It sits above the Llandeilo beds. Bala limestone runs twenty to forty feet thick. Most of North Wales recognises that bed. It matches the Lake District's Coniston limestone. Hirnant limestone crowns the type section. Slates 1,400 feet thick part the two limestones. Volcanic rocks lie below them. Snowdon's tuffs reach thousands of feet thick. South Wales shows its own Bala beds. Trinucleus beds and Dicranograptus shales appear there. Graptolites mark the upper and lower parts.
britannica-1911-balfour-arthur-james:
Arthur James Balfour (born 1848) was a British statesman, born on 25 July 1848 and schooled at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge. He entered Parliament in 1874 as a Conservative for Hertford. In 1878 he served as private secretary to his uncle, Lord Salisbury, and went with him to the Congress of Berlin.

The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, tracks his rise through Irish office and the leadership of the Commons to the premiership, then into opposition after the defeat of 1906. It covers the tariff reform split, his Insular Free Trade pamphlet, and his books, among them Defence of Philosophic Doubt and The Foundations of Belief.
britannica-1911-bank-notes:
Bank-notes, for the purpose of this entry, means all paper substitutes for metal money, whether issued by banks, governments, or other financial bodies. Early notes were simple printed forms with the amounts filled in by hand, usually for £40 or more, printed on watermarked paper. Little was done at first to stop imitation, yet forgery stayed rare.

Small notes of £1 and £2, spread at the end of the 1700s, changed that: forgery ran rife, with 352 people convicted in England in a single year. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, follows the contest between note makers and counterfeiters ever since. Engine-turned engraving and special watermarks held one side. Photography gave the other side a dangerous new tool. Defences such as Henry Bradbury's of 1856 answered it.
britannica-1911-bannister-charles:
Charles Bannister was an English actor and singer with a fine bass voice. He lived from seventeen thirty eight to eighteen o four. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Gloucestershire, he first acted in London in seventeen sixty two.

Bannister won fame as a singer at Ranelagh and as an actor too. Garrick was so struck that he engaged him for Drury Lane theatre. His son John Bannister, born in seventeen sixty, also took the stage. John first trained as a painter, then acted at the Haymarket in seventeen seventy eight. He became the best low comic actor of his day in England.
britannica-1911-barbary-pirates:
The Barbary pirates were sea robbers of the north coast of Africa who fell on the shores and trade of Europe for ages. The 1911 Britannica entry traces mere sea theft back through the fall of Rome, the wild years of invasion, and the wars of faiths in the middle ages. It was ever there by the side of great strife.

When the Berber royal houses sank in a late age, sea theft flared to a peak, with one town as its most famed haunt. But the true Barbary powers, the entry says, rose in a later age still. They grew to their height, then sank by slow steps, and were put down for good in the early part of the age of steam. Their reach struck not just the inland sea but the open ocean as well.
britannica-1911-bareges:
Barèges is a town of south-western France, in the department of Hautes-Pyrénées, in the valley of the Bastan, 25 miles south of Bagnères-de-Bigorre by road. It stands 4,040 feet up and is hardly inhabited in winter. Its fame is its warm sulphurous springs, running from 75 to 111 degrees Fahrenheit.

Those waters became widely known in 1675, when Madame de Maintenon visited with the duke of Maine, son of Louis XIV. Used for drinking and in baths, they were valued for wounds, ulcers, scrofula, gout, and skin diseases. A military hospital dates from 1760. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that embankments and replanting had cut the old risk of avalanches and floods, and that the light fabric called barège takes its name from the town.
britannica-1911-barmecides:
The Barmecides, more accurately the Barmakids, were a noble Persian family that rose to great power under the Abbasid caliphs. Barmak, the founder, was a Persian fire-worshipper, said to be a native of Khorasan. About 736 he rebuilt and adorned his city of Balkh after a rebellion, and the family prospered from there.

His grandson Yahya became vizier to the caliph Mahdi and tutor to Harun al-Rashid, and Yahya's sons Fadl and Jafar held high office under Harun. Jafar is the Giafar of the Arabian Nights. The 1911 Britannica entry tells the romantic story of their fall. A formal marriage between Jafar and the caliph's sister Abbasa was meant to keep propriety. In fact the terms were broken, and Harun had Jafar beheaded.
britannica-1911-barnim-dukes:
Barnim is the name of thirteen dukes who ruled over parts of the duchy of Pomerania. The 1911 Britannica entry picks out the most important of them. Barnim I, called the Good (about 1209–1278), succeeded his father in Pomerania-Stettin in 1220. He fought long wars. In 1250 he had to accept the supremacy of the margrave of Brandenburg.

In 1264 Barnim I united the whole of Pomerania under his rule and turned to its inner improvement: German settlers and customs, new towns, and generous gifts to the church. The entry goes on to Barnim III, called the Great, who won military distinction against the emperor Louis IV's party, with a victory in August 1332 singled out.
britannica-1911-barrington-daines:
Daines Barrington (1727–1800), an English lawyer, antiquary, and naturalist, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the fourth son of the first Viscount Barrington. Trained in law, he became a Welsh judge in 1757 and later second justice of Chester. The entry judges him a poor judge, yet praises the book that made his name among historians of law and old customs.

That book, Observations on the Statutes, covered old laws from Magna Carta to the reign of James I and proposed reshaping the statute book. Barrington also edited Orosius with King Alfred's Saxon version, wrote tracts on reaching the North Pole, and published Miscellanies in 1781. His papers ranged oddly and widely, from an account of the child Mozart in London to studies of birdsong and the language of birds. He died in March 1800.
britannica-1911-barrois-charles:
Charles Barrois (1851– ), a French geologist born at Lille on 21 April 1851, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He studied geology at Lille under Jules Gosselet and took his doctorate in science. His first large work, published in 1876, covered the Upper Cretaceous rocks of England and Ireland, and it was dedicated to Gosselet, the teacher who had trained him.

Barrois's chalk research set a lasting pattern. Working out the fossil zones in the Chalk and Upper Greensand of Britain in detail for the first time, he produced results that later workers built on and largely confirmed. He joined the French Geological Survey in 1876 and became professor at Lille in 1877. Other studies covered rocks in the Ardennes, Spain, and Brittany. Medals from the Geological Society of London and election to the Academy of Sciences followed.
britannica-1911-barry-james:
James Barry (1741–1806), an English painter born at Cork, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father, a builder and coastal trader, meant him for the sea, but the boy hated sailor life and turned to drawing instead. At school in Cork he was treated as a prodigy. Before leaving for Dublin at twenty-two, he painted large pictures for his father's house, among them Aeneas escaping from Troy and Daniel in the lions' den.

Patronage opened the next stage. A painting of St Patrick baptizing the king of Cashel won Barry the support of Edmund Burke, whose help sent him to Paris and Rome in 1765. After returning in 1771 he painted Venus and Jupiter and Juno on Mount Ida. Later he spent seven years covering the great room of the Society of Arts in the Adelphi with six historical paintings, working for expenses alone.
britannica-1911-barry-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Barry (1795–1860), an English architect born in London, the son of a stationer, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He was trained in an architects' office until 1817, then spent three years travelling in Greece, Italy, Egypt, and Palestine to study buildings. Back in London from 1820, he made his name first with St Peter's church at Brighton, finished in 1826.

Italian style marked Barry's early fame. The Travellers' Club in Pall Mall in 1831 and the larger Reform Club in 1837 set a new pattern for London clubhouses. He also built Bridgewater House, schools and halls in Birmingham, Manchester, and Halifax, and rebuilt the Treasury buildings. His masterwork, the Houses of Parliament at Westminster, occupied 1840 to 1860. Knighted in 1852, he died at Clapham in May 1860 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
britannica-1911-barthelemy-jean-jacques:
Jean Jacques Barthélemy (1716–1795), a French writer and numismatist born at Cassis in Provence, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. While studying for the priesthood he turned to oriental languages and classical antiquities, above all coins. In Paris from 1744 he assisted Gros de Boze, keeper of the royal medals, and succeeded him in 1753. Three years of research in Italy with the ambassador Choiseul won him a powerful patron and valuable posts.

One book, worked on for thirty years, made Barthélemy's fame. Voyage du jeune Anacharsis, published in four volumes in 1787, sends a young Scythian through the republics, colonies, and islands of Greece to learn from them. The entry also records his election to the French Academy in 1789, his brief arrest in the Revolution, and his return to the medal collection he had enriched.
britannica-1911-barthelemy-saint-hilaire:
Jules Barthélemy Saint-Hilaire (1805–1895), a French philosopher and statesman born in Paris, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He began as a political journalist, opposing the king's reactionary policy in Le Globe from 1826 to 1830 and signing the journalists' protest in the revolution of 1830. In 1833 he left politics for ancient philosophy and began a translation of Aristotle that occupied him, on and off, for most of his life.

Scholarship and office alternated after that. The Aristotle work won him a chair at the Collège de France in 1838. He sat as a republican deputy in 1848, reported on the proposed Suez canal from Egypt in 1855, and helped make Thiers president in 1871. As foreign minister in 1880–1881 he actively promoted the French protectorate over Tunis. Books on the Vedas, Buddhism, and Mohammed are also listed.
britannica-1911-barytes:
Barytes, also called barite or heavy spar, is a mineral described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is composed of barium sulphate and is widely distributed. Weight gives it its name: the Greek word barys means heavy, and its specific gravity of 4.5 is about twice that of salt and of many similar glassy minerals. The entry notes that the mineral is usually found in a fairly pure state, with only small replacements by strontium or calcium compounds.

Crystals and occurrences take up most of the article. Barytes crystals are orthorhombic, often perfectly formed in varied shapes, with very perfect cleavage, the way a mineral splits along flat planes. The mineral can be colourless, white, yellow, brown, bluish, or greenish, and also occurs granular, earthy, or in rounded crested masses. It is common in metal-bearing veins, especially those yielding lead and silver ores, and in beds of iron ore.
britannica-1911-basilides:
Basilides was a leading teacher of Gnosticism, an early religious movement mixing Christian, Jewish, and Greek ideas, who lived at Alexandria in the early second century. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates his activity before AD 138, since Agrippa Castor already wrote against him under Hadrian. Basilides wrote a commentary in twenty-four books on “his” gospel, though which gospel is unknown. His son Isidorus also wrote, on the attached soul, the prophet Parchor, and ethics.

Sources and a scholarly quarrel fill most of the article. Only fragments of Basilides survive, gathered by Hilgenfeld. Irenaeus sketches the school's teaching one way, while the Philosophumena ascribed to Hippolytus gives a quite different, strongly monistic account, treating all things as coming from one source. Which version represents Basilides himself had long been disputed. Recent opinion decided against the Philosophumena, whose author likely mixed his own views into the systems described.
britannica-1911-basnage-jacques:
Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), a French Protestant divine born at Rouen in Normandy, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of a noted lawyer, studied classical languages at Saumur and theology at Geneva, and served as pastor at Rouen from 1676. When the edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685, Basnage gained the king's leave to retire to Holland. He settled as a pastor at Rotterdam and then at The Hague.

Exile made Basnage a diplomat as well as a preacher. Heinsius placed him at The Hague in 1709 largely for civil affairs. Basnage then handled secret negotiations with France at the congress of Utrecht with success. He later advised on the Triple Alliance of 1717 and calmed French fears about a Protestant rising in the Cevennes. His many writings are headed by historical works on the Reformed churches and the Jews.
britannica-1911-basses-alpes:
Basses-Alpes was a department of south-eastern France, formed in 1790 from the northern portion of Provence, as described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It covered about 2698 square miles and held 113,126 people in 1906. The Durance river crosses its west, fed by the Ubaye, Bléone, and Asse, while the Verdon forms part of its southern limit. Five arrondissements, with chief towns Digne, Barcelonnette, Castellane, Forcalquier, and Sisteron, organized it.

Poverty of the land is the entry's main theme. The district is poor and hilly, rising to the Aiguille de Chambeyron at 11,155 feet above the Ubaye headwaters. Mountain pastures had been damaged by the shepherds who rented them, and forests thinned, though replanting was under way. The soil was dry under the southern sun. Railways were few and short. The Col de l'Argentière pass toward Cuneo in Italy, crossed by Francis I in 1515, closes the account.
britannica-1911-basses-pyrenees:
Basses-Pyrénées was a department of south-western France, formed in 1790, as described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Two-thirds of it came from Béarn and the rest from Basse-Navarre, Soule, and Labourd, the Basque country of France in its west. It covered 2977 square miles at the angle of the Bay of Biscay, bordered Spain to the south, and held 426,817 people in 1906.

Mountains dominate the south. The western Pyrenees rise from the Rhune at 2950 feet to the peak of Anie at 8215 feet and Ossau at 9465 feet along the Spanish frontier. Forts guard the upper Nive and Aspe valleys, where passes cross into Spain. Most rivers run north-west to the Adour through the Gave de Pau, Bidouze, and Nive, while heaths and plateaus fill the north-east and fertile valleys the west.
britannica-1911-bassianus-joannes:
Joannes Bassianus was an Italian jurist of the twelfth century, profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Little is known of his origin, though one writer made him a native of Cremona. He taught in the law school of Bologna, learning first as the pupil of Bulgarus and then teaching Azo, two of the school's famous names. His Summary on the Authentica survived. Savigny judged it a precious work of the Gloss-writers, scholars who explained Roman law with marginal notes.

Ingenious teaching devices made Bassianus famous. His Law-Tree, Arbor Arborum, drew legal actions as fruit on a tree. Forty-eight civil actions hang on one side, and 121 praetorian, or equitable, actions on the other. A notation system let a student sort any action under its proper head at once. His lectures on the Pandects and the Code, collected by a pupil, have unfortunately perished.
britannica-1911-bastide-jules:
Jules Bastide (1800–1879), a French publicist born in Paris, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied law briefly, then worked as a timber merchant. In 1821 he joined the French Carbonari, the secret society plotting against the restored monarchy, and he took a prominent part in the Revolution of 1830. For his share in the Paris rising of June 1832, at General Lamarque's funeral, he was sentenced to death, but he escaped to London.

Journalism and one brief ministry fill the rest. Back in Paris, Bastide was acquitted in 1834 and wrote for the republican National, becoming its editor in 1836. In 1847 he founded the Revue nationale with Buchez. After the February revolution of 1848, his knowledge of foreign affairs won him a secretarial post in the provisional government and then the foreign ministry itself under the executive commission. He gave up the post at the end of 1848 and retired after the 1851 coup.
britannica-1911-bathonian-series:
Bathonian series is a geological name set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands for the Great Oolite series of England. The name comes from the Bath Oolite, a limestone so much quarried near Bath that William Smith first studied its beds there. The term was first used in 1843 and then fixed in a narrower sense by d'Orbigny in 1849, a history of naming that the entry gives in some detail.

Order of the beds fills the middle. In English use the Bathonian holds, from the top down, the Cornbrash, the Forest Marble with Bradford Clay, the Great or Bath Oolite, the Stonesfield Slate, and the Fullers' Earth. It matches the upper part of the German Dogger, of Middle Jurassic age. Rocks of this age are found across Europe and as far as Greenland, Africa, India, and South America. The famed Caen stone of Normandy is one of them.
britannica-1911-bathycles:
Bathycles was an Ionian sculptor of Magnesia, known for one great work in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Spartans hired him to make a marble throne for the statue of Apollo at Amyclae. The work dates to about 550 BC, in the early age of Greek art in stone. 

What we know comes from a text. Pausanias, the Greek travel writer, gives a full account of the monument in the third book of his work. The entry calls that account of the greatest value, since it shows the character of Ionic art at that early time. The throne bore scenes from myth cut in relief, flat carving on its sides, and free-standing figures made in the round to support it.
britannica-1911-batteux-charles:
Charles Batteux (1713–1780), a French philosopher and writer on aesthetics, the study of beauty and taste, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Vouziers and trained in theology at Reims, he came to Paris in 1739. He taught in colleges, then took the chair of Greek and Roman philosophy at the Collège de France. In 1746 he published Les Beaux-Arts réduits à un même principe, his bid to find one rule behind all theories of beauty. Its views were widely taken up.

Fame and a fall frame his later years. A Horace translation in 1750 confirmed his name. His Cours de belles lettres fed into the Principes de la littérature of 1774. Its rules for writing are called somewhat pedantic, fussy over small points. In his Histoire des causes premières he attacked abuse of power in philosophy so freely that he lost his chair.
britannica-1911-bayly-thomas-haynes:
Thomas Haynes Bayly (1797–1839) was an English songwriter and dramatist born at Bath. He studied at Winchester and at St Mary Hall, Oxford, at first with the church in mind. A visit to Dublin showed him his gift for ballads, and from 1824 he built a wide name in England.

Songs such as “I’d be a butterfly,” “She wore a wreath of roses” and “Gaily the troubadour” kept his name alive. Bayly also wrote two novels and many plays, of which Perfection, staged by Madame Vestris, did best. Money troubles over his wife’s Irish estates hurt his health, and he died in April 1839.
britannica-1911-beattie-james:
James Beattie, a Scots poet and thinker, fills a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Kincardine in seventeen thirty five, he was the son of a small farmer. His father died while he was young, but a brother sent him to college. He won funds at Marischal College in Aberdeen. School posts led to a chair in moral thought there in seventeen sixty.

With Reid and Campbell he formed a club that met to test the thought of David Hume. His Essay on Truth in seventeen seventy hit Hume head on and won wide fame. The text grants that book no worth as deep thought. King George the Third gave him a wage for life on a London trip. His long poem The Minstrel met with great praise in its day.
britannica-1911-bell-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Bell (1774–1842) was a Scottish anatomist born at Edinburgh, youngest son of a clergyman. His brothers included the anatomist John Bell and the jurist G. J. Bell. Trained at Edinburgh’s high school and university, he studied anatomy under John and published A System of Dissections while still a pupil in 1798.

Bell’s engravings of the brain and nerves, drawn from his own dissections, won praise for their skill and finish. Moving to London in 1804, he announced in his New Idea of the Anatomy of the Brain how nerves serve different functions by their links to the brain. He later took the Edinburgh chair of surgery and died near Worcester in 1842.
britannica-1911-bellegarde-heinrich-jose:
Heinrich Joseph Johannes, Count von Bellegarde (1756–1845), was an Austrian soldier and statesman born at Dresden. After brief Saxon service he joined Austria in 1771 and won notice as a dragoon colonel in the Turkish War of 1788–1789. He fought in the Netherlands in 1793–1794 and on the archduke Charles’s staff in Germany and Italy.

Bellegarde besieged Alessandria, stood at the decisive battle of Novi, and led the Austrian right at bloody Caldiero in 1805. In 1809 he commanded the main army’s right wing and fell back into Bohemia after Eckmühl. Later campaigns in Italy mixed soldiering with skilled negotiation, and he held high posts until weak eyes forced his retirement in 1825.
britannica-1911-belles-lettres:
Belles-lettres, French for “fine literature,” names the more artistic and imaginative kinds of writing. Poetry and romance fall under it, set against drier and more exact studies. Swift seems to have been the first to use the term in English, in 1710.

The entry is a bare definition, and it makes its point by contrast. Belles-lettres covers work valued for style, feeling and invention rather than for fact or proof. A history or a science text aims at exact knowledge, while a poem or novel aims at shaped beauty of language. That dividing line, between the pleasing and the precise in writing, is all the short note records.
britannica-1911-benares:
