Benares, the holy city of the Hindus, gives its name to a district and division in the United Provinces of India. It ranks among the most ancient cities in the world. Its old name Varanasi has no known source, while Kasi, still in common Hindu use, is said to mean “bright.”

Buddha came to Sarnath, near the present city, in the sixth century B.C. to found his teaching, and a Chinese pilgrim of the seventh century A.D. counted thirty Buddhist monasteries there. Hinduism has since taken Buddhism’s place, and the city now holds over 1,500 temples along a four-mile sweep of the Ganges. The entry goes on to the district, its people and its history under Hindu kings.
britannica-1911-benedictines:
Benedictines, or Black Monks, are monks who live by the Rule of Saint Benedict of Nursia. Subiaco in the Abruzzi was their cradle, where Benedict founded twelve monasteries. He then moved to Monte Cassino, the house from which his Rule and order spread across the West.

For four or five centuries each monastery stood alone, with no bond between houses. Reform movements such as Cluny later drew houses together, while the Carolingian age tried to force one strict pattern on all. In England the order flourished greatly; the Reformation wrecked it across much of northern Europe. Figures for 1905 still count over 4,000 choir monks and nearly 2,000 lay brothers.
britannica-1911-bennett-john-hughes:
John Hughes Bennett (1812–1875) was an English physician and pathologist born in London. Educated at Exeter and articled to a Maidstone surgeon, he began medical study at Edinburgh in 1833 and graduated with the highest honours four years later. Study in Paris and Germany followed.

Back at Edinburgh in 1841, Bennett lectured on histology and pressed the microscope’s worth in studying disease. He took the chair of the institutes of medicine in 1843 and held it with great energy until his health failed. His many books include Lectures on Clinical Medicine, a work on cod-liver oil, and Leucocythaemia of 1852; he had published the first recorded cure of that blood disease in 1845.
britannica-1911-berenice-princesses:
Berenice, or Bernice, is the Macedonian form of the Greek name Pherenice. Seven princesses bore it, and the entry treats them in two groups: five Egyptian and two Jewish. The first Berenice was mother of Ptolemy Philadelphus, and her ability won her divine honours after death.

Darker stories follow. A second Berenice, married to Antiochus of Syria under a peace deal, was murdered with her son by the cast-off queen Laodice. A third, wife of Ptolemy III, vowed her hair for her husband’s safe return from Syria; when it vanished from the temple, the astronomer Conon placed it among the stars. The Jewish pair end with the Berenice who followed Titus to Rome and was sent home when he became emperor.
britannica-1911-bergues:
Bergues is a town of northern France in the department of Nord, where the Colme canal meets the canals to Dunkirk and to Furnes in Belgium. It lies five miles south-south-east of Dunkirk by rail and counted 4,499 people in 1906. Small as it is, Bergues holds sights worth the stop.

Its belfry, raised in the mid-1500s and restored in the 1800s, is called the finest in French Flanders. The brick church of St Martin is Gothic work of the 1600s with a modern front, and the town hall keeps a library and a good picture collection. Brewing and malting, brush-making and oil works are the town’s trades, plain industries for a canal town.
britannica-1911-bernard-jacques:
Jacques Bernard (1658–1718), a French theologian and publicist born at Nions in Dauphiné, was driven from France for preaching Reformed doctrine against royal orders. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him to Holland, where he became a pensionary minister at Gouda and turned to the periodical press that made his name.

He ran a monthly history of Europe from 1686 to 1688, then Lettres historiques until 1698, and later continued Bayle's Nouvelles de la république des lettres until 1710. At Leiden he also held a chair of philosophy and mathematics and ministered to the Walloon church. He died there in 1718.
britannica-1911-bernard-of-chartres:
Bernard of Chartres (about 1080–1167), surnamed Sylvestris, was a scholastic philosopher at the school of Chartres in France. John of Salisbury, quoted in this 1911 Britannica entry, called him the most perfect Platonist of the age, and the entry places him and his brother Theodore among the school's leading figures.

Working from Plato's Timaeus, Bernard held that ideas truly exist and are stored for ever in the mind of God. He tried to reconcile Plato and Aristotle, and to build a symbolism of numbers around the Trinity and the ideas of unity, plurality, and likeness. Only fragments survive, from his Megacosmus and Microcosmus.
britannica-1911-bernauer-agnes:
Agnes Bernauer (died 1435) was the daughter of an Augsburg baker. About 1432 she was secretly married to Albert. He was the son of Ernest, Duke of Bavaria-Munich. Ernest did not know the marriage was lawful. He pressed his son to marry and reproached him over Agnes. Albert then declared that she was his lawful wife.

During Albert's absence she was seized on Ernest's order. She was condemned to death for witchcraft. On 12 October 1435 she was drowned in the Danube near Straubing. Albert later had her remains buried in that town. The story lived long in popular memory. It gave material to dramas by Böttger, Hebbel, and Otto Ludwig.
britannica-1911-bernician-series:
Bernician Series is a geology term for the lower part of the Carboniferous System. It names the rocks below the Millstone Grit. S. P. Woodward proposed the term in 1856 in his Manual of Mollusca. He took the name from Bernicia, the old province on the Anglo-Scottish border. The series is much the same as the Dinantien of later French writers.

The 1911 Britannica entry tracks how the term shifted in use. In 1875 Professor Lebour joined Tate's calcareous and carbonaceous groups under the name Bernician. Later he spoke of all Northumberland Carboniferous rocks as the Bernician type. The entry calls that wider use the most satisfactory one. Woodward's matching term for the upper rocks was Demetian.
britannica-1911-bertram-charles:
Charles Bertram (1723–1765) was an English literary impostor, born in London, son of a silk dyer. By 1747 he taught English at the Danish naval cadet school in Copenhagen. That year he wrote to the antiquary William Stukeley with a claim. He said he had found a manuscript by a monk, Richard of Westminster. It claimed to correct the Roman Itinerary of Antoninus for Britain. Clever copies soon followed.

The forgery deceived the palaeographers of the day, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Stukeley read an account of it to the Society of Antiquaries in 1756. Bertram printed the full text at Copenhagen in 1757. Proof of the fraud came only in 1866 and 1867, in the Gentleman's Magazine. Yet a translation still entered Bohn's Antiquarian Library in 1872. The fake misled many writers on Roman Britain.
britannica-1911-bes:
Bes, or Besas, was an Egyptian god of recreation. The 1911 Britannica article shows him as a dwarf with a large head, goggle eyes, and a protruding tongue. A shaggy beard, a bushy tail, and bow legs complete the figure. He usually wears a tall crown of feathers. A Bes-like mask was found among twelfth-dynasty remains. His earliest clear temple image stands at Deir el Bahri, about 1500 BC.

His ugliness was thought to scare away evil spirits. In his cheerful side he plays the harp or flute and dances. He guards children and childbirth in the birth-houses of temples. His image marks mirrors, ointment vases, and amulets. Unusually for Egyptian art, he is shown full faced, not in profile. Links to Punt and Ethiopia close the article.
britannica-1911-bessarion-johannes:
Johannes Bessarion (about 1395–1472) was a Greek scholar and titular patriarch of Constantinople. He was born at Trebizond and educated at Constantinople. In 1423 he went to hear Gemistus Pletho teach Plato in the Peloponnese. He joined the order of St Basil and took the name Bessarion. In 1437 he became archbishop of Nicaea. He then sailed to Italy with the emperor to seek church union.

At Ferrara and Florence he backed the Roman church, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Pope Eugenius IV made him a cardinal in reward. He settled in Italy for good. There he patronized scholars and collected books and manuscripts. His library, rich in Greek manuscripts, went to Venice. It formed the core of the famous library of St Mark.
britannica-1911-besseges: Bessèges is a town of south-eastern France in the department of Gard, standing on the river Cèze, 20 miles north of Alais by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry is only two sentences long. It gives the town a population of 7,662 in the 1906 census and states plainly why the place matters: Bessèges is important for its coal-mines, its blast-furnaces, and its iron-works. No history, buildings, or other trades are mentioned; the entry names only the mining and iron work.
britannica-1911-bethesda-wales:
Bethesda is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an urban district of Carnarvonshire in North Wales. The village lies five miles from Bangor, on a branch of the London and North-Western railway, near the lower end of the fine Nant Ffrancon, the valley of the Ogwen stream. It held 5,281 people in 1901. Its scriptural name comes, as often in Wales, from the Nonconformist church from which the settlement took its title.

Great slate quarries belonging to Lord Penrhyn give the place its work and its shape. A narrow gauge railway links the quarries with Port Penrhyn, at the mouth of the Cegid stream. The article is brief, but its facts fix the pattern of a Welsh slate village: a chapel name, a peer's quarries, and a small port.
britannica-1911-bichromates-and-chromate:
Bichromates and chromates are salts of chromium acids, treated together in this 1911 Britannica chemistry article. Chromium trioxide dissolves in water to give a solution held to contain chromic acid. Its normal salts are the chromates. Extra proportions of the trioxide give bichromates and trichromates in a series. The article sets out the general formulae for that series. It then takes the salt families one by one.

The alkaline chromates are made by fusing a chromium compound with an alkaline carbonate and an oxidizer. Chrome-ironstone serves as a raw source in that process. Most chromates are yellow in colour. The article details tests, reactions, and uses for each group in turn. It closes with the unstable perchromates, formed from a blue peroxide compound. Those salts break down fast into oxygen and potassium bichromate.
britannica-1911-bituriges:
Bituriges were a Celtic people of Gaul, ranked by Livy as the most powerful there in Tarquinius Priscus's time. At some unknown date they split into two branches. The Bituriges Cubi held the modern diocese of Bourges, across Cher, Indre, and part of Allier. The Bituriges Vivisci held the Gironde coast strip instead. The name is supposed to mean rulers of the world, or perpetual kings. In Caesar's day the Cubi accepted Aedui supremacy over them.

Their chief town was Avaricum, modern Bourges. In Vercingetorix's revolt of 52 BC that town resisted desperately before Caesar stormed it. Its people were put to the sword, the 1911 Britannica entry recounts. The tribe submitted the next year, and Augustus placed it in Aquitania in 28 BC. Pliny calls them liberi, pointing to a measure of freedom under Rome. The Vivisci capital was Burdigala, modern Bordeaux, already a wine centre then.
britannica-1911-bizet-georges:
Georges Bizet (1838–1875) was a French musical composer, born at Bougival near Paris on 25 October 1838. His father was a singing-master. The boy showed musical gifts early and entered the Paris Conservatoire. He studied under Halévy and swept up prizes for organ and fugue. In 1857 he won the Grand Prix de Rome with his cantata Cloris et Clotilde. That same year he shared first prize in Offenbach's operetta contest with Lecocq.

After his three Rome years he returned to Paris as pianist and accompanist. His first opera, Les Pêcheurs de perles, reached the Théâtre Lyrique in September 1863. The 1911 Britannica entry closes with Carmen and its strange early fate. Bizet died of a heart affection on 3 June 1875, three months after the Paris production. He lived just long enough to know Vienna had accepted the opera. London's immense success came in 1878, after his death.
britannica-1911-blair-james:
James Blair (1656–1743) was a Scottish churchman who shaped church and college life in colonial Virginia. Born in Scotland and educated at Edinburgh, he was sent out by the bishop of London as a missionary in 1685. He held parishes at Henrico, Jamestown, and finally Bruton Church at Williamsburg until his death.

From 1689 Blair was the bishop's commissary for Virginia, the colony's highest church office, charged with visiting parishes and keeping clergy in order. He also sat on the Virginia council and long served as its president. Charges he brought helped remove three governors. His greatest service, the entry says, lay in founding education in the colony, work the later pages set out in detail.
britannica-1911-blomfield-charles-james:
Charles James Blomfield (1786-1857) was an English churchman and scholar, and his career is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bury St Edmunds, he won high honors at Trinity College, Cambridge, and became a fellow in 1809. His first work was an edition of the Prometheus of Aeschylus in 1810.

The entry follows his move from study into church posts, then to bishop of Chester in 1824, where he pushed through needed reforms. In 1828 he moved to the bishopric of London and held it for twenty-eight years. There his drive widened the reach of the church, and he stood out as a strong speaker in the House of Lords.
britannica-1911-blount-charles:
Charles Blount was an English author born in a suburb of London, son of a knight who wrote a famed tale of his own trips to the east. His father gave him a strict schooling, and is said to have had a hand in his sons first great work. That book set out the views of the ancients on the soul of man after this life.

The work gave great offense by its doubts, the 1911 Britannica entry says. A bishop had it banned, and a hot zealot burned it, though a new issue was let pass in time. Blount was a fan of a famed thinker of doubt, and put out that mans last words as cuts from his great book. A tract on the root of image worship drew sharp fire as an attack on priest craft.
britannica-1911-blunt-john-james:
John James Blunt, an English divine who lived from 1794 to 1855, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Newcastle under Lyme in Staffordshire, he was educated at Saint John College, Cambridge. He took his degree with honours in mathematics and won a fellowship in 1816. In 1818 he was appointed a travelling bachelor and spent time in Italy and Sicily.

 He was Hulsean lecturer in 1831 and 1832 while he held a curacy in Shropshire. In 1834 he became rector of Great Oakley in Essex in that period. In 1839 he was appointed Lady Margaret professor of divinity at Cambridge. In 1854 he declined the bishopric of Salisbury when it was offered to him. His chief book was Undesigned Coincidences in the Writings of the Old and New Testaments, first out in 1833 and in fuller form in 1847.
britannica-1911-bois-brules:
Bois Brûlés, or Brulés, is the French rendering of Sichangu, the Indian name of a sub-tribe of the Dakota, in the Teton river division of North America. The entry is very brief. Its main point is one of naming and of who the name came to cover in Canada.

By 1869 the name was most often tied to the half-breed people of Manitoba who rose to brief fame in Riel's Rebellion. By then, the entry says, they had lost all purity of tribal blood. They were also called Metis, or half-castes, and most of them were descended from French-Canadians. Readers are sent to the Red River article for the rebellion itself.
britannica-1911-boissard-jean-jacques:
Jean Jacques Boissard (1528–1602) was a French antiquary and Latin poet who built a famed collection of Roman remains. Born at Besançon, he studied at Louvain, fled a harsh master, crossed Germany, and spent years in Italy, often very poor. Italy gave him his taste for old things.

He gathered choice monuments from Rome and its area, sailed to the Greek islands, and, after illness cut that tour short, finished his collection in Rome. Back home, his Protestant faith could not be openly held, so he settled at Metz and died there in 1602. His books include Poemata (1574), Emblemata (1584), lives of famous men with portraits, and a topography of ancient Rome issued from 1597 to 1602.
britannica-1911-bongars-jacques:
Jacques Bongars (1554–1612) was a French scholar who spent his career as a diplomat for Henry of Navarre, later Henry IV. Born at Orleans and raised in the reformed faith, he studied at Marburg, Jena, Orleans, and Bourges. Time in Rome and a tour of eastern Europe widened his training.

He joined the service of Ségur Pardaillan, Henry's envoy, and in 1587 was sent to the princes of northern Europe. He also went to England to beg Queen Elizabeth's help for Henry. From 1593 he stood as the French king's man at the imperial courts. He spent health and money freely to curb Habsburg power and worked on until Henry's murder in 1610. His writings include an abridged Justin and collections of crusade-era histories, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-bonnet-charles:
Charles Bonnet (1720–1793) was a Swiss naturalist and thinker from Geneva who made his name studying insects and plant life. Born to a French family driven into Switzerland by religious persecution in the 1500s, he trained in law but loved natural science. A book read at sixteen turned him to insect life, and with Réaumur's work and live specimens he added many findings of his own.

In 1740 he showed by experiment that aphids can breed without mating, the fact now called parthenogenesis, and was made a corresponding member of the Paris academy. In 1741 he turned to regrowth of lost parts in the freshwater hydra, and in 1742 he found that caterpillars and butterflies breathe through pores called stigmata. He entered the Royal Society in 1743, and later work ranged over plants, sight, and the philosophy of nature.
britannica-1911-bootes:
Boötes, the Ploughman, is a star group of the northern sky known since the earliest Greek records. Its Greek name means a ploughman, from the word for an ox. Eudoxus in the 300s B.C. and Aratus in the 200s name it, and the entry links it to hints in Homer, Hesiod, and perhaps the book of Job.

Greek picture-makers drew a walking man, club in his right hand, his left holding the leash of two dogs barking at the Great Bear. Ptolemy listed 23 stars in it, Tycho 28, and Hevelius 52. Beyond bright Arcturus, the entry picks out fine double stars, the yellow and blue pair epsilon, the yellow and purple xi, and the irregular variable W Boötis. A long roll of other names for the group, Greek, Arab, and later, closes the account.
britannica-1911-booth-charles:
Charles Booth (born 1840) was a Liverpool shipowner who spent his fortune mapping London poverty street by street. Born at Liverpool, he joined the family firm of Alfred Booth and Company, in the Brazil trade, in 1862 and later chaired the Booth Steamship Company. His spare time and large sums went to the facts of social questions.

The fruit was Life and Labour of the People in London (1891–1903). The work sets out how poverty, misery, and wrongdoing stand against steady earnings and comfort, class by class. Striking maps colour each street by its degree of want. The facts came from school-board visitors' records, from Booth's own directed inquiries, and from poor-law officers and the Charity Organization Society. The entry turns last to his kindred study of the aged poor.
britannica-1911-borda-jean-charles:
Jean Charles Borda (1733–1799) was a French mathematician and sea astronomer whose instruments served the mapping of the earth. Born at Dax, schooled at La Flèche, he took a cavalry commission young. In 1756 his paper on the motion of projectiles won him a seat in the Academy of Sciences.

He fought at Hastembeck, then joined the navy and charted the Azores and Canary Islands with an admired map. Taken by a British squadron in 1782, he was freed on parole at once and sent home. His studies in hydrodynamics helped marine engineering, and his improved reflecting and repeating circles served astronomy at sea. With Delambre and Méchain he worked on the measure of a meridian arc, using instruments mostly of his own design.
britannica-1911-boucher-de-crevecur-de-p:
Jacques Boucher de Crèvecœur de Perthes (1788–1868) was a French customs officer who became a founder of Stone Age studies. Born at Rethel in the Ardennes, he entered the customs service in 1802, served six years in Italy, and rose fast at home. In March 1825 he followed his father as director of customs at Abbeville and stayed there for life.

His leisure went to what he called antediluvian man. About 1830 he found flints in the Somme valley gravels that he took for human work, but he made the find public only in 1846. That year he reported a worked flint tool lying with remains of elephant and rhinoceros at Menchecourt. The later pages tell how the learned world first doubted, then accepted, his proof of man's great antiquity.
britannica-1911-bridaine-jacques:
Jacques Bridaine (1701–1767) was a French Roman Catholic preacher born at Chuslan in the department of Gard on 21 March 1701. He studied at Avignon, first in the Jesuit college and then at the Sulpician seminary of St Charles. Ordained in 1725, he joined the Missions Royales, a body set up to win French Protestants back to the Catholic faith.

For more than forty years he preached as a missioner in nearly every town of central and southern France, winning goodwill and many converts. His Paris sermons of 1744 struck hearers hard for their force and plain sincerity. He died at Roquemaure, near Avignon, on 22 December 1767, leaving spiritual songs printed in 1748 and often reprinted, plus five volumes of sermons issued at Avignon in 1823.
britannica-1911-bridgittines:
Bridgittines were an order of Augustinian canonesses founded by St Bridget of Sweden about 1350 and approved by Urban V in 1370. The order was double in form: each convent of women had a small house of canons beside it to serve as chaplains, yet rule rested with the abbess. That rare setup shapes the whole account.

Houses spread widely in Sweden and Norway, reaching 80 in all lands, and the order did much for learning and letters in the north. Its head house at Vadstena by Lake Vetter held out until 1595. In England the rich convent of Syon at Isleworth, founded by Henry V in 1415, was restored under Mary. Driven abroad under Elizabeth, wandering to the Low Countries, Rouen and at last Lisbon in 1594 before returning to England in 1861. The house, now at Chudleigh in Devon, claims an unbroken life since before the Reformation.
britannica-1911-brigantes:
Brigantes, a Celtic name read as mountaineers or free and privileged folk, were a people of northern Britain before and during the Roman advance. Their land ran from the Humber on the east and the Mersey, or perhaps the Ribble, on the west up to the Wall of Antoninus. That sweep took in most of Yorkshire and all of Lancashire, Durham, Westmorland, Cumberland and part of Northumberland, with York as chief town.

First contact with Rome came under Claudius, when Publius Ostorius Scapula beat them in battle. Under Vespasian they submitted to Petillius Cerealis, yet full conquest waited until the days of Antoninus Pius. Their goddess Brigantia is named on stone inscriptions, as is a god Bergans, and a branch of the tribe also settled in south-east Ireland by the river Barrow.
britannica-1911-brignoles:
Brignoles is a town in the department of Var in south-eastern France, 36 miles by rail north of Toulon. It held 3639 people in 1906. The town sits 754 feet above the sea in a fertile valley, on the right bank of the Carami river, a setting that feeds its farm trade.

Inside stands the old summer palace of the counts of Provence, fitting the town's old name Villa Puerorum, since the counts' children were often raised there. Trade runs briskly, above all in prunes sold as prunes de Brignoles. The town was sacked more than once in the religious wars of the 16th century. Twelve miles north-west lies St Maximin, a starting point for the pilgrimage to Sainte Baume, where St Mary Magdalene is said to have taken refuge, 20 miles away by road.
britannica-1911-brindley-james:
James Brindley (1716–1772) was an English engineer born at Thornsett, Derbyshire, in 1716 to parents in very humble circumstances. He had little or no schooling. Apprenticed at seventeen to a millwright near Macclesfield, he soon set up on his own as a wheelwright at Leek and won fame for clever repair of all kinds of machinery.

In 1752 he built an engine to drain coal pits at Clifton, and in 1755 finished machinery for a silk mill at Congleton. His great chance came in 1759, when the duke of Bridgewater wanted better outlets for his coal: Brindley advised a canal from Worsley to Manchester. Its crown was an aqueduct carrying the canal 39 feet above the river Irwell at Barton. Success brought more schemes, an extension to the Mersey at Runcorn and the Grand Trunk Canal joining Trent, Humber and Mersey.
britannica-1911-brisson-mathurin-jacques:
Mathurin Jacques Brisson (1723–1806) was a French zoologist and natural philosopher born at Fontenay le Comte on 30 April 1723. The first half of his life went to natural history, the study of animals. His published works in that field include Le Regne animal of 1756 and a great Ornithologie of 1760, on birds.

After the death of Reaumur (1683–1757), whose assistant he had been, Brisson left natural history behind. He became professor of natural philosophy, the study of matter and force, at Navarre and later at Paris. His chief work in that second career was Poids specifiques des corps of 1787. On the specific weights of bodies, backed by several other books on physical subjects that held repute for a time. He died at Croissy near Paris on 23 June 1806, closing a life split cleanly between two sciences.
britannica-1911-brooke-frances:
Frances Brooke (1724–1789) was an English novelist and dramatist whose maiden name was Moore, born in 1724. Her novels won considerable popularity in their day. Three titles carry her reputation in the short entry, spanning fourteen years of work, while her plays and her translations from French have sunk from view.

Chief among the novels are The History of Lady Julia Mandeville of 1763, Emily Montague of 1769 and The Excursion of 1777. The notice sets those dates and titles as the record worth keeping, calls her dramatic pieces and translations forgotten, and closes with her death in January 1789. Compact as it is, the account tells a reader exactly which books to seek and which parts of her output time has left behind.
britannica-1911-brooke-sir-james:
Sir James Brooke, who lived from 1803 to 1868, was an English soldier who became raja of Sarawak. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens at his birth near Bath. His father served the East India Company in Bengal. James joined that service too and sailed for India about 1825. A grave wound in the Burmese war sent him home in 1826.

A voyage to China in 1830 changed his course. Among the islands he saw rich lands torn by war and piracy. He formed a plan to bring those peoples under settled rule. Wealth left by his father let him buy a yacht, the Royalist. He spent three years training its crew of twenty men. In October 1838 he sailed from the Thames for Borneo. The head of the entry stops as he reaches the island, with his great venture just begun.
britannica-1911-browne-james:
James Browne (1793–1841) was a Scottish man of letters born at Whitefield in Perthshire in 1793. Educated at Edinburgh and at St Andrews, where he studied for the church, he instead turned to writing and law. A Sketch of the History of Edinburgh for Ewbank's Picturesque Views of that city came out from 1823 to 1825, early proof of his pen.

In 1826 he joined the Faculty of Advocates and took a doctorate of laws from King's College, Aberdeen. His works include a critical examination of Macculloch on the Highlands and Islands (1826), a French study of Egyptian hieroglyphs printed at Paris in 1827. A History of the Highlands and Highland Clans from 1834 to 1836. Appointed editor of the Caledonian Mercury in 1827. He became sub-editor of the seventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica two years later, contributing a large number of its articles before his death in April 1841.
britannica-1911-browne-maximilian-ulysse:
Maximilian Ulysses Browne, Count von Browne (1705–1757), was an Austrian field marshal born at Basel on 23 October 1705. His father, an Irish exile of 1690 in imperial service, was made a count of the Empire in 1716, and an uncle rose to field marshal in the Russian army. Family influence and a marriage into the Martinitz family pushed the young officer up so fast that at twenty-nine he was colonel of an infantry regiment.

He earned the speed in the field. Distinction in the Italian campaign of 1734 came first. Further credit in the Tirolese fighting of 1735 and in the unlucky Turkish war raised him to general officer. By 1740 he was a lieutenant field marshal commanding the Silesian garrisons when Frederick II and the Prussian army overran the province. His careful use of such resources as he had is where the account dwells as it opens the Silesian war.
britannica-1911-browne-sir-james:
Sir James Browne (1839–1896) was an Anglo-Indian engineer and administrator, son of Robert Browne of Falkirk in Scotland. Educated at the military college at Addiscombe, he received a commission in the Bengal engineers in 1857. Frontier service came fast: the expedition against the Mahsud Waziris in 1860, with mention in despatches, and the Umbeyla campaign of 1863, where he was three times mentioned.

In January 1875 he became superintendent of works for building the Indus bridge, rose to lieutenant-colonel in 1877. He served as political officer with Sir Donald Stewart in the Afghan War of 1878-1879, fighting in several engagements and receiving the C.B., and he became colonel in 1881. He led the Indian engineer contingent sent to Egypt in 1882 and fought at Tell-el-Kebir. He was engineer in chief of the Sind-Pishin railway from 1884, was knighted K.C.S.I. in 1888, and became quarter-master-general for India in 1889.
britannica-1911-bruges:
Bruges, in Flemish Brugge, a name meaning the bridge or place of bridges, is the capital of West Flanders in Belgium, with 53,728 people in 1904. The city holds some of the finest monuments of the great age of the Flemish communes. Its medieval appearance is better preserved as a whole than that of any other Belgian city.

The cathedral of St Sauveur and the church of Notre-Dame, early Pointed Gothic work of the 13th and 14th centuries, lead the sights. The cathedral was much injured by fire in 1839 yet keeps fine proportions, pictures and monumental brasses. Notre-Dame holds Michelangelo's marble Virgin and Child and the gilded copper effigies of Charles the Bold and Mary of Burgundy. The hospital of St Jean, caring for the sick since the 12th century, holds Memling's chief works, including the famed reliquary of St Ursula. The market hall of 1561-1566 rises on an older site.
britannica-1911-brunet-jacques-charles:
Jacques Charles Brunet (1780–1867) was a French bibliographer born in Paris on 2 November 1780, son of a bookseller. In 1802 he printed a supplement to the bibliographical dictionary of rare books by Duclos and Cailleau from 1790. In 1810 came the first edition of his Manuel du libraire et de l'amateur des livres, in three volumes, the work that made his name.

Successive editions of that great bibliographical dictionary rapidly won recognition as the first book of its class in European literature. He died on 14 November 1867. Other works named are new bibliographical researches of 1834, researches on the original editions of Rabelais of 1852, and an edition of the French poems of J. G. Alione d'Asti from the early 16th century, dated 1836. A supplement to the Manuel's fifth edition, by Deschamps and G. Brunet, appeared in 1878-1880, after his death.
britannica-1911-bryce-james:
James Bryce (1838–) was a British jurist, historian and politician. This 1911 Britannica biography traces his career. He was born at Belfast on 10 May 1838. He studied at Glasgow and at Trinity College, Oxford. In 1862 he became a fellow of Oriel. He practised briefly at the bar in London. Then Oxford called him back as regius professor of civil law. He held that chair from 1870 to 1893.

His book The Holy Roman Empire made his name in 1864. His great work was The American Commonwealth, in 1888. It studied United States institutions as history and law. The book at once became a classic. Bryce was a Liberal member of parliament from 1880. He held office under Gladstone and later cabinets. He was chief secretary for Ireland in 1905. In February 1907 he became British ambassador at Washington. The entry also notes his climb of Mount Ararat in 1876.
britannica-1911-builders-rites:
Builders rites are customs tied to the laying of foundation stones for buildings. Their custom entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Coins and newspapers are oft placed in a hole beneath the stone. The plain view says such goods record the event for later finders.

The entry argues a deeper and older reason must lie behind the rite. In old times living victims were chosen as a gift to the gods. Grimm held that men walled live beasts and men into foundations. That grim gift was meant to ensure the building would stand firm. Skeletons found under two round towers in Ireland back that claim.
britannica-1911-bulfinch-charles:
Charles Bulfinch, an American builder, fills a life of town works in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Boston in seventeen sixty three, he was the son of a rich doctor. He learned at Boston Latin School and at Harvard in his youth. Years of travel and study in Europe shaped his craft. In seventeen eighty seven he set up in Boston as its first pro builder.

His first works span a stage house and the new State House of the town. For twenty one years he led the town board as its chief. Drain, light, watch, and street works all grew new in his hands. In eighteen eighteen he took charge of the Capitol works at Washington. There he built the dome hall and the west front to his own plans.
britannica-1911-burbage-james:
James Burbage, an English actor who died in fifteen ninety seven, was said to be born at Stratford. He was a member of the earl of Leicester's company of players. By fifteen seventy four he stood at the head of that company of actors. In fifteen seventy six he got a lease of land at Shoreditch. There he built the house known for twenty years as The Theatre.

That house was the first theatre ever built in London, the entry says. Burbage also had a hand in a second house near by, the Curtain. Later, against much local ill will, he began the Blackfriars theatre in fifteen ninety six. That house became the most famed home of the rising drama of the age. His son Richard was more famed than his father as an actor. Richard played all the great parts in Shakespeare's plays on stage.
britannica-1911-burney-charles:
Charles Burney is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English writer on music and a church organist. Born in Shrewsbury in seventeen twenty six, he learned music from local teachers and then in London. He wrote stage music while still a young man.

The entry follows his posts in London and in Norfolk and his growing plan for a full history of music. Ill health sent him to the country, where his health came back. He later took music degrees at Oxford. To gather facts for his history he toured the main courts and towns of Europe. His travel books and his history made his lasting name.
britannica-1911-butler-charles:
Charles Butler is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Butler was a British lawyer and writer of many works, born in London in 1750. He was educated at Douai and entered Lincoln's Inn in 1775. He built a strong practice as a conveyancer, a drafter of property deeds.

After the Roman Catholic Relief Act of 1791, he was called to the bar. In the last year of his life he took silk and became a bencher of his inn. His writing output was enormous, running to about fifty volumes. The entry names his Reminiscences and his studies of biblical subjects. His Book of the Roman Catholic Church of 1825 stirred a public dispute. He also wrote lives of Erasmus, Grotius, Bossuet, and Fenelon. Readers meet a Catholic lawyer whose pen served both his profession and his faith.
britannica-1911-byron-henry-james:
Henry James Byron, an English playwright who lived from 1834 to 1884, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Manchester, the son of a British consul. In 1858 he entered the Middle Temple to study law. He soon gave up all show of legal study and joined a touring company as an actor.

As an actor he never did well, though he played for years, mostly in his own pieces. As a writer he was tireless, and he was the first editor of the comic paper Fun. His early wins came in burlesque, and in 1865 he helped run a London theatre. His great hit was Our Boys, which ran at the Vaudeville from 1875 to 1879. That was a run without match at the time.
britannica-1911-cadoudal-georges:
Georges Cadoudal, leader of the Chouans in the French Revolution, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from 1771 to 1804. He was born near Auray and had a fair schooling. When the Revolution broke out, he stayed true to his royalist and Catholic teaching.

From 1793 he raised a rebellion in the Morbihan against the new government. It was quickly put down. He then joined the army of the revolted Vendeans. He fought at Le Mans and at Savenay in December 1793. Back in Morbihan, he was arrested and held at Brest. He escaped and began the fight once more. His party met defeat after defeat. More than once he was forced to take refuge in England. Still he kept up the struggle. The article traces a die-hard foe of the Revolution who would not yield.
britannica-1911-calais-and-zetes:
Calais and Zetes, twin brothers in Greek myth, are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They were the winged sons of Boreas, the north wind, and Oreithyia. Sailing with the Argonauts, they came to Salmydessus in Thrace. There they freed their sister Cleopatra, whom her husband Phineus had thrown into prison with her two sons.

The article gives more than one form of the tale. In one form the brothers saved Phineus from the Harpies and died in the chase. In another, Heracles slew them near the island of Tenos after a quarrel on the voyage. The gods were said to have changed them into winds. The entry ends by noting that, like the Harpies, the pair plainly stand for winds in human shape.
britannica-1911-calculating-machines:
The hosted text for this record opens in mid-article. It drops straight into the working of planimeters and integrators. Those are the calculating instruments this part of the 1911 Britannica article treats. A planimeter measures the area of a drawn figure. The text explains how repeated measurement improves the result. It also sets a limit on the figure's size.

An integrator works on the same idea in a wider form. It evaluates a definite integral from a plotted curve. The integral equals the area under that curve. The text shows how a planimeter can solve harder problems. It does so by turning them into questions of area. Integraphs take the process one step further. They draw the solution of a differential equation as a curve. Lord Kelvin first suggested the idea, the text says. No truly useful integraph has yet been built, it adds.
britannica-1911-cales:
Cales, the modern Calvi, was an ancient city of Campania. It stood on the Via Latina, in Italy. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its history and remains. The city first belonged to the Aurunci tribe. Rome took it in 335 B.C. A colony with Latin rights followed at once. Some 2500 citizens settled there as colonists. For long it was the centre of Roman power in Campania.

Cales served as an important base against Hannibal. The quaestor for southern Italy had his seat there. Its rich farmland made the city prosperous. Its black glazed pottery was exported as far as Etruria. After the Social War it became a municipium. In the 5th century it became a bishop's see. The entry describes its 12th-century cathedral in detail. It notes carved portals, marble mosaic work, and early Christian grottos. Remains of an amphitheatre and theatre also survive nearby.
britannica-1911-cannes:
Cannes, a seaport of France on the Mediterranean in the Alpes Maritimes, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies south west of Nice, with about twenty four thousand people in 1906. The town faces south on a slope to the sea, and ranges of hills shield it from the north winds.

Before 1831 Cannes was little more than its old quarter, with a castle and a hill church. Lord Brougham's notice that year changed its fate. It grew into a large town and one of the most fashionable winter resorts in the south of France, much loved by English visitors. Fine villas crowd the country round it, built of a soft stone that is sawn, not hewn. A good quay and a promenade along the beach are praised. To the east the town runs on to Golfe Jouan, where Napoleon landed in 1815 on his return from Elba.
britannica-1911-cantharides:
Cantharides, or Spanish flies, the common blister-beetles of European pharmacy, are described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. They are bright, shining golden-green or bluish beetles. The insect runs from half an inch to an inch long. The female is broader and altogether larger than the male.

The beetle is native to southern Europe, found in Spain, France, Germany, Italy, Hungary, and southern Russia, and also got in Siberia. It turns up now and then in the south of England. The insects feed on the leaves of ash, lilac, privet, and jasmine. Their presence is known by a strong, unpleasant smell that carries far. They are gathered at late evening or early morning, while dull and bedewed. Collectors shake them from the trees onto cloths spread below. They are then killed, dried, and stored in glass-stoppered bottles, guarded with care against mites.
britannica-1911-caradoc-series:
The Caradoc series is a set of rocks in Shropshire, England. It is a series of sandstones and shales. This 1911 Britannica article defines its beds. R. I. Murchison introduced the name in 1839. He took it from Caer Caradoc in Shropshire. Later work has modified the limits Murchison set. C. Lapworth defined its members by graptolite zones. Those zones match the Bala series of North Wales.

Geologists use Bala and Caradoc as interchangeable names. Both mean the top substage of the Ordovician system. The article lists the beds in descending order. The Trinucleus shales come first in that list. Acton Scott beds, Longville flags and Chatwell sandstones follow. Soudley sandstones, Harnage shales and Hoar Edge grits close it. In the Corndon district the series wears other names. There it appears as ashes, shales and grit groups. The article maps the series across several districts in turn.
britannica-1911-carales:
Carales was the most important ancient city of Sardinia. Its Greek name was Karalis, and its modern heir is Cagliari. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its history. It stood on the south coast of the island. Its founding is generally credited to the Carthaginians. Punic tombs survive in numbers near the modern town. They lie by the cemetery and on the plateau north-west.

Carales enters Roman history in the Second Punic War. It probably gained full Roman civic rights from Julius Caesar. In imperial times it was the island's chief town. Its fine sheltered harbour explains much of that rank. A detachment of the Misenum fleet was stationed there. In the 4th and 5th centuries it likely held the governor's seat. The city was the hub of Sardinia's road system. Roads ran from it to Olbia, Othoca and Sulci. The entry closes with the hill of the medieval town.
britannica-1911-carbonates:
Carbonates are the salts of carbonic acid. This 1911 Britannica article treats the whole chemical family. Many carbonates occur in nature as minerals. Cerussite, the lead carbonate, is one named example. Malachite and azurite are basic copper carbonates. Calamine is the zinc carbonate of the list. Witherite, strontianite, calcite and dolomite also appear.

Most metals form carbonates, the article says. Aluminium and chromium are the named exceptions. The alkali metals yield two types of salt. One type is the acid carbonate, or bicarbonate. The other is the normal carbonate of the textbooks. The article gives the formulas of both types. It then works through the group metal by metal. The making and properties of each salt are set out. Sodium carbonate closes the list of named natural salts.
britannica-1911-cardinal-virtues:
The cardinal virtues are the chief virtues of conduct. The phrase comes from cardo, Latin for a hinge. They are the fixed points on which conduct turns. This 1911 Britannica entry gives the classic list. Socrates and Plato name four such virtues. They are Prudence, Courage, Temperance and Justice. The Republic sets them out as the frame of the good life.

The entry notes one striking omission from the list. Benevolence plays no part in the ancient four. Yet it stands at the centre of Christian ethics. It also anchors modern theories of altruism, the entry adds. Two charges are brought against Plato's list. It is arbitrary, the critics say. Its virtues also overlap and are not truly distinct. St Ambrose first adapted the list to Christian theology. The Roman Church counts them as natural virtues. They stand against the theological virtues, Faith, Hope and Charity.
britannica-1911-carey-henry-charles:
Henry Charles Carey (1793–1879) was an American economist. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and doctrine. He was born in Philadelphia on 15 December 1793. His father, Mathew Carey, was a publisher and reformer. At twenty-eight Henry succeeded him in the firm of Carey & Lea. That firm was long the most conspicuous in America. He died in Philadelphia on 13 October 1879.

Mathew Carey had written early essays favouring protection. Henry's life-work spread the same theory of tariffs. He retired from business in 1838. His Principles of Political Economy appeared from 1837 to 1840. It became the standard American statement of the protectionist school. That school has dominated the country's tariff system since, the entry says. Smaller works treated wages, credit, interest and slavery. In 1858–1859 he gathered all into The Principles of Social Science. The three volumes crowned his lifelong labours.
britannica-1911-carloman-frankish-prince:
Carloman is the name of three Frankish princes. This 1911 Britannica article treats them in one entry. The first Carloman (d. 754) was a son of Charles Martel. He became mayor of the palace with his brother Pippin in 741. He ruled the eastern part of the Frankish kingdom. He won wars against troublesome neighbours on his borders. He also worked to reform and strengthen the church.

In 747 that Carloman laid down his office. He retired to a monastery he founded on Monte Soracte. Visitors troubled him there, so he moved to Monte Cassino. He died at Vienne on 17 August 754. The second Carloman (751–771) was Charlemagne's brother. The two became joint kings of the Franks in 768. Trouble over the Aquitaine war split them before his early death. The third was a son of Louis the Stammerer. He became king of France with his brother Louis III.
britannica-1911-carmelites:
The Carmelites are one of the four mendicant orders. In England they are called White Friars. That name comes from the white mantle over their brown habit. This long 1911 Britannica article examines their origins. It gives much space to the order's own foundation stories. Those stories were believed in the 17th and 18th centuries. They claimed that Elias founded a hermit community on Mount Carmel.

That community, the stories said, lasted unbroken to Christian times. Its members heard Peter preach at Pentecost and were converted. They built a chapel to the Virgin on Carmel. In 1668 the Bollandist Papenbroek rejected these tales as fables. A fierce controversy followed that rejection in print. The Carmelites appealed to the Inquisition against his volumes. Spain censured the offending books, but Rome did not. In 1698 a decree imposed silence on both parties. The article calls the whole affair a curiosity of history.
britannica-1911-carnutes:
Carnutes is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Celtic people of central Gaul who lived between the Seine and the Loire. Their land matched the later dioceses of Chartres, Orléans, and Blois, and other Gauls saw it as the political and religious centre of the nation. Their chief towns were Cenabum, modern Orléans, and Autricum, modern Chartres. Livy counted them among the tribes that followed Bellovesus into Italy in early times.

The entry follows the Carnutes through Caesar's wars. In 52 B.C. they joined Vercingetorix's rebellion, and Rome punished the killing of merchants at Cenabum by burning the town and killing or enslaving its people. They sent 12,000 men to relieve Alesia but shared the Gallic defeat. Under Augustus they gained the rank of a free allied community, keeping their own institutions. In 275 Aurelian raised Cenabum to a city and renamed it Aurelianum, the root of Orléans.
britannica-1911-carroll-charles:
Charles Carroll (1737–1832) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an American political leader of Irish ancestry, born at Annapolis, Maryland. He was educated in French Jesuit colleges and studied law at Bourges, Paris, and London. He returned to Maryland in February 1765, when an estate called Carrollton was settled on him. He always signed his name as “Charles Carroll of Carrollton.”

Before and during the War of Independence he led the patriot cause in Maryland, serving on committees of correspondence and safety and in the provincial and constitutional conventions. In 1776 Congress sent him with Samuel Chase and Benjamin Franklin on a failed mission to win Canada over. He sat in the continental congress from 1776 to 1779 and signed the Declaration of Independence on 2 August 1776. He outlived every other signer, dying at Baltimore in November 1832 after years in the Maryland and United States senates.
britannica-1911-cartier-jacques:
Jacques Cartier (1491–1557) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French navigator born at St Malo in Brittany, the discoverer of the St Lawrence river. Nothing is known of his early life. On 20 April 1534 he sailed from St Malo with two ships and sixty one men, sent to look for a north west passage to the East. He reached Newfoundland on 10 May and entered the strait of Belle Isle.

Cartier worked down the west coast of Newfoundland, was driven by a storm into the gulf, and named Brion Island after Admiral Chabot. He mistook the Magdalen and Prince Edward islands for the mainland shore. Sailing north along New Brunswick, he found that Chaleur Bay was no strait. During ten days in Gaspé Harbour he made friends with Huron-Iroquois men from Quebec and carried two of them off with him. The entry follows the voyage harbour by harbour.
britannica-1911-caryatides:
Caryatides is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an architectural term from ancient Greece. The word is the plural of Caryatis, a woman of Caryae in Laconia, passed through Latin from the Greek. In architecture it names the draped female figures used as piers or supports in a building. Human figures thus take the place of plain columns, carrying the structure above them on their heads.

The entry gives two famous cases. Caryatides appear in the porticos of the Erechtheum at Athens and in the Treasury of Cnidus at Delphi. Both are works of classical Greek building, and the entry points readers to the article on Greek Art and its figures for the visual evidence. The definition is brief, but it fixes the term's origin in the women of one Laconian town and its sense in the vocabulary of classical architecture.
britannica-1911-casas-grandes:
Casas Grandes is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small village in Chihuahua, Mexico, famed for the ruins of early native buildings near its site. The village stands on the Casas Grandes river, about 150 miles north west of the city of Chihuahua. The ruins lie half a mile away. They are built of sun dried blocks of mud and gravel, some 22 inches thick, formed and dried in place.

The main building runs 800 feet from north to south and 250 feet east to west. It seems to have joined three separate piles by galleries and lower ranges. Rooms ranged from mere closets to wide courts, and walls rose perhaps six or seven storeys. Some walls still stand 40 to 50 feet high. A smaller building, set around a square court some 450 feet away, adds to the plan. The exact layout stays obscure, and the entry says so.
britannica-1911-cassiterides:
The 1911 Britannica article on the Cassiterides examines the Tin Islands of ancient geography, islands placed somewhere near the west coasts of Europe. Herodotus had dimly heard of them, and later writers set them off the north-west coast of Spain as small islands with tin and lead mines.

The article argues that no real place fits the reports. Tin in fact came from north-west Spain and from Cornwall, neither of which matches the tale, and the Scillies hold no tin worth naming. It concludes that the name most likely records the first vague Greek knowledge that tin was found overseas somewhere in the far west.
britannica-1911-castres:
Castres, a town in the south-west of France, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Agout in the department of Tarn. In 1906 its commune held just over twenty-eight thousand people. Old houses line the river, and wide streets cross the west of the town.

The article notes the old church of Saint Benoît and the town hall in a former palace. It lists trades such as cloth weaving, tanning, and the making of ware and machines. A short history tells how the town grew round an abbey and passed through the wars of the Albigenses.
britannica-1911-cathelineau-jacques:
Jacques Cathelineau is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cathelineau was a French Vendean chief in the Revolution who lived from 1759 to 1793. He travelled Anjou as a pedlar and dealer in smuggled goods. His strength and deep piety gave him great sway over the peasants. They called him the saint of Anjou.

The article tells how priests and royal exiles drew him into revolt. He gathered peasants and smugglers and took a castle and its cannon. In March 1793 his band took town after town. His force grew and joined other Vendean chiefs to take more towns. To end rivalry among the chiefs, he was named head of all the rebels. In 1793 the royal forces tried to take Nantes. Cathelineau entered the town but was killed there, and his army broke up.
britannica-1911-causses:
Causses is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the limestone table lands south of the central plateau of France, sloping west from the Cévennes. The name comes from the Latin calx, lime, through a local French form. The causses spread across parts of six departments, among them Lozère, Aveyron, and Lot. They are dry, sterile, and treeless, most starkly in the east, where the Causse Méjan rises to nearly 4200 feet.

Deep river gorges now split what was once one table land, the Tarn, Dourbie, and Jonte cutting through it. The summits have no running water, since rain sinks through the porous soil or drains into deep fissures. The people of the higher causses, the Caussenards, farm sheltered hollows and keep sheep. From the sheep's milk they make Roquefort cheeses. The entry paints a hard, waterless country that its people work by pockets and by grazing.
britannica-1911-cazotte-jacques:
The 1911 Britannica article on Jacques Cazotte (1719-1792) gives the life of a French author. He was born at Dijon. He was trained by the Jesuits. He held a public post at Martinique. He came back to Paris in 1760. He then appeared in print for the first time. A mock romance and a song made him popular.

The article lists his romances and his fantastic oriental tales. His most popular work is a tale of 1772. In it the hero raises the devil. Cazotte wrote with great ease and speed. Later he took up prophecy with the Illuminati. He was arrested in August 1792. He was executed the next month.
britannica-1911-cebes:
Two Greek thinkers bear one name in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cebes of Cyzicus was a Stoic of the age of Marcus Aurelius. Cebes of Thebes was a pupil of Socrates and of Philolaus. Plato sets the Theban as a speaker in his Phaedo tale. There he seeks truth with zeal, keen in talk, slow to judge.

Three talks are laid to the Theban's name by old lists. Two are lost, and the third is the famed Tabula work. Most scholars deny that he wrote that last work, the entry says. Its words and stuff show marks of a later age, they hold. The work reads a picture of life hung in a shrine. True learning, it teaches, is the shaping of character.
britannica-1911-celebes:
Celebes is one of the four Great Sunda Islands in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It belongs to the Dutch East Indies. Its outline is wildly irregular, like a starfish with torn rays. Four great peninsulas jut from a small central nucleus.

Three large gulfs cut deep between those arms of land. The gulf of Tomini is by far the largest of the three. Chains of smaller islands continue each peninsula out to sea. With those islands, Celebes covers some seventy-eight thousand square miles. Its people are estimated at two million in all. The naturalist Wallace praised its scenery in strong terms. Nowhere in the archipelago, he wrote, had he seen such gorges and chasms. In the Maros district the cliffs run sheer or overhanging. Some of those precipices stand five or six hundred feet high.
britannica-1911-celestine-popes:
Celestine is the name borne by five popes, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. Celestine the First held the papacy from 422 to 432, the first of the five. At his accession the strife left by the Eulalius faction had not yet died down. He rose above that strife, and his reign as bishop of Rome was a peaceful one.

When the teachings of Nestorius were reported to him, Celestine charged Cyril of Alexandria to pursue the matter. The emperor Theodosius the Second called a general council at Ephesus, to which Celestine sent his envoys. He had hard dealings with bishops in Africa over appeals to Rome. To root out Pelagian teaching he sent the deacon Palladius to Britain. He also charged Palladius to preach in Ireland, and he was the first pope known to take a direct hand in the churches of Britain and Ireland.
britannica-1911-celestines:
Celestines is the subject of a religious order article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Celestines were an order founded near 1260 by Peter of Morrone. Peter later became Pope Celestine the Fifth. The order sought to unite the hermit life with life in common. His first followers lived as hermits on a mountain in the Abruzzi. The rule of Saint Benedict formed the basis of their life, with added strict rules.

The article says the order spread fast in the founder's lifetime. In time it held about a hundred fifty monasteries in Italy, with others in France, Bohemia, and the Netherlands. The French houses formed their own group, with its head house in Paris. The revolutions of France and of the eighteen hundreds destroyed their houses. By 1911 the Celestine order seems no longer to exist. Its monks wore a black habit.
britannica-1911-cenobites:
Cenobites is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on monks who live in common. The word comes from two Greek words, one meaning common and one meaning life. Cenobites live together in a convent or community. They live under a rule and under a superior. The entry sets them against hermits and anchorets, who live alone in isolation.

Two great families of orders stand as the chief examples. In the East the Basilians hold that place. In the West the Benedictines do. The entry gives no history of either. Instead it points the reader onward. Cross references lead to the articles on the Basilian monks, the Benedictines, and Monasticism itself. The whole definition fits in a few lines, but it fixes the term that names the communal half of monastic life.
britannica-1911-ceres:
Ceres was an old grain queen of Italy. Her name may mean the one who makes, from roots for grow and make. When Greek gods were brought to Rome past a great drought, the Greek grain queen took her place in Rome. Or, as the entry puts it, Greek rites and tales were grafted on to her cult.

Her rites were Greek in tongue and form, and Greek born wives served as her staff. Plain folk were her chief flock, and her shrine by the great ring was kept by their chiefs. Her chief feast with games ran each spring for a week. A fall fast in her name came in late days.
britannica-1911-cevennes:
Cévennes is a mountain range of southern France, treated in this 1911 Britannica article. It forms the southern and eastern fringe of the central plateau, and part of the divide between the streams flowing to the Atlantic and those flowing to the Mediterranean. The range is a narrow ridge some 320 miles long, with high plateaus and side ranges branching from it.

Its northern part, under names such as the mountains of Charolais and Lyonnais, nowhere rises above 3,320 feet. The central part holds the highest point of the whole range, the Mont de Mézenc at 5,755 feet. Farther south lies the part to which the name Cévennes is most strictly given, in Lozère and Gard. In the south the range divides the cold, bare Causses table lands from the sunny lowland of Languedoc, where the olive, vine, and mulberry thrive.
britannica-1911-chagres:
Chagres is a village in Panama, on the Atlantic coast of the Isthmus. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it at the mouth of the Chagres river. Columbus found the port in 1502 on his voyages, it says. Traffic across to Panama on the Pacific side ran through it for ages.

When Porto Bello faded, Chagres became the chief Atlantic port there. Gold seekers bound for California in 1849 raised it to its peak. The Panama railway in 1855 drew that traffic to Colon instead. The town then shrank to poor huts with little past glory left. A castle at the river mouth marks its old defense role.
britannica-1911-charity-and-charities:
Charity and Charities, a long essay in the 1911 Britannica, treats giving as both a habit of mind and a form of work. Charity, or love, stands for the rule of the good life. From that habit springs the shared and private effort to help others. Where the habit is weak, the effort drifts and lacks a clear aim. Where it is strong, help rests on close study of social needs.

The essay holds that sound rules for good work can be found by study of how social life has grown. It then sorts out near words that are often mixed up. Some stress family love, some grace or favour, and some a gift owed as a duty. Alms paid from duty are set apart from the kindness the Bible calls mercy. Readers get a clear frame for judging such work.
britannica-1911-charles-i-king-of-naples:
Charles the First was king of Naples and Sicily and count of Anjou. He lived from twelve twenty six to twelve eighty five. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the seventh child of Louis the Eighth of France and Blanche of Castile.

Charles gained Anjou and Maine in twelve thirty two, then wed Beatrice of Provence. With help from his brother the French king, he took that county as well. In twelve forty eight he joined the crusade to Egypt with Louis. He was captured there, then freed for ransom and sent home. Back in Provence he put down town revolts and cut their free rights.
britannica-1911-charles-ii-king-of-naple:
Charles the Second lived from 1250 to 1309 and was king of Naples and Sicily. The 1911 Britannica life makes him son of Charles the First of that line. In 1284 a sea fight off Naples ended with his capture at war. Ruggiero di Lauria took him for Peter of Aragon in that battle. When his father died, Charles was still a prisoner in Aragon hands.

In 1288 Edward the First of England brokered a peace for his release. Charles was to keep Naples alone, with Sicily left to Aragon. He also had to make his cousin Charles of Valois drop Aragon. Valois had been given that crown by the pope but never held it. Charles left three sons and sixty nobles as hostages for the pact.
britannica-1911-chartered-companies:
Chartered companies are trading firms that hold rights from a crown charter. The 1911 Britannica entry sets out what such a charter does in law. It grants set rights and lays set duties on the firm. It also fixes the lands where those rights may be used in trade. Such firms are old, but their form has changed with the times.

In Britain the first such charters went to foreign groups, not English ones. Branches of the Hanseatic League held them in the early days. Queen Elizabeth shut their London yard, the Steelyard, in the year 1597. That step ended 700 years of foreign chartered trade in England. All English trading firms trace their roots to the Merchants of the Staple.
britannica-1911-chartres:
Chartres, a city of north-western France, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is the capital of the department of Eure-et-Loir. It lies south-west of Paris, on the railway to Le Mans. Its people numbered 19,433 in 1906. The city is built on the left bank of the Eure river.

It stands on a hill crowned by its famous cathedral. The spires of that church are a landmark in all the country around. To the south-east stretches the fruitful plain of Beauce. Beauce is called the granary of France. Chartres is the commercial centre of that plain. The Eure divides into three branches at this point. Several bridges cross it, some of them ancient. Remains of the old walls fringe the river in places. The Porte Guillaume, a gateway flanked by towers, is the most complete of them. It dates from the fourteenth century.
britannica-1911-chastellain-georges:
Georges Chastellain (d. 1475) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Burgundian chronicler, a native of Alost in Flanders. His surname came from ancestors who were burgraves, or châtelains, of the town. The entry works out his birth date from his own words. He was a schoolboy at Louvain in 1430, so his birth falls nearer 1415 than 1405. He saw active service in the Anglo French wars and won the name L'adventureux.

In 1434 Philip the Good, duke of Burgundy, rewarded his military service with a gift. After the peace of Arras in 1435 he left soldiering for diplomacy. He spent ten years in France, serving great lords and running missions to the duke. He then entered Philip's own household and joined the ducal council in 1457. His household titles, pantler and carver, hide the real work. He was a diplomatist, employed on errands between two hostile courts.
britannica-1911-chaudesaigues:
Chaudes-Aigues is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a village of central France, in the department of Cantal. It stands at the foot of the Aubrac mountains, 19 miles south south west of St Flour by road. The village counted 937 people in 1906. Its commune counted 1558. The village is celebrated for its hot mineral springs. Their heat runs from 135 to 177 degrees Fahrenheit. At their hottest they rank as the hottest springs in France.

The water holds bicarbonate of soda. It is used in medicine, for rheumatism and other ills. It is also put to work in daily life. People wash fleeces in it and hatch eggs with its heat. In winter it heats the houses of the town. A cold chalybeate spring, the Condamine, lies nearby. The Romans knew the warm springs, and Sidonius Apollinaris mentioned them. The entry joins medicine, housekeeping, and a long history in one small place.
britannica-1911-chauncy-charles:
Charles Chauncy (1592–1672) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the president of Harvard College. He was born at Yardley Bury in Hertfordshire and educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow. He served as vicar at Ware and then at Marston St Lawrence. He refused to observe Archbishop Laud's regulations. The court of high commission suspended and imprisoned him in 1634, for opposing a rail around the communion table.

His recantation in 1637 left him lasting self reproach. That year he emigrated to America. He was associate pastor at Plymouth, then pastor at Scituate from 1641 to 1654. From 1654 until his death he was president of Harvard, succeeding Henry Dunster. Cotton Mather called him a most incomparable scholar. His writings include The Plain Doctrine of the Justification of a Sinner, of 1659. The entry closes with his son Isaac, a voluminous theological writer in England.
britannica-1911-chaves:
Chaves is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of northern Portugal, in the district of Villa Real. It stands eight miles south of the Spanish frontier, on the right bank of the river Tamega. Its population in 1900 was 6388. Chaves is the ancient Aquae Flaviae. It is famous for hot saline springs that are still in use. A fine Roman bridge of eighteen arches spans the Tamega.

In the sixteenth century the town held 20,000 people. It was long one of the principal frontier fortresses of Portugal. Its present name comes from that role: chaves means keys, the keys of the north. One of its churches holds the tomb of Alphonso I of Portugal. In 1830 the town gave a marquis's title to Pinto da Fonseca, a leader of the Miguelite party. The entry joins Roman remains, spa waters, and border defence in one short account.
britannica-1911-chechenzes:
Chechenzes is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a people of the eastern Caucasus, occupying the whole of west Daghestan. The Georgians know them as Khists. They call themselves Nakhtche, “people.” The entry calls them a wild, fierce people. They fought desperately against Russian invasion in the eighteenth century under Shamyl and others. They fought on in the nineteenth under Khazi Mollah. Some in the mountain districts were still independent.

Their character, as the entry gives it, mixes generosity and hospitality with quick revenge. The women wear rich robes, pink silk trousers, and silver bracelets. Their houses, though, are mere hovels of earth, boughs, and stones. Before Russian rule every man was equal, and communes governed themselves by popular assembly. Justice lay in the hands of the wronged. Murder could be paid for only by death, unless the killer submitted to a ritual of brotherhood on the Koran.
britannica-1911-cheremisses:
Cheremisses, also called Tcheremisses, are a Finnish people living in scattered groups across eastern Russia, in governments such as Kazan, Viatka, Perm and Ufa. They call themselves Mori or Mari, and their language belongs to the Finno-Ugrian family. The entry puts their number at some 240,000. Two physical types are described, one dark and flat faced, the other short, fair and white skinned.

Those on the right bank of the Volga are called Hill Cheremis, and the entry calls them taller and stronger than the left bank groups. The people farm and keep horses and cattle, and they are usually monogamous. Their faith mixes Shamanism, Islam and Christianity. Marriage by forced abduction of the bride, coin breastplates and hooded head-dresses trimmed with glass jewels are described in detail.
britannica-1911-chlorates:
Chlorates are the metal salts of chloric acid, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. All of them are solids that dissolve in water. The potassium salt dissolves least of them all. They can be made by more than one route, such as soaking a metal oxide in water and filling the mix with chlorine gas.

Heat breaks all chlorates down and frees oxygen from them. Strong sulphuric acid on them frees a gas called chlorine peroxide. The chief salt of the group is potassium chlorate, first got in 1786. In modern works it is made by the use of electric current in a hot salt bath. It forms large white tablets with a bright shine. Its uses take in the making of oxygen and matches, fireworks, and medicine.
britannica-1911-chosroes:
Chosroes is a common Persian king name, meaning with a good name. Its kings entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was borne by a famed king of Iranian legend first. Two Sassanid kings who bore the name are treated in the entry.

Chosroes the First, called the Blessed, ruled from five thirty one to five seventy nine. He first made an endless peace with the emperor Justinian of Rome. Roman wins in Africa and Sicily then drew him back to war. In five forty he invaded Syria and sacked the city of Antioch. He moved its people to a new city near Ctesiphon built for them.
britannica-1911-chretien-de-troyes:
Chretien de Troyes is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French medieval poet. He was a native of Champagne in France. He is the most famous French poet of his age. Few exact details of his life are known today. Opinion differs on the dates of his poems. He wrote the Chevalier de la Charrette for a patron. That patron was Marie, countess of Champagne. 

He wrote the Conte del Graal for another patron. That was Philip, count of Flanders, who died in 1191. The tale is also known by the name Perceval. Philip had been regent of France from 1180 to 1182. The Grail poem was likely made in that period. Chretien called it the best tale told at the royal court. He left that poem unfinished at his death or rest. At least three later writers added to it over time.
britannica-1911-churchill-charles:
Churchill, Charles (1731–1764) was an English poet and satirist, born in Vine Street, Westminster, in February 1731 and educated at Westminster school. His father held a curacy and lectureship at St John's, Westminster, and the son followed him into orders after a hasty Fleet marriage. He became curate at South Cadbury, then succeeded his father at Rainham in 1758. Pay under 100 pounds a year forced him to teach in a girls' school as well.

The Rosciad, published in March 1761, made his name with a reckless, exact satire on London actors and actresses, Garrick alone escaping censure among leading men. Debt, a failed marriage and scandal marked these years, and protests from his parishioners led him to resign his offices in 1763. He then worked closely with John Wilkes on the North Briton. The Prophecy of Famine in 1763 turned his wit on Scottish influence and Lord Bute.
britannica-1911-chuvashes:
Chuvashes, or Tchuvashes, are a tribe found in eastern Russia, forming about one fourth of the population of the government of Kazan. They also live in scattered communities through Simbirsk, Samara, Saratov, Orenburg and Perm. Some identify them with the Burtasses of the Arab geographers, and many authorities think them descendants of the ancient Bolgars. In looks they generally resemble the Finns, round headed, flat featured and light eyed, though Tatar contact has marked them.

Their number is put at some half a million in the entry's count. In dress they are thoroughly Russianised, and they are nominally Christians in faith. Yet they cling to many old Shamanistic practices alongside that formal faith, the entry notes. Their language belongs to the Tatar or Turkish group of tongues. It has been strongly influenced by the Finno-Ugrian idioms spoken around it, a point the entry closes on.
britannica-1911-cis-sutlej-states:
Cis-Sutlej States, an old name for the southern part of the Punjab in India, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name came into use in 1809, when the Sikh chiefs south of the Sutlej river came under British protection. It covered the land south of that river and north of the Delhi territory. The Himalayas bound it on the east.

Before 1846 most of that land was independent, watched only by a British political officer at Umballa. After the first Sikh War the full rule of the tract passed to that officer. In 1849 the Punjab was annexed, and the Cis-Sutlej charge was folded into the new province. By 1862 shifts of districts made the old name unfit, and the tract became the Umballa division. Patiala, Jind, and Nabha got their own agency in 1901.
britannica-1911-clark-john-bates:
John Bates Clark was an American man of wealth lore who was born at Providence in eighteen forty-seven. He was schooled at Brown, at Amherst, and at two schools past the sea. In eighteen seventy-seven he took a chair of that lore at a small school in the north west. Posts at two more schools came in turn.

In eighteen ninety-five he took the chair at a great school in New York. His books span more than twenty years of work. Themes run from the thought of wealth, to pay, to funds and their gains, to the sway of great firm groups and lone trade rule.
britannica-1911-clark-sir-james:
Sir James Clark, who lived from 1788 to 1870, was an English physician born at Cullen in Banffshire. The 1911 Britannica article says he was schooled at Fordyce and at the universities of Aberdeen and Edinburgh. He served six years as an army surgeon. He then spent time in travel on the continent. His aim was to study mineral waters and the air of health resorts. He lived in Rome for seven years.

Clark set up practice in London in 1826. In 1835 he became physician to the duchess of Kent. Two years later he was made physician in ordinary to Queen Victoria. In 1838 he was given a baronetcy. His chief books deal with the force of climate on long illness, with tables of weather data, and with consumption of the lungs. The first came out in 1829 and the second in 1835.
britannica-1911-classified-list-of-artic:
Classified List of Articles is a subject index to the encyclopaedia's own contents, arranging article titles under broad heads and smaller groups. A warning at its head states plainly that the lists that follow are highly incomplete and are work in progress. Anthropology and Ethnology opens the portion hosted here, with a note sending readers to Archaeology for ancient anthropology. General Subjects and Terms then lists heads from Anthropology itself through tattooing, totemism, tribe and wampum.

A second group, Races and Tribes, runs alphabetically through peoples of every continent, from the Ababda and Abipones to Aztecs, Basques, Bedouins, Berbers and Blackfoot. Cross references in brackets direct readers between related heads, as the opening note does for religious customs.
