The value of the piece lies in that map of coverage rather than in any single subject. Readers can trace how the 1911 edition sorted human knowledge into classes and names.
britannica-1911-clay-charles:
Charles Clay (1801-1893) was an English surgeon based in Manchester. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his training in Manchester and Edinburgh. He qualified in 1823 and built a general practice at first. In 1839 he moved to Manchester as a surgeon who operated and advised.

His name rests on one bold operation above all. In 1842 he first carried out ovariotomy with full success. By 1865 he could report 111 cases with deaths just above thirty percent. That record helped prove the operation could be made safe. He also wrote on geology and on the coinage of the Isle of Man.
britannica-1911-cleanthes:
Cleanthes, a Stoic thinker born about three hundred and one years before the common count, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Assos in the Troad, he was at first a boxer. He came to Athens with just four small coins to his name. There he heard a Cynic teach, then the Stoic head of the school.

All the while he kept himself by night work. He bore water for a man who kept a garden plot. That toil won him a byname tied to the well. His slow pace won him a rude name as well, that of the ass. Yet his high worth won such love that he took the school on the death of its head in two sixty three. He kept up his hand work all the same. His pupils held a king of Macedon, who gave him a large gift of coin.
britannica-1911-cleethorpes:
Cleethorpes, a watering place in Lincolnshire in England, is given a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies within the borough of Great Grimsby, a few miles south east of that town, and its urban district held more than twelve thousand people in 1901. The town faces east to the North Sea, though its shore of fine sand, good for bathing, belongs in truth to the estuary of the Humber. 

A pier stands there, and the sea wall runs for about a mile as a promenade. Its church shows mostly Norman work, with older work in the tower, and crowds came from the midland counties and the north.
britannica-1911-clemenceau-georges:
Georges Clemenceau is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Clemenceau was a French statesman born in the Vendee in 1841. He trained as a doctor and settled in Montmartre in Paris in 1869. After the revolt of 1870 he was named mayor of that unruly district. He won a seat in the National Assembly in 1871 as a Radical.

The article tells how he tried in vain to stop the killing of two generals by the Commune crowd. He was cleared of blame, but the charge led to a duel and a short prison term. He gave up his posts and left politics for a time. He came back through the Paris city council. In 1876 he won a seat in the Chamber of Deputies. His force and sharp speech soon made him leader of the Radical group.
britannica-1911-clement-jacques:
Clément, Jacques (1567–1589) was the murderer of the French king Henry III, born at Sorbon in the Ardennes and become a Dominican friar. Civil war raged in France, and Clément became an ardent partisan of the League, his mind apparently unhinged by religious fanaticism. He talked of exterminating the heretics and formed a plan to kill the king. League heads encouraged him with promises of earthly reward for success and eternal bliss for failure.

With letters for the king he left Paris on 31 July 1589 and reached St Cloud, where Henry was besieging Paris. Admitted next day, he said he had a confidential message, and as Henry read the letters he stabbed him with a dagger hidden beneath his cloak. Attendants killed the assassin at once, and Henry died early the following day. League partisans in Paris regarded Clément as a martyr, and even his canonisation was discussed.
britannica-1911-cleomenes:
Cleomenes is the name of three Spartan kings of the Agiad line, and the entry treats them in turn under one head. Cleomenes I, son of Anaxandridas, succeeded about 520 B.C. and crushed the Argives near Tiryns, burning some 6,000 of them in a sacred grove where they had fled. That victory secured Sparta the undisputed hegemony of the Peloponnese. His moves in central Greece fared worse, as the next episodes show.

In 510 he marched to Athens to help expel the Peisistratidae, then returned to back Isagoras and the oligarchs against Cleisthenes. Blockaded in the Acropolis, he was forced to capitulate, and a second expedition broke up at Eleusis. He secured his colleague Demaratus's deposition by bribing the Delphian priestess, then fled when the bribe was discovered. Recalled about 488 B.C., he shortly afterwards killed himself in a fit of madness.
britannica-1911-clergy-reserves:
Clergy Reserves, in Canada, were lands set apart by the act of 1791, which established the provinces of Upper and Lower Canada. One eighth of all the crown lands was reserved for the support of a Protestant clergy, the entry states. Owing to the wording of the imperial act, the amount is often stated as one seventh instead. Clergy sometimes claimed that larger share for themselves under the act's terms.

Those reservations blocked the economic development of the province for many years after their creation. They also caused much bitter political and ecclesiastical controversy in Canadian public life. In 1854 the Canadian parliament secularised the reserves at last, ending their church purpose. Proceeds were applied to other purposes, chiefly educational, the entry says in closing. Land policy, church support and schooling thus meet in this short Canadian notice.
britannica-1911-cleves:
Cleves is a town of Germany in Prussia, formerly capital of its own duchy, 46 miles north-west of Düsseldorf and twelve miles east of Nijmwegen. Its people numbered 14,678 in 1900, and it lies neatly built in Dutch style on three small hills near the Rhine. A canal, the Spoykanal, joins it to that river two miles away. The old castle of Schwanenburg, once home of the dukes, has a massive tower 180 feet high.

That tower carries the legend of the Knights of the Swan, immortalised in Wagner's Lohengrin, and the restored castle now serves as court and prison. The collegiate church of about 1340 holds fine ducal monuments, and manufactures cover boots, shoes, tobacco and machinery. Beautiful woods and mineral wells make Cleves a favourite summer resort. The duchy passed to Brandenburg by the treaty of Xanten in 1614.
britannica-1911-clinton-henry-fynes:
Henry Fynes Clinton is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a British scholar of classics and dates born in seventeen eighty one. He came of an old noble line and was schooled at Westminster and Oxford. Greek and Roman texts and annals formed his life study.

The entry notes his twenty years as a member of parliament for a small borough. His fame rests on great date books that set Greek time in order. Those works put the study of old dates on a firm base at last. Later research fixed some of his calls, but the worth stands high. Short forms of both great works came out near the end of his life.
britannica-1911-clones:
Clones is a market town of County Monaghan, Ireland, 64 and a half miles south-west by west from Belfast and 93 and a half miles north-west from Dublin. Lines from Dublin, Belfast, Londonderry, Enniskillen and Cavan converge here, making it an important junction on the Great Northern railway. Its urban district counted 2,068 people in 1901, and it stands on a slight elevation. The market place, called the Diamond, occupies the summit of that rise.

A considerable agricultural trade, corn mills and farm implement works support the town, while a former lace industry is extinct. Clones was the seat of an abbey founded in the 6th century by Saint Tighernach, to whom the Protestant parish church is dedicated. Abbey remains include a 12th century nave and tower and a shrine cut from a block of red sandstone. A round tower 75 feet high also survives.
britannica-1911-cloves:
Cloves are the dried, unexpanded flower buds of Eugenia caryophyllata, a tree of the natural order Myrtaceae, named from the French clou, a nail, for their shape. The clove tree is a beautiful evergreen of 30 to 40 feet, with large oval leaves and crimson flowers in terminal clusters. Buds turn from pale to green to bright red, when they are ready for collecting. Each clove is rather more than half an inch long.

The tree is native to the Moluccas, or Spice Islands, and cloves formed a rich trade from early in the Christian era. The Portuguese held the principal portion of that trade for nearly a century after rounding the Cape of Good Hope. In 1605 the Dutch expelled them from the Moluccas and tried to extirpate clove trees in the native islands. Production was to be concentrated in the Amboyna islands under a complete Dutch monopoly.
britannica-1911-cocceius-johannes:
Cocceius, Johannes (1603–1669), strictly Koch, was a Dutch theologian born at Bremen, who studied at Hamburg and Franeker under teachers including Sixtinus Amama. In 1630 he became professor of biblical philology at the Gymnasium illustre in his native town. Transferred to Franeker in 1636, he held the chair of Hebrew and from 1643 the chair of theology also. In 1650 he succeeded Spanheim the elder as professor of theology at Leiden, where he died on 4 November 1669.

His chief services as an oriental scholar lay in Hebrew philology and exegesis, and he led the covenant or federal theology. He spiritualised the Hebrew scriptures so far that it was said Cocceius found Christ everywhere in the Old Testament and Grotius nowhere. Before the Fall as after it, he taught, God and man stood in covenant, works first and then grace. He held millenarian views and founded a school of theologians called Cocceians after him.
britannica-1911-cockle-sir-james:
Sir James Cockle is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the fourteenth of January 1819, he was an English lawyer and worker in maths. He was schooled at Charterhouse and at Trinity College, Cambridge, and entered the Middle Temple in 1838.

The article follows two careers in one life. At law he built a sound practice on the midland circuit. In 1863 he was made chief justice of Queensland, and he held that post till 1879. His lasting fame, the text says, rests on maths, not law. He worked on hard sums in algebra and on the theory of changing forms. He led learned groups in Queensland, London, and the star science world. A book of his studies was given to the British Museum in 1897.
britannica-1911-coelom-and-serous-membra:
The coelom is the body cavity in human anatomy. The entry divides it into the pericardium, the two pleurae, the peritoneum and the two tunicae vaginales. The pericardium is a closed sac at the centre of the chest. It holds the heart. Like all serous membranes, it has an inner and an outer layer.

The inner layer clings to the heart itself. Its smooth cells give a fresh heart its glossy look. The outer layer is double, with a tough fibrous coat outside. That coat joins the sheaths of the great vessels and the diaphragm. The entry then works through each cavity in long detail. It cites a wide range of anatomy books at the close. The scale suits a reference entry for medical readers.
britannica-1911-cohoes:
Cohoes is a city of Albany county, New York, about nine miles north of Albany. It stands where the Mohawk and Hudson rivers meet. Its people grew from 22,509 in 1890 to 24,709 in 1910. Railways, electric lines and two canals served it. The Erie and Champlain canals both reached the town.

Making things ruled its life. Hosiery and knit goods led all other trades by far. Factory output in 1905 came to more than ten million dollars. Hosiery alone made up about forty per cent of that sum. The city ranked fifth in the land for that trade among towns of its size. Cotton cloth, valves, paper and beer plants added breadth. The Falls of the Mohawk gave power. The town began as part of a Dutch grant from 1629. It became a city in 1870.
britannica-1911-coinage-offences:
Coinage offences strike at a right held by the sovereign power alone in every state. The making of money belongs to that power. Any breach of it draws stern punishment, since it can harm the state. In Britain the law on false coin was set in order by an act of 1861. The entry walks through that act part by part.

False making of gold or silver coin heads the list of crimes. Gilding or washing base metal to pass as gold or silver counts as well. Buying or selling false coin below its face value is a crime. So is bringing false coin into the country with knowledge of its nature. Making or mending the tools of the trade is banned too. The entry then turns to the United States. There the same acts draw fines and hard labour.
britannica-1911-colbert-de-croissy-charl:
Charles Colbert, marquis de Croissy (1625–1696), was a French diplomat and younger brother of Jean Baptiste Colbert. Like his brother, he began in the war office of Le Tellier. In 1656 he bought a post at the parlement of Metz. In 1658 he became intendant of Alsace. There he had to set in order land newly joined to France.

His brother's backing at court won him missions abroad. He served in Germany and Italy from 1659 to 1661. Later intendancies took him to Soissons, Amiens and Paris. In 1668 he turned for good to diplomacy. He spoke for France at Aix-la-Chapelle. That August he went as ambassador to London. There he was to fix a firm alliance with Charles II. He arranged the Dover meeting between Charles and his sister. He also formed the plan of taking land in peace by the chambers of reunion.
britannica-1911-colle-charles:
Charles Collé (1709–1783) was a French dramatist and song-writer, the son of a notary, born at Paris. Song rhymes caught his fancy early in life. He worked first in a notary's office, then in the finance office of a receiver-general. That post held him for near twenty years. At about seventeen he met Alexis Piron, a master of light verse.

Piron and Panard set his true path. For a time he wrote verses whose merit lay in their lack of sense. The younger Crébillon pulled him away from that trick. In 1729 the Caveau society gave his gift for popular song a stage. Its members included Helvétius, Duclos and Rameau. Later work struck a note of love of country that won him a pension. His journal and memoirs, kept from 1748 to 1772, close the record of sources.
britannica-1911-colombes:
Colombes is a town of France in the department of Seine, seven miles north-west of Paris. Its people numbered 28,920 in 1906. A church of the 1500s stands there with a tower from the 1100s. A race-course draws crowds to the town. Villas and boarding schools fill much of its ground.

Trade plays a smaller part. Makers turn out oil, vinegar and measuring tools. A castle once stood on the site. Henrietta Maria, queen of Charles I of England, died in that castle. That single royal link is the town's chief mark in the past. The entry stays close to those facts. It gives place, count, sights and trades, and no long civic history. Proximity to Paris shapes the town more than any event of its own.
britannica-1911-coma-berenices: Coma Berenices, meaning Berenice's Hair, is a star group in the northern sky. It was first named by Callimachus and by Eratosthenes in the third century before Christ. It is not among the forty eight star groups listed by Ptolemy. A tale says Conon named it to console Queen Berenice for a lost lock. That lock of her hair had been stolen from a temple of Venus. The finest member of the group is a wide double star. Its two parts shine orange and blue in the sky.
britannica-1911-commercial-treaties:
Commercial treaties, contracts between states about trade, are the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. A treaty of this kind is a two-sided act, the article stresses. Each party enters definite arrangements toward the other, rather than granting mere concessions. Lesser forms, such as an agreement, an exchange of notes, or a convention, cover one subject. A treaty usually covers several matters, commercial or political.

Trade and navigation were often governed by such arrangements in ancient times. Treaties between Carthage and Rome from 509 and 348 before Christ still survive in text. Aristotle notes that nations were linked by commercial treaties. Under the Roman empire, law and usage took over such matters. When imperial power shrank, written agreements became needful again. The article cites tenth-century treaties that protected Russian merchants at Constantinople.
britannica-1911-condensation-of-gases:
Condensation of gases is the subject of a physics entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It deals with what happens as a gas is squeezed at a fixed warmth. Two cases may occur as the volume keeps shrinking. The gas may keep filling its space in one even state.

Or it may split into two distinct phases, each even in itself. Which case occurs turns on the warmth of the substance. A limit called the critical temperature decides the outcome. Above that limit the space stays in one phase. Below it the substance can divide. The entry then turns to finding the weights of elements and compounds.
britannica-1911-conder-charles:
Charles Conder (1868-1909) was an English artist born in London. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his boyhood passed in India with his father. State service in Australia came first, but art won him by 1890. Paris study led to a post with a French art society in 1893.

His name spread through fan designs in a Watteau like style in London. A small set of fans and critics prized his soft pastoral scenes. Galleries at home and abroad bought his work in time, it says. The Luxembourg ranks among those that took his art on show. Ill health dogged his last years before death in 1909.
britannica-1911-conduction-electric-gase:
Electric conduction through gases treats how air and other gases carry a charge. Air in its normal state conducts to a very small extent only. That fact was fixed for sure only in the early 1900s. Physicists had chased the point for more than a hundred years. Charged bodies were known to lose their charge with time, even when well insulated.

Some held that the leak ran through dust in the air. Dust struck the body, took some charge and flew off with it. Faults in insulation took the blame from most men of science. Coulomb made careful tests in 1785 and allowed for those faults. He still found a real loss through the air itself. The vast entry runs to some 225,000 bytes of tests and gear. Tables of values for metals such as aluminium fill its later pages. It is a full lab record, not a short summary.
britannica-1911-connective-tissues:
Connective tissues are the binding and supporting tissues of the animal body, and an anatomy entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines the group. Such tissues occur very widely through the organs of the body. Their mark is a high share of substance lying between the cells. That substance may be even in structure throughout.

More often the substance is made, in whole or part, of fibrous elements. The group takes in a set of named types. Areolar tissue, fat tissue, and reticular tissue belong to it. White fibrous tissue and elastic tissue are members too. Cartilage and bone round out the list. All of them grow from the same layer of cells in the embryo. All do a like task, to connect and support the other tissues of the body.
britannica-1911-cook-james:
James Cook (1728–1779) was an English naval captain and explorer born at Marton in Yorkshire on 28 October 1728. His father was a farm labourer who rose to bailiff. At twelve the boy was set to a haberdasher at Staithes. He then served Whitby shipowners for years in the Norway, Baltic and Newcastle trades. In 1755, by then a mate, he joined the royal navy.

Sir Hugh Palliser backed his rise to master of a string of ships. He served in the Saint Lawrence and sounded and surveyed that river. His chart of the channel from Quebec to the sea went into print. In 1762 he helped retake Newfoundland and surveyed its coast. In 1763 he became marine surveyor of that coast under Governor Palliser. The long entry follows his great voyages from there. It credits him with fixing the outlines of the southern globe.
britannica-1911-copper-pyrites:
Copper-pyrites, or chalcopyrite, is a sulphide of copper and iron and a key ore of copper. Its name joins the Greek word for copper with the word pyrites. Agricola used the German form as far back as 1546. Henckel set the name chalcopyrite in print in 1725. The ancients lumped the mineral with other kinds under the broad name pyrites.

The mineral forms in the tetragonal system, but its shape lies so near a cube that men missed that fact until 1822. Fine measurement in that year set the matter right. Crystals most often take a tetrahedral look. One set of faces is dull and lined, while its mate set is bright and smooth. Joining of the two sets gives a figure much like a cube. Change in the stone brings tarnish in rich, shifting colours. Blue most often leads that play of hue.
britannica-1911-coprolites:
Coprolites are the fossilized droppings of extinct animals. Their name joins Greek words for dung and for stone. Dr William Buckland first saw their true nature. Twisted bodies in the Lias of Gloucestershire caught his eye. They had the form that soft matter takes in passing through the guts of reptiles or fishes. Men had long called them fossil fir cones and bezoar stones.

Dr W. Prout tested Buckland's guess in the lab. The bodies proved to be made of calcium phosphate and carbonate in the main. Bits of unbroken bone sat in them at times. Buckland gave them their name on that proof. He also held that they could serve farms well, for the phosphate they hold. The Lias kind look like oblong pebbles or kidney potatoes. Most run two to four inches long. Later finds came in immense quantities in some beds.
britannica-1911-copying-machines:
Copying machines are devices of many kinds for making copies of pen or pencil writing. The plainest path serves when one copy will do. A man writes with copying ink, thickened with sugar or gum. He lays a damped sheet of thin paper on the page. A press then squeezes the two as one. The print comes through in reverse and must be read from the back of the thin sheet.

Other paths give many copies at once. Thin white sheets are stacked with sheets of carbon paper between them. A sharp style writes on the top sheet and marks all below. The hectograph takes a third path, akin to lithography. Writing in aniline ink moves to a plate of jelly-like stuff. From that plate fresh sheets take the print in turn.
britannica-1911-coquerel-athanase-lauren:
Athanase Laurent Charles Coquerel (1795-1868) was a French Protestant divine born in Paris on 17 August 1795. His early schooling came from his aunt, Helen Maria Williams, an Englishwoman known for her translations and her Letters from France. He finished his studies for the ministry at the Protestant seminary of Montauban. In 1816 he was ordained as a minister.

In 1817 Coquerel was asked to serve as pastor of the chapel of St Paul at Jersey. He declined, since he would not sign the Thirty-nine Articles of the Church of England. For the twelve years after, he lived in Holland. He preached to Calvinist congregations at Amsterdam, Leiden, and Utrecht. In 1830, at the call of Baron Cuvier, he came to Paris as pastor of the Reformed Church.
britannica-1911-cordes: Cordes is the subject of a short town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cordes is a town in southern France, in the Tarn district northwest of Albi. By 1906 its people numbered near sixteen hundred. The town covers the top and slopes of a lone hill. It was a planned fortress town founded by Raymond the Seventh, count of Toulouse, in the first half of the twelve hundreds. Many houses of the thirteen and fourteen hundreds form its chief attraction. A church of the same ages survives.
britannica-1911-corrupt-practices:
Corrupt practices is a term of English election law in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. As defined by the great act of 1883, it covers five kinds of wrong. They are bribery, treating, undue influence, and personation. Aiding or procuring personation counts as a corrupt practice too.

Parliament had legislated against election corruption for over a century. Statutes on the subject run from 1729 through a chain of later acts. The act of 1883 folded in the act of 1854 and repealed all that went before. The article then spells out who counts as guilty of bribery. Giving or promising money to sway a voter heads the list. So does offering a voter an office, a place, or a job. Paying a third person to win votes or secure a member's return is bribery as well. The definitions reach both the hand that gives and the hand that takes.
britannica-1911-corybantes:
Corybantes is the subject of a myth article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In Greek myth the Corybantes were beings half divine and half demonic. They stand to the Asiatic Great Mother of the Gods as the Curetes stand to Rhea. From their first place in literature they are often confused with the Curetes. They differ by their Asiatic origin and by the wilder nature of their rites.

The article lists varied tales of their birth, as sons of Cronus, of Zeus, or of the Great Mother herself. Their names and number were unclear even to the ancients. Their rite centred on a frenzied dance with flute music, drums, and clashing metal. Wild cries and self wounding led to a state of rapture and collapse. In art they appear, two or three at a time, fully armed and dancing before the Great Mother. They sometimes appear with the child Dionysus.
britannica-1911-coutances:
Coutances is a town of north-west France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Manche. It stands seven miles east of the English Channel and 58 miles south of Cherbourg. Its people numbered 6,089 in 1906. The town sits in beauty on the right bank of the Soulle. A granite rise lifts it, crowned by the famed cathedral of Notre-Dame.

Men have long argued the date of that church. Traces of Romanesque work survive in its walls. In the main it is Gothic, from the first half of the 1200s. Slender turrets mass round its western towers. An eight-sided central tower forms a lantern within. Rose windows with stained glass of the 1300s light the nave and choir. Two more churches earn a note. Saint Pierre mixes Renaissance work with Gothic, and Saint Nicolas dates from the 1500s and 1600s.
britannica-1911-couthon-georges:
Georges Couthon (1755–1794) was a French revolutionary born at Orcet, a village near Clermont in Auvergne. He studied law and became an advocate at Clermont in 1785. In that period men noted his honesty, kind heart and charity. His health was frail, and both his legs were paralysed. In 1787 he sat in the provincial assembly of Auvergne.

At the outbreak of the Revolution he served on the town council of Clermont-Ferrand. A pamphlet, L'Aristocrate converti, showed him as a liberal and a friend of constitutional monarchy. Fame came fast. In 1791 he led the town tribunal and entered the Legislative Assembly. The king's flight to Varennes soured his views in the meantime. Hostility to the crown marked him from then on. A health trip to Flanders drew him close to Dumouriez. In September 1792 he won a seat in the Convention.
britannica-1911-coverdale-miles:
Miles Coverdale (about 1488–1569) was an English translator of the Bible and bishop of Exeter. He was born of Yorkshire parents and studied philosophy and theology at Cambridge. In 1514 he was ordained priest at Norwich. He then entered the convent of Austin friars at Cambridge. There the prior, Robert Barnes, swayed his thought for good.

At Cambridge he met Sir Thomas More and Thomas Cromwell. Deep study of the Scriptures began in those years. He joined the men who met at the White Horse tavern to debate points of faith. When Barnes faced a heresy charge, Coverdale went to London to help frame his defence. Soon after, he left the convent and preached against confession and the worship of images. From 1528 to 1534 he spent most of his time abroad, with care. In 1534 a first book from his hand came into print. The entry then traces his Bible work.
britannica-1911-cowes:
Cowes is a seaport and watering-place in the Isle of Wight, 12 miles south-east of Southampton. West Cowes and East Cowes face each other across the mouth of the river Medina. West Cowes held 8,652 people in 1901 and East Cowes 3,196. The port between them is the chief port of the island. It is the headquarters of the Royal Yacht Squadron, founded in 1812.

Steamships link the towns to Southampton and Portsmouth on set runs. A steam ferry and a floating bridge cross the Medina, 600 yards broad at that point. Houses rise in fine order on gentle wooded slopes behind the harbour. Villas dot the lanes round about. Two forts of Henry VIII gave the towns their start. He built them in 1540, one on each side of the river mouth, to guard the coast. The east fort has gone. The west fort stands and serves as the yacht club's house.
britannica-1911-craggs-james:
James Craggs, an English politician who lived from 1657 to 1721, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was a son of Anthony Craggs of Holbeck, in Durham. He was baptized in June 1657. After following various callings in London, he entered high service.

Craggs was a person of considerable financial ability. He entered the service of the duchess of Marlborough. Through her influence he became member of parliament for Grampound in 1702. He held that seat until 1713. He was in business as an army clothier. He held several official positions as well. In 1715 he became joint postmaster-general. In all these capacities he made the most of his chances. He amassed a great deal of money by them. He also grew his wealth by mixing in the affairs of the South Sea Company.
britannica-1911-creon-of-thebes:
Creon of Thebes, a figure of Greek legend, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. He was the son of Menoeceus. After the death of Laius, he became king of Thebes. He was husband of his sister Jocasta, the widowed queen.

At that time Thebes suffered under the Sphinx. Creon offered his crown, and the hand of the queen, to any man who solved the fatal riddle. Oedipus, the son of Laius, did not know his own parentage. He solved the riddle and married Jocasta, his mother. Their sons were Eteocles and Polyneices. The brothers agreed to reign in turn, year by year, after their father's death. Eteocles, as the elder, took the throne first. At the year's end he refused to give it up. His brother then attacked him at the head of an army of Argives.
britannica-1911-cressent-charles:
Cressent, Charles is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French furniture maker and sculptor. More important still, he was a pupil of André Charles Boulle, the great master of marquetry. From such training came work that justifies calling him the best decorative artist of the age.

The article describes what set his work apart. Cressent also created the gilded bronze mounts that enrich his furniture. His female figures at the corners of tables are among the finest work of the age. The Louvre and the Wallace Collection hold much of his work.
britannica-1911-crichton-james:
James Crichton, called the Admirable Crichton, who lived from 1560 to about 1582, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Son of Scotland's lord advocate, he was born most likely at Eliock in Dumfriesshire. He took two degrees at St Andrews by the age of fifteen. By 1577 he was in Paris, and tales of his gifts grew fast.

The entry keeps a cool head about those tales. His vast memory and skill in tongues seem real, and Scaliger praised him highly. But his surviving works show few marks of rare power, and grand claims by Urquhart need discount. Sure facts are two years in the French army and a stay at Genoa in 1579. At Venice he beat all comers in debate save one. Two great debates at Padua in 1581 close the tale.
britannica-1911-critius-and-nesiotes:
Critius and Nesiotes were two Greek sculptors of uncertain school who worked in the time of the Persian Wars. When Xerxes carried off to Persia the statues of Harmodius and Aristogiton made by Antenor, the pair were commissioned to replace them. Coins and reliefs have let scholars match their work. Two statues at Naples, long restored wrongly as gladiators, are known as copies of their tyrannicides.

Lucian praised the pair's figures as closely knit, sinewy, hard, and severe in outline. Those words, the entry says, fit the Naples copies well. Critius also made a statue of the armed runner Epicharinus. Replacing a stolen civic monument is the act that fixed both names in the record. Their school stays unknown, and no other works are listed for Nesiotes.
britannica-1911-croft-sir-james:
Sir James Croft, who died in 1590, was an English soldier and official from an old Herefordshire family. He sat for his county in parliament in 1541 and governed Haddington in 1549. In 1551 he became lord deputy of Ireland, where he gained a name for a conciliatory temper but achieved little. The entry calls him a double-dealer all his life. Mary jailed him in the Tower for treason, and Elizabeth freed and favoured him.

Croft governed Berwick, where John Knox visited him in 1559, and worked for the Scottish Protestants. Suspected of secret dealings with Mary of Guise, he spent ten years out of office. Elizabeth made him a privy councillor in 1570 and later sent him to treat for peace with the duke of Parma. Private dealings with Parma on that mission sent him to the Tower again. Freed before the end of 1589, he died on 4 September 1590.
britannica-1911-croll-james:
James Croll (1821–1890), a Scottish man of science, was born to a peasant family at Little Whitefield in Perthshire on 2 January 1821. Ill health barred him from manual work after a wheelwright's apprenticeship, and he turned to shop-keeping and insurance. Largely self-taught, he became keeper of the Andersonian Museum in Glasgow in 1859. That post led him into physical science, and he soon wrote for leading journals.

Croll's essay of 1864 on the physical cause of climate change in geological epochs won him a post on the Scottish Geological Survey. His book Climate and Time of 1875 argued that earth's revolutions owe much to cosmic causes, and it stirred warm controversy. Later works treated stellar evolution and the basis of evolution itself. The entry notes that his ice-age theory was later abandoned, yet calls his work under hardship heroic. He died on 15 December 1890.
britannica-1911-crusades:
Crusades is the name for the wars fought to free the Holy Land from Muslim rule, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The name comes from the cross worn as a badge by the crusaders on campaign. By likeness the word is also given to any campaign waged in the same spirit. The text opens by asking what the Crusades meant, in their own age and in ours.

One view sees them as the high wave of a surge of religious revival in western Europe. An other view sees them as a chief chapter in the long meeting of East and West. The eye of history, the text argues, must weigh them more as a meeting of two worlds, ruled by an age that prized the next world above this one.
britannica-1911-cujas-jacques:
Jacques Cujas (1520–1590) was a French jurisconsult born at Toulouse, the son of a fuller. He taught himself Latin and Greek, then studied law under Arnoul Ferrier. His lectures on Justinian won fame, and in 1554 he became professor of law at Cahors. Called to Bourges, he was driven out by a rival's stirring of the students. Valence took him in, and there his name spread across Europe.

Students such as Joseph Scaliger and de Thou gathered to Cujas at Valence. Posts, pensions, and offers from Charles IX, Henry III, and Pope Gregory XIII failed to move him for long. He ended his days at Bourges in 1590, refusing all part in the religious wars. His merit, the entry says, was to turn from weak commentators to Roman law itself. He collected over 500 manuscripts. His usual answer on the wars was that they had nothing to do with the praetor's edict.
britannica-1911-culdees:
The Culdees were an ancient monastic order with settlements in Ireland and Scotland. Older writers, above all Presbyterians, fondly pictured them as keepers of a pure early Christianity free of Rome. Hector Boece made them heirs of the Irish and Iona monks of earlier centuries. The entry states that Bishop William Reeves disproved both views. Their Irish name, Céle Dé, means God's comrade or sworn ally.

In the 800s Culdee communities appear at nine Irish places, Armagh and Clonmacnoise among them, as annexes to regular monasteries. They cared for the poor and the sick and took part in the music of worship. From Ireland they crossed to Scotland late in that century, filling gaps left at Iona. Their life there matched that of secular canons more than of cloistered monks. In Ireland the Culdees of Armagh lasted until the dissolution of 1541.
britannica-1911-currie-james:
James Currie was a Scottish doctor and the editor of Burns, son of a minister in a border shire. Lured by tales of wealth in America, he went to Virginia as a youth. He spent five hard years there. Much of that time he was ill, and his trade deals never paid.

War between the colonies and England killed his last hope there, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He sailed home through long delays, then read medicine at Edinburgh. He took his degree at Glasgow and settled at Liverpool. There he rose to a post at the town sick house. His chief book set out case notes on cold and warm water as a cure for fevers. It holds the first full count in English of heat readings in sick care.
britannica-1911-customs-duties:
Customs duties are taxes laid on goods brought into or sent out of a land. The 1911 Britannica article ranks them among the most old of all taxes. They stay in all lands one of the most common ways to raise funds for the state. In an island land like Britain, such taxes came in time to be laid in the seaports alone. So they fell on foreign trade, where fair rules could be made to hold.

That plain state was reached by slow steps. For long, dues were laid on goods that passed between England and Scotland. Tolls at bridges, ferries, and town gates are of the same breed. Such town tolls on farm goods are still a common form of tax on the continent of Europe. The wide spread of the practice gave the English tongue its word customs. The piece ends with guides to kindred heads.
britannica-1911-cy-pres:
Cy-près is a rule explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is Anglo-French for so near. The rule belongs to the court of chancery and its handling of charitable trusts. When a giver's stated purpose cannot be carried out, the court acts.

Instead of letting the gift fail, the court applies the funds to a kindred purpose. The new purpose must lie as near the old one as may be. The article gives an old case. A fund was left in part to free British slaves in Turkey and Barbary. No such slaves existed, so that share went to the will's other charities. The rule holds only where a general intent to give is clear. A gift for one fixed object alone, if that object fails, passes to the next of kin. American courts widely took up the same rule.
britannica-1911-cyanic-acid-and-cyanates:
Cyanic Acid and Cyanates is a chemistry article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a sharp, unstable acid and the salts formed from it. Cyanic acid was found by the chemist Wohler in 1824. It can be made by heating its own polymer, cyanuric acid, in a stream of carbon dioxide.

The entry stresses how hard the acid is to keep. The liquid is very volatile and smells much like acetic acid. It stays stable only below the freezing point of water. At that point it quickly turns into a mix of cyanuric acid and a white powder called cyamelide. In water it breaks down at once into carbon dioxide and ammonia. The related gas cyanogen chloride is noted as very poisonous. The piece gives chemists the basic handling facts for a tricky substance.
britannica-1911-cyclopes:
Cyclopes, the round-eyed ones, are beings of Greek myth described in more than one way, and this 1911 Britannica entry sorts the versions. In Homer they are huge cave-dwellers with one eye, eaters of men who live a herdsman's life in the far west. They know no law or order and fear neither gods nor men. The most famous of them is Polyphemus.

In Hesiod they are three sons of Uranus and Gaea, named Brontes, Steropes, and Arges. As storm gods they forged thunder and lightning for Zeus, in thanks for their release from Tartarus. Apollo later slew them for making the bolt that killed Asclepius. Later tales moved their home to Etna or other volcanic isles, where they help Hephaestus at his forge. A third kind are the giant builders of the great walls of Mycenae and Tiryns.
britannica-1911-d-arblay-frances:
Frances d'Arblay, better known as Fanny Burney, an English novelist and diarist who lived from 1752 to 1840, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. She was born at King's Lynn in Norfolk, the daughter of a famed music teacher. Her mother came of a French refugee family. Fanny was the fourth child in a family of six.

One brother became an admiral who sailed with Captain Cook, and another became a known classical scholar. In 1760 the family moved to London, where her father was a fashionable music master. Her mother died in 1761, when Fanny was nine. Her sisters were sent to school in Paris, but Fanny was left to educate herself, the entry stresses. That fact frames the account of her later writing life.
britannica-1911-dalou-jules:
Jules Dalou, a French sculptor who lived from 1838 to 1902, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a pupil of Carpeaux and Duret, and mixed the liveliness of one with the sound craft of the other. He first showed work at the Salon in 1867. In 1871, when the Commune rose in Paris, he fled to England.

In England he taught at South Kensington and helped shape the new British school of sculpture. His clay groups there included a French peasant woman and two women of Boulogne. Back in France from 1879, he made large public works, among them the Triumph of the Republic in Paris. The entry praises his taste, skill, and rich sense of form.
britannica-1911-damocles:
Damocles was one of the courtiers of the elder Dionysius of Syracuse. He spoke in outsized terms of the happiness of his master. Dionysius, the story says, answered with an invitation to a rich banquet. Damocles took his seat in state at the feast. Above him hung a naked sword, held by a single hair. The tale ends at that seat, with the sword over his head.

Cicero in the Tusculans, Horace in the Odes, and Persius all carry the story, and the entry cites those three sources. Nothing more is told of Damocles himself, his birth, rank, or later life. The whole entry is the one scene and its telling in three Roman authors. A courtier's flattery, a tyrant's lesson, and a sword on a hair make up the record. The name lives by that single image alone.
britannica-1911-danton-george-jacques:
George Jacques Danton (1759–1794) was a leading actor in the French Revolution, born at Arcis-sur-Aube on 26 October 1759. His family, of respectable rank and modest means, gave him a good schooling. He built a sound practice as an advocate at the Paris bar. When revolution came he led the Cordeliers club of his district, the centre of the popular cause pushed to its extreme. His robust, impetuous temper made him its natural chief.

Danton took no traced part in the great risings of 1789, the Bastille or the march on Versailles. In 1790 he defended Marat from arrest and took command of his district's national guard battalion. Posts in the government of Paris followed in 1791. Only in 1792, the entry stresses, did he rise to the height of a great revolutionary chief. The long life that follows traces that rise and his fall.
britannica-1911-darboy-georges:
Georges Darboy (1813–1871) is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was archbishop of Paris, born at Fayl-Billot in Haute Marne. He studied with honours at the seminary at Langres and was made priest in 1836. He was made bishop of Nancy in 1859, and in 1863 he rose to the archbishopric of Paris.

Darboy stood firm for the rights of bishops against Rome. When war with Prussia broke out, he set up relief for the wounded and stayed at his post through the siege. The communists seized him as a hostage in April 1871. On the 27th of May he was shot in prison at La Roquette. He died giving a blessing and words of pardon.
britannica-1911-de-loutherbourg-philip-j:
Philip James de Loutherbourg (1740–1812) was an English artist, born at Strassburg on 31 October 1740. His father, of a Polish family, painted miniatures there. The son spent most of his life in London and took British nationality. He shaped the scenery of the English stage and left a mark on the artists who came after him. He had been meant for the Lutheran ministry and was schooled at the university of Strassburg.

The call did not suit him, and he chose painting instead, studying under Vanloo in Paris. His skill grew fast, and he became known in high society. In 1767 he was elected to the French Academy below the age the rules required. He painted landscapes, sea storms, and battles, and his first show held twelve pictures, among them Storm at Sunset, Night, and Morning.
britannica-1911-dee-wales:
Dee is a river of Wales and England known in Welsh as Dyfrdwy. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows it from Bala Lake to the sea. It leaves that lake and runs northeast past Corwen. It then bends east past Llangollen and north to Chester.

A narrow fair valley holds the river for thirty-five miles. Berwyn slopes wall it in on the south side. The Vale of Llangollen in that stretch holds wide fame. A canal aqueduct built by Telford strides across it there. The full course runs about seventy miles with a long fall. Below Chester a straight cut channel leads to the estuary. At low tide that mouth turns to broad bare sands. A Kingsley ballad made those sands a byword for danger.
britannica-1911-dekker-edward-douwes:
Edward Douwes Dekker (1820-1887) was a Dutch writer known as Multatuli. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his path from Amsterdam to service in Java. Revenue posts there rose until he served at Lebak in 1857. What he saw of Dutch rule abuses filled him with anger there.

He quit his post and went home to expose the system in print. Papers and pamphlets drew little heed until Max Havelaar in 1860. That novel laid bare forced labor abuse in the Dutch Indies. All Europe read it, though some called its picture overdrawn. Satire books and seven volumes of Ideas followed in later years.
britannica-1911-delescluze-louis-charles:
Louis Charles Delescluze is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French journalist. He lived from 1809 to 1871. He was born at Dreux on the second of October 1809. He studied law in Paris in his youth. Early he developed a strong democratic bent of mind. He played a part in the July revolution of 1830. 

In 1836 he was forced to take refuge in Belgium. Returning in 1840, he settled in Valenciennes. After the revolution of 1848 he removed to Paris. There he started a newspaper of democratic and social views. His zeal so far outran his discretion in that work. He was twice imprisoned and fined for the paper. The paper was suppressed, and he fled to England. He was arrested in Paris in 1853 on a later visit. He was deported to French Guiana after that arrest.
britannica-1911-delille-jacques:
Jacques Delille was a French poet who lived from seventeen thirty eight to eighteen thirteen. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Aigue Perse in Auvergne, a child born out of wedlock, he taught school. He won note for verse that hinted things through long roundabout phrases.

Delille rendering of the Georgics of Virgil in seventeen sixty nine made him famed. Voltaire urged his name for the next free Academy seat in France. He was elected at once but kept out till seventeen seventy four. His Jardins poem of seventeen eighty two proved his own gift as a poet. The Revolution later cut him down to poverty in his old age.
britannica-1911-demochares:
Demochares (about 355-275 B.C.), a nephew of Demosthenes, was an Athenian orator and statesman of the decline. He first appears in 322, speaking in vain against handing over Demosthenes and the other anti-Macedonian orators to Antipater. Banished in 303 for mocking a fulsome decree in honour of Demetrius Poliorcetes, he was recalled in 298 and spent four years fortifying Athens and stocking it with food and ammunition.

Fresh banishments and returns mark his later career, and in 280 he won a public monument for his uncle. His public services, recorded after his death, were cuts in spending, careful finance, and successful begging missions to Egypt and Macedonia. Cicero credits him with a history of his own times, written in an orator's rather than a historian's style.
britannica-1911-elmes-james:
Elmes, James (1782–1862), was a British architect, civil engineer, and writer on the arts, born in London on 15 October 1782. He was educated at Merchant Taylors' school and studied building under his father and architecture under George Gibson. As a student at the Royal Academy he gained the silver medal in 1804. He designed many buildings in London and served as surveyor to the port of London.

Elmes is best known as a writer on the arts. In 1809 he became vice-president of the Royal Architectural Society, but partial loss of sight forced him to resign that office and the port surveyorship in 1828. He died at Greenwich on 2 April 1862. His books include Sir Christopher Wren and his Times and Lectures on Architecture. He also wrote a General and Biographical Dictionary of the Fine Arts and a Treatise on Architectural Jurisprudence.
britannica-1911-empedocles:
Empedocles (about 490–430 B.C.) was a Greek philosopher and statesman born at Agrigentum in Sicily, of a noted family. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Empedocles article within it. Empedocles himself helped end an oligarchic rule at Agrigentum and was invited to become king, an honour he refused.

Of his poem on nature about 400 lines survive, in uneven fragments, out of an original 5000, and fewer than 100 verses of his hymns of purification remain. The entry shows him as at once statesman, prophet, physicist, physician, and reformer, a figure his age took for more than a mere man. Another has him leap into the crater of Etna, hoping to be thought a god, until the volcano cast up his brazen sandals and betrayed him.
britannica-1911-eperjes:
Eperjes is a town of Hungary, capital of the county of Sáros, 190 miles north-east of Budapest by rail, with a population of 13,098 in 1900. It stands on the left bank of the river Tarcza and was almost wholly rebuilt after a great fire in 1887. It is the seat of a Greek-Catholic bishop and holds a fine late Gothic cathedral of the 18th century.

The town makes cloth, table-linen, and earthenware, and trades in wine, linen, cattle, and grain. The entry also covers its county neighbours. Eperjes was founded about the mid 12th century by a German colony and made a royal free town in 1347. Its darkest fame is the “butchery of Eperjes” of 1687, when General Caraffa's tribunal condemned many citizens accused of Protestantism to death.
britannica-1911-epimenides:
Epimenides was a poet and prophet of Crete who lived in the 6th century B.C., though many fabulous stories are told of him and his very existence is doubted. While tending his father's sheep he is said to have fallen asleep in the Dictaean cave near Cnossus. From that sleep he did not wake for fifty-seven years, the story runs. When a pestilence struck Athens after the murder of Cylon, Solon called him in to purify the city.

The only reward Epimenides would take was a branch of the sacred olive and a promise of lasting friendship between Athens and Cnossus. He died in Crete at a great age; his countrymen, who later honoured him as a god, said he lived nearly three hundred years. The entry counts him, with Melampus and Onomacritus, among the founders of Orphism.
britannica-1911-epithelial-endothelial-a:
Epithelial, endothelial, and glandular tissues in anatomy are the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Every body surface that may meet foreign matter is covered by a guard layer of cells. Those cells are bound close to one another to form unbroken sheets. Such sheets are called epithelium. The article explains how growths outward or inward from these surfaces form further structures.

In that way arise the central nervous system and the sense organs. The glands, the hairs, and the nails also grow from surface layers. The cells have clear marks under the microscope. Their outline is sharp, their nucleus large and round, and their living matter often holds many granules. The article sorts the cells by shape: flat, cube-like, tall, and hair-bearing forms all appear. Some membranes are one cell thick, as in much of the gut. Others have many layers.
britannica-1911-equites:
Equites, or horsemen, were a corps of horse in early Rome. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the root as equus, the Latin word for horse. In time they grew from a mere arm of war to a rank. Under the empire they took up an army role once more. Custom says Romulus first raised them as three troops of horse.

Each troop bore the name of one of the three old tribes. Ten squadrons of thirty men made up each troop in full. The whole corps bore the name celeres, or the swift, in old speech. Livy limits that name to a guard of Romulus in his text. Servius Tullius found six troops and added twelve more to them.
britannica-1911-espagnols-sur-mer-les:
Les Espagnols sur Mer is the name for a sea fight off Winchelsea on 29 August 1350, as told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A Spanish trade fleet, armed and led by Don Carlos de la Cerda, was sailing home from Flemish ports. On the way it had seized English trade ships and thrown their crews into the sea. King Edward the Third of England vowed to strike back.

Edward set his meet point at Winchelsea and sailed on his ship the Cog Thomas on 28 August. His wife and her ladies waited in a convent on shore. His sons, the Black Prince and John of Gaunt, sailed with him, as did many nobles. The English fleet, put by Stow at 50 ships, lay at anchor and waited for the Spanish fleet to come in sight.
britannica-1911-essenes:
Essenes, a monastic order among the Jews before Christianity, are traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They first show in history in the time of Jonathan the Maccabee, from 161 to 144 before Christ. How much older they may have been, no means can tell for sure. Sources grant them an age that no date can fix.

The name shows in Greek in two forms in old books. Josephus uses one form fourteen times and the other six times in his works. Philo uses the second form alone in the three places cited. Other writers from Synesius to Porphyry split between the two forms in turn. One guess ties the name to a place called Essa named by Josephus. That root is not much in favour now among scholars. Lightfoot holds the name means the silent ones in its sense.
britannica-1911-etampes:
Etampes is a town of northern France south of Paris. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its churches, keep, and trades. It is the chief town of its district in Seine et Oise. Its count in 1906 was about eighty-seven hundred.

The town straggles long between the rail line and a small river. A ruined keep from the twelfth century looks down on it. The chief church shows a fine Romanesque tower and spire. A walled ring still guards part of that old church. Two houses named for royal favorites show Renaissance grace. Flour mills, iron works, and shoe shops give local work. Town markets trade in grain and sheep from the farms. A church council there in 1130 backed a pope in a split.
britannica-1911-etaples:
Étaples, a town of northern France, is sketched in a short place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It stands in Pas-de-Calais on the right bank of the Canche estuary, three miles from the Straits of Dover. By rail it lies 17 miles south of Boulogne. Its count in 1906 was 5,136 people. The town had a small fishing and trade port, and boat building went on there.

An old church holds a statue of the Virgin held dear by sailors. A bridge more than 1,600 feet long crosses the Canche. Near the shore, Le Touquet and Paris-Plage drew French and English guests for golf, tennis, and bathing. Finds near the town hint it may sit on the old Gallo-Roman port of Quentovicus. In 1492 Henry the Seventh of England and Charles the Eighth of France signed a treaty there.
britannica-1911-eubulides:
Eubulides of Miletus was a Greek philosopher who succeeded Eucleides as head of the Megarian school. Nothing is known of the events of his life. Indirect signs make him a contemporary of Aristotle, whom he attacked with great bitterness. Tradition also counts Demosthenes among his pupils. His fame rests chiefly on a set of noted syllogisms tied to his name. The entry calls them false and captious, more verbal quibbling than logic.

Yet those puzzles still show real snags in language and in explaining sense impressions. Eubulides also wrote a treatise on Diogenes the Cynic. A number of comedies are credited to him as well. The entry is one of the briefest lives in this stretch of the volume. It points readers to the article on the Megarian school for the wider setting. No dates for his birth or death are offered.
britannica-1911-eucratides:
Eucratides was king of Bactria, about 175 to 129 B.C., who seized the throne by rebellion against the house of Euthydemus. Rival dynasts in Sogdiana, Aria and Drangiana challenged him, most known only from their coins. In the west Mithradates I of Parthia took two provinces from him. His great foe was Demetrius of India, who besieged him in a fortress with a huge army. Eucratides broke out and conquered much of western India.

Apollodorus credited him with rule over a thousand towns. His coins, struck with Greek and Indian legends, style him the great King Eucratides. They confirm his sway over Bactria, Sogdiana, Kabul and the western Punjab. He founded a Greek city, Eucratideia, in Bactria. Returning from India about 150 B.C., he was murdered by the son he had made co-regent. Under that son the kingdom lost its lands north of the Hindu Kush.
britannica-1911-eumenes:
Eumenes is a double life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name belongs to two rulers of Pergamum in Asia Minor. Each king gets his own short account in the entry. Their reigns fall in the third and second centuries before Christ.

Eumenes the First took power from his uncle Philetaerus in the year 263 before Christ. His one great act was a victory near Sardis over Antiochus Soter. That win secured the districts around his capital. Eumenes the Second ruled from 197 to 159 and stood as a loyal ally of Rome. He helped defeat Antiochus of Syria at the battle of Magnesia. Rome rewarded him with wide lands as far as the Taurus range. The entry gives readers a brief guide to a small kingdom that grew by Roman favor.
britannica-1911-eumenides: Eumenides is a kind name for the Furies of Greek myth. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica breaks the word down from Greek roots meaning kindly and well disposed. The Furies, also called the Erinyes, were feared powers of revenge. Calling them the kindly ones was a soft name meant to avoid their wrath. The name also titles a famed play by Aeschylus. That play praised the old faith and the old ruling class of Athens. It stood against the newer rule of the people in the age of Pericles.
britannica-1911-euripides:
Euripides (480 to 406 before Christ) was the great Greek writer of tragedies, and this 1911 Britannica entry begins with the legends around his birth. He was born, by the tale, on the very day of the Greek victory at Salamis, where his Athenian parents had fled for safety.

Comic poets liked to taunt him that his mother Clito had sold herbs for a living. He was meant at first for the life of an athlete, a calling he later spoke of with scorn. He also tried painting. At twenty-five he brought out his first play, the Peliades. Though his fame was great, he won the first prize only five times in a career of about fifty years.
britannica-1911-explosives:
Explosives are substances which, under certain treatment, break down violently and generate force. They sort loosely into propellants and detonators, but the line will not hold sharp. The same substance may serve either role under changed conditions. A propellant burns fast and evenly, swelling a small volume into a large one of gas. Heat freed in the burning expands those gases further. A detonator wrecks a small area without throwing matter far.

Time, the article stresses, is the key factor in the difference. Plain burning can turn explosive when contact between fuel and oxygen supplier grows, as in gas and dust blasts. Heat alone does not make an explosion; aluminium and magnesium give great heat yet no blast without gas. True explosives are either mechanical mixtures or endothermic compounds. Endothermic bodies store energy taken in at their making, and release it as gas when they break down.
britannica-1911-extenuating-circumstance:
Extenuating circumstances, in law, are facts that lessen the gravity of a crime, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains how courts treat them. An offence has been committed with no legal justification, yet the facts around it cut down its blame, in punishment or in moral weight.

The entry sets out English practice first: the jury cannot fix punishment, which rests with the judge within set limits. Juries often add a rider to a guilty verdict, urging mercy for grave provocation, and in murder cases that plea goes to the Home Office. A judge may also weigh facts from the trial itself. French law, the entry adds, gives the jury the sole right and duty in such questions.
britannica-1911-false-pretences:
False Pretences is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a crime in English law. The crime is the taking of goods, money, or bonds from a person by a false claim, with fraud in mind. The law of 1861 made it a chargeable wrong.

The article draws a sharp line between this crime and theft. In theft the owner does not mean to part with his goods. Here the owner is tricked into handing them over for good. The false claim must deal with a fact that stands at the time. A bare promise to pay later does not count. The piece traces the crime from a law of Henry the Eighth. It ends with a note on law in the United States.
britannica-1911-fatimites:
Fatimites, or Fatimides, names a dynasty claiming descent from Fatima, daughter of the prophet Mahomet, and her husband the caliph Ali. It is also called Obaidi, after Obaidallah, its first sovereign, and Alawi, a title shared with other dynasties of the same claimed ancestry. Three rulers in north-western Africa came before the annexation of Egypt: al-Mahdi Obaidallah from 909, al-Qaim Mahommed from 934, and al-Mansur Ismail from 945.

The dynasty rose on widespread loyalty to the prophet's family, held by many to own the sovereignty by right. Its supporters backed the line of Ismail, son of Jafar al-Sadiq, though the claimed pedigree was later disputed at Bagdad. Rival accounts made the founder a heretic's scion or even a Jew. The long entry follows the caliphs' rule and closes by judging their practice close to orthodox Islam in most doctrine.
britannica-1911-fauriel-claude-charles:
Claude Charles Fauriel (1772-1844), French historian, philologist and critic, was born at St Etienne on 21 October 1772. Son of a poor joiner, he was well educated at Oratorian colleges. He served twice in the army, then in municipal office, and from 1797 to 1799 gave himself to hard study of Greek and Italian literature and history, ancient and modern. In Paris he became private secretary to Fouche, minister of police.

Fauriel resigned in 1802, in part because Napoleon, made consul for life, had broken strict republican principles. Articles on Madame de Stael's work on literature began a close friendship with her. Her circle and that of Madame de Condorcet shaped his life of love, friendship and learning. The entry follows his later scholarship and the posthumous papers, memoirs and correspondence by which his thought is known, including fragments on the close of the Consulate published in 1886.
britannica-1911-fearne-charles:
Charles Fearne (1742-1794), English jurist, was son of Charles Fearne, judge-advocate of the admiralty. He was born in London in 1742 and educated at Westminster school. He took up the law, and his talents fitted him to succeed as a barrister. Yet he neglected practice and spent his attention and inheritance on scientific experiments. He hoped for discoveries that would repay the cost. The hope failed, and he died in 1794 leaving his family in need.

Fearne's fame rests on one book, his Essay on the Learning of Contingent Remainders and Executory Devises. A decision of Lord Mansfield in Perrin v. Blake called it forth. The essay had the effect of reversing that decision. It passed through numerous editions as a legal authority. A volume of his posthumous works was published by subscription in 1797. That volume was issued for his widow's benefit.
britannica-1911-felix-popes:
Felix is the name borne by five popes, gathered here in one entry. Felix I held the see from January 269 until his death in January 274. Claimed as a martyr, he was probably confused with another bishop of the name. He appears in the Antioch dispute over Paul of Samosata. The emperor Aurelian gave the church building to the bishop recognized by Rome. Felix II, an antipope, was raised to the chair in 356 while Liberius was banished.

The entry follows each bearer of the name in turn. Felix III, from a powerful Roman family, died in 492. Felix IV, a native of Beneventum, is linked with the church of Saints Cosimo and Damiano. He died after a short reign. Felix V was the name taken by Amadeus, duke of Savoy, a rival pope. In the end he accepted a settlement, lands and a cardinal's rank.
britannica-1911-fellows-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Fellows, a British digger of old ruins, fills a life of travel in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Nottingham in seventeen ninety nine, he showed art skill as a boy of fourteen. Sketches from a trip to Newstead Abbey made the front page of a Byron life. He settled in London, then spent years in Italy, Greece, and the Levant. In eighteen thirty eight he set Smyrna as his base for work in Asia Minor.

He found the ruins of Xanthus, the old chief town of Lycia, on that first push. Print of his diary stirred such zeal that the British Museum backed a fresh trip. More trips found a host of old towns and sent cases of carved stone to London. Xanthus, Pinara, Patara, and Myra stand out in that list.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-i-of-naples:
Ferdinand the First, also called Don Ferrante, was king of Naples from 1423 to 1494 in the years of his life. His reign is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the natural son of Alphonso of Aragon and Naples. By his father's will he took the throne in 1458. Pope Calixtus the Third said the line of Aragon was dead and the realm a fief of the church.

The pope died before he could press the claim, and the next pope knew Ferdinand as king. But John of Anjou used the unrest of the barons to invade and seek the throne of his house. Ferdinand was beat hard at Sarno in 1460. With help from Sforza and from the Albanian chief Skanderbeg he won through and by 1464 held the realm firm.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-ii-of-naples:
Ferdinand the Second, who lived from 1469 to 1496, was king of Naples. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his short fight for the throne. He was a grandson of the first Ferdinand of Naples. His father Alphonso gave up the crown to him in 1495.

France under Charles the Eighth was then marching on Italy. Treason inside Naples made the city hard to hold. Ferdinand fled to Ischia as the French drew near. When Charles left with most of his army, the king returned. Townsfolk stung by occupation welcomed him back with warmth. A great Spanish captain helped him clear the last French posts. He died in September 1496, soon after that full recovery.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-ii-of-the-two-:
Ferdinand the Second (1810-1859), king of the Two Sicilies, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Palermo, the son of Francis the First, he was in his early years thought to hold liberal ideas. His free and easy manners made him popular with the poor of Naples. He came to the throne in 1830.

The article says his first edict promised fair justice, sound finances, and care to heal the wounds of the kingdom. Those words, it argues, were meant only to lull unrest to sleep. He did a little for trade and growth, but taxes stayed heavy and corruption flourished in every office. In the end he set up a rule by one man's will, harsher than that of any king before him. The entry calls him shrewd by nature, but poorly schooled and steeped in superstition.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-iv-of-naples:
Ferdinand the Fourth of Naples, who lived from 1751 to 1825, gets a long life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Third son of Don Carlos of Bourbon, he was born at Naples in 1751. When his father took the Spanish throne in 1759, the boy became king of Naples under a regency led by Tanucci. That regent let his schooling slide and fed his love of sport.

His first act as king in his own right was to drive out the Jesuits. In 1768 he wed Maria Carolina, a daughter of the empress Maria Theresa. Bright and proud, she soon held full sway over her idle husband and ruled in fact. Tanucci was cast off in 1777 and Sir John Acton rose in his place. When the French royal pair were beheaded, the court joined the first coalition against France in 1793.
britannica-1911-fergusson-james:
James Fergusson, who lived from 1808 to 1886, was a Scottish writer on building and design. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from Ayr to Calcutta. He went east as a partner in a trade house. Work at an indigo plant let him retire in about ten years. In India he grew drawn to the old temples and ruins. Few in Britain then knew or grasped that work.

His first book, on the rock cut temples of India, came out in 1845. A broad handbook of building history followed in 1855. He then grew it into a full history of the art. Indian and eastern building later got a book of its own in 1876. A history of modern building, from the rebirth of old styles onward, came in 1862. The entry shows a man who turned trade wealth into a life of study.
britannica-1911-fibres:
Fibres is a 1911 Britannica article on the thread-like parts used in making goods. The word comes from a Latin term, fibra. It may link to filum, a thread, or to findere, to split. Fibres are the structural parts of animal and plant tissue that makers use.

For sorting, they fall into four groups. Textile fibres come first, then paper-making fibres. Brush fibres and a mixed group follow. Textile fibres are mostly products of the living world. In animals they serve to protect, as wool and hairs do. In plants they serve as parts of the tissue, as in flax and hemp. The text notes one exception from the mineral world. That is asbestos, a fibrous mineral. Trade and craft readers get a scheme for sorting the raw stuff of much making.
britannica-1911-flach-geofroi-jacques:
Geofroi Jacques Flach (1846– ) was a French jurist and historian born at Strassburg on the 16th of February 1846. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his career from a law degree in 1869 to the chair of comparative legislation at the Collège de France. His early theses tried a new idea for France, explaining points of law through history.

The Franco-German War turned him for two years to rebuilding the library and museum at Strassburg, wrecked by Prussian shells. Settling in Paris, he taught comparative law and studied the laws of lands as far apart as Ireland, Hungary, Russia, and Japan. His great work, Les Origines de l'ancienne France, traced how feudal law grew as great landowners took over the work of the state. A first volume dealt with lordship, a second with towns, feudal rule, and knighthood.
britannica-1911-fleetwood-charles:
Charles Fleetwood, who died in 1692, was an English soldier and politician. He was third son of Sir Miles Fleetwood of Aldwinkle in Northamptonshire. Admitted to Gray's Inn in November 1638, he joined the earl of Essex's life-guard when the Great Rebellion began. He was wounded at the first battle of Newbury, gained a regiment in 1644 and fought at Naseby. By 1646 he sat in parliament for Marlborough.

In the quarrel between army and parliament Fleetwood played a chief part. He was said to be the main author of the plot to seize King Charles at Holmby, though he took no part in the king's trial. Made a governor of the Isle of Wight in 1649, he rode as lieutenant-general of horse in Cromwell's Scottish campaign and helped win Dunbar. Recalled to command the forces in England, he helped gain the final triumph at Worcester, as the entry follows his rise.
britannica-1911-flores-east-indies:
Flores is the subject of an island entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is an island of the Dutch East Indies, part of the chain that extends east of Java. Its length, greatest breadth, and area are all given. Slate, chalk, sandstone, and volcanic rock are found across the island.

Several volcanoes on Flores are active, the entry notes. Lofty summits on the south coast are named with their heights. One lesser peak is described as constantly active and forming a peninsula. The thickly wooded interior was little explored at that time. The coasts and their harbours are treated next in the full entry.
britannica-1911-foli-allan-james:
Allan James Foli (1837-1899), born Foley, was an Irish bass singer. He was born at Cahir in Tipperary on 7 August 1837. Trained first as a carpenter, he studied singing under Bisaccia at Naples. He made his first appearance at Catania in 1862. From opera in Paris he was engaged by Mapleson for the season of 1865. He appeared with much success in various parts, winning a wide public.

Foli sang Daland in the first performance of The Flying Dutchman in England in 1870. He also sang in the first performance of Gounod's Redemption in 1882. The entry praises his vigorous, straightforward singing. He was as distinguished in oratorio as in opera, and in great request at ballad concerts. He died on 20 October 1899.
britannica-1911-forbes:
Forbes is a municipal town of Ashburnham county, New South Wales, Australia. It stands 289 miles west by north from Sydney, on the Lachlan river, with a station on the Great Western railway. Its population in 1901 was 4,313. The town's weight as a trade centre comes from its position, handy between the northern and southern markets of the state. Steam-sawing and flour mills, breweries and wool-scouring works are its industries.

The country around Forbes yields good quantities of cereals, lucerne, wine and fruit. That is the whole of the short entry: a young Australian inland town fixed by its river, its railway and its place between two markets. Its mills, breweries and wool works, and the crops and vines of its district, stand as the signs of its Edwardian growth. No history or buildings are described in the hosted text beyond these plain facts.
britannica-1911-forres:
Forres is a royal burgh in Elginshire in the north of Scotland. The town stands on the Findhorn river, west of Elgin, with its port at Findhorn to the north. The entry notes its size at the last counts and calls it one of the old towns of the north. Its Gaelic name is glossed as near water.

The bulk of the piece gives the town tale. Kings died or were slain there in old times, and Macbeth is said to have killed Duncan at its first castle. A later royal castle stood for years and was burnt in thirteen ninety. The text also notes the town hall and a tall stone raised to a brave surgeon.
britannica-1911-fourier-s-series:
Fourier's series, in mathematics, are series that proceed by sines and cosines of multiples of a variable. The multiples stand in the ratio of the natural numbers. Such series can stand for a function of the variable between set finite limits. Bernoulli, Lagrange and others had seen their value, above all in the theory of vibrations, and had debated their properties. Fourier was the first to grasp the arbitrary character of the functions the series can represent, and to try in earnest to prove the representation sound.

The long technical article follows that proof and its critics. It treats Dirichlet's conditions, the trouble at a point of discontinuity, and later work by Dircksen, Bessel and Lipschitz. Many later studies tried to free the function from Dirichlet's restrictions. No full set of needful and sufficient conditions had yet been won. It is a piece of higher analysis.
britannica-1911-fourmies:
Fourmies is a town of northern France, in the department of Nord. It stands on a tributary of the Sambre, 39 miles south-east of Valenciennes by rail. Its population in 1906 was 13,308. It is one of the chief centres in France for wool combing and spinning, and it produces a great variety of cloths. The glass-works of Fourmies date from 1599 and were the first set up in the north of France, giving the town an industrial past of three centuries.

Iron is worked nearby, and there are important forges and foundries, while enamel-ware is also made. In 1891 labour troubles at Fourmies brought military intervention and bloodshed, the dark event of the town's modern record. A board of trade arbitration and a school of commerce and industry stand among its public institutions. The short entry stands in a hosted file that opens with pages of the Fourier's Series article.
britannica-1911-fowler-charles:
Charles Fowler (1792-1867), English architect, was born at Cullompton in Devon on 17 May 1792. After five years of apprenticeship at Exeter he went to London in 1814 and joined the office of David Laing. He stayed there until he began practice for himself. His first important work was the court of bankruptcy in Basinghall Street, finished in 1821. The next year he won first premium for a design for the new London Bridge, though another man's design was built in the end.

Fowler designed a bridge across the Dart at Totnes and the markets of Covent Garden and Hungerford in London. He also built the new market at Gravesend, Exeter lower market, several churches, the Devon lunatic asylum of 1845, the London fever hospital of 1849 and the hall of the Wax Chandlers. The entry lists a practical career in iron, glass and stone, serving the markets, hospitals and asylums of the Victorian city.
britannica-1911-francis-i-of-the-two-sic:
Francis I (1777-1830), king of the Two Sicilies, was the son of Ferdinand IV and Maria Carolina of Austria.
