Lascaris, Joannes, also called Janus, was a Greek scholar born about 1445, and the 1911 Britannica gives him a life sketch. He came from Bithynia, likely the younger brother of Constantine Lascaris. After the fall of Constantinople he moved to Florence. At the court of Lorenzo de Medici he acted as a go-between with Sultan Bayezid the Second. He bought Greek books for the Medici library.

When the Medici were driven out, Lascaris moved to Paris in 1495 and taught Greek in public. Louis the Twelfth sent him on missions, among them to Venice. In 1515 Leo the Tenth put him in charge of the Greek college at Rome. He later helped build the royal library at Fontainebleau. The entry lists works he edited, from a Greek anthology of 1494 to studies of Homer, before his death at Rome in 1535.
britannica-1911-lazarites:
Lazarites, also called Lazarists, are the subject of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name covers the Congregation of Priests of the Mission in the Roman Catholic Church. Their work grew from missions to common people led by Saint Vincent de Paul. He worked with five other priests on the estates of the Gondi family.

The entry dates their firm start to sixteen twenty four, when the group settled in Paris. Church approval came two years later. A papal bull in sixteen thirty two set the group up as a congregation. Saint Vincent de Paul stood at its head. The text traces how that small band became a lasting order.
britannica-1911-leixoes:
Leixões, a seaport and harbour of refuge in northern Portugal, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies three miles north of the mouth of the Douro, in the parish of Matozinhos. It is the main port of the city of Oporto, joined to it by an electric tramway. The harbour is artificial, covering over 220 acres. It admits vessels of any size, with nearly fifty feet of water at the entrance.

Cargo moves between ships in the basin and Oporto entirely by lighter. Besides Oporto's wine and other goods, large numbers of emigrants for South America board here. The trade of the port is mainly in British hands. Many British ships call at Leixões on the voyage between Lisbon and Liverpool, London, or Southampton. The parish held 7,690 people in 1900.
britannica-1911-leleges:
Leleges is the name Greek writers gave to an early people, or peoples, of the Greek lands. An article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes up the problem of who they were. In Homer they are allies of the Trojans, though they do not appear in the formal list of forces. Their home is not fixed there. They are kept apart from the Carians, with whom later writers mixed them up.

The article notes their king Altes and their town Pedasus, which Achilles sacked. The town name turns up in several places, from the Troad to Caria and Messenia. One early writer gave the Leleges the coast of Caria from Ephesus to Phocaea, with the islands of Samos and Chios. A later writer still found them living as serfs in south Caria. The entry shows a name spread thin across many shores.
britannica-1911-lelong-jacques:
Jacques Lelong is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lelong was a French bibliographer, born at Paris in 1665. He was a priest of the Oratory and librarian to his order in Paris. He spent his life in seclusion among books and died in 1721.

His first great work was the Bibliotheca sacra of 1709. It indexed every edition of the Bible known to him. In 1719 came his history of French books, the Bibliotheque historique de la France. That huge volume held 17,487 items, some with useful notes attached. The entry admits the work is far from complete. Lelong hoped his friend Desmolets would carry it on, but another scholar took up the task. Fevret de Fontette spent fifteen years rewriting it, reaching 29,143 items in two volumes. Readers meet a quiet priest who mapped a nation's whole literature.
britannica-1911-lemaitre-francois-elie-j:
François Élie Jules Lemaître (1853- ) was a French critic and dramatist, and this 1911 Britannica entry surveys his output. He was born at Vennecy in the Loiret and became a professor at the university of Grenoble. By then his literary criticism had already made him known. In 1884 he gave up his post to devote himself wholly to literature.

He followed Weiss as drama critic of the Journal des Débats and later held the same post on the Revue des Deux Mondes. His studies of writers were gathered as Les Contemporains in seven series, and his theatre pieces as Impressions de théâtre in ten. The entry praises his sketches of modern authors for their insight, their surprise judgments, and their gay, fresh style. He also published poems, tales, and a string of plays from 1889 onward.
britannica-1911-lemonnier-pierre-charles:
Lemonnier, Pierre Charles, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French star gazer. Born in Paris on the 23rd of November 1715, he was a teacher's son. His first noted sighting of the sky was made before age sixteen. A fine moon map he made won him Academy entry in 1736.

That same year he went on a land-measuring trip to Lapland. Maupertuis and Clairault were his mates on that cold trip north. Back home he pressed for English tools and ways in his field. That push did much to reform French star work of his day. He was first to show the wobble of the earth's axis in sun tables. In 1741 he set a transit tool in use at Paris.
britannica-1911-lenfant-jacques:
Jacques Lenfant, who lived from 1661 to 1728, was a French Protestant divine born at Bazoche. The 1911 Britannica article says his father was a pastor who left France when the edict of Nantes fell. Lenfant studied at Saumur and Geneva, then finished his course at Heidelberg. There in 1684 he was ordained minister of the French Protestant church. When the French invaded in 1688 he withdrew to Berlin. In 1689 he became a minister of the French church there, and held the post till his death.

Lenfant wrote many works, chiefly on church history. His best known book is the history of the council of Constance, printed in 1714. It leans on the great labours of Hardt but has merits of its own. All sides praised its fairness. He wrote thirty-two works in all. He died at Berlin on the seventh of August 1728.
britannica-1911-leo-johannes:
Johannes Leo (about 1494-1552), known as Leo Africanus, wrote the Description of Africa. That book long ranked as the best guide to Muslim Africa. Born most likely at Granada of noble Moorish stock, he learned much at Fez. Travel began young across the Barbary states.

Journeys of 1513 to 1515 took him to Timbuktu and the Niger lands. Egypt and Constantinople followed. On the way home about 1520, pirates seized him near Gerba. He was given as a slave to Pope Leo X. The pope freed his mind with a pension and stood sponsor at his baptism. Leo taught Arabic at Rome and wrote in Latin and in Italian. His Africa book came out at Rome in March 1526.
britannica-1911-leochares:
Leochares was a Greek sculptor of the 300s B.C. He worked with Scopas on the Mausoleum about 350 B.C. For Philip of Macedon he made gold and ivory statues of the royal house. Philip set them in the Philippeum at Olympia. With Lysippus he made a bronze lion-hunt group at Delphi.

Other works named are statues of Zeus, Apollo, and Ares. A Vatican statuette of Ganymede borne off by an eagle matches a group Pliny ascribes to him. The copy is much restored and poor in craft. Still, its Attic traits back the link. Close likeness in head and pose ties the Apollo Belvidere to the same hand, some argue. A fine Alexander at Munich is also held a copy of his Olympia portrait.
britannica-1911-leotychides:
Leotychides was a Spartan king of the Eurypontid house. He took the throne in 491 B.C. His claim beat that of Demaratus, with help from Cleomenes. He joined the second raid on Aegina. Ten hostages were seized there and left with Athens for safe keeping.

In spring 479 he led the Greek fleet of 110 ships. The fleet lay first at Aegina, then at Delos. In August he struck the Persian post at Mycale. The land army was crushed and the beached fleet wiped out. In 476 he marched on Thessaly to punish the Aleuadae. A bribe bought his retreat. Trial at Sparta followed. He fled to a temple at Tegea and took exile. His house was razed and his grandson took the throne.
britannica-1911-leptines:
Leptines was an Athenian speaker known for one law. His rule barred grants that freed men from state festival costs. Citizens and resident aliens both fell under it. One line alone kept the grant: the heirs of Harmodius and Aristogeiton. Festival funds were the aim. The treasury and the citizens were both short of cash.

Demosthenes spoke against the law in 354 B.C. His speech backed a plan to test each grant case by case. It warned that scrapping grants would brand Athens as thankless and false. It also charged a fault in form. An older law that backed the grants still stood unrepealed. Solon's rules barred a new law till the clash was cleared. The law was most likely struck down. Nothing more of Leptines is known.
britannica-1911-lesches: Lesches is the reputed maker of the Little Iliad, one of the cyclic poems of Greece. Custom makes him a man of Pyrrha in Lesbos, set about 660 B.C. The poem took up the tale where the Iliad stops. It opened with Ajax and Odysseus in strife for the arms of Achilles. From there it ran to the fall of Troy. A summary in Proclus ends it with the wooden horse inside the walls.
britannica-1911-leslie-charles:
Charles Leslie (1650-1722) was an Irish churchman who would not swear to new rulers. Dublin was his birthplace in July 1650. His father had held two Irish sees. Enniskillen school and Trinity College formed him. Law came first, then orders in 1680. A chancellor's post at Connor came in 1687.

Public debate with the Catholic bishop of Clogher opened his long war of words. Loyal to the Stuarts, he lost his post rather than swear to William and Mary. Twenty years of pamphlets followed. Quakers, Jews, Socinians, Catholics, and Deists all drew his fire. A warrant in 1710 sent him to the Pretender at Bar-le-Duc. Italy held him till 1721. Home at last, he died at Glaslough on 13 April 1722. His church works filled two folio volumes in 1721.
britannica-1911-lever-charles-james:
Charles James Lever (1806–1872) was an Irish novelist, and the schoolboy start of his life fills a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Dublin on the thirty first of August 1806. He was the second son of a Dublin architect and builder. His descent was purely English, the entry notes.

Lever was schooled at private schools, where he cut a wild figure. He wore a ring, smoked, read novels, and led every breach of discipline. His pranks at Trinity College, Dublin, fill a store of tales. From that store, the best scenes of his novels are drawn. He took a medical degree there in 1831, after years of escapades. One college friend became the model for Frank Webber in Charles O’Malley. That character stands at the head of a line of gay young heroes in fiction.
britannica-1911-levites:
Levites is a Bible article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a holy caste in old Israel. The Levites claimed descent from Levi, a son of Jacob. In the full grown system they kept the temple service at Jerusalem.

The article sets out the grades within that service. All Levites shared the blood, but the true priesthood sat with the sons of Aaron alone. The mass of Levites served as lesser hands who could not come near the altar. No lay man might step in on pain of death. The piece argues that this strict scheme came late. In the days of the kings, it says, no such hard line held. Then each Levite counted as fit for priestly work in his own right.
britannica-1911-limoges:
Limoges is a town of west-central France. It heads the department of Haute-Vienne. Orleans lies 176 miles north by the road to Toulouse. Town count in 1906 was 75,906. The commune held 88,597. A hill on the right bank of the Vienne holds the town.

Two old parts split the ground. The Cité, low on the slope, keeps tight streets and old houses. The upper town holds the Rue de la Boucherie and its strong butchers' guild. Ring roads sit where walls once stood. The cathedral leads the Limousin in fame. Work began in 1273. Choir came in 1327 and transept by the mid-1500s. Nave work ran again from 1875 to 1890. A fine Renaissance screen stands inside. Four bridges and a rail viaduct cross the Vienne. Two bridges date to the 1200s.
britannica-1911-linton-william-james:
William James Linton is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in 1812, he was an English wood engraver, a republican, and an author. At sixteen he was bound to a wood engraver as a trainee.

The article follows his rise to the front rank of his craft. His early work showed in a picture Bible of 1833. In 1842 he went into firm with a partner, and the firm was hired by a new picture paper. His partner died the next year, leaving him with two households to feed. All the while he threw his weight into free state causes. He helped expose the opening of Mazzini's letters by the post office in 1844. That act won him the friendship of the Italian leader.
britannica-1911-lobo-francisco-rodrigues:
Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, a Portuguese writer of pastoral verse who lived from about 1575 to about 1627, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. All that is known of his life is that he was born of rich, noble parents at Leiria. He lived at ease in its scenic neighbourhood, reading philosophy and poetry.

He studied at the university of Coimbra and took a degree about 1600, and visited Lisbon from time to time. Tradition says he drowned on the Tagus on a journey there. His first and last books were written in Spanish, the tongue then favoured by polite society. His eclogues and prose pastorals, though, were composed wholly in Portuguese. His Primavera appeared in 1601, with its second part in 1608 and its third in 1614.
britannica-1911-loches:
Loches, a town in France on the Indre River, is drawn in full in a 1911 Britannica place entry. It sits at the foot of a rock crowned by a great castle of the Anjou house. A wall more than a mile round guards the fort hill. The church of Saint Ours, the royal lodge, and the keep stand inside it. Its folk count for nineteen oh six was three thousand seven hundred fifty one.

Stone peaks on the church roof and fine carve work on its west door draw praise. The lodge holds the tomb of Agnes Sorel. The keep held famed state captives in iron cages in past days. Trade spans brandy, tan work, wine, wood, and farm goods. Past notes trace the town to a church house of near the year five hundred.
britannica-1911-los-angeles:
Los Angeles is a city and county seat in southern California state. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies along the small Los Angeles river in San Gabriel foothills. A thin strip joins the main city to its ocean front at San Pedro.

Counts show fast growth, from eleven thousand in eighteen eighty to three hundred nineteen thousand. That last count, from nineteen ten, shows a near threefold leap in ten years. Three rail lines, steamers, and five electric rail systems serve the city. A long breakwater at San Pedro Bay has much improved the harbour. Federal work deepened the bar and built inner harbour works there.
britannica-1911-lotteries:
Lotteries is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on games of chance run by states and towns to raise money. The surviving text deals at length with France, where the royal lottery was at last shut down in 1836. A law of May 1844 still let lotteries be held for charity and the fine arts. In 1878 Paris sold twelve million one-franc tickets to fund prizes for the great Exhibition and trips for working men.

The article also tracks the rules across Europe. Lotteries were shut down in Belgium in 1830, Sweden in 1841, and Switzerland in 1865. France let banks and towns raise loans whose repayment was set by lot. That loan practice was barred in Germany and England. It harked back to older loans where the rate of interest was fixed by chance. Readers get a clear map of how states weighed easy revenue against public morals.
britannica-1911-lucas-sir-charles:
Lucas, Sir Charles is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English soldier of the Civil War. He was a son of Sir Thomas Lucas of Colchester, in Essex, and he died in 1648. As a young man he served in the Netherlands under his brother. In the Bishops' War he led a troop of horse for King Charles the First.

He was knighted in 1639. At the outbreak of the Civil War he took the king's side, as a matter of course, and was wounded at Powick Bridge, the first cavalry fight. Early in 1643 he raised a regiment of horse and beat Middleton at Padbury. In January 1644 he led the attack on Nottingham. On Prince Rupert's advice he was made lieutenant-general of the northern army.
britannica-1911-lyell-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Lyell, a British geologist born on 14 November 1797 on his family estate in Scotland, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Charles Lyell of Kinnordy in Forfarshire. His father knew plants well and turned Dante into English. The plant Lyellia took its name from him.

Love of nature, most of all insects, marked the boy early. At Exeter College, Oxford, talks by Dr Buckland drew him to the study of rocks. He took his first degree in 1819 and then trained for the law. Trips to France and Scotland fed his field work. By 1827 he had left the law for good to follow science.
britannica-1911-macdonell-james:
James Macdonell, who lived from 1841 to 1879, was a British journalist born at Dyce in Aberdeenshire. The 1911 Britannica article says he lost his father young and took a clerk's post in 1858. He began to write for the Aberdeen Free Press. In 1862 he joined the Daily Review at Edinburgh. At the age of twenty-two he was editor of the Northern Daily Express.

In 1865 Macdonell moved to London and joined the Daily Telegraph. He stayed ten years and served as its special reporter in France in 1870 and 1871. From 1873 he wrote leaders for The Times. He died in London on the second of March 1879. His book on France since the First Empire came out after his death. Though left unfinished, the article calls it a shrewd and sound account of French public life.
britannica-1911-mackay-charles:
Charles Mackay, a Scottish writer and newsman, fills a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Perth in 1814 and schooled in London and Brussels. At sixteen he served a Belgian ironmaster and wrote for local papers. Back in London he joined the staff of the Morning Chronicle. He stayed there from 1835 to 1844 and made his name by hard work.

His book on crowd delusions came out in 1841 and still drew readers. A book of verse in 1846 made his literary fame at last. Some songs from it, set to music, won wide love with crowds. He later ran the Glasgow Argus and the Illustrated London News. During the American Civil War he wrote for The Times from the field.
britannica-1911-mackintosh-sir-james:
Sir James Mackintosh, a Scottish publicist, was born at Aldourie near Inverness in seventeen sixty five. He came of old Highland families on both sides of his house. In seventeen eighty he went to college at Aberdeen and made a famed friend. That friend was Robert Hall, afterwards a famous preacher in England. In seventeen eighty four Mackintosh went to Edinburgh to study medicine.

He took his medical degree in seventeen eighty seven, joining the ferment of that city. In seventeen eighty eight he moved to London in a time of high politics. The trial of Warren Hastings and the king's illness filled the news then. Events in France drew his mind far more than his practice did. In April seventeen ninety one he published his answer to Burke on France. That work was the only worthy answer to Burke, the entry says.
britannica-1911-macklin-charles:
Charles Macklin, an Irish actor and playwright who lived from about 1699 to 1797, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His real name was McLaughlin. After an adventurous youth he came to Bristol, where he first appeared on stage as Richmond in Richard the Third. By 1733 he was at Drury Lane in London.

A quarrel between the manager and the leading actors won Macklin better parts, and when those parts were taken back he moved to the Haymarket, then returned to Drury Lane. He acted there near continuously till 1748, then played two seasons in Dublin and came back to Covent Garden. He played a great number of parts, chiefly in comedy. Shylock was his greatest role, and Iago and the Ghost in Hamlet were also in his repertory. At the end of 1753 he left the stage to open a tavern, which failed.
britannica-1911-maclaren-charles:
Charles Maclaren lived from 1782 to 1866 and was a Scottish editor. The brief 1911 Britannica life opens at Ormiston in Haddingtonshire. He was the son of a farmer and dealer in cattle there. Near self taught, he became a clerk in Edinburgh as a young man. In 1817 he helped found the Scotsman newspaper in that city.

He served as first editor of the Scotsman at its founding. A clerk's post in the custom house drew him away soon after. He took the editor's chair again in 1820 and held it till 1845. That same year he was made editor of the sixth Britannica. From 1864 he led the Geological Society of Edinburgh till his death.
britannica-1911-malines:
Malines is an old city in Belgium, seat of the sole chief church post in that land since fifteen fifty-nine. Its count of folk in nineteen four was past fifty-eight thousand. It lies on a stream past the way from one great town to the next. Its name is thought to mean the line of the sea, which once came up to it.

Its weight comes from its post as the faith heart of the land. Its great church, built past two ages and more, is one of the finest church builds in Europe. Its vast tower was meant to rise far past its height. The church holds a famed paint by a great hand, and its carved oak stand is of note. Trade runs in cloth and rail freight.
britannica-1911-mallet-du-pan-jacques:
French journalist Jacques Mallet du Pan, born near Geneva in seventeen forty nine, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from an old Huguenot family, and his father was a Protestant minister. He was schooled at Geneva. Through Voltaire's help he won a teaching post at Cassel.

He soon quit that post and went to London to work on a political journal. After its editor was jailed, he carried the work on alone. He later changed its title and then merged it with a Paris journal, whose political side he led. When revolt broke out in France he sided with the royalists. The king sent him to seek help from German princes. Exiled in seventeen ninety seven, he later set up a new journal in London.
britannica-1911-manners-charles:
Charles Manners (1857- ) was an English singer and opera manager, and this short 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. His real name was Southcote Mansergh, and he was born in London, the son of an Irish colonel. He had a fine bass voice and was trained for music in Dublin and at the Royal Academy of Music in London. He began singing in opera in 1881.

In 1882 he scored a great success as the sentry in Iolanthe at the Savoy. Engagements in opera followed in England and America. In 1890 he married the singer Fanny Moody, already a leading soprano. In 1897 the two formed the Moody-Manners opera company. It did well in the provinces and mounted London seasons in 1902. The entry says their venture, backed by other fine artists, had real weight in the English music of the day.
britannica-1911-marcellus-popes:
Marcellus is a church article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about two popes who bore that name. The piece gives a short life of each man in turn. Both reigns were brief, and both men died in the year their rule began or soon after.

The first Marcellus most likely took office in May 308, under the ruler Maxentius. His harsh penance rules for lapsed Christians sparked unrest in Rome. He was banished in 309 and died that same year. The second Marcellus was born in 1501 and was elected on the ninth of April 1555. He had led the strict party and helped guard papal rights at Trent. Death took him on the last day of that April, before his reform plans bore fruit.
britannica-1911-marcion-and-the-marcioni:
Marcion and the Marcionite Churches, in the 1911 Britannica, is a church history essay on the strongest rival to Catholic order of its age. Between 130 and 180 the loose Christian groups of the empire hardened into fixed churches, schools, and sects. The Marcionite body stood next to Catholicism in weight and took in all believers, of any rank or learning.

Marcion held that the pure gospel had been spoiled in the circles of his time. His aim was to purge false Jewish strands and restore Paul's sense of the message, Paul being the one apostle who read Christ aright. The entry is firm that this makes him no Gnostic, since he set salvation by faith, not by secret knowledge. His two-god view is then laid out, from sources written by foes such as Tertullian.
britannica-1911-marius-of-avenches:
Marius of Avenches is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a sixth century bishop who wrote a short chronicle of his age. Marius was born near Autun, probably in 530, and became bishop of Avenches about 573. He was a skilled goldsmith as well as a churchman, sat at the council of Macon in 585, and moved his see from Avenches to Lausanne. He died on the last day of 593 or 594.

His Chronicon takes up where the chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine leaves off and runs from 455 to 581. Though he drew on older sources, the work still holds value for the history of Burgundy. Marius dated events by the years of the Roman consuls and the East Roman emperors, since he saw his land as still under the rule of the empire. The sole surviving copy rests in the British Museum.
britannica-1911-marquette-jacques:
Jacques Marquette, a French Jesuit missionary and explorer, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Laon in sixteen thirty seven, he went to Canada in sixteen sixty six. He was sent to the upper lakes of the Saint Lawrence. There he worked at missions around Lake Superior and the straits.

In sixteen seventy three he was chosen with Louis Joliet to explore the Mississippi river. The French had begun to hear of that river from Native peoples of the central prairies. Their route lay up Green Bay and along Lake Michigan. The entry follows the voyage that reopened that great river to French knowledge.
britannica-1911-mascaron-jules:
Jules Mascaron, a French preacher of great fame, gets a life note in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Marseilles in sixteen thirty four, he was the son of a court lawyer of Aix. He joined the French Oratory while still a young man. Town fame as a speaker spread to Paris in short time. In sixteen sixty six he was called to preach at the royal court.

King Louis the Fourteenth held his speech as a gift that did not age. He rose to bishop of Tulle, then to the larger see of Agen. Court calls for sad rite speeches still came to him oft. His speech for Turenne in sixteen seventy five ranks as his best work. Late years went to church care at Agen, where he died in seventeen oh three.
britannica-1911-matachines:
Matachines are bands of masked players in Mexico, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out their show. The Spanish word stands for a clown or a masked dancer. The bands roam from town to town in the weeks of Lent, most of all near the Rio Grande. They play a set drama drawn from the tale of Montezuma.

The players wear wild dress in the native style. Rattles serve them as their band. The Monarch is Montezuma himself. Malinche is the native woman who was close to Cortes. The Bull is the ill willed clown of the play, in hide and horns. An old man and an old woman round out the cast. With a choir of dancers they play the loss of his folk by the king, his lure back, the glad reunion, and the slaying of the Bull.
britannica-1911-mathews-charles:
Charles Mathews, an English actor who lived from 1776 to 1835, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in London in June 1776. His father was a grave bookseller who served as well as a minister in a chapel of Lady Huntingdon. The boy was schooled at Merchant Taylors' School and formed his love of the stage as his father's apprentice.

In 1794 his father let him take a stage post in Dublin, though with a sore heart. For years he had to make do with poor parts at low pay. In May 1803 he first played London, at the Haymarket, and from then his career was one long triumph. He had a rare gift of mimicry and could hide his own self with no change of dress at all. His one-man shows, the At Homes, began in 1818 and were rich in humour.
britannica-1911-measles:
Measles, an acute catching disease that falls mostly on children, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Old names for it include Morbilli and Rubeola. Arab doctors such as Rhazes wrote of it in the tenth century. For long it was held to be a kind of smallpox.

Once that error fell away, measles and scarlet fever stayed mixed up in the minds of doctors. Sydenham gave accounts of London outbreaks in 1670 and 1674. Even that sharp watcher had not yet split the two diseases with full clarity. A Palermo doctor may have made that split a century before him. The germ that causes measles had not been pinned down for sure when the entry was written. Its course runs through set stages.
britannica-1911-melville-sir-james:
Melville, Sir James is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Scottish courtier, envoy, and writer of memoirs. James Melville lived from 1535 to 1617. He was the third son of Sir John Melville of Raith in Fife, who was put to death for treason in 1548. In 1549 the young Melville went to France as a page to Mary Queen of Scots.

He fought on the French side at Saint Quentin in 1557, was hurt, and was taken prisoner. He then ran missions for King Henry the Second of France. When Mary came back to Scotland in 1561 she gave him a pension and a post in her household. She also sent him to smooth her planned marriage with Darnley before Queen Elizabeth. The piece gives a vivid sense of a man who served rival rulers in a dangerous age.
britannica-1911-meryon-charles:
Charles Méryon, a French etcher who lived from 1821 to 1863, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Paris, son of an English physician and a French dancer. His mother died while he was young. He entered the French navy and sailed round the world in a corvette.

On the coast of New Zealand he made pencil drawings of the landscape. Years later those studies served him for etchings of the same scenes. Still a lieutenant, he left the navy to follow his bent for art. Finding himself colour-blind, he chose etching as his craft. He learned its technique in the workshop of Bléry, a master he never ceased to thank. Poor and too proud to ask his kin for help, he ground out hack work for bread. His own great work was a series of etchings of Paris, made from 1850 to 1854.
britannica-1911-mesomedes: Mesomedes of Crete, a Greek lyric poet of the second century, is covered in a brief life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a freedman of the emperor Hadrian and is said to have writ a praise poem on Antinous. Two short poems by him survive in the Greek Anthology, and a hymn to Nemesis also survives. That hymn holds special value because the old music signs are writ above the words.
britannica-1911-metrocles:
Metrocles was a Greek thinker of the Cynic school. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ties his life to his master Crates. He had first followed the views of Theophrastus at Athens. Crates won him over to the hard Cynic way of life.

His sister Hipparchia fell in love with that same master. Her match is a famed sidelight on Cynic scorn for comfort. Metrocles held the joys of life at a very low price. Only Crates stopped him from killing himself in his youth. He taught the same views by word and by deed. Menippus of Sinope sat among his pupils in time. Weighing old age pains against its joys, he chose death. He drowned himself when life held nothing he much cared for.
britannica-1911-michelet-jules:
Jules Michelet, who lived from 1798 to 1874, was a French historian born in Paris. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his family Huguenot roots and a master printer father. The boy helped at the press in his father shop as a lad at work. A place at the imperial printing office was his for the taking instead.

His father chose school, and the Lycee Charlemagne brought out his gifts in full. He passed the university exam in 1821 and took a history chair at College Rollin. Marriage came in 1824 as patrons such as Cousin and Villemain backed his rise. Republican fire had burned in him since childhood, the entry stresses.
britannica-1911-mieres: Mieres, a town of northern Spain in the province of Oviedo, is described in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gazetteer entry. It stands on the river Caudal, twelve miles by rail south-east of Oviedo. Its people numbered 18,083 in 1900. The town is the chief place of a hilly, fertile, well-wooded district. Coal, iron, and copper are mined there in quantity. Sulphur and cinnabar are found in smaller amounts. Mieres holds large iron foundries and chemical works. It trades in fruit, cider, timber, and live stock.
britannica-1911-mignons-les:
Les Mignons were the favored young men of King Henry III of France. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the French word mignon means favorite in plain use. Parisians gave it a sharp edge for this court group in particular. A writer of the time calls them hated for pride and strange dress.

Huge royal gifts to them stirred still more public anger in Paris. The Guise family fanned that ill will for its own ends, it says. From 1576 attacks on the group grew in talk and in print. Historians later repeated scandal tales without proof, the entry warns. Dukes of Joyeuse and Épernon were the best known of them.
britannica-1911-miller-william-hallowes:
William Hallowes Miller was a British worker in the study of stones and crystals, born in Wales. He went to college at Cambridge, came out high in maths, and was made a fellow there. For some years he taught in the college and put out works on the science of waters at rest and in flow.

The 1911 Britannica entry stresses his turn to the study of crystal forms. On the post falling free, he took the chair of the science of stones at Cambridge and held it for near forty years. His chief book on crystal study came out in those years, and he was made a fellow of the Royal Society. He helped set new state standards of length and weight, and edited a key primer in his field.
britannica-1911-mills-roger-quarles:
Roger Quarles Mills is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an American lawmaker born in 1832 in Kentucky. He was born in Todd county in March 1832. He went to Texas as a boy in 1839. He read law and was called to the bar young. A special act let him in before age twenty one. In 1861 he joined the Confederate army for war.

He fought as a private at Wilson Creek at first. As colonel he led a Texas regiment in hard fights. He led a brigade for part of one great battle. He sat in the national House from 1873 to 1892. He sat in the Senate from 1892 to 1899. Tariff was his special study in all that time. He was held the top voice on tariffs in Congress. A bill that bore his name cut duties in 1888.
britannica-1911-miltiades:
Miltiades is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It covers two Athenian leaders of one famed house in old Greece. The first was a foe of a tyrant who ruled Athens in his day. A plea for aid from a far tribe gave him a realm of his own.

The entry tells how he walled off his new realm at its neck of land. Foes seized him once, but a great king won his release by threat. The second man of the name went out to rule that same realm in turn. He is the famed victor of the great battle of Marathon. His clash with Persia fills the rest of the short double tale.
britannica-1911-misiones:
Misiones, a tract of north Argentina, is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Paraguay and Brazil bound it north, Brazil east and south, and Paraguay and an Argentine province west. Great rivers form its lines on three sides. Its area is past eleven thousand square miles. Its count is put at near thirty nine thousand.

The land is of rough, broken face. Low hills run its length and part its streams. Those streams flow north to one great river and south to a second. Most of the land is clad in wood and in thick growth of the hot zone. The air is of the warm belt. The soil is held to be rich past the norm, yet its goods stay close to the ground they grow on.
britannica-1911-moderatus-of-gades:
Moderatus of Gades, a Greek philosopher of the new Pythagorean school, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He lived at the same time as Apollonius of Tyana. He wrote a great work on the doctrines of the Pythagoreans. In it he tried to show that the followers of Pythagoras added nothing to their founder's views. They only borrowed and restated his wording, he held.

Recent writers have given Moderatus a false weight, the entry argues. They cast him as a forerunner of the Alexandrian school of thought. One scholar has shown that the ground for that view is wholly unsound. Moderatus is thus left as a minor yet curious figure of a kind of thought almost gone since the fifth century before Christ. A fragment of his writing survives in a later collection.
britannica-1911-molasses: Molasses is the syrup drained from raw sugar, or drawn off in refining. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that American use covers both forms. English use more often calls the refined form treacle instead, it says. Old spellings like melasses and molassos trace back to Portuguese and French words. The root ties to a Latin word for syrup made from honey. Molasse, a soft green sandstone name from the Alps, must not be confused with it.
britannica-1911-monophysites:
Monophysites held that Christ had one joined nature, not two. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows their long church fight. The name comes from Greek words for one and for nature. Their stand grew in the great debates of the fifth and sixth centuries.

A council at Chalcedon in 451 set a two nature rule. Followers of Cyril of Alexandria saw that rule as a split of Christ in two. Riots shook Palestine and Egypt as bishops were cast out. One emperor backed the group for a short reign. A later edict tried to shelve the whole dispute in 482. Rome read the edict as a slight and broke with the East. The breach lasted for decades, the entry shows.
britannica-1911-montceau-les-mines: Montceau les Mines is a short place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a town in east central France, on a main rail line. The town owes its growth to coal, as the centre of a rich coal basin. A canal and many rail lines link the pits to the town. Its works include cloth mills, iron and copper foundries, and shops that build machines. Counts for the town and the wider commune are both given.
britannica-1911-montgomery-james:
James Montgomery is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a British poet and journalist. He was born in 1771 at Irvine in Ayrshire, Scotland. His father was a Moravian minister. Part of his youth was spent in Ireland. He was schooled at Fulneck in Yorkshire, a Moravian school near Leeds. He went on to edit the Sheffield Iris for over thirty years.

His work as a reform minded editor brought real risk. He was jailed twice, in 1795 and in 1796. His poem The Wanderer of Switzerland came out in 1806. It dealt with the French hold on that land. Lord Byron praised his gift in strong terms. A harsh review in Edinburgh cut the other way. The entry weighs both sides of his early fame.
britannica-1911-montserrat-west-indies:
Montserrat is an island in the British West Indies, one of the presidencies of the Leeward Islands colony, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes it. It lies south-west of Antigua, eleven miles long and seven broad, with an area of about thirty-two square miles. Its people, mostly Black, numbered 12,215 in 1901. The island is a cluster of rugged volcanic peaks rising from the Caribbean Sea, their tops clothed with forest.

The still active Soufrière, at three thousand feet in the south, is the highest point. The average heat is eighty-one degrees, softened by cool sea breezes, and rain averages ninety-four inches a year. Water is plentiful and the roads are well kept. The chief products are sugar and lime-juice, both raw and concentrated, and minerals are found as well. Schooling is compulsory.
britannica-1911-morphy-paul-charles:
Paul Charles Morphy is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Morphy was an American chess player born in New Orleans in 1837. His father was a judge who loved chess. The boy learned the moves at age ten. In less than two years he could beat all the amateurs of his home city.

The article follows his rise while he still read law at school. He won first prize at the first American chess congress in New York in 1857. He then sailed to Europe and won match after match. In Paris he beat the German champion by a wide score. He also beat eight strong players at once while blindfold. He came home in 1859 intending to practise law. War and failing health ended those plans, and he died in 1884.
britannica-1911-mossamedes: Mossamedes is a town in Portuguese West Africa and the chief town of its own district. It stands on the south side of a small bay that gives good mooring for ships. Its count of folk is given as about five thousand. A rail line of more than a hundred miles starts at the port. The line crosses dry coast land to a rich high plain. The town is also the base for a large trade in fish. The entry is a short note from the nineteen eleven work.
britannica-1911-muspratt-james:
James Muspratt (1793–1886) was a British chemical manufacturer, and the wild start of his career fills a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Dublin on the twelfth of August 1793. At fourteen he was apprenticed to a wholesale druggist. A quarrel with his master ended that training in 1810.

In 1812 Muspratt went to Spain to fight in the Peninsular War. He could not gain a cavalry commission, so he followed the army on foot. Fever laid him up at Madrid, and he barely escaped capture by the French. He reached Lisbon and joined the navy there. Harsh discipline on his second ship drove him to desert. The entry follows a restless youth who later built a great chemical business.
britannica-1911-myrmidones:
Myrmidones is a legend article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a race of men in Greek tale. In Homer's time they dwelt in Phthiotis, in Thessaly. Old tales give their first home as the island of Aegina. From there they crossed to Thessaly with Peleus.

The article sets out two tales behind their name. One traces it to a forebear, a son of Zeus and Eurymedusa. Zeus wooed her in the shape of an ant. The other tale says the men of Aegina died in a plague. At the prayer of King Aeacus, Zeus turned ants into men to fill the island again. The word myrmidon has passed into English from these tales. It now names a follower who carries out orders with no mercy and no thought.
britannica-1911-nayler-james:
James Nayler, who lived from 1618 to 1660, was an English Puritan turned Quaker. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Ardsley in Yorkshire. In 1642 he joined the parliament army as a quartermaster. In 1651 he took up Quaker ideas. Slowly he came to hold that he was Christ come again. A small band of followers gathered round him.

In October 1655 he rode into Bristol on horseback in mimic of Christ. His followers sang hosannas as they went on foot and on horse. He was seized at the High Cross and tried by parliament. The sentence was savage: whipping, branding with a B, and his tongue bored with hot iron. Two years of hard labour followed the pain. Freed, he was taken back by the Quakers. He died on a road trip to Yorkshire in 1660.
britannica-1911-nazarenes:
The Nazarenes were a small Jewish Christian sect of the fourth century. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places them in Syria and the Decapolis. Epiphanius is the chief source on them. He said they traced their seat at Pella to the flight from Jerusalem. That flight came just before the siege of the year 70. He calls them Jews pure and simple. Yet they owned the new covenant as well as the old.

Jerome adds that they held Christ as God's son, born of Mary. His sharp verdict was that they tried to be both Jews and Christians. In his view they ended as neither. They read Matthew's gospel in its Aramaic form and kept the law's rules on sabbaths and foods. Unlike stricter sects, they owned Paul as an apostle. The entry takes them to be the Ebionites under another name.
britannica-1911-north-west-territories:
The North West Territories began as a general name for British lands north west of the Saint Lawrence. The British North America Act of eighteen sixty seven made way for their entry into Canada. Manitoba was formed out of that district in eighteen seventy as a province. The land that remained kept the name North West Territories for its rule. It was placed under the governor of Manitoba for the time.

In eighteen seventy six the district of Keewatin was set up as a unit. In eighteen eighty two four new districts were organized across the west. Two of those, with changes, became the province of Saskatchewan in nineteen o five. The other two became the province of Alberta in that same year. What is left holds four districts under an administrator at Ottawa. Its people are in the south chiefly Chipewyan, and Eskimo in the north.
britannica-1911-obsequies: Obsequies is a short word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the rites and acts held at a burial, most of all grand ones. The word was formed in church Latin on the shape of an older term. Its root means to follow close after a great person. That root gave old English a word for meek and ready service. That sense is lost now, save in one word for a fawning manner.
britannica-1911-offenbach-jacques:
Jacques Offenbach, a French composer who lived from 1819 to 1880, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is famed for light opera, the opera bouffe. Born at Cologne to German Jewish parents, he showed a gift for music at a very early age. In 1833 he was sent to Paris to study the cello.

Offenbach joined the orchestra of the Opera Comique in 1834 and rose to conductor at another house. His first hit as a composer came in 1848 with a song in a play by Musset. From then on he fought without pause for fame. His first full work came out in 1853, and a crowd of light pieces followed. In 1855 he took a small Paris theatre and refilled it night after night. His fame peaked with La Grande Duchesse de Gerolstein in 1867, called the most popular light opera ever writ.
britannica-1911-ohnet-georges:
Georges Ohnet, a French novelist crowds loved, is sketched in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris in 1848, he first ran two Paris papers as editor. Plays came first in his work, writ with a partner's help. He held Georges Sand high and scorned the new truth-school of tales. His own tales took a plain and hopeful cast of mind.

His run of novels was called Battles of Life as a set. Serge Panine of 1881 won a crown from the Academy. The Ironmaster of 1882 won still wider fame with the public. Critics called his work unreal and flat, yet crowds bought it. Stage forms of his tales ran long and drew full houses. The Ironmaster held the Gymnase stage for a whole year.
britannica-1911-otis-james:
James Otis was an American friend of freedom who lived from seventeen twenty-five to seventeen eighty-three. He was born at West Barnstable in Massachusetts and trained at Harvard. He rose to fame at the bar in Boston. A book on Latin verse by him was held in high regard.

His great hour came in the writs case of seventeen sixty-one. He held a post that bound him to speak for the Crown, so he gave it up. He then spoke for the folk against broad search writs. His plea went past the case to the rights of the folk in America as a whole.
britannica-1911-outram-sir-james:
Sir James Outram, an English general and a hero of the Indian Mutiny, lived from 1803 to 1863. His life fills an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of an engineer of Butterley Hall in Derbyshire. His father died in 1805, and his mother moved to Aberdeenshire in 1810. The boy went from school there to a cadetship in India in 1819.

His drive drew note at once at Bombay. In 1820 he became acting adjutant to a battalion at Poona. In 1825 he was sent to Khandesh, where he raised a light corps from the Bhil tribes. He won them by his skill and daring as a hunter, and used them to check raids and theft. Ill health dogged his early years, yet each bout seemed to leave him with a frame of iron.
britannica-1911-paddington-new-south-wal: Paddington, a municipality in New South Wales, Australia, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies three miles south east of Sydney, as a suburb of that city, in Cumberland county. The entry gives it 22,034 people in 1901. It is a busy industrial suburb, given to brewing, tanning, soap boiling, and other trades. Its town hall is one of the finest in the colony, and it has a fine free library. Paddington returns one member to parliament.
britannica-1911-parrot-fishes:
Parrot-Fishes, more truly called Parrot-Wrasses, get a fish entry in the 1911 Britannica. They form the family Scaridae, close kin to the wrasses, with eight genera in all. Large scales, from 21 to 25 along the side, mark them at a glance. So do fixed counts of spines and rays in their fins. Their teeth set them apart most of all.

The jaw teeth are fused into a sharp edged beak like a parrot's. With it the fish scrape coral for the polyps inside, or cut tough seaweed, and throat teeth grind the food to pulp. Near one hundred species live in warm seas of the Indo-Pacific and Atlantic. Their bright colours fade at death. Most are good to eat, though some turn poisonous after feeding on coral. Many pass three feet in length.
britannica-1911-parsees:
Parsees, or Parsis, are described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article as the followers of Zoroaster in India. The entry calls them descendants of ancient Persians who moved to India after the Arab conquest of their country in the eighth century. They first landed at Sanjan on the coast of Gujarat, where Hindu rulers took them in kindly.

Inside, the article notes that their home speech is Gujarati, which they have used in writing and journalism. Their move to Bombay dates only from British rule there. In 1901 there were 94,000 Parsees in all India, most of them in the Bombay area and Baroda. The entry also describes their dress, their homes, and the free public place allowed to women.
britannica-1911-parton-james:
James Parton (1822-1891) was an American writer of lives, born in Canterbury, England. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes he came to the United States at age five. He taught school in Philadelphia and New York before writing full time. In 1875 he settled at Newburyport, Massachusetts, where he died.

He was the most popular biographer of his day in America, it says. Lives of Horace Greeley, Aaron Burr, and Andrew Jackson came first. Lives of Franklin, Jefferson, and Voltaire followed in later years. He also wrote books of famed Americans for young readers. His wife Sara wrote popular novels under the name Fanny Fern.
britannica-1911-paschal-popes:
Paschal is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on two popes and one anti-pope. Paschal the First held the post from 817 to 824. A native of Rome, he was raised to the post by clergy acclaim. That came before the emperor's sanction had been got for it.

His ties with the imperial house never grew warm or close. He also failed to win the love of the Roman nobles. He died in Rome while imperial agents probed a dark affair. Two great men had been seized, blinded, and then beheaded there. Paschal had shielded the killers but denied a hand in the crime. The folk of Rome refused him burial in St Peter's church. His church building work in Rome is also told.
britannica-1911-pasiteles:
Pasiteles was a sculptor whose workshop shaped Roman taste in the days of Julius Caesar. A short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls him the chief name of the Neo-Attic school. His shop met a strong Roman demand for copies of famed Greek works. His pupils Stephanus and Menelaus also left signed works that still survive.

The entry notes that the shop worked from early Dorian models. Its polish made the figures fine but somewhat smooth and school-like. Pliny is cited for the facts that Pasiteles came from Magna Graecia, in the south of Italy. Pliny also says that Rome granted him the rights of a citizen.
britannica-1911-patarenes: Patarenes, or Paratelli, is a name first used in Milan about 1058. It named the strong foes of marriage among the clergy. The party took its name from the quarter of the city where its members met to plan their acts. That quarter was the Pataria, the ragmen's quarter, from a local word for a rag. In the 1200s the Cathari took the name for their own and said it came from a Latin word for to suffer.
britannica-1911-patenotre-des-noyers-jul:
Jules Pâtenôtre des Noyers (born 1845) was a French diplomat from Baye in Marne. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his training at a top Paris school for teachers. He taught at Algiers for some years before joining the foreign service in 1871. Field posts then took him across Asia, Africa, and beyond.

His key task came in 1884 as minister to China. He had to settle French control in Annam and Tongking after fighting there. A first round of talks failed and fighting resumed. The next year he signed a peace at Tien-tsin that secured the French claim. Later posts took him to Morocco, Washington, and Madrid.
britannica-1911-patrocles:
Patrocles (about 312-261 BC) was a Macedonian general who also wrote on lands and seas. He lived in the reigns of Seleucus I and Antiochus I. In 285 he held command of the fleet of Seleucus. He then made a voyage of exploration on the Caspian Sea. His aim was to find trade routes, above all a path to the peoples of northern India.

Patrocles came to hold that the Caspian was a gulf or inlet of the sea. He held too that ships could enter it from the Indian Ocean. No copy of his work stands, and even its title is unknown. All we know of it comes through Strabo. After the death of Seleucus, Antiochus sent him to put down a revolt in Asia Minor. He lost his life in a fight with the Bithynians.
britannica-1911-paul-popes:
Paul is the name borne by five popes, and their reigns are set out in one article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Paul the First held the see from 757 to 767. He followed his brother Stephen the Third. His reign is marked by a close bond with Pippin, king of the Franks, to whom he sent books. He strove in vain to heal the rift with the East.

Paul the Second, born Pietro Barbo at Venice in 1417, reigned from 1464 to 1471. Meant for trade, he took orders under his uncle, Pope Eugenius the Fourth, and rose to cardinal. He was picked to follow Pius the Second, to the surprise of all. He ruled at once that pledges set for a new pope bind him as counsel only, not as law. He checked the grasping policy of Venice and clashed with Louis the Eleventh of France.
britannica-1911-peacock-sir-barnes:
Sir Barnes Peacock (1810-1890) was an English judge who did his great work in India, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born the son of a solicitor, practised as a special pleader, and was called to the bar in 1836. In 1844 he won wide notice by finding the flaw that overturned the conviction of Daniel O'Connell and his fellow defendants.

In 1852 he went to India as legal member of the governor-general's council. There he pushed law reform with energy, though at times with too little care for native feeling. He backed the annexation of Oudh and stood by Lord Canning through the Mutiny. In 1859 he became chief justice of the Supreme Court. Back in England from 1870, he sat on the judicial committee of the privy council, where his Indian knowledge made him invaluable.
britannica-1911-pelagius-popes:
Pelagius is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on two popes of that name. Pelagius the First held the post from 555 to 561. A Roman by birth, he first shows up as a deacon at Constantinople. There he served as envoy for Pope Silverius at the imperial court.

The emperor Justinian sent him to Antioch in 542 on church work. He also took part in the synod at Gaza that year. Back in Rome, he used his wealth to aid the poor. That won him great love among the folk of the city. Left as vicar in 544, he dealt with Totila the Goth with tact. His care saved the folk from murder and outrage, the text says.
britannica-1911-pelissier-aimable-jean-j:
Aimable Jean Jacques Pelissier, who lived from 1794 to 1864, was a marshal of France and duke of Malakoff. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his birth at Maromme to a prosperous artisan family. School at La Fleche and Saint Cyr led him into the artillery in 1815. A fine exam in 1819 won him a place on the general staff.

Aide service in Spain in 1823 and the Morea in 1828 broadened his field craft. Algeria took him in 1839, and rank rose on his return from that tour. Staff years in Paris and Oran followed, with a lead part in hard operations. The entry notes the severity that marked his name before Crimea made it famed.
britannica-1911-penates:
Penates were Roman gods of the food store and the kitchen in this 1911 Britannica faith entry. Their name rests on a Latin word for food and goods kept by. The store room stood by the main hall in old homes. Pure folk alone might step into that shrine like space. The gods had no names of their own as a rule.

Kin gods called Lares stood close by them in the home shrine. Each house held two Penates but just one Lar, the text says. Images of the pair danced with a drink horn raised in joy. Dawn prayers, meal blessings, and burnt bits of food marked the rite. Set days each month and two feasts in the year held rites of their own.
britannica-1911-pendleside-series:
The Pendleside Series, in geology, is a set of shales in the English Midlands. The shales lie between the top part of the Carboniferous Limestone and the Millstone Grits. They run from Stoke-on-Trent to Settle. The set starts with black limestones at its base. Black shales with lime-rich nodules come next, and they pass into sandy shales with hard sandstones. In places the set is 1,000 to 1,500 feet thick.

Where the Pendleside Series is thickest, the Millstone Grits reach their full thickness as well. The set is rich in fossils, with forms such as Productus giganteus among them. The best spots to study it are the west slope of Pendle Hill and the valley of the Hodder. Other good spots are Mam Tor and the Edale valley in Derbyshire, and sites in north Staffordshire, North Wales, and the Isle of Man.
britannica-1911-penrith-new-south-wales:
Penrith is a municipality of Cumberland county in New South Wales in Australia, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It stands on the Nepean River, 34 miles by rail west of Sydney. Penrith and the next township of Saint Marys are chiefly remarkable for their link with the railway. The iron tube bridge that carries the line over the Nepean is the best of its kind in the colony.

The viaduct over Knapsack Gulley is called the most remarkable work of its kind in Australia. Large engineering works and railway fitting shops stand at Penrith in the text. The town is also the junction for all the western goods traffic of the colony. The inhabitants of both towns are mainly railway employees in their work. Their counts in 1901 were 3,539 for Penrith and 1,840 for Saint Marys, small towns built on the traffic of the line.
britannica-1911-pericles:
Pericles, an Athenian statesman who lived from about 490 to 429 before Christ, gets a long entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was the son of Xanthippus and Agariste, and kin through his mother to Cleisthenes and the Alcmaeonid house. His teachers were among the ablest of the day. Damon taught him music, Zeno showed him the power of argument, and Anaxagoras shaped his calm cast of mind.

His first recorded act came in 463, when he helped charge Cimon with bribery, a charge the entry doubts was meant in earnest. The attack on the Areopagus belongs chiefly to Ephialtes, not to Pericles. When Ephialtes was killed, Pericles took the lead in the state. Athens then pushed outward hard, with 200 ships sent to aid Egypt against Persia, and wars round Megara mark his ascendancy.
britannica-1911-pescadores:
Pescadores, a group of islands thirty miles west of Formosa, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name means fishers in the old Spanish form. A channel parts the islands from Formosa near the tropic of Cancer. The Japanese call the group Hōkō tō.

The islands number forty eight, and twenty one of them hold people. Their coast line runs to about ninety nine miles, and their land to about eighty six square miles. About 55000 people live there, mostly Chinese. The soil lies flat and yields little. Strong north east winds sweep the isles for half the year, and typhoons cross their path. Storm days average 237 a year in the count given. Fishing is the chief work, and dried fish go out as exports.
britannica-1911-peter-des-roches:
Peter des Roches is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a bishop of Winchester. He died in 1238, having served under John and Henry the Third. A Poitevin by birth, he was a foreign favourite at court. Such men drew much of the kings' ill fame, the entry says.

He got the chamberlain post late in the reign of Richard. In 1205, by John's sway, he was picked for the Winchester see. The pick was fought, but the pope backed it on appeal. Peter stood by his king through the whole ban on the land. In 1213 he was made justiciar in place of Geoffrey Fitz Peter. At Lincoln in 1217 he led a wing of the royal host.
britannica-1911-pherecrates:
Pherecrates was a Greek poet of the Old Attic Comedy, a peer of famed comic writers of his age. The 1911 Britannica entry says he first worked as an actor, then won a prize for a play in his early years. One more firm date stands: a late play of wild men, staged some years on.

The entry says he, like a poet he copied, left off mocking named men for broad themes, though bits of his plays still jab at known men. He was famed for a rich fancy, and for pure, fine speech that won him a name for the most Attic style. He gave his name to a new verse measure used in Greek tragic song and by Horace, and parts of his plays still stand in print.
britannica-1911-phosphates:
Phosphates, in chemistry, are the salts of phosphoric acid. Phosphoric oxide joins with water in three shares to form three acids. They are meta-, pyro-, and ortho-phosphoric acid, the last being the common form. Each acid gives rise to sets of salts of its own. The salts of the common acid are the most key, and phosphates are spread wide in the world of minerals.

Common phosphoric acid can be made in more than one way. It can be made by boiling the oxide in water, or by the action of nitric acid on red phosphorus. It can also be drawn from a mineral phosphate by the use of sulphuric acid. The acid most often forms a thin syrup. When that syrup is drawn down in a vacuum, it sets into hard, clear prisms. Those prisms melt at 41.7 degrees.
britannica-1911-phthalazines:
Phthalazines are a group of ring compounds in organic chemistry. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives how the parent kind is made. The ring holds carbon and nitrogen in a fused pair of loops. The group matches a kin group called cinnolines in its atom count.

The parent stuff forms when a brominated wood spirit kin meets hydrazine. A second path cuts down a chlorine bearing form with strong acid. The stuff acts as a base and joins with alkyl salts. Air and a strong oxidant turn it into a two acid product. Zinc and acid break it down into a diamine instead. A sister form with oxygen in the ring also gets full treatment. Such notes served bench chemists who built new dyes and drugs.
britannica-1911-pichegru-charles:
Charles Pichegru is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a French general who lived from 1761 to 1804. He was born in February 1761, the son of a labourer. Friars at Arbois gave the boy a sound schooling. One master took him to a school for arms at Brienne. In 1783 he joined a regiment of artillery. He rose there to a junior officer rank.

When revolt began he led a party in Besancon. His well kept troops drew note in the Rhine army. Staff work led to rank as a brigade chief. In 1793 envoys sought new chiefs who could win fights. With Hoche he won back Alsace for the republic. He then led the army of the North. Three great drives in one year mark that command.
britannica-1911-pinto-fernao-mendes:
Fernao Mendes Pinto, a Portuguese traveller who lived from 1509 to 1583, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Montemor-o-Velho, of poor parents. After service in Lisbon and Setubal, he sailed for India in 1537. For twenty one years he travelled, fought, and traded across China, Tartary, Pegu, and nearby lands.

In 1542 and 1543 he was among the first Europeans to visit Japan, where he brought the musket. He was thirteen times a captive and seventeen times sold as a slave, yet came through each blow. He served as soldier, sailor, merchant, doctor, envoy, and mission helper. He was a friend of Saint Francis Xavier, whom he lent funds to build the first Jesuit house in Japan. In 1554 he joined the Jesuits himself at Goa.
britannica-1911-pipe-fishes:
Pipe-fishes, a group of small fishes, are the subject of a nature article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. With the sea-horses they form a family of their own. Their name comes from the shape of the snout, drawn out into a long tube. It ends in a narrow mouth that opens upward and has no teeth.

The article describes a long, thin, snake-like body and tail. Hard coverings wrap them, split into neat segments in rows. Ridges run along the body, so that a cut across it shows corners, not the round or oval shape of most fishes. A back fin is always present and does most of the work of swimming. The belly fins are always absent, and the other fins may or may not grow. The males of one kind carry the young in a pouch under the tail.
britannica-1911-pisces:
Pisces, the fishes, is the twelfth sign of the zodiac in astronomy, as a 1911 Britannica entry states. Its mark shows two fishes tied together by their tails in the sky. Eudoxus and Aratus named the star group in early Greek times of science. Ptolemy listed thirty eight stars in it, with later counts close to that figure.

Greek tale says Aphrodite and Eros leapt into the Euphrates to escape the monster Typhon. Changed into two fishes in the water, they won safety from his rage. The entry judges that tale a Greek dress on an older Egyptian story. Bright double stars in the group are picked out for observers.
britannica-1911-plumptre-edward-hayes:
Edward Hayes Plumptre, English divine and scholar, was born in London on 6 August 1821 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a scholar of University College at Oxford. There he took a double first class degree in 1844 and won a fellowship at Brasenose College the same year. He was ordained in 1847.

At King College in London he served as chaplain and then as a teacher of pastoral work. A stall at St Paul came to him in 1863. From 1869 to 1874 he helped revise the Old Testament for the authorized version. He gave the Boyle lectures in 1866 and 1867 on Christ and Christendom. In 1881 he became dean of Wells, and he died in 1891.
britannica-1911-potgieter-everhardes-joh:
Everhardes Johannes Potgieter, a Dutch prose writer and poet who lived from 1808 to 1875, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Zwolle in Overyssel in June 1808, he began life in a merchant's office at Antwerp. In 1831 he made a journey to Sweden. He told of it in two volumes, published at Amsterdam from 1836 to 1840.

Potgieter then settled in Amsterdam and traded on his own account, with a growing bent toward literature. With Heije and Bakhuizen van den Brink he founded a review, De Muzen, in 1834. It was soon replaced by De Gids, the leading magazine of Holland, in which he wrote many articles and poems. After his death in 1875, a full edition of his works appeared in eight volumes.
britannica-1911-pradier-james:
James Pradier, who lived from 1792 to 1852, was a French sculptor. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places him before the Romantic wave. He was born at Geneva and joined the French Academy. His manner matched the drawing room classic style of Canova at Rome.

A Niobe group of 1822 leads the list of his works. The Three Graces and a Psyche came in the same early years. He carved the Fame figures on the great Paris triumphal arch. A relief by him also marks the Carrousel arch in Paris. His Prometheus stands in the Tuileries Gardens for all to see. Late works include an Atalanta and a Sappho in the Louvre. He also made a statue of Rousseau for his home city.
britannica-1911-precession-of-the-equino:
Precession of the equinoxes is a slow shift of the equinox in the sky, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The shift runs from east to west, against the way the planets move. The equinox is the point where the equator and the ecliptic cross in the heavens. Both of those great circles are in slow but steady motion, and that is why the point moves.

Part of the motion comes from the pull of the planets on the earth. That pull turns the plane of the orbit of the earth by slow degrees. The rate at the time of writing is given as 46.7 seconds of arc per century. The text works through the axis of this turn and the parts of the circle where the drift runs south or north. It is a dry, exact piece for readers who need the maths of the sky.
britannica-1911-procrustes: Procrustes is a short myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of a robber in Greek legend who lived near Eleusis. He kept two beds, one very long and one very short, for guests he seized. Tall guests were laid on the short bed and cut down to fit it. Short guests were stretched on the long bed until they died. The hero Theseus slew him in the end. His name lives on in a phrase for a harsh fixed rule that forces all to fit.
britannica-1911-pyrites:
Pyrites is a stone article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a term for a group of metal bearing sulphur stones. In its strict sense it names one stone of iron and sulphur, formed in cube shapes. In wider use it heads a whole group, with kin named for copper, arsenic, and other metals.

The article traces the name to a Greek word for fire. The stone throws sparks when struck hard, as with flint. Lumps of it found in old graves hint at its use to make fire in early times. It was even used in old wheel lock guns. The text sets this stone apart from a near kin with a different inner form. Its hardness is given at about six on the scale. Its weight runs well above that of the kin stone.
britannica-1911-quinones:
Quinones are a group of compounds in organic chemistry, and this 1911 Britannica entry defines them and shows how they are made. In a quinone, two hydrogen atoms of a benzene ring are replaced by two oxygen atoms. The swap can sit in the ortho or the para positions, giving orthoquinones or paraquinones. Metaquinones, the entry notes, seem never to have been isolated on their own.

The paraquinones, the true quinones, are made by treating hydrocarbons or certain benzene compounds with chromic acid. Work by Pechmann in 1888 showed that one class of compounds turns into paraquinones under warm caustic alkali. The entry also reports Bayrac's route to coloured offshoots of the paraquinones from a mixture in acetic acid. Chemical formulae are given throughout in the style of the day.
britannica-1911-quinoxalines:
Quinoxalines, a family of compounds in organic chemistry, are described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Each one joins a benzene ring with a pyrazine ring. They are kin to the cinnolenes, phthalazines, and quinazolines. They form when ortho-diamines are condensed with diketones. The parent compound, quinoxaline, results when glyoxal is used. Other members arise from ketonic acids or chloroketones.

The article sets out the family's main reactions and products. Diamino forms arise when cyanogen is condensed with diamines. Those amino forms pass easily into dioxy forms with weak acid. The group as a whole acts as a weak base. The members resist agents that cause oxidation. They are, though, readily reduced to hydro forms. Keto forms arise from mono-alkyl diamines with ketonic acids. Azonium bases form when dihydro forms are oxidized with ferric chloride.
britannica-1911-rennell-james:
James Rennell is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a British map maker born in Devon in seventeen forty two. His father, a gun officer, died in war soon after his birth. The boy went to sea as a cadet at age fourteen.

The entry tells how he left the navy to survey lands in Bengal for a great trade company. He gave thirteen years to that work and was badly hurt in a clash. He then spent more than fifty years in London on map research. His atlas of Bengal and his first sound map of India made his name. Books on old lands and on sea currents fill out his long list.
britannica-1911-rennes:
Rennes is a town in the west of France, once chief town of Brittany and now chief of its shire. Its count of folk past the town bounds was past seventy-five thousand. It stands where two streams meet and where rail lines join for Paris and the coast. A great fire in the past age razed most of it.

The town was built once more on a straight plan in dark stone. The old town on a hill holds the chief builds. A great church was built new in a Greek style on the site of two old ones. The old law house, with carved work and paints, is its finest build.
britannica-1911-renwick-james:
James Renwick, who lived from 1662 to 1688, was a Scottish covenanting leader and son of a weaver. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from Moniaive to study at Edinburgh university. About 1681 he joined the Cameronian wing of the Covenanters and rose fast. Theology study at Groningen led to his ordination as minister in 1683.

Back in Scotland he preached in the fields and was declared a rebel by the council. He helped frame the bold declaration of 1684 that disowned Charles the Second. Refusal to abjure that text was made a death offence by the state. Unlike some allies, he held back from the Argyll rising of 1685.
britannica-1911-ribbon-fishes:
Ribbon fishes form a family of sea fishes, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes them. They are known by a long, flat, tape like body, a short head, and a narrow mouth. Their teeth are weak, and a high fin runs the whole length of the back. No anal fin is present, and the tail, when present, splits in two bundles of rays.

All their traits mark them as fish of very great depths, the text says. They are so frail that they are found at the surface or cast ashore in a hurt state as a rule. The rays of their fins and the skin that joins them are thin and brittle. Young fish of the family have some fin rays drawn out to a strange length. Just two genera make up the family, Regalecus, the oar fish, and Trachypterus.
britannica-1911-rice-james:
James Rice, who lived from 1843 to 1882, was an English writer of novels. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Northampton. He read law at Cambridge and joined the bar in 1871. In 1868 he bought the weekly Once a Week. The venture lost money but brought him a key friend. Walter Besant had written for the paper.

The two men then wrote as a pair for ten years. Their first joint novel, Ready-money Mortiboy, came out with no names on it. Rice supplied the lead figure and the core plot. A stream of books followed at a fast pace. The Golden Butterfly of 1876 won the widest fame of the set. Other titles include My Little Girl and The Seamy Side. Short tales filled several books of their own. Rice died at Redhill in April 1882, still in his thirties.
britannica-1911-rich-claudius-james:
Claudius James Rich (1787–1821) was an English traveller and scholar, and the opening of his life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses his gift for tongues. He was born near Dijon on the twenty eighth of March 1787. His youth was spent at Bristol. Early on he mastered Latin and Greek, and then Hebrew, Syriac, Persian, and Turkish as well.

In 1804 Rich went to Constantinople, where he polished his Turkish. He moved on to Alexandria as aide to the British consul general there. There he gave himself to Arabic and its dialects, and to Eastern manners and customs. Leaving Egypt, he travelled by land to the Persian Gulf in disguise as a Mameluke. He passed through Damascus on that journey. He even entered the great mosque there without being found out.
britannica-1911-riddles:
Riddles is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on what it calls the oldest form of humour. A riddle springs from a likeness seen in nature, the text says. A man notes the likeness, puts it as a query, and the riddle is made. The Sphinx's riddle on the three stages of man's life is the prime case.

The entry gives a second old riddle whose sense turns on lice. Homer is said to have died vexed at failing to solve it. Men then made a game of riddles, with bets laid on the answer. The text cites Tonga, West Africa, and Samson's riddle to the Philistines. In tales and songs, a hero's fate may hang on his skill at the game.
britannica-1911-rivington-charles:
Charles Rivington is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rivington was a British publisher who lived from 1688 to 1742. He was born at Chesterfield in Derbyshire. He came to London as a bookseller's apprentice. In 1711 he took over the publishing business of Richard Chiswell. At his shop he dealt almost wholly in church and school books.

The article tells how he printed one of Whitefield's earliest works and an edition of a famed devotional book. In 1736 he founded a company of booksellers to rival an older group. In 1741 he published the first volume of Richardson's Pamela. He died in 1742 and was followed by his two sons. One son went to America and traded in New York. The other stayed and became the great church publisher of his day. The firm kept a church society's agency for over seventy years.
britannica-1911-robert-king-of-naples:
