Robert is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Robert was king of Naples who lived from 1275 to 1343. He was a son of Charles the Second of Anjou. In youth he took part in campaigns to wrest Sicily from Aragon. Those efforts failed, like those of his father and grandfather. Peace was agreed in 1302, leaving Sicily in rival hands.

The article tells how he gained the throne in 1309 ahead of a nephew with a prior claim. The pope crowned him at Avignon. He became the known leader of the papal party in Italy and fought in all its wars. He gained overlordship over Rome, Florence, and other cities at times. He was counted the most powerful Italian prince of his day. He was a man of learning and a generous patron. The poet Petrarch admired him greatly.
britannica-1911-robert-of-jumieges:
Robert of Jumiéges (died about 1070) was a Norman archbishop of Canterbury. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his path from Rouen to an abbey at Jumiéges. Close friendship with Edward the Confessor brought him to England in 1042. He became bishop of London in 1044 under that king.

He led the foreign party at court against Earl Godwine power. In 1051 Edward named him archbishop over a chapter choice already made. When Godwine returned in 1052, Robert fled England in haste. He was outlawed and removed, and died back at Jumiéges. William later used his treatment as a pretext for invasion.
britannica-1911-rollin-charles:
Charles Rollin, a French historian and teacher who lived from 1661 to 1741, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Paris, son of a cutler. At twenty two he became a master at the College du Plessis. In 1694 he was made rector of the university of Paris, where he revived the study of Greek.

He held that post two years instead of one, a rare honour. In 1699 he became principal of the College de Beauvais. Rollin held Jansenist views and defended the claimed wonders at the tomb of Deacon Paris. Those opinions cost him his posts. His writing dates mostly from his later years, when he was forbidden to teach. His Ancient History, printed from 1730 to 1738, taught readers for generations. His work on studies was more original and of real weight.
britannica-1911-roncesvalles: Roncesvalles is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a village of northern Spain. It stands in Navarre on the river Urrobi, 3,220 feet up among the Pyrenees. Its population in 1900 was only 152. The village is famous in history and legend for the defeat of Charlemagne and the death of Roland in 778. Its small collegiate church holds curious relics linked with Roland and draws many pilgrims. The battle is said to have been fought in the Val Carlos and the pass of Ibaneta.
britannica-1911-rose-hugh-james:
Hugh James Rose, an English divine who lived from 1795 to 1838, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Little Horsted in Sussex in June 1795. He read at Trinity College, Cambridge, and took his degree in 1817. He took orders and held livings at Buxted and then Horsham.

A trip to Germany fed four addresses he gave at Cambridge against rationalism. Printed in 1825, they stirred sharp debate on both sides of the sea. Rose rose through church posts in Suffolk, Essex, and London. Ill health cut short a divinity chair at Durham after one year. In 1836 he became principal of King's College, London. A bout of influenza then broke his health for good. He died at Florence in December 1838. A high churchman, he had founded the British Magazine in 1832. Through it he joined hands with the leaders of the Oxford movement.
britannica-1911-royle-john-forbes:
Royle, John Forbes is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British botanist. Born at Cawnpore in India in 1799, he entered the service of the East India Company as an assistant surgeon. He turned to botany and geology and made large collections in the Himalaya mountains. He studied the medical properties of Indian plants, work printed in 1837.

The article follows his posts in India and London. For nearly ten years he ran the East India Company's botanic garden at Saharanpur in the Himalayas. In 1837 he became professor of materia medica at King's College, London, holding the chair until 1856. At the East India House he built a large museum of technical products from the East Indies. The article names his books, above all the Illustrations of the Botany of the Himalaya Mountains.
britannica-1911-ruby-mines:
Ruby Mines is a district in the Mandalay division of Upper Burma, along the Irrawaddy river. The 1911 Britannica article gives its total area as 5,476 square miles, with a count of 87,694 in 1901. The land forms part of the Shan plateau, a mass of hills that run north and south. Kachins and Palaungs make up large shares of its folk. Rain at Mogok averages ninety-eight inches a year.

Mogok, the chief town, stands in a valley 4,000 feet above the sea. It is the heart of the ruby trade. The Ruby Mines Company works large open pits there with power pumps and washers. Ruby earth is dug out in bulk, washed, and crushed by machine. Spinels and sapphires come up with the rubies. In 1904 the yield of rubies alone was 200,000 carats, worth eighty thousand pounds.
britannica-1911-ryle-john-charles:
John Charles Ryle (1816–1900) was an English bishop, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his church posts in order. He was born at Macclesfield on the tenth of May 1816. He was educated at Eton and at Christ Church, Oxford. In 1836 he was named a Craven Scholar there.

Ryle held a curacy at Exbury in Hampshire, then a string of livings. He was rector at Winchester and at Helmingham, and vicar of Stradbroke from 1861. He became an honorary canon of Norwich in 1872 and dean of Salisbury in 1880. Before he could take up the dean post, he was raised to the new see of Liverpool. He held that see until he resigned, three months before his death in 1900. The entry notes his strong support of the evangelical school.
britannica-1911-sadducees:
Sadducees were a Jewish party named in the New Testament and in other old writings. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica weighs what those sources say. Josephus and the Talmud also speak of the group. Their mark was a refusal of some beliefs held by the Pharisees.

The Pharisees taught hope of life after death and belief in angels. The Sadducees denied both points and held to the written law alone. The entry calls them strict keepers of the old way in their own eyes. Yet most surviving accounts come from their rivals, so the picture may be bent. Notes also link the group to Jews who took up Greek ways in daily life.
britannica-1911-samoyedes:
The Samoyedes, a people spread over a vast tract of the north, are described in a 1911 Britannica article. The head of the hosted text first ends a piece on an Aegean isle, but the Samoyedes section follows in full. They live from the Altai hills down the Ob and Yenisei basins. Their land runs to the shores of the Arctic Ocean.

The text splits them into three main groups. The Yuraks live on the coast from the Yenisei to the White Sea. The Tavghi live between the Yenisei and the Khatanga. The Ostiak group lives more to the south, mixed in with Ostiaks in the woods of Tobolsk and Yeniseisk.
britannica-1911-scabies: Scabies, or the itch, is a disease of the skin caused by a small animal that lives on man. The mite, Sarcoptes scabei, digs under the outer skin at any part of the body. It is hard to find on the face or scalp of grown men and women. It most often starts in the clefts of the fingers. Its marks are scattered pimples, torn at the top by the scratch of the man who bears it. The cure named is soap and water, and an ointment of sulphur.
britannica-1911-schouler-james:
James Schouler, an American lawyer and historian born in 1839, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born in West Cambridge, Massachusetts, in March 1839. His father edited the Boston Atlas, a leading Whig journal of New England. The son graduated at Harvard in 1859, studied law in Boston, and was admitted to the bar in 1862. In 1869 he moved to Washington and published a law journal for three years.

Back in Boston from 1874, Schouler gave himself to office practice and to writing. He lectured at Boston University, at Washington, and at Johns Hopkins. In 1896 he led the American Historical Association. His legal treatises cover property, bailments, executors, and wills. He is best known as a historian, for his six-volume history of the United States under the Constitution.
britannica-1911-scilly-isles:
Scilly Isles, a group of small islands off Cornwall, get a full survey entry in the 1911 Britannica. They lie 25 miles west of Land's End and form an outer part of the Cornish granite heights. Old claims that they were the Tin Islands of Herodotus are now dropped. Their shores are wild, with sheer cliffs and caves cut by the Atlantic.

Reefs and shoals make the seas round them a risk in rough weather, and wrecks there have been grim. In 1707 Sir Cloudesley Shovel died when his flagship and two more warships were lost. A churchyard on St Mary's holds 311 dead from the wreck of the Schiller in 1875. Lights have cut the risk since, Bishop Light of 1858 among them. The land is all granite, the air mild, and gardens on Tresco seem almost subtropical.
britannica-1911-shambles: Shambles, a slaughter-house or place where butchers kill animals for food, is defined in this short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. In the singular, the word properly means a bench or stall where butchers show meat for sale in a market. It appears in Old English as a word for foot-stool. Its root is a Latin word for a step or bench. A distinct word, shamble, meaning to walk awkwardly, comes from a Dutch word for stumbling.
britannica-1911-sidi-bel-abbes:
Sidi-Bel-Abbes is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a town in Oran, Algeria. It stands on the Mekerra river, 1,552 feet above the sea. The town count for 1906 is 24,494 folk. Three-fourths of them are French or Spaniards, the entry says.

A wall with bastions and a ditch rings the walled town. Barracks hold room for six thousand troops on the site. The town is the home post of a Foreign Legion regiment. Two broad, tree-lined streets cross it from gate to gate. Wheat, tobacco, and alfa grass form its chief trade goods. Vines and olive groves spread in the lands round it.
britannica-1911-silures:
Silures is a 1911 Britannica article on a powerful tribe of ancient Britain. The Silures held land close to the modern counties of Monmouth, Brecon, and Glamorgan. They were a warlike people. They made a fierce stand against the Roman conquest, which began about the year 48.

A legionary fortress, Isca Silurum, was planted in their midst. By the year 78 they were overcome. Their town, Venta Silurum, became a Romanized town. It was like Silchester, but smaller, the text says. Its massive Roman walls still stand today. Digging there has laid bare a town hall and a market square. A temple, baths, and an amphitheatre have also come to light. Many snug houses with mosaics were found as well. A carved stone shows the town was the seat of the tribe's council under Rome.
britannica-1911-simcoe-john-graves:
John Graves Simcoe, who lived from 1752 to 1806, was a British soldier. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica adds that he was the first lieutenant governor of Upper Canada. He was born at Cotterstock in February 1752. Simcoe went to Eton at fourteen, then to Merton College, Oxford. In 1775 he first saw active service at Boston. In 1776 he took command of the Queen's Rangers.

His war in America ended at the surrender of Yorktown in 1781. He went home on parole and married in 1782. In 1790 he entered parliament for Saint Mawes in Cornwall. Late in 1791 he was named to govern the new province of Upper Canada. He reached Kingston in July 1792 and proclaimed the government there. The first assembly of the province met that September at Newark. His ideas of rule were military and aristocratic, the entry warns.
britannica-1911-skene-william-forbes:
William Forbes Skene is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Scottish writer on the past born in eighteen hundred and nine. His father was a friend of the great novelist Walter Scott. School in Edinburgh and study in Germany shaped his love of Celtic tongues.

The entry tells how he worked as a law clerk while he wrote on the Highlands. His first book traced the roots and past of the Highland folk. His chief work told the tale of Celtic Scotland in three large books. That work ranks as a top gift to Scots history in its century. High honours and a royal post as realm chronicler crowned his years.
britannica-1911-skin-diseases:
Skin diseases, the article holds, do not differ in kind from the diseases of other organs. Like other organs, the skin is made of cells set on a frame of connective tissue. Blood vessels feed it, and nerves link it to the rest of the body. Yet the skin also has traits of its own. Some come from its build, and some from its open place on the body.

Unlike the kidney, to which the article compares it, the skin has no depth turned inward. All of it lies open, so its processes are one-sided. If a disease spreads, it must spread across the surface. Spread that runs the same way in all directions tends to give skin patches a round shape. The skin's large area and open place also expose it to more kinds of irritation and attack.
britannica-1911-skinner-james:
James Skinner, a British soldier of fortune in India who lived from 1778 to 1841, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in India, he was the son of a British officer and a Rajput mother. At age eighteen he joined the Mahratta army and soon showed a gift for war. He served there until 1803, when war broke out and he would not fight his own folk.

Skinner then joined Lord Lake and raised a corps of light horse known as Skinner Horse, or the Yellow Boys. It became the most famed such corps in India at that time. He fought at the siege of Bharatpur and won a land grant and high rank in British service. His deep knowledge of the folk of India made his counsel prized by each new governor general. He died at Hansi in 1841.
britannica-1911-skittles:
Skittles is a game of pins and throws, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Players hurl a flat oval missile, called the cheese, at a set of wooden pins. The game is old and wide spread, with kin in France and Germany under other names. In early days in England, sheep's joints were thrown in place of the cheese.

As played in England, nine large pins stand in a square, three to a side. The player stands about twenty-one feet off and may take one step as he throws. The aim is to fell the most pins in the fewest throws. In the east of England only four pins are used. In the Dutch form the mid pin, the king, is the mark. In Germany balls are rolled, and that form grew into bowling in America.
britannica-1911-sleidanus-johannes:
Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556) was a German historian, the writer of the years of the Reformation. He was born at Schleiden, near Aix-la-Chapelle. He studied old tongues and books at Liége and Cologne, and law at Paris and Orleans. While among the scholars of Liége, he took up the Protestant faith. He entered the service of Cardinal du Bellay and was used in the vain talks of the French court. Those talks sought a pact with the German Protestants against the emperor Charles V.

In 1542 Sleidanus settled at Strassburg. He had long made a habit of copying all papers on the Reformation that he could reach. Martin Bucer saw that store and urged Philip of Hesse to name him the historian of the Reformation. The heads of the Schmalkalden league agreed in time, with pay and a full use of the papers he needed.
britannica-1911-slovenes:
Slovenes is the subject of a peoples entry in the 1911 Britannica. The Slovenes are a Slavonic folk of about one million souls. The main mass of them lives in Austria lands. They hold Carniola and parts of Carinthia and Styria. A part of north Istria is also held by them. Small groups live over the border in Italy. More live in the far south west of Hungary.

Italians bound them on the south west side. Germans bound them on the west and north sides. Past signs show they once held more land than now. On the east they have lost ground to the Magyars. On the south kindred Croats lie next to them. That south bound is hard to fix in sharp lines. Speech shades from one folk into the next there. In towns they are much mixed with Germans. Only in Carniola do they stand fairly solid alone.
britannica-1911-small-isles:
Five islands in the Inner Hebrides make up the parish called the Small Isles. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists them as Canna, Sanday, Rum, Eigg, and Muck. They lie in a crescent between Skye and the mainland of Scotland. Moor, pasture, and hills cover most of their ground.

Sea birds thrive there in large numbers. Eider ducks, puffins, shearwaters, and gulls are all common on the coasts. Fishing for cod, ling, and herring supports local life. Each isle gets its own notes on size, rock type, farms, and harbors, with Rum noted for its high peaks and red deer.
britannica-1911-snow-shoes:
Snow-shoes is a gear article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about footgear made for travel over snow. Each tribe of American Indians had its own shape of shoe. The plainest forms come from the far north.

The article compares shapes from north to south. Eskimo shoes run short, in a triangle or near round form. Farther south the shoe grows longer and thinner. The Cree hunting shoe runs near six feet long, with the toe turned up. Shoes for white lumbermen and trackers get their own notes. The frame is one bent strip of tough wood, most often hickory. Webbing of hide strips fills the frame, with a gap for the toe. The text ends with the slide step used in walking, and with racing in Canadian clubs.
britannica-1911-solesmes:
Solesmes, a village of western France, is the subject of a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It stands on the left bank of the Sarthe, 29 miles west of Le Mans by road. A priory was set up there in 1010 under the abbey of La Couture of Le Mans. Shut at the revolution, it came back as a Benedictine monastery in 1830 and rose to an abbey in 1837, a seat of learning famed for music.

A nunnery beside it was also left empty after the associations law was passed. The rebuilt monastery stands as a tall mass of buildings on the river bank. Its church holds two famed works of carved stone made between about 1490 and 1550. One shows the burial of Christ, with eight figures round the tomb, the other the burial of the Virgin.
britannica-1911-sophocles:
Sophocles, a Greek tragic poet, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from 495 to 406 before Christ. He was born at Colonus, in the neighbourhood of Athens. His father's name was Sophillus. The family burial place lay on the road to Decelea, near the city.

The date of his birth fits a famed tale of his youth. The young Sophocles was a pupil of the musician Lamprus. He was chosen to lead the boys' chorus at the feast for the victory of Salamis. That victory fell in the year 480 before Christ. The time of his death is fixed by hints in later plays. The Frogs of Aristophanes alludes to it. A lost play of Phrynichus does the same. Both plays were staged in the year 405 before Christ. That was shortly before the capture of Athens. A legend adds that Lysander allowed him funeral honours.
britannica-1911-sorel-agnes:
Agnes Sorel, mistress of King Charles the Seventh of France, who lived from about 1422 to 1450, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was born to a family of the lesser nobility at Fromenteau in Touraine. As a girl she served Isabel of Lorraine, queen of Sicily. From 1444 until her death she was the open mistress of the king.

Sorel was the first woman to hold that near official place at the French court. Her rise dates from the feasts at Nancy in 1444, the first bright court of the reign. The king gave her wealth, castles, and lands, and the state of a queen. Her sudden death, soon after the birth of her fourth child, was blamed on poison. Some blamed the Dauphin, the next Louis the Eleventh, and the charge was later used against Jacques Coeur as well.
britannica-1911-sosigenes:
Sosigenes was a Greek student of the stars and of number, most likely of Alexandria. He did his work in the first century B.C. Pliny says that Julius Caesar used him in the reform of the Roman calendar in 46 B.C. Sosigenes wrote three books, which he took care to correct. From a second note in Pliny, men take it that he held a bold view of Mercury. He held that Mercury moves round the sun, a view his peer Cicero also names.

The article warns that this Sosigenes is not the man of the same name who taught in a later age. That second Sosigenes was a thinker of the school of Aristotle, who lived at the end of the 2nd century A.D. He taught Alexander of Aphrodisias, the most famed of those who wrote on Aristotle.
britannica-1911-sotades:
Sotades was a Greek satirist of Maronea in Thrace, or of Crete, and his life is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the chief of the writers of coarse mocking poems in the Ionic tongue. The verse form of those poems took his name and was called sotadic. He lived in Alexandria in the reign of Ptolemy the Second.

For a fierce attack on the king, at the time of his marriage to his own sister, Sotades was thrown in prison. He got free and fled to the island of Caunus. There the admiral of Ptolemy caught him. He was shut in a chest of lead and cast into the sea. All but a few true scraps of his work are lost. The scraps kept in Stobaeus are held by most to be false, and Ennius turned some such poems into Latin.
britannica-1911-spherulites:
Spherulites, in petrology, are small rounded bodies common in glassy igneous rocks, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article describes them. They show in obsidian, pitchstone, and rhyolite as globules about the size of millet seed or rice grains. They have a duller shine than the glassy base around them. Through a lens they prove to have a radiating fibrous build.

Under the microscope a spherulite is round in outline, made of thin fibres spreading outward. The fibres are crystalline and react on polarized light. Between crossed nicols a black cross appears in the spherulite. As the stage is turned, the cross stays steady, with four bright sectors between its arms. That shows the fibres are doubly refracting with straight extinction. Spherulites are commonest in acid glassy rocks, but they occur in basic glasses like tachylyte too. Sometimes they make up the whole rock mass.
britannica-1911-spires:
Spires, called Speyer in German, is a town and bishopric in Germany, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it. The town is the capital of the Bavarian palatinate. It stands on the left bank of the Rhine, where the Speyerbach flows in. Its count in 1905 came to 21,823 people.

The main streets are broad but irregular in plan. The town looks less old than it is, the entry notes. The French burned Spires in 1689, and most old buildings were lost. The cathedral alone stands as a great survivor of that fire. It is a vast basilica of red sandstone. The entry calls it one of the noblest works of Romanesque building now standing. The church holds a special place among the old churches of the Rhineland.
britannica-1911-sponges:
Sponges is a zoology article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The sponges, or Porifera, form a somewhat separate branch of the animal kingdom. The branch holds a vast number of sea and fresh-water creatures. All share a set of body features found in no other animals.

The article warns readers against a common picture. The bath sponges sold in shops are the best-known members of the group. Yet they are among its most highly organized and least typical kinds. The history of sponge study begins with Aristotle. He knew several kinds and noted that Greek warriors padded their helmets with them. Their fixed life, odd growth, and weak powers puzzled later ages. Readers get an opening survey of a strange and ancient branch of animal life.
britannica-1911-st-bertrand-de-comminges:
St Bertrand-de-Comminges, a hill village of France, is drawn in a site entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands at the foot of the Pyrenees in Haute-Garonne. The Garonne River flows a mile from its left bank site. Its famed cathedral crowns an lone hill above the village homes. Bishop Bertrand began that church late in the eleventh century.

The front and first bay keep the round Romanesque style of that start. Nave and choir rose later in the pointed Gothic style. Bertrand de Goth, later Pope Clement the Fifth, drove that work. Wood carving of rare skill fills the choir screen and stalls. A white marble tomb of a bishop rests in the church. Rome founded the town on that hill in 72 before Christ.
britannica-1911-st-maur-des-fosses:
Saint Maur des Fosses is a south eastern suburb of Paris, on the right bank of the Marne. It lies seven miles from the centre of the city of Paris. Its people numbered twenty eight thousand and sixteen in nineteen o six. Saint Maur and the homes round it cover a peninsula formed by a loop in the Marne. A canal crosses the neck of that loop of river.

In the reign of Clovis the Second a monastery called Les Fosses was founded there. The fuller name came when the body of Saint Maurus was brought to that house. About the same time a pilgrimage to Notre Dame des Miracles began there. That pilgrimage still takes place each year, the entry notes. In fourteen sixty five a peace treaty was signed at Saint Maur. It ended the War of the Public Weal between king and barons.
britannica-1911-staines:
Staines is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Staines is a market town in Middlesex in England. It stands on the river Thames where the Colne joins it, west of London. Two railways serve the town. By 1901 its people numbered near seven thousand. Breweries and mustard mills employ many hands. A rifle range for volunteers opened in 1892.

The article notes that a British village stood here at a Thames crossing on the main road to the southwest. That crossing was among the earliest to be bridged. Oaks from Windsor forest were granted for bridge repair in 1262. The present bridge, opened in 1831, followed three failed bridges in forty years. The town name may come from a stone marking the limit of London's rule over the lower Thames. Nearby lies Runnymede, where King John signed Magna Carta.
britannica-1911-stalactites:
Stalactites, hanging masses formed by very slow dripping water, are the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to drip. Such growths are seen under bridges, arches, and old buildings. Water seeping through joints dissolves tiny amounts of lime from the mortar. Part of the water then evaporates in the air.

The lime solution grows over-full, and a deposit forms at the drip point. As drops keep falling from the same spot, a small column of white calcite grows slowly downward. Ice stalactites form in the same way in frosty weather. Other minerals also grow in this form, among them limonite, fluorspar, opal, and chalcedony. Those are small, rarely more than two or three inches long. The article lists three conditions for perfect growth: a slow trickle, steady evaporation, and freedom from disturbance.
britannica-1911-standish-miles:
Miles Standish, also spelled Myles, was an American colonist born about 1584. The 1911 Britannica life places his birth in Lancashire, in a good house. Next to nothing firm is known of him before the year 1620. That year he sailed to New England in the Mayflower with his wife Rose. He became the chief soldier and guard of the Plymouth colony at once.

In 1625 the colony sent him to London on colony business in vain. Three years later he was one of eight men who bought out the backers. They pledged a large sum to take full charge of the venture. In 1631 he settled at Duxbury with Brewster and others of the band. A tall stone shaft and bronze figure there now mark his name.
britannica-1911-stannaries:
Stannaries, in the 1911 Britannica, is a law and custom entry on the tin mines of Cornwall and Devon. The name comes from the Latin word for tin. Stannary courts held a sway of their own over tinners, who by old charters stood free of all other courts save in cases of land, life, and limb. The customs ran back past the charter of Earl Edmund, though no one can say how far.

Twenty-four stannators met as a kind of parliament and chose a speaker. The Cornish met at Truro and the Devon men on Dartmoor, and the last Cornish meeting sat in 1752. The entry tracks later acts that merged the courts in 1855 and shut them in 1896, passing their work to county courts. Free tinners could work waste land for a toll of tin.
britannica-1911-stansfeld-sir-james:
Sir James Stansfeld is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Halifax on the fifth of October 1820, he was an English public man and the son of a county court judge. He was schooled at University College, London, and called to the bar in 1849.

The article follows his work for the cause of Italy. Through his wife's father he met Mazzini in 1847 and became his close friend. From 1859 he sat for Halifax for more than thirty six years. Garibaldi chose him as an adviser on a visit to England. In 1864 French charges over a plot against Napoleon the Third rocked his post. He barely escaped blame in the house and gave up his office. Later posts came, and he led the local government board.
britannica-1911-starley-james:
James Starley is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Starley was a British inventor who lived from 1830 to 1881. He was a farmer's son from Sussex. At age eighteen he ran away toward London. On the way he found work as a gardener at Lewisham. He had a gift for small machines and fixed watches and clocks for neighbours.

The article tells how sewing machines drew his inventive mind. He worked for a London sewing machine firm and improved their machines. In 1857 he moved to Coventry to make machines. That firm was the seed of the great bicycle works that later centred on Coventry. In 1868 the firm began to make bicycles from a Paris model. Starley designed a tricycle and a balance gear for it. He died in 1881.
britannica-1911-stephen-popes:
Stephen is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on the name shared by nine popes. The first Stephen was bishop of Rome from about 254 to 257, following Lucius the First. He broke church fellowship with Cyprian and some Asiatic bishops over their view on rebaptising heretics. He also pressed for the return of two Spanish bishops who had repented.

The second Stephen was pope from March 752 to April 757. He was still a deacon when chosen, within days of the death of Zacharias. The chief trouble of his rule came from Aistulf, king of the Lombards, who pressed hard on Rome. After failed missions to Aistulf and to the emperor, Stephen set out in weak health to seek aid. Pippin received him in France in early 754, and he wintered at Saint Denis.
britannica-1911-stephen-sir-james:
Sir James Stephen, who lived from 1789 to 1859, was an English historian and a high official in the colony office. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born in London on the third of January 1789. His father wrote books on slavery in the West India colonies. Stephen read law at Cambridge and built a large practice as a chancery barrister. He then served as counsel to the trade board and the colony office.

In 1834 he became under-secretary for the colonies, a post he held until 1847. On leaving, he was made a knight of the Bath. In 1849 Cambridge gave him the chair of modern history. His best known books were studies of church lives and talks on the past of France, given in two volumes in 1851.
britannica-1911-stephen-sir-james-fitzja:
Sir James Fitzjames Stephen, an English lawyer, judge, and publicist who lived from 1829 to 1894, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in London in March 1829. He was the third child and second son of Sir James Stephen. He spent three years at Eton, from 1842 to 1845.

He then spent two years at a college in London. In October 1847 he entered Trinity College, Cambridge. For all his rare vigour of mind and body, he won no usual honours there. He took none of the scholastic prizes, and none of the athletic ones. The only studies then pursued in earnest were mathematics and classics. Neither drew him in its academic form, and he cared nothing for sport. Yet his Cambridge time bore fruit in other ways, the text says. The portrait is of force ripening outside the prize lists.
britannica-1911-stewart-charles:
Charles Stewart was an American naval officer whose career a 1911 Britannica entry follows. He urged President Madison to send the navy to sea in the war of 1812. Harbour defence alone was not his plan for the young sea force. Placed in command of the Constellation, he was held fast by blockade at Norfolk.

In 1813 he took command of the famed frigate Constitution for war service. In February 1815 he captured the Cyane and the Levant in one fight. Later commands took him to the Mediterranean, the Pacific, and home squadrons in turn. He retired in 1855 and died at Bordentown in New Jersey in 1869.
britannica-1911-stillman-william-james:
William James Stillman is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Stillman was an American painter and journalist who lived from 1828 to 1901. He was born at Schenectady in New York. His parents were Seventh Day Baptists, and his early faith training swayed him all his life. He graduated at Union College in 1848 and studied art under a noted landscape painter.

The article tells how he went to England in 1850 and met Ruskin and Turner. He fell under the sway of Rossetti and Millais and came home known as the American Pre-Raphaelite. In 1852 he was sent to Hungary on a vain errand to dig up hidden crown jewels. He then painted landscapes in the Adirondacks and in New York. There he started an art journal that drew leading writers as contributors. When it failed for lack of funds, he moved to Cambridge.
britannica-1911-stocks-and-shares:
Stocks and shares are the subject of a finance entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. A share, in the financial sense, is the right to take part in the profits of a joint stock venture. The entry sets out what company law in the United Kingdom required firms to state. That includes the capital and how it is divided into shares.

Company figures show a trend in recent years, the entry notes. Firms tended to register with smaller nominal capital than before. There was also a trend to lower the value of single shares. The text uses those trends to explain how share ownership spread to smaller holders in that period.
britannica-1911-stockton-on-tees:
Stockton-on-Tees is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a port and mill town in Durham, England. It stands on the north bank of the Tees river, on a main rail line. Its count in 1901 was 51,478.

The article names a town hall, a public library, and quays that take ships of deep draught. Steel works, blast furnaces, and iron and brass works anchor its trade. Ship building in iron is a major line as well. Goods sent out in 1900 were valued at more than four hundred thousand pounds. The town grew up around a castle of the bishops of Durham. A charter may have come from King John in 1214, though no trace of it lasts.
britannica-1911-stone-edward-james:
Edward James Stone is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a British star scholar born in London in eighteen thirty one. He won school prizes that took him to two colleges in turn. He took a high maths rank at Cambridge and a fellowship at once.

The entry tells how he rose to chief aide at the royal star house. His great task there was to hone the base counts of star science. He fixed the gap to the sun from views of Mars on two far coasts. Views of Venus in transit backed his count with a like result. Work on the moon pull and mass fills out his list of feats.
britannica-1911-straw-and-straw-manufact:
Straw and its manufactures are the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Straw, from a word for strewing, is the stalky residue of grain plants such as wheat, rye, oats, and barley. It is the raw material of several trades. It serves for thatching roofs and for making paper. It is also used in straw mosaic, mats, mattresses, baskets, and artificial flowers.

Those uses are small beside straw's place in hats and bonnets for both sexes. Wheaten straw is the most important material for plaited head-gear. Only certain areas grow straw fit for plaiting. Good plait straw needs a long pipe between the knots, a clear golden colour, and no brittleness. The most valuable straw grows in Tuscany. From it come the Tuscan plaits and Leghorn hats. Tuscan straw is sorted into three grades, the finest being called Pontederas Semone.
britannica-1911-strickland-agnes:
Agnes Strickland (1806-1874), an English writer of history, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the third daughter of a Suffolk gentleman of Reydon Hall. Her first efforts in print were tales of history in verse, in the style of Walter Scott. From verse she passed to prose histories, written in a simple style for the young.

Her great work, planned with her sister, was the Lives of the Queens of England. It ran from Matilda of Flanders to Queen Anne, in twelve books printed between 1840 and 1849. The article calls her a warm partisan of royalty and the church. It also praises her hard study of official records and other public papers, from which she drew rich extracts. Her pages gave lively pictures of the manners and customs of each age. She also edited the letters of Mary, Queen of Scots.
britannica-1911-stuart-moses:
Moses Stuart, an American scholar of the Bible born in seventeen eighty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Wilton, Connecticut, he was raised on a farm. He took top marks at Yale in seventeen ninety nine. He was let to the bar, taught at Yale for two years, then took a church post in New Haven.

In eighteen ten he was made a teacher of holy letters at a new school for church men at Andover. There he met a hard task. He knew at the start next to nothing of Hebrew and not much more Greek. In two years he wrote a Hebrew grammar for his class. The boys copied it day by day from his hand script. The entry shows a man who learned his field by teaching it, and then reshaped that field for a nation.
britannica-1911-sturt-charles:
Charles Sturt, who died in eighteen sixty nine, was an English explorer in New South Wales and South Australia. Born in England, he joined the army and rose to captain. He landed in Australia with his regiment, the Thirty Ninth. There he grew keen on the map problems of the day. A first trip in eighteen twenty eight led to the finding of the Darling river.

A second trip made Lake Alexandrina known, and Sturt came back from it near blind. A third trip, in eighteen forty four and forty five, brought hard suffering. He came back quite blind and never fully got his sight back. He served as surveyor general of South Australia and later as chief secretary. He retired on a pension to Cheltenham in England.
britannica-1911-submarine-mines:
Submarine mines, weapons of war set in the water, are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A mine is a charge of explosive stuff, moored at or below the surface. Its blast is meant to put a hostile ship out of action at once. The entry sets the mine against the torpedo: a mine cannot move, save for the special drifting kind that rides the tide.

That split in terms came only in 1870, the article notes. Before then the word torpedo served for all charges fired in the water. Mines fall into two main classes, those that can be controlled and those that cannot. The first are fired by electricity from a station on shore, joined to them by covered cables. Switching off the current makes such mines harmless in a moment, a great gain for the defence of harbours.
britannica-1911-sully-james:
James Sully is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English psychologist. He was born in 1842 at Bridgwater. He was educated at colleges in Taunton and London. He also studied at Gottingen and at Berlin. He was at first destined for the Nonconformist ministry. In 1871 he adopted a literary and philosophic career. From 1892 to 1903 he held a chair at University College, London. That chair covered the philosophy of mind and logic.

Carveth Read succeeded him in that post in 1903. Sully belonged to the associationist school of psychology. His views had great affinity with those of Alexander Bain. His monographs are ably and readably written, the entry says. His work on pessimism is named as one such book. His textbooks are models of sound exposition. The Human Mind of 1892 is the most important of them.
britannica-1911-sumner-charles:
Charles Sumner, an American statesman who lived from 1811 to 1874, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Boston, he finished at Harvard College in 1830 and at Harvard Law School in 1834. There, in close friendship with Joseph Story, he fell in love with the study of law.

At twenty three Sumner was admitted to the bar, wrote for a law journal, and edited law texts and Story's rulings. A month in Washington in 1834 filled him with disgust for politics as a career, and he went home set on the practice of law. Three years in Europe changed his scale. He gained a ready command of French, German and Italian, met leading statesmen, and learned the systems of law and rule on the continent. In England, Lord Brougham said he had never met a man of Sumner's age with such legal knowledge.
britannica-1911-sunnites:
Sunnites, one of the two main divisions of Islam, are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name means, in plain words, those of the path. They follow the directions of the Prophet and take the orthodox tradition, as well as the Koran, as a source of doctrine and law. The other division is the Shi'ites, whose main seat is Persia.

The article maps where each body holds sway. The Sunnites rule in Arabia, the Turkish Empire, the north of Africa, Turkestan, and Afghanistan. They also form the mass of Muslims in India and the east of Asia. Orthodox Islam, it says, keeps the form of doctrine fixed in the tenth century by a great scholar. The attacks of free reason, aided by Greek philosophy, were beaten back with the weapons of school logic borrowed from the Greeks themselves.
britannica-1911-swinburne-algernon-charl:
Algernon Charles Swinburne is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English poet and critic born in London in eighteen thirty seven. His father was an admiral from an old northern house. The boy left London at once and grew up far from city life.

The entry paints two homes that split his youth in stark halves. Half the year was spent on a mild isle off the south coast. The other half was spent in the bleak north with his grandfather. Sea cliffs and lush vales by his isle home mark his verse for life. Many of his finest pieces were penned in a house by a bay there.
britannica-1911-syme-james:
James Syme was a Scottish surgeon who lived from seventeen ninety nine to eighteen seventy. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Edinburgh, the son of a signet writer and landowner, he studied early. His father lost most wealth in bids to work minerals on his land.

Syme entered university at age fifteen and took arts classes for two years. He began medical study in eighteen seventeen with a bent for chemistry. Trials led him to find a coal tar fluid that melts india rubber. That fluid could proof silk and cloth, an idea Mackintosh soon patented. In eighteen eighteen he became aide in the dissecting room of Robert Liston.
britannica-1911-symeon-metaphrastes:
Symeon Metaphrastes, the most famed Byzantine writer of saints lives, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Scholars long clashed on when he lived, with dates spread across five centuries. Most now place him in the later half of the tenth century. Very little is known of his own life.

His fame rests on a great set of saints lives set out by the twelve months of the year. About one hundred fifty lives make up the set. Some were taken whole from older sets, while others were recast in new form. That recasting is what his name Metaphrastes points to. A chronicle, a set of church laws, letters, and poems are also linked to his name, with less sureness. Greeks honour him as a saint on the twenty eighth of November.
britannica-1911-tachylytes:
Tachylytes are the glassy forms of the basic igneous rocks, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes them for students of rock science. The Greek roots of the name mean easily fused. In plain terms they are basaltic obsidians. They are black in colour, dark brown in the thinnest slices, with a pitch-like shine. They are often full of tiny holes and sometimes carry small balls of crystal growth.

They are very brittle and break down fast under the hammer. Small crystals of felspar or olivine can at times be seen in them with the naked eye. All tachylytes weather fast, and as their iron rusts they turn dark brown or red. The entry stresses that they form only where cooling was quick. They are far less common than the acid volcanic glasses, since basic rocks tend more strongly to crystallise as they cool.
britannica-1911-tages: Tages was a minor Etruscan god and founder of the art of divination in Etruria, said to be a grandson of Jupiter. His myth entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how a boy like being sprang from a furrow as a field near Tarquinii was ploughed. The ploughman Tarchon cries drew all the people of Etruria to hear the boy teach divination. Then the boy vanished, and his teaching passed by mouth before it was written as the twelve books of Tages.
britannica-1911-tassie-james:
James Tassie (1735-1799), a Scottish gem engraver and modeller, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of humble parents near Glasgow, he worked in his early years as a stonemason. A show of paintings gathered in Glasgow by the printer brothers Foulis turned his mind to art. He joined the academy they had founded and became one of its most famed pupils.

The article tells how a trip to Dublin for work changed his path. There he met a doctor who had been testing ways to copy antique engraved gems in coloured pastes. Working as his assistant, Tassie helped perfect an enamel hard and fine enough for gems and medallions. The doctor urged him to try his luck in London, and he went in 1766. The start was hard, but he worked on with great care and destroyed every flawed casting.
britannica-1911-tennant-charles:
Charles Tennant, a Scottish works chemist born in seventeen sixty eight, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ochiltree in Ayrshire, he set up as a bleacher at Darnley. In seventeen ninety eight he won a right for a bleach fluid made from a sharp gas, lime, and water.

The fluid used cheap lime in place of costly potash. That was its edge over the French fluid then in wide use. When he sued men who stole the plan, the right was held void. His writ was thin, and the plan had been used near Nottingham before his date. Next year he won a right for bleach dust, a far more handy form. For its make he founded the great St Rollox works at Glasgow.
britannica-1911-thames:
Thames, the chief river of England, is mapped in words in a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It rises in small streams among the Cotswold Hills in Gloucestershire. Its source is most often placed at Thames Head near Cirencester, though some claim the Seven Springs, the head of the Churn, instead.

The entry gives the river's length as just over two hundred miles in all, and its widths at set points. It is a narrow stream at Oxford, wider at Teddington, and broad at Gravesend and at the Nore. Heights and fall are given too, from the source down to Lechlade and on to London. Its drainage ground covers more than five thousand square miles, counting the Medway, which joins its mouth. The river also forms long stretches of county bounds, a role the account follows from its start.
britannica-1911-tibeto-burman-languages:
Tibeto-Burman Languages is the subject of a tongue entry in the 1911 Britannica. The family holds a long chain of dialects. Those tongues run from Tibet in the north to Burma. They run west to Kashmir and east to China provinces. First come the tongues of Tibet itself in the list. Those are spoken all over Tibet and near districts. A second set, the Himalayan group, comes next.

That group is spoken in the south Himalayan hills. Some of its tongues stay close to Tibetan in frame. Others struck out on new lines of growth. Old folk tongues of the hills may have shaped them. A third small group lies north of the Assam vale. A fourth group, the Bodo, runs south from Bhutan. A fifth group fills the Naga hills to the west. A sixth group runs down the long hill chain south.
britannica-1911-tilden-samuel-jones:
Samuel Jones Tilden, who lived from 1814 to 1886, was an American statesman. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at New Lebanon, New York. Ill health cut short his time at Yale. He read law in New York City and joined the bar in 1841. His rise there was swift. In the rail crash years half the northern railways were at some time his clients.

He sat in the state assembly and in two state conventions. In 1848 he joined the free soil revolt of the Barnburners. Through the civil war he backed the Union cause with warmth. In 1866 he took charge of the state Democratic party. That post set him against the Tweed ring of New York City. He dug into the ring's bank records to prove how the spoils were split, and won the governorship in 1874.
britannica-1911-title-guarantee-companie:
Title guarantee companies are firms that insure the ownership of land. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica frames them as a shield for owners and lenders. Their skill lies in probing the risk in a deed's past. Such firms grow where land titles rest on public record. Where records tangle with claims and debts, a clean title is hard to prove. Only the United States raised these firms to a large scale.

Other lands solve the puzzle in other ways. Australia needs no such probe, since the state lists and backs each title. In lands with no state list, deeds pass from hand to hand in private. In America, deeds and loans must be put on record by law. Wills, suits, tax debts, and workmen's claims crowd those records too. In big cities the pile grew so vast that checking a title became slow and dear.
britannica-1911-towneley-charles:
Charles Towneley (1737-1805) was an English archaeologist and collector of marbles, and his life is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Towneley, the family seat near Burnley in Lancashire, he was educated at Douai. In 1765 he left England to study ancient art, chiefly at Rome.

The entry tells how, with the artist Gavin Hamilton and a banker in Rome, he built a splendid set of antiquities, housed in two Westminster houses bought for the purpose. His only publication was an account of an ancient helmet found at Ribchester. After his death the British Museum bought his marbles, bronzes, coins, and gems for about 28,000 pounds.
britannica-1911-townley-james:
James Townley (1714–1778) is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English playwright, born in London, the second son of a merchant. He was schooled at Merchant Taylors' School and at St John's College, Oxford. He took holy orders and was made priest in 1738. He then taught at Merchant Taylors' School, and from 1753 was grammar master at Christ's Hospital. In 1760 he became head master of Merchant Taylors'.

Townley kept a keen love of the stage all his life. Men said that many of David Garrick's best shows and revivals owed much to his help. He was the hidden writer of High Life below Stairs, a two act farce shown at Drury Lane in 1759. He held his headmastership until his death in 1778.
britannica-1911-townshend-charles:
English politician Charles Townshend, born in seventeen twenty five, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of the third Viscount Townshend. His mother was famed for wit and for plain speech, traits her son shared.

He was schooled at Leiden and at Oxford. At Leiden he fell in with a small set of English youths who later made names in many fields. He sat in Parliament for Great Yarmouth from seventeen forty seven. In seventeen fifty three he drew notice with a lively speech against a marriage bill. Two years later he wed a rich widow, the eldest daughter of the Duke of Argyll. That match served the aim his speech had mocked.
britannica-1911-tralles:
Tralles was an old town of Caria in Asia Minor, set out in a 1911 Britannica entry on its past. It stood on the Eudon stream, a branch of the Maeander river. Tales called it a colony of Argives and Thracians, and it lay long under Persian rule. Later kings enlarged and renamed it, and it passed to Rome in 133 before Christ.

One Roman poet mocked it as a far off backwater town in a famed line. Yet rich folk lived there, and fine works of art have been dug from the site. Two prized marble heads in the Constantinople museum came from Tralles. Digs in 1904 and chance finds kept adding proof of its past wealth.
britannica-1911-treaties:
Treaties is a 1911 Britannica article on the formal deals made between states. A treaty, it says, is a contract between two or more states. The Latin term tractatus came into this use late. It grew common only from the end of the seventeenth century.

Older terms, such as convention publica and foedus, held the field before that. In modern diplomatic speech, treaty is kept for the weightier deals. Deals made by a congress rank highest of all. Lesser deals on minor points are called conventions. The article states that it will ignore that fine split. It goes on to note that the making of treaties is a very early practice. Nations have bound themselves by such pledges since the dawn of their dealings. Readers get the base terms of diplomacy set out in plain words.
britannica-1911-trematodes:
Trematodes, or flukes, are flat worms named for their fish like shape. They form one of three groups in their tribe. Two or more suck discs mark their frame, which gives them their Greek name of pierced with holes. They live as guests on hosts in youth and in ripe age alike.

Their frame shows less loss from that life than most guest kinds. Organs match those of free kin part for part. Grip tools and a thick skin that guards past host saps are their chief new traits. Sense parts show the sole clear loss. Plates show the beasts in a group view.
britannica-1911-tupper-sir-charles:
Canadian statesman Charles Tupper, born at Amherst, Nova Scotia, in eighteen twenty one, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was son of a clergyman and was educated at Horton Academy. He then studied medicine at Edinburgh University, where he took his medical diplomas.

In eighteen fifty five he was returned to the Nova Scotia Assembly for Cumberland county. He held posts in the provincial government across the next decade. In eighteen sixty four he became prime minister of Nova Scotia. He held that office until the Union Act took force in eighteen sixty seven. He led the Nova Scotia delegation to the union conferences at Charlottetown and Quebec. He also led it to the final conference in London that settled the terms of union.
britannica-1911-turle-james:
James Turle is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Turle was an English organist and composer, born at Taunton in 1802. He began as a choir boy at Wells Cathedral. In 1817 he came to London as a pupil of the organist at Westminster Abbey.

After years as deputy, he took the Abbey post himself in 1831. He held it until his death in 1882, a span of half a century. The entry calls him a great organist in his day. He also composed a good deal of church music that stayed well known. A closing note names his son, who edited the journal Notes and Queries. The piece is brief, but it marks a long life spent at one great organ.
britannica-1911-turner-charles:
Charles Turner is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English engraver. He lived from 1773 to 1857. He was born at Woodstock in the year 1773. He entered the schools of the Royal Academy in 1795. He engraved in stipple in the manner of Bartolozzi. His finest plates, however, are in mezzotint work. In that method he engraved many famed pictures.

He engraved Turner's Wreck and many Liber Studiorum subjects. He rendered Reynolds's Marlborough Family in that method too. Many of Raeburn's best portraits passed through his hands. He also worked after Lawrence, Shee, and Owen. The entry calls him an admirable engraver of his time. His touch was large, broad, and masterly in character. He reproduced with great fidelity each painter's own traits. In 1828 he was elected associate of the Royal Academy. He died on the first of August 1857.
britannica-1911-turner-sir-james:
Sir James Turner is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a Scot who served as a soldier and wrote on war. He lived from 1615 to 1686. He was schooled for the church at first. He chose arms instead and joined the Swedish army. That army was then the best school of war in Europe. He saw much service in the Thirty Years War.

He came home in 1640 with the rank of captain. He served with Scot forces in Ireland and in England. He was taken at Preston and again at Worcester. He spent years abroad in royalist plots after those defeats. At the return of the king he was knighted. Harsh acts against church rebels cost him his command in Scotland. His book on the art of war, from 1683, closes the entry.
britannica-1911-twelve-tables: Twelve Tables is a brief law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the earliest written code of Roman law. The laws were set out on tables of wood, engraved or painted. At first there were ten tables. Two more were added later, holding extra matter, and the whole code took the name Lex XII Tabularum, the Law of the Twelve Tables. For the substance of the code the short entry sends the reader on to the articles on Roman law and on Rome itself.
britannica-1911-urban-popes:
Urban is the subject of a group life entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name was borne by eight popes in all. The first Urban was bishop of Rome from 222 to 230. He came after Calixtus and was followed by Pontianus. Most of the space shown goes to Urban the Second. He held the papal throne from 1088 to 1099. He was born of knightly rank near Reims in France.

Urban the Second had trained with the monks of Cluny. He served as a legate in Germany for the prior pope. As pope he held fast to a reform plan. He fought sale of church posts and wedlock for priests. He faced a rival pope who held Rome for years. In 1095 he called a great council at Clermont. There his call for the First Crusade marked his reign.
britannica-1911-ursins-marie-anne-de-la-:
Marie Anne de la Tremoille, Princess des Ursins, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in sixteen forty two, she was the daughter of the duke of Noirmontier. She wed young, to the Prince de Chalais. Her husband fled France after a fatal duel and died soon after in Spain.

The widow then settled in Rome, the entry explains. In sixteen seventy five she wed Flavio Orsini, duke of Bracciano. That match was far from calm, but he left her his wealth. It also brought years of lawsuits with a rival claimant. In the end she sold the title and estates and took the name Princess des Ursins.
britannica-1911-ursulines:
Ursulines is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a religious order for women. Angela Merici founded the order at Brescia in November 1535. Its first aims were the schooling of girls and the care of the sick and needy. Pope Paul the Third approved it in 1544.

In 1572, at the urging of Charles Borromeo, the order was declared a religious order under the rule of Saint Augustine. In France, most sisters took on enclosure and solemn vows, while others kept the first, freer plan. The entry notes Ursulines in Canada by the sixteen thirties, teaching Indian children. At its height early in the seventeen hundreds, the order held some twenty groups, three hundred fifty convents, and up to twenty thousand nuns.
britannica-1911-uses:
Uses, the old trust in land, are pinned down in a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A use was a fair claim on land held by another man. Early law barred a man from leaving his land by will. Church houses could not take land into their hands either. Men dodged the ban by grants made to the use of others.

The grantee held the bare legal hold on the land. The true gain went to the one named in the use. The chancellor's court gave force to that fair claim in law. Abuse of the dodge brought the famed Statute of Uses in 1536. That law failed of its aim, the entry plainly notes. From its failure grew the modern law of trusts in full.
britannica-1911-usher-james:
James Usher, an Anglican divine and archbishop who lived from 1581 to 1656, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in the parish of Saint Nicholas in Dublin on 4 January 1581, he came of the house of Nevill. His surname came from an ancestor who served as usher to John Plantagenet in Ireland in 1185. 

In 1594 Usher entered the newly founded university of Dublin, whose charter his uncle the archbishop had just won. He proved a diligent student with a bent for disputed points of theology. He graduated in 1600 and became a fellow of Trinity College in Dublin. On the death of his father in 1598 he gave up the family estate to his younger brother. He kept only a small rent charge for his own support and made ready to take orders.
britannica-1911-valenciennes:
Valenciennes, a town in the north of France, is described in a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town stands in the Nord department on the Scheldt, where the Rhonelle joins it. It lies thirty miles south east of Lille by rail. The counts for 1906 gave the town 25,977 people and the commune 31,759.

The Scheldt splits into two arms at the town, one of them made into a port. Of the old walls, pulled down in 1892, the Tour de la Dodenne and the citadel still stand. The entry stresses trade and work. The town sits at the heart of a rich coal field. Foundries, forges, mills, and wire works line the river bank. Beet growing feeds sugar works and stills nearby.
britannica-1911-variolites:
Variolites is the subject of a rock article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name comes from a Latin word for smallpox. In the study of rocks it names a group of dark green basic rocks from melted stone. On weathered surfaces they show pale spots that give a pock marked look. Those spots can be grey, pale green, violet, or yellow. The main rock is usually dark green.

The article says variolites stand closest to the basalts. They are nearly always much decayed and fine grained. Later changes can hide their first make up. The spots are round and often about a quarter inch across. They have a radiating structure and are sometimes ringed in zones. Some kinds are merely glassy forms of basalt with round knots. Dike edges in western Scotland hold large brown knots of this kind, easy to see in hand specimens.
britannica-1911-wages:
Wages is a term of economic science for the reward of labour. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it common yet hard to define with care. It builds the word from a Latin term for a pledge, wadium. The plain sense is clear: wages pay a man for his work. Yet Adam Smith warned that labour is an abstract thing to grasp.

Most folk grasp the worth of a good far more fast than of work. A heap of goods is a plain thing the hand can touch and see. A sum of labour is a notion, clear enough but less plain. From the worker's side the sum is not mere output in goods. It counts all the pain, strain, and vexation bound up in toil.
britannica-1911-waldenses:
Waldenses were members of a Christian sect that arose in the south of France about 1170, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The piece opens with the valleys of the sect in Italy, south west of Turin. The chief of these is the Val Pellice, watered by the stream of that name. Side glens such as Angrogna and Rora join it near the town of Torre Pellice.

To the north west of Pinerolo lies the valley of Saint Martin, watered by the Germanasca stream. At Perrero that valley splits into the Prali glen and the Massello glen. Massello is called the wildest of all the Waldensian valleys in the text. The valleys as a whole hold no high or snowy peaks, the piece notes. With one or two exceptions they are fertile and well wooded.
britannica-1911-watt-james:
James Watt, Scottish engineer and maker of the modern condensing steam engine, was born at Greenock on 19 January 1736 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father was a small merchant who lost his trade and fortune. Watt was thrown early on his own strength. A taste for mechanics took him to London at nineteen.

There he learned the trade of making fine instruments, though hard work and lean living hurt his frail health. Back in Scotland in 1756 he fixed star instruments for Glasgow professors. The city guilds barred him from opening a shop, since his training time was short. The college took him in during 1757 as its maker of maths instruments. That shelter let his great work begin.
britannica-1911-wattignies:
Wattignies, a village of France, is the subject of a battle entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The fight there took place in October seventeen ninety three, during the French Revolutionary Wars. Allied troops, chiefly Austrians under Coburg, were besieging Maubeuge. A French army gathered near Avesnes to relieve the town.

The entry sets out both plans in clear detail. Coburg placed a covering force across the road to Maubeuge, with troops on a ridge and on the Wattignies plateau. The French commander Jourdan hid his move behind a line of woods. He sent strong forces against both wings and a feint at the centre. The text then follows how the plan played out.
britannica-1911-wells-david-ames:
Wells, David Ames is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American economist. He was born in Springfield, Massachusetts, on the seventeenth of June 1828 and died in 1898. He graduated at Williams College in 1847. The next year he joined the staff of the Springfield Republican, and at that time he devised a machine for folding newspapers.

He then moved to Cambridge and took a science degree. From 1850 to 1865 he issued an Annual of Scientific Discovery with George Bliss. An essay of his on the national debt won him the chair of a national revenue commission in 1865. That body's work laid the base of fair, scientific taxation in the United States. From 1866 to 1870 he served as special commissioner of revenue and printed weighty yearly reports.
britannica-1911-wentworth-william-charle:
William Charles Wentworth was an Australian leader who lived from seventeen ninety-three to eighteen seventy-two. He was born on Norfolk Isle, where his father was a state surgeon. He was schooled in England and at Cambridge. On trips home he crossed the Blue Hills and won note for bold feats.

Back in Sydney as a lawyer, he co-founded a paper that pled for self rule. He spoke for freed men who had served their time, against the proud set who shut them out. His drive helped shape the frame of rule of eighteen forty-two. He led the grazier party and helped found the chief school of Sydney.
britannica-1911-wheatstone-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Wheatstone is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English physicist. He lived from 1802 to 1875. He is called the practical founder of modern telegraphy. He was born at Gloucester in February 1802. His father was a music seller in that city. In 1806 the family removed to London. His education was carried on in several private schools. He showed no remarkable attainments at those schools.

He was marked mainly by a morbid shyness and sensitiveness. About 1816 he was sent to his uncle in the Strand. That uncle was a musical instrument maker by trade. The boy was to learn that trade from him. But, with his father's leave, he read books instead. He spent more time in reading than at work. For some years he made experiments in acoustics. He followed his own ideas in that field of study.
britannica-1911-whitelocke-sir-james:
Whitelocke, Sir James, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English judge. Born on the 28th of November 1570, he was a London merchant's son. He was schooled at Merchant Taylors and at Oxford. There he became a fellow of his college and a barrister.

He ran the estates of three colleges before his rise in law. In 1610 he sat in the Commons for the borough of Woodstock. In 1620 he was made chief justice for Chester and knighted. Four years later he took a seat on the king's bench court. He died at Fawley Court on the 22nd of June 1632. His journal was brought out by the Camden Society in 1858.
britannica-1911-wilkins-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Wilkins, an English Oriental scholar who lived from about 1749 to 1836, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Frome in Somersetshire. In 1770 he went to India as a clerk in the East India Company's service. There he was drawn to the study of Eastern tongues, above all Sanskrit.

Wilkins set up a printing press for those languages in India. He took a large share in the bench work of cutting the type himself. Back in England from 1786, he kept up his Sanskrit studies. He became librarian to the Company and an examiner at its college at Haileybury. The article calls him a pioneer, the first Englishman to master Sanskrit. He made a Sanskrit grammar and rendered several sacred books of the East. In 1833 he was knighted for his services to Eastern learning.
britannica-1911-xenocrates:
Xenocrates of Chalcedon, a Greek philosopher, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in the year 396 before Christ. He headed the Academy at Athens from 339 to 314 before Christ. In early youth he moved to Athens. He became a pupil of the Socratic Aeschines.

He soon joined himself to Plato instead. He went with Plato to Sicily in the year 361 before Christ. On his master's death, he visited Hermias at Atarneus, in company with Aristotle. In the year 339, he succeeded Speusippus as head of the school. He beat his rivals Menedemus and Heracleides by a few votes. Three times he served on an Athenian embassy. Once he went to Philip, and twice to Antipater. Soon after the death of Demosthenes, he took offence at Macedonian sway in Athens. The article traces a loyal pupil who became a school head in hard times.
britannica-1911-xerxes:
Xerxes is the subject of a kings article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The hosted text opens with the tail of a book list for the writer Xenophon. It then turns to Xerxes itself. Xerxes is the Greek form of a Persian royal name. In the Old Testament the name appears as Ahasuerus. It was borne by two Persian kings of one royal house.

The article gives most space to Xerxes the First. He was a son of Darius the First and Atossa, daughter of Cyrus the Great. He was named heir ahead of older half brothers born before Darius became king. He came to the throne in October of the year 485 before Christ. His first task was to put down a revolt in Egypt. That revolt had broken out before he took power.
britannica-1911-yorke-charles:
Charles Yorke, an English lord chancellor who lived from 1722 to 1770, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was the second son of Philip Yorke, first earl of Hardwicke. He was born in London in December 1722. He was educated at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.

His gifts for letters showed early. With his brother Philip he worked on the Athenian Letters. In 1745 he published a treatise on the law of forfeiture for high treason. It defended his father's handling of the Scottish Jacobite peers. The next year he was called to the bar. His father was lord chancellor at the time. Yorke gained a sinecure post in the Court of Chancery in 1747. He entered parliament that year as member for Reigate. The article traces a rise eased by birth, yet backed by real legal talent.
bryusov-the-republic-of-the-southern-cro:
A polar republic dies of a mysterious disease of contradiction in the title story of Valery Bryusov's story collection, given here in English. Bryusov led the Russian Symbolists, and his tales mix utopias, plagues, and the occult with decadent polish. Madness spreads through a perfectly planned Antarctic city like a logical infection.

Other stories in the set range across history and fantasy with the same stylish control. Bryusov wrote prose the way his movement wrote verse: dense, musical, and deliberately strange. English readers meet a side of Russian fiction far from the great realist novels. The collection shows symbolism attempting the short story with full ambition. Strange and unlike anything else of its period, it rewards adventurous readers.
buddy-and-brighteyes-pigg-bed-time-stori:
Howard R. Garis wrote bedtime tales of two small pigs, Buddy and Brighteyes Pigg, first run in the Evening News of Newark. A run of short tales fills the book, each a night's read. Buddy in a cabbage patch opens the set. Brighteyes and Mrs. Hoptoad come next.

Sammy Littletail, ball play, and Sister Sallie fill the early run. Dr. Pigg and Uncle Wiggily step in at the sixth tale. Fourth of July, a tight rope walk, and a tin can trap crowd the mid-run. Burglar fox, deep hole, and groundhog tricks raise the stakes late. Berry bush, cow herding, horseback rides, and sand house builds keep the tone soft. Falls downhill and baths close the list in the copy held here. Small scrapes, quick saves, and home by dark form the stock of each night.
bunyan-characters-1st-series:
Alexander Whyte, minister of St George's Free Church in Edinburgh, delivered Bunyan Characters as lectures on the people of The Pilgrim's Progress, printed in 1893. His introduction lingers on the word character, used once in the New Testament for Christ as the express image of the Father. From that text he builds a method: study Bunyan's persons to study souls.

The first series treats Christian himself, the Interpreter, Evangelist, Obstinate and Pliable, Faithful, Talkative, and Hopeful among others. Whyte quotes Goodwin, Pusey, and Thomas Shepard on truth without love making hypocrites. His lectures became devotional classics in Scotland, read as seriously as Bunyan himself, and they assume a congregation that knew the allegory by heart.
bunyan-characters-2nd-series:
Alexander Whyte continued his St George's lectures in Bunyan Characters, second series, printed in 1894, opening with Ignorance, the brisk young talker in religion who was alive without the law once. Whyte warns that a few more such gentlemen would make pilgrimage fashionable. The series turns to the second part of Bunyan's allegory, Christiana's journey.

Christiana, overcome by the King's letter bidding her follow her husband, begs her visitor to carry her and her children to worship the King. Mr Fearing trembles at the wicket gate until Goodwill takes him by the collar and bids him peace. Whyte's pulpit psychology treats Bunyan's figures as parishioners he has counseled for years.
bunyan-characters-3rd-series:
Alexander Whyte, minister of St. George's Free Church in Edinburgh, devoted this third series of Bunyan Characters lectures to John Bunyan's Holy War. Whyte opens by ranking the books: Pilgrim's Progress tells the soul's journey, while Holy War, published in 1682, tells its battles. The town of Mansoul is besieged, taken, and retaken, and Whyte reads the siege as a map of the Christian life.

Lecture by lecture he walks through Bunyan's soldiers, captains, and assaults, drawing lessons for faith under attack. Macaulay's praise of Holy War as nearly the best allegory ever written gets quoted early. Whyte writes as a preacher to preachers, warm, urgent, and certain that Bunyan's war still describes his hearers.
burlesques:
William Makepeace Thackeray collected his Burlesques, the parodies that first showed his comic gift in magazines. Notes by Eminent Hands mimics the novelists of the day in fake masterpieces: George de Barnwell after Bulwer-Lytton, Codlingsby after Disraeli, and others in the manners of popular romancers and military tale-tellers. A Plan for a Prize Novel gives the recipe away.

Then come the Jeames papers, the diary and letters of C. Jeames de la Pluche, a footman speculating in railway shares and writing his lords-and-liveries English. Major Gahagan's tremendous adventures in India close the volume in tall-tale style. Thackeray's targets are literary humbug and social climbing, and the imitations are so exact that the laughter doubles as criticism. Few parodists have loved their victims this knowingly.
burned-bridges:
Bertrand W. Sinclair wrote a north-west novel, put out by Grosset and Dunlap in 1919. Five fresh prints ran from August 1919 to February 1920, a mark of hot sale. Ralph P. Coleman drew the front plate: a man feels a girl's heart hammer at his breast. North of Fifty-Three heads Sinclair's past work.

The first problem heads the chapter list. The man and his mission come next. A lone cabin, slow doubt for Mr. Thompson, and fresh meets fill the early run. A slip of the axe and its fruits mark the heart. Maid and man, a minister's man's job, and a fortune with a flitting turn the tale. Partners, the restless foot, and a world made small close the heads in view. Wild land, church work, and love form the stakes the heads lay out.
buttercup-gold-and-other-stories:
Ellen Robena Field dedicated Buttercup Gold and Other Stories, copyrighted in 1894 by the Bangor Kindergarten Association, to the dear kindergarten children and her little friend Alice Caro Wing. Longfellow and Lowell supply the mottoes about children as living poems and God's apostles. The tales are nature stories for the very young.

Flowers, birds, and seasons speak in short chapters meant for kindergarten telling: a homesick bird is cheered by a singer promising the sun is smiling and trying to make the flowers glad. Field wrote from the Froebel kindergarten movement, which taught through story, song, and garden. The book preserves that movement's voice at its most earnest and sweet.
buttered-side-down-stories:
Edna Ferber published Buttered Side Down in 1912, her first book of stories, after years as a newspaper reporter in Wisconsin and Chicago.
