The title states her rule of life: things tend to fall buttered side down, and her heroines, mostly working girls, learn to laugh and carry on anyway. Her pages fill with salesgirls, stenographers, actresses, and traveling saleswomen in small hotels and city shops.

Ferber writes with quick wit and a warm eye for the talk and dress of her time. The tales mix romance with rent money, and success, when it comes, is earned at a counter or a desk. The book launched a career that led to Show Boat and a Pulitzer Prize for So Big.
by-rock-and-pool-on-an-austral-shore-and:
Louis Becke wrote tales of the South Seas, put out at New York in 1901. New Amsterdam Book Company set the book out on Fifth Avenue. Pacific Tales and By Reef and Palm head his past work on the title page. The title tale gives the set its name and first place.

Solepa follows. Fisher folk of Nukufetau come next, a tale of isle life at work. Mrs. Maclaggan's Billy brings a change of key. An Island Memory and A Hundred Fathoms Deep dive back to sea ground. On a Tidal River and Denison heads fill the list in the copy held here. Becke's stock is shore trade, reef risk, and isle folk met at close range. Salt air and lagoon calm run through the set, tale by tale.
caesar-dies:
Talbot Mundy wrote a novel of Rome under the emperor Commodus. Golden Antioch opens the tale, laid like a jewel at a mountain's throat. Streets near four miles long cross the city, paved in granite and lined with marble posts. Gay crowds take the air in chariots, litters, and on foot.

Fruit in open shops and bloom in town gardens paint the scene in green and white. Slave groups wait on rich owners in the throng. Two breeds stand split in that crowd. Romans, less rich and less schooled yet no less loose, look down on the town folk — yet love the town, the tale owns. Court rot and street shine form the ground a Caesar's fall will shake. The title gives the end away from the first page.
california-sketches-new-series:
O. P. Fitzgerald wrote a second set of California sketches, dated 1883, with a front word by Bishop George F. Pierce. Six prints of the first set had sold out, by the author's own note. Friends' calls and his own push brought this encore, though he owns he hates encores.

Much of the song sits in a low key, he warns. Sketches from real life must do so, since all lives are sad tales in his view. Bearded men in rough dress, with steel nerves and fire hearts, front the book in verse. Few fair women, fleet as shades, stand with them. Past joy and pain trod again form the path: hills of youth walked a second time. Nashville, September 1881, signs the author's word to the reader.
cambridge-pieces:
Cambridge Pieces collects Samuel Butler's earliest published writings, most of them written while he was an undergraduate at St John's College, Cambridge. R A Streatfeild edited the volume, issued in London in 1914, long after Butler's death. Several pieces first appeared in the Eagle, a college magazine, in 1858. They show a clever student testing his voice.

An essay on English composition argues for clear, plain prose over swollen style. A tour narrative and a mock translation from Herodotus follow. Butler offers variations on the shield of Achilles and a playful prospectus for a Great Split Society. Skits on examinations, two deans, and Napoleon at St Helena add satire. A memoir by A T Bartholomew on Butler and the Simeonites, a college religious group, closes the book.
cambridge-sketches:
Frank Preston Stearns's Cambridge Sketches recalls the distinguished men he knew in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Stearns regrets that he never introduced himself to more of them, since at the time he had no expectation of writing about them, yet their acquaintance raised his idea of human nature.

Some of his subjects enjoy world-wide celebrity, Stearns notes, while others, famed in their day, now seem headed for oblivion. All, he insists, deserve honour from humankind and from their age. Charles Sumner fronts the volume, and the sketches that follow mix memory, anecdote and character. Readers of New England history will find Stearns warm, unpretentious and observant.
camps-quarters-and-casual-places:
Archibald Forbes wrote a set of pieces from a war writer's life, with a note dated London, June 1896. Thanks at the front name the houses that first ran the pieces: Routledge, the Nineteenth Century, the Contemporary Review, and McClure's Magazine. Wedlock under fire opens the list of near twenty pieces.

Golden feet in Burma, German war prayers, and a bride cake tale fill the early run. A Balaclava in Forbes's own form and a boast of how he saved France mark the war side. Christmas in a cavalry camp gives the soft beat. Cawnpore and Lucknow as they stand now get two slots. Bismarck in the Franco-German war gets a long one. War of the future, royal nerve in fight, and odd fairs fill the frame's spread of war and peace.
canada-and-the-states:
Sir E. W. Watkin's Canada and the States gathers his recollections from 1851 to 1886, years spent crossing the Atlantic on railway and political business. Watkin dedicates the book informally to Lady Watkin, who bore the anxieties of home life during his many long absences on the American continent.

The recollections touch the Maritime Provinces, their hardy population, harbours, fisheries and seamen, and the question of their place beside Canada and the United States. Watkin writes as a businessman and member of Parliament, not as a detached historian, and his pages carry the practical concerns of railways, trade and empire. Readers interested in Anglo-Canadian relations will find his first-hand view unusually concrete.
canterbury-pieces:
Samuel Butler's Canterbury Pieces gathers short early writings from his years in New Zealand, edited by R A Streatfeild and published in London in 1914. Butler had emigrated to Canterbury in 1859, just as Charles Darwin's Origin of Species appeared. That book seized his attention at once. The pieces here grew out of colonial newspaper debates that followed.

A dialogue on Darwin's theory opens the volume, dated from Christchurch in 1862. Letters from 1863 argue with a newspaper leader called Barrel-Organs. Darwin Among the Machines then imagines machines evolving like living things, an idea Butler later expanded. A note on Shakespeare's Tempest and a piece on English cricketers close the set. Readers see a young Butler learning to argue, joke, and doubt in print.
cape-cod-stories:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Cape Cod Stories, also published as The Old Home House, opens at the Orham post-office. Cap'n Jonadab Wixon and Barzilla Wingate each find a long envelope sealed with a crest and a letter D. The two old salts narrate the tales in thick Cape dialect. Two Pairs of Shoes leads the contents.

The Count and the Manager, The Mare and the Motor, and The Love of Lobelia 'Ankins follow, with The Antiquers and His Native Heith among the twelve. Lincoln's Cape is a place of retired sea captains, summer visitors, and small schemes. Motors meet mares, antiquers meet their match, and the post-office stove hears all. His humour is gentle and his dialect lovingly phonetic. The stories made Lincoln the chronicler of a vanishing Cape Cod, read aloud in parlours for a generation.
captain-cook-his-life-voyages-and-discov:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote a life of Captain James Cook, in a text dated 1871. Humble roots front the tale. Cook's father rose from farm lad to bailiff on Mr. Thomas Skottowe's farm of Airy-Holme, near Ayton in Yorkshire. His mother was a cottager's girl. James was born at Marton, near Stockton, on 27 October 1728.

Nine children filled the house. James outlived all save one sister, wed to a Redcar fisherman. Rise from such stock to high fame marks Cook out, Kingston holds, among all Englishmen of like path. School, shop, and sea steps fill the youth part in the book's plan. Three great world runs form the heart, by the title's word. Charts, new lands, and a hard death at the last give the life its shape for young readers.
captain-scraggs-or-the-green-pea-pirates:
Peter B. Kyne wrote a comic sea tale of a coastwise skipper, first run in the Sunset Magazine. Rights years on the print run from 1911 to 1919. Gordon Grant drew the plates. Grosset and Dunlap put out the book at New York. Cappy Ricks heads Kyne's past work.

Scraggs in a rage throws his brown derby down and jumps on it, in the front plate's jest. Great snakes, he yells in one plate, and falls back at his cabin wall. One plate shows him burst from a ring of wild folk and run for the beach. Tabu names crowd the plate list's edge in view. Green peas give the pirates their odd flag in the title: a cargo joke turned crew name, in the book's own terms. Port talk, short hauls, and a hot head form the stock.
carlyle-reminiscences:
Thomas Carlyle, the Sage of Chelsea, wrote his Reminiscences in bursts of grief right after his wife's death in 1866. His friend and biographer James Froude published them in 1881. The pieces were never meant as a finished book, which gives them their raw force.

Carlyle recalls his father, his early friend Edward Irving, and the Scotland of his youth, now vanished. He writes of London fame and of Jane Welsh Carlyle with love and regret. The prose is tender, gloomy, and vivid by turns. Publication stirred scandal, since Carlyle spared neither himself nor others in these pages.
catalan-s-constant-to-1-500-000-places:
Thomas Papanikolaou computed Catalan's constant to 1,500,000 digits on October 26, 1996, and this file prints them. The run used a Sun Sparc20 and took seven days, seven hours, and about a quarter of an hour. Papanikolaou says he verified the earlier million-digit value by LiDIA comparison before extending it.

The method is Greg Fee's algorithm from the 1990 ISSAC proceedings, using the standard series for Catalan's constant sped up by an Euler transform and only integer arithmetic in the main loop. A companion file gives 300,000 places by Fee himself. The digits fill the file in long blocks, a reference monument to 1990s computational number theory rather than a text to read.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-ferr:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Ferrières describes a Benedictine abbey in the diocese of Orléans. It has been most unfortunate for historians, having lost its archives, charters and all that would aid a reconstruction of its history. Legend has therefore had full play around its origins.

The most accurate account available, the entry says, comes from an obscure eighteenth-century Benedictine, Dom Philippe Mazoyer. Mazoyer traces a chapel of Our Lady of Bethlehem at Ferrières, dates the abbey no earlier than King Dagobert's reign, and dismisses the Acts of St. Savinian and a Clovis charter dated 508 as false. The entry weighs these claims against the church's ancient stonework.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-s:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Solesmes describes a Benedictine monastery in the Sarthe, near Sablé in France. Geoffrey, lord of Sablé, founded it in 1010 as a priory under Le Mans' St-Pierre de la Couture. War with England brought two pillagings and one fire that almost wholly burned it.

Apart from those disasters its history ran uneventfully for centuries, until rebuilding began late in the fifteenth century. Prior Philibert de la Croix changed the church from basilica to Latin cross form. His successor Jean Bougler, prior from 1505 to 1556, finished the church, added the tower, and rebuilt cloisters, sacristy and library. Under Bougler the two famous Saints of Solesmes statue groups were set in the transept chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abipones:
The Abipones were an Indian tribe of Guaycuru stock who once roamed the east bank of the Parana. They were later gathered between the Bermejo, the Salado, and the Parana in present-day Argentina. Their customs matched those of South American tribes generally: clanship, elaborate animism, and great sway for medicine men over private and tribal affairs. Chiefs were chosen or imposed through striking deeds and shaman craft, and the lance was their favoured weapon.

By 1641 they had horses from Spanish settlers, and mounted raids made them dangerous to colonization. Jesuits undertook to tame them in the early eighteenth century. Fathers Casado and Sanchez laboured at the task, and above all Martin Dobrizhoffer, a missionary in Paraguay for eighteen years, whose history of the Abipones remains the chief source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abrahamites:
Abrahamites is a name borne by three distinct groups, and this entry keeps them apart. First came Syrian heretics of the ninth century, called Brachiniah by the Arabs after Ibrahim of Antioch, their head, who denied Christ's divinity and was linked by some to the Paulicians. Second were Bohemian Deists who claimed Abraham's religion before his circumcision, believed in one God, and rejected the Trinity, original sin, and endless punishment.

From the Bible those Bohemian Abrahamites accepted just the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer. When they refused to adopt a tolerated religion, Joseph II banished them in 1783 to Transylvania, though some later became Catholics. Third were monks of St. Abraham's in Constantinople, martyred in 832 under Emperor Theophilus for defending holy images against the Iconoclasts. The entry cites the Kirchenlexikon for all three.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-the-a:
Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament in the accepted order, and this long entry questions whether its title came from the author at all. Cornely thought the author affixed it, but the entry judges it far more likely added later, like the Gospel headings. The title itself misleads, since the book holds neither the acts of all apostles nor all the acts of any one apostle.

It opens with the forty days after the Resurrection, when Christ spoke of the kingdom of God, promised the Holy Ghost, and ascended. Peter advises choosing a successor to Judas, and Matthias is chosen by lot. At Pentecost the Holy Ghost descends with the gift of tongues, Peter explains the miracle as the power of Jesus Christ, and many converts are baptized. The entry then follows authorship, sources, and text through modern scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adamites:
Adamites were an obscure sect, perhaps from the second century, professing Adam's primeval innocence regained. St. Epiphanius and St. Augustine mention them by name and describe their practices; their church they called Paradise, condemned marriage as foreign to Eden, and stripped themselves naked during common worship; they cannot have been numerous.

Accounts of their origin differ. Some make them an offshoot of the Carpocratian Gnostics, with a sensual mysticism and complete emancipation from moral law, a view Theodoret held, linking them to licentious sects Clement of Alexandria describes. Others see misguided ascetics striving to kill carnal desire by simpler manners and abolishing marriage. Similar practices revived in Europe later, among the Brethren of the Free Spirit, the Beghards, and Bohemian Picards, whom Ziska nearly exterminated in 1421.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-admiral-sands:
Benjamin F. Sands was a rear-admiral of the United States Navy, born at Baltimore on 11 February 1812. He died at Washington on 30 June 1883, of non-Catholic parents, and became a convert in 1850 after marrying Henrietta French, a Catholic. Appointed midshipman on 1 April 1828, he rose through successive grades to rear-admiral on 27 April 1871, retiring at sixty-two in 1874.

In the Civil War he commanded several important posts with conspicuous success; in 1867 he became superintendent of the Naval Observatory at Washington. Under him until 1874, the observatory rose to equal the most celebrated in Europe. His notes became From Reefer to Rear Admiral. Son James Hoban Sands, born in 1845, also became a rear-admiral, famed for daring and seamanship, and the entry follows both careers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aguas-calient:
Aguas Calientes, Latin Aquae Calidae, is a Mexican see dependent on Guadalajara. Leo XIII erected it by decree on 27 August 1899, carving it from Guadalajara. The province of Aguas Calientes forms it. Its first bishop, Jose Maria Portugal, a Friar Minor, was born in Mexico on 24 January 1838.

Portugal had been made Bishop of Sinaloa in 1888, transferred to Saltillo in 1898, and to Aguas Calientes on 9 June 1902. An inland Mexican state, it covers 2,950 square miles. Its capital, also Aguas Calientes, lies 300 miles northeast of Mexico City on a 6,000-foot plateau, with a population of 30,000 in 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albanenses: The Albanenses were a Manichaean group, followers of a dualist faith built on two eternal powers, good and evil. They lived in Albania probably around the eighth century. Little is known about them beyond their place among the sects that kept the original Manichaean teaching alive. They held a strict, unyielding form of that teaching, refusing any softening of the claim that the evil power is eternal and fully equal to the good. The entry points readers to related groups such as the Bogomiles, the Cathars, and the Paulicians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albigenses:
The Albigenses, named from Albi in southern France, were a medieval religious movement whose entry sets out their beliefs, history, organization, and the Church's response. They held that two opposed powers coexist: a good power that made the spiritual world and an evil power that made the material world. Their doctrines and morals followed from that stark division.

The sect divided its members into the perfect, the few who had received the initiation rite called the consolamentum, and the ordinary believers. The entry traces the movement's origin and history, its organization and liturgy, and the attitude of the Church toward it. It covers the sect's system whole, from its dualist first principles to its clash with the medieval Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-of-:
Alexander of Hales was a Franciscan theologian and philosopher, counted among the greatest scholastics. He was born at Hales in Gloucestershire toward the end of the twelfth century and died at Paris in 1245. Schooled at home and probably at Oxford, he went to the University of Paris, where he took master's degrees first in arts and then in theology. Later writers styled him the Irrefragable Doctor, the Fount of Life, and the Monarch of Theologians.

His chief work, the Summa of Universal Theology, was begun about 1231 and left unfinished. It made him the first to attempt a systematic account of Catholic doctrine after Aristotle's metaphysical and physical works reached the schools. His theology broadly matches that of Bonaventure and Thomas, beginning from what the mind can know of God. In psychology he kept to the older Augustinian teaching, with its threefold division of the soul's powers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-de-:
Alexandre de Rhodes was a French missionary and author, born at Avignon in March 1591 and dead at Isfahan in Persia in November 1660. He entered the Jesuit novitiate at Rome in April 1612, intending to devote his life to converting the infidels, and was sent to the East Indies. He began mission work in 1624, winning great success in Cochin China. By 1627 he went to Tongking, where he converted 6,000 people in three years, including several bonzes, Buddhist monks.

When persecution drove Rhodes from Tongking in 1630, his new converts carried on the work of evangelization. Recalled to Rome, he gained permission to work in Persia instead. Amid a busy missionary life he still wrote. His works include a two-book history of Tongking published at Lyons in 1652 and an account of the glorious death of Andrew the Catechist in 1653. He also wrote a catechism in Latin and Tongkingese printed at Rome in 1658.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-de-va:
Alfonso de Valdés was a Spanish humanist and chancellor of Emperor Charles V, born at Cuenca about 1500, dead at Vienna in October 1532. His talents won early advancement, and he accompanied Charles to the coronation at Aachen in 1520 and the Diet of Worms in 1521. From 1522 he was secretary of the imperial chancellery. He drafted state papers including the 1525 Pavia report and a sharp 1526 letter to Clement VII urging an ecumenical council.

After Rome's capture and sack in 1527, Valdés wrote the dialogue Lactantius, attacking the pope as a disturber of peace. The papal nuncio accused him before the Inquisition, but Charles protected him. Valdés admired Erasmus and spread his ideas in Spain. He travelled with the emperor through Italy, Germany, and the Netherlands in 1529, and in October 1531 wrote from Brussels congratulating the Swiss Catholics on their victory over Zwingli. His brother was Juan Valdés of the Naples movement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-breadbo:
Altar breadboxes hold the unleavened hosts used at Mass, made of wood, tin, britannia, silver, or other metal. A round flat weight, covered if needed with silk or linen and fitted with a knob, rests on the breads to keep them from bending or curving. The cover must fit tightly, so the breads stay dry and clean.

The box for the large hosts is sized to fit them, while a larger box holds the small particles given at the communion of the laity. Together these plain vessels keep the breads flat, dry, and clean until the moment of consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-candles:
Altar candles at Mass and other liturgical functions must be beeswax. The pure wax from flowers stands for Christ's pure flesh from his Virgin Mother, the wick for his soul, and the flame for his divinity. Only beeswax carries the first meaning, though other candles share the other two.

Seven candles burn at a pontifical high Mass, the seventh somewhat higher than the rest. A solemn high Mass takes six, a sung high Mass at least four, and a low Mass by a priest only two. A bishop's low Mass usually takes four, and bishops may use a hand candle, the bugia, before Mass except on Good Friday and Holy Saturday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altars-in-the:
In Old Slavonic and Russian, altar, sometimes spelled oltar, means the whole space behind the iconostasis around the altar, matching the Greek bema and the Latin sanctuary. The Russian Orthodox or Ruthenian Greek Catholic altar is thus the sanctuary, not merely the Latin altar, which Slavonic and Russian call prestol, the throne. The Greek altar itself, he hagia trapeza, has stayed practically unchanged and unadorned, unlike Latin altars.

The entry follows the Greek consecration service through hymns, psalms, and the blessing of holy water. Greek practice thus keeps the altar simpler and the sanctuary's meaning wider than the Latin use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amazones:
Amazonas, or Manãos, is a South American diocese dependent on San Salvador of Bahia. Amazonas, Brazil's largest state, lies south of British Guiana, Venezuela, and Colombia, between Peru west and Pará east, covering 732,250 square miles with only 207,600 people in 1900. Manãos, the capital, is its chief port, and Amazonas, once part of Pará, became a state in 1850.

Erected a see by Leo XIII on 27 April 1892, it counts 350,000 Catholics and 800 Protestants. It has 24 parishes, 19 secular priests, 13 regular priests, 41 churches or chapels, and 105 Catholic schools. A vast state with a thin population, its church counts far outnumber its priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosio-mora:
Ambrosio Morales, Spanish historian born at Cordova in 1513, died in 1591. After Salamanca and Alcalá studies he took Holy Orders, won Alcalá's Belles-Lettres chair, and in 1574 became Castile's chronicler, commissioned to continue Ocampo's Crónica General de España. Ten years' labour brought it to Castile and León's union under Ferdinand I, his pupil Sandoval continuing to 1079.

More talented and better trained than Ocampo, Morales remains an old-time chronicler. He shows little tendency to test facts, link cause and effect, or philosophize, and his style is rather wearisome. His other writings cover Spain's cities' antiquities and a royal journey for Philip II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-american-fede:
The American Federation of Catholic Societies unites the Catholic laity, parishes, and groups under the bishops to defend and advance their religious, civil, and social concerns. Laity, parishes, and groups keep their own life while still acting together. It destroys no group's freedom and never interferes with any activity, seeking union for cooperation and economy of forces. It is not political and asks no privileges or favours for Catholics.

Its principal object is encouraging the Christian education of youth. Cooperation without control is its whole method: united strength, untouched freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ammonites:
The Ammonites were a people very closely akin to the Hebrews, called Bén'ámmî, Son of my people, marking descent from Israel's near kin. Their country lay east of the Jordan, originally from the Jordan to the wilderness and from the Jabbok south to the Arnon, land later falling to Reuben and Gad. Their chief city Rabbath-Ammon, distinct from Moab's namesake, lay in a fertile, well-tilled valley. The royal city flourished under a wealthy king in David's time, well fortified, though it fell to Joab's attack.

Moab and Ammon's close blood kinship is admitted by all. The Moabite Stone's almost-Hebrew language witnesses their racial affinity with Israel. Israel's distinction against its nearest relatives traced to Ammon's treatment of Israel marching to Palestine while struggling toward nationhood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amorrhites:
An ancient people named often in the Old Testament, the Amorrhites take their name from a word whose sense scholars still dispute. Many once read it as highlanders. Yet the article warns that the name predates both the Bible and the Hebrew people, so a Hebrew root proves little, even though these people often lived in hill country.

In the Bible the name stretches at times to cover all the early inhabitants of Canaan. At other times it marks one people among them, feared as tall warriors and foes of Israel. Outside the Bible, Babylonian, Egyptian, and Assyrian records apply a similar name across Syria and Palestine from very early times. By the days of Solomon and later leaders, the Amorrhites had blended into the general population of Palestine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anchorites:
Anchorites, from a Greek word meaning I withdraw, are also called hermits, or desert dwellers. In Christian terms they are men who try to defeat the flesh and the devil by taking away their ally, the world. Scripture sanctions the impulse, in John the Baptist in the desert and in Christ withdrawing again and again into solitude.

The article insists this life is no empty trance. A soul freed from distracting cares and fixed on divine thoughts lives, it says, the happiest life open to man on earth. It then sorts hermits into kinds. Some take vows or community life and serve a church with the bishop's approval. Others adopt the hermit's habit on their own authority and live under no rule. Against abuses by this last class the Holy See issued strict laws, cited here from Benedict XIV and Ferraris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-of-rho:
Andrew of Rhodes, also called Andrew of Colossus, theologian, died in 1440. Greek by birth, of schismatic parents, he had no early education but afterwards studied Latin, Greek, and theology. Study of the early Fathers convinced him that truth lay with the Latin Church. He abjured his error, professed the faith, and entered the Dominican order.

He led an apostolic life, urging fellow-Greeks to reunite with Rome. In 1413 he was made Archbishop of Rhodes. At Basle he delivered an oration in the pope's name. At Ferrara-Florence he was one of six theologians answering the Greeks' objections, proving the Church could add the Filioque to the Creed and that the Greek Fathers agreed. Eugene IV sent him to Cyprus, where he made peace between Latins and Greeks and overcame Nestorian, Eutychian, and Monothelite heresies. He wrote a dialogue for Cardinal Bessarion replying to Mark of Ephesus on Roman rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angels-of-the:
The angels of the churches are the figures addressed in the Apocalypse. Saint John sees seven candlesticks and, in their midst, the Son of Man holding seven stars. The candlesticks represent the seven Churches of Asia, and the stars are the angels of those Churches. John is bidden to write to each angel, giving praise or blame.

Origen reads these angels as the Churches' guardians, a reading Dean Alford supports. Saint Epiphanius explicitly rejects this view and, following the passage's imagery, explains them as the bishops. Scripture also likens a teacher to a star, as in Daniel 12:3. Saint Augustine's reason for reading the angels as the prelates is that John speaks of them as losing their first charity, which angels cannot do.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annates:
Annates are a church benefice's first year's revenue, paid to the Curia, in medieval times to bishops. As administration centred in Rome, benefices were increasingly granted directly by the pope. This held for bishoprics, monasteries, and smaller livings, canonicates, and parishes. On such occasions the treasury took a tax from the new holder's income. Since the fifteenth century, that tax has been called annates.

A prescriptive right to such gifts grew out of the custom. In the first half of the thirteenth century, a scale was fixed for liable dioceses and abbeys on appointment or confirmation. During the thirteenth century, many cathedrals also took a year's income from vacant benefices for bishops. Exceptionally, bishops levied this annate on all diocesan benefices falling vacant within a period. In 1306 Clement V reserved a year's revenues from all English and Scottish benefices vacant, or falling vacant within three years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antidicomaria:
The Antidicomarianites were an Eastern sect, flourishing about 200 to 400, named as Mary's opponents. At first the Ebionites held that Our Lord was merely Joseph and Mary's son. Even its own adherents came to find that teaching repugnant. It was changed to say that, though Our Lord was born of Mary through the Holy Ghost, Joseph and Mary afterwards lived in wedlock and had many other children. The sect rejected the formula ever-Virgin Mary, used in the Greek and Roman Liturgies.

Tertullian gives the earliest reference to the sect, and Origen expressly mentions its doctrines. Certain Arians, Eudocius and Eunomius, strongly backed the teaching. Toward the end of the fourth century the sect reached its greatest development in Arabia. Saint Epiphanius gave it the name Antidicomarianites in particular, writing against it with the doctrine's history and proofs of its falsity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipodes:
Earth-roundness and men with feet toward ours drew the early Fathers only where they touched one human race, hence shared original sin and redemption. Augustine shows this: As to the Antipodes fable, men on earth's far side, walking feet toward ours, there is no reason for believing it. Its affirmers claim no actual information; they merely conjecture.

A singular eighth-century exception: Zachary's 748 letter to Boniface shows Germany's Apostle invoking censure on Vergilius. Vergilius, supposed the Irish Ferghil, later Salzburg's archbishop, held that beneath the earth lay another world, men, sun, and moon. Zachary told Boniface to expel him if the teaching held. That Vergilius was ever tried, condemned, or forced to retract is baseless assumption. The Church deserves esteem for upholding human brotherhood for all; yet the Irish monk, centuries ahead of his age, stands with Galileo as warning against hasty ecclesiastical censure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-da-fo:
Antonio da Fonseca Soares, better known in religion as Antonio das Chagas, lived from 1631 to 1682 and moved from soldiering to the Franciscan order. Born at Vidigueira in Portugal, he served as a common soldier and fled to Bahia in Brazil after a duel. He lived carelessly until the writings of Louis of Granada turned him toward religious life. Illness in 1662 hardened his resolve, and he entered the Franciscans that May, taking his new name.

He soon won fame across Portugal for poetry and ascetical writing, prose and verse on the spiritual life, praised for learning joined to elegant style. The article places him among the classics of Portuguese letters, and lists works published after his death, including Sparks of Divine Love and Spiritual Works. Much of his writing stayed unpublished, yet his reputation rested on a virtuous life and a polished pen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apaches:
The Apaches, a North American Indian people of Athapascan language stock, are traced here from a supposed home in northwestern Canada southward to California, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. Oñate in 1598 first mentions them by this name. From their first appearance in history, the article says, they were noted for restlessness and fierceness, opposed to fixed homes and a terror to more peaceful peoples. That harsh framing is the encyclopedia's own voice.

Catholic mission work among them is called a sad history. Franciscans laboured from 1629, when Father Benavides established Santa Clara de Capo on the edge of Apache country. An Apache chief named Sanaba was converted, yet the tribe is described mainly as despoilers of Christian Pueblo Indians. Jesuits in Upper California met them early in the eighteenth century, and their raids near Arizona reservations won them the label Iroquois of the West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apelles:
Apelles, founder of a Gnostic sect, died at a great age late in the second century, and almost all we know of him comes from hostile witnesses. Fragments of his opponent Rhodon, preserved by Eusebius, and Tertullian's Prescription against Heretics supply the record. At Rome he broke from Marcion, whose most famous pupil he had been, and travelled to Alexandria, where he met the seer Philumene and treated her utterances as inspired.

He gathered her oracles in a book called Manifestations and wrote a long work, Syllogisms, attacking Mosaic theology, the teaching of Moses in the Old Testament. Gnosticism, the movement he joined, claimed secret saving knowledge beyond ordinary faith. His moral character is judged differently by Rhodon's plain portrait of an aged teacher and by Tertullian's tales of early scandal, told, the article notes, not without exaggeration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aphraates:
Aphraates, called the Persian Sage, heads the long roll of Syriac writers whose works survive, and his life must be pieced together from his own writings. Born of pagan parents in the later third century, very likely on the frontier of the Persian empire, he converted to Christianity. He embraced religious life and later became a bishop, taking the Christian name Jacob. That name caused centuries of confusion, since his works were long assigned to Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, who died in 338.

Only in the tenth century was the Persian Sage finally identified as Aphraates. A British Museum manuscript dated 1364 calls him bishop of the monastery of Mar Mattai, along the eastern shore of the Tigris near modern Mosul. Its ruins, now Sheikh Matta, can still be seen. The entry untangles a long case of mistaken identity and sets a fourth-century Syriac author in his frontier world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostles:
Apostles, from Greek apostello, to send forth, means in root sense one dispatched on a mission. In classical writers the word is rare and in the Greek Old Testament it occurs once, but in the New Testament it appears about eighty times. This article supplies brief essential information under seven heads. They are the name, its various meanings, the origin of the apostolate, the office and required qualities of apostles, and their authority and privileges. It also covers their relation to bishops and the origin of their feasts.

Linked articles fill out single apostles. The entry thus works as a hub, defining the office and tracing how twelve men commissioned by Christ became the model for later church authority. It sorts the many uses of a word that ranges from the Twelve to missionaries in general. Readers who want the whole framework in one place will find it here.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-chu:
Apostolic Churches takes its name from an epithet, apostolikos, found as early as about 110 in Ignatius's letter to the Trallians. There he greets that church in apostolic character, after the manner of the apostles. From the end of the second century the word grows common in phrases such as apostolic man, apostolic writing, and apostolic churches. In a broad sense every orthodox church could be called apostolic, since each stood in some connection with the apostles, and Tertullian sometimes uses the phrase that way.

Usually, however, western writers of the second to the fourth century mean something narrower: the ancient local churches founded by an apostle, or at least governed by one. They therefore enjoyed special dignity as witnesses to true teaching. Irenaeus often appeals to such churches. The entry sorts loose and strict uses of a proud title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-ind:
Apostolic indulgences are those the Roman pontiff, as successor of Peter, prince of the apostles, attaches to crosses, crucifixes, chaplets, rosaries, images, and medals. He blesses them by his own hand or through delegates. The general principles of indulgences apply here too, but since these are among the most frequent and abundant indulgences now in use, they merit separate, fuller treatment. Some are plenary, remitting all temporal punishment due to sin, and others partial, remitting part of it.

Possession of a blessed object is not by itself the condition for gaining its indulgences. It enables the holder to gain them by performing certain set good works or acts of piety, much as local or personal limits shape other indulgences. The entry explains a practice woven into daily Catholic devotion: a blessed medal or rosary becomes, through the pope's blessing, a channel for indulgences earned by prayer and good deeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-argyll-and-th:
Argyll and the Isles joins two Scottish dioceses with tangled histories. Argyll, founded about 1200 and separated from Dunkeld, covered western Dunkeld beyond the Drumalban mountains, with the Isle of Lismore, where its cathedral stood. Its first bishop was Harold, chaplain to Dunkeld's bishop, chosen for his knowledge of Gaelic. The Diocese of the Isles covered islands off Scotland's west coast, formerly under Norway and joined to the Scottish crown in 1206.

The archbishop of Trondheim kept jurisdiction over the islands. In the mid-fourteenth century the Hebrides were separated ecclesiastically from the Isle of Man, which fell under Canterbury and later York. A century and a half later Alexander VI, at James IV's request, united the See of the Isles with the abbacy of Iona. The two offices were held thereafter by one person, with the new diocese's cathedral at Iona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aristides:
Aristides, a Christian apologist of Athens in the second century, wrote a defence of Christianity presented to Emperor Hadrian at Athens in 126. Eusebius reports that Hadrian, staying in Greece from 123 to 127, had himself initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries. Local Christians then faced persecution, probably from pagan zeal stirred by the emperor's act. Two apologies were written for the occasion, one by Quadratus and one by Aristides.

Jerome calls Aristides a most eloquent philosopher and says his Apology was woven from philosophers' sayings and later imitated by Justin Martyr. Jerome adds that the work survived in his own day and was highly thought of, and Eusebius in the fourth century says it circulated widely among Christians. The entry follows a lost-then-found defence from imperial court to later readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ashes:
Ashes in liturgy raise a hard question: what did their use first mean? Christian ritual surely borrowed from Jewish practice, kept in details of synagogue ceremony to this day, but Jewish custom itself needs explaining. Old Testament passages link ashes, efer, with mourning: the mourner sat or rolled in ashes, sprinkled his head, or mingled food with them. Yet efer might often better read as dust, since the same phrases occur with afar, which certainly means dust.

Dust may first have come from the grave, as a sign the living felt one with the dead. Or humiliation and neglect of cleanliness may have been the dominant idea, since a like show of grief appears among Aryan peoples, as in Homer's Iliad. The entry weighs grave dust against humiliation, tracing a mourning sign from Jewish custom into Christian liturgy without forcing a single origin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asperges:
Asperges, from Latin aspergere, to sprinkle, is the ceremony of sprinkling the people with holy water before the principal Sunday Mass. It is named for the words intoned at its start, taken from Psalm 51 through the year, except at Eastertide, when Vidi aquam, from Psalm 117, is sung instead. It precedes any other ceremony before Mass, such as blessing palms or candles.

The celebrant, wearing vestments of the day's liturgical colour, performs it, and it is dropped when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed. Many rubricists think only the sprinkling of the altar, not the congregation, should then be omitted. After singing the antiphon the priest recites Psalm 51 or 118 by season, sprinkling altar front and platform, then himself, then ministers and choir. Lastly he sprinkles the congregation, usually walking through the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attaliates:
Michael Attaliates, probably born in Attalia in Pamphylia, reached Constantinople in the 1130s and rose to the highest offices. He served, among other posts, as judge of the empire's supreme court. In 1072 he compiled a handbook of Byzantine law for Emperor Michael Parapinakes, filling gaps in the great Basilica law books. Five years later he founded a poorhouse and monastery in the capital and wrote its rule.

That rule is prized for what it shows of eleventh-century Byzantine daily life, including a catalogue of the house library. Around 1079 he published a history of Byzantium from 1034 to 1079, written as an eyewitness to palace coups. The entry praises his sound judgment and fairness, ranking him above his successor Psellos. It closes by tracing the later printings of his law book, his monastery rule, and his history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-autos-sacrame:
Autos sacramentales were a form of Spanish drama, a play about the mystery of the Eucharist. The form belongs peculiarly to Spain, though it recalls England's morality plays. Its characters were usually allegories: Faith, Hope, Air, Sin, Death, and the Virtues, Vices, and Elements, . Some plays held no human character at all. Earlier religious plays at Christmas and Easter were simple dialogues, but the first true auto on the Eucharist was Gil Vicente's Auto de San Martin.

Through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the autos grew richer until Calderon brought them to their height. They were staged in the streets during the feast of Corpus Christi, after a solemn procession, with music and splendor at public cost with the Church's blessing. Allegory had long gripped the Spanish people, and the plays held strong popular favor. Charles III forbade their public staging in 1765, yet they lingered in smaller towns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxilius-of-n:
Auxilius of Naples is the name, probably fictitious according to Hefele, of a churchman behind remarkable writings on Pope Formosus and his fate. Auxilius was a Frank, ordained priest or perhaps only deacon at Rome by Formosus, who later lived at Naples. After Formosus died, the papacy sank into deep humiliation. Stephen VI abused the dead pope's memory and body, and Stephen was strangled in prison in 897. Six popes in turn owed their rise to party strife.

Sergius III, who overthrew the last of them in 904, held Formosus's elevation illegal and his orders null and void. Auxilius, a follower of Formosus, answered about 908 to 911 with a learned defense of Formosus and of his orders' validity. Morinus first printed two of the works in 1665. A Monte Cassino necrology notes an Auxilius, deacon and monk, who died on 25 January, and he may be the same man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-averroes:
Averroes, Abul Walid Mahommed Ibn Achmed Ibn Roschd, was a philosopher, astronomer, and writer on jurisprudence. He was born at Cordova in 1126 and died at Morocco in 1198. His father and grandfather had both served as cadi, judge in civil affairs, in Andalusia. He studied jurisprudence, medicine, mathematics, philosophy, and theology, and he won favor at court under the caliphs Abu Jacub Jusuf and his son.

He held civil offices at Morocco, Seville, and Cordova. Then he fell from favor and was banished with other learned men. Shortly before his death the edict against philosophers was recalled, but many of his works had already burned, so he left no school. Moorish rule in Spain soon ended, and Averroism passed wholly into Hebrew and Latin channels, shaping Christian Europe to the modern era. His Commentaries on Aristotle won him the name Commentator, and his medical Colliget appeared in the 1527 Latin Aristotle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-azores:
The Azores, Portuguese Acores, meaning Falcons, are an archipelago in the Atlantic Sargasso Sea. The nine islands run from southeast to northwest between the 37th and 40th parallels and the 24th and 32nd meridians. They form three groups: Sao Miguel and Santa Maria in the southeast, Fayal, Pico, Sao Jorge, Terceira, and Graciosa, and Flores and Corvo in the northwest. They span 922 square miles, from Sao Miguel at 288 to Corvo at no more than five.

Volcanic in origin, they show broken shapes, with Pico's volcano rising 8,500 feet and the Vara in Sao Miguel above 5,500. Extinct craters, called caldeiras, mark the ranges, and one on Graciosa forms a lake of pitch. Mineral springs abound on nearly every island. The Diocese of Angra holds 110 parishes, a cathedral chapter of twelve canons, and a seminary training 120 students. Its secular clergy number 353, while Angra city holds 11,000 people and Ponta Delgada 6,000 more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-azymes:
Azymes, from Greek azymos, without leaven, are the unleavened cakes used by Jews in sacrifices and rites. The Law commanded them in offerings, and prescribed them for the Passover, when Israel left Egypt in haste. Because they were quick to prepare, they also served ordinary life for unexpected guests and in times of need. At the Exodus itself they won the name bread of affliction. In First Corinthians, unleavened bread stands as a type of sincerity and truth.

Unleavened cakes belonged especially to the Feast of Azymes, the solemn feast, instituted to recall deliverance from Egyptian bondage. It began on the fifteenth of Abib, or Nisan, the month of new corn, and ran seven days, with first and last days specially solemn. No other bread was allowed during the whole feast. Though first distinct, the Feast of Azymes and the Passover are often treated as one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-azymites:
Azymites, from a privative and zyme, leaven, is a term of reproach Greeks have used since the eleventh century against Latins. The Latins, with Armenians and Maronites, celebrate the Eucharist with unleavened bread. A few Latin writers retorted with Fermentarians and Prozymites. The West has always held consecration valid with leavened or unleavened bread, so Latin bitterness had cause.

Whether Christ's Last Supper bread was leavened or not remains open. Early Church usage is so scant and contradictory that many theologians call the problem insoluble. By the ninth century unleavened bread was universal. Greeks, stressing the gap between Jewish and Christian Pasch, used leavened bread. Photius, alert to Latin faults, never pressed the point, but two centuries later the quarrel resumed under a less scrupulous patriarch. Modern Russians claim the crusade against azyms, though treatises tied to Leontius of Kiev seem from a later pen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balearic-isle:
The Balearic Isles are a Spanish group in the western Mediterranean, four larger islands and eleven smaller ones. Majorca, Minorca, Iviza, and Formentera lead the group, and Palma is the capital. In 1900 the province covered 1,936 square miles and held 311,649 people, almost all Catholic. The islanders were Iberians, famed in antiquity as slingers. Carthage subdued them in the seventh century BC, and Mago, Hannibal's brother, built Mahon in 206 BC.

Metellus conquered the islands in 123 to 122 BC and founded Palma and Pollentia. Vandals followed in 426, then Byzantine rule under Justinian, a Frankish spell under Charlemagne, and Arab rule from 798. About 1230 James I of Aragon took them, and from 1276 to 1343 they formed the independent kingdom of Majorca. Minorca spent most of 1708 to 1783 under England, returning to Spain by the Peace of Versailles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptistines:
Baptistines covers three groups named for St John the Baptist: hermits, missionary priests, and sisters. The French hermits were founded about 1630 by Michel de Saint-Sabine, who reformed and united hermits across dioceses. Each diocese gained a visitor, four majors, and a secretary, and its brothers met yearly under the bishop. Metz in 1633 and Cambrai in 1634 first made his statutes obligatory.

Jean-Baptiste carried the reform to Vienne, Lyons, Geneva, Le Puy, and Langres, and died at Angers in 1691. The missionary priests, founded by the Genoese Domenico Olivieri, evangelized cities and countryside. The sisters kept rigorous cloister in Italy, rising at midnight for Matins, sleeping clothed, going barefoot, and fasting always. Several of their convents survived in Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bardesanes-an:
Bardesanes, or Bar-Daisan, was a Syrian poet, astrologist, and philosopher, born at Edessa in 154 and dead there in 222. His name means Son of the Daisan, the river of Edessa, and his wealthy parents were Persian or Parthian. He was schooled with the Osrhoenic crown prince at Abgar Manu VIII's court. Driven to Hierapolis, paganism's stronghold, he learned Babylonian astrology in a heathen priest's house, a training that marked his life.

At twenty-five he heard Bishop Hystaspes of Edessa, was baptized, and entered the diaconate or priesthood. When his boyhood friend Abgar IX took the throne in 179, Bardesanes took his place at court. He left a son, Harmonius, and is called the Parthian, the Babylonian, and the Armenian by different ancient writers. His teaching set a living, knowing light against a dead, ignorant darkness, with evil flowing from nature alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barnabites:
Barnabites is the popular name for the Regular Clerics of St Paul, a title Paul III gave the order in 1535. Three Italian noblemen founded it: Anton Maria Zaccaria, Barthélemy Ferrari, and Jacopo Morigia of Milan. Second among regular clerics after the Theatines, it began as a congregation in 1530. Clement VII approved it in 1533, and Paul III's bulls of 1535 and 1543 freed it from diocesan jurisdiction.

Julius III's bulls of 1550 confirmed its privileges and made it a religious order in the strict sense, though members still said Congregation. The name Barnabites came from Milan's church of St Barnabas, gained in the order's earliest years. St Charles Borromeo presided in 1579 over the commission that fixed the order's constitution for good. The general also extends to any bishop the privilege of a monthly Mass for a stated intention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomites:
Bartholomites were Armenian monks who fled to Italy after Egypt's sultan invaded their country in 1296. The first band landed at Genoa, where a church of St Bartholomew gave them their name. Others settled across Italy, from Parma and Florence to Rome, Milan, Naples, and Bologna, growing numerous and prosperous. At first they kept St Basil's Rule and the Armenian Liturgy, with Clement V's acknowledgment of the right.

In time they took the Roman Liturgy, a Dominican-like habit, and St Augustine's Rule in place of Basil's. Innocent VI approved the change in 1356 and joined their monasteries into one congregation under a superior-general. Superiors first served for life, then, from 1474, were elected every three years. Their Genoa church still preserves the celebrated Holy Face of Edessa, a portrait of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilides:
Basilides names martyrs entered on 10, 12, and 28 June in old martyrologies. Eusebius devotes a whole chapter to Basilides and Potamiana of Alexandria, under Septimius Severus. Basilides, a court officer, led Potamiana to execution, shielding her from the mocking rabble. She thanked him, promising to entreat the Lord for him after her death.

Called to swear an oath soon after, he refused, openly confessed himself Christian, and was imprisoned. Christians visiting him heard that Potamiana had appeared three days after her death and crowned him, promising the Lord would soon take him. Baptized, he was beheaded the next day, and the present Roman martyrology lists him on 30 June. The Roman Basilides of 10 and 12 June, martyred on the Via Aurelia, is likely the same martyr twice entered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedictine-a:
Jumièges, a Benedictine abbey on the north bank of the Seine in Normandy, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Founded in 634 by St. Philibert, a courtier turned monk, it soon held nearly a thousand monks under its second abbot, St. Achard. Patronage from the dukes of Normandy made it a centre of religion and learning.

Its schools produced scholars of note, and its monks carried its influence across northern France. Viking raids, rebuilding, and later decline all figure in its long story, though the entry keeps its focus on foundation and flourishing. The abbey stands in the piece as a model of early Norman monastic life.

Lindores, a Benedictine abbey on the River Tay near Newburgh in Fife, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. David, Earl of Huntingdon, founded it about 1191. He was a younger brother of King William the Lion. Monks of the Tironensian branch, brought from Kelso, built a church nearly two hundred feet long, richly endowed by its founder with ten parish churches.

The entry dismisses a romantic foundation tale, repeated by Walter Scott, as unproven fiction, preferring the plainer record. Guido, prior of Kelso, became first abbot and nearly finished the buildings. Lindores appears here as a well-endowed Scottish house with a sober, documented start.

Lobbes, a Benedictine abbey in Hainault, Belgium, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. St. Landelin, a converted brigand, founded it about 650 on the very ground where his crimes had been done, hoping the place might gain by his change of life. He soon resigned as abbot to live austerely, leaving St. Ursmer to preach to the still pagan Belgians.

Lobbes was luckier than most houses in keeping its ancient annals, so its history survives in unusual detail. The entry draws on those annals for abbots, schools, and fame in learning. A house born from one man's repentance thus becomes one of Belgium's best-recorded monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bequests-for-:
Bequests for Masses in the United States receive a legal entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, centred on New York courts. The Court of Appeals there affirmed that prayer for the dead is a Catholic doctrine entitled to the same legal respect as any other faith's observance. Yet in Holland v. Alcock it still voided a gift for Masses, for want of a definite beneficiary.

Later cases and a statute of 1893 restored the old doctrine of charitable uses, changing the ground again. The entry follows this zigzag through Williams, Holland, O'Conner, and Bowman, showing judges and lawmakers correcting each other. It is a case study in how American law learned to handle a Catholic gift.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-sylve:
Bernard Sylvester, more properly of Tours, was a twelfth-century philosopher of Neo-Platonic bent, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Little is known of him beyond his work. Between 1145 and 1153 he wrote On the Universe of the World, dedicating it to Thierry of Chartres, a dedication suggesting he studied at the famous school of Chartres.

The treatise blends Plato's cosmology with medieval learning, picturing the world shaped by divine mind and nature. It must not be confused with the work of Bernard of Chartres, who died in 1125. The entry is a short, careful note separating two Bernards and their books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berno-apostle:
Berno, Apostle of the Obotrites, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. The Obotrites were a Slav tribe, called Wends, living along the Baltic in Mecklenburg. Three bishoprics raised in their land in the tenth century had stood empty through most of the eleventh, until Duke Henry the Lion subdued the people and restored them.

In 1155 Henry chose Berno, a Cistercian monk of Amelungsborn, as Bishop of Mecklenburg. From there Berno preached, built churches, and planted Christian life among a people fresh from paganism. The entry presents a missionary bishop rebuilding a church that invasion had emptied.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bestiaries:
Bestiaries, medieval books on animals, receive a compact entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. In these books the traits of beasts, real and fancied alike, were read as religious symbols. Lions and eagles stand beside griffins, dragons, sirens, and unicorns, all pointing to Christ, the devil, virtues, and vices.

The habit came from antiquity and above all from the ancient East, where Eastern and Greco-Roman writing tied animals to gods and human life. Christian writers took the beast lore and turned each creature into a moral lesson. The entry presents a medieval world where natural history doubled as preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethlehemites:
Bethlehemites, the name of two military orders devoted to Our Lady of Bethlehem, receive a long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Matthew Paris notes the first, whose English house Henry III allowed at Cambridge in 1257, though founder and origin stay unknown. Their habit matched the Dominicans, with a red five-rayed star on the cape.

The second order, founded by Pius II in 1459 to fight the Turks, wore white with a red cross and followed a rule like the Knights of St. John. Endowed with suppressed orders' property, it died when Lemnos fell again to the Turks. The entry also notes a later hospital order of Bethlehem in the Americas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bible-societi:
Bible societies, Protestant groups founded to print and spread the Bible worldwide, receive a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. They spring from the Protestant principle of Scripture alone as the rule of faith, a formula the entry traces to Chillingworth. Heroic efforts to put a Bible in every tongue follow from taking that formula literally.

Early societies for the poor, for soldiers and sailors, and for the American colonies came first. Then came the great British and Foreign Bible Society of 1804, founded by Nonconformist ministers and laymen after a revival against religious apathy. The entry follows its translations, agents, and Catholic objections in a long, critical survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-anti:
Biblical antiquities, the study of ancient Israel's inner life, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It defines archaeology narrowly, excluding chronology, geography, and natural history, and focusing on records, homes, social and religious life, manners, and customs. Monumental remains and written sources anchor the survey.

From tents to houses, villages, and walled cities, the entry follows settlement growth, clan and tribe organization, and the standing a man held in his clan. Flocks gave way to trade by the early monarchy. The piece is a vast handbook of daily life behind the Bible's stories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-mary-anne-:
Blessed Mary Anne de Paredes, called the Lily of Quito, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Quito in 1618 to a noble Toledo father and a Spanish mother of high family, she died there in 1645. Unusual signs in the heavens at her birth were attested in her beatification process, the entry says.

From infancy she showed a pull toward prayer, fasting, and devotion to the Virgin, living as a recluse in her sister's house rather than entering a convent. Fasts, vigils, and charity marked a short life that made her Ecuador's beloved saint. The entry presents a girl mystic of the Andes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-cuneg:
Blessed Cunegundes, a Poor Clare honoured as patroness of Poland and Lithuania, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1224, daughter of King Bela IV of Hungary and niece of St. Elizabeth, she died at Sandeck in 1292. With reluctance she married Boleslaus II, Duke of Cracow, and soon after, the pious couple vowed perpetual chastity before the Bishop of Cracow.

When Boleslaus died in 1279, Cunegundes refused the kingdom's government, sold all her goods for the poor, and entered the Poor Clares at Sandeck, which she had founded. Thirteen years of prayer, penance, and heroic humility followed, never letting anyone dwell on her former queenship. Alexander VIII approved her cult in 1690, and she became Poland's chief patroness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-jean-:
Blessed Jean Eudes, French missionary and founder of the Eudists, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Ri in France in 1601, brother of the historian François Eudes, he died at Caen in 1680. A vow of chastity at fourteen and Jesuit schooling at Caen led him to the Oratory in 1623, under Bérulle and Condren.

Ordained in 1625, he laboured heroically among plague victims, then preached missions across Normandy for decades. He founded the Congregation of Jesus and Mary, the Eudists, for seminaries, and the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity for fallen women. His liturgical devotion to the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary crowns the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boni-homines:
Boni Homines, or Bonshommes, was a popular name shared by at least three religious orders. The Grandmont order, founded by Stephen of Muret for austere hermits under Augustine's rule, held more than sixty houses by the late twelfth century, chiefly in Aquitaine, Anjou, and Normandy. English kings, then rulers of Normandy, favored these friars, whose oldest house stood at Vincennes.

The Fratres Saccati, or Brothers of Penitence, also bore the name, with houses at Saragossa and Valenciennes by Innocent III's time and a London house by 1257. Edmund of Cornwall later founded their Ashridge monastery. A third use came when the Minims took over the Vincennes house and inherited the Bonshommes name. Grandmont's houses were suppressed at the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-jubil:
The Book of Jubilees, an apocryphal writing also called Little Genesis, retells biblical history on a rigid calendar of jubilee periods. Every event falls in a stated week, month, and year of a forty-nine-year jubilee, on a scheme of sevens. Seven days make the week, four times seven the month, and fifty-two times seven the year of 364 days. Its author claims heavenly authority for this impossible solar year.

Little Genesis means lesser authority, not lesser size, since the book runs longer than canonical Genesis. It is also called the Apocalypse of Moses and the Life of Adam, and Kufale in Ethiopic. Written first in Hebrew, it survives complete only in Ethiopic, with Greek and Latin fragments. Dillmann edited the Ethiopic text in 1859, Ceriani the Latin version in 1861, and Charles produced the standard English edition in 1902.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bourges:
Bourges, archdiocese of the Cher and Indre departments, traces its church to Saint Ursinus near the close of the third century. After the Concordat of 1802 it became metropolitan over Clermont, Saint-Flour, and Limoges, adding Tulle and Le Puy in 1822. Duchesne dates Ursinus by counting back from Leo, twelfth bishop in 453, past the mission of the twelve bishops in 250.

Fifteen saints stand among Leo's successors to the ninth century, including Sulpicius II, who gave his name to Paris's Saint-Sulpice. Later bishops include Guillaume de Donjeon, the theologian Giles of Rome, and Jean Coeur, under whom the university rose. Bourges still claims the primacy of Aquitaine, kept its title despite Clement V, and hosted councils in 1225, 1438, and 1528.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bridgewater-t:
The Bridgewater Treatises, eight works on God's power, wisdom, and goodness in creation, came from the Earl of Bridgewater's will. Francis Henry Egerton, eighth earl, died in 1829 leaving eight thousand pounds to the Royal Society's president, to pay writers of works proving design from nature, arts, sciences, and literature.

President Davies Gilbert, advised by Canterbury, London's bishop, and a friend of the earl, split the fund among eight authors. Chalmers wrote on man's moral frame, Prout on chemistry and digestion, Kirby on animals, Bell on the hand, Buckland on geology, Kidd on man's body, Whewell on astronomy, and Roget on physiology. Critics faulted the choices, and the books, once famed in apologetics, are now nearly forgotten.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brigittines:
The Brigittines, or Order of Saint Saviour, founded by Saint Bridget of Sweden at Vadstena in 1346, joined monks and nuns under an abbess called Sovereign. Bridget, a Swedish princess wed to Ulf of Mercia, was widowed in 1344 and received the rule in vision two years later. With King Magnus's help she built a double house, where her daughter Katherine became first abbess after her death in 1375.

Monks and nuns shared a chapel but lived in separate wings, passing food and clothes through a turnstile, with the confessor alone crossing to the nuns. The abbess ruled all temporal affairs for both houses, while the monks' superior guided the nuns in spiritual things. The Rule capped choir nuns at sixty, with thirteen priests for the apostles, four deacons for the doctors, and eight lay brothers, matching the apostles and seventy-two disciples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-o: The Brothers of Our Lady of Lourdes, founded at Renaix, Flanders, in 1830 by the Belgian priest Etienne Modeste Glorieux, teach youth and care for the sick and infirm. Approved by Leo XIII in 1892, the congregation counts 518 members, with its mother-house at Oostacker, Belgium, and thirty filial houses. One house stands in the United States, at South Park in the Seattle diocese. Thirteen brothers there run a house of studies and a day and boarding school for boys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bruges:
Bruges, chief town of West Flanders, grew from a marsh burg into a wealthy merchant city under the counts of Flanders. Nicholas I reconciled Charles the Bald with Baldwin Bras-de-Fer in 863, forgiving his abduction of Judith and granting him the northern marches. Baldwin built a stronghold on an old burg of 366, housing Saint Donatian's relics, and checked the Northmen, drawing merchants and artisans to settle.

Arnulph the Great, count from 918 to 989, endowed Saint Donatian's chapter, founded collegiate churches, and built or restored eighteen great monasteries. Baldwin IV's charter of liberties spurred trade until walls had to stretch in 1039. Crusaders added fame and relics: Robert II brought Saint Basil's relics, Thierry of Alsace brought the Holy Blood, and Baldwin IX carried Bruges's name to the Latin East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buenos-aires:
Buenos Aires, federal capital of Argentina and second city of the Latin world, holds 1,100,000 people on the Plata's right bank. The river's mouth spans over 108 miles, narrowing to about 43 miles at the city, which stands some 65 feet above sea level. With a death rate of 14 per thousand, it ranks in sanitation with the world's most advanced cities, and snow never falls there.

Its climate swings sharply, with north winds bringing humid heat and storms, then the cold, dry Pampero sweeping the sky clean with ozone. Mean temperature stands near 62 degrees, with highs at times reaching 95. From 300 settlers in 1580, the city grew to 11,118 in 1744, 177,787 in 1869, 663,854 in 1895, and 1,109,202 by July 1907. Growth runs 46 per thousand yearly, mostly from immigration, with Italians the largest foreign group.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cades:
Cades, or Cadesbarne, stood on the extreme southern border of Palestine, its Hebrew name Qadesh meaning Holy. After Sinai it holds the chief place in the story of Israel's forty years in the desert. From Cades spies scouted Canaan, and the gloomy report of all but Caleb and Joshua stirred a mutiny. That mutiny condemned the people to thirty-eight more years of wandering.

At Cades Mary, the sister of Moses, died. Water flowed a second time from the rock, and after that Moses and Aaron were barred from the Promised Land for want of trust. From Cades Moses also asked the King of Edom for passage, and on refusal the people turned aside through the Arabah valley. Scholars differ on how long the stay at Cades lasted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cainites:
The name Cainites covers both the descendants of Cain and a sect of Gnostics and Antinomians. Genesis lists nine of Cain's line in direct descent: Henoch, Irad, Maviael, Mathusael, and Lamech, whose children by Ada were Jabel and Jubal and by Sella were Tubalcain and Noemi. Cain built a city named for his son Henoch, and the names of Lamech's children read as trades: Jabel the shepherd, Jubal the musician, and Tubalcain the smith.

The names' roots are disputed, some Hebrew, some Babylonian or Sumerian, and four Sethite names match Cainite ones, with Henoch and Lamech identical in both lines. Read in English, the passage suggests the rise of polygamy and the spread of crafts under figures of speech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cana-canaanit:
Canaan names both a person and a land. In the Old Testament Canaan is a son of Ham. The land of Canaan is the country of his descendants, a name found as Kinahhi in the Amarna letters two centuries before Moses and as Ka-n-'-na in older Egyptian records. When Phoenician traders stood high among the Canaanites, the word also came to mean merchant or trader.

Scholars derive the name from a root meaning low, humble, or subjected, reading the land of Canaan as the low land, though biblical tradition traces the land's name to the person Canaan. Noah's curse made Canaan a servant of servants to his brothers Shem and Japheth, a figure that fits the name's sense of servant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candles:
The candle, from the Latin candela, came into English as a church term, likely by the eighth century. In classical times it meant any taper with a wick, often papyrus, cased in wax or animal fat. Candles, like incense and lustral water, served pagan worship and rites for the dead. The Church took them into her service early, as she took other things indifferent in themselves that could grace worship.

Tapers borne before pope or bishop in procession, or carried with the Gospel book to the pulpit, likely adapted a secular honor paid to high Roman officials. Masses of candles and lamps marked the Easter vigil from near-apostolic times, and Eusebius tells how Constantine's pillars of wax turned night into day. Daytime burning in cemeteries drew rebuke at Elvira about 300 as a superstitious abuse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-fac:
A faculty in law is authority, privilege, or permission for an act. Broadly it is any power to act validly or lawfully, whether from one's own right or another's favor. Strictly it means a superior with jurisdiction granting a subordinate church rights that common law denies him, to act validly, lawfully, or at least safely, in the outer or inner forum.

Faculties split first by object. Jurisdiction covers sins, censures, vows, irregularities, and marriage bars; licenses cover acts like reading banned books or saying two Masses in a day; and precautionary grants cover cases where theologians disagree. By source they are apostolic, from the pope or Roman congregations; episcopal, from a diocesan bishop; or regular, from religious superiors. General faculties cover undesignated persons, particular ones named persons or cases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canticle-of-c:
The Canticle of Canticles, also called the Song of Songs, stands among the three books of Solomon in the Hebrew, Greek, and Christian canons. Its name means the most excellent song. The entry reads it as a lyrico-dramatic exchange between Solomon and the Sulamitess. A wedding-day passage at its center uses procession, wreath, and bridal bed to mark the marriage.

Later sections work through the allegorical reading, the literary form, and the book's unity. They take up hard passages and questions of age and authorship. They weigh the state of the Hebrew text, where scholars such as Gratz, Bickell, Budde, and Cheyne argue over mistakes and changes. The entry thus joins a close reading of the love poetry to the history of its interpretation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-captivities-o:
The captivities of the Israelites cover the successive exiles that broke the Hebrew kingdoms. They run from the Assyrian captivity of the north to the Babylonian exile of Judah and the Roman captivity after the fall of Jerusalem. The entry opens with the northern kingdom under Jeroboam II, prosperous on the surface. Beneath that bloom, in the prophets' picture, lay calf worship, high-place rites, and moral corruption.

Later sections follow the ten tribes into exile and Assyrian pressure on Judah. They recount the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile with its effects. They trace the prelude to restoration. Finally they reach the Roman captivity, when captives filled mines and arenas. Children under seventeen were sold as slaves, and rebel leaders John and Simon were paraded in Titus's triumph. The sweep joins political narrative to prophetic judgment across many centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capuchinesses:
Capuchinesses belong to the Poor Clares who keep the original observance, founded at Naples in 1538 by Maria Longo. Longo had embraced the Third Order of St. Francis, founded a hospital where she served the sick, and worked to rescue fallen women. She built a convent called Santa Maria in Gerusalemme and became its superior.

Theatine fathers first directed the convent, then Capuchins took over its direction. On Capuchin advice the sisters adopted the primitive Rule of St. Clare in 1538, with constitutions modeled on the Capuchin Friars and obedience to the Capuchin vicar-general. A Rome foundation followed in 1576, houses spread across Europe and South America, and exiled French sisters opened a German novitiate at Vaals in Holland in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caraites:
Caraites are a Jewish sect that follows the text of the Bible, the Miqra, while rejecting rabbinical tradition and the Talmud. Their Hebrew name means followers of the Bible. Older doubters of tradition, such as the Sadducees, foreshadowed them. Caraism in the strict sense began with Anan, who died about 780 and gave the movement its early name, Ananism.

The sect grew among Jews until the tenth century, when Saadia al-Fayyumi answered it with force. An eleventh-century struggle in Spain, shaped by Joseph Faussol and Judah ben Ezra, drove Caraism almost wholly from Western Europe, though it held on in the East. Its Sabbath law is strict, its views on cleanliness recall Essenism, and in practice it has taken over many rabbinical customs it rejects in theory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-virt:
The cardinal virtues are the four chief virtues, with the rest of the moral virtues turning on them as on a hinge. The word itself comes from cardo, a hinge. The entry finds its early uses in Ambrose and Augustine, with a supposed Jerome use resting on a work not truly his. Thomas Aquinas draws out the senses of cardinal, generic and specific, from this hinge image.

Four conditions mark every moral virtue: sound judgment, service to the common good, restraint within measure, and firmness. Those four conditions yield four distinct virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, whose roots the entry traces to Greek thought through Plato, Aristotle, and the reporters of Socrates. Later writers from Peter Lombard to Thomas carry the fourfold scheme into Christian moral teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-cong:
Catholic congresses are public gatherings where Catholics meet to discuss matters close to their hearts. Some assemblies speak as delegates of a whole country, while others gather as members of one association pursuing its own aims. Taken together, they show that modern Catholic life is not confined to church devotions. Men of every rank, calling, age, and nation took part, stirred by the nineteenth-century revival in church life.

The first large congress met among German Catholics in the revolutionary year 1848. The article traces the movement's growth through France and other countries. It covers its international congresses, and its national, religious, sociological, political, and educational forms. Cheaper travel, wider social interests, and modern political freedom all helped make such gatherings possible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-dire:
A directory, in its church sense, is a guide for the daily recitation of the Office and Mass. The Latin directorium means guide. Yet by the later Middle Ages the word had a special use: books that told clergy which Mass and Office to say each day of the year. Clement Maydeston gave the title Directorium Sacerdotum to his reordered Sarum Ordinal in the early fifteenth century, and similar guides appeared across Europe.

Each diocese has its own calendar. So a directory had to fit the diocese or group of dioceses it served. The article follows the word from these liturgical guides to its modern confusion with the secular sense. It surveys present-day directories, including those of the United States and Canada, with their sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-indi:
From the first discoveries, the governments of Catholic Spain and France treated the spiritual welfare of America's Indigenous peoples as a central concern. Early patents for exploration and settlement said so plainly. The 1532 grant to Ayllón for the Florida coast made bringing the inhabitants to the faith the chief motive of the enterprise. It ordered that priests, vestments, and all needs of worship be paid from the colony's revenues.

The article surveys the missions that followed, region by region. It moves from Maryland and the Ohio country to New Mexico, California, and the Columbia region. It closes with a roll of missionary martyrs, Franciscans and others killed in Texas, California, and elsewhere between the sixteenth century and 1833.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-soci:
Catholic societies exist in great numbers around the world, some international, some national, some diocesan, and some parochial.
