Individual societies are treated under their own titles elsewhere in the encyclopedia; this article deals only with societies in general. It defines a society as a lasting, voluntary association of people who pledge themselves to work together for a particular good of soul or body.

The piece roots the right of association in natural law and recalls how the early Church worked under the guise of a private corporation in pagan Rome. Once free, it encouraged guilds and fraternities. These stayed under church supervision. The article then distinguishes societies for laymen from those for clerics. For clerics, the most complete form is the religious order bound by perpetual vows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-trut:
Catholic Truth Societies are treated here in the order they were founded in each country. In England the society lived twice: Cardinal Vaughan first launched it while rector of St. Joseph's Missionary College, but it lapsed when he became Bishop of Salford in 1872. A separate group of priests and laymen then raised twelve pounds to print prayer cards, and Vaughan suggested they take the old society's name and place.

Formally established on 5 November 1884 under Vaughan's presidency, the revived society spread small devotional works and defended Catholic truth, later under Cardinal Bourne. The article follows the same pattern in Ireland, Australia, and the United States, where societies fought false textbook statements and built links with agencies in fifteen foreign countries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cedes:
Cedes, Hebrew Qedesh meaning sanctuary, names two cities of Palestine. The better known, Cedes in Naphtali or in Galilee, was a Levitical city and a place of refuge. Its name suggests it was already sacred before the Hebrew occupation. Barac made it his home, and there he and Debbora gathered an army chiefly from Naphtali, Zabulon, and Issachar before facing Sisara near Mount Thabor.

Later history was less kind: under King Phacee of Israel it was taken by Tiglath-pileser, and its people were carried captive to Assyria. During the Maccabean wars Jonathan beat the generals of Demetrius II near the city, and in the great Jewish rebellion Titus camped beneath its walls before taking Gishala. A second Cedes, in Issachar, is distinguished from it in the sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestines:
The Celestines were a group of extreme Spiritual Franciscans of the Marches, so called because Celestine V took them under his special protection. They must not be confused with the Benedictine Celestine hermits, the order the same pope had founded about 1254 before becoming pope. In the autumn of 1294 Pietro da Macerata, Pietro da Fossombrone, and other Spirituals lately returned from Armenia reached the papal curia at Aquila.

There Celestine allowed them to live apart as hermits, following the Rule of St. Francis, as a separate fraternity free of the Minorite superiors. They obeyed Celestine and, under him, Pietro da Macerata, renamed Liberato, while his companion took the name Angelo Clareno. Cardinal Nicholas Orsini became their protector, and they were called the Poor Hermits of the Lord Celestine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cemeteries:
Cemeteries takes its name from the Greek koimeterion, a sleeping place, used in early literature almost only for Jewish and Christian burial grounds. Though the word now means a separate, park-like enclosure apart from any churchyard, it once applied to any single tomb or whole graveyard. It was the usual term for the subterranean burial places now called catacombs. An imperial edict of 259 already speaks of their so-called cemeteries as a distinctive name.

At first Gospel converts were content to share the graves of their Jewish brethren without distinction. But that arrangement could not last. The article follows burial through the early history of cemeteries, burial in churches, and medieval and monastic cemeteries. It closes with the consecration of cemeteries and sources on burial law in America, England, and Quebec.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cham-chamites:
Cham, or Ham in the Authorized Version, was Noah's son and father of one of three great races in the Genesis 10 table. Wherever the Bible lists Noah's three sons, Cham stands between Sem and Japhet. Genesis 9:24 calls him the younger son, so the order does not follow age. The only recorded incident of his life after the Flood comes in Genesis 9:21-24. Cham finds his father drunk and naked in his tent and tells his brothers, who cover the patriarch respectfully.

Noah's response shows Cham's great irreverence on that occasion. Shem and Japhet receive his blessing with their posterity, but the curse falls not on Cham himself, rather on his son Chanaan and his descendants, foretelling their servitude. The Chamites, descended from Cham, divide into four families in Genesis 10:6-20: Chus, Mesram, Phuth, and Chanaan. The Cushites spread through the Euphrates and Tigris valleys, Arabia, and Africa, while Mesram is Egypt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charity-and-c:
Charity joins love of God with love of neighbour. As a virtue it disposes a person to love God above all creatures and to love self and neighbour for God's sake. When God infuses that power into the soul it is supernatural; when it grows from repeated acts it is natural. The history that follows runs from the apostolic age through the persecutions. It continues from Constantine to Gregory the Great, through the Middle Ages, and from the late fifteenth century down to today.

Early Christian teaching made the slave a brother in Christ, commanding mild treatment, rest on holy days, and family life. Later centuries brought hospital orders such as St. Lazarus, founded against plague in the twelfth century and dissolved by Innocent VIII. After the Reformation, confiscation of monastic charity and harsher secular landlords deepened distress, above all in England, while giving fell among all classes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chartres:
The French department of Eure-et-Loir forms the Diocese of Chartres. Suppressed in 1802 and placed under Versailles, the see was restored in 1822 as a suffragan, or subordinate diocese, of Paris. Its bishops are traced back to the age of Constantine. The list runs through saints such as Solennis, who helped convert Clovis, to Fulbert, the poet and teacher of 1007 to 1029, whose name is bound up with the cathedral.

Later bishops include Saint Yves, jailed by Philip I, John of Salisbury, once secretary to Becket, and Clausel de Montals. The entry honours the cathedral's relic, the veil said to have been given by Charles the Bald and raised as a standard against the Norman Rollo in 911. By 1900 the diocese ran a foundling asylum, seventeen infant schools, seventeen orphanages, and twenty-one hospitals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-nam:
An entry on Christian names, the forenames given at baptism, whose meaning Camden already saw fading in the sixteenth century. Strictly, a Christian name is not just a personal label set against a family surname, but the name imposed at christening. To christen is to baptise, as the old English form for emergency baptism shows.

Names carried omens in Hebrew thought, given for a child's trait or a parent's hope. A changed state called for a changed name, as Abram became Abraham at the covenant of circumcision. The entry weighs whether naming at baptism came from the apostles, citing Paul, called Saul before conversion. It rejects the claim, since Acts names him Saul well after his baptism and Paul only later. It then traces Christian naming through saints, feasts, and customs across the centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christobal-mo:
An entry on Cristóbal Morales, a Spanish composer born at Seville in January 1512 and dead at Málaga in June 1553. From September 1535 to April 1540 he sang in the papal choir at Rome. Trained in the Netherlands school, he belonged to the group of sixteenth-century Spaniards, with Victoria, Encina, Ribera, and Peñalosa, whose music won Spain a renown that later faded.

Morales wrote in a markedly original style, and many counterpoint devices he invented came into general use after him. His works include masses for four, five, and six voices, Lamentations settings, many motets for three to six voices, and Magnificats in Gregorian modes for four and six voices. Ambros judged the Magnificats his most finished works, and his music survives in the papal archives, in Proske's Musica Divina, and in Eslava's Lira Sacra.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronological:
An entry on the chronological lists of the popes, a body of literature running from the second century to the present day. The article does not discuss every catalogue, and it sends readers to the Liber Pontificalis for the most famous of them. Its aim is narrower: to show, briefly, what grounds the names and lengths of reign for the popes of the first two centuries.

Irenaeus, writing between 175 and 190, lists the series from Peter to Eleutherius to prove that bishops inherit apostolic teaching against heretical novelties. He gives names only, not reign lengths. That gap is filled above all by the Liberian Catalogue, edited in 354, which lists Roman bishops from Peter to Liberius with reign lengths, consular dates, emperors, and details. Its earlier part, to Pontian in 230 to 235, is held to be the work of Hippolytus of Portus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cinites:
The Cinites, also called Kenites, were a tribe or family often named in the Old Testament. Their origin and even the origin of their name remain obscure. Hobab, a relative of Moses, was a Cinite, and the Cinites seem to have belonged to the Madianites. They worshipped Yahweh, and some scholars credit them with shaping much of Israel's monotheistic theology.

Friendly to Israel throughout, the Cinites aided the wanderers in the desert and joined the march on Chanaan. One clan under Haber settled in the north at the time of Barac and Debbora. Jahel, who slew Sisara, was Haber's wife. The Rechabites, a Cinite clan, kept nomadic habits as ascetics. South and north alike, the Cinites lived near Israel without recorded enmity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercians-i:
Saint Stephen Harding, third Abbot of Citeaux from 1109 to 1133, was an Englishman, and his hand in shaping the young order made an English monastic colony natural. In November 1128, with William Giffard, Bishop of Winchester, monks settled at Waverley near Farnham in Surrey. Five houses sprang from Waverley before 1152, some with offshoots of their own.

The northern foundations proved more vigorous in monastic expansion. William, sent from Clairvaux by Saint Bernard in 1131, founded Rivaulx in Yorkshire. Walter Espec gave the land, and by 1143 three hundred monks had entered, including Saint Aelred, called the Saint Bernard of England. Fountains, founded in 1132 by Benedictines of Saint Mary's, York, seeking a sterner monastic observance, soon produced Newminster and Meaux. In 1138 thirteen Savigny houses, among them Furness and Jervaulx, joined the order, and by 1152 England counted fifty-four Cistercian monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-de-sai:
Claude de Sainctes, a French controversialist, was born at Perche in 1525 and died at Crevecoeur in 1591. At fifteen he joined Saint-Cheron's Canons Regular. and took his theology doctorate at the College de Navarre in 1555. His erudition carried him to Poissy in 1561, where Catholics met Huguenots with Beza and Father Lainez present. He then went to Trent as deputy for the University of Paris with Simon Vigor.

He published against the spoliation of Catholic churches, against Calvin and Beza, and a Eucharist treatise, exhaustive in scope. Through the Cardinal of Lorraine he became Bishop of Evreux in 1575 and published the Rouen council records of 1581 in French. Backing the League, he fled when royal troops seized Evreux. Papers approving the murder of Henry the Third brought a death sentence for treason at Caen, commuted by Henry the Fourth to life imprisonment. He died two months later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clementines:
The Clementines are the curious religious romance that has come down in two forms as composed by Pope Saint Clement the First. The Greek form, the Homilies in twenty books, survives in only two manuscripts. The Latin form, the Recognitions, is Rufinus's translation from the Greek; he died in 410. Two later epitomes of the Homilies exist, with a partial Syriac translation. It covers the first three Recognitions and Homilies ten to fourteen. 

Curious rather than admirable, the writings matter chiefly for theories nineteenth-century scholars built on them. Their existence became known in 1572 and 1578 through the Jesuit Turrianus. The first edition, by Cotelier in 1672, lacked the twentieth book and part of the nineteenth. Dressel's 1853 edition first used the complete Vatican manuscript. The Recognitions, very popular in the Middle Ages, tell of Clement and his father Faustus, said to have originated the Faust legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conflict-of-i:
Klemens Löffler's entry treats the Conflict of Investitures, German Investiturstreit, the struggle between popes and German kings Henry IV and Henry V from 1075 to 1122. Banning investiture only occasioned the fight. The real issue, at its height, was whether imperial or papal power would rule Christendom. Gregory VII, ardent and powerful, sought God's Kingdom on earth under papal guidance. He claimed supreme authority in spiritual and secular affairs, trusting Peter's successor could act only by justice, goodness, and truth.

Henry ignored Gregory's ban, naming bishops in Germany and Italy. To general astonishment he came as penitent seeking pardon. Papal supporters ignored the reconciliation, electing Rudolf of Rheinfelden king. Gregory's deposition and Guibert's election as Clement III followed, with Henry crowned emperor by his antipope. Victor III, milder, succeeded Gregory. Henry V, first backed by the pope, later forced success. Peace yielded investitures with ring and staff to the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conimbricense:
John Cassidy's entry explains the Conimbricenses, the Jesuits of Coimbra in Portugal. The college roll at various times listed two hundred Jesuits, professors and students alike. Toward the end of the sixteenth century and the start of the seventeenth, long commentaries on Aristotle's works went forth from the school. Professors dictated these notes to students, never intending publication, yet they were published, but fraudulently.

To explain and disown false, unauthorized printings, Father Claudius Acquaviva, General of the Society of Jesus, charged Father Peter Fonseca, head of the Portuguese province, with overseeing revision for publication. Fonseca, widely known for learning, took up the task. The Coimbra notes on Aristotle's Physics appeared in 1591, with more volumes on other works following. A prefatory note denied any link with a Frankfurt 1604 volume claiming the Conimbricenses name. Later printings added Aristotle's Greek text, and de Backer lists each printing exactly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-celtes:
Joseph Sauer's entry follows Conrad Celtes, properly Conrad Pickel or Meisel, called Protusius in Latin. A German humanist, he was born at Wipfeld in Lower Franconia on 1 February 1459 and died at Vienna on 4 February 1508. He studied at Cologne from 1477 and Heidelberg from 1484, where Dalberg and Agricola stimulated him. Then he wandered as a travelling scholar, lecturing on humanism at Erfurt, Rostock, and Leipzig. At Leipzig he issued his first work, Ars versificandi et carminum, in 1486, plus an edition of Seneca.

That same year he reached Rome, befriending Pomponius Laetus, then travelled Italy, meeting Marsilio Ficino at Florence, Beroaldus at Bologna, and Sabellicus with printer Aldus Manutius at Venice. Returning to Germany, Frederick III crowned him Poet Laureate at Saxon Elector Frederick's instance. His lectures advanced and spread humanistic learning as lastingly as his learned associations, which gathered scholars across German lands and carried classical study into universities and courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consitutio-ro:
Andrew Meehan's entry follows Romanos Pontifices, born from Pius IX's restoration of England's hierarchy on 29 September 1850 through Universalis ecclesiae. Transition raised disputes over rule and discipline, chiefly between bishops and religious orders. Bishops defended hierarchy's rights, while superiors resisted giving up old rights. Chief disputes covered regulars' exemption from bishops, bishops' right to divide regulars' parishes and place secular priests over new missions, and regulars' duty in parish work to attend conferences and synods.

Further points touched appeals, bishops' relations with religious in parish duties, and temporal goods. It states that regulars, though subject to the Holy See under canon law, fall under bishops over small communities. In parish work regulars stand subject to episcopal watch, visits, rule, and correction. Sources print it in the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore and Acta Apostolicae Sedis, with Vaughan's life and Taunton's Law of the Church on the English dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coptic-bibles:
Eugène Hyvernat's entry surveys Coptic Bible versions across four dialects: Bohairic, formerly Memphitic; Fayumic; Sahidic, formerly Theban; and Akhmimic. No Bohairic manuscript, and probably no Fayumic one, predates the ninth century, while some Sahidic and Akhmimic codices appear as old as the fifth, even the fourth, century. In the ninth century Bohairic flourished in Northern Egypt, particularly Bohairah province southwest of Alexandria and the Nitrian monasteries. Sahidic meanwhile spread through Upper Egypt, or Sahid, including Cairo, superseding Fayumic in Fayum province, ancient Crocodilopolis, and Akhmimic around Akhmim, ancient Panopolis.

Versions exist in all four dialects, and all agree on their great value. The Bohairic version's only complete Old Testament books extant are the Pentateuch, Prophets with Lamentations, Psalms, and Job. The Sahidic version was known until recently almost only in fragments, several hundred manuscripts, chiefly from Amba Shnudah's monastery, Shenoute, near Sohag.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-correctories:
Anthony Maas's entry treats correctories, Latin Vulgate texts fixed by scholars in the thirteenth century. Scribes' slips, critics' guesses, and added notes and new wordings spoiled Saint Jerome's text at an early date. About 550 Cassiodorus tried to clean up the Latin text. Charlemagne gave the same job to Alcuin, who gave back a fixed copy in 801.

Similar attempts followed from Theodulphus, Bishop of Orléans, and Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1070 to 1089. Stephen Harding, Abbot of Cîteaux from 1109 to 1134, and Deacon Nicolaus Maniacoria did the same work early in the thirteenth century. Dominican correctories go back to the order's 1236 general chapter, which gave the France province a fixed Latin Bible text. Franciscan correctories begin with Roger Bacon, first to set out rules for fixing the Latin Vulgate. The Correctorium Sorbonicum may come from William of Brittany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmas-indico:
Cosmas Indicopleustes, a Greek merchant traveller of the sixth century, sailed the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf from his home in Alexandria. Business carried him south to Cape Guardafui, and he gathered reports of lands farther east, though whether he reached India himself stays uncertain. Late in life he entered the monastery of Raithu on Sinai.

There he wrote the Christian Topography, a twelve-book account of the universe as he pictured it and of the regions he knew. Earth, in his scheme, forms a rectangular floor beneath a vaulted heaven, ringed by ocean, with no antipodes on the far side. Merchants' notes give the book its lasting worth, outliving a cosmology no later geographer adopted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-av:
The Council of Avranches, held on 27 and 28 September 1172, faced the aftermath of St Thomas Becket's murder in the English Church. Henry II of England, after penance, won absolution from censures incurred by the assassination and swore fidelity to Pope Alexander III through his legate.

Discipline followed absolution: no benefice carrying the cure of souls might go to a child, nor a father's church to a priest's son. Every parish gained an assistant priest, and the Advent fast won commendation, above all for clergy. The council thus paired royal reconciliation with parish reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coutances:
A diocesan entry describes Coutances, the see covering the whole department of La Manche in Normandy, as a suffragan of Rouen. Enlarged in 1802 with the former Diocese of Avranches, its bishops since 1854 have borne the double title of Coutances and Avranches.

The entry runs through the bishops in order, from the legendary fourth-century names to Leontianus, the first known to history. It pauses on Saint Lo, on Geoffroy de Montbray, builder of the cathedral and founder of abbeys, and on Hugues de Morville, founder of the Hotel-Dieu. A parallel history of Avranches follows, with its own saints and founders, and a bibliography closes the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crusades:
A monumental entry defines the Crusades as expeditions undertaken under solemn vow to free the Holy Places from Muslim rule. The name comes from the cloth cross worn as a badge by participants. Later the word stretched to cover any vowed war against Muslims, pagans, heretics, or the excommunicated. Such wars ranged from Spain's long fight with the Moors to campaigns against Prussians and Albigensians.

Its core is the Eastern Crusades, told in ten movements. These run from origins under Urban II at Clermont in 1095, through the founding of Christian states and their fall, to the capture of Constantinople in 1204. Later movements cover thirteenth-century campaigns and the long Ottoman struggle into the fifteenth century. It closes with the Crusades' legacy in exploration, from Marco Polo to Columbus and Vasco da Gama, and in the spread of European culture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-culdees:
This entry tackles the Culdees, a word one scholar calls the best-abused in Scottish church history. In Irish it was Ceile-De, companion or even spouse of God, Latinized as Colidei and anglicized as Culdees. In Scotland it often appears as Kelidei. Etymology, persons, doctrines, rules, and privileges have all sparked controversy and partisan zeal.

All agree the early Culdees lived apart from the mass of the faithful, devoted to religion in community. Scottish writers preferred derivations from worshippers of God, or from words for shelter or church, unwilling to trace the name to Ireland. The entry defends the Irish derivation as easiest and now generally accepted, and follows the Culdees through Irish and Scottish monastic history, separating fact from patriotic legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyclades:
A geographical entry presents the Cyclades, a group of islands in the Aegean Sea. The ancients gave the name only to Delos and eleven neighbours, including Andros, Naxos, Paros, and Syros. Myth called them nymphs turned to rock for refusing sacrifice to Poseidon. In fact they are remnants of an ancient continent lost in the tertiary age.

Successively Cretan, Dorian, and Ionian, they fell to Athens under Miltiades, were plundered by Saracens, and became a Venetian duchy after the Fourth Crusade before Turkish conquest in the sixteenth century. Now a department of Greece, they count about 130,000 people, producing silk, wine, cotton, fruit, sponges, Parian marble, and Naxian emery. Latin and Greek sees, suffragan to Rhodes and Naxos, are also surveyed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deaconesses:
A historical entry examines deaconesses, women set apart to aid clergy in the early Church. The New Testament offers no certain formal office. Phoebe in Romans is called diakonos, but that may mean only service. The widows of First Timothy may have been deaconesses. Pliny's letter to Trajan in AD 112, mentioning tortured ministrae, hints at an early technical office.

By the mid-fourth century women certainly exercised definite functions under the name diakonoi or diakonissai. Sections cover history and consecration, where deaconesses are distinguished from widows. They cover functions such as instructing and baptizing women catechumens and charitable care. They also cover the modern Protestant revival begun by Pastor Fliedner at Kaiserswerth in 1833, inspired by Elizabeth Fry and spread through Germany and America. The story runs from doubt in the first century to clear proof in the fourth, and then to new life in the nineteenth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delatores:
A short entry explains delatores, Latin for denouncers, a term the Synod of Elvira about 306 used to stigmatize Christians who accused their brethren. Its canon 73 ruled that if a Christian was outlawed or executed on another Christian's denunciation, the delator suffered perpetual excommunication. No distinction appears between true and false accusation, though the synod likely meant accusation of Christianity before a heathen judge.

False accusation of a bishop, priest, or deacon drew the same penalty under canon 75, while false witness generally was punished under canon 74 in proportion to the charge. Arles in 314 decreed likewise against false accusers. During persecutions apostates sometimes denounced fellow Christians, as Pliny's letter to Trajan shows, and Diocletian's persecution saw brethren denounce ecclesiastics to heathen judges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denes:
An entry on the Déné peoples, also called Athapaskans, the northernmost native family of North America. Three groups make up the family: a southern group of Apache and Navaho peoples, a small Pacific group, and a far larger northern group. Northern territory runs from the Churchill River and northern Saskatchewan to Eskimo fishing grounds and across most of Alaska.

Latest reliable counts put the southern group at twenty-seven thousand, three hundred and sixty-five. The Pacific group stood at eight hundred and forty-six, and the northern group at nineteen thousand, three hundred and ninety. Life in dense forest and bleak waste kept numbers low for the area claimed. Epidemics and disorders after white newcomers arrived nearly wiped out whole tribes, and the closing pages list the main northern tribes and the works that describe them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devises-and-b:
A legal history entry on gifts and bequests for Masses, traced from England to the United States. Before the Reformation, Masses for donors' souls stood firm in England. A 1532 statute voided land uses meant for a perpetual priest, save short leaseholds. Edward the Sixth's 1547 statute seized property already given for priests, anniversaries, and church lights.

English judges went further without a statute. They struck down gifts of land or goods for such superstitious uses as against public policy, even legacies for prayers or raising poor children Catholic. Those statutes and that doctrine, the entry stresses, do not apply in the United States. Drafting advice closes the piece: write wills in clear words that fit local trust statutes and the run of decided cases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didacus-ximen:
Didacus Ximenes was a Spanish Dominican of the sixteenth century. He won note as a theologian, a philosopher, and a student of the stars, and he died in 1560. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he took a law degree at Salamanca and served as rector of the College of Cuenca. Then he left a rising legal career for the Dominican habit after a strange summons from an unknown friar.

In 1559 he was chosen as companion to Archbishop Carranza of Toledo. Carranza sent him on order business to Segovia, though his efforts there came to nothing. His chief writings were a perpetual calendar for the Dominican office and a Spanish work on the learning proper to religious life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dispersion-of:
The Dispersion of the Apostles is a feast honoring the missionary work of the Twelve. It is kept as a double major feast on 15 July. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces its first sign to a sequence written by Godescalc, who died in 1098 while a monk of Limburg. Godescalc also brought the feast to Aachen when he served as provost of the church of Our Lady there.

William Durandus, bishop of Mende, mentions it in the later thirteenth century, and through the Middle Ages it was kept across Spain and Italy. Its purpose, as Godescalc set it, is to mark the apostles leaving Jerusalem for the ends of the earth. Modern mission societies still keep it with solemnity in Germany, Poland, and parts of France, England, and America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dives: Dives comes from the Latin word for a rich man, though Scripture never uses it as a personal name. Medieval readers gave the name to the rich man of the parable of Lazarus in Luke chapter 16. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that many have taken the parable for real persons and events. Jerusalem guides still point out the House of Dives, though any real house must have vanished long ago.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-attrib:
The divine attributes are the perfections of God viewed one by one, so that the mind can grasp what it means to call God all-perfect. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that each attribute is a facet of the one divine substance, treated apart for the sake of order. Our natural knowledge of God comes by reasoning from created things, which mirror their maker darkly, as Saint Paul wrote to the Romans.

From the world we learn of God's power and godhead, and from these hints theology builds its ordered account. The entry moves through the chief attributes, ending with God as one, simple, unchanging spirit, blessed in himself and raised unspeakably above all that exists or can be thought. It is a systematic map of classical teaching on the nature of God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-double-monast:
Double monasteries are houses holding communities of both men and women, dwelling side by side under one superior and sharing one church for their offices. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the reason, that priests of the male house could tend the spiritual needs of the nuns more closely than separate houses would allow. The system arose almost with monasticism itself, and like it began in the East.

Communities of women gathered around founders in Egypt and elsewhere, and the life of Saint Pachomius tells much of nuns under his rule. In some houses a high wall split the church lengthwise to part nuns from canons, and similar walls likely served elsewhere. No such communities survive today in the Western Church, the entry notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-druzes:
The Druzes are a small Muslim sect of Syria, known for their opposition to the Maronites, a Catholic people of the Lebanon slopes. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry derives their name from Dorazy, a Persian at the court of the caliph El Hakim in Egypt about 1015. They later cut all ties with him and called themselves Unitarians, for the stress they lay on the unity of God.

Their story opens with Dorazy reading in a mosque a book that made the mad Fatimite caliph an incarnation of God. The furious crowd chased him into the valley lying between Hermon and the southern Lebanon. Later strife with the Maronites was stayed chiefly by English and French intervention. The entry cites Wortabet, Churchill, and Socin on a secretive faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duties-of-rel:
Duties of relatives flow from the general law of charity, to love one's neighbor as oneself, with a special stress laid by kinship. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that nearer kinship gives the command a sharper edge, setting an order of preference for relatives in keeping the law. Saint Thomas teaches that the strength of affection follows the closeness of the bonds that join us. No bond comes before the family, and none lasts longer.

Ordinarily, then, we owe more love to kin than to mere friends, whatever excellences friends may hold. This holds both for natural affection and for the supernatural act of charity. Theologians have worked out the order in detail, and the entry cites Slater, Rickaby, and d'Annibale, closing with Saint Paul's warning that one who neglects his own household denies the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-roman-c:
This entry takes the early Roman Christian cemeteries singly, following the great Roman roads that Christians lined with their dead. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry begins at the Vatican, where the first popes lay near the body of Saint Peter. Anacletus, second successor of Peter, raised a small chapel over the apostle's body, and popes were buried there down to Zephyrinus, who died in 217.

From Zephyrinus the papal burials moved to the cemetery of Saint Callistus, and the entry follows road by road through the catacombs of Rome. Epitaphs found near Peter's tomb open the survey, and the great histories of Von Reumont, Grisar, and Gregorovius close it, with Duchesne's critical edition of the papal book as guide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eastern-churc:
Eastern Churches are the Christian bodies that grew from the Eastern half of the Roman world. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry roots the split in the empire's own division, first by Diocletian, then by the sons of Theodosius, Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West. It was fixed at last by Charlemagne's rival empire in 800. Western churches gather around Rome or broke from her at the Reformation.

Eastern churches look back to Constantinople and the Eastern Empire. The entry surveys their rites, patriarchates, and tangled histories, and it ends in hope, that old quarrels over the Filioque and unleavened bread may be buried in dust. Eastern Christians, it suggests, may one day find that a union never truly broken only waits to be registered anew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ebionites:
The Ebionites were one or more early Christian sects tainted with Jewish errors. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the name as a transliteration of an Aramaic word for poor men. It first appears in Irenaeus, without a gloss on its sense. Origen and Eusebius tied it to poverty of mind, poverty of the Law they clung to, or poor views of Christ, but the entry judges these guesses wide of the historic origin.

Tertullian, Hippolytus, and Epiphanius add to the picture of a sect clinging to the Law while holding a low view of Christ. The Ebionites lingered in hamlets of Syria and Palestine before fading into obscurity. Farther east their influence may be traced among the Mandeans, and some writers link them to the roots of Islam, a claim the entry reports with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastes:
Ecclesiastes is the book of Scripture that usually follows Proverbs, its Hebrew name Qoheleth matching the Greek for preacher. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry warns that preacher here means no pulpit speaker before a crowd. It means a solemn herald of weighty truths, with Solomon as the herald of wisdom. The word itself may be a plain noun for proclamation, a poetic trumpet blast, or a personal name like others in Ezra.

The entry surveys the book's teaching on vanity, wisdom, and the fear of God, and it lists commentaries Catholic and Protestant, from Zapletal to Zockler. For readers facing its riddles, it offers a guide that keeps both the Hebrew roots and the long train of interpreters in view.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical addresses follow rules that come to us from Italy, where fitting forms for church correspondence were fixed. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that other Catholic nations took those rules with changes to suit local custom, yielding differences worth learning. Before any address is written, the paper itself must be white, no other color being allowed.

The proper Italian sheet is called palomba, used by the Roman congregations and watermarked with a dove. Elsewhere, protocol or ministerial paper may serve. The entry then works through openings and closings for each rank, warning that a shortfall in form falls short of what is due. Battandier and Parisi stand among its sources.

A diocese, parish, monastery, or religious community keeps its documents, records, and memorials in ecclesiastical archives, which cover its origin, growth, rights, and constitutions. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds that the word also names the place where such papers are kept. Archive comes from the Latin archium, itself drawn from the Greek archeion, the senate house or council house of the Greeks.

Cicero used tabularium and Pliny tablinum, while Pomponius Mela seems first to use archium for archives. Tertullian uses archivum twice. The entry then treats the care, housing, and use of church records, citing Lucidi, Van Espen, and Muehlbauer. For archivists and historians, it states what a church archive is and why its papers matter.

Ecclesiastical censures are medicinal and spiritual penalties laid by the Church on a baptized, offending, and stubborn person. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that they strip him, wholly or in part, of certain spiritual goods until he gives up his stubbornness. The name reaches back to republican Rome, where censors kept the register of citizens and ruled manners and morals with absolute power in their sphere.

Roman censors could degrade a citizen from his class for faults of morals or means. The Church took the name and shaped it to its own discipline. The entry traces censures through canon law to modern handbooks, citing Wernz, Laurentius, Lega, and Taunton. For students of church discipline, it sets out a penalty meant to heal rather than merely to punish.

Ecclesiastical conferences are meetings of clergy to discuss their state of life, above all questions of moral theology and liturgy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry seeks their roots in the gatherings of Egyptian desert hermits, who met as early as the third century to talk of asceticism and the hermit life. Later monasteries held similar meetings among monks, though these share little with today's pastoral conferences.

The direct ancestors are the quasi-synodal meetings ordered by decrees of the nineteenth century and earlier councils. The entry traces those decrees and the present form of conferences, citing the acts of recent councils, Lucidi, and Thomassin. For priests, it explains a custom that keeps learning and counsel alive among the clergy.

The law bends for clergy and for consecrated objects and places through ecclesiastical privileges. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry lists the clergy's privileges, personal inviolability, a special court, freedom from certain burdens, and the right to proper maintenance. These are known as the privileges of canon, forum, immunity, and competence.

Clergy also take precedence over laity in religious assemblies and processions, with a special place in church, the presbytery. Honors grow with higher order or office. The entry traces the privilege of canon from early days, when wounding a cleric drew severe penances and at times excommunication, and it cites Wernz, Laurentius, and Sagmuller.

Ecclesiastical property in the United States turns on a clash between church teaching and civil law. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry quotes the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore, which decreed that full ownership and dominion over church goods reside in the Church, to be held holily and inviolably. In English-speaking lands, however, the state as a rule denies that inherent right.

The state claims supreme dominion over temporal goods and refuses to own the Church as a corporation able to hold property in her own name. Civil power thus deals only with single persons. The entry cites Taunton, Smith, and Baart on the dangers when bishops cannot control temporal goods by church rules, a problem American Catholics know well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-sykes:
Edmund Sykes was an English priest and martyr, born at Leeds and put to death at York Tyburn on 23 March 1587. Trained at Reims and ordained in 1581, he worked in his native Yorkshire until illness wore him down. An apostate named Webster betrayed him, and in weakness he once went to a Protestant service, though he refused to repeat the act.

Banished after months in prison, he sailed abroad, made a pilgrimage to Rome to atone for his lapse, and chose to return to the English mission. His own brother then betrayed him to the Council of the North, and at the Lent assizes he was condemned as a traitor for his priesthood. The entry is a stark, moving tale of failure, repentance, and a second, fatal return.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elcesaites:
The Elcesaites, also called Helkesaites, were Gnostic Ebionites whose faith mixed heathen superstition with Christian teaching and Judaism. Hippolytus tells how, under Pope Callistus, Alcibiades of Apamea in Syria came to Rome. He brought a book said to have come from Parthia through a just man named Elchasai. Its contents, so the tale ran, had been revealed by an angel ninety-six miles tall.

That angel was the Son of God, attended by his sister the Holy Ghost, of the same vast size. Alcibiades proclaimed a new forgiveness of sins, dated to the third year of Trajan, in the year 100. It was to be won by a baptism that could wash even the grossest sinners clean. Scholars debate whether Elchasai truly lived under Trajan and whether Alcibiades invented the book himself. Origen, writing about 246, found the sect quite new, and the entry weighs these early witnesses with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-election-of-t:
Election of the popes is the subject of this entry, which starts from a plain point: the pope is chief pastor because he is Bishop of Rome. An election to the papacy is therefore, first of all, an election to the Roman bishopric. The right to elect has always belonged to the Roman Church, and the choice itself belongs to the clergy, now chiefly to the cardinals as the leading Roman clergy.

Should the college of cardinals ever die out, the duty would fall to the remaining Roman clergy, not to bishops in council. A pope cannot name his successor: Benedict II is said to have drawn up such a paper and then burned it. A pope may suggest a fit man to the cardinals, as Gregory VII did for Victor III, but that hint does not bind their choice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emigrant-aid-:
Emigrant aid societies are the subject of this entry, which opens by admitting how thin the early records are. The first American law on immigration came on 2 March 1819, when Congress ordered a record of arrivals with their ages, sex, trades, and birthplaces. Ireland supplied a large share of arrivals from the early eighteenth century, though before the Revolution those emigrants were nearly all Presbyterians, with few Catholics among them.

Arthur Young wrote in the 1770s that emigration in Ireland seemed tied to Presbyterianism and the linen trade, and that Catholics seemed rooted to their parishes. In 1728 Lieutenant Governor Gordon of Pennsylvania reported orders to guard against crowds of foreigners, Irish Papists, and convicts. The earliest American body for immigrants' care was the Charitable Irish Society of Boston, founded on 17 March 1737 to relieve countrymen struck by sickness, shipwreck, age, or accident.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-encratites:
The Encratites, literally abstainers, were early Christians who shunned wine, animal food, and marriage, and this entry traces a tendency found in several sects, chiefly Gnostic. Their abstinence rested on a false view of matter as evil, a view older than Christianity, seen in Pythagorism, Essenism, and Indian asceticism. Paul speaks of people forbidding marriage and meats, but Irenaeus first names a sect of Encratites.

Irenaeus ties their start to Saturninus and Marcion. By rejecting marriage they charge the Creator, who made male and female, and by shunning animal food they show ingratitude to the maker of all things. Tatian, a disciple of Justin, added a denial that Adam could be saved, calling marriage corruption and fornication. Clement of Alexandria devoted a book to fighting false continency. Hippolytus notes that the Encratites agreed with the Church on God and Christ, differing chiefly in their harsh ascetic rules.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eperies:
Eperies was a diocese of the Greek Ruthenian rite, suffragan to Gran, cut off from Munkacs in 1818. Its bishops were Gregory Tarkovics from 1818 to 1841, Joseph Garganecs from 1843 to 1875, Nicholas Toth from 1876 to 1881, and John Valyi from 1882. The city of Eperies, called Presov, was founded by a German colony in the twelfth century on the Tarcza, a tributary of the Danube.

Capital of Saros county in Hungary, with eleven thousand people, it is famed for sugar factories, mineral waters, and a rock salt mine at Sovar. The diocese held a hundred and sixty thousand Ruthenian Catholics, with two hundred and twelve priests, nearly all married. It had a hundred and ninety parishes across six counties, a hundred and ninety churches, and twenty-five chapels. It had twenty-four parish schools with twenty-eight thousand pupils, plus a boys' college, two Basilian convents, and a seminary of forty students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-glo:
Episcopal gloves are a liturgical adornment reserved for bishops and cardinals, worn only at pontifical Mass and only until the washing of hands before the sacrifice. Other churchmen, including abbots, may not use them without a special papal privilege. Today they are knitted by machine or hand from silk thread, with a cross on the back and an embellished border at the wrist.

Their colour must match the liturgical colour of the day, but they are never black, since they are not used on Good Friday or at Masses for the dead. At consecration the consecrator puts them on the new bishop just after the blessing. The custom grew up at Rome probably in the tenth century, though it appeared somewhat earlier outside Rome, first in France, whence it spread everywhere. The chief reason was likely a wish to adorn the bishop's hands fittingly, rather than any practical need.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-sub:
Episcopal subsidies are contributions the faithful owe toward the support of religion, above all in their own diocese. This entry sorts them into ordinary and extraordinary kinds. A bishop may ask his subjects, above all his clergy, for diocesan needs, and such gifts should as far as possible be voluntary rather than strict taxes.

Among them is the cathedraticum, a fixed yearly sum from diocesan churches. In the United States it forms bishops' chief revenue. Other kinds are pensions imposed under law, hospitality on canonical visitations, seminary contributions, and chancery fees. The surplus of chancery fees goes to charity, not to the bishop himself. The chief extraordinary levy is the charitable subsidy. It is asked of churches, benefices, and beneficed clergy, but not of lay people, and only for a reasonable and evident cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-of-st:
The Epistle of Saint James is treated here in order: author and genuineness, canonicity, contents, occasion, readers, style, and time and place. The author is commonly identified with the Lord's brother, Bishop of Jerusalem, and internal evidence points to him, since he alone meets the letter's conditions. The view that the Lord's brother is James son of Alpheus is the most probable.

Outside evidence starts rather late. Parallels exist with the Apostolic Fathers, Clement of Rome, Hermas, Justin, and Irenaeus, though the tie to Romans is doubtful. Its later recognition in the West is explained by its address to Jewish Christians, so it spread little among Gentile churches. From the middle of the third century writers cite it as the Lord's brother's work. In the East, Eusebius and Epiphanius explain doubts about its origin and canonicity. Theodore of Mopsuestia doubted it too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erasmus-darwi:
Erasmus Darwin Keyes, a soldier and convert, was born at Brimfield, Massachusetts, on 29 May 1810, and died at Nice, France, on 14 October 1895. West Point took him in, and he graduated in 1832 with a lieutenant's commission in the Third Artillery. Service in the South during the Nullification troubles followed, and from 1837 to 1841 he served as military aide to General Scott.

Scott made him military secretary in January 1860. In May 1861 he became colonel of the 11th Infantry, soon after brigadier-general of volunteers. At the first battle of Bull Run he fought, and a corps in the Army of the Potomac came under his command. Gallantry at Fair Oaks won him the brevet of brigadier-general in the regular army. He resigned in May 1864, went to California, and became a Catholic at San Francisco in 1866.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-essenes:
The Essenes were one of three leading Jewish sects Josephus mentions as flourishing in the second century before Christ, with the Pharisees and Sadducees. The only ancient authorities are Philo, Josephus, and a scanty notice in Pliny. Philo styles them Essaei, deriving it from hosios, holy, and Josephus styles them Essaei and Esseni. Their numbers were about 4000, and their chief residence was along the west side of the Dead Sea, away from the shore.

They also dwelt in other secluded parts and small towns of Palestine, yet some were found in cities. The sect arose about 150 before Christ and disappeared towards the end of the first century after Christ. They worshipped a single God, creator and ruler of everything, all-powerful and all-knowing. They esteemed Moses so highly that blaspheming his name meant death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eucharistic-c:
Eucharistic Congresses are gatherings of ecclesiastics and laymen for celebrating and glorifying the Holy Eucharist. They seek better means of spreading knowledge and love of it worldwide. The Real Presence in the Eucharist is a principal dogma of the Catholic Faith, the most precious treasure Christ left His Church, centre of worship and source of piety.

Chiefly, these congresses have focused the faithful's thoughts on the mystery of the altar. They have also made known the means by which devotion towards the Holy Eucharist may be promoted in people's hearts. The promoters believe that the recent spread of Eucharistic devotion, works of adoration, Confraternities of the Blessed Sacrament, and frequent Communion is largely due to these gatherings. Bishop Gaston de Ségur inspired the first congress, held at Lille, France, on 21 June 1881.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eutyches:
Eutyches was a fifth-century archimandrite, head of a monastery outside Constantinople, whose name stuck to the teaching of one nature in Christ after the Incarnation. Aged seventy in 448, he had ruled some three hundred monks for thirty years. He was no scholar, but he had weight through Chrysaphius, minister of Theodosius II, to whom he had stood godfather. A fierce foe of Nestorianism, he denounced a supposed revival of it at Constantinople.

Eusebius of Dorylaeum counter-charged him with heresy before Flavian's synod. Eutyches refused to leave his monastery, which he called his tomb, and would confess Christ only as of two natures, not in two natures, with flesh not the same as ours. The synod condemned and deposed him. His cause then split the East, drew in Pope Leo, and led through the stormy council of Ephesus in 449 to the definition of Chalcedon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-extravagantes:
Extravagantes is the name for certain papal decretals that lie outside the canonical collections of special authority. They are not in Gratian's Decree of about 1140, nor in the three official collections: Gregory IX's Decretals, the Sixth Book, and the Clementines. The term first covered documents Gratian had left out, though they still bound the whole Church. Bernard of Pavia gathered such pieces between 1187 and 1191.

Today the name covers two collections in all editions of the Corpus Juris. They are the Extravagantes of John XXII and the Extravagantes communes, ordered by Jean Chappuis in his Paris edition of 1499 to 1505. The communes hold decretals from Martin IV through Sixtus IV, including Boniface VIII's famed Unam Sanctam. Neither collection has official value like the three great ones, and some pieces were already repealed. Yet many still bind the whole Church, such as Paul II's Ambitios against alienating church goods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-asse:
The Feast of Asses was a medieval church pastime centred on Balaam's ass. It grew from a sermon in which Hebrew prophets testified to Christ. By the eleventh century the sermon had become a metrical dramatic dialogue. The crowd loved Balaam's ass best, giving the feast its name.

At Beauvais a girl with a child rode a draped ass to church. After the Introit a Latin prose praised the ass in song. At Mass's end the priest brayed thrice, and the people answered in kind. The feast later merged into the Feast of Fools and Corpus Christi plays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-tabe:
The Feast of Tabernacles was one of the three great Hebrew feasts. Families lived seven days in leafy booths of branches and foliage. It recalled the tents of the long wilderness years after the Exodus. It also thanked God for the harvest and the Promised Land.

The feast opened on the seventh month's fifteenth day. Every male Israelite went up to Jerusalem for the great celebration. After the Exile, water drawn from Siloe was poured on the altar. On the eighth day booths were broken up and people went home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-formularies:
Formularies were medieval books of model documents, with blank spaces left for the names, dates, and facts of each new case. Offices that issued many papers of the same kind naturally fell into fixed wording. Those models let minor officials draft important deeds correctly, since every clause already carried a settled meaning. The result was a trained art of drafting, called dictare, taught in monastic and church schools from the fifth to the ninth centuries.

The models cover royal decrees, court papers, sales, gifts to churches, manumissions of slaves, dowries, wills, and church acts like consecrations and excommunications. Because most surviving models were copied from real deeds, they are a rich source for historians of law, institutions, manners, and language, and for spotting forged charters by their faulty style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-quino:
Francis Quinones, also spelled Quignonez, was a Spanish Franciscan cardinal born in the Kingdom of Leon about 1482 and dead at Veroli in Italy on 5 November 1540. Son of Diego Fernandez de Quinones, Count of Luna, he was schooled as a page of Cardinal Ximenes. At sixteen he entered the Friars Minor at Los Angeles in Spain, taking the name Francis of the Angels in 1498.

In 1521 Leo X gave him leave to go to the American missions with Father Glapion, confessor of Charles V, but Glapion died that year. Quinones became commissary general of the Ultramontane Franciscans, then minister general from 1523 to 1527. As general he visited convents in Spain, Italy, and Belgium and promoted studies and discipline. In 1524 he sent twelve missionaries to Mexico, including Juan Juarez, later the first bishop within the present United States.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-jos:
Francisco Jose de Goya y Lucientes, born at Fuendetodos in Aragon on 31 March 1746 and dead at Bordeaux on 16 April 1828. He was Spain's great painter and etcher of an age of tumult. His father, a small landowner, gave him scant schooling, but a monk of Santa Fe may have wakened his art. At fourteen he painted frescoes at Fuendetodos, studying soon after with Martinez at Saragossa. At twenty he made his way to Rome as a bullfighter, painted little in Italy, yet won a Paris prize for Hannibal seeing Italy from the Alps.

Back in Spain in 1775, Mengs commissioned tapestry sketches for the Prado and Escorial, bringing Goya to court. There he lived among princes, married Josefa Bayeu, and became the brightest member of the king's brother's circle. He died at Bordeaux, one son surviving him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-tor:
Francisco Torres, called Turrianus, was a Hellenist and polemicist born at Herrera in Palencia about 1509 and dead at Rome on 21 November 1584. Nephew of the Bishop of the Canaries, he studied at Salamanca and stayed at Rome with Cardinals Salviati and Seripando. He was sent by Pius IV to the Council of Trent in 1562, and became a Jesuit on 8 January 1567. He taught at the Roman College, helped revise the Sistine Vulgate, and counted Hosius and Baronius among his literary associates.

 He defended the Immaculate Conception, papal authority over councils, the divine authority of bishops, communion under one kind for the laity, the authenticity of the Apostolic Canons and Pseudo-Isidorian decretals. He helped restore the feast of the Presentation, suppressed by Pius V. He wrote more than seventy books, chiefly polemics against Protestants and translations of Greek Fathers found hidden in libraries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-alonzo-b:
Fray Alonzo Benavides, also spelled Benavidez, was Archbishop of Goa in the Portuguese Indies, a prelate of high rank whose life remains very imperfectly known. Born on the island of San Miguel, he professed in the Franciscan convent of Mexico in 1603 and served as master of novices at Puebla. He became Custos of the Missions of New Mexico. He returned to Spain in 1630, where he corresponded with the Venerable Maria de Agreda, and on returning to America was made Archbishop of Goa. The date and place of his death are still unknown.

 To stir interest in those remote regions he wrote and issued two booklets, full of exaggerations about Indian numbers but otherwise of the highest value for New Mexico's ethnography and ethnology. They were judged as encouraging guides that also carry much accurate information from personal knowledge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-french-cathol:
French Catholics in the United States tells the little-written story of French-Canadian immigrants and their Church. By the time of writing they numbered nearly 1,200,000 souls, the leading element in several dioceses and a weighty presence across the Eastern states. The article gathers their numbers, parishes, and progress over fifty years.

Migration began before American independence, when French Canadians fought in Washington's armies and won land on Lake Champlain called the Refugees' Tract. A new wave followed the Quebec rebellion of 1837, and the chief influx came after the Civil War, in which French Canadians gave 40,000 soldiers to the Union. Their papers and parish records supply most of what the article can prove.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fringes:
Fringes, in the Bible, are the tassels ordered for the corners of Jewish garments in Numbers and Deuteronomy. The Lord told Moses that Israel should wear fringes with a thread of blue, so that seeing them they would recall all the commandments. The entry untangles a term that English Bibles render loosely, since the Hebrew points to twisted cords and tassels rather than mere trimming.

Four tassels hung from a large square cloak, one thread longer than the rest, knotted and wound by set rules. The woman healed by touching the hem of Christ's cloak likely touched such a tassel. Rabbis later fixed minute rules for spinning and tying them, and Pharisees drew blame for enlarging their fringes to show their piety. The article reads law, custom, and gospel together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fulbert-of-ch:
Fulbert of Chartres, bishop and teacher, made his school France's most famous school. Born of humble parents between 952 and 962, he studied at Reims under Gerbert, later Pope Sylvester II. In 990 he opened his school at Chartres, drawing pupils from France, Italy, Germany, and England. His students called him the venerable Socrates.

Made bishop in 1007 through King Robert, his old fellow student, Fulbert kept teaching and warned pupils against reason set above faith. Ironically, his pupil Berengarius of Tours pushed that path furthest. When fire took the cathedral about 1020, Fulbert rebuilt it in greater splendor with gifts from kings, including Canute of England. His letters, hymns, and sermons still serve historians of his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fundamental-a:
Fundamental Articles names a Protestant effort to split Christian doctrine into essentials and non-essentials. During the seventeenth century, divines of the Reformed churches sought a rule for the split, hoping it might ground reunion or answer Catholic charges. The entry follows the idea from its first form to its place in English debate.

George Cassander, a Catholic writing in 1561, first argued that the Apostles' Creed held the true foundations of faith. Louvain teachers and Calvin alike rejected him, but Protestants took the tool up again. It let them claim unity on fundamentals despite splits, and hope for salvation before the Reformation. Catholic writers, in turn, labored to show the whole distinction worthless.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-funeral-dues:
Funeral Dues explains the parish priest's right to offerings at the burial of his people. The right runs two ways: an offering when a parishioner is buried in his own parish, and a fourth share, the quarta funeralis, when he is buried elsewhere. The rule rests on simple justice, since the priest served the dead in life and should not lose all reward for that care.

Trent named the fourth portion, but older names abound, from canonical portion to justice itself. The custom reaches back to Anglo-Saxon soul-shot, a mortuary gift left while the grave stood open. Burial itself can never be sold, the article stresses, yet fixed scales, extra services, and local custom may warrant fees. The poor, it adds, must always be buried free of charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-druil:
Gabriel Druillettes, a Jesuit missionary born in France in 1610, carried the faith to the Abnaki of Maine and the Montagnais of Canada. He entered the Society at Toulouse in 1629 and reached Canada in 1643. After learning Algonquin, he shared winter hunts with the Montagnais, then took a mission on the Kennebec in August 1646.

Druillettes became the first white man to travel from the Saint Lawrence to the sea by the Chaudière and Kennebec, meeting English agent John Winslow at Coussinoc. Twice he served as French envoy, treating at Boston in 1650 and at New Haven in 1651 for trade and defense against the Iroquois. Later he paddled the Saguenay toward the North Sea, reaching Kekouba twenty-nine days from Tadousac.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gennadius-of-:
Gennadius of Marseilles, a priest of the late fifth century, is remembered for carrying on Saint Jerome's catalogue of famous Christian writers. Nothing of his life survives save his own last biography, where he lists eight books against heresies, five against Nestorius, ten against Eutyches, and three against Pelagius. A letter on his faith to Pope Gelasius, who reigned from 492 to 496, dates him firmly.

Of all his works, only the catalogue itself surely survives, with lost translations of Evagrius and Timothy Aelurus beside it. A treatise on church doctrines, long passed as Augustine's, is now given to Gennadius, likely a fragment of his anti-heresy books. His pages praise Semipelagians warmly, call full Pelagians heretics, and treat Augustine himself with a cool, teasing edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gentiles:
Gentiles, from the Latin for nations, collectively names the peoples distinct from the Jews in both Testaments. The Hebrew Goyim, Greek ethne, and Vulgate Gentes all mark the same divide. Jews, as Abraham's children, stood as God's chosen people before Christ, while other nations, worshiping other gods and living loosely, gave the word a scornful edge in Scripture and Talmud.

Since Christianity spread, theological speech uses Gentiles for those who are neither Jews nor Christians. The entry notes one local twist: American Mormons apply the word to all outside their own sect. A short piece, it fixes a term that shifts with the speaker, from Bible translation to modern sectarian use, and points readers toward the article on proselytes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-hermes:
George Hermes, a philosopher and theologian born in Westphalia in 1775, tried to ground Christian truth on reason alone. Kant and Fichte had shaken his faith at Münster, and his 1805 Inquiry into the Inner Truth of Christianity sought harmony between reason and revelation. Its favor won him Münster's theology chair in 1807, where students loved his teaching and colleagues elected him dean three times before 1819.

Hermes's rationalist methods stirred opposition at Münster, notably over his refusal to keep Latin in dogmatic lectures, and he advised the Prussian ministry on Bonn's new faculty. After his death at Bonn in 1831, Gregory XVI condemned the Hermesian system in 1835, placing his Introductions and Dogmatic on the Index. A further decree in 1836 named his divergences from Catholic doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-piside:
George Pisides, a Byzantine poet of the seventh century's first half, sang Heraclius's wars for the emperor's court. A Pisidian by birth and friend of Patriarch Sergius and Emperor Heraclius, he served as deacon at Saint Sophia's, archivist, guardian of sacred vessels, and referendary. He evidently marched with Heraclius against Persia in 622, when the true Cross, seized at Jerusalem, was recovered.

About five thousand verses survive, mostly trimetric iambics, mixing theology, morals, and war chronicle. His poems cover the Persian expedition, the Avars' 626 attack on Constantinople, Heraclius's triumph over Chosroes, the Resurrection, and the long Hexaemeron on creation, dedicated to Sergius. Later ages preferred him even to Euripides, though Finlay judged his verse correct yet dull and courtly. He stands as his century's sole poet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georgr-henry-:
George Henry Miles, a dramatist and man of letters born at Baltimore in 1824, won the stage's great prizes before thirty. Graduated from Mount Saint Mary's in 1842, he practiced law briefly, but verse and story pulled him away. His Truce of God ran serially, Loretto won the Catholic Mirror's fifty-dollar prize in 1849, and his tragedy Mahommed won Edwin Forrest's thousand-dollar prize in 1850, ending his legal career.

De Soto succeeded at Broadway in 1859, the same season his comedy Mary's Birthday played, and Señor Valiente opened in New York, Boston, and Baltimore on one night. His Seven Sisters, on secession, ran at Laura Keene's in 1860 to 1861, while Cromwell stayed unfinished. Fillmore sent him to Spain in 1851, and after 1864 Europe he published Glimpses of Tuscany, Christine, and Christian Poems. Professor of English at Mount Saint Mary's from 1859, he died near Emmitsburg in 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germans-in-th:
Germans in the United States, numbering no fewer than twelve million by birth or descent, counts all German speakers from Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and Luxemburg. The story opens in autumn 1683. Franz Daniel Pastorius and his Mennonite weavers from Crefeld founded Germantown, Pennsylvania, building a church and a school where Pastorius's primer became the first original schoolbook printed in Pennsylvania.

Rosicrucians, German Friends at Cresheim, and Dunkers at Conestoga and Ephrata followed, and Pennsylvania Germans produced Taylor, Lick, Yerkes, Fritz, Wanamaker, Schwab, and Frick. Palatines landed in 1707, and fifty-two more with three Holsteiners appealed to Queen Anne in 1708. About three thousand Palatines crossed in 1709 and 1710. New Berne in North Carolina, Germanna in Virginia, and Strasburg in the Shenandoah mark their spread, crowned by the great January 1710 expedition from England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gift-of-mirac:
The gift of miracles is one of the extraordinary graces St. Paul lists in his First Epistle to the Corinthians, among the charismata, or graces freely given. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sets it apart from the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and from the fruits of the Spirit. Unlike those, it need not go with personal holiness, since it is given chiefly for the good of others.

Christ promised the gift to his disciples. Paul speaks of it as abiding in the Church, confirming faith and making doctrine credible. Yet no person holds it as a lasting power of soul, since working wonders belongs to divine omnipotence alone. The grace comes only passingly, as God moves someone to act, whether through prayer, through fitting means, or through relics and shrines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-of-fo:
Godfrey of Fontaines, called Godefridus de Fontibus and Doctor Venerandus, was a scholastic philosopher and theologian born near Liège in the thirteenth century. He became canon of his native diocese, and of Paris and Cologne, and in 1300 was elected to the See of Tournai, which he declined. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a staunch supporter of Thomism, original enough to differ from the master.

He taught theology at Paris during the last quarter of the century, as a master of theology and member of the Sorbonne. He left that body a valuable collection of manuscripts. His notable XIV Quodlibeta show a theologian and philosopher who was also canonist, jurist, moralist, and controversialist. He took an active part in the disputes stirring Paris. He opposed Thomas on the mendicant orders' privileges, yet admired his teaching, differing on individuation and on essence and existence in material things.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greek-rites:
Greek Rites is an article insisting that rite, language, and religion are three things always kept apart. A rite is a set order of words and acts for the Eucharist, the Hours, and other sacraments and sacramentals. A Catholic Encyclopedia article shows why language is no clue to rite.

The Roman and Gallican Uses are both written in Latin yet are completely different rites. The Roman Rite stays Roman in Old Slavonic in Dalmatia or in Greek in Italy. In the East nearly all liturgies were originally written in Greek, and even the Armenian, Nestorian, and Abyssinian exceptions are modified derivations from Greek originals. At the head of all Eastern liturgies stand the foundations of Alexandria and Antioch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guastallines:
Luigia Torelli, Countess of Guastalla, born about 1500 and widowed twice by twenty-five, gave up her inherited principality to Fernando Gonzaga and turned to religious foundations. In 1536 she joined the Angelicals, a congregation she had founded and endowed, taking the name Paola Maria. She worked with them among women alongside the Barnabites.

When Paul III imposed enclosure on the Angelicals, whose calling had been active charity for the sick and orphans, she founded a second Milan community, the Daughters of Mary, for noble orphans. Eighteen girls were provided for in the endowment, staying twelve years before choosing the world with a dowry or the religious life. The sisters, in black garb with a gold ring showing a hand holding a cross, took no solemn vows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guelphs-and-g:
Guelph and Ghibelline were the names of the two factions that split and battered Italy through much of the later Middle Ages. Behind them lay the old question of the two powers, spiritual and temporal, each independent in its own sphere. There was also the clash between a feudal nobility of foreign descent and a rising commercial, municipal democracy rooted in Roman law.

The names themselves came from Germany, from Welf of Bavaria and Waiblingen, castle of the Hohenstaufen, first shouted as war cries at Weinsberg in 1140. Carried into Italy, Guelph came to mean the party of the Church and the communes, Ghibelline the party of the emperor and the old aristocracy. The entry insists, though, that local grudges, like Florence's Buondelmonti and Amidei feud of 1215, often mattered more than principle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guido-gorres:
Guido Görres, son of the historian Johann Joseph Görres, was born at Coblenz in 1805 and became a historian, publicist, and one of Germany's foremost Catholic lyric poets. After studies at Bonn and Munich and a prize from the French Academy in 1830, he wrote lives of Nicholas of Flüe and Joan of Arc. With Count Pocci he made an illustrated church festival calendar for the young.

From 1838 he edited the Historisch-politische Blätter, defending Catholic rights in Germany until his death in 1852, while his poems, Marian songs, Christmas pieces, and a life of St. Cecilia in verse won wide popularity. He also translated the Imitation of Christ, edited Brentano's fairy tales, and published a study of Siegfried and the dragon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haudriettes:
Paris's Haudriettes began early in the fourteenth century when Jeanne, wife of Etienne Haudry, secretary to St. Louis, thought her husband dead on pilgrimage to Compostela. Gathering pious women under her roof, she vowed perpetual chastity and a life serving the poor. On Etienne's return in 1329 he won her a dispensation on condition the community keep his house and funds for twelve poor women.

A chapel and then a hospital followed, and Cardinal d'Ailly framed statutes approved in 1414. After slackening, Cardinal de La Rochefoucauld reformed the house under Gregory XV, adding poverty to chastity and obedience and the Augustinian rule. Moved to Saint-Honoré in 1622, the sisters became Daughters of the Assumption, and the Revolution ended the congregation for good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hebrew-names:
Hebrew names mattered deeply to their bearers, since a name was felt to be nearly the person himself. This entry studies divine, personal, and place names as a key to Israel's religion and society. Parents, often the mother, chose a child's name for some mark, as Edom for red or Jacob for supplanter, given at birth or later at circumcision. Cities took names from founders or conquerors.

Divine names open the study. Yahweh comes from the verb to be and is best read as he is. El and Elohim are found among all Semitic peoples, and Shadday, once perhaps fecundity or highness, later means simply Almighty. Personal names divide into pure Hebrew forms, simple or compound, and hebraicized foreign names, with many old patriarchal names reshaped in passing between tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helie-de-bour:
Périgord Franciscan Hélie de Bourdeilles, born about 1423 at his family's castle, became Archbishop of Tours and cardinal while keeping religious poverty. Made Bishop of Périgueux at twenty-four on Charles VII's request in 1447, he spent years as an English prisoner for defending church immunity. He moved to Tours in 1468 and received the red hat from Sixtus IV in 1483.

A friend of St. Francis of Paula, his name stands in the Franciscan martyrology for 5 July. He defended church rights against the state and pressed for abolishing the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges in two treatises of 1484 and 1486. He also left a Latin defence of Joan of Arc, bound in manuscript with the record of her rehabilitation, before his death at Artannes in 1484.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-augustu:
Henry Augustus Rawes, educated at Houghton-le-Spring and Trinity College, Cambridge, served as an Anglican curate and warden of the House of Charity in Soho. He entered the Catholic Church at Edinburgh in 1856. A year later he joined the English Oblates of St. Charles, was ordained, and took charge of the poor Potteries district of Notting Hill. There he spent his own fortune building the Church of St. Francis of Assisi. He served as superior of the congregation from 1880 until his death in 1885.

Rawes wrote sermons and devotional works marked by a mystical strain, including the allegory Homeward and a study of the Beloved Disciple. His hymns, collected above all in Foregleams of the Desired, are praised for poetic beauty and depth of devotion. He translated Leo XIII's encyclical on Catholic philosophy along with treatises of Aquinas on the Eucharist and the Lord's Prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heriger-of-lo:
Heriger of Lobbes, born about 925, worked as a medieval theologian and historian, studied at the cathedral school of Liège, and became a Benedictine at Lobbes. He served as scholasticus of its school and went to Rome with his friend Bishop Notger in 989. Elected abbot of Lobbes in 990, he amassed unusual learning from Fathers and classical writers and wrote more critically than most contemporaries. As hagiographer he sometimes sank to an ascetical novelist's level. He died on 31 October 1007.

Heriger's chief work, the Gesta of the bishops of Liège, reaches only to St. Remaclus's death in 667 and was continued to 1048 by Anselm of Liège. His other writings include lives of Berlendis, Landoald, and Ursmar and a treatise on the Body and Blood of Christ compiled from the Fathers. An arithmetical work on the abacus was published with Gerbert's mathematical works. Most of his writings appear in Migne's Patrology, volume 139.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hernando-cort:
Hernando Cortés was the Spanish conqueror of Mexico, born at Medellín around 1485 and dead near Seville in 1547. Restless at school in Salamanca, he sailed for the West Indies, served in the Antilles, and quarrelled bitterly with Governor Velázquez of Cuba, who had first favoured him. That break shaped the daring expedition that followed.

Cortés landed in Mexico, marched inland with striking speed, and took the Aztec capital after desperate fighting, though the Crown later probed his conduct and curbed his power. His letters to the emperor remain a vivid first-hand record of the conquest. The entry follows his swift movements, his clashes with rivals such as Narváez, and his later years, including the failed Algiers expedition of 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hethites:
The Hethites, called Hittites in the Authorized Version, were a people of north-western Asia. The Hebrew Bible calls them Hittim, Egyptian monuments say Khuti or Kheta, and cuneiform records say Hatti. For centuries they were known only from scanty Bible allusions. Then Egyptian and Assyrian documents, studied in the later nineteenth century, revealed a great empire, and fresh finds at its homeland kept adding to the picture almost daily.

The trail began with carved figures noticed near Ibreez in the eighteenth century and stone slabs covered in strange characters found at Hamah by Burckhardt in 1812. At first no one could read them. The entry follows the slow unravelling of Hittite history from those early sightings. It voices the hope that Hittite history might soon grow as famous as Egypt's and Assyria's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hieronymites:
The Hieronymites were a religious congregation formed in Spain and Italy in the fourteenth century by joining several groups of hermits. They took St. Jerome as model and patron. But the entry is firm that Jerome himself founded no order and wrote no monastic rule, and later claims of a direct link rest on no solid basis. Popes approved the new congregation and imposed the Rule of St. Augustine upon it.

In Spain the cradle of the congregation was San Bartolome de Lupiana, where the first prior, Fernando Pecha, won bulls from Gregory XI in October 1373 confirming the order. The pope received their vows and gave them their habit of white tunic with brown scapular and mantle.
