Solemn blessings opening the Sermon on the Mount, the Eight Beatitudes of Matthew chapter 5, verses 3 to 10, are the Gospel text expounded here. Four recur in slightly different form in Luke chapter 6, verse 22, at a sermon's start parallel to Matthew 5 to 7, matched there by four woes in verses 24 to 26. Matthew's fuller account and pride of place fit the First Gospel's spiritual view of the Messianic kingdom.

Poetic parallelism of thought and phrase, hallmark of biblical poetry, makes the Beatitudes perhaps the only strictly poetical sayings of the Lord. Text, translation, and each blessing's sense follow: poor in spirit, mourners, meek, hungry for justice, merciful, pure of heart, peacemakers, and persecuted. Their promise of the kingdom crowns Christian ethics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-machabees:
Priestly rebels who won Jewish freedom give this entry its family. Mathathias launched the revolt against Antiochus IV Epiphanes of Syria, and his house ruled the commonwealth until Herod the Great overthrew it. Machabee began as the surname of Judas, third son of Mathathias, then spread to all his descendants and to all who joined the rising.

Hammer explains the name best, from Aramaic maqqaba, earned by Judas's valour against Israel's foes. Hasmoneans, from ancestor Hashmon, serves as the family name in old Jewish writers and now labels Simon's dynasty. Martyrs of Second Machabees, chapter 6 and 7, also bear the name, linking war and witness in one proud title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-organic-a:
Napoleon's law for public worship, voted with the Concordat itself, is the subject here. Seventy-seven articles touched Catholicism and forty-four Protestantism, presented to Tribunate and legislative body together and published as law on 8 April 1802 under one title and preamble. French governments down to 1905 treated them as inseparable from the Concordat.

Pius VII protested on 24 May 1802 that they had issued without his knowledge and needed change before he could accept them. Catholic articles fall under four titles, the first covering the Church's government in relation to state rights and constitution. State approval for papal acts, seminaries, and appointments shows a concordat fenced by police power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-synods-of:
Church councils at Arles, across five centuries, are gathered here in order. The first, in 314, aimed to end the Donatist row, backing Rome’s council of 313: Caecilian of Carthage stood rightly chosen, Donatus of Casae Nigrae stood cast out. Twenty-two rules on abuses since Diocletian’s persecution rank among early church law’s key texts.

A council of 353, with two papal envoys present, leaned Arian, drawn into shunning communion with Athanasius and refusing to condemn Arius, to Pope Liberius’s grief. The synod of 443, or 452, framed fifty-six rules, mostly repeats of old discipline: new converts barred from high orders, married men seeking priesthood vowing continence, and rules for making bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ursulines:
Angela de Merici's teaching order for girls, the first of its kind for women in the Church, is the subject here. Convinced of a divine call to found an educational institute, Angela spent seventeen years guiding young women known as the Company of Saint Ursula. They lived at home with their families yet met at set times for conferences and devotions. 

Hindrances at last gave way, and in 1535 twelve members formed a community with episcopal approval, Angela as superioress. Enthusiasm carried the movement swiftly through Italy, Germany, and France, with houses soon multiplying, each independent. Constitutions fitted to the institute's special work followed, shaping girls' schooling for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theatines:
Clerks Regular known as Theatines, founded to recall clergy and laity to holy living, are introduced here. Gaetano dei Conti di Tiene, Paolo Consiglieri, Bonifacio da Colle, and Giovanni Pietro Carafa, later Paul IV, founded the order. Carafa, Bishop of Chieti or Theate in the Abruzzi, gave the congregation its distinctive name among later-modelled groups such as Jesuits, Barnabites, and Somaschi. 

Gaetano consecrated the order to the Cross as its emblem. Foundation fell on the Finding of the Holy Cross, 3 May 1524, approved by Clement VII on 24 June in the brief Exponi Nobis. Solemn profession before Saint Peter's papal altar followed on 14 September. Reform of clergy, preaching, and pastoral care fill the order's early story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodoric-thi:
Schoolman Theodoric of Chartres, lover of the classics, fought a lone battle for good Latin and Greek learning. Born in France early in the twelfth century, he died at Chartres about 1150. He likely learned at Chartres under his brother Bernard and led its school in 1121. Paris teaching came next, with John of Salisbury among his pupils, and Chartres teaching again in 1141.

His books were the Eptateuchon on the seven liberal arts, De Sex Dierum Operibus, and a note on De Inventione Rhetorica ad Herennium. The first still lies in manuscript at Chartres, the rest saw print in 1884 and 1890. He loved the classics with zeal, took an interest in nature lore through Herman's Ptolemy Planisphere, and held a Platonic view of reality that gave ideas full being.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theological-c:
Church judgments that brand teachings harmful to faith or morals are the censures explained here. They differ from canonical censures such as excommunication, suspension, and interdict, which punish offenders. Theological censure judges doctrine, not persons, and the Church has claimed that right from Saint Paul onward.

Paul declared anathema on perverters of Christ's Gospel and warned against profane novelties and false knowledge. Newman saw the teaching office work in two ways: stating truth plainly and condemning error. Popes, councils, Roman congregations, universities, and special commissions all share in the task, down to Pius X's condemnation of Modernism. Grades of censure, from heretical to rash, fill the rest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-willia:
Thomas William Allies, an English writer born in 1813, moved from Anglican ministry to Catholic letters. A lonely boy at a country parsonage, he loved books more than company. He won the Newcastle Scholarship at Eton at sixteen, studied at Oxford, and took Anglican orders. His poetry and philosophy blended in a mind that prized clear thought.

Newman's departure from the Church of England in 1845 left Allies without his guiding star, yet he pressed on. His Journal drew a sharp rebuke from the Bishop of Oxford. On 11 September 1850 he converted, giving up his living, his work and his prospects with a wife and three sons to face the world. He then gave his mind to Catholic truth in a long career as a writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tithes:
Tithes are the tenth part of the increase from land and stock, set apart for the clergy or for religious and charitable uses. The word comes from the Anglo-Saxon teotha, meaning a tenth. Scripture already shows the custom: Abraham gives tithes of spoil to Melchizedek, and Jacob vows a tenth of all he gains. Under the Mosaic Law the tenth of field produce, tree fruit and firstborn livestock went to God.

God in turn assigned the tithes to the Levites for their service in the tabernacle. Later law divided tithes into predial tithes from crops, mixed tithes from cattle, milk, cheese and wool, and personal tithes from work or trade. Charlemagne's capitularies first enforced payment by civil law, and English statutes from Westminster in 1285 onward recognized the tithe as a legal charge on the land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tralles:
Tralles was a titular see subject to Ephesus in Asia Minor, founded, so tradition says, by Argians and Thracians on a slope of Mount Messogis in the Meander valley. It ranked among the richest and most populous cities of Lydia, and King Attalus kept a splendid palace there. Zeus Larasios was its local god, with Apollo Pythius and others also worshipped.

An earthquake destroyed Tralles, and Augustus rebuilt it as Caesarea. Christianity came very early: Ignatius of Antioch, writing to its church, notes that Bishop Polybius visited him at Smyrna and warns the people against Docetism, showing a church already well organized. Its bishops run from Heracleon in 431 to John in 1230. About 1270 Andronicus rebuilt and repeopled it to 36,000 souls, but the Turks soon retook and demolished it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trocmades:
A titular see of Galatia Secunda, suffragan of Pessinus, named for no city any geographer or historian mentions. Hierocles gives a "regio Trocnades" instead, likely the Galatian name of a tribe on the left bank of the Sangarius, centred near the present village of Kaimez.

All the episcopal lists up to the thirteenth century place the see among Pessinus's suffragans, the latest calling it Lotinou, perhaps Plotinou after St. Plotinus. Le Quien lists four bishops. They run from Cyriacus at the Robber Synod of Ephesus in 449 to Constantine in 879. A Cyriacus said to have attended Nicaea in 325 is absent from the authentic lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-troyes:
A diocese covering the Department of Aube, re-established in 1802 as a suffragan of Paris. At first it also held Yonne, and its bishop bore the titles of Troyes, Auxerre and Châlons-sur-Marne. Châlons became a separate see in 1822, and Auxerre passed to Sens, leaving Troyes a suffragan of Sens.

Its bishop list, known since the ninth century, is judged trustworthy by Duchesne. Among its bishops are St. Lupus, who forced the Huns to spare Troyes and was carried off as Attila's hostage, and St. Prudentius, who wrote against Gottschalk, while the Lirey Winding Sheet, once exposed here, is now honoured at Turin. The diocese also honours Saint Mathia and Saint Helena as patronesses of the town, their relics found at Troyes in 980 and transferred there in 1209.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-universities:
This general entry treats universities as a whole, while particular Catholic foundations get their own articles. It runs in five parts: origin and organization, academic work and development, Renaissance and Reformation, the modern period, and Catholic action. The name is sometimes given to the famed schools of Athens and Alexandria, but universities properly arose in the Middle Ages. Legends long credited Oxford to King Alfred, Paris to Charlemagne, and Bologna to Theodosius II.

For thirteenth-century foundations dates and charters can be fixed, but the earliest beginnings stay obscure. The entry follows the schools from cathedral and monastic roots through the dialectical method and Scholasticism, shaped by Peter Lombard and crowned in St Thomas's Summa. At Bologna the new learning turned practical, toward civil and canon law under Irnerius and Gratian. Later parts carry the story through humanism, reform, and the modern Catholic university.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vannes:
Vannes covers the Department of Morbihan in Brittany and was restored by the Concordat of 1802. It was formed from the old Diocese of Vannes, minus parishes east of the Oust River given to Rennes. It also took the district of Roche-Bernard from Nantes, the southern part of old St Malo, and the district of Gourin from Quimper. It answered to Tours until 1859 and since then to Rennes.

Morbihan holds more monuments of old Gallic worship than any part of France, with the famed long avenues of menhirs at Carnac. By tradition St Clair, first Bishop of Nantes, died in the third century while preaching in the region. The entry follows the diocese's bishops, its shrines, and its modern parishes, a compact history of a Breton see rich in stone and legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-christoph:
Christopher Bales, also called Bayles or Evers, was a priest and martyr born at Coniscliffe near Darlington about 1564, executed on 4 March 1590. He entered the English College at Rome on 1 October 1583, but poor health sent him to Reims, where he was ordained on 28 March 1587. Sent to England on 2 November 1588, he was soon seized, racked, and tortured by Topcliffe, and hung by his hands for twenty-four hours at a time, bearing all with patience.

Tried at last for high treason, on the charge of ordination overseas and coming to England to exercise his office, he put a question to Judge Anderson. He asked whether St Augustine, Apostle of the English, was also a traitor. The judge answered no, but said the act had since been made treason by law. Bales suffered on 4 March 1590, about Easter, in Fleet Street, London.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edward-jo:
Edward Jones was a priest and martyr born in the Diocese of St Asaph in Wales at an unknown date, who died in London on 6 May 1590. Raised Anglican, he was received into the church at the English College, Reims, in 1587, ordained priest in 1588, and went to England the same year. In 1590 a priest-catcher posing as a Catholic seized him in a Fleet Street shop.

Jailed in the Tower and brutally tortured by Topcliffe, he at last admitted he was a priest and had been an Anglican. Those admissions were used at his trial, yet he mounted a skilful and learned defence, arguing that a confession wrung out by torture could not lawfully convict. The court praised his courageous bearing but convicted him of high treason as a priest entering England, and he suffered the same day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-d:
William Davies was one of the most celebrated Welsh priests to suffer under Elizabeth, executed at Beaumaris in July 1593. Born in North Wales, he reached Reims in 1582, was ordained in 1585. Laboured with great zeal in Wales until his arrest at Holyhead in 1592, while sending four students by way of Ireland to Valladolid.

Thrown into a foul dungeon in Beaumaris Castle, he frankly owned that he was a priest. His patience won easier confinement, and he could celebrate Mass and receive visitors, Catholics seeking counsel and Protestant ministers coming to dispute. Condemned at the assizes, he intoned the Te Deum, a hymn of praise, which his companions took up. After examinations at Ludlow and Bewdley, where he outwitted attempts to trap him into a Protestant service, he was put to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veneration-of:
This long doctrinal article defends the Catholic veneration, or reverent honour, of sacred images against the charge of idolatry. It opens with the First Commandment's apparent ban on graven things, noting the golden calf as proof of how easily Israel might slide from making a statue to worshipping it.

Insists the law's thrust is against strange gods and adoration, not against every picture. From there the survey moves through the Old Testament, the early Church, and the iconoclast controversies, distinguishing the honour paid to an image from worship owed to God alone. Later sections describe popular devotion in practice, icons crowned, incensed, and kissed, lamps burning before them. Images reputed not made by hands, while arguing that such reverence passes through the image to the holy person it portrays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-versailles:
Versailles is a French diocese covering Seine-et-Oise, created in 1790 by the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and maintained by the Concordat of 1802, losing Eure-et-Loir to restored Chartres in 1822. It was pieced together from parts of the old dioceses of Paris, Chartres, Rouen, Sens, Beauvais, Senlis, and Evreux.

The town itself was a mere village when Louis XIII bought it in 1632 and built a small château. Under Louis XIV, Mansart raised the great palace from 1661, Lenôtre laid out the gardens. Lebrun directed the interiors; the king lived there constantly from 1682. French monarchs resided at Versailles for over a century, and there the 1783 treaty recognized American independence and, in 1789, the Third Estate constituted itself a national assembly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-canes:
Vincent Canes, in religion John Baptist, was an English Franciscan controversialist who died in London in June 1672. Raised Protestant on the Nottingham and Leicestershire borders, he embraced Catholicism at twenty, went to Douai, joined the Friars Minor. Became lecturer in philosophy and then professor of theology in their convent.

Back in England he laboured strenuously for the faith and was chosen by Catholics to answer Dr Stillingfleet. His ability as a controversialist was strengthened, the entry notes, by an absence of bitterness toward opponents, and his elegant, graceful style made his writings effective. His works include The Reclaimed Papist of 1655, Fiat Lux of 1662, a plea for moderation and quiet after England's religious tumults. Dedicated to the Countess of Arundel, and Infallibility of 1665 as its appendix.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-votive-office:
A votive office is an office not entered in the general calendar but adopted to satisfy a special devotion. By Pius X's constitution Divino Afflatu of November 1911 all votive offices were abolished. Before that action such an office might be celebrated, under rules the entry summarizes, either by privilege or by custom predating St Pius V's bull.

They were called votive because recitation remained optional in principle, as the object of a privilege, even when, after the privilege was obtained, it became accidentally obligatory. They differed from offices ad libitum properly so called. Held a place in a calendar under the rubric ad libitum and might be indicated at will by the compiler of the Ordo. Two classes existed: votive offices granted to petitioners but obligatory after concession, such as the Office of the Blessed Sacrament for Thursdays, and others the entry goes on to detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-waldenses:
The Waldenses were a religious group arising in the second half of the twelfth century and living on, much changed, to the present day. Their name comes from Waldes, their founder, with variants Valdesii and Vallenses. Their vow of extreme poverty earned them the name Poor, their Lyons origin Leonistae, and their sandals or wooden shoes Sandaliati, Insabbatati, and Sabotiers.

Some Waldenses claimed apostolic origins, with Paul founding their Piedmont valley churches on his way to Spain. Later sections follow their structure, a yearly synod checking districts, taking men into ministry, and casting out the unworthy. The Lombard communities, more radical than the French, who held sacramental validity depended on the minister's worthiness and rejected the Catholic Church as Satan's community.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wales:
Wales is the western portion of Great Britain between the Irish Sea and the Dee, the English border counties, the Severn estuary, the Bristol Channel, and St George's Channel. Its name was given not by its inhabitants but by Teutonic occupiers, meaning territory of the alien race. The Welsh have ever called themselves Cymry, and their country in poetry alone Gwalia.

After a 330-year invasion, Angles, Saxons, and Jutes drove the earlier Britons into the western hills, and the entry follows Welsh history, language. Religion from pre-Aryan nature worship and Celtic deities, equations of Greek and Latin gods, through Roman occupation and Llandaff, the oldest episcopal see, to Cardiff's recognition as capital. Its religion sections trace nature cults deifying abstract ideas rather than material objects, and the long Christian story that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-henry:
William Henry Coombes was an English priest and scholar who escaped Revolutionary France and served one parish for nearly forty years. Born in 1767, he died in 1850. Raised at Meadgate in Somerset under his Douai-trained uncle, he entered Douai at twelve, took orders in 1791, and fled from Dourlens to England in October 1793 as the Revolution raged. A doctor of theology, he worked with Bishop Douglass at Old Hall seminary as teacher and vice-president.

From 1810 Coombes served Shepton Mallet until retiring to Downside monastery in 1849. Friends called him spiritual, self-denying, and deeply learned. His books include Sacred Eloquence from Basil and Chrysostom, and an Escape from France memoir with the sufferings of Pius VI. Lives of Saint Francis de Sales and Saint Jane Frances de Chantal, and The Essence of Religious Controversy of 1827 complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-co:
William of Conches was a twelfth-century thinker who carried Arab science and Platonic cosmology into Christian schools. Born about 1100, he taught theology at Paris, then about 1122 became tutor to Henry Plantagenet. A friend's warning about the risks in his Platonic realism as applied to theology turned him toward philosophy and the natural science of the Arabs. When and where he died is uncertain.

Authorship of his works is debated, but he likely wrote glosses on Plato's Timaeus, a commentary on Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue called Dragmaticon, and a treatise, Magna de Naturis Philosophia. A pupil of Bernard of Chartres, he shared the Chartrain love of Plato, humane letters, and nature study. He ranks among the first medieval Christian thinkers to use Arab physics and physiology, reaching him through Constantine the African's translations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ju:
William of Jumièges, surnamed Calculus, was an eleventh-century Benedictine historian of the Normans. Practically nothing is known of his life beyond Norman birth, monkhood at the royal abbey of Jumièges, and death about 1090. His fame rests wholly on the Historia Normannorum in eight books, the chief source for Norman history from 851 to 1137. An early manuscript survived at Rouen until the Revolution and now sits in Paris's Bibliothèque Nationale.

William built his first four books on Dudon of Saint Quentin, praising his predecessor yet pruning his romancing and errors and using all that was sound. Only seven books are William's own, running to 1087; an anonymous hand added the eighth, reaching Abbot Boson's death in 1137. Ordericus Vitalis and Thomas Walsingham drew heavily on him, and the work first reached print at Frankfurt in 1603.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-williamites:
Williamites was the name of two small religious families, one rooted at Monte Vergine and one at Maleval. The Monte Vergine branch sprang from William of Vercelli's houses in Naples, including a double house at Guglieto. Celestine III confirmed the congregation in November 1197. By 1611 it counted forty-five houses; Benedict XIV confirmed new constitutions in 1741, and in 1879 the mother-house alone joined the Cassinese Congregation, keeping its white habit.

The Hermits of Saint William were founded by Albert, companion and biographer of Saint William of Maleval, and Renaldus, a physician at Maleval. It spread swiftly over Italy, Germany, France, Flanders, and Hungary until Gregory IX softened its harsh rule in 1229. Many houses took Benedictine or Augustinian rule, and in 1256 Alexander IV's new Augustinian Hermits drew some away while others stayed apart, numbering fifty-four houses in three provinces by 1435.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yellow-knives:
The Yellow Knives are a sub-arctic Déné people, called Copper Indians by Hearne and Red Knives by Mackenzie and Franklin. About five hundred strong, they now roam the bleak wastes northeast of Great Slave Lake, though 250 years ago they hunted along the Coppermine River. Their name comes from knives they once made from copper scattered on a mountain slope, which drew Hudson Bay fur traders and prompted Hearne's trek to the Coppermine's mouth.

Legend says a woman showed them the copper, then sank into the ground, taking most of it with her. When whites first met them, they were bold and unscrupulous, often bullying gentler neighbours until bloody revenge fell on them. Remote habitat has left them among the least civilized-touched tribes. They are now Catholics, served by Oblate missionaries from two missions on Great Slave Lake's north shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zionites:
Zionites were a sect of visionary fanatics who flourished in the eighteenth century at Ronsdorf in the Duchy of Berg, now in Prussia's Rhine province. The sect sprang from a Philadelphian society founded at Elberfeld in 1726 by Elias Eller and Pastor Daniel Schleiermacher.

The society's prophetess was Anna van Bushel, a baker's daughter, who had dreams, visions, and apparitions. After his wife's death Eller married her; she called herself mother of Zion, her husband father of Zion, and prophesied she would bear the world's saviour. Her first child was a daughter, but Eller consoled the society with Scripture texts; a son born in 1733 died two years later. In 1737 the sect left Elberfeld and founded Ronsdorf, raised to city rank in 1745 through Eller's influence. Eller took the chief offices, lived in great pomp, and governed tyrannically until death.
cato-maior-de-senectute-with-introductio:
Cicero's dialogue on old age, spoken by the elder Cato to Scipio and Laelius, appears here in a school and university edition prepared by James S. Reid of Cambridge and revised for American students by Francis W. Kelsey of Michigan. The Latin text stands substantially as Reid left it, with variant readings noted.

A long introduction treats Cicero as a writer on philosophy, then the dialogue's date, Greek sources, purpose, form, and speakers. Notes below the text work line by line through grammar, usage, and Roman life, often at generous length, since the editors aimed at broad and exact Latin scholarship. Cato's answers to the four charges against old age — weakness, idleness, failing memory, and nearness to death — anchor the reading.
cattle-brands-a-collection-of-western-ca:
Andy Adams gathered fourteen western tales in 1906 under a camp-fire frame, two of them reprinted from Leslie's Monthly. The first, Drifting North, follows a trail herd waterbound on the South Canadian. It runs two weeks behind schedule. Its owner rides out impatiently from Dodge, with a buyer waiting on his hands.

Round-ups in winter, a college vagabond among cowboys, the ransom of Don Ramon Mora, and the passing of Peg-Leg fill the middle of the book. Adams writes from inside the work: brands, river crossings, night guards, and the talk of men around a wagon. The stories prize loyalty and nerve, and they record a cattle kingdom already passing when he wrote.
cautionary-tales:
Hilaire Belloc's 1907 volume gathers his comic verse for children, drawn by B. T. B., and it is frank from the start: asked whether the verses are true, the introduction answers that they are not. Jim runs from his nurse and is eaten by a lion. Matilda tells lies. Henry King swallows string.

Rebecca slams doors until a marble bust ends the habit, and Lord Lundy weeps his way out of a career. Two beast books follow the tales, with short rhymes on the python, porcupine, scorpion, vulture, and bison. Each poem hands a dreadful fate to a small fault, played strictly for laughter. The mock-serious tone is the whole point.
celibates:
Celibates, by George Moore, collects three long stories about people who renounce love, in a 1915 New York printing with an introduction by Temple Scott. Scott looks back twenty years to the book's first publication in 1895 and finds the Moore of both dates the same artist. Moore, he says, is never a reporter or a philosopher, but a man expressing himself through whatever personalities stir his imagination to create.

The three tales study their celibates from inside. One is a young woman artist in London. One is a man whose single passion curdles into religion and routine. Others turn purity into a kind of self worship. Moore writes desire denied with slow, exact attention to rooms, clothes, and weather of mind. The introduction warns that fact matters less here than rendering, at the moment English fiction was learning new candor.
celtic-religion-in-pre-christian-times:
Edward Anwyl, professor of Welsh and comparative philology at Aberystwyth, published his short study with Constable in 1906. He begins by fixing his terms: Celtic means the lands where Celtic speech was used in historic times. Speech, he warns, is not the same as race, and older peoples lived in Gaul and Britain long before.

Later chapters trace the phases of Celtic civilisation and tie religion to daily work. Farming had its patron god Amaethon, metalwork its Gofannon, and rivers, springs, and forests all drew worship. Gaulish counterparts of Mercury and Minerva show Roman influence at work. Anwyl builds from language, legend, and archaeology rather than from classical writers alone.
cenci-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas recounted the Cenci horror in this piece from his Celebrated Crimes, dated by its heading to 1598. Dumas starts as a tourist in Rome, following a guide through St. Peter in Montorio, before the story takes him: Francesco Cenci, a rich Roman noble of monstrous cruelty, kept his family in terror, and his daughter Beatrice became the center of the case. The family turned on the tyrant, and murder answered tyranny.

Rome then tried the Cenci, and pope and people took opposite sides on the executions that followed. Dumas tells the tale as documented melodrama, with the famous portrait of Beatrice hanging over it. His Celebrated Crimes series mined real dossiers for exactly this mixture: history, pity, and judicial cruelty in gorgeous prose.
charmides:
Plato's Charmides, in Benjamin Jowett's translation with his analyses and introductions, stages Socrates fresh from the battle of Potidaea meeting the beautiful young Charmides in a wrestling school. The question is temperance, sophrosyne, and each definition fails in turn: quietness, modesty, doing one's own business, self-knowledge. Critias, the boy's guardian and a future tyrant, defends the argument.

Jowett's introduction notes the dialogue's puzzle: Plato here asks whether a knowledge of knowledge is possible or useful, almost in Aristotle's spirit, though elsewhere he identifies good and knowledge. The Charmides matters for that puzzle and for its portrait of Socratic irony playing on Athenian beauty and ambition just before the city's great war.
checkmates-for-three-pieces: William Brett Fishburne's Checkmates for Three Pieces is a data file of chess endgame positions rather than a prose book. Each line gives one board position in FEN, a compact notation that records where the pieces stand and whose move it is. Every position uses only three pieces: the two kings plus a queen or a rook. The side to move faces checkmate, the trapped king with no legal escape.
chess-history-and-reminiscences:
H. E. Bird's Chess History and Reminiscences condenses his forty-six years at the board into one gossipy volume. Bird, an English master, admits in his preface that the work is the essence of a much larger one. He mixes what can be discovered about the origin of chess with his own memories. The dedication honours an opponent and patron of nearly forty years.

Three Indian traditions compete in his account of the game's invention. Progress runs through China, Egypt, Persia, and Arabia into medieval Europe. Chaucer, Caxton, and Elizabeth's reign mark the English chapters. Philidor's ascendency introduces the modern masters, Simpson's club, and the congresses of Bird's own century. Specimens of play and a review of Steinitz follow. Bird writes as a participant, not a scholar, and his reminiscences of players' temperaments are the book's living core.
children-s-hour-with-red-riding-hood-and:
Watty Piper edited a 1922 story hour for young children, opening with Little Red Riding Hood in a gentle version. Grandmother, in this telling, jumps out of bed and hides in a closet when the wolf comes. The basket of eggs, butter, and cake still goes through the wood. Flower-picking still delays the child on her path.

Other tales follow in the same plain style. A false bride pronounces her own doom before a king, in a story of swapped brides. The Babes in the Wood are left to an uncle who promised to father them, then schemes for their money. The book was made to be read aloud, with large print and famous illustrations in its original form.
chinese-sketches:
Herbert A. Giles knew China from eight years of travel and consular work when he gathered these sketches, first printed in a Shanghai newspaper. Giles opens with the death of the young emperor in January 1875 and the secret accession of a child successor. Other pieces take up customs, names, examinations, and street life as he met them with pencil and notebook in hand.

His preface fights the English habit of calling the Chinese a degraded race. Giles answers that he found a hardworking, sober, and happy people, placed between Western wealth and Western misery. The sketches mix reportage, folklore, and argument. They read as one informed foreigner's attempt to correct his countrymen, anecdote by anecdote.
chippings-with-a-chisel-from-twice-told-:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's sketch, drawn from Twice-Told Tales, remembers a summer at Edgartown on Martha's Vineyard. There he befriended a travelling carver of tombstones. The man had come from inland Massachusetts hunting work. Islanders, Hawthorne notes, remember their dead long and dearly, yet live so healthily that a resident stone-cutter might starve.

The burial ground becomes their text. Elder stones carry death's-heads, cross-bones, scythes, and hour-glasses, likely carved in London. Slabs of plain slate mark a plainer taste. Rough island rock, cut by friends' unskilled hands, moves Hawthorne most. Talk turns sceptical: the carver's trade itself is questioned, and heavy marble is called a mistaken symbol. Thoughts, the sketch argues, should soar like the butterfly, not linger with its husk.
chivalry-dizain-des-reines:
James Branch Cabell's linked tales of queens appeared in a 1921 edition, opened by an essay on the chivalric code itself. Every age, that essay argues, lives by catchwords that spare it hard thought. Chivalry's code put God, honour, and a knight's mistress above all else. It asked piety, obedience, and a modified chastity, but never poverty.

The tales then test the code on real courts. Queens command, flatter, and send men to war. One queen orders a malingering marquess from his bed to lead troops against the Scots. His illness, she notes, is the one that killed Iscariot. Hastings must rise anyway. Cabell writes medieval romance with a modern, ironic smile, in prose dressed for pageantry.
chocolate-and-cocoa-recipes-and-home-mad:
Walter Baker and Company of Dorchester issued a recipe book in 1909 as a compliment to customers, its mills pictured from the air. Maria Parloa wrote the chocolate and cocoa half. Janet McKenzie Hill wrote the home-made candy half. An essay first traces cacao from Mexico, where Spaniards under Cortez found it in 1519.

Consumption figures make the firm's case. Americans kept about an ounce per head in 1860. By 1908 they kept over sixteen ounces. Liebig is quoted calling chocolate a perfect food. Recipes then take over: drinks, cakes, frostings, and Mrs. Lincoln's chocolate caramels among them. Exact measures rule every page. The book is advertising, but of the useful kind, made to live in a kitchen.
christmas-eve-on-lonesome-and-other-stor:
John Fox Jr. published five Kentucky mountain tales in 1911, illustrated by four artists and dedicated to Thomas Nelson Page. The title story rides with Buck through snow on Christmas Eve. Buck has served a prison term for a crime another man swore onto him. He is riding to kill that enemy, whose window glows red above the hollow called Lonesome.

A prison chaplain's text — vengeance is mine, saith the Lord — rings against Buck's own answer: mine. The Pardon of Becky Day turns on forgiveness demanded at a gate, and a dying woman's curse held in reserve. The Army of the Callahan, A Crisis for the Guard, and Christmas Night with Satan complete the set. Feud country supplies the weather, inside and out.
chronicles-of-the-canongate-1st-series:
Walter Scott framed Chronicles of the Canongate through Mr Chrystal Croftangry, an elderly Edinburgh gentleman who edits other people's manuscripts. The publisher's crisis of 1826 had ended Scott's anonymity, as his 1827 introduction explains. The first series contains two long tales plus that introduction and an appendix on the Theatrical Fund dinner.

The Highland Widow tells of Elspat MacTavish, whose son's soldiering ends on the scaffold. The Two Drovers follows English and Scottish cattle men whose quarrel turns on honor and a concealed dirk. Bruce's vengeance in the Highland pass appears inside the widow's back-story of cateran raids. Scott's late tales trade his early romance for tragic compression, and they still cut deep.
cicely-and-other-stories:
Cicely and Other Stories, by Annie Fellows Johnston, gathers five tales for young readers from the author of the Little Colonel series. The contents list Cicely, Alida's Homeliness, The Hand of Douglas, Elsie's Palmistry Evening, and Their Ancestral Latch-String. Thirteen illustrations are listed by page, with a frontispiece.

Cicely opens amid the whir of sewing machines in Madame Levane's workroom. The stories turn on girls facing plain, hard choices about pride, looks, and loyalty. One scene has an old man counsel a girl named Mary Lee not to spoil her friend's pleasure by going home on impulse. Browning's poem Saul enters that advice, as it might in a household where books are close at hand.
cinderella-and-other-stories:
Cinderella, and Other Stories, by Richard Harding Davis, is a story collection first placed in Scribner's Magazine, Harper's Magazine, and Harper's Weekly. The title story is no fairy tale. It opens at the Hotel Salisbury on Broadway, where the servants have set a date for their annual ball and concert.

Four more stories follow it in the contents: Miss Delamar's Understudy, The Editor's Story, An Assisted Emigrant, and The Reporter who Made Himself King. The ball story levels all ranks for a night, from the night clerk to the hall boy asked to play a banjo solo. A far grimmer note sounds in a later tale, where a small boy sinks into sleep on cold steps behind a sailors' boarding house.
cinderella-or-the-little-glass-slipper-a:
Anonymous authors fill this children's story collection headed by Cinderella, or the Little Glass Slipper, printed without credits for its many contributors. The contents run to dozens of short pieces: Fanny's Telephone Order, Sir Gobble, A Sad Thanksgiving Party, Mean Boy, Naughty Pumpkin's Fate, The Ice-King's Reign, and Christmas in California among them. Moral tales and holiday stories mix freely.

One story follows Hiram, who catches shrimp early and late to buy his mother a ring costing three dollars and twenty-two cents. Another sets four dolls before a dressing-case mirror at a children's party. The volume typifies nineteenth-century Sunday-school and gift-book fare: brief, improving, and varied enough to hold a child's whole winter of evenings.
cleek-the-man-of-the-forty-faces:
Cleek: the Man of the Forty Faces, by Thomas W. Hanshew, is a detective novel whose hero is named in its title as a master of many faces. It opens in London street traffic. A young constable, P.C. Collins, spots a Frenchwoman threading the maze of vehicles at Dead Man's Corner and springs to pilot her to the kerb.

She thanks him in broken English, marvels at London policemen, and asks the way to the Abbey of Westminster. Collins, susceptible and pleased, is hooked on the spot. Later pages reach back into case history: a chevalier who would not reply to a steward's letter, and six hundred marks sent in place of a rash promise of wealth.
clotelle-a-tale-of-the-southern-states:
William Wells Brown, who escaped slavery himself, wrote Clotelle as a tale of the southern states built from the legend of Thomas Jefferson's enslaved daughter. His contents announce the machinery of the system chapter by chapter: the slave's social circle, the negro sale, the slave speculator, the slave-holding parson, and today a mistress, tomorrow a slave. Clotelle, the quadroon heroine, is sold away from her mother and lover.

The middle chapters move through slave hunts, prisons, and self-sacrifice, with servants carrying compliments between great houses in the ordinary courtesies that slavery hollowed out. Brown revised the novel across four versions over fourteen years. It stands among the first novels published by an African American.
cobwebs-and-cables:
Cobwebs and Cables, by Hesba Stretton, is a two part novel whose author note reserves American publication to Dodd, Mead & Company alone. Part I opens with a chapter called Absconded and moves through Phebe Marlowe, Felicita, Upfold Farm, and the Old Bank. Fraud is its engine: a confession and a second fraud stand in the chapter list.

Part II begins after many years. Canon Pascal, Felicita's refusal, a London curacy, and a grave at Engelberg carry the older generation's sins forward. Alice Pascal stands at its heart. In one scene Felix tells his mother that as long as he can remember, he has loved Alice. A father's sin and haunting memories close in before the end.
collected-essays-volume-v-science-and-ch:
Collected Essays, Volume V: Science and Christian Tradition, by Thomas Henry Huxley, gathers his fighting essays of 1887 to 1891. The contents list Science and Pseudo-Science, An Episcopal Trilogy, and The Value of Witness to the Miraculous. Agnosticism gets three entries in a row: the essay of 1889, a rejoinder, and Agnosticism and Christianity.

A prologue from Controverted Questions, 1892, admits the essays' origin. Most were written in reply to attacks, and they bear the mark of that origin in their tone. Huxley calls polemic useful, sometimes necessary, and always more or less of an evil. The Keepers of the Herd of Swine and a closing attack on Mr. Gladstone's controversial methods end the volume.
comedy-of-marriage-and-other-tales:
Comedy of Marriage and Other Tales, by Guy de Maupassant, opens in dramatic form. A contents glimpse names pieces called Cake, Corsican Bandit, and The Duel, and gives the play its French title, La Paix du Ménage. Its persons are Monsieur de Sallus, Madame de Sallus, and Jacques de Randol, and its time is Paris, 1890.

Jacques slips into the drawing room unannounced and kisses Madame de Sallus on the hair. She protests at the imprudence; the servants will think he does not count. His visits last five minutes before some other admirer, impatient for his departure, arrives. If you only were my wife, he sighs. A later scene turns on another woman, Gilberte, whose word a pleading man demands before he will shape his life.
complete-works-of-plutarch-volume-3-essa:
Plutarch's essays and miscellanies fill this third volume of his complete works in English, the Moralia beyond the famous Lives. The contents divide into philosophical essays and literary essays. The philosophical set opens with an attack on Epicurus, arguing that his doctrine makes a pleasant life impossible, and continues against the Stoics.

The Symposiacs preserve table talk on dozens of questions, and short pieces treat fate, the eating of flesh, and Plato's problems. The literary essays include the Life and Poetry of Homer, advice on how a young man ought to hear poems, and the Banquet of the Seven Wise Men. The Malice of Herodotus closes the list, a prosecution of the father of history for bias. The old translation's thee-and-thou manner is part of the flavour.
condensed-novels-new-burlesques:
Bret Harte turned parodist in Condensed Novels: New Burlesques, shrinking the popular novels of his day into mocking miniatures. Rupert the Resembler deflates Anthony Hope's Prisoner of Zenda romances, with a hero proud of resembling everybody and being nobody. The Stolen Cigar Case imitates Conan Doyle, and other pieces take off Hall Caine, Marie Corelli, and Kipling, their authors' names printed in coy dashes.

Harte copies each writer's tricks so exactly that the joke needs no explaining: the mannerisms were the message all along. These burlesques first made his name in California magazines. Read beside his mining tales, they show a second gift, literary mimicry sharp enough to wound and fond enough to entertain.
connor-magan-s-luck-and-other-stories:
Connor Magan's Luck and Other Stories, by M. T. W., was published in Boston by D. Lothrop & Company in 1881. Fourteen stories fill the table. Why Mammy Delphy's Baby Was Named Grief stands among them. So do Sammy Sealskin's Enemy, Nannette's Live Baby, and Brothers For Sale. A Story of a Clock, Naughty Zay, and The Legend of the Salt Sea fill out the list.

The title story throws twelve-year-old Connor into a spring freshet on the Ohio River. The coffee-colored flood has swallowed the landmarks and floats trees, timbers, and bridge wreckage toward the Gulf. Connor shouts his luck, tosses his brimless hat, and pushes off in the skiff where his father Tim waits. In Naughty Zay, a little rebel calmly postpones running away until after dinner, the smell of fricassee having settled the question.
corporal-sam-and-other-stories:
Short tales by Sir Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, signed 'Q', make up this story book. The title tale follows Sergeant David Wilkes and men of the First Regiment of Foot as they haul a gun into place on Mount Olia. War, the sea, and Cornish life supply most of the settings.

Ten more tales stand in the contents list. Among them are The Copernican Convoy, Red Velvet, The Jew on the Moor, and My Christmas Burglary. Others turn on a mayor, a doctor, and news said to come from Troy. The mix gives readers brief, varied scenes of risk, duty, and local character, each told in a plain, brisk style.
cousin-hatty-s-hymns-and-twilight-storie:
Simple hymns and short tales for children fill this Boston book of 1851. The preface, dated Boston, December 4, 1850, says most verses were first written for one dear child. Friends urged print so that other children might take the same pleasure.

Morning and evening hymns stand beside tales of a cat, a spider, a bee, and a monkey. Bible children such as Samuel and Moses appear, as do Hagar and Ishmael. Lessons on anger, selfishness, and cross looks are told in plain rhyme. Seasons, Christmas, and the New Year each get a piece. The whole is a gentle home book, meant to teach faith and good conduct to the very young.
cowmen-and-rustlers-a-story-of-the-wyomi:
A tale of the Wyoming cattle ranges by Edward S. Ellis fills this book, its title page dated MCMIV. The Whitney household in Maine opens the story on a bright winter night. A warning from the woods and flight over the ice soon move the action west and into danger.

Thirty-five chapters track fights between cowmen and rustlers. Burned ranches, a truce flag, a hostage, and hot pursuit fill the middle. A band the book calls the Dog Indians adds a further threat. The closing chapters clear up a missing man and a strange deed. Ellis writes brisk frontier action for young readers, with the cattle war as its engine.
crime-and-its-causes:
Crime studied as a social fact fills this book by William Douglas Morrison of H. M. Prison, Wandsworth. Swan Sonnenschein of London and Charles Scribner's Sons of New York issued it in 1902. Press notices at the front praise it as an early English work of strict scientific method on the topic.

Morrison tests common claims about why men break the law. He argues that if want vanished from England and Wales, crime would not drop much. Hard cases, he says, are too often taken as types of the whole criminal class. Chapters work through causes one by one in a calm tone. The book helped found criminology as a study in English.
critical-miscellanies-vol-2-of-3-essay-1:
An essay on the French moralist Vauvenargues by John Morley fills this file, the first essay of his Critical Miscellanies, volume two. Macmillan of London and New York issued the volume in 1905. A contents list maps the essay by page, from the sway of Pascal to the beauty of its subject's nature.

Morley tells a short, hard life: birth, scant schooling, Paris, and friendship with Voltaire. He sets Vauvenargues against Pascal and La Rochefoucauld, whose maxims he found too bleak. Character, will, and warm feeling stand at the core of the man's thought. Morley praises a plea for a sane, normal view of human ties. The essay is a fine sample of Victorian life-and-letters criticism.
critiques-and-addresses:
Speeches and essays by Thomas Henry Huxley, dated 1873, make up Critiques and Addresses. Huxley says in his preface that the pieces deal chiefly with schooling, science, and philosophy. They mark, in his phrase, the high-water mark of his work since 1870.

Two papers come from his year on the London School Board, from which ill health forced him to resign. Other pieces take up skull types in old tombs, from Scandinavia to pre-Roman Britain and Gaul. Long heads and broad heads are sorted tribe by tribe. The book joins the public man of science with the field worker. Readers see how Huxley argued in hall and print in the same strong voice.
crowded-out-and-other-sketches:
Sketches of Canadian life by S. Frances Harrison, written under the name Seranus, fill this book. The title sketch, Crowded Out, stands first among ten pieces. Harrison's preface offers the set to her Canadian public with due fear and humility.

She says some tales are true and some are works of fancy. French Canada fills much of the book: Monsieur, Madame, and a pea-green parrot; the tale of Delle Josephine Boulanger; the prisoner Dubois, known as an agitator. The Bishop of Saskabasquia and the Foxley family add other shades of colonial life. Harrison held that every town and class has its own deep stamp. The sketches try to catch that stamp for Canada.
crucial-instances:
Edith Wharton's Crucial Instances gathers seven stories, opening with The Duchess at Prayer. Wharton asks whether the reader has ever questioned the shuttered front of an old Italian house, a motionless mask as smooth and mute as a priest's face behind which buzz confessional secrets.

Other houses declare their activities, Wharton writes, but the old palace down its narrow street stays as closed as death, its tall windows like blind eyes. Contents also include The Angel at the Grave, The Recovery, Copy: A Dialogue, The Rembrandt, The Moving Finger, and The Confessional. Readers of Wharton will find these instances finely observed studies of conscience and society.
daddy-do-funny-s-wisdom-jingles:
Short verses in the voice of an old plantation storyteller fill Ruth McEnery Stuart's book of jingles. The Century Company of New York holds copyrights from 1910 to 1913, and G. H. Clements drew the pictures. Stuart inscribes the book to the memory of enslaved men who guarded homes in the war years.

Daddy speaks on roosters, wrens, mules, and watermelons, each in a page or two. Judge Owl, the mosquito, and the scarecrow get their own short pieces. A weather prayer opens the set, and incubator chickens close one rhyme with a sigh for lost mothers. The dialect verse shows how white writers of 1913 framed Black speech for young readers, a frame now read with care.
dangerous-ages:
A novel of women at three ages fills Rose Macaulay's Dangerous Ages, issued by Boni and Liveright of New York in 1921. Macaulay had won notice with Potterism, and she inscribes this book to her mother. A line at the front, from Mr Cradock, says that all ages are dangerous to all people.

The tale opens on Neville's birthday, at dawn in a creepered house full of birds. Mrs Hilary's birthday follows, then family life, roots, and seaweed. Gerda and Nan carry the young side of the house, while the mother and the daughter face each other in twin chapters. Youth to youth, the dream, and time fill the close. Macaulay writes a bright, sharp study of growing old and staying young.
dante-the-central-man-of-all-the-world-a:
Lectures on Dante, given to students at the New York State College for Teachers at Albany in 1919 and 1920, fill this book by John T. Slattery. P. J. Kenedy and Sons of New York published it in 1920, with a preface by John H. Finley. Slattery thanks the college heads who urged the talks into print.

Five lectures make the course: Dante and his time, Dante the man, and then the Inferno, the Purgatorio, and the Paradiso. Slattery quotes Ruskin, who called Dante the central man of all the world. Scenes such as Farinata rising from his fiery tomb get close reading. The book is a plain guide for students who meet the great poem for the first time.
darrel-of-the-blessed-isles:
A North Country tale by Irving Bacheller fills Darrel of the Blessed Isles, issued in 1903 with pictures by Arthur I. Keller. Bacheller lists Eben Holden and D'Ri and I among his books, and inscribes this one to his father's memory. A prelude and thirty-seven chapters make the whole.

Darrel is a clock tinker, and the tale turns on his craft and his odd wisdom. The Linley schoolhouse, a rustic museum, and a Christmas adventure fill the middle. Trove, the young hero, carries home a scarf knit by Polly as a keepsake of his first term. Trouble, evidence, and the law take the close. Bacheller writes warm village fiction, full of dialects, clocks, and snow.
david-crockett-his-life-and-adventures:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this biography of David Crockett for the American Pioneers and Patriots series. Abbott says plainly in his preface that Crockett was no model man. He presents him instead as a representative frontiersman whose wild life shows a whole class of early Americans. The narrative runs from Crockett's birth in Tennessee to his fame.

Early chapters cover a runaway boyhood, work as a farm labourer, and a scant schooling. Marriage and settlement follow, then soldiering under Andrew Jackson in the Creek War. Abbott takes Crockett through Indian warfare, a justice of the peace's bench, and election to Congress. Hunting tales, bear fights, and tall talk fill the later pages. The book closes with Crockett's restless move west and his death in Texas, told as popular history.
david-poindexter-s-disappearance-and-oth:
Julian Hawthorne's David Poindexter's Disappearance and Other Tales gathers mystery stories rooted in real cases. Hawthorne notes that English state trials hold many strange stories, but that local cases of small legal notice can stimulate imagination just as much.

The title tale retells the disappearance of David Poindexter, much discussed near the scene of its events, in the simple form in which Hawthorne heard it years before. Other tales in the contents include Ken's Mystery, When Half-Gods Go, the Gods Arrive, Set Not Thy Foot on Graves, and My Friend Paton. Readers who enjoy Victorian mystery with a documentary flavour will find Hawthorne's handling quiet and effective.
dead-men-tell-no-tales:
A sea mystery by E. W. Hornung fills this 1899 tale of twenty chapters. Love on the ocean opens it, on a long clipper voyage of the old sort. Hornung notes that love came easy, and went as easy, when Sydney or Melbourne lay four months away.

A mysterious cargo, a silent sea, and a sole survivor follow in the chapter heads. The narrator's lady gives orders he must obey with his life at stake, and he totters over a plank above a beck toward a lit cottage. The woman Braithwaite stands gaunt in the door in one dread scene. The statement of Francis Rattray closes the book. Hornung, who made Raffles, here works the sea tale of crime.
death-at-the-excelsior-and-other-stories:
Eight early tales by P. G. Wodehouse fill this set, grouped for Project Gutenberg. The contents give each tale's first date, from 1910 to 1921. A title tale of 1914 opens the book in a bare boarding-house room.

Captain John Gunner lies dead on that floor, his teeth bared in a grin, while a policeman and a gaunt landlady look down. Misunderstood, The Best Sauce, and Concealed Art follow in a lighter vein. Two Jeeves tales stand in the list, with Cyril Bassington-Bassington kept from the stage by fifty-seven cables in one of them. The set shows Wodehouse young: part crime tale, part the comic manner that made his name.
debate-on-woman-suffrage-in-the-senate-o:
Speeches for and against votes for women fill this Senate pamphlet, printed at Washington in 1887. The debate ran in the second session of the Forty-ninth Congress, on December 8, 1886, and again in January 1887. Senators Blair, Brown, Dolph, Vest, and Hoar are named on the title page.

Blair opens by moving a joint resolution for a change in the Constitution to extend the vote to women. The text of that amendment is read out in full. Later speech turns to women's work and shopping, and to shops where a woman's care and taste once ruled the counters. The pamphlet keeps the words as spoken. It is a plain record of the first great Senate fight over the suffrage amendment.
deeds-that-won-the-empire-historic-battl:
Battle tales of the British Empire fill W. H. Fitchett's book of historic scenes. John Murray of London issued this copy, after a first edition of November 1897 and a twenty-ninth impression in October 1914. Reprints of 1917 and 1921 are also noted on the title page.

The fight off Cape St Vincent and the heights of Abraham open the set. Nelson and the Nile, the Shannon and the Chesapeake, and the breaches of Badajoz and Ciudad Rodrigo follow. Waterloo gets eight full sections, from the rival hosts to the Old Guard and the great defeat. Trafalgar closes the book in three parts. Plans of the great fights serve the reader. Fitchett writes brisk, patriotic history for the general reader.
definitions-essays-in-contemporary-criti:
Definitions, essays in contemporary criticism by Henry Seidel Canby, gathers the work of a Yale English professor who also edited the Literary Review of the New York Evening Post. Canby thanks the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's, the Century, the Nation, and the North American Review for leave to reprint. His preface explains the title. Literature in a civilization trying to be sophisticated and democratic at once has too many sources for one theory. Each essay opens a door by defining its term.

An informal definition, Canby says, is his whole method: approach a word like fiction, poetry, or realism through the books that embody it, and let writer and reader enter together. This first series surveys the literary scene of the early nineteen twenties. It asks what novelists, poets, and critics are trying to do.
derues-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas retells the career of Antoine Derues, the Paris poisoner, as one tale in his Celebrated Crimes series. The story opens in September 1751 with schoolboys at Chartres, where the young Derues is already marked out by cruelty and cunning. Dumas follows the boy as apprenticeship and marriage carry him to the capital.

In Paris Derues becomes a grocer with a reputation for piety, and Dumas shows how the mask serves the crimes. The poisoning of Madame de Lamotte and her son, the concealment of the bodies, the arrest, and the trial are laid out step by step. Derues went to his execution in 1777 still protesting innocence. The tale suits readers who like their true crime dressed in a novelist's pacing and scene-setting.
derzhavin-spiritual-odes:
Russia's great eighteenth-century poet Gavrila Derzhavin speaks in his Spiritual Odes, given here in Russian. Derzhavin bridged classicism and the age of Pushkin, serving empresses while writing verse of startling personal force. His famous ode God stands among the landmarks of Russian poetry, translated across Europe in his lifetime.

Odes to God and meditations on death combine lofty philosophy with sudden, intimate feeling. A courtier who had seen favor and disgrace alike, Derzhavin writes about power's vanity from inside the palace. The Russian text preserves his bold, uneven music exactly. Modern Russian poetry effectively begins on this foundation stone. Readers with Russian will find the odes grand, strange, and unexpectedly tender.
desperate-remedies:
Thomas Hardy says in his prefatory note that this was his first published story, written when he was still feeling his way to a method. He admits its machinery frankly: mystery, entanglement, surprise, and moral crookedness carry the interest. The chapter headings keep a strict ledger of time, from the events of thirty years down to the events of three hours.

The tale is a sensation novel of the 1870 pattern. A young woman thrown on her own resources takes service in a great house, loves where she should not, and falls within the reach of a steward with a buried secret. Hardy lets coincidence and concealment do the work his later novels give to character and place. Readers of the Wessex books come here to watch the apprentice test his tools.
dick-in-the-everglades:
Florida wilds fill A. W. Dimock's tale for boys, issued by Frederick A. Stokes Company of New York under copyright of 1909. Thirty-two half-tone pictures, from photographs by J. A. Dimock, fill the book. Dick and his chum Ned go to sea, live on a sponger, and are caught in a waterspout before the hunt begins.

The capture of a manatee, harpooning from a canoe, and ghosts and alligators stand in the contents. Camps hear deer in shallow water by night, and the soft tread of some cat-like beast. Outlaws, a bear, crocodile country, Seminoles, a prairie on fire, and a fight with a panther crowd the list. Dick's rescue and Molly and the manatee close it. The book is a photo-filled tour of the Glades.
diet-and-health-with-key-to-the-calories:
Eating by number fills Lulu Hunt Peters's book of 1918, issued by the Reilly and Lee Company of Chicago. Peters, a doctor, had chaired the public health work of the California Federation of Women's Clubs, Los Angeles District. She inscribes the book, by permission, to Herbert Hoover, and her small nephew Dawson Hunt Perkins drew the pictures.

A key to the calories stands in the title, and side notes share the page with the text. Peters treats gaining and losing weight in one book, since lack of food knowledge, she says, founds both. A club plan in the text fines members who fail to shed a pound a week, the money to the Red Cross. The tone is brisk, funny, and strict.
directions-for-cookery-in-its-various-br:
Cookery in all its branches fills Miss Eliza Leslie's book, in a tenth edition with improvements and added receipts, dated 1840. A contents roll runs from soups to perfumery. Meats, poultry, fish, vegetables, pickles, sweetmeats, pastry, cakes, and home-made liquors each get a full part.

Soups open the work, with a plain rule: always use soft water, and somewhat less than a quart of water to a pound of meat for common soup. Preserves get the same care: green gages are boiled gently a quarter of an hour, cooled, boiled again next day, and jarred with syrup under brandy paper. Food for the sick has its own part. The book is a working kitchen bible of early America.
disease-and-its-causes:
What disease is, and what causes it, fills W. T. Councilman's book of 1913. Henry Holt of New York and Williams and Norgate of London issued it. Councilman was professor of pathology at Harvard University. Chapter heads map the whole body and its tie to the world round it.

Living matter and its cells come first, with the amoeba as the type of a one-celled animal. Fit to a changing world, surfaces of the body, glands, fluids, nerves, heart, and blood fill the survey. A later passage treats germs too small to catch: a fluid passed through porcelain filters that hold back the smallest bacteria still gave the disease when inoculated. The book is a clear, calm tour of pathology for lay readers.
doe-osti-17014406-fy26-cellular-silicone:
John Blessinger of Los Alamos National Laboratory summarized fiscal year 2026 friction tests on cellular silicone foam in this report, issued September 27, 2026. The foam is a soft, air filled padding, and the tests measured its static friction, the grip that must be overcome before sliding starts. Samples of varied porosity, meaning varied air content, were compared across test setups.

An opening addendum corrects the prior year analysis, which had used a wrong sample surface area and so scaled every friction value badly. Recalculated values follow. The main body then reports static friction results by porosity and closes with conclusions and a plan for future test work.
doe-osti-17056541-advancing-atomic-physi:
Tilo Doeppner of Lawrence Livermore led project 24-ERD-044 on atomic physics at extreme pressure, reported in September 2026. Models in wide use seem to understate how easily tightly bound electrons leave atoms in dense carbon and beryllium, based on recent National Ignition Facility experiments. That error skews predictions of how hot, dense matter absorbs and moves energy.

The project paired x-ray scattering, which probes electron behavior in dense plasma, with precision radiography that measures x-ray absorption. New analysis methods read plasma temperature with less reliance on theory, cutting uncertainty in the scattering readings. Together the work tests rival predictions and aims to ground better models for stars, planets, and fusion targets.
doe-osti-17065278-solar-desalination-pri:
Official rules govern the Solar Desalination Prize, a United States Department of Energy contest run by the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation. The prize seeks systems that use sunlight to make fresh water from salt water. Its stated application deadlines fall on August 10, 2027, and August 10, 2028, at 5 p.m. Eastern Time.

Four phases structure the contest: Innovation, Teaming, Design, and Test. Early phases pick promising concepts and help form mixed skill teams around them. Later phases require working prototypes of solar thermal desalination systems, tested at real facilities, with site visits by the Energy Department. Winners gain cash prizes plus mentoring and training through the American-Made Network.
doe-osti-17076820-site-evaluation-to-sup:
Femi Omitaomu and Brandon Miller of Oak Ridge, with Ross Hays and Nipun Popli of Idaho, evaluated sites for the Energy Department Reactor Pilot Program in this June 30, 2026 report. The program will place qualified test reactors at chosen sites, so siting limits and advantages must be mapped early. A siting tool named ORSAGE supplied updated data sets for the work.

Site categories were compared against major siting criteria aligned with Nuclear Regulatory Commission practice. Four demonstration clusters then get detailed treatment: Idaho National Laboratory, the Texas A&M RELLIS Campus, Abilene Christian University, and Orangeville, Utah. Conclusions and next steps close the report, which was prepared for the Systems Analysis and Integration Campaign.
doe-osti-17121546-multiscale-modeling-va:
Chaitanya Bhave and Idaho National Laboratory colleagues model how palladium leaks through the silicon carbide shell of TRISO fuel particles, in an August 2025 NEAMS report. TRISO particles are tiny fuel kernels wrapped in layers, and the silicon carbide layer is the main barrier. Palladium, a fission product, can attack and cross that layer at high heat.

Models at several scales are linked. Atom and mesoscale work quantifies how grain boundaries in the carbide speed palladium flux. An engineering scale model then computes penetration across a whole particle layer. A simpler reduced order model is derived and checked against an empirical correlation. A final part applies Bayesian uncertainty methods, adding grain aspect ratio effects, and validates the chain against experimental data sets.
doe-osti-2584725-development-of-a-reliab:
Livermore internship report LLNL-TR-2006465, by Laura Leos from a winter 2025 materials science placement, redesigns the jig used to pot photoconductive semiconductor switches. Potting seals these delicate switches in epoxy against mechanical stress, moisture, and high voltage. The existing compression jig fit only one switch style and clamped with binder clips, applying uneven pressure that let potting material leak.

The replacement is a universal, micrometer-driven compression jig, cross-compatible with varied switch designs so one tool pots them all. The process it serves bonds nickel-gold plated copper electrodes to the device's contacts and injects EP30 epoxy openly through a PEEK ring, supporting the weak bond while it cures. Known roadblocks are named honestly: epoxy leaking into the optical path, and misalignment of the electrode bond. The report is a compact piece of process engineering, measured by whether the next batch of switches comes out sealed and straight.
doe-osti-2585501-soft-catching-high-velo:
Jack Borg of Sandia National Laboratories wrote report SAND2025-09717, printed in August 2025, on catching fast projectiles without wrecking them. In gas gun and powder gun tests, researchers often need the sample back for study after the shot. The catch must absorb the impact gently, so nearly all the damage in the sample comes from the test itself, not from being stopped.

Borg reviews methods used at lower speeds, such as nylon parachute fabric in catch tanks for shots up to about 700 meters per second. The report then explores a method for the much harder case of materials launched near 3,000 meters per second. Chapters cover the Flying Pig project and two diagnostics, optical beam ranging and photonic Doppler velocimetry, before closing with future concepts and conclusions.
doe-osti-2586447-advancements-in-neams-t:
Nicholas Wozniak, Gang Yang, Ahmed Abdelhameed, and colleagues at Argonne National Laboratory report progress on reactor simulation tools in ANL/NEAMS-25/1. The work sits in the Department of Energy's NEAMS program, which builds advanced modeling for nuclear reactors. The target problem is core bowing in liquid metal-cooled fast reactors, where heat and radiation gradients bend fuel assemblies and feed back on reactivity.

The team is building a MOOSE-based workflow that couples radiation transport, fluid flow, heat transfer, and mechanics. This year it assessed the Griffin reactor physics code for bowing calculations and coupled physics and thermal solvers on single- and multi-assembly problems based on the ABR-1000 design. Supporting checks used an IAEA verification problem with swelling and creep, plus a small core benchmark from the Japan Atomic Energy Agency. Fast Flux Test Facility data was identified for validation.
doe-osti-2588022-securing-flexible-deman:
Dane Christensen of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory presented these slides, dated December 2, 2024, on securing flexible demand. As the grid grows more distributed and intelligent, loads that can shift in time become a resource: flexible demand. The deck lays out the vocabulary first, from demand-side management and demand response to virtual power plants, which aggregate homes and devices into something a grid operator can dispatch.

Federal rules frame the opportunity, including FERC Order 841 on storage and Order 2222 on distributed energy aggregations in markets. A Texas case from August 20, 2024 shows why flexibility matters: locational prices in the Texas interconnect spiked toward 5,000 dollars per megawatt-hour. Smart thermostats are the mass-market wedge. Adoption already reaches 32 percent of United States homes, led by Nest at 18 percent, Honeywell at 9 percent, and Ecobee at 5 percent.
doe-osti-2588956-fy25-moose-usability-im:
Emily Shemon, Yinbin Miao, Shikhar Kumar, and colleagues at Argonne National Laboratory wrote this report, ANL/NEAMS-25/3, on fiscal 2025 usability improvements to MOOSE, the laboratory's multiphysics simulation framework. Capability gets the glory in scientific software, but usability decides whether anyone outside the core team can run the thing. This year's work takes three concrete bites out of that problem.

First, 3D meshing capabilities were extended inside the framework. Second, geometry support for Monte Carlo tools was initiated, so MOOSE models can feed neutron transport codes more directly. Third, the MOOSE and Workbench user input interactions were enhanced. An example threaded through the meshing work shows the payoff. TRISO particles are placed and packed inside fuel compacts. Finite element meshes are then generated from those locations. Thermomechanical analysis is handed off to the BISON fuel performance code.
doe-osti-2588976-detonation-waves-in-hig:
Ralph Menikoff and Edward Kober of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this monograph, LA-UR-25-29410, on detonation waves in high explosives. It is a full reference work, running to ten chapters plus an index, that collects the theory a modeler needs to simulate how a detonation starts, runs, and fails.

Four parts structure the book. An introduction leads into the mathematical description: reactive flow equations, shock wave relations, and the planar detonation wave. Phenomena and experiments come next. Chapters treat shock initiation, the ignition and growth concept built on hotspots, diameter and curvature effects, and failure diameter with corner turning and dead zones. The final part turns to calibration, fitting equation of state models and reaction rate models to data. Power-law relations between run distance, time, and pressure appear in the initiation analysis. For the laboratory that invented much of this science, the volume is a baseline text.
doe-osti-2997453-591-mhz-srf-cavity-desi:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229008-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-143, by Wencan Xu, A. Blednykh, Z. Conway, and co-authors, presents the second design round for a radio-frequency cavity for the Electron-Ion Collider. The cavity is a single superconducting cell running at 591 megahertz, for the collider's Electron Storage Ring. That ring's beam loses up to 10 megawatts to synchrotron radiation, which the radio system must replace.

Eighteen such cavities will supply that power for a 2.5 ampere electron beam. Work covered shaping the cavity for a tight impedance budget, checking multipacting, the electron avalanches that can block operation, and damping higher-order modes that threaten beam stability. The larger beam pipe stays at 137 millimeters. One gain in this round: the peak surface electric field came down against the first design.
doe-osti-2997488-2025-status-report-fibe:
Savannah River National Laboratory status report SRNL-STI-2025-00660, by Thanh-Tam Truong, dated September 2025, tracks the fiberboard cushioning inside the Model 9975 shipping package. Fiberboard absorbs shocks and insulates the inner container, but it degrades over decades in storage at the site's K-Area Complex. Samples have aged up to 20 years under accelerated heat and humidity.

Measurements of heat conduction, energy absorption, weight, size, and density feed aging models that give a rate of change for each property at a given storage condition. The site's storage evaluations assumed rates of 0.5 percent per year for several properties across a 40-year life. Those models supported extending the rated storage life of packages holding 3013 containers from 20 years to 40 years. The report keeps the property data and the rate fits current for the next review.
doe-osti-2997615-humate-amendment-inject:
Evan Koelker, Holly VerMeulen, and Sophia Fuentes continue tests of injecting humate, a natural organic extract, to treat polluted groundwater, in Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2025-00566 dated September 2025. The Lost Lake Aquifer Zone under the site's M-Area holds trichloroethylene and tetrachloroethylene from past operations. Pilot injections ran from 2017 to 2020 before low flow rates and spills stopped them.

New bench work compares two products, Huma-K and BorreGro, in batch mixtures and soil columns. Huma-K varied from sample to sample because its extraction process leaves impurities, while BorreGro was made more consistently, favoring it for field use. Samples were pH-adjusted and left overnight before checks. The studies decide whether a fresh field injection trial is worth attempting, and with which product.
doe-osti-2997983-gridlab-d-technical-sup:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory technical support document, by Laura Hinkle, Carolyn Goodman, and Robert Pratt, dated September 2025, explains the house model inside the GridLAB-D grid simulator. The model, called the equivalent thermal parameter model, treats a house as two linked heat stores: indoor air and the building's mass. Planners use thousands of these houses to test how home heating and cooling loads bend under price or control signals.

Chapters derive the model's second-order equation in closed form, set its boundary conditions, and rewrite it in state-space form for the simulator. Parameter definitions then cover house geometry, envelope insulation values for walls, ceiling, floor, windows, and doors, thermal mass, and heating and cooling system design. One formula sums each surface's area divided by its resistance, plus air leakage, into a single loss coefficient. The document is the reference behind the simulator's residential load numbers.
doe-osti-2999880-sphenix-heavy-flavor-je:
Xuan Li, Jakub Kvapil and Zhiwan Xu report in LA-UR-25-30173, issued 14 October 2025, on teaching computers to spot jets from heavy quarks at the sPHENIX detector. sPHENIX, at Brookhaven's collider, studies the quark-gluon plasma, matter so hot that protons melt. Jets born from bottom and charm quarks lose energy in that plasma in telling ways, but first the jets must be correctly labelled by their starting quark.

Two machine learning taggers were trained on simulated proton-proton collisions at 200 giga-electronvolts. One uses a long short-term memory network, which reads jet parts in sequence. The other uses an attention-based network, which weighs which parts matter most. For bottom quark jets, both beat the traditional method of simple cuts on measured values. The report details the training samples, the input variables chosen, tuning steps, and side-by-side performance, as groundwork for later plasma studies.
doe-osti-3001405-high-fidelity-self-lear:
Michael Zeifman and Kurt Roth of Fraunhofer USA file the report for award DE-EE0009696, submitted 31 October 2025, on software that turns houses into a power plant. A virtual power plant needs forecasts household by household. It must know how much each home will draw, and how far heating, water heater and car charger loads can flex without annoying anyone. The team built models that calibrate themselves from thermostat, meter and weather history.

Components include a thermal model for homes with forced air heating and cooling, and a solar generation predictor. Probabilistic models cover electric water heating and vehicle charging. Gains are better accuracy over longer horizons than prior models. Optimisation costs grow linearly with households, where model predictive control grows quadratically. One optimiser can reshape a community's load curve while cutting home bills under time of use prices. A comfort model predicts tolerated discomfort, keeping flexibility honest.
doe-osti-3002139-materials-signatures-of:
Zach Brubaker, Duncan Moseley, Chad Parish, and eight colleagues close a research project in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4177, dated October 2025. The project studied the material fingerprints of tiny metallic particles. Such particles matter in nuclear forensics, where their makeup can point to how and where material was made. The report is the final account of a laboratory-directed research effort.

The team pushed several tools: transmission Kikuchi diffraction for crystal maps, nanotomography for 3D particle views, and atomic force microscopy for surface traits.
