New workflows move and slice many particles at once; for 316L steel, slicing throughput rose fivefold. The group also made test particles by controlled heating and combustion synthesis. Together, the methods read a particle's history faster and in more detail.
doe-osti-3002239-hfir-high-power-heu-neu:
Aaron Holzaepfel, Kevin Burg, David Chandler, and colleagues run reactor physics calculations in a September 2025 Oak Ridge report. The reactor is the High Flux Isotope Reactor, and the question is a high-power test cycle on its current highly enriched uranium fuel. Running at 95 megawatts would preview conditions planned for future low-enriched fuel.

Earlier analyses showed the replacement silicide fuel must run at 95 megawatts to match what today's fuel delivers at 85. Two MCNP computer models were built for the test cycle. One carries a representative load of beam tube experiments. The other swaps in aluminum dummy rods, since many experiments cannot qualify for the hotter cycle. A third model at 85 megawatts anchors comparisons. Results cover cycle length and uranium-235 burnup patterns.
doe-osti-3002999-load-data-for-mk279-pro:
Kyle Winter and Sivana Torres collect firing data in Sandia report SAND2025-13958, printed November 2025. The data cover Mk279 Mod1 projectiles shot from an RD24 barrel at different powder loads. The goal is a reference table: future testers who use this projectile as a calibrated impactor can pick a load to reach a target speed.

Tables pair each powder charge with the measured average velocity. The authors flag a limit plainly: the shot count at each load was too small for the averages to be statistically firm. More shots per load are needed before the numbers carry high confidence. The short report is a working lab record, published so later ballistic test planning starts from measured data rather than fresh trial and error.
doe-osti-3005922-heu-systems-at-low-temp:
Rowan Johnson of Texas A&M and Los Alamos, with George McKenzie of Los Alamos, present a slide deck dated September 2025 on highly enriched uranium systems at low temperature. The Nuclear Criticality Safety Program sponsors the work, with Lawrence Livermore collaborating. The concern is transport: fissile material packages can end up in cold environments, bounded at minus 40 degrees Celsius by federal shipping rules.

MCNP calculations tested how reactivity changes as assemblies are inserted and reflectors added, across fast and thermal spectrum cases. Reactivity rose steadily with insertion and reflector growth in the fully inserted design, though it wobbled at low reflector heights while staying safely subcritical. The deck is candid about model limits: thermal contraction and low-temperature scattering data for aluminum are missing. Experiments are planned, aimed at an international benchmark entry.
doe-osti-3005930-deimos-and-graphite-tsl:
Slides by Nicholas Thompson and four Los Alamos colleagues (LA-UR-25-26447) were presented July 9, 2025 at the 1st Reactor Graphite Workshop. They examine how graphite's thermal scattering law, or TSL, handles porosity in the Deimos critical assembly. Deimos runs at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center in Nevada, and its graphite parts are not fully dense. The deck first gives an overview of the center and the Deimos and Theta assemblies.

Calculations then test how pore fraction changes the results. For an infinite lattice, porosity in the TSL had no visible effect, which the authors link to mid-range neutron spectra and small graphite sections. For Deimos itself, the effect ran about 15 to 20 pcm per percent of porosity between 0 and 30 percent. Nominal and 30 percent porosity TSLs differ by roughly 500 pcm, a gap the deck calls measurable across the planned benchmark set.
doe-osti-3006202-corrected-moments-in-an:
ARM technical report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-327, dated April 2026, documents CMAC, Corrected Moments in Antenna Coordinates, a software chain that cleans up weather radar data. Nine authors are listed, led by S. M. Collis, J. J. Helmus, and Z. S. Sherman. The chain first calculates fields that help identify what kind of scatterer sits at each radar gate, then applies a fuzzy logic identification. Corrections and retrievals follow, including dealiasing of folded velocities.

Worked cases close the report. One covers a severe weather night with embedded tornadoes passing over the BNF site. Another revisits May 20, 2025, when supercells crossed the Huntsville metro area during the ARM Summer School and an EF1 tornado damaged the hotel hosting instructors. A figure shows CSAPR2 radar reflectivity at 3.5 degrees for that night, matching the observed damage. The report serves users who need corrected radar moments rather than raw sweeps.
doe-osti-3006492-destructive-analysis-of:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4291, dated October 2025, documents a destructive method for assaying uranium in TRISO fuel particles. Ten authors are listed, led by Kayron Rogers, Tamara Keever, and Christopher Hobbs. The method crushes the particles, burns off the coatings, and leaches the uranium into nitric acid. One pictured batch, UCO500-01T+, came from Standard Nuclear.

Uranium content is then measured two ways: Davies-Gray titration and isotope dilution mass spectrometry. Filter paper samples are also checked by gamma spectrometry, and micrographs record the particles after treatment. An appendix gives quality control data for both methods. Titration results are plotted against the certificate value of reference material CRM 112-A. Mass spectrometry results are plotted against NIST 3164 with its expanded uncertainty band. The report closes with a conclusion section and acknowledgements.
doe-osti-3007476-fy25-cellular-silicone-:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-31737, by John Blessinger and James Valdez, sums up fiscal 2025 friction testing of cellular silicone foam, a soft padding material. Sled tests dragged foam samples across two track surfaces, Macor ceramic and 304 stainless steel, while surface roughness was recorded. An appendix lists every completed test in the year's matrix.

The test matrix covered foams of 67 and 70 percent porosity under compressive stresses that included 2 and 8 pounds per square inch, with repeat runs at set sliding times. Results are reported as mean friction coefficients with spread bands against the stress in the foam. The data feed design work wherever this foam must slide, grip, or seal under load.
doe-osti-3010209-solvated-ionic-liquid-b:
DOE Basic Energy Sciences final report for award DE-SC0023440, by Daniel Kuroda of Louisiana State University, dated December 22, 2025, covers solvated ionic liquid electrolytes studied from September 2022 to August 2025. These are lithium salts dissolved in glyme solvents at concentrations so high the liquid behaves like an ionic liquid.

Infrared spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and molecular dynamics together showed charge moving by ion hopping through charged aggregates, a mechanism like proton conduction in water and largely independent of viscosity. Longer glymes, diglyme through tetraglyme, chelate lithium more strongly and improve stability. The results give battery designers a molecular picture for building high-voltage electrolytes on purpose.
doe-osti-3011801-applying-social-science:
Social science methods assess a community energy outreach program in a National Renewable Energy Laboratory case study by Lis Blanco, Shannon Anderson, and Lauren Reichelt. The Gap Region Outreach Project sat inside the Energy to Communities program. The authors set out a framework others can reuse for judging gaps, reach, and impact in technical assistance work.

Interviews and listening sessions gathered the evidence. In total, 143 people from 115 groups took part, split between 60 community based groups and 55 government agencies across four priority regions. Qualitative content analysis and iterative feedback loops turned the sessions into program adjustments.
doe-osti-3011899-ion-conducting-polymer-:
Ion conducting polymers coated onto copper nanoparticles are designed to raise carbon dioxide conversion efficiency in a phase 1 CRADA report. Bob Allen, Danielle Henckel, and Michael McGraw of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory are the technical contacts. The target reaction turns carbon dioxide into ethylene at the electrode interface. Polymer structure governs both reactivity and selectivity in earlier published work.

One polymer was polymerised in place on the particles. It is a dimethylaminopropyl methacrylamide with a glass transition near 150 degrees C. Monomer at 6 weight percent relative to copper and AIBN initiator were mixed in methanol and dried under vacuum. The mixture then heated to 65 degrees C in a sonicator bath for twelve hours under nitrogen. Products were stored under nitrogen.
doe-osti-3012214-wrs-capabilities-bookle:
Capabilities of the Weapons Research Services division at Los Alamos National Laboratory are laid out in a booklet by Ellen Schaeffer, LA-UR-25-32295. The division acts as the information backbone of the lab's weapons programs and manages the nation's largest store of classified weapons data. The booklet is meant for lab staff and partners across the nuclear security enterprise.

Four pillars shape the work: integrated cyber assurance, data stewardship, knowledge access and transfer, and software solutions. A hub called PRIDE runs mission critical software that speeds business work across the enterprise. Standards and rules for classifying, protecting, and distributing weapons data sit with the division.
doe-osti-3012401-transmission-cost-alloc:
Transmission cost allocation practices across United States grid operators are reviewed in a technical brief from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The authors are Fritz Kahrl, Josh Schellenberg, and Lisa Schwartz, with Pacific Northwest National Laboratory coauthors. Costs reach customers through two main processes, generator interconnection and transmission planning. FERC Order 1000 sorts projects by driver: reliability, economic, or public policy.

Those drivers are hard to isolate in practice, which complicates allocation. New England offers a worked example. FERC approved ISO-NE's long term transmission planning and cost allocation proposal on July 8, 2024. States select solutions with a benefit to cost ratio above 1.0. Costs then spread across the footprint on a load ratio share basis.
doe-osti-3012649-from-viruses-to-protist:
Gibert, Jean Philippe, of Duke University, with Jonathan Shaw, David Weston, Dale Pelletier of Oak Ridge, and Steven Wilhelm of the University of Tennessee, wrote this technical report for award SC0020362. The team studied how warming affects protists and viruses, two overlooked controls on microbes in peatlands. Sphagnum mosses lock away about a quarter of all land carbon as peat, helped by microbes that supply them nitrogen.

Combining genomics, math models, field warming experiments, and lab microcosms, the team linked cell traits to heat performance in protists and mapped how predator-prey ties shift with temperature. They charted the virus community living on Sphagnum over ten months and found trait shifts in field protist communities under warming. The results feed models of how peatland carbon storage may respond as the climate warms.
doe-osti-3013105-power-of-quantum-witnes:
Supartha Podder of Stony Brook University wrote this project final report for award DE-SC0023179 on the power of quantum witnesses. In quantum complexity theory, a witness is the evidence offered to prove an answer, and QMA is the quantum counterpart of the classical class NP. Whether quantum witnesses are genuinely stronger than classical ones remains an open question after decades of work.

Podder's project attacked the question from three sides: comparing quantum and classical witnesses, asking how easily quantum witnesses can be copied, and testing whether they illuminate other problems. Work on distributed verification, where an untrusted quantum data center must prove its results, showed cases where quantum help gives an exponential advantage. The report lays out next steps for the multi-verifier setting.
doe-osti-3013241-existing-methods-for-gr:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-5D00-94961, by Pranav Sharma, Vahan Gevorgian, Shahil Shah, and eight co-authors from five labs and grid operators, dated November 2025, reviews methods for assessing grid strength. Grid strength describes how firmly voltage and frequency hold when disturbed. As inverter-based solar, wind, and batteries replace spinning generators, weak-grid pockets have triggered real instability events.

The report catalogs steady-state and dynamic assessment methods and the metrics behind them. It then examines hydropower's special role: hydro plants are synchronous machines that stiffen the grid, and they can run as synchronous condensers, spinning without generating to supply strength and inertia. Grid operators in Australia and elsewhere are already exploring that service. The review gives planners a common vocabulary for a fast-changing problem.
doe-osti-3013776-floating-photovoltaics-:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-82657, dated January 2026, studies floating solar panels on hydropower reservoirs in the United States. Twenty authors took part. They came from INL, NREL, Oregon State University, and industry partners. Floating panels put solar cells on water instead of land. The lakes behind dams already have grid links, roads, and calm, managed water.

As of 2023 the country had just 26 floating solar sites, with 36 megawatts in all. The report maps how much could be built on reservoirs under federal rules. It works through costs, down to substation upgrades sized by plant size and grid voltage. Later chapters look at how cover levels change lake surface heat and the life in the water. Permit rules for federal waters close the study. Developers get a full siting picture.
doe-osti-3013970-dc-fast-charging-test-p:
Argonne report ANL/TAPS-25/6, by Payas Vartak and Sam Thurston, dated December 2025, recommends standardized test procedures for DC fast charging of light-duty electric vehicles. Fast charging results are hard to compare today because labs measure at different points and run different sequences. Argonne drafted the procedure from its Next Gen Profiles project testing experience.

The draft builds on SAE J2953-4 and ISO 12906:2024, and pairs the charge test with the SAE J1634 discharge procedure so the two run back to back, saving time. Measurement points are specified explicitly: ideally at the battery inlet, point P3, because readings at the charger-side point P2 fold in conversion and wiring losses. The goal is a practical standard that manufacturers and test authorities can both run without heavy extra effort.
doe-osti-3014981-energy-101-hydropower-s:
Energy 101: Hydropower is a slide deck by Elise DeGeorge and Maddy Crouse. It teaches hydropower fundamentals. The deck was produced when the laboratory operated as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. It opens with the three terms that set a site's potential. Head is the vertical drop. Flow is the water passing through. Efficiency splits among the penstock, the turbine, and the motor.

Project types follow in turn. Small hydro means under 10 megawatts on existing dams, canals, or pipelines. Run-of-river systems borrow part of a stream and return it. Conventional dam hydropower stores water in reservoirs. In-conduit systems place a turbine inside a pipeline. They capture pressure instead of wasting it at a reducing valve. A closing section lists federal incentives. They run from the production and investment tax credits to depreciation and clean energy bonds.
doe-osti-3015226-carbon-nanotube-field-e:
A University of Missouri final report under award DE-SC0022145, dated January 29, 2026, tests carbon nanotube cathodes for radio-frequency sources. Kovaleski, Maschmann, and Weatherford wrote it. Nanotubes have a tall, thin, conductive shape. That shape makes them natural electron emitters. The project ties how a cathode is built to how well it emits.

Two geometries were compared on five-by-five millimeter silicon substrates. One was dense nanotube forests of varying height. The other was patterned pillars cut by ultraviolet photolithography. Swept from zero to minus 250 volts, forest emitters produced currents between 36.8 microamps at the low end and 572.34 microamps at the high end. Pillars gave currents between 39.4 microamps and 317.51 microamps. Taller samples generally emitted more. A static run held emission fairly stable over 4.5 hours. Three emission regions emerged. The last ends in exponential Fowler-Nordheim tunneling. Fabrication faults, though, left few viable pillars at heights matching the forests.
doe-osti-3016087-evaluation-of-novel-bat:
Max Schulze was the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5700-98630, and Reeja Jayan is also named on the record. The project evaluated new battery chemistries meant for long duration energy storage, storage that can discharge for many hours. The partner's SeaLion coating for battery electrodes was the technology under test.

Coated graphite and lithium cobalt oxide electrodes were built into half-cell coin cells and run through standardized test protocols. The aim was to benchmark the coated cells against strong commercial chemistries already on the market. Early electrochemical results go back to the partner, so it can tune the coating deposition settings for a second round of electrodes. Grid storage developers get an early, lab-checked read on whether the coating helps cells perform.
doe-osti-3017545-etipp-success-stories-s:
Bryan Mentlik, with Clayton Pokorny, presented these ETIPP success story slides on October 22, 2025. ETIPP is the Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project, an Energy Department program that lends national laboratory analysis to coastal, remote, and island communities. The slides answer a practical question for towns considering the program: what does success actually look like?

Expectations are set plainly. Communities can expect deep analysis of technologies they are weighing, with pros, cons, trade-offs, sizing, and reliability needs. Cost analysis stays high level, with breakeven timing. Policy obstacles and utility relationship building are part of the package. What communities should not expect is a finished project: the analysis informs their own decisions, and sometimes it shows a favored project should not proceed. The deck argues that a well-supported no is also a success, because it saves a small community real money.
doe-osti-3017549-geothermal-assessment-s:
Geoffrey Mibei, Hyunjun Oh, Bryan Mentlik, and Rebecca Meadows presented this geothermal assessment for Shelter Island in July 2025. Shelter Island received the work through a federal technical assistance program. The deck starts with geothermal basics, then moves to a conceptual analysis and a high-level feasibility judgment for the island, closing with next steps.

Resource types covered range from medium and low temperature hydrothermal systems to enhanced and advanced geothermal in dry or superhot rock. A long section focuses on closed loop geothermal heat pumps, the most plausible island option. The assessment also weighs groundwater risks honestly. One example: leaking propylene glycol, a common loop fluid, can deplete oxygen, disturb microbial communities, and harm drinking water sources. Community decision makers get the geology, the options, and the cautions in one sitting.
doe-osti-3017551-reopt-key-findings-pres:
Gustavo Campos, Bryan Mentlik, and Rebecca Meadows presented these REopt findings for Shelter Island in July 2025. REopt is the National Laboratory of the Rockies software that sizes solar and storage to minimize life-cycle cost. The community directed the study toward distributed, behind-the-meter systems. Eight Shelter Island sites, commercial and residential, got a preliminary analysis.

Assumptions are printed on the slides: a four percent discount rate, three percent inflation, five percent yearly electricity cost escalation, and a twenty-five year analysis period. Rooftop solar was costed at 2,265 dollars per kilowatt, carport solar at 4,458. Three sites went to deep dive: a home, a school, and the recycling center. One case saves an average of 12,000 dollars a year over the project life, with payback near nine years. The school-scale case also cut indirect carbon emissions by 4.3 tonnes a year, a seventy percent drop.
doe-osti-3017762-data-centers-gap-analys:
Ellie Estreich, Luke Lavin, and Ilya Chernyakhovskiy of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presented these gap analysis slides in February 2026. The work sits in a Grid Deployment Office project on planning for large loads. Large loads, above all data centers, are expected to drive near-term electricity demand growth in the United States, but with significant uncertainty attached.

The team analyzes gaps in understanding how large loads affect the grid and customers. They also categorize mitigation options for connecting big loads to the bulk power system in the near term. One structural problem anchors the deck: grid infrastructure has historically taken five years or more to plan, permit, site, and build. Research questions cover what drives load growth, which siting factors matter, and where data is missing. The laboratory audience is told plainly where its modeling should add value next.
doe-osti-3018060-fy25-ion-exchange-proce:
Amy M Westesen, Austin A Bachman, and Krusha D Bhakta of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory led this January 2026 report on ion exchange processing for Hanford's West Area Risk Management project. Fourteen authors are named in all. Ion exchange is a cleanup workhorse: contaminated liquid passes through engineered media that grab specific radioactive elements and let the rest flow on.

The year's work centered on crystalline silicotitanate, the leading medium for this duty. Batch contact tests with simple strontium simulants generated data across solution conditions, and overall strontium removal by the medium was assessed. Prior work on how feed displacement and hydroxide concentration change performance feeds directly into these runs. The results set operating choices for treating West Area streams: contact times, feed preparation, and what removal to expect. Cleanup managers get fresh numbers for a process that runs at the heart of Hanford's risk reduction work.
doe-osti-3019689-summary-report-from-the:
Sandra D Taylor, Mavis Boamah-Agyemang, Eric Borguet, and an organizing committee summarized a conference in this report, prepared January 20, 2026. The Interfaces for Energy and the Environment Conference met May 19 to 23, 2025, in Richland, Washington. It was the inaugural edition, hosted at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Interfacial science cuts across energy and environmental research, but its practitioners are scattered across chemistry, physics, and geoscience. The conference gave them one room. Young-Shin Jun assembled the summary.

Themes ran from interface structure and charge transfer theory to nucleation, growth, and dissolution. Computation and new analytical techniques formed a second thread. The report's back half is the abstract and program books, preserved as appendices. For the field, the value is a snapshot of where interfacial science stood in 2025. It shows which methods are converging, and which energy problems, from batteries to mineralization, now turn on interface behavior.
doe-osti-3020534-summer-2025-solar-indus:
Summer 2025 Solar Industry Update is a slide deck by David Feldman, Jarett Zuboy, and co-authors from the National Laboratory of the Rockies and DOE's Solar Energy Technologies Office. It was presented on August 19, 2025. The deck tracks global and United States solar deployment, system pricing, manufacturing, and policy. In the first half of 2025, China installed 212 gigawatts of solar, up 107 percent year over year, and India added 19.4 gigawatts, up 70 percent.

United States installations were roughly flat at 20.7 gigawatts, and Germany's shrank 14 percent. The United States also installed about 5.8 gigawatt-hours of grid energy storage in the first quarter of 2025. On policy, the deck explains how the newly passed budget law changed federal incentives. The homeowner solar credit ends in 2026, corporate credits phase down later, and limits on Chinese content begin in 2026.
doe-osti-3020694-fall-2025-solar-industr:
Fall 2025 Solar Industry Update, a slide deck by David Feldman, Jarett Zuboy, Matthew Heine, and co-authors from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, was presented on November 19, 2025. It updates global deployment, United States installations, system pricing, and manufacturing. The headline shift: after a record first half, China installed 28 gigawatts in the third quarter of 2025, down 52 percent year over year, following market-based pricing reforms.

India installed a record 29.5 gigawatts in the first nine months of 2025, challenging the United States for second place among markets. Solar supplied 8.2 percent of United States electricity over the twelve months through August 2025, up from 6.9 percent in 2024. Average prices ran $3.2 to $4.2 per watt for residential systems and $1.1 per watt for utility-scale. Domestic panel manufacturing rose 126 percent year over year.
doe-osti-3021917-american-made-solar-pri:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory final report for CRADA 615, by Shiva Poudel, Aaqib A. Peerzada, and Jaime T. Kolln, dated October 2025, reports an American-Made Solar Prize project with Edgeli on faster grid interconnection for distributed energy resources. Every community solar array, rooftop system, and charging depot must be studied before a utility lets it connect, and those studies are a bottleneck. The project automated the data work behind them.

Software routines converted geographic data into network databases and power flow models automatically. Scenarios then produced full-year hourly hosting capacity values, all 8,760 hours, plus voltage and thermal impacts for specific projects, spanning community solar, rooftop solar, and vehicle charging. A grid upgrade module mapped violations to fixes such as reconductoring and transformer replacement, choosing the least-cost option. The tools are slated to become web services inside utility queue management systems.
doe-osti-3021968-waste-to-energy-potenti:
Slide deck by Anelia Milbrandt, Sydney Harris, Michael Talmadge, and co-authors from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated January 9, 2026, weighs waste-to-energy options for Guam. The island territory covers about 210 square miles with limited landfill space, and city waste projections run through 2040. Turning waste into power, heat, fuels, or chemicals could stretch landfill life and hold disposal costs steady.

The deck surveys market-ready routes: combustion, gasification, pyrolysis, anaerobic digestion with landfill gas recovery, and turning fats and greases into biodiesel or renewable diesel. Advanced options include hydrothermal liquefaction and carbonization of organic waste. As a mainland comparison, it profiles a textile recycling pilot in Fairfax County, Virginia, launched in early 2025 with Helpsy. The pilot collected nearly 49 tons of textiles by October 2025, far beyond early expectations.
doe-osti-3022279-tru-bison-simulation-ov:
An INL slide deck, INL/MIS-25-88951, by Alexander Swearingen, Tiankai Yao, and Colby Jensen, surveys BISON fuel performance simulations of transuranic-bearing metallic fuel tests. The focus is experiment X501, whose minor actinide fuel elements carry an average makeup of uranium with 20.2 percent plutonium, 9.1 percent zirconium, 1.2 percent americium, and 1.3 percent neptunium, at 60 percent uranium-235 enrichment, irradiated over cycles 163A through 167A.

The deck maps the BISON material models used for this fuel system, from thermal conductivity and expansion to burnup-driven solid swelling, then sets simulation against measurement. For element G591 the predicted cladding diametral strain matches profilometry in shape and size. The match is tempered by a profilometry error near 0.35 percent strain, about the size of the strain itself.
doe-osti-3022895-virtual-power-plant-arc:
INL report INL/RPT-26-89692, by Megan Culler, Remy Stolworthy, and Robert Edsall with a ScottMadden team, examines the architecture of virtual power plants and how to design them to withstand attack. A virtual power plant aggregates rooftop solar, batteries, and controllable loads into a resource a utility can dispatch like a conventional plant. FERC Order 2222 accelerates that model by opening wholesale markets to such aggregations.

The security problem is structural. These systems run on consumer-owned devices, public internet links, and multi-vendor platforms, creating attack surfaces unlike a fenced power station. The report singles out platform-to-grid conduits as high-consequence paths: an attacker reaching authenticated platform systems inherits centralized leverage with distributed consequences. Real incidents and threat patterns support practical guidance for utilities, regulators, and aggregators on bounding those paths and failing safely.
doe-osti-3022910-llnl-carbon-storage-pro:
LLNL quarterly report LLNL-TR-2007292, by Allan Chang, Tiziana Bond, and Matteo Cusini, reports progress in the lab's carbon storage targeted research program. It covers the first quarter of 2025. Two tasks advance in parallel: predicting the earthquakes that carbon injection might trigger, and building fiber optic sensors that can sniff out leaking carbon dioxide.

On the modeling side, the team extended the open-source GEOS simulator to couple reservoir poromechanics with quasi-dynamic earthquake physics. Faults are treated as lower-dimensional surfaces with contact constraints. The capability is aimed at high-resolution hazard estimates for storage sites. On the sensing side, work optimized laser-drilled holes in hollow-core fibers and tested fiber survival under hot, pressurized brine. It also checked splice repeatability and light throughput ahead of adding Bragg grating reflectors.
doe-osti-3023172-utah-forge-coreflooding: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory submission LLNL-TR-2003421, by W Kottkamp, M Davila Ordonez, M Smith, and K Kroll in March 2026, is a data package rather than a narrative report. It holds results from core-flooding experiments at 100 and 200 degrees for the Utah FORGE geothermal project, using core taken from well 16A(78)-32. Nearly all of the file is raw measurement tables from those runs, with only a short introduction ahead of the data.
doe-osti-3023391-developing-methane-emis:
Elena S F Berman of Kairos Aerospace led this methane survey project for the National Energy Technology Laboratory under award DE-FE0032310, running October 2023 through September 2025. Erin Wetherley, Petr Yakovlev, Evan Sherwin, and Adam Brandt joined her, with Stanford University and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory among the partners. The goal was an emissions inventory for the Anadarko and Haynesville basins built by fusing three kinds of evidence.

Aircraft found the plumes first, then the GHGSat satellite looked again at the same spots. In 52 follow-up images, the satellite detected no plumes at the targeted locations, but it did catch 28 emissions from other sources, ranging from 213 to 2,153 kilograms per hour. A second-year high-frequency campaign revisited sub-regions to learn how long large gas losses last.
doe-osti-3023671-osl1-delivery-lens-desi: Shamaar Howard and Lucas Taylor of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory gave this slide update on the OSL1 delivery lens design. It was filed as LLNL-TR-2006242, with slides dated April 26, 2024. Beyond the title slide, the deck is mostly lens prescription tables. Rows cover elements such as LENS_15 and LENS_16 and glass codes such as C79-80, given as long columns of numbers with no explanatory text. Readers get the current design figures themselves rather than a written account of the changes.
doe-osti-3024235-combustion-synthesis-of:
Evgeny Shafirovich of the University of Texas at El Paso closes award DE-EE0010429, covering March 2023 through December 2025, submitted February 25, 2026. The project used combustion synthesis to make nanoscale magnesium borides for hydrogen storage, aiming at hydrides that release and recharge hydrogen at mild temperatures and pressures. The work complemented the HyMARC consortium, and students trained at both El Paso and Sandia National Laboratories.

Testing at Sandia brought a sober result: borides richer in boron than MgB2 gave no significant improvement in hydrogen uptake. Heat analysis of MgB2 and MgB4 decomposition showed a multi-step path through intermediate MgB7 and MgB20 phases. The authors read that pattern as high thermodynamic stability in the boron-rich phases, which explains why the stored hydrogen would not move as hoped.
doe-osti-3025202-powered-by-rev-slides:
Galen Maclaurin and Gabe Zuckerman of the National Laboratory of the Rockies gave this slide talk on March 24, 2026, introducing the reV model under the banner Powered By reV. Electricity demand is growing fast, the opening slides note, mostly driven by data centers, citing the Energy Information Administration's 2025 short-term outlook. Growth on that scale forces new generation and transmission, which run straight into siting and interconnection fights.

reV is an open-source geospatial platform for weighing barriers and openings for energy deployment at regional to continental scale. Its research questions ask how social, ecological, and technical factors shape siting, and how cost and grid connection drive what actually gets built. Example exclusions include urban areas for wind and pumped hydro, plus technology-specific setbacks from structures, roads, transmission rights-of-way, and water features.
doe-osti-3025691-data-center-power-syste:
Shahil Shah, Vahan Gevorgian, Przemyslaw Koralewicz, Robb Wallen, Barry Mather, Ben Kroposki, and Jen Kurtz presented these slides in March 2026 on the power systems inside data centers. The deck traces the chain from the grid connection point to the racks, through uninterruptible power supplies, power supply units, bus converters, and voltage regulators. It asks what such loads do to grid reliability.

Hardware detail is concrete. Existing power supply units take single-phase input and are generally rated at 3 or 5.5 kilowatts; the industry is pushing units of 12 kilowatts and above, possibly with three-phase input. Inside, a power factor correction stage makes about 400 volts DC and a second converter steps down to 48 volts. Laboratory work includes megawatt-scale emulation of AI load profiles and performance testing of a multi-megawatt UPS.
doe-osti-3028125-microstructure-amp-mech:
Geeta Kumari, Caleb Massey, Peeyush Nandwana, and eight Oak Ridge National Laboratory colleagues measured what thermal aging does to additively manufactured 316H stainless steel, in ORNL/TM-2025/4138, dated September 2025. The builds were made by laser powder bed fusion and then scaled up, a step that can change microstructure and strength. Reactor designers need those properties after aging, not just fresh off the printer.

Fracture testing shows the laboratory craft involved. Specimen halves were photographed, crack lengths measured in pixels and converted to millimeters against the undeformed edge, and load-displacement records turned into fracture resistance curves. Because the specimens were small and the tests hot, direct crack growth measurement was impractical. The team used a modified curve normalization method from the Hertzberg reference to build each J-R curve.
doe-osti-3030409-microstructure-and-mech: LPBF 316H got thermally aged again, and this DOE text scales microstructure builds. The pages detail the mechanical findings. The materials folks get their data. The properties were mechanical. The data were material. The again were aged. The builds were SS.
doe-osti-3030828-energy-101-transportati:
Prateek Joshi, Carishma Gokhale-Welch, and Maddy Crouse of the National Laboratory of the Rockies built this Energy 101 slide deck on transportation, dated March 2025. It was made for the Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project, which helps remote and island communities plan energy work. The deck teaches basics: vehicle types, fuels, public transit, and planes, ships, and trains, with case studies and links for deeper reading.

Four electric vehicle kinds open the tour. Battery electrics run 100 to 400 miles per charge, plug-in hybrids mix plug power with an engine, plain hybrids recharge by braking, and fuel cell cars turn hydrogen into electricity. Later slides cover renewable diesel from fats and oils, and power-to-liquids fuel made from hydrogen and carbon dioxide that fits current engines.
doe-osti-3031081-microgrids-slides:
Ian Baring-Gould, Michael Ingram, and Trent Dillon of the National Laboratory of the Rockies teach this March 2026 training on microgrids. A microgrid is a local power system that can run alone when the main grid fails. The slides open with resilience: what energy service really means, from reliability and power quality to voltage, frequency, and clean waveforms that electronics need.

Case studies ground the ideas, and breakout talks let students apply them. The Bronzeville community microgrid in Chicago gets a full page. ComEd built it for about 25 million dollars, per a 2018 estimate, with roughly 24 million dollars in added funding from the Energy Department and partners between 2016 and 2020. A 4 million dollar federal SHINES award backed its solar and battery work.
doe-osti-3362552-transient-fuel-testing-:
Jason L. Schulthess, Colby B. Jensen, Nicolas E. Woolstenhulme, and David W. Kamerman of Idaho National Laboratory present these July 2025 slides on transient fuel testing in TREAT. TREAT is a reactor built to pulse: it can slam a test fuel sample with a burst of energy that mimics an accident, then watch what happens. Fuel safety research exists to keep core material contained, the first of three defense layers ahead of the vessel and the building.

Fuel behavior fights on two fronts, the slides say: fuel-cladding interaction and fission gas behavior. Test gear ranges from cheap static capsules to flowing loops with active cooling, all built in a cartridge style that swaps between platforms. In-situ instruments ride inside the reactor during shots, and the facility links straight to hot cells for after-test exams.
doe-osti-3363285-new-energy-infrastructu:
John Brewer, Brandon Seedorf, and Nicholas Messina of the National Energy Technology Laboratory present this slide deck. It is the New Energy Infrastructure Outlook (DOE/NETL-2026/5338, March 31, 2026). The deck surveys energy projects under development in the continental United States. Its data run through December 31, 2025. It focuses on projects making real progress toward commercial operation.

Sections cover power plant projects and proposed nameplate capacity by region. Others cover AC and DC transmission, natural gas pipelines, and liquefied natural gas projects. Fuel stockpiles and proposed data centers get sections too. The authors caution that early stage projects may never be built. A listing as announced does not signal committed capital. Status runs from announced to under construction.
doe-osti-3363302-powered-by-erad-slides:
Aadil Latif and Gayathri Krishnamoorthy of the National Laboratory of the Rockies present these April 2026 slides on ERAD, the Energy Resilience Analysis tool for Distribution systems. ERAD is a free, open source Python toolkit. It estimates the energy and service impacts of hazards such as earthquakes and flooding. It uses a graph based model of grid connectivity. The model includes the critical services that depend on the grid.

The pitch targets a planning gap: more than 3,000 distribution utilities face siloed, single hazard studies whose results cannot be compared across investments. ERAD instead models damage probabilistically at asset level. The slides find pole upgrades cheap and often selected, undergrounding costly but valuable in severe scenarios, and substations the highest impact assets to protect.
doe-osti-3364329-novel-and-rugged-electr:
A DOE STTR Phase I final report from Cyentech Consulting of Cypress, Texas, led by Shubin Zeng under award DE-SC0025769, covers February 2025 to May 2026. The project designed a rugged wireless system to watch carbon dioxide plumes stored deep underground. Sensors must survive for years downhole, where batteries die and cables fail, so the design moves both data and power through the steel well casing itself.

Four tasks structure the work. A loop antenna senses the plume electromagnetically. A toroidal antenna handles wireless communication along the casing. A third task transfers power through the casing into a supercapacitor. Control electronics tie the module together. Models included a 600-meter steel casing in surrounding rock. Phase I results support a monitoring system that could verify stored carbon stays put.
doe-osti-3365155-the-scaling-and-units-o:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-24170, by Joshua D. Carmichael and Jonas A. Kintner and issued May 20, 2026, settles a units question that can silently corrupt explosion monitoring. The subject is the elastic response term for Rayleigh waves, surface waves that roll along the ground, as output by the widely used Computer Programs in Seismology package. The authors care most about Rayleigh waves from atmospheric explosions.

The term's scaling is inconsistent across the literature, and the software's output mixes units: kilometers, kilometers per second, grams per cubic centimeter. Converted properly, an elastic response of one in those mixed units equals 10 to the 87th power in meters per newton. The paper walks through the Airy phase formula term by term so analysts can convert with confidence instead of propagating a scaling error into yield estimates.
doe-osti-3367361-generative-ai-for-grid-: Slide deck NLR/PR-5D00-98379 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, by Ben Kroposki and Seong Choi, argues generative AI belongs in grid control rooms. It opens with the February 2021 Texas freeze, when demand hit 69 gigawatts against a typical winter peak of 57, then traces control rooms from analog panels to digital systems. NERC compliance rules currently bar cloud services, so the deck explains pre-training a language model inside utility walls. The hosted text is the deck itself, about twenty slides, and the description reflects that presentation format.
doe-osti-3374537-megawatt-mayhem-grid-op:
Report INL/RPT-25-87430 from Idaho National Laboratory, dated September 2025, looks at the strain that very large new loads place on the United States power grid. Six lab authors wrote it, led by Luis Fernando Enriquez-Contreras and Timothy R. McJunkin. Data centers drive most of the growth. Their draw is huge, fast to build, and unlike the steady load of a classic factory.

The report sorts the problems grid operators face. Planning suffers because load growth now outruns the old forecast cycle. Normal operations must track sharper swings in demand. Stress events raise reliability fears when many large loads act at once. One section covers automatic generation control, which shifts plant output to hold grid frequency steady. Slow thermal plants ramp far more slowly than hydro units or batteries, a gap operators must plan around.
doe-osti-3374777-pixe-state-of-the-art-s:
Sandia National Laboratories paper SAND2026-22256R, by Patrick Jojola and dated June 2, 2026, surveys particle-induced X-ray emission, known as PIXE. In PIXE, a beam of protons or heavier ions knocks inner electrons out of target atoms. Outer electrons drop in to fill the gaps. The atoms then emit X-rays at energies unique to each element. Reading that spectrum names the elements present and, with care, their amounts.

The method is fast and can sense trace levels of many heavier elements at once. Users range from geology and art studies to chip plants and forensics. The paper then turns to limits. Background glow can hide small peaks, and overlapping lines confuse the fit. At high count rates, piled-up pulses fake extra peaks. Sample thickness and mix also skew the numbers, so honest results need solid correction methods.
doe-osti-3377406-tank-14h-annulus-sample:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2026-00223, Revision 0, dated June 2026, gives lab results for samples drawn from the annulus of waste Tank 14H. J. R. Dekarske, J. M. Cutler, and W. C. Benson ran the analyses. The annulus is the thin gap between the tank's inner and outer walls. Material caught there hints at leaks and salt creep. Knowing its makeup guides how the tank farm watches and handles the vessel.

Work split between bulk chemistry and radiochemistry. Gamma counts ran on high purity germanium detectors. Each count ran long enough to hold the cesium-137 error at the method mark of 5.00 percent. Iodine-129 took a longer path: filtrates were acidified, treated twice with ammonium molybdophosphate to strip cesium, then reduced so the iodine could fall out as silver iodide. That cake was filtered and counted on a thin-window photon detector. Results feed the site's tank records.
doe-osti-3377460-system-advisor-model-sa:
A National Laboratory of the Rockies slide deck, by Maddy Crouse and dated August 2025, introduces the System Advisor Model, known as SAM. The deck was made when the lab still ran as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. SAM is free software for techno-economic study of energy systems. It pairs performance models with finance models. Users can size a system, price its output, and test how incentives shift the sums.

The technology list is wide: solar, wind, storage, geothermal, marine energy, fuel cells, and hybrid builds. Finance forms run from home and business ownership to power purchase deals and merchant plants. Lawmakers and utilities form one user class; project developers another. Key outputs get plain glosses: simple payback, capacity factor, levelized cost of energy, and net present value. The deck ends on training and help routes for new users. It serves as the lab's standard first tour of the tool.
doe-osti-3377461-pvwatts-calculator-slid:
A National Laboratory of the Rockies slide deck, by Maddy Crouse and dated July 2025, introduces the PVWatts Calculator. The deck was made when the lab ran as NREL. PVWatts estimates the output of grid-tied solar systems. Homeowners, building owners, installers, and makers use it for quick sums. It answers how a roof or ground array would fare at a site, and what that power is worth.

Six inputs describe the system: direct current size, module type, array type, system losses, tilt, and azimuth. Three refine the design for advanced users: the DC-to-AC size ratio, inverter efficiency, and ground coverage ratio. Results come back as hourly output and energy cost. Users can shift the site or the array angle and watch the year change. The tool pairs with the System Advisor Model for full study. Access is web-based, with a developer interface.
doe-osti-3377462-energy-101-marine-energ:
A National Laboratory of the Rockies slide deck in the Energy 101 series, by Tessa Greco and dated March 2025, teaches the basics of marine energy. The deck was made when the lab still ran as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Marine energy draws power from ocean tides, currents, and waves, plus river flow and sea temperature gaps. The deck calls it one of the largest untapped sources. Its stress falls on steadiness: the sea generates day and night.

That steadiness suits coastal towns. Many towns burn shipped-in diesel at high cost. A case study follows Igiugig, an Alaska village on a salmon river. Its people, the Igyararmiut, have lived from that river for more than 8,000 years. Slides credit the village with leadership and a path to near-total renewable power. Other uses span fish farms, research craft, and ocean sensors. Workforce training for remote sites closes the lesson.
doe-osti-3377464-energy-101-microgrids-s:
A National Laboratory of the Rockies slide deck in the Energy 101 series, dated February 2025, teaches the basics of microgrids. Daniel Olis, Michael Callahan, Maddy Crouse, and Marsha Sanchez share the byline. The deck was made when the lab still ran as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. A microgrid joins local generators, storage, and a control system into one small network. It can link to the main grid or cut loose and island, keeping power on through an outage.

Local sources near the user carry the name distributed energy resources. The list runs from solar and wind to combined heat and power, batteries, and electric vehicles. Demand response and efficiency count too. Each microgrid is tailored to its site and needs. Uses span shops, campuses, and towns, bought for lower cost, stronger reliability, or both. The lesson closes with the lab's own study lines on single and networked microgrids.
doe-osti-3377650-energy-101-solar-slides:
Energy 101: Solar is a teaching slide deck by Maddy Crouse of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated February 2025. It opens with basic terms: irradiance is the solar power hitting a surface at one moment, while insolation is that energy added up over a period. A typical peak irradiance at midday in summer in a sunny area is about one kilowatt per square meter.

Later slides cover the parts of sunlight that reach the ground and then turn to concentrated solar power, which uses reflectors to focus sunlight into heat. That heat can drive steam turbines or be stored for ten hours or more. The Crescent Dunes project near Tonopah, Nevada, is given as an example, with a generating capacity of 110 megawatts.
doe-osti-3377664-powered-by-dgen-webinar:
Paritosh Das, a senior research scientist at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, presents the Powered by dGen webinar in slides dated May 21, 2026. The session explains why forecasting rooftop solar and other local energy gear is hard. Many adoption choices are made by single households and firms. And they do not decide on price alone.

Das shows how the dGen model folds buyer behavior into grid planning. There, adoption shapes grid upgrades, capacity purchases, and hosting capacity work. Two applied examples anchor the talk. One animates rooftop solar adoption feeder by feeder for the Orlando Utilities Commission service area. The other describes lab support for ISO New England. For that grid operator, dGen helped build the long-term forecast of local generation growth.
doe-osti-3377778-reopt-energy-decision-s:
Maddy Crouse of the National Laboratory of the Rockies introduces REopt, an energy decision support tool, in slides dated July 2025. The deck was produced while the laboratory operated as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. REopt answers a practical question for a building or campus: will distributed energy resources work for your site, and what will they save?

The tool weighs local energy resources, site consumption, utility costs, technology costs, and financial incentives all at once, rather than one at a time. That matters, the slides argue, because the nation's supply is shifting toward wind, solar, and geothermal power, with more capacity behind the meter. A results section defines terms such as net present value and energy bill savings in plain language for first-time users.
doe-osti-3377799-energy-101-utilities-sl:
Energy 101: Utilities is a teaching deck from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated March 2025, by Michael Ingram, Douglas Gagne, Chandralata Shah, Rachel Shepherd, and Maddy Crouse. It was produced while the laboratory operated as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The subject is the electric utility system itself, explained from the ground up.

The slides start with the grid: power plants generate electricity, and substations, transformers, and power lines carry it to customers. Local grids interconnect for reliability and trade, forming larger networks that match supply to demand. In the United States that means thousands of miles of high-voltage lines and millions of miles of low-voltage lines, linking thousands of plants to hundreds of millions of customers. Later material covers utility types and how customers work with their utility.
doe-osti-3377894-energy-101-distributed-:
Energy 101: Distributed Energy Resources and Controllable Loads is a March 2025 teaching deck from the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Seven authors are printed: Douglas Gagne, Rebecca O'Neil, Emma Stewart, Andy Hoke, Maddy Crouse, Emma Elgqvist, and Michael Coddington. It was produced while the laboratory operated as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.

The deck defines its two subjects. A distributed energy resource, per IEEE in 2018, is a power source not directly connected to the bulk system. Examples include solar, wind, combined heat and power, storage, and small hydro. Controllable loads, per a 2014 NIST framing, can be shifted by direct control or price signals. They include demand response, electric vehicles, smart thermostats, and water heaters. Microgrids and an appendix on electricity bill structure round out the material.
doe-osti-3377980-durability-of-abc-team-:
Durability of ABC Team Wall Assemblies, Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2026/4614 from May 2026, by Emishaw Iffa and Andre Desjarlais, tests how advanced retrofit wall systems hold up over time. The study uses a field test facility in Hollywood, South Carolina. The site was chosen to represent a mixed-humid coastal climate, designated Zone 3. Moisture and heat moving through the walls are the measures that matter. It is a hygrothermal test.

A baseline wall of typical uninsulated wood-frame construction anchors the comparison. Retrofits tested against it include Tremco and Dryvit prefabricated panel systems, named Revitalite and Fedderlite. They also include reinforced fiberglass plastic panels developed at Oak Ridge. Vacuum insulated panels integrated with foam insulation, by Home Innovation Research Labs and Oak Ridge, complete the set. The goal is long-term durability evidence before such systems are sold for home retrofits.
doe-osti-3383100-microgrid-design-toolki:
Maddy Crouse of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Sarah Jewel and John P. Eddy of Sandia National Laboratories, introduces the Microgrid Design Toolkit in slides dated July 2025. The toolkit is decision support software developed by Sandia. It is offered free through the Department of Energy. It gives microgrid designers the information they need to identify designs that balance performance, reliability, and cost.

The toolkit fits the early stage of design, when choices are still open. Search algorithms work through large design spaces from user inputs and site factors. They handle topology optimization, the physical arrangement and connections of components. Designers explore a trade space of candidate solutions. They compare performance, reliability, and cost in result views and graphs. They take away quantitative evidence for a decision, such as whether to replace a generator and what size its successor should be.
doe-osti-3384929-modern-on-boarding-to-l:
Samuel Herts of Oak Ridge National Laboratory's National Center for Computational Sciences wrote Modern On-boarding to Large Repositories in report ORNL/TM-2026/4598, dated July 2026. The subtitle states the method: large language models as expert introduction. The problem is familiar to any big computing center: a new developer joins a huge, old codebase and needs months to find anything.

Herts studies whether a language model, loaded with the repository, can serve as the patient expert who answers the newcomer's first hundred questions. The work used resources of the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, home of some of the largest scientific codes in the world. On-boarding speed matters there because the codes outlive their authors, and every new maintainer starts as a stranger to millions of lines.
doe-osti-3387419-matlib-1-2-2-nuclear-ma:
MatLib-1.2.2: Nuclear Material Properties Library, dated May 2026, documents the material property set used by the FAST fuel performance code. Four Pacific Northwest National Laboratory authors are printed, K. J. Geelhood, W. G. Luscher, C. E. Goodson, and D. F. Wray. J. Corson and J. J. Whitman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission join them. The work was prepared for the commission's Office of Nuclear Regulatory Research. It was developed under the NQA-1-2017 quality standard.

A fuel code is only as good as the properties it feeds on. Those include how a cladding alloy conducts heat, swells, or creeps at temperature. MatLib gathers those properties for the materials in light-water and research reactor fuel. They run from oxide and mixed oxide fuels to zirconium alloys. Some draw on the Metallic Fuels Irradiation and Physics Database. This release is the documented state of that library.
doe-osti-3394708-impact-01-assembly-over:
David M. Sanches and Calvin Myer Downey of Idaho National Laboratory present the IMPACT-01 assembly in conference slides, INL/CON-25-88012, dated September 2025. IMPACT-01 is an irradiation capsule for the Advanced Test Reactor. It carries three uranium-10 percent zirconium fuel designs in a stainless steel capsule: slotted fuel, annular fuel, and a sodium-bonded baseline.

The slides follow the build at the Materials and Fuels Complex. Three fuel slugs were made from down-blended EBR-II highly enriched uranium, depleted uranium, and zirconium at three target enrichments. They were arc melted and drop cast, then machined. The sodium-bonded slug carries a splashguard on internal threads. Weld development used orbital autogenous TIG welding with a Swagelok M200 power supply. A five-foot leadout section routes the instrument leads out of the core. It has handling rings, a tungsten shine shield, and a hermetic seal path.
doe-osti-3399502-aluminum-4047-vendor-re:
An Aluminum 4047 Vendor Review, Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-26865 issued July 31, 2026, is a six-slide follow-up to an October 2024 review of filler metal suppliers. R. Bruce Madigan and Michael David McAninch of Gray Beards Engineering prepared it for three laboratory staff: Joris Erich Hochanadel, Kevin Daniel Martinez, and Mark Joseph Cola. The work ran under a contract dated March 4, 2026. Alloy 4047 is a silicon-rich aluminum welding filler.

The criteria are specific. A maker must control its process from ingot to packaged wire. The wire must sell off the shelf in small quantities so stock stays fresh. It comes in 0.047-inch diameter on small spools, ideally five pounds and no more than sixteen. Lincoln Electric meets every criterion, fully manufactured in North America. Hobart and AlcoTec qualify on all but smelting control, with origin not guaranteed. All vendors warned that 4047 is more prone to porosity than other 4000-series fillers.
doe-osti-3399768-building-a-trusted-roam:
Ryan Cryar and Robert Fitzgerald of the National Laboratory of the Rockies present Building a Trusted Roaming Hub in slides dated April 16, 2026. Roaming is what lets an electric vehicle driver charge on any network with one account. Today's charging networks are fragmented: every connection between networks is a custom integration, hundreds of bilateral agreements, with no unified trust layer for roaming or data exchange.

The hub replaces that tangle with one connection. It acts as a switchboard, storing no data and dictating no policy, but verifying that messages move securely between the right platforms. In software terms it is a REST application programming interface implementing the OCPI 2.3.0 specification, written in Rust on the Axum framework. The laboratory frames its role as building the security foundation for Plug and Charge, roaming, and smart charging, on zero trust principles.
doe-osti-3400806-ziacore-critical-experi:
Nicholas William Thompson's Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-26997, issued August 5, 2026, describes the ZiaCore critical experiment. ZiaCore is a Laboratory Directed Research and Development project to develop and demonstrate key technologies for future nuclear energy systems. Its reactor design is a uranium dioxide fueled microreactor. It is moderated by graphite and zirconium hydride and cooled by heat pipes.

The project split into three tasks: design the reactor, develop the zirconium hydride and heat pipe components, and run a critical experiment with a representative core section. The experiment used the Deimos testbed. Its inner region was replaced by a vacuum chamber holding graphite core blocks, a sodium heat pipe, and three quartz-encapsulated hydride rods. It also held 42 fuel pins, heaters, and thermocouples under multilayer insulation. Around it sat the Deimos outer region with HALEU TRISO fuel cups and moderator rods. The team performed the approach to critical.
doe-osti-3401689-exergetic-de-risking-ne:
Report NLR/TP-5500-98777 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated July 2026, presents the EXERGETIC project on geothermal hybrid power plants. Fifteen authors from the Rockies lab, Florida State University, a thermal firm, and Clemson University took part. The work tests hybrid designs in a virtual digital twin before any plant is built.

Modeled cases cover geothermal plants from 1 to 100 megawatts, paired with solar heat and underground thermal storage. Adding solar heat cuts the geothermal heat needed for the same power output. Readers get a low-risk way to judge hybrid designs, controls, and plant size before field work begins.
doe-osti-3409107-powered-by-sam-slides:
Janine Keith of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presents a short slide set, dated July 21, 2026, on SAM, the System Advisor Model. SAM is free software for performance and cost analysis of energy systems. It runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux, with a Python package called PySAM.

Development began in 2004 with the Department of Energy, the Rockies lab, and Sandia. Slides list who uses SAM results: engineers, developers, utilities, and grid modelers. A new model run starts every 1.4 minutes, per the deck. New users get a quick map of what SAM does and who leans on it.
doe-osti-3424627-online-and-offline-anal:
Argonne milestone report, dated July 2026, compares ways to measure chloride salts in nuclear fuel work, both live and offline. Amber Polke leads a seven-author Argonne team. The milestone code is M3FT-26AN080502017. Molten salt reactors need salt chemistry reads they can trust.

Voltammetry tracked uranium states in a uranium chloride salt mix across a wide strength range. Scan rates reached 3000 millivolts per second in the test shown. A thermal probe is also being tuned for fuel checks. It reads temperature gaps between samples. Salt makers get more than one way to verify what is in the pot.
doe-osti-3484649-pfas-interpretability-s:
Los Alamos slide set LA-UR-26-27573, by Lucy Liu and issued August 21, 2026, presents work on making PFAS model results easier to interpret. PFAS are a large family of industrial chemicals tracked for health risk. The slides come from a university intern project with the lab.

One method tries every single-atom move between molecule clusters to raise a score. The search uses three clusters and up to 100 passes in the code shown. Best moves are kept one step at a time. Such tools could show which parts of a molecule drive model warnings. The hosted set is slides only, so details stay at outline level.
doe-osti-3484655-metropolis-hastings-sli:
Los Alamos slide set LA-UR-26-27632, by Lucy Liu and issued August 24, 2026, teaches the Metropolis-Hastings sampling method. The method builds Markov chains that sample hard probability distributions. Slides come from a university intern project with the lab.

One rule of thumb sets proposal spread at twice the target spread. That choice aims for an acceptance rate near one quarter. The rule was derived for a Gaussian case, the slides caution. Standard variance misleads for chain samples, so effective sample size is covered. Students get practical tuning guidance, with limits stated in plain view.
doe-osti-3625676-regulatory-compliance-a:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-7A40-100263, dated August 2026, closes CRADA CRD-23-24436 with FarmAfield Labs. William Tokash and Grant Ellwood were the lab contacts, and the report date is March 11, 2026. The work ran from January 2024 to January 2026. It gave strategy support for placing solar and heat pump projects through a rural project channel in Nebraska.

Tasks began with a review of FarmAfield's tools, sites, and past work with ranch customers. Later tasks mapped deployment choices by state and by utility type. Nebraska public power district rules shaped much of the study. One part worked through community solar terms, where a share starts at a set monthly energy amount. Credits were tied to market value, minus the worth of past output and of assigned capacity. The report closes on what target customers could save under each route, and what still needs study.
doe-osti-3798027-2025-csewg-meeting-minu:
Brookhaven report BNL-230125-2026-INRE, dated August 2026, holds the minutes of the 2025 Cross Section Evaluation Working Group meeting. The meeting ran January 6 to 9, 2026, and D. Brown is the named compiler. The group tends the ENDF nuclear data library, the standard file set behind reactor and shielding codes. Sessions covered the library's status, the European JEFF-4.0 release, and fission and decay data at several labs.

Talks trace new measurements, fresh evaluations, and fixes to older files. One thread follows fission product yields at Los Alamos and a new framework built on them. Another debates how unresolved resonance data should carry its uncertainty. The minutes keep questions and replies in near-verbatim form, forming the record the teams will build on next year.
doe-osti-3893550-zpr-zppr-critical-exper:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-24/26 Revision 1, dated September 2026, preserves the design record of the lab's fast critical experiment facilities. Richard Lell is the printed author. The ZPR and ZPPR machines ran assemblies whose drawers held fuel and moderator plates in set patterns. Modern analysts still simulate those experiments, but a model is only trustworthy if it matches what was actually built. The report assembles as-built detail for ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9, and ZPPR.

Chapters cover each machine's physical traits, operating measurements, corrections, and core compositions. A long section treats the drawer master records: their traits, figure evolution, labelling rules, and limits. Reactor logbooks for each facility get their own review. The final guidance is practical. Rather than modelling every neglected feature one by one, analysts should build a single model holding all of them. The gap between that model and the reference run gives the total bias in one step.
dolly-dialogues:
Anthony Hope's Dolly Dialogues present twenty short conversations between the narrator and Miss Dolly Foster, a married flirt of perfect assurance. The first, A Liberal Education, opens with Dolly crying ingratitude at a smart young man passing their seat. Titles like Retribution, My Last Chance, and The Other Lady map the game.

Dolly teases, confesses, and corners her partner while husbands, lovers, and rivals pass through the talk. Hope, who wrote The Prisoner of Zenda, shows his other gift here: society comedy in pure dialogue, hardly a line wasted. Dolly's bashful, knowing smiles drive men to angry patronage and back. The dialogues were 1890s drawing-room favorites and still sparkle.
donatello-by-lord-balcarres:
Lord Balcarres, the Earl of Crawford, studies the Florentine sculptor Donatello in a 1903 book from Duckworth in London and Scribner's in New York, with plates of the works. The front matter even lists the old spellings the printers have fixed. Donatello's bronze and marble figures fill churches and squares across Italy, and the author treats him as a master above his peers.

Chapters take up the works in turn, from the Padua cross onward. Balcarres praises Donatello's children most: where Michelozzo's are dull and della Robbia's always sweet, Donatello alone grasped the whole mind of a child, he writes. Play, work, sorrow, and comedy all show in the young faces. The book pairs close looking with strong judgment, and it asks readers to see a fifteenth-century sculptor as a keen watcher of life.
dorothy-dainty-s-gay-times:
Amy Brooks wrote and drew the pictures for Dorothy Dainty's Gay Times, a 1908 volume in her Dorothy Dainty series for girls. Dorothy is a lovely, well-loved child at a fine stone house with vine-covered balconies. Twelve chapters follow her school days and play days with friends like Nancy, Arabella, Patricia, and Flossie.

The first day at school opens the book, and a school entertainment, a party, and two sleigh rides follow. One chapter turns on a necklace, and another on an unexpected trip. In a late scene, little Flossie hears the dread word quarantine and steals Uncle Harry's baby away in her arms to save it, crossing the lawn in secret. Brooks writes a sheltered world where small scrapes loom large and love sets them right. Young readers get gentle fun with a warm heart at the center.
douglass-life-and-times:
Life and Times of Frederick Douglass, first published in 1881 and revised in 1892, is his third and fullest autobiography. Douglass had become a statesman of Reconstruction, a marshal, a diplomat, and the leading Black voice in America. This is the capstone of his life's writing.

He retells his enslavement and escape, then follows his public career through the Civil War and beyond. His meetings with Lincoln, his recruiting of Black troops, and his posts in Washington fill the second half. Douglass looks back with pride and continued fight. The book completes the greatest life story written by an American born enslaved.
dr-bullivant-from-the-doliver-romance-an:
Nathaniel Hawthorne sketches an old Boston doctor in Dr. Bullivant, a short piece from his posthumous set The Doliver Romance and Other Pieces. The doctor, Hawthorne says at once, was not great enough to earn a memorial for his own sake after a century and a half. He serves instead as a lens on early New England life.

The sketch argues that we paint the Puritans too dark. At a cold distance we see only stern peaks and gray mist, Hawthorne writes, and miss the green hollows and warm spots of their world. Gloom ruled the age, he grants, but deep and solid happiness lived beside the frolic of the mind. Through Bullivant's sociable figure, the town's mix of old settler stock and new blood from the eastern world comes into view. The piece is brief, rich, and pure Hawthorne in voice.
dramatic-romances:
Robert Browning's Dramatic Romances, in the Porter and Clarke edition drawn from Crowell's 1898 Poetic Works, gathers the great monologues and tale-poems. My Last Duchess opens the muster of voices: a duke showing a portrait and burying a wife in a sentence. The Pied Piper of Hamelin follows as the volume's child's story, with the Incident of the French Camp and The Patriot for the crowd's two faces. Count Gismond, In a Gondola, and The Flight of the Duchess carry the romance half of the title. The Last Ride Together carries its philosophy.

Browning's method is the book: speakers who reveal more than they intend, in verse that thinks at talking speed. Porter and Clarke's notes made this the standard American school Browning. Readers get the essential Browning in one volume, the poems through which most English readers first hear that famous, rapid, sidelong voice.
drift-from-two-shores:
Bret Harte called this gathering Drift from Two Shores, fourteen short pieces from his California years and after. The Man on the Beach opens the book with a solitary figure living beside a river mouth near Trinidad Head, indifferent miners his only neighbors. Other titles promise saints of the foothills, a ghost of the Sierras, a hoodlum band, a tramp, an office seeker, and a sleeping-car experience.

Harte ranges from mining camps to city avenues, mixing sketches, tales, and character studies. Some pieces run only a few pages; each turns on a revealed trait or a quiet reversal. For readers sampling Harte beyond his two or three famous stories, this miscellany shows the variety he could manage inside a single volume.
dutch-courage-and-other-stories:
Jack London's Dutch Courage and Other Stories, printed in New York in 1924, gathers ten tales of the sea and the trail. The title story opens in the high mountains. Young Gus Lafee and Hazard Van Dorn find a white flag already planted on a rock wall a mile above camp. Gus throws down his towel in disgust at being scooped.

Other tales roam far. They tell of a typhoon off Japan, a lost poacher, and the banks of the Sacramento. An able seaman named Chris Farrington stars in one. Others face boarders at sea and anchor in Yeddo Bay. In one talk, an old sailor mourns the old times. The sea was once one constant glorious adventure, he says, when a boy shipped out and met Spanish galleons in weeks. London writes youth, risk, and salt water with a hard shine.
duty-and-other-irish-comedies:
Seumas O'Brien fills a 1916 volume with five Irish one-act comedies: Duty, Jurisprudence, Magnanimity, Matchmakers, and Retribution. Duty was first played at the Abbey Theatre, Dublin, on December 17, 1913, and the book prints the cast: Arthur Sinclair as Head Constable Mulligan, with Fred O'Donovan, Sydney J. Morgan, J. M. Kerrigan, J. A. O'Rourke, and Una O'Connor.

The scene is the back kitchen of a country public house on a Sunday night. Micus Goggin and Padna Sweeney beg Mrs. Cotter to fill their pewter pints again, and she refuses: the police might call any minute. The comedy turns on the Royal Irish Constabulary men who must enforce the closing law in the town they live in. O'Brien writes the talk thick and musical, and the laughs carry a sting about law, drink, and duty in small-town Ireland.
eating-in-two-or-three-languages:
Irvin S. Cobb, back from war reporting overseas, plans a campaign of eating in this 1919 humor book from George H. Doran of New York. The day he lands, he vows, will be a great day for waiters and a hard day for cooks. Green corn, asparagus, fried chicken with Virginia ham, and cantaloupe loaded with vanilla ice cream all stand on his list.

Wartime food rules under H. Hoover haunt the jokes. Cobb dreams of defying the food chief mid-bite, and plays the returning American as a starved man loose in a rich land. French and shipboard meals give him the other languages of the title. One set piece has a restaurant boss parade a live lobster from table to table, poking it under each new party's nose to prove it is no clockwork fake. The book is pure Cobb: warm, greedy, and quick with a line.
edinburgh-picturesque-notes:
Robert Louis Stevenson, born in Edinburgh, wrote these picturesque notes on his native city, here in the 1903 Seeley people's edition. He walks the reader through the Old Town and New Town, the castle hill, closes, wynds, and gardens. History sits close beside daily street life in every chapter.

Stevenson recalls famous residents, executions, kirks, and the windy views toward the Firth of Forth and the May lighthouse. He loves the city's beauty while noting its dirt, poverty, and stern past. Anyone who wants Edinburgh explained by one of its most gifted sons, with affection and clear eyes, will find the short book rewarding.
edna-s-sacrifice-and-other-stories:
Frances Henshaw Baden opens her story set on a wet September night, with three days of rain keeping four women indoors and bored to their wits' end. Nell, Floy, Aunt Edna, and the narrator have read all that is readable, played the piano to complaint, and worn out backgammon. That frame opens Edna's Sacrifice, the title tale.

Four more stories follow: Who Was the Thief?, The Ghost, The Two Brothers, and What He Left. A parting scene in one tale has Frank begging Susie to wed him before he returns to W—, while she pleads with him not to talk so. Love, duty, and family pride drive the plots in the genteel manner of the day. Baden writes for the parlor reader: sentiment high, morals clear, and each small storm of feeling brought safe to shore.
edward-fane-s-rosebud-from-twice-told-ta:
Nathaniel Hawthorne asks readers to rebuild a young woman out of an old one in Edward Fane's Rosebud, a tale from Twice Told Tales. He calls it a hard exercise of fancy: to gaze at a figure of sad age and restore the graces time snatched away, without losing the face's identity. Some old women, he grants, seem never to have been young at all.

His subject is the Widow Toothaker, a nurse of great repute who has breathed the air of sickrooms and dying breaths for years. Her sable widow's dress seems part of her being. Hawthorne rolls the years back to her dewy youth, then lets each sadder year settle again on the figure. The rosebud of the title is the token of that lost spring. The tale is short and tender, a study of how sorrow writes itself in wrinkles that a skilled eye can read backward.
elder-conklin-and-other-stories:
Frank Harris's Elder Conklin and Other Stories gathers American tales of the prairie and the mining West. The title story opens after supper, as the Elder's daughter and the new schoolmaster step onto the verandah of a frame house on a roll in the prairie.

Cottonwood Creek runs below, fringed with trees, and the sun sinks like a ball of orange fire beyond spears of yellow maize. Other stories include The Sheriff and His Partner, A Modern Idyll, Eatin' Crow, and The Best Man in Garotte. Harris writes with a journalist's eye and a storyteller's warmth. Readers of Western short fiction will find these tales vigorous and unpolished in the best sense.
elves-and-heroes:
Donald A. Mackenzie retells the fairy and heroic lore of the Scottish Highlands in Elves and Heroes, dated 1909 and given to Miss Yule of Tarradale. His preface pushes back at the literary Celt of Arnold and Renan, all mist and melancholy. The Gael of the old tales, he insists, was no ineffectual dreamer.

Highland poetry, Mackenzie writes, has more light than shadow, much symbolism but no vagueness, and pictures in minute detail. The verse tales that follow bear him out. Finn and his hunters chase for three days round Knockfarrel and Ussie Loch, and come home at even with meagre burdens, while the winter spell breaks under a golden sun. Elves, heroes, and the peat-fire world between them fill the book. It is folklore retold as literature, by a Scotch journalist who loved the old material and trusted its cheer.
emerson-s-wife-and-other-western-stories:
Florence Finch Kelly gathers fourteen Western tales in Emerson's Wife and Other Western Stories, from A. C. McClurg of Chicago in 1911, with color pictures by Stanley L. Wood. Colonel Kate appears twice in the contents, winning her spurs and sheltering a protégée. Other tales tell of the Kid of Apache Teju, a blaze on Pard Huff, and the rise, fall, and redemption of Johnson Sides.

The title tale opens with Nick Ellhorn waking in a strange room with curiosity but no surprise and no memory. The frontispiece shows Nick shouting defiance: want my guns, then come and take them.
