In another tale, a reformed man wears out three or four pocket testaments, always keeping one on him, sober and respectable ever since, but not nearly so interesting. Kelly writes the mining and ranch West with a woman's eye for its converts and strays.
english-fairy-tales:
Joseph Jacobs's English Fairy Tales collects the folk tales of England, answering those who said English folk had no fairy tales of their own. Jacobs found traces of some 140 tales in the country, a quarter of them collected in the ten years before publication.

The preface notes that France and Italy were likewise said to lack folk tales until 1870, yet within fifteen years over a thousand tales had been collected in each. Jacobs hopes his volume will stir equal activity in England, and begs readers to send him more. Children and folklorists will find here the classic English collection, with its playful invitation to knock, take down the key and walk in.
english-satires:
Oliphant Smeaton picks the typical over the complete in English Satires, an anthology running from Langland to Lowell. His preface says the aim is representative, not exhaustive. The pieces mark each era's special character and the trend of satiric development across the centuries.

Langland's pilgrimage in search of Do-well opens the book, then Chaucer's monk and friar and Lydgate's London Lackpenny. Pope appears in talk of writing for nothing but to write, asking if Dennis be alive or dead. Smeaton thanks C. H. Herford for revising his introduction and dedicates the volume to Alexander Balloch Grosart. Clough's Spectator ab Extra and Calverley's verses close the collection, by kind permission. The introduction frames satire as a national habit of mind.
english-villages:
P. H. Ditchfield reads the English village from its stones in English Villages, written at Barkham Rectory in May 1901. Twenty-three chapters run from prehistoric remains, tumuli, and pit dwellings through Roman relics and Anglo-Saxon villages. The Domesday Book, Norman castles, and monasteries follow, then the manor house and the parish church in loving detail.

Ditchfield, a rector and antiquary, lingers on church plate, brasses, the parish chest, stained glass, and bells. The medieval village, its sports, its inn, and its superstitions close the tour. Plates show stocks and whipping-post, Anne Hathaway's cottage, and tithe barns. An appendix lists books and documents for readers who want to write their own parish history.
enoch-soames-a-memory-of-the-eighteen-ni:
Max Beerbohm invents Enoch Soames, a forgotten poet of the eighteen-nineties, and mourns that Holbrook Jackson's thorough history of the decade omits him entirely. Soames wrote obscure books with titles like Fungoids and a preface urging readers to lean near to life. Nobody read them, and Beerbohm claims to be the only mourner.

The story turns fantastic when Soames, desperate to know his future fame, bargains with the devil to visit the British Museum a hundred years hence. He drones that the museum will still stand where it stands, and finds his reward waiting there. Beerbohm's tale mixes parody, pity, and a perfect literary hoax: later readers hunted catalogs for Soames's works.
enquire-within-upon-everything-the-great:
Enquire Within Upon Everything promises the whole of domestic life between two covers, here in its eighty-ninth edition of 1894, its total issue past one million one hundred and eighty-eight thousand copies. The editor's motto covers modeling a flower in wax, curing a headache, making a will, getting married, and burying a relative. Robert Kemp Philp built the book; Houlston and Sons of Paternoster Square kept revising it.

Numbered paragraphs answer everything, from kite-swimming to life-belts, and an index points enquirers to them. Companion volumes crowd the front pages: dictionaries of daily wants, useful knowledge, and medical knowledge. The great Victorian standby taught households etiquette, cookery, and law in one alphabetical rush. Few books were reprinted so often.
ensign-knightley-and-other-stories:
A. E. W. Mason opens his story collection with a siege in Ensign Knightley and Other Stories, published in 1901. The title tale begins at eleven at night on May 13th, 1680, in Tangier. Surgeon Wyley of the ship Bonetta finds officers at bassette in the Main-Guard while the Moors entrench beneath the walls. The Henrietta Redoubt has fallen that day.

Fourteen more stories follow: The Man of Wheels, The Coward, The Deserter, The Shuttered House, and How Barrington Returned to Johannesburg. A wreck tale lands a sailor on Tresco, emptying his sea-boots on a settle and dreading the name of the Golden Ball. Mason mixes soldiers, sailors, and strays, all caught at the moment luck turns.
eric-brighteyes:
H. Rider Haggard wrote Eric Brighteyes as a saga of Viking Iceland, and dedicated it to the Empress Frederick, whose dying husband had found pleasure in his stories. Eric, a golden-haired hero of great strength, loves Gudruda the Fair. Her father Asmund opposes the match. So does the witch-born Swanhild, who wants Eric herself. The berserk Skallagrim instead becomes his sworn companion. Deeds fill the chapter heads: winning the sword Whitefire, riding down Golden Falls, outlawry, and a-viking to London town.

Haggard imitates the Icelandic sagas' manner, fate-heavy and laconic, while loading the plot with witchcraft, sea fights, and a wedding feast that ends in blood. Eric's doom is foretold and unavoidable. The book stands beside King Solomon's Mines as proof of Haggard's second gift, the northern romance.
essays-and-lectures:
Oscar Wilde's Essays and Lectures, in its fourth Methuen edition of 1913, collects his early criticism and platform talks, pieces he never meant to reprint. The literary executor's preface says only the closing Poems in Prose are excepted from that judgment. The Rise of Historical Criticism, Wilde's Oxford prize essay, opens the volume.

Lectures on the English Renaissance of art, house decoration, and the craftsman follow, plus a lecture to art students and the sketch London Models. Wilde argues that art shapes life more than life shapes art, and that criticism itself is creative. Readers can watch his epigrammatic style forming here, years before the plays made it famous across London.
essays-and-tales:
Joseph Addison's periodical essays fill this Cassell volume of 1888, drawn from the Tatler and the Spectator. The introduction explains the plan of the series: an earlier volume took the Isaac Bickerstaff papers, another the Sir Roger de Coverley set. This one leaves Addison speaking alone, on subjects from public credit to household superstitions.

The contents show his range in one list. Six papers examine wit, two celebrate the ballad of Chevy Chase, and others treat friendship, censure, genius, and good nature. The Vision of Mirza gives the volume its most famous allegory, a dream of human life as a bridge over a tide. Short tales like Theodosius and Constantia close the set. These are the essays that taught English prose its ease.
evelyn-innes:
Moore's novel Evelyn Innes was first published in 1898. George Moore dedicates it to Arthur Symons and W. B. Yeats, writers he calls kindred spirits. This copy is the Essex Library reprint of 1929. The opening chapter enters the world of early music in London.

Mr. Innes, Evelyn's father, repairs an Elizabethan virginal by candlelight. He adjusts its jacks, tunes it, and plays Byrd and Morley. His grey hair and burning eyes mark him as a dreamer for old instruments. A sixteenth-century organ lately gained fills his thoughts. The scene builds a household ruled by early music. That devotion forms the ground of Evelyn's own musical life.
everybody-s-business-is-nobody-s-busines:
Daniel Defoe published Everybody's Business Is Nobody's Business in 1725 under the name Andrew Moreton, Esquire, as this fifth edition's title page shows. Its subtitle promises private abuses and public grievances, exemplified in the pride, insolence, and exorbitant wages of women servants and footmen. A proposal for amendment accompanies the complaint.

Defoe, speaking as a master of a family, tells how a visitor's fine lady proved a common servant-wench asking eight pounds a year, dressed cleaner than her mistress. He also proposes clearing London's streets of shoe-cleaner vermin by employing the starving industrious poor instead. The pamphlet shows Defoe the social engineer, half indignant, half scheming, in his last productive decade.
fables:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these Fables across his career, and they were gathered in print in the 1890s, after his death. Like Aesop, he tells short tales of animals, sailors, devils, and kings, each ending in a moral that often turns the expected lesson on its head. A tadpole and a frog debate progress. A devil keeps an inn. A singer and his song meet their reckoning.

Stevenson packs wit, dread, and tenderness into a page or two at a time. Some tales read as jokes with teeth; others, like the tale of the man and the yellow paint, feel like small parables about art itself. Readers who know him from Treasure Island will find the same clear spring of story, here at its most concentrated.
fables-for-the-times:
Phillips's Fables for the Times retells beast fables with a sharp modern edge. Henry Wallace Phillips wrote the pieces, and T. R. Sullivant drew the pictures. The contents list about twenty short fables. Old favorites such as The Fox and the Grapes sit beside new coinages.

The Baa-Sheep and the Lion opens the book and returns at the end. In it a sheep under a lion's paw begs to hear the lion sing first. The lion roars a Wagner selection while the sheep weeps. His tears, he claims, mourn the ruin of so fine a voice by wool nearby. Other titles include The Ambitious Hippopotamus and The Horse and the Oyster. Phillips aims Aesop's form at the manners of his own times.
famous-americans-of-recent-times:
Parton's Famous Americans of Recent Times profiles eleven public figures of the age before the Civil War. James Parton wrote lives of Jackson, Burr, and Franklin as well. The title page is dated 1867. Most papers first ran in the North American Review, his note says.

Henry Clay, Daniel Webster, and John C. Calhoun lead the contents. John Randolph and Stephen Girard follow among the statesmen and givers. James Gordon Bennett stands for the press with his New York Herald. Charles Goodyear and Commodore Vanderbilt represent invention and capital. Henry Ward Beecher and his church close the main run. Theodosia Burr and John Jacob Astor end the volume. Parton opens Clay's life by noting how war's end makes its men seem distant.
famous-men-of-the-middle-ages:
John H. Haaren, a New York school superintendent, and A. B. Poland wrote Famous Men of the Middle Ages as history for young readers. Their preface argues that children learn the past best through lives, as peaks give shape to a landscape. Clear stories replace dates and king lists. The book served elementary classrooms as reading text and history.

Teuton gods and the Nibelung legends open the volume, mixing myth with history. Alaric the Visigoth, Attila the Hun, and Genseric the Vandal march through the chapters. Theodoric, Clovis, and Justinian show kingdoms rising from the empire's wreckage. Mohammed, Charles Martel, Pepin, and Charlemagne carry the story into a new Europe of faith and empire. Harun-al-Raschid of Baghdad adds the Muslim world in its golden age. Teachers liked the design: one vivid life per chapter, told plainly enough for a child to retell after one reading.
famous-modern-ghost-stories:
Scarborough's Famous Modern Ghost Stories anthologizes the modern supernatural tale. Dorothy Scarborough, a Columbia lecturer, selected the stories and wrote the introduction. Her own study of the supernatural in fiction stands behind the choices. The book is dated 1921 and dedicated to Ashley Horace Thorndike.

Her introduction is titled The Imperishable Ghost. Algernon Blackwood's The Willows opens the fiction. Mary E. Wilkins Freeman and Robert W. Chambers follow. Leonid Andreyev's Lazarus and W. F. Harvey's The Beast with Five Fingers deepen the set. Anatole France, Fitz-James O'Brien, and Ambrose Bierce all appear. Poe's Ligeia and Maupassant's A Ghost close the range. Scarborough maps the ghost story as a living modern form.
fancy-s-show-box-from-twice-told-tales:
Hawthorne's Fancy's Show-Box is a short morality piece from his Twice-Told Tales. Nathaniel Hawthorne asks whether guilt can stain the soul without a deed. Crimes plotted and resolved on, yet never done, form his question. Earthly courts judge acts alone, he grants from the start.

Heaven's court may weigh guilty thoughts as deeds' shadows, he proposes. The soul can pollute itself in a midnight chamber or at prayer in church. Such crimes seem carnal, yet need no hand to complete them. Hawthorne calls this a fearful truth if it holds. He then illustrates it by an imaginary example. Mr. Smith, long a pattern of moral excellence, warms himself with wine. The tale that follows tests thought against innocence.
fantastic-fables:
Ambrose Bierce collected Fantastic Fables in 1899, very short satirical tales modeled on Aesop but aimed at modern politics, business, law, and religion. The contents list pieces such as The Moral Principle and the Material Interest, The Ingenious Patriot, and Two Kings. Each fable runs a page or less and ends in a sting.

Politicians promise, officials dodge, big nations bully small ones, and reformers expose themselves, all in Bierce's dry, exact prose. Animals still talk, but senators, editors, and financiers now share the stage with them. Readers who enjoy the bitter wit of his Devil's Dictionary will find the same mind here, working in miniature and rarely sparing anyone.
far-above-rubies:
MacDonald's Far Above Rubies is a short novel of a young poet's inner life. George MacDonald opens with Hector Macintosh, a man of about twenty-five. Hector bears a Celt's gifts and some of their disabilities, the narrator says. He regards only the ideal and shuns lesser authority.

His delight is embodying his thoughts in verse, his natural form. He attempts it only in his own chamber's retirement. No friend can tempt him to share these cherished matters. He dwells on love and friendship in the abstract alone. Of neither has he had the smallest direct experience, MacDonald notes. His ideals of both passions are of the purest sort. The tale tests such sealed idealism against real life.
fashionable-philosophy-and-other-sketche:
Oliphant's Fashionable Philosophy and Other Sketches collects short satirical pieces. Laurence Oliphant also wrote Piccadilly and Altiora Peto. This text follows the 1887 William Blackwood and Sons edition, priced one shilling. His preface jokes that railway travel seldom breeds serious thought.

Station bookstall fare shaped his modesty, he says. Only the first and third sketches try to stir reflection. Even those merely suggest ideas for the reader to develop. One piece, The Sisters of Thibet, came from the Nineteenth Century Review. Correspondents had mistaken its satire for his own travels, he notes. He corrects that error with thanks to the editor. The sketches glance at fashionable thought with a raised eyebrow.
father-brown-stories:
Chesterton's Father Brown Stories collects detective tales of the priest sleuth. G. K. Chesterton wrote the stories among his eighty-five varied volumes. This Penguin Popular Classics copy carries the record date 1927. A life sketch of Chesterton opens the volume.

Gilbert Keith Chesterton was born in London in 1874, it says. Slow and awkward at school, he was marked as idiot or genius. He left the Slade School of Art without a degree for publishing. He claimed to have read ten thousand novels in six years. With Hilaire Belloc he formed the Chesterbelloc of Shaw's nickname. The sketch praises his paradox, pun, and oratory. The stories within made Father Brown a classic detective of reason and faith.
fenimore-cooper-s-literary-offences:
Mark Twain's most famous piece of literary criticism opens with the praise he means to destroy. Professors Lounsbury and Brander Matthews and the novelist Wilkie Collins call Cooper's Pathfinder and Deerslayer perfect works of art. Twain replies that the professors cannot have read the books, and proceeds to the evidence.

There are nineteen rules, he says, governing romantic fiction, and Cooper violated eighteen of them in The Deerslayer. In two-thirds of a page he counts 114 offences against literary art out of a possible 115. The rules are then applied one by one: the tale must accomplish something, its people must talk like humans, its woodcraft must be possible. The essay is demolition performed as comedy, and it fixed Cooper's reputation for a century.
fifty-famous-fables:
Lida Brown McMurry retold Fifty Famous Fables as a reader for children, drawing on the old Aesop tradition. Each short tale uses animals or country folk to act out a single fault or virtue. The stories are grouped under plain moral headings. A brief telling keeps every episode within a few pages.

Young readers meet the tortoise and the ducks, the shepherd boy who cried wolf, and the goose that laid golden eggs. Other tales warn against pride, greed, quarrelling, and deceit. Some praise deeds over words and urge contentment with one's lot. McMurry's groupings make the lesson of each story easy to find and discuss. The book served schools and families who wanted classic fables in simple modern English.
fifty-famous-people-a-book-of-short-stor:
Fifty Famous People, a book of short stories by James Baldwin, tells true incidents from great lives for young readers. Baldwin's prefatory note makes a careful claim: the stories are not biographical, but they are about real persons who actually lived and played their parts in history. Each, he says, has a basis of truth and an ethical lesson, and he has given good measure, a few more than fifty people, into the bargain.

The contents open with bird stories and schoolroom pieces, speaking a piece and writing a composition among them. Benjamin Franklin's whistle, the famous bought lesson in paying too much for a pleasure, stands for the method. Caliphs and poets, the Ettrick Shepherd, and kings and inventors follow in short chapters sized for reading aloud. Baldwin believed children delight in the real when it is told as story. He built the book to prove that doctrine false.
fifty-one-tales:
Dunsany dreams in short form in Fifty-One Tales, printed in 1915. Lord Dunsany fills the book with brief tales of gods, death, and strange cities. The contents list reads like a spell book: Charon, The Death of Pan, The Sphinx at Giza, The Raft-Builders, and Death and Odysseus among them.

The sampled tale sends a man from a black-thatched cottage through rooms of black velvet and black marble. Magicians whisper and do not look up as he passes. In the third room a silk pavilion stands with its curtains drawn, the holy of holies of that dark place, with still forms crouched on each side. The dread builds from hush and stone. Across the book, Dunsany's tales are short, strange, and set at the edge of myth.
figures-of-earth-a-comedy-of-appearances:
Cabell spins a sly romance in Figures of Earth, a comedy of appearances printed in 1921. James Branch Cabell tells of Manuel, who leaves the mire to seek his fate. Frank C. Papé drew the illustrations. The book falls in three parts: the Book of Credit, the Book of Spending, and the Book of Cast Accounts.

Manuel's road runs through marvels with dry names. Chapters treat the economics of Math, the crown of wisdom, the halo of holiness, and the feather of love. In the sampled pages, Manuel keeps a hut in the forest. He makes the proper soup, sets candles under umbrellas in the set manner, and calls three times at sunset that supper is ready. A voice answers that it is coming, and the woods fall still. Cabell's tale joins quest romance to a cool, mocking wit.
filipino-popular-tales:
Fansler gathers the tales of an archipelago in Filipino Popular Tales, printed in 1921. Dean S. Fansler collected the stories in the Philippines from 1908 to 1914, and edited them with comparative notes. None, his preface says, had been in print before. He sets the islands at the meeting point of East and West, near China and Japan, tied to Malay and Indian worlds, and ruled from the West for three centuries.

That place, he argues, makes the tales rich for study. The notes weigh each story against the tale stock of the world. One note takes up a hero with a magic ring who sets out to seek his fortune. Fansler places the tale in the Bride Wager group, and sorts it against the types Von Hahn had named. The book serves two readers at once: the child of the fireside and the scholar of the folk tale.
five-tales:
John Galsworthy gathered Five Tales in 1919. His contents page itself tells a publishing story. The fifth tale in this edition is Indian Summer of a Forsyte, later moved into The Forsyte Saga. The other tales are The First and Last, A Stoic, The Apple Tree, and The Juryman. The First and Last opens in a barrister's firelit library, where Keith Darrant rests from court and a family crisis assembles itself offstage.

Galsworthy's tales turn on conscience under pressure: a brother's crime, an old clerk's loyalty, a young man's holiday love, a juror's doubt. His method is quiet accumulation, detail by detail, until duty and desire cannot both be served. Readers of the Forsytes will find Soames's world here in concentrated, short-story form.
flames:
Hichens opens Flames with a study of a soul in 1897. Robert Hichens gives his hero, Valentine Cresswell, a first chapter named for him: The Saint of Victoria Street. Refinement, not religion, ruled the young man. It held him back from most of the sins of his age with a curious ease.

Each age, the book says, passes its special sins in review, like troops, before a man decides what regiment he will join. Valentine had joined none. The trumpets of vice rang in his ears in vain. He pitied the poor creatures who hastened at their summons, and chose to be master of his soul. The sampled middle brings in Cuckoo, a woman with a sunless past, and Julian, whom she judges. The novel sets its pure saint and its fallen woman on one scale, and weighs what each may say to the other.
flower-fables:
Louisa May Alcott wrote Flower Fables as a girl of sixteen, and it became her first published book, in 1854. She wrote the tales for Ellen Emerson, the daughter of her father's friend Ralph Waldo Emerson. The hosted text gathers her fairy stories, each built around flowers, elves, and the small moral weather of kindness, pride, and patience.

In the title tale, the elf Thistledown must learn gentleness before the flower spirits will welcome him. Other tales follow a violet, a little bud, and fairy queens through trials that test their hearts. Alcott's love of nature and her gift for plain, warm telling show early here, years before Little Women made her famous. The book stays sweet without going soft.
fly-leaves: Charles Stuart Calverley's 1884 verse book gathers light and reflective poems on morning and evening, shelter, the palace, first love and sad memories. Schoolmasters, railway stations, examinations, the beach and the organ all supply subjects, treated with wit and a sharp ear for metre. The collection moves easily between humour and tenderness, never settling long in either mood.
foes:
Johnston writes of friendship turned to enmity in Foes, printed in 1918. Mary Johnston sets her novel in Scotland, at Glenfernie House and in a glen below it. English Strickland, the tutor, sits on a door-stone with Mother Binning as the tale opens. She spins and dreams, and tells him what a bonny day lets her see.

The sampled pages find a man far from that glen, kept from a sea strand in Holland. Elspeth fills his thoughts: what she does this April day, how the trees bud in the glen at home. Alexander's challenge lies on the floor by his foot. He loves her again as he sits there, and with a strange sense of having loved her long ago, and more than once. Johnston's tale joins a feud of men to a love that feels older than one life.
food-remedies-facts-about-foods-and-thei:
Daniel's booklet treats everyday foods as medicine, giving each one's uses in sickness and health. It appeared in London in 1908 as the second of the Healthy Life Booklets. Orange pips, crushed and taken in hot water, are offered as a harmless sedative. A marmalade drink is said to relieve neuralgia and pains in the head.

Parsley gets a long entry: useful for the kidneys, and its bruised leaves are applied to nursing mothers' painful breasts. Florence Daniel opens with a Talmud saying about crediting one's sources, then admits her own sources are too tangled to name one by one. The tone stays practical throughout, closer to a herbal than to a cookbook.
footprints-on-the-sea-shore-from-twice-t:
Hawthorne's sketch follows a solitary September ramble along a rocky shore near his home. He goes out because the forest is too far for a daily escape, while the sea lies within reach. He watches the waves, the sea-birds, and his own footprints washing away in the sand.

By evening the sea turns melancholy and the distant sails look astray and not of earth. His spirit wanders and comes shivering back, and he asks not to be grudged the day. The sea has been his companion, the birds his friends, and the wind has told him secrets. Nathaniel Hawthorne promises the day's calm will still be felt tomorrow in the crowded street at noon.
four-arthurian-romances:
Chretien de Troyes, court poet of twelfth-century France, wrote the four verse romances gathered here in English prose: Erec et Enide, Cliges, Yvain, and Lancelot. Chretien effectively invented Arthurian romance, turning Welsh legend into courtly French storytelling. Knights leave Arthur's court to test love against adventure.

Erec must prove marriage has not softened him, Yvain the lion knight goes mad and is healed by service, and Lancelot rides in a cart for Guinevere's sake. The scholarly notes discuss even the chastity-testing horn at Arthur's court. Chretien's irony and psychology shaped Malory and every Arthurian writer after him. These translations let modern readers meet the source, graceful, strange, and foundational.
four-max-carrados-detective-stories:
Bramah's blind detective Max Carrados solves four cases in this collection. The Coin of Dionysius opens in a coin dealer's back office on a rainy night, where Baxter expects an important caller. The Knight's Cross signal problem and the tragedy at Brookbend Cottage follow.

Carrados works through his friend Carlyle, who brings him clients and eyes. In one case Carlyle delivers a young man whose sister needs protection from a man named Creake. Bramah remarks that every man carries the life of any other in his hands daily, unnoticed. Ernest Bramah published the four stories in 1914.
four-weird-tales:
Blackwood gathers four weird tales in this 1907 collection, opening with The Insanity of Jones. John Enderby Jones, a clerk, plainly sees himself as the inheritor of a long series of past lives. Each body, he believes, was determined by the behaviour of the one before it.

The Man Who Found Out and The Glamour of the Snow follow, and Sand closes the book. In Sand, a traveller is trailed down a hotel corridor by Richard Vance of Birmingham. Algernon Blackwood lets the voice come unpleasantly close behind his man. The knowledge Jones carries, the preface to his tale insists, is not too welcome.
freckles:
Gene Stratton-Porter, an Indiana writer and naturalist, wrote Freckles, published in 1904, one of her best-loved novels. Its hero is Freckles, a young orphan with one hand, raised in a children's home with no knowledge of his family. He is hired to guard a stretch of precious timber in the Limberlost swamp, walking a lonely line each day against thieves who want the trees.

In the swamp he finds beauty, birdsong, and work that gives him pride. He also finds the Swamp Angel, a girl whose singing and kindness match his love of the wild place, and a friend in the Bird Woman who studies nature. A logging boss's plot and a question of birth drive the tale to its close. The book helped save the real Limberlost in readers' hearts.
friendly-fairies:
Gruelle wrote and drew these fairy tales for young children. The first story tells of three little gnomes under a fallen tree. They rescue a lost boy who followed a hunt. Other tales feature talking woodland creatures. Sally Migrundy lives in a tiny cottage by a stream. Johnny Cricket sees Santa Claus.

The stories stay gentle and brief. Each one turns on a small kindness or a small wonder. Mr. and Mrs. Thumbkins appear among the fairy folk. A wishbone, a fairy ring, and a happy rattle supply the magic. Gruelle's own pictures run through the book. The tone suits reading aloud at bedtime.
friends-in-council-first-series:
Arthur Helps's Friends in Council, First Series, presents moral and social discussion in the form of conversations among friends. Helps was born at Streatham in July 1813, went to Eton at sixteen and then to Trinity College, Cambridge, graduating in 1835.

He served as aide to two cabinet ministers, published Essays Written in the Intervals of Business in 1841, and took a post settling French, Danish and Spanish claims. Friends in Council applies that experience to questions of conduct, work and society, in dialogue rather than lecture. Readers who enjoy Victorian essays in conversational dress will find Helps thoughtful, urbane and quietly wise.
frontier-stories:
Harte collected these tales of the California frontier in one volume. The first story, Flip, opens on a heat-blasted mountain terrace. An outlaw gambler hides under a stage-coach to escape a sheriff. Other tales are set at mining camps and missions. Found at Blazing Star and In the Carquinez Woods follow. A Blue-Grass Penelope shifts a classic waiting-wife plot west.

A Ship of '49 recalls the gold rush voyage. Left Out on Lone Star Mountain closes the list. Harte writes miners, gamblers, and drifters with dry irony. His California is vivid, harsh, and sentimental at once. The stories helped fix the West in readers' minds. Each tale is complete in itself.
fugitive-pieces:
Byron's first book of verse, Fugitive Pieces, is reproduced here from the first edition. It was printed in private in the autumn of 1806, when Byron was eighteen years old. A bibliographical note by Marcel Kessel tells the story of that printing. The poems nearly doubled in size during a pause in the press work. Byron found pieces he thought lost and wrote new ones. This facsimile was issued for the Facsimile Text Society by Columbia University Press in 1933.

The poems are young work: love lyrics, satires, and pieces to friends. The note traces dates and states with care. Readers get both the verse and the evidence of how it first reached print.
gallantry-dizain-des-fetes-galantes:
Cabell's Gallantry, subtitled Dizain des Fetes Galantes, is a set of ten linked comedies of love and manners. James Branch Cabell frames them in the style of the age of the second George. An introduction by Louis Untermeyer opens the volume. The tales bear titles such as Simon's Hour, Love at Martinmas, and The Casual Honeymoon. An afterpiece, Love's Alumni, closes the set. Cabell dedicates the book to James Robinson Branch as a model of gallantry in its highest sense.

The epistle dedicatory, addressed to Mrs. Grundy, sets the arch tone. Courtiers scheme over seats in Parliament and marriages in the dialogue. Wit, not plot, carries the pieces.
gallegher-and-other-stories:
Gallegher and Other Stories, by Richard Harding Davis, collects the newspaper tales that made his name, in an 1891 Scribner's volume illustrated by Charles Dana Gibson. Davis opens his title story in a newsroom worn down by office boys. So many sleepy, lazy, and too smart boys had passed through that the staff called them all by one name, until Gallegher arrived and became an individual at once.

Around Gallegher, Davis sets A Walk Up the Avenue, My Disreputable Friend Mr Raegen, The Other Woman, and The Trailer for Room No 8. Three Van Bibber stories close the book, following his elegant young man of society through swan boats, a burglar, and duty as best man. Davis wrote from inside the newspaper world he had just conquered, and the copy boy who solves a crime became the pattern for a generation of reporter heroes.
galton-memories:
Francis Galton published Memories of My Life in 1908, summing up one of the most varied careers in Victorian science. Galton was Darwin's cousin, and his interests seemed endless. Travel, weather, heredity, and measurement all drew his restless mind.

He recalls exploring in southwest Africa, mapping weather patterns, and inventing the fingerprint method for identification. His work on heredity and human ability, which he named eugenics, fills later chapters and now draws sharp criticism. Galton writes with dry humor about his many failures and fixes. The memoir shows the making of modern statistics, for better and for worse.
geoffrey-monmouth-history-kings-britain-:
Geoffrey of Monmouth completed his History of the Kings of Britain around 1136, and it became a medieval bestseller. J. A. Giles's translation is the text here, from his Six Old English Chronicles. Geoffrey claimed to translate a very ancient book in the British tongue. What he really did was invent much of Britain's past.

From Brutus of Troy, his kings run through Lear, Cymbeline, and the long line to Arthur, whose reign fills the book's center. Merlin's prophecies thread the story. Shakespeare drew Lear and Cymbeline from Geoffrey's pages, and Arthur's world starts here. Historians scolded the book for centuries while everyone read it. It is myth-making of the first order.
gildas-on-the-ruin-of-britain-giles:
Gildas, a British monk of the sixth century, wrote On the Ruin of Britain as a sermon of blame against his own kings and priests. J. A. Giles translated the Latin for the modern reader. The work is the only connected narrative source for Britain after the Romans left. Everything else for those years is scraps and saints' tales.

Gildas tells of Roman rule, the coming of the Saxons as hired swords, their revolt, and the wars of Ambrosius and the siege of Badon. Then he turns on the five kings of his day and scourges their sins. His Latin is hot, tangled, and full of scripture. Later ages mined him for Arthur's age, though he never names Arthur.
glasses:
Henry James opens Glasses with a narrator resolving, pen in hand, to follow a thread of colored beads back to a first impression at Folkestone. The story he reconstructs concerns Flora Saunt, a beautiful young woman whose face all London watches through opera glasses. She sustains fifty tentative glasses at the theater with admirable serenity.

Flora is secretly going blind and hides her glasses, the instruments of her vanity and shame, behind subterfuges her friend gradually perceives. James studies the terror of being seen versus the need to see, in a society that prices a woman's face. The 1916 Secker text preserves the tale's delicate cruelty: a small subject worked to novella depth.
glimpses-of-unfamiliar-japan-first-serie:
Lafcadio Hearn went to Japan in 1890 as a journalist and stayed for life. This first series of Glimpses of Unfamiliar Japan gathers his early sketches, dedicated to two friends whose kindness, he says, alone made his stay in the Orient possible. Chapters begin with his first day in the Orient and a pilgrimage to Enoshima. Others treat the market of the dead and the Bon-Odori dance for the dead.

Hearn dwells on shrines, ghosts, and old customs: the great shrine at Kitzuki, the cave of the children's ghosts, and fox lore. He writes as a lover of the old Japan he saw fading. His prose is lush and exact at once. The book helped fix the image of Japan in Western minds, and it still reads as a tender record of a world in change.
glimpses-of-unfamiliar-japan-second-seri:
Hearn's second series of Japanese sketches opens in a Japanese garden, by his small house near a river in Matsue. The house proved too small in the hot season, so he moved to a quiet street behind the old castle, into a former samurai residence. Chapters cover the household shrine, women's hair, and the diary of an English teacher, for Hearn taught English in Japan.

Two strange festivals, a dancing girl, and a trip from Hoki to the Oki islands fill the middle of the book. Essays on souls, on ghosts and goblins, and on the Japanese smile show his deep study of local belief. The book closes with Sayonara, a farewell. Together with the first series, it forms Hearn's best-loved portrait of the Japan he made his home.
goldsmith-english-men-of-letters-series:
William Black wrote this life of Oliver Goldsmith for the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley and published in 1878. Goldsmith gave English letters The Vicar of Wakefield, The Deserted Village, and She Stoops to Conquer. Black's chapters run from school and college through idleness and foreign travel to the early struggles of a hack writer in London.

Later chapters treat The Citizen of the World, an arrest for debt, The Traveller, and Goldsmith in society. Black ends with increasing difficulties and the end. Goldsmith's charm, folly, and kindness are the heart of the book: a man always in debt, always at ease in talk, and able to write with a grace that still feels fresh. The life is short and warm, a good first meeting with its subject.
govdocs-archive_org-PaulFosterCaseGreatS:
Paul Foster Case, an American occultist and founder of the Builders of the Adytum, wrote The Great Seal of the United States. His subject is the history, symbolism, and message of the national emblem. Case read public symbols as carriers of hidden teaching. The Great Seal, with its pyramid and eye, drew him strongly.

He traces the seal's making in the 1780s and reads its parts: the eagle, the shield, the unfinished pyramid, and the Latin mottos Annuit Coeptis and Novus Ordo Seclorum. For Case the seal announces a new age for mankind. The book decodes the nation's emblem for readers of his school, in the archive's collection.
govdocs-archive_org-SpanishUFOFiles_Span:
Spain investigated unidentified flying objects through official channels for decades, and its files on those cases were later released to the public. The Spanish UFO Files gather that material: reports and investigations kept in the government's own records.

The papers cover sightings brought to official attention and the inquiries that followed, recorded in the dry language of state paperwork. Read together, they show how a modern government handled reports it could not easily explain. For UFO researchers, official releases like these matter because they rest on documents rather than retellings, and claims can be checked against the record.
govdocs-archive_org-TheFBIAndCISPES_The_:
In July 1989 the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence issued its report on the FBI's investigation of CISPES, the Committee in Solidarity with the People of El Salvador. The inquiry, from the 101st Congress, reviewed how the Bureau had treated an American group opposed to United States policy in Central America.

The report sets out what the FBI did, on whose authority, and where the committee found fault with the investigation. It became part of the wider record of 1980s fights over domestic surveillance of political groups. Readers get Congress's own oversight findings, drawn from the Bureau's files and testimony.
govdocs-archive_org-Volume3Part2HowHelpC:
Cisco Wheeler, who presented herself as a survivor of Illuminati mind control, wrote Deeper Insights into the Illuminati Formula as a companion to the conspiracy literature around that book. Part 2, How Help Comes About, turns from the alleged system itself to escape from it.

Wheeler writes about how help supposedly reaches people caught in the programming she describes, drawing on her own claimed experience. The volume assumes readers know the earlier Illuminati Formula books and their framework of handlers, alters, and secret networks. It is held as an archive holding, without endorsement, as part of the 1990s mind-control literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BankRobberies_B:
The FBI's King assassination file, MURKIN, generated teletypes long after the shooting, as agents ran down leads to build and close the case. This teletype, dated November 14, 1968, reports a registration-records check at a motel in Indiana, under file 44-38861.

Agents were looking for any record of James Earl Ray or his associates at the motel, and the check found none. Negative results fill much of the MURKIN file, because proving where Ray had not been mattered to a case built on his movements. The single teletype is preserved as issued, one page of the Bureau's legwork.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurkeJW_Burke_J:
On June 8, 1977, an angry citizen wrote to J. W. Burke Jr. about the House Select Committee on Assassinations, then in the first year of its reinvestigation of the Kennedy and King murders. The author's name is garbled in the scan, but the temper survived intact.

The letter denounces the committee as dishonest and irresponsible, a charge the HSCA heard from both directions: some thought it a whitewash, others a witch hunt. Citizen mail in the files shows the second investigation never enjoyed the public's full trust. The single letter is preserved as written, heat and all, for researchers of the committee's reception.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli:
A news article reports a demand from Maryland Governor Marvin Mandel. Mandel ordered Baltimore Police Commissioner Donald Pomerleau to deliver a full report on his department's secret intelligence and surveillance activities. The governor wanted the covert work of the city police brought into the open.

The demand put a police commissioner under public pressure from his own governor. Domestic intelligence units in American cities operated with little oversight in this period, and Baltimore's was no exception. The article records the moment that secrecy was challenged from the top of state government.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FoxJames_Fox_Ja: A personal letter dated August 6, 1991 was written to a man named David. The writer enclosed a copy of another letter and mentioned Sciambra, a member of Jim Garrison's staff, and the judge in the Shaw case. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text, so the letter survives as an unsigned note among researchers still trading Shaw case material in 1991.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GochenauerJames: nsia-GochenauerJames Gochenauer James: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JohnsonHaynes_J:
Haynes Johnson reported from New Orleans for the Washington Star in 1967 on two vacant offices on Lafayette Square. One had been used by Cuban exiles. The other was the headquarters of Guy Banister Associates, the detective agency of a former FBI man. Johnson explains their place in the Kennedy assassination story.

An address can carry a case. The square put exile politics and Banister's office within steps of each other, and Oswald's New Orleans summer ran through that ground. Johnson's article walks readers through the geography while the Garrison investigation made it famous.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KirkwoodJames_K: James Kirkwood's interview with Clay Shaw survives in this file, under the heading 'Surviving.' Shaw was the New Orleans businessman whom District Attorney Jim Garrison put on trial in 1969 over the Kennedy assassination. He was acquitted. Beyond the title and Kirkwood's name, the file gives little detail about when the interview was made or what Shaw said in it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LeavelleJames_L: Canada's Maclean's magazine devoted its November 22, 1993 issue to the Kennedy assassination, thirty years after Dallas. The special issue appeared under the line 'JFK — 30 Years Later.' Anniversary issues like this one gathered essays, photographs, and argument about the case for a general audience. The file preserves the issue as a record of how the anniversary was marked in print, though the evidence here does not list its individual articles.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Queries_Queries: A letter filed under the heading 'Queries' concerns geese donated to Peace Corps projects. The project was nicknamed 'Geese for Peace.' The letter discusses the publicity the donations generated. Geese went abroad as breeding stock and as symbols, and the press noticed. The file gives the project, the nickname, and the letter's concern with coverage. It does not name the writer, so the letter stands as one page of that project's correspondence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Sources_Sources: Days after President Kennedy was shot in November 1963, FBI staff in Dallas faced a legal problem. Their report, filed as DL 89-43 and linked to Anton Pavrlka Jr., records the search for a federal statute that actually covered an assassination. At the time, killing a president was not clearly a federal crime. The report shows investigators working through the law books while the case was already underway.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Turtles_Turtles: nsia-Turtles Turtles: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Witnesses_Witne: Howard Leslie Brennan was the witness who said he saw a rifleman in the Texas School Book Depository window. A study examines his Warren Commission testimony, given in March 1964. Brennan's account helped the commission place a shooter in that building. Because so much rested on his words, researchers have tested them for decades. The study works through what he said and how well it holds up.
govdocs-archive_org-the-odessa-signal-si: The Odessa Signal SIGMA 6 UMBRA: the declassified government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated material, filed, an obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers, a single volume.
govdocs-archive_org-topdeclassified_Top_:
The CIA wrote the Human Resource Exploitation Training Manual in 1983 to teach its officers the work of interrogation. It covers techniques for questioning prisoners and human sources, set out in the agency's own calm, procedural language.

Once secret, the manual was later declassified and became one of the most notorious training texts of the Cold War. Human rights groups cite it in debates over coercive questioning, because later detention programs echoed its methods and its euphemisms. The library presents the full text as an archive holding. Readers can study exactly what the agency taught its people, rather than rely on summaries or accusations about it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH: CHILE: The Barnes House - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records, filed. An obscure item and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Colombia set up a Truth Commission to account for decades of armed conflict, alongside a special court and a unit hunting for the disappeared. A Constitutional Court ruling said all three bodies could see every record they needed. This briefing book reports that the promise ran into a wall.

Despite the ruling, Colombia's armed forces kept key files off limits. The blocked records included military intelligence files tied to serious abuses. Those same agencies were linked to illegal paramilitary groups and drug traffickers. The posting shows how access to paper can decide whether a truth process can do its job.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
How should a military choose targets for cyber operations? Michael Martelle edited this briefing book, number 683, published in September 2019. It presents a freedom of information release on that question.

The released material discusses considerations inside United States military targeting doctrine as applied to cyberspace. Targeting rules decide what may be hit, what must be avoided, and who approves. Seeing those considerations in an official release helps readers understand how cyber attacks are planned as formal military operations, not improvised hacks. Releases of this kind are uncommon, since targeting doctrine is usually kept classified.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia-int:
Gina Haspel ran a CIA black site where detainees were tortured, and cables from that program were later declassified. The evidence for this posting centers on the legal cover the program needed. Top CIA lawyer John Rizzo worked the Justice Department for secret opinions approving the proposed methods.

Those opinions were ultimately repudiated by the Justice Department itself, but only years later. That sequence is the core of the record: lawyers blessed harsh methods in secret, the blessing was withdrawn long after the acts, and the cables survived to be read. The posting ties Haspel's name to the paper trail of the program she oversaw.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Ira: Iran's 1979 Revolution Revisited: Failures (and a Few Successes) - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the records and readers.
government-and-administration-of-the-uni:
Westel W. Willoughby and William F. Willoughby wrote this study for the Johns Hopkins University Studies in Historical and Political Science, in the ninth series. Both were young scholars; William worked at the U.S. Department of Labor. The book opens with first principles: forms of rule from absolute monarchy to republic, and the necessary and optional functions of a government.

It then traces colonial governments and their tie to England, the steps toward union, and the Articles of Confederation. Later parts take up the Constitution and the working of the federal machine. The brothers write in a clear, teaching style, with heads and summaries to guide a student. The volume is a period piece of the new political science in America, keen to describe its own government as a system that could be studied like any other.
grandma-s-memories:
Mary D. Brine, author of Grandma's Attic Treasures, published Grandma's Memories in 1888 and dedicated it to those whose faces are turned toward the sunset. The book is a life in verse and picture, told by a grandmother looking back. The pictures carry the story in their titles: Grandma's a maiden, Grandma now is a bride, and at last a kiss falls on Grandma's thin cheek from a grandchild.

Lullabies, girlhood woes, courtship, and the hush of a baby's breath pass in short, tender poems. The tone is sweet and a touch sad, as such books were meant to be. Brine wrote for the parlor and the gift table, and her verses were much loved. The volume is a small monument to the Victorian cult of grandmotherhood, all rocking chair, memory, and love.
great-catherine-whom-glory-still-adores:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Great Catherine, a short play about Catherine the Great of Russia, prefaced by an author's apology for his title. Shaw confesses that Catherine's diplomacy and conquests bore him. Her character fascinates him instead. In his portrait she outplays every statesman at court intrigue. Her favorite Patiomkin fools her with sham villages built for her tours.

The play brings a stiff young English officer, Captain Edstaston, into Catherine's court. He represents respectable England in a palace run on appetite and wit. Claire and the Princess Dashkoff move through the court scenes. Catherine toys with the captain's prudery while ruling Russia between love affairs. Shaw treats history as farce with a serious edge. Readers get an empress shown as a great comic performer, shrewder than the diplomats who thought they managed her.
great-sea-stories:
Joseph Lewis French edited Great Sea Stories for Brentano's in 1921, adding it to his line of anthologies of ghosts, mystery, and the psychic. The contents raid the great sea novels. Charles Kingsley gives Spanish Bloodhounds and English Mastiffs, from Westward Ho! Captain Marryat gives the club-hauling of the Diomede, from Peter Simple. Michael Scott gives the cruise of the Torch, from Tom Cringle's Log.

Charles Reade's Hard Cash gives a merchantman and a pirate; an anonymous piece tells the mutiny of the Bounty. Cooper's Red Rover, Melville's Moby Dick, and Hugo's Ninety-three all stand here in extract. The book is a lifeboat of the classics: storm, chase, wreck, and whale, chosen for readers who want the salt without the long calms. It still serves as a tasting menu of sea fiction.
greek-and-roman-ghost-stories:
Lacy Collison-Morley, a former scholar of St. John's College, Oxford, gathered these tales of the supernatural from the classics in 1912. He says the collection began at the suggestion of the novelist Marion Crawford, whose wide reading in the classics supplied more than one story. The pieces were put together over years of casual browsing, he adds, and may interest others who share the amusement. Chapters first treat the power of the dead to return to earth.

Then come the belief in ghosts in Greece and Rome, stories of haunting, and necromancy, the calling up of the dead. Pliny's haunted house and other famous tales stand here in English. Collison-Morley writes with a scholar's care and a fan's delight. The little book proves that ghost stories are as old as letters, and that the ancients feared and wondered much as we do.
green-bays-verses-and-parodies:
Arthur Quiller-Couch, who signed himself Q, gathered his Oxford verses in Green Bays, a thin book of verses and parodies. Most of the pieces were written at Oxford and first appeared in the Oxford Magazine; a few come from The Speaker and from his own novels. The contents open In a College Garden and pass to The Splendid Spur, The White Moth, and a set called Irish Melodies. A piece asks why this volume is so thin.

Sapphics for Lady Jane, a triolet, songs, and the mock-serious Doom of the Esquire Bedell fill the book. Q parodies the styles of older poets with a scholar's ear and a friend's malice. The Latin motto plays on the laurel and the bay of his title. It is a young don's jeu d'esprit, light, learned, and meant for readers who know the originals by heart.
grey-roses:
Henry Harland, author of The Cardinal's Snuff-Box, gathers short tales in Grey Roses, here in a fifth edition of 1911. Its motto, taken from Parashkine, sets the key: the conception was a rose, but the achievement is a rose grown grey. The contents lead with The Bohemian Girl and Mercedes, then A Broken Looking-Glass, The Reward of Virtue, and A Re-Incarnation. Flower o' the Quince and When I Am King follow.

Harland's tales are set among artists, exiles, and lovers in London, Paris, and Spain. They are told in a fine, wistful prose that prizes mood over plot. Disappointment runs through them like a scent: bright hopes dimming into grey. Harland edited The Yellow Book in its famous days, and his own fiction shares its polish. The tales suit a slow evening and a taste for the 1890s.
grim-tales:
E. Nesbit was famed for bright tales for young readers, such as her books of child quests. In 1893 she showed a far more dark face in this set of horror tales. The change shocked some fans who knew just the gay side of her pen.

The best known tale, 'Man-Size in Marble,' turns on two stone knights in a church who may not stay still. Dread in wed life, in homes, and in love runs through the set as its core theme. The set is the dark twin of her famed books for the young.
grimm-s-fairy-stories:
Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm gathered the tales in this book from the mouths of German folk, and their collection became the best-loved story book in the world. This edition of 1922 has colored pictures by John B. Gruelle and pen-and-ink sketches by R. Emmett Owen. The contents open with The Goose-Girl and The Little Brother and Sister. Hansel and Grethel, Little Snow-White, and Cinderella follow in the famous order.

Rapunzel, Briar Rose, Rumpelstiltskin, and the Frog Prince are all here, with the Valiant Little Tailor and Little Red-Cap. The tales are told in the plain, brisk English that children have known for a century. Cruelty and wonder stand side by side, as in the old tellings. This is a handsome gift edition of tales no childhood has lacked for two hundred years.
half-past-seven-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson's Half-Past Seven Stories gathers bedtime tales, illustrated in colour by Dorothy Hope Smith. Anderson dedicates the book to Sarah Davis Anderson, whose young admirers called her Aunt Sally, in tribute to a loving heart that made many little ones happy.

Contents include The Little Lost Fox, The Big Bobsled, The Jolly Roger, The Old Woman Who Lived on the Canal, Two o' Cat, The Fairy Lamp, and The Animals' Birthday Party. Later tales bring Dr. Philemon Pipp the patent medicine man, Ole Man Pumpkin, the Norway spruce, and the hole that ran to China. Children will find these stories whimsical, warm and made for reading aloud.
hans-brinker-or-the-silver-skates:
Mary Mapes Dodge set Hans Brinker, or The Silver Skates in Holland, announcing in her preface a book of travels joined to a domestic tale. Hans and his sister Gretel Brinker are poor, honest children whose father Raff lies injured and senseless after a fall from a dike. A famous skating race offers silver skates as its prize.

The children seek the surgeon Dr Boekman, visit Amsterdam and Haarlem at Saint Nicholas season, and learn their father's hidden story. Dodge checked her Dutch customs, dress, and scenery with scrupulous care and Dutch friends' help. Generations of American children learned Holland from this book: canals, windmills, tulip mania, and the boy who held the dike.
hawaiian-folk-tales:
Thomas G. Thrum compiled these Hawaiian folk tales at Chicago in 1907, with sixteen illustrations from photographs. His note says the legends had been a feature of The Hawaiian Annual for years, and that repeated requests now bring them into book form. Several tales are new here. The famous shark legend was furnished for the purpose from the papers of the Hawaiian Historical Society.

The tales tell of gods, chiefs, sharks, and spirits of the islands, in the form in which Hawaiian tellers passed them down and Thrum's Annual had printed them. Thrum was the islands' great almanac maker, a settler who spent his life recording their lore. The book is uneven as literature, as such gatherings are, yet precious as record. Much of old Hawaii survives in pages like these, gathered before the last native tellers were gone.
hawthorne-english-men-of-letters-series:
Henry James, who signs himself Junr. on the title page, published this study of Nathaniel Hawthorne in 1879, in the English Men of Letters series. He says at once that the sketch must take the form of a critical essay rather than a biography. The data for a life of Hawthorne are, he notes, the reverse of copious, and Hawthorne's career was tranquil and uneventful in any case. The contents run from early years through early writings to Brook Farm and Concord.

Then come the three American novels, England and Italy, and the last years. James, a young American in Europe, judges the older master with love and a touch of patronage, finding his world thin beside Europe's richness. The book is now read as much for James as for Hawthorne: two great novelists, one weighing the other, in prose already unmistakably Jamesian.
he-walked-around-the-horses:
H. Beam Piper published He Walked Around the Horses in Astounding Science Fiction in April 1948. A note before the tale states its ground: the story is based on an authenticated, documented fact. A man vanished, right out of this world. In November 1809, an Englishman named Benjamin Bathurst vanished, inexplicably and utterly. He was on his way to Hamburg from Vienna, where he had served as his government's envoy to what Napoleon had left of the Austrian Empire.

At an inn in Perleberg, in Prussia, while examining a change of horses, Bathurst stepped out of his secretary's sight around the horses, and was never seen again. Piper's tale, told in letters and reports, sends him into a parallel world whose history forked from ours. The puzzle is worked with a historian's care. It is one of Piper's best-loved stories, and an early jewel of the alternate-history kind.
heart-histories-and-life-pictures:
T. S. Arthur's Heart-Histories and Life-Pictures came out in New York in 1853. His introduction argues that every heart has its history, sad or bright. We cross paths daily with sober faces whose stories we never ask. Arthur wrote, he says, to awaken sympathy rather than to win literary elegance.

The Book of Memory opens the tales with an old man's counsel to Edwin. Memory, he warns, records every act on pages that cannot be erased. Jenny Lawson, The Wife, and The Married Sisters treat women's lots. Unredeemed Pledges and Going to the Springs mix money and fashion. Arthur dates his preface from Philadelphia in December 1852. The pictures are brief and direct, built to make readers kinder to the strangers beside them.
hebrew-life-and-times:
Harold B Hunting wrote this study of ancient Hebrew life, issued in 1921. It was made for Bible study groups and young readers. Hunting starts with shepherds on the edge of the desert. He then moves through tents, farms, villages, kings, and prophets in short, clear chapters.

Each chapter ends with questions for group talk and study. The book links home life to law, worship, and war. It shows how farming, towns, and exile changed old customs over time. Readers who want the daily world behind the Bible stories will find a plain and useful guide.
heckewelder-lenape-dialogues:
Words, Phrases, and Short Dialogues in the Lenape tongue appeared in 1819. Heckewelder gathered the material at Moravian stations on the frontier. Missionaries there had to preach and teach in the people's own language.

Word lists give the core terms of daily Lenape life and speech. Useful phrases cover travel, trade, food, and greetings between strangers. Short talks between speakers show the tongue in real use. The slim book was a working tool, not a work of show. Today it keeps early Lenape speech on record for new students of the tongue. Linguists still value its plain, field-gathered forms and phrases.
helen-s-babies:
John Habberton's Helen's Babies begins with a letter that traps a bachelor. Harry Burton, salesman of white goods, aged twenty-eight, is choosing where to spend his fortnight's vacation. His sister Helen writes from Hillcrest: come to us, she says, since Tom and she are invited away. The man she needs is an uncle for ten days. Budge and Toddie, her two toddlers, are the babies of the title, promised by the subtitle to be innocent, crafty, angelic, impish, witching, and impulsive by turns.

Inside, Harry's journal of the ten days became one of America's best-selling comic books. The children wreck his books, his courtship prospects, and his dignity in rotation. He records it all with a salesman's eye. Readers get the Victorian nursery's favorite comedy here.
hell-fer-sartain-and-other-stories:
John Fox Jr wrote these Kentucky mountain stories, collected under the title of the first, 'Hell fer Sartain.' The contents promise tales of dances, feuds, courtship, and preaching: Through the Gap, Courtin' on Cutshin, Preachin' on Kingdom-Come, and The Passing of Abraham Shivers among them. Fox renders mountain speech in heavy dialect throughout.

The opening story explains its creek's name at a Christmas dancing party where Rich Harp and Harve Hall carry old grudges into the room. Others follow moonshiners, mountain preachers, and young lovers in the Cumberland hills Fox knew from his family's Kentucky home. His stories helped define the local-color picture of Appalachia for magazine readers of the 1890s.
hero-tales:
James Baldwin retold these hero tales for young readers. The hosted copy came from Scribner's, with a 1904 copyright and a 1914 printing. The tales draw on Greek myth, northern saga, and French song. Apollo, Hercules, Siegfried, and Charlemagne all appear among the heroes.

Each tale is short, clear, and told in simple prose. Readers meet the golden apple, the forging of Balmung, and the pass at Roncevaux. Baldwin keeps the wonder while trimming the old texts to school size. The book served as a first door into the great story hoards of Europe for many school children of its day.
hieroglyphic-tales:
Horace Walpole printed these tales at his own Strawberry Hill press in 1785. He calls the first a new Arabian night's entertainment. A princess climbs a great mountain to gather goat's eggs for her freckles. Walpole jokes that learned men need not believe what they claim.

Kings are kicked into the sea and queens play blindman's buff with the senate. Each short tale piles absurd acts on absurd acts. Sense is the last thing on offer, and that is the point. Readers meet Walpole at his most playful, mocking grave tales and grave men alike.
hindoo-tales-or-the-adventures-of-ten-pr:
Dandin, a Sanskrit author, wrote the tales known as the Adventures of Ten Princes. P W Jacob freely translated them into English, in a London edition of 1873. Jacob warns that the Sanskrit original was left unfinished. He cut and softened some parts for English readers of his day.

Ten princes tell of quests, tricks, and strange turns of fate. Deceit, quick wit, and blind belief all play their part. Jacob notes that some turns match tales in the Arabian Nights. The stories give a lively picture of old Hindu manners, courts, and morals.
hinton-scientific-romances-first-series:
Charles Howard Hinton, a British mathematician, issued his Scientific Romances in essays between 1884 and 1886. Hinton coined the word 'tesseract' for a four-dimensional cube. His tales were the first great push to make the fourth dimension known to general readers.

The essays mix story and study: flat worlds, beings who pass through solid walls, and drills for picturing four dimensions. Hinton thought training the mind to see past three dimensions could free it. His work fed later writers of higher-space fiction, and Abbott's Flatland appeared in the same years.
historical-miniatures:
August Strindberg wrote these twenty brief episodes from world history. Claud Field translated them into English. A preface by the critic Maximilian Harden, from 1907, presents the set. Harden calls Strindberg a philosopher and poet at his visions of the past.

Julian the Apostate and Peter the Hermit walk these pages. Attila, Luther, Alcibiades, and Eginhard appear as well. Pharaohs and Czars, Athens and Henry the Eighth's England set the scenes. Each miniature is short, sharp, and built on one strong moment. Strindberg treats great lives as flashes of character, not as chronicles.
historical-mysteries:
Andrew Lang collected these essays on famous unsolved cases, in a second edition of 1905. Lang starts with the strange case of Elizabeth Canning. Fourteen pieces follow, each a puzzle from the record. Lang weighs tales, trials, and ghosts with a cool, amused eye.

Kaspar Hauser, the child of Europe, gets a full chapter. The Gowrie conspiracy, the cardinal's necklace, and the Chevalier d'Éon follow. Daniel Dunglas Home's séances pose, for Lang, twin puzzles of science and society. Saint-Germain the deathless closes the main set. Readers who like history's loose ends will find them probed with style.
history-of-kershaw-s-brigade-with-comple:
D Augustus Dickert, a veteran, wrote this history of Kershaw's Brigade. The brigade served South Carolina in the Civil War, on the Confederate side. The book was privately published by his neighbor Elbert Aull, a small-town editor. A modern introduction calls it rare, valuable, and long overdue for reprint.

Dickert gives complete rolls of the companies, man by man. Life sketches, incidents, and anecdotes fill out the record. One scene shows a soldier crossing a railroad under hundreds of bullets on a desperate errand. The tone is proud and mournful at once. Veterans' families get names and deeds kept that official lists would lose.
history-of-the-united-states:
Charles A Beard and Mary R Beard wrote this history of the United States together. Macmillan published it at New York in 1921. The contents open with the colonial period and the great migration. Agencies of colonization and colonial life frame the first chapter.

The Beards treat politics as the crest of deeper forces. Land, trade, slavery, and industry drive their long story. Lincoln's hard question to Douglas, and Douglas's lame reply, get sharp telling. The pair argue that a territory could kill slavery by unfriendly laws. Students of their day got a bracing, economic reading of the nation's past in one volume.
holidays-at-the-grange-or-a-week-s-delig:
Emily Mayer Higgins wrote this book of games and stories, copyrighted in 1886. A party gathers at Wyndham Grange for a Christmas week. Each chapter is a day of the holiday. Parlor games fill the hours between tales.

The guests play Consequences, Rhymes, and Cento on the first nights. A fairy wood tale and a rhyming game follow. Orikama, or the White Water-Lily, adds an Indian tale to the set. Higgins packs in charades, riddles, and fireside fun for hosts. Families of the time got a ready-made week of Christmas sport in one thick volume.
home-geography-for-primary-grades:
C C Long wrote this geography text for primary grades. Long divides the subject into home geography and world geography. Home knowledge, he argues, must come from direct observation. What a child sees nearby becomes the base for picturing far lands.

The hill a pupil climbs daily may stand for the Andes or Alps. Lessons treat rivers, rain, slopes, and valleys in simple terms. One river lesson is cast as a poem, the stream telling its own tale. Vapor rises, falls as rain, and runs back to the sea, Long explains. Teachers get a method built on the schoolyard, not the map alone.
homeburg-memories:
George Fitch published these small-town memories in 1915. Homeburg is his comic everytown of trains, bands, and weekly papers. Chapters salute the 4:11 train and the friendly fire-fiend. The town's two four-hundredths and its leisure class get gentle roasting.

The Homeburg Weekly Democrat anchors the longest chapter. One citizen notes the paper, cut in two, fits his wife's pantry shelves exactly. The marine band, the telephone exchange, and a school election follow. Fitch writes with a son's fondness for his father, to whom the book is given. Readers get Midwestern humor at its warmest, before the auto age fully landed.
homespun-tales:
Kate Douglas Wiggin gathered three long stories in Homespun Tales, all set in an imaginary village in York County, Maine. Wiggin explains in her introduction that two first appeared as decorated gift-books. The Saco River runs through the first tale and through her summers. She calls the river its real principal character. A meeting house and a church society anchor the second.

Rose o' the River follows a country girl and a river-driving romance. The Old Peabody Pew tells of a Dorcas Society that scrubs its church clean and of Nancy Wentworth returning at nightfall to mend a pew tied to her lost love. Village neighbors, hymn singing, and parish pride fill the pages. Readers get Wiggin's Maine at its warmest: small places, stubborn hearts, and kindness treated as a form of local knowledge.
hospital-sketches:
Louisa May Alcott, not yet famous for Little Women, nursed Union soldiers in Washington and turned the work into Hospital Sketches. James Redpath published the book in Boston in 1863, after the sketches ran in the Commonwealth newspaper. Alcott hides inside a mask, Miss Tribulation Periwinkle, and calls her family the Periwinkles. Five cents from each copy went to war orphans.

Obtaining Supplies shows her fighting red tape to reach the hospital. A Forward Movement carries her to the wards, where a day and a night of nursing fill two chapters. Wounded men arrive in batches, and she washes, feeds, writes letters, and sits with the dying. Off Duty gives the nurses' meals, jokes, and sorrows between the crises. A postscript sums up what the work taught her about courage and waste. Civil War readers value the sketches as a nurse's record, unsparing about pain that glory talk hides.
houses-and-house-life-of-the-american-ab:
Lewis Henry Morgan wrote this study of Native American houses and house life. It formed part five of his Ancient Society manuscript, on house architecture. The work appears here as the fourth volume of Contributions to North American Ethnology. One chapter first ran as Montezuma's Dinner in 1876.

Morgan describes great communal houses where each family holds one room. Wardrobes hang from a log beneath the rafters in his account. Work, cooking, eating, and sleeping share that single large space. Aztec and mound-builder houses get their own chapters. Morgan argues that house form mirrors social form. The book remains a base text of American anthropology.
hugo-a-fantasia-on-modern-themes:
Arnold Bennett published this fantasia on modern themes in 1906. Hugo, its hero, rules a vast London establishment with a dome. Sealed rooms give the first part its name and its mystery. Hugo is rich, secretive, and used to obedience in all things.

Ravengar, his enemy, refuses to believe his death threat is real. Hugo tells him he will be dead by this time tomorrow. The scene's chill is pure Bennett stagecraft in prose. Shops, flats, and modern London hum behind the melodrama. Bennett classed the book with his fantasias, beside The Grand Babylon Hotel. It shows his lighter, swifter gift at full stretch.
hume-english-men-of-letters-series:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this life and study of David Hume for the English Men of Letters series. John Morley edited the series, and Macmillan issued the volume in 1879. Part One gives Hume's life, from early writings to the History of England. Part Two expounds the philosophy in ten chapters.

Contents of the mind, impressions, and mental operations come first. Language and necessary truths follow, then miracles and theism. The soul and immortality close the main course. Huxley parses even verb forms: silver shone is a memory, silver will shine an expectation. A scientist reads the great sceptic with rare sympathy and precision.
hunt-popular-romances-west-england-1865-:
Robert Hunt, a Cornish man of science, made this first set of the folk tales of the west of England in 1865. He heard most of the tales in Cornwall, from miners, fish wives, and old folk. His aim was to save the lore of old Cornwall before it died out.

The set holds the famed tale of the Mermaid of Zennor, who lured a choir man to the sea. Giants, saints, mine sprites, and strange dreams fill the rest of the Cornish store. Hunt's work is the chief book of the folk lore of the Cornish coast.

Robert Hunt brought out the second set of his Cornish folk tales in 1865, in the Hotten print of that year. It stands as mate to the first set of the same year. Hunt spent years in the lanes and ports of Cornwall to gather his store.

More drolls, as Cornish folk name their sly tales, fill this set with fresh lore. Saints, giants, sea tales, and old rites of the Cornish year all find a place here. With the first set, it forms the full record of old Cornwall as its folk told it.
hunting-sketches:
Anthony Trollope wrote Hunting Sketches as short character studies of the fox-hunting field he loved. His eight sketches sort the crowd by type. There are men who hunt and dislike it, men who love it, and the lady who rides to hounds. The hunting farmer, the man who never jumps, the hunting parson, and the master of hounds complete the field. A closing piece teaches how to ride to hounds.

Trollope insists the men who dislike hunting outnumber its lovers, since fashion and business drag many into the field. Gates, rails, and pretty sporting pictures get his dry practical treatment. Barsetshire's creator knew this world from his own saddle, and the sketches mix comedy, class observation, and genuine riding instruction.
i-saw-three-ships-and-other-winter-tales:
Arthur Quiller-Couch, signing as Q, wrote these winter tales of Cornwall. The title tale turns on Young Zeb and a stranger. Three ships, a chest of drawers, and a dance in borrowed shoes mark its chapters. Zeb sells his soul and wins it back before the third ship comes.

A Christmas Eve opening sets the west-country mood. Cake, cider, crowding, and geese dancing prolong the feast till carols end it. The Haunted Dragoon and A Blue Pantomime follow. The Two Householders and The Disenchantment of Elizabeth close the set. In one scene Zeb hides the stranger under evil-smelling weed in a jowter's cart. Q writes his home coast with love and a ghost-story gleam.
idle-hour-stories:
Eugenia Dunlap Potts of Kentucky published Idle Hour Stories herself in Lexington in 1909. She dedicated the book to her late son George, who had watched the tales take shape. The contents list more than twenty short pieces, plus a few poems at the end.

Tales range from a ghost at Crestdale to a Christmas gift and a case in a Pullman car. Some draw on old Kentucky life, farm girls, and courtship. Others turn on a singer, an iron box, or a first jury case. The mix is light home reading in a warm local voice.
if-winter-comes:
A. S. M. Hutchinson published If Winter Comes in Boston in 1921, and it was reprinted many times that fall. The title quotes Shelley's line on winter and spring. The novel is built in four parts named for three women, Mabel, Nona, and Effie. Its hero is Mark Sabre of Penny Green.

Sabre is met at thirty-four, with a look back to his marriage in 1904. Nicknamed Puzzlehead at school, he puzzles over right and wrong in home life. War, scandal, and divided love press on him as the parts unfold. The book became a best seller on Sabre's moral strain.
ilka-on-the-hill-top-and-other-stories:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published this story collection, with Ilka on the Hill-Top as the first tale, in a second edition in 1891. Other tales are Annunciata, Under the Glacier, and A Knight of Dannebrog. One piece is called a philosophical fairy tale. The book was first issued in New York in 1881.

The title tale opens on a summer ride in the Tyrol. A father and son ride farm horses toward Ginzling as light fades over the Alps. Later tales move to love, loss, and fate under ice and sea. Boyesen writes of Norse and Alpine folk with a close eye.
imaginations-and-reveries:
George William Russell, who wrote as AE, gathered twenty-five years of articles and tales in Imaginations and Reveries. In his preface he says no single theme holds the book. Art pulled him one way, while work for Irish life pulled him another. He followed each mood as it came.

Essays and tales range over Irish nationalism, land for small holders, and the spirit in daily life. Russell argues for freedom of the person against the weight of the state. Other pieces turn inward, toward light and faith. The book shows a writer split, by his own account, between Ireland and eternity.
